# Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity

> Why does search use the angle between embeddings, not the distance?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity/
- Related: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your food app recommends the same popular restaurant to almost everyone, even people whose taste points elsewhere. The interviewer asks:

> What is the difference between a dot product and cosine similarity, and which would you use here?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app describes each customer and each restaurant with two taste numbers: how much they lean towards **spicy** food and towards **healthy** food. A customer who likes both equally is (1, 1); one who loves spicy, healthy food is (4, 3). Real systems use hundreds of dimensions learned by a model (embeddings), but the maths is identical and 2-D lets us draw it.

#### "How similar are these two things?" as a number

To recommend restaurants, retrieve documents for a RAG system or find near-duplicate products, you need one number that says how alike two items are. Once items are vectors, similarity becomes arithmetic. The choice of arithmetic decides who gets recommended.

### The idea

Think of two arrows. Cosine only asks whether they point the same way. The dot product also rewards length, so a very long arrow can win even when it points the wrong way.

[Figure: Three arrows from one point. The customer and the small restaurant point almost the same way. The popular restaurant is much longer but points elsewhere.]

_You (1, 1). Popular (4, 0.5). Small (1, 1.2). Dot product picks popular, 4.5 against 2.2. Cosine picks small, 0.996 against 0.79._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Make the restaurant much longer without changing its angle. Then rotate it until it sits at 90° from the customer.

#### Move the vectors, watch the three measures

Make the restaurant longer without changing its angle: the dot product grows, the cosine doesn't move, and the distance changes. Rotate it to 90° from the customer: the dot product and cosine hit zero.

**Now say why:** which measure ignored the extra length, and why did two of them hit zero at 90°?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

In ML every item (a customer, a restaurant, a sentence) becomes a **vector**: a list of numbers. The **dot product** a·b multiplies matching entries and adds them; geometrically it is |a| |b| cos θ, so it grows when vectors point the same way _and_ when they are long. **Cosine similarity** divides out the lengths and keeps only the direction (−1 to 1). **Euclidean distance** measures the straight-line gap. Which one you use changes what "similar" means: dot product favours big, popular items; cosine compares taste regardless of size. Every linear model, attention layer and vector search is built on these three operations. What you'll be able to do after this: compute a dot product, norm and cosine by hand, explain the geometry, and choose between dot product, cosine and Euclidean for a similarity search.

#### Vectors, length and the dot product

$$ {a\cdot b = \textstyle\sum_i a_i b_i} = {\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert\cos\theta}, \qquad {\lVert a\rVert = \sqrt{a\cdot a}} $$

Mathematics for Machine Learning §3.1–3.4 (norms, inner products, angles) [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/).

- **dot product**: Multiply matching entries and add: (4, 3)·(2, 1) = 4×2 + 3×1 = 11. One number from two vectors.

- **the same, geometrically**: Length of a times length of b times the cosine of the angle between them. Big when both are long and point the same way; zero when perpendicular; negative when opposite.

- **length (L2 norm)**: ‖a‖ = √(a·a) = √(4² + 3²) = 5: Pythagoras in any number of dimensions.

1. A customer a and a restaurant b, drawn as arrows from the origin.

2. Drop a perpendicular from a's tip onto b's line. The shadow's length is ‖a‖ cos θ: how much of a points along b.

3. The dot product is that shadow times b's length. That's why it measures "agreement in direction, scaled by size".

4. The cosine alone ranges from 1 (same direction) through 0 (unrelated) to −1 (opposite).

#### Cosine = dot product of unit vectors

$$ {\cos\theta} = {a\cdot b} \,/\, {(\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert)} $$

- **cosine similarity**: How aligned two vectors are, from −1 to 1, ignoring how long they are.

- **dot product**: The raw agreement.

- **divide out both lengths**: Equivalent to scaling both vectors to length 1 first, then taking the dot product.

#### Three ways to compare vectors

| Measure | Formula | Cares about | Used in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dot product** | Σ aᵢbᵢ | Direction and length | Linear models (w·x), attention scores (q·k), matrix-factorisation recommenders, maximum-inner-product search |
| **Cosine similarity** | a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖) | Direction only | Text and sentence embeddings, semantic search, RAG retrieval |
| **Euclidean distance** | ‖a − b‖ | Absolute position | k-NN, k-means, when magnitudes are meaningful |

For unit-length vectors (‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1), all three agree on the ranking: ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2 cos θ. That's why many embedding models normalise outputs, and vector databases then use the cheapest one (dot product).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Dot product vs cosine in recommenders and search

- **Dot product** when vector length carries real signal: in matrix factorisation, a longer item vector often encodes popularity or quality, and ranking by dot product deliberately favours it. Two-tower recommenders typically score by dot product for this reason.

- **Cosine** when length is an artefact: text embeddings of a long vs short document about the same topic should match. Most sentence-embedding models and RAG pipelines use cosine (or normalise and use dot product).

- **Euclidean** when absolute position matters and features are on comparable, scaled units (see k-NN); in high dimensions all distances concentrate, which hurts every measure.

Whatever the embedding model was trained with is the right choice: a model trained with a cosine loss should be queried with cosine.

#### The dot product is everywhere

- **Linear and logistic regression:** the score is w·x + b (Linear Regression).

- **Neural network layers:** each neuron computes a dot product of its weights with its input.

- **Attention:** query·key dot products, scaled by 1/√d, decide which tokens attend to which.

- **Vector search:** nearest neighbours by cosine or inner product over millions of embeddings (HNSW, IVF; see k-NN).

#### Where to go next

- **Other ways to measure length:** vector and matrix norms cover L1, L2 and more, and why L1 gives sparse weights.

- **Dot products and closest points:** orthogonality and projections shows how this idea becomes least squares.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Recommend whatever has the highest dot product"

The dot product rewards length. If a restaurant's vector is long simply because it's popular (its embedding was trained on many orders), it wins for almost everyone, even customers whose taste points elsewhere. A customer u = (1, 1) who likes spicy and healthy equally gets a dot product of 4.5 with a popular, mostly-spicy restaurant (4, 0.5), but only 2.2 with a small restaurant (1, 1.2) that matches their taste almost exactly. Cosine similarity flips the order: 0.79 vs 0.996. Neither is always right; they answer different questions (see In practice).

#### Caveats

- Cosine ignores magnitude entirely: two customers who order 1 and 100 times a month with the same taste look identical.

- Cosine on raw, unscaled features is dominated by big-unit features, like any distance.

- A zero vector has no direction; cosine is undefined (libraries add a tiny ε).

## Say it

### What is the difference between a dot product and cosine similarity, and which would you use here?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does attention divide by √d?

Dot products of random d-dimensional vectors have variance growing with d, so softmax would saturate; dividing by √d keeps scores in a usable range (Vaswani et al. 2017).

Follow-up 2 of 3

How are cosine and Euclidean related?

For unit vectors, ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2 cos θ, so ranking by one is ranking by the other.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What does orthogonal mean for features?

Zero dot product: the directions share no component. Orthogonal (uncorrelated, centred) features make linear models easier to interpret.

#### The 30-second answer

A dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them; geometrically it's the product of the lengths times the cosine of the angle, so it measures alignment scaled by magnitude. Cosine similarity divides by both lengths, so it compares direction only and ranges from −1 to 1. Euclidean distance measures absolute separation. For normalised vectors they all rank the same. I use cosine for text embeddings where length is an artefact, dot product where magnitude carries signal like popularity in recommenders, and Euclidean for scaled feature spaces like k-NN.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Cosine similarity is a distance." It's a similarity; 1 − cos is a dissimilarity, but not a true metric.

- "Dot product and cosine always give the same ranking." Only for equal-length vectors.

**Key terms and sources**

Vectors as lists of features, length (norm), the dot product, cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and why embeddings and recommenders run on them · built from Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_ (ch. 2–3) and Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, _Deep Learning_ (ch. 2) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | An ordered list of numbers; a point or arrow in space. |
| **Norm ‖a‖** | Length; L2 by default, L1 = sum of absolute values. |
| **Dot product** | Σ aᵢbᵢ = ‖a‖‖b‖cos θ. |
| **Cosine similarity** | Dot product of unit vectors; angle only. |
| **Orthogonal** | Dot product 0: perpendicular, unrelated directions. |

#### Sources

1. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, Cambridge University Press 2020, free at [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/) (ch. 2–3).

2. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, ch. 2, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

3. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention is all you need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) (scaled dot-product attention).

# Vector and Matrix Norms

> What's the difference between L1 and L2 norms, and why does L1 give sparse weights?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/vector-and-matrix-norms/
- Before this: Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity (`fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity`)
- Related: Regularized Linear Models (`fundamentals/regularized-linear-models`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your regression has 500 features, and you want most of the weights to go to zero. A teammate switches between L1 and L2 penalties and gets very different results. You also want to stop exploding gradients. The interviewer asks:

> What's the difference between L1 and L2 norms, and why does L1 give sparse weights?

#### Why it matters

The norm you choose decides what "small" means. That choice sets which weights regularisation removes, when gradient clipping activates and how far a layer can amplify its input. This builds on vectors and length.

### The idea

Think of getting from one place to another in a city. L2 is the straight-line distance, as a bird flies. L1 is the distance by road on a grid, adding every block. L∞ only cares about your longest stretch. It's the same trip, measured by different rules.

[Figure: Three norms for the vector 3, minus 4. L1 is 7, the sum of absolute values. L2 is 5, the straight-line length. L infinity is 4, the largest value.]

_The same vector, (3, −4), measured three ways._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the vector to (3, 0), then (3, 3). Then lower the clip limit.

#### Compare the unit balls

Diamond is L1, circle is L2 and square is L∞, each drawn at radius 2. The dot is your vector. Clipping scales the whole vector, so the direction is unchanged.

Set the vector to **(3, 0)**: all three norms agree, because only one value is non-zero. Set it to **(3, 3)**, and they differ. L1 counts every value, while L∞ only sees the biggest.

**Now say why:** why do the three norms agree when only one value isn't zero?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **norm** measures size. **L2** is straight-line length, **L1** adds absolute values, and **L∞** takes the largest entry. Each has a different "unit ball". L1's is a diamond with corners on the axes, so penalised solutions tend to land where some weights are exactly zero. For matrices, **Frobenius** treats all entries like one long vector, and the **spectral norm** is the most a matrix can stretch any vector.

#### Measuring size

| Norm | How | Where it's used |
|---|---|---|
| **L2** | Square root of the sum of squares. | Ridge and weight decay, gradient clipping, Euclidean distance. |
| **L1** | Sum of absolute values. | Lasso, for sparse weights. Less sensitive to single large values. |
| **L∞** | The largest absolute value. | Limits on any single value, like adversarial attacks. |
| **Frobenius** | L2 of all a matrix's entries. | Low-rank error, matrix factorisation. |
| **Spectral** | The largest singular value. | How much a layer can amplify. Spectral normalisation in GANs. |

##### Why L1 gives zeros

Regularisation asks for the lowest loss inside a norm's ball. The loss's contours usually first touch L1's diamond at a corner, and corners sit on an axis, where other weights are exactly zero. L2's circle has no corners, so its weights shrink but rarely reach zero.

The gradient tells the same story. L2's pull weakens as a weight approaches zero. L1's pull stays constant, so it can push a small weight all the way to zero.

##### A rule every norm follows

- It's zero only for the zero vector.

- Scaling a vector scales its norm.

- The triangle inequality holds: going directly is never longer than going via another point.

#### The maths

$$ {\|x\|_p} = \Big(\sum_i |x_i|^{{p}}\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad {\|A\|_F} = \sqrt{\sum_i \sigma_i^2}, \qquad {\|A\|_2} = \sigma_{\max} $$

Worked example: for x = (3, −4), L1 = 7, L2 = 5 and L∞ = 4. See the SVD lesson for singular values.

- **the p-norm**: One formula covers them all. p = 1 gives L1, p = 2 gives L2, and as p grows it approaches the largest entry.

- **the power**: A higher p gives more weight to the largest entries.

- **Frobenius norm**: Treats a matrix as one long vector. It also equals the square root of the sum of squared singular values.

- **spectral norm**: The most the matrix stretches any unit vector, equal to its largest singular value.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Gradient clipping:** if the gradient's L2 norm exceeds a limit, scale the whole gradient down. Direction stays the same, and only the step size changes.

- **Scale your features:** norms add values across features, so a feature in large units can dominate. Standardise before using a norm penalty.

- **Normalise embeddings:** dividing by the L2 norm makes the dot product equal cosine similarity.

- **Spectral normalisation:** dividing a layer's weights by its spectral norm limits how much it can amplify.

- **Check for divergence:** tracking the norm of weights and gradients is a quick health check during training.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "L2 is better because it's smooth"

It sounds right, since smooth functions are easier to optimise. But they do different jobs. L2 shrinks all weights and keeps them, while L1 removes some entirely. If you want a small set of features, L2 won't give you one. Choose by the outcome you want, and consider elastic net for both.

## Say it

### What's the difference between L1 and L2 norms, and why does L1 give sparse weights?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does gradient clipping use the norm rather than clipping each value?

Clipping each value separately changes the gradient's direction, whereas scaling by the norm keeps it. Per-value clipping is simpler, and some use it, but norm clipping keeps pointing where the gradient said to go, with only a smaller step.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Lasso picks one of two highly correlated features. Why?

The L1 penalty doesn't care how weight is split, in total, between two identical features, so it can land on either, often zeroing the other. Which one it picks can change between samples. Elastic net adds some L2, which spreads weight more evenly.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When would you prefer the spectral norm to Frobenius?

When you care about the worst case: the most a matrix can stretch any input. That matters for stability and Lipschitz limits. Frobenius is about total energy across all directions, which is what matters for low-rank approximation error.

#### The 30-second answer

A norm measures size. L2 is straight-line length, and L1 is the sum of absolute values. L1 gives sparse weights because its unit ball is a diamond with corners on the axes, so the loss's contours tend to touch it where some weights are exactly zero. In terms of gradients, L1 keeps a constant pull towards zero, while L2's pull fades. For matrices, Frobenius treats all entries as one vector, and the spectral norm is the largest singular value, which limits how much a layer can amplify.

**Key terms and sources**

L1, L2 and max norms for vectors, Frobenius and spectral norms for matrices, and how they drive regularisation, gradient clipping and stability. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/)

- [Kolter and Do, CS229 Linear Algebra Review](https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/cs229-linalg.pdf)

- [Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

- Regularised linear models on this site

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Matrices as Transformations

> What does a matrix actually do to space, and what does its determinant measure?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/matrices-as-transformations/
- Before this: Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity (`fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your recommendation model stacks two linear layers with no activation between them, and the second layer adds nothing. The interviewer asks:

> What does a matrix do to a vector, and why do two linear layers act like one?

**Running example:** two customer features, spicy and healthy taste (as in the previous lesson). A layer of a recommendation model multiplies every customer vector by a 2×2 matrix W. We watch what W does to the whole space by tracking the unit square and the two axis arrows.

#### Grids of numbers that nobody can read

Weight matrices, covariance matrices, attention matrices: ML is full of them, and staring at the numbers tells you little. Seeing a matrix as a **transformation of space** turns it into a picture you can reason about: what it stretches, what it destroys, whether it can be undone.

### The idea

Think of a matrix as a rule that moves every point on a rubber sheet. Its columns say where the two axis arrows land. The determinant says how much area changes, and zero means the sheet was flattened onto a line, which can't be undone.

[Figure: A unit square on the left becomes a slanted parallelogram on the right. On the far right, a flattened line shows a matrix with determinant zero.]

_Illustrative. Straight lines stay straight, and the origin stays put._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Pick the squash preset, then drag the entries until the two column arrows point the same way.

#### Drag the entries, watch the plane move

Faint grid: the original space. Coloured grid and square: the same space after W. Teal arrow = first column, orange = second column.

**Now say why:** what happens to the determinant and the rank, and why can't this matrix be undone?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A matrix is a **function that moves every vector**: rotate, stretch, shear, squash or flip space, always keeping straight lines straight and the origin fixed. Its **columns** tell you where the two axis arrows land, so you can read a matrix by looking at it. Multiplying matrices = doing one transformation after another. The **determinant** is how much areas get scaled (negative if space is flipped, zero if it's squashed flat). A zero determinant means information is lost: the matrix has **rank** below full and no **inverse**. In ML, every dense layer is a matrix: Wx moves your data into a new space before the non-linearity bends it. What you'll be able to do after this: read a 2×2 matrix as a picture, compute a determinant and say what it means, explain rank and invertibility, and connect W x + b to a layer.

#### Matrix times vector

$$ {W x} = x_1 {\begin{pmatrix} w_{11}\\ w_{21}\end{pmatrix}} + x_2 {\begin{pmatrix} w_{12}\\ w_{22}\end{pmatrix}} $$

The column view of matrix–vector multiplication: Wx is a combination of W's columns with weights x. Strang, _Introduction to Linear Algebra_, ch. 1–2; MML §2.2.

- **the moved vector**: Where customer x lands after the layer.

- **first column**: Where the arrow (1, 0) lands. Multiply it by x’s first coordinate.

- **second column**: Where the arrow (0, 1) lands. Multiply it by x’s second coordinate, then add.

#### The determinant is the area-scaling factor

$$ {\det W} = {w_{11} w_{22}} - {w_{12} w_{21}} $$

- **determinant**: The factor by which W scales every area (volume in higher dimensions).

- **main diagonal**: Stretching along the axes enlarges area.

- **off-diagonal**: Mixing the axes tilts the square into a parallelogram, which takes area away.

det = 0: the unit square collapses to a line or point, so some different inputs map to the same output, and the transformation can't be reversed. The number of dimensions that survive is the **rank**. det < 0: space is flipped like a mirror image.

#### A small zoo of transformations

| Matrix | Does | Determinant |
|---|---|---|
| [[2, 0], [0, 0.5]] | Stretch x by 2, squash y by half | 1 (area kept) |
| [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]] | Rotate by θ | 1 |
| [[1, 1], [0, 1]] | Shear: slide the top sideways | 1 |
| [[1, 2], [0.5, 1]] | Columns parallel: squash onto a line | 0 (rank 1, not invertible) |
| [[0, 1], [1, 0]] | Swap the axes (a reflection) | −1 (orientation flipped) |

#### Composition, order and inverses

- **Composition:** applying B then A is the single matrix AB (read right to left). Determinants multiply: det(AB) = det A · det B.

- **Order matters:** rotate-then-shear and shear-then-rotate land in different places, so in general AB ≠ BA.

- **Inverse:** W⁻¹ undoes W, and exists exactly when det W ≠ 0. For 2×2: W⁻¹ = (1/det) · [[w₂₂, −w₁₂], [−w₂₁, w₁₁]].

- **Stacked linear layers collapse:** W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, one matrix. Without a non-linearity between them, a deep linear network is just one linear map, which is why activations matter.

#### Trace and change of basis

##### Trace

The trace is the sum of a matrix's diagonal entries. It looks simple, but it also equals the sum of the eigenvalues, so it doesn't change when you change coordinates. In ML, it appears in the Frobenius norm, since ‖A‖²F = tr(AᵀA), and in the total variance of a dataset, which is the trace of its covariance matrix.

##### Change of basis

The same transformation looks different in different coordinates. If P's columns are the new axes, the matrix in those coordinates is P⁻¹AP. Determinant, trace, rank and eigenvalues all stay the same, as they describe the transformation itself. Picking the eigenvectors as your axes makes the matrix diagonal, which is what eigendecomposition does.

Next: matrix multiplication and shapes, and linear independence and rank.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Matrices in ML

- **Dense layers:** h = σ(Wx + b): a linear transformation, a shift, then a bend.

- **Linear regression:** the normal equations solve (XᵀX)w = Xᵀy; if XᵀX is singular (perfectly correlated features, rank-deficient), there's no unique solution, which is what ridge regularisation fixes (Regularized Linear Models).

- **Covariance matrices:** describe how features vary together; their eigenvectors give PCA (next lesson).

- **Low-rank matrices:** LoRA and recommender embeddings deliberately use rank-r factors (SVD lesson).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Matrix multiplication is just a recipe of rows times columns"

Memorising row-times-column works for computing, but hides the meaning, and leads to classic mistakes: assuming AB = BA (order matters: rotating then shearing ≠ shearing then rotating), or expecting every matrix to have an inverse. With the transformation view these are obvious: two moves in a different order end in different places, and a move that squashes the plane onto a line can't be undone because points that landed on top of each other can't be separated again.

## Say it

### What does a matrix do to a vector, and why do two linear layers act like one?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What does a determinant of zero mean for linear regression?

XᵀX is singular: some feature is a linear combination of others (perfect multicollinearity), so infinitely many weight vectors fit equally well. Drop a feature or add regularisation.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why do neural networks need non-linear activations?

A composition of linear maps is linear: W₂W₁ is a single matrix, so without activations depth adds nothing.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the rank of a matrix?

The number of linearly independent columns (equivalently rows): the dimension of the output space the matrix can reach.

#### The 30-second answer

A matrix is a linear transformation: its columns say where the basis vectors land, and multiplying a vector combines those columns. Multiplying matrices composes transformations, so order matters. The determinant is the factor by which areas or volumes scale; zero means the space is squashed into fewer dimensions, the matrix is rank-deficient and has no inverse. In ML, every dense layer computes Wx + b, linear regression's normal equations need XᵀX to be invertible, and low-rank structure is exploited by PCA, matrix factorisation and LoRA.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "AB equals BA." Generally not.

- "Every square matrix can be inverted." Only if its determinant is non-zero.

**Key terms and sources**

Matrix–vector multiplication, columns as "where the axes go", composition, the determinant, rank and inverses, and why a neural-network layer is a matrix · built from Deisenroth et al., _Mathematics for Machine Learning_ (ch. 2, 4), Strang, _Introduction to Linear Algebra_, and 3Blue1Brown's _Essence of Linear Algebra_ · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Linear transformation** | Keeps lines straight and the origin fixed; any matrix. |
| **Determinant** | Area/volume scaling factor; sign = orientation. |
| **Rank** | Number of independent columns: dimensions that survive. |
| **Singular matrix** | det = 0; not invertible. |
| **Identity I** | The "do nothing" matrix. |

#### Sources

1. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, CUP 2020, [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/) (ch. 2, 4.1).

2. G. Strang, _Introduction to Linear Algebra_, 5th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press 2016.

# Matrix Multiplication and Tensor Shapes

> How do you reason about tensor shapes and the cost of matrix multiplication in a model?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/matrix-multiplication-and-tensor-shapes/
- Before this: Matrices as Transformations (`fundamentals/matrices-as-transformations`)
- Related: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your attention model runs fine on 1,024 tokens, but runs out of memory at 4,096. A teammate says that's only four times longer. Elsewhere, a loss looks fine, yet the model doesn't train, and it turns out to be a shape bug. The interviewer asks:

> How do you reason about tensor shapes and the cost of matrix multiplication in a model?

#### Why it matters

Shape errors are the most common bug in model code, and the cost of multiplication decides your GPU bill. If you can follow the shapes through a model, you can read any architecture, and predict what breaks at a larger scale. This builds on matrices as transformations.

### The idea

Think of shipping containers through a chain of ports. Each crane fits one container size, so the output of one step has to fit the next. And it can be much cheaper to ship in a smart order, even if everything ends up in the same place.

[Figure: Multiplying matrices. Inner sizes must match, the outer sizes give the result, and the cost is m times n times p.]

_Inner sizes must match, and outer sizes give the result._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Double the tokens, and watch the multiplications. Then change the heads.

#### Follow the shapes through attention

Heads shown are 2, 4, 8 and 12, using the nearest head count that divides the embedding size. One attention layer, ignoring the projections. Assumes 4 bytes per score, and no optimised attention methods.

Double the tokens from **1,024** to **2,048**. Multiplications and memory go up four times. Now change the heads: multiplications stay the same, because each head uses a smaller piece of the embedding, but the score matrices take more memory.

**Now say why:** why does doubling the tokens quadruple the cost of attention?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

To multiply matrices, the **inner sizes must match**: (m × n)(n × p) gives m × p, at a cost of about **m × n × p** multiplications. Most model bugs and cost surprises come from this. **Order matters** for cost, though not for the result. In attention, scores form a T × T matrix for T tokens, so **doubling the length quadruples** the cost.

#### Reading shapes

##### Three ways to see a product

- **Dot products:** each output entry is a row of A dotted with a column of B.

- **Combining columns:** each output column is a mix of A's columns, with weights from B.

- **Composition:** apply B, then A. That's why order matters, and AB usually differs from BA.

##### Shapes in a model

| Step | Shape | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Input batch | [B, d] | Batch dimension first, by convention. |
| Linear layer | [B, d] × [d, k] gives [B, k] | Has d × k weights, plus k for bias. |
| Token sequence | [B, T, d] | Batch, tokens, features. |
| Attention scores | [B, h, T, T] | h heads, comparing every token with every other. |

##### Broadcasting

Libraries stretch dimensions of size 1 automatically. A [B, 1] tensor plus a [1, k] tensor gives [B, k]. It's useful, and it's also a silent source of bugs: [B] minus [B, 1] gives [B, B], not an error.

##### Order changes the cost

(AB)C and A(BC) give the same answer, but can cost very different amounts. Multiply a matrix by a vector first, when you can. That's why backpropagation multiplies from the output backwards, keeping one small vector rather than building full matrices.

#### The maths

$$ \underbrace{{A}}_{m \times n}\,\underbrace{{B}}_{n \times p} = \underbrace{{C}}_{m \times p}, \qquad {C_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik}B_{kj}, \qquad {\text{cost} \approx mnp} $$

Example: A is 10 × 100, B is 100 × 5, C is 5 × 50. (AB)C costs 5,000 + 2,500 = 7,500. A(BC) costs 25,000 + 50,000 = 75,000: ten times more for the same answer.

- **left matrix**: Its number of columns must equal B’s number of rows.

- **right matrix**: Its number of rows must match, and its columns decide the output width.

- **each output entry**: A dot product of a row of A with a column of B, using n multiplications.

- **total cost**: m × p outputs, each with n multiplications. Multiply two n × n matrices, and it’s about n³.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Comment your shapes:** write them next to each line, or use a tool that checks them. It saves hours.

- **Watch for quiet broadcasting:** check shapes before adding or subtracting, particularly with loss functions.

- **Think in batches:** matrix operations on a batch are much faster on a GPU than looping, because they run in parallel.

- **Vector first:** applying A then B to a vector costs far less than computing AB first.

- **Estimate before you scale:** count how cost grows with tokens, batch and width. This is what limits context length.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It's four times longer, so four times the memory"

It sounds right, since most things grow in proportion. But attention compares every token with every other, so the score matrix grows with the square of the length. Four times the tokens means sixteen times the scores. That's what limits context length, and why people look for more efficient attention methods.

## Say it

### How do you reason about tensor shapes and the cost of matrix multiplication in a model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How many parameters does a linear layer from 768 to 3072 have?

768 × 3072 = 2,359,296 weights, plus 3,072 for the bias, so 2,362,368. Each output has one weight per input, plus a bias. It's a useful habit for spotting where a model's parameters really are.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does adding attention heads not increase the score multiplications?

Each head works on d divided by h features. There are h heads, each costing T² × d/h, and the h cancels. The score matrices do multiply, though, so memory rises. Multi-head attention gives several views at about the same compute.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What goes wrong if you subtract a [B] tensor from a [B, 1] tensor?

Broadcasting makes both [B, B], and you get a B × B matrix of all pairs, with no error. If it's a loss, the value looks reasonable, while the model trains badly. Check shapes, or squeeze the extra dimension first.

#### The 30-second answer

For matrices to multiply, the inner sizes must match: m by n times n by p gives m by p, at about m times n times p multiplications. I track shapes through a model with batch first. A linear layer takes B by d to B by k. Attention scores are batch, heads, tokens, tokens, so doubling the tokens quadruples cost. Multiplication is associative, so order doesn't change the result, but it can change the cost hugely. That's why backprop keeps multiplying a vector instead of building whole matrices.

**Key terms and sources**

How to track shapes through a model, what each multiplication costs, how the order matters, and how batches, broadcasting and attention use it. · checked 6 Nov 2026

# Linear Independence, Basis and Rank

> What is the rank of a matrix, and why do correlated features break linear regression?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/linear-independence-basis-and-rank/
- Before this: Matrices as Transformations (`fundamentals/matrices-as-transformations`)
- Related: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your linear regression has weights in the millions, with opposite signs on height in cm and height in inches. A colleague also one-hot encoded a category with all its columns, and included an intercept. The solver warns about a singular matrix. The interviewer asks:

> What is the rank of a matrix, and why do correlated features break linear regression?

#### Why it matters

Rank explains many practical failures: unstable regression weights, the dummy variable trap, models with more features than rows, and why large embedding matrices can be compressed. See SVD and low rank for how to use this.

### The idea

Think of directions to a friend's house. "Two blocks north, then one east" gets you there. Adding "also go 200 metres north" tells you nothing new, and now there are many ways to describe the same trip. Rank is how many directions really add something.

[Figure: Three cases. Independent features have full rank and unique weights. Near dependent features keep rank, but weights are unstable. Dependent features lose rank, and there are no unique weights.]

_Rank is the number of directions that really add something._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the correlation from 0.90 to 0.99, then to exactly 1.00.

#### Correlate two features

Two standardised features. The area is the determinant of the correlation matrix, 1 − ρ². Figures come from the formula, not a simulation. In practice, rank is judged numerically, so very high correlations behave as if rank were lost.

Move from **0.90** to **0.99**. Inflation goes up about ten times, even though the features already looked similar. Then try exactly **1.00**: the rank drops, and no unique weights exist.

**Now say why:** why do weights become unstable before rank is actually lost?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Vectors are **independent** if none can be built from the others. The **rank** of a matrix is how many of its columns are truly independent: the real number of dimensions in its data. If a feature is a mix of others, the matrix is **rank-deficient**, and many different weights fit equally well. Nearly-dependent features aren't quite as bad, but they still make weights unstable. Regularisation and removing features both help.

#### Building blocks

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Span** | All the vectors you can build by mixing a set. | Two non-parallel arrows reach anywhere in a plane. |
| **Independent** | None can be built from the others. | Height in cm and weight. Not height in cm and height in inches. |
| **Basis** | The smallest set that reaches everything in a space. | (1, 0) and (0, 1) for a plane, but other pairs work too. |
| **Rank** | The number of independent columns, which always equals the number of independent rows. | A 1,000 × 50 data matrix has rank 50 at most. |

##### Column space and null space

- **Column space:** every output Ax can produce. If b isn't in it, Ax = b has no exact solution, which is why regression uses least squares.

- **Null space:** every x where Ax = 0. Add one of these to a solution, and you get another solution that fits equally well.

- **Rank-nullity:** rank + null space size = number of columns. Each lost column dimension adds a direction you can't measure.

##### When features break regression

- **Exact dependence:** height in cm and in inches. XᵀX can't be inverted, and there's no single answer.

- **Near dependence:** strongly correlated features. An answer exists, but small changes in data swing the weights.

- **Dummy variable trap:** one-hot columns for all k categories add up to the intercept column. Drop one, or use regularisation.

- **More features than rows:** rank can't exceed the number of rows, so there are infinitely many perfect fits.

#### The maths

$$ {\mathrm{rank}(A)} + {\dim(\mathrm{null}(A))} = {n}, \qquad {\mathrm{VIF}_j} = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2} $$

As R² approaches 1, VIF grows without limit. At exactly 1, the matrix has lost rank, and the weight isn’t defined.

- **rank**: How many independent directions the columns really cover.

- **null space size**: How many independent directions the matrix wipes out. Weights along these can’t be determined from the data.

- **number of columns**: The two always add up to this.

- **variance inflation factor**: R² is how well other features predict feature j. A VIF of 10 means the variance of its weight is 10 times what it would be, if it were uncorrelated with the others.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Prediction vs explanation:** collinearity may not hurt predictions on similar data, as the mix of weights still works. It does hurt when you try to interpret individual weights.

- **Fixes:** remove one feature, combine them, use ridge, or use PCA.

- **Check:** look at VIF, and at the matrix's singular values. Very small ones mean you're close to losing rank.

- **Numerical rank:** real data rarely has exact zeros. Count singular values above a small threshold.

- **Low-rank data is useful:** many large matrices have a much smaller true rank, which is why compression, recommenders and LoRA work.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The correlation is only 0.9, so it's fine"

It sounds right, since the features are still different. But at 0.9, each weight's variance is already over five times higher, and at 0.99 it's about fifty times higher. Weights can flip sign between samples. Whether that matters depends on your goal: predictions may hold, while explanations won't.

## Say it

### What is the rank of a matrix, and why do correlated features break linear regression?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why do the rows and columns always have the same rank?

It's a basic theorem: the number of independent rows always equals the number of independent columns. It's why a 1,000 × 50 matrix can't have rank above 50, and why more features than rows always leaves a non-trivial null space.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Does multicollinearity hurt predictions?

Not much, if new data has the same correlation, because errors in individual weights cancel out in the combination. It hurts interpretation, and predictions when that correlation changes in production. So it matters most for understanding, and for shifting data.

Follow-up 3 of 3

You have 100 rows and 1,000 features. What happens to linear regression?

The rank is at most 100, so there are infinitely many weights that fit perfectly, and no unique solution. Use regularisation, such as ridge or lasso, reduce the features, or use a minimum-norm solution through the pseudoinverse. Each of those picks one answer.

#### The 30-second answer

The rank is the number of truly independent columns, which is the real dimension of the data. If a feature is a mix of others, the matrix loses rank, XᵀX can't be inverted, and many sets of weights fit equally well. That's what the null space means: directions you can't determine from the data. With strong but not perfect correlation, a solution exists, but weights are unstable, with variance inflated by one over one minus R squared. I'd drop or combine features, or use ridge. Predictions may be fine, but weights can't be trusted.

**Key terms and sources**

Linear independence, span, basis, rank, column and null space, and how they explain collinearity, the dummy variable trap and low-dimensional embeddings. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Kolter and Do, CS229 Linear Algebra Review](https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/cs229-linalg.pdf)

- [Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

- Linear regression on this site

# Orthogonality and Projections

> Why is least squares a projection, and why are orthogonal matrices so useful?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/orthogonality-and-projections/
- Before this: Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity (`fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity`), Linear Independence, Basis and Rank (`fundamentals/linear-independence-basis-and-rank`)
- Related: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're asked to explain least squares without the usual calculus. Your dataset's predictions can only be combinations of its features, and no combination hits y exactly. The interviewer asks:

> Why is least squares a projection, and why are orthogonal matrices so useful?

#### Why it matters

This single picture explains linear regression, PCA, residuals, and why QR is the stable way to solve least squares. Once you see it as geometry, the formulas become easy to remember. See rank and dot products first.

### The idea

Think of the sun straight overhead, casting a pole's shadow on flat ground. The shadow is the closest point on the ground to the top of the pole, and the line from pole top to shadow makes a right angle with the ground. Regression's predictions are y's shadow on what your features can produce.

[Figure: Least squares as a projection. Xw can only reach the column space. Predictions are the closest point to y in that space. The residual is at right angles to it.]

_The residual at right angles is the whole idea._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Rotate the line through the point, then at right angles to it. Move the point anywhere.

#### Project a point onto a line

Blue is the line, green is the projection and red is the residual. Move anything: the residual · line value stays at zero.

Rotate the line until it passes through the point. The error falls to **zero**, which is like a regression fitting perfectly because y is in the column space. Now rotate it to be at right angles to the point: the projection is zero, meaning the feature tells you nothing about y.

**Now say why:** why must the shortest error be at right angles to the line?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Vectors are **orthogonal** if their dot product is zero: they share no direction. **Projection** finds the closest point on a line or subspace, and the error is always at right angles to it. **Least squares is exactly this**: your predictions are the projection of y onto the space of what your features can produce. **Orthogonal matrices** only rotate or reflect, keeping lengths, which makes them very stable.

#### The closest point

##### Why right angles

To find the closest point to b on a line, drop a perpendicular. Any other point on the line is farther away. So the leftover error, b minus the projection, must be orthogonal to the line. That single condition gives every formula here.

##### From a line to least squares

1. Xw can only produce vectors in X's column space.

2. y usually isn't in that space, so no w fits exactly.

3. The closest achievable point is y's projection onto the column space.

4. The residual y − Xw must be orthogonal to every column of X: Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0.

5. Rearranging gives the **normal equations**: XᵀXw = Xᵀy.

That explains a fact about regression with an intercept: residuals sum to zero, because the residual is orthogonal to the all-ones column.

##### Orthogonal matrices

Q has orthonormal columns, and QᵀQ = I. So its inverse is just its transpose, and it never changes a vector's length. It can't amplify errors, which makes it numerically stable.

##### Gram-Schmidt and QR

Take the columns one at a time. Subtract each column's projection onto those before it, then scale to length 1. This gives an orthonormal basis Q, and the coefficients form an upper triangular R, so **A = QR**. Least squares then becomes the easy triangular system Rw = Qᵀy.

#### The maths

$$ {\hat b} = \frac{{a^\top b}}{{a^\top a}}\,a, \qquad {P} = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top, \qquad {\hat y = Py} $$

Example: project b = (2, 3) onto a = (1, 0). The result is (2, 0), and the residual (0, 3) is orthogonal to a.

- **the projection**: The closest point to b along the direction a.

- **how much b points along a**: The dot product measures overlap.

- **normalising**: Divides out a’s own length, so scaling a doesn’t change the result.

- **projection matrix**: Projects onto X’s column space. Applying it twice changes nothing: P² = P.

- **predictions**: Regression predictions are y projected onto what X can produce.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use QR for regression:** solving through XᵀX squares the condition number, so QR is more stable. See solving Ax = b.

- **Check residuals:** if residuals correlate with a feature, the fit isn't really least squares, or there's a bug.

- **PCA:** PCA projects onto the directions that keep the most variance.

- **Orthogonal initialisation:** starting a layer's weights as orthogonal keeps signal lengths steady, which helps deep and recurrent networks.

- **Orthogonal features:** if features are orthogonal, each weight can be computed separately, and removing one doesn't change the others.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just solve the normal equations"

It sounds right, since they're the textbook formula, and for small, well-behaved problems they're fine. But forming XᵀX squares the condition number, which can destroy accuracy on correlated features. QR uses the same geometry on X itself, and that's why libraries use it.

## Say it

### Why is least squares a projection, and why are orthogonal matrices so useful?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why do the residuals sum to zero in regression with an intercept?

The intercept column is all ones, and the residual is orthogonal to every column. A dot product with all ones is just the sum, so it must be zero. Without an intercept, this needn't hold.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the difference between orthogonal and uncorrelated?

Orthogonal means the dot product is zero. Uncorrelated means the covariance is zero, which is the dot product after subtracting the means. So for centred data, they're the same. For uncentred data, they can differ.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why is P squared equal to P?

Once a point is in the space, it's already its own closest point, so projecting again doesn't move it. Algebraically, the middle XᵀX cancels with its inverse. It's a useful test of whether a matrix is a projection.

#### The 30-second answer

Xw can only produce vectors in the column space of X. y usually isn't there, so least squares finds the closest point, which is y's projection onto that space. The residual must be orthogonal to every column, giving X transpose times y minus Xw equals zero, which is the normal equations. Orthogonal matrices have Q transpose Q equal to the identity, so they keep lengths, and their inverse is just the transpose. That's why QR, built with Gram-Schmidt, is a stable way to solve least squares.

**Key terms and sources**

Orthogonal vectors and matrices, projecting onto a line and subspace, least squares as a projection, Gram-Schmidt and QR. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

# Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

> Which directions does a matrix only stretch, and why does PCA care?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors/
- Before this: Matrices as Transformations (`fundamentals/matrices-as-transformations`)
- Related: Principal Component Analysis (`fundamentals/pca`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're running PCA on customer data where orders and app sessions move together. The interviewer asks:

> What is an eigenvector, and how does PCA use eigenvectors?

**Running example:** the covariance matrix of two customer features, orders per month and app sessions per month, both standardised. They move together (correlation 0.5), so the covariance matrix is [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]. What directions does it single out? (The same data appears in the PCA lesson.)

#### Finding a matrix's natural axes

A matrix mixes coordinates, which makes it hard to understand. But many matrices have a hidden set of axes along which they act simply: stretch this way by 1.5, that way by 0.5, nothing else. Find those axes and the matrix becomes a list of stretches. In ML those axes are the directions of greatest variance in data, the most important pages on the web, or the directions in which training is unstable.

### The idea

Think of stretching a rubber sheet with arrows drawn on it. Most arrows swing to a new direction. A few stay on their own line and only get longer or shorter. Those are eigenvectors, and how much they stretch is the eigenvalue.

[Figure: Three arrows before and after a matrix. Two eigenvector arrows stay on their lines and only change length. A third arrow swings to a new direction.]

_Illustrative, using the lesson's covariance matrix: one direction stretches by 1.5, the other by 0.5._

### Play

**Try to break it.** On the covariance matrix, find the arrows that stay on their line. Then switch to rotation 45° and look for them again.

#### Which arrows stay on their line?

Teal: 24 unit vectors around the circle. Orange: where the matrix sends each one (thin line joins input to output). Green: eigen-directions, where input and output stay on the same line.

For the covariance matrix, every arrow swings towards the diagonal except two: along (1, 1) the matrix stretches by 1.5, along (1, −1) it shrinks to 0.5. Those are the directions in which "orders and sessions together" vary most and least: the first and second principal components, with variances 1.5 and 0.5 (75% and 25% of the total).

**Now say why:** why does the rotation have no such arrows, while the covariance matrix has two perpendicular ones?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Most vectors get knocked off their direction when a matrix acts on them. **Eigenvectors** are the special directions that stay on their own line, only stretched or shrunk; the stretch factor is the **eigenvalue** λ, so Av = λv. For a symmetric matrix (like a covariance matrix) the eigenvectors are perpendicular and the eigenvalues real: the matrix is just "stretch along these axes". That is exactly PCA: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the principal components, and the eigenvalues are the variances along them. Repeatedly multiplying by A pulls any vector towards the top eigenvector (**power iteration**), the idea behind PageRank. What you'll be able to do after this: define eigenvectors geometrically, compute them for a 2×2 matrix, explain why covariance eigenvectors are PCA, and describe power iteration.

#### The eigen-equation

$$ {A v} = {\lambda v}, \qquad {\det(A - \lambda I) = 0} $$

MML §4.2; Strang ch. 6. Worked example: A = [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]] gives (1 − λ)² − 0.25 = 0, so λ = 1.5 with v = (1, 1)/√2 and λ = 0.5 with v = (1, −1)/√2.

- **the matrix acting on v**: Apply the transformation to a candidate direction v.

- **just a stretched v**: The result points along v itself, scaled by λ. λ > 1 stretches, 0 < λ < 1 shrinks, λ < 0 flips, λ = 0 squashes v to zero.

- **how to find λ**: Av = λv means (A − λI)v = 0 has a non-zero solution, so A − λI must be singular: its determinant is zero. For a 2×2 matrix that’s a quadratic in λ.

#### Symmetric matrices: the spectral theorem

$$ {A} = {Q}\,{\Lambda}\,{Q^{\top}} $$

Spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices: real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors (MML Theorem 4.15). In practice libraries compute eigen-decompositions with QR-type algorithms (`numpy.linalg.eigh` for symmetric matrices).

- **any symmetric matrix**: For example a covariance matrix.

- **rotate to the eigen-axes**: Q’s columns are orthonormal eigenvectors. Qᵀ rotates the data into eigen-coordinates.

- **stretch along each axis**: Λ is diagonal: the eigenvalues. Nothing but independent stretches.

- **rotate back**: Q rotates back. So A = rotate, stretch, rotate back.

#### Multiply repeatedly and you find the top eigenvector

Write the start vector as a mix of eigenvectors. Each multiplication scales the λ = 1.5 part by 1.5 and the λ = 0.5 part by 0.5, so the smaller part shrinks by a factor of 3 every step relative to the larger; after normalising, the vector swings onto the top eigenvector. The speed depends on the ratio of the top two eigenvalues. Brin & Page's original PageRank is the principal eigenvector of the web's link matrix, computed exactly this way at scale [Brin & Page 1998](http://infolab.stanford.edu/~backrub/google.html).

#### The Rayleigh quotient: why PCA picks the top eigenvector

For a symmetric A, the **Rayleigh quotient** R(x) = xᵀAx / xᵀx says how much A stretches along x. It always lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues, and it reaches the largest exactly at the top eigenvector.

Example: for A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], R(1, 0) = 2, while R(1, 1) = 3, the top eigenvalue.

This explains PCA. The variance of data projected onto a unit vector w is wᵀΣw, which is the Rayleigh quotient of the covariance matrix. So the direction of most variance must be Σ's top eigenvector, and that variance is its eigenvalue.

Next: positive definite matrices look at what the signs of the eigenvalues mean.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Eigenvectors in ML

- **PCA:** principal components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix; eigenvalues are explained variances (PCA).

- **Optimisation:** eigenvalues of the loss Hessian are curvatures; gradient descent diverges when the learning rate exceeds 2/λmax (Gradient Descent), and a large ratio λmax/λmin (condition number) makes it zig-zag.

- **Graphs:** spectral clustering uses eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian; PageRank uses the top eigenvector of the link matrix.

- **RNN stability:** repeatedly multiplying by a recurrent weight matrix explodes or vanishes depending on whether its largest eigenvalue magnitude is above or below 1.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Every matrix has real eigenvectors you can see"

A rotation by 45° moves every direction; it has no real eigenvectors (its eigenvalues are complex). A shear has only one eigen-direction. Non-symmetric matrices can have eigenvectors that aren't perpendicular. The tidy picture, perpendicular axes and real stretches, is guaranteed only for **symmetric** matrices, which luckily include covariance matrices, Hessians and graph Laplacians: most of the matrices ML cares about.

## Say it

### What is an eigenvector, and how does PCA use eigenvectors?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How is PCA related to eigenvectors?

PCA's components are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, sorted by eigenvalue; each eigenvalue is the variance along its component. In practice computed via SVD of the centred data.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Can eigenvalues be negative or complex?

Yes in general; rotations have complex ones. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues; covariance matrices (positive semi-definite) have non-negative ones.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the link to exploding/vanishing gradients?

Multiplying by the same matrix many times scales components by λᵗ: |λ| > 1 explodes, |λ| < 1 vanishes.

#### The 30-second answer

An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction the matrix only stretches, Av = λv, and the eigenvalue is the stretch factor. You find eigenvalues from det(A − λI) = 0. Symmetric matrices, like covariance matrices, have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors, so they decompose as QΛQᵀ: rotate, stretch, rotate back. In ML, the covariance eigenvectors are PCA's principal components with eigenvalues as variances, Hessian eigenvalues describe curvature and set the maximum stable learning rate, and power iteration finds the top eigenvector, as in PageRank.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Eigenvectors are always perpendicular." Only guaranteed for symmetric (normal) matrices.

- "An eigenvector is unique." Any non-zero multiple is also an eigenvector; we usually normalise.

**Key terms and sources**

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Eigenvector** | A non-zero v with Av = λv: a direction only stretched. |
| **Eigenvalue** | The stretch factor λ. |
| **Characteristic equation** | det(A − λI) = 0. |
| **Spectral theorem** | Symmetric A = QΛQᵀ, orthonormal eigenvectors, real eigenvalues. |
| **Power iteration** | Repeated multiplication + normalisation → top eigenvector. |
| **Condition number** | λmax/λmin (symmetric positive definite): how stretched the problem is. |

#### Sources

1. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, CUP 2020, [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/) (ch. 4: eigendecomposition, spectral theorem).

2. G. Strang, _Introduction to Linear Algebra_, 5th ed., 2016, ch. 6.

3. S. Brin & L. Page, "The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual web search engine", WWW 1998, [stanford.edu](http://infolab.stanford.edu/~backrub/google.html).

# Positive Definite Matrices

> What is a positive definite matrix, and where does it show up in ML?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/positive-definite-matrices/
- Before this: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors (`fundamentals/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors`)
- Related: Convexity & Local Minima (`fundamentals/convexity-and-local-minima`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your Gaussian process crashes with "matrix not positive definite". Separately, you built a correlation matrix from data with missing values, and an optimiser is rejecting it. The interviewer asks:

> What is a positive definite matrix, and where does it show up in ML?

#### Why it matters

This one idea connects covariance, convexity, kernels and numerical stability. Whenever a library complains that a matrix "isn't positive definite", this is what it means, and it's usually a real data problem. See eigenvalues first.

### The idea

Think of a valley with a single lowest point. Walk any direction from the bottom, and you go up. That's positive definite. A long flat trough is semi-definite, and a mountain pass, up one way and down another, is indefinite. The matrix describes the shape of the land.

[Figure: Three shapes. Positive definite is a bowl with all eigenvalues positive. Semi-definite is a trough with some eigenvalues zero. Indefinite is a saddle with mixed signs.]

_The signs of the eigenvalues decide the shape._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise b from 1 to 2.5, then lower a below zero.

#### Shape the bowl

The curve shows points where xᵀAx = 1. An ellipse means positive definite. Open curves mean a saddle or flat direction. Ridge shows the λ that would lift the lowest eigenvalue just above zero.

Raise b from **1** to **2.5**. The features are now "too correlated" for those variances, and one eigenvalue goes negative. A real covariance matrix can't do that, so if yours does, something's wrong with how it was computed.

**Now say why:** why can't a real covariance matrix have a negative eigenvalue?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A symmetric matrix is **positive definite** if xᵀAx is above zero for every non-zero x, which means all its eigenvalues are positive. Picture a bowl with one lowest point. **Semi-definite** allows flat directions, and **indefinite** gives a saddle. That's why this matters: a **positive definite Hessian means a true minimum**, covariance matrices are always semi-definite, and you can factor these matrices quickly with Cholesky.

#### Bowls and saddles

| Type | Eigenvalues | Shape of xᵀAx | Meaning for a Hessian |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Positive definite** | All above 0 | A bowl | A true local minimum |
| **Semi-definite** | All 0 or above | A trough with flat directions | Flat directions, so it's not unique |
| **Indefinite** | Mixed signs | A saddle | A saddle point |
| **Negative definite** | All below 0 | An upside-down bowl | A local maximum |

##### How to test for it

- **Try Cholesky:** the practical method. It succeeds if and only if the matrix is positive definite, and it's cheap.

- **Eigenvalues:** check they're all positive. This is clear, but slower.

- **For a 2 × 2:** the top-left entry and the determinant must both be positive.

##### Where it shows up

- **Covariance:** xᵀΣx is the variance of a combination of features, and variance can't be negative. So Σ is always semi-definite.

- **Gram matrices:** XᵀX is always semi-definite, and it's positive definite when X has full column rank.

- **Ridge regression:** adding λI lifts every eigenvalue by λ, which makes XᵀX + λI positive definite, so it always has an inverse.

- **Kernels:** a valid kernel must produce a semi-definite matrix, as if it were dot products in some space.

- **Sampling:** if Σ = LLᵀ, then Lz has covariance Σ when z is standard normal.

#### The maths

$$ {x^\top A x} > 0 \;\; \forall x \neq 0 \;\iff\; {\lambda_i(A) > 0} \;\iff\; {A = LL^\top} $$

These three statements are equivalent for symmetric matrices. Example: [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it’s positive definite. [[1, 2], [2, 1]] has eigenvalues 3 and −1, so it’s indefinite.

- **the quadratic form**: A single number from a vector and a matrix. It’s positive in every direction.

- **the eigenvalues**: All are positive, as each one is the value of the form along an eigenvector.

- **Cholesky exists**: The matrix factors into a lower triangular L times its transpose, like a matrix square root.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **"Matrix not positive definite" errors:** common causes are duplicate rows, features with more columns than rows, or rounding errors. Check your data before anything else.

- **Add jitter:** adding a small value to the diagonal, like 1e-6, is a standard fix for numerical problems in Gaussian processes. It's a repair for rounding, not for bad data.

- **Pairwise deletion breaks it:** computing correlations with missing data on different rows can produce a matrix that's no longer semi-definite.

- **In deep learning:** real Hessians are usually indefinite, with many saddle points and flat directions, so these tidy guarantees rarely hold.

- **Use Cholesky when you can:** it takes about half the work of LU, and it's stable for these matrices.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "All entries are positive, so it's positive definite"

It sounds right, given the name. But it's about directions, not entries. [[1, 2], [2, 1]] has only positive entries, yet its eigenvalues are 3 and −1, so it's indefinite. And [[2, −1], [−1, 2]] has negative entries, and it's positive definite. Check the eigenvalues, or try Cholesky.

## Say it

### What is a positive definite matrix, and where does it show up in ML?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is a covariance matrix always positive semi-definite?

For any weights w, wᵀΣw is the variance of the combination wᵀx, and variance can't be negative. It's only semi-definite, not definite, if some combination has zero variance, like when one feature is an exact mix of the others.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How does ridge regression help with a singular matrix?

Adding λI adds λ to every eigenvalue. A zero eigenvalue becomes λ, so the smallest eigenvalue is at least λ, and the matrix is positive definite and invertible. It also reduces the condition number, which makes the solution more stable.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Your Gaussian process fails with a Cholesky error. What do you check?

First, duplicate or almost-duplicate points, since those make rows nearly identical. Then the kernel's length scale, as very long scales make everything look alike. Adding a small jitter to the diagonal fixes pure rounding problems, but check the data first.

#### The 30-second answer

A symmetric matrix is positive definite if x transpose A x is positive for every non-zero x, which is the same as all eigenvalues being positive. Geometrically, it's a bowl with one minimum. Semi-definite allows flat directions, and indefinite is a saddle. It appears in many places. A positive definite Hessian means a true local minimum. Covariance matrices are always semi-definite, because variance can't be negative. Ridge's lambda I makes X transpose X positive definite. The practical test is Cholesky, which succeeds only for positive definite matrices.

**Key terms and sources**

Quadratic forms, positive definite and semi-definite matrices, how to test for them, and their role in covariance, convexity, kernels and sampling. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Kolter and Do, CS229 Linear Algebra Review](https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/cs229-linalg.pdf)

- [Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

- [Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/)

- Convexity on this site
