# SVD & Low-Rank Approximation

> How LoRA and compression keep most of a matrix with a fraction of the numbers.

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/svd-and-low-rank/
- Before this: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors (`fundamentals/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

You need to fine-tune a huge language model, and a teammate suggests training only a low-rank update to its weights. The interviewer asks:

> What is SVD, and what do you get by keeping only the top k singular values?

**Running example:** a 32 × 32 grayscale icon of a delivery scooter (1,024 pixel values), with a little random noise added, as if from a cheap camera. We compress it with the SVD and ask how many components we need, and whether dropping components can even remove noise.

#### Big matrices with little real information

A ratings matrix of 10 million users × 100,000 restaurants, a 12,288 × 12,288 weight matrix in a language model, an image: these are huge, but their content is often driven by a few underlying factors (taste profiles, dominant directions, shapes). We want to find those factors, store less, and throw away the noise. The eigendecomposition only works for square (and nicely behaved) matrices; the SVD works for **any** matrix.

### The idea

Think of a picture as a stack of transparent layers, sorted from most to least important. The first few layers give you almost the whole picture. Later layers add fine detail, and eventually mostly noise. SVD finds those layers for any matrix.

[Figure: A matrix equals a sum of layers, drawn darker for the most important layer and fainter for later layers.]

_Illustrative. Each layer is one rank-one term, and its singular value says how much it matters._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Slide the rank up from 1 and watch the error against the clean icon. Keep going all the way to 32.

#### Keep k singular values

Left: noisy image and its rank-k reconstruction. Right: the singular values, kept in teal.

The first singular value alone carries 74% of the energy; five carry 96%. Error against the noisy image falls steadily to zero at k = 32 (you reproduce the noise exactly). Error against the **clean** icon is lowest around k = 8 (13%, below the 18.7% error of the noisy image itself) and then rises again as later components add noise back. Truncation is a denoiser: the signal lives in a few strong directions, the noise is spread thinly over all of them.

**Now say why:** why does the error against the clean icon stop falling and then rise, even as you keep more of the image?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Every** matrix, any shape, can be written as A = UΣVᵀ: a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation. The stretches, the **singular values** σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ …, say how important each direction is. Keep only the top k and you get the **best possible rank-k approximation** of A (Eckart–Young), stored in k(m + n + 1) numbers instead of m × n. Real data is often nearly low-rank, so a small k captures most of it and drops noise. That idea is PCA (SVD of centred data), matrix-factorisation recommenders (users × items ≈ low-rank), and LoRA (fine-tune a huge weight matrix by learning a rank-r update BA). What you'll be able to do after this: describe the three factors of the SVD, explain rank-k truncation and its error, compute the storage saving, and connect it to PCA, recommenders and LoRA.

#### The decomposition

$$ {A} = {U}\,{\Sigma}\,{V^{\top}} = {\textstyle\sum_{i} \sigma_i\, u_i v_i^{\top}} $$

MML §4.5. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA, and V's columns are its eigenvectors (Eigenvalues).

- **any m × n matrix**: Our 32 × 32 image, or a users × items ratings table.

- **left singular vectors**: Orthonormal columns: the output-side directions (column patterns of the image).

- **singular values**: A diagonal of non-negative stretches σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0: how much each direction matters.

- **right singular vectors**: Orthonormal columns: the input-side directions (row patterns).

- **a sum of rank-1 layers**: Equivalently, A is a sum of simple outer products σᵢ uᵢ vᵢᵀ, each a rank-1 “layer”, from most to least important.

#### The best rank-k approximation

$$ {A_k = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^{\top}}, \qquad {\lVert A - A_k\rVert_F = \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{i>k} \sigma_i^2}}, \qquad {k(m + n + 1)} $$

C. Eckart & G. Young, "The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank", _Psychometrika_, 1936; MML Theorem 4.25.

- **rank-k approximation**: Keep the first k terms of the sum.

- **its error**: Frobenius distance to A: exactly the root-sum-of-squares of the dropped singular values. No other rank-k matrix does better.

- **what you store**: k columns of U, k of V and k singular values: k(m + n + 1) numbers. For our 32 × 32 image and k = 5: 325 instead of 1,024.

#### LoRA: fine-tune with a rank-r update

$$ h = {W_0}\,x + {B}\,{A}\,x $$

Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models", Eq. 3 [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685#page=4).

- **frozen pretrained weights**: A d × k matrix, never updated.

- **d × r**: Trainable, initialised to zero so training starts from the pretrained model.

- **r × k**: Trainable, random Gaussian initialisation. With r ≪ d, B and A together have r(d + k) parameters instead of d·k.

The authors hypothesise that the change in weights during fine-tuning has a low "intrinsic rank". On GPT-3 175B, LoRA "can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times" compared with full fine-tuning with Adam [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685), and "a very low rank (i.e., r in Figure 1 can be one or two) suffices even when the full rank (i.e., d) is as high as 12,288" [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685#page=2). Because BA has the same shape as W₀, it can be merged after training: no extra inference latency.

#### SVD and eigendecomposition, and very large matrices

##### How they connect

- **Scope:** eigendecomposition needs a square matrix, and may need complex numbers. SVD works for any matrix, and always gives real values.

- **The link:** AᵀA = VΣ²Vᵀ. So A's right singular vectors are the eigenvectors of AᵀA, and its eigenvalues are the squared singular values.

- **When they match:** for a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix, SVD and eigendecomposition are the same.

- **PCA:** for centred data X with n rows, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are σ²/(n − 1). Libraries often use the SVD of X, which avoids forming XᵀX and squaring its condition number.

##### Randomised SVD

A full SVD is too slow for very large matrices, and you usually only want the top k directions. So multiply A by a small random matrix, which captures most of its top directions with high probability. Then run an exact SVD on that much smaller matrix. With fast-decaying singular values, this gets close to the true result at far lower cost.

Next: the pseudoinverse uses SVD to solve systems with no ordinary inverse, and norms define the error sizes used here.

## In practice

### In practice

#### SVD across ML

- **PCA:** the SVD of the centred data X = UΣVᵀ gives the principal components (rows of Vᵀ) and variances σ²/(n − 1) (PCA).

- **Recommenders:** approximate the users × items ratings matrix by user factors × item factors of rank k (matrix factorisation, popularised by the Netflix Prize). Missing ratings need special solvers (alternating least squares, SGD), not plain SVD.

- **Latent semantic analysis:** truncated SVD of a term–document matrix finds topics.

- **Pseudo-inverse and least squares:** the SVD gives the stable solution to linear regression even when XᵀX is singular.

- **Model compression:** replace a big weight matrix by its rank-k factors to save memory and compute.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Compress by keeping a subset of rows or pixels"

Dropping rows, columns or pixels throws away specific parts of the data. The SVD instead keeps the most important _patterns_ spread across all pixels. And there's a guarantee no ad-hoc scheme has: among all rank-k matrices, the truncated SVD is closest to A (Eckart–Young, 1936), with error equal to the root sum of squares of the dropped singular values.

#### Caveats

- Full SVD costs O(min(mn², m²n)); for big matrices use randomised or truncated SVD (`TruncatedSVD`, `svds`).

- Low rank works only if the data really is close to low rank; a full-rank weight change (e.g. a new language) needs larger r, as the LoRA authors note.

- Singular vectors are directions of variance, not guaranteed to be interpretable features.

## Say it

### What is SVD, and what do you get by keeping only the top k singular values?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

SVD vs eigendecomposition?

Eigendecomposition needs a square matrix and may not exist or be orthogonal; SVD exists for every matrix and always has orthonormal factors. Singular values of A are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How does PCA use SVD?

Centre X, compute its SVD; the right singular vectors are the principal directions and σ²/(n − 1) the variances. It avoids forming the covariance matrix and is more stable.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does LoRA work?

Fine-tuning updates appear to have low intrinsic rank; a rank-r update BA with r ≪ d captures most of it, cutting trainable parameters and optimizer memory, and it can be merged into W₀ at inference.

#### The 30-second answer

The singular value decomposition writes any matrix as UΣVᵀ: orthonormal input directions, non-negative singular values, and orthonormal output directions, or equivalently a sum of rank-one layers ordered by importance. Keeping the top k gives the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm, by the Eckart–Young theorem, with error equal to the root sum of squares of the dropped singular values, and storage of k(m + n + 1) numbers. It underlies PCA, matrix-factorisation recommenders, latent semantic analysis and LoRA, which fine-tunes a large model by learning a low-rank update BA.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "SVD only works on square matrices." It works on any shape.

- "Keeping more components is always better." Against noisy data, too many components reproduce the noise.

**Key terms and sources**

The singular value decomposition, rank-k truncation and the Eckart–Young theorem, compression and denoising, and how low rank powers PCA, recommenders and LoRA · built from Deisenroth et al., _Mathematics for Machine Learning_ (ch. 4), Eckart & Young (1936) and Hu et al., "LoRA" (2021) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SVD** | A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix. |
| **Singular value** | Non-negative stretch σᵢ; importance of a direction. |
| **Rank** | Number of non-zero singular values. |
| **Truncated SVD** | Keep the top k terms. |
| **Eckart–Young** | Truncated SVD is the best rank-k approximation. |

#### Sources

1. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, CUP 2020, [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/) (ch. 4.5–4.6).

2. C. Eckart & G. Young, "The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank", _Psychometrika_ 1, 1936.

3. E. Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models", ICLR 2022, [arXiv:2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

# Solving Ax = b: LU, QR, Cholesky and the Pseudoinverse

> Why shouldn't you invert a matrix to solve Ax = b, and what is the pseudoinverse?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/solving-linear-systems/
- Before this: SVD & Low-Rank Approximation (`fundamentals/svd-and-low-rank`), Orthogonality and Projections (`fundamentals/orthogonality-and-projections`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

A teammate's regression code computes the inverse of XᵀX directly. It's slow, and with correlated features the weights come out badly wrong. Some of your problems also have more unknowns than equations. The interviewer asks:

> Why shouldn't you invert a matrix to solve Ax = b, and what is the pseudoinverse?

#### Why it matters

On paper, you write the inverse. Software almost never computes one. Knowing why helps you pick methods, understand numerical warnings and explain what a library's linear regression really does. This uses SVD and QR.

### The idea

Think of finding a word's page. You could copy out the whole dictionary into a lookup table, just to look up one word. Or you could sort things into easy steps and go straight to it. Inverting builds the table. Factoring does the easy steps.

[Figure: Choosing a method. LU suits general square systems. Cholesky suits positive definite matrices at half the cost. QR suits least squares. SVD handles rank problems.]

_Factor into easy pieces, rather than computing an inverse._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Slide ε down to 0.000001, and change b by a tiny amount.

#### Nudge a nearly singular system

Solves A = [[1, 1], [1, 1 + ε]] with b = (2, 2 + ε), whose exact solution is (1, 1), then adds your change to b's second value. Exact arithmetic, using the formula directly. Digits lost is the rule of thumb log₁₀(κ).

Slide ε down to **0.000001**. The two equations are nearly the same, so a tiny change in b sends the solution far away. The maths is correct: the problem itself is unstable. Better methods won't rescue an unstable problem, but regularisation changes the question to one that's stable.

**Now say why:** why can't a better algorithm fix a badly conditioned problem?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Don't compute A⁻¹ to solve Ax = b: it's slower and less accurate than **factoring** A into easy pieces. Use **LU** for general square matrices, **Cholesky** for positive definite ones, **QR** for least squares and **SVD** when rank is in doubt. The **condition number** tells you how much errors get amplified. The **pseudoinverse** extends the idea to any matrix, giving the least-squares answer with the smallest weights.

#### Factor, then solve

The idea: split A into matrices that are easy to solve, like triangular or orthogonal ones. Triangular systems take only about n² work, by substituting one line at a time.

| Method | Form | Use it for | Approximate cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LU** | A = LU, with row swaps | General square systems. Reuse the factors for many b. | ⅔n³ operations |
| **Cholesky** | A = LLᵀ | Positive definite: covariance, ridge, Gaussian processes. | ⅓n³, half of LU |
| **QR** | A = QR | Least squares, when it's well behaved. | About 2mn² |
| **SVD** | A = UΣVᵀ | Rank-deficient or nearly so. The most robust, and the slowest. | Several times QR |

##### Why not invert?

- **Cost:** computing A⁻¹ then multiplying takes about three times the work of an LU solve.

- **Accuracy:** it generally adds more rounding error.

- **Memory:** the inverse of a sparse matrix is usually dense, so you can lose all the savings.

##### Condition number

The condition number κ is the largest singular value divided by the smallest. It's how much a small change in the data can be amplified in the answer. As a rule of thumb, you lose about log₁₀(κ) digits of accuracy.

**The normal equations square it:** κ(XᵀX) = κ(X)². If κ(X) is 10⁸, XᵀX has about 10¹⁶, which is beyond double precision. That's why libraries use QR or SVD for regression.

##### The pseudoinverse

When there's no inverse, take the SVD, invert the non-zero singular values and leave the zeros at zero. That gives A⁺. It handles every case:

- **Too many equations:** A⁺b is the least-squares answer.

- **Too few equations:** of infinitely many exact answers, A⁺b has the smallest norm.

It also connects to ridge: as λ shrinks to zero, the ridge solution approaches A⁺b.

#### The maths

$$ {A^{+}} = V\,{\Sigma^{+}}\,U^\top, \qquad {\kappa(A)} = \frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}, \qquad {\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \le \kappa(A)\,\frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}} $$

Example: if κ = 1,000 and your data has 0.1% noise, the answer could be wrong by up to 100%.

- **the pseudoinverse**: Works for any matrix, even non-square ones. If A has an inverse, A⁺ equals it.

- **inverting the singular values**: Each non-zero σ becomes 1/σ, and zeros stay zero. Very small values should be treated as zero, as 1/σ would blow up.

- **the condition number**: How close the matrix is to losing rank. An orthogonal matrix has κ = 1, the best possible.

- **what it means**: A relative error in b can grow by up to κ times in x.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use a solver:** call solve, not inv. For regression, call a least-squares function.

- **Scale your features:** features in very different units raise the condition number. Standardising is an easy fix.

- **Reuse factors:** if you solve for many b, factor once, then each solve is cheap.

- **Choose a cutoff:** pseudoinverse functions treat tiny singular values as zero. That threshold matters when you're near rank deficiency.

- **Very large systems:** direct methods grow with n³, so use iterative methods such as conjugate gradient, or gradient descent, for huge or sparse problems.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "My matrix isn't singular, so inverting is safe"

It sounds right, since the inverse exists. But being invertible isn't the same as being safe. A nearly singular matrix has an inverse, and it amplifies every rounding error and bit of noise. Check the condition number, and solve by factoring. Regularisation helps where the problem itself is unstable.

## Say it

### Why shouldn't you invert a matrix to solve Ax = b, and what is the pseudoinverse?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why do the normal equations lose accuracy?

Forming XᵀX squares the condition number. A condition number of 10⁸, which is manageable, becomes 10¹⁶, close to the limit of double precision. QR works on X directly, so it avoids this. Normal equations remain faster, and they're fine for well-conditioned problems.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does the pseudoinverse give when there are more unknowns than equations?

Of the infinitely many exact solutions, it gives the one with the smallest norm. Interestingly, gradient descent started at zero converges to this same solution for linear regression, which is one way of explaining implicit regularisation.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When would you use gradient descent instead of a direct solve?

When n is so large that n³ or even storing the matrix is too expensive, or when the data is sparse or arrives in batches. Direct methods are exact and can be better for small dense problems. Conditioning still matters, since badly conditioned problems also slow gradient descent.

#### The 30-second answer

I wouldn't invert. Computing the inverse costs about three times an LU solve, and it's less accurate. I'd factor A into easy pieces: LU for general matrices, Cholesky for positive definite ones at half the cost, QR for least squares and SVD if the rank is in doubt. The condition number, largest over smallest singular value, says how much errors get amplified, and normal equations square it, which is why libraries use QR or SVD. The pseudoinverse inverts only the non-zero singular values, giving the least-squares answer with the smallest norm.

**Key terms and sources**

How computers actually solve linear systems: LU, QR, Cholesky and SVD, the condition number, and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Boyd and Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/vmls/)

- [Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data](https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

- [Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/)

- [Kolter and Do, CS229 Linear Algebra Review](https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/cs229-linalg.pdf)

# Matrix Calculus

> How do you differentiate a matrix expression, like the least-squares loss?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/matrix-calculus/
- Before this: Matrix Multiplication and Tensor Shapes (`fundamentals/matrix-multiplication-and-tensor-shapes`), Derivatives, Gradients & the Chain Rule (`fundamentals/derivatives-and-chain-rule`)
- Related: Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

## Intuition

### The situation

In an interview, you're asked to derive the least-squares solution on a whiteboard. Your hand-written gradient for a custom loss also trains badly, and you suspect a missing transpose. The interviewer asks:

> How do you differentiate a matrix expression, like the least-squares loss?

#### Why it matters

Interviews often ask you to derive a gradient, and every training loop relies on them. Thinking in shapes turns a messy sum into a few lines. This uses derivatives and the chain rule and tensor shapes.

### The idea

Think of a mixing desk with hundreds of sliders, and one volume meter. The gradient tells you, for each slider, how much the meter moves if you nudge it. Calculus works as usual, one slider at a time. Matrices are just tidy bookkeeping, and their shapes tell you when you've made a mistake.

[Figure: Derivatives by shape. A scalar of a vector has a gradient. A vector of a vector has a Jacobian. The second derivative of a scalar has a Hessian.]

_The shape tells you which derivative you've got._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the weights towards (1, 2), and compare the formula with the numerical value.

#### Check the formula numerically

Fixed example: X = [[1, 0], [1, 1], [1, 2]] and y = (1, 3, 5), which fits exactly at w = (1, 2). The numerical gradient nudges each weight by 0.0001 either way. This check also finds bugs in hand-written gradients.

Move the weights towards **(1, 2)**, and the gradient falls to zero as the loss does. Comparing against nudged values like this is called a **gradient check**, and it's the standard way to test a gradient written by hand.

**Now say why:** why does the gradient vanish exactly at the best fit?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Matrix calculus is ordinary calculus, organised by **shape**. A scalar function of a vector has a **gradient**, the same shape as the vector. A vector function of a vector has a **Jacobian**. The second derivative of a scalar gives a **Hessian**. A few identities cover most ML, like ∇‖Xw − y‖² = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y). Setting this to zero derives least squares, and multiplying Jacobians is all **backpropagation** does.

#### Derivatives by shape

| Input → output | Derivative | Shape | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vector → scalar | **Gradient** | n | Loss with respect to weights. |
| Vector → vector | **Jacobian** | m × n | A layer's outputs with respect to its inputs. |
| Vector → scalar, twice | **Hessian** | n × n | The curvature of the loss. |

##### Identities worth knowing

| Function | Gradient with respect to x |
|---|---|
| aᵀx | a |
| xᵀx | 2x |
| Ax | A (a Jacobian) |
| xᵀAx | (A + Aᵀ)x, or 2Ax when A is symmetric |
| ‖Ax − b‖² | 2Aᵀ(Ax − b) |

A helpful check: in one dimension, ax² has derivative 2ax. The matrix version looks similar, and the shapes tell you where the transpose goes.

##### Deriving least squares

1. Loss: L(w) = ‖Xw − y‖².

2. Gradient: ∇L = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y).

3. Set to zero: XᵀXw = Xᵀy, the normal equations.

4. Hessian: 2XᵀX, which is semi-definite. So the loss is convex, and this is a true minimum.

##### Why backpropagation runs backwards

The chain rule multiplies Jacobians: J₃J₂J₁. Each may be enormous. Starting from the output, you keep a vector and multiply it by one Jacobian at a time. This is called a **vector-Jacobian product**, and it doesn't require forming any full Jacobian. So one backward pass costs about as much as a forward pass, however many parameters there are.

#### The maths

$$ {L(w)} = \|Xw - y\|^2 \;\Rightarrow\; {\nabla L} = 2X^\top{(Xw - y)}, \qquad {\nabla^2 L} = 2X^\top X $$

Layout warning: books differ on whether a gradient is a row or a column. This site uses columns, which is the common convention in ML. Let shapes guide you.

- **the loss**: A single number from n weights, so its gradient has n entries.

- **the gradient**: Xᵀ maps the errors back to one value per weight. Shapes: [n, m] × [m] gives [n].

- **the residual**: The current errors. When they’re orthogonal to X’s columns, the gradient is zero, matching the projection picture.

- **the Hessian**: It doesn’t depend on w, so curvature is the same everywhere. It’s semi-definite, so the loss is convex.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Check shapes first:** most mistakes show up as a shape mismatch, so write shapes under each step.

- **Gradient check:** compare hand-written gradients against finite differences, using central differences with a small step.

- **Autograd does the rest:** frameworks compute these for you, but you still need this to debug them, reason about memory and read papers.

- **Hessians are huge:** n weights give n² entries, so large models use Hessian-vector products, or approximations, instead.

- **Forward vs reverse mode:** reverse suits many inputs and few outputs, like a loss. Forward suits few inputs and many outputs.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Autograd does this, so I don't need it"

It sounds right, since frameworks compute gradients for you. But interviews ask you to derive them, and debugging exploding gradients, memory use and custom losses all need this understanding. You'll also read papers written in this notation. Autograd saves effort, but it doesn't replace understanding.

## Say it

### How do you differentiate a matrix expression, like the least-squares loss?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the gradient of xᵀAx when A isn't symmetric?

(A + Aᵀ)x. Only the symmetric part of A contributes to the value, so that's what appears. When A is symmetric, it simplifies to 2Ax. Example: for A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] and x = (1, 1), the gradient is (6, 8).

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why is reverse mode used for training?

There are millions of inputs (weights) and one output (loss). Reverse mode computes all those gradients in a single backward pass. Forward mode would need one pass per weight. The cost is memory, as you have to store intermediate values from the forward pass.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you find a bug in a gradient?

Run a gradient check: nudge each weight by a small amount in each direction, compute the loss change, and compare with the gradient. Use a small random model and a few weights, as it's slow. Differences usually come from a wrong transpose, a missing factor of two, or a non-smooth function.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd think in shapes. A scalar loss of n weights has an n-length gradient. For L equals the norm of Xw minus y squared, the gradient is 2 X transpose times Xw minus y. Shapes confirm it: n by m times m gives n. Setting it to zero gives the normal equations, and the Hessian, 2 X transpose X, is semi-definite, so it's a true minimum. For a vector output, you get a Jacobian. Backprop is a chain of Jacobians, multiplied from the output, so you only keep a vector and never form the full matrices.

**Key terms and sources**

Gradients, Jacobians and Hessians, the key identities, layout conventions, deriving least squares and why backpropagation multiplies from the output. · checked 6 Nov 2026

# Linear Algebra Practice

> Shapes, rank, eigenvalues, least squares, SVD and gradients: can you do them by hand?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Linear algebra
- Type: Interview · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/linear-algebra-practice/
- Before this: SVD & Low-Rank Approximation (`fundamentals/svd-and-low-rank`)
- Quiz topic: `la`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Say your approach out loud, then open the answer and compare the method, not just the number.

**Tools for this page:** check shapes first, then ask what's independent. For symmetric matrices, the eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant, which is a quick check.

Question 1 · Easy · shapes

### A is 3 × 4, and B is 4 × 2. What shape is AB? Can you compute BA?

Answer: **AB is 3 × 2. BA isn't defined.**

1. For AB, the inner sizes match: 4 and 4. The result takes the outer sizes: 3 × 2.

2. For BA, the inner sizes are 2 and 3, which don't match.

Even when both are defined, AB usually differs from BA.

Question 2 · Easy · rank

### What's the rank of [[1, 2], [2, 4]]?

Answer: **1**

1. The second row is twice the first, so there's only one independent row.

2. Check: the determinant is 1 × 4 − 2 × 2 = 0, so it can't have rank 2.

Rows and columns always have the same rank.

Question 3 · Easy · cosine

### What's the cosine similarity between (1, 0) and (1, 1)?

Answer: **About 0.707**

1. Dot product: 1 × 1 + 0 × 1 = 1.

2. Lengths: 1 and √2.

3. Cosine: 1 / √2 ≈ 0.707, an angle of 45°.

Length doesn't affect cosine similarity.

Question 4 · Medium · eigenvalues

### Find the eigenvalues of [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Is the matrix positive definite?

Answer: **3 and 1, so yes**

1. Solve (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0, so 2 − λ = ±1.

2. λ = 3 with eigenvector (1, 1), and λ = 1 with eigenvector (1, −1).

3. All eigenvalues are positive, so it's positive definite.

The eigenvalues add up to the trace, 4, and multiply to the determinant, 3. That's a quick check.

Question 5 · Medium · least squares

### You fit one constant w to y = (1, 2, 6), using least squares. What's w, and how does this relate to projection?

Answer: **w = 3, the mean**

1. X is the all-ones column, so XᵀX = 3, and Xᵀy = 9.

2. w = 9 / 3 = 3.

3. The prediction (3, 3, 3) is y's projection onto the all-ones direction, and the residual (−2, −1, 3) sums to zero, so it's orthogonal to it.

This is why the mean minimises squared error.

Question 6 · Medium · multiplication cost

### A is 10 × 100, B is 100 × 5 and C is 5 × 50. How much do (AB)C and A(BC) cost?

Answer: **7,500 and 75,000 multiplications**

1. (AB)C: 10 × 100 × 5 = 5,000, then 10 × 5 × 50 = 2,500. Total: 7,500.

2. A(BC): 100 × 5 × 50 = 25,000, then 10 × 100 × 50 = 50,000. Total: 75,000.

Same result, at ten times the cost.

Question 7 · Hard · SVD

### A matrix has singular values 5, 3 and 1. What's the error of its best rank-2 approximation, and what share of the energy does it keep?

Answer: **Error 1, and about 97% of the energy**

1. The best rank-2 keeps 5 and 3, and drops 1 (Eckart-Young).

2. Frobenius error: √(1²) = 1. Spectral error: 1.

3. Energy kept: (25 + 9) / (25 + 9 + 1) = 34/35 ≈ 97.1%.

Energy uses squared singular values, not the values themselves.

Question 8 · Hard · gradient

### What's the gradient of f(x) = xᵀAx, with A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] at x = (1, 1)?

Answer: **(6, 8)**

1. A is symmetric, so ∇f = 2Ax.

2. Ax = (2 + 1, 1 + 3) = (3, 4).

3. 2Ax = (6, 8).

Check numerically: f(1, 1) = 7. Nudging x₁ by 0.01 gives f ≈ 7.0602, a slope of about 6.

**More practice and sources**

8 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 6 Nov 2026

Keep practising

Review vectors, rank, SVD and matrix calculus.

# Derivatives, Gradients & the Chain Rule

> How backprop is just the chain rule, applied carefully.

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Calculus and optimisation
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/derivatives-and-chain-rule/
- Related: Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`)
- Quiz topic: `calc`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model has billions of weights, and nudging each one to measure its effect would take billions of passes for a single step. The interviewer asks:

> How does backpropagation use the chain rule?

**Running example:** a one-neuron model predicting whether a delivery will be late. Input x (distance, scaled), weight w, bias b; the neuron computes z = wx + b, then the probability a = σ(z) = 1/(1 + e−z), and the loss is the squared error L = (a − y)² against the true label y. Training needs ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b.

#### Which way should each weight move?

A model has thousands to billions of weights and one number, the loss, that says how wrong it is. To improve, each weight must move in the direction that reduces the loss, by an amount that matches how sensitive the loss is to it. Derivatives give exactly that sensitivity, and the chain rule makes it computable for deep, nested models.

### The idea

Think of a row of gears. Turn the first one, and the last one moves by the product of every gear ratio in between. The chain rule is that product. Backprop walks the gears backwards from the loss to find how much each weight matters.

[Figure: A chain from weight w to score z to probability a to loss L, with a slope on each link. Multiplying the slopes 1, 0.21 and 1.38 gives about 0.30.]

_From the lesson's one-neuron example, with w = 1, x = 1, b = −0.2 and y = 0._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Here z is the neuron's score before the sigmoid. Raise w and x until z is above about 5, for example w = 3 and x = 2.

#### Chain rule vs finite differences

Push |z| above about 5 (e.g. w = 3, x = 2): the sigmoid saturates, ∂a/∂z collapses towards 0 and the gradient vanishes even though the prediction may be badly wrong. That's the vanishing-gradient problem in miniature.

**Now say why:** why does the gradient vanish even when the prediction is badly wrong?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **derivative** answers "if I nudge this input a little, how much does the output change?". With many inputs (every weight in a model), each has a **partial derivative**, and together they form the **gradient**: an arrow pointing in the direction where the loss rises fastest. Training walks the other way. Models are long chains of simple steps (multiply, add, squash, compare to the target), and the **chain rule** says the sensitivity through a chain is the **product of the local sensitivities**. **Backpropagation** computes all of them in one backward pass by reusing shared products, so a gradient costs about as much as one forward pass. What you'll be able to do after this: differentiate a loss with respect to a weight by hand, explain what the gradient vector means, apply the chain rule on a computation graph, and check a gradient numerically.

#### Derivative, partial derivative, gradient

$$ {f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim_{h\to 0} \tfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}}, \qquad {\nabla_\theta L = \bigl(\tfrac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_1}, \dots, \tfrac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_n}\bigr)} $$

MML §5.1–5.2. Useful rules: d(x²)/dx = 2x; dσ(z)/dz = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)); d(log x)/dx = 1/x.

- **derivative**: The slope of f at x: how much f changes per unit nudge of x, in the limit of tiny nudges.

- **tiny nudge h**: Compare f just to the right of x with f at x, divided by the size of the nudge.

- **gradient**: For a function of many variables, list one partial derivative per variable (hold the others fixed). The gradient points uphill, steepest first; its length is how steep.

#### The chain rule

$$ {\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}} = {\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}} \cdot {\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}} \cdot {\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}} $$

The multivariate chain rule, MML §5.2.2. Backpropagation applies it systematically from the loss backwards (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, _Nature_ 1986).

- **what we want**: How the loss changes when we nudge the weight.

- **loss vs prediction**: ∂L/∂a = 2(a − y): how wrong the prediction is, and in which direction.

- **sigmoid’s slope**: ∂a/∂z = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)): at most 0.25, tiny when the neuron is saturated.

- **pre-activation vs weight**: ∂z/∂w = x: a weight matters in proportion to its input.

#### Forward: compute values. Backward: multiply local slopes.

1. The neuron as a chain of simple steps: a computation graph.

2. Forward pass: plug in numbers. With w = 1, x = 1, b = −0.2 and a true label y = 0 (on time), the model predicts 0.69 probability of late and the loss is 0.48.

3. Backward pass: at each step compute the local slope. ∂L/∂a = 2(a − y) = 1.38; ∂a/∂z = a(1 − a) = 0.21; ∂z/∂w = x = 1 and ∂z/∂b = 1.

4. Multiply along the path: ∂L/∂w ≈ 0.30. Positive, so increasing w would increase the loss: training will decrease w. In a big network, the shared products (here ∂L/∂z) are computed once and reused for every weight feeding into z.

#### Why the gradient is steepest, and what happens at kinks

##### Why the gradient points the steepest way

The rate of change in a unit direction u is the **directional derivative**: ∇f · u. A dot product is largest when both vectors point the same way, so the steepest increase is along the gradient, and the steepest decrease is directly against it. At right angles to the gradient, the function doesn't change at all, at first order. That's why contour lines are perpendicular to gradients.

Example: if ∇f = (3, 4), its length of 5 is the steepest slope available. The direction (1, 0) gives a slope of only 3.

##### Points with no derivative

ReLU has a kink at 0, and so does |w| in L1 regularisation. Neither has a true derivative there. A **subgradient** is any slope that stays below the function at that point. For |w| at 0, anything from −1 to 1 qualifies. In practice, frameworks simply pick one value, such as 0 for ReLU at 0, and this causes little trouble as inputs rarely land exactly on the kink.

Next: automatic differentiation and Taylor series and curvature.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Gradients in practice

- **Autodiff:** PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow record the computation graph in the forward pass and apply the chain rule backwards automatically (reverse-mode automatic differentiation).

- **Cost:** reverse mode computes the gradient of one scalar loss with respect to all parameters for a small constant multiple of the forward cost (Goodfellow et al. §6.5), which is why it beats finite differences by a factor of n.

- **Loss and activation choices:** cross-entropy with a sigmoid gives ∂L/∂z = a − y, cancelling the saturating σ′ term; squared error with a sigmoid doesn't. That's one reason classifiers use cross-entropy (see Entropy & KL).

- **Gradient checking:** compare backprop to finite differences on a tiny model when you write custom layers.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Estimate each partial derivative by nudging each weight"

Finite differences, (L(w + h) − L(w))/h, work for one weight and are a great way to **check** a gradient. But a model with n weights needs n + 1 forward passes per step: for a 7-billion-parameter model, 7 billion passes to take one step. They're also numerically fragile: too large an h is inaccurate, too small loses precision to rounding. Backpropagation gets all n partial derivatives exactly for the price of roughly one forward and one backward pass.

## Say it

### How does backpropagation use the chain rule?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Derive ∂L/∂z for sigmoid + cross-entropy.

L = −[y log a + (1 − y) log(1 − a)], a = σ(z): ∂L/∂a = (a − y)/(a(1 − a)), ∂a/∂z = a(1 − a), so ∂L/∂z = a − y.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why reverse mode, not forward mode?

Reverse mode costs about one backward pass per scalar output, whatever the number of inputs: ideal for one loss and millions of parameters. Forward mode costs one pass per input.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What causes vanishing and exploding gradients?

Multiplying many local derivatives: values below 1 shrink exponentially (saturated sigmoids/tanh), above 1 grow. Fixes: ReLU-type activations, careful initialisation, normalisation, residual connections, gradient clipping.

#### The 30-second answer

A derivative measures how much an output changes for a small change in an input; with many parameters, the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives and points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss, so we step against it. Models are compositions of simple functions, and the chain rule says the derivative through a composition is the product of local derivatives. Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backwards over the computation graph, reusing intermediate products, so all parameter gradients cost about one extra pass. Saturating activations make local derivatives tiny, which causes vanishing gradients.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Backprop is an optimisation algorithm." It computes gradients; the optimiser (SGD, Adam) uses them.

- "The gradient points to the minimum." It points to the steepest local increase.

**Key terms and sources**

Derivatives as sensitivity, partial derivatives, the gradient vector, the chain rule, computational graphs, and backpropagation on a single neuron · built from Deisenroth et al., _Mathematics for Machine Learning_ (ch. 5), Goodfellow et al., _Deep Learning_ (ch. 6.5) and Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Derivative** | Local rate of change of a function. |
| **Partial derivative** | Rate of change in one variable, others fixed. |
| **Gradient** | Vector of partials; points uphill. |
| **Chain rule** | Derivative of a composition = product of local derivatives. |
| **Backpropagation** | Reverse-mode chain rule over a computation graph. |
| **Vanishing gradient** | Products of small local slopes shrink the gradient towards 0. |

#### Sources

1. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, CUP 2020, [mml-book.github.io](https://mml-book.github.io/) (ch. 5).

2. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, §6.5, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

3. D. Rumelhart, G. Hinton & R. Williams, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", _Nature_ 323, 1986.

# Automatic Differentiation

> How does automatic differentiation work, and why does training use reverse mode?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Calculus and optimisation
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/automatic-differentiation/
- Before this: Derivatives, Gradients & the Chain Rule (`fundamentals/derivatives-and-chain-rule`)
- Related: Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`)
- Quiz topic: `calc`

## Intuition

### The situation

A model has a million weights and one loss. A teammate suggests working out each gradient by nudging each weight, since it's so simple. Elsewhere, your model trains fine at inference size, but it runs out of memory as soon as you turn training on. The interviewer asks:

> How does automatic differentiation work, and why does training use reverse mode?

#### Why it matters

Every training framework is built on this. Understanding it explains why training needs far more memory than inference, what a computation graph is, and why some operations break gradients. It follows on from the chain rule.

### The idea

Think of a chain of factories, and you want to know how each raw material affects the final price. You could change one material at a time and rerun everything. Or you could run once, then walk backwards from the price, asking each factory how much it passed on. One walk answers it for every material.

[Figure: Three ways to get a gradient. Numerical nudges each input, and is slow and inexact. Symbolic manipulates formulas, which can grow huge. Automatic applies the chain rule to each operation, and is exact and fast.]

_Reverse-mode automatic differentiation is what frameworks use to train._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Change x and y, and check the gradients by hand. Then compare passes with many weights and many outputs.

#### Trace both passes

The top half computes the worked example exactly. The bottom half counts passes for a full gradient. A backward pass usually costs a small multiple of a forward pass, and it needs stored values.

Set the weights to **10** and the outputs to **100**. Now forward mode needs fewer passes. So forward mode isn't bad: it's right when inputs are few and outputs are many. Training is simply the opposite case.

**Now say why:** why does a backward pass need values from the forward pass?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Automatic differentiation** breaks a program into small operations with known derivatives, then applies the chain rule by machine. It gives exact gradients, unlike nudging values, and it doesn't produce giant formulas. **Forward mode** pushes derivatives along with values, one input at a time. **Reverse mode** runs the program, then goes backwards from the output. With millions of inputs and one loss, **reverse mode gets every gradient in one backward pass**. The cost is memory, because intermediate values must be stored.

#### Three ways to get a gradient

| Method | How | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Numerical** | Nudge each input, and see what changes. | One or two runs per input, and rounding errors. Good for checking. |
| **Symbolic** | Manipulate formulas, like in algebra software. | Formulas can grow huge, and code with loops is hard to handle. |
| **Automatic** | Apply the chain rule to each operation as the code runs. | Exact up to rounding, at a small multiple of the run's cost. |

##### Worked example: f(x, y) = xy + x, at (2, 3)

| Step | Value (forward pass) | How much f changes with it (backward pass) |
|---|---|---|
| a = xy | 6 | df/da = 1 |
| f = a + x | 8 | df/df = 1 |
| y | 3 | df/dy = df/da × x = 2 |
| x | 2 | df/dx = df/da × y + 1 = 4 |

One forward pass and one backward pass gave both gradients.

##### Forward or reverse?

- **Forward mode:** carries a derivative with each value. One pass gives the effect of **one input on all outputs**.

- **Reverse mode:** records operations, then works back from the output. One pass gives the effect of **all inputs on one output**.

Training has millions of inputs and one loss, so reverse mode wins by a huge margin. Backpropagation is reverse mode applied to a neural network.

##### What can break it

- **Steps with no useful gradient:** argmax, rounding and sampling have zero or undefined gradients. Hence tricks like softmax and reparameterisation.

- **Leaving the graph:** converting to another library, or detaching a tensor, stops gradients flowing.

- **In-place changes:** changing a stored value can make the backward pass wrong, so frameworks often raise an error.

#### The maths

$$ {\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}} = {v^\top} J_k J_{k-1} \cdots J_1, \qquad {\text{reverse: } (v^\top J_k) J_{k-1} \cdots}, \qquad {\text{forward: } J_k \cdots (J_1 u)} $$

Same product, different order. With many inputs and one output, multiplying from the output keeps things small. See the shapes lesson on why order changes cost.

- **the gradient**: What the chain rule gives: a product of one Jacobian per step.

- **the starting vector**: For a single loss, it’s just 1.

- **reverse mode**: Multiply from the left. Each step is a vector times a matrix, so you never hold a whole Jacobian. One pass gives every weight’s gradient.

- **forward mode**: Multiply from the right, starting with one input direction u. It needs a pass for each input.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Memory:** the backward pass needs values from the forward pass, so training uses much more memory than inference. That's why large models run out of memory only in training.

- **Gradient checkpointing:** store only some values and recompute the rest. You trade compute for memory.

- **Disable it for inference:** turning off gradient tracking saves the memory and time of recording operations.

- **Accumulating gradients:** frameworks add to existing gradients, so clear them each step, or use this on purpose to simulate larger batches.

- **Hessian-vector products:** running reverse over forward mode gives curvature information, without building the full Hessian.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Autodiff is just numerical differentiation done quickly"

It sounds right, since both give numbers rather than formulas. But numerical differentiation nudges inputs and needs a run per input, with rounding error. Automatic differentiation applies exact derivative rules to each operation, and needs one backward pass. They're different methods, and numerical is mainly useful for checking the other.

## Say it

### How does automatic differentiation work, and why does training use reverse mode?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Is automatic differentiation the same as numerical differentiation?

No. Numerical nudges inputs and measures the change, needing a run per input, with rounding error. Automatic applies exact derivative rules to each operation. Numerical differentiation is still useful for checking that automatic gradients are right.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does training use so much more memory than inference?

The backward pass needs values from the forward pass, so they must stay in memory until used. Inference discards them as it goes. Gradient checkpointing reduces this by storing only some, and recomputing the rest.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When is forward mode better?

When there are few inputs and many outputs, such as measuring how one hyperparameter affects many values. Also for a Jacobian-vector product, where you only need one direction. Forward mode uses little extra memory, as it doesn't store a record for a backward pass.

#### The 30-second answer

Automatic differentiation breaks a program into simple operations with known derivatives, and applies the chain rule to them. It's exact, unlike numerical differentiation, and avoids the formula growth of symbolic methods. Forward mode gives the effect of one input on all outputs per pass. Reverse mode records the operations, then goes back from the output, giving the effect of all inputs on one output. Training has millions of weights and one loss, so reverse mode gets every gradient in a single backward pass. The cost is memory, as it must store intermediate values.

**Key terms and sources**

Computational graphs, forward and reverse mode, why training uses reverse mode, how it differs from numerical and symbolic differentiation, and its memory cost. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/)

- Backpropagation on this site

- Matrix calculus on this site

# Taylor Series and Curvature

> What does a Taylor expansion tell you about optimisation, and why does curvature limit the learning rate?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Calculus and optimisation
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/taylor-series-and-curvature/
- Before this: Derivatives, Gradients & the Chain Rule (`fundamentals/derivatives-and-chain-rule`), Matrix Calculus (`fundamentals/matrix-calculus`)
- Quiz topic: `calc`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your training was stable at a learning rate of 0.001, but it blows up at 0.01. A teammate asks why a small change can cause that, and whether there's a principled limit. The interviewer asks:

> What does a Taylor expansion tell you about optimisation, and why does curvature limit the learning rate?

#### Why it matters

Taylor is the idea behind most of optimisation. It tells you why gradients work only locally, why learning rates have a limit, and how saddle points and Newton's method fit together. See derivatives and matrix calculus first.

### The idea

Think of driving at night with short-range headlights. The road ahead looks straight, so you can trust that for a short distance. If the road bends sharply, you can only safely go a little before the picture is wrong. The straight-road picture is the gradient, and the bend is the curvature.

[Figure: Local approximations. First order gives a line, which leads to gradient descent. Second order gives a bowl or saddle, which leads to Newton's method.]

_Each order adds detail, but only near the point you started from._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Make the step large. Then move the point near x = 0, where the curve bends the other way.

#### Approximate a curve

The curve is f(x) = x⁴ − 3x² + x, a made-up function. Blue is the tangent, and green is the second-order approximation. The red dot is where you start, and the purple dot is where the step lands. Safe learning rate is 2 ÷ f″(x), valid only near this point.

Move to a point near **x = 0**. Curvature is negative, so the approximation opens downwards, and there's no safe-rate formula here. Then make the step large, and see both approximations leave the curve. That's why learning rates must stay small on a curving loss.

**Now say why:** why must the learning rate shrink as curvature grows?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Near a point, any smooth function looks like a simple polynomial. The **first-order Taylor approximation** is a straight line, and it's why gradient descent works: for a small step, the loss falls along the negative gradient. The **second-order** version adds curvature through the Hessian. Curvature is what limits your learning rate: on a curve with second derivative L, steps above **2/L** diverge.

#### Local pictures of a function

| Order | Shape | It tells you | Leads to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First** | Tangent line or plane | Which way is downhill. | Gradient descent |
| **Second** | A bowl or saddle | How fast the slope changes. | Newton's method |

##### Why gradient descent lowers the loss

By first-order Taylor, L(w + Δ) ≈ L(w) + ∇Lᵀ Δ. Choose Δ = −η∇L, and the change is −η‖∇L‖², which is negative. So a small enough step always reduces the loss, unless the gradient is zero. "Small enough" is the catch: the line is only accurate nearby.

##### Why curvature limits the learning rate

Take a simple quadratic with second derivative L, so L(w) = ½Lw². A gradient step gives w ← (1 − ηL)w.

- **η below 1/L:** moves steadily towards the minimum.

- **η between 1/L and 2/L:** overshoots, but still shrinks.

- **η above 2/L:** each overshoot is bigger than the last, and the loss explodes.

With many dimensions, the sharpest direction sets the limit, so the largest Hessian eigenvalue decides the largest safe learning rate. Flat directions then move slowly, which is the problem of ill-conditioning.

##### Reading the Hessian at a flat point

When the gradient is zero, the second-order term decides what you have. All-positive eigenvalues mean a minimum, all-negative a maximum and mixed signs a saddle. See positive definite matrices.

#### The maths

$$ {f(x+\Delta)} \approx {f(x)} + {\nabla f(x)^\top \Delta} + {\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta^\top H(x)\,\Delta} $$

Worked example: f(x) = x² near x = 3, with Δ = 0.1. Value 9, slope term 0.6, curvature term 0.01. The total of 9.61 is exactly 3.1², since a quadratic’s approximation is exact.

- **the value nearby**: What you’d like to estimate, a small step Δ away.

- **where you are**: The starting value.

- **the slope term**: The first-order change. This gives gradient descent.

- **the curvature term**: The second-order change, using the Hessian H. This gives Newton’s method, and it decides what kind of flat point you’re at.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **When training diverges:** the learning rate is probably above 2 divided by the sharpest curvature. Lower it, or use warm-up, which lets the model reach flatter regions first.

- **Sharp vs flat minima:** the sharper the region, the smaller the safe step. Large learning rates can't settle in very sharp regions.

- **You rarely compute the Hessian:** Hessian-vector products or tracking the loss are far cheaper ways of learning about curvature.

- **Non-smooth losses:** Taylor assumes smoothness. Clipping and normalising tame sudden changes.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The gradient points downhill, so a bigger step gets there faster"

It sounds right, as the direction is right. But the gradient is only accurate nearby. On a curved loss, a big step passes the minimum and lands higher up the other side. Above 2/L, each step is worse than the last. Direction and step size are separate questions.

## Say it

### What does a Taylor expansion tell you about optimisation, and why does curvature limit the learning rate?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is the safe limit 2/L and not 1/L?

Each step multiplies the distance by 1 − ηL. At 1/L, you land exactly on the minimum in one step on a quadratic. Between 1/L and 2/L you overshoot, but the size of 1 − ηL stays below 1, so you still converge. Above 2/L it exceeds 1, and you diverge.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How does ill-conditioning follow from this?

The sharpest direction limits your learning rate, while the flattest direction wants a large one. With a large ratio between them, the condition number, progress along flat directions is painfully slow, and you get zig-zagging. Momentum and second-order methods address this.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does the first-order approximation guarantee a lower loss?

Only for small enough steps. It's a local statement, and curvature can make a larger step go uphill. That's why training can diverge, and why methods like line search exist.

#### The 30-second answer

A Taylor expansion approximates a function near a point with a polynomial. First order is the gradient term, and it's why gradient descent works: a small step along the negative gradient changes the loss by minus eta times the squared gradient norm. Second order adds curvature, through the Hessian. On a quadratic with second derivative L, a gradient step multiplies the distance by one minus eta L, so above 2 over L it diverges. In many dimensions, the largest Hessian eigenvalue sets the limit. At a flat point, the Hessian's signs distinguish minima and saddles.

**Key terms and sources**

First and second-order Taylor approximations, what the Hessian says about curvature, and how they explain gradient descent, learning rate limits and saddle points. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/)

- [Boyd and Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/vmls/)

- [Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning, slides for chapter 4](https://mnassar.github.io/deeplearninghandbook/slides/04_numerical.pdf)

- Learning rate schedules on this site

# Gradient Descent, Momentum & Adam

> Why does a slightly bigger learning rate make training explode?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Calculus and optimisation
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/gradient-descent/
- Before this: Derivatives, Gradients & the Chain Rule (`fundamentals/derivatives-and-chain-rule`)
- Quiz topic: `calc`

## Intuition

### The situation

Someone raises the learning rate slightly, and your training loss explodes to NaN. The interviewer asks:

> Why can a larger learning rate make training diverge, and how do momentum and Adam help?

**Running example:** training two weights of a delivery-time model whose loss is a narrow valley: L(θ) = ½(θ₁² + 10 θ₂²). It's 10 times steeper in θ₂ than in θ₁ (curvatures 1 and 10), the shape you get when features have very different scales. Every run starts at (−4, 2); "converged" means the loss drops below 0.0001.

#### Minimising a loss you can't solve on paper

Linear regression has a formula for the best weights; neural networks, logistic regression and most models don't. What we can always compute is the gradient (previous lesson): the uphill direction. Gradient descent turns that into an algorithm. The art is the step size and how to deal with valleys of very different steepness.

### The idea

Think of walking down a narrow valley in fog. You can only feel the slope under your feet. Take steps that are too big and you bounce from wall to wall, climbing higher each time. Momentum is like a heavy ball that keeps rolling along the valley floor, and Adam adjusts your stride to the steepness in each direction.

[Figure: Oval contour lines of a narrow valley, with a path that zig-zags from wall to wall as it moves towards the centre.]

_Illustrative. Plain gradient descent zig-zags across a valley that's much steeper in one direction than the other._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Choose gradient descent with η = 0.19, then move to η = 0.21. Then try momentum and Adam at 0.21.

#### Same valley, three optimisers

Contours of L = ½(θ₁² + 10θ₂²). Start (−4, 2), minimum at the centre.

| η | 0.01 | 0.05 | 0.1 | 0.19 | 0.21 | 0.3 | 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gradient descent | > 200 | 111 | 54 | 58 | diverges | diverges | diverges |
| Momentum | 93 | 78 | 103 | 117 | 96 | 112 | diverges |
| Adam | > 200 | 179 | 105 | 84 | 79 | 99 | 85 |

Steps to reach loss < 0.0001. Plain gradient descent is fastest at a well-chosen η but fails completely beyond 0.2. Momentum is stable over a wider range (it diverges only at 0.5 here) and is much better at small η (93 steps vs never). Adam converges for every η from 0.05 to 0.5 because its step size is normalised per parameter: the steep θ₂ and shallow θ₁ directions move at similar speeds. Its weakness shows at η = 0.01: steps are about η in size, so it crawls from 4 units away.

**Now say why:** why does such a small change blow up plain gradient descent, while the other two still converge?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Gradient descent** repeats one step: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), walking downhill on the loss. The **learning rate** η is everything: too small crawls, too large overshoots and **diverges** (for a quadratic, beyond 2/λmax, where λmax is the steepest curvature). When the loss is a long, narrow valley (**ill-conditioned**), plain gradient descent zig-zags across it. **Momentum** keeps a running velocity so consistent directions build up speed and oscillations cancel. **Adam** also divides each parameter's step by a running estimate of its gradient size, so every direction moves at a similar pace, which makes it robust to the learning rate. In practice gradients come from small random **mini-batches** (SGD), which adds noise. What you'll be able to do after this: write the update rules for GD, momentum and Adam, explain divergence and the 2/λ rule, explain why momentum and Adam help on narrow valleys, and pick a learning rate sensibly.

#### The update rule

$$ {\theta_{t+1}} = {\theta_t} - {\eta}\,{\nabla L(\theta_t)} $$

Goodfellow et al. §4.3; MML §7.1.

- **new parameters**: Where the weights go after one step.

- **current parameters**: Where they are now.

- **learning rate**: η: how big a step to take. The most important hyperparameter in deep learning.

- **gradient**: Uphill direction; subtracting it goes downhill. Steeper slope → bigger step.

#### Three optimisers

| Optimiser | Update | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **(S)GD** | θ ← θ − η g | Step against the (mini-batch) gradient |
| **Momentum** | v ← β v + g; θ ← θ − η v | Velocity accumulates consistent directions, damps oscillation (β ≈ 0.9) |
| **Adam** | m ← β₁m + (1 − β₁)g; v ← β₂v + (1 − β₂)g²; θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) | Momentum plus per-parameter step scaling by recent gradient size; bias-corrected |

Adam's update and defaults (η = 0.001, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 10⁻⁸) are from Kingma & Ba, Algorithm 1 [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.6980#page=2), who describe the effective step as "approximately bounded by the stepsize hyperparameter" and invariant to rescaling the gradient.

#### Why plain gradient descent zig-zags

The ratio of steepest to shallowest curvature is the **condition number** (here 10). Gradient descent's best learning rate is limited by the steep direction, so progress along the shallow direction is slow, and in between it bounces from wall to wall. Fixes: **scale your features** (often the cause of ill-conditioning; see Feature Scaling), use **momentum** (bounces cancel, the valley direction accumulates), use **adaptive methods** like Adam (rescale each direction), and use **normalisation layers** in networks.

#### Nesterov, AdaGrad and RMSProp: how Adam came about

| Method | What it adds | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Momentum** | Keeps a running average of past gradients, which smooths zig-zags. | Can overshoot. |
| **Nesterov** | Measures the gradient at the point momentum is about to reach, so it can correct earlier. | A small change in practice for noisy gradients. |
| **AdaGrad** | Divides each weight's step by the root of its summed squared gradients, which suits rare features. | The sum only grows, so steps can shrink too far. |
| **RMSProp** | Uses a decaying average instead of a sum, so old gradients are forgotten. | No momentum term. |
| **Adam** | Combines momentum with RMSProp's scaling, and corrects for starting at zero. | Can generalise less well in some settings. See AdamW. |

These per-weight scales use squared gradients, not true curvature. For that, see Newton's method.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Mini-batches, schedules and warm-up

- **Stochastic gradient descent:** estimate the gradient from a mini-batch (e.g. 32–4,096 examples) instead of the whole dataset. Much cheaper per step; the noise can even help escape poor regions.

- **Learning-rate schedules:** start larger, decay later (step, cosine, linear decay) so early progress is fast and late steps settle.

- **Warm-up:** start from a small η and ramp up over the first steps; common for Transformers, where Adam's early estimates are noisy.

- **AdamW:** Adam with decoupled weight decay (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019), the standard for training large language models.

#### Recipe

1. Scale inputs; use sensible initialisation.

2. Start with Adam/AdamW (η ≈ 1e-3 for small nets, smaller for big ones) or SGD + momentum (η ≈ 0.1 with schedules, common for vision).

3. Run a learning-rate range test or a coarse log-scale search (Hyperparameter Tuning).

4. If the loss explodes or turns NaN: lower η, add warm-up or gradient clipping.

5. If it plateaus: decay η, check data and scaling.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Bigger learning rate, faster training"

Along a direction with curvature λ, one gradient step multiplies the distance to the minimum by (1 − ηλ). If η > 2/λ, that factor is below −1: each step overshoots further than the last, and the loss explodes. The steepest direction sets the limit: here λmax = 10, so any η above **0.2** diverges, while the shallow direction (λ = 1) would happily take steps 10× bigger. With η = 0.21, plain gradient descent blows up to a loss of about 10¹⁷ in 200 steps; with η = 0.1 it converges in 54.

## Say it

### Why can a larger learning rate make training diverge, and how do momentum and Adam help?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does Adam need bias correction?

m and v start at zero, so early averages are biased towards zero, most strongly when β₂ is close to 1; dividing by (1 − βᵗ) corrects it. Without it, early steps can be far too large (Kingma & Ba §3, §6.4).

Follow-up 2 of 3

SGD vs Adam: which generalises better?

An active debate: well-tuned SGD with momentum is often preferred for image classification; Adam/AdamW dominates Transformers and LLMs. Tune both if it matters.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What batch size?

Larger batches give less noisy gradients and better hardware use but need larger learning rates (often scaled roughly linearly) and warm-up; very large batches can hurt generalisation.

#### The 30-second answer

Gradient descent updates parameters by subtracting the learning rate times the gradient. The learning rate must be below about 2 over the largest curvature or it diverges, and when curvatures differ a lot, an ill-conditioned problem, plain GD zig-zags and crawls along the shallow direction. Momentum averages gradients into a velocity, which damps oscillation and accelerates consistent directions. Adam combines momentum with per-parameter scaling by a running RMS of the gradient, plus bias correction, so it's robust to learning-rate choice and gradient scale. In practice we use mini-batch SGD or AdamW with learning-rate schedules, warm-up and clipping.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "A higher learning rate always trains faster." Past 2/λmax it diverges.

- "Adam needs no tuning." Its learning rate still matters a lot.

**Key terms and sources**

The update rule, the learning rate and when it diverges, ill-conditioning and zig-zags, mini-batch SGD, momentum, and Adam's adaptive step sizes · built from Goodfellow et al., _Deep Learning_ (ch. 4, 8), Deisenroth et al., _MML_ (ch. 7) and Kingma & Ba, "Adam" (2015) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Learning rate η** | Step size multiplier. |
| **Divergence** | Loss grows each step; for quadratics when η > 2/λmax. |
| **Condition number** | λmax/λmin of the curvature (Hessian). |
| **Momentum** | Exponentially averaged gradient used as velocity. |
| **Adam** | Momentum + per-parameter scaling by RMS gradient, bias-corrected. |
| **SGD** | Gradient estimated from a random mini-batch. |

#### Sources

1. D. Kingma & J. Ba, "Adam: a method for stochastic optimization", ICLR 2015, [arXiv:1412.6980](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980).

2. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, ch. 4 and 8, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

3. M. P. Deisenroth, A. A. Faisal & C. S. Ong, _Mathematics for Machine Learning_, CUP 2020, ch. 7.

4. I. Loshchilov & F. Hutter, "Decoupled weight decay regularization", ICLR 2019, [arXiv:1711.05101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101).

# Newton's Method and Second-Order Optimisation

> What is Newton's method, and why isn't it used to train deep networks?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Calculus and optimisation
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/newton-and-second-order-methods/
- Before this: Taylor Series and Curvature (`fundamentals/taylor-series-and-curvature`), Gradient Descent, Momentum & Adam (`fundamentals/gradient-descent`)
- Related: Gradient Boosting (`fundamentals/gradient-boosting`)
- Quiz topic: `calc`

## Intuition

### The situation

A colleague says Newton's method converges in very few steps and doesn't need a learning rate, so why not train your deep model with it? Meanwhile, your logistic regression solver uses something called L-BFGS. The interviewer asks:

> What is Newton's method, and why isn't it used to train deep networks?

#### Why it matters

This is a common interview question, and the answer explains why deep learning uses Adam, not a seemingly better method. These ideas are still used directly in logistic regression and gradient boosting. See Taylor series first.

### The idea

Think of hiking down a valley. Gradient descent only feels the slope underfoot, so it takes cautious steps. Newton also has a map of how the land curves, and jumps straight to the bottom of the local bowl. It's a great jump, but drawing that map for a million-dimensional land is impossibly costly.

[Figure: Comparing methods. Gradient descent uses the slope, and it's cheap per step. Newton uses exact curvature, and is costly. L-BFGS approximates curvature from history, and sits between them.]

_Newton wins per step, and loses on what each step costs._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the condition number, then raise the weights.

#### Compare the two methods

On a pure quadratic, using gradient descent's best fixed learning rate, to reduce the error a million times. Real losses aren't quadratic, so Newton needs several steps. Assumes 4 bytes per number.

Raise the condition number: gradient descent's steps grow in proportion, and Newton's stay at one. Now raise the weights: the memory needed for the Hessian grows a hundred times for every tenfold increase. Newton wins per step, and loses on what each step costs.

**Now say why:** why does the Hessian's memory grow so much faster than the gradient's?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Gradient descent only uses slope, so it needs a learning rate and struggles when curvature differs by direction. **Newton's method** jumps to the minimum of the local quadratic: w − H⁻¹g. It's scale-free and converges very fast near a solution. But with n weights, the Hessian has **n² entries and n³ solving cost**, and it can head towards saddle points. So deep learning sticks to first-order methods, while **L-BFGS** and Newton-style boosting work well on smaller or convex problems.

#### Using curvature

##### Where the step comes from

Take the second-order Taylor approximation, and jump straight to its minimum by setting its gradient to zero: g + HΔ = 0, so Δ = −H⁻¹g. It scales each direction by its curvature, taking long steps where the loss is flat and short ones where it's sharp.

##### How it compares

| | Gradient descent | Newton | L-BFGS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Uses** | Slope | Slope and exact Hessian | Slope and recent history |
| **Learning rate** | Needs tuning | Natural step of 1 | Usually a line search |
| **Memory** | n | n² | About 2mn, for m past steps |
| **Cost per step** | n, per example | n³ to solve | About mn |
| **Near the solution** | Steady | Very fast, doubling correct digits | Fast |

##### Why deep learning doesn't use it

- **Size:** a million weights gives a trillion Hessian entries.

- **Saddle points:** Newton looks for any flat point, so with mixed-sign curvature, it can move towards a saddle.

- **Noise:** mini-batches give noisy curvature estimates, and approximate curvature methods are sensitive to this.

##### Where these ideas are used

- **Logistic regression:** Newton's method, as IRLS, and L-BFGS are common solvers, as the problem is convex and small enough.

- **Gradient boosting:** XGBoost-style trees use first and second derivatives of the loss per example. See gradient boosting.

- **Adam:** it divides by a running estimate of squared gradients, which acts as a rough per-weight scale. It isn't true curvature, but it has a similar spirit.

#### The maths

$$ {w_{t+1}} = w_t - {H^{-1}}\,{g}, \qquad {w_{t+1}} = w_t - (H + \lambda I)^{-1} g $$

Example: f(x) = x² − 4x. At x = 10, g = 16 and H = 2, so the step is 8, and you land on the minimum at x = 2 in one go.

- **Newton’s update**: Jumps to the minimum of the local bowl. On a true quadratic, it lands there in one step.

- **the inverse Hessian**: Shrinks steps in sharp directions, and stretches them in flat directions. In practice, you solve a system rather than computing an inverse.

- **the gradient**: Which way the loss changes, as in gradient descent.

- **damped Newton**: Adding λI keeps the system well behaved when curvature is small or negative. Larger λ makes it act more like gradient descent.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Small, convex problems:** L-BFGS is often a great default, because it needs no learning rate.

- **Don't store the Hessian:** Hessian-free methods use conjugate gradient with Hessian-vector products, so they only need matrix-vector operations.

- **Natural gradient:** similar in spirit, using the Fisher matrix. K-FAC approximates it for neural networks.

- **Damping and line search:** plain Newton can overshoot far from the solution. Both make it more robust.

- **Full batch:** L-BFGS expects fairly accurate gradients, so it suits full or large batches rather than noisy ones.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Newton's is better because it converges in fewer steps"

It sounds right, as fewer steps looks like less work. But steps aren't the cost: each one needs the full Hessian. With a million weights, that's four terabytes, plus an n³ solve, while a gradient step costs almost nothing. What matters is total time to a good result, and on large models, first-order methods win.

## Say it

### What is Newton's method, and why isn't it used to train deep networks?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does Newton's method have no learning rate?

The Hessian scales each direction by its curvature, so it already knows how far to go in the quadratic model. A natural step size is 1. In practice, damping or a line search reduce it when the approximation isn't trustworthy, particularly far from the solution.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why might Newton's method be attracted to saddle points?

It solves for where the gradient is zero, and a saddle has zero gradient too. With a negative curvature direction, the step can go towards the saddle instead of away. Gradient descent doesn't have this attraction. Damping or using absolute curvature can help.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How does XGBoost use second derivatives?

It approximates the loss with a second-order Taylor expansion around current predictions. Each example gives a gradient and a Hessian, and these determine leaf values and how good a split is. It makes the same procedure work for many losses, and it's cheap because the Hessian is per example, not per weight.

#### The 30-second answer

Newton's method jumps to the minimum of the local quadratic, using w minus H inverse g. It accounts for curvature, so it needs no learning rate, and converges very quickly near a solution. It's not used for deep networks for three reasons. With n weights, the Hessian takes n squared memory and n cubed to solve. It can move towards saddle points, since it finds any flat point. And mini-batch curvature is noisy. So we use first-order methods. L-BFGS approximates it using recent gradients, and it works well on convex problems. XGBoost also uses second derivatives per example.

**Key terms and sources**

Newton's step, why it handles ill-conditioning, its cost, quasi-Newton methods like L-BFGS, and where second-order ideas are used in ML, such as XGBoost. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning, slides for chapter 8](https://mnassar.github.io/deeplearninghandbook/slides/08_optimization.pdf)

- [CS231n, Neural Networks Part 3](https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-3/)

- [Boyd and Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/vmls/)

- [XGBoost paper, Chen and Guestrin (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754)

- Taylor series on this site
