# Sampling and Bias

> What sampling methods would you use, and how can selection or survivorship bias ruin a dataset?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/sampling-and-bias/
- Before this: Descriptive Statistics and Outliers (`fundamentals/descriptive-statistics-and-outliers`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

You built a churn model using only customers active today, and it looks great. In production, it fails. A survey of a million users also reports high satisfaction, while reviews are getting worse. The interviewer asks:

> What sampling methods would you use, and how can selection or survivorship bias ruin a dataset?

#### Why it matters

Most ML failures in the real world begin here. A model learns from the data it's given, and a very large biased dataset simply gives you a confident wrong answer. See correlation vs causation for a related problem.

### The idea

Think of checking a soup. A random spoonful tells you about the whole pot, if it's stirred, and more spoonfuls make you surer. But if you only taste from the top, and the salt has sunk to the bottom, a thousand spoonfuls will still be wrong. Bias is the unstirred pot.

[Figure: Two kinds of error. Random noise shrinks as the sample grows. Bias stays the same however large the sample.]

_A bigger sample can't fix who's missing._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the sample to 100,000. Then set the appearing chance to 1.

#### Sample with a rare group

Illustrative: the main group's mean is 10, and the rare group's is 30, both with a standard deviation of 5. The two noise figures are standard errors without any bias.

Raise the sample to **100,000**. Noise nearly disappears, while the biased estimate doesn't move at all. You're now very sure of a wrong answer. Set the appearing chance to **1**, and the bias is gone.

**Now say why:** why doesn't a larger sample fix the estimate?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A sample is only useful if it represents the population you care about. **Random error** shrinks with more data, but **bias doesn't**. **Stratified sampling** guarantees rare groups are represented, and reduces noise. **Cluster sampling** saves money, at the cost of more noise. The big risk is **selection bias**: data you have because of some process that also relates to the outcome. Survivorship bias, feedback loops and non-response are all forms of it.

#### Getting a fair sample

| Method | How | Use it when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simple random** | Everyone has an equal chance. | You have a full list, and no rare groups. | Rare groups may barely appear. |
| **Stratified** | Split into groups, and sample within each. | Groups differ, or some are rare. | You need to know the groups, and reweight if you oversample. |
| **Cluster** | Pick whole groups, like cities. | Reaching individuals is costly. | People within a cluster are alike, so you get less information per person. |
| **Systematic** | Take every kth item. | Simple logging streams. | A pattern in the data can line up with k. |

##### Bias you'll meet in ML

| Bias | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Selection** | Who's in the data depends on something related to the outcome. | A loan model only sees repayment for people who were approved. |
| **Survivorship** | You only see those who lasted. | Studying only customers who stayed, to explain why people churn. |
| **Non-response** | Those who answer differ from those who don't. | Ratings come mostly from very happy or very unhappy users. |
| **Feedback loop** | The model decides which data you collect next. | A recommender only learns about items it already shows. |
| **Time** | Your sample period isn't typical. | Training on festival-week orders. |

##### What helps

- **Ask who's missing** before looking at any results.

- **Random exploration:** serving some random choices gives unbiased data for feedback loops.

- **Reweight:** if you know how groups differ from the population, use inverse-probability weights.

- **Compare with a known total:** check your sample's mix against what you know about all users.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{Error}^2} = {\text{Bias}^2} + {\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}, \qquad {SE_{\text{strat}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\text{within}}^2}{n}}, \qquad {SE_{\text{random}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\text{within}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{between}}^2}{n}} $$

This is why a survey of a million biased responses can be worse than one of a thousand random ones.

- **total squared error**: How far your estimate tends to be from the truth.

- **the bias term**: Doesn’t depend on n. More data won’t reduce it.

- **the sampling noise**: Shrinks as n grows, and this is the only part more data can fix.

- **stratified sampling**: Removes the differences between groups from its noise, with proportional allocation.

- **simple random sampling**: Noise also includes how much the groups differ.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Train and serve mismatch:** if training data comes from a different source than production, measure it with drift checks.

- **Stratified splits:** with rare labels, split so each fold keeps the same share. See cross-validation.

- **Oversampling:** sampling rare classes more often for training is fine, but the model's probabilities then need correcting.

- **LLM logs:** feedback comes from people who bother to respond. Evaluate on a random sample of traffic as well.

- **Sensitive decisions:** a model trained only on past approvals may never learn about groups that were rarely approved.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We have millions of rows, so it's representative"

It sounds right, as big samples feel safe. But size only removes random noise. If your data comes from those who stayed, or from items you already show, millions of rows give a precise picture of the wrong group. Ask who's missing, whatever the size.

## Say it

### What sampling methods would you use, and how can selection or survivorship bias ruin a dataset?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How would you check for survivorship bias?

Ask what would make something disappear from your data, and whether that's linked to what you're measuring. Then find a source that includes those who left, like sign-up logs. For a churn model, sample users as of a past date, including those who've since gone, and not just today's active users.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Stratified or cluster sampling: what's the difference?

Stratified sampling takes some from every group, so it reduces noise when groups differ. Cluster sampling takes whole groups, and skips the others, to save cost, and it increases noise, as people within a group are alike. A stratified sample covers all groups, and a cluster sample doesn't.

Follow-up 3 of 3

You have a million ratings. Why might they still be misleading?

Those who rate aren't typical, often being very happy or unhappy, and the system only shows some items. So a big sample shrinks noise, but not that bias. I'd compare against a random survey, and model who's likely to respond, or weight by exposure.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd start with who the population is, and who might be missing. Random error shrinks with more data, but bias doesn't. Simple random sampling suits most cases. Stratified sampling guarantees rare groups appear and removes between-group noise. Cluster sampling is cheaper, but noisier. The main risk is selection bias, where being in the data depends on something related to the outcome. For example, a loan model only sees outcomes for approved people. I'd use some random exploration, reweighting and checks against known totals.

**Key terms and sources**

Random, stratified and cluster sampling, how selection, survivorship and non-response bias arise, and why training data so often differs from the real world. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Barr, OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/)

- [Bruce, Bruce and Gedeck, Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, contents excerpt](https://toc.uni.li/FLMF048415.pdf)

- [DataCamp statistics interview questions](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/statistics-interview-questions)

# Confidence Intervals & the Bootstrap

> What does 95% confidence actually promise?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/confidence-intervals-and-bootstrap/
- Before this: Expectation, Variance & Covariance (`fundamentals/expectation-and-variance`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

You report 87% accuracy on 500 test rows, and a stakeholder asks how sure you are. The interviewer asks:

> What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean, and when would you use the bootstrap?

**Running example:** delivery times in minutes, simulated from a right-skewed distribution (log-normal: median 30 minutes, true mean 34.0 minutes, a long tail of slow deliveries). Operations samples n deliveries and reports the average delivery time with a 95% interval.

#### A number without an error bar is a guess

"Average delivery time: 33.1 minutes" from 30 deliveries could easily be 36 on the next 30. "Model accuracy 87.2%" on 500 test rows has an uncertainty of about ±3 points. Interviewers and stakeholders ask "how sure are you?" and a confidence interval is the standard answer, provided you know what it means and when it's off.

### The idea

Think of throwing a ring at a hidden peg. Once it lands, it either circles the peg or it doesn't. The 95% describes how good your throw is: about 95 of every 100 throws land around the peg.

[Figure: Eight horizontal intervals around a vertical line marking the true mean. Seven cross the line. One misses it and is drawn in red.]

_Illustrative. Each line is one sample's interval, and most of them cover the true mean._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at n = 10 and read the coverage. Then move up to n = 100.

#### Draw 100 samples, build 100 intervals

Each horizontal line is one sample's 95% t-interval; the orange vertical line is the true mean (34.0 min). Red lines miss it.

With skewed data the t-interval under-covers for small n: about 92.5% at n = 10 and 93.7% at n = 30 instead of 95%, approaching 95% by n = 50–100 as the central limit theorem kicks in. Intervals also narrow like 1/√n. For heavy tails or tiny samples, report this caveat, transform the data (log), or use the bootstrap.

**Now say why:** why do intervals on skewed data miss more often when the sample is small?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Any number computed from a sample (a mean, a median, an accuracy) would come out different on another sample. Its spread across samples is the **sampling distribution**; its standard deviation is the **standard error**, σ/√n for a mean. The **central limit theorem** says means are roughly Gaussian for large n, so mean ± 1.96 × SE gives a **95% confidence interval**: a procedure that captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples (not "95% chance the truth is in this one interval"). With small or skewed samples coverage drops below 95%. The **bootstrap** resamples your own data thousands of times to get intervals for any statistic, no formula needed. What you'll be able to do after this: compute a CI for a mean, state its correct interpretation, explain when it's unreliable, and build a bootstrap CI for a median or a model metric.

#### Standard error and the CLT

$$ {\mathrm{SE}(\bar x)} = {s}\,/\,\sqrt{n}, \qquad {\bar x \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\,\mathrm{SE}} $$

Wasserman, _All of Statistics_ §6.3.2, §7; the central limit theorem (Blitzstein & Hwang §10.3) makes x̄ approximately Gaussian for large n whatever the shape of the data.

- **standard error of the mean**: How much the sample mean varies from sample to sample. Shrinks like 1/√n: four times the data halves it.

- **sample standard deviation**: Spread of individual deliveries, estimated from the sample.

- **95% interval**: Sample mean ± about 2 standard errors (1.96 from the Gaussian; a slightly larger t value for small n).

#### Resample your own data to see the sampling distribution

Efron (1979) noticed that if your sample is representative, drawing samples _from your sample_ (n draws with replacement) mimics drawing new samples from the population. Compute the statistic on each of, say, 2,000 resamples; the spread of those values estimates its sampling distribution. The simplest 95% interval takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (the percentile bootstrap); refinements such as BCa correct for bias and skew.

One sample of 50 deliveries, 2,000 bootstrap resamples. There's no simple formula for the standard error of a median or a 90th percentile; the bootstrap doesn't need one.

#### Small samples: the t-interval

With a small sample, your estimate of the spread is itself uncertain, so 1.96 standard errors is too narrow. Use the t-distribution's multiplier instead: about 2.13 with 15 degrees of freedom, and 2.78 with 4. It approaches 1.96 as the sample grows.

See t-tests and z-tests for why, and the central limit theorem for why these intervals work at all.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Error bars for models and metrics

- **Test-set metrics:** accuracy p on n test rows has SE ≈ √(p(1 − p)/n): 87% on 500 rows is ±2.9 points (95%). Small test sets can't separate models 1–2 points apart.

- **Bootstrap a metric:** resample test rows to get intervals for AUC, F1 or MAE; resample both models' predictions together to compare them fairly (paired).

- **Bagging:** the bootstrap is literally how random forests make each tree's training set (Random Forest).

- **A/B tests:** intervals for the difference between variants (next lesson).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "There's a 95% chance the true mean is in my interval"

In the frequentist framework, the true mean is a fixed number; this particular interval either contains it or doesn't. The 95% describes the **procedure**: if you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the truth. The lab in the Intuition tab shows 100 such intervals at once. (A Bayesian credible interval does support the "95% probability" reading, given a prior.)

#### Caveats

- Both methods assume independent observations; repeated orders from the same customer need clustered or block resampling.

- The bootstrap can't invent information: with n = 10 the interval is unreliable too; extreme statistics (max, min) bootstrap badly.

- "Statistically significant" isn't "important": a tiny difference can have a tight interval with lots of data.

## Say it

### What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean, and when would you use the bootstrap?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How many test examples do I need to measure accuracy to ±1 point?

95% half-width 1.96√(p(1 − p)/n) ≤ 0.01; at p ≈ 0.85, n ≈ 1.96² × 0.1275 / 0.0001 ≈ 4,900.

Follow-up 2 of 3

When does the bootstrap fail?

Tiny samples, dependent data (use block bootstrap), statistics at the extremes (max), and heavy-tailed distributions without enough data.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Confidence interval vs credible interval?

Frequentist: a procedure with 95% coverage over repetitions. Bayesian: given the prior and data, the parameter lies in the interval with 95% posterior probability.

#### The 30-second answer

A statistic like a sample mean varies from sample to sample; its standard deviation is the standard error, s over root n for a mean. By the central limit theorem the mean is roughly Gaussian, so mean plus or minus about two standard errors is a 95% confidence interval, meaning the procedure captures the true value in 95% of repeated samples, not that this interval has a 95% probability. With small or skewed samples, coverage falls short. The bootstrap resamples the observed data with replacement thousands of times to estimate the sampling distribution of any statistic, such as a median, AUC or F1, and the percentiles give an interval.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "There's a 95% chance the true value is in this interval" (for a frequentist CI).

- "Non-overlapping intervals are needed for a significant difference." Overlapping CIs can still differ significantly; test the difference directly.

**Key terms and sources**

Sampling distributions, standard error, the central limit theorem, what a 95% confidence interval does and doesn't mean, coverage with skewed data, and bootstrap intervals for any statistic · built from Wasserman, _All of Statistics_ (ch. 6–8), Efron (1979), Efron & Tibshirani, _An Introduction to the Bootstrap_, and Blitzstein & Hwang (ch. 10) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Sampling distribution** | How a statistic varies across repeated samples. |
| **Standard error** | Std dev of a statistic; s/√n for a mean. |
| **Central limit theorem** | Means of many independent draws are approximately Gaussian. |
| **Coverage** | How often the interval procedure contains the truth. |
| **Bootstrap** | Resampling the data with replacement to estimate sampling variability. |

#### Sources

1. L. Wasserman, _All of Statistics_, Springer 2004, ch. 6–8.

2. B. Efron, "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife", _Annals of Statistics_ 7(1), 1979; B. Efron & R. Tibshirani, _An Introduction to the Bootstrap_, Chapman & Hall 1993.

3. J. Blitzstein & J. Hwang, _Introduction to Probability_, 2nd ed., 2019, §10.3 (central limit theorem), [stat110](https://projects.iq.harvard.edu/stat110).

Delivery times are simulated (log-normal) with fixed seeds; intervals and bootstraps are computed live in your browser.

# Hypothesis Tests, p-values & A/B Testing

> Why peeking at your A/B test every day breaks it.

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/hypothesis-testing-and-ab-tests/
- Before this: Confidence Intervals & the Bootstrap (`fundamentals/confidence-intervals-and-bootstrap`)
- Related: Randomisation and Assignment (`fundamentals/randomisation-and-assignment`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

After a week, your new checkout button converts at 10.4% against 10.0%, and the product manager wants to ship it. The interviewer asks:

> How would you run an A/B test, and what does the p-value mean?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app tests a new checkout button. 10% of visitors to checkout currently place an order (conversion rate). The product team hopes the new button lifts it to 11%, a 10% relative lift. How many users does the test need, and how do we read the result?

#### Is a 0.4-point lift real?

After a week, B converts at 10.4% and A at 10.0%. With a few thousand users per arm, a difference that size appears by chance alone fairly often. Shipping on noise wastes effort and can hurt the product; ignoring real wins leaves money on the table. Hypothesis testing gives a disciplined way to decide, and its failure modes are classic ML and product-sense interview questions.

### The idea

Think of a coin you suspect is biased. A few heads in a row proves little. An A/B test asks how surprising your result would be if nothing had changed. And flipping until you like the answer doesn't count.

[Figure: A bell curve showing results if nothing changed. A marker shows the observed result, and the shaded tail beyond it is the p-value.]

_Illustrative. The p-value assumes no real difference, so it isn't the chance that B is better._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare checking once at day 20 with checking daily and stopping at the first p below 0.05. Neither arm has any real difference here.

#### Checking every day inflates false positives

A/A tests: both arms are identical (10% conversion, 500 users per arm per day, 20 days). Lines show the z-statistic over time for 30 of the tests; the band is ±1.96.

With no real difference at all, a single check at the planned end gives about **5%** false positives, as designed. Checking every day and stopping at the first p < 0.05 gives about **25%**: the z-statistic wanders, and with 20 looks it will often cross 1.96 at some point. Johari, Pekelis & Walsh show that with continuous monitoring and an unlimited horizon a false positive is eventually guaranteed, and propose "always valid" p-values that allow stopping at any time [arXiv:1512.04922](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04922). Fixes: pre-commit to a sample size, use sequential tests (alpha-spending, mSPRT), or Bayesian methods with care.

**Now say why:** why does looking more often create false wins when nothing changed?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An A/B test randomly splits users between the old version (A) and a new one (B) and asks whether the difference in a metric is real or noise. Assume **no difference** (the null), compute how surprising the observed difference would be under that assumption: that's the **p-value**. If p < 0.05 you call it significant, accepting a 5% false-positive rate (type I error). **Power** is the chance of detecting a real effect; it depends on effect size, variance and sample size, so small lifts need big samples, decided **before** the test. The classic mistake is **peeking**: checking daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives from 5% to about 25%. What you'll be able to do after this: run a two-proportion test, interpret a p-value correctly, compute the sample size for a target lift, and explain why peeking, multiple metrics and novelty effects mislead.

#### Null, test statistic, p-value

$$ {z} = {(\hat p_B - \hat p_A)} \,/\, {\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)\,(1/n_A + 1/n_B)}}, \qquad {p = 2\,(1 - \Phi(|z|))} $$

The two-proportion z-test (Wasserman §10.1–10.2). With 5,000 users per arm, 10.4% vs 10.0% gives z ≈ 0.66 and p ≈ 0.51: not distinguishable from noise.

- **test statistic**: How many standard errors apart the two conversion rates are.

- **observed difference**: B’s rate minus A’s rate.

- **standard error under the null**: Using the pooled rate p̄ of both arms: the spread the difference would have if there were no real effect.

- **p-value**: Two-sided: the probability, assuming no real difference, of a |z| at least this large. Small p = the data would be surprising if nothing changed.

#### Two kinds of error, and power

| | No real effect | Real effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Declare a win (p < α)** | Type I error (false positive), rate α = 5% | Correct: probability = power |
| **No win** | Correct | Type II error (false negative), rate β = 1 − power |

$$ {n} \approx {(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2}\,{\bigl[p_A(1-p_A) + p_B(1-p_B)\bigr]} \,/\, {(p_B - p_A)^2} $$

Standard normal-approximation sample size for two proportions; see Kohavi, Tang & Xu (2020). For 10% → 11%: n ≈ 14,750 users per arm.

- **users per arm**: For a two-sided test at α = 0.05 with 80% power.

- **the two error rates**: 1.96 for α = 0.05 two-sided, 0.84 for 80% power. Stricter tests or more power need more users.

- **variance of the metric**: Noisier metrics need more data.

- **minimum detectable effect, squared**: Halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the sample size.

#### Power calculator

With 10,000 users per arm, the test has only a 64% chance of detecting a real 10% → 11% lift; 14,750 per arm reaches 80%. A 5% relative lift needs about 57,800 per arm; a 20% lift only about 3,800. Small lifts on low conversion rates are expensive to detect, which is why teams set a minimum detectable effect and the duration **before** launching.

#### Which test do I use?

| Question | Data | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Two groups differ? | Numbers | Welch's t-test |
| The same subjects changed? | Numbers | Paired t-test |
| Two rates differ? | Yes or no | Two-proportion z-test |
| Are two categories related? | Categories | Chi-squared |
| Three or more group means differ? | Numbers | ANOVA |
| Small, skewed data, or an unusual statistic? | Any | Mann-Whitney or a permutation test |

##### Report the effect size too

A p-value tells you whether there's evidence of a difference, not how large it is. With enough data, tiny effects become significant. So report the difference with its interval, and a standardised size if you're comparing across metrics, like Cohen's d: the difference in means divided by the standard deviation.

## In practice

### In practice

#### More things that break A/B tests

- **Multiple comparisons:** testing 20 metrics or segments at α = 0.05 gives about one false "win" by chance. Pick a primary metric in advance; correct for multiplicity (Bonferroni, Benjamini–Hochberg).

- **Sample ratio mismatch:** if the split isn't the planned 50/50, assignment or logging is broken; Kohavi et al. recommend checking this first.

- **Novelty and primacy effects:** users react to change itself; run long enough (full weekly cycles).

- **Interference:** in marketplaces (riders, restaurants) treatment users can affect control users; randomise by city or time (switchback tests).

- **Unit of randomisation vs analysis:** randomising users but analysing orders understates variance (orders from one user are correlated).

Kohavi, Tang & Xu, _Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments_, Cambridge University Press 2020.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "p = 0.03 means a 97% chance B is better"

The p-value is computed _assuming_ there's no difference; it can't be the probability that there is one. The American Statistical Association's statement lists the correct reading and the common misreadings: "P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model"; they do not measure "the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone"; and "a p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result" [ASA 2016](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108). Report the effect size with a confidence interval alongside the p-value.

## Say it

### How would you run an A/B test, and what does the p-value mean?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your test is significant at p = 0.04 after you checked it daily. Ship?

Not yet: daily peeking inflates false positives well above 5%. Re-run with a fixed horizon or analyse with a sequential method; also check effect size and guardrail metrics.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you choose the sample size?

From baseline rate, MDE, α and power: n ≈ (1.96 + 0.84)² [p₁(1 − p₁) + p₂(1 − p₂)]/(p₂ − p₁)² per arm, then convert to duration using traffic, rounding up to full weeks.

Follow-up 3 of 3

The test is flat but you believe the feature helps. What now?

Check power (was it sized to detect a realistic effect?), segment heterogeneity (pre-registered only), metric sensitivity and variance reduction (CUPED), and implementation bugs.

#### The 30-second answer

An A/B test randomises users into control and treatment and tests the null hypothesis of no difference. The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as large if the null were true; below the significance level, typically 0.05, we reject the null, accepting a 5% false-positive rate. Before launching, I'd fix the primary metric, the minimum detectable effect and the sample size for 80% power; small lifts on low baselines need tens of thousands of users per arm. I'd avoid peeking or use sequential methods, correct for multiple metrics, check sample-ratio mismatch, and report the effect size with a confidence interval, not just the p-value.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "p = 0.03 means 97% chance B is better."

- "Not significant means no effect." It may be underpowered.

- "Let's run until it's significant."

**Key terms and sources**

Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics and p-values, significance, type I and II errors, power and sample size, the peeking problem, and how online experiments are run · built from the ASA Statement on p-values (2016), Kohavi, Tang & Xu, _Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments_ (2020), Johari et al. (2017) and Wasserman, _All of Statistics_ (ch. 10) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Null hypothesis** | No difference between variants. |
| **p-value** | P(data at least this extreme \| null true). |
| **α / significance level** | Tolerated false-positive rate (often 5%). |
| **Power** | P(detect \| real effect of the planned size), often 80%. |
| **MDE** | Minimum detectable effect the test is sized for. |
| **Peeking** | Repeatedly checking and stopping early on significance. |

#### Sources

1. R. Wasserstein & N. Lazar, "The ASA statement on p-values: context, process, and purpose", _The American Statistician_ 70(2), 2016, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108).

2. R. Kohavi, D. Tang & Y. Xu, _Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing_, Cambridge University Press 2020.

3. R. Johari, L. Pekelis & D. Walsh, "Always valid inference: bringing sequential analysis to A/B testing", [arXiv:1512.04922](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04922); "Peeking at A/B tests", KDD 2017.

# T-Tests and Z-Tests

> What's the difference between a t-test and a z-test, and when would you use a paired test?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/t-tests-and-z-tests/
- Before this: Hypothesis Tests, p-values & A/B Testing (`fundamentals/hypothesis-testing-and-ab-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

You compared two models on the same 10 folds, and a colleague ran an unpaired test, finding no significant difference. Someone else used a z-test on just 8 samples, and is very confident. The interviewer asks:

> What's the difference between a t-test and a z-test, and when would you use a paired test?

#### Why it matters

The t-test is the most commonly used statistical test. It's the basis of comparing model scores and user metrics, and a common interview question. This builds on hypothesis tests, and gives you what the z-test leaves out.

### The idea

Think of two runners. You could compare a group of runners on one shoe with another group on another shoe, but people differ hugely. Better, have the same people run in both pairs. Their own speed cancels out, so you can see the difference between the shoes. That's why pairing helps.

[Figure: Three tests. A z-test assumes a known spread. A t-test estimates the spread, with heavier tails. A paired test uses differences within the same subjects.]

_Choose by what you know, and how the data was collected._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the samples to 3, and compare t with z. Then raise the correlation.

#### Run the same data as unpaired and paired

Calculated exactly from the summary numbers. The z-test uses the same statistic, wrongly treating the sample's spread as known, so its p-value is too small at low n.

Set the samples to **3**: t's cutoff rises to 2.78, and z's p-value is too low. Raise them to **200**, and the cutoff is nearly 1.96. Then drag the correlation up. The difference and spreads don't change, yet the paired test gets much stronger.

**Now say why:** why does correlation between pairs make the test stronger?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Both tests ask how many standard errors a difference is from zero. A **z-test** assumes you know the population's spread. A **t-test** estimates it from the sample, which adds uncertainty, so it uses a **t-distribution with heavier tails**. With a large sample, they match. Use a **paired test** when measuring the same things twice, as removing differences between subjects makes it far more sensitive. Use **Welch's** version as your default for two groups.

#### Which test, and why

| Test | Question | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **One-sample** | Does this mean differ from a target? | Is average delivery time different from 30 minutes? |
| **Two-sample (Welch)** | Do two separate groups differ? | Do users on A and B spend different amounts? |
| **Paired** | Did the same subjects change? | Two models scored on the same 50 test folds. |
| **Two-proportion z** | Do two rates differ? | Conversion in an A/B test. |

##### Why t has heavier tails

With a small sample, your estimate of the spread is itself noisy. Sometimes it's too small, making the statistic look bigger than it should. The t-distribution allows for this, by making extreme values more likely. The smaller the sample, the stronger the correction: the 5% cutoff is 2.78 with 4 degrees of freedom, and approaches 1.96 as the sample grows.

##### Degrees of freedom

These count how many values are free to vary. After you've used the sample's mean, the last value is fixed, so a one-sample test has n − 1. Think of it as how much information you have left to estimate the spread.

##### Why pairing is powerful

People or test sets differ a lot from each other. A paired test works on each subject's difference, so those differences cancel. The more correlated the pairs, the larger the gain. When comparing two models, always use the same test data, and pair the results.

##### What the tests assume

- **Independence:** this is the serious one. Correlated rows make it far too optimistic.

- **Roughly Normal averages:** fine with large samples, thanks to the central limit theorem. With small, skewed samples, consider a non-parametric test.

- **Equal variances:** the classic version assumes this, and Welch's doesn't, so prefer Welch's.

#### The maths

$$ {t} = \frac{{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}}{{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}}}, \qquad {t_{\text{paired}} = \frac{\bar d}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}}, \qquad {s_d^2 = s_1^2 + s_2^2 - 2\rho s_1 s_2} $$

Worked example: n = 16, mean 52, s = 8, testing against 50. SE = 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so t = 1, with 15 degrees of freedom. That’s not significant.

- **the t statistic**: How many standard errors apart the two means are.

- **the observed difference**: The signal you’re checking.

- **the standard error**: Noise in the difference, using spreads estimated from the sample.

- **the paired version**: Works on each pair’s difference, and has n − 1 degrees of freedom.

- **why pairing helps**: Strong positive correlation ρ makes the spread of the differences much smaller.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **In A/B tests with many users:** t and z give almost the same answer, so the difference rarely matters at scale.

- **Comparing models:** use the same test set, and a paired test on per-example or per-fold results. Cross-validation folds overlap, so they aren't truly independent, and results can be overconfident.

- **Check independence first:** treating many events from one user as separate samples is the most common way these tests go wrong.

- **One-sided tests:** only use them if you decided the direction beforehand, and the other direction would truly make no difference.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Use a t-test whenever the sample is under 30"

It sounds right, as it's a popular rule. But you almost never know the true spread, so a t-test is the right choice at any size, and it simply converges to z. Thirty also doesn't guarantee Normal averages, as skewed data can need far more. The more important question is whether your samples are independent.

## Say it

### What's the difference between a t-test and a z-test, and when would you use a paired test?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does the t-test use n − 1 degrees of freedom?

Estimating the spread uses the sample's own mean, which uses up one piece of information. Given the mean, the last value is determined. So you have n − 1 values free to vary, and this sets the shape of the t-distribution, which has heavier tails with fewer degrees of freedom.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you test whether model B is better than model A?

Score both on the same test examples, and compare with a paired test on per-example results, like a paired t-test, a McNemar test for accuracy or a bootstrap of the differences. Pairing removes the difficulty of each example. Report the effect size too, not only significance.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When does a t-test mislead you?

When samples aren't independent, like many clicks from one user, as it underestimates noise. Also with small samples from very skewed or heavy-tailed data, and when you've run many tests, or stopped early. Independence is the most serious, as a larger sample doesn't fix it.

#### The 30-second answer

Both ask how many standard errors a difference is from zero. A z-test assumes the population's spread is known, while a t-test estimates it, adding uncertainty, so it uses a t-distribution with heavier tails. With large samples, they match. For two groups, I'd default to Welch's t-test, which doesn't assume equal variances. If I'm measuring the same subjects twice, like two models on the same test folds, I'd use a paired test: differences between subjects cancel, which makes it much more sensitive. The key assumption is independence.

**Key terms and sources**

One-sample, two-sample and paired t-tests, degrees of freedom, Welch's correction, how the t differs from z, and when to use each. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Barr, OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/)

- [Bruce, Bruce and Gedeck, Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, contents excerpt](https://toc.uni.li/FLMF048415.pdf)

- [Wasserman, All of Statistics](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~larry/all-of-statistics/)

# Chi-Squared Tests and ANOVA

> When would you use a chi-squared test or ANOVA, and why not just run many t-tests?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/chi-squared-tests-and-anova/
- Before this: T-Tests and Z-Tests (`fundamentals/t-tests-and-z-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

You've tested five versions of a recommendation model. A colleague ran t-tests on every pair, and celebrates one significant result. Another wants to know whether a user's plan type is related to whether they churn. The interviewer asks:

> When would you use a chi-squared test or ANOVA, and why not just run many t-tests?

#### Why it matters

Not every question is about two means. You might compare several model versions, or check whether two categories are related. These are the standard tools, and knowing which to choose is a common interview question.

### The idea

Think of noise in a classroom. If you wonder whether groups differ, you could compare every pair of students, and something will look different by chance. Or you could ask once: is the difference between groups larger than the ordinary variation within them? That single question is ANOVA.

[Figure: Choosing a test. Chi-squared compares observed and expected counts for categories. ANOVA compares the variation between groups with the variation within them.]

_Chi-squared is for counts, and ANOVA is for group means._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the gap to 0, and raise the groups to 20. Then raise the gap.

#### Compare many groups

Illustrative: each group has a standard deviation of 1, and means rise evenly. The false-win figure assumes independent tests with no real differences, so treat it as a guide. Pairwise tests that share groups are correlated.

Set the gap to **0** and raise the groups to **20**. All groups are identical, yet pairwise testing almost guarantees you'll "find" a difference. ANOVA doesn't, as its F statistic stays low.

**Now say why:** why does F stay small when the groups are identical?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

The **chi-squared test** compares the counts you got with the counts you'd expect, so it suits categories, like plan type against churn. **ANOVA** compares means across many groups at once, by asking whether differences between groups are large compared with the noise within them. Running every pair of t-tests instead inflates false positives. A significant ANOVA only says that **some group differs**, so you follow up to find which.

#### Two tests for two situations

| Your data | Question | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Two categories | Are they related? | Chi-squared test of independence |
| One category | Does it match an expected split? | Chi-squared goodness of fit, as in SRM checks |
| A number, across 3 or more groups | Do the means differ? | One-way ANOVA |

##### Chi-squared, in steps

1. Work out each cell's expected count if the two variables were unrelated: row total × column total ÷ grand total.

2. For each cell, compute (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, and add them up.

3. Compare with a chi-squared distribution with (rows − 1)(columns − 1) degrees of freedom.

Use counts, not percentages. If expected counts are very small, under about 5, use Fisher's exact test. For a 2 × 2 table, chi-squared equals the two-proportion z-test squared.

##### ANOVA, in one idea

Split total variation into two parts. **Between groups** measures how far group means are from the overall mean. **Within groups** measures the noise inside each group. If the groups really are the same, the two should be about equal, and their ratio, the **F statistic**, is close to 1.

##### After a significant result

ANOVA doesn't say which group differs. Follow up with pairwise tests, corrected for multiple comparisons, such as Tukey's test. With only two groups, ANOVA gives the same answer as a t-test, since F = t².

#### The maths

$$ {\chi^2} = \sum_{\text{cells}} \frac{({O} - {E})^2}{{E}}, \qquad {F} = \frac{{\text{variance between groups}}}{{\text{variance within groups}}} $$

Worked example: A converts 40 of 100, and B converts 60 of 100. Expected is 50 in each cell. χ² = 4 × 10²/50 = 8, with 1 degree of freedom, so p ≈ 0.005.

- **chi-squared**: The total surprise across all cells. Larger means a bigger gap from what you’d expect.

- **observed counts**: What you actually saw.

- **expected counts**: What you’d see if the variables were unrelated.

- **the F statistic**: A signal-to-noise ratio. Around 1 means no sign of a real difference.

- **between groups**: How spread out the group means are.

- **within groups**: Ordinary noise inside each group.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **A/B/n tests:** if you only compare each variant with control, Dunnett's test or a simple correction is often better than ANOVA. See multiple testing.

- **Feature selection:** chi-squared and F scores give quick filters for feature importance, but they only see simple relationships.

- **Effect sizes:** with large samples, tiny differences become significant. Report how large the relationship is, like Cramér's V or η².

- **Independence:** both assume independent observations. Repeated events from one user break this.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "ANOVA was significant, so the best-looking group wins"

It sounds right, as ANOVA found a difference. But it only says the groups aren't all equal. It doesn't say which differs, or that the top group beats the next one. Follow up with corrected pairwise comparisons, and look at effect sizes.

## Say it

### When would you use a chi-squared test or ANOVA, and why not just run many t-tests?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the connection between chi-squared and the two-proportion z-test?

For a 2 × 2 table, they're the same test: chi-squared equals z squared, with the same p-value. Chi-squared generalises to more rows and columns. The z-test also gives you a direction, and a confidence interval for the difference.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does ANOVA use variances to compare means?

If all group means were equal, their spread would only reflect noise, and it would match the noise inside groups. If the means differ, their spread grows beyond that. So comparing the two variances tests whether the means differ. It's the same logic as signal against noise.

Follow-up 3 of 3

ANOVA is significant, but no pairwise test is. What's going on?

It can happen. ANOVA pools evidence across all groups, while corrected pairwise tests are stricter, each with less power. It suggests something differs, without enough data to say which. You could look at a planned contrast, such as a trend across ordered groups, or collect more data.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd use chi-squared for categories: it compares observed counts with those expected if the variables were unrelated. I'd use ANOVA to compare a number's mean across three or more groups: it compares variation between groups with variation within them. Running all the pairwise t-tests instead inflates false positives. With five groups, that's ten tests, and up to a 40% chance of a false win. A significant ANOVA only says some group differs, so I'd follow up with corrected pairwise tests, like Tukey's.

**Key terms and sources**

Chi-squared tests for categories, ANOVA for comparing many group means, why repeated t-tests inflate false positives, and how to follow up. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Barr, OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/)

- [Bruce, Bruce and Gedeck, Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, contents excerpt](https://toc.uni.li/FLMF048415.pdf)

- [KDnuggets on statistical concepts for interviews](https://www.kdnuggets.com/2021/02/10-statistical-concepts-data-science-interviews.html)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Non-Parametric and Permutation Tests

> What do you do when a t-test's assumptions fail, and how does a permutation test work?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/non-parametric-and-permutation-tests/
- Before this: T-Tests and Z-Tests (`fundamentals/t-tests-and-z-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have 10 users in each group, and revenue is very skewed. One big spender in group A makes A's mean larger, while most of B's users spend more. A t-test says there's no difference. The interviewer asks:

> What do you do when a t-test's assumptions fail, and how does a permutation test work?

#### Why it matters

Real metrics are often messy: revenue, session length, latency. These tests give you a reliable option when the usual assumptions don't hold, and they explain what AUC really measures. See t-tests first.

### The idea

Think of a race where you only note who finished ahead of whom. A runner who's an hour behind counts just the same as one who's a second behind, so one extreme time can't skew the result. To test for luck, you could also shuffle team labels, and see how often a shuffled team does as well.

[Figure: Two approaches. Rank tests use order, not size, so outliers matter less. Permutation tests shuffle labels to build the null, for any statistic.]

_Fewer assumptions, at the cost of some detail._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag A's largest value down to 12, and up to 500. Then lower the shift.

#### Add an outlier to a small test

Illustrative: A is 3 to 11, plus your largest value. B is 4 to 13, with your shift added to each. Mann-Whitney uses a Normal approximation with tie correction. Permutation uses 4,000 seeded shuffles.

Lower A's largest value to **12**. The t-test recovers, as there's no extreme value left to distort things. The ranks barely change between these two settings, which is the point of using them. Notice that at 200, a permutation test on **means** also fails, as the outlier dominates every shuffle. A test is only as robust as its statistic, so try a permutation test on medians or ranks in that case.

**Now say why:** why does the rank test barely change?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

When data is small, skewed or full of outliers, a t-test can mislead. **Rank tests**, such as Mann-Whitney, replace values with their ranks, so one extreme value can't dominate. Mann-Whitney's U is directly tied to **AUC**: both give the chance that a random item from one group beats one from the other. **Permutation tests** build the null by shuffling group labels, so they need few assumptions, and work for any statistic.

#### Two ways to avoid assumptions

##### Rank tests

1. Pool both groups, and sort all the values.

2. Replace each value with its rank. A huge outlier just becomes the top rank.

3. Check whether one group's ranks are unusually high.

| Instead of | Use | Situation |
|---|---|---|
| Two-sample t-test | **Mann-Whitney U** | Two separate groups |
| Paired t-test | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** | The same subjects, twice |
| One-way ANOVA | **Kruskal-Wallis** | Three or more groups |
| Pearson correlation | **Spearman** | Relationships that rise steadily, but not in a straight line |

##### What Mann-Whitney actually tests

It's often described as comparing medians, but that's only true under extra assumptions. In general, it tests whether a random value from one group tends to beat one from the other. That chance is U ÷ (n₁n₂), which is exactly the AUC, if the groups are positives and negatives.

##### Permutation tests

1. Compute your statistic on the real data, like the difference in means.

2. Shuffle the group labels randomly, and recompute it.

3. Repeat thousands of times, to see what chance alone produces.

4. The p-value is how often a shuffled result is at least as extreme as the real one.

The logic is direct: if the groups really don't differ, the labels are arbitrary. It works for any statistic, like medians, ratios or a model's AUC gain.

##### The trade-offs

- **Lost precision:** rank tests discard sizes, so they don't say "how much". Report an effect size too.

- **Totals matter:** if a few whales drive revenue, a rank test may miss a change that you care about, as it ignores how big those values are.

- **Some power loss:** on truly Normal data, a t-test is slightly better, though the rank test's loss is small.

- **Bootstrap or permutation?** Permutation tests a null hypothesis. The bootstrap estimates uncertainty, as in confidence intervals.

#### The maths

$$ {U} = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} \mathbb{1}[{x_i > y_j}] + \tfrac12\mathbb{1}[x_i = y_j], \qquad {\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{U}{n_1 n_2}}, \qquad {p \approx \frac{\#\{|T_{\text{shuffled}}| \ge |T_{\text{real}}|\} + 1}{R + 1}} $$

Worked example: with 10 and 15 items and U = 75, AUC = 75 ÷ 150 = 0.5, so neither group tends to beat the other.

- **the U statistic**: Counts how many pairs from the two groups have x beating y.

- **one comparison**: Only the order matters, not how far apart the values are.

- **its link to AUC**: Divide by the number of pairs to get the chance that x beats y. 0.5 means no difference.

- **permutation p-value**: The share of R shuffles that are at least as extreme as the real result. Adding 1 keeps it above zero.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Choosing:** with large samples, a t-test on means is usually fine, thanks to the central limit theorem, and answers the question about totals. Use rank tests for small samples, or when a typical user matters more than the total.

- **Comparing models:** permutation tests on paired predictions, swapping which model gets each example's result, are a simple way to test a metric's difference.

- **Check your unit:** shuffle at the level you randomised, like users, not events. Otherwise, you underestimate noise.

- **Cost:** permutation needs thousands of recomputations, so it can be slow on expensive statistics.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Mann-Whitney compares medians"

It sounds right, as it's in many cheat sheets. But it only compares medians if the two distributions have the same shape. In general, it tests whether a value from one group tends to beat one from the other. Two groups can have the same median, and still get a significant result.

## Say it

### What do you do when a t-test's assumptions fail, and how does a permutation test work?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How is Mann-Whitney related to AUC?

AUC is the chance that a random positive scores above a random negative. U counts pairs where one group's value beats the other's, with ties as a half. So U ÷ (n₁n₂) is exactly AUC, and testing whether AUC differs from 0.5 is the same as a Mann-Whitney test.

Follow-up 2 of 3

When would you not use a rank test, even with skewed data?

When you care about the total. If you want to raise revenue, a change that moves a few very large spenders matters, and a rank test could miss it entirely. With large samples, a test on the mean is fine even for skewed data, or you could use the bootstrap.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the difference between a permutation test and the bootstrap?

A permutation test shuffles labels without replacement, assuming no group difference, to get a p-value. The bootstrap resamples with replacement from the data as it is, to estimate uncertainty, like a confidence interval. They answer related but different questions.

#### The 30-second answer

When data is small, skewed or has outliers, I'd consider Mann-Whitney, which ranks the pooled values, so one extreme value can't dominate. It tests whether one group tends to beat the other, and U over n1 n2 is the same as AUC. A permutation test shuffles the group labels thousands of times to build the null, then asks how often a shuffle is at least as extreme as the real result. It needs few assumptions, and works for any statistic. But a rank test ignores size, so if totals matter, such as revenue, I'd keep looking at the mean.

**Key terms and sources**

Rank tests like Mann-Whitney, the link with AUC, permutation tests, and when these are better than a t-test. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [DataCamp statistics interview questions](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/statistics-interview-questions)

- [Wasserman, All of Statistics](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~larry/all-of-statistics/)

- ROC and PR AUC on this site

# Inference for Regression

> How do you interpret a regression coefficient, its p-value and R², and how do you check the model's assumptions?

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/inference-for-regression/
- Before this: T-Tests and Z-Tests (`fundamentals/t-tests-and-z-tests`), Linear Independence, Basis and Rank (`fundamentals/linear-independence-basis-and-rank`)
- Related: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

A regression on delivery time shows distance with a coefficient of 3 and p below 0.001, with R² of 0.85. A manager concludes that the model is excellent and that distance causes delays. Its residual plot shows a clear curve. The interviewer asks:

> How do you interpret a regression coefficient, its p-value and R², and how do you check the model's assumptions?

#### Why it matters

Often you need to explain a model, not just predict: which factors matter, and by how much? This is where regressions are most often misread. See linear regression for how it's fitted.

### The idea

Think of a weather forecast with a score. A good score says the forecast tracks the temperature overall. It doesn't say why, or where it goes wrong. For that, you look at its errors: if it's always too cold in summer, the score hid a pattern. Residuals are those errors.

[Figure: Reading a regression. The coefficient is the expected change per unit. The standard error is how noisy it is. Residuals show whether the model fits.]

_Numbers summarise a fit, and residuals show what they miss._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch to curved data with low noise. Then try the funnel.

#### Fit a line, then read the residuals

Our seeded simulation, using ordinary least squares with x from 0 to 10. Left: data and fit. Right: residuals against predictions. Standard errors are the classic kind, which assume constant noise.

Switch to the **curved** pattern, with low noise. R² looks strong, and the slope is highly significant, yet the residuals show an obvious curve. The numbers said it's good, and the plot says the model's wrong. Always look at both.

**Now say why:** how can R² be high while the model is wrong?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A regression gives a **coefficient** for each feature: the expected change in the outcome per unit, **holding the others fixed**. Its **standard error** tells you how noisy that is, which gives a t-test and a confidence interval. **R²** is the share of variance explained, not whether the model is right. Check **residual plots**: patterns there reveal missing curves or unequal noise. And a significant coefficient doesn't prove cause.

#### Reading the output

| Output | What it says | What it doesn't say |
|---|---|---|
| **Coefficient** | Expected change in y per unit of x, with other features held fixed. | That x causes it. That it's the most important feature. |
| **Standard error** | How much the coefficient would vary across samples. | That the model is correctly specified. |
| **p-value** | How surprising this coefficient is if the true value is zero. | How large or useful the effect is. |
| **R²** | The share of variance in y explained. | Whether the model's right, or will predict well on new data. |

##### Worked reading

Say delivery time = 12 + 3 × distance in km, with a standard error of 1 on the slope. Each extra km is linked to about 3 more minutes, for similar orders. t = 3 ÷ 1 = 3, and the 95% interval is about 1 to 5 minutes.

##### What residual plots tell you

Residuals should look like shapeless noise. Plot them against predictions.

| You see | It means | Try |
|---|---|---|
| A curve | A straight line doesn't fit. | Transform features, or add terms. |
| A funnel | Noise grows with size (heteroscedasticity). Standard errors are wrong. | Robust standard errors, or a log transform. |
| Long tails or a few far points | Outliers, which may have high influence. | Investigate, or use a robust loss. |
| A pattern over time | Errors aren't independent. | Time-series methods, or clustered standard errors. |

##### Common traps

- **Correlated features:** collinearity inflates standard errors, so each feature can look insignificant, while the model predicts well.

- **Comparing sizes:** a coefficient's size depends on units. Standardise features before comparing them.

- **R² always rises:** adding any feature raises training R². Use adjusted R² or a test set.

- **Significance with huge data:** a tiny, useless effect can have a small p-value. Look at the interval.

#### The maths

$$ {\hat\beta} \pm t^* \cdot {SE(\hat\beta)}, \qquad {SE(\hat\beta)} = \frac{{\hat\sigma}}{{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}}}, \qquad {R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2}} $$

This is for a single feature. With many, the standard error also grows with collinearity, by the variance inflation factor.

- **the coefficient and its interval**: The estimate, plus or minus a margin of about two standard errors.

- **the standard error**: Noise in the slope.

- **residual noise**: More scatter around the line means a less certain slope.

- **the spread of x**: A wide range of x pins the slope down better. More data helps here as well.

- **R squared**: 1 minus the share of variance left in the residuals.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Say "linked to", not "causes":** a coefficient describes an association, unless the design supports a causal claim. See causal inference.

- **Robust standard errors:** when noise isn't constant, they correct your intervals, without changing the fit.

- **Regularised models:** ridge and lasso coefficients are biased on purpose, so these simple p-values don't apply.

- **Tree models:** use permutation importance or SHAP, but remember these also describe the model, not causes.

- **Test data:** high R² in training says little about new data. Use a test set when the goal's prediction.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "High R² and low p-values mean the model is right"

It sounds right, since both numbers look good. But a straight line can explain a lot of a curve, with a strong slope, while being clearly the wrong shape. And with lots of data, even tiny effects give small p-values. Look at residuals, and test on new data.

## Say it

### How do you interpret a regression coefficient, its p-value and R², and how do you check the model's assumptions?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you interpret a coefficient of 3 on distance?

Each extra km is linked to about 3 more minutes, holding the other features fixed. It's not necessarily causal, and it may not hold outside the data's range. Its interval tells you how certain you are, and its size depends on the units used.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Is a high R² always good?

No. It can be high with a wrong model, as with curved data, or on training data from overfitting. And a low R² can still be useful: in noisy behaviours, a small explained share can be valuable. Look at residuals, a test set and what the decision needs.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A feature's p-value is high. Should you drop it?

Not automatically. It could be collinear with another feature, which inflates its standard error, so together they may matter. Or it may have a real but small effect, with too little data. Check VIF, look at the interval, and compare models on validation data.

#### The 30-second answer

A coefficient is the expected change in the outcome per unit of that feature, holding the others fixed. Its standard error gives a t-test and an interval: about plus or minus two standard errors. R squared is the share of variance explained, not proof that the model's right. So I'd check residual plots: a curve means a straight line doesn't fit, and a funnel means noise varies, so standard errors are off. Collinearity inflates standard errors. And I'd say a feature's linked to the outcome, not that it causes it, unless the design supports that.

**Key terms and sources**

Reading coefficients and their standard errors, confidence intervals, what R² does and doesn't say, residual plots, and common traps. · checked 6 Nov 2026

- [Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Barr, OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/)

- [Bruce, Bruce and Gedeck, Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, contents excerpt](https://toc.uni.li/FLMF048415.pdf)

- Linear regression on this site

# Correlation vs Causation

> When the data says the opposite of the truth: confounders and Simpson's paradox.

- Track: Fundamentals › Maths for ML › Statistics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/correlation-vs-causation/
- Before this: Hypothesis Tests, p-values & A/B Testing (`fundamentals/hypothesis-testing-and-ab-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `stats`

## Intuition

### The situation

Customers who use live order tracking reorder far more often, and someone wants to push tracking on everyone. The interviewer asks:

> How can correlation mislead you, and how do you estimate a causal effect?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app notices that customers who use live order tracking reorder far more often. Should it push tracking on everyone to increase reorders? A simulation where we control the truth answers it: tracking has **no effect** on reordering, but engaged customers are more likely both to use tracking and to reorder. A real medical dataset shows the same trap in Simpson's paradox.

#### Prediction questions vs intervention questions

"Which customers will reorder?" is a prediction question: any correlated signal helps. "Will customers reorder more _if we make them_ use tracking?" is a causal question: only the effect of changing tracking matters. ML engineers are asked the second kind constantly, and answering it with the tools for the first is one of the most expensive mistakes in industry.

### The idea

Think of umbrellas and wet streets. They rise and fall together, but handing out umbrellas won't make it rain. Rain causes both. A hidden common cause like this can make two things look linked when neither affects the other.

[Figure: Engagement sits at the top with arrows to using tracking and to reordering. A dashed line between tracking and reordering shows a correlation with no arrow of cause.]

_From the lesson's simulation: engagement drives both tracking use and reordering._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Look at all patients, then split them by stone size.

#### Simpson's paradox: kidney stones

| | Open surgery (A) | Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B) |
|---|---|---|
| Small stones | 93% (81/87) | 87% (234/270) |
| Large stones | 73% (192/263) | 69% (55/80) |
| All patients | 78% (273/350) | 83% (289/350) |

A was better for small stones _and_ for large stones, yet worse overall. The confounder is stone size: doctors gave the riskier open surgery mostly to large, harder cases, so A's overall rate is dragged down by case mix. The study was observational, not randomised, so even the subgroup comparison isn't proof [Charig et al., BMJ 1986](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1339981/). Which table to trust depends on the causal story, not on the numbers: here stone size affects both treatment choice and outcome, so compare within size.

**Now say why:** how can one treatment win in both groups and still lose overall?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. A hidden **confounder** can drive both (engaged customers both use live tracking _and_ reorder more), the arrow can point the other way (**reverse causation**), or the data may only include a skewed subset (**selection bias**). Confounding can even flip a comparison: in **Simpson's paradox** a treatment wins in every subgroup and loses overall. **Randomisation** (A/B tests) breaks every hidden link and is the gold standard; without it you must adjust for the confounders you can measure and argue there are no others. ML models learn correlations, so they predict well but don't tell you what will happen if you _intervene_. What you'll be able to do after this: name the ways correlation misleads, explain Simpson's paradox with real numbers, say why randomisation works, and keep "predictive" and "causal" claims apart in interviews.

#### Four ways a correlation can mislead

1. The data shows that tracking users reorder more.

2. **Confounding:** engagement causes both. Tracking may do nothing, yet the correlation is strong.

3. **Reverse causation:** customers who already order often are the ones who find and use the feature.

4. **Selection bias:** if the dataset only includes some customers (survey responders, retained users), correlations inside it can be created by who got in. A fourth trap is pure chance across many tested pairs.

5. **Randomisation** assigns tracking by coin flip, so nothing about the customer can influence who gets it. Any remaining difference must be caused by tracking (or noise).

#### How to get a causal answer

1. **Randomised experiment (A/B test):** the gold standard; treatment can't depend on anything about the unit (A/B Testing).

2. **Adjust for observed confounders:** stratification, regression with the confounders as inputs, matching, or inverse-propensity weighting. Valid only if there are no _unmeasured_ confounders, an assumption you must argue from domain knowledge.

3. **Natural experiments:** difference-in-differences (a policy changed in one city but not another), instrumental variables, regression discontinuity (a sharp eligibility cut-off).

4. **Causal diagrams:** draw the assumed causes (Pearl's DAGs) to decide which variables to adjust for, and which _not_ to (adjusting for a consequence of the treatment, a mediator or a collider, creates bias).

Hernán & Robins, _Causal Inference: What If_ (free online); Pearl & Mackenzie, _The Book of Why_.

#### Pearson, Spearman, and going further

- **Pearson** measures straight-line relationships. Outliers can strongly affect it.

- **Spearman** is Pearson on ranks, so it measures any steadily rising or falling relationship, and it's robust to outliers.

Example: for x = 1 to 5 and y = x³, Spearman is exactly 1, as the order always agrees, while Pearson is about 0.94. A zero correlation of either kind doesn't mean no relationship: y = x² on symmetric x has a Pearson of 0.

When you can't run an experiment, see causal inference without an experiment.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What this means for models

- **Feature importance isn't causal:** a feature can be important because it's a proxy for a confounder (zip code for income). Changing it won't change the outcome.

- **Shortcut learning:** models latch onto spurious correlations (a hospital's scanner model predicting disease) that break when the setting changes.

- **Feedback loops:** a recommender's training data is caused by its own past recommendations; observed clicks reflect exposure, not only preference.

- **Uplift modelling:** to decide _whom to treat_ (send a coupon), model the difference in outcome with vs without treatment, trained on randomised data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Tracking users reorder 25 points more, so tracking drives reorders"

20,000 simulated customers per study. Engagement drives both tracking use and reordering; in the second setting tracking also has a real positive effect.

With **no** real effect, the naive comparison shows a 25.5-point lift. Comparing customers of similar engagement shrinks it to 2.6 points (some confounding remains within the coarse bands), and the randomised test shows 0.8 points, within noise. With a real effect, the naive estimate (33.7) is still far too high, while randomisation (8.5) recovers the true size. Adjusting only works for confounders you _measured_; randomisation also handles the ones you didn't.

## Say it

### How can correlation mislead you, and how do you estimate a causal effect?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Users who use feature X retain better. How would you test if X causes retention?

Randomised rollout or encouragement design (randomly prompt some users to try X); if impossible, compare similar users with matching/propensity scores, look for a natural experiment, and state the unmeasured-confounder risk.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Explain Simpson's paradox with an example.

Kidney stones: open surgery had higher success for small and for large stones, but lower overall, because it was mostly used on large stones, which have worse outcomes regardless.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Should you control for every variable you have?

No: controlling for mediators removes part of the effect you want, and controlling for colliders creates bias. Use a causal diagram to choose.

#### The 30-second answer

Correlation can come from a confounder that causes both variables, from reverse causation, from selection bias, or from chance. Confounding can even reverse a comparison, as in Simpson's paradox, where a treatment wins in every subgroup but loses overall because of case mix. The cleanest way to estimate a causal effect is randomisation, because nothing about the unit can influence assignment. Without it, adjust for measured confounders with stratification, regression, matching or propensity weighting, and argue there are no unmeasured ones, or use natural experiments like difference-in-differences. Predictive models learn correlations, so feature importance isn't a causal effect.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The model shows feature X drives churn." It shows association.

- "More data will remove confounding." Bias doesn't shrink with sample size.

**Key terms and sources**

Confounders, Simpson's paradox, selection bias and reverse causation, randomisation, adjusting for observed confounders, and what it means for ML models and feature importance · built from Charig et al., _BMJ_ (1986), Pearl & Mackenzie, _The Book of Why_ (2018), Hernán & Robins, _Causal Inference: What If_ (2020) and Kohavi et al. (2020) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Confounder** | A common cause of treatment and outcome. |
| **Simpson's paradox** | A trend in every subgroup reverses when groups are combined. |
| **Selection bias** | Distortion from how units entered the data. |
| **Randomised controlled trial** | Treatment assigned by chance; breaks confounding. |
| **Collider** | A common effect; conditioning on it creates spurious association. |

#### Sources

1. C. Charig, D. Webb, S. Payne & J. Wickham, "Comparison of treatment of renal calculi by open surgery, percutaneous nephrolithotomy, and extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy", _BMJ_ 292, 1986, [PMC1339981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1339981/).

2. J. Pearl & D. Mackenzie, _The Book of Why_, Basic Books 2018.

3. M. Hernán & J. Robins, _Causal Inference: What If_, Chapman & Hall/CRC 2020, [free online](https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/).
