# Bandits vs A/B Tests

> Why not use a multi-armed bandit instead of an A/B test, so fewer users see the worse version?

- Track: Fundamentals › A/B Testing › Beyond the fixed test
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/bandits-vs-ab-tests/
- Before this: Reading the Result: Significance and Decisions (`fundamentals/reading-ab-results`)
- Quiz topic: `ab`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're choosing between two checkout designs. Each user on the worse one costs money, so someone suggests a multi-armed bandit: it shifts traffic to the winner as you go. The interviewer asks:

> Why not use a multi-armed bandit instead of an A/B test, so fewer users see the worse version?

#### Why it matters

Every user in the losing group has a cost, known as **regret**. Bandits come up in interviews because they seem to remove that cost for free. They don't: you give up something else.

### The idea

Think of two restaurants in a new town. An A/B test eats at each one 20 times, and then you know exactly how they compare. A bandit tries both and goes back more often to whichever seems better. You eat better meals, but you'll never know quite how much worse the other place is.

[Figure: Two methods. An A/B test splits traffic evenly and gives a precise effect. A bandit shifts traffic to the winner, losing fewer conversions but measuring the effect less precisely.]

_You're trading measurement for reward._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set B equal to A, then raise it. Compare conversions lost with the margin of error.

#### Run both on the same traffic

Our simulation: option A converts at 10%, with instant feedback and beliefs updated every 100 users, averaged over 40 seeded runs. Test and roll sends the first 10% of users 50/50, then everyone to the better arm. Margin of error is the 95% half-width from the final group sizes, for comparison only, as it ignores the adaptive allocation. Conversions lost is against always showing the better option.

Set B to **10%**, the same as A. There's no winner, so nothing's lost, and a bandit can still drift towards one arm by chance. Then raise B: the bandit saves conversions, but look at its margin of error.

**Now say why:** why does a bandit measure the lift less precisely?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An A/B test splits traffic evenly to **learn** as clearly as possible. A **bandit** shifts traffic towards the winner as it goes, to **earn** more during the test. **Thompson sampling** picks each arm in proportion to the chance it's best. Bandits lose fewer users to the worse option, but measure effects less precisely and handle slow outcomes poorly. Use them for short-lived choices, and A/B tests for lasting decisions.

#### Explore or exploit

##### Thompson sampling

1. For each arm, keep a belief about its conversion rate, based on results so far.

2. When a user arrives, draw one random value from each belief.

3. Show the arm with the highest draw, then update its belief with what happened.

At first, the beliefs are wide, and traffic is mixed. As one arm pulls ahead, it gets nearly all the traffic, but a weaker arm with an uncertain rate can still get tried.

##### How they compare

| | A/B test | Bandit |
|---|---|---|
| **Main goal** | Measure the effect. | Maximise reward during the run. |
| **Users on the worse arm** | Half, until the test ends. | Falls over time. |
| **Effect estimate** | Precise and easy to explain. | Noisier, and needs care, as traffic share changed with the results. |
| **Slow outcomes** | Fine: wait, then read. | Poor: it needs quick feedback to adapt. |
| **Guardrails and segments** | Straightforward. | Harder, as the worse arm gets little data. |

##### When to use which

- **Bandit:** short-lived choices like headlines and promotions, many variants, quick rewards, and where measuring the exact effect isn't important.

- **A/B test:** lasting product decisions, long-term or several metrics, and whenever you need to explain and defend the size of the effect.

##### A middle option

**Test and roll:** run a short A/B test, then send everyone to the winner. Feit and Berman show that, with the profit-maximising test size, its regret grows at the same rate as Thompson sampling's. Their test is much smaller than a usual hypothesis test, since the aim is to pick well rather than prove a difference.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{Regret}} = \sum_{t=1}^{N} \left({\mu^*} - {\mu_{a_t}}\right), \qquad {p_i} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1 + s_i,\; 1 + f_i) $$

The Beta distribution suits yes or no outcomes. It starts flat, and narrows with more data.

- **regret**: The reward you lost by not always showing the best arm.

- **best arm’s true rate**: Unknown during the run.

- **rate of the arm shown**: For the arm picked for user t.

- **the belief for an arm**: With s successes and f failures so far. Thompson sampling draws from this for each arm, and shows the highest.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Rewards must arrive quickly:** clicks suit bandits. Retention measured a month later doesn't.

- **Watch for changes over time:** if weekend users behave differently, an early leader can capture the traffic for the wrong reason. Keep some minimum traffic on every arm.

- **Log the probabilities:** record the chance each arm had for each user, so you can correct your analysis afterwards.

- **Contextual bandits:** these choose by user features, moving closer to a recommender.

- **Don't use one where you need a reason:** leadership asks "how much did it help?", and a bandit answers that less well.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A bandit is simply a better A/B test"

It sounds right, since it loses less during the run. But it answers a different question: which option earns more right now, not how much better one is. For a lasting product decision, you usually need an exact effect across slow and guardrail metrics, and a bandit gives you weaker evidence for those.

## Say it

### Why not use a multi-armed bandit instead of an A/B test, so fewer users see the worse version?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not use bandits for everything, if regret is lower?

Because many decisions need a precise effect size across several metrics, including slow ones like retention. Bandits give the weaker arm too little data for that. They also assume the reward arrives quickly, and that arms stay stable over time.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the difference between epsilon-greedy and Thompson sampling?

Epsilon-greedy explores at random a fixed share of the time, even once an arm is clearly bad. Thompson sampling explores in proportion to uncertainty, so exploration fades as evidence builds. Thompson sampling usually wastes less.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why can't you read a bandit's result with a normal A/B test formula?

Because traffic share depended on earlier results. An arm that got lucky early receives more traffic, so simple averages can be biased, and the samples aren't independent. You need methods that account for the allocation, using the logged probabilities.

#### The 30-second answer

A bandit shifts traffic to the better option as it learns, so fewer users see the worse one. Thompson sampling does this by showing each arm according to the chance it's best. But you pay in measurement: the weaker arm gets little traffic, so the effect estimate is noisier, and guardrails and segments are harder. It also needs quick feedback. I'd use a bandit for short-lived choices like headlines, and an A/B test for lasting decisions where I need to know the size of the effect.

**Key terms and sources**

How multi-armed bandits and Thompson sampling trade clean measurement for lower regret, and when to choose each. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Feit and Berman, Test and Roll: Profit-Maximizing A/B Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00457)

Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Explanations are ours, built from these sources and standard statistics.

# Running Many Tests at Once

> Your teams want to run 50 tests this month, but you only have so many users. How do you run them together?

- Track: Fundamentals › A/B Testing › Beyond the fixed test
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/running-many-tests-at-once/
- Before this: Randomisation and Assignment (`fundamentals/randomisation-and-assignment`), Multiple Testing and Segments (`fundamentals/multiple-testing`)
- Quiz topic: `ab`

## Intuition

### The situation

Twelve teams want to test changes this month, and each test needs two weeks of full traffic. Running them one by one would take half a year. Someone proposes running them all at once, on the same users, and a colleague says that will invalidate them all. The interviewer asks:

> Your teams want to run 50 tests this month, but you only have so many users. How do you run them together?

#### Why it matters

Traffic is what limits how many ideas you can test. Google built its overlapping system because a single layer of tests, with each query in at most one, couldn't scale. Interviewers often ask whether overlapping tests invalidate each other. The honest answer is "usually not, and here's how you'd check".

### The idea

Think of a school trying a new maths book and a new lunch menu at once. Flip one coin per pupil for each change, and about half of the new-book pupils also get the new menu, so the menu affects both sides of the book comparison equally. Trouble only comes if the two changes affect each other, like two new timetables for the same lesson.

[Figure: Three ideas. Overlap keeps all the traffic. Layers stop clashes. Interactions are the risk to check.]

_Overlap by default, and isolate what could clash._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set a negative interaction. Then switch to separate users.

#### Overlap two tests

Illustrative, ignoring noise. Overlap assumes a 50/50 split in B. With separate users, each test gets an equal share of the traffic. False alarms assume every pair of tests is checked once, with no real interactions.

A and B each add 1 point alone, and together they lose 1 point of that. **Overlapping** tests each report 0.5, which adds up to the real gain of 1.0 from shipping both. Each test also keeps all the traffic. With **separate users**, each test reports 1.0, which adds up to a wrong 2.0, and each gets only a tenth of the traffic. So overlap is often more honest about the combined launch. Its weak spot is shipping only one: if A launches alone, the real gain is 1.0, not the 0.5 it reported. Now set tests to 50: that's 1,225 pairs, so about 61 false alarms at 5% if you check them all.

**Now say why:** why do overlapping tests add up to the real combined gain?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

If every test needed its own users, ten tests would get a tenth of the traffic each, and take ten times as long. So large platforms let tests **overlap**: each test hashes users with its own salt, so one person can be in many tests at once. Other tests then act like extra noise, which affects both groups equally. The risk is an **interaction**, where two changes together do something neither does alone. Serious ones appear to be rare, and **layers** keep changes that could clash from reaching the same user.

#### Overlap, layers and interactions

##### Why overlap is usually safe

With a different salt per test, being in treatment for test A tells you nothing about test B. So about half of A's treatment group and half of A's control group are in B's treatment. B affects both sides of A equally, on average.

##### Layers and domains

| Idea | What it is | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Layer** | A group of settings. A user is in at most one test per layer | Changes that could clash, such as two tests of the same button |
| **Domain** | A slice of traffic set aside from the rest | Big changes that touch many layers at once |
| **Launch layer** | A layer across all traffic for gradual rollouts | Features about to launch, kept apart from ordinary tests |

A user gets a fresh, independent bucket in each layer, so tests in different layers overlap, while tests in the same layer never do. PlanOut's namespaces solve the same problem: each one centres on one kind of unit, such as users, and experiments take a share of its traffic.

##### How common are interactions?

Microsoft looked at hundreds of thousands of test-pair and metric combinations across four products, each running hundreds of tests a day. Three products showed no abnormal interactions. In the fourth, about 1 in 50,000 showed one, and none had significant effects pointing in opposite directions. They concluded that most tests don't interact, or do so only weakly. Your product may differ, especially in a small part of the product with many changes at once.

##### Finding one

You can compare A's effect among users in B's treatment and control. But that's hard, as an interaction estimate has twice the standard error of a main effect, so it needs about **four times the users**. With many tests, there are also many pairs to check, so you need multiple testing corrections.

#### The maths

$$ {\hat\tau_A} = {\tau_A} + {p_B}\,{I}, \qquad {\text{both vs neither}} = \tau_A + \tau_B + I $$

A standard two-by-two factorial result. The interaction’s estimate has twice the standard error of a main effect, on the same users.

- **what test A measures**: A’s effect, averaged over everyone in test A, some of whom also have B.

- **A on its own**: The effect of A for users who don’t have B.

- **B’s share**: The share of users in B’s treatment, usually a half.

- **the interaction**: How much more or less the two changes do together than the sum of their separate effects.

- **shipping both**: The real gain if both launch. At a 50/50 split, the two measured effects add up to exactly this.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Isolate what clearly clashes:** if two changes touch the same element, or could break each other, put them in one layer. A colour test and a background test could make text unreadable together.

- **Reset salts:** use a new salt for each test, so effects from an earlier test don't carry over into the next.

- **Scan automatically:** check pairs that share a surface, correct for multiple tests, and treat an alarm as a lead to follow up.

- **Test before launching together:** for two big launches at once, run them as a planned two-by-two test on the combination.

- **Watch for coupling in systems:** tests can also interact through shared caches, models and logs, where hashing can't help.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Overlapping tests invalidate each other"

It sounds right, as users get several changes at once. But with independent assignment, each other test is balanced across your two groups, so it adds a little noise and no bias on average. An interaction can still shift what you measure, so isolate changes that could clash, and scan for the rest.

## Say it

### Your teams want to run 50 tests this month, but you only have so many users. How do you run them together?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Doesn't overlap add noise to each test?

A little, because other tests add to the variance of your metric. But they're balanced across your groups, so they don't bias the comparison, and the extra noise is usually tiny compared with the gain from having all the traffic.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does an interaction need about four times the users?

A main effect compares two halves of the users. An interaction is a difference of differences across four quarters, which doubles its standard error. Sample size depends on its square, so that's four times.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Two teams want to launch big changes to the same page next week. What do you do?

Run a planned two-by-two test across both, or at least keep them in the same layer until one has launched. Then compare each change alone and both together, because the combination is what users will see.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd let tests overlap. Each test hashes the user with its own salt, so being in one test tells you nothing about another, and other tests affect both groups equally. Each test then keeps all the traffic. The risk is an interaction, where two changes together differ from the sum of each. Microsoft's analysis across four products found these were very rare. For changes that could clash, I'd use layers, so a user is in at most one test per layer, and tests in different layers overlap. I'd scan for interactions automatically, knowing they need about four times the users to detect and need multiple testing corrections.

**Key terms and sources**

Why overlapping tests are usually safe, layers and domains, what an interaction does to your results, and how to detect one. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Tang, Agarwal, O'Brien and Meyer, Overlapping Experiment Infrastructure (KDD 2010)](https://research.google/pubs/overlapping-experiment-infrastructure-more-better-faster-experimentation/)

- [Jeng, A/B Interactions: A Call to Relax (Microsoft, 2023)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/articles/a-b-interactions-a-call-to-relax/)

- [Bakshy, Eckles and Bernstein, Designing and Deploying Online Field Experiments (PlanOut, WWW 2014)](https://hci.stanford.edu/publications/2014/planout/planout-www2014.pdf)

# Heterogeneous Effects and Uplift Modelling

> Your coupon test is flat overall. Could it still work for some users, and who should get it?

- Track: Fundamentals › A/B Testing › Beyond the fixed test
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/heterogeneous-effects-and-uplift/
- Before this: Multiple Testing and Segments (`fundamentals/multiple-testing`), Reading the Result: Significance and Decisions (`fundamentals/reading-ab-results`)
- Quiz topic: `ab`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have budget to send a coupon to 20% of users. A colleague trains a model on who's most likely to buy, and plans to send it to the top 20%. Last quarter's test of the same coupon was flat overall. The interviewer asks:

> Your coupon test is flat overall. Could it still work for some users, and who should get it?

#### Why it matters

Many ML systems choose who gets something: a coupon, a notification, a retention call. Interviewers often move from A/B tests to this question. The usual mistake is to train a model on who's likely to buy, then send them the coupon. Many would have bought anyway, so the money is wasted.

### The idea

Think of a doctor with a limited supply of a medicine. Giving it to patients who'd recover anyway is a waste, and so is giving it to those it can't help. The medicine belongs with those it changes the outcome for. Those aren't the same as the patients most likely to recover.

[Figure: Three steps. Run a randomised test. Model each user's uplift. Check it on held-out random data.]

_You're ranking by the change you cause, not by who buys._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Treat 20%, then raise the model error. Then move the share to 100%.

#### Who gets the coupon?

Our simulation of 20,000 users with a fixed seed. The numbers are invented: middling buyers gain the most, the keenest buyers can lose out, and about 18% of users are harmed. Green: by uplift. Grey dashed: at random. Red: by likely buyers. The uplift score here is the true effect plus error. Real data never shows you the true effect.

Treating 20% of users, **targeting likely buyers** gives about −168 extra purchases: you reach sure things and sleeping dogs, so the campaign does harm. **Random** targeting gives about 303. Even a noisy **uplift model** gives about 505. Set the model's error to 0 and it rises to 658. Now move the share to 100%. All three lines meet at about 1,515, because everyone gets treated, so the ranking stops mattering. The value of a model is in choosing who not to treat.

**Now say why:** why does targeting likely buyers do so badly?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An A/B test gives one average, but a change may help some people and hurt others. **Heterogeneous effects** are those differences. If you can only treat some users, you should target those whose behaviour the treatment **changes**, not those most likely to buy anyway. **Uplift models** estimate each user's effect, using a randomised test as training data. You can never see one person's effect directly, so you evaluate on a held-out randomised group, by checking whether top-ranked users really show a larger gap between treatment and control.

#### Target the change

##### Four kinds of user

| Group | Without a coupon | With a coupon | Should you treat them? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Persuadable** | Doesn't buy | Buys | Yes: this is the only group that pays back |
| **Sure thing** | Buys | Buys | No: you give away margin |
| **Lost cause** | Doesn't buy | Doesn't buy | No: you pay for nothing |
| **Sleeping dog** | Buys | Doesn't buy | No: contact makes it worse, such as a reminder to cancel |

This is the standard way to explain uplift modelling. In reality, you estimate each user's chance of being helped, because you can't sort people into these groups directly.

##### Three ways to build one

| Learner | How it works | Weak spot |
|---|---|---|
| **S-learner** | One model, with treatment as a feature. Predict with it on and off, then subtract | A regularised model can ignore treatment altogether |
| **T-learner** | Two models, one per group. Subtract their predictions | Errors from two models stack up, especially with few treated users |
| **X-learner** | Fit two models, compute each user's imputed effect from the other group's model, model those, then blend them | More steps, and it needs care when the data is thin |

Künzel et al. found the X-learner performed well in simulations, but none of the learners was best everywhere. **Causal forests** instead extend random forests to estimate effects directly, and split the data so that the same users don't both choose the splits and estimate the effects.

##### Evaluating without seeing the truth

1. Keep a held-out set from a randomised test.

2. Rank its users by predicted uplift.

3. In each slice, compare treated and control users. A good model shows larger gaps at the top.

4. Plot the cumulative gain against the share treated: an uplift or Qini curve. Compare it with treating at random.

#### The maths

$$ {\tau(x)} = {E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]}, \qquad {\hat\tau_T(x) = \hat\mu_1(x) - \hat\mu_0(x)} $$

Notation as in Künzel et al. These estimates need randomised data, or strong assumptions when treatment wasn’t random.

- **the conditional effect**: The average effect for users who look like x.

- **two outcomes you can’t both see**: Each user’s result with and without treatment. One is always missing, so this has to be estimated over groups.

- **the T-learner**: Fit one model on treated users and another on control users, then subtract their predictions.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Train on random data:** if past targeting was by rule, treated and control users differ. Keep a random holdout to supply clean training data.

- **Effects are small:** individual effects are harder to predict than outcomes, so uplift models need a lot of data. The public Criteo benchmark has 13.9 million samples.

- **Plan your segments:** mining many segments finds false winners. See multiple testing, and confirm a finding with a new test.

- **Include the cost:** treat a user only when the expected gain beats the cost. A coupon that's used by a sure thing costs margin.

- **Keep testing the policy:** compare the model's targeting with a simple rule in a live A/B test. Keep a share at random, or you'll lose your training data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Send it to the people most likely to buy"

It sounds right, since they're your best customers. But they were likely to buy anyway, so the coupon gives away margin for nothing, and some may even respond badly. What matters is the change the coupon causes, which only a randomised test can teach a model.

## Say it

### Your coupon test is flat overall. Could it still work for some users, and who should get it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not target users with the highest predicted purchase probability?

They're the most likely to buy without help. The coupon then costs you margin for no extra sales. What you want is the change the coupon causes, which a response model doesn't estimate.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you evaluate an uplift model, if the true effect is never seen?

Use a randomised held-out set. Rank users by predicted uplift, split them into slices, and compare treated and control results in each slice. The cumulative gain against the share treated gives the uplift or Qini curve, which you compare with random targeting.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A test is flat overall, but a model finds a segment with a big lift. Do you ship to them?

Not yet, because searching for a segment finds false winners. Check that the segment holds on held-out data and makes sense, then run a new test on that segment alone.

#### The 30-second answer

An average can hide who benefits. If I can only treat some users, I want those whose behaviour changes, not those likely to buy anyway, because sure things give away margin and sleeping dogs can be harmed. So I'd run a randomised test, then train an uplift model to estimate each user's effect. A T-learner fits one model per group and subtracts them, an S-learner uses one model with treatment as a feature, and an X-learner and causal forests are more advanced. You can't observe one person's effect, so I'd evaluate on a held-out randomised set: rank by predicted uplift, and check that top slices show larger gaps between treatment and control, using an uplift or Qini curve. Then I'd test the targeting policy live.

**Key terms and sources**

Why an average can hide who benefits, targeting uplift rather than response, T, S and X learners, causal forests, and how to evaluate uplift without seeing it directly. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Künzel, Sekhon, Bickel and Yu, Metalearners for Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03461)

- [Wager and Athey, Estimation and Inference of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects using Random Forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.04342)

- [Athey and Imbens, Recursive Partitioning for Heterogeneous Causal Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.01132)

- [Gutierrez and Gérardy, Causal Inference and Uplift Modeling: A Review (2017)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v67/gutierrez17a.html)

- [Diemert et al., A Large Scale Benchmark for Uplift Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.10106)

# A/B Testing Practice

> 12 by-hand questions: sample size, intervals, SRM, CUPED, multiple testing, peeking, launch rules and uplift.

- Track: Fundamentals › A/B Testing › Beyond the fixed test
- Type: Interview · 40 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/ab-testing-practice/
- Before this: Running Many Tests at Once (`fundamentals/running-many-tests-at-once`), Heterogeneous Effects and Uplift Modelling (`fundamentals/heterogeneous-effects-and-uplift`)
- Quiz topic: `ab`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. The numbers are small enough to work out by hand, so try each one first, then open the answer and compare.

**The toolkit:** users per group ≈ 16σ²/δ²; SE of a difference = √(p₁q₁/n + p₂q₂/n); χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; design effect = 1 + (m − 1)ρ; CUPED removes ρ² of the variance; Bonferroni = α/m; rule of thumb = 355 × skewness²; corrected β = β/(G + 1).

Question 1 · Easy · sample size

### Checkout converts at 10%. You want to detect a rise of 1 point, at 5% significance and 80% power. You get 20,000 eligible users a day. How many users per group, and how long do you run?

Answer: **About 14,400 per group, and at least 1 full week**

1. σ² = 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09.

2. 16 × 0.09 ÷ 0.01² = 14,400 per group, so 28,800 in total.

3. 28,800 ÷ 20,000 = 1.44 days.

4. Round up to a full week, to cover weekly patterns.

Why not stop at 1.44 days? You'd miss weekend behaviour, and you can't see whether the effect fades.

Question 2 · Easy · reading a result

### 40,000 users per group. Control converts at 5.0%, and treatment at 5.5%. The smallest lift worth shipping is 0.3 points. Give the 95% interval and the decision.

Answer: **0.19 to 0.81 points: significant, but it crosses the bar, so it's a judgement call**

1. SE = √(0.05 × 0.95 ÷ 40,000 + 0.055 × 0.945 ÷ 40,000) ≈ 0.158 points.

2. Interval = 0.5 ± 1.96 × 0.158 = 0.19 to 0.81.

3. It's above zero, so it's probably real. It also includes values below 0.3.

What would settle it? More data, which narrows the interval until it clears the bar or falls below it.

Question 3 · Easy · SRM

### A 10/90 test should give 10,000 and 90,000 users. You got 10,300 and 89,700. Is that a problem?

Answer: **Yes: χ² = 10, p ≈ 0.0016, so stop and investigate**

1. χ² = 300² ÷ 10,000 + 300² ÷ 90,000 = 9 + 1 = 10.

2. With 1 degree of freedom, p ≈ 0.0016, well below a 0.01 cutoff.

3. Don't read the main metric. Slice the mismatch by browser, version and day.

Note that you must compare with the planned 10/90, not with 50/50.

Question 4 · Medium · ratio metrics

### You assign by user and analyse click-through per page view, using the simple formula. Users have 20 views each, and the correlation within a user is 0.05. What's the real false-positive rate of a test at 5%?

Answer: **About 16%**

1. Design effect = 1 + (20 − 1) × 0.05 = 1.95.

2. The real standard error is √1.95 ≈ 1.40 times larger than the formula says.

3. Your 1.96 cut-off is really 1.96 ÷ 1.40 = 1.40 real standard errors.

4. Two-sided, that's p ≈ 0.16.

The fix is the delta method, or a bootstrap over users.

Question 5 · Medium · CUPED

### A test needs 300,000 users per group, which is 4 full weeks. The correlation between before and during is 0.6. What does CUPED save?

Answer: **36% of the variance: 192,000 users, or about 3 weeks after rounding up**

1. ρ² = 0.36, so 64% of the variance remains.

2. 300,000 × 0.64 = 192,000 users per group.

3. 4 × 0.64 = 2.56 weeks, which rounds up to 3.

What about users with no history? They get no reduction, so the real saving depends on how many have past data.

Question 6 · Medium · multiple testing

### Six metrics give p-values of 0.001, 0.008, 0.012, 0.041, 0.2 and 0.6, at α = 5%. How many pass Bonferroni, and how many pass Benjamini-Hochberg?

Answer: **Bonferroni: 2. Benjamini-Hochberg: 3**

1. Bonferroni's threshold is 0.05 ÷ 6 = 0.0083, which 0.001 and 0.008 pass.

2. Benjamini-Hochberg's thresholds are 0.0083, 0.0167, 0.025, 0.033, 0.042 and 0.05.

3. The third p-value, 0.012, is below 0.025. The fourth, 0.041, is above 0.033.

4. The largest passing rank is 3, so the top three pass.

With no correction, four would pass at 0.05.

Question 7 · Medium · peeking

### A test plans 5 equally spaced looks. At the first look, z = 3.0. Do you stop under Pocock? Under O'Brien-Fleming?

Answer: **Pocock: yes. O'Brien-Fleming: no**

1. Pocock's threshold is about 2.41 at every look, and 3.0 is above it.

2. O'Brien-Fleming's first threshold is 2.04 × √5 ≈ 4.56, and 3.0 is below it.

3. Stopping at the first z above 1.96 with 5 looks would give about 14% false wins.

If Pocock stops here, is the estimate fair? It's likely too high, because stopping early selects a moment when noise was pushing it up.

Question 8 · Medium · heavy tails

### Revenue per user has a skewness of 12. Capping brings it to 4. What does the rule of thumb ask for in each case?

Answer: **About 51,000 per group uncapped, and about 5,700 capped**

1. 355 × 12² = 51,120.

2. 355 × 4² = 5,680.

3. This only covers the normal approximation. Do a power calculation too, and use the larger number.

What might the cap hide? Any change that only affects spending above it.

Question 9 · Hard · launch rule

### You have 1 success metric and 4 guardrails, at α = 5% and β = 20%, using one-sided tests. What level and power does each use, and how many more users does that take?

Answer: **α stays at 5%, with 96% power per metric: about 1.9 times the users**

1. With one success metric, α ÷ 1 = 5%. Guardrails aren't corrected for α.

2. Corrected β = 0.2 ÷ (4 + 1) = 0.04, so 96% power.

3. (1.645 + 1.751)² ≈ 11.5, against (1.645 + 0.842)² ≈ 6.2.

4. 11.5 ÷ 6.2 ≈ 1.9 times.

Why correct power? All guardrails must pass, so more of them means more chances to fail by accident.

Question 10 · Hard · interference

### Riders share a fixed number of cars. A 50/50 test makes treated riders 10% more likely to win a car than control riders, and total bookings don't change. Roughly what happens to each group, and what does the A/B test report?

Answer: **Treatment up about 5%, control down about 5%. The test reports about +10%, while the real gain is 0**

1. The total is fixed, so any gain for one group is a loss for the other.

2. With equal groups, a 10% gap needs about +5% and −5%.

3. The test compares winners with losers, so it counts control's loss as a gain.

What would you run instead? A switchback or a city-level test, which gives less bias at the cost of far more variance.

Question 11 · Hard · overlap

### Tests A and B overlap, each 50/50. A alone adds 2 points, and B alone adds 1. Together, they add only 2. What does each test report, and what's the real gain from shipping both?

Answer: **A reports +1.5, B reports +0.5, and the real gain from both is +2**

1. The interaction I = 2 − (2 + 1) = −1.

2. Test A reports 2 + (½ × −1) = 1.5.

3. Test B reports 1 + (½ × −1) = 0.5.

4. They add up to 2, which is the real gain from shipping both.

If only A ships, its real gain is 2, not the 1.5 it reported.

Question 12 · Hard · uplift

### A coupon costs ₹20, and each extra purchase earns ₹200. Purchase rates without and with the coupon: group A, 30% and 31%. Group B, 5% and 20%. Group C, 60% and 60%. Group D, 50% and 45%. Who gets it?

Answer: **Only group B**

1. Group A: 0.01 × ₹200 = ₹2, which is less than ₹20.

2. Group B: 0.15 × ₹200 = ₹30, which is more than ₹20.

3. Group C: no gain, so it loses ₹20.

4. Group D: it loses sales as well as the coupon cost.

Note that a response model would pick C first, as it has the highest purchase rate.

**More practice and sources**

12 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 7 Nov 2026

Keep practising

Uses the lessons in this section, from Randomisation to Uplift Modelling, and the launch decision rule. The scenarios and numbers are invented, so the answers are worked examples.

# Encoding Categorical Features

> 400 pincodes and a 'late order' flag: how do you encode them without leaking the answer?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Data and features
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/categorical-encoding/
- Quiz topic: `feat`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model has a pincode column with 400 values. One-hot means 400 sparse columns, and replacing each pincode with its average late rate looks great in training but falls apart in test. The interviewer asks:

> How would you encode a categorical feature with 400 values?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app predicts two things from order data (simulated): **delivery delay** in minutes from the restaurant's cuisine (6 categories) and the distance; and whether an order will be **late** (about 25% are) from the delivery **pincode** (400 pincodes, about 7 training orders each) and the distance. Each pincode has a small real effect on lateness, so there's some genuine signal to find, and plenty of noise to fool a careless encoder.

#### Labels aren't numbers

A linear model multiplies each input by a weight; a distance-based model subtracts inputs. Neither can do anything with "Chinese" or "560034". Every categorical column needs an encoding, and the choice quietly decides what the model can learn: whether categories get an artificial order, how many columns you create, and whether target information leaks into the features.

### The idea

Think of replacing each pincode with its track record. A record from three orders means little, so you pull it towards the overall average. And a record that includes the very order you're predicting gives away the answer, so you compute it from other orders.

[Figure: A scale of late rate. A pincode with 2 late orders out of 3 has a raw rate of 67 percent. Shrunk towards the 25 percent global rate, it becomes 30 percent.]

_Worked from the lesson's example of 2 late orders out of 3, with smoothing m = 20._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Choose naive encoding with low smoothing and read the test log loss. Then switch to cross-fitted.

#### Naive vs cross-fitted target encoding

Logistic regression on [encoded pincode (as log-odds), distance], 3,000 training orders, 20,000 test orders. Plot: training rows' encoded value vs their label (jittered): with naive encoding, late rows (top) sit visibly further right because their own label is inside their feature.

Naive encoding makes the model **worse than ignoring pincode altogether**: test log loss 0.58–0.63 (depending on m) against 0.539 for distance alone, and AUC 0.63–0.65 against 0.683. The model gave the encoded column a large weight because, on the training rows, it partly contained the answer. Cross-fitted encoding gets a small, honest weight and slightly beats the baseline: log loss **0.536**, AUC **0.689**, close to what the weak true pincode signal allows. Smoothing helps the naive version a little but doesn't cure it; cross-fitting does.

**Now say why:** why does the naive version look so useful to the model, yet do worse than ignoring pincode altogether?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Models need numbers, but "cuisine" and "pincode" are labels. **One-hot** encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column: safe, no fake order, but it explodes with thousands of categories. **Ordinal** encoding (1, 2, 3…) is compact but tells a linear model that "Biryani" is 4× "Chinese", so use it only for truly ordered categories or for tree models. **Target encoding** replaces each category with the average target for that category; it handles thousands of pincodes in one column, but it is a leak waiting to happen: compute it with **cross-fitting** (out-of-fold) and **smoothing** towards the global mean, or the model learns noise. Plan for categories you've never seen. What you'll be able to do after this: choose an encoder for a column by its cardinality and the model, explain why naive target encoding overfits, write the smoothing formula, and handle unseen and rare categories.

#### Three basic encoders

1. A categorical column: each order has a cuisine.

2. **One-hot:** one 0/1 column per category. No order is implied, and a linear model gets a separate weight for each cuisine. (Drop one column when the model has an intercept, to avoid perfect collinearity.)

3. **Ordinal:** one integer per category. Compact, but a linear or distance-based model treats the integers as quantities with an order and spacing that aren't real. scikit-learn: estimators "would interpret the categories as being ordered, which is often not desired".

4. **Target encoding:** replace each category with the average target (here, average delay) for that category. One column regardless of cardinality, and it carries exactly the information the model wants, which is also why it can leak.

Quote from scikit-learn's preprocessing guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html#encoding-categorical-features).

#### Target encoding, done safely

For 400 pincodes, one-hot means 400 sparse columns with ~7 examples each. Target encoding compresses each pincode to one number: its late rate. But a pincode with 3 orders, 2 of them late, gets 0.67, mostly noise. The fix is **shrinkage** towards the global rate:

$$ {S_i} = {\lambda_i}\,{\tfrac{n_{iY}}{n_i}} + (1 - {\lambda_i})\,{\tfrac{n_Y}{n}}, \qquad {\lambda_i} = \tfrac{n_i}{{m} + n_i} $$

scikit-learn's `TargetEncoder` formula for binary targets [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html#target-encoder); the blending idea is from Micci-Barreca (2001).

- **encoded value**: The number that replaces pincode i.

- **trust in the category**: λ_i = n_i / (m + n_i): close to 1 for pincodes with many orders, close to 0 for rare ones.

- **category’s own rate**: Late orders in pincode i divided by its orders.

- **global rate**: The overall late rate, the safe fallback; unseen pincodes get exactly this.

- **smoothing strength**: m acts like m imaginary orders at the global rate. scikit-learn’s smooth='auto' sets it from the within- and between-category variance (empirical Bayes).

Shrinkage alone is not enough. If a training row's own label is part of its pincode's average, the feature contains that row's answer. The model learns to trust the feature far too much, and the trust doesn't transfer to new orders. **Cross-fitting** fixes this: split training data into k folds and encode each fold with statistics computed from the other k − 1. scikit-learn's `fit_transform` does exactly this, which is why "`fit(X, y).transform(X)` does not equal `fit_transform(X, y)`" and why "training data should always be trained and transformed with `fit_transform(X_train, y_train)`" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html#target-encoder).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Pick by cardinality and model

| Situation | Encoder |
|---|---|
| Few categories (< ~15), any model | One-hot (`OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist")`) |
| Truly ordered (S/M/L, rating bands) | Ordinal with the real order |
| Tree ensembles | Native categorical support, or ordinal codes |
| Many categories (pincodes, restaurant IDs) + linear/NN | Target encoding (cross-fitted, smoothed), or learned embeddings |
| Huge or open-ended vocabularies (user agents, search terms) | Feature hashing; frequency encoding |
| Rare categories | Group into "other" (`min_frequency`, `max_categories`) |

A benchmark of encoders across 24 datasets (Pargent, Pfisterer, Thomas & Bischl, _Computational Statistics_, 2022) found that regularised target encoding (with 5-fold cross-fitting) "consistently provided the best results" across lasso, random forests, boosting, k-NN and SVMs; traditional encodings could compete only on datasets with fewer levels, and integer encoding did poorly even with gradient boosting. [arXiv:2104.00629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00629)

#### New, rare and missing categories

- **Unseen at prediction time:** a new restaurant opens. One-hot with `handle_unknown="ignore"` (or `"infrequent_if_exist"`) gives an all-zero row; target encoding returns the global mean; scikit-learn's `TargetEncoder` does this automatically [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html#target-encoder).

- **Rare categories:** group them into one "infrequent" level (`min_frequency`, `max_categories`), so the model doesn't memorise them.

- **Missing:** treat "missing" as its own category; it's often informative (chapter on missing values).

- **Drift:** category frequencies change (new pincodes as the app expands). Monitor the share of unseen categories in production.

#### Frequency, hashing and embeddings

##### Frequency / count encoding

Replace a category by how often it occurs. No target, so no target leak; useful when popularity itself matters (busy pincodes). Collisions: different categories with the same count look identical.

##### Feature hashing

Hash the category string into one of k buckets (`FeatureHasher`). Fixed memory, handles open-ended vocabularies and unseen values, but unrelated categories can collide in a bucket.

##### Learned embeddings

Neural networks learn a dense vector per category (entity embeddings). Similar restaurants end up close together. Needs a lot of data per category.

##### CatBoost's ordered target statistics

Encodes each row using only rows that come before it in a random permutation: the same goal as cross-fitting, built into the booster (see Gradient Boosting).

#### The whole recipe

1. Per column, check **cardinality**, whether it's **ordered**, and rare/unseen rates.

2. Low cardinality → one-hot; ordered → ordinal; high → cross-fitted target encoding, hashing or native categorical support.

3. Put encoders in a `ColumnTransformer` inside the `Pipeline`, so everything is refitted per CV fold.

4. Decide behaviour for **unseen** and **rare** values up front.

#### Scenarios

##### "10,000 restaurant IDs, logistic regression"

Cross-fitted, smoothed target encoding (or hashing); group restaurants with < 20 orders; unseen → global mean.

##### "Same data, LightGBM"

Use native categorical handling or ordinal codes; consider target encoding only if categories are very many and sparse.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just number the categories"

Linear regression on delay = distance + cuisine, 600 training orders. Bars: true extra delay per cuisine (grey) and what the model learned (coloured). Ordinal forces the learned effects onto a straight line in the arbitrary order 1–6.

With ordinal codes the model can only learn "each step up the list adds k minutes", so test error is **4.90 minutes**; with one-hot it learns each cuisine's own effect and reaches **3.06**, essentially the noise floor. Tree models are different: they split on thresholds and can carve any group out of an ordinal code with a few splits, so ordinal codes (or native categorical support, as in LightGBM, CatBoost and HistGradientBoosting) work for them when categories are few. With many categories, even gradient boosting did worse with integer codes than with regularised target encoding in a 24-dataset benchmark (Pargent et al. 2022).

#### Caveats

- One-hot with many columns is fine for linear models with regularisation and sparse matrices; the "explosion" is a memory/speed problem more than an accuracy one.

- Target encoding gives one number per category: it can't express interactions (pincode × time of day) unless you encode the combination.

- Cross-fitting makes training-time encodings slightly noisier than test-time ones (which use all training data); this mismatch is small and intended.

- Always evaluate the whole pipeline in CV; an encoder fitted outside CV leaks just like feature selection (see Cross-Validation & Leakage).

## Say it

### How would you encode a categorical feature with 400 values?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Why does naive target encoding overfit?

Each training row's label is included in its own category's mean, so the feature partly contains the answer, especially for rare categories. The model learns to over-trust it, and that trust doesn't hold on new data. Cross-fitting removes the row's own label; smoothing reduces noise for rare categories.

Follow-up 2 of 4

One-hot vs ordinal for tree models?

Trees split on thresholds, so ordinal codes work and are compact; one-hot with many categories makes each split very unbalanced and can hurt. Many libraries handle categories natively.

Follow-up 3 of 4

The dummy variable trap?

With an intercept, k one-hot columns are perfectly collinear (they sum to 1); drop one for unregularised linear models. Regularised models and trees don't care.

Follow-up 4 of 4

How do you handle a category never seen in training?

One-hot: all zeros or an "infrequent" bucket; target encoding: global mean; hashing: falls into some bucket; plus monitoring the unseen rate.

#### The 30-second answer

It depends on cardinality and the model. For a few unordered categories I'd one-hot encode, handling unknown categories. For ordered categories, ordinal encoding in the real order. Tree models can use ordinal codes or native categorical support. For high-cardinality columns with linear models or neural nets, I'd use target encoding: replace each category with its average target, shrunk towards the global mean for rare categories, and computed out-of-fold so a row's own label never enters its feature; otherwise the model overfits. Alternatives are hashing, frequency encoding or learned embeddings. Everything sits inside the pipeline so it's refitted within cross-validation.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "I label-encode everything." Not for linear or distance-based models.

- "Target encoding on the full dataset, then split." That leaks.

- "One-hot pincodes for a KNN." 400 sparse dimensions break distances.

**Key terms and sources**

One-hot, ordinal, target encoding (with smoothing and cross-fitting), frequency and hashing encoders, and what trees need · built from scikit-learn's preprocessing guide, Micci-Barreca (2001) and Pargent et al. (2022) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### Pincode → late order: test log loss (this page's simulation; lower is better)

naive target encoding, m = 1

0.634

naive target encoding, m = 20

0.587

distance only (ignore pincode)

0.539

cross-fitted target encoding, m = 20

0.536

Illustrative simulation: 400 pincodes, 3,000 training orders.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cardinality** | Number of distinct categories in a column. |
| **One-hot / dummy encoding** | One binary column per category. |
| **Ordinal encoding** | One integer per category. |
| **Target (mean) encoding** | Category → smoothed average target. |
| **Cross-fitting** | Encode each training fold with statistics from the other folds. |
| **Feature hashing** | Map categories to a fixed number of buckets by a hash. |

#### What this page is built from

1. scikit-learn, [Preprocessing: encoding categorical features](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html#encoding-categorical-features) (OneHotEncoder unknown/infrequent handling, OrdinalEncoder caveat, TargetEncoder formula and cross-fitting).

2. D. Micci-Barreca, "A preprocessing scheme for high-cardinality categorical attributes in classification and prediction problems", _SIGKDD Explorations_ 3(1), 2001.

# Missing Values & Feature Scaling

> Slow kitchens hide their prep time. Does it matter how you fill the gap, and when must you scale?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Data and features
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/missing-values-and-scaling/
- Quiz topic: `feat`

## Intuition

### The situation

Prep time is missing for a third of your orders, and it turns out slow kitchens stop reporting it. A teammate fills every gap with the mean. The interviewer asks:

> How do you handle missing values and feature scaling?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app predicts a delivery score from two features: distance and restaurant prep time (correlated: far restaurants also tend to be slower). Prep time is missing for 28–40% of orders, under three different simulated mechanisms. Test data has the same missingness, as it would in production. A separate example uses order values in rupees, with a few huge corporate catering orders, for the scaling section.

#### Most models can't take a blank

Real tables have holes: a restaurant didn't report prep time, a customer skipped the rating, a sensor dropped out. Most scikit-learn models refuse NaN. Dropping incomplete rows throws data away and, worse, can bias the sample (the dropped rows may be systematically different). Filling them in is easy to do badly. And feature scales are a second, related trap: a column in rupees next to a column in kilometres can dominate any distance or penalty.

### The idea

Think of a form with a blank answer. You can pencil in a good guess, but the blank is a clue too: slow kitchens hide their times. So you fill the gap and keep a note that it was blank.

[Figure: A row with a blank prep time becomes a row with a guessed prep time and a new column flagging that it was missing.]

_Illustrative. This is imputation plus a missing indicator._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the reason to slow kitchens hiding it (MNAR), and try mean fill. Then add the indicator, and try regression fill.

#### Which fill works under which mechanism?

Linear regression, 2,000 training and 10,000 test orders. Teal: observed prep times; orange: imputed ones (for training rows). Under MNAR, the orange points sit where the hidden slow kitchens are not.

| Mechanism | mean | mean + indicator | regression | regression + indicator |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MCAR (28% missing) | 1.814 | 1.812 | 1.653 | 1.652 |
| MAR (37%) | 1.954 | 1.915 | 1.797 | 1.799 |
| MNAR (40%) | 2.271 | 1.663 | 2.067 | 1.588 |

Test RMSE (lower is better; 1.00 if nothing were missing). Regression imputation wins whenever prep time can be predicted from distance. The indicator does nothing under MCAR (missingness carries no information) but cuts the error from 2.27 to 1.66 under MNAR, because "prep time not reported" now tells the model "probably a slow kitchen".

**Now say why:** why does the indicator help more here than a smarter guess?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Before choosing how to fill a gap, ask **why it's missing**. If values are missing at random, a simple fill loses little; if missingness depends on the missing value itself ("customers who give bad ratings often don't rate"), the fact that it's missing is **information**, so add a **missing indicator** column. Model-based imputation (predict the missing feature from the others) beats the mean when features are correlated. Gradient-boosted trees can take NaN directly. **Scaling** matters for anything distance- or penalty-based (k-NN, SVM, k-means, PCA, regularised linear models, neural nets) and not for trees; with outliers, use a robust or quantile scaler. Both steps are learned from data, so both go **inside the pipeline**. What you'll be able to do after this: name the three missingness mechanisms with examples, pick an imputer and justify an indicator column, choose a scaler for skewed data with outliers, and say which models don't care.

#### Three reasons a value goes missing

| Mechanism | Missingness depends on | Delivery example |
|---|---|---|
| **MCAR**: missing completely at random | Nothing (pure chance) | A logging bug drops prep time for random orders |
| **MAR**: missing at random | Other observed features | Far-away restaurants (known distance) use an old app that doesn't report prep time |
| **MNAR**: missing not at random | The missing value itself | Slow kitchens stop reporting prep time because it looks bad |

Terminology from Rubin (1976) and Little & Rubin, _Statistical Analysis with Missing Data_. You usually can't prove which mechanism holds from the data alone; domain knowledge decides.

#### Impute the value, and keep the fact that it was missing

For prediction (not for estimating population averages), you don't need the "true" missing value; you need features that let the model predict well. Two things help: a good guess for the value (use correlated features), and an **indicator** saying the value was guessed, which lets the model learn that "missing" itself means something. Statistics textbooks often warn against indicators because they bias coefficient estimates; for predictive accuracy under MNAR they're one of the most effective tricks.

#### Who needs scaling, and which scaler

scikit-learn: "many elements used in the objective function of a learning algorithm (such as the RBF kernel of Support Vector Machines or the l1 and l2 regularizers of linear models) may assume that all features are centered around zero or have variance in the same order. If a feature has a variance that is orders of magnitude larger than others, it might dominate the objective function" [preprocessing guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html).

##### Needs scaling

- k-NN, k-means, DBSCAN (distances)

- SVMs with RBF kernels

- PCA (variance)

- Ridge, lasso, regularised logistic regression (penalty treats all weights alike)

- Neural networks (optimisation)

##### Doesn't care

- Decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees (threshold splits are unchanged by monotone rescaling)

- Naive Bayes (per-feature distributions)

- Unregularised linear regression (predictions; coefficients rescale)

1,000 order values: 990 everyday orders (median ₹401) and 10 corporate catering orders of ₹20,000–50,000.

Ten catering orders inflate the mean to ₹832 and the standard deviation to ₹3,860, so **StandardScaler** squeezes all everyday orders into −0.20 to 0.30, and **MinMaxScaler** into 0 to 0.04: the model can barely tell a ₹150 order from a ₹1,000 one. **RobustScaler** uses the median and interquartile range (₹309), so everyday orders spread over −1.1 to 5.2 and the catering orders sit far out (around 80), still extreme but no longer squashing everyone else. scikit-learn: "If your data contains many outliers, scaling using the mean and variance of the data is likely to not work very well" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html). A **quantile** transform maps values to ranks, removing the outlier effect entirely, at the cost of distorting distances. For skewed money values, a log transform before scaling is often the simplest fix.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The imputation toolbox

| Method | What it does | scikit-learn |
|---|---|---|
| Drop rows / columns | Only if few rows are affected and missingness is MCAR, or a column is mostly empty | pandas `dropna` |
| Simple fill | "a provided constant value, or … mean, median or most frequent" | `SimpleImputer` |
| Missing indicator | Extra 0/1 column: "preserving the information about which values had been missing can be informative" | `add_indicator=True`, `MissingIndicator` |
| k-NN imputation | Average of the nearest complete rows | `KNNImputer` |
| Model-based (round-robin) | "models each feature with missing values as a function of other features" (still experimental) | `IterativeImputer` |
| Native NaN support | Trees learn which branch missing values take | `HistGradientBoosting*`, XGBoost, LightGBM |

Quotes from scikit-learn's imputation guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/impute.html).

#### Fit on training data, in the right order

- **Fit imputers and scalers on training folds only.** A mean or median computed on all rows leaks test information (see Cross-Validation & Leakage). scikit-learn's pitfall example: forgetting to apply the train-fitted scaler to the test set gave a test MSE of 62.8 instead of 0.90 [common pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html).

- **Order:** impute, then scale, so the scaler sees the final values; encode categorical columns in their own branch of a `ColumnTransformer`.

- **Same transform in production:** save the fitted pipeline, not just the model. Recomputing means on live data silently shifts every feature.

- **Placeholder values:** "−1" or "999" for missing look like real numbers to a linear model; convert them to NaN first.

#### The whole recipe

1. **Profile missingness:** share per column, and whether it correlates with other features or the target.

2. **Decide the mechanism** with domain knowledge; if it might be MNAR, add indicators.

3. **Pick an imputer:** median for robustness, iterative/KNN when features are correlated, or let gradient-boosted trees handle NaN.

4. **Pick a scaler** if the model needs one: standard by default, robust or log + standard with outliers, quantile for heavy tails.

5. **Wrap it all in a Pipeline** and cross-validate the whole thing.

#### Scenarios

##### "Income is missing for 30% of loan applicants"

Likely MNAR (people with unusual incomes skip it): median or model-based fill plus an indicator; check whether the indicator is predictive; consider gradient boosting with native NaN handling.

##### "Our k-NN recommender ignores rating counts"

Unscaled features: popularity counts in thousands dwarf 1–5 ratings. Log-transform counts and standardise everything.

Next: feature engineering.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Fill with the mean and move on"

Mean imputation keeps every row, but it puts all the missing orders at one prep-time value, flattening the relationship with the target. Under MNAR it's worse: if slow kitchens hide their prep time, the observed mean is too low, and every slow kitchen gets imputed as average. In our simulation the observed mean prep time is 0.05 under MCAR but −0.48 under MNAR (true mean 0): the visible data is already biased before you fill anything.

#### Caveats

- Single imputation makes the filled values look more certain than they are; if you need valid confidence intervals (inference, not prediction), use multiple imputation.

- Indicators double the feature count for many sparse columns; add them where missingness is common or plausibly informative.

- If missingness changes in production (a new app version starts reporting prep time), models that learned "missing = slow" break. Monitor missing rates.

- `IterativeImputer` is still marked experimental in scikit-learn.

## Say it

### How do you handle missing values and feature scaling?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Mean or median imputation?

Median for skewed data or outliers; mean when roughly symmetric. Both shrink variance and ignore correlations, so prefer model-based fills when other features predict the missing one.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Why add a missing indicator?

So the model can learn that missingness itself predicts the target (MNAR or informative missingness), and so imputed values aren't mistaken for real ones.

Follow-up 3 of 4

Standardisation vs min-max?

Standardisation centres and scales by sd, good default; min-max maps to [0,1], useful for bounded inputs but very sensitive to outliers; robust scaling uses median/IQR.

Follow-up 4 of 4

Do tree models need scaling or imputation?

No scaling. Imputation depends on the library: modern gradient boosting handles NaN natively; classic scikit-learn random forests historically needed imputation (recent versions accept NaN in some estimators).

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd ask why values are missing: completely at random, at random given other features, or not at random, where missingness depends on the value itself. For prediction, I'd impute with the median or a model-based imputer that uses correlated features, and add a missing indicator when missingness might be informative; under MNAR the indicator often matters more than the fill. Gradient-boosted trees can handle NaN natively. For scaling, distance- and penalty-based models such as k-NN, SVMs, k-means, PCA, regularised linear models and neural networks need it; trees don't. With outliers I'd use a log transform or a robust scaler instead of standardisation. Imputers and scalers are fitted on training data only, inside the pipeline.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "I drop rows with missing values." Only if few and MCAR.

- "I scale using the whole dataset's mean." That leaks test data.

- "Trees need standardised features." They don't.

**Key terms and sources**

Why values go missing (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), dropping vs imputing, missing-value indicators, model-based imputation, and when and how to scale (standard, min-max, robust, quantile) · built from scikit-learn's imputation and preprocessing guides, Rubin (1976) and Little & Rubin · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **MCAR / MAR / MNAR** | Missing by chance / because of observed data / because of the missing value itself. |
| **Imputation** | Filling missing values with estimates. |
| **Missing indicator** | 0/1 column recording that a value was missing. |
| **Standardisation** | (x − mean) / sd. |
| **Robust scaling** | (x − median) / IQR. |
| **Quantile transform** | Map values to ranks, then to a target distribution. |

#### What this page is built from

2. scikit-learn, [Preprocessing data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html) (scalers, outliers, quantile and power transforms).

3. scikit-learn, [Common pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) (inconsistent preprocessing).

4. D. Rubin, "Inference and missing data", _Biometrika_ 63, 1976; R. Little & D. Rubin, _Statistical Analysis with Missing Data_, 3rd ed., Wiley 2019 (MCAR/MAR/MNAR; background).

Data simulated with fixed seeds; every model is fitted live in your browser.

# Feature Engineering

> How would you create useful features for a model, and how do you avoid leaking the future?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Data and features
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/feature-engineering/
- Before this: Missing Values & Feature Scaling (`fundamentals/missing-values-and-scaling`), Encoding Categorical Features (`fundamentals/categorical-encoding`)
- Quiz topic: `feat`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're predicting orders per hour. A linear model using the raw hour does badly, as it can only draw one straight line through the day. A teammate's new "average orders this week" feature gives a huge jump in score. The interviewer asks:

> How would you create useful features for a model, and how do you avoid leaking the future?

#### Why it matters

On tabular data, better features often help more than a fancier model. They're also a very common topic in practical interviews. This follows encoding and missing values and scaling.

### The idea

Think of giving someone directions. "Walk 3 km north-north-east" and "go to the station" point to the same place, but one is far easier to act on. Features work the same way: the same information, expressed so the model can use it.

[Figure: Three common recipes. Ratios allow fair comparisons. Windows capture recent behaviour. Cycles keep 11 pm near midnight.]

_Every feature must be computed as of the prediction time._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Use only the raw hour. Then try each of the other options alone.

#### Help a linear model learn the day

Our seeded simulation: orders per hour with lunch and dinner peaks, plus noise. It's fitted with linear regression on 2,000 rows, and scored on 2,000 others. The dashed line is the true pattern, and the orange line is the model.

Try each option on its own. The model and the data haven't changed, only how the hour is expressed. A tree could find these peaks with raw hour, by splitting several times, but it would still need enough data to do so.

**Now say why:** why does the same model do so much better with the same information?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A model can only learn from what you give it, and the way you express something decides how easily it can use it. Good features come from **asking how the outcome really happens**: ratios, recency, counts over time, and cycles like hour of day. Tree models find many interactions themselves, while linear models need more help. The big danger is **leakage**: any feature using information you wouldn't have at prediction time looks great, then fails in production.

#### Common recipes

| Type | Example | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| **Ratios** | Cancelled orders ÷ total orders | Comparable across big and small users. |
| **Recency** | Days since the last order | Recent behaviour often predicts best. |
| **Windows** | Orders in the last 7 and 30 days | Captures level and trend. |
| **Cycles** | Sine and cosine of the hour | 11 pm and midnight are close, though 23 and 0 aren't. |
| **Interactions** | Distance × rain | One feature's effect depends on another's. |
| **Transforms** | Log of income | Tames long tails, particularly for linear models. |
| **Aggregates** | A restaurant's average preparation time | Brings in group-level knowledge. |
| **Missing flags** | "No phone given" | Being missing can itself be a signal. |

##### Different models need different help

- **Linear models:** only add up what they're given, so they need interactions, curves and scaling.

- **Trees and boosting:** handle thresholds and many interactions, and ignore scale. But they struggle to make a smooth ratio, or to extrapolate a trend.

- **Neural networks:** learn features from raw text and images, and on tabular data they still benefit from good inputs.

##### Leakage: the main way this goes wrong

A feature leaks if it contains information you wouldn't have at prediction time.

- **From the future:** a 30-day average that includes days after the prediction moment.

- **From the label:** a "refund issued" field in a model that predicts complaints.

- **From the test set:** computing averages or target encodings on all the data, before splitting.

Always compute a feature **as of the prediction time**. If a new feature gives a huge, sudden jump in score, suspect leakage first. See cross-validation and leakage.

#### The maths

$$ {x_{\sin}} = \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi \cdot \text{hour}}{24}\right), \qquad {x_{\cos}} = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi \cdot \text{hour}}{24}\right), \qquad {x_{7d}(t)} = \sum_{k=1}^{7} \text{orders}(t - k) $$

With a cycle encoding, a linear model can represent a single daily peak. Two daily peaks need a second pair at 12 hours, as the lab shows.

- **the sine part**: Places each hour on a circle, so 23:00 and 00:00 end up near each other.

- **the cosine part**: Both are needed, as sine alone gives two hours the same value.

- **a window feature**: It only counts days before t. Including t or later would leak the future.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Start from the domain:** ask someone who knows the process what would predict the outcome, before generating thousands of features.

- **Same code in training and serving:** computing a feature differently in each causes training-serving skew.

- **Fit inside the fold:** anything learned from data, like means or encodings, must be computed from training folds only.

- **Keep a baseline:** add features in groups, and check the validation score, so you can see what actually helps.

- **Count the cost:** each feature needs computing, monitoring and maintaining in production.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The new feature raised our score a lot, so ship it"

It sounds right, as that's the goal. But a sudden large jump is the classic sign of leakage. An average that includes the current week contains the very thing you're predicting. Check when each value is really known, and test on a strictly later period, before you trust it.

## Say it

### How would you create useful features for a model, and how do you avoid leaking the future?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How would you encode hour of day?

Sine and cosine of a 24-hour cycle, so 23:00 and 00:00 are close. With a tree, a raw hour often works, as it can split on ranges. If there are several daily peaks, add a 12-hour cycle, or flags for known peaks, which a linear model can use directly.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A new feature raised AUC from 0.75 to 0.99. What do you do?

Suspect leakage. Check when that value becomes known compared with the prediction time, and how it's computed. Look at importance, read some rows, and try it on a strictly later time period. Real features rarely produce a jump that large.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Do tree models need feature engineering?

Less than linear models, as they don't need scaling, and they find thresholds and many interactions. But they can't easily make ratios, as this needs many splits, and they can't extrapolate trends. Good domain features still often help the most.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd start by asking how the outcome really happens, then express that: ratios for fair comparisons, recency, windows of counts, cycles for time, and interactions. Linear models need more of this, while trees find thresholds and interactions, but not smooth ratios or trends. The main risk is leakage, so I'd compute every feature as of the prediction time, and fit anything learned from data on training folds only. If a feature gives a sudden huge jump, I'd suspect a leak first. I'd use the same code in training and serving.

**Key terms and sources**

Turning raw data into signal: ratios, dates and cycles, aggregates and interactions, what different models need, and how to avoid leakage. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [scikit-learn user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

- [Google Machine Learning Crash Course](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course)

- [Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning, contents](https://unilibrary.zetech.ac.ke/bib/5958)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.
