# Feature Selection

> How do you choose which features to keep, and how can selecting features leak information?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Data and features
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/feature-selection/
- Before this: Feature Engineering (`fundamentals/feature-engineering`), Cross-Validation & Data Leakage (`fundamentals/cross-validation-and-leakage`)
- Quiz topic: `feat`

## Intuition

### The situation

A colleague has 1,000 candidate features and 50 rows. They pick the 10 most correlated with the label, then cross-validate, and report 90% accuracy. You rerun it with shuffled labels, and it still scores far above 50%. The interviewer asks:

> How do you choose which features to keep, and how can selecting features leak information?

#### Why it matters

This error is easy to make and it produces beautiful results that vanish in production. In production, each feature also has a cost to compute and monitor. This builds on cross-validation.

### The idea

Think of picking the best stock pickers from 1,000 people after the year is over, then saying they beat the market that year. Of course they did: that's how you picked them. To test them fairly, you must choose first, then watch next year.

[Figure: Three families. Filters score features one by one. Wrappers try subsets with the model. Embedded methods select during training.]

_Whichever you use, selection must happen inside each fold._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the noise features to 3,000. Then keep fewer of them.

#### Select from pure noise

Our seeded simulation, averaged over 8 runs. All features are random, and so are the labels. It uses 5-fold cross-validation, and a nearest-centroid classifier on the features with the largest correlation with the label.

Raise the noise features: the wrong method looks better and better, with no signal at all. The right method stays near the true **50%**. It's often slightly below, as holding out a fold tips the class balance a little against it. If your results depend on which way you do it, the higher number is the false one.

**Now say why:** why can a model look good when there's no signal at all?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Fewer features can mean a simpler, cheaper and sometimes better model. **Filter** methods score features one at a time. **Wrapper** methods try subsets with the model. **Embedded** methods select during training, as Lasso does. The classic trap is **choosing features using all the data, and then cross-validating**: with enough noise features, you can score far above chance on pure randomness. Selection must happen inside each fold.

#### Three families

| Family | Examples | Good | Weak |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Filter** | Correlation, chi-squared, mutual information | Fast, and independent of the model. | Looks at one feature at a time, so it misses interactions and redundancy. |
| **Wrapper** | Forward selection, recursive elimination | Uses the actual model, and catches interactions. | Slow, and easy to overfit. |
| **Embedded** | Lasso, tree importance | Happens during training. | Tied to that model, and unstable with correlated features. |

##### The leak

1. Take thousands of features that are pure noise.

2. Pick those most correlated with the label, using all the rows. By chance, some look strong.

3. Cross-validate on just those. They look predictive, because they were chosen using the same labels you're now testing on.

The fix is simple: make selection a **step inside the fold**, computed only from training rows. A pipeline makes this automatic. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman call this the wrong and the right way to do cross-validation.

##### Do you need selection at all?

- **For accuracy:** regularised models and boosting often cope well with extra features, so selection may add little.

- **For cost and simplicity:** this is often the real reason. Fewer features means less to compute, monitor and explain.

- **For stability:** a feature that drifts or breaks is a risk. Removing fragile ones can make a model safer.

##### Correlated features

If two features carry the same signal, either can be dropped, and which one is chosen can change between runs. So a removed feature isn't necessarily useless. It may only be redundant.

#### The maths

$$ {\min_w \|Xw - y\|^2 + \lambda \|w\|_1}, \qquad {\text{Gain}(j \mid S)} = {\text{score}(S \cup \{j\})} - {\text{score}(S)} $$

Whichever method you use, keep a test set out of it, or run the whole selection inside each fold.

- **Lasso**: An embedded method. The L1 penalty pushes some weights to exactly zero.

- **forward selection’s gain**: How much a feature adds, given those already chosen.

- **score with the feature**: Must be measured on validation data.

- **score without it**: Stop when added features no longer help.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use a pipeline:** put selection inside it, so cross-validation refits it on each fold.

- **Start by removing the obvious:** constant columns, near duplicates, IDs and anything unavailable at serving time.

- **Group features:** judge related features together, by source or cost. Dropping a whole source saves more than dropping one column.

- **Check it holds up:** if the chosen set changes a lot across folds or time, the selection isn't reliable.

- **Be careful with importance:** correlated features can hide each other, so test by removing and retraining.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We selected features first, so the model is simpler and the score is fair"

It sounds right, as cross-validation came afterwards. But the test folds' labels already helped choose the features, so those rows were never unseen. With enough features, this produces high scores from pure noise. Put selection inside the pipeline, so it's refit in every fold.

## Say it

### How do you choose which features to keep, and how can selecting features leak information?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does selecting before cross-validation give optimistic scores?

The labels of future test folds influenced which features were chosen. With many features, some correlate with those labels by chance. So test rows aren't really unseen. With random labels and many features, you can get scores far above chance. Selecting inside each fold fixes it.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Would you remove a feature with a low importance score?

Not without testing. It may be correlated with another feature, hiding its value, or matter only for some groups. I'd remove it, retrain and compare on validation data, and also weigh the cost of computing and maintaining it.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Filter methods missed a useful pair of features. How?

They score features one at a time. With an XOR-style pattern, each is useless alone, and together they predict perfectly. Trees and wrapper methods can find that pair, since they evaluate features in combination.

#### The 30-second answer

There are three families. Filter methods score each feature alone, which is fast, but misses interactions and redundancy. Wrapper methods try subsets with the model, which is slow and can overfit. Embedded methods like Lasso select during training. The main trap is selecting with all the data, then cross-validating: with many noise features, you can score far above chance on random labels. So I'd make selection a step inside each fold. Accuracy often isn't the main reason to select. Cost and reliability often are.

**Key terms and sources**

Filter, wrapper and embedded methods, why selection can leak into your evaluation, and when you shouldn't bother. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/)

- [scikit-learn on feature selection](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_selection.html)

- [ISLR](https://www.statlearning.com/)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Linear Regression

> What does least squares actually minimise, and when does it break?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Linear models
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/linear-regression/
- Quiz topic: `lin`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have 12 flats with their size and price, and you need to predict the price of a new one. You could draw endless lines through them. The interviewer asks:

> What is linear regression, and how is it fitted?

**Running example:** 12 flats in one city, size in m² and price in ₹ lakh (illustrative numbers). Goal: predict the price of a flat from its size.

#### Draw the "best" straight line through a cloud of points

You have flats you know the price of, and a new flat you don't. Plot price against size and the points roughly follow a line. Linear regression turns "roughly follows a line" into a precise answer: _which_ line, and _why_ that one.

1. Twelve flats. Bigger flats cost more, but not perfectly: the points scatter around a trend.

2. A candidate line: price ≈ 0.85 lakh per m² × size + 9.6 lakh. Any line makes a prediction ŷ for every size.

3. The vertical gaps between each point and the line are the errors, called **residuals**: y − ŷ.

4. Least squares squares each residual (literally: the red squares) and adds them up. Big misses count much more than small ones.

5. The fitted line is the one with the smallest total squared error. For these 12 flats, no other straight line does better.

That's the whole idea. Everything else on this page is _how_ to find that line, _why_ squares, and _when_ to distrust it.

### The idea

Think of a stiff rod held by a spring to every data point. The further away a point is, the harder its spring pulls. The rod settles where the total pull balances out, and that's the least-squares line.

[Figure: Points scattered around a straight line, with a short vertical gap from each point to the line.]

_Illustrative. Squaring the gaps means big misses count far more than small ones._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the slope and intercept until the red squares are as small as you can get them. Then snap to the least-squares line.

#### Feel the bowl: move the line, watch the loss

Illustrative data: 12 flats. The red squares are the squared residuals; their total area (÷ 12) is the MSE. Notice that slope and intercept trade off: a steeper slope needs a lower intercept.

**Now say why:** why does a steeper slope need a lower intercept, and how close did you get to the best line?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of features, ŷ = w·x + b, and picks the weights that make the **sum of squared errors** as small as possible. There's a closed-form answer (the normal equation) and an iterative one (gradient descent). Under Gaussian noise, least squares is exactly maximum likelihood. It's simple, fast and interpretable, and it breaks in predictable ways: outliers, curved relationships, and correlated features. What you'll be able to do after this: derive and explain the loss, solve it two ways, read the assumptions, spot when the line is lying to you, and answer the classic follow-ups.

#### A weighted sum of features

With one feature, the model is a line: slope w and intercept b. With many features (size, floor, age, distance to metro), it's the same idea in more dimensions: each feature gets a weight, and the prediction is the weighted sum plus a bias.

$$ {\hat{y}} = {w_1}{x_1} + {w_2}{x_2} + \dots + {b} \qquad {\hat{\mathbf y} = X\theta} $$

CS229 writes hθ(x) = θ⊤x with x0 = 1 standing in for the bias [CS229 §1](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf) · hover any symbol.

- **prediction**: The model's guess: the predicted price ŷ.

- **weights**: One number per feature: how much the price moves when that feature goes up by one unit, holding the others fixed. Here about 0.85 lakh per m².

- **features**: The inputs for one flat: size, and any other columns you have.

- **bias / intercept**: The prediction when every feature is zero. Often not meaningful on its own (a 0 m² flat), but it lets the line sit at the right height.

- **all rows at once**: Stack every flat as a row of X, with an extra column of 1s for the bias. Then all predictions are one matrix product: ŷ = Xθ.

"Linear" means linear in the **weights**, not necessarily in the raw inputs. You can feed in x², log(x) or a product of two features and it is still linear regression.

#### Choose the weights that minimise the sum of squared residuals

$$ {J(\theta)} = {\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}}{\big(}{\theta^{\top}x^{(i)}} - {y^{(i)}}{\big)^2} $$

The least-squares cost function, CS229 §1 [CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf). The mean squared error (MSE) is the same thing divided by n.

- **the cost**: One number that scores a choice of weights θ. Lower is better.

- **prediction**: The model's prediction for example i: θᵀx⁽ⁱ⁾.

- **the truth**: The real price of flat i.

- **squared miss**: Square the residual: no cancelling, and big misses cost much more than small ones.

- **over all examples**: Add up across all n training flats. The ½ is just there so the derivative comes out clean.

J is a bowl: a smooth, convex function of the weights with a single lowest point. That's why linear regression always has one best answer (or a flat valley of equally good answers when features are redundant), and why the methods below can find it reliably.

#### The normal equation: set the slope of the bowl to zero

At the bottom of a bowl, the gradient is zero. Differentiate J, set it to zero, and you get a linear system you can solve in one shot [CS229 §1.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf):

$$ {\theta^{*}} = {(X^{\top}X)^{-1}}\,{X^{\top}\mathbf{y}} \qquad {\text{if } X^{\top}X \text{ is invertible}} $$

From X⊤Xθ = X⊤y, CS229 §1.2 and footnote 3 on invertibility.

- **best weights**: The weights that minimise J exactly.

- **undo the feature overlap**: XᵀX shows how the features move together (p × p). Its inverse untangles how much each feature contributes on its own.

- **feature–target overlap**: How much each feature moves together with the target.

- **needs an inverse**: Only works if XᵀX is invertible: fails when features are perfectly redundant (size in m² and in ft²) or when there are more features than rows. Nearly redundant features make it numerically shaky; that's what Ridge fixes.

1. Think of all 12 prices as one vector in 12-dimensional space. Every choice of weights gives a prediction vector Xθ, and all of them lie on a flat surface: the space spanned by the feature columns.

2. The real prices y are almost never on that surface. No line passes through every point.

3. The best you can do is the point on the surface closest to y. That's ŷ = Xθ*.

4. "Closest" means the leftover error is perpendicular to the surface: Xᵀ(y − Xθ) = 0. Rearranged, that is exactly the normal equation. Least squares is a projection.

##### What breaks: cost and conditioning

Inverting XᵀX costs about p³ operations, fine for hundreds or thousands of features, painful for millions. And when features are nearly collinear, tiny changes in the data swing the weights wildly; scikit-learn: the least-squares estimate "becomes highly sensitive to random errors in the observed target, producing a large variance" [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html). Libraries solve via QR or SVD rather than an explicit inverse for stability.

#### Gradient descent: small steps against the slope

Instead of solving the system, start anywhere and repeatedly nudge each weight in the direction that lowers J. For least squares the update is the **LMS rule**: move each weight by the error times its feature [CS229 §1.1](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf).

$$ {\theta_j} := {\theta_j} + {\alpha}\,{\big(y^{(i)} - h_\theta(x^{(i)})\big)}\,{x^{(i)}_j} $$

- **one weight**: Weight j, updated in place.

- **learning rate**: Step size α. Too small: painfully slow. Too big: overshoots and diverges.

- **the error**: How wrong the prediction was on this example: truth minus prediction.

- **the feature**: Weights on features that were large for this example move more. That's also why feature scale matters so much.

##### Try it: learning rate and feature scaling

Full-batch gradient descent on our 12 flats, starting from w = b = 0. With raw sizes (45–170), the slope and the intercept need wildly different step sizes, so any learning rate small enough not to blow up crawls on the intercept. Standardise the feature (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and the bowl becomes round: a few steps suffice.

#### Least squares = maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise

Assume each price is the true line plus random noise ε that is Gaussian, independent, and has the same spread σ for every flat. Ask which weights make the observed prices most probable. Take the log of that probability and you get [CS229 §1.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf):

$$ {\ell(\theta)} = {n\log\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}} - {\tfrac{1}{\sigma^{2}}}\cdot{\tfrac12\sum_{i}\big(y^{(i)} - \theta^{\top}x^{(i)}\big)^2} $$

- **log-likelihood**: How probable the data is under weights θ (on a log scale). Higher is better.

- **a constant**: Depends on n and σ, not on θ. It doesn't affect which θ wins.

- **a positive scale**: Also doesn't change which θ wins.

- **the least-squares cost**: Maximising the likelihood means minimising exactly this sum of squares. Squared error isn't arbitrary: it's what Gaussian noise implies.

This also explains the weakness. Gaussian noise almost never produces a point far from the line, so least squares treats a far point as very informative and bends to reach it:

Dashed line: the original fit. One mislabelled or unusual flat drags the whole line. Fixes: inspect residuals, use a robust loss (Huber, absolute error), or transform the target (e.g. log price).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Two ways to the same answer, plus a statistics toolkit

| Approach | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Closed form** (normal equation, or QR / SVD) | Solve XᵀXθ = Xᵀy directly | Up to a few thousand features; exact answer in one shot. scikit-learn's `LinearRegression` uses a least-squares solver |
| **Gradient descent** / SGD | Repeatedly step the weights downhill on the loss | Huge data or many features; streaming data; the same machinery that trains neural nets |
| **Statistical inference** (e.g. statsmodels) | Same fit, plus standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals | When you need to explain or test the coefficients, not just predict |

All three minimise the same squared-error loss. scikit-learn's docs: `LinearRegression` "fits a linear model with coefficients w = (w₁, …, wp) to minimize the residual sum of squares" [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).

#### R²: how much of the variation the line explains

$$ {R^{2}} = 1 - {\textstyle\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2} \,\big/\, {\textstyle\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2} $$

- **R²**: Share of the target's variance explained by the model. 1 is perfect; 0 means no better than predicting the mean.

- **what the model misses**: Sum of squared residuals around the fitted line.

- **what a dumb model misses**: Sum of squared differences from the mean of y: the error of always predicting the average.

For our flats R² ≈ 0.99 (the illustrative points are very linear). Anscombe's sets all score 0.67 while being completely different, so R² alone is never enough. Report an error in the target's units too (RMSE or MAE: "off by ₹3 lakh on average"), and evaluate on held-out data. Training R² always goes up when you add a feature, even a useless one.

#### Fitting a linear regression you can trust

1. **Plot first.** Scatter the target against key features; Anscombe's lesson.

2. **Split the data** into train and test (or use cross-validation) before anything else.

3. **Engineer features:** logs for skewed quantities like prices, polynomial or interaction terms where the relationship bends, one-hot encoding for categories.

4. **Scale features** if you use gradient descent or regularization (not needed for plain closed-form OLS predictions).

5. **Fit** by least squares (closed form for small p, gradient descent for big data).

6. **Check residuals:** residuals vs fitted (curve? funnel?), outliers, high-leverage points.

7. **Evaluate on held-out data** with RMSE or MAE in real units, plus R².

8. **If the weights are unstable or there are many features,** move to Ridge, Lasso or Elastic Net.

#### Use it, or reach for something else?

##### Use linear regression when

- You need a fast, explainable baseline for a numeric target

- You need coefficients you can explain to stakeholders

- Data is small, or features are already well engineered

- The relationship is roughly linear (or linear after a log)

##### Reach for something else when

- Many correlated features or p ≈ n → Ridge / Lasso / Elastic Net

- Strong non-linearities and interactions → gradient boosting, random forests

- Heavy outliers → Huber or quantile regression

- A yes/no target → logistic regression

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Make the errors add up to zero" picks terrible lines

The obvious first idea: choose the line whose errors sum to zero, so the misses above and below cancel out. Try it. Every line through the average point (102.75 m², ₹97.2 lakh) has residuals that sum to exactly zero, no matter how wrong its slope is:

The first number stays at 0 for every slope, even a flat or downhill line. Positive and negative errors cancel, so "sum of errors" can't tell a good line from a bad one. Absolute or squared errors can't cancel, so they can.

##### What breaks: errors that cancel

You need a loss where every miss counts as a cost. The two natural choices are |error| (least absolute deviations) and error² (least squares). Least squares won historically because it's smooth, has a closed-form solution, and matches the maths of Gaussian noise (see the Maths tab). Its price is sensitivity to outliers, since a miss of 10 costs 100.

#### Same line, same R², four completely different stories

In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe built four small datasets that share the same mean of x (9), mean of y (7.50), correlation (0.816), regression line (y = 3.00 + 0.500x) and R² (0.67). Fit linear regression to each and the software reports the same numbers four times. Now look at them:

–

Real data: [Anscombe's quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anscombe%27s_quartet) (Anscombe, 1973). The orange line is the fitted line, identical for all four.

The assumptions behind the usual statistics (standard errors, p-values, prediction intervals) are often remembered as **LINE**:

| Assumption | Means | How to check / fix |
|---|---|---|
| **L**inearity | The mean of y really is linear in the features | Residuals vs fitted plot shows no curve; add x², logs, interactions (set II) |
| **I**ndependence | Errors don't depend on each other | Watch for time series and grouped data; use time-aware or mixed models |
| **N**ormality | Errors are roughly Gaussian | Q-Q plot of residuals; matters mostly for small-sample inference, not for the fit itself |
| **E**qual variance | Error spread is the same for all x (homoscedasticity) | Funnel-shaped residuals → transform y (log) or use weighted least squares |

Plus two practical ones: no extreme outliers or high-leverage points (sets III and IV), and features not too collinear (see the normal equation in the Maths tab, and the Regularized Linear Models lesson). For pure prediction you need fewer of these. For interpreting coefficients, you need the right form and independent errors, and equal variance for the usual standard errors. Normal errors matter mainly with small samples.

#### Why least squares, and what can bias it

##### Gauss-Markov: why least squares is a good default

Suppose the model's form is right, errors average zero whatever the features are, errors have equal variance and aren't correlated, and no feature is a perfect mix of the others. Then least squares has the lowest variance among all **linear, unbiased** estimators. Normal errors aren't needed.

Note those two words. A biased method like ridge can still have lower total error, by accepting some bias for less variance.

##### Omitted-variable bias

Leave out a feature that affects y **and** is correlated with a feature you kept, and the coefficient you kept absorbs part of its effect.

$$ {\tilde\beta_1} = {\beta_1} + {\beta_2}\,{\delta} $$

The standard result for two features, in expectation.

- **the slope you get**: From a model that leaves out x₂.

- **the true effect of x₁**: Holding x₂ fixed.

- **the left-out feature’s effect**: How much x₂ moves y.

- **how they’re linked**: The slope when you regress x₂ on x₁. If it’s zero, there’s no bias.

**A worked example, with illustrative numbers.** Say price truly rises ₹0.7 lakh per m², and being central adds ₹20 lakh. Central flats tend to be smaller, so "central" falls by 0.005 per extra m². Leave out "central", and the slope becomes 0.7 + 20 × (−0.005) = 0.6. The model now understates what size is worth.

- **For prediction:** this may do no harm, as long as the link between the features stays the same in production.

- **For explanation:** it can be badly misleading, and can even flip a sign. No test on your data can reveal a variable you never measured, so this needs domain knowledge, or an experiment or causal design.

- **Correlated features:** to measure this problem, see VIF in inference for regression.

#### Polynomial features: more wiggle, and the overfitting trap

Add x², x³, … as extra columns and fit them with the same least squares. The model is still linear in its weights, but can now bend. Each extra degree lowers the training error. Watch what happens on new data:

–

Illustrative data: a smooth curve plus noise. ● training points, ● test points. With degree 9 and 10 points, the curve passes through every training point (training error 0) and swings wildly in between.

##### Two fixes

Choose the complexity with held-out data (cross-validation), or keep the flexible model and penalise large weights. The second fix is Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net, the next lesson.

#### What to keep

**The lesson:** linear regression is a projection: it finds the closest prediction a weighted sum of features can make, measured by squared error. It is exact, fast and explainable, and it is the base that ridge, lasso, logistic and softmax regression (and every neural network's last layer) build on.

- **Coefficients are "holding the others fixed".** With correlated features, a coefficient can even flip sign compared with a one-feature fit. Don't read them as causal effects.

- **Squared loss is outlier-sensitive.** One bad row can move the line (see the outlier lab in the Maths tab).

- **Linear in weights ≠ linear world.** If residuals curve, add features or use a more flexible model.

- **Extrapolation is risky.** The line knows nothing outside the range of x it saw.

## Say it

### What is linear regression, and how is it fitted?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why squared error and not absolute error?

Squared error is smooth and convex with a closed-form solution, and it's the maximum-likelihood loss under Gaussian noise. Absolute error (least absolute deviations) is the MLE under Laplace noise, is more robust to outliers, and predicts the conditional median instead of the mean, but it has no closed form and isn't differentiable at zero.

Follow-up 2 of 6

When does the normal equation fail?

When XᵀX isn't invertible: perfectly collinear features (e.g. a one-hot encoding with every category kept plus an intercept, the "dummy variable trap"), or more features than examples. Near-collinearity makes it numerically unstable. Fixes: drop or combine features, use the pseudo-inverse (SVD), or add a ridge penalty, which makes XᵀX + λI invertible.

Follow-up 3 of 6

Normal equation or gradient descent?

Normal equation for small to medium p (exact, no tuning). Gradient descent or SGD when n or p is huge, data streams in, or the model is part of something bigger. Gradient descent needs scaled features and a tuned learning rate.

Follow-up 4 of 6

What are the assumptions, and which matter for prediction?

Linearity, independent errors, normal errors, equal variance (LINE), plus limited multicollinearity and no extreme outliers. For pure prediction, linearity (a correct functional form) and representative data matter most. Normality and equal variance matter mainly for valid standard errors, p-values and intervals.

Follow-up 5 of 6

How do you interpret a coefficient?

The expected change in y for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the other features constant. Correlated features make that "holding constant" unrealistic and the coefficients unstable, so be careful with interpretation and never read them as causal without a causal design.

Follow-up 6 of 6

Does adding a feature always increase R²?

On training data, yes (or keeps it the same), even for pure noise. That's why you use adjusted R² or, better, held-out error.

#### The 30-second answer

Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of features plus a bias, and fits the weights by minimising the sum of squared residuals. That has a closed-form solution, the normal equation θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, which is a projection of y onto the span of the features, or you can use gradient descent at scale. If the noise is Gaussian, least squares is exactly maximum likelihood. Its weak spots are outliers, non-linearity, and collinear features, which is where regularization comes in.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Start with the model ŷ = Xθ and why we need a loss where errors can't cancel. Write J(θ) = ½Σ(θᵀx − y)², a convex bowl. Solve two ways: normal equation (exact, about p³ cost, needs XᵀX invertible) or gradient descent (LMS update, needs feature scaling and a sensible learning rate). Justify squares via Gaussian maximum likelihood, and note the price: outlier sensitivity. Then the assumptions (LINE), why R² alone can lie (Anscombe), and polynomial features with the overfitting trade-off that motivates Ridge and Lasso.

#### What not to say

- "Linear regression can only fit straight lines." It's linear in the weights; polynomial and log features bend it.

- "The features need to be normally distributed." The assumption is about the _errors_, not the features.

- "High R² means the model is right." See Anscombe's quartet.

- "A bigger coefficient means a more important feature." Only if the features are on the same scale, and not under strong collinearity.

**Key terms and sources**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Residual** | y − ŷ for one example. |
| **OLS** | Ordinary least squares: minimise the sum of squared residuals. |
| **Normal equation** | XᵀXθ = Xᵀy, the closed-form solution. |
| **Design matrix X** | One row per example, one column per feature (plus a column of 1s). |
| **Learning rate** | Step size in gradient descent. |
| **Multicollinearity** | Features that are (nearly) linear combinations of each other. |
| **Homoscedasticity** | Error variance that's the same everywhere. |
| **R² / RMSE / MAE** | Share of variance explained / root mean squared error / mean absolute error. |
| **Overfitting** | Fitting training noise so well that new-data error goes up. |

# Regularized Linear Models

> Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net: why does L1 zero out weights while L2 only shrinks them?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Linear models
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/regularized-linear-models/
- Before this: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`), Maximum Likelihood & MAP (`fundamentals/mle-and-map`)
- Quiz topic: `lin`

## Intuition

### The situation

With 22 flats and 10 features, your model says each extra bedroom makes a flat cheaper. The interviewer asks:

> What is the difference between Ridge and Lasso?

**Running example:** predicting flat prices again (continuing Linear Regression), but now with only **22 flats** and **10 features**: five real ones (size, bedrooms, age, floor, distance to metro) and five pure junk (the flat number's last digit, listing weekday, photos in the ad, owner's birth month, agent ID parity). Size and bedrooms are 95% correlated. Data is simulated so we know the truth; test error is measured on 400 fresh flats.

#### Least squares believes every feature, even the useless and the redundant

Fit ordinary least squares (OLS) to the 22 flats and something odd happens: it says each extra **bedroom makes a flat cheaper**. That's not economics, it's collinearity. Size and bedrooms carry almost the same information, so OLS can trade one off against the other freely, and small quirks of the sample decide the split. Draw a different 22 flats and watch:

Coefficients on standardised features (₹ lakh per standard deviation). The true effects are positive for both. OLS's split between size and bedrooms jumps around, and even goes negative. Ridge (λ = 0.3) keeps both positive and stable from sample to sample.

Two problems at once: **variance** (weights swing with the sample) and **overfitting** (with 10 features and 22 rows, OLS also fits the junk). Tibshirani's diagnosis from 1996 still holds: OLS estimates "often have low bias but large variance; prediction accuracy can sometimes be improved by shrinking or setting to 0 some coefficients" [Tibshirani 1996, p. 267](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=2).

### The idea

Think of charging a model for its weights. Ridge charges more for bigger weights, so every weight shrinks but none disappears. Lasso charges the same for every unit, so small weights can't justify the cost and drop to exactly zero.

[Figure: Left: a diamond for Lasso, with the best point landing on a corner, so one weight is exactly zero. Right: a circle for Ridge, with the best point on the curve, so both weights shrink but neither reaches zero.]

_Tibshirani's picture: the budget's shape decides whether the best point lands on a zero._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Choose Ridge and raise the strength, then do the same with Lasso. Watch how many features are kept, and how many junk ones survive.

#### Turn the dial and watch the weights

Bars: coefficients on standardised features; the hollow tick is the OLS value. Bottom chart: test MSE on 400 fresh flats versus α for the chosen method (dot = current α). Simulated data with known truth: price rises with size and bedrooms, falls with age and metro distance, rises slightly with floor; the last five features are pure noise. Fitted by coordinate descent with scikit-learn's objective scaling.

Things to look for. **Ridge** pulls size and bedrooms toward each other and shrinks junk, but zeros nothing; its best test MSE (about α = 0.1) beats OLS clearly. **Lasso** around α ≈ 1–2 keeps size, age, floor and metro distance, drops the junk (all five are gone by α = 2), and drops bedrooms too (it picks one of the correlated pair). It gets the best test error of the three. **Elastic Net** keeps size and bedrooms together, the grouping effect, at the cost of keeping some junk at these settings. Push any of them too far and everything shrinks to nothing: high bias, rising test error.

**Now say why:** why does Lasso reach exact zeros when Ridge never does?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Plain least squares trusts every feature completely, so with many or correlated features its weights become huge, unstable and overfit. Regularization adds a price on the size of the weights. **Ridge** (an L2 penalty) shrinks all of them smoothly and fixes collinearity. **Lasso** (an L1 penalty) shrinks and sets some to exactly zero, so it selects features. **Elastic Net** mixes both, so correlated features enter or leave together. One knob, λ, trades bias for variance, and you choose it by cross-validation. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why L1 gives zeros and L2 doesn't (geometrically and algebraically), pick between the three, and tune them properly.

#### Three ideas you need first

##### Bias–variance trade-off

Test error ≈ bias² + variance + noise. OLS is unbiased but, with few rows and many correlated features, has huge variance. Accepting a little bias (pulling weights toward zero) can cut variance a lot, and lower total error.

##### Standardise the features

A penalty on weight size only makes sense if features share a scale. Otherwise "size in m²" and "size in km²" get penalised completely differently. Subtract each feature's mean, divide by its standard deviation, and don't penalise the intercept.

##### Norms: two ways to measure "how big are the weights"

**L2**: ‖β‖₂² = β₁² + β₂² + … (the squared length). **L1**: ‖β‖₁ = |β₁| + |β₂| + … (the sum of absolute values). They sound similar. The difference in their shapes (a circle versus a diamond) is the whole story of the Lasso section.

#### Fit the data, but pay for every unit of weight

$$ \min_{\beta}\ {\|\mathbf y - X\beta\|_2^2} + {\lambda}\,{P(\beta)} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad {\min_\beta \|\mathbf y - X\beta\|_2^2 \ \text{ s.t. } P(\beta)\le t} $$

The penalised and constrained forms are equivalent; Tibshirani defines the lasso in the constrained form [p. 268](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=3).

- **fit the data**: The usual least-squares error. Alone, it lets weights grow as large as they like.

- **the price**: λ ≥ 0 sets how expensive weight is. λ = 0 gives back OLS; λ → ∞ forces every weight to 0.

- **how weight is measured**: The norm of the weights: L2 for Ridge, L1 for Lasso, a mix for Elastic Net. The shape of this norm decides the behaviour.

- **same thing, as a budget**: Equivalently: minimise the error subject to the weights staying inside a budget t. Each λ matches some t. This view gives the geometry in the Lasso section.

#### An L2 penalty, and a matrix that's always invertible

$$ {\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}} = \big({X^{\top}X} + {\lambda I}\big)^{-1}{X^{\top}\mathbf y} $$

Minimiser of ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖²; scikit-learn's `Ridge` objective [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).

- **ridge weights**: The solution has a closed form, just like OLS.

- **the features' overlap**: XᵀX, the same matrix as in the normal equation. With collinear features it is nearly singular, so its inverse explodes.

- **the ridge**: Adding λ to the diagonal (the ridge) makes the matrix well conditioned and always invertible, even with more features than rows.

- **feature–target overlap**: Unchanged from OLS.

That's why Ridge fixes the sign flip from the start of this lesson. scikit-learn: with ridge, "the coefficients become more robust to collinearity." Zou and Hastie give a nice reading of it: the ridge operator is "decorrelation followed by direct scaling shrinkage": it shrinks the correlations between features by 1/(1 + λ), then scales [Zou & Hastie 2005, p. 308](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf#page=8). Correlated features end up sharing the credit roughly equally.

##### What it can't do

Ridge "does not set any coefficients to 0 and hence does not give an easily interpretable model" [Tibshirani 1996, p. 267](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=2). The five junk features get small weights, but never zero. Try it in the Play lab, in the Intuition tab.

#### Why L1 lands on exact zeros: the diamond

Swap the squares for absolute values, and Lasso does something Ridge never does: it sets weights to **exactly** zero. Tibshirani's picture explains why [§2.3, p. 270](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=5):

1. Two weights, β₁ and β₂. On the left the budget is an L1 budget; on the right, an L2 budget.

2. OLS sits at the unconstrained best point, outside the budget in both cases.

3. Moving away from OLS, the squared error rises in elliptical contours: every point on one ellipse has the same error.

4. The allowed region: a **diamond** for L1 (|β₁| + |β₂| ≤ t), a **circle** for L2.

5. The solution is where the growing ellipses first touch the region. The diamond has corners on the axes, and an ellipse often hits a corner first, which means one weight is exactly zero. The circle has no corners, so the touching point almost never lies on an axis. In more dimensions the diamond has even more corners and edges, so many weights hit zero.

##### The same thing algebraically

With uncorrelated (orthonormal) features you can solve both exactly, and the difference is plain. Ridge _scales_ each OLS weight by a constant factor; Lasso _subtracts_ a constant and stops at zero ("soft thresholding") [Tibshirani 1996, §2.2](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=4):

$$ {\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}}_j = \hat\beta_j \,/\, (1+\lambda)} \qquad {\hat\beta^{\text{lasso}}_j = \operatorname{sign}(\hat\beta_j)\,\big(|\hat\beta_j| - \lambda\big)}{_{+}} $$

Orthonormal design (XᵀX = I), with the penalties scaled to give these simple forms · hover any symbol.

- **ridge: scale**: Divide the OLS weight by 1 + λ. Big or small, every weight shrinks by the same proportion, and never reaches zero.

- **lasso: shift and cut**: Move the OLS weight λ closer to zero; if it would cross zero, stop at zero. Any weight smaller than λ is deleted.

- **the cut-off**: (·)₊ means max(·, 0). This is where exact zeros come from.

x-axis: the OLS weight. y-axis: what each method returns. Dashed: OLS (no shrinkage). Everything inside the green flat zone (|β̂| ≤ λ) becomes exactly zero under Lasso.

#### Why Lasso alone isn't enough

Zou and Hastie list three situations where Lasso struggles [Zou & Hastie 2005, p. 302](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf#page=2):

1. **More features than rows (p > n):** "the lasso selects at most n variables before it saturates." With 20,000 genes and 70 patients, it can keep at most 70.

2. **Correlated groups:** "the lasso tends to select only one variable from the group and does not care which one is selected." In our flats it keeps size and drops bedrooms.

3. **Correlated features, n > p:** "the prediction performance of the lasso is dominated by ridge regression."

Elastic Net adds a little L2 to the L1. The L1 part still produces zeros; the L2 part makes the problem strictly convex, which produces the grouping effect: "strongly correlated predictors tend to be in or out of the model together" [abstract](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf#page=1). The authors' image: "like a stretchable fishing net that retains 'all the big fish'".

$$ \min_{\beta}\ {\tfrac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf y - X\beta\|_2^2} + {\alpha}{\rho\,\|\beta\|_1} + {\alpha}{\tfrac{1-\rho}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2} $$

scikit-learn's `ElasticNet` objective, with `l1_ratio` = ρ [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html). Zou and Hastie also rescale the naive solution by (1 + λ₂) to undo "double shrinkage" [p. 307](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf#page=7).

- **fit, averaged**: Mean squared error with a ½ (scikit-learn's scaling: 1/(2n)).

- **overall strength**: α: how much penalty in total.

- **the L1 share**: ρ (l1_ratio) of the penalty is L1: this part creates zeros. ρ = 1 is pure Lasso.

- **the L2 share**: The remaining 1 − ρ is ridge: it stabilises the fit and groups correlated features. ρ = 0 is a ridge penalty.

scikit-learn's one-line summary: "Lasso is likely to pick one of these at random, while elastic-net is likely to pick both" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Three penalties, one recipe

| Method | Penalty | Origin | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ridge** | λ‖β‖₂² | Hoerl & Kennard, 1970 | Shrinks every weight smoothly; never exactly zero; fixes collinearity |
| **Lasso** | λ‖β‖₁ | Tibshirani, 1996 | Shrinks and sets some weights to exactly zero: feature selection |
| **Elastic Net** | mix of both | Zou & Hastie, 2005 | Sparse like Lasso, but keeps correlated groups together |

In scikit-learn they're `Ridge`, `Lasso` and `ElasticNet`, with `RidgeCV`, `LassoCV` and `ElasticNetCV` to pick the strength by cross-validation. The same penalties appear everywhere else in ML: `LogisticRegression` is L2-regularised by default, and "weight decay" in neural networks is an L2 penalty. [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

#### λ is a hyperparameter: pick it with cross-validation

The training error always prefers λ = 0 (OLS fits the training rows best). So you can't choose λ on training error. Standard practice is k-fold cross-validation over a grid of λ values (log-spaced, as in the lab), then refit on all the training data with the winner. Two common choices: the λ with the lowest CV error, or the largest λ within one standard error of it (the "one-standard-error rule", a simpler model at almost the same accuracy). `RidgeCV`, `LassoCV` and `ElasticNetCV` do this for you.

##### Classic mistakes

- Not standardising: the penalty then punishes features for their units.

- Fitting the scaler on all data before splitting: test-set information leaks into training.

- Penalising the intercept: shifts every prediction toward zero for no reason (libraries don't, if you let them fit it).

- Comparing α across libraries or models: scikit-learn's Ridge has no 1/n factor, its Lasso has 1/(2n), and LogisticRegression uses C = 1/strength [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).

**Go deeper: the Bayesian view**

Regularised least squares is maximum a posteriori estimation. A Gaussian prior on each weight (most weights small, any value possible) gives Ridge; a Laplace prior (a sharp peak at zero with heavier tails) gives Lasso. The sharp peak at zero is the probabilistic version of the diamond's corners. λ corresponds to how tight the prior is relative to the noise. This is standard textbook material (e.g. ESL ch. 3).

#### Regularised regression, start to finish

1. Split off a test set. Build a pipeline: impute → one-hot → **standardise** → model, so scaling is learned on training folds only.

2. Pick the penalty from your goal: stability with correlated features → Ridge; a small, readable model → Lasso; many correlated features or p > n → Elastic Net.

3. Cross-validate α (and ρ for Elastic Net) on a log grid.

4. Refit on all training data, evaluate once on the test set.

5. Interpret carefully: Lasso's zeros mean "not needed given the others", not "no effect"; which of two correlated features survives can change between samples.

#### Pick by goal

| Situation | Start with |
|---|---|
| Many correlated features, you want stable predictions, all features plausible | **Ridge** |
| You believe only a few features matter and want a short, readable model | **Lasso** |
| More features than rows, or groups of correlated features (genes, sensors, one-hot blocks) | **Elastic Net** |
| Lots of data, few well-chosen features | Plain OLS is fine; a light ridge rarely hurts |
| Not sure | Elastic Net with ρ cross-validated over [0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1] covers all three |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just drop the bad features by hand" (subset selection)

The classic fix is to try subsets of features and keep the best one (forward, backward or best-subset selection). It gives a small, readable model. But it's all-or-nothing, and that makes it unstable:

##### What breaks: a discrete choice is a jumpy choice

"Subset selection provides interpretable models but can be extremely variable because it is a discrete process: regressors are either retained or dropped from the model. Small changes in the data can result in very different models being selected and this can reduce its prediction accuracy" [Tibshirani 1996, p. 267](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=2). Best-subset search also grows as 2p: 10 features means 1,024 models, 40 means about a trillion.

Regularization replaces "in or out" with a continuous dial.

#### What to keep

**The lesson:** regularization trades a little bias for a lot less variance by charging for weight. The shape of the charge decides the behaviour: L2's round ball shrinks smoothly, and L1's corners produce exact zeros.

- **Lasso selection isn't stable inference.** Which of two correlated features survives can flip between samples. Use stability selection or the bootstrap if you need to trust the selected set.

- **Shrunken coefficients are biased.** Good for prediction, misleading for effect sizes. A common trick is to refit OLS on Lasso's selected features ("relaxed lasso").

- **No penalty fixes a wrong model.** If the relationship is non-linear, regularising a linear model just makes it a more stable wrong model.

- **The simulation here is small** (22 rows, 10 features), chosen to make the effects visible. With lots of data and few features, OLS and the regularised fits converge.

## Say it

### What is the difference between Ridge and Lasso?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why does L1 produce zeros and L2 doesn't?

Geometrically, the L1 ball is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the error contours usually touch it first at a corner. The L2 ball is round, so the touching point is almost never on an axis. Algebraically, the L1 penalty's gradient doesn't vanish near zero (it's ±λ), so small weights get pushed all the way to zero (soft thresholding). The L2 gradient 2λβ fades as β → 0, so it only scales weights down.

Follow-up 2 of 6

Why must you standardise before regularising?

The penalty compares weights across features. If one feature is in metres and another in millimetres, the same effect needs weights 1000× apart, so the penalty would crush one and ignore the other. Standardising puts all features on a common scale, so the penalty is fair. Fit the scaler on training data only.

Follow-up 3 of 6

What happens as λ → 0 and λ → ∞?

λ → 0 gives OLS (low bias, high variance). λ → ∞ drives every coefficient to zero, so the model predicts the mean (high bias, zero variance). The best λ, found by CV, sits in between.

Follow-up 4 of 6

Lasso with two highly correlated features?

It tends to keep one and zero the other, somewhat arbitrarily, and which one can change with the sample. Ridge splits the weight between them. Elastic Net keeps both with similar weights (the grouping effect).

Follow-up 5 of 6

Can you use Lasso for feature selection, then OLS?

Yes, that's the relaxed lasso or post-lasso OLS: it reduces Lasso's shrinkage bias on the kept features. But the selection itself is noisy, so validate the final model on held-out data, and don't treat the p-values of the refit as if the features had been chosen in advance.

Follow-up 6 of 6

How does this relate to neural networks?

Weight decay is an L2 penalty on the weights (with a subtlety: for adaptive optimisers like Adam, AdamW applies decoupled weight decay rather than adding λ‖w‖² to the loss). L1 penalties are used less but appear in sparsity work. Same idea everywhere: limit capacity to generalise better.

#### The 30-second answer

Regularized regression adds a penalty on weight size to least squares to cut variance and overfitting. Ridge uses an L2 penalty: it shrinks all coefficients smoothly, never to zero, and handles collinearity because XᵀX + λI is always invertible. Lasso uses L1: its diamond-shaped constraint has corners on the axes, so it sets some coefficients exactly to zero and does feature selection, but with correlated features it arbitrarily keeps one and can select at most n features. Elastic Net mixes the two to get sparsity plus grouping. You standardise features and tune λ by cross-validation.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Problem: OLS has high variance with many or correlated features (show the sign flip). Bias–variance framing. Penalised objective ‖y − Xβ‖² + λP(β), equivalent to a budget. Ridge: closed form (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, decorrelates and shrinks. Lasso: diamond geometry, soft thresholding in the orthonormal case, exact zeros. Elastic Net: Zou & Hastie's three Lasso failures and the grouping effect. Practicalities: standardise, don't penalise the intercept, cross-validate λ, beware α conventions. Evidence: prostate data, Elastic Net 0.381 vs OLS 0.586 test MSE.

#### What not to say

- "Ridge does feature selection." It never zeros a weight.

- "Lasso tells you which features truly matter." It tells you a small set that predicts well; with correlated features the choice is fragile.

- "Regularization always improves test error." Only if λ is tuned; too much λ underfits.

- "You don't need to scale features for Lasso." You do.

**Key terms and sources**

Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net · built from Tibshirani (1996), Zou & Hastie (2005) and scikit-learn's docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### A real benchmark: prostate cancer data

Zou and Hastie compared all the methods on a classic dataset: predicting log prostate-specific antigen from 8 clinical measures, 67 training patients, 30 test patients, tuning by tenfold cross-validation [Zou & Hastie 2005, Table 1](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf#page=11):

##### Test mean squared error (↓ better)

OLS · all 8 variables

0.586

Ridge · all 8

0.566

Lasso · 5 variables

0.499

Elastic Net · 5 variables

0.381

Standard errors are large (0.105–0.188) with a 30-patient test set, so treat the ranking as indicative, not definitive. The authors conclude "the elastic net is the winner among all the competitors in terms of both prediction accuracy and sparsity. OLS is the worst method."

And Tibshirani's original claim for the lasso: simulations "suggest that the lasso enjoys some of the favourable properties of both subset selection and ridge regression. It produces interpretable models like subset selection and exhibits the stability of ridge regression" [abstract, p. 267](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/j_royal_stat_soc_b1996.pdf#page=2).

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Regularization** | Adding a penalty on model complexity (here, weight size) to the training loss. |
| **Ridge / L2** | Penalty λΣβ²; smooth shrinkage, never zero. |
| **Lasso / L1** | Penalty λΣ\|β\|; shrinkage plus exact zeros (feature selection). |
| **Elastic Net** | Weighted mix of L1 and L2 (α, l1_ratio). |
| **Soft thresholding** | sign(b)·max(\|b\| − λ, 0): Lasso's update. |
| **Grouping effect** | Correlated features get similar weights and enter or leave together. |
| **Multicollinearity** | Features that are nearly linear combinations of each other. |
| **Coordinate descent** | Optimise one weight at a time; the standard Lasso / Elastic Net solver. |
| **Weight decay** | The neural-network name for an L2 penalty. |

2. H. Zou & T. Hastie, [Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/courses/stat527/s13/readings/zouhastie05.pdf), JRSS-B 67 (2005) 301–320: Lasso's limits, grouping effect, prostate benchmark.

# Logistic Regression

> Why is a classifier called regression, and what does log-loss punish?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Linear models
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/logistic-regression/
- Before this: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`), Maximum Likelihood & MAP (`fundamentals/mle-and-map`)
- Quiz topic: `lin`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have 20 students, their hours studied, and whether each one passed. You need a yes or no, and how sure you are. The interviewer asks:

> What is logistic regression, and why is it called regression?

**Running example:** 20 students, hours studied, and whether each passed the exam (illustrative data). Goal: given hours, predict the _probability_ of passing.

#### Predict yes or no, and how sure you are

Spam or not, churn or not, default or not, click or not: a huge share of real ML problems have a yes/no answer. You want two things: a decision, and a **probability** you can rank, threshold and trust ("82% likely to default" is far more useful than "yes"). The target is 0 or 1, which breaks the tool from the last two lessons.

### The idea

Think of a judge weighing evidence. Each fact adds or takes away points, and the total can be any number. A curve then squashes that total into a chance between 0 and 100%.

[Figure: Evidence adds up to a score, a curve squashes the score, and out comes a chance between 0 and 100 percent]

_Illustrative. In the model, the points are the weights and the curve is the sigmoid._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Here w is how much each hour counts, and b is where the judge starts. Lower log-loss means a better fit. Drag w as high as it goes.

#### w sets the steepness, b sets where it crosses 50%

Each student's contribution to the loss is drawn as a red bar: the bar is long when the curve gives low probability to what actually happened. Notice that a very steep curve (large w) gets punished hard for the few students on the "wrong" side.

**Now say why:** why does the steepest curve get punished, even though it looks so confident?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Logistic regression is a **classifier**. It models the **log-odds** of the positive class as a weighted sum of features and squashes that through a sigmoid to get a probability between 0 and 1. It is trained by maximum likelihood, which is the same as minimising **log-loss** (cross-entropy): a convex problem with one best answer and no closed form. Its decision boundary is a straight line (a hyperplane), its weights read as odds multipliers, and with regularization its probabilities are often well calibrated. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why it's called "regression", why we don't use squared error, derive the gradient, interpret a coefficient as an odds ratio, and handle separable data, thresholds and calibration.

#### Probability, odds and log-odds

Three ways to say the same thing. A probability p lives in [0, 1]. The **odds** p / (1 − p) live in [0, ∞): p = 0.8 is odds of 4 ("4 to 1"). The **log-odds** (the **logit**) log(p / (1 − p)) live on the whole real line, from −∞ to +∞, with 0 meaning a coin flip.

That last scale is the key: a weighted sum of features can be any real number, and so can log-odds. So we let the linear part predict the log-odds.

#### A linear model for the log-odds, squashed into a probability

$$ {h_\theta(x)} = {g}\big({\theta^{\top}x}\big) = 1\,/\,\big(1 + e^{-\theta^{\top}x}\big) \qquad {\log\!\big(h/(1-h)\big) = \theta^{\top}x} $$

CS229 §2.1 [CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf). The derivative is neat: g′(z) = g(z)(1 − g(z)), which keeps the gradient simple.

- **the probability**: h(x) = P(y = 1 | x): the model's probability of a pass.

- **the sigmoid**: g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Maps any real number to (0, 1): very negative → near 0, 0 → 0.5, very positive → near 1.

- **the logit**: θᵀx: an ordinary weighted sum of features, exactly like linear regression. It can be any real number.

- **the same thing, inverted**: Solve for the linear part: log-odds = θᵀx. Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds scale. That's where “regression” in the name comes from.

#### Maximum likelihood gives log-loss, not squared error

Treat each label as a coin flip with probability h(x). The probability of all the observed labels is a product; take its log and you get the log-likelihood [CS229 Eq. 2.1](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf). Its negative is **log-loss**, also called binary cross-entropy:

$$ {\ell(\theta)} = {\sum_{i=1}^{n}}\Big[{y^{(i)}\log h(x^{(i)})} + {(1-y^{(i)})\log\big(1-h(x^{(i)})\big)}\Big] $$

- **log-likelihood**: How probable the observed passes and fails are under θ. Maximise it (or minimise its negative, the log-loss).

- **when y = 1**: Only this term is active for a pass: log of the predicted pass probability. Predict 0.99 → about 0; predict 0.01 → −4.6.

- **when y = 0**: Only this term is active for a fail: log of the predicted fail probability.

- **over all students**: Add over the n examples. One term per example, one active part per term.

##### Feel the penalty

Squared error never exceeds 1, so a confident wrong answer costs at most 1. Log-loss goes to infinity as p → 0: a model that says "1% chance" about something that happened is punished severely. That's a difference in how hard each punishes a confident mistake. Both are proper scoring rules: each is best when you report the true probability.

##### Why not squared error? The shape of the loss

Both losses on our 20 students as the weight w changes (bias kept so the curve crosses 50% at the fitted threshold). Log-loss (orange) is a single convex valley. Squared error on sigmoid outputs (purple) flattens into a plateau for wrong-sign weights and is non-convex there: gradients vanish, and an optimiser can stall. With log-loss, the gradient is simply (prediction − label) × feature, and it never vanishes while the model is wrong.

#### The gradient is (label − prediction) × feature, again

Differentiate the log-likelihood using g′ = g(1 − g), and nearly everything cancels [CS229 Eq. 2.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf):

$$ {\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\ell(\theta)} = {\big(y - h_\theta(x)\big)}\,{x_j} $$

- **slope for weight j**: How the log-likelihood changes when weight j moves, for one example.

- **the error**: Label minus predicted probability. If the model said 0.9 and the student passed, the error is only 0.1.

- **the feature**: Scaled by the feature value, just like linear regression's LMS rule.

That's the same form as the least-squares update, but it isn't the same algorithm: h is now the sigmoid of θᵀx. CS229 asks whether the match is a coincidence and answers with generalized linear models (see the family tree below): both are GLMs with their natural "canonical" link. Unlike linear regression, setting the gradient to zero has **no closed-form solution**, so we iterate: gradient descent, Newton's method or L-BFGS. The log-loss is convex, so they all reach the same optimum, when one exists (perfectly separable data has none).

#### Each weight is an odds multiplier

Because the model is linear in the log-odds, one extra unit of a feature adds w to the log-odds, which **multiplies the odds by ew**, no matter where you start.

Fitted on our 20 students. The odds ratio is constant, but the change in _probability_ isn't: one extra hour moves P(pass) a lot near 50% and very little near 0% or 100%. Interview trap: "a coefficient of 0.86 means 86% more likely" is wrong; it means the odds multiply by e0.86 ≈ 2.36.

#### With two features, the boundary is a straight line

1. Now two features: hours studied and hours slept. Each dot is a student (illustrative).

2. P = 0.5 exactly where the logit is zero: 0.9·study + 0.8·sleep − 9.5 = 0. That's a straight line, the **decision boundary**.

3. Every probability level is a line parallel to it. Probability changes only as you move across the lines, never along them.

4. The weight vector is perpendicular to the boundary and points toward higher pass odds. In more dimensions the boundary is a flat hyperplane.

A straight boundary is both the strength and the limit. If the classes are separated by a curve (a ring, an XOR pattern), plain logistic regression can't follow it. Add features (squares, products, splines), or use a non-linear model. That's exactly what a neural network's hidden layers do before its final logistic or softmax layer.

#### Perceptron, GLMs, and softmax

**The perceptron: logistic regression with a hard step**

Replace the sigmoid with a hard threshold (output 1 if θᵀx ≥ 0, else 0) and use the same update θj := θj + α(y − h(x))xj, and you get the perceptron (1950s–60s). It finds a separating line if one exists, but CS229 notes "it is difficult to endow the perceptron's predictions with meaningful probabilistic interpretations" [CS229 §2.2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf). Logistic regression is the smooth, probabilistic version.

**Generalized linear models: why sigmoid, and why the same gradient**

Linear and logistic regression are both GLMs: pick an exponential-family distribution for y given x, model its natural parameter as θᵀx, and predict its mean. Gaussian y gives linear regression (identity link); Bernoulli y gives logistic regression, and writing the Bernoulli in exponential-family form produces the sigmoid on its own. Poisson y (counts) gives Poisson regression. Every GLM with the canonical link has the gradient (y − prediction)·x, which answers the "coincidence" above [CS229 §3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf).

More than two classes? Give each class its own weight vector and replace the sigmoid with a softmax. That's the next lesson.

GLMs have their own lesson: see Generalised Linear Models.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Still a workhorse

Logistic regression is the default baseline for binary classification and still production-grade in credit scoring, medical risk scores, fraud and click-through-rate models, wherever probabilities and explainability matter. In scikit-learn it's `LogisticRegression` (L-BFGS by default, and **L2-regularised by default**, with `C = 1`); statsmodels' `Logit` gives the unregularised fit with standard errors; `SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss")` trains it on streams. scikit-learn notes the default penalty explicitly: "Regularization is applied by default, which is common in machine learning but not in statistics" [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).

#### 0.5 is a default, not a law

On our 20 students with the fitted model. Lower the threshold and you catch more passers (recall up) but also more failers (precision down). Pick the threshold from the costs: missing a fraud costs far more than reviewing a false alarm, so fraud models use low thresholds.

**Calibration** means "of all cases predicted at 70%, about 70% are positive." Logistic regression is good at this by construction. scikit-learn: it "is more likely to return well calibrated predictions by itself as it has a canonical link function for its loss," which in the unpenalised case gives the "balance property" [scikit-learn calibration docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html). The guarantee weakens with strong penalties, a mis-specified model, or resampled training data (e.g. after oversampling the rare class). Check a reliability curve, and recalibrate if needed.

#### Shipping a logistic regression

1. Split train/test (stratified, so both keep the class ratio).

2. Encode categories (one-hot), standardise numeric features (needed for the penalty and for fast convergence).

3. Fit with L2 (default) and cross-validate C; try L1 or Elastic Net if you want feature selection.

4. Evaluate with metrics that fit the problem: log-loss and ROC-AUC for ranking quality, PR-AUC when positives are rare. Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

5. Check calibration (a reliability curve); recalibrate if you resampled or regularised heavily.

6. Choose the threshold from business costs, on validation data.

7. Explain with odds ratios (ew per unit, or per standard deviation for standardised features).

#### Use it, or reach for something else?

##### Use logistic regression when

- You need probabilities and a strong, fast baseline

- You need to explain decisions (regulated domains like credit and health)

- Data is high-dimensional and sparse (text with TF-IDF, one-hot features)

- Latency or memory is tight

##### Reach for something else when

- Strong non-linear interactions in tabular data → gradient boosting

- Images, audio, raw text → neural networks (with a logistic/softmax output layer)

- More than two classes → softmax regression (or one-vs-rest)

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just run linear regression on the 0s and 1s"

Fit a straight line to the 0/1 labels and call anything above 0.5 a pass. It sort of works on tidy data. Then one diligent student who studied a lot (and passed, obviously) joins the dataset:

Purple: least-squares line on 0/1 labels. Orange: logistic curve. The extra student is an easy, correct "pass", yet the straight line tilts to reach them, its 0.5 crossing slides right, and it starts misclassifying students it got right before. The logistic fit barely moves. (Axis shows 0–20 hours; points further right are off-screen.)

##### What breaks

A line predicts values below 0 and above 1, which aren't probabilities. Its squared error punishes being "too right" (predicting 1.4 for a sure pass), so easy points far from the boundary drag the fit. CS229 makes the same point: "it is easy to construct examples where this method performs very poorly" and "it also doesn't make sense for hθ(x) to take values larger than 1 or smaller than 0" [CS229 §2](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf).

#### Perfectly separable data: the weights run to infinity

If a line separates passes from fails perfectly, the likelihood keeps improving as the sigmoid gets steeper, with no finite best weight. The optimiser just keeps going:

Same 20 students, but relabelled so everyone with ≥ 3.75 hours passed (perfectly separable). Gradient descent, learning rate 0.5. Without a penalty, w keeps growing and the curve becomes a step with fake 100%/0% certainty. With an L2 penalty (λ = 0.05) it converges to a finite, sensible slope.

This is one big reason scikit-learn regularises by default. The strength is set by `C`, the _inverse_ of the penalty: small C means strong regularization [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html). With many features, separable data is common, and the same L1/L2/Elastic Net trade-offs from the last lesson apply.

#### What to keep

**The lesson:** logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds, trained with log-loss. Convex, fast, calibrated-ish, explainable, and the building block (as the output layer) of most neural classifiers.

- **Linear boundary only.** Interactions and curves must be engineered in.

- **Separable data and many features** need regularization, or weights explode.

- **Class imbalance** doesn't break the model but does break accuracy and the 0.5 threshold. Use class weights or threshold tuning, and remember that reweighting shifts the probabilities.

- **Collinear features** make individual odds ratios unstable, exactly as in linear regression.

## Say it

### What is logistic regression, and why is it called regression?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why is it called regression if it's a classifier?

It's a regression model for the log-odds (a GLM with a logit link): it predicts a continuous quantity, the probability, and classification only happens when you apply a threshold.

Follow-up 2 of 6

Why log-loss and not MSE?

Log-loss is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood, so it's the principled choice. With a sigmoid output it's convex in the weights and gives the clean gradient (h − y)x. MSE on sigmoid outputs is non-convex with flat regions where gradients vanish, and it penalises a confident wrong prediction by at most 1, so those mistakes push back only weakly during training.

Follow-up 3 of 6

How do you interpret a coefficient?

A one-unit increase in the feature, holding others fixed, adds w to the log-odds, so it multiplies the odds by ew. The effect on probability depends on where you are on the curve: largest near 0.5.

Follow-up 4 of 6

What happens with perfectly separable data?

The maximum-likelihood estimate doesn't exist: weights grow without bound while the loss keeps falling toward zero. Regularization (scikit-learn's default L2) or early stopping gives finite, sensible weights.

Follow-up 5 of 6

Is the decision boundary linear?

Yes, in the features you give it: θᵀx = log(t/(1 − t)) for threshold t. Add polynomial or interaction features to get curved boundaries in the original space.

Follow-up 6 of 6

How would you handle class imbalance?

Keep log-loss, but use class weights or resampling, evaluate with PR-AUC or recall at a fixed precision rather than accuracy, and tune the threshold. If you reweight or resample, the predicted probabilities shift, so recalibrate if you need true probabilities.

#### The 30-second answer

Logistic regression is a linear classifier. It models the log-odds of the positive class as a linear function of the features, and the sigmoid turns that into a probability. It's trained by maximum likelihood, which means minimising log-loss: convex, solved iteratively with gradient descent or L-BFGS, with gradient (prediction − label) × feature. Coefficients are log odds ratios, the decision boundary is a hyperplane, and in practice it's L2-regularised, which also handles separable data. It's called regression because it regresses the log-odds.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Problem: binary target, want calibrated probabilities. Why not linear regression (outputs outside [0, 1], easy points drag the fit). Odds and log-odds; model logit = θᵀx; sigmoid. Bernoulli likelihood → log-loss; why not MSE (non-convex, vanishing gradients, weak penalty for confident errors). Gradient (y − h)x, no closed form, convex optimisation. Interpretation via odds ratios. Boundary is linear; feature engineering for curves. Separable data → infinite weights → regularization (C). Threshold from costs; calibration and the balance property.

#### What not to say

- "It outputs a class." It outputs a probability; the class comes from your threshold.

- "Coefficient 0.5 means 50% more likely." It's +0.5 log-odds, an odds ratio of about 1.65.

- "It can't do non-linear problems." Not with raw features, but with engineered features it can.

- "There's a closed-form solution like linear regression." There isn't; it's solved iteratively.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Stanford CS229 notes (§2–3), scikit-learn's linear-model and calibration docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Sigmoid / logistic function** | g(z) = 1/(1 + e−z), squashes to (0, 1). |
| **Logit / log-odds** | log(p/(1 − p)); the linear part of the model. |
| **Odds ratio** | ew: how the odds multiply per unit of a feature. |
| **Log-loss / binary cross-entropy** | −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], averaged. |
| **Decision boundary** | Where p = threshold; a hyperplane θᵀx = const. |
| **Calibration** | Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. |
| **C (scikit-learn)** | Inverse regularization strength. |
| **GLM** | Generalized linear model: exponential-family response with a linear predictor. |

#### What this page is built from

1. A. Ng, T. Ma et al., [Stanford CS229 lecture notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf), §2 (logistic regression, perceptron, multi-class) and §3 (GLMs).

2. scikit-learn, [Linear models user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html): LogisticRegression objective, C, default regularization, solvers.
