# Softmax Regression

> How does logistic regression handle many classes, and why does every LLM end with it?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Linear models
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/softmax-regression/
- Before this: Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`), Entropy, Cross-Entropy & KL Divergence (`fundamentals/entropy-cross-entropy-kl`)
- Related: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `lin`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're sorting fruit into apple, orange or banana. A teammate turns scores into probabilities by dividing each by the total, and then one score goes negative. The interviewer asks:

> What is softmax regression, and how is it trained?

**Running example:** sort 27 fruits into apple, orange or banana from two measurements: length (cm) and "yellowness" (0–1, from a colour sensor). Illustrative data, generated with a fixed seed.

#### More than two answers, and one probability for each

Digit recognition (10 classes), intent detection (dozens), product categories (thousands), next-token prediction (over 100,000): most real classification has more than two classes. You want a probability for every class, all of them between 0 and 1, summing to exactly 1. Logistic regression gives one probability for one yes/no question. How do you get a proper distribution over K options?

### The idea

Think of a vote share. Each class gets a score, and raising e to that score makes it positive and widens the lead. Dividing by the total then gives shares that add up to 100%.

[Figure: Three scores, 2, 1 and minus 1, become probabilities of 71, 26 and 4 percent after softmax. They add up to 100 percent.]

_Worked from the scores 2, 1 and −1. Percentages are rounded._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Add 3 to every logit. Then raise the temperature, and then lower it.

#### Move the scores, watch the distribution

Things to try. Add the same amount to every logit: nothing changes (the Maths tab shows why). Raise T: the distribution flattens toward uniform. Lower T: it sharpens toward the single biggest logit. That's exactly the "temperature" knob in LLM sampling.

**Now say why:** why does adding the same amount change nothing, and what does temperature really do?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Softmax regression extends logistic regression to K classes. Each class gets its own weight vector and its own score (a **logit**); the **softmax** exponentiates the scores and normalises them, so they're positive and sum to 1. It's trained with **cross-entropy**, and the gradient is beautifully simple: (predicted probability − one-hot label) × features. With two classes it reduces exactly to the sigmoid. And it's not just classical ML: the last layer of every LLM is softmax regression over its vocabulary. What you'll be able to do after this: derive softmax and its gradient, explain why logits are shift-invariant, implement it without overflow, compare it with one-vs-rest, and connect temperature to LLM sampling.

#### One score per class, then turn scores into probabilities

Give each class k its own weight vector θk. For a fruit with features x, each class gets a score tk = θkᵀx: how much the features look like that class. These raw scores are called **logits**. They can be any real number, so we need a function that turns K arbitrary numbers into a probability distribution. CS229 points out the two problems with using them directly: θkᵀx "is not necessarily within [0, 1]" and "the summation of θkᵀx's is not necessarily 1" [CS229 §2.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf).

Notation: the label is often written **one-hot**, a vector with a 1 in the true class's slot and 0 elsewhere. A banana is (0, 0, 1).

#### Exponentiate the scores, then normalise

$$ {P(y=i\mid x)} = {\exp({\theta_i^{\top}x})} \,\Big/\, {\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\theta_j^{\top}x)} $$

CS229 Eqs. 2.9–2.10 [CS229 §2.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf). "Softmax" because it's a smooth version of "argmax": the biggest score gets most of the probability, but the others keep some.

- **probability of class i**: The model's probability that this fruit is class i.

- **exponentiate**: e^(score): always positive, and it stretches differences: a score 1 higher means a 2.7× bigger number.

- **normalise**: Divide by the sum over all K classes, so the probabilities add up to exactly 1.

- **the logit**: Class i's score: θᵢᵀx, a weighted sum of the features, one weight vector per class.

#### Adding a constant to every logit changes nothing

$$ {\mathrm{softmax}(t + c)_i} = {e^{c}\,e^{t_i} \,/\, \textstyle\sum_j e^{c}\,e^{t_j}} = {\mathrm{softmax}(t)_i} $$

- **shifted scores**: Add the same number c to every class's logit.

- **factor out**: e^(t+c) = e^c · e^t: the same factor e^c appears on top and in every term of the sum.

- **identical output**: It cancels. Softmax depends only on the differences between logits.

Two consequences. First, the parameters are **redundant**: add the same vector to every θk and predictions don't change, so one class's weights can be fixed at zero without losing anything. Regularization also pins this down. Second, it gives the standard trick for computing softmax without overflow:

Computed live in your browser with 64-bit floats. e1000 overflows to Infinity, and Infinity / Infinity is NaN. e−1000 underflows to 0, and 0 / 0 is also NaN. Subtracting the largest logit first makes the biggest exponent e0 = 1: same answer, no overflow. Every library does this, and computes log-softmax as t − max − log Σ et − max (the log-sum-exp trick).

#### Cross-entropy, and the cleanest gradient in ML

Maximum likelihood again: maximise the probability the model gives to the true class. For one example the loss is just −log of that probability [CS229 §2.3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf):

$$ {\ell_{\text{ce}}} = -\log{\phi_{y}} \qquad {\nabla_{\theta_i}\ell_{\text{ce}}} = {\big(\phi_i - \mathbb{1}\{y=i\}\big)}\,{x} $$

With φ = softmax of the logits; in vector form, ∂ℓ/∂t = φ − ey (CS229 Eq. 2.17).

- **cross-entropy loss**: For one example with true class y.

- **the true class's probability**: Only the probability of the correct class appears. Predict 0.9 for it → loss 0.105; predict 0.01 → 4.6.

- **gradient for class i's weights**: How to change θᵢ, from CS229 Eq. 2.18.

- **prediction − truth**: φᵢ minus 1 if i is the true class, else 0. Push up the true class by (1 − its probability); push every other class down by its probability.

- **the features**: Scaled by the input, exactly like linear and logistic regression.

–

Using the trained model from the next section. Bars: predicted probability φ (filled) and the one-hot label (outline). The gradient on each class's logit is φ − label: negative means "raise this score", positive means "lower it". Confident and correct → tiny gradient; confused → big push.

#### Straight-edged regions, one per class

1. 27 fruits by length and yellowness. Bananas are long and yellow; apples and oranges differ mainly in colour.

2. After training (gradient descent on cross-entropy, a light L2 penalty), each point of the plane is assigned to the class with the biggest logit. These are the decision regions.

3. Region edges are where two logits tie: θaᵀx = θbᵀx, which is a straight line. So softmax regression is still a linear classifier: K classes, regions bounded by straight lines.

4. Curved class shapes need engineered features, or hidden layers in front: a neural network is learned features plus this same softmax layer.

**Go deeper: two classes = the sigmoid**

With K = 2 and logits (t₁, t₂): P(class 1) = et₁ / (et₁ + et₂) = 1 / (1 + e−(t₁ − t₂)) = σ(t₁ − t₂). Binary softmax is exactly logistic regression, with weight vector θ₁ − θ₂ (the redundancy from the section above, in action). In GLM terms, softmax is the canonical response function of the multinomial distribution, just as the sigmoid is for the Bernoulli [CS229 §3](https://cs229.stanford.edu/main_notes.pdf).

For the wider family, see Generalised Linear Models.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Two ways to go multi-class

| Approach | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **One-vs-rest (OvR)** | Train K separate binary logistic regressions ("apple vs not", …), predict the highest | Simple and parallel, but the K probabilities don't sum to 1 and weren't trained together (see Softmax vs one-vs-rest below) |
| **Multinomial / softmax** | One model, K weight vectors, a single softmax, a single cross-entropy loss | Coherent probabilities; the standard choice; it's the output layer of neural classifiers and LLMs |

scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` fits the multinomial (softmax) model for multi-class problems with its default solver, and uses a coefficient matrix W with one row per class; the old liblinear solver "cannot learn a true multinomial (multiclass) model" [scikit-learn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html). In PyTorch, it's a `nn.Linear` layer followed by `CrossEntropyLoss`, which applies the softmax internally.

#### OvR's probabilities don't add up

Both models trained on the same 27 fruits. OvR runs three independent "this class vs the rest" logistic regressions; their outputs answer three different questions, so they can sum to more or less than 1. Softmax's outputs are one coherent distribution. Both usually pick the same winner; the difference shows up when you use the probabilities (ranking, thresholds, expected cost).

#### Every LLM ends with softmax regression

A language model's last step is exactly this lesson. The network turns the context into a hidden vector (4,096 numbers in Llama 3.1 8B), and a final linear layer produces one logit per token in the vocabulary: 128,256 of them. Softmax turns those into next-token probabilities, and training minimises cross-entropy against the actual next token [Llama 3.1 8B config (a copy that needs no login)](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Llama-3.1-8B/raw/main/config.json). That one output matrix alone holds 4,096 × 128,256 ≈ 525 million weights: softmax regression with 128,256 classes.

$$ {q_i} = \exp({z_i / {T}}) \,\Big/\, \textstyle\sum_j \exp(z_j / T) $$

Temperature softmax as used in knowledge distillation, Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, [Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531) (2015), where a high T exposes the teacher's "dark knowledge" in the small probabilities of wrong classes. The same knob controls randomness in LLM sampling.

- **softened probability**: The probability of class (or token) i at temperature T.

- **logits ÷ T**: Divide every logit by T before the softmax.

- **temperature**: T = 1: the normal softmax. T > 1: flatter, more random, lets low-probability options through. T < 1: sharper. T → 0: always the top choice (greedy).

#### Training a softmax classifier

1. Encode labels as integers (or one-hot); stratified train/test split.

2. Standardise features; add engineered features if classes have curved shapes.

3. Compute logits t = Wx + b, then the loss with a fused, stable log-softmax + cross-entropy (never take the log of a softmax you computed separately).

4. Optimise with L-BFGS (small data) or SGD/Adam (large); add L2 regularization (it also removes the redundancy in the logits).

5. Evaluate with per-class precision and recall, a confusion matrix, macro-F1 for imbalanced classes, and log-loss for probability quality.

6. For decisions, use argmax, or thresholds and costs per class; check calibration if probabilities feed decisions.

#### Use it, or reach for something else?

##### Use softmax regression when

- Classes are mutually exclusive and you need coherent probabilities

- You want a fast, interpretable multi-class baseline (e.g. text with TF-IDF)

- You're building the output layer of any neural classifier

##### Use something else when

- Items can carry several labels → one sigmoid per label

- Classes are ordered (ratings 1–5) → ordinal regression

- Boundaries are strongly non-linear in tabular data → gradient boosting

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Divide each score by the total"

The first idea: just normalise, pk = tk / Σ tj. Scores of (2, 1, 1) give (0.5, 0.25, 0.25). Looks fine, until a score is negative or the scores sum to zero:

Apple and orange scores fixed at 2.0 and 1.0. Plain division produces negative "probabilities", values above 1, or a division by zero as banana's score moves. Softmax always gives a valid distribution, and keeps the order of the scores.

##### What breaks

Plain normalisation needs every score to be positive. Exponentiating first fixes that (et > 0 always), and it has a deeper reason: it's what you get by extending the logistic model's log-odds idea to K classes.

#### What to keep

**The lesson:** softmax regression is logistic regression for K classes: one logit per class, exponentiate and normalise, cross-entropy loss, gradient φ − y. It's linear, convex, and the output layer of almost every modern classifier and language model.

- **Mutually exclusive classes only.** If an item can have several labels at once (multi-label tagging), use independent sigmoids per label, not one softmax.

- **Softmax probabilities are not automatically calibrated**, especially in big neural nets, which tend to be overconfident. Temperature scaling on a validation set is the usual fix.

- **Huge K is expensive.** The normaliser sums over every class; with very large vocabularies, training uses tricks like sampled softmax, and inference often only needs the top few logits.

- **Linear boundaries**, just like logistic regression.

## Say it

### What is softmax regression, and how is it trained?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

Derive the gradient of softmax + cross-entropy with respect to the logits.

ℓ = −ty + log Σj etj. ∂ℓ/∂ti = −1{i = y} + eti/Σ etj = φi − 1{i = y}. So the gradient vector is φ − one-hot(y), and with respect to θi it's (φi − 1{i = y})·x.

Follow-up 2 of 5

Why subtract the max logit?

exp overflows for logits above about 709 in float64 (far less in float16), and very negative logits underflow to 0, both producing NaN. Softmax is invariant to adding a constant, so subtracting the max gives identical results with the largest exponent equal to 1.

Follow-up 3 of 5

Softmax vs sigmoid outputs?

Softmax: one distribution over mutually exclusive classes (sums to 1). Independent sigmoids: one yes/no probability per label, for multi-label problems. For exactly two exclusive classes, softmax over two logits equals a sigmoid of their difference.

Follow-up 4 of 5

What does temperature do?

Dividing logits by T > 1 flattens the distribution (more diverse samples, exposes small probabilities, used in distillation); T < 1 sharpens it; T → 0 is argmax. The ranking of classes never changes.

Follow-up 5 of 5

One-vs-rest or multinomial?

Multinomial gives coherent, jointly trained probabilities and is the default in modern libraries. OvR is simpler to parallelise and can be fine for ranking, but its scores don't sum to 1 and aren't comparable across classes without recalibration.

#### The 30-second answer

Softmax regression is multinomial logistic regression. Each class has a weight vector that gives a logit; softmax exponentiates and normalises the logits into a probability distribution. It's trained by minimising cross-entropy, the negative log probability of the true class, and the gradient with respect to the logits is just predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label. It's convex and linear in its decision boundaries, reduces to the sigmoid for two classes, and in practice you subtract the max logit for numerical stability. It's also exactly the output layer of neural classifiers and LLMs.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Need: a distribution over K exclusive classes. Logits tk = θkᵀx; why not divide by the sum (negatives); exponentiate and normalise. Shift invariance → redundancy and the max-subtraction trick. Cross-entropy from maximum likelihood; gradient φ − y times x. Binary case = sigmoid of the logit difference. Decision regions with straight edges. Versus one-vs-rest: incoherent probabilities. Temperature, and the LLM output layer (Llama 3.1 8B: 128,256 classes).

#### What not to say

- "Softmax probabilities are the model's true confidence." Often overconfident; calibrate.

- "Softmax is non-linear, so the model is non-linear." The decision boundaries are linear in the features.

- "Use softmax for multi-label." Use independent sigmoids.

- "Higher temperature changes which class is most likely." It never changes the ordering, only the spread.

**Key terms and sources**

Multinomial logistic regression · built from Stanford CS229 notes (§2.3, §3), scikit-learn's docs and Hinton et al. (2015) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Logit** | A class's raw score θkᵀx, before softmax. |
| **Softmax** | exp(ti) / Σ exp(tj): logits → probability distribution. |
| **Cross-entropy** | −log(probability of the true class); averaged over examples. |
| **One-hot** | Label vector with 1 in the true class, 0 elsewhere. |
| **Log-sum-exp trick** | Subtract the max logit before exponentiating to avoid overflow. |
| **Temperature** | Divide logits by T to flatten (T > 1) or sharpen (T < 1) the distribution. |
| **One-vs-rest** | K independent binary classifiers instead of one joint softmax. |
| **Multinomial logistic regression** | Another name for softmax regression. |

# Generalised Linear Models

> How would you predict counts or insurance costs, and what do linear and logistic regression have in common?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Linear models
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/generalised-linear-models/
- Before this: Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`), Maximum Likelihood & MAP (`fundamentals/mle-and-map`)
- Quiz topic: `lin`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're predicting support calls per hour. A linear regression gives good overall error, but predicts minus two calls at quiet times. Some teams were also observed for ten days, and others for a hundred. The interviewer asks:

> How would you predict counts or insurance costs, and what do linear and logistic regression have in common?

#### Why it matters

Not everything is a number on a straight line. Calls per hour can't be negative. Costs have long tails. GLMs handle these simply, stay explainable, and are widely used in insurance and demand modelling. They also explain why logistic regression has the loss it has.

### The idea

Think of a score and a translator. The model always produces a simple linear score. The link is the translator that turns it into the right kind of answer: a probability, a positive count or any number. Change the translator, and the same machinery handles a new problem.

[Figure: One recipe, three models. Linear regression uses no link. Logistic regression uses a logit for probabilities. Poisson regression uses a log for counts.]

_All three share a linear score. They differ in the distribution and the link._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the growth to 0.6. Then set it to 0.

#### Fit a line and a GLM to counts

Our seeded simulation. Counts are drawn from a Poisson distribution with a mean of exp(−1 + b × x), for x from 0 to 10. The GLM is fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares.

The orange line is least squares, and the green curve is the GLM. Set growth to **0**: both are then flat, and agree. The bigger the growth, the worse a straight line fits. Add rows, and the multiplier gets closer to the true value.

**Now say why:** why can the GLM never predict a negative count?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **GLM** has three parts: a distribution for the outcome, a linear score, and a **link** that connects them. Linear regression uses a normal distribution and no link. Logistic regression uses Bernoulli and the logit. **Poisson regression** uses counts and the log, so predictions can't be negative, and each coefficient multiplies the rate. The loss in each case comes from maximum likelihood.

#### One recipe, many models

| Outcome | Distribution | Link | Model | Loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Any real number | Normal | Identity | Linear regression | Squared error |
| Yes or no | Bernoulli | Logit | Logistic regression | Log loss |
| Counts | Poisson | Log | Poisson regression | Poisson deviance |
| Positive, long-tailed | Gamma | Log | Gamma regression | Gamma deviance |

##### What a coefficient means with a log link

The prediction is exp(score), so a coefficient b **multiplies** the rate by eb for each unit. If b = 0.4, each unit multiplies the rate by about 1.49. It's an increase of 49%, however large the rate already is.

##### Why not fit a line to counts?

- A line can predict negative counts.

- Counts often grow by percentages, which a line can't capture.

- The spread of counts grows with their mean, so the equal-spread assumption fails.

##### Two practical details

**Exposure.** If one shop was observed for 10 days and another for 100, more counts in the second doesn't mean a higher rate. Add log(exposure) to the score with a fixed coefficient of 1. This is called an **offset**.

**Overdispersion.** Poisson assumes the variance equals the mean. Real counts often vary more, which makes standard errors too small. A quasi-Poisson or negative binomial model handles it.

##### GLM or trees?

Boosting usually predicts better when there are many interactions, and many libraries offer a Poisson objective too. A GLM is simpler and easier to explain, which matters when regulators or stakeholders ask questions.

#### The maths

$$ {y \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)}, \qquad {\log \mu} = {w^\top x}, \qquad {\mu = \exp(w^\top x)} $$

Weights are fitted by maximum likelihood, commonly using iteratively reweighted least squares. With a log link, a weight’s effect is multiplicative.

- **the distribution**: What kind of outcome this is. Here, counts.

- **the link**: Connects the mean of the outcome to the score.

- **the linear score**: Features and weights, as in linear regression.

- **the prediction**: The inverse of the link. An exponential is always positive.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Match the outcome:** counts suit Poisson, and positive long-tailed amounts suit Gamma.

- **Handle exposure:** use an offset whenever observation time or population differs.

- **Check dispersion:** compare the variance with the mean. If it's much bigger, consider negative binomial.

- **Watch for excess zeros:** many more zeros than Poisson expects can mean two processes, such as "never buys" and "buys sometimes".

- **Evaluate with the right metric:** squared error can mislead for counts, so check deviance too.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "For counts, just take the log of y and use linear regression"

It sounds right, as it's simple, and it often looks fine. But log(0) is undefined, and counts often include zeros. It also models the mean of the log, rather than the log of the mean, so converting back gives biased predictions. A Poisson GLM avoids both problems.

## Say it

### How would you predict counts or insurance costs, and what do linear and logistic regression have in common?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the difference between a GLM and a linear regression on log(y)?

Log(y) models the mean of the log, while a GLM models the log of the mean. These aren't the same. Log(y) also fails when y is zero, which is common in counts. A Poisson GLM handles zeros naturally.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your Poisson model's coefficient for a promotion is 0.3. What does that mean?

With a log link, the promotion multiplies the expected count by e^0.3, about 1.35, holding other features fixed. That's roughly a 35% rise, whatever the starting rate. It's an association unless the promotion was randomised.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you handle different observation periods?

Add log(exposure) as an offset, with its coefficient fixed at 1. The model then predicts a rate per unit of exposure. Without it, shops observed for longer would simply look busier.

#### The 30-second answer

A GLM has three parts: a distribution for the outcome, a linear score, and a link between them. Linear regression is normal with an identity link, and logistic regression is Bernoulli with a logit. For counts, I'd use Poisson with a log link: predictions stay positive, and each coefficient multiplies the rate by e to the b. I'd add log exposure as an offset if observation time differs, and check for overdispersion, which makes standard errors too small. If there is, I'd use negative binomial.

**Key terms and sources**

One framework for linear, logistic and Poisson regression: a distribution, a link and a linear score, plus exposure and overdispersion. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [ISLR, including Poisson regression](https://www.statlearning.com/)

- [scikit-learn on generalized linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html#generalized-linear-models)

- [CS229 syllabus](https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-summer2019.html)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Decision Trees

> How does a tree choose its questions, and why does a deep tree memorise noise?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Tree-based models
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/decision-trees/
- Quiz topic: `trees`

## Intuition

### The situation

A lender wants loan rules it can read, learned from 160 past borrowers. The interviewer asks:

> How does a decision tree choose its splits?

**Running example:** a lender's loan book, simulated: 160 past borrowers with annual income (₹ lakh) and credit score, and whether they repaid. The true rule is a mix of thresholds, plus 10% label noise (people are unpredictable). Test accuracy is measured on 600 new applicants. A second, 1-D example (delivery time vs distance) shows regression trees.

#### A loan officer's rules, learned from data

An experienced loan officer thinks in rules: "score above 690 and income above ₹6 lakh: approve; score above 780: approve almost regardless; otherwise, be careful." A linear model can't express "and" and "otherwise" without hand-built features. A decision tree learns exactly this kind of nested rule directly from past borrowers, and you can print it and read it.

### The idea

Think of a game of twenty questions. Each yes-or-no question splits the group, and you always ask whichever question leaves each side the least mixed. Then you repeat on each side.

[Figure: A small decision tree. First question: credit score above 690? If no, be careful. If yes, a second question: income above 6 lakh? Yes means approve, no means be careful.]

_Illustrative, based on the lesson's loan officer rules._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the threshold until the weighted Gini is as low as you can get it, then snap to the best split. Then switch to the other feature.

#### Move the threshold, watch the impurity

The algorithm does exactly this for every feature, sorts the values once, and sweeps the threshold, which costs about O(features × n log n) per level [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). Then it recurses on each child.

Information gain is mutual information between a split and the label.

**Now say why:** why does the algorithm prefer this threshold, and which feature would it choose first?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions ("credit score > 690?", "income > ₹6 lakh?") and predicts the majority class (or the mean value) of whatever ends up in each leaf. It's built **greedily**: at every node, try every feature and threshold and keep the split that most reduces **impurity** (Gini, entropy, or squared error). Grown fully, a tree memorises the training data, so you limit depth, require minimum leaf sizes, or **prune**. Trees are readable, need almost no preprocessing, and handle non-linear patterns; they're also unstable and blocky, and those weaknesses are exactly what Random Forest and Gradient Boosting fix. What you'll be able to do after this: compute a split by hand, explain Gini vs entropy, show why a deep tree overfits, describe pruning, and say what trees are bad at.

#### Nodes, splits, leaves, and impurity

A **node** holds some borrowers and asks one question about one feature: xj ≤ t? Yes goes left, no goes right. A **leaf** stops asking and predicts the share of repayers there (classification) or the mean target (regression). To choose questions, we need a number for how mixed a node is, its impurity. For a node where a share p repaid:

$$ {H_{\text{Gini}} = \textstyle\sum_k p_k(1-p_k)} \qquad {H_{\text{ent}} = -\textstyle\sum_k p_k\log p_k} \qquad {H_{\text{MSE}} = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum (y-\bar y)^2} $$

scikit-learn's impurity definitions [tree guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

- **Gini impurity**: Σ p_k(1 − p_k) over classes. The chance two randomly drawn borrowers from this node have different labels. 0 when pure; 0.5 at a 50/50 mix (two classes).

- **entropy**: −Σ p_k log p_k. Bits of surprise. 0 when pure; 1 bit at 50/50. Splitting on entropy “is equivalent to minimizing the log loss” (scikit-learn).

- **regression: squared error**: For numeric targets: the variance of the target in the node. A leaf predicts the mean, which minimises it.

All three are 0 for a pure node and peak at 50/50. Gini and entropy are curved (strictly concave), so a split that makes one child purer always reduces them a bit; plain misclassification error is flat-sided and often can't tell good splits apart. Gini and entropy almost always pick the same split; Gini is slightly cheaper (no logarithm).

#### Greedily pick the split that reduces impurity the most

$$ {G(\theta)} = {\tfrac{n_{L}}{n}}\,{H(Q_L)} + {\tfrac{n_{R}}{n}}\,{H(Q_R)}, \qquad {\theta^{*} = \arg\min_{\theta=(j,t)} G(\theta)} $$

scikit-learn's formulation [tree guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). Greedy because finding the globally best tree "is known to be NP-complete", so practical algorithms choose the locally best split at each node.

- **split quality**: The impurity after the split: the children's impurities, weighted by how many borrowers go to each. Lower is better.

- **left share**: Fraction of the node's borrowers that answer yes (x_j ≤ t).

- **left impurity**: How mixed the yes-group is.

- **right share**: Fraction that answer no.

- **right impurity**: How mixed the no-group is.

- **the chosen split**: Try every feature j and every threshold t between sorted values; keep the one with the lowest G. Information gain is just parent impurity minus G.

#### Grow big, then cut back the weakest branches

Stopping rules (max depth, min leaf size) decide early and can miss a useful split hiding behind a weak one. CART's alternative: grow a large tree, then prune it with **minimal cost-complexity pruning**:

$$ {R_\alpha(T)} = {R(T)} + {\alpha}\,{|\widetilde{T}|} $$

scikit-learn: "A non-terminal node with the smallest value of αeff is the weakest link and will be pruned" [tree guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). Choose α by cross-validation (scikit-learn's `cost_complexity_pruning_path` lists the candidate α values).

- **penalised risk**: What pruning minimises: the tree's error plus a price per leaf.

- **the tree's error**: Total impurity (or misclassification) of the leaves on the training data.

- **price per leaf**: α ≥ 0 (ccp_alpha in scikit-learn). α = 0 keeps the full tree; a large α prunes it to a stump.

- **number of leaves**: |T̃|: more leaves, more penalty. Branches whose improvement is worth less than α per extra leaf get cut, weakest link first.

#### Predict numbers with a staircase

Delivery time vs distance with a rush-hour bump around 6 km (simulated). Split by squared error; each leaf predicts the mean of its points, so the fit is a step function. Depth 3–4 follows the bump; depth 10 chases noise. Beyond 10 km the tree just repeats its last step: trees "are not good at extrapolation" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### CART, ID3, C4.5

| Algorithm | Splits | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **ID3** (Quinlan, 1986) | Multi-way, categorical features only | Information gain (entropy) |
| **C4.5 / C5.0** (Quinlan) | Multi-way; discretises continuous features | Gain ratio; converts trees to if–then rule sets |
| **CART** (Breiman et al., 1984) | Always binary | Gini or entropy for classification, squared error for regression; cost-complexity pruning. scikit-learn "uses an optimized version of the CART algorithm" |

Summary from scikit-learn's tree guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). Every modern tree ensemble (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) is built on CART-style binary trees.

#### Scaling, categories, missing values, importance

##### No scaling needed

Splits compare a feature with a threshold, so any monotonic transform (log, standardise) gives the same tree. Trees "require little data preparation" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

##### Categorical features

CART can split a category set into two groups; scikit-learn's trees currently need encoding (one-hot or ordinal). LightGBM, CatBoost and scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting handle categories natively.

##### Missing values

scikit-learn trees support NaN with `splitter='best'`: the training split decides which side missing values go to; if none were seen, they go "to the child with the most samples" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

##### Feature importance

Impurity-based importance (total impurity decrease per feature) is free but biased toward high-cardinality features and computed on training data. Prefer permutation importance on held-out data for decisions.

#### Training a single tree you can trust

1. Start shallow (scikit-learn suggests `max_depth=3`) to read the structure.

2. Tune max_depth, min_samples_leaf (try 5) or ccp_alpha with cross-validation.

3. For imbalanced classes, use class weights or balanced sampling; trees "create biased trees if some classes dominate".

4. Inspect: print the rules (`export_text`), check that the splits make domain sense.

5. If accuracy matters more than one readable tree, move to an ensemble: Random Forest (variance) or Gradient Boosting (bias).

#### A single tree, or something else?

##### Use a single tree when

- The rules themselves are the product (eligibility checks, triage guidelines)

- You need a quick, explainable baseline

- Regulation demands a transparent model and a small tree is accurate enough

##### Use an ensemble when

- Accuracy matters most: gradient boosting is the tabular default

- You want robustness with little tuning: Random Forest

- Smooth or linear relationships: consider linear models too

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Keep splitting until every leaf is pure"

With enough questions you can isolate every borrower in their own leaf: 100% training accuracy. But 10% of the labels are noise, so a tree that fits every point has memorised the noise. In the lab below, training accuracy climbs to 100% as depth grows, while test accuracy peaks at depth 4 (≈ 84.5%) and then falls. scikit-learn: decision trees "can create over-complex trees that do not generalize the data well. This is called overfitting" [tree guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

#### Each split adds a rectangle

Every boundary is horizontal or vertical: each split looks at one feature. Deep trees carve tiny boxes around single noisy borrowers. Raising min_samples_leaf (no leaf may hold fewer than m borrowers) is a gentler brake than capping depth; scikit-learn suggests "min_samples_leaf=5 as an initial value" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html).

#### A slightly different sample, a different tree

–

Four samples of 160 borrowers from the same population, a depth-4 tree on each. The top split stays near a credit score of 690, but the lower boxes move around a lot. scikit-learn: "small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree being generated. This problem is mitigated by using decision trees within an ensemble" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). High variance is the price of flexibility, and averaging many trees (Random Forest) is the cure.

#### Strengths and weaknesses, side by side

##### Strengths

- Readable rules ("white box")

- Captures interactions and thresholds automatically

- No scaling; mixed feature types; fast prediction (O(depth))

- The building block of the strongest tabular models

##### Weaknesses

- Overfits unless constrained

- Unstable: small data changes, different tree

- Axis-aligned, blocky boundaries; a diagonal boundary needs many steps

- Can't extrapolate; struggles with XOR / parity-type patterns

## Say it

### How does a decision tree choose its splits?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

Gini vs entropy?

Both are concave impurity measures that are 0 for pure nodes and maximal at a uniform mix; they choose the same split in most cases. Gini is slightly faster (no log); entropy corresponds to minimising log-loss. Misclassification rate is a poor splitting criterion because it's not strictly concave.

Follow-up 2 of 5

Why are trees greedy, and what's the downside?

Finding the optimal tree is NP-complete, so each split is chosen locally. A split that looks useless alone (XOR) can enable great splits below it, and greedy search misses it.

Follow-up 3 of 5

How do you stop a tree from overfitting?

Pre-pruning (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, min_impurity_decrease) or post-pruning (cost-complexity with ccp_alpha), chosen by cross-validation, or ensembles.

Follow-up 4 of 5

Do trees need feature scaling? Can they handle missing values?

No scaling: splits are threshold comparisons, invariant to monotonic transforms. Modern implementations (recent scikit-learn trees, XGBoost, LightGBM, HistGradientBoosting) learn which branch missing values take.

Follow-up 5 of 5

What's the complexity?

Training about O(features × n log n) per level; prediction O(depth), about O(log n) for a balanced tree.

#### The 30-second answer

A decision tree recursively splits the data with yes/no questions on single features. At each node it greedily picks the feature and threshold that most reduce impurity (Gini or entropy for classification, squared error for regression), and leaves predict the majority class or mean. Fully grown trees overfit, so we limit depth, set a minimum leaf size, or use cost-complexity pruning tuned by cross-validation. Trees are interpretable and need no scaling, but they're unstable, blocky and can't extrapolate, which is why we usually use them inside ensembles like random forests or gradient boosting.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Trees find the optimal decision rules." They find greedy, locally optimal splits.

- "Impurity-based importance tells you causal impact." It's biased and descriptive only.

- "Deeper is better." Train accuracy, yes; test accuracy usually not.

**Key terms and sources**

CART, Gini and entropy, pruning, regression trees · built from scikit-learn's tree guide, Breiman et al. (1984) and Quinlan (ID3/C4.5) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Impurity** | How mixed a node is: Gini, entropy, or squared error. |
| **Information gain** | Parent impurity − weighted child impurity. |
| **CART** | Classification and Regression Trees: binary splits, Gini/MSE, cost-complexity pruning. |
| **max_depth / min_samples_leaf** | Pre-pruning limits on tree size. |
| **Cost-complexity pruning** | Minimise error + α × leaves; post-pruning. |
| **Stump** | A depth-1 tree: one split. The classic boosting weak learner. |

#### What this page is built from

1. scikit-learn, [Decision Trees user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html) (formulation, criteria, pruning, complexity, missing values, ID3/C4.5/CART, practical tips).

2. L. Breiman, J. Friedman, R. Olshen & C. Stone, _Classification and Regression Trees_, Wadsworth, 1984 (CART, cost-complexity pruning; background).

3. J. R. Quinlan, "Induction of decision trees", _Machine Learning_ 1 (1986) (ID3); _C4.5: Programs for Machine Learning_, 1993 (background).

4. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, _The Elements of Statistical Learning_, §9.2 (tree-based methods; background).

Loan and delivery data are simulated with fixed seeds; every tree on this page is grown live in your browser by a small CART implementation (exhaustive search over midpoints).

# Random Forest

> How do many wobbly trees make one steady prediction?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Tree-based models
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/random-forest/
- Before this: Decision Trees (`fundamentals/decision-trees`)
- Quiz topic: `trees`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your deep decision tree changes completely when a single applicant is relabelled. The interviewer asks:

> How does a random forest improve on one deep tree?

#### Eight loan applicants, four features

Everything on this page uses the same tiny dataset. A bank wants to predict whether an applicant will repay. The numbers are made up for teaching , but the labs in this lesson run real computations on them.

| # | credit score | income (k/mo) | debt ratio | years at job | repaid? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

One feature, credit score, separates these eight perfectly (650 and below never repaid). Remember that; it is what makes plain bagging fail, as The answer that sounds right shows.

#### One decision tree is sharp but unstable

A decision tree asks yes/no questions about features until it reaches a leaf with an answer. Grown deep, it fits its training data almost perfectly, so its bias is low. The catch is variance: scikit-learn's own docs warn that "small variations in the data might result in a completely different tree being generated" [sklearn trees](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html). Watch it happen with one relabelled applicant.

1. Trained on the eight rows, the best first question is "credit ≤ 650?". It splits the data perfectly.

2. Now relabel one applicant, #6, from not repaid to repaid. Nothing else changes.

3. The tree's first question flips to a different feature entirely, "debt ratio ≤ 0.42?", because that is now the perfect split.

4. Ask both trees about a new applicant with credit 640 and a debt ratio of 0.20. They disagree.

5. That is high variance: the model's answer depends heavily on which exact rows it happened to see.

High variance means the error you see on new data is mostly noise from the particular sample, not a lack of capacity. The classic fix for variance is averaging. The rest of the page is about how to average trees so that it actually works.

### The idea

Think of asking a crowd for an estimate. A crowd only beats one person if people make different mistakes, because mistakes that differ cancel out. A forest makes its trees disagree: each one sees different rows, and each split sees only a few features.

[Figure: Three different trees built from different rows and features. Two vote yes and one votes no, and the forest's combined answer is yes.]

_Illustrative. Different rows and features make the trees disagree, and the combined answer is steadier._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the correlation between trees to 0.9 and add as many trees as you can. Then lower the correlation.

#### Averaging only cancels mistakes that differ

Here is the one equation the whole method follows from. Average B trees whose predictions each have variance σ² and are correlated with each other by ρ [ESL Eq. 15.1, p. 588](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/):

$$ {\mathrm{Var}\big(\bar f\,\big)} = {{\rho}\,\sigma^{2}} + {\frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^{2}} $$

Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, _Elements of Statistical Learning_, §15.2 · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **error from wobble**: The variance of the averaged prediction: how much the forest’s answer would wobble if you redrew the training data. This is the part averaging can shrink.

- **the floor**: ρσ² does not depend on B. However many trees you add, this part stays. If the trees are perfectly correlated (ρ = 1), averaging gives exactly one tree’s variance.

- **shrinks with trees**: (1 − ρ)σ²/B goes to zero as B grows. This is the only part that more trees can remove.

- **correlation**: So the lever is ρ. Lower the correlation between trees and the floor drops. That is the entire reason random forests add randomness.

Set ρ to 0.9 (very similar trees, like plain bagging with one dominant feature) and B to 500: the variance only drops to about 0.9. Set ρ to 0.3: it drops to about 0.3. The forest's job is to **lower ρ without making each tree much worse**. Breiman calls these two quantities the correlation and the strength of the trees, and the random-features section shows his bound with both.

Why only variance? Bagged trees are identically distributed, so the average has the same bias as one tree. ESL: "the only hope of improvement is through variance reduction" ESL p. 588. That is also why forests use deep, low-bias trees.

**Now say why:** why can't more trees fix high correlation, and what does a forest do to lower it?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A single decision tree is accurate on the data it saw but changes wildly when the data changes a little. A random forest grows hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows and each choosing every split from a random handful of features, then lets them vote. The randomness makes the trees disagree, and averaging trees that disagree cancels their mistakes. After this you can derive why it works (the variance formula), explain every knob (n_estimators, max_features, bootstrap, oob_score), and answer the usual interview follow-ups.

#### Gini impurity: how mixed is a group?

At each node, a tree (CART, which scikit-learn implements) tries every feature and every threshold, and keeps the split whose two children are the least mixed. Mixedness is measured with Gini impurity: 0 when a group is all one class, 0.5 when two classes are 50/50 [sklearn §1.10.7](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#classification-criteria).

$$ {G(\theta)} = {\tfrac{n_{L}}{n}}\,{H(L)} + {\tfrac{n_{R}}{n}}\,H(R),\qquad {H(Q)=\sum_k p_k\,(1-p_k)} $$

scikit-learn's mathematical formulation for classification trees [sklearn §1.10.7](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#mathematical-formulation) · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **split score**: G is the score of one candidate split: lower is better. The tree computes it for every feature and threshold and keeps the minimum.

- **share going left**: The fraction of the node’s rows that answer yes and go to the left child.

- **left impurity**: How mixed the left child is. Each child is weighted by its size, so a tiny pure child does not count as much as a big one.

- **share going right**: The same for the right child. The two weights add up to 1.

- **Gini of a group**: For one group: add up p(1 − p) over the classes, where p is the share of each class. All one class gives 0; half and half gives 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5.

##### Try it on the eight applicants

Try every feature: only credit score reaches 0. A greedy tree will always take it first, and that is about to matter.

#### Every tree trains on a resampled copy of the data

1. Start with the N = 8 training rows.

2. Draw 8 rows at random, putting each one back before the next draw. scikit-learn does exactly this with `randint(0, n, n)` [_forest.py](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py).

3. Some rows get picked twice or more, so this tree effectively weights them more.

4. Some rows are never picked. They are "out of bag" for this tree, which gives a free test set (see the out-of-bag section).

How many rows does a tree miss? Each draw misses a given row with probability 1 − 1/N, and there are N independent draws:

$$ {P(\text{row never drawn})} = {\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\Big)}^{{N}} \;\longrightarrow\; {e^{-1}\approx 0.368} $$

Standard bootstrap result; Breiman: "about one-third of the instances are left out" [Breiman 2001, p. 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=8).

- **chance a row is left out**: The probability that one particular row never appears in the bootstrap sample.

- **miss once**: On a single draw, N rows are equally likely, so this row is missed with probability 1 − 1/N.

- **N draws**: The N draws are independent, so the misses multiply: raise it to the power N.

- **about 36.8%**: As N grows this tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368. So each tree sees about 63.2% of the distinct rows, and about a third are out of bag, exactly Breiman’s “about one-third”.

##### Why keep bootstrapping once features are random?

Breiman gives two reasons: bagging "seems to enhance accuracy when random features are used", and the left-out rows give running estimates of error, strength and correlation [p. 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=8). scikit-learn: `bootstrap=True` by default; turn it off and every tree sees all rows (as Extra-Trees do).

#### Hide the star feature sometimes

This is the move that turns bagging into a random forest. Before each split, the tree may only look at m features drawn at random from all p. It picks the best split among those m, and the next node draws a fresh m [ESL Alg. 15.1](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/).

1. At the root, the tree could consider all four features, and credit score would win every time.

2. Instead, draw m of them at random. Here m = 2, and credit score is not among them.

3. The node splits on the best of what it was offered. It is a weaker split than credit score, on purpose.

4. Every child node draws its own fresh m. Credit score will still be used, just not always first, and not always in the same place.

5. That forced variety is what lowers the correlation ρ between trees.

##### Check it: grow 60 trees with m features per split

Same experiment as the bagging lab in The answer that sounds right, but now you choose m. With m = 4 it is plain bagging. Watch the first-split feature spread out as m drops.

##### The trade-off, in Breiman's own bound

Lower m means less correlated trees, but each tree is also a bit weaker. The authors put it plainly: "Reducing m reduces both the correlation and the strength" [Breiman & Cutler](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests/cc_home.htm). Breiman's Theorem 2.3 bounds the forest's error with exactly these two numbers:

$$ {PE^{*}} \;\le\; {\frac{{\bar\rho}\,\big(1-{s}^{2}\big)}{{s}^{2}}} $$

Breiman 2001, Theorem 2.3 [p. 6](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=6). He adds that the bound "is likely to be loose".

- **forest error**: PE* is the forest’s generalization error: the chance it misclassifies a new example.

- **mean correlation**: ρ̄ is the average correlation between trees (of their margins). Random features push this down.

- **strength**: s is the strength: on average, how much more often the trees vote for the right class than for the best wrong class. Stronger trees push the bound down.

- **the c/s² ratio**: Breiman’s summary: the ratio correlation / strength² should be small. The bound is loose, but it says what to aim for.

##### What m to use

| Source | Classification | Regression |
|---|---|---|
| Inventors' recommendation (via ESL) | ⌊√p⌋, min node size 1 | ⌊p/3⌋, min node size 5 |
| scikit-learn default | "sqrt" | 1.0 = all features (plain bagging) |
| Breiman's 2001 experiments | m = 1 and m = ⌊log₂p + 1⌋, picked by out-of-bag error | |

Sources: ESL §15.3, p. 592; [sklearn ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#random-forests), which also notes 0.3 "is a typical default in the literature" for regression; Breiman p. 9.

##### It is not very sensitive to m

Across Breiman's 20 datasets, the average absolute difference in test error between m = 1 and the larger m was under 1%. "It was surprising that using a single randomly chosen input variable to split on at each node could produce good accuracy" [p. 11](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=11). ESL adds that the best m is problem-dependent and worth tuning (their Figure 15.3: m = 6 beats the default 2).

##### What breaks without it

Set m = p and you are back to bagging: scikit-learn calls `max_features=1.0` "equivalent to bagged trees". On data with one dominant feature, like ours, the trees stay correlated and the variance floor ρσ² stays high.

#### Vote, or average the probabilities

For regression the forest averages the trees' numbers. For classification the original paper lets each tree cast one vote [Def. 1.1, p. 2](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=2).

$$ {\hat f^{\,B}_{\mathrm{rf}}(x)} = {\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}}\,{T(x;\,{\Theta_b})} $$

ESL Eq. 15.2, p. 589 · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **forest prediction**: The random forest’s prediction at input x, using B trees.

- **average over trees**: Add up the B trees’ outputs and divide by B. Every tree counts equally; no tree is trusted more than another.

- **one tree**: T(x; Θ_b) is tree number b’s output for x.

- **its randomness**: Θ_b holds everything random about tree b: which rows it drew and which features each split was offered.

Here is a detail many explanations miss: **scikit-learn does not take a majority vote.** Its classifier averages each tree's predicted class probabilities ("in contrast to the original publication") [sklearn ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#random-forests); the code divides the summed `predict_proba` by the number of trees [_forest.py](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py). Usually they agree. Not always:

##### Do more trees overfit?

No. Breiman's Theorem 1.2: as trees are added the error converges to a limit, "this result explains why random forests do not overfit as more trees are added" [p. 4](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=4). More trees only cost time.

##### But the forest itself can still overfit

ESL is careful here: adding trees does not overfit, but the limit, an average of fully grown trees, "can overfit the data" and "incur unnecessary variance"; controlling depth gives small gains in some studies, though full trees "seldom cost much" ESL §15.3.4, p. 596. The authors' site says "Random forests does not overfit" [Breiman & Cutler](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests/cc_home.htm). Both are right about different things: B does not overfit; depth and leaf size can.

#### Every row is a test row for about a third of the trees

1. Take one training row, applicant #2.

2. Look at the forest. Each tree trained on its own bootstrap sample, so some trees saw #2 and some did not.

3. Let only the trees that never saw #2 predict it. For them, #2 is genuinely new data.

4. Do this for every row and compare with the truth. That error rate is the out-of-bag (OOB) error, a test-set estimate without holding any data back.

Breiman cites evidence that the OOB estimate "is as accurate as using a test set of the same size as the training set", and notes it is unbiased once you run past the point where the error has converged [p. 8](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=8). ESL: almost identical to N-fold cross-validation, so you can stop adding trees once OOB error stabilizes ESL §15.3.1, p. 592. In scikit-learn: `oob_score=True`, available only with `bootstrap=True`.

#### Shuffle a column and see how much worse it gets

1. Measure the fitted forest's error on rows it did not train on (out-of-bag or a validation set).

2. Randomly shuffle one feature's column. This breaks its link to the label but keeps its distribution.

3. If error jumps, the model leaned on that feature. The numbers here are illustrative.

4. If error barely moves, the model did not need it. Repeat for every feature.

$$ {i_j} = {s} - {\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} s_{k,j}} $$

[sklearn permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html); Breiman's original version permutes each variable in the out-of-bag rows [p. 19](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=19).

- **importance of feature j**: How much the score drops when feature j is scrambled.

- **original score**: The model’s score on the data with nothing shuffled.

- **average over K shuffles**: Shuffle column j K times (scikit-learn’s n_repeats) and average the scores, so one lucky shuffle does not decide.

| | Impurity importance (MDI) · `feature_importances_` | Permutation importance |
|---|---|---|
| Computed from | how much each feature's splits reduced Gini, on the training data | score drop when the feature is shuffled, on held-out data |
| Speed | free, already computed | needs extra predictions (K × features) |
| Known bias | favours features with many unique values; can rank useless features high when the model overfits | correlated features share the credit, so both can look unimportant |

##### Do not trust the default bar chart blindly

scikit-learn: impurity-based importances "favor high cardinality features" and are computed on training data, so they "do not necessarily inform us on which features are most important" for new data [sklearn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#feature-importance-evaluation). Strobl et al. (2007) showed the measures are unreliable when predictors differ in scale or number of categories, and a 2008 follow-up found bias toward correlated predictors [Strobl 2007](https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2105-8-25). For correlated features, scikit-learn suggests clustering them and keeping one per cluster.

To explain a model properly, see SHAP, permutation importance and partial dependence. To compare combination methods, see ensembles.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Everything in one picture

1. Start with N training rows and p features.

2. Make B bootstrap samples, one per tree.

3. Grow each tree to full depth on its sample, offering only m random features at every split. Trees are independent, so they train in parallel (`n_jobs`).

4. To predict, run the input down every tree and combine: vote (paper) or average probabilities (scikit-learn); average for regression.

5. The rows each tree left out give the OOB error and permutation importances for free.

6. That is the whole method. Every piece exists to keep the trees strong but decorrelated.

#### When to use it

**Reach for it** as a strong, low-effort baseline on tabular data, when you want a built-in validation score (OOB), robustness to label noise, and trivial parallelism. **Look elsewhere** when the last point of accuracy matters (try gradient boosting), when you must extrapolate beyond the training range, or when the data are images, text or audio.

### The answer that sounds right

#### Just average many trees? They come out the same

Idea one: train 100 trees and average them. On the same data, a tree-growing algorithm with no randomness builds the same tree 100 times. The average of 100 identical answers is that answer.

Idea two, bagging (Breiman, 1996): give each tree a different bootstrap sample, the rows drawn at random with replacement [Breiman 1996](https://statistics.berkeley.edu/node/1781). Better, but there is a trap. When one feature is much stronger than the rest, most samples still split on it first, so the trees stay similar.

1. Bootstrap sample 1 repeats row 1 and leaves out row 3. Its best first split is still credit score.

2. Sample 2 is different again. The threshold moves a little, from 670 to 655, but the question is the same.

3. Sample 3: same story. Credit score separates any sample of these rows perfectly, so it usually wins. Only now and then does a sample happen to let another feature tie.

4. The trees make the same mistakes on the same applicants. Averaging only helps when their mistakes differ.

##### Check it yourself: grow 60 bagged trees

This grows 60 one-split trees, each on its own bootstrap sample, letting every split consider all four features (that is plain bagging). It counts which feature each tree splits on first.

#### The lesson, and where it bends

**The lesson.** Averaging reduces variance only as far as the averaged models disagree. A random forest is a recipe for cheap disagreement: random rows per tree, random features per split, deep trees that are individually low-bias. Everything else (OOB error, importance, parallelism) falls out of that design.

- **It does not reduce bias.** The average has a single tree's bias, so if deep trees cannot represent the pattern, more trees will not help (ESL p. 588).

- **Default importances mislead.** Use permutation importance on held-out data, and watch correlated features.

- **Regression forests cannot extrapolate.** Every leaf predicts an average of training targets, so the forest never predicts beyond the range of y it saw.

- **Size and latency.** Hundreds of deep trees take memory and per-prediction time; limit depth or leaf size if it matters (sklearn).

- **Usually behind tuned boosting on accuracy** in recent tabular benchmarks, but far less sensitive to settings.

##### What came after

**Extra-Trees** (Geurts et al., 2006) go further: random features and random thresholds, and by default no bootstrap, trading a bit more bias for a bit less variance [Geurts 2006](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-006-6226-1). **Gradient boosting** (XGBoost, LightGBM) takes AdaBoost's sequential route and now usually leads tabular benchmarks.

## Say it

### How does a random forest improve on one deep tree?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 7

Why random features at each split, isn't bootstrapping enough?

Bootstrapping alone (bagging) still lets one strong feature win the top split in almost every tree, so trees stay correlated and the ρσ² floor stays high. Hiding features at random forces different trees to use different structure, lowering ρ. The bagging and random-features labs show it on our data.

Follow-up 2 of 7

Random forest vs gradient boosting?

Forest: deep trees trained independently and in parallel, averaged; reduces variance; few hyperparameters; robust to label noise. Boosting: shallow trees trained sequentially, each correcting the last; reduces bias; usually more accurate when tuned, but more sensitive to settings and noise (Breiman's Table 4 shows AdaBoost's sensitivity).

Follow-up 3 of 7

Does adding more trees overfit?

No: error converges as trees are added (Breiman Thm 1.2), more trees only cost time. But the forest can still overfit through very deep trees; that is controlled with depth or leaf size, not tree count (ESL §15.3.4).

Follow-up 4 of 7

What is OOB error, and why about 37%?

Each bootstrap sample misses a row with probability (1 − 1/N)^N → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. Predicting each row with only the trees that never saw it gives a test-like error estimate, close to N-fold cross-validation, without a holdout.

Follow-up 5 of 7

How would you choose max_features?

Start from the defaults (√p classification; scikit-learn uses all features for regression, the literature often ⌊p/3⌋ or 0.3). Smaller m → more decorrelated but weaker trees. Tune it with OOB or cross-validated score; Breiman found results fairly insensitive to it.

Follow-up 6 of 7

Which feature importance would you trust?

Permutation importance on held-out data. The default impurity-based importance is computed on training data and favours high-cardinality features. With correlated features, both methods split the credit, so group correlated features first.

Follow-up 7 of 7

Does a random forest need feature scaling?

No. Splits compare a feature with a threshold, so any monotone rescaling of a feature gives the same splits.

#### The 30-second answer

"A random forest is many deep decision trees whose predictions are averaged. A single deep tree has low bias but high variance. Averaging reduces variance, but only if the trees make different mistakes, so the forest decorrelates them two ways: each tree trains on a bootstrap sample of the rows, and each split only considers a random subset of features. That keeps a dominant feature from making every tree the same. Bonus: the rows each tree didn't see give a free out-of-bag error estimate. The trade-off: it reduces variance, not bias, and tuned boosting often beats it on accuracy."

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Problem: a deep tree overfits and is unstable; change a few rows and you get a different tree. Intuition: average many trees, like asking many people and taking the majority, which only helps if they think independently. Mechanism: (1) B bootstrap samples, (2) grow each tree deep, at every split choosing among m random features (√p for classification), (3) vote or average. Why it works: the variance of an average is ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, so more trees remove the second term and random features lower ρ, the floor. Evidence: Breiman's 2001 paper matched AdaBoost across 20 datasets while being far more robust to label noise. Limitation: no bias reduction, biased default importances, no extrapolation.

#### What not to say

- "Random forests can't overfit." Say: more trees don't overfit; deep trees still can.

- "Random forest reduces bias." It reduces variance; bias stays at the level of one tree.

- "It picks random features per tree." That is Ho's random subspace method; random forests resample features at every split.

- "scikit-learn takes a majority vote." It averages class probabilities.

- "feature_importances_ tells you what matters." Only with caveats; prefer permutation importance.

**Key terms and sources**

Leo Breiman's 2001 method, as it runs in scikit-learn today · 16 sources · checked 27 Oct 2026

#### Five ways people already randomized ensembles

Breiman's paper opens by listing the tricks it builds on [Breiman 2001, p. 1–2](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=1). Each injects randomness somewhere different.

1. Bagging (Breiman, 1996): each tree sees a bootstrap sample of the rows, then they vote.

2. AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire, 1996) takes the opposite road. No randomness: each new tree focuses on the rows the previous ones got wrong. It was the accuracy leader at the time.

3. Three ideas randomize the features instead: Amit and Geman searched a random set of features at each node, Ho gave each whole tree a random feature subset, and Dietterich picked randomly among the K best splits. Breiman says Amit and Geman most shaped his thinking.

4. The random forest combines bagging with a fresh random feature subset at every single split, and grows each tree to full depth without pruning.

Before random forests, these randomized ensembles were less accurate than AdaBoost: Breiman notes that random split selection beats bagging, "but none of these three forests do as well as Adaboost" [Breiman 2001, p. 7](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=7). Closing that gap was the goal.

#### Does it work?

##### One tree vs forest vs AdaBoost (Breiman, 2001)

Test-set error, lower is better. Forest-RI with 100 trees; AdaBoost with 50; m chosen by out-of-bag error between 1 and ⌊log₂p + 1⌋; "one tree" is the average single tree in the forest [Table 2, p. 10–11](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=10).

The forest cuts the average single tree's error by about 1.8× (glass) to 9× (vowel) and matches AdaBoost, beating it on some datasets and trailing on others. Across all 20 datasets in the table the two stay within a few points of each other.

##### With 5% of labels flipped

Breiman flipped 5% of the training labels and measured how much each method's test error rose [Table 4, p. 16](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=16):

| Dataset | AdaBoost | Random forest |
|---|---|---|
| breast cancer | +43.2% | +1.8% |
| votes | +48.9% | +6.3% |
| ionosphere | +27.7% | +3.8% |
| soybean | +26.9% | +3.2% |

These are 4 of the table's 9 datasets, where AdaBoost suffered most. The effect was small on glass (+1.6%), and on ecoli AdaBoost (+7.5%) was slightly better than the forest (+7.9%).

Why: AdaBoost keeps raising the weight of rows it gets wrong, and mislabelled rows are always wrong, so it "will concentrate increasing weight on these noisy instances and become warped". A forest weights no row specially.

##### Fast, too

Each split searches only m features. On the zip-code data with m = 1, 100 forest trees took 4.0 minutes versus almost three hours for 50 AdaBoost trees, about 40× faster (a 250 MHz Mac in 2000) [p. 11](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf#page=11).

##### Update · my check (27 Oct 2026)

Twenty-five years on, tree ensembles still do well on tables. A 45-dataset NeurIPS 2022 benchmark found tree-based models such as XGBoost and random forests remain state of the art on medium-sized (~10K rows) tabular data, ahead of deep learning [Grinsztajn et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.08815). The NeurIPS 2025 TabArena benchmark finds gradient-boosted trees still strong, deep models catching up with large tuning budgets, and TabPFNv2 excelling on small datasets (≤10K rows) [TabArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16791). In those benchmarks, tuned boosting usually edges out random forests on accuracy; forests win on how little tuning they need. A review of RF tuning agrees the defaults "work reasonably well" in most cases, with tuning adding some gains [Probst et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.03515).

#### Key terms

Bootstrap sample

N rows drawn with replacement from N; about 63.2% distinct rows.

Bagging

Bootstrap aggregating: one model per bootstrap sample, then vote or average.

m / max_features / mtry

How many randomly chosen features each split may consider.

Out-of-bag (OOB)

Rows a tree did not train on; used to estimate test error and importance.

Strength (s)

How much more the trees vote for the right class than the best wrong one, on average.

Correlation (ρ)

How alike the trees' predictions or errors are. Lower is better for averaging.

Gini impurity

Σ p(1 − p): 0 for a pure node, 0.5 for a 50/50 two-class node.

MDI

Mean decrease in impurity, scikit-learn's default `feature_importances_`.
