# Naive Bayes

> Its core assumption is almost always wrong. Why does it still classify so well?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Other classic classifiers
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/naive-bayes/
- Before this: Probability Basics & Bayes' Rule (`fundamentals/probability-and-bayes`)
- Quiz topic: `clf`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're building a spam filter from 100 messages. Almost every message is unique, so you can't just count how often each whole message is spam. The interviewer asks:

> What is naive about naive Bayes?

**Running example:** a small spam filter. Its training mail has 40 spam and 60 ham messages, and a vocabulary of six words. The counts below are illustrative (made up to be easy to follow), and every probability on the page is computed live from them. Later chapters use simulated numeric data for Gaussian naive Bayes.

#### Reverse the question

| word | free | win | offer | meeting | project | lunch | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **count in spam** | 30 | 20 | 25 | 2 | 3 | 0 | 80 |
| **count in ham** | 4 | 1 | 5 | 30 | 35 | 25 | 100 |

We want P(spam | this message). That's hard to estimate directly: almost every message is unique. The reverse is easy to count: how often does the word "free" appear in spam? Bayes' rule turns the easy direction into the one we need. The only obstacle is that a message has many words, and counting every combination of words is hopeless. Naive Bayes removes that obstacle with one bold assumption.

### The idea

Think of a detective who treats every clue as if it were independent of the others. That's rarely true, because clues are often linked. But it makes the case easy to work through, and the detective usually names the right suspect, just with too much confidence.

[Figure: The words free, offer and meeting each multiply the spam score and the ham score separately, giving a 76 percent chance of spam.]

_From the lesson's spam example, with Laplace smoothing._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Build a message with the word "lunch" in it, and set the smoothing as low as it goes. Then raise it.

#### One unseen word must not veto everything

"lunch" never appeared in our spam, so the raw estimate P(lunch | spam) = 0/80 = 0. Any message containing "lunch" then gets P(spam) = 0, however spammy its other words. The fix is to add α imaginary occurrences of every word:

$$ {\hat\theta_{yi}} = ({N_{yi}} + {\alpha}) \,/\, ({N_y + \alpha n}) $$

scikit-learn: the smoothing priors "account for features not present in the learning samples and prevent zero probabilities" [naive Bayes guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).

- **smoothed estimate**: P(word i | class y) used by Multinomial naive Bayes.

- **count of word i in y**: How many times word i appeared in class-y training mail. 0 for lunch in spam.

- **pseudo-count**: α = 1 is Laplace smoothing; α < 1 is Lidstone smoothing. Treat it as a hyperparameter.

- **total words in y, plus α per word**: N_y + αn: n is the vocabulary size (6 here), so the probabilities still sum to 1.

Bars: each word's log-likelihood ratio, log P(word | spam) − log P(word | ham). Right = evidence for spam, left = for ham. Set α = 0 and pick "free win lunch".

With α = 0, "free win lunch" scores P(spam) = **0**, a certain "ham", even though two of its three words are strongly spammy: "lunch" vetoes the spam class. With α = 0.1 it's 0.41, and with Laplace α = 1 it's **0.76**. Words that are never seen in _either_ class at prediction time are simply skipped.

**Now say why:** why can one unseen word overrule everything else in the message?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Naive Bayes classifies by asking "which class makes this input most likely?", using Bayes' rule. It makes one big simplification: given the class, every feature is **independent**, so the likelihood is just a product of one-feature probabilities you can count from data. That makes it tiny, instant to train, and good with little data, which is why it was the classic spam filter. Two practical fixes are mandatory: **smoothing** (an unseen word must not zero out a class) and **log space** (products of many small numbers underflow). The independence assumption is almost always false, yet the **ranking** of classes often survives; the **probabilities** don't: they're pushed towards 0 and 1. What you'll be able to do after this: classify a message by hand, explain smoothing with a concrete failure, pick the right variant, and explain why naive Bayes can be accurate but badly calibrated.

#### Bayes' rule, term by term

$$ {P(y \mid x)} = {P(y)}\;{P(x \mid y)} \,/\, {P(x)} $$

- **posterior**: What we want: the probability the message is class y (spam or ham) given its words x.

- **prior**: How common the class is before reading anything: 40 of 100 training messages were spam, so P(spam) = 0.4.

- **likelihood**: How probable these words are if the message were class y. This is the part we have to model.

- **evidence**: P(x): the same for every class, so for choosing the class we can ignore it and just compare numerators.

#### Given the class, treat every feature as independent

$$ {\hat y} = \arg\max_y\ {P(y)}\ {\prod_{i=1}^{n}} {P(x_i \mid y)} $$

scikit-learn: naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem "with the 'naive' assumption of conditional independence between every pair of features given the value of the class variable" [naive Bayes guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).

- **predicted class**: Pick the class with the biggest score. P(x) is dropped because it's the same for all classes.

- **prior**: Class frequency in training data.

- **the naive product**: Instead of one impossible joint probability, multiply one small probability per feature. With 50,000 words that's 50,000 numbers per class instead of 2^50,000.

- **one-feature likelihood**: Estimated by counting: how often word i appears in class y. Gaussian NB uses a per-class mean and variance instead.

1. A new message with three words from our vocabulary.

2. Start each class with its prior: 40% of training mail was spam, 60% ham.

3. Multiply by P("free" | class). With Laplace smoothing (try it in the Play lab): spam (30 + 1)/(80 + 6), ham (4 + 1)/(100 + 6).

4. Then "offer" and "meeting", each as if it were independent of the others given the class.

5. Compare the two products. Divide each by their sum to get probabilities: about 0.76 spam. "free" and "offer" pull towards spam; "meeting" pulls hard towards ham.

#### Products underflow; sums don't

A 1,000-word email multiplies 1,000 probabilities, each maybe 0.001. The product, 10−3000, is far below the smallest positive double (about 10−308), so the computer stores 0 for both classes and can't compare them. Taking logs turns the product into a sum, which keeps the comparison exact:

$$ {\text{score}(y)} = {\log P(y)} + {\sum_{i} \log P(x_i \mid y)} $$

- **class score**: A log score per class: compare these, the biggest wins. Exponentiate and normalise (softmax) only if you want probabilities.

- **log prior**: log 0.4 for spam, log 0.6 for ham.

- **sum of log likelihoods**: Each word adds its log probability. The bars in the lab are differences of these terms between the two classes.

Seen this way, Multinomial naive Bayes is a **linear model** in the word counts: each word has a weight (its log probability per class). It's the same functional form as logistic regression; only the way the weights are found differs (counting vs optimising).

#### Gaussian naive Bayes: one bell curve per feature per class

$$ {P(x_i \mid y)} = {(2\pi\sigma_{y}^2)^{-1/2}}\ \exp\!\Bigl({-(x_i - \mu_{y})^2 / (2\sigma_{y}^2)}\Bigr) $$

scikit-learn's GaussianNB likelihood (σ and μ per class and feature) [naive Bayes guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).

- **one-feature likelihood**: For numeric feature i: how likely its value is under class y.

- **normaliser**: Makes the bell curve integrate to 1; it depends on the class variance.

- **squared distance from the class mean**: Measured in units of that class's standard deviation for this one feature. Means and variances are estimated by maximum likelihood.

Multiplying per-feature bell curves is a Gaussian with a **diagonal** covariance: its contours are ellipses aligned with the axes. It can't represent "these two features move together". Raise the correlation below and compare with a full-covariance Gaussian model (quadratic discriminant analysis), which can:

Shading: Gaussian NB's decision regions. Ellipses: the 2σ contour each model fits for each class (orange dashed = NB, axis-aligned; violet = full covariance). Simulated: 200 training and 4,000 test points.

With uncorrelated features both models score 76.1%. At correlation 0.95, naive Bayes gets **95.0%** and the full model **99.9%**: the classes are separated along a diagonal direction that only the correlation reveals. Naive Bayes still does reasonably, which is the theme of this page: wrong assumption, decent decisions.

For shared and full covariances, see LDA and QDA.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Generative vs discriminative

There are two ways to build a classifier. **Discriminative** models (logistic regression, SVMs, trees) learn P(y | x) or the boundary directly. **Generative** models learn how each class produces data, P(x | y) and P(y), then use Bayes' rule. Naive Bayes is the simplest generative classifier. Ng & Jordan (2001) compared it with its discriminative twin, logistic regression: logistic regression has the lower error with lots of data, but naive Bayes "may also approach its (higher) asymptotic error much faster" [NIPS 2001](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2001/hash/7b7a53e239400a13bd6be6c91c4f6c4e-Abstract.html). With little data naive Bayes often wins; with lots, logistic regression catches up and passes it.

#### The naive Bayes family

| Variant | Feature type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GaussianNB** | Continuous | Per-class mean and variance per feature |
| **MultinomialNB** | Counts (word counts, TF-IDF also works in practice) | The classic text classifier; smoothing α |
| **BernoulliNB** | Binary present/absent | "explicitly penalizes the non-occurrence of a feature i that is an indicator for class y, where the multinomial variant would simply ignore a non-occurring feature" |
| **ComplementNB** | Counts, imbalanced classes | Uses statistics from the complement of each class; "regularly outperforms MNB (often by a considerable margin) on text classification tasks" (Rennie et al. 2003) |
| **CategoricalNB** | Categorical (ordinal-encoded) | Its own categorical distribution per feature |

All from scikit-learn's naive Bayes guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html). Every variant supports `partial_fit`, so it can learn from a stream in batches.

#### A text classifier, step by step

1. **Vectorise**: word counts (CountVectorizer) or TF-IDF.

2. **Choose the variant**: Multinomial or Complement for counts, Bernoulli for short texts as presence/absence, Gaussian for numeric features.

3. **Tune α** by cross-validation (try 0.01–1).

4. **Train**: one pass of counting, O(n × features).

5. **Calibrate** if you'll threshold or average the probabilities.

#### When to use it

##### Use naive Bayes when

- Text classification baseline: spam, topics, sentiment, routing tickets

- Very little training data, or data arrives as a stream

- You need training and prediction to be nearly free

##### Reach for something else when

- You need trustworthy probabilities (calibrate or use logistic regression)

- Features interact strongly: trees, boosting

- Plenty of data: logistic regression, boosting or fine-tuned transformers usually win on text

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just count P(x | y) for whole messages"

Modelling P(x | y) exactly means estimating the probability of every possible combination of words. With only our 6 words treated as present/absent there are 26 = 64 combinations per class; with a realistic 50,000-word vocabulary there are 250,000. You will never see most combinations even once, so their counted probability is 0, and any new message would get probability zero under both classes. Exact Bayes is right in theory and impossible in practice.

#### Correlated features are counted twice

Suppose a tokenizer produces "free", "FREE" and "free!" as separate features, and they always appear together. They're one piece of evidence, but naive Bayes treats them as three independent ones and multiplies the same likelihood ratio three times. The class it picks often stays the same; the confidence explodes.

Simulated: one numeric feature, class 0 ~ N(0, 1), class 1 ~ N(1.5, 1), equal priors. Violet: the true probability. Red: naive Bayes after copying the feature k times. Same 0.5 crossing, so the same decisions; a steeper, overconfident curve.

Accuracy stays at **77.4%** for any number of copies, while log loss rises from 0.47 to 1.02 at 5 copies, and the predictions it is "more than 95% sure" about are right only 83.8% of the time. This is Domingos & Pazzani's point: naive Bayes can be optimal under zero–one loss even when the independence assumption is clearly violated, because classification only needs the right class to come out on top, not the right probability [Machine Learning 29](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1007413511361). scikit-learn: naive Bayes "is known to be a decent classifier, [but] it is known to be a bad estimator, so the probability outputs from predict_proba are not to be taken too seriously" [naive Bayes guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).

##### The fix when you need probabilities

Calibrate the outputs on held-out data (`CalibratedClassifierCV` with isotonic or sigmoid calibration), or switch to logistic regression. Ranking metrics like ROC-AUC are unaffected by this kind of overconfidence; log loss and Brier score are not. See Probability metrics.

#### Caveats

##### Strengths

- Trains in one counting pass; predicts instantly; tiny model

- "require a small amount of training data" (scikit-learn)

- Handles thousands of sparse features; streams with partial_fit

- A strong, honest baseline for text

##### Weaknesses

- Overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities

- Double-counts correlated features

- Can't model interactions ("free" is spammy unless next to "lunch")

- Usually beaten by logistic regression or boosting once data is plentiful

## Say it

### What is naive about naive Bayes?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why is it called "naive"?

Because of the conditional independence assumption: given the class, knowing one feature tells you nothing about another. It's almost never true (words co-occur), but it turns an impossible estimation problem into many easy ones.

Follow-up 2 of 6

What is Laplace smoothing and why do you need it?

Adding α pseudo-counts to every feature count (α = 1 is Laplace). Without it, a word never seen with a class gives that class probability zero for any message containing it, no matter what else the message says.

Follow-up 3 of 6

Why does it classify well if the assumption is wrong?

Classification needs only the correct class to have the highest score. Violated independence distorts the scores, often by pushing them to extremes in the same direction, so the argmax frequently survives (Domingos & Pazzani 1997). The probabilities don't.

Follow-up 4 of 6

Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?

A generative–discriminative pair: Multinomial NB is linear in the counts, like logistic regression. NB fits weights by counting, LR by optimising the conditional likelihood. NB converges faster with little data; LR reaches lower error with more data and gives better-calibrated probabilities (Ng & Jordan 2001).

Follow-up 5 of 6

Multinomial vs Bernoulli NB?

Multinomial models word counts and ignores absent words. Bernoulli models presence/absence and penalises the absence of an indicative word. Bernoulli can do better on short texts; Multinomial on longer documents.

Follow-up 6 of 6

How do you handle continuous features?

Gaussian NB (per-class mean and variance per feature), or discretise into bins and use Categorical/Multinomial NB. Strongly non-Gaussian features may need a transform first.

#### The 30-second answer

Naive Bayes is a generative classifier: it uses Bayes' rule, P(y | x) ∝ P(y) P(x | y), and assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(x | y) factorises into a product of per-feature probabilities that you estimate by counting. You smooth the counts so unseen features don't give zero probability, and you compute in log space to avoid underflow. It's very fast and works well with little data, especially for text, but because the independence assumption is usually wrong, it double-counts correlated evidence and its probabilities are overconfident even when its classifications are good.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Naive Bayes assumes features are independent." Conditionally independent _given the class_.

- "Its predict_proba is a reliable risk score." It's typically overconfident; calibrate first.

- "Smoothing is optional." Without it, one unseen word zeroes out a class.

**Key terms and sources**

Bayes' rule, the independence assumption, Laplace smoothing, log space, Gaussian/Multinomial/Bernoulli/Complement variants, why it classifies well but estimates badly · built from scikit-learn's naive Bayes guide, Domingos & Pazzani (1997), Ng & Jordan (2001) and Rennie et al. (2003) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Why a wrong model works

##### Optimal decisions despite violated independence

Domingos & Pazzani (1997) showed that the naive Bayes classifier is optimal under zero–one loss for a far larger set of problems than those where independence holds, because it only needs the true class to get the highest score. Their experiments on UCI datasets found it competitive with decision-tree and rule learners even where features were clearly dependent [Machine Learning 29](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1007413511361). They also note the corollary: the probability estimates themselves can be far off.

##### Faster to its (higher) error than logistic regression

Ng & Jordan (2001): discriminative logistic regression has the lower asymptotic error, but generative naive Bayes approaches its own asymptote with far fewer examples; in their analysis, a number that grows only logarithmically with the number of features, versus linearly for logistic regression. On UCI datasets they observed the two regimes: naive Bayes ahead at small training sizes, logistic regression ahead later [NIPS 2001](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2001/hash/7b7a53e239400a13bd6be6c91c4f6c4e-Abstract.html).

##### This page's simulations

log loss, 1 copy of the feature

0.47

log loss, 3 copies

0.68

log loss, 5 copies

1.02

Accuracy was 77.4% in all three. Lower log loss is better. Illustrative simulation, from the double-counting lab.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Prior / likelihood / posterior** | P(y), P(x \| y), P(y \| x). |
| **Conditional independence** | Given the class, features carry no information about each other. |
| **Laplace / Lidstone smoothing** | Add α (= 1 / < 1) pseudo-counts so nothing has probability 0. |
| **Generative vs discriminative** | Model P(x \| y) and P(y) vs model P(y \| x) directly. |
| **Calibration** | Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. |

1. scikit-learn, [Naive Bayes user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html) (assumption, decision rule, Gaussian/Multinomial/Bernoulli/Complement/Categorical variants, smoothing, "bad estimator" caveat).

2. P. Domingos & M. Pazzani, "On the optimality of the simple Bayesian classifier under zero-one loss", _Machine Learning_ 29, 103–130, 1997, [doi:10.1023/A:1007413511361](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1007413511361).

3. A. Ng & M. Jordan, "On discriminative vs. generative classifiers: a comparison of logistic regression and naive Bayes", [NIPS 2001](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2001/hash/7b7a53e239400a13bd6be6c91c4f6c4e-Abstract.html).

4. J. Rennie, L. Shih, J. Teevan & D. Karger, "Tackling the poor assumptions of naive Bayes text classifiers", ICML 2003 (Complement NB; cited by scikit-learn).

# Discriminant Analysis: LDA and QDA

> How do LDA and QDA classify, and when would you choose them over logistic regression or naive Bayes?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Other classic classifiers
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/discriminant-analysis/
- Before this: Naive Bayes (`fundamentals/naive-bayes`), Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `clf`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have a small dataset with a few numeric features and three classes. Logistic regression's weights jump between samples, as the classes are well separated. A colleague suggests a model that describes each class as a bell curve instead. The interviewer asks:

> How do LDA and QDA classify, and when would you choose them over logistic regression or naive Bayes?

#### Why it matters

These are simple, fast baselines, and they show how generative classifiers work. Interviewers also like the comparison with logistic regression and naive Bayes. One warning: LDA can also mean Latent Dirichlet Allocation, a topic model. That's something different.

### The idea

Think of describing each team by the average player and how players vary. To place a new player, ask which team's description fits best. If you assume all teams vary the same way, you need few numbers and get a straight dividing line. Let each team vary in its own way, and the line can curve, but you need more data.

[Figure: Three assumptions. LDA shares one covariance. QDA gives each class its own. Naive Bayes keeps only the diagonal.]

_More flexible needs more data, so it's a bias-variance choice._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the classes' correlations to opposite values. Then lower the rows to 5.

#### Which assumption fits?

Our seeded simulation: two Gaussian classes. Scores are averaged over 20 runs, each tested on 2,000 new points. The chart shows one run.

Set class B's correlation to **−0.7**, and see QDA's curved boundary pull ahead. Now return it to 0.7, and lower rows to **5**: LDA's simpler estimate is more reliable. Naive Bayes ignores correlation, so it trails whenever correlation matters.

**Now say why:** why does a shared covariance give a straight boundary?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Instead of learning a boundary directly, these models describe each class as a **Gaussian**, then use Bayes' rule. **LDA** gives every class the same covariance, so its boundaries are straight. **QDA** gives each class its own, so its boundaries are curved, but it has many more numbers to estimate. **Gaussian naive Bayes** is QDA with only the diagonal of each covariance. The choice is a bias-variance trade-off, and LDA can also project data down to at most K − 1 dimensions.

#### One family, three assumptions

| Model | Covariance | Boundary | Numbers to estimate for covariance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LDA** | One, shared by all classes | Straight | p(p + 1) / 2 |
| **QDA** | One per class | Curved | K × p(p + 1) / 2 |
| **Gaussian naive Bayes** | One per class, diagonal only | Curved, but ignores correlation | K × p |

With 50 features and 2 classes, for example, LDA estimates 1,275 covariance numbers, QDA 2,550, and naive Bayes 100. That's why more flexible isn't always better on small data.

##### Why LDA's boundary is straight

Each class's score contains a term that's quadratic in x. With a shared covariance, that term is the same for all classes, so it cancels when you compare them. Only a linear part remains. In QDA, the covariances differ, so it stays.

##### LDA or logistic regression?

Both draw straight boundaries, but they fit them differently.

- **LDA** assumes Gaussian classes with a shared shape. If that's close to true, it uses data efficiently, which helps with few rows. It stays stable when classes are well separated, where logistic regression's weights can run away.

- **Logistic regression** makes fewer assumptions. It's usually safer with outliers, categorical features or non-Gaussian data.

##### Too many features

The covariance estimate becomes unreliable when features approach the number of rows. **Shrinkage** pulls it towards a simpler matrix, which often helps a lot.

##### LDA for dimensionality reduction

With K classes, the class means lie in at most K − 1 dimensions, so LDA can project onto those. Unlike PCA, it uses the labels: it looks for directions that separate classes, rather than directions with the most variance. It's the same LDA used differently, so the number of dimensions you keep doesn't affect its predictions.

#### The maths

$$ {\delta_k(x) = -\tfrac12 \log|\Sigma_k| - \tfrac12 (x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k) + \log \pi_k}, \qquad {\delta_k(x) = x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k - \tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k + \log\pi_k} $$

Both come from Bayes’ rule with Gaussian classes, as in the scikit-learn guide. π is the share of each class.

- **the QDA score**: Each class has its own covariance. Choose the class with the highest score.

- **the LDA score**: With one shared Σ, the quadratic term cancels, and the score is linear in x.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Scale for the shrinkage:** LDA's predictions don't depend on scale, but shrinkage towards a simpler matrix can.

- **Check the assumption loosely:** heavy outliers or categorical features suit logistic regression or trees better.

- **Use shrinkage with many features:** especially if features are close to the number of rows.

- **Try QDA only with enough rows per class:** it estimates a full covariance for each class.

- **Remember the base rates:** the class share π is part of the score, so a change in class balance changes decisions.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "QDA is more flexible, so it's always better"

It sounds right, as curves can fit anything a line can. But QDA estimates a full covariance for each class. With few rows, those estimates are noisy, and a simpler model does better on new data, even if its assumption is slightly wrong. Compare them on validation data.

## Say it

### How do LDA and QDA classify, and when would you choose them over logistic regression or naive Bayes?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is LDA limited to K − 1 dimensions?

It only uses the directions that separate the class means. K points lie in a space of at most K − 1 dimensions. Two classes give one direction, however many features you have.

Follow-up 2 of 3

LDA vs PCA?

Both project data onto fewer dimensions. PCA ignores labels, and keeps the directions with the most variance. LDA uses labels, and keeps the directions that best separate classes. So PCA could keep a high-variance direction that says nothing about the class.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How is naive Bayes related to QDA?

Gaussian naive Bayes is QDA with each covariance restricted to its diagonal. That removes correlations, so it estimates far fewer numbers. It's more stable with little data, but it can't use correlation between features.

#### The 30-second answer

LDA and QDA are generative: they model each class as a Gaussian, and use Bayes' rule. LDA shares one covariance across classes, so the quadratic term cancels, and boundaries are straight. QDA gives each class its own, so boundaries curve, but it has far more to estimate, so it needs more data. Gaussian naive Bayes is QDA with diagonal covariances. Compared with logistic regression, LDA is more efficient if the Gaussian assumption holds, while logistic regression is safer if it doesn't. With many features, I'd use shrinkage. LDA can also project data to at most K minus 1 dimensions.

**Key terms and sources**

Modelling each class as a Gaussian: shared or separate covariance, linear or curved boundaries, shrinkage, LDA as dimensionality reduction, and how they compare. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [scikit-learn on linear and quadratic discriminant analysis](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/lda_qda.html)

- [ISLR, chapter on classification](https://www.statlearning.com/)

- [CS229 syllabus, generative learning](https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-summer2019.html)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# k-Means Clustering

> How do you split customers into groups when nobody has labelled them?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Unsupervised learning
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/k-means/
- Quiz topic: `unsup`

## Intuition

### The situation

Marketing wants three campaigns, one per kind of customer, but no column says which kind each customer is. The interviewer asks:

> How does k-means work, and does it always find the best clustering?

**Running example (shared by the unsupervised lessons):** a food-delivery app wants to group its customers without any labels. Each customer has two numbers, orders per month and average basket size, both standardised (mean 0, standard deviation 1). The simulated base has 180 customers drawn from three hidden segments: occasional small orders, frequent small orders, and occasional big orders. The algorithm never sees the segment; we use it only to score the result (adjusted Rand index, ARI: 1 = perfect agreement, 0 = chance).

#### Group customers when nobody has labelled them

Marketing wants three campaigns, one per kind of customer. There's no column saying which kind each customer is; that's the thing we want to discover. Clustering finds groups of points that are close to each other and far from other groups. k-means is the simplest and most used clustering method: fast, easy to explain, and the baseline every other method is compared with.

### The idea

Think of opening three shops in a town. Each customer goes to their nearest shop. Then each shop moves to the middle of its customers. Customers re-choose, shops move again, and you repeat until nothing changes.

[Figure: Three groups of customers, each with a marked centre in the middle of its group.]

_Illustrative. The assign and move steps repeat until the groups stop changing._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Run start A until no points switch, and note the inertia. Then reset and run starts B and C.

#### Step through Lloyd's algorithm on the customers

k = 3, random starting centroids (three random customers). Grey points: not assigned yet. Watch the inertia fall at every step until nothing switches.

**Now say why:** why doesn't every start reach the same answer, and how would you protect against a bad one?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

k-means splits data into k groups by placing k **centroids** and repeating two steps: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. Each step lowers the **inertia** (total squared distance to centroids), so it always converges, but only to a **local** minimum that depends on where you started, which is why **k-means++** seeding and several restarts matter. You must choose k yourself (elbow, silhouette, or business sense), and because it measures squared Euclidean distance to a centre, it assumes round, similar-sized clusters: elongated, curved or uneven groups break it. What you'll be able to do after this: run Lloyd's algorithm by hand, explain why it converges and why it gets stuck, pick k with two methods, and name the shapes k-means can't handle.

#### Centroids and inertia

Describe each group by its **centroid**, the average customer in it. A good grouping keeps every customer close to their own group's centroid. k-means measures this with the inertia, the within-cluster sum of squares:

$$ {J} = {\sum_{j=1}^{k}}\ {\sum_{x_i \in C_j}}\ {\lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2} $$

scikit-learn: k-means works by "minimizing a criterion known as the inertia or within-cluster sum-of-squares" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means).

- **inertia**: One number for the whole clustering. Lower is better; 0 only if every point sits exactly on its centroid.

- **over the k clusters**: Add up the cost of each cluster.

- **over its members**: Every point x_i assigned to cluster j.

- **squared distance to the centroid**: Squared Euclidean distance from the point to its cluster’s centroid μ_j. Squaring punishes far points heavily.

#### Alternate two easy problems

Minimising inertia over groupings and centroids together is hard. But each half is easy on its own:

1. Nine customers and two starting centroids (◆), placed badly on purpose.

2. **Assign:** with centroids fixed, the best grouping is obvious: each point joins its nearest centroid. The middle customer joins the right one.

3. **Update:** with the grouping fixed, the best centroid is obvious too: the mean of its points (the mean minimises the sum of squared distances).

4. Assign again with the new centroids: the middle customer is now closer to the left centroid and switches. Update again.

5. Neither step can increase inertia, and there are finitely many groupings, so this always stops. That's Lloyd's algorithm.

scikit-learn: "Given enough time, K-means will always converge, however this may be to a local minimum. This is highly dependent on the initialization of the centroids" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means). The algorithm is from Lloyd (1957 report, published 1982).

#### Local minima, and k-means++

A bad start can trap Lloyd's algorithm: two centroids share one true group while another centroid sits between two groups, and no single assign/update step can fix it. **k-means++** (Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007) picks the first centroid at random, then each next one with probability proportional to its **squared distance** from the nearest centroid chosen so far, so starts are spread out.

Five well-separated groups of 40 customers each, k = 5, a single run per seed. Try seeds until you find a stuck run: one big group split in two and two groups merged.

On this data, a single run with random starts got stuck in **15 of 50** seeds; with k-means++, in **6 of 50**. The worst random run had inertia 697, against 53.4 for the right answer. The fix that always works is cheap: run several starts and keep the lowest inertia (scikit-learn's `n_init`). Arthur & Vassilvitskii proved k-means++ seeding alone is expected to be within a factor of 8(ln k + 2), i.e. O(log k), of the optimal inertia [SODA 2007](https://theory.stanford.edu/~sergei/papers/kMeansPP-soda.pdf).

#### Elbow and silhouette

Inertia always falls as k grows (k = n gives inertia 0), so you can't pick k by minimising it. Two common aids:

- **Elbow:** plot inertia against k and look for the bend where adding a cluster stops helping much.

- **Silhouette:** for each point, a = mean distance to its own cluster, b = mean distance to the nearest other cluster; s = (b − a) / max(a, b), between −1 and 1. Average over points; higher means tighter, better-separated clusters.

On the customers, inertia drops from 583 (k = 1) to 314 (k = 2) to **97** (k = 3), then only to 83 at k = 4: a clear elbow at 3. The silhouette peaks at k = 3 too (0.64). Real data is rarely this clean; often there's no sharp elbow, and the right k is the one the business can act on (three campaigns, not seven). scikit-learn's caution about the silhouette: it is generally higher for convex clusters than for density-based ones, so don't use it to compare k-means with DBSCAN.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The clustering toolbox

| Method | Finds | You choose | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| **k-means** | Round, similar-sized groups | k | this one |
| **Hierarchical** | A tree of nested groups | linkage, where to cut | next |
| **DBSCAN / HDBSCAN** | Any shape; marks noise | density (eps, min_samples) | DBSCAN |
| **Gaussian mixtures** | Elliptical groups, soft membership | k, covariance type | lesson 4 |

scikit-learn ships all of these with the same fit/predict interface [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html).

#### The whole recipe

1. **Scale** features (StandardScaler); consider PCA first if there are many.

2. **Fit** with k-means++ and several starts (`n_init`), for a range of k.

3. **Choose k** with the elbow and silhouette, then sanity-check that the clusters mean something to the business.

4. **Describe** each cluster by its centroid (in original units) and size.

5. **Check stability:** refit on a resample; clusters that change a lot aren't real.

Cost: each Lloyd iteration is O(n·k·d). For millions of rows, `MiniBatchKMeans` updates centroids from small random batches, trading a little inertia for big speed-ups [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#mini-batch-k-means).

#### When to use it

##### Use k-means when

- You want a quick segmentation with a fixed number of groups

- Groups are roughly blob-shaped after scaling

- Data is large and you need speed

##### Reach for something else when

- Shapes are curved or density varies: DBSCAN/HDBSCAN

- You need probabilities of membership: GMM

- You want a hierarchy or don't know k: hierarchical clustering

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just try every possible grouping and keep the best"

The number of ways to split 180 customers into 3 non-empty groups is about 3180 / 6, roughly 1085, more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Finding the grouping with the lowest inertia exactly is NP-hard in general. So every practical method is a **heuristic** that finds a good grouping, not a guaranteed best one. k-means is the heuristic that won because each step is cheap and provably helps.

#### Round, similar-sized clusters only

Assigning each point to the nearest centre draws straight boundaries halfway between centroids (a Voronoi diagram). scikit-learn: "Inertia makes the assumption that clusters are convex and isotropic, which is not always the case. It responds poorly to elongated clusters, or manifolds with irregular shapes" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#k-means).

Same algorithm, best of 10 starts, true k given. Round groups: perfect. Moons: k-means cuts straight across both (ARI 0.21). Tilted groups: it slices them crosswise (ARI 0.62).

##### Also breaks on

- Groups of very different sizes or spreads (the boundary sits halfway, cutting into the big group)

- Unscaled features (one feature in rupees dominates the distance)

- Outliers (squared distance lets one far point drag a centroid)

- Very high dimensions: distances concentrate (see k-NN)

##### What to use instead

- Curved or noisy shapes: DBSCAN / HDBSCAN

- Elliptical or overlapping groups, soft membership: Gaussian mixtures

- Outliers: k-medoids or trimming

- High dimensions: reduce first with PCA

#### Caveats

##### Strengths

- Fast, simple, scales to millions (mini-batch)

- Centroids are easy to describe ("the average frequent small-basket customer")

- Assigning new points is instant

- A strong first baseline; also used for vector quantisation and as an initialiser (GMMs, IVF indexes in vector search)

##### Weaknesses

- You must pick k

- Local minima: needs k-means++ and restarts

- Assumes round, similar-sized clusters; sensitive to scale and outliers

- Every point is forced into a cluster; no notion of noise

## Say it

### How does k-means work, and does it always find the best clustering?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why does k-means converge?

The assignment step minimises inertia for fixed centroids; the update step minimises it for fixed assignments (the mean minimises squared distance). Inertia never increases and there are finitely many assignments, so it stops, typically in a few dozen iterations.

Follow-up 2 of 6

How do you choose k?

Elbow on inertia, average silhouette, gap statistic, or BIC with a GMM, plus stability across resamples and whether the business can use that many groups.

Follow-up 3 of 6

What is k-means++?

Seeding that picks each new centroid with probability proportional to D(x)², the squared distance to the nearest chosen centroid. It spreads starts out and is O(log k)-competitive in expectation.

Follow-up 4 of 6

When does k-means fail?

Non-convex shapes, different cluster sizes or densities, unscaled features, outliers, and high dimensions. Also it always assigns every point; there's no noise label.

Follow-up 5 of 6

k-means vs GMM?

k-means is like a GMM with equal, spherical covariances and hard assignments in the zero-variance limit. GMMs learn shape (covariance), give soft probabilities, and can be compared by BIC.

Follow-up 6 of 6

Complexity?

O(n·k·d) per iteration; usually few iterations. Mini-batch k-means for very large n.

#### The 30-second answer

k-means partitions data into k clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squared distances to the centroids. Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then set each centroid to the mean of its points. Each step can only lower the objective, so it converges, but to a local minimum that depends on initialisation, so we use k-means++ seeding and multiple restarts. You choose k with the elbow method, silhouette score, or domain needs. It assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters and needs scaled features; for other shapes use DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "k-means finds the optimal clustering." It finds a local minimum.

- "Pick the k with the lowest inertia." That's always k = n.

- "k-means works on any distance." The mean update is tied to squared Euclidean distance; for other distances use k-medoids.

**Key terms and sources**

Inertia, Lloyd's algorithm, k-means++, choosing k (elbow, silhouette), and where k-means fails · built from scikit-learn's clustering guide, Lloyd (1982) and Arthur & Vassilvitskii (2007) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### This page's simulations

stuck runs, random start (of 50)

15

stuck runs, k-means++ (of 50)

6

stuck runs, k-means++ with 10 starts

0

Five-group data, single runs per seed. The last row picks the lowest-inertia run of 10 k-means++ starts, checked for all 50 seeds. Illustrative simulation.

##### A guarantee for the seeding

k-means++ is O(log k)-competitive in expectation: the expected inertia after seeding alone is at most 8(ln k + 2) times the optimum [Arthur & Vassilvitskii 2007](https://theory.stanford.edu/~sergei/papers/kMeansPP-soda.pdf). Lloyd iterations then only improve it. It's the default initialisation in scikit-learn.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Centroid** | Mean of a cluster's points. |
| **Inertia (WCSS)** | Sum of squared distances from points to their centroids. |
| **Lloyd's algorithm** | Alternate assign-to-nearest and move-to-mean until stable. |
| **k-means++** | Seeding proportional to squared distance from chosen centroids. |
| **Silhouette** | (b − a)/max(a, b): cohesion vs separation, −1 to 1. |
| **ARI** | Adjusted Rand index: agreement with known labels, corrected for chance. |

#### What this page is built from

1. scikit-learn, [Clustering user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html) (inertia, Lloyd steps, local minima, k-means++, assumptions, mini-batch, silhouette, adjusted Rand index).

2. D. Arthur & S. Vassilvitskii, "k-means++: the advantages of careful seeding", SODA 2007, [PDF](https://theory.stanford.edu/~sergei/papers/kMeansPP-soda.pdf) (8(ln k + 2) bound).

3. S. Lloyd, "Least squares quantization in PCM", _IEEE Trans. Information Theory_ 28(2), 1982 (the algorithm; background).

# Hierarchical Clustering

> What if you don't know k? Build every grouping at once and cut the tree.

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Unsupervised learning
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/hierarchical-clustering/
- Before this: k-Means Clustering (`fundamentals/k-means`)
- Quiz topic: `unsup`

## Intuition

### The situation

Marketing sees three customer segments today, but one might split into weekday and weekend users. You don't want to commit to one number of groups. The interviewer asks:

> How does hierarchical clustering work, and how do you pick the number of clusters?

**Running example:** the same food-delivery customers as the k-means lesson (standardised orders per month and basket size, three hidden segments). The dendrogram lab uses 36 of them (12 per segment) so every leaf is visible; the linkage lab uses all 180, plus a "two moons" shape to show where linkages disagree.

#### "How many segments?" depends on how closely you look

At a glance there are three kinds of customers. Look closer and the "frequent small orders" group might split into weekday and weekend users. k-means makes you pick k up front and gives one answer. Hierarchical clustering builds **all** the answers at once, from n clusters of one down to a single cluster, as a tree you can cut at any level.

### The idea

Think of building a family tree from the bottom up. Everyone starts alone, then the closest pairs join, then the closest groups, until one family remains. Cut the tree at any height, and you get that many groups.

[Figure: A tree of merges over six customers. A dashed cut across the tree gives two clusters, and a lower cut would give more.]

_Illustrative. Higher joins mean the groups were further apart._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the cut height up and down and watch the cluster count. Then switch from Ward to single linkage.

#### Read a dendrogram and choose the cut

Vertical lines are clusters; the dashed line is your cut. The longest vertical stretch with no merge is where the data "wants" to be cut: clusters that stay separate over a wide range of heights.

With Ward linkage on these 36 customers, the last merges happen at heights 2.07, 2.47, then **9.45** and 10.13: a huge jump between 3 clusters and 2. Any cut in that gap gives the three hidden segments exactly (ARI 1.0). Heights aren't comparable across linkages (Ward heights are on a variance scale), so compare the _shape_ of the tree, not the numbers.

**Now say why:** why does the same data give such a different tree under single linkage?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Start with every customer as its own cluster, then repeatedly **merge the two closest clusters** until one is left. Record each merge and its height (how far apart the merged clusters were) and you get a **dendrogram**, a tree of every possible grouping. You choose the number of clusters afterwards by **cutting** the tree, ideally where there's a big jump in merge height. What "closest clusters" means is the **linkage**: single (nearest pair) follows chains and odd shapes but snowballs; complete (farthest pair) and average are in between; **Ward** (smallest increase in variance) gives even, round clusters like k-means. The cost is O(n²) memory and up to O(n³) time. What you'll be able to do after this: read a dendrogram, choose a cut, explain the four linkages and when each fails, and compare hierarchical clustering with k-means.

#### Merges, heights and the dendrogram

1. Five customers, each its own cluster. On the right, an empty dendrogram: leaves at the bottom, merge height going up.

2. The closest pair, A and B, merges first. Draw a bracket at the height equal to their distance.

3. Next closest: C and D, a little farther apart, so a slightly higher bracket.

4. Now the closest clusters are {A, B} and {C, D}. How far apart two _groups_ are is the linkage choice (see below). They merge, higher up.

5. Finally E, far from everyone, joins at the top. n points always take exactly n − 1 merges.

6. A horizontal cut crosses three vertical lines, giving three clusters: {A, B}, {C, D}, {E}. A higher cut gives two; a lower one, five.

#### Greedy merging under a chosen cluster distance

Agglomerative clustering is greedy: each merge is the best one available now and is never undone. Everything about the result follows from one choice: how to measure the distance between two clusters A and B. The four standard linkages:

$$ {\min_{a,b} d(a,b)} \qquad {\max_{a,b} d(a,b)} \qquad {\tfrac{1}{|A||B|}\textstyle\sum_{a,b} d(a,b)} \qquad {\tfrac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\lVert \mu_A - \mu_B\rVert^2} $$

scikit-learn: Ward "minimizes the sum of squared differences within all clusters. It is a variance-minimizing approach"; complete "minimizes the maximum distance between observations of pairs of clusters"; average uses "the average of the distances between all observations of pairs of clusters"; single uses "the distance between the closest observations of pairs of clusters" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hierarchical-clustering). Ward (1963) introduced the variance criterion.

- **single: closest pair**: Distance between the two nearest members. Follows chains and curved shapes; snowballs through bridges and noise.

- **complete: farthest pair**: Distance between the two farthest members. Prefers compact clusters of similar diameter; sensitive to outliers.

- **average: mean of all pairs**: Average distance over every pair, one from each cluster. A middle ground; works with any distance metric.

- **Ward: added variance**: How much the total within-cluster sum of squares grows if A and B merge. The same objective as k-means, so it gives round, even-sized clusters. Euclidean only.

#### No linkage wins everywhere

| Linkage | Customers (ARI, sizes) | Two moons (ARI) |
|---|---|---|
| Ward | 0.98 · 60/61/59 | 0.42 |
| average | 0.98 · 60/61/59 | 0.42 |
| complete | 0.98 · 60/61/59 | 0.64 |
| single | 0.57 · 60/119/1 | 1.00 |

Single linkage is the only one that traces the curved moons (it just follows the chain of nearest neighbours), and the only one that fails on the noisy round segments, for the same reason. Ward, average and complete prefer compact groups: good segments, wrong moons. This trade-off is why density-based methods (DBSCAN, HDBSCAN) exist: they keep single linkage's shape-following but add a density threshold that stops one bridge point from chaining clusters together. HDBSCAN is, in fact, single linkage on a density-adjusted distance.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Agglomerative (bottom-up) is the standard

Hierarchical clustering can be **agglomerative** (start with singletons, merge) or **divisive** (start with everything, split). Agglomerative is what libraries implement: scikit-learn's `AgglomerativeClustering` and SciPy's `scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage`, which also draws dendrograms. It's popular where the hierarchy itself is meaningful: biology (gene expression heatmaps, taxonomies), document and product catalogues, and customer segmentation where marketing wants coarse and fine levels.

#### O(n²) memory, up to O(n³) time

The straightforward algorithm keeps an n × n distance matrix (O(n²) memory: 100,000 points means 1010 distances, about 80 GB as doubles) and searches it at each of n − 1 merges. Faster algorithms exist for specific linkages (O(n²) time for single linkage via a minimum spanning tree, for example), but the memory still limits plain hierarchical clustering to tens of thousands of points. scikit-learn: agglomerative clustering "is computationally expensive when no connectivity constraints are added between samples: it considers at each step all the possible merges"; with a connectivity matrix (only merge neighbours, e.g. a k-nearest-neighbour graph or adjacent pixels) it "can also scale to large number of samples" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hierarchical-clustering). For very large data: cluster a sample, or run k-means into a few hundred micro-clusters first and build the hierarchy on their centroids.

#### The whole recipe

1. **Scale** features; choose a distance (Euclidean for Ward; any metric for average/complete/single).

2. **Pick a linkage:** Ward for even, round groups; average for non-Euclidean distances; single only for chain-like shapes on clean data.

3. **Build the full tree** and plot the dendrogram.

4. **Cut** at a big jump in height (or at a distance threshold that means something), and check the clusters make sense.

5. **Mind the size:** sample or pre-cluster beyond ~10–20k points.

#### When to use it

##### Use hierarchical clustering when

- The hierarchy itself is useful (taxonomies, coarse and fine segments)

- You don't know k and want to explore

- n is in the thousands and you have a meaningful custom distance

##### Reach for something else when

- Hundreds of thousands of points: k-means, mini-batch, HDBSCAN

- Noisy data with arbitrary shapes: HDBSCAN

- You need to score new points often: k-means or GMM

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Merge the two closest points, always"

The simplest definition of distance between clusters is the distance between their two closest members (single linkage). It sounds natural, and it can follow curved shapes. But one stray customer sitting between two segments is enough to bridge them: once the bridge merges, the two segments become one. On all 180 customers, single linkage cut at 3 clusters gives sizes **60 / 119 / 1**: one real segment, two segments chained together, and a lone outlier as the "third cluster" (ARI 0.57). scikit-learn calls single linkage "the most brittle linkage option" for this "rich getting richer" effect [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hierarchical-clustering).

#### Caveats

##### Strengths

- No k needed up front; one tree gives every k

- The dendrogram is a readable picture of the structure

- Deterministic (no random starts)

- Average/complete/single work with any distance, even precomputed

##### Weaknesses

- O(n²) memory, slow beyond tens of thousands of points

- Greedy: an early bad merge is never undone

- Results depend heavily on linkage

- No natural way to assign new points (unlike k-means' nearest centroid)

## Say it

### How does hierarchical clustering work, and how do you pick the number of clusters?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

How do you choose where to cut?

Look for the largest vertical gap in the dendrogram (clusters that persist across many heights), use a distance threshold with domain meaning, or pick k and validate with silhouette or stability.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Single vs complete vs average vs Ward?

Single: closest pair, chaining, finds elongated shapes, brittle to noise. Complete: farthest pair, compact clusters, outlier-sensitive. Average: compromise, works with any metric. Ward: minimal variance increase, even sizes, Euclidean only.

Follow-up 3 of 4

Hierarchical vs k-means?

Hierarchical needs no k up front, is deterministic and gives a tree, but costs O(n²) memory and can't easily assign new points. k-means is fast and scalable but needs k, restarts, and round clusters.

Follow-up 4 of 4

How do you scale it?

Connectivity constraints (kNN graph), sampling, or pre-clustering into micro-clusters (BIRCH or k-means) and running hierarchy on those.

#### The 30-second answer

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, recording each merge height in a dendrogram. You get flat clusters by cutting the tree, usually at a large gap in merge heights, so you don't fix k in advance. The linkage defines cluster distance: single uses the closest pair and can follow arbitrary shapes but chains through noise; complete uses the farthest pair; average the mean pairwise distance; Ward merges the pair that least increases within-cluster variance and gives k-means-like round clusters. It's deterministic but needs O(n²) memory and up to O(n³) time, so it suits small to medium datasets.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Merge heights mean the same across linkages." Ward heights are on a different scale.

- "Hierarchical clustering scales like k-means." The distance matrix is O(n²).

- "Single linkage is the default." Ward is scikit-learn's default.

**Key terms and sources**

Agglomerative clustering, dendrograms, single/complete/average/Ward linkage, cutting the tree · built from scikit-learn's clustering guide, SciPy's hierarchy docs and Ward (1963) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### Cluster sizes on the 180 customers (k = 3)

Ward: largest cluster

61

single: largest cluster

119

single: smallest cluster

1

True segments: 60 each. Illustrative simulation; matches scikit-learn's description: "single linkage is the worst strategy, and Ward gives the most regular sizes" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hierarchical-clustering).

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Agglomerative / divisive** | Bottom-up merging / top-down splitting. |
| **Dendrogram** | Tree of merges; vertical position = merge height. |
| **Linkage** | The rule for distance between clusters. |
| **Cut** | A height (or k) that turns the tree into flat clusters. |
| **Connectivity constraint** | Only allow merges between neighbours; speeds it up and respects structure. |

#### What this page is built from

# DBSCAN

> How do you find curved clusters and flag the points that belong nowhere?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Unsupervised learning
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/dbscan/
- Before this: k-Means Clustering (`fundamentals/k-means`)
- Quiz topic: `unsup`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your deliveries follow curved roads, and stray GPS pings land everywhere. k-means cuts straight across both roads. The interviewer asks:

> How does DBSCAN find clusters, and what is its main weakness?

**Running example:** the same food-delivery app, now looking at **where** orders are delivered. Simulated GPS points (standardised): 200 deliveries along two curved roads that wrap around each other (the "two moons" shape), plus 20 stray pings scattered at random (GPS errors). A second map has a dense city-centre cluster beside a sparse suburb. We want the roads found as two clusters and the stray pings flagged.

#### Clusters that aren't round, and points that belong nowhere

Deliveries follow roads, so the clusters are long and curved, and a k-means centroid in the middle of a curve sits where nobody lives. k-means on the two roads scores ARI 0.21: it cuts straight across both (see the k-means lesson). It also forces every GPS error into some cluster. We need a method that follows dense regions wherever they go and is allowed to say "this point is noise".

### The idea

Think of finding crowds at a fair. Wherever people stand packed together, you can walk from person to person and stay in the same crowd. Someone standing alone belongs to no crowd at all.

[Figure: Two curved roads of dense points wrap around each other. A few scattered grey points don't belong to either and are marked as noise.]

_Illustrative, based on the lesson's two roads and stray GPS pings._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Try eps at 0.25, 0.30 and 0.35. Watch how many clusters it finds and how many points become noise.

#### eps is everything

Big dots: core points. Small dots: border points. Grey: noise. The circle (top left) shows eps to scale.

With min_samples = 10: eps = 0.30 finds both roads exactly (ARI 1.0) and flags 4 stray pings as noise; the other 16 strays lie close enough to a road to be absorbed as border points. eps = 0.25 breaks a road into pieces (3 clusters); eps = 0.35 merges both roads into one. A 20% change in eps flips the answer. scikit-learn: eps "is crucial to choose appropriately for the data set and distance function and usually cannot be left at the default value" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#dbscan).

**Now say why:** why does such a small change in eps swing the result from fragments, to two roads, to one blob?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

DBSCAN says a cluster is a region where points are packed densely, separated from other clusters by sparse space. A point with at least **min_samples** neighbours within radius **eps** is a **core** point; core points within eps of each other join the same cluster, points near a core point join it as **border** points, and everything else is **noise**. So it finds clusters of **any shape**, figures out how many there are, and flags outliers, none of which k-means can do. Its weakness is one global density: **eps** is hard to set, and when clusters have different densities, no single eps works. **HDBSCAN** fixes that by trying all densities and keeping the most stable clusters. What you'll be able to do after this: classify points as core/border/noise by hand, pick eps with a k-distance plot, explain why DBSCAN finds curved clusters, and say when to switch to HDBSCAN.

#### Core, border and noise

1. Eight delivery points. Two settings: eps (a radius) and min_samples (how many points must be inside that radius).

2. Draw a circle of radius eps around a point. It contains 5 points including itself, at least min_samples = 4, so it's a **core point**: it's inside a dense region.

3. Check every point the same way: four more have at least 4 points within eps, so they are cores too. Core points within eps of each other are linked, and everything linked forms one cluster, whatever its shape.

4. These two points have too few neighbours to be cores (3 and 2 inside their circles), but each lies within eps of a core point, so they join the cluster as **border points**. Border points belong to a cluster but can't extend it.

5. The lone point has no core within eps. It's **noise** (label −1 in scikit-learn): DBSCAN refuses to force it into a cluster.

Definitions from scikit-learn: a core sample has "min_samples other samples within a distance of eps"; "Any sample that is not a core sample, and is at least eps in distance from any core sample, is considered an outlier by the algorithm" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#dbscan). (scikit-learn's min_samples counts the point itself.) Original algorithm: Ester, Kriegel, Sander & Xu, KDD 1996.

#### A cluster is a connected dense region

$$ {N_\varepsilon(p) = \{\,q : d(p,q) \le \varepsilon\,\}} \qquad {|N_\varepsilon(p)| \ge \text{min\_samples}} \qquad {p \to p_1 \to \dots \to q} $$

- **eps-neighbourhood**: All points within distance eps of p, including p itself.

- **core condition**: p is a core point if its neighbourhood holds at least min_samples points: p sits in a dense region.

- **density-reachable**: q belongs to p’s cluster if you can walk from p to q in eps-sized hops, where every point you hop from is a core point.

A cluster is a maximal set of points that are density-connected through core points. The number of clusters comes out of the data; nobody sets k. The algorithm is a flood fill: pick an unvisited core point, start a cluster, and keep adding the neighbours of every core point you reach.

#### The k-distance plot

For every point, compute the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour (k = min_samples − 1, so the circle around it holds min_samples points), sort those distances and plot them. Points inside clusters have small k-distances; noise points have large ones. The curve is flat, then bends sharply upward: eps near the bend separates "dense enough" from "noise". This heuristic is from the original DBSCAN paper.

Sorted distance from each of the 220 points to its k-th nearest neighbour. The dashed line marks eps = 0.30, the value that worked above.

For k = 9 the curve is nearly flat up to about the 85th percentile (0.25), then climbs: 0.30 at the 90th, 0.36 at the 95th, 0.48 at the 99th. The bend sits close to the eps that separated the roads. It's a guide, not a guarantee: with clusters of different densities there is no single bend.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The density-based family

| Method | Idea | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| **DBSCAN** (1996) | One density threshold; core/border/noise | eps, min_samples |
| **OPTICS** (1999) | Orders points by reachability; extract clusters at many eps | min_samples (max eps) |
| **HDBSCAN** (2013) | Hierarchy over all densities; keeps the most stable clusters | min_cluster_size, min_samples |

All three are in scikit-learn (`DBSCAN`, `OPTICS`, `HDBSCAN`) [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html). Typical uses: geospatial data (pickup hotspots, store locations), anomaly detection (noise points are the anomalies), and clustering embeddings after UMAP (see t-SNE & UMAP).

#### Speed, scaling and determinism

- **Cost:** one neighbourhood query per point. With a KD-tree or ball tree in low dimensions that's roughly O(n log n); otherwise O(n²). scikit-learn's implementation can build a full pairwise matrix that "will consume n² floats" when trees can't be used [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#dbscan).

- **Scale features:** eps is one radius in every direction, so unscaled features make it meaningless. For GPS, use haversine distance in metres.

- **High dimensions:** distances concentrate (see k-NN), so density is hard to define; reduce dimensions first.

- **Order:** core points and noise are deterministic, but a border point within eps of two clusters goes to whichever reaches it first, so "results can differ when data is provided in a different order" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#dbscan).

#### The whole recipe

1. **Scale** features or choose a meaningful distance (haversine for GPS, cosine for embeddings).

2. **Set min_samples** from domain sense (a common rule of thumb: about 2 × dimensions, at least 4 or 5); larger means fewer, denser clusters and more noise.

3. **Pick eps** at the bend of the k-distance plot; try a few values around it.

4. **Inspect noise:** is it really noise, or a sparse cluster? If densities differ, switch to HDBSCAN.

#### When to use it

##### Use DBSCAN / HDBSCAN when

- Clusters have odd shapes (geography, trajectories)

- You expect noise and want outliers flagged

- You don't know how many clusters there are

- HDBSCAN: densities vary

##### Reach for something else when

- Clusters are round and k is known: k-means is simpler and faster

- You need soft membership: GMM

- Very high-dimensional raw features: reduce first

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Link every pair of points closer than some distance"

Linking any two points within distance eps (single linkage cut at eps) follows curves too. But one chain of stray GPS pings between the two roads links them into one cluster, and isolated pings become their own tiny "clusters". DBSCAN's fix is the min_samples rule: only **core** points can extend a cluster, and a stray ping in a sparse area isn't a core, so it can't act as a bridge. Density, not just distance, decides what's connected.

#### A dense centre and a sparse suburb

120 deliveries packed in the city centre, 60 spread across a suburb next to it. min_samples = 5.

eps = 0.15 finds the centre but throws away **54 of the 60** suburb deliveries as noise. eps = 0.4 keeps the suburb but merges it with the centre into one cluster. The compromise, eps = 0.3, keeps them apart but hands 11 suburb deliveries to the centre and drops 7 as noise. scikit-learn: "DBSCAN assumes that the clustering criterion (i.e. density requirement) is globally homogeneous" and "may struggle to successfully capture clusters with different densities" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hdbscan).

**Go deeper: how HDBSCAN removes eps**

HDBSCAN (Campello, Moulavi & Sander, PAKDD 2013) "explores all possible density scales": it replaces raw distance with a **mutual reachability distance** (the larger of the two points' core distances and their actual distance, which pushes sparse points apart), builds a single-linkage tree on it (via a minimum spanning tree), and condenses the tree, dropping splits smaller than `min_cluster_size`. It then keeps the clusters that persist longest as density changes (their **stability**). Each cluster effectively gets its own eps. scikit-learn: it "relies solely on the choice of min_samples, which tends to be a more robust hyperparameter" [clustering guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hdbscan). In practice it's the better default; use plain DBSCAN when you know the density scale (e.g. "a hotspot is ≥ 10 orders within 200 m").

#### Caveats

##### Strengths

- Any cluster shape

- No k: the number of clusters comes from the data

- Built-in outlier detection (noise label)

- Few parameters with physical meaning (a radius and a count)

##### Weaknesses

- Very sensitive to eps

- Can't score new points without refitting (scikit-learn)

- One global density: fails on clusters of different densities

- Struggles in high dimensions

- Border points between clusters are assigned arbitrarily

## Say it

### How does DBSCAN find clusters, and what is its main weakness?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

How do you choose eps and min_samples?

min_samples from domain sense or ~2 × dimensions; eps from the bend of the sorted k-distance plot with k = min_samples − 1, then check the clusters and noise share. If no single bend exists, use HDBSCAN.

Follow-up 2 of 5

DBSCAN vs k-means?

DBSCAN: any shape, no k, noise label, but eps-sensitive and single-density. k-means: round clusters, needs k, every point assigned, fast and simple.

Follow-up 3 of 5

What are border points and why are they ambiguous?

Non-core points within eps of a core. A border point near two clusters goes to whichever cluster reaches it first, so it can depend on data order.

Follow-up 4 of 5

How would you use it for anomaly detection?

Run it on a batch, and treat noise points (label −1) as candidates. scikit-learn's DBSCAN only labels the data it was fitted on, and can't score new points, so you refit on each batch. To score new points one by one, use a method built for that, such as LOF in novelty mode or Isolation Forest. HDBSCAN also gives outlier scores (GLOSH).

Follow-up 5 of 5

Complexity?

About O(n log n) with spatial indexes in low dimensions, O(n²) worst case or in high dimensions.

#### The 30-second answer

DBSCAN is density-based clustering. A point with at least min_samples neighbours within radius eps is a core point; clusters are groups of core points reachable from each other through eps-hops, plus border points within eps of a core; everything else is noise. It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, infers the number of clusters, and flags outliers. The catch is eps: results are very sensitive to it, you pick it from the bend of a k-distance plot, and because it's one global density it fails when clusters have different densities. HDBSCAN fixes that by building a hierarchy over all densities and keeping the most stable clusters, so it only needs a minimum cluster size.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "DBSCAN needs the number of clusters." It doesn't.

- "DBSCAN handles clusters of any density." Any shape, yes; different densities, no.

- "Noise points are errors to delete." They might be a real sparse cluster.

**Key terms and sources**

Density-based clustering: core, border and noise points, eps and min_samples, the k-distance plot, varying density and HDBSCAN · built from Ester et al. (1996), scikit-learn's clustering guide and Campello et al. (2013) · checked 28 Oct 2026

##### Recognition

The DBSCAN paper (Ester, Kriegel, Sander & Xu, KDD 1996) received the SIGKDD Test of Time award in 2014; it remains one of the most-cited clustering papers.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **eps** | Neighbourhood radius. |
| **min_samples** | Points needed within eps (including itself) to be a core point. |
| **Core / border / noise** | Dense point / non-dense point near a core / everything else. |
| **Density-reachable** | Reachable by eps hops through core points. |
| **k-distance plot** | Sorted distances to the k-th neighbour; its bend suggests eps. |
| **HDBSCAN** | Hierarchical DBSCAN over all densities; picks stable clusters. |
