# Stationarity, ARIMA and Exponential Smoothing

> What is stationarity, and how do ARIMA and exponential smoothing produce a forecast?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Time series
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/stationarity-arima-and-smoothing/
- Before this: Time-Series Forecasting Basics (`fundamentals/forecasting-basics`)
- Quiz topic: `ts`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have two years of daily orders, and a benchmark to beat. A colleague fits a model on the raw series, and reports a great fit, but its residuals still show a clear pattern. Another keeps differencing until the plot looks flat. The interviewer asks:

> What is stationarity, and how do ARIMA and exponential smoothing produce a forecast?

#### Why it matters

Forecasting Basics covers benchmarks and honest backtests. Interviewers often go further, and ask what stationarity means, or how you'd choose p, d and q. These two model families are also strong choices for a single series with little data.

### The idea

Think of steering a car. Exponential smoothing is like checking your position often, and trusting recent checks most. ARIMA is more like correcting from how far you've drifted and how wrong your last corrections were. Both work best once you've removed the road's overall slope.

[Figure: Three ideas. Differencing removes trend and season. ARIMA uses past values and past errors. Exponential smoothing tracks level, trend and season.]

_Neither family contains the other, so compare them with a backtest._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Difference a series at φ = 0. Then try α near 0 and α = 1.

#### See stationarity, then smooth a series

Our seeded simulation of 300 steps: today = φ × yesterday + noise, plus the trend. φ = 1 is a random walk. The top chart shows the series, and the bars show the ACF at lags 1 to 10.

Our seeded simulation: a level of 50 jumps to 70 halfway through, with noise. Catching up means getting within 2 of the new level.

In the first lab, tick **difference** at φ = 1, and the slow ACF disappears. Then set φ to **0**, which is already stationary, and keep the tick: a false pattern appears at lag 1. That's why over-differencing is a real mistake. In the second lab, try α near 0 and α = 1, and find the balance between smoothing and reacting.

**Now say why:** why does differencing a stationary series create a false pattern?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A series is **stationary** if its behaviour doesn't depend on when you look, so trends and seasons break it. **Differencing** usually fixes that. **ARIMA** then predicts a differenced series from its own past values and past errors. **Exponential smoothing** takes another route, and tracks a level, a trend and a season using weighted averages that favour recent data. Forecast uncertainty grows with the horizon, so a single number is never the whole answer.

#### The pieces

##### Stationarity

In a stationary series, the statistical properties don't depend on the time you observe it. So a series with a trend or a season isn't stationary. Cycles of no fixed length can be, as you can't predict where the peaks will be.

**Differencing** replaces each value with its change from the one before, which removes a changing level. A **seasonal difference** subtracts the value one season ago, such as the same weekday last week. More than two ordinary differences is almost never needed, and too many add false patterns.

##### Reading ACF and PACF

The **ACF** gives the correlation between a series and itself at each lag. The **PACF** gives the same after removing the effect of the lags in between.

| What you see | What it suggests |
|---|---|
| ACF falls slowly, and the first value is large | Not stationary, so difference it. |
| ACF decays, and PACF has a last clear spike at lag p | AR(p): an ARIMA(p, d, 0). |
| PACF decays, and ACF has a last clear spike at lag q | MA(q): an ARIMA(0, d, q). |
| Both decay | A mix of the two. The plots can't give p and q, so compare models. |

##### Choosing the model

- **d:** use a test. KPSS assumes the series is stationary, so a small p-value suggests differencing. ADF assumes the opposite, so a large p-value suggests differencing.

- **p and q:** minimise AICc, for models with the same d. Differencing changes the data being fitted, so AICc can't compare different d.

- **Check:** residuals should look like noise, with no ACF pattern left.

##### Exponential smoothing

| Method | Tracks | Its forecast looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple** | Level | A flat line. |
| **Holt** | Level and trend | A straight line. |
| **Damped trend** | Level and a fading trend | A line that flattens out. |
| **Holt-Winters** | Level, trend and season | A repeating pattern. Additive if the swings stay constant, and multiplicative if they grow with the level. |

**ETS** is the statistical version of these methods. It gives the same point forecasts, and adds prediction intervals.

##### ARIMA or exponential smoothing?

Neither family contains the other. Linear smoothing models are special cases of ARIMA, and simple smoothing matches ARIMA(0, 1, 1). But multiplicative smoothing models have no ARIMA equivalent, and some ARIMA models have no smoothing equivalent. AICc can't compare across the two families, so compare them with a backtest.

##### Why intervals widen

Errors build up as you forecast further ahead. For a naive forecast, the spread grows with the square root of the horizon. As an illustration, if the one-step standard deviation is 10 orders, a 95% interval is about ±20 at one step, and about ±39 at four steps.

#### The maths

$$ {y'_t} = {c} + {\sum_{i=1}^{p}\phi_i\, y'_{t-i}} + {\sum_{j=1}^{q}\theta_j\, e_{t-j}} + {e_t}, \qquad {\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}} $$

From Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, chapters 8 and 9.

- **the differenced series**: The value after differencing d times. This is the I in ARIMA.

- **a constant**: Together with d, this sets the long-run behaviour of the forecast.

- **the AR part**: Today depends on the last p values.

- **the MA part**: Today also depends on the last q forecast errors.

- **the new shock**: The part of today that nothing could have predicted.

- **simple smoothing**: The new level mixes the latest value with the old level. A large α reacts quickly, and a small α smooths more.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Plot first:** a transform like a log can steady a series whose swings grow with its level.

- **Start with a benchmark:** a model that can't beat seasonal naive isn't worth keeping.

- **One series or many:** these models fit one series at a time. With thousands of related series, boosting on lag features often does better, and is simpler to run as one model.

- **Use a damped trend for long horizons:** a straight line continues forever, which is rarely believable.

- **Report intervals:** check they contain the actual values about as often as they claim.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Keep differencing until the series looks flat"

It sounds right, as stationarity is the goal. But each extra difference adds noise, and can create patterns that aren't real. A stationary series gets a false lag-1 correlation of about −0.5 if you difference it. One or two differences are almost always enough, and a test can tell you when to stop.

## Say it

### What is stationarity, and how do ARIMA and exponential smoothing produce a forecast?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How would you tell if a series is stationary?

Plot it, and look for a trend, a season or changing spread. Look at the ACF too: a slow decay suggests non-stationary. Then confirm with a test such as KPSS, where a small p-value suggests differencing, or ADF, where the null hypothesis is the opposite.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not just keep differencing until it looks flat?

Too many differences add false patterns, and increase the variance. If you difference a stationary series, you get a lag-1 correlation of about −0.5. One or two differences are almost always enough.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the difference between AR and MA?

AR predicts from past values, so a shock's effect fades gradually. MA predicts from past errors, so a shock's effect ends after q steps. That's why the ACF of an MA(q) series has a last clear spike at lag q, while an AR series decays.

#### The 30-second answer

A stationary series behaves the same whenever you look at it, so trends and seasons break it, and differencing usually fixes that. ARIMA predicts the differenced series from its past values and past errors. I'd choose d with a test, read p or q from the ACF and PACF if the pattern is clear, and otherwise compare AICc for the same d. Exponential smoothing tracks a level, trend and season with weighted averages. Neither family contains the other, so I'd compare them with a backtest, against seasonal naive, and report intervals, which widen with the horizon.

**Key terms and sources**

Stationarity, differencing, ACF and PACF, what AR, MA and ARIMA models do, exponential smoothing from simple to Holt-Winters, and why intervals widen. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, ARIMA (chapter 9)](https://otexts.com/fpp3/arima.html)

- [Same book, exponential smoothing (chapter 8)](https://otexts.com/fpp3/expsmooth.html)

- [Same book, prediction intervals (section 5.5)](https://otexts.com/fpp3/prediction-intervals.html)

# Classification Metrics

> Your fraud model is 99.8% accurate. Why is your manager unhappy?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/classification-metrics/
- Before this: Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your fraud model is 99.8% accurate, and your manager is unhappy. About 200 of every 100,000 transactions are fraud. The interviewer asks:

> Your fraud model is 99.8% accurate. Is it good?

**Scenarios used throughout:** card-fraud detection (0.2% of transactions are fraud), cancer screening (1% have the disease), spam filtering (40% of mail is spam), and a customer-support intent classifier with a rare but costly "cancel subscription" class. Scores come from a simple model of a classifier (illustrative); every number on the page is computed live from it.

#### "Our fraud model is 99.8% accurate." Your manager is unhappy. Why?

Out of every 100,000 card transactions, about 200 are fraud. A model that **never flags anything** is right on the 99,800 legitimate ones: 99.8% accuracy, and it catches zero fraud. One number told you nothing about the thing you care about. Classification metrics exist to ask the right question about the right mistakes.

### The idea

Think of a smoke alarm that never rings. It's right almost every day, and it's useless. Precision asks how many alarms were real fires. Recall asks how many fires set off the alarm.

[Figure: A confusion matrix. Precision reads across the flagged column, true positives out of everything flagged. Recall reads across the real positives row, true positives out of all real positives.]

_Every metric in this lesson is built from these four counts._

### Play

**Try to break it.** On Fraud, slide the threshold down until recall is high, and watch precision. Then switch to Spam and do the same.

#### Slide the threshold, watch the trade-off

–

Lower the threshold and you flag more: recall rises, precision falls. Raise it and the reverse. There's no free lunch, so the right threshold depends on what each kind of mistake costs. That's the subject of Thresholds & Misclassification Costs.

**Now say why:** why does the same threshold move give such different precision on rare fraud and common spam?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Every classification metric is a ratio built from four counts: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. **Accuracy** hides rare classes. **Precision** asks "when I flag, am I right?" **Recall** asks "of what's out there, how much do I catch?" **Specificity** and **NPV** ask the same about negatives. **F1** balances precision and recall and ignores true negatives. Precision depends on how common the positive class is; recall doesn't. For many classes, **macro**, **micro** and **weighted** averaging answer different questions. What you'll be able to do after this: compute and explain every metric from a confusion matrix, pick the one a scenario needs, and spot the accuracy trap instantly.

#### Four counts: the confusion matrix

1. Every prediction lands in one of four boxes: what the model said (columns) versus what was true (rows).

2. **True positive (TP):** it was fraud and we flagged it.

3. **False negative (FN):** it was fraud and we missed it. Statisticians call this a type II error.

4. **False positive (FP):** it was legit and we flagged it, a false alarm. Type I error.

5. **True negative (TN):** legit and let through.

6. Rows add up to what's really there; columns add up to what the model flagged. Every metric on this page is some ratio of these four numbers.

#### Each metric divides by a different "out of what?"

$$ {\text{Precision} = \tfrac{TP}{TP+FP}} \quad {\text{Recall} = \tfrac{TP}{TP+FN}} \quad {\text{Specificity} = \tfrac{TN}{TN+FP}} \quad {\text{NPV} = \tfrac{TN}{TN+FN}} $$

Standard definitions, as in scikit-learn's metrics guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Recall, sensitivity, hit rate and true positive rate are four names for one thing.

- **precision (PPV)**: Out of everything I flagged, how much was really positive? TP / (TP + FP). Low precision = many false alarms. Spam filters live and die on this.

- **recall (sensitivity, TPR)**: Out of all real positives, how many did I catch? TP / (TP + FN). Low recall = missed cases. Cancer screening lives and dies on this.

- **specificity (TNR)**: Out of all real negatives, how many did I correctly leave alone? TN / (TN + FP). 1 − specificity is the false positive rate.

- **NPV**: Out of everything I called negative, how much was really negative? TN / (TN + FN). Matters when a negative result sends someone home.

#### A 95%-specific test, and most of its positives are false

Recall and specificity describe the test itself. Precision mixes the test with the **base rate**: when positives are rare, even a small false-positive rate on the huge negative group swamps the true positives. That's Bayes' rule:

$$ {\text{PPV}} = {\text{rec}\cdot\pi} \,\Big/\, \big({\text{rec}\cdot\pi} + {(1-\text{spec})\,(1-\pi)}\big), \quad {\pi = \text{prevalence}} $$

- **precision (PPV)**: Probability that a flagged case is really positive.

- **true positives per person**: Recall × prevalence: the share of the population that is positive and caught.

- **false positives per person**: (1 − specificity) × (1 − prevalence): small rate × huge group.

- **prevalence**: How common positives are. Drop it from 10% to 0.1% and precision collapses, even though the test is unchanged.

Screening scenario: a good test (90% sensitive, 95% specific) at 1% prevalence flags about 495 healthy people for every 90 sick ones, so precision is about 15%. That's why screening positives get a second, more specific test. Same test in a high-risk clinic (20% prevalence): precision about 82%.

#### F1: the harmonic mean, and what it ignores

$$ {F_1} = {2PR \,/\, (P+R)} = {2TP \,/\, (2TP + FP + FN)} $$

- **F1**: One number between 0 and 1 that is high only when precision and recall are both high.

- **harmonic mean**: 2PR / (P + R). Dominated by the smaller of the two: precision 1.0 and recall 0.1 give F1 = 0.18, not 0.55.

- **in counts**: 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN). True negatives never appear: F1 doesn't care how well you handle negatives.

The harmonic mean punishes imbalance; you can't buy a good F1 with one great number. If the two errors aren't equally costly, use F-beta (next lessons), not F1.

##### F1's blind spots

It ignores true negatives, and it changes if you swap which class you call "positive"; MCC doesn't have either problem [Chicco & Jurman 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941312). By default scikit-learn returns F1 = 0 when there are no positive predictions and no positives; the `zero_division` parameter controls this [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

#### Macro, micro and weighted

Support tickets go to **billing** (600), **technical** (350) or **cancel subscription** (50). Cancel is rare but the most expensive to miss: an unhandled cancel is a lost customer. Compare two models:

Micro-averaging pools all decisions, so with every class included it equals accuracy [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html); it's dominated by big classes. Macro-averaging gives every class equal weight, so the rare class counts as much as billing. Weighted averages by support. Model A looks fine on micro and weighted, and macro exposes it.

| Average | Question it answers | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **micro** | How good is a random single decision? | Every prediction matters equally; multi-label tagging |
| **macro** | How good is the model on a typical class? | Rare classes matter as much as common ones (support intents, rare diseases) |
| **weighted** | Macro, but proportional to class size | Reporting overall quality on imbalanced data without letting tiny classes dominate |
| **per class (None)** | Everything, unsummarised | Always look at this before trusting any average |

scikit-learn notes that macro "may over-emphasize the typically low performance on an infrequent class", and that a weighted F can fall outside the range between precision and recall [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### A report, not a number

In practice you print a per-class report (scikit-learn's `classification_report`: precision, recall, F1 and support for every class) next to the confusion matrix, and pick one **headline metric** that matches the cost of mistakes in your scenario, plus a **guardrail** (e.g. "maximise recall subject to precision ≥ 80%"). The sections below build each piece.

#### Top-k accuracy, and multi-label metrics

##### Top-k accuracy

Correct if the true label is among the k highest-scored classes; accuracy is the k = 1 case [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Use it when a human or a later step picks from a short list: ImageNet top-5, product category suggestions, autocomplete.

##### Multi-label (several tags per item)

**Subset accuracy**: all tags exactly right (harsh). **Hamming loss**: fraction of individual tag decisions that are wrong (lenient). **Jaccard**: |predicted ∩ true| / |predicted ∪ true| per item. Plus per-tag precision and recall with micro or macro averaging.

##### Worked example: one article, true tags {politics, economy, india}

| Predicted tags | Subset accuracy | Jaccard | Hamming loss (5 possible tags) |
|---|---|---|---|
| {politics, economy, india} | 1 | 1.00 | 0.0 |
| {politics, economy} | 0 | 0.67 | 0.2 |
| {politics, sports} | 0 | 0.25 | 0.6 |

Missing one of three tags already scores 0 on subset accuracy; Jaccard and Hamming give partial credit.

#### Which metric, in which situation

| Scenario | Headline metric | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Cancer screening (first test) | Recall / sensitivity | A miss can be fatal; false alarms get a cheap follow-up test |
| Confirmatory diagnosis | Specificity, precision | A false positive means unnecessary treatment |
| Spam filter | Precision (at good recall) | Losing a real email is worse than letting one spam through |
| Fraud (0.2%) | Recall at a fixed precision (or alerts per day) | Review capacity is limited; accuracy is meaningless here |
| Content moderation | Precision for auto-removal, recall for the human-review queue | Two thresholds, two jobs |
| Support intents with a rare costly class | Macro-F1 + per-class recall | Micro and accuracy hide the rare class |
| Balanced classes, equal costs (e.g. cats vs dogs) | Accuracy is fine | Its weakness only appears with imbalance or unequal costs |
| Imbalanced, need one fair number | MCC or balanced accuracy | Use all four cells (see Thresholds & Costs) |

### The answer that sounds right

#### Accuracy: (TP + TN) / everything

With rare positives, the do-nothing baseline already scores near 100%, and a genuinely useful model can even score _lower_ because its false alarms cost accuracy points. With balanced classes (spam), accuracy is informative again.

##### What breaks

Accuracy "cannot be considered a reliable measure" on unbalanced data, because it gives "an overly optimistic estimate" [Chicco & Jurman 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941312). Always compare against the majority-class baseline, and use metrics that look at the positive class directly.

#### What to keep

- **All of these depend on the threshold.** For threshold-free comparison, use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC (next lesson).

- **Precision and NPV depend on prevalence**, so they don't transfer between populations (a clinic vs the general public, a test set rebalanced to 50/50 vs production). Recall and specificity do transfer, if the positives themselves look the same.

- **Small classes give noisy metrics.** Recall on 50 "cancel" tickets moves 2 points per ticket; report confidence intervals (Choosing the Right Metric).

- **Metrics are proxies for costs.** When you can put a price on each error, optimise expected cost directly.

## Say it

### Your fraud model is 99.8% accurate. Is it good?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

Your fraud model has 99.8% accuracy. Is it good?

Can't tell: fraud is about 0.2%, so "never flag" also scores 99.8%. I'd look at recall and precision on the fraud class, the confusion matrix, PR-AUC, and alert volume against review capacity.

Follow-up 2 of 5

Precision or recall for cancer screening? For spam?

Screening: recall, since a miss is very costly and false positives get a cheap follow-up. Spam: precision, because sending a real email to spam is worse than letting one spam through. In both I'd set a floor on the other metric.

Follow-up 3 of 5

Why is precision low even though the test is accurate?

Base rate. With 1% prevalence, 5% false positives on the 99% healthy group outnumber the true positives on the 1%. PPV = rec·π / (rec·π + (1 − spec)(1 − π)).

Follow-up 4 of 5

Macro vs micro F1?

Micro pools all decisions (equals accuracy for single-label multi-class), so big classes dominate. Macro averages per-class F1 equally, so a failing rare class drags it down. Use macro when every class matters; always inspect per-class numbers.

Follow-up 5 of 5

Why the harmonic mean for F1?

It's dominated by the smaller value, so you can't get a high F1 with one strong and one weak component. Precision 1.0 and recall 0.1 give F1 ≈ 0.18.

#### The 30-second answer

I start from the confusion matrix. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data because the majority-class baseline already scores high. Precision measures how many flagged items are right, and recall how many real positives I catch; which one I prioritise depends on the scenario's costs: recall for screening, precision for spam. F1 balances them but ignores true negatives. Precision also depends on prevalence, so it shifts between populations. For multi-class problems I report per-class metrics and choose macro averaging when rare classes matter.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "High accuracy, so the model is good." Check the baseline and the class balance.

- "F1 is always the right metric for imbalance." It ignores TN and unequal costs.

- "Precision is a property of the model." It's also a property of the population (prevalence).

**Key terms and sources**

Built from scikit-learn's model-evaluation guide and Chicco & Jurman (2020) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Formula / meaning |
|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | (TP + TN) / N |
| **Precision, PPV** | TP / (TP + FP) |
| **Recall, sensitivity, TPR** | TP / (TP + FN) |
| **Specificity, TNR** | TN / (TN + FP) |
| **FPR / FNR** | FP / (FP + TN) = 1 − specificity; FN / (FN + TP) = 1 − recall |
| **NPV** | TN / (TN + FN) |
| **F1** | 2PR / (P + R) |
| **Support** | Number of true instances of a class |
| **Prevalence** | Share of positives in the population |
| **Macro / micro / weighted** | Average of per-class scores / pooled counts / support-weighted average |

#### What this page is built from

1. scikit-learn, [Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) (precision/recall/F, averaging, top-k, Hamming, Jaccard).

2. D. Chicco & G. Jurman, [The advantages of the Matthews correlation coefficient over F1 score and accuracy in binary classification evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941312), BMC Genomics 21:6 (2020).

3. T. Fawcett, "An introduction to ROC analysis", _Pattern Recognition Letters_ 27 (2006): definitions of TPR, FPR and related terms.

4. Interview angle: [DataLemur ML interview questions](https://datalemur.com/blog/machine-learning-interview-questions).

Scenario scores come from a simple, illustrative model of a classifier (positives' and negatives' scores as two overlapping bell curves), with expected counts computed exactly.

# ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC

> Why can a 0.98 ROC-AUC fraud model still be nearly useless?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/roc-auc-vs-pr-auc/
- Before this: Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Model A gets 70% recall at 40% precision, and model B gets 60% at 55%. Your threshold could change next quarter, so you need a comparison that doesn't depend on it. The interviewer asks:

> When would you use PR-AUC instead of ROC-AUC?

**Scenarios:** fraud detection (0.2% fraud), credit default ranking (about 5% default), rare-disease screening, and ad click prediction. Scores come from the same simple model as Classification Metrics: positives' and negatives' scores as two overlapping bell curves, separated by d standard deviations (illustrative, computed exactly).

#### Precision and recall change with the threshold. How do you compare models?

Model A gets recall 70% at precision 40%; model B gets recall 60% at precision 55%. Which is better? It depends on the threshold each was run at, and the threshold depends on business costs that may change next quarter. You want a score for the model's **ranking** itself: how well it orders cases from most to least likely, across every possible threshold.

### The idea

Think of ranking a huge pile of CVs. ROC-AUC asks how often a good CV ranks above a bad one, across the whole pile. PR-AUC asks how good the top of the pile is, which is all you'll actually read. When good CVs are rare, the two tell different stories.

[Figure: Two small charts for the same model with rare positives. The ROC curve hugs the top left and looks excellent. The precision-recall curve falls away quickly and looks much weaker.]

_Illustrative, for a model with rare positives._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Keep the model quality fixed and push the prevalence of positives down as far as it goes. Watch both scores.

#### Change the class balance, watch which curve cares

The ROC curve (left) doesn't move when you change prevalence, because both of its axes are rates within a class. The PR curve (right) sinks, because precision mixes in how many negatives there are. A random model's PR-AUC equals the prevalence; scikit-learn: "With random predictions, the AP is the fraction of positive samples" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

**Now say why:** why does one score hold steady while the other collapses?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Threshold metrics judge one operating point; curves judge them all. The **ROC curve** plots recall against false positive rate as the threshold sweeps. Its area (**ROC-AUC**) is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative, and it **doesn't change with class balance**. The **precision–recall curve** plots precision against recall, and its area (**average precision, PR-AUC**) **drops as positives get rarer**, because precision does. So ROC-AUC measures ranking quality in general, and PR-AUC measures how useful the top of the ranking is when positives are rare. Gini (2·AUC − 1) and KS are the credit-scoring dialects of the same idea. What you'll be able to do after this: read both curves, explain AUC as a probability, say which to report for a given scenario, and explain why a 0.98 ROC-AUC fraud model can still be nearly useless.

#### Sweep the threshold, plot each point

1. Axes: false positive rate (share of negatives flagged) across, true positive rate (share of positives caught) up. A model that guesses at random lies on the diagonal.

2. A strict threshold flags only the most confident cases: few false alarms, low recall. Bottom-left.

3. Loosen it: recall rises faster than false alarms if the model ranks well.

4. Very lenient: almost everything is flagged. Top-right.

5. Joining every threshold gives the ROC curve. The area under it is the ROC-AUC, here 0.921 for a model whose classes are separated by 2 standard deviations.

#### AUC = the chance a random positive outranks a random negative

$$ {\text{AUC}} = {P\big(s(x^{+}) > s(x^{-})\big)} = {\tfrac{1}{n_{+}n_{-}}\textstyle\sum_{i\in +}\sum_{j\in -}\mathbb 1[s_i > s_j]} $$

The probability interpretation and its equivalence to the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney statistic [Fawcett 2006, via the ROC article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic).

- **ROC-AUC**: The area under the ROC curve, between 0 and 1. 0.5 = random ordering; 1 = every positive above every negative.

- **a ranking probability**: Pick one positive and one negative at random: AUC is the probability the positive gets the higher score. That's why it is threshold-free and prevalence-free.

- **how it's computed**: Count positive–negative pairs ranked correctly (ties count half) and divide by the number of pairs: the Mann–Whitney U statistic, normalised.

Green: positives' scores; red: negatives'. The overlap is where ranking mistakes happen. AUC says nothing about where you'd put a threshold, or whether the scores are calibrated probabilities. Multiply every score by 10 and AUC is unchanged.

#### PR-AUC: how good is the top of the list?

$$ {\text{AP}} = \sum_{n}{(R_n - R_{n-1})}\,{P_n} $$

scikit-learn's definition, which deliberately does not interpolate: linear interpolation of the PR curve "provides an overly-optimistic measure of classifier performance" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Davis & Goadrich (2006) showed why straight-line interpolation is wrong in PR space.

- **average precision**: A step-wise area under the precision–recall curve.

- **recall gained**: How much recall increases from threshold n−1 to n: the width of each step.

- **precision there**: The precision at threshold n: the height of the step. AP is the precision averaged over the points where you catch new positives.

Two facts connect the curves. Davis and Goadrich proved that one curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space, so if model A is better everywhere, both views agree. But "an algorithm that optimizes the area under the ROC curve is not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve" [Davis & Goadrich, ICML 2006](https://mlanthology.org/icml/2006/davis2006icml-relationship). When curves cross, the two areas can rank models differently, and PR-AUC weights the high-score region your business actually uses.

#### Gini, KS and partial AUC

##### Gini (credit risk)

Gini = 2·AUC − 1: twice the area between the ROC curve and the diagonal, rescaled so random = 0 and perfect = 1 [ROC article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic). Banks report scorecards in Gini. Not the same as the Gini impurity used in decision trees.

##### KS statistic (credit risk)

The maximum gap between the cumulative score distributions of "goods" and "bads", equal to max(TPR − FPR) over thresholds: the furthest vertical distance from the ROC curve to the diagonal. That's the same point Youden's J picks. Practitioner rules of thumb vary (often 0.3–0.7 is called acceptable in credit risk) and aren't a formal standard.

##### Partial AUC: only the region you'll use

If you can only ever tolerate a 1% false positive rate (screening a whole population, fraud alerts), the rest of the ROC curve is irrelevant. Partial AUC integrates only up to that FPR; scikit-learn exposes it as `roc_auc_score(..., max_fpr=0.01)` (standardised) [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

##### Multi-class AUC

One-vs-rest (each class vs all others, then average) or one-vs-one (every pair of classes, then average; Hand & Till 2001). In scikit-learn: `multi_class='ovr'` or `'ovo'`, with macro or prevalence-weighted averaging [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Which curve, in which situation

| Scenario | Report | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud detection (0.2%) | PR-AUC + precision@k (alerts per day) | Positives are rare and analysts only see the top of the list; ROC-AUC looks great regardless |
| Rare-disease screening | PR-AUC, plus sensitivity at a fixed specificity | Same imbalance problem; clinicians pick an operating point |
| Credit default ranking (≈5%) | ROC-AUC / Gini, KS | Industry standard for ranking power; cut-offs set later by policy |
| Ad click prediction | ROC-AUC **and** log-loss | AUC for ranking ads; log-loss because bids use the probability itself (see Probability Metrics) |
| Balanced problem (≈50/50) | ROC-AUC | Both curves tell a similar story; ROC is easier to compare across datasets |
| Comparing across test sets with different class balance | ROC-AUC | PR-AUC changes with prevalence, so it isn't comparable between datasets |
| Only low false-positive rates are usable | Partial AUC (max_fpr) | Ignore the region you'll never operate in |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "ROC-AUC is 0.98, ship it"

ROC-AUC uses the false positive _rate_: false alarms divided by all negatives. With 99,800 legitimate transactions, a 1% false positive rate is still 998 false alarms, and against 200 frauds that wrecks precision, yet it barely moves ROC. Saito and Rehmsmeier showed that on imbalanced data "the visual interpretability of ROC plots… can be deceptive with respect to conclusions about the reliability of classification performance" [Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4349800/). See it in the Play lab, in the Intuition tab: push prevalence down and ROC-AUC doesn't move, while PR-AUC collapses.

#### What to keep

- **AUC measures ranking, not calibration.** A model with perfect AUC can output probabilities that are all wrong by a factor of 10.

- **AUC hides the operating point.** Two models with equal AUC can differ a lot at the threshold you'll actually use. Report the metric at your operating point too.

- **AUC estimates are noisy, and the measure itself has critics.** Hand (2009) argues AUC implicitly uses different cost assumptions for different classifiers when comparing them, and proposed the H-measure as a coherent alternative [Hand 2009, via the ROC article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic). Bootstrap confidence intervals are cheap; use them.

- **PR-AUC isn't comparable across different prevalences**, so always quote the baseline (the prevalence) next to it.

## Say it

### When would you use PR-AUC instead of ROC-AUC?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Why doesn't ROC-AUC change with class imbalance?

Both axes are rates within a class: TPR divides by positives, FPR by negatives. Changing how many negatives there are doesn't change either rate. Precision divides by everything flagged, so it mixes the classes and moves with prevalence.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Your fraud model has ROC-AUC 0.98. Is it good?

Maybe not. At 0.2% prevalence even a 1% FPR means about 5 false alarms per real fraud. I'd check PR-AUC (against a 0.002 baseline), precision at the recall we need, and alert volume against analyst capacity.

Follow-up 3 of 4

What's the AUC of a random model, and of a model that's always wrong?

Random: 0.5 ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC equal to the prevalence. AUC 0 means a perfectly inverted ranking: flip the scores and you have a perfect model. An AUC below 0.5 usually means a sign bug.

Follow-up 4 of 4

Gini vs AUC vs KS?

Gini = 2·AUC − 1, the same information rescaled. KS = max(TPR − FPR), the best single-threshold separation (also where Youden's J peaks). Credit risk teams report Gini and KS; ML teams usually report AUC.

#### The 30-second answer

ROC-AUC is the probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative. It's threshold-free and doesn't depend on class balance, which makes it good for comparing ranking quality. PR-AUC, or average precision, summarises precision across recall levels; its baseline is the prevalence, so it drops when positives are rare. With heavy imbalance, like fraud, ROC-AUC can look excellent while precision at any useful recall is poor, so I'd report PR-AUC plus precision at the operating point. Neither one measures calibration.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "AUC 0.9 means 90% accuracy." It's a ranking probability, not accuracy at any threshold.

- "PR-AUC 0.3 is bad." Compare it with the prevalence: 0.3 against a 0.002 baseline is strong.

- "High AUC means good probabilities." AUC ignores calibration.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Fawcett (2006), Davis & Goadrich (2006), Saito & Rehmsmeier (2015), Hand (2009) and scikit-learn's docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ROC curve** | TPR vs FPR across all thresholds. |
| **ROC-AUC** | Area under it = P(random positive outscores random negative). |
| **PR curve** | Precision vs recall across thresholds. |
| **Average precision (PR-AUC)** | Σ (Rn − Rn−1) Pn; baseline = prevalence. |
| **Gini** | 2·AUC − 1. |
| **KS statistic** | max(TPR − FPR) = largest gap between the classes' cumulative score distributions. |
| **Partial AUC** | Area over a restricted FPR range. |
| **DET curve** | A ROC variant plotting false negative rate vs false positive rate on normal-deviate axes (used in biometrics and speaker verification). |

#### What this page is built from

2. J. Davis & M. Goadrich, [The relationship between Precision-Recall and ROC curves](https://mlanthology.org/icml/2006/davis2006icml-relationship), ICML 2006.

3. T. Saito & M. Rehmsmeier, [The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4349800/), PLOS ONE 10(3) (2015).

# Thresholds & Misclassification Costs

> Why flag at 0.5, when a missed fraud costs 100 reviews?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/thresholds-and-costs/
- Before this: Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your code flags fraud at 0.5, which treats a missed ₹20,000 fraud and a ₹200 manual review as equally bad. The interviewer asks:

> How do you choose a classification threshold?

**Scenarios with real-world-style costs** (illustrative): fraud (missed fraud ₹20,000; reviewing a false alarm ₹200), cancer screening (a miss is 100× worse than a follow-up test), loan approval (approving a defaulter ₹2,00,000; rejecting a good customer ₹30,000 of lost interest), spam (losing a real email 10× worse than one spam in the inbox). Scores come from the same calibrated model as the earlier lessons.

#### Why flag at 0.5?

Most code says `predict = proba >= 0.5`. That treats a missed ₹20,000 fraud and a ₹200 manual review as equally bad. Change the threshold and the business outcome changes by lakhs. In our fraud scenario, the cost per 100,000 transactions is about **₹28.7 lakh at 0.5** and **₹10.9 lakh at the cost-optimal threshold**: same model, same data, different line.

### The idea

Think of deciding when to call a doctor. A wasted visit costs a little, and a missed illness costs a lot, so you call even when you're only somewhat worried. A threshold works the same way: you act once acting is the cheaper bet.

[Figure: A U-shaped curve of total cost against the threshold. The lowest cost sits well to the left of the usual 0.5 default.]

_Illustrative. When misses cost far more than false alarms, the best threshold sits well below 0.5._

### Play

**Try to break it.** On Fraud, drag the threshold until you find the lowest cost. Then switch to Spam and find it again.

#### Cost, Youden, F1 and F2 on the same model

–

Two patterns to notice. First, the cost curve's minimum lands exactly on CFP/(CFP + CFN), because these probabilities are calibrated. Second, **Youden's J always picks the threshold where the probability equals the prevalence** in this model. It agrees with the cost optimum only when the cost ratio happens to mirror the class ratio: almost exactly in cancer screening (100:1 costs, 99:1 classes), badly in spam and fraud.

**Now say why:** why does the best threshold move so far between the two, even though neither model changed how it works?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A model gives scores; a **threshold** turns them into decisions, and the right threshold depends on what each mistake **costs**. If the probabilities are calibrated and you can price the errors, the cost-optimal rule is simple: flag when p ≥ CFP / (CFP + CFN). **Youden's J** (sensitivity + specificity − 1) picks a threshold as if a miss and a false alarm were equally bad _per class_; **F-beta** lets you say recall is β times as important as precision. When you need one fair number on imbalanced data, **MCC** and **balanced accuracy** use all four cells of the confusion matrix. And reweighting classes during training is just threshold moving in disguise. What you'll be able to do after this: turn business costs into a threshold, explain why "0.5" is arbitrary, and choose between Youden, F-beta, MCC, kappa, G-mean and expected cost for a scenario.

#### A cost matrix: put a price on each cell

| | predict positive | predict negative |
|---|---|---|
| actually positive | CTP (often 0) | CFN: the miss |
| actually negative | CFP: the false alarm | CTN (often 0) |

Elkan's observation: from a decision-making point of view, a 2×2 cost matrix has essentially **one** degree of freedom, the ratio of the two error costs [Elkan, IJCAI 2001](https://mlanthology.org/ijcai/2001/elkan2001ijcai-foundations). You don't need exact rupee values; you need a defensible ratio ("a missed fraud costs about 100 reviews").

#### Flag when the expected cost of flagging is lower

For one case with calibrated probability p of being positive: flagging costs (1 − p)·CFP in expectation (it might be a false alarm); not flagging costs p·CFN (it might be a miss). Flag when the first is smaller:

$$ \text{flag if }\ {(1-p)\,C_{FP}} \le {p\,C_{FN}} \iff {p \ge C_{FP} \,/\, (C_{FP} + C_{FN})} $$

Bayes-optimal decision with zero cost for correct decisions; the threshold result is Elkan's (2001) [IJCAI 2001](https://mlanthology.org/ijcai/2001/elkan2001ijcai-foundations). It only holds if p is a calibrated probability (see Probability Metrics).

- **expected cost of flagging**: If you flag, you pay C_FP only when it is actually negative, with probability 1 − p.

- **expected cost of not flagging**: If you let it through, you pay C_FN only when it is actually positive, with probability p.

- **the threshold**: Solve for p: flag whenever p ≥ C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN). Fraud: 200 / 20,200 ≈ 0.0099, so flag anything above 1%. Spam: 10 / 11 ≈ 0.91.

#### Sensitivity + specificity − 1

$$ {J} = {\text{sensitivity}} + {\text{specificity}} - 1 = {\text{TPR} - \text{FPR}} $$

Youden (1950). scikit-learn: balanced accuracy with `adjusted=True` "in the binary case… is also known as Youden's J statistic, or informedness" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

- **Youden's J (informedness)**: From 0 (no better than chance) to 1 (perfect). Also called informedness or bookmaker informedness.

- **sensitivity**: Recall on positives.

- **specificity**: Recall on negatives. J gives both classes equal weight regardless of how many cases are in each.

- **on the ROC curve**: TPR − FPR: the vertical distance from the ROC curve to the diagonal. Its maximum is the KS statistic, and the threshold there is the classic “optimal cut-off”.

##### When Youden is right, and when it isn't

Maximising J is equivalent to minimising cost when CFN × prevalence = CFP × (1 − prevalence), i.e. when the total cost at stake in each class is equal. It's a sensible default for diagnostic tests with no cost information, and wrong whenever one error is far more expensive than the class ratio suggests.

#### "Recall is β times as important as precision"

$$ {F_\beta} = (1+{\beta^{2}})\,PR \,/\, (\beta^{2}P + R) = {(1+\beta^2)TP \,/\, \big((1+\beta^2)TP + FP + \beta^2 FN\big)} $$

scikit-learn's formula [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

- **F-beta**: A weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall.

- **β²**: β = 2 weights recall more (screening, finding all relevant documents); β = 0.5 weights precision more (spam, auto-actions). β = 1 is F1.

- **in counts**: β² multiplies the false negatives: larger β makes misses more expensive. True negatives still never appear.

#### MCC, balanced accuracy, G-mean and Cohen's kappa

$$ {\text{MCC}} = {(TP\cdot TN - FP\cdot FN)} \,/\, {\sqrt{(TP{+}FP)(TP{+}FN)(TN{+}FP)(TN{+}FN)}} $$

Matthews (1975). Chicco & Jurman: MCC "produces a high score only if the prediction obtained good results in all of the four confusion matrix categories", and should be preferred to accuracy and F1 for binary evaluation [BMC Genomics 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941312).

- **Matthews correlation**: The correlation between predictions and truth, from −1 (inverse) through 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Uses all four cells.

- **agreement minus disagreement**: TP·TN − FP·FN: positive only if the right-diagonal outweighs the wrong one.

- **normaliser**: The geometric mean of all four row and column totals, so MCC is high only if the model does well on both classes.

Three fraud models on 100,000 transactions (0.2% fraud):

Green = best in each row. "Never flag" scores 99.8% accuracy, beating model A, yet every metric designed for imbalance exposes it: balanced accuracy 0.5, MCC 0, kappa 0, G-mean 0. Between the two real models, the metrics disagree, because each encodes a different view of which mistake matters more.

| Metric | Definition | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Balanced accuracy** | (sensitivity + specificity) / 2; macro-averaged recall | You want "accuracy" that isn't fooled by imbalance; equals Youden's J rescaled |
| **MCC** | Correlation between prediction and truth | One honest summary of a binary confusion matrix; symmetric in the classes |
| **G-mean** | √(sensitivity × specificity) | Imbalanced-learning papers; punishes neglecting either class |
| **Cohen's kappa** | (accuracy − chance agreement) / (1 − chance agreement) | Originally for agreement between human annotators; scikit-learn notes it's designed for "comparing labelings by different human annotators, not a classifier versus a ground truth" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) |

## In practice

### In practice

#### Four ways teams choose a threshold

| Approach | What it assumes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimise expected cost** | You can price (or ratio) the errors; probabilities are calibrated | Fraud, credit, insurance, anything with money attached |
| **Fix one rate, optimise the other** | A hard constraint: "recall ≥ 95%", "≤ 500 alerts a day", "precision ≥ 90%" | Screening programmes, alert queues with fixed capacity |
| **Maximise Youden's J** | Sensitivity and specificity matter equally | Diagnostic test cut-offs in medicine |
| **Maximise F1 / F-beta** | Only the positive class matters; β sets recall vs precision | Information retrieval, detection tasks with no clear costs |

#### Reweighting during training is (mostly) a threshold shift

Two common ways to "handle imbalance": give positives weight w in the training loss, or train normally and lower the threshold afterwards. For a well-specified probabilistic model (like logistic regression), weighting positives by w multiplies the predicted odds by w. So a threshold of 0.5 on the weighted model is the same decision as a threshold of 1/(1 + w) on the unweighted one.

##### Prefer threshold moving when

- You need calibrated probabilities (weights distort them)

- Costs change over time: re-pick the threshold, no retraining

- You want one model serving several cost policies

##### Class weights / resampling help when

- The model has limited capacity and should spend it on the rare class (trees, small nets)

- The training loss would otherwise ignore positives entirely

- Then recalibrate before using the probabilities

#### Choosing a threshold in practice

1. Get calibrated probabilities on a validation set (check a reliability curve).

2. Agree the cost ratio CFN : CFP with the business, or the hard constraint (capacity, minimum recall).

3. Start from p* = CFP/(CFP + CFN); verify by computing expected cost across thresholds on validation data.

4. If there are constraints, pick the best threshold that satisfies them.

5. Report the confusion matrix and the money at that threshold, plus a threshold-free metric for model comparison.

6. Re-check when prevalence or costs change (fraud patterns, new pricing); the threshold is a business setting, not a model property.

#### Which criterion, in which situation

| Scenario | Choose the threshold by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Card fraud | Expected cost (₹), capped by analyst capacity | Clear money on both errors; alerts are a budget |
| Loan approval | Expected profit / cost per decision | Asymmetric and quantifiable; regulators also want a fixed, documented cut-off |
| Cancer screening | Minimum sensitivity (e.g. ≥ 95%), then best specificity; Youden as a no-cost default | Lives can't be priced comfortably; a constraint is easier to agree |
| Spam | High threshold (F0.5 or cost ratio 10:1) | False positives (lost email) are the expensive error |
| Search / retrieval without costs | F1 or F2 | Only the positive class is of interest |
| Reporting one honest score on imbalanced data | MCC (or balanced accuracy) | Uses all four cells; not fooled by the majority class |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Pick the threshold that maximises F1"

Maximising F1 is popular because it needs no cost numbers. But F1 has a hidden opinion: misses and false alarms are equally costly _relative to the positives_, and true negatives don't matter. In our scenarios, the F1-optimal threshold costs **2.1×** the optimum for fraud and **2.6×** for cancer screening. Any metric you maximise encodes a cost assumption; better to choose the assumption on purpose.

#### What to keep

- **p* = CFP/(CFP + CFN) needs calibrated probabilities.** With an overconfident model, tune the threshold empirically on validation data instead.

- **Costs are often per-case** (a ₹2 lakh fraud vs a ₹500 one). Then use example-dependent costs: flag if p·amount ≥ review cost.

- **Every "optimal threshold" metric hides a cost assumption**: Youden (equal per-class weight), F1 (TN don't matter, P and R equal), accuracy (all errors equal).

- **MCC and kappa are hard to explain** to non-technical stakeholders; translate the chosen operating point into counts and money.

## Say it

### How do you choose a classification threshold?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Missing fraud costs 100× a false alarm. What threshold?

p* = 1/(1 + 100) ≈ 0.0099: flag anything with at least about 1% fraud probability, assuming calibrated probabilities. Then check alert volume against review capacity.

Follow-up 2 of 4

What is Youden's J and when would you use it?

Sensitivity + specificity − 1, i.e. TPR − FPR; its maximum on the ROC curve is a common "optimal" cut-off in diagnostics. It weights the two classes equally regardless of size, so it's right only when the total cost at stake in each class is equal. Use it when there's no cost information.

Follow-up 3 of 4

MCC vs F1?

F1 ignores true negatives and changes if you swap which class is positive; MCC uses all four cells, is symmetric, and is 0 for random or constant predictions. On imbalanced data MCC is the more honest single number.

Follow-up 4 of 4

Class weights or threshold tuning for imbalance?

For calibrated probabilistic models they're nearly equivalent: weighting positives by w ≈ moving the threshold to 1/(1 + w). Threshold tuning keeps probabilities calibrated and lets you change policy without retraining. Weights help low-capacity models focus on the rare class; recalibrate afterwards.

#### The 30-second answer

The threshold is a business decision, not a model property. If the model's probabilities are calibrated and I can estimate the costs of a false positive and a false negative, I flag when p is at least C_FP over C_FP plus C_FN, which minimises expected cost. Without costs, I'd use a constraint like minimum recall, Youden's J if sensitivity and specificity matter equally, or F-beta to weight recall versus precision. For a single summary on imbalanced data I prefer MCC or balanced accuracy over accuracy and F1. Class weighting during training is essentially threshold moving, so I usually train normally, calibrate, then pick the threshold.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The default threshold is 0.5 so that's what we use." It's only optimal when the costs are equal and the probabilities are calibrated.

- "Maximise F1 to choose the threshold." Only if F1's hidden cost assumption fits.

- "Kappa is the standard metric for classifiers." It was designed for annotator agreement; MCC is usually clearer.

**Key terms and sources**

Youden's J, cost matrices, F-beta, MCC, balanced accuracy, G-mean and Cohen's kappa · built from Elkan (2001), Chicco & Jurman (2020), Fawcett (2006) and scikit-learn's docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cost matrix** | Price of each (prediction, truth) outcome. |
| **Cost-optimal threshold** | p* = CFP / (CFP + CFN) for calibrated p. |
| **Youden's J / informedness** | Sensitivity + specificity − 1 = TPR − FPR. |
| **F-beta** | Weighted harmonic mean; β > 1 favours recall. |
| **MCC** | Correlation between predicted and true labels (−1 to 1). |
| **Balanced accuracy** | Mean of per-class recall. |
| **G-mean** | √(sensitivity × specificity). |
| **Cohen's kappa** | Agreement corrected for chance. |
| **Threshold moving** | Changing the decision threshold after training instead of reweighting. |

#### What this page is built from

1. C. Elkan, [The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning](https://mlanthology.org/ijcai/2001/elkan2001ijcai-foundations), IJCAI 2001 (cost matrix, one degree of freedom, optimal threshold); summary in [Cost-sensitive machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost-sensitive_machine_learning).

2. W. J. Youden, "Index for rating diagnostic tests", _Cancer_ 3 (1950); J as informedness in the [ROC article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic).

3. D. Chicco & G. Jurman, [MCC vs F1 and accuracy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941312), BMC Genomics 2020.

4. scikit-learn, [Metrics and scoring](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html): balanced accuracy (adjusted = Youden's J), MCC, Cohen's kappa, F-beta.

5. Interview angle: [DataLemur](https://datalemur.com/blog/machine-learning-interview-questions).

# Regression Metrics

> RMSE went up 9× but MAE barely moved. Is the model worse?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/regression-metrics/
- Before this: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Two orders get stuck in traffic. Your ETA model's RMSE jumps ninefold, while its MAE barely moves. The interviewer asks:

> How do you choose between RMSE and MAE?

**Scenarios:** food-delivery ETA (minutes), house prices (₹), demand forecasting for a slow-moving item (units per day), salary prediction, stocking inventory to a service level, energy load. Data is illustrative; every metric is computed live.

#### "RMSE went up 9×, but MAE barely changed. Is the model worse?"

A delivery app's ETA model is off by about 2 minutes on a normal day. Then two orders get stuck in a traffic jam: 95 and 80 minutes instead of the predicted 33 and 30. RMSE jumps from 1.8 to 17.1 minutes; MAE goes from 1.7 to 6.6; the median error doesn't move at all. All three are "correct". They just answer different questions, and choosing between them is choosing what you want the model to be good at.

### The idea

Think of a restaurant's average bill. One huge party drags the mean up, but barely moves the median. RMSE behaves like the mean: a few huge misses dominate it. MAE behaves like the median.

[Figure: On a normal day RMSE is 1.8 and MAE is 1.7 minutes. With two orders stuck in traffic, RMSE jumps to 17.1 while MAE only reaches 6.6.]

_From the lesson's ETA example, in minutes._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Slide the constant prediction and find where each metric is lowest.

#### Each metric is minimised by a different summary of the target

If you could only predict one number for every case, which number would each metric reward? MSE is minimised by the **mean**, MAE by the **median**, pinball loss at level α by the **α-quantile**. That's the deep reason the metric choice matters: it decides what your model is trained and judged to predict. Drag the constant and watch each loss bottom out at a different place:

23 right-skewed delivery times (most 20–35 min, a few long ones). Curves scaled to a common height. The long tail pulls the mean above the median; a service-level target ("promise a time we beat 90% of the time") is a quantile. scikit-learn calls these "strictly consistent scoring functions": pick the metric for the statistic you want predicted [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

**Now say why:** why does each metric reward a different number, and what does that mean for what your model will learn to predict?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Every regression metric is a different way to average errors, and each one quietly rewards a different prediction. **MSE/RMSE** square errors, so big misses dominate and the best constant prediction is the **mean**. **MAE** treats every unit of error equally and rewards the **median**. **Pinball loss** rewards a chosen **quantile** (e.g. "enough stock 90% of days"). **R²** compares you with predicting the average and can go negative. **MAPE** is a percentage but explodes near zero and favours under-forecasting; **WAPE** and **MASE** fix that for demand forecasting. **RMSLE** cares about ratios and punishes under-prediction more. What you'll be able to do after this: pick the metric that matches what the business actually wants predicted (mean, median, quantile, ratio), and explain why a model's RMSE and MAE can tell opposite stories.

#### Errors, and three ways to average them

$$ {\text{MAE} = \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum|y_i - \hat y_i|} \qquad {\text{MSE} = \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum(y_i - \hat y_i)^2} \qquad {\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}}} $$

- **MAE**: Mean absolute error: the average size of a miss, in the target's own units (“off by 1.7 minutes”). Every minute of error counts the same.

- **MSE**: Mean squared error: squares each miss first, so a 10-minute miss costs 100 and a 1-minute miss costs 1. Units are squared (minutes²), hard to read.

- **RMSE**: Square root of MSE: back in minutes, but still dominated by the biggest misses. Always ≥ MAE; the gap tells you how uneven the errors are.

#### R²: better than predicting the average?

$$ {R^2} = 1 - {\textstyle\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2} \,/\, {\textstyle\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2} \qquad {\bar R^2 = 1 - (1-R^2)\,\tfrac{n-1}{n-p-1}} $$

scikit-learn: a constant model that always predicts the average "would get an R² score of 0.0", and R² "can be negative (because the model can be arbitrarily worse)" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

- **R²**: Share of the target's variance the model explains. 1 is perfect; 0 equals always predicting the mean; negative means worse than that.

- **your squared errors**: The model's residual sum of squares.

- **the mean's squared errors**: Total sum of squares: the error of the dumbest sensible model, a constant at the average.

- **adjusted R²**: Penalises extra features: with n rows and p features it only rises if a new feature helps more than chance would. Use it to compare models with different feature counts on training data.

##### R² is not comparable across datasets

It depends on how spread out the target is. In the traffic-jam example, R² fell from 0.87 to 0.04 because the jams made the denominator huge, not only because errors grew. A model with RMSE ₹5 lakh can have R² 0.9 on all-India house prices and 0.2 within one housing society. Report an error in real units next to R². scikit-learn also notes that explained variance ignores systematic offset, so R² "should be preferred in general" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

#### MAPE, sMAPE, WAPE and MASE for forecasting

Business teams love percentages ("we're 8% off") because they compare across products of different sizes. MAPE averages |error| / |actual|, and that denominator is the problem:

14 days of demand. On a zero-demand day, |error| / 0 is infinite; scikit-learn divides by a tiny ε instead, so a single zero turns MAPE into an astronomical number [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). WAPE divides total error by total demand, so zeros are harmless. MASE divides by the error of a naive "same as yesterday" forecast: below 1 means you beat naive.

##### MAPE's two biases

**Near zero:** tiny actuals give huge percentages. **Asymmetry:** under-forecasting can cost at most 100% (predict 0 for an actual 100), but over-forecasting is unbounded (predict 200 → 100%, 400 → 300%). So optimising MAPE pushes forecasts low, which for inventory means stock-outs.

##### What forecasters use instead

Hyndman and Koehler showed the common measures "can give infinite or undefined values in commonly occurring situations" and proposed **MASE**, the mean absolute scaled error, for comparing accuracy across series [Hyndman & Koehler 2006](https://www.doi.org/10.1016/J.IJFORECAST.2006.03.001). Retail teams also use **WAPE** (volume-weighted). sMAPE bounds the range but has its own asymmetry.

$$ {\text{MASE}} = {\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum|y_t - \hat y_t|} \,\Big/\, {\tfrac{1}{T-1}\textstyle\sum_{t=2}^{T}|y_t - y_{t-1}|} $$

- **MASE**: Your forecast's MAE divided by a benchmark MAE. Scale-free, works with zeros, and 1 means “as good as naive”.

- **your errors**: Mean absolute error of the forecast on the evaluation period.

- **naive forecast's errors**: The in-sample mean absolute change from one period to the next: the error of predicting “same as last period” (or same as last season for seasonal data).

#### When the business wants a quantile, not an average

An e-grocery store doesn't want to stock the _average_ demand; it wants enough to cover demand on 90% of days. A delivery app promising "arrives by 7:40" wants a time it beats 90% of the time. Train and judge those models with **pinball loss**:

$$ {\ell_\alpha(y,\hat y)} = {\alpha\,\max(y - \hat y, 0)} + {(1-\alpha)\,\max(\hat y - y, 0)} $$

scikit-learn's `mean_pinball_loss`; with α = 0.5 it "equals half of MAE" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Use the same α in the training loss (e.g. gradient boosting with `loss="quantile"`).

- **pinball loss at level α**: Asymmetric absolute error. α = 0.5 gives half the MAE (the median); α = 0.9 targets the 90th percentile.

- **under-prediction**: When the actual is above the prediction, pay α per unit: with α = 0.9, running out costs 9× more…

- **over-prediction**: …than overstocking, which costs only 1 − α = 0.1 per unit. The best constant is the point with 90% of outcomes below it.

#### RMSLE, and deviance for counts and claims

##### RMSLE: errors as ratios

RMSE on log(1 + y). Predicting ₹50k for a ₹1 lakh salary and ₹50 lakh for a ₹1 crore salary are the same error. scikit-learn notes it suits targets with exponential growth and "penalizes an under-predicted estimate greater than an over-predicted estimate" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Example: actual 100, predict 50 → 0.68; predict 150 → 0.40.

##### Poisson / Gamma / Tweedie deviance

For counts (calls per hour, claims per policy) and positive skewed amounts (claim sizes), use the deviance of the matching distribution. Tweedie with power 0 is MSE, 1 is Poisson, 2 is Gamma; at power 2 the deviance "is thus only sensitive to relative errors" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Insurance pricing teams use exactly this.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The metric menu

| Metric | Formula idea | Rewards predicting the… | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MSE / RMSE** | mean of squared errors | mean | target units (RMSE) |
| **MAE** | mean of absolute errors | median | target units |
| **Median AE, max error** | median / max of \|errors\| | typical case / worst case | target units |
| **Pinball (quantile) loss** | asymmetric absolute error | chosen quantile | target units |
| **R²** | 1 − SSres/SStot | mean (relative to a constant) | unitless, ≤ 1 |
| **MAPE / sMAPE** | mean of \|error\| / \|actual\| | a low-biased forecast | percent |
| **WAPE** | Σ\|error\| / Σ\|actual\| | median-ish, volume-weighted | percent |
| **MASE** | MAE / MAE of a naive forecast | median, scale-free | < 1 beats naive |
| **RMSLE** | RMSE of log(1 + y) | ratios (geometric) | log units |
| **Poisson / Tweedie deviance** | likelihood-based | mean of counts / claims | deviance |

#### Which metric, in which situation

| Scenario | Report | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery ETA | MAE + P90 absolute error (or pinball at 0.9 for the promise) | Customers feel minutes linearly; rare jams shouldn't dominate the headline, but the tail matters for promises |
| House price estimate | MAE in ₹ and median % error; RMSE if big misses are costly | Explainable to buyers; prices are skewed, so percentage errors also help |
| Demand forecasting (retail) | WAPE or MASE; pinball for stocking decisions | Zeros and mixed scales break MAPE; stocking is a quantile decision |
| Energy / load forecasting | RMSE (+ MAPE for reporting) | Large errors cause outages or expensive spot buying, so squaring fits; loads are never near zero |
| Salary, population, prices across orders of magnitude | RMSLE (or MAE on log target) | Ratios matter more than absolute rupees |
| Insurance claims, call volumes | Poisson / Tweedie deviance | Counts and zero-inflated amounts |
| Reporting to non-technical stakeholders | MAE (or WAPE) in real units + a baseline | "Off by 1.7 minutes, vs 4.2 for the old rule" |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "RMSE is the standard, report RMSE"

Same model, same 20 ordinary orders. RMSE is dominated by the two jams; the median absolute error ignores them completely; MAE sits in between. R² collapses because the jams also blow up the spread of actual times. None of these is "wrong": RMSE is right if a 60-minute miss really is 3,600× worse than a 1-minute one (it rarely is), MAE if every minute late costs the same.

#### What to keep

- **Train with the loss you'll be judged on.** A model trained on MSE predicts means; judging it on MAE or a quantile will look worse than a model trained for that target.

- **Always show a baseline**: predicting the mean (R² = 0), the median, last period's value (MASE = 1).

- **Look at the error distribution** (by segment, by size, the tail), not just one average.

- **Scale-dependent metrics** (MAE, RMSE) can't be compared across products or datasets; use scale-free ones (MASE, WAPE, R²) with care.

## Say it

### How do you choose between RMSE and MAE?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

MAE vs RMSE: when each?

RMSE when large errors are disproportionately bad (squaring) or you need the mean; MAE when every unit of error costs the same and you want robustness to outliers (it targets the median). RMSE ≥ MAE always; a big gap signals a few large errors.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Why is MAPE problematic?

Division by the actual: undefined at zero and huge near zero, and asymmetric. Under-forecasts are capped at 100% while over-forecasts are unbounded, so minimising MAPE biases forecasts low. Use WAPE, MASE or sMAPE (with care).

Follow-up 3 of 4

Can R² be negative?

Yes, on data where the model does worse than predicting the mean (typically test data, or models without an intercept). Training R² of OLS with an intercept is between 0 and 1.

Follow-up 4 of 4

How would you evaluate a model that sets inventory levels?

As a quantile problem: choose the service level (say 95%), train with pinball loss at α = 0.95, evaluate with pinball loss and actual coverage (did demand exceed the forecast about 5% of days?), and translate into stock-out and holding costs.

#### The 30-second answer

The metric decides what the model should predict. MSE and RMSE are minimised by the mean and are dominated by large errors; MAE is minimised by the median and is robust to outliers; pinball loss targets a chosen quantile, which is what you want for service levels or stocking. R² compares against predicting the mean and isn't comparable across datasets. For forecasting, MAPE breaks near zero and favours under-forecasting, so I'd use WAPE or MASE, and RMSLE when ratios matter. I always report the error in real units against a simple baseline.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "RMSE is the best regression metric." It's best for one goal (predicting means, punishing big misses).

- "R² of 0.6 is bad." It depends on the domain and the target's spread.

- "MAPE is fine, it's a percentage." Not with zeros, and not if under-forecasting is costly.

**Key terms and sources**

MAE, MSE, RMSE, R², MAPE, sMAPE, WAPE, MASE, RMSLE, pinball loss and more · built from scikit-learn's docs and Hyndman & Koehler (2006) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **MAE / MSE / RMSE** | Mean absolute / squared / root mean squared error. |
| **MedAE, max error** | Median and worst absolute error. |
| **R², adjusted R²** | Variance explained vs a constant; adjusted for feature count. |
| **MAPE, sMAPE** | Mean (symmetric) absolute percentage error. |
| **WAPE** | Σ\|error\| / Σ\|actual\|. |
| **MASE** | MAE relative to a naive forecast's in-sample MAE. |
| **RMSLE** | RMSE on log(1 + y). |
| **Pinball / quantile loss** | Asymmetric absolute error targeting a quantile. |
| **Tweedie deviance** | Family covering MSE (0), Poisson (1), Gamma (2). |

#### What this page is built from

1. scikit-learn, [Metrics and scoring: regression metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) (R², MAPE ε, MSLE, pinball, Tweedie, D², consistent scoring functions).

2. R. J. Hyndman & A. B. Koehler, [Another look at measures of forecast accuracy](https://www.doi.org/10.1016/J.IJFORECAST.2006.03.001), International Journal of Forecasting 22 (2006).

3. Interview angle: [Interview Query](https://interviewquery.com/p/linear-regression-interview-questions); [DataLemur](https://datalemur.com/blog/machine-learning-interview-questions).

Delivery, demand and skewed-time data are illustrative.
