# Ranking Metrics

> How do you score a search page, a recommendation list, or a RAG retriever?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/ranking-metrics/
- Before this: Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`)
- Related: Design a recommendation system (`system-design/recommendation-system`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Two search engines return the same 10 products in a different order. Accuracy-style metrics score them the same, but users don't see them the same. The interviewer asks:

> Which metrics would you use to evaluate a ranked list?

**Scenarios:** an e-commerce search for "wireless earbuds under ₹3,000" with graded relevance labels (3 = perfect, 2 = good, 1 = loosely related, 0 = irrelevant), and a RAG retriever that must find the one chunk containing the answer. Lists and labels are illustrative; metrics are computed live.

#### Two search engines return the same 10 products in a different order

Accuracy-style metrics see the same set and score them identically. Users don't: they look at the first few results, and a perfect match in position 1 is worth far more than one in position 9. A RAG system is even stricter: if the chunk with the answer isn't in the top 5 passed to the LLM, the answer is lost no matter what's at position 6. Ranking metrics put a number on "the right things, near the top".

### The idea

Think of a shop window. Items at the front get seen, and items at the back barely do. Ranking metrics give more credit for putting good items near the front, and they differ in how much.

[Figure: Bars for result positions 1 to 5. Each position counts for less: 1, 0.63, 0.5, 0.43 and 0.39.]

_The standard log discount used in DCG, 1 ÷ log₂(position + 1)._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare Engine A and Engine C at a cut-off of 10, then change the cut-off to 3. Then look at the ideal order.

#### Three engines, one query, every metric

Binary metrics count grade ≥ 2 ("good" or better) as relevant. There are 5 such items in the catalogue for this query, one of which no engine retrieved in its top 10 (so recall never reaches 100%). NDCG uses the grades (0–3) directly as gains, with the ideal order built from all labelled items.

**Now say why:** why can two engines tie on one metric and differ on another?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Search, recommendations and RAG retrieval return an **ordered list**, and users mostly look at the top. Ranking metrics score the list, not single predictions. **Precision@k**: how much of the top k is relevant. **Recall@k**: how much of everything relevant made the top k (the key RAG retriever metric). **MRR**: how high the first relevant result is. **MAP**: precision averaged at every relevant hit. **NDCG**: graded relevance with a position discount, normalised against the ideal order, the standard for search. Offline metrics are a proxy; online behaviour (clicks, conversions) is the truth. What you'll be able to do after this: compute every metric by hand on a ranked list, choose the right one for search vs RAG vs recommendations, and explain why NDCG needs graded labels.

#### Relevance labels and the cut-off k

You need a judgement for each (query, item) pair: **binary** (relevant or not; RAG gold chunks, clicked or not) or **graded** (0–3 from human raters, or purchase > add-to-cart > click). And a **cut-off k**: how many positions matter (what fits on the first screen, how many chunks fit in the prompt). Every metric below is "@k". Choose k from the product, not habit.

#### Precision@k, Recall@k and hit rate

$$ {P@k = \tfrac{\#\text{rel in top }k}{k}} \qquad {R@k = \tfrac{\#\text{rel in top }k}{\#\text{rel total}}} \qquad {HR@k = \mathbb 1[\#\text{rel in top }k \ge 1]} $$

- **precision@k**: Share of the top k that is relevant. What the user sees on the first screen.

- **recall@k**: Share of all relevant items that made the top k. For RAG, the gold chunk must be in the k chunks sent to the LLM: this is the retriever's key metric.

- **hit rate@k**: 1 if at least one relevant item is in the top k, else 0, averaged over queries. Common for recommendations (“did the user's next purchase appear in our 10 suggestions?”).

Recall@k needs to know every relevant item, which is easy when there's one gold answer (RAG evaluation sets) and hard for open catalogues, where it's estimated by pooling results from several systems (the TREC approach).

#### Reciprocal rank and MRR

$$ {\text{MRR}} = {\tfrac{1}{|Q|}\textstyle\sum_{q\in Q}} \,1\,/\,{\text{rank}_q} $$

scikit-learn notes that with exactly one relevant label per sample, label-ranking average precision "is equivalent to the mean reciprocal rank" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

- **mean reciprocal rank**: Average over queries of 1 / (position of the first relevant result).

- **over queries**: |Q| queries in the evaluation set.

- **rank of the first hit**: First relevant at position 1 → 1.0; at 2 → 0.5; at 5 → 0.2; none found → 0. Steep: moving from 1st to 2nd halves the score.

RAG retriever evaluation: 8 questions, each with one gold chunk. The table shows the rank where each retriever placed it (— = not in the top 20).

Retriever X often puts the gold chunk first but sometimes misses it entirely; Y rarely ranks it first but almost always gets it into the top 5. If you pass 5 chunks to the LLM, Y's Recall@5 matters more than X's higher MRR. If you show one answer (a FAQ bot), MRR, or even Recall@1, is the metric.

#### Average precision and MAP

$$ {AP@k} = {\tfrac{1}{\min(k,\,R)}}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} P@i\cdot{\text{rel}(i)} $$

The standard IR definition (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, _Introduction to Information Retrieval_, ch. 8); it's the ranking version of the area under the precision–recall curve from the ROC vs PR lesson.

- **average precision@k**: For one query: average of precision@i taken at each position i where a relevant item appears.

- **only at hits**: rel(i) is 1 at relevant positions, 0 elsewhere, so precision is sampled exactly where the user finds something useful.

- **normaliser**: Divide by the number of relevant items (capped at k in the @k version), so missing relevant items costs you. MAP is the mean of AP over queries.

#### DCG and NDCG

$$ {\text{DCG}@k} = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\text{rel}_i} \,/\, {\log_2(i+1)} \qquad {\text{NDCG}@k = \text{DCG}@k \,/\, \text{IDCG}@k} $$

Järvelin & Kekäläinen introduced cumulated gain, its discounted version, and normalisation against the ideal ranking [ACM TOIS 2002](https://trepo.tuni.fi/bitstream/10024/65718/1/cumulated_gain_based_indicators_2002.pdf). scikit-learn: "Use NDCG when [the ground truth] has graded relevance" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html). Log base and gain function vary between libraries: always say which you used.

- **discounted cumulative gain**: Sum of the gains of the top k items, each discounted by its position.

- **gain**: The relevance grade of the item at position i (some use 2^rel − 1 to reward top grades more strongly).

- **position discount**: Divide by log₂(i + 1): position 1 counts fully, 2 counts 63%, 3 counts 50%, 10 counts 29%.

- **normalise**: Divide by the DCG of the ideal ordering (IDCG), so NDCG is between 0 and 1 and comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant items.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Labels are a proxy; users are the truth

##### Offline (before launch)

- NDCG / MAP / Recall@k on labelled queries

- Fast, repeatable, cheap to compare 50 models

- Labels can be stale, biased toward what the old system showed, or miss new items

##### Online (after launch)

- Click-through rate, conversion, add-to-cart, dwell time, "zero-result rate", reformulation rate

- A/B test against the current system

- Clicks have **position bias** (people click the top regardless), so raw CTR flatters whatever is shown first

Beyond accuracy, recommenders also track **coverage** (how much of the catalogue ever gets recommended), **diversity** (are the top 10 all the same item in different colours?) and **novelty**. A list that maximises NDCG with ten near-duplicates is a bad product.

#### Which metric, in which situation

| Scenario | Offline metric | Why |
|---|---|---|
| E-commerce / web search | NDCG@10 (graded) | Grades and positions both matter; first screen dominates |
| RAG retriever | Recall@k (k = chunks passed to the LLM), + MRR | The answer must be in the context; order matters less once it's in |
| FAQ bot / "I'm feeling lucky" / voice assistant | MRR or Recall@1 | Only the first answer is used |
| Recommendations ("next purchase") | Hit rate@k, Recall@k, + coverage/diversity | Usually one held-out positive per user; avoid an all-bestseller list |
| Binary relevance with several relevant items (document retrieval) | MAP | Rewards finding all of them early |
| Legal / patent / medical literature search | Recall@k with large k | Missing a relevant document is the costly error |
| Feed ranking at scale | NDCG offline, CTR / dwell / retention online | Offline to iterate, online to decide |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Use precision@10"

Precision@10 counts relevant items in the top 10, so it can't tell "perfect match first" from "perfect match tenth", and it treats a loosely related accessory like the exact product. In the Play lab, in the Intuition tab, engines A and C have the same precision@10 but very different NDCG. Position and grade both matter, which is what MRR, MAP and NDCG add.

#### What to keep

- **Average over queries, then look at the worst queries.** A great mean can hide queries that return nothing useful.

- **NDCG values aren't comparable** across different gain functions, log bases, k, or label sets.

- **Relevance labels age**: new products, new documents, new user intents. Refresh them.

- **Offline wins don't always transfer online.** Treat offline metrics as a filter for what's worth an A/B test.

## Say it

### Which metrics would you use to evaluate a ranked list?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

How would you evaluate the retriever in a RAG system?

Build a set of questions with gold chunks (or answer-containing passages). Measure Recall@k at the k you actually pass to the LLM, plus MRR and latency. Then evaluate end-to-end answer quality separately, since good retrieval doesn't guarantee a good answer.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Why the log discount in NDCG?

It models declining attention down the list, smoothly: position 1 counts fully, position 10 about 29%. Normalising by the ideal DCG makes scores comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant items.

Follow-up 3 of 4

MRR vs MAP?

MRR only cares about the first relevant item, right for single-answer tasks. MAP rewards ranking all relevant items early, right when users want several.

Follow-up 4 of 4

Offline NDCG improved but online CTR didn't. Why?

Stale or biased labels, position bias in the click data the labels came from, a mismatch between label grades and what users want, diversity or latency changes, or a difference too small to show up in the test. Check per-segment results and run the test long enough.

#### The 30-second answer

Ranking metrics score an ordered list at a cut-off k. Precision@k and Recall@k ignore order within the top k; MRR looks at the position of the first relevant result; MAP averages precision at each relevant hit; NDCG uses graded relevance with a logarithmic position discount, normalised by the ideal ranking. For a RAG retriever I'd use Recall@k with k equal to the number of chunks in the prompt, plus MRR; for search, NDCG@10; for single-answer systems, MRR. Then I'd validate online with an A/B test on clicks or conversions, keeping position bias in mind.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Accuracy for search." Order and position are the whole point.

- "NDCG with binary labels is the same as MAP." They weight positions differently.

- "High offline NDCG means users will be happy." Validate online.

**Key terms and sources**

Precision@k, Recall@k, Hit Rate, MRR, MAP and NDCG · built from Järvelin & Kekäläinen (2002), Manning et al.'s _Introduction to IR_ and scikit-learn's docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P@k / R@k** | Share of top k that's relevant / share of relevant found in top k. |
| **Hit rate@k** | At least one relevant in top k. |
| **MRR** | Mean of 1 / rank of the first relevant result. |
| **AP / MAP** | Precision averaged at each relevant position / mean over queries. |
| **DCG / NDCG** | Position-discounted graded gain / normalised by the ideal order. |
| **IDCG** | DCG of the best possible ordering. |
| **Position bias** | Users click higher results more, regardless of relevance. |

#### What this page is built from

1. K. Järvelin & J. Kekäläinen, [Cumulated gain-based evaluation of IR techniques](https://trepo.tuni.fi/bitstream/10024/65718/1/cumulated_gain_based_indicators_2002.pdf), ACM TOIS 20(4) (2002).

2. C. Manning, P. Raghavan & H. Schütze, _Introduction to Information Retrieval_, ch. 8 (evaluation: precision, recall, MAP), Cambridge University Press 2008.

3. scikit-learn, [Metrics and scoring: ranking metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) (DCG/NDCG, LRAP ≈ MRR, coverage error).

4. [Discounted cumulative gain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounted_cumulative_gain) (common log₂(i + 1) form).

Search results, grades and RAG ranks are illustrative.

# Probability Metrics

> The model ranks perfectly, so why are the bids wrong?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/probability-metrics/
- Before this: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC (`fundamentals/roc-auc-vs-pr-auc`), Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your ad model bids price = P(click) × value. It ranks ads perfectly, but it says 4% when the true rate is 2%, so every bid is double what it should be. The interviewer asks:

> How do you check whether a model's probabilities can be trusted?

**Scenarios:** ad click-through prediction for bidding, insurance and credit risk pricing, medical risk scores shown to patients, weather forecasting (where the Brier score was born), and deep-network confidence. Predictions come from a simple model (illustrative) whose calibration you can break and fix live; the published results are from Guo et al. (2017).

#### "The model ranks perfectly, so why are we losing money on bids?"

An ad platform bids **price = P(click) × value of a click**. If the model says 4% when the true rate is 2%, every bid is double what it should be. The model can still _rank_ ads perfectly, so its AUC looks great. Ranking metrics can't see this error. You need metrics that check whether the numbers themselves are right.

### The idea

Think of a weather forecaster. When they say 70% chance of rain, it should rain on about 70% of those days. That's calibration. A forecaster can order days perfectly by rain risk and still get the chances wrong.

[Figure: A reliability diagram. A dashed diagonal shows perfect calibration. An overconfident model's curve sits below it at high predictions and above it at low ones.]

_Illustrative. A reliability diagram compares what a model says with what really happens._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the temperature away from 1 in both directions, and watch AUC, log-loss and the diagram. Then apply temperature scaling.

#### Reliability diagram: break the calibration, watch which metrics notice

10% positives; predictions computed over 20,000 cases. Left: reliability diagram (bars = observed frequency per confidence bin; diagonal = perfect; red = gap). Right: how many predictions fall in each bin. Overconfidence (T < 1) pushes predictions toward 0 and 1, so bars sit below the diagonal on the right. AUC never changes with T, because temperature doesn't change the order.

**Now say why:** why can AUC stay put while the probabilities become badly wrong?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

When decisions use the probability itself (pricing, bidding, risk scores, the cost thresholds from Thresholds & Costs), you need probabilities that are **right**, not just well ranked. **Calibration** means "of all cases predicted 70%, about 70% happen". **Log-loss** and the **Brier score** are proper scoring rules: they're best only when predicted probabilities equal the true ones, so they reward both sharpness and calibration. A **reliability diagram** and the **expected calibration error (ECE)** isolate calibration. Key insight: you can wreck calibration without changing **AUC at all**. Modern deep networks tend to be overconfident, and a one-parameter fix, **temperature scaling**, usually repairs it. What you'll be able to do after this: read a reliability diagram, explain why AUC can't detect miscalibration, choose between log-loss, Brier and ECE, and calibrate a model properly.

#### Calibration and sharpness

##### Calibration

Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: P(y = 1 | p̂ = p) = p for every p. Guo et al.: "given 100 predictions, each with confidence of 0.8, we expect that 80 should be correctly classified" [Guo et al. 2017, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=2).

##### Sharpness (resolution)

Predictions far from the base rate. Always predicting the base rate (say 10%) is perfectly calibrated and useless. Good probabilistic models are both calibrated and sharp.

#### Two proper scoring rules and one calibration error

$$ {\text{LL} = -\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum\big[y\log\hat p + (1-y)\log(1-\hat p)\big]} \quad {\text{BS} = \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum(\hat p - y)^2} \quad {\text{ECE} = \textstyle\sum_m \tfrac{|B_m|}{n}\,\big|\text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m)\big|} $$

ECE as defined by Guo et al., Eq. 3 [p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=3); Brier score: Brier (1950); scikit-learn calls it "strictly proper", achieving "the best score only when the estimated probabilities equal the true ones" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).

- **log-loss**: Negative log-likelihood: −log of the probability given to what happened. Unbounded: a confident wrong prediction (p = 0.001 for an event that happens) costs 6.9. Strictly proper.

- **Brier score**: Mean squared difference between predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome. Bounded between 0 and 1, gentler on confident mistakes. Also strictly proper.

- **expected calibration error**: Bin predictions by confidence, compare each bin's average confidence with its observed frequency, and take the weighted average gap. Measures calibration only, not sharpness.

#### Murphy's decomposition: reliability − resolution + uncertainty

$$ {\text{BS}} = {\text{REL}} - {\text{RES}} + {\text{UNC}} $$

Murphy (1973), via the [Brier score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score) article. scikit-learn's warning follows from it: "A lower Brier loss, for instance, does not necessarily mean a better calibrated model" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html); a sharper model can win on resolution while being worse calibrated. The **Brier skill score** 1 − BS / BSbase-rate rescales it so that predicting the base rate scores 0.

- **Brier score**: Lower is better.

- **reliability**: Calibration error: how far each group's predicted probability is from what actually happened. 0 = perfectly reliable. Lower is better.

- **resolution**: How much the groups' outcome rates differ from the overall base rate: sharpness that's real. Higher is better, so it's subtracted.

- **uncertainty**: ō(1 − ō) for base rate ō: how hard the problem is. Fixed by the data; no model changes it.

#### Platt scaling, isotonic regression, temperature scaling

$$ {\hat q_i} = \max_k\ \mathrm{softmax}\big({z_i} \,/\, {T}\big)^{(k)} $$

Guo et al., Eq. 9: "temperature scaling does not affect the model's accuracy" [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=6).

- **calibrated confidence**: The new probability for input i.

- **the logits**: The model's raw scores before the softmax: untouched.

- **one temperature**: A single scalar T > 0 fitted by minimising log-loss on a held-out validation set. T > 1 softens overconfident outputs. Because dividing by T doesn't change the argmax, accuracy is unchanged.

| Method | What it fits | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Platt scaling** | A logistic regression on the model's score (2 parameters) | Binary classifiers with sigmoid-shaped distortion (SVMs, boosted trees); small validation sets |
| **Temperature scaling** | One parameter on the logits | Neural networks, multi-class; the default first try |
| **Isotonic regression** | Any monotonic step function | Large validation sets and odd-shaped distortions; can overfit small sets |
| **Histogram binning** | One probability per score bin | Simple, robust; can change class predictions |

In scikit-learn: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid" | "isotonic")`, fitted on data the model wasn't trained on. Logistic regression is often well calibrated already: it "is more likely to return well calibrated predictions by itself" thanks to its canonical link [scikit-learn calibration docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Bigger, more accurate, and worse calibrated

Guo et al. found that "modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated": a 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-100 is more accurate than a 5-layer LeNet, but its average confidence is far above its accuracy. Depth, width, batch normalisation and less weight decay all made calibration worse; their explanation is that networks keep lowering training log-loss by growing more confident after they already classify the training data correctly [Guo et al. 2017, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=3).

##### ECE on CIFAR-100 (ResNet-110), before and after post-hoc calibration (↓ better)

uncalibrated

16.53%

histogram binning

2.66%

isotonic regression

4.99%

temperature scaling

1.26%

matrix scaling

25.49%

15 bins. Matrix scaling has too many parameters for 100 classes and overfits the validation set [Table 1, p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=6). Across vision and NLP datasets, uncalibrated ECE was "typically between 4 to 10%", and temperature scaling was best on the vision tasks [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599#page=7).

#### Which metric, in which situation

| Scenario | Report | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ad click prediction for bidding | Log-loss + calibration (predicted/actual CTR ratio by segment) | Bids multiply by p; a 2× bias doubles spend |
| Credit default, insurance claims pricing | Brier / log-loss + reliability by score band; AUC/Gini for ranking | Prices and capital depend on the probability level, not just the order |
| Weather forecasts ("70% chance of rain") | Brier score and its decomposition | Where it came from: Brier, _Monthly Weather Review_, 1950 |
| Medical risk shown to patients or doctors | Calibration plot + Brier | A "12% risk" must mean 12%; patients act on the number |
| Deep-network classifier confidence (abstain / route to a human) | ECE + log-loss; temperature-scale first | Overconfidence makes "only answer when sure" unreliable |
| Fraud alert ranking with a capacity limit | PR-AUC; calibration matters less | Only the order of the top alerts is used (unless costs use p) |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "AUC is 0.92, the probabilities must be fine"

AUC only looks at the **order** of the scores. Squash or stretch every probability with any monotonic function (make them all twice as confident) and the order, and the AUC, are unchanged, while every probability is now wrong. The Play lab, in the Intuition tab, proves it: move the temperature and AUC stays fixed at its value while log-loss, Brier and ECE all move.

#### What to keep

- **ECE depends on binning** (number of bins, equal-width vs equal-count) and is noisy with few samples per bin; it also ignores sharpness. Report it with log-loss or Brier, never alone.

- **Calibrate on held-out data**, never the training set, and re-check after data drift.

- **Resampling and class weights break calibration** (see Thresholds & Costs); recalibrate afterwards.

- **Calibration is about groups, not individuals.** "70%" being right on average says nothing about any one case, and can hide miscalibration within subgroups (check fairness-relevant segments).

## Say it

### How do you check whether a model's probabilities can be trusted?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Log-loss vs Brier: which?

Both are proper. Log-loss is unbounded and harshly punishes confident mistakes, which suits systems where a 0.1% prediction for a frequent event is catastrophic, and it's what models are trained on. Brier is bounded, gentler, decomposes into reliability, resolution and uncertainty, and is common in forecasting and medicine.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Can a model have high AUC and poor calibration?

Yes. Any monotonic distortion of the scores keeps AUC identical while making probabilities wrong. Conversely, predicting the base rate for everyone is perfectly calibrated with AUC 0.5.

Follow-up 3 of 4

How does temperature scaling work, and why doesn't it change accuracy?

Divide the logits by a scalar T fitted to minimise validation log-loss. It rescales confidence but keeps the logits' order, so the argmax (and accuracy) is unchanged.

Follow-up 4 of 4

What's wrong with ECE?

It depends on the binning scheme, is biased with few samples, ignores sharpness, and only looks at the top-class confidence. Pair it with log-loss or Brier and a reliability diagram.

#### The 30-second answer

When decisions use the probability itself, like bidding, pricing or risk thresholds, I check calibration as well as ranking. AUC can't detect miscalibration because it only depends on order. Log-loss and Brier are proper scoring rules that reward both calibration and sharpness; a reliability diagram and ECE isolate calibration. Modern neural networks tend to be overconfident, and temperature scaling, one parameter fitted on validation data, usually fixes that without changing accuracy. For other models I'd use Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Softmax outputs are probabilities." They sum to 1, but they're often miscalibrated.

- "Lower Brier means better calibrated." It also rewards sharpness.

- "Calibrate on the training set." Use held-out data.

**Key terms and sources**

Log-loss, Brier score, reliability diagrams, ECE and calibration methods · built from Guo et al. (2017), Brier (1950), Murphy (1973) and scikit-learn's docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Calibration** | Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. |
| **Proper scoring rule** | Expected score is optimised by reporting the true probability (log-loss, Brier). |
| **Log-loss / NLL / cross-entropy** | −mean log probability of what happened. |
| **Brier score** | Mean squared error of probabilities. |
| **Reliability diagram** | Observed frequency vs predicted confidence, per bin. |
| **ECE / MCE** | Weighted average / maximum gap between confidence and accuracy over bins. |
| **Temperature scaling** | Divide logits by a fitted T. |
| **Platt / isotonic** | Sigmoid / monotonic step-function recalibration. |

#### What this page is built from

1. C. Guo, G. Pleiss, Y. Sun & K. Weinberger, [On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599), ICML 2017 (ECE, reliability diagrams, temperature scaling, Table 1).

2. G. W. Brier, "Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability", _Monthly Weather Review_ (1950); A. H. Murphy, "A new vector partition of the probability score" (1973); summary in [Brier score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score).

3. scikit-learn, [Metrics and scoring](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html) (log-loss, Brier, strictly proper) and [Probability calibration](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html).

4. A. Niculescu-Mizil & R. Caruana, "Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning", ICML 2005 (Platt vs isotonic; background).

The live lab uses an illustrative two-bell-curve score model with 10% positives; the published numbers are Guo et al.'s.

# Choosing the Right Metric

> Which metric would you use for X? Twelve scenarios to practise.

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Evaluation metrics
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/choosing-the-right-metric/
- Before this: Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`), Regression Metrics (`fundamentals/regression-metrics`), Ranking Metrics (`fundamentals/ranking-metrics`), Probability Metrics (`fundamentals/probability-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `metrics`

## Intuition

### The situation

A team raises their recommender's offline NDCG by 4% and ships it. Engagement goes up, but returns and refund complaints go up more. The interviewer asks:

> Which metric would you use?

#### The model improved. The business got worse.

Here's an illustrative story. A team raises their recommender's offline NDCG by 4% and ships it. Engagement goes up; returns and refund complaints go up more, because the model learned to push cheap, clicky items. Nothing was wrong with NDCG. It just wasn't the whole goal. The metric question in interviews ("how would you evaluate this?") is really asking: do you know what success means here, and how would you know you'd achieved it?

### The idea

Think of a shop that rewards staff only for sales. Sales rise, and so do returns. Any metric becomes a target that gets chased, so start from how the output is used, and keep guardrails on what mustn't get worse.

[Figure: Three layers. A model metric to iterate quickly, a business metric that must move, and guardrails that must not get worse.]

_From the lesson's three layers._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set a new model just slightly above the old one and shrink the test set. Then grow the test set until the difference looks real.

#### Metric differences need error bars

A test set is a sample. An accuracy measured on n examples has a standard error of about √(p(1 − p)/n), so a 95% interval is roughly ±1.96 of those. Before celebrating a new model, check the gap is bigger than the noise:

Normal approximation, treating the two accuracies as independent (conservative). Both models are usually scored on the same test set, so a paired test (McNemar's test on the examples where they disagree, or a paired bootstrap) is tighter and is the standard recommendation (Dietterich, 1998). The point stands: at n = 1,000, a 1-point accuracy gain is inside the noise.

- **Bootstrap** any metric (AUC, NDCG, F1): resample the test set with replacement 1,000 times, recompute, read off the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

- **Rare classes make it worse**: recall on 50 positives moves 2 points per example.

- **Don't tune on the test set**: every look at it is a chance to overfit; keep a validation set for choices and touch the test set once.

**Now say why:** when can you trust that one model really is better?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Pick the metric from **what the model's output is used for**: a decision with asymmetric costs, a ranked list, a number, or a probability that feeds another calculation. Pair one **headline model metric** with the **business metric** it's meant to move and a few **guardrails** that must not get worse. Always compare against a baseline, and check whether a difference is bigger than the noise: on 1,000 test examples, 91% vs 90% accuracy is not a real win. What you'll be able to do after this: answer "which metric would you use for X?" for any scenario in under a minute, with a reason, and challenge a claimed improvement that's within noise.

#### Model metric, business metric, guardrails

| Layer | Example (fraud) | Example (search) | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model metric** (offline) | PR-AUC; recall at 500 alerts/day | NDCG@10 | Fast to compute; used to iterate and choose models |
| **Business metric** (online) | ₹ fraud losses prevented | Conversion, revenue per search | What you actually care about; slow and noisy |
| **Guardrails** | Good customers blocked per 10,000; review queue length | Latency, zero-result rate, return rate | Must not get worse while the main metric improves |

Online experimentation practice formalises this as an overall evaluation criterion plus guardrail metrics (Kohavi, Tang & Xu, _Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments_, 2020).

#### Start from how the output is used

1. Don't start from the model type. Start from what someone or something does with the output.

2. **A yes/no decision:** the costs of the two errors decide the metric (Classification Metrics, Thresholds & Costs).

3. **A ranked list:** what matters is the top of the list and how many items get used (Ranking Metrics, ROC vs PR).

4. **A number:** which summary of the outcome you want predicted: mean, median, quantile, ratio (Regression Metrics).

5. **A probability used in a calculation:** it must be calibrated, not just well ranked (Probability Metrics).

## In practice

### In practice

#### A metric plan for any project

1. **Write down the decision** the model supports, and who acts on it.

2. **Price the errors** (or rank them): which mistake is worse, roughly by how much?

3. **Choose one headline offline metric** that matches the output type and the error costs.

4. **Name the business metric** it should move, and 2–3 **guardrails** (latency, fairness across segments, complaints, coverage).

5. **Set baselines**: majority class, current system, a simple heuristic.

6. **Report with uncertainty** (CIs or bootstrap) and **by segment** (new vs returning users, regions, rare classes).

7. **Validate online** with an A/B test before declaring victory; re-check when data or costs drift.

#### All six lessons on one table

| Situation | Metric | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Balanced classes, equal costs | Accuracy | Classification |
| Misses are costly | Recall (at a precision floor), F2 | Classification, Thresholds |
| False alarms are costly | Precision, F0.5 | Classification, Thresholds |
| Costs known | Expected cost; threshold p* = CFP/(CFP+CFN) | Thresholds |
| One fair number, imbalanced | MCC, balanced accuracy | Thresholds |
| Many classes, rare ones matter | Macro-F1 + per-class recall | Classification |
| Ranking quality, any balance | ROC-AUC (Gini, KS) | ROC vs PR |
| Ranking with rare positives | PR-AUC, precision@k | ROC vs PR |
| Search with graded relevance | NDCG@k | Ranking |
| RAG retrieval | Recall@k, MRR | Ranking |
| Numeric, typical error | MAE (median) | Regression |
| Numeric, big misses costly | RMSE (mean) | Regression |
| Service level / stocking | Pinball loss at α | Regression |
| Forecasts with zeros / many series | WAPE, MASE | Regression |
| Probabilities used in calculations | Log-loss, Brier, ECE + reliability diagram | Probability |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Optimise the metric everyone reports"

Goodhart's law, in Marilyn Strathern's phrasing: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Optimise accuracy on imbalanced data and you get "never flag". Optimise MAPE and forecasts drift low. Optimise click-through and you get clickbait. Every metric in this section has a way to be gamed, so choose it knowing how, and watch the guardrails.

## Say it

### Which metric would you use?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Model B is 0.4% more accurate than A. Ship it?

Depends on the test-set size and variance: compute a confidence interval or a paired test. Also check per-segment results, latency and cost, and whether accuracy is even the right metric for the task.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Offline metrics improved but online metrics didn't. Why?

The offline metric is a poor proxy for the business goal, training–serving skew, stale or biased labels, feedback effects (the new model changes the data), novelty effects, or a test that's too small. Investigate by segment.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's a guardrail metric?

A metric that must not get worse while you optimise the main one: latency, error rates, fairness gaps, complaint rate, unsubscribe rate. It protects against Goodhart-style gaming of the headline metric.

#### A 4-step answer template

First, how is the output used: a decision, a ranking, a number, or a probability. Second, which mistake is worse and roughly by how much. That gives me the headline metric, for example recall at a precision floor for fraud, with PR-AUC to compare models. Third, the business metric it should move and the guardrails, like blocked good customers and review queue length. Fourth, baselines and uncertainty: compare with the current system using bootstrap intervals, then confirm with an A/B test.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "I'd use accuracy" (without checking balance and costs).

- "The new model is better because its metric is higher" (without error bars or a baseline).

- "Offline metrics are enough" (for anything user-facing).

**Key terms and sources**

A decision guide, 12 interview scenarios, and "is the difference real?" · built from the six metric lessons, Kohavi et al. (2020) and Dietterich (1998) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### What this page is built from

1. The six lessons of this section and their sources (scikit-learn, Fawcett, Davis & Goadrich, Saito & Rehmsmeier, Elkan, Chicco & Jurman, Hyndman & Koehler, Järvelin & Kekäläinen, Guo et al., Brier, Murphy).

2. R. Kohavi, D. Tang & Y. Xu, _Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing_, Cambridge University Press, 2020 (overall evaluation criterion, guardrail metrics).

3. T. G. Dietterich, "Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms", _Neural Computation_ 10 (1998) (McNemar's test, paired comparisons).

4. M. Strathern, "Improving ratings: audit in the British University system", _European Review_ 5 (1997) (the common phrasing of Goodhart's law).

# The Bias–Variance Trade-off

> Two models are equally wrong for opposite reasons. How do you tell which, and fix it?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/bias-variance/
- Before this: Linear Regression (`fundamentals/linear-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

A straight-line model misses your delivery curve the same way every time. A degree-15 model fits its training data, but gives a completely different wiggle on each new sample. The interviewer asks:

> What is the bias–variance trade-off?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app predicts delivery time (minutes) from distance (km). The true relationship is a known smooth curve, and each delivery adds random noise with a standard deviation of 4 minutes (traffic, a slow lift, a chatty customer). A training set is 25 deliveries spread over 0–10 km. Because we know the truth, we can redraw the training set again and again and measure bias and variance exactly, something you can never do with real data.

#### Two different ways to be wrong

A straight-line model misses the curve: it's wrong in the same direction every time, no matter which 25 deliveries it sees. A wiggly degree-15 polynomial passes near every training delivery, but each new training set gives a completely different wiggle. Both have bad test error, for opposite reasons, and they need opposite fixes. Telling them apart is one of the most practical skills in ML, and the most-asked "fundamentals" interview topic.

### The idea

Think of archery. Bias is every arrow landing together in the wrong spot. Variance is arrows scattered all over the target. Making a model more flexible usually trades the first problem for the second.

[Figure: Two archery targets. On the left, arrows cluster tightly but away from the centre, which is high bias. On the right, arrows scatter widely around the centre, which is high variance.]

_Illustrative. Test error adds these two to noise you can't remove._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at degree 1 and move up to the highest degree. Watch the thin lines, and read bias² and variance at each step.

#### See bias and variance by refitting on many samples

Thin lines: the same model trained on 20 different samples of 25 deliveries. Thick green: the truth. Dashed: the average of 60 fits. Numbers average over 60 training sets and 41 test distances in 0.5–9.5 km.

Degree 1: all twenty lines agree with each other (variance 1.06) and all miss the curve the same way (bias² 8.1). Degree 15: the average of the fits sits almost exactly on the truth (bias² 0.07), but individual fits swing wildly, especially near the ends (variance 9.0). The best expected error is at **degree 4**: 18.9, against the floor of 16 set by noise.

**Now say why:** why does total test error fall and then rise, even though training error keeps falling?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A model's expected error on new data splits into three parts: **bias²** (how far its _average_ prediction is from the truth: too simple a model is wrong the same way every time), **variance** (how much its predictions jump around when you train it on a different sample: too flexible a model chases noise), and **irreducible noise** (no model can remove it). Making a model more flexible lowers bias and raises variance, so test error is U-shaped in complexity. You move along the U with model size, regularisation and features, and you **shrink variance** with more data, averaging (bagging) or stronger regularisation. Modern over-parameterised models add a twist: past the point where they fit the training data exactly, test error can fall again (**double descent**). What you'll be able to do after this: state and read the decomposition, diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from train/validation curves, pick the right fix for each, and explain double descent without overclaiming.

#### The decomposition

Imagine training the same kind of model on many different training sets drawn from the same world. At a test input x, look at the prediction f̂(x) across all those models. For squared error:

$$ {\mathbb{E}\bigl[(y - \hat f(x))^2\bigr]} = {\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)] - f(x)\bigr)^2} + {\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\hat f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)])^2\bigr]} + {\sigma^2} $$

The standard decomposition for squared loss, e.g. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, _The Elements of Statistical Learning_ §7.3; named and analysed for neural networks by Geman, Bienenstock & Doursat (1992). It's an identity: the cross terms vanish because the new label's noise is independent of the training set.

- **expected test error**: Averaged over training sets and over the noise in the new point’s label. What you actually care about.

- **bias²**: Squared gap between the average prediction (over training sets) and the true value f(x). Systematic error from the model being too simple or wrongly shaped.

- **variance**: How much predictions at x scatter around their own average when the training set changes. Error from the model being sensitive to the particular sample.

- **irreducible noise**: σ², the variance of the label around the truth. Here σ = 4 minutes, so 16. No model can beat it.

**Go deeper: why the cross terms vanish**

Write y − f̂ = (y − f) + (f − E f̂) + (E f̂ − f̂). Square and take expectations. y − f is the new point's noise: mean zero and independent of the training set, so it's uncorrelated with the other two terms. (f − E f̂) is a constant at fixed x, and E[E f̂ − f̂] = 0, so their product averages to zero. What's left is noise + bias² + variance. For other losses (0–1 loss in classification) the decomposition isn't this clean, but the intuition carries over.

#### The U-shaped test-error curve

Stacked: noise (grey, 16), bias² (orange) and variance (violet) for each polynomial degree, computed from 60 simulated training sets each.

| Degree | 1 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 10 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bias² | 8.14 | 7.15 | 0.46 | 0.04 | 0.05 | 0.07 |
| variance | 1.06 | 1.82 | 2.41 | 3.44 | 5.96 | 9.04 |
| total | 25.2 | 25.0 | 18.9 | 19.5 | 22.0 | 25.1 |

Bias falls off a cliff at degree 4, when the polynomial can finally bend the way the truth does; after that it's essentially zero, and each extra degree only adds variance. A useful rule from this: once bias is gone, extra flexibility is pure cost. A fresh-sample check agrees: simulated test error was 18.2 at degree 4 and 22.2 at degree 12.

#### Keep the flexible model, tame it with λ

Instead of choosing a smaller model, keep degree 15 and add a ridge penalty λ‖w‖² (see Regularized Linear Models). λ is a continuous dial between the two failure modes:

For the degree-15 model: λ = 10−6 gives total 22.4 (variance-dominated), λ = 0.01 gives **19.5**, and λ = 100 gives 56.9 (bias² 40: the curve is flattened). The regularised flexible model nearly matches the best hand-picked degree (18.9) without having to guess the right degree. That's why "big model + regularisation, tuned by validation" is the default modern recipe.

#### Variance shrinks with n; bias doesn't

Lines show 20 degree-12 fits at this n. With few points the flexible model is chaotic; with many, it settles onto the truth.

With 10 deliveries the degree-12 model's expected error is 512 (variance 493); with 200 it's 16.8, and both models approach the noise floor of 16. Variance falls roughly like 1/n; bias stays wherever the model's shape puts it (the straight line would stay biased forever). Practical reading of a **learning curve** (train and validation error against n): a big gap between them that shrinks with n means variance, so more data helps; both high and close together means bias, so more data won't help; change the model.

#### Double descent: past the interpolation threshold

Deep networks have far more parameters than training points and fit the training data exactly, yet generalise well. That seems to contradict the U-curve. Belkin, Hsu, Ma & Mandal (2019) showed the U is only the left half of the picture: as capacity grows, test error first follows the U, peaks around the **interpolation threshold** (just enough parameters to fit the training data exactly), and then **decreases again**, often below the classical sweet spot.

1. Below the threshold: the classical U. Test error falls (less bias), then rises (more variance) as training error drops.

2. Near the threshold the model has just enough parameters to pass through every training point, and the only way to do it is a wild, high-norm fit. Test error peaks.

3. Add even more parameters: many functions now fit the data exactly, and the training method picks a smooth, low-norm one among them. Test error falls again, while training error stays at zero.

4. The classical picture isn't wrong; it describes the left part of a longer curve.

Their evidence: random-feature models on 10,000 MNIST images peak at exactly N = n = 10,000 features, then improve "dramatically" past it, beating the classical sweet spot; two-layer networks, random forests and boosting show similar shapes [Belkin et al. 2019, pp. 4–8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.11118#page=4). Their explanation: past the threshold, the minimum-norm interpolating solution acts as a strong implicit regulariser (smoothness). Caveats from the same paper: regularisation and early stopping hide the peak, which is why practitioners rarely see it. And it doesn't license dropping validation: you still pick models by held-out error.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The knobs that move you along the trade-off

| Knob | More flexible (less bias, more variance) | Less flexible |
|---|---|---|
| Model size | Higher polynomial degree, deeper trees, more layers | Fewer parameters |
| Regularisation | Smaller λ / larger C, less dropout | Larger λ, early stopping |
| Neighbours | Small k in k-NN | Large k |
| Features | More and richer features | Fewer features |

Two things reduce variance _without_ adding much bias: **more training data**, and **averaging many models** (bagging, random forests). Boosting does the opposite: it starts from high-bias weak learners and reduces bias step by step. See Random Forest and Gradient Boosting.

#### Diagnose, then fix

| Symptom | Diagnosis | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Train error high, validation ≈ train | High bias (underfitting) | Bigger model, better features, less regularisation, boosting, train longer |
| Train error low, validation much higher | High variance (overfitting) | More data, stronger regularisation, smaller model, bagging/ensembles, early stopping, data augmentation, feature selection |
| Both near a floor you can't beat | Irreducible noise | Better labels or new information (features), not a new model |

#### When it matters

##### Scenario: model is great offline, poor in production

Check leakage and distribution shift first (next lesson); if validation was honest and the gap is train vs validation, it's variance: regularise, simplify, get more data.

##### Scenario: more data didn't help

Both errors high and close: a bias problem. Add features or capacity; more rows of the same features won't move it.

To diagnose this on a real model, see learning curves and debugging.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Pick the model with the lowest training error"

Training error falls every time you add flexibility, all the way to zero when the model can pass through every point. But low training error only shows low bias; it hides variance completely. A model that has memorised 25 deliveries, noise included, will be confidently wrong on the 26th. That's why model choice uses held-out data (the next lesson), never training error.

#### Caveats

- The clean three-way split holds for squared error. For classification losses there are several competing definitions; the intuition (systematic vs sample-driven error) still holds.

- You can't compute bias and variance on real data (you don't know the truth or have many training sets); you infer them from train/validation gaps and learning curves.

- "Complexity" isn't just parameter count: regularisation, early stopping and the training algorithm all change effective capacity. Double descent is the clearest example.

- Variance also comes from the training procedure (random seeds, data order), not only from the sample.

## Say it

### What is the bias–variance trade-off?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

How do you tell bias from variance in practice?

Compare training and validation error, and plot learning curves. Large gap that narrows with more data: variance. Both high and close: bias.

Follow-up 2 of 5

How do bagging and boosting relate to bias and variance?

Bagging averages many high-variance, low-bias models (deep trees) to cut variance. Boosting adds weak, high-bias learners sequentially to cut bias, and needs regularisation (shrinkage, early stopping) to control variance.

Follow-up 3 of 5

How does regularisation affect the trade-off?

It constrains the model (shrinks weights), increasing bias slightly and reducing variance; tuned well, total error falls.

Follow-up 4 of 5

What is double descent?

Beyond the interpolation threshold, increasing capacity can lower test error again, because among the many interpolating solutions the training algorithm finds low-norm, smooth ones (Belkin et al. 2019). Explicit regularisation and early stopping usually hide the peak.

Follow-up 5 of 5

Does more data always help?

It reduces variance; it doesn't reduce bias. If you're bias-limited, more of the same data won't help.

#### The 30-second answer

For squared error, expected test error decomposes into bias squared, variance and irreducible noise. Bias is the error of the average model: too simple a model misses the pattern consistently. Variance is how much the model changes with the training sample: too flexible a model fits noise. Increasing complexity lowers bias and raises variance, so test error is U-shaped and we pick complexity with validation data. High bias shows as high training and validation error; high variance as a large gap between them. Fix bias with more capacity or features; fix variance with more data, regularisation, smaller models or bagging. Modern over-parameterised models can show double descent, where error falls again past the interpolation threshold.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Overfitting means high bias." It's high variance.

- "Zero training error means the model is overfit." Usually, but interpolating models can generalise well (double descent).

- "You can measure bias and variance on your dataset directly." You can only estimate them indirectly.

**Key terms and sources**

Underfitting vs overfitting, the decomposition of test error, model complexity, regularisation, more data, and double descent · built from Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman (ESL §2.9, §7.3), Geman, Bienenstock & Doursat (1992) and Belkin et al. (2019) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

Mean squared error in minutes², 25 training deliveries, 60 simulated training sets. Lower is better. Illustrative.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Bias** | Average prediction minus truth, over training sets. |
| **Variance** | Spread of predictions across training sets. |
| **Irreducible error** | Noise variance σ² in the labels. |
| **Underfitting / overfitting** | Bias-dominated / variance-dominated error. |
| **Learning curve** | Train and validation error against training-set size. |
| **Interpolation threshold** | Smallest capacity that fits the training data exactly. |
| **Double descent** | Test error falling again beyond the interpolation threshold. |

# Cross-Validation & Data Leakage

> How did a model score 86% on pure noise, and how do you make sure yours isn't?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/cross-validation-and-leakage/
- Before this: The Bias–Variance Trade-off (`fundamentals/bias-variance`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your cross-validation says 0.92 AUC, and production says 0.70. Nothing in the code threw an error. The interviewer asks:

> What is data leakage, and how does cross-validation help you avoid it?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app's data team. Three simulated situations, each with a known true answer so the leak is visible: (1) predicting whether a customer will churn from 10,000 behavioural signals that are in fact pure noise (true accuracy 50%); (2) trying many model variants and keeping the one with the best validation score; (3) predicting a rider's "safe driver" badge from repeated trip records, several per rider.

#### The score you report is a prediction too

"Validation accuracy 86%" is a claim about data the model hasn't seen. If any information about that data leaked into training, the claim is wrong, and nothing in the code will tell you. scikit-learn: testing on the training data "is a methodological mistake: a model that would just repeat the labels of the samples that it has just seen would have a perfect score but would fail to predict anything useful on yet-unseen data" [cross-validation guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html). Every technique on this page exists to keep the scoring data genuinely unseen.

### The idea

Think of a practice exam where you've already seen the answer key. You'll score brilliantly, and the score tells you nothing. Leakage is any way the answers reach your model before it's tested, and it often looks like good hygiene.

[Figure: Five rows of five blocks. In each row, a different block is held out for validation while the other four train the model.]

_5-fold cross-validation: each block gets one turn being held out._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Select features on all the rows, then cross-validate, and read the accuracy. The labels here are random, so the truth is 50%. Then select inside each fold.

#### Feature selection outside CV finds signal in noise

200 customers, 10,000 random features, random churn labels. Pick the 25 features whose class means differ most, then classify with nearest centroid. Generated in your browser (takes a second).

Selecting on all rows: CV accuracy **86.5%** on data with no signal at all. Selecting inside each training fold: **51%**, the truth. With 10,000 random features, some will separate the two classes in these 200 rows by pure chance; selecting them with the validation rows included bakes that chance into the "test". scikit-learn's own version of this experiment: 0.76 accuracy when selecting on all data vs 0.5 when splitting first [common pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage). The same leak, smaller, happens with scaling, imputation, target encoding and SMOTE fitted before the split.

**Now say why:** how did pure noise score so well, when no line of code looks wrong?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An evaluation is only honest if the data used to score the model played **no part** in building it. **k-fold cross-validation** rotates which slice is held out, so every row is tested once and the estimate is less noisy than a single split. The split must copy how the model will meet new data in production: **stratify** rare classes, keep each **group** (patient, customer, device) on one side, and never let a model see the **future**. **Leakage** is any information at training time that won't exist at prediction time: preprocessing or feature selection fitted on all rows, tuning on the test set, duplicated or related rows across the split, or features that are recorded after the outcome. Leaks don't crash anything; they just give you a great score that vanishes in production. What you'll be able to do after this: choose the right splitter for a dataset, explain nested CV, spot the five common leaks, and reproduce three of them with numbers.

#### Train, validation, test, and k-fold

1. Start with all the labelled data.

2. Set aside a **test set** first and don't touch it until the very end. It's your one honest final exam.

3. Split the rest into k = 5 folds. Train on four (teal), validate on the fifth (orange), and rotate so every fold is the validation set once.

4. Average the five validation scores. The spread across folds tells you how much the score depends on the particular split.

5. Use the CV score to choose models and settings; report the test score once, for the final choice.

$$ {\mathrm{CV}_k} = {\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}} {\mathrm{Score}\bigl(}{\hat f^{(-j)}}{,\ \text{fold}_j\bigr)} $$

scikit-learn also notes leave-one-out "often results in high variance as an estimator for the test error" and costs n fits [cross-validation guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html).

- **the CV estimate**: Estimated performance of the whole training procedure on unseen data.

- **average over folds**: k separate train/validate runs; scikit-learn: “most authors and empirical evidence suggest that 5 or 10-fold cross validation should be preferred to LOO”.

- **model trained without fold j**: Fitted on everything except fold j, including every preprocessing step.

- **score on fold j**: Accuracy, AUC, RMSE… computed only on the held-out rows.

#### Cross-validate the whole pipeline, split like production

Two rules cover almost everything:

1. **Everything that learns from data goes inside the fold.** Scaling, imputation, encoding, feature selection, resampling, target encoding, PCA and the model itself are one pipeline, refitted on each training fold and only applied to its validation fold. In scikit-learn that means a `Pipeline` passed to `cross_val_score` or `GridSearchCV`.

2. **The validation fold must look like the future.** If production sees new customers, validation must contain customers the model never saw; if production sees next month, validation must be later than training.

Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich & Stitelman define leakage as "the introduction of information about the data mining target that should not be legitimately available to mine from", and recommend a strict "learn-predict separation" [ACM TKDD 2012](https://doi.org/10.1145/2382577.2382579).

#### Tune inside, score outside

If you choose hyperparameters with the same CV loop that produces the score you report, the score is optimistic (the same leak as tuning on test, in a milder form). **Nested CV** wraps the whole tuning procedure (e.g. a `GridSearchCV`) inside an outer loop: each outer fold is scored by a model whose settings were chosen using only the other folds. Varma & Simon (2006) showed that tuning and estimating in one CV loop gives a biased error estimate, and that the nested procedure "gives an estimate of the error that is very close to that obtained on the independent testing set" [BMC Bioinformatics 7](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-7-91). It costs kouter × kinner × grid fits; with plenty of data, a single untouched test set does the same job.

##### Target leakage: features that encode the answer

A feature recorded _after_ or _because of_ the outcome: "refund issued" when predicting fraud, "account closed date" when predicting churn, "treatment given" when predicting diagnosis. CV can't catch it (it's present in every fold); only asking "would I have this value at prediction time?" does. Leaks like these are a recurring theme in data-mining competitions; Kaufman et al. survey several, including KDD Cup cases [TKDD 2012](https://doi.org/10.1145/2382577.2382579). A warning sign: a single feature with suspiciously high importance, or validation accuracy far above what domain experts manage.

Choosing features is a common way to leak: see feature selection.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Choose the splitter that matches production

| Data | Splitter | Why |
|---|---|---|
| i.i.d. rows, balanced | `KFold(shuffle=True)` | Plain rotation |
| Rare classes | `StratifiedKFold` | Each fold keeps "approximately the same percentage of samples of each target class" |
| Several rows per patient / customer / device | `GroupKFold`, `StratifiedGroupKFold` | "ensures that the same group is not represented in both testing and training sets" |
| Time-ordered data | `TimeSeriesSplit` (or a date cut-off) | Train on the past, test on the future; shuffled CV on time series gives "poor estimates of generalization error" |
| Tuning + honest estimate | Nested CV | Inner loop tunes, outer loop scores (see the Maths tab) |

Quotes from scikit-learn's cross-validation guide [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html), which adds: "While i.i.d. data is a common assumption in machine learning theory, it rarely holds in practice."

#### The whole recipe

1. **Split first**, by the production rule (time cut-off, groups, or stratified random), and lock the test set away.

2. **Put every learned step in a Pipeline**; never call fit on validation or test rows.

3. **Cross-validate the pipeline** (5 or 10 folds, with the matching splitter) to compare models and tune.

4. **Audit features** for timing: would each one exist at prediction time?

5. **Evaluate once on the test set.** If it's much worse than CV, look for leakage before blaming overfitting.

#### Scenarios

##### "CV said 0.92 AUC, production says 0.70"

Check, in order: preprocessing fitted on all rows, groups split across folds, time order ignored, features not available at prediction time, then genuine distribution shift.

##### "Which CV for churn with monthly snapshots per customer?"

Time-based split (train on earlier months, validate on later) and keep each customer on one side, or validate on customers who signed up later.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Prepare the data first, then cross-validate"

The most common leak looks like good hygiene: scale, impute, select features or balance classes on the full dataset, then run CV on the result. But every one of those steps learned something from the rows that will later be the validation folds. scikit-learn: "Data leakage occurs when information that would not be available at prediction time is used when building the model … The general rule is to never call `fit` on the test data" [common pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage). How big can it get? The Leak 1 section shows a model scoring 86% on pure noise.

#### Try enough models and one will look good

Every variant is a coin-flip model (true accuracy 50%). Each dot is one variant's validation accuracy on the same 50 rows.

With 50 validation rows, a single coin-flip model already scored 58% here by luck; the best of 10 scored 62%, of 100 68%, and of 1,000 **70%**. On 10,000 fresh rows, the "winner" scores 50%: it was never better, just luckier on that sample. Hyperparameter searches, feature experiments and "let me try one more thing" all do this. scikit-learn: tuning against the test set means "knowledge about the test set can 'leak' into the model and evaluation metrics no longer report on generalization performance" [cross-validation guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html). The cure: choose on validation/CV, and report a test set used once. With small data and heavy tuning, use nested CV.

#### The same rider in train and test

40 riders × 8 trips. Each rider's trips share a personal "signature" (phone, route, riding style) but the badge is random: trip features carry no real signal about it. Strip: each square is a rider; split = trips of that rider on both sides.

Random K-fold: **92.5%**. The model just recognises the rider from their other trips in the training folds. GroupKFold: **47%**, the honest coin flip. scikit-learn's example is the same: a model "flexible enough to learn from highly person specific features … could fail to generalize to new subjects. GroupKFold makes it possible to detect this kind of overfitting" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#group-k-fold). Same story for medical images (several scans per patient), sessions per user, near-duplicate documents, and augmented copies of one image.

##### Time leaks

If production predicts next week, validation must be later than training. Shuffled CV on time-ordered data tests on rows "artificially similar (close in time) to training samples" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html). Also watch features computed with future data: a 30-day rolling average that includes days after the prediction, "total orders this month" used on day 3, or a customer's lifetime value as of today.

#### Caveats

- CV estimates the performance of the _procedure_ (pipeline + tuning), not of one fitted model.

- Fold scores aren't independent (training sets overlap), so the fold spread understates the true uncertainty; don't over-read small differences between models.

- No splitter fixes distribution shift you didn't anticipate (a new city, a new app version). Validate on the most production-like slice you have.

- Nested CV is expensive; critics (e.g. Wainer & Cawley 2021) argue it's often overkill when comparing a few model types. Use it when tuning is heavy and data is small.

## Say it

### What is data leakage, and how does cross-validation help you avoid it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

Why not leave-one-out?

It costs n fits and its estimate has high variance, since the n models are nearly identical; 5- or 10-fold is the usual recommendation.

Follow-up 2 of 5

What is nested cross-validation and when do you need it?

An inner CV tunes hyperparameters; an outer CV scores the tuned procedure. You need it when you report a performance estimate after heavy tuning on small data; otherwise the estimate is optimistically biased.

Follow-up 3 of 5

Give examples of data leakage.

Scaling or SMOTE before splitting; feature selection on all data; target encoding without out-of-fold estimates; duplicate users/patients across folds; random splits on time series; features like "refund issued" for fraud.

Follow-up 4 of 5

How would you detect leakage?

Scores too good to be true, one dominant feature, big CV-to-production gap, performance that drops when you switch to grouped or time-based splits, and feature-timing audits.

Follow-up 5 of 5

Should you oversample before or after splitting?

After, and only on the training fold (inside the pipeline). Oversampling first puts copies or interpolations of validation rows into training.

#### The 30-second answer

Cross-validation estimates how a modelling procedure performs on unseen data by rotating held-out folds and averaging the scores, usually 5- or 10-fold, with a separate test set used once at the end. The split must mirror production: stratified for rare classes, grouped when there are several rows per entity, and time-based for temporal data. Data leakage is any information at training time that wouldn't exist at prediction time; the common forms are fitting preprocessing or feature selection on all rows, tuning on the test set, related rows on both sides of the split, and features recorded after the outcome. The fix is to put every learned step in a pipeline that's refitted inside each fold, split by the production rule, use nested CV when tuning heavily, and audit features for timing.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "I scaled the whole dataset, then cross-validated." That's a leak.

- "I tuned on the test set to get the best model." The test score is now optimistic.

- "Shuffled K-fold is fine for time series." It leaks the future.

**Key terms and sources**

Hold-out sets, k-fold, stratified, grouped and time-series splits, nested CV for tuning, and the leaks that make offline scores lie · built from scikit-learn's cross-validation and common-pitfalls guides, Varma & Simon (2006) and Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich & Stitelman (2012) · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### Leaked vs honest scores (this page's simulations; truth is 50% in all three)

feature selection on all rows

86.5%

… inside each fold

51.0%

riders split randomly

92.5%

… grouped by rider

47.2%

Illustrative simulations with no real signal. scikit-learn's own feature-selection example: 0.76 leaked vs 0.5 honest [common pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage).

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Hold-out / test set** | Data kept aside and used once for the final score. |
| **k-fold CV** | Rotate k validation folds; average the scores. |
| **Stratified / grouped / time-series split** | Keep class ratios / keep groups together / train on past only. |
| **Nested CV** | Inner CV for tuning inside an outer CV for scoring. |
| **Data leakage** | Training-time information unavailable at prediction time. |
| **Target leakage** | A feature recorded after, or because of, the outcome. |

1. scikit-learn, [Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html) (k-fold, LOO, stratified, group, time-series splits, i.i.d. caveats, test-set leakage).

2. scikit-learn, [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) (data leakage definition, feature-selection example, pipelines).

3. S. Varma & R. Simon, "Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection", _BMC Bioinformatics_ 7:91, 2006, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2105-7-91) (nested CV).

4. S. Kaufman, S. Rosset, C. Perlich & O. Stitelman, "Leakage in data mining: formulation, detection, and avoidance", _ACM TKDD_ 6(4), 2012, [doi](https://doi.org/10.1145/2382577.2382579).
