# Class Imbalance

> 2% fraud: should you SMOTE it, weight it, or just move the threshold?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/class-imbalance/
- Before this: Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`), Thresholds & Misclassification Costs (`fundamentals/thresholds-and-costs`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

About 2% of your orders are fraud, and the default threshold flags almost nothing. A teammate wants to balance the classes to 50/50. The interviewer asks:

> How do you handle a 2% positive class?

**Running example:** the food-delivery app's fraud screen. Each order has two risk signals (standardised); about **2%** of orders are fraudulent. Training data: 6,000 simulated orders (106 fraud); a validation set of 4,000 for choosing thresholds; a test set of 20,000 (1.92% fraud). The model is logistic regression throughout, so the only thing that changes between experiments is how we handle the imbalance. This lesson builds on Classification Metrics, ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC and Thresholds & Costs.

#### The rare class is the one you care about

Fraud, churn, defaults, rare diseases, machine failures, click-through: the event you want to catch is the minority. Three things go wrong at once. **Accuracy** rewards ignoring it (always "legit" = 98%). A default threshold of 0.5 flags almost nothing, because with a 2% base rate few orders ever look more than 50% likely to be fraud. And with only ~100 positive examples, the model has little to learn the minority pattern from. People lump all three under "imbalance", but they need different fixes.

### The idea

Think of airport security. Very few bags are dangerous, but you don't pretend half of them are. You keep an honest risk score for every bag, then decide how risky a bag must be to open, based on what a miss and a search each cost.

[Figure: Orders ranked from low risk to high risk. The default cut at 0.5 catches almost nothing. A much lower cut catches far more of the rare fraud.]

_Illustrative. Ranking orders and deciding where to cut are two separate jobs._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at a threshold of 0.5 and read the recall and the cost. Then slide it down until the cost is as low as you can get.

#### Move the threshold, not the data

Same trained model, only the cut changes. Try 0.31 (best F1 on validation) and 0.02–0.03 (the cost-optimal t* ≈ 0.024 from the Maths tab).

On the test orders, the default 0.5 costs ₹2,44,000 (most fraud slips through), the F1-best 0.31 costs ₹1,96,960, and the cost-optimal 0.02 costs ₹1,03,560 while catching 84% of fraud: the same model, less than half the cost, and no resampling involved.

Elor & Averbuch-Elor (2022) tested this at scale on 73 imbalanced datasets: with a tuned threshold, "balancing the data and optimizing the decision threshold yield comparable prediction performance" except for very weak classifiers, and they recommend tuning the threshold because it is simpler and cheaper to compute. For the strong models (XGBoost, CatBoost), balancing didn't improve AUC at all: "best prediction is achieved by using a strong classifier and balancing the data is not required nor beneficial" [arXiv:2201.08528, §4–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.08528#page=5). scikit-learn's `TunedThresholdClassifierCV` chooses the threshold by cross-validation.

**Now say why:** why did this help so much without touching the model or the data?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

When 2% of orders are fraud, a model that always says "legit" is 98% accurate and useless. The usual reflex is to "fix the imbalance" by reweighting or resampling the training data. On our data, and in recent large studies, that reflex mostly **doesn't improve ranking** (AUC is unchanged), **breaks the probabilities** (the model now thinks fraud is 10× more common than it is), and only **moves the decision threshold**, something you can do directly. The reliable recipe: use a proper metric (PR-AUC, log loss, cost), train a strong model on the real data, then **choose the threshold** from costs or a validation set. Resampling still helps weak learners and fixed-threshold systems, and only inside the training fold. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why accuracy fails, compare weights/resampling/SMOTE/thresholds with numbers, undo resampling's damage to probabilities, and answer "how would you handle imbalanced data?" without the standard wrong answer.

#### Probabilities, thresholds and the base rate

A probabilistic classifier outputs p = P(fraud | order). A good one is **calibrated**: among orders it scores 0.3, about 30% are fraud, so its average prediction matches the base rate (here 1.9%). Turning p into a decision needs a **threshold** t: flag if p ≥ t. Ranking quality (AUC) doesn't depend on t; precision, recall and F1 do. The cost-optimal threshold, if a missed fraud costs CFN and a false alarm CFP, is:

$$ {t^{*}} = {C_{FP}} \,/\, ({C_{FP}} + {C_{FN}}) $$

Derived in Thresholds & Costs. Note what this says: the imbalance doesn't need "fixing" to catch fraud; a calibrated model plus the right threshold already accounts for both the base rate and the costs.

- **best threshold**: Flag an order when its fraud probability exceeds this. Requires calibrated probabilities.

- **cost of a false alarm**: E.g. ₹20 of a reviewer’s time and an annoyed honest customer.

- **cost of a missed fraud**: E.g. a ₹800 chargeback. With these numbers t* = 20/820 ≈ 0.024: flag anything with more than a 2.4% fraud chance.

#### Separate ranking from deciding

A classifier does two jobs: **rank** orders by risk, and **decide** where to cut. Imbalance mostly hurts the decision (a default cut of 0.5 is wrong for rare events), and the decision is cheap to fix after training. Ranking is only hurt when there are too few minority examples to learn from, and reweighting or duplicating the same ~100 fraud cases adds no new information about them. So: get the best ranking you can on the real distribution, keep the probabilities honest, and choose the cut with the costs. Reach for resampling only when you can't control the cut, or your model is weak.

#### Correct the probabilities back

Undersampling is sometimes necessary for speed (billions of negatives, as in click prediction). Then correct the predicted probabilities for the sampling rate. If you kept a fraction β of the negatives:

$$ {p} = {\beta}\,{q} \,/\, \bigl({\beta}\,{q} - {q} + 1\bigr) $$

Prior-shift correction for undersampling, e.g. Dal Pozzolo et al., "Calibrating probability with undersampling for unbalanced classification" (IEEE SSCI 2015). Applying it is equivalent to subtracting log(1/β) from the model's log-odds.

- **corrected probability**: The fraud probability on the real, imbalanced population.

- **model output**: What the model trained on the undersampled data predicts.

- **negatives kept**: β = negatives kept / negatives available. Here 106 / 5,894 ≈ 0.018.

On our data the correction brings the average prediction from 21.3% back to 2.9% and log loss from 0.378 to 0.062, close to the uncorrected model's 0.057, with the same AUC. Class weights can be undone the same way (shift the intercept by log of the weight ratio). Better still: calibrate on untouched validation data (`CalibratedClassifierCV`).

## In practice

### In practice

#### The menu of fixes

| Approach | What it does | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Better metric** | Judge by PR-AUC, recall at fixed precision, log loss, expected cost; not accuracy | scikit-learn metrics |
| **Threshold moving** | Keep the model, choose t from costs or validation | `TunedThresholdClassifierCV`, manual |
| **Class weights** | Multiply the loss of minority errors | `class_weight="balanced"`, `scale_pos_weight` |
| **Random over/undersampling** | Duplicate minority / drop majority rows (training fold only) | imbalanced-learn |
| **SMOTE and variants** | Synthesise minority points between minority neighbours | imbalanced-learn |
| **More minority data / better features** | Address the real bottleneck: few examples | labelling, data collection |

imbalanced-learn describes the problem as the decision function tending "to favour the class with the larger number of samples" [imbalanced-learn](https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/introduction.html). Whether that "favouring" is a bug or correct Bayesian behaviour is exactly the question this lesson answers.

#### Five ways to handle the same 2% fraud

Plot: test orders grouped by predicted probability (10 bins); each dot compares the average prediction with the actual fraud rate in that bin. On the diagonal = calibrated. Logistic regression in every case; trained in your browser.

| Method | AUC | Mean predicted | Log loss | F1 @ 0.5 | Best t | F1 @ best t |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| No correction | 0.934 | 1.9% | 0.057 | 0.315 | 0.31 | 0.430 |
| Class weights | 0.934 | 21.4% | 0.336 | 0.182 | 0.96 | 0.426 |
| Oversample | 0.934 | 21.4% | 0.337 | 0.182 | 0.96 | 0.428 |
| Undersample | 0.934 | 21.3% | 0.378 | 0.173 | 0.98 | 0.432 |
| Undersample + correction | 0.934 | 2.9% | 0.062 | 0.426 | 0.55 | 0.431 |

Every method ranks equally well (AUC 0.934), and every method reaches the same F1 (~0.43) once its threshold is tuned. The difference is all in the probabilities: the three corrections inflate the average fraud prediction elevenfold and multiply log loss by about six. At the default 0.5 threshold they flag over 3,000 of 20,000 orders with 10% precision, worse F1 than not correcting at all. The resampled models only "need" a threshold of 0.96–0.98 to get back to where the plain model was at 0.31.

#### Synthetic minority points, and when they help

1. A few fraud orders (red) among many legit ones.

2. SMOTE (Chawla et al., 2002) picks a minority point and finds its k nearest minority neighbours (default k = 5).

3. It places a synthetic fraud order at a random point on the segment to one neighbour.

4. Repeat until the minority class is as large as you asked for. Unlike duplication, the new points fill the space between real ones.

SMOTE spawned more than 100 variants (Borderline, SVM-SMOTE, ADASYN…). The 2022 evidence is sobering: with a fixed threshold, the sophisticated SMOTE variants were "not more effective than the simple random oversampler" for strong boosted trees, and with a tuned threshold, balancing at all brought them no gain; SMOTE did help weak learners (MLP, SVM, decision trees, AdaBoost) and fixed-threshold setups [Elor & Averbuch-Elor 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.08528#page=6). Synthetic points can also land in the majority region and blur the boundary, and on categorical or high-dimensional data, interpolation can create impossible rows.

#### The whole recipe

1. **Pick the metric from the decision:** expected cost, recall at a precision floor, or PR-AUC; log loss/Brier if probabilities matter. Not accuracy.

2. **Split with stratification** (and groups/time if relevant) so every fold has minority cases.

3. **Train a strong model on the real distribution** (gradient boosting, well-regularised logistic regression).

4. **Check calibration**; calibrate on validation data if needed.

5. **Choose the threshold** from costs (t* = CFP/(CFP + CFN)) or by validation.

6. **Only then** try class weights or resampling, inside the CV pipeline, and keep them only if the chosen metric improves. Correct the probabilities if you use them.

7. **Collect more minority examples** if recall is capped: that's the one fix that adds information.

#### Scenarios

##### Fraud screen with a review team of fixed size

Rank by score and review the top N per day: only ranking matters (PR-AUC, precision@N). No resampling or threshold tuning needed.

##### Ad click prediction feeding a bid

Probabilities feed money: calibration is critical. Undersample negatives for speed if you must, then apply the prior correction and check log loss.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Balance the classes to 50/50 and the model will notice fraud"

The standard advice is to oversample fraud, undersample legit orders, or weight fraud 50× in the loss. It does change the output: at threshold 0.5 the model now flags far more orders. But look at what it costs (see Compare the fixes, in the In practice tab): the model now believes 21% of orders are fraud, when the true rate is 1.9%. Its ranking of orders is **exactly as good as before** (AUC 0.934 in every case). All the "fix" did was distort the probabilities so that 0.5 lands where a lower threshold would have landed on the original model. van den Goorbergh et al. (2022) found the same in clinical risk models: all correction methods "led to poor calibration, but not to better discrimination" [JAMIA 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382395/).

#### Caveats

- **When resampling/weights do help:** weak or high-bias models, systems where you can't set the threshold, extremely rare classes where the loss barely "sees" the minority during training (e.g. neural nets with mini-batches containing no positives), and undersampling for compute.

- Our demo uses a linear model, where reweighting mostly shifts the intercept. With flexible models, weights can also change the shape of the boundary, for better or worse; always validate.

- "Imbalance" is often a proxy for the real problem: few minority examples, overlapping classes, or label noise. Resampling fixes none of these.

- Never resample before the train/test split, and never evaluate on resampled data.

## Say it

### How do you handle a 2% positive class?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 5

Does oversampling or SMOTE improve the model?

It changes where the model cuts, not how well it ranks: AUC is typically unchanged for strong models, and probabilities become miscalibrated. It can help weak learners or when the threshold is fixed. It must happen inside the training fold only.

Follow-up 2 of 5

Class weights vs threshold tuning?

For a linear model, weights mostly shift the intercept, which is equivalent to a threshold change but corrupts probabilities. Threshold tuning keeps calibration and can be re-tuned without retraining.

Follow-up 3 of 5

Why is accuracy misleading, and what would you use?

The majority-class baseline already scores 98%. Use precision/recall/F1 at a chosen threshold, PR-AUC for ranking, log loss/Brier for probabilities, or business cost.

Follow-up 4 of 5

How do you fix probabilities after undersampling?

Apply the prior correction p = βq / (βq − q + 1) with β the fraction of negatives kept, or recalibrate on untouched validation data.

Follow-up 5 of 5

When is imbalance a real problem?

When there are very few minority examples to learn from, classes overlap heavily, or the training procedure rarely sees positives (mini-batches). Then more data, better features, focal loss or sampling-for-batches help.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd pick a metric that reflects the decision, such as expected cost, recall at a fixed precision or PR-AUC, because accuracy is meaningless with a 2% base rate. Then I'd stratify the splits, train a strong model on the real distribution, check calibration, and choose the threshold from the error costs or on validation data, since the default 0.5 is the main thing imbalance breaks. Class weights and resampling mostly just shift the threshold while distorting the probabilities; recent studies found they don't improve AUC for strong models and that a tuned threshold matches them. I'd use them inside the training folds only for weak models or fixed-threshold systems, correct the probabilities afterwards, and prioritise getting more minority examples.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Always SMOTE imbalanced data." It often doesn't help strong models and breaks calibration.

- "Balance the test set too." Evaluate on the real distribution.

- "Resample, then split." That leaks copies of test rows into training.

**Key terms and sources**

Why rare classes are hard, what actually goes wrong, and what each fix really does: class weights, over- and undersampling, SMOTE, threshold moving and prior correction · built from Elor & Averbuch-Elor (2022), van den Goorbergh et al. (2022), Chawla et al. (2002) and the scikit-learn / imbalanced-learn docs · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### F1 on 73 datasets, CatBoost (Elor & Averbuch-Elor 2022, Table 3)

no balancing, threshold 0.5

0.444

no balancing, tuned threshold

0.532

random oversampling

0.525

SMOTE

0.529

Mean F1, higher is better; ± about 0.02 [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.08528#page=5). For a weak MLP the picture flips: baseline 0.303 with a tuned threshold vs 0.411 with SMOTE.

##### Clinical risk models

van den Goorbergh et al. (JAMIA 2022), logistic regression with random under/oversampling and SMOTE on ovarian-tumour data plus simulations: corrections strongly overestimated the minority-class probability, did not improve AUROC, and the sensitivity/specificity gains were matched by simply shifting the threshold [PMC9382395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382395/). A 2024 follow-up extended this to machine-learning models with the same conclusion for calibration [arXiv:2404.19494](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19494).

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Base rate / prevalence** | Share of the minority class in the population. |
| **Calibration** | Predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. |
| **Threshold moving** | Choosing the probability cut-off instead of using 0.5. |
| **Class weights** | Scaling each class's contribution to the loss. |
| **Random over/undersampling** | Duplicate minority / drop majority training rows. |
| **SMOTE** | Synthetic minority points interpolated between minority neighbours. |
| **Prior correction** | Mapping resampled-model probabilities back to the true base rate. |

2. R. van den Goorbergh, M. van Smeden, D. Timmerman & B. Van Calster, "The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models", _JAMIA_ 29(9), 2022, [PMC9382395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382395/).

# Hyperparameter Tuning

> Grid, random or Bayesian: how do you spend 30 expensive training runs?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/hyperparameter-tuning/
- Before this: Cross-Validation & Data Leakage (`fundamentals/cross-validation-and-leakage`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

Each trial of your ETA model means training it and running 5-fold cross-validation, so you can only afford a few dozen trials. The interviewer asks:

> How do you tune hyperparameters efficiently?

**Running example:** tuning the food-delivery app's ETA model. Each trial means training the model with one setting and scoring it with 5-fold CV, which takes minutes, so the budget is a few dozen trials. The labs use stand-in validation-loss functions with a known optimum (simulated) so we can measure exactly how close each search method gets.

#### Expensive, noisy, black-box optimisation

You want the settings that minimise validation loss, but you can't take a gradient of "train a model and cross-validate it" with respect to the learning rate; each evaluation costs real time; and the result is noisy (fold randomness). So tuning is a search problem with a tiny budget. The question is how to spend each trial.

### The idea

Think of finding the best dish in a city with only a few meals to spare. A grid keeps returning to the same few streets. Random search covers more ground. Bayesian optimisation heads towards what's been good so far, and successive halving takes one bite of many dishes before committing.

[Figure: Left, a grid of nine trials that tests only three distinct values of each setting. Right, nine random trials that test nine distinct values.]

_Illustrative. If only one setting really matters, random search tests far more values of it._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare grid and random at 9, 16 and 25 trials. Watch the distinct values of the setting that matters, and the best loss.

#### Spend each trial on new information

Background shading: validation loss, which depends only on the horizontal setting (the vertical one is irrelevant). The tick marks on the bottom axis show which values of the important setting each method actually tested.

Over 2,000 simulated problems with a random optimum, the average best loss with 9 trials was 0.075 for the grid and **0.049** for random search; with 25 trials, 0.027 vs **0.006**. Bergstra & Bengio (2012) showed the same on real models: random search found models "as good or better within a small fraction of the computation time", because the score functions have "low effective dimensionality" [JMLR 13](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/bergstra12a.html).

**Now say why:** why does the same budget go further when the trials aren't lined up in a grid?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Hyperparameters (learning rate, depth, regularisation strength…) are set before training, so you choose them by trying settings and scoring each with cross-validation. **Grid search** tries every combination, which wastes trials when only one or two parameters matter. **Random search** samples settings and, for the same budget, explores many more distinct values of the parameters that matter. **Bayesian optimisation** fits a cheap model of "score as a function of settings" and picks the next trial where improvement looks most likely. **Successive halving / Hyperband** start many settings on a small budget and only keep training the promising ones. Whatever you use, tune on validation folds and judge the winner on data the search never saw. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why random beats grid, describe the BO loop and expected improvement, explain successive halving's budget trick, and set up tuning without fooling yourself.

#### Parameters, hyperparameters, search spaces

- **Parameters** are learned from data by training (weights, split thresholds). **Hyperparameters** are chosen before training (λ, max_depth, learning rate, number of trees, k in k-NN).

- **Search space:** a range for each hyperparameter, and a **scale**. Rates and regularisation strengths vary over orders of magnitude, so search them on a **log scale** (λ ∈ 10−4…102), not linearly.

- **Objective:** the cross-validated metric you actually care about (scikit-learn's `scoring=`).

#### Model the score, then choose where to look

Random search ignores what earlier trials revealed. Bayesian optimisation (BO) fits a **surrogate model** to the trials so far, usually a Gaussian process (GP) that gives, for every untried setting, a predicted loss and an uncertainty. An **acquisition function** then trades off "predicted to be good" (exploit) against "we know little here" (explore). The classic choice is expected improvement:

$$ {\mathrm{EI}(x)} = {(y^{*} - \mu(x))}\,{\Phi(z)} + {\sigma(x)\,\varphi(z)}, \qquad z = (y^{*} - \mu(x))/\sigma(x) $$

Expected improvement for minimisation with a GP surrogate (μ mean, σ standard deviation, y* best observed), as used by Snoek, Larochelle & Adams, "Practical Bayesian optimization of machine learning algorithms", NeurIPS 2012 [arXiv:1206.2944](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.2944).

- **expected improvement**: How much better than the current best we expect setting x to be, averaging over the surrogate’s uncertainty. Run the next trial where this is largest.

- **predicted gain**: Best loss so far minus the predicted loss at x. Large when the surrogate thinks x is good.

- **chance it’s better**: Φ(z): probability that x beats the current best under the surrogate.

- **uncertainty bonus**: σ(x) φ(z): large where the surrogate is unsure, which pulls trials into unexplored regions.

Dashed grey: the true validation loss over log₁₀ λ (unknown to the optimiser; it has a second, worse dip on the left). Orange: GP mean ± 2σ. Violet (bottom): expected improvement; the next trial goes at its peak.

Averaged over 100 runs from random starts, BO's distance from the best possible loss shrank to 0.0005 by the 8th trial and to zero by the 10th; random search was still 0.014 away after 15 trials. On cheap or high-dimensional problems the advantage shrinks, and BO's own overhead grows with the number of trials (a GP is cubic in trials). Popular tools often use a tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE, Bergstra et al. 2011, the default in Optuna) instead of a GP; same loop, different surrogate.

#### Successive halving and Hyperband

Many trials are hopeless after a few epochs. Successive halving starts many settings with a small budget, keeps the best fraction, and multiplies their budget: scikit-learn calls it "a tournament among candidate parameter combinations", where in each round "the number of resources per candidate is multiplied by `factor` and the number of candidates is divided by the same factor" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/grid_search.html#successive-halving-user-guide).

81 settings; rounds of 81 × 1 epoch, 27 × 3, 9 × 9, 3 × 27, 1 × 81 (factor 3). Grey: curves of settings that were dropped; green: survivors.

Averaged over 500 simulated problems, successive halving used 405 epochs (6% of training all 81 to completion) and picked a setting with final loss 0.217, against 0.205 for the true best; random search with the same 405 epochs (5 full runs) picked 0.268. On any single problem either can win (in problem C above, one of random search's five full runs happened to be the best setting); the average is what matters. The risk: a slow starter (low learning rate, strong regularisation) gets cut early. **Hyperband** (Li et al.) hedges by running several successive-halving "brackets" with different aggressiveness, and reported "over an order-of-magnitude speedup" over Bayesian optimisation on deep-learning and kernel problems [JMLR 18, arXiv:1603.06560](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06560).

## In practice

### In practice

#### The search methods

| Method | Idea | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Grid search** | All combinations of chosen values | `GridSearchCV` |
| **Random search** | Sample settings from distributions | `RandomizedSearchCV` |
| **Bayesian optimisation** | Model score vs settings, pick the most promising next trial | Optuna (TPE), scikit-optimize, SMAC, Ax |
| **Successive halving / Hyperband** | Many settings on small budgets, keep the best, give them more | `HalvingRandomSearchCV`, Optuna pruners, Ray Tune |

scikit-learn lists two advantages of random search: "A budget can be chosen independent of the number of parameters and possible values" and "Adding parameters that do not influence the performance does not decrease efficiency" [model-selection guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/grid_search.html).

#### The tuned score is optimistic

The best CV score among many trials is biased upward: some of its lead is luck on those folds (the Cross-Validation lesson shows 1,000 coin-flip models reaching 70% on a validation set). scikit-learn: "it is recommended to split the data into a development set (to be fed to the GridSearchCV instance) and an evaluation set to compute performance metrics" [docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/grid_search.html). With small data, use nested CV. And watch the leaderboard of trials: if the top 20 settings score within noise of each other, pick the simplest or most regularised one.

#### The whole recipe

1. **Start from good defaults** and tune only the hyperparameters that matter most (learning rate, regularisation, capacity).

2. **Define ranges on the right scale** (log for rates and penalties).

3. **Random search** for a quick, robust baseline (30–60 trials); **Bayesian optimisation** when trials are expensive and dimensions few; **successive halving / pruning** for iterative learners (boosting rounds, epochs).

4. **Score with CV** using the metric you care about; use early stopping inside each trial for boosting and neural nets.

5. **Evaluate the final pick once** on held-out data.

#### Scenarios

##### "Each training run takes 2 hours, 4 hyperparameters"

Bayesian optimisation (TPE/GP) with ~30 trials, plus pruning on intermediate validation loss.

##### "LightGBM, 1M rows, quick runs"

Random search (50–100 trials) with early stopping on boosting rounds; tune on a subsample first, confirm on full data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Try every combination on a grid"

A 3 × 3 grid over two hyperparameters costs 9 trials, but tests each hyperparameter at only **3** distinct values. If only one of the two really matters (common: Bergstra & Bengio found that "for most data sets only a few of the hyper-parameters really matter"), six of those nine trials are repeats of the same three values of the important one. Grids also grow exponentially: 5 values × 6 hyperparameters = 15,625 fits, before cross-validation multiplies that by 5.

#### Caveats

- Tuning rarely beats better data or features; gains over sensible defaults are often small for gradient boosting.

- Random search's advantage relies on low effective dimensionality; with one hyperparameter, a fine grid is fine.

- BO needs sensible priors/ranges and struggles with many dimensions, categorical choices and parallel trials (TPE handles these better than GPs).

- Early-stopping methods assume early performance predicts final performance; resource-dependent hyperparameters (e.g. learning rate schedules) break that.

## Say it

### How do you tune hyperparameters efficiently?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Why is random search better than grid search?

With low effective dimensionality, a grid tests the important hyperparameter at only √n (for 2-D) distinct values; random search tests n. It also lets you set the budget independently of dimension (Bergstra & Bengio 2012).

Follow-up 2 of 4

How does Bayesian optimisation work?

Fit a surrogate (GP/TPE) to (settings, score) pairs; compute an acquisition function (expected improvement, UCB) that balances predicted quality and uncertainty; evaluate the maximiser; refit; repeat.

Follow-up 3 of 4

What is Hyperband?

Successive halving run in several brackets with different trade-offs between number of configurations and budget per configuration, so you don't have to guess how aggressive to be.

Follow-up 4 of 4

How do you avoid overfitting during tuning?

Score with CV on a development set, evaluate the final model once on a held-out set (or nested CV), prefer simpler settings when scores tie, and limit the number of trials relative to data size.

#### The 30-second answer

Hyperparameters are chosen by searching settings and scoring each with cross-validation. Grid search is exhaustive but wasteful, because usually only a few hyperparameters matter and a grid tests each at few distinct values; random search with the same budget explores many more values and is a strong default. Bayesian optimisation fits a surrogate model, such as a Gaussian process or TPE, to past trials and uses an acquisition function like expected improvement to pick the next one, which helps when trials are expensive. Successive halving and Hyperband start many configurations cheaply and only continue the promising ones. I search rates and penalties on a log scale, use early stopping inside trials, and evaluate the chosen model on data the search never touched.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "I tune on the test set." Then the test score is no longer honest.

- "Grid search is the most thorough, so it's best." Not per trial spent.

- "Search the learning rate from 0.001 to 0.3 in steps of 0.01." Use a log scale.

**Key terms and sources**

Grid vs random search, Bayesian optimisation with a Gaussian process and expected improvement, successive halving and Hyperband, and honest evaluation of tuned models · built from Bergstra & Bengio (2012), Snoek, Larochelle & Adams (2012), Li et al. (2018) and scikit-learn's model-selection guide · checked 28 Oct 2026

#### Evidence

##### Kernel classifier on CIFAR-10 (Li et al., Hyperband paper)

In the time Bayesian optimisers evaluated about 3 configurations, Hyperband's first bracket evaluated over 250 and found a good one in about 20 minutes; the paper reports it "over 30× faster than Bayesian optimization methods and 70× faster than random search" on this task, and around 6× faster on a random-features task [pp. 18–19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.06560#page=18). The authors also note their most aggressive bracket alone often beat full Hyperband.

##### This page's simulations

Lower is better; one important and one irrelevant hyperparameter. Illustrative.

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Hyperparameter** | Setting chosen before training. |
| **Surrogate model** | Cheap model of score vs settings (GP, TPE, random forest). |
| **Acquisition function** | Rule for choosing the next trial (EI, UCB). |
| **Successive halving** | Keep the best 1/η, multiply their budget by η, repeat. |
| **Hyperband** | Several successive-halving brackets with different starting budgets. |
| **Pruning** | Stopping unpromising trials early (Optuna's term). |

# Learning Curves and Debugging Models

> Your model isn't good enough. How do you decide whether to get more data, or change the model?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/learning-curves-and-debugging/
- Before this: The Bias–Variance Trade-off (`fundamentals/bias-variance`), Cross-Validation & Data Leakage (`fundamentals/cross-validation-and-leakage`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model's validation error is too high. Your manager offers budget to double the labelled data. An engineer wants a much bigger model instead. Nobody has checked which problem you have. The interviewer asks:

> Your model isn't good enough. How do you decide whether to get more data, or change the model?

#### Why it matters

Teams can spend months on the wrong fix. This is a common interview question, as it shows whether you diagnose before acting. It builds on bias and variance.

### The idea

Think of a student who failed an exam. If they also fail the practice papers, more papers of the same kind won't help them. They need better teaching. If they ace the practice papers but fail the exam, they memorised answers, so they need more varied practice. Check which it is before you act.

[Figure: Three patterns. Both errors high means underfitting. A large gap means overfitting. Both near the noise floor means you may be near the limit.]

_Diagnose first, as the fixes for these are opposites._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Add rows at degree 1. Then try degree 12 with few rows.

#### Diagnose a model

Our seeded simulation: y = sin(3x) plus noise, with x between −1 and 1, fitted by least squares. Errors are mean squared errors, and the median of 15 runs. Validation uses 500 new rows. The diagnosis uses simple thresholds, as a guide.

The dashed line marks the noise floor, the vertical line marks the rows you have, and the bottom axis counts rows. Start at degree **1**, and add rows: nothing improves. Now try degree **12** with few rows: there's a large gap, which closes as rows grow. Degree **5** gets close to the floor, and no model goes reliably below it.

**Now say why:** why doesn't more data help a straight line fit a curve?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Plot training and validation error **as data grows**. If both are high and close together, the model is too simple, and **more data won't help**. If training error is low and there's a large gap, it's overfitting, and **more data or regularisation should help**. If both level off near the noise in your labels, you may be near the limit. It saves weeks of collecting data that was never going to help.

#### Reading the curves

| What you see | Diagnosis | Helps | Doesn't help |
|---|---|---|---|
| Both errors high and close | **Underfitting** | Better features, a more flexible model, less regularisation. | More rows. |
| Training low, large gap | **Overfitting** | More rows, regularisation, simpler model, fewer features. | A more flexible model. |
| Both low and close | **Good fit** | Check slices and production behaviour. | More tuning, probably. |
| Both level off, even with flexible models | **Noise or missing information** | Cleaner labels, new information. | More tuning. |
| Good offline, poor in production | **Shift or leakage** | Check leakage and drift. | Any of the above. |

##### Why it works: a little learning theory

Training minimises the error on your sample, called **empirical risk**. What you want is low error on new data. The gap between them grows with a model's **capacity**, meaning how many patterns it could fit, and shrinks as data grows. Measures like **VC dimension** make this formal. It's why a flexible model needs more data.

##### Modern exception

Large neural networks can fit training data perfectly and still generalise, which classic capacity bounds don't explain well. So use these curves for diagnosis, rather than treating the theory as a law. See bias and variance, which covers double descent.

##### A debugging order

1. **Check the data:** read rows and labels. Check the splits, and whether any feature leaks.

2. **Set a baseline:** compare against a simple rule, or a simple model.

3. **Try to overfit a small sample:** if a flexible model can't, there's a bug, or the features carry no signal.

4. **Plot the learning curve:** decide between more data and a better model.

5. **Look at the errors:** group mistakes by segment. A few causes often explain many errors.

6. **Estimate the ceiling:** how well could an expert do? It tells you how much gain remains.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{Validation error}} \approx {\text{Training error}} + {\text{Gap}(\text{capacity},\, n)}, \qquad {\text{Error} \geq \text{noise}} $$

This is a way to think about it, not an exact equation. Formal bounds exist, and are often loose in practice.

- **what you care about**: Error on data that the model hasn’t seen.

- **what you can reduce directly**: If it’s high, the model is underfitting.

- **the gap**: It grows with capacity, and shrinks with more data.

- **the floor**: Label noise sets a limit that no model can beat on average.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use sampled subsets:** train on 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of your rows. That's cheap, and often enough to see the trend.

- **Keep validation fixed:** otherwise the curves aren't comparable.

- **Check for label noise:** have two people label the same rows. Their disagreement suggests a realistic ceiling.

- **Split time correctly:** if the data changes over time, a random split will make things look better than they are.

- **Fix one thing at a time:** keep a log, so that you know what actually helped.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "More data always helps"

It sounds right, as more data rarely hurts. But if the model is too simple, the errors are already close together, and adding rows changes almost nothing. You'd spend the budget and see no gain. A learning curve from your current data tells you this cheaply.

## Say it

### Your model isn't good enough. How do you decide whether to get more data, or change the model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your boss wants to double the labelled data. How do you decide?

Plot a learning curve using subsets of the current data. If validation error is still falling as rows grow, more data should help, and you can roughly extend the trend. If it's flat, spend the money on features, labels or a different approach.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why try to overfit a small sample?

A flexible model should nearly memorise a small sample. If it can't, something's broken: mislabelled data, a bug in the pipeline, a bad learning rate, or features with no signal. It's a quick test that rules out many problems.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Training error is lower than the label noise. Is that a problem?

It means the model is fitting noise, at least partly, because noise can't really be predicted. Validation error will tell you how much it matters. Some overfitting like this can be harmless, as with some large models, so judge by validation performance.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd plot training and validation error as the data grows. If both are high and close, it's underfitting, so more rows won't help, and I'd add features or flexibility. If training is low with a large gap, it's overfitting, so more rows or regularisation should help. If both level off near the label noise, I'd improve the labels, or find new information. Before that, I'd check the data and leakage, compare with a baseline, and try overfitting a small sample to rule out bugs. Then I'd look at the errors by segment.

**Key terms and sources**

Reading train and validation curves, what capacity means, when more data helps, and a step-by-step way to debug a model. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [scikit-learn on validation and learning curves](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/learning_curve.html)

- [CS229 syllabus](https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-summer2019.html)

- [ISLR](https://www.statlearning.com/)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Explaining Models: SHAP, Permutation Importance and PDPs

> How would you explain what your model learned, and why it made a particular prediction?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/explaining-models/
- Before this: Random Forest (`fundamentals/random-forest`), Cross-Validation & Data Leakage (`fundamentals/cross-validation-and-leakage`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your delivery-time model is accurate, but operations want to know why one order was predicted at 68 minutes, and which features matter overall. A colleague shows the tree's built-in importance chart, with an order ID near the top. The interviewer asks:

> How would you explain what your model learned, and why it made a particular prediction?

#### Why it matters

People ask why a model refused a loan or flagged an order. Debugging also starts here, as an important feature that shouldn't be there often means data leakage. Getting a number is easy. Reading it correctly is the skill.

### The idea

Think of a team that won a prize. To split it fairly, you ask how much each person added, trying them joining in every possible order, and you average. Shapley values do this for features. The shares always add up to the whole prize.

[Figure: Three tools. Permutation importance answers which features matter overall. Partial dependence shows how a feature moves predictions. SHAP explains one prediction.]

_Each answers a different question, and none of them shows cause._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the interaction to 5. Then set rain to 0.

#### Share credit for one prediction

A made-up model: minutes = 20 + 2 × distance + 10 × rain + 8 × peak + interaction × distance × rain. The baseline uses distance 5, no rain and peak 0.3. Absent features take these values. Shares are exact, from every ordering.

Raise the interaction to **5**. Part of the effect now exists only when distance and rain act together, and Shapley values split that part between them. Now set rain to **0**: it matches the baseline, so it gets exactly zero credit.

**Now say why:** why does rain get no credit when it matches the baseline?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Permutation importance** shuffles one feature, and measures how much the score drops: which features the model relies on overall. **Partial dependence** shows how predictions change as one feature changes. **SHAP** explains a single prediction, splitting the gap from a baseline fairly among features. All of them **explain the model, not the world**, so they don't show cause, and correlated features can mislead each one.

#### Which tool answers which question

| Question | Tool | How it works | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Which features does the model rely on? | **Permutation importance** | Shuffle one column, and measure the score's fall. | Correlated features hide each other. |
| How does a feature move predictions on average? | **Partial dependence** | Set the feature to each value for all rows, and average. | Averages hide interactions. Can create unrealistic rows. |
| Does the effect differ across rows? | **ICE plots** | One line per row. Their average is the PDP. | Hard to read with many rows. |
| Why this prediction? | **SHAP** | Share the gap from the baseline among features. | Depends on the baseline, and on how absent features are handled. |
| Why this prediction, simply? | **LIME** | Fit a small linear model on nearby perturbed samples. | Results depend on its settings, and can be unstable. |

##### Shapley values, in one idea

Imagine the features as a team, sharing credit for a prediction. A feature's contribution can depend on which others are already present. So average its added value across **every order** in which features could join. The result is the only way of sharing that meets three properties:

- **Local accuracy:** the contributions add up exactly to the prediction minus the baseline.

- **Missingness:** a feature that's absent gets no credit.

- **Consistency:** if a model comes to rely on a feature more, its credit shouldn't fall.

Trying every order is exponential. So practical tools use shortcuts, and TreeSHAP makes it fast for tree models.

##### Why built-in tree importance can mislead

Impurity-based importance is calculated on training data, and it favours features with many values, like IDs. It can rank a useless feature highly, so prefer permutation importance on held-out data.

##### How correlated features fool each tool

- **Permutation:** shuffle one of two twin features, and the model still has the other, so both look unimportant.

- **PDP and SHAP:** these can evaluate impossible combinations, like a 6-foot-tall child. The model's answer on those rows means little.

Group correlated features first, or look at them together.

#### The maths

$$ {\phi_i} = \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{i\}} {\frac{|S|!\,(|F| - |S| - 1)!}{|F|!}}\; {\big[v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)\big]}, \qquad {f(x) = \phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i} $$

From Lundberg and Lee (2017), building on Shapley’s work in game theory. SHAP sets absent features using expected values, and independence is a common simplifying assumption.

- **feature i’s Shapley value**: Its fair share of the gap between this prediction and the baseline.

- **the weight**: The share of all orderings in which exactly the features in S come before i.

- **its added value**: How much the prediction changes when i joins the features in S.

- **local accuracy**: The baseline plus all the contributions gives exactly the prediction.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use them to find leaks:** if one feature dominates, ask if it could really be known at prediction time.

- **Evaluate first:** explaining a poor model tells you little, so check its score on held-out data.

- **Say it correctly:** "the model's prediction rose because of X", not "X causes delays". Changing X in the real world may do nothing. See causal inference.

- **Check stability:** retrain with a different seed. If the explanations change a lot, trust them less.

- **Simple models help:** if a small model does nearly as well, it may be easier to justify than a complex one with an explanation attached.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "SHAP says this feature causes the outcome"

It sounds right, as the number looks precise. But SHAP describes what the model does with its inputs. A feature can be a proxy for something else, and changing it may change nothing in the real world. To learn what a change would do, run an experiment or a causal analysis.

## Say it

### How would you explain what your model learned, and why it made a particular prediction?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why might two important features both look unimportant?

If they're strongly correlated, shuffling one leaves the other available, so the score barely falls, and both seem unimportant. Group correlated features, permute them together or remove one, and compare. It's a known weakness of permutation importance.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A feature has a large SHAP value. If you change that feature, will the outcome change?

Not necessarily. SHAP explains the model's output. It could be a proxy for something else, or the model may have learned a correlation. To know whether changing it changes real outcomes, you need an experiment or a causal analysis.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not use a tree model's built-in feature importance?

Impurity importance is computed on training data, so it can reward overfitting, and it favours features with many unique values. A random ID can look important. Permutation importance on held-out data avoids that, though it has its own issue with correlated features.

#### The 30-second answer

It depends on the question. For which features matter overall, I'd use permutation importance on held-out data: shuffle a feature, and measure the score drop. For how a feature moves predictions, I'd use partial dependence, with ICE to reveal interactions. For one prediction, I'd use SHAP, which splits the gap from a baseline fairly among features, and always adds up. I'd watch correlated features, which hide each other or create unrealistic rows. And these explain the model, not the world, so they don't show cause.

**Key terms and sources**

Global and local explanations: permutation importance, partial dependence and ICE, SHAP and LIME, how each can mislead, and why none shows cause. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Lundberg and Lee, A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874)

- [scikit-learn on permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html)

- [scikit-learn on partial dependence and ICE](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/partial_dependence.html)

- [Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning: SHAP](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/shap.html)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Classical ML Practice

> Ensembles, metrics, odds, Gini and leakage: can you answer these quickly?

- Track: Fundamentals › Classical ML › Core concepts
- Type: Interview · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/classical-ml-practice/
- Before this: The Bias–Variance Trade-off (`fundamentals/bias-variance`), Classification Metrics (`fundamentals/classification-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `mlcore`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Say your approach out loud, then open the answer and compare the method, not just the number.

**Tools for this page:** ask what the model is reducing, bias or variance, then which errors cost most, and whether any step used data it shouldn't have.

Question 1 · Easy · trees

### Does a random forest mainly reduce bias or variance? What about gradient boosting?

Answer: **Random forest: variance. Boosting: mainly bias**

1. A forest averages many deep, nearly independent trees, which smooths out their noise.

2. Boosting adds shallow trees one by one, each fixing earlier errors, which lowers bias.

3. Boosting also overfits more easily if you add too many trees.

That's why forests need little tuning, while boosting needs a learning rate and early stopping.

Question 2 · Easy · regularisation

### What's the practical difference between L1 and L2 regularisation?

Answer: **L1 can make weights exactly zero. L2 shrinks them all**

1. L1 has a constant pull towards zero, so small weights get removed.

2. L2's pull weakens near zero, so weights rarely reach zero.

So L1 also selects features, while L2 handles correlated features more steadily.

Question 3 · Easy · starting point

### You have 5,000 rows of tabular data. What do you try first, and why?

Answer: **A simple baseline, then gradient boosting**

1. Logistic regression, or a similar simple model, sets a baseline and catches data problems.

2. Gradient boosting usually does very well on tabular data, with little preparation.

Getting a sound validation split matters more than the model choice.

Question 4 · Medium · metrics

### TP = 80, FP = 20 and FN = 40. What are precision, recall and F1?

Answer: **Precision 0.80, recall 0.67, F1 0.73**

1. Precision: 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80.

2. Recall: 80 ÷ 120 ≈ 0.67.

3. F1: 2 × 0.80 × 0.67 ÷ (0.80 + 0.67) ≈ 0.73.

Which matters more depends on the cost of each error.

Question 5 · Medium · imbalance

### A fraud model scores 99% accuracy, and 1% of transactions are fraud. Is that good?

Answer: **Not necessarily. Predicting "not fraud" always gets 99%**

1. Accuracy here says almost nothing.

2. Check precision and recall, or PR-AUC, on the fraud class.

3. Choose a threshold from the costs of each kind of error.

Resampling isn't always needed. Class weights and a good threshold often do enough.

Question 6 · Medium · logistic regression

### In logistic regression, a feature has a coefficient of 0.7. What does this mean?

Answer: **Each unit multiplies the odds by about 2**

1. Coefficients act on the log odds.

2. e^0.7 ≈ 2.01.

3. So each extra unit about doubles the odds, holding other features fixed.

It doesn't double the probability. That depends on where you start.

Question 7 · Hard · decision trees

### A node is 50 yes and 50 no. A split gives one side 40 yes, 10 no, and the other 10 yes, 40 no. What's the fall in Gini impurity?

Answer: **0.18**

1. Parent: 1 − 0.5² − 0.5² = 0.50.

2. Each child: 1 − 0.8² − 0.2² = 0.32.

3. Weighted child average: 0.32, so the fall is 0.50 − 0.32 = 0.18.

Trees choose the split with the largest such fall.

Question 8 · Hard · leakage

### You scale all the data, choose features, then cross-validate, and get 95%. In production, it's 70%. What likely happened?

Answer: **Leakage through preprocessing and selection**

1. Scaling and especially selection used rows from the test folds.

2. Move every step that learns from data into a pipeline, fit on training folds only.

3. Also check for time leakage, and whether production data has shifted.

Selecting with test labels is the most damaging of these.

**More practice and sources**

8 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 6 Nov 2026

Keep practising

Review gradient boosting, regularisation, classification metrics, logistic regression, decision trees and leakage.

# From Perceptron to MLP

> Why can't one neuron learn XOR, and what does a hidden layer add?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Neural network basics
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/perceptron-to-mlp/
- Before this: Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`)
- Quiz topic: `nn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your delivery model scores orders with one weighted sum, but orders run late in two separate rush-hour bands. No single straight line can capture that. The interviewer asks:

> Why can't a single neuron learn XOR, and what does a hidden layer add?

**Running example (all Deep Learning lessons):** the food-delivery app predicts whether an order will arrive **late** from two numbers: the **distance** (0–10 km) and the **hour** it was placed (10:00–23:00). Orders run late when they're far away, and also during the lunch rush (around 13:00) and dinner rush (around 20:30), even when they're close.

#### Some patterns can't be separated by one straight line

Logistic regression scores an order as w₁·distance + w₂·hour + b and says "late" when the score is positive. That's a single straight boundary across the (distance, hour) plane. But "late" here is two separate bands of hours plus a far-away region: no single line can carve that out. We need a model that can learn curved, multi-part boundaries without us hand-crafting features like "is it rush hour?".

### The idea

Think of drawing fences on a map. One neuron can only draw one straight fence. Each hidden unit draws its own fence, and the output combines them, so together they can fence off odd shapes.

[Figure: Left: one straight line can't separate a band of late orders. Right: several lines from hidden units together fence the band off.]

_Illustrative, based on the lesson's rush-hour bands._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start with 0 hidden units, then try 2, 4 and 16. Watch the boundary and compare train and test accuracy.

#### Add hidden units, watch the boundary bend

Each run trains a tanh MLP in your browser (600 full-batch Adam steps on log loss, fixed seed). Shaded regions: predicted late (orange) or on time (teal); dots: test orders.

Logistic regression is stuck near **72%** test accuracy: its one straight line can't follow the rush-hour bands. Two hidden units barely help (75%), four get most of the shape (86%), and sixteen reach **89%**. Notice the 16-unit model is at 98% on the training orders: more capacity also means more room to overfit, which the Regularisation lessons later in this track deal with.

**Now say why:** what does each extra hidden unit add, and when does adding more stop helping?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **neuron** takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an **activation function**. One neuron (a **perceptron** or logistic regression) can only draw a straight line between classes, so it fails on patterns like XOR. Stack neurons into a **hidden layer** and the network can bend its boundary: each hidden unit draws one line, and the output combines them. Without a non-linear activation, any stack of layers collapses back into one linear layer. With one, a wide enough single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function (**universal approximation**), and in practice **deeper** networks get there with far fewer units. What you'll be able to do after this: write the forward pass of an MLP, explain why it needs a non-linearity, count its parameters, and explain why width and depth help.

#### One neuron

$$ a = {f}\big({w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2} + {b}\big) $$

Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) used a step function and a simple error-driven update rule; logistic regression is the same neuron with a sigmoid and log loss (Logistic Regression).

- **weights**: How much each input matters, learned from data. For our example, one weight for distance and one for hour.

- **bias**: Shifts the threshold: how big the weighted sum must be before the neuron fires.

- **activation**: A non-linear squashing function: step (perceptron), sigmoid, tanh, ReLU. Without it, the neuron is just a linear function.

#### The multi-layer perceptron (MLP)

$$ {\mathbf{h} = {\phi}(W_1 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1)}, \qquad {\hat{p} = \sigma(\mathbf{w}_2^{\top} \mathbf{h} + b_2)} $$

Parameters: 2 × 16 + 16 for the hidden layer plus 16 + 1 for the output = 65. "Fully connected" or "dense" layer = this matrix-product-plus-bias layer. Goodfellow et al. ch. 6.

- **hidden layer**: A layer of neurons computed together as a matrix product: each row of W₁ is one hidden unit’s weights. With 16 hidden units and 2 inputs, W₁ is 16 × 2.

- **element-wise non-linearity**: Applied to every hidden unit separately (tanh in our lab, ReLU or GELU in most modern networks).

- **output layer**: Combines the hidden units into one score; a sigmoid turns it into the probability that the order is late.

#### Each hidden unit draws a line; the output combines them

1. The (distance, hour) plane. The late orders sit in two horizontal bands (the rush hours) and a vertical strip on the right (far away).

2. A single neuron can only split the plane with one straight line. Whatever line it picks, it misclassifies a big chunk.

3. Give the network a hidden layer. Each hidden unit learns its own line and outputs "which side am I on" (smoothly, through tanh or ReLU).

4. The output neuron learns to combine those yes/no signals: late inside a band or past the far line. With smooth activations the corners round off, and more units give a finer boundary.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Universal approximation, and why we still go deep

- **Universal approximation:** an MLP with one hidden layer and a non-linear activation can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as you like, given enough hidden units (Cybenko 1989 for sigmoids; Hornik 1991 for general activations). It says such a network _exists_, not that training will find it, or how many units it needs.

- **Depth is more efficient:** some functions need exponentially many units in a shallow network but only polynomially many in a deep one (Goodfellow et al. §6.4.1). Each layer can reuse the features of the layer below: edges → shapes → objects in vision.

- **Depth is harder to train:** gradients have to pass through every layer, so they can vanish or explode. That's why the next lessons cover initialisation, vanishing gradients and normalisation.

**Counting parameters** (a common interview warm-up): a dense layer from n inputs to m outputs has n·m weights + m biases. An MLP 784 → 256 → 10 (MNIST) has 784·256 + 256 + 256·10 + 10 = **203,530** parameters.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just stack linear layers"

Two linear layers in a row, W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂, equal one linear layer (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂). A 100-layer network with no activation is still a straight-line model. The fix is the activation function between layers: it's what lets each layer bend the space before the next one looks at it.

Minsky and Papert's 1969 book _Perceptrons_ showed that a single-layer perceptron can't compute XOR. Multi-layer networks could, but nobody had a good way to train their hidden weights until backpropagation was popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams in 1986 (the chain rule lesson).

## Say it

### Why can't a single neuron learn XOR, and what does a hidden layer add?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why can't a single perceptron learn XOR?

XOR's positive points (0,1) and (1,0) sit on opposite corners; no single straight line separates them from (0,0) and (1,1). Two hidden units (one for OR, one for AND) plus an output (OR and not AND) solve it.

Follow-up 2 of 3

If one hidden layer is universal, why use deep networks?

Universality may need an impractically large layer; depth lets layers reuse lower-level features, giving exponentially more efficient representations for many functions, and deep nets generalise better in practice.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What happens if all weights are initialised to zero?

Every hidden unit computes the same thing and gets the same gradient, so they stay identical forever (symmetry is never broken). Weights must start random (initialisation lesson).

#### The 30-second answer

A neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies a non-linear activation. One neuron is a linear classifier, so it can't solve XOR-like patterns. An MLP stacks layers of neurons: each hidden unit carves the input space with one boundary and later layers combine them, so the network can learn curved, multi-part boundaries. The non-linearity is essential, because stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map. By the universal approximation theorem, one wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function, but deeper networks usually represent the same function with far fewer parameters, at the cost of being harder to train.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "More layers always means better." Deeper nets are harder to optimise and can overfit.

- "Universal approximation means a network will learn any function." It's an existence result, not a guarantee about training or data.

**Key terms and sources**

The artificial neuron, the perceptron and its XOR limit, hidden layers, why a non-linearity is essential, the universal approximation theorem and why depth helps · built from Rosenblatt (1958), Minsky & Papert (1969), Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), Cybenko (1989), Hornik (1991) and Goodfellow et al., _Deep Learning_, ch. 6 · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Perceptron** | One neuron with a step activation; a linear classifier. |
| **Hidden layer** | Neurons between input and output; learn intermediate features. |
| **Dense / fully connected** | Every input connects to every unit: Wx + b. |
| **Activation function** | The non-linearity applied to each unit (next lesson). |
| **Universal approximation** | One wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. |

#### Sources

1. F. Rosenblatt, "The perceptron: a probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain", _Psychological Review_ 65(6), 1958.

2. M. Minsky & S. Papert, _Perceptrons_, MIT Press 1969.

3. D. Rumelhart, G. Hinton & R. Williams, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", _Nature_ 323, 1986.

4. G. Cybenko, "Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function", _Mathematics of Control, Signals and Systems_ 2, 1989.

5. K. Hornik, "Approximation capabilities of multilayer feedforward networks", _Neural Networks_ 4(2), 1991.

6. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, ch. 6, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

# Activation Functions

> Why did ReLU replace sigmoid, and what do LLMs use now?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Neural network basics
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/activation-functions/
- Before this: From Perceptron to MLP (`fundamentals/perceptron-to-mlp`)
- Quiz topic: `nn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your deep network uses sigmoid in every layer, and its early layers barely learn. The interviewer asks:

> Why did ReLU replace sigmoid, and what do LLMs use now?

**Running example:** the late-delivery network from the previous lesson. Each hidden unit receives a pre-activation z = w·x + b computed from distance and hour; what matters here is the spread of those z values across orders, and what the activation does to them.

#### The non-linearity also sits on the gradient's path

We need a non-linearity between layers, or the network collapses to a linear model. But in backprop every layer multiplies the gradient by the activation's slope f′(z) (backpropagation lesson). If those slopes are small, the gradient reaching early layers is tiny and they barely learn; if they're exactly zero, the unit stops learning altogether. So choosing an activation is choosing how gradients flow.

### The idea

Think of a volume knob that stops responding at both ends. Sigmoid behaves like that: push it far either way, and turning it further changes nothing, so no learning signal gets through. ReLU stays responsive across its whole positive side.

[Figure: Left: a sigmoid curve is flat at both ends, where its slope is almost zero. Right: ReLU is flat below zero and keeps a slope of one above it.]

_Illustrative. Backprop multiplies the gradient by this slope at every layer._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Choose sigmoid and push the mean of the pre-activations far from zero. Then switch to ReLU and make the mean strongly negative.

#### Where do your pre-activations land on the curve?

Teal: f(z). Orange: f′(z). Grey area: the distribution of pre-activations z across orders (normal with the mean and spread you set). Computed exactly by numerical integration.

With z centred at 0 and spread 1, sigmoid's average slope is only **0.21**, and **no** unit passes even half the gradient: through ten sigmoid layers the gradient shrinks by roughly 0.207¹⁰ ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁷. Tanh does better (average 0.61; 62% of units pass at least half), and ReLU passes exactly half the inputs at full strength. Now push the mean to −3: **99.9%** of ReLU units are dead, leaky ReLU still passes 0.01 of the gradient everywhere, and GELU keeps an average slope of 0.03 with 38% of units stuck. Put the mean back to 0 and widen the spread to 4: **40%** of tanh units are saturated (slope below 0.005).

**Now say why:** how does each activation get stuck, and what does that do to the gradient?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

The activation is the non-linearity that makes a network more than a linear model, and its **slope** decides how much gradient flows back through each unit. **Sigmoid** and **tanh** saturate: for large inputs their slope is almost 0, and sigmoid's slope is never above 0.25, so gradients shrink layer after layer. **ReLU** (max(0, z)) has slope exactly 1 for positive inputs, which made deep networks trainable, but a unit whose input is always negative gets zero gradient and **dies**. **Leaky ReLU** keeps a small slope there; **GELU** is a smooth ReLU used in BERT and GPT; and **SwiGLU**, a gated unit, is the feed-forward activation in LLaMA-style LLMs. What you'll be able to do after this: compare activations by output range, slope and failure mode, explain vanishing gradients through saturating units and dead ReLUs, and say which activation goes where.

#### Sigmoid and tanh

$$ {\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}}, \qquad {\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1} $$

Goodfellow et al. §6.3.2: sigmoidal units saturate across most of their domain, which makes gradient-based learning hard; their use as hidden units is now discouraged.

- **sigmoid**: Squashes to (0, 1). Fine for an output probability; poor in hidden layers: not zero-centred, and its slope σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) peaks at only 0.25.

- **tanh**: A rescaled sigmoid with range (−1, 1): zero-centred, slope up to 1 at z = 0. Still saturates: at z = 3 its slope is about 0.01.

#### ReLU and its descendants

$$ {\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)}, \quad {\mathrm{Leaky}(z)=\max(\alpha z, z)}, \quad {\mathrm{GELU}(z)= z\,\Phi(z)} $$

- **ReLU**: Slope exactly 1 for z > 0, so gradients pass through unchanged; cheap to compute; outputs exact zeros (sparse). Made deep supervised nets trainable without pre-training (Glorot, Bordes & Bengio 2011; Nair & Hinton 2010).

- **leaky ReLU**: A small slope α (often 0.01) for z < 0, so a unit pushed negative still gets some gradient and can recover (Maas et al. 2013).

- **GELU**: Weights the input by the probability that a standard normal is below it: a smooth ReLU that is slightly negative near zero. Used in BERT and GPT-2/3 (Hendrycks & Gimpel 2016).

**Dying ReLU:** if a large update or a big negative bias pushes a unit's input below zero for every training example, its output and gradient are zero everywhere, and it never recovers. A too-high learning rate can kill a large share of units. Fixes: leaky ReLU / GELU, careful initialisation, lower learning rate.

#### Gated linear units: SwiGLU

$$ \mathrm{FFN}_{\mathrm{SwiGLU}}(x) = \big({\mathrm{Swish}(xW)} \otimes {xV}\big){W_2} $$

Shazeer, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", 2020 [arXiv:2002.05202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202): in T5 experiments GEGLU and SwiGLU gave the best perplexities among feed-forward variants. SwiGLU is used in PaLM and LLaMA. It has three weight matrices instead of two, so the hidden width is usually cut to about ⅔ to keep the parameter count equal. Covered again in the Transformers lessons.

- **Swish gate**: Swish(z) = z·σ(z) (also called SiLU), computed from one projection xW. It decides how much of each feature passes.

- **value path**: A second, purely linear projection xV. The gate multiplies it element-wise.

- **down projection**: Projects back to the model width, like the second layer of a normal MLP block.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Cheat sheet

| Activation | Range | Max slope | Failure mode | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sigmoid** | (0, 1) | 0.25 | saturates, not zero-centred | binary output, gates (LSTM) |
| **Tanh** | (−1, 1) | 1 | saturates | RNN/LSTM state |
| **Softmax** | probabilities | – | overflow (subtract max) | multi-class output, attention |
| **ReLU** | [0, ∞) | 1 | dying units | CNNs, MLP default |
| **Leaky ReLU** | (−∞, ∞) | 1 | extra hyperparameter α | GANs, when ReLUs die |
| **GELU** | ≈ [−0.17, ∞) | ≈ 1.13 | slightly costlier | BERT, GPT, ViT |
| **SwiGLU** | (−∞, ∞) | – | 3 matrices | LLaMA-style LLM FFN |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Sigmoid everywhere, like the output"

Through 10 sigmoid layers the gradient is multiplied by at most 0.25 ten times: 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 9.5 × 10⁻⁷, before even counting the weights. The early layers effectively stop learning. That's the vanishing gradient problem, and it's a big reason deep networks were so hard to train before ReLU (vanishing & exploding gradients).

## Say it

### Why did ReLU replace sigmoid, and what do LLMs use now?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is zero-centred output helpful?

If all inputs to a layer are positive (sigmoid outputs), the gradients for that layer's weights all share a sign per unit, so updates zig-zag. Tanh or zero-mean activations avoid this; normalisation layers also help.

Follow-up 2 of 3

ReLU isn't differentiable at 0. Is that a problem?

Not in practice: frameworks use a subgradient (0 or 1) at exactly 0, and inputs are almost never exactly 0.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you detect dead ReLUs?

Log the fraction of units whose output is zero for every example in a batch (or over an epoch), per layer. A rising fraction suggests the learning rate is too high or the initialisation/bias is off.

#### The 30-second answer

Activations add the non-linearity, and their derivative scales every gradient that flows back. Sigmoid and tanh saturate, and sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so in deep stacks gradients vanish. ReLU has slope 1 for positive inputs, is cheap, and made deep nets trainable, but units can die if their inputs stay negative; leaky ReLU and GELU keep some gradient there. Today CNNs mostly use ReLU, transformers use GELU, and modern LLMs use gated units like SwiGLU in their feed-forward blocks. Sigmoid and softmax stay at the output for probabilities.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "ReLU solves vanishing gradients completely." It helps a lot, but deep nets still need good initialisation, normalisation and residual connections.

- "Use softmax in hidden layers." It's for outputs and attention weights.

**Key terms and sources**

Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and its variants, GELU and gated units like SwiGLU: what each does to the signal and to the gradient, and why modern networks use the ones they do · built from Glorot, Bordes & Bengio (2011), Nair & Hinton (2010), Maas et al. (2013), Hendrycks & Gimpel (2016), Shazeer (2020) and Goodfellow et al. §6.3 · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. V. Nair & G. Hinton, "Rectified linear units improve restricted Boltzmann machines", ICML 2010.

2. X. Glorot, A. Bordes & Y. Bengio, "Deep sparse rectifier neural networks", AISTATS 2011.

3. A. Maas, A. Hannun & A. Ng, "Rectifier nonlinearities improve neural network acoustic models", ICML Workshop 2013.

4. D. Hendrycks & K. Gimpel, "Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)", [arXiv:1606.08415](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08415), 2016.

5. N. Shazeer, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", [arXiv:2002.05202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202), 2020.

6. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, §6.3, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).
