# Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning

> Only 15 labelled examples? Reuse a model trained on 1,000.

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › CNNs
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/transfer-learning/
- Before this: ResNets and Skip Connections (`fundamentals/resnets-and-skip-connections`)
- Quiz topic: `cnn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your delivery app launches in a new city with only 15 labelled orders, and you already have a model trained on 1,000 orders from another city. The interviewer asks:

> With only 15 labelled examples, how would you reuse a pre-trained model?

**Running example:** the late-delivery model was trained on **1,000 orders from city A**. The app launches in **city B**, where the rush hours are a little different (lunch peaks around 12:30, dinner around 21:00) and distance matters slightly less. City B has only a few labelled orders so far. Train a new model, or reuse city A's?

#### Small datasets can't train big models

A model trained from scratch on 15 or 30 examples has to discover everything ("rush hours exist", "distance matters") from almost no evidence. But a related task already taught a network those ideas. Reusing it is like hiring someone who knows the food business and only needs to learn the new city.

### The idea

Think of hiring someone who already knows the food business and teaching them your city, instead of training a complete beginner. You keep what they know, and you adjust gently, so you don't wipe out what made them valuable.

[Figure: A row of pre-trained layers shown as frozen, followed by one new head that gets trained.]

_Illustrative. Early layers tend to be general, and later ones specific to the task._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at 15 orders and compare from scratch, frozen features and fine-tuning. Then move up to 200.

#### City B accuracy, by how many labelled orders it has

All models: 16 tanh hidden units. Source model trained on 1,000 city-A orders. Test: 500 city-B orders. Frozen = only the output layer trains; fine-tune = all layers from city-A weights with learning rate 0.01 instead of 0.05. Fixed seeds.

With only **15** city-B orders, a model from scratch reaches **69%**; reusing city A's hidden layer and training just a new output layer reaches **89%**, already better than city A's model unchanged (85%). Fine-tuning everything is close behind (85%): with so little data, updating every weight is riskier than updating a few. At **200** orders the picture flips: from scratch catches up (93%) and **fine-tuning wins (95%)**, because it can adapt the hidden features to city B's different rush hours, which a frozen layer can't.

**Now say why:** why does the best choice change as you get more data?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Features learned on a big dataset (ImageNet photos, web text) are useful far beyond it: early layers learn general things like edges and colours, later layers more task-specific ones. So instead of training from scratch, start from a **pre-trained** model. With little data, **freeze** it and train only a new output layer (**feature extraction**). With more data, **fine-tune** all layers with a **small learning rate**, often unfreezing from the top down. Transfer works best when the new task resembles the original, and it is how almost every vision, language and speech model is built today. What you'll be able to do after this: choose between from-scratch, frozen features and full fine-tuning for a given dataset size, and describe a safe fine-tuning recipe.

#### Three ways to use a pre-trained network

| Option | What trains | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Use as-is** | nothing | the tasks are the same (or zero-shot models) |
| **Feature extraction** | a new head on frozen features | little target data; similar domain |
| **Fine-tuning** | all (or the top) layers, small learning rate | more target data, or the domain differs |
| **From scratch** | everything, random init | lots of data and a very different domain |

Razavian et al. (2014) showed that off-the-shelf CNN features plus a linear classifier were a strong baseline across many vision tasks; Kornblith et al. (CVPR 2019) found that better ImageNet models generally transfer better, especially with fine-tuning.

#### Which layers transfer?

- Yosinski et al. (NeurIPS 2014) [arXiv:1411.1792](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1792): first-layer features (Gabor-like edges, colour blobs) are **general**; higher layers become **specific** to the original task. Transferability drops as the tasks become less similar, yet transferred features beat random ones even for distant tasks, and fine-tuning transferred weights improved generalisation.

- So: freeze more layers when data is scarce and the domain is close; unfreeze more (from the top down) as data grows or the domain drifts.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Fine-tuning without wrecking the pre-trained weights

1. Replace the head with one sized for the new classes; keep the pre-trained preprocessing (same normalisation, image size or tokenizer).

2. Train the head first with the body frozen (a few epochs), so random head gradients don't damage the body.

3. Unfreeze the top blocks (or everything) with a learning rate 10–100× smaller than from scratch; **discriminative learning rates** (smaller for lower layers) and **gradual unfreezing** come from ULMFiT (Howard & Ruder 2018).

4. Use warmup, early stopping and light regularisation; small datasets overfit within a few epochs.

For BERT-style models the usual setting is AdamW with learning rates of 2e-5 to 5e-5 for 2–4 epochs (Devlin et al. 2019). Very large models are often adapted with parameter-efficient methods like LoRA instead of full fine-tuning (covered in the LLMs track).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just fine-tune the whole model at your normal learning rate"

It sounds right, since more training usually helps. But pre-trained weights are already near a good solution, and large steps destroy useful features. With very little data, fine-tuning everything can also overfit, so you start with the head, then unfreeze from the top with a learning rate 10 to 100 times smaller.

## Say it

### With only 15 labelled examples, how would you reuse a pre-trained model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why a lower learning rate for fine-tuning?

The pre-trained weights are already near a good solution; large steps destroy useful features (catastrophic forgetting) before the new head has learned anything.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Medical X-rays with an ImageNet model: freeze or fine-tune?

The domain is far from ImageNet, so fine-tune more layers (keep early layers or use small rates there), and consider domain-specific pre-trained models.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's negative transfer?

When the source task is so different that pre-trained features hurt compared with training from scratch; validate against a from-scratch baseline.

#### The 30-second answer

Transfer learning reuses a model pre-trained on a large dataset. Early layers learn general features like edges and textures, later layers more task-specific ones. With little target data and a similar domain, I freeze the backbone and train a new head; with more data or a different domain, I fine-tune, starting with the head, then unfreezing from the top with a learning rate 10 to 100 times smaller, often with discriminative learning rates, keeping the original preprocessing. It massively reduces the data and compute needed, and it's how nearly all modern vision and language models are deployed.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Fine-tuning with the original learning rate." It erases what was learned.

- "Always freeze everything." With enough data, fine-tuning beats frozen features.

**Key terms and sources**

Reusing a network trained on a big dataset for a new task: feature extraction (freeze and train a new head), fine-tuning (update everything, gently), which layers transfer, how much data you need, and the usual recipe · built from Yosinski et al. (NeurIPS 2014), Razavian et al. (2014), Kornblith et al. (CVPR 2019), Howard & Ruder (ACL 2018) and Devlin et al. (2019) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. J. Yosinski, J. Clune, Y. Bengio & H. Lipson, "How transferable are features in deep neural networks?", NeurIPS 2014, [arXiv:1411.1792](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.1792).

2. A. Razavian, H. Azizpour, J. Sullivan & S. Carlsson, "CNN Features off-the-shelf: an Astounding Baseline for Recognition", CVPR Workshops 2014, [arXiv:1403.6382](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6382).

3. S. Kornblith, J. Shlens & Q. Le, "Do Better ImageNet Models Transfer Better?", CVPR 2019, [arXiv:1805.08974](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.08974).

4. J. Howard & S. Ruder, "Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification" (ULMFiT), ACL 2018, [arXiv:1801.06146](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.06146).

5. J. Devlin, M.-W. Chang, K. Lee & K. Toutanova, "BERT", NAACL 2019, [arXiv:1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805).

# RNNs and Backprop Through Time

> Why can't a plain RNN remember a word from 50 steps ago?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Sequence models
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/rnns-and-backprop-through-time/
- Before this: Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`)
- Quiz topic: `seq`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model reads reviews one word at a time. By the end of a long review, it has lost track of what "cold" referred to. The interviewer asks:

> Why can't a plain RNN remember a word from 50 steps ago?

**Running example (Sequence and Transformer lessons):** the app reads restaurant reviews. Take "_the biryani was cold but the naan was great_". To judge it, a model must remember "cold" belongs to the biryani, and that "but" flips the tone, even if many words sit between them.

#### Inputs that come in order, with any length

An MLP takes a fixed-size input. Reviews, sentences, delivery-tracking events and audio are sequences of different lengths where order matters ("not good" ≠ "good, not"). We need a model that reads one step at a time, carries a memory forward, and reuses the same weights at every position, just as a CNN reuses a filter at every pixel.

### The idea

Think of reading a review with a single sticky note. After each word, you rewrite the note from what's on it and the new word. Early details get fainter with every rewrite, until they're gone.

[Figure: Words pass through a chain of hidden states. The memory of the first word fades at each step.]

_Illustrative. The same weights are reused at every step._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the recurrent weight scale below 1 and read the gradient at 10 and 50 steps back. Then push it above 1, and try the linear RNN.

#### How much gradient reaches earlier words?

A 32-unit RNN with random recurrent weights scaled to the chosen size, random inputs, 60 steps, fixed seed. Curve: size of ∂h60/∂ht for each earlier step t (log scale); band = 0.1–10.

With weight scale 1 and tanh, the gradient falls below 10⁻³ about **22 steps** back: words further away barely influence learning. At 0.7 the horizon shrinks to **11 steps**. Push the scale up to about 1.4 and the gradient survives 50 steps (still 0.1), but the network now sits at the edge of chaos: at 2 the gradient _grows_ backwards (about 12 at 50 steps), so tiny changes to early words swing the output wildly. The linear RNN shows the pure exponential: at scale 1.5 the gradient explodes to about **6 × 10⁹**. The useful middle ground is narrow and drifts as the weights train, which is why gated cells that make the memory path explicit won out.

**Now say why:** why does a small change in the scale make the gradient vanish or explode?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An **RNN** processes a sequence one item at a time, keeping a **hidden state** ht that mixes the new input with the previous state, using the **same weights at every step**. That lets one small network handle sequences of any length. To train it, we **unroll** it into a deep network with one layer per time step and run ordinary backprop through it: **backpropagation through time (BPTT)**. The catch: the gradient from step T back to step t is a product of T − t Jacobians of the same recurrent matrix, so it **vanishes** or **explodes** exponentially. Plain RNNs struggle to remember more than about 10–20 steps, which is why LSTMs, GRUs and then attention took over. What you'll be able to do after this: write the RNN update, explain BPTT and truncated BPTT, and explain why long-range memory fails.

#### One update, repeated

$$ {h_t} = \tanh\!\big({W_{hh}\,h_{t-1}} + {W_{xh}\,x_t} + b\big), \qquad {\hat{y}_t = W_{hy}\,h_t} $$

The Elman network (1990). Goodfellow et al. ch. 10.

- **new hidden state**: The memory after reading word t: a vector, e.g. 128 numbers.

- **recurrent weights**: How the previous memory feeds the next one. The same W_hh is used at every step: that sharing is what makes the network work for any length.

- **current input**: The embedding of word t, projected by W_xh.

- **output**: Optional at each step (tagging every word) or only at the end (one sentiment score).

#### Unroll it, then backprop through time

1. The review arrives one word at a time.

2. Each step computes a new hidden state from the word and the previous state, with the same W_hh every time. Unrolled, it looks like a deep network with one layer per word, sharing weights.

3. A loss is computed at the end (e.g. sentiment) or at every step.

4. Backprop through time: run normal backprop through the unrolled graph. Because W_hh is shared, its gradient is the sum of its gradients at every step.

5. The signal from the loss to an early word passes through one Jacobian per step. Multiply many of them and it vanishes (or explodes), exactly like a very deep plain network.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Practical fixes and where RNNs stand today

- **Truncated BPTT:** backprop only through the last k steps (e.g. 50–200) while carrying the hidden state forward; cheaper, but can't learn dependencies longer than k.

- **Gradient clipping** for explosions (Pascanu et al. 2013; vanishing & exploding gradients).

- **Gated cells** (LSTM, GRU) for vanishing: next lesson.

- **Bidirectional RNNs** read the sequence both ways when the whole input is available (tagging, encoding).

- **Today:** Transformers replaced RNNs for most language tasks because RNNs process steps one after another (no parallelism over time) and forget long-range context. Recurrent ideas returned in state-space models (e.g. Mamba), which keep a fixed-size state with linear-time processing.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The hidden state carries everything forward, so an RNN can remember any length"

It sounds right, since the hidden state does flow through every step. But each step multiplies it by the same weights and squashes it, so the gradient linking a late loss to an early word shrinks or explodes exponentially. In practice, a plain RNN remembers only tens of steps.

## Say it

### Why can't a plain RNN remember a word from 50 steps ago?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why can't an RNN be parallelised over time?

h_t depends on h_{t−1}, so step t can't start until step t − 1 is done. Transformers compute all positions at once.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does truncated BPTT give up?

Gradients from more than k steps back, so the model can't learn dependencies longer than the window (it can still carry information forward in the state).

Follow-up 3 of 3

Many-to-one vs many-to-many?

Sentiment of a review: read all words, one output at the end. Tagging: one output per word. Translation: an encoder RNN reads, a decoder RNN writes (seq2seq).

#### The 30-second answer

An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time, updating a hidden state h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t−1} + W_xh x_t + b) with the same weights at every step, so it handles any length. Training unrolls it into a deep network over time and backpropagates through every step; the shared weight's gradient is summed across steps. The gradient from a late loss to an early step is a product of many Jacobians of W_hh and tanh slopes, so it vanishes or explodes exponentially; in practice plain RNNs remember only tens of steps. We use truncated BPTT, gradient clipping, and gated cells like LSTMs, and Transformers largely replaced RNNs because they parallelise over the sequence and attend directly to distant tokens.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Each time step has its own weights." They're shared.

- "RNNs have unlimited memory." In theory the state can carry anything; in practice gradients limit what's learned.

**Key terms and sources**

Recurrent neural networks read a sequence one step at a time with a hidden state as memory; training unrolls them and backpropagates through every step, which makes gradients vanish or explode over long sequences · built from Elman (1990), Rumelhart et al. (1986), Werbos (1990), Bengio, Simard & Frasconi (1994), Pascanu et al. (2013) and Goodfellow et al. ch. 10 · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. J. Elman, "Finding Structure in Time", _Cognitive Science_ 14, 1990.

2. P. Werbos, "Backpropagation through time: what it does and how to do it", _Proc. IEEE_ 78(10), 1990.

3. Y. Bengio, P. Simard & P. Frasconi, "Learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is difficult", _IEEE Trans. Neural Networks_ 5(2), 1994.

4. R. Pascanu, T. Mikolov & Y. Bengio, "On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks", ICML 2013, [arXiv:1211.5063](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.5063).

5. I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio & A. Courville, _Deep Learning_, MIT Press 2016, ch. 10, [deeplearningbook.org](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

# LSTM and GRU

> How do gates let a network remember for hundreds of steps?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Sequence models
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/lstm-and-gru/
- Before this: RNNs and Backprop Through Time (`fundamentals/rnns-and-backprop-through-time`)
- Quiz topic: `seq`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your review says "the biryani was cold", then 40 words about delivery, then "overall I'd order again". A plain RNN has forgotten "cold" by the end. The interviewer asks:

> How do gates let a network remember for hundreds of steps?

**Running example:** the review "_the biryani was cold but … [40 more words about the delivery] … overall I'd order again_". To score it, the model must remember "cold" across 40+ words, then weigh it against "order again".

#### A memory that's rewritten every step fades fast

In a plain RNN, ht = tanh(W ht−1 + …): every step multiplies the old memory by W and squashes it. As the previous lesson showed, the gradient reaching 50 steps back is around 10⁻⁶. We need a path where the memory is kept by default and only changed deliberately.

### The idea

Think of swapping the sticky note for a notebook. Nothing gets rewritten unless you choose to. One gate decides what to erase, and another decides what to add, so old notes survive by default.

[Figure: A straight memory line runs across the top. Gates along it decide what to forget and what to add, so memory is kept by default.]

_Illustrative. The output gate, not shown, decides what to expose at each step._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the forget-gate bias up and down, and compare what the LSTM keeps after 50 and 200 steps with the plain RNN.

#### How much survives after many steps?

Green: gradient kept along the LSTM cell state, the product of forget-gate values (each ft = σ(bf + noise from the input), fixed seed). Red: the plain 32-unit tanh RNN from the previous lesson (weight scale 1). Log scale.

With bf = 4 the forget gate averages about 0.98, and the LSTM keeps about **40%** of the signal after 50 steps and still about **1.4%** after 200 (56% with bf = 6), while the plain RNN is down to about **10⁻⁶** at 50 steps. Slide bf down to 0 (f ≈ 0.5) and the LSTM forgets almost immediately: memory is a choice the gate makes, which training learns per slot and per input.

**Now say why:** why does the LSTM keep so much more, and what happens when its forget gate is low?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A plain RNN overwrites its memory at every step and its gradients fade within tens of steps. An **LSTM** adds a separate **cell state** ct, a memory conveyor belt that is changed only by **addition** and by a multiplicative **forget gate**. Learned **gates** (sigmoids between 0 and 1) decide what to forget, what to write and what to reveal. When the forget gate stays near 1, information and gradients pass through hundreds of steps almost unchanged, like a residual connection through time. The **GRU** merges the gates into an update gate and a reset gate, with no separate cell: fewer parameters, usually similar accuracy. What you'll be able to do after this: write the LSTM and GRU equations, explain each gate, and explain why gating fixes vanishing gradients.

#### The LSTM cell

$$ {f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_f)},\;\; {i_t = \sigma(W_i[\cdot]+b_i)},\;\; {\tilde{c}_t = \tanh(W_c[\cdot]+b_c)} \\[6pt] {c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t}, \qquad {h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t),\;\; o_t = \sigma(W_o[\cdot]+b_o)} $$

Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, _Neural Computation_ 1997 (with the forget gate from Gers et al. 2000). An LSTM layer has 4 weight matrices: about 4× the parameters of a plain RNN of the same size. Olah's "Understanding LSTM Networks" (2015) is the classic visual walkthrough.

- **forget gate**: For each memory slot, a number between 0 and 1 from a sigmoid: how much of the old cell state to keep. Added by Gers et al. (2000); 1 means keep everything.

- **input gate**: How much of the new candidate to write.

- **candidate**: What could be written: a tanh of the input and previous hidden state, like a plain RNN’s update.

- **cell state update**: Old memory times the forget gate PLUS gated new content. The plus is the key: no squashing on the memory path.

- **output gate**: How much of the (squashed) memory to reveal as the hidden state h_t, which the next layer and the gates see.

#### An additive memory path

Along the cell state, ∂ct/∂ct−1 = ft (element-wise). There's no weight matrix and no tanh slope in the way: if the network learns f ≈ 1 for a slot, that slot's memory and its gradient pass through unchanged, exactly like the identity path in a ResNet. A common trick is to initialise the forget-gate bias to 1 so the cell starts out remembering (Jozefowicz et al. 2015).

## In practice

### In practice

#### The GRU: fewer gates, similar results

$$ {z_t = \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1},x_t])},\;\; {r_t = \sigma(W_r[h_{t-1},x_t])},\;\; \tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W[r_t\odot h_{t-1}, x_t]),\;\; {h_t = (1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t} $$

Cho et al., EMNLP 2014. Chung et al. (2014) found GRUs comparable to LSTMs on music and speech modelling; Jozefowicz et al. (2015) found neither consistently better across many tasks. GRUs have 3 weight matrices instead of 4.

- **update gate**: Blends old state and new candidate in one go: z near 0 keeps the old state (like forget ≈ 1, input ≈ 0).

- **reset gate**: How much of the old state to use when computing the candidate: lets the unit ignore the past for a fresh start.

- **interpolation**: The new state is a weighted average of old and candidate: again an additive, gated memory path, but no separate cell state and no output gate.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "An LSTM remembers because it has more memory"

It sounds right, since an LSTM does have more parameters. But the fix is the shape of the path, not its size. Along the cell state, the derivative is just the forget gate, with no weight matrix or tanh slope in the way. When the network learns a forget gate near 1, information and gradients pass through almost untouched.

## Say it

### How do gates let a network remember for hundreds of steps?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why sigmoid for gates and tanh for content?

Gates are fractions (0 to 1, "how much to let through"); content can be positive or negative, so tanh keeps it centred in (−1, 1).

Follow-up 2 of 3

Do LSTMs fully solve exploding gradients?

No; the paths through the gates and hidden state can still explode, so gradient clipping is still standard.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How many parameters does an LSTM layer have?

4 × (hidden × (hidden + input) + hidden): four gate/candidate blocks, each with a weight matrix over [h, x] and a bias.

#### The 30-second answer

An LSTM adds a cell state that is updated additively: c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t, with sigmoid gates deciding what to forget, what to write, and with an output gate what to expose as h_t. Because the derivative along the cell is just the forget gate, the network can keep information and gradients for hundreds of steps by learning f near 1, which fixes the vanishing-gradient problem of plain RNNs, much like a residual connection through time. A GRU merges this into an update gate that interpolates old and new state plus a reset gate, with fewer parameters and usually similar accuracy. Both have largely been replaced by Transformers for language, but are still used for streaming and small on-device models.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "LSTMs have perfect long-term memory." The gates must learn to keep information, and very long contexts still degrade.

- "GRU is always better because it's smaller." Neither wins consistently.

**Key terms and sources**

Gated recurrent cells: the LSTM's cell state and its forget, input and output gates, the simpler GRU with update and reset gates, why an additive memory path stops gradients vanishing, and LSTM vs GRU in practice · built from Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997), Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins (2000), Cho et al. (2014), Chung et al. (2014), Jozefowicz et al. (2015) and Olah, "Understanding LSTM Networks" (2015) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. S. Hochreiter & J. Schmidhuber, "Long Short-Term Memory", _Neural Computation_ 9(8), 1997.

2. F. Gers, J. Schmidhuber & F. Cummins, "Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM", _Neural Computation_ 12(10), 2000.

3. K. Cho et al., "Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation", EMNLP 2014, [arXiv:1406.1078](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078).

4. J. Chung, C. Gulcehre, K. Cho & Y. Bengio, "Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling", [arXiv:1412.3555](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3555), 2014.

5. R. Jozefowicz, W. Zaremba & I. Sutskever, "An Empirical Exploration of Recurrent Network Architectures", ICML 2015.

6. C. Olah, ["Understanding LSTM Networks"](https://colah.github.io/posts/2015-08-Understanding-LSTMs/), 2015.

# Seq2seq and Bahdanau Attention

> How did attention fix translation of long sentences?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Sequence models
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/seq2seq-and-attention/
- Before this: LSTM and GRU (`fundamentals/lstm-and-gru`)
- Quiz topic: `seq`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're translating restaurant notes into French, and your encoder–decoder works on short sentences but falls apart on long ones. The interviewer asks:

> How did attention fix translation of long sentences?

**Running example:** the app translates restaurant notes for a French-speaking courier: "_the cold biryani arrived late_" → "_le biryani froid est arrivé en retard_". French puts the adjective after the noun, so the word order changes.

#### Input and output are both sequences, of different lengths

Translation, summarisation, speech-to-text and question answering map one sequence to another with no one-to-one word correspondence: 5 English words become 7 French words in a different order. An RNN tagger, which outputs one label per input step, can't do that.

### The idea

Think of a translator. The old way is to read the whole sentence, memorise it, and translate from memory. Attention lets the translator glance back at the original for every word they write.

[Figure: An English sentence on top and French underneath, with lines linking each French word to the English word it looks at. The lines for cold and biryani cross, because French puts the adjective after the noun.]

_Illustrative, using the lesson's sentence. The crossed lines show the change in word order._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Step through each French word and see which English word gets the most weight. Then change the softmax temperature.

#### The alignment for our sentence

Scores are dot products between hand-set decoder and encoder vectors chosen to mimic what a trained model learns (illustrative, not trained). Rows: French output words; columns: English source words; darker = more weight. The selected row is outlined.

Producing **froid**, the decoder puts most of its weight on **cold**, and producing **biryani** it looks at **biryani**: the alignment crosses, handling the word-order swap with no rule about adjectives. Lower the temperature and the attention becomes almost a hard pointer; raise it and the weights spread over every word, blurring the context. "en retard" (two French words for "late") shows that one output can align to one input even when the lengths differ.

**Now say why:** why do the weights handle the word-order change without any rule telling them to?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Seq2seq** models handle tasks where both the input and output are sequences of different lengths, like translation or summarisation: an **encoder** RNN reads the input, a **decoder** RNN writes the output one token at a time. The original design squeezed the whole input into **one fixed-size vector**, a bottleneck that hurt long sentences. **Bahdanau attention** removed it: at each output step the decoder scores every encoder state, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and reads a weighted average (the **context vector**). The weights form a soft **alignment** between output and input words, learned without any alignment labels. This idea, with the RNNs removed, became the Transformer. What you'll be able to do after this: describe an encoder–decoder, explain the bottleneck, and compute attention weights and a context vector.

#### Encoder–decoder (seq2seq)

- **Encoder:** an RNN/LSTM reads the source words and produces a hidden state per word; the last one summarises the sentence.

- **Decoder:** another RNN starts from that summary and generates the output one word at a time, feeding each generated word back in, until it emits an end token.

- Sutskever, Vinyals & Le (NeurIPS 2014) used deep LSTMs and found that **reversing the source sentence** helped, because it put the first source words close to the first target words; Cho et al. (2014) introduced the encoder–decoder with the GRU.

#### Bahdanau attention: look back at every word

$$ {e_{ij} = \mathrm{score}(s_{i-1}, h_j)}, \qquad {\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_k \exp(e_{ik})}}, \qquad {c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij}\, h_j} $$

Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate", ICLR 2015 [arXiv:1409.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473): with a bidirectional encoder and attention, English→French quality was comparable to the phrase-based system of the time and, unlike the plain encoder–decoder, held up on long sentences. Luong et al. (EMNLP 2015) introduced simpler dot-product variants.

- **score**: How relevant is source word j for producing output word i? Bahdanau used a small neural net on the decoder state and encoder state (additive attention); Luong et al. used a dot product.

- **attention weights**: A softmax over all source words: positive weights that sum to 1. This row of weights is the soft alignment.

- **context vector**: A weighted average of encoder states, recomputed for every output word and fed to the decoder alongside its own state.

## In practice

### In practice

#### From attention-on-RNNs to attention-only

- Attention fixed the bottleneck but the RNNs still processed words one at a time, slow to train and still forgetful inside each encoder.

- Vaswani et al. (2017) kept the attention and removed the recurrence: every word attends to every other word directly (self-attention), all positions computed in parallel. That is the Transformer.

- The "query" (decoder state) / "key" (encoder state used for scoring) / "value" (encoder state averaged) roles in Bahdanau attention are exactly the Q, K, V of Transformer attention.

For greedy and beam search, see Decoding and Sampling.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "One vector for the whole sentence"

Whether the source has 5 words or 50, the decoder only sees one fixed-size vector. Long sentences don't fit: Cho et al. and Bahdanau et al. both found translation quality **dropped sharply as sentence length grew**. The reversing trick only moves the problem: whichever words end up far from where they're needed get forgotten.

## Say it

### How did attention fix translation of long sentences?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Additive vs dot-product attention?

Additive (Bahdanau) scores with a small MLP: vᵀ tanh(W s + U h). Dot-product (Luong) uses sᵀh or sᵀWh: cheaper and the basis of Transformer attention.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What is teacher forcing?

During training, the decoder is fed the true previous word rather than its own prediction; it speeds training but causes a train–test mismatch (exposure bias).

Follow-up 3 of 3

How is the output generated at inference?

Greedily or with beam search, one token at a time, until an end-of-sequence token.

#### The 30-second answer

A seq2seq model has an encoder RNN that reads the input and a decoder RNN that generates the output token by token. Originally the decoder only got the encoder's final hidden state, a fixed-length bottleneck that made long sentences fail. Bahdanau attention fixes it: at each decoding step, score the decoder state against every encoder state, softmax the scores into weights, and feed the weighted average of encoder states, the context vector, to the decoder. The weights act as a learned soft alignment between output and input. Removing the RNNs and keeping only attention gave the Transformer.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Attention was invented by the Transformer paper." It came from Bahdanau et al. (2014) for RNN translation.

- "Attention weights are hard alignments." They're soft (a probability distribution over source positions).

**Key terms and sources**

Encoder–decoder models for sequence-to-sequence tasks, the fixed-length bottleneck, and the first attention mechanism, which lets the decoder look back at every input word when producing each output word · built from Sutskever, Vinyals & Le (2014), Cho et al. (2014), Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio (ICLR 2015), Luong et al. (2015) and Vaswani et al. (2017) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. I. Sutskever, O. Vinyals & Q. Le, "Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks", NeurIPS 2014, [arXiv:1409.3215](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215).

2. K. Cho et al., "Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation", EMNLP 2014, [arXiv:1406.1078](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078).

3. D. Bahdanau, K. Cho & Y. Bengio, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate", ICLR 2015, [arXiv:1409.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473).

4. M.-T. Luong, H. Pham & C. Manning, "Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation", EMNLP 2015, [arXiv:1508.04025](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.04025).

5. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

# Self-Attention (Q, K, V)

> What do Q, K and V do, and why divide by √d?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/self-attention/
- Before this: Seq2seq and Bahdanau Attention (`fundamentals/seq2seq-and-attention`), Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity (`fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity`)
- Related: Attention Is All You Need (`papers/attention-is-all-you-need`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your review says "the biryani was cold but the naan was great". An RNN has to carry "biryani" along to reach "cold", and a CNN only sees nearby words. The interviewer asks:

> What do Q, K and V do, and why divide by √d?

**Running example:** the review "_the biryani was cold but the naan was great_": 9 tokens. Which food was cold, which was great? A good representation of "cold" should contain "biryani", and "great" should contain "naan".

Where this lesson sits in the Transformer: the highlighted box. Every Attention & Transformers lesson shows this map.

Full walkthrough: The Transformer, End to End.

#### Words need context from anywhere in the sentence

"Cold" means nothing until you know what was cold. An RNN has to carry "biryani" through the hidden state to reach "cold"; a CNN only sees nearby words. We want each word to look directly at every other word and decide, from the content, which ones matter: the attention idea from seq2seq, applied within one sequence.

### The idea

Think of a room where each word asks a question. The query is what a word is looking for, the key is the label every word wears, and the value is what it hands over. "Cold" asks what's cold, biryani's label matches, so "cold" takes in most of biryani.

[Figure: The word cold sends out a question. Biryani's key matches best, so biryani's value gets the largest share. Naan and was get smaller shares.]

_Illustrative. The shares come from a softmax over the query–key scores._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Click each word and see who it attends to. Compare "cold" with "great", and then look at "was".

#### Who does each word attend to?

4-dimensional hand-set keys (noun-ness, adjective-ness, verb-ness, which clause) and queries chosen to mimic a trained head: illustrative, not trained. Bars and percentages: softmax(q·k/√4) over all 9 tokens; small numbers under each word: its scaled score q·k/√4.

The query for **cold** looks for a noun in its own clause: the biggest weight goes to **biryani**, and the "naan" key, a noun in the other clause, gets much less. **Great** does the reverse and picks **naan**. The token's new vector is mostly the value of the food it describes, which is exactly the context a later layer needs. Nothing about word order was hard-coded: the clause feature stands in for what positional encodings provide in a real model.

**Now say why:** how does the same formula send "cold" to biryani and "great" to naan, with no rule about food?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

In **self-attention**, each token asks a question (its **query**), every token advertises what it contains (its **key**), and the match between a query and each key, a dot product, decides how much of each token's **value** to blend in. Scores are divided by **√d** (the key size) so they don't grow with dimension and push the softmax into near one-hot outputs with tiny gradients. The result: every token's new vector is a weighted mix of all tokens, so "cold" can pull in information from "biryani" no matter how far apart they are. All tokens are computed at once as matrix products, which is fast on GPUs, but the score matrix is **n × n**, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length. What you'll be able to do after this: compute attention by hand, explain Q, K and V, justify the √d scaling, and state attention's cost.

#### Scaled dot-product attention

$$ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = {\mathrm{softmax}}\!\Big({\frac{{Q}\,{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}}\Big)\,{V}, \qquad Q = XW_Q,\; K = XW_K,\; V = XW_V $$

Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, Eq. 1 [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762). Jay Alammar's "The Illustrated Transformer" is the classic visual guide.

- **queries**: Each token’s embedding times a learned matrix W_Q: what this token is looking for. Stacked into an n × d matrix.

- **keys**: Embeddings times W_K: what each token offers to be matched on.

- **scaled scores**: Every query dotted with every key: an n × n table of relevance, divided by √d_k to keep the scale steady.

- **softmax per row**: Each row becomes weights that are positive and sum to 1: how much token i attends to each token j.

- **values**: Embeddings times W_V: the content actually passed along. The output for token i is its weighted average of values.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Parallel, direct, and quadratic

- **Direct paths:** any two tokens interact in one step, whatever their distance (an RNN needs n steps).

- **Parallel:** all n tokens are computed together with matrix multiplies, so training uses GPUs efficiently.

- **Quadratic cost:** the score matrix is n × n: 4,096 tokens → about 16.8 million scores per head per layer. Long-context models use tricks like FlashAttention (exact, memory-efficient), sparse or sliding-window attention.

- **Order-blind:** attention treats its inputs as a set; position must be added separately (positional encodings).

### The answer that sounds right

#### Without scaling, the softmax saturates

If query and key entries are roughly independent with variance 1, their dot product over d dimensions has variance d. With d = 64, raw scores have a standard deviation of 8, and the softmax turns into a near one-hot: the gradient of everything except the top score almost vanishes. Dividing by √d brings the standard deviation back to 1 (Vaswani et al., §3.2.1).

2,000 random rows: a query and 9 keys with independent standard-normal entries, fixed seed. With uniform attention the top weight would be 1/9 ≈ 11%.

With scaling, the score spread stays near **1** at every d and the top weight stays moderate (around 35%). Without it at d = 64, the spread is **8**, the average top weight is about **87%** and about a third of rows (36%) are essentially one-hot; at d = 1,024, 79% are.

## Say it

### What do Q, K and V do, and why divide by √d?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why separate Q, K and V projections?

What a token looks for, what it is matched on and what it passes on are different roles; separate matrices let the model learn asymmetric relations (A attends to B without B attending to A).

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the complexity?

O(n² · d) time and O(n²) memory for the score matrix per head, versus O(n · d²) for the projections.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Self-attention vs cross-attention?

Self: Q, K, V from the same sequence. Cross: queries from one sequence (decoder), keys and values from another (encoder output).

#### The 30-second answer

Self-attention lets every token build its representation from all tokens. Each token's embedding is projected into a query, a key and a value. The attention weights for token i are a softmax over the dot products of its query with every key, divided by root d_k, and its output is the weighted sum of the values. Scaling keeps the score variance near one, otherwise the softmax saturates and gradients vanish. It's computed for all tokens at once as softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, so it's parallel and connects distant tokens directly, but it costs O(n²) in sequence length and is order-agnostic, so positional information has to be added.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Divide by d." It's √d, from the variance argument.

- "Attention weights explain the model." They're one signal; they don't fully explain predictions.

**Key terms and sources**

How every token builds a new representation by looking at every other token: queries, keys and values, scaled dot-product attention, why the scores are divided by √d, and the n² cost · built from Vaswani et al. (NeurIPS 2017), Bahdanau et al. (2015), Alammar, "The Illustrated Transformer" (2018) and Goodfellow et al. · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. D. Bahdanau, K. Cho & Y. Bengio, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate", ICLR 2015, [arXiv:1409.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473).

3. J. Alammar, ["The Illustrated Transformer"](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/), 2018.

4. T. Dao et al., "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness", NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2205.14135](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135).

# Multi-Head Attention

> Why several heads, and what do they cost at long context?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/multi-head-attention/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

With one attention head, "cold" has to split its attention between "biryani", what is cold, and "was", the verb before it. The signals blur together. The interviewer asks:

> Why several heads, and what do they cost at long context?

**Running example:** the same review, "_the biryani was cold but the naan was great_". To understand it, a word may need to know _which food it describes_ and _which word came right before it_ at the same time.

Where this lesson sits: inside the attention box of each Transformer layer.

Full walkthrough: The Transformer, End to End.

#### One head, one weighted average

A single attention head gives each token one probability distribution over the other tokens. If "cold" needs both "biryani" (what is cold?) and "was" (the verb just before it), one distribution has to split its weight and the two signals get blurred into one average. We want several independent looks.

### The idea

Think of several readers going through the same text, each with their own highlighter. One marks food, another marks grammar. Then they combine their notes, instead of one highlighter trying to do both jobs.

[Figure: The same sentence twice. One head highlights biryani for the word cold, and another highlights was, the word just before it.]

_Illustrative. Heads aren't told their jobs. Each learns its own pattern._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between the two heads, and compare what "cold" and "naan" attend to in each.

#### Two heads, two different jobs

Rows: the token doing the looking (query); columns: the token looked at (key); darker = more weight. Hand-set heads that mimic patterns found in trained models (illustrative).

Head 1 ties adjectives and verbs to the food they describe: "cold" → biryani, "great" → naan. Head 2 ignores meaning and just looks one word back: a positional head. After concatenation, the next layer gets both facts for every word. Studies of BERT found exactly such heads: some attend to the previous or next token, some to delimiters, some follow syntactic relations like objects of verbs (Clark et al. 2019); and many heads can be pruned with little loss, while a few specialised ones matter most (Voita et al. 2019; Michel et al. 2019).

**Now say why:** what would be lost if both patterns had to share one set of weights?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

One attention head produces one weighted average per token, so it can only follow one kind of relationship at a time. **Multi-head attention** splits the model width d into h heads of size d/h, runs attention separately in each (with its own WQ, WK, WV), **concatenates** the results and mixes them with an output matrix WO. Different heads learn different jobs (one links adjectives to nouns, another looks at the previous word, another follows syntax), at the **same cost** as a single full-width head: the parameter count stays 4d². The expensive part at long context is the n × n score matrix per head and the cached keys and values, which is why LLMs share keys and values across heads (**MQA/GQA**). What you'll be able to do after this: write multi-head attention, explain why multiple heads help, and compute the parameters, score-matrix size and KV-cache memory.

#### Split, attend, concatenate, mix

$$ \mathrm{MHA}(X) = {\mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_h)}\,{W_O}, \qquad {\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(XW_Q^{(i)},\, XW_K^{(i)},\, XW_V^{(i)})} $$

Vaswani et al. (2017) used h = 8 heads of size 64 with d = 512: "multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions". In code, all heads are computed in one batched matrix multiply.

- **one head**: Ordinary scaled dot-product attention, but with its own projections into a d/h-dimensional subspace. With d = 512 and 8 heads, each head works in 64 dimensions.

- **concatenate**: Stack the h head outputs side by side: back to d dimensions.

- **output projection**: A d × d matrix W_O that mixes information across heads.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Parameters stay the same; memory grows with n²

Score matrix = n² × heads × 2 bytes (what naive attention would hold for one sequence). KV cache = 2 × n × d × 2 bytes per layer for standard multi-head attention; with grouped-query attention using 8 key/value heads it shrinks by heads ÷ 8.

For a 7B-class model (d = 4,096, 32 heads) at 8,192 tokens, the attention weights are **67 million** per layer whatever the head count, but storing the full score matrix would take **4.3 GB per layer**, which is why FlashAttention computes it in tiles without ever storing it. During generation the cached keys and values take **134 MB per layer** (4.3 GB over 32 layers) per sequence; grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads cuts that 4× to 34 MB. At 131,072 tokens the naive score matrix would need 1.1 TB per layer.

#### Sharing keys and values: MQA and GQA

- **Multi-query attention (MQA):** all heads share a single key and value projection; the KV cache shrinks by a factor of h and decoding speeds up, with a small quality cost (Shazeer 2019).

- **Grouped-query attention (GQA):** groups of query heads share one KV head (e.g. 32 query heads, 8 KV heads): close to full multi-head quality with most of MQA's speed (Ainslie et al. 2023). Used in LLaMA 2 70B, LLaMA 3 and Mistral.

- Why it matters: generating each token re-reads the whole KV cache, so its size, not the FLOPs, often limits serving speed.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "More heads means more parameters"

It sounds right, since each head has its own projections. But with d fixed, each head works in a smaller space of size d ÷ h, so the total stays at 4d². Adding heads changes how attention gets divided, not how many weights you have. The real cost at long context is the n-by-n score matrix and, during generation, the KV cache.

## Say it

### Why several heads, and what do they cost at long context?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Does adding heads add parameters?

No, if d is fixed: each head gets d/h dimensions. 8 heads of 64 cost the same as 1 head of 512.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Can you have too many heads?

Yes: with a fixed width, each head gets too small a subspace to represent useful queries and keys; very small head sizes hurt.

Follow-up 3 of 3

KV cache size for one sequence?

2 (K and V) × layers × tokens × KV heads × head size × bytes per value. GQA and MQA reduce the KV-head count.

#### The 30-second answer

Multi-head attention runs h attention operations in parallel, each with its own query, key and value projections into a subspace of size d over h, then concatenates the outputs and mixes them with an output projection. Each head gives a separate attention pattern, so different heads can track different relations, like coreference, the previous token or syntax, instead of blending them into one average. The parameter count stays 4 d squared regardless of h. The cost that grows is the n-by-n score matrix and, during generation, the KV cache, which is why modern LLMs use FlashAttention and share keys and values across heads with grouped-query or multi-query attention.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Each head sees a different part of the sentence." Each head sees the whole sentence, in a different learned subspace.

- "More heads means more parameters." Not at fixed d.

**Key terms and sources**

Running several attention operations in parallel, each in its own smaller subspace, so different heads can track different relationships; the projections, concatenation and output matrix; head specialisation; and the memory cost of attention at long context, including MQA/GQA · built from Vaswani et al. (2017), Clark et al. (2019), Voita et al. (2019), Michel et al. (2019), Shazeer (2019) and Ainslie et al. (2023) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. K. Clark, U. Khandelwal, O. Levy & C. Manning, "What Does BERT Look At? An Analysis of BERT's Attention", BlackboxNLP 2019, [arXiv:1906.04341](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04341).

3. E. Voita et al., "Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned", ACL 2019, [arXiv:1905.09418](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09418).

4. P. Michel, O. Levy & G. Neubig, "Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?", NeurIPS 2019, [arXiv:1905.10650](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10650).

5. N. Shazeer, "Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need", [arXiv:1911.02150](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150), 2019.

6. J. Ainslie et al., "GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints", EMNLP 2023, [arXiv:2305.13245](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245).

# Positional Encodings (incl. RoPE)

> How does a Transformer know word order, and why RoPE?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/positional-encodings/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

"The biryani was cold but the naan was great" and "the naan was cold but the biryani was great" use the same words, with opposite meanings for each dish. Plain self-attention can't tell them apart. The interviewer asks:

> How does a Transformer know word order, and why RoPE?

**Running example:** "_the biryani was cold but the naan was great_" vs "_the naan was cold but the biryani was great_": same words, opposite meaning for each dish. Without position, plain self-attention can't tell them apart.

Where this lesson sits: positions enter right after the token embeddings (RoPE applies them inside every attention layer).

Full walkthrough: The Transformer, End to End.

#### Attention is order-blind

Scores q·k depend only on the two tokens' contents. Permute the input and the outputs are permuted the same way: self-attention is permutation-equivariant. For a bag of words that's fine; for language, "dog bites man" ≠ "man bites dog". RNNs got order for free by reading in sequence; Transformers have to be told.

**One exception worth knowing:** a GPT-style decoder uses a causal mask, so each token sees only itself and earlier tokens. That already leaks some order: the token at position 2 sees 3 tokens, the one at position 7 sees 8. Explicit position information is still added because the mask alone doesn't directly say "one word back" vs "ten words back". Section 6 shows models that lean on this anyway.

### The idea

Think of giving each word a clock hand, turned according to its position. Any two words a fixed distance apart have the same angle between their hands, wherever they sit. That's RoPE: attention sees how far apart words are, not just where they are.

[Figure: Two clock faces. On each, two hands sit the same angle apart, even though their absolute positions differ, because the gap between the words is the same.]

_Illustrative. Each pair sits the same angle apart, because each pair's gap is the same._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the query and key positions together, keeping the gap between them the same. Then change the gap.

#### RoPE: rotate queries and keys by position

$$ {\big(R_{{m\theta}}\, q\big)^{\!\top}\big(R_{n\theta}\, k\big)} = {q^{\top} R_{(n-m)\theta}\, k} $$

Su et al., "RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding", 2021 [arXiv:2104.09864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864): RoPE encodes absolute position with a rotation matrix and makes the attention score depend on relative position. Used in LLaMA (Touvron et al. 2023), PaLM, Mistral, Qwen and most open LLMs.

- **rotation by position**: Split the query (and key) into 2-D pairs; rotate pair i by angle m·θ_i for a token at position m, with θ_i = 10000^(−2i/d) as in the sinusoids.

- **rotated query and key**: Applied inside every attention layer, to Q and K only (not V), instead of adding anything to the embeddings.

- **only the offset matters**: Rotations compose: rotating q by m and k by n gives the same dot product as rotating q by m − n alone. The score depends on the relative position.

A fixed 8-dimensional query and key (4 rotating pairs, θi = 10000−2i/8). The circle shows pair 1 of the rotated query (teal) and key (orange); the score uses all 4 pairs.

Shift both positions by 40 and the score is identical: only m − n matters. Change the gap instead (move n) and the score changes. That's why RoPE models generalise across positions within the trained range: "the adjective two words before the noun" looks the same at the start or the end of a document.

**Now say why:** why does the score depend on the gap, and not on the absolute positions?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Attention compares every token with every other but has no idea of **order**: shuffle the words and each token gets the same weights. So position must be injected. The original Transformer **added** fixed **sinusoidal** vectors to the embeddings; BERT and GPT-2 **learned** one vector per position. Most modern LLMs use **RoPE**: rotate each pair of query and key dimensions by an angle proportional to the token's position. Then the attention score depends only on the **relative distance** between two tokens, which is what language mostly cares about. Extending a model to longer contexts usually means adjusting these position schemes. Newer models also rotate only part of each head, skip RoPE in some layers, or add a learned distance bias instead. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why position is needed, compare absolute, learned, relative, RoPE and ALiBi, and show why RoPE gives relative positions, and say what recent models use instead of full RoPE.

#### Sinusoidal positional encoding

$$ {PE_{({pos},\,2i)} = \sin\!\Big(\frac{pos}{{10000^{2i/d}}}\Big),\qquad PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big)} $$

Vaswani et al. (2017), §3.5: chosen because PE(pos + k) is a linear function (a rotation) of PE(pos), which may let the model attend by relative position; learned embeddings performed nearly identically in their tests. A small detail: the paper also multiplies the token embeddings by √dmodel before adding the encoding, most likely so the two are on a similar scale and position doesn't swamp meaning.

- **position**: The token’s index in the sequence: 0, 1, 2, …

- **frequency per dimension pair**: Each pair of dimensions uses a different wavelength, from 2π up to about 10000·2π: fast waves tell nearby positions apart, slow waves encode coarse position.

- **sine and cosine**: Even dimensions use sine, odd use cosine. The vector is added to the token embedding.

Top: the encoding for positions 0–63 (rows) × 64 dimensions (columns), orange = +1, blue = −1. Bottom: cosine similarity between PE(p) and PE(p + k) for k = 0…100. d = 64.

Neighbouring positions get similar vectors and similarity falls with distance. Move p from 20 to 150: the similarity values for +1, +10 and +50 stay the same (0.97, 0.66 and 0.49 for d = 64), because sinusoidal similarity depends only on the offset, not on where you are in the sentence.

## In practice

### In practice

#### ALiBi and context extension

- **ALiBi** (Press et al., ICLR 2022): no position vectors at all; subtract a penalty proportional to distance from each attention score. Trained on short sequences, it extrapolated to longer ones at test time.

- **Position interpolation** (Chen et al. 2023): to run a RoPE model on 4× longer inputs, squeeze the positions (divide them by 4) so the angles stay in the trained range, then fine-tune briefly; later methods (NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) rescale the frequencies instead.

- Long-context models combine these with attention optimisations; position handling is usually the first thing to change when extending context.

#### Partial RoPE, NoPE layers and learned bias

RoPE in every attention layer is still the most common choice in open-weight LLMs. But recent models increasingly change it in three ways.

- **Partial RoPE: rotate only some dimensions.** MiniMax-M3 rotates 64 of the 128 dimensions in each head and leaves the rest unchanged. That halves the precomputed sine and cosine tables; the KV cache doesn't shrink, because keys are stored in full. Khan et al. (2026) found that rotating about 10% of the dimensions in 1B–8B models gave training loss close to full RoPE, though full RoPE was better on some evaluations.

- **NoPE layers: no explicit position at all.** Because of the causal mask, a token that spreads its attention evenly gives the first token a weight of 1/3 at position 2, 1/4 at position 3, and so on. That fraction is a position signal a later layer can read. Kazemnejad et al. (NeurIPS 2023) found that small decoders without any position encoding handled longer-than-trained inputs better than RoPE on most of their synthetic tasks. In practice models mix the two: SmolLM3 drops RoPE from every 4th layer, which its authors report helped long context without hurting short context.

- **Learned relative bias, again.** Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026) uses no RoPE. It adds a learned bias to each attention score, chosen by the distance between the two tokens and the query, which is T5's 2019 idea brought back.

In Raschka's count of open-weight architectures (Nov 2026), the share using full RoPE in every layer fell from 2025 to 2026, and among RoPE models partial RoPE went from a minority to a majority. The groups are small, so read this as a direction, not a rule.

Even a layer that skips RoPE isn't position-blind: its inputs come from earlier layers that did use position.

### The answer that sounds right

#### Learned absolute positions don't extrapolate

BERT and GPT-2 learn one vector per position (512 and 1,024 positions). Simple and effective, but a model has never seen position 1,025 and has no vector for it, and absolute position is often less useful than "how far apart are these two words?". Relative schemes (Shaw et al. 2018; T5's relative biases) add a learned term to each attention score that depends on the distance i − j.

The table also gets expensive. In GPT-2 Medium, 1,024 position vectors are about 0.3% of the weights. Stretch the table to about 100,000 positions and it would be more than 22% of the model (Raschka, 2026), and every one of those vectors has to be trained.

## Say it

### How does a Transformer know word order, and why RoPE?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 7

Why is RoPE applied to Q and K but not V?

Position should affect _who attends to whom_ (the scores), not the content that is passed along.

Follow-up 2 of 7

Added vs multiplied position information?

Sinusoidal and learned encodings are added once to the input; RoPE multiplies (rotates) inside every attention layer, so relative position is present at every layer.

Follow-up 3 of 7

Why multiple frequencies?

Fast-rotating pairs distinguish nearby positions; slow ones cover long ranges without repeating, like the hands of a clock.

Follow-up 4 of 7

Can a decoder learn position with no positional encoding?

Partly. The causal mask means each token sees a different number of earlier tokens, and attention can turn that count into a position signal. This is NoPE. It extrapolates well in small studies, and models like SmolLM3 skip RoPE in some layers, but most models still keep RoPE in most layers.

Follow-up 5 of 7

What is partial RoPE, and why use it?

Rotate only some of each head's dimensions (MiniMax-M3 rotates 64 of 128) and leave the rest untouched. It halves the sine and cosine tables and leaves some dimensions for pure content matching. The KV cache stays the same size.

Follow-up 6 of 7

Two RoPE codebases pair dimensions differently. Which is right?

Both. The RoFormer paper and original LLaMA pair neighbouring dimensions (1,2), (3,4); most code now pairs the first half with the second half, (1,5), (2,6), because it's simpler to vectorise. Reorder the features and the scores are identical. But you can't load weights trained with one convention into code using the other.

Follow-up 7 of 7

Are the RoPE sine and cosine tables learned or stored?

Neither: they're computed once from the positions and frequencies and shared by every head, query and key. They're cheap enough that nobody saves them with the weights.

#### The 30-second answer

Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without position information a Transformer can't reliably tell word order (a decoder's causal mask leaks only a little). The original paper added fixed sinusoidal encodings at different frequencies to the embeddings; BERT and GPT-2 learned absolute position embeddings, which can't go beyond the trained length. Most modern LLMs use RoPE: rotate each 2-D pair of query and key dimensions by an angle proportional to position, so the dot product depends only on the relative offset. ALiBi instead adds a distance penalty to the scores. To extend context, people interpolate or rescale RoPE frequencies and fine-tune. Recent models also use partial RoPE, skip RoPE in some layers, or use a learned distance bias.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Transformers know order from the input sequence." An encoder like BERT doesn't at all; a decoder gets only a weak signal from its causal mask.

- "Every modern LLM uses RoPE in every layer." Many now use partial RoPE, skip it in some layers, or use a learned distance bias.

- "RoPE lets any model handle unlimited length." It still degrades beyond the trained range unless rescaled.

**Key terms and sources**

(NoPE, NeurIPS 2023), the SmolLM3 report (2025), Khan et al. (partial RoPE, 2026) and Raschka's "Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs" (Nov 2026) · checked 16 Nov 2026

# The Transformer Block

> What's inside one block, and where do the parameters go?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/transformer-block/
- Before this: Multi-Head Attention (`fundamentals/multi-head-attention`), BatchNorm vs LayerNorm vs RMSNorm (`fundamentals/normalisation-layers`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

A teammate stacks attention layers and nothing else, and the model is weak. Attention only produces weighted averages. The interviewer asks:

> What's inside one block, and where do the parameters go?

**Running example:** each token of "_the biryani was cold but the naan was great_" enters as a vector. One block lets "cold" pull in "biryani" (attention), then processes the combined vector (feed-forward), and adds the result back to what it already had.

Where this lesson sits: the dashed box that repeats N times.

Full walkthrough: The Transformer, End to End.

#### Mixing across tokens isn't enough

Attention only produces weighted averages of value vectors: on its own it's nearly linear in the values, and it never transforms a token's features with a non-linearity. Stacking attention alone would be weak. We need a unit that alternates communication between tokens with computation on each token, and that can be stacked dozens of times without training falling apart.

### The idea

Think of a meeting followed by desk work. In attention, tokens share what they know. In the feed-forward layer, each works alone on what it heard. Everything gets added to one running document, so nothing is lost along the way.

[Figure: A vertical residual stream on the left. Attention and feed-forward sub-layers each add to it, and the block repeats.]

_Illustrative. The block keeps its shape, so you can stack N of them._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare GPT-2 small, BERT-base and LLaMA-7B, then change the number of layers. Look at attention against FFN parameters.

#### Where do the parameters go?

Attention 4d² per block (Q, K, V, O); FFN 2·d·dff (GELU) or 3·d·dff (SwiGLU); embeddings V·d (plus learned positions for GPT-2/BERT; LLaMA has untied input and output embeddings). Biases and norms are ignored (under 0.1%). Changing N shows what a deeper version of the same width would cost.

The formula reproduces the published sizes: **GPT-2 small ≈ 124M**, **BERT-base ≈ 109M** (110M with biases, token-type and pooler weights), **LLaMA-7B ≈ 6.74B**. In every block the FFN holds **twice as many** parameters as attention, so across the stack about two-thirds of the non-embedding parameters are FFN. In small models the embedding table is a big share (32% for GPT-2 small); in LLaMA-7B it's under 4%.

**Now say why:** why do most of the parameters sit in the feed-forward layers, when attention gets all the attention?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A Transformer is the same **block** stacked N times. Each block has two sub-layers: **multi-head self-attention**, which mixes information _across tokens_, and a position-wise **feed-forward network** (an MLP applied to each token separately, usually 4× wider), which transforms information _within_ each token. Each sub-layer is wrapped as x + Sublayer(Norm(x)): a **residual connection** plus **layer normalisation**. Modern LLMs use **pre-norm** with RMSNorm and a SwiGLU FFN. Surprisingly, about **two-thirds of the parameters** sit in the FFNs, not in attention. What you'll be able to do after this: draw a Transformer block, explain each part's role, compare pre- and post-norm, and count a model's parameters.

#### Inside one block (pre-norm)

1. The residual stream: each token's vector flows straight up through the block. Everything else only adds to it.

2. Sub-layer 1: normalise a copy, run multi-head attention across all tokens, and add the result back to the stream. Here "cold" picks up "biryani".

3. Sub-layer 2: normalise again, run the feed-forward network on each token separately (expand to 4d, non-linearity, project back), and add that back too.

4. The block outputs vectors of the same shape it received, so blocks stack: attention lets tokens exchange information, the FFN processes what each token now holds.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The feed-forward network

- Original: FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2 with inner width 4d (2,048 for d = 512). GPT and BERT use GELU.

- Modern LLMs use **SwiGLU** (Shazeer 2020): three matrices, inner width about (8/3)d so the parameter count matches (activation functions).

- What it does: Geva et al. (EMNLP 2021) showed FFN layers act like **key–value memories**: the first matrix detects input patterns, the second writes associated outputs, often promoting likely next tokens.

- Mixture-of-Experts models replace one FFN with many expert FFNs and route each token to a few of them.

### The answer that sounds right

#### Where the norm goes matters

$$ {x_{l+1} = \mathrm{Norm}\big(x_l + F(x_l)\big)} \qquad\text{vs}\qquad {x_{l+1} = x_l + F\big(\mathrm{Norm}(x_l)\big)} $$

Details: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm vs RMSNorm and learning-rate warmup.

- **post-norm (2017)**: The original Transformer normalises after adding the residual. The norm sits on the residual path, so gradients near the input are badly scaled at initialisation; training needs a careful warmup.

- **pre-norm (GPT-2 onwards)**: Normalise only the branch input; the residual path stays a clean identity from bottom to top. Stable at depth and less dependent on warmup (Xiong et al. 2020). Standard in LLMs, usually with RMSNorm.

## Say it

### What's inside one block, and where do the parameters go?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does the FFN act per token?

Mixing across positions is attention's job; the FFN applies the same MLP to each position independently, so it's cheap to parallelise and its cost is linear in sequence length.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Rough FLOPs per token?

About 2 × parameters for a forward pass (one multiply-add per weight), ~6 × parameters for training (Kaplan et al. 2020), plus the attention term that grows with context length.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What is the "residual stream" view?

Treat the residual as a shared channel: every sub-layer reads from it and writes an update into it; interpretability work analyses what each layer adds.

#### The 30-second answer

A Transformer block has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention, which moves information between tokens, and a position-wise feed-forward network, usually four times wider, which transforms each token independently. Each is wrapped in a residual connection with layer normalisation; modern models use pre-norm, x plus F of Norm x, which keeps the residual path an identity and trains stably at depth, typically with RMSNorm and a SwiGLU FFN. The block preserves shape, so you stack N of them. Per block, attention has 4 d squared parameters and the FFN 8 d squared, so about two-thirds of the parameters are in the FFNs.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Most parameters are in attention." Most are in the FFNs.

- "LayerNorm normalises across the batch." Across features of each token.

**Key terms and sources**

The repeating unit of every Transformer: multi-head attention and a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation; pre-norm vs post-norm; what the FFN does; and where the parameters go · built from Vaswani et al. (2017), Xiong et al. (2020), Geva et al. (EMNLP 2021), Shazeer (2020), Radford et al. (2019), Devlin et al. (2019) and Touvron et al. (2023) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. R. Xiong et al., "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture", ICML 2020, [arXiv:2002.04745](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745).

3. M. Geva, R. Schuster, J. Berant & O. Levy, "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories", EMNLP 2021, [arXiv:2012.14913](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14913).

4. N. Shazeer, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", [arXiv:2002.05202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202), 2020.

5. A. Radford et al., "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), OpenAI 2019; J. Devlin et al., "BERT", NAACL 2019, [arXiv:1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805).

6. H. Touvron et al., "LLaMA", [arXiv:2302.13971](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971), 2023; J. Kaplan et al., "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models", [arXiv:2001.08361](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361), 2020.
