# Encoder vs Decoder vs Encoder-Decoder

> BERT vs GPT vs T5: what's actually different?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/encoder-decoder-architectures/
- Before this: The Transformer Block (`fundamentals/transformer-block`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have three jobs: classify a review, generate a reply and translate a note. A colleague asks which of BERT, GPT and T5 to use. The interviewer asks:

> BERT vs GPT vs T5: what's actually different?

**Running example:** three jobs on restaurant text: **classify** a review as positive or negative, **generate** a reply to it, and **translate** a note ("the cold biryani arrived late" → French).

Where this lesson sits: the attention box, and in particular its **mask**.

Full walkthrough: The Transformer, End to End.

#### Understanding and generating need different views

To classify a review, every word should see the whole review, including words after it ("not" changes what comes before it as well as after). To _generate_ text one word at a time, a word must not see the future: during training, if token 5 could look at token 6, predicting token 6 would be trivial and the model would learn nothing usable at generation time.

### The idea

Think of reading a finished book, writing a new one, and translating. A reader can flip to any page. A writer can only see what's written so far. A translator reads the original while writing the new text. Those are the three attention masks.

[Figure: Three grids showing which tokens can see which. The encoder sees everything, the decoder only earlier tokens in a triangle, and cross-attention sees all of the source.]

_The same attention, with different masks deciding who can see whom._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between encoder, decoder and cross-attention, and select different query tokens. Watch which tokens they can see.

#### Who can see whom?

Rows: queries; columns: keys. Teal = allowed, red = masked. In cross-attention, the rows are the decoder's French tokens and the columns the encoder's English tokens.

In the **decoder**, "cold" (token 4) sees only **"the biryani was cold"**: 45 of the 81 pairs are allowed (the lower triangle). In the **encoder** it sees all 9 tokens, including "but … great". In **cross-attention**, every French token may look at every English token, which is how the decoder reads the source sentence.

**Now say why:** what would go wrong if a token could see the future during training?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

The same block becomes three kinds of model depending on **which tokens may attend to which**. An **encoder** lets every token see every other token (bidirectional); it's trained to fill in masked words and is great for classification and embeddings (BERT). A **decoder** uses a **causal mask**: each token sees only itself and earlier tokens, so it can be trained to predict the next token and then **generate** text (GPT, LLaMA). An **encoder–decoder** encodes the input bidirectionally, then a causal decoder generates the output while attending to the encoder through **cross-attention** (original Transformer, T5). Today's LLMs are almost all decoder-only. What you'll be able to do after this: draw the three attention masks, match each family to its training objective and uses, and explain cross-attention.

#### A mask added to the attention scores

$$ \mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} + {M}\Big)V, \qquad {M_{ij} = \begin{cases}0 & j \le i\\ -\infty & j > i\end{cases}} $$

Vaswani et al. (2017), §3.2.3: masking in the decoder "ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i". Because all positions are still computed in parallel, a decoder trains on every next-token prediction in a sequence at once.

- **mask**: 0 where attention is allowed, −∞ where it isn’t. After the softmax, −∞ becomes a weight of exactly 0.

- **causal mask**: For a decoder, position i may attend to j only if j ≤ i: the lower triangle of the n × n score matrix.

#### Three families, three training objectives

| Family | Attention | Pre-training objective | Examples | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoder-only** | bidirectional | masked language modelling: predict ~15% hidden tokens | BERT, RoBERTa | classification, NER, embeddings / retrieval |
| **Decoder-only** | causal | next-token prediction | GPT series, LLaMA, Mistral | generation, chat, in-context learning |
| **Encoder–decoder** | bidirectional encoder + causal decoder + cross-attention | span corruption / denoising | original Transformer, T5, BART | translation, summarisation |

BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) masked 15% of input tokens; T5 (Raffel et al. 2020) framed every task as text-to-text with span corruption; BART (Lewis et al. 2020) trained a denoising autoencoder.

For encoders in detail, read BERT and Masked Language Models.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Why LLMs are decoder-only

- **One simple objective** on any text: every token is a training example, no corruption scheme needed.

- **Generation is native:** the same causal model that trains on next-token prediction generates at inference, reusing cached keys and values for earlier tokens.

- **Scales and generalises:** with prompting, one decoder handles classification, translation and reasoning. Wang et al. (ICML 2022) found causal decoders trained on next-token prediction gave the best zero-shot generalisation right after pre-training, while encoder–decoders did better after multitask fine-tuning.

- Encoders are still the workhorse for **embeddings** and retrieval, where the bidirectional view and small size win.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "BERT, GPT and T5 are basically the same model at different sizes"

It sounds right, since they're all built from the same blocks. But the attention mask and the training objective differ, and that decides what each can do. BERT sees the whole text and predicts hidden tokens, so it isn't built to generate. GPT only sees earlier tokens and predicts the next one, so generating text is natural.

## Say it

### BERT vs GPT vs T5: what's actually different?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Can BERT generate text?

Not naturally: it never learned left-to-right prediction and its bidirectional attention sees the future. It's built for understanding.

Follow-up 2 of 3

In cross-attention, which side gives Q, K and V?

Queries come from the decoder; keys and values come from the encoder output.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why is training a decoder efficient despite generating one token at a time at inference?

With teacher forcing and the causal mask, all next-token predictions in a sequence are computed in one parallel forward pass.

#### The 30-second answer

The three families differ mainly in the attention mask. Encoders like BERT use bidirectional attention and masked-language-model pre-training, which suits classification and embeddings. Decoders like GPT and LLaMA use a causal mask so each token only sees earlier tokens, trained on next-token prediction, which makes generation natural and lets them train on every position in parallel. Encoder–decoders like the original Transformer and T5 encode the input bidirectionally and generate with a causal decoder that reads the encoder through cross-attention, which suits translation and summarisation. Modern LLMs are decoder-only because the objective is simple, it scales, and prompting covers most tasks.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "GPT has an encoder." GPT-style LLMs are decoder-only.

- "The causal mask is only used at inference." It's essential during training to stop the model from seeing the answer.

**Key terms and sources**

The three Transformer families: bidirectional encoders (BERT) for understanding, causal decoders (GPT, LLaMA) for generation, and encoder–decoders (original Transformer, T5, BART) for sequence-to-sequence; the attention masks that define them, their training objectives, and why decoder-only won for LLMs · built from Vaswani et al. (2017), Devlin et al. (2019), Radford et al. (2018, 2019), Raffel et al. (T5, JMLR 2020), Lewis et al. (BART, 2020) and Wang et al. (ICML 2022) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. J. Devlin, M.-W. Chang, K. Lee & K. Toutanova, "BERT", NAACL 2019, [arXiv:1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805).

3. A. Radford et al., "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training" (GPT), OpenAI 2018; "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), 2019.

4. C. Raffel et al., "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer" (T5), _JMLR_ 21, 2020, [arXiv:1910.10683](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683).

5. M. Lewis et al., "BART", ACL 2020, [arXiv:1910.13461](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.13461).

6. T. Wang et al., "What Language Model Architecture and Pretraining Objective Work Best for Zero-Shot Generalization?", ICML 2022, [arXiv:2204.05832](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05832).

# The Transformer, End to End

> Walk a sentence through a whole Transformer, with shapes.

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Attention and Transformers
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/transformer-end-to-end/
- Before this: The Transformer Block (`fundamentals/transformer-block`), Positional Encodings (incl. RoPE) (`fundamentals/positional-encodings`)
- Related: Attention Is All You Need (`papers/attention-is-all-you-need`)
- Quiz topic: `attn`

## Intuition

### The situation

An interviewer hands you the marker and asks you to go through a whole Transformer on the board, from raw text to the next word. The interviewer asks:

> Walk a sentence through a whole Transformer, with shapes.

**Running example:** a GPT-2-small-sized model (d = 768, 12 layers, 12 heads, vocabulary 50,257) reads "_the biryani was cold but the naan was_" and predicts the next word. Shapes below are for one sequence of n tokens.

### The idea

Think of an assembly line. Text goes in and becomes ids, then vectors. The vectors pass through identical stations that keep their shape, and a final station turns each one into a score for every word in the vocabulary.

[Figure: A pipeline: text becomes n ids, then an n by 768 matrix, passes through 12 blocks and a norm keeping that shape, then a linear layer gives n by 50,257 logits.]

_Shapes for one sequence of n tokens, in a GPT-2-small-sized model. The last shape is the logits._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between GPT-2 small and LLaMA-7B. Then raise the batch size and sequence length, and watch the logits tensor and KV cache.

#### Tensor shapes through the model

Shapes for one forward pass. KV cache = 2 × layers × B × n × d × 2 bytes (multi-head attention; LLaMA-7B has 32 layers and d = 4,096).

For one 8-token sentence in GPT-2 small, every hidden tensor is 1 × 8 × 768 and the logits are 1 × 8 × 50,257. Push n to 4,096 with a batch of 8 on LLaMA-7B: the KV cache alone is about **17 GB**, which is why serving long contexts is limited by memory (Pope et al. 2022; multi-head attention).

**Now say why:** why does the KV cache grow so fast, and where does its memory go?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Text is split into **tokens**, each token id is looked up in an **embedding** table (n × d), **position** information is added (or applied as RoPE), and the vectors pass through **N identical blocks**: each lets tokens exchange information with **causal multi-head attention**, then processes each token with a **feed-forward network**, both as residual updates with normalisation. A final norm and a **linear layer to the vocabulary** turn each position's vector into **logits**; a **softmax** on the last position gives the next-token probabilities. Pick a token, append it, repeat, reusing cached keys and values. Every arrow in that pipeline is one of the lessons in this track. What you'll be able to do after this: walk through a Transformer forward pass with shapes, explain generation with a KV cache, and compare the decoder-only design with the 2017 encoder–decoder.

#### A decoder-only Transformer, bottom to top

1. The text is split into tokens (sub-word pieces) and mapped to integer ids: here 8 tokens. Tokenisation is covered in the LLMs track.

2. Each id selects one row of the embedding table (V × d): the sequence becomes an 8 × 768 matrix, one vector per token.

3. Position information is added (GPT-2: a learned 1,024 × 768 table) or applied inside attention as RoPE (LLaMA). Without it the model can't tell word order.

4. N = 12 identical pre-norm blocks. In each, causal multi-head attention lets every token read the earlier ones (12 heads, each with an 8 × 8 score matrix), then a 4× wider MLP processes each token; both add their output to the residual stream. Shape stays 8 × 768 throughout.

5. A final LayerNorm, then a linear layer (often the embedding matrix reused, "tied") maps each position's vector to 50,257 logits, one per vocabulary token.

6. Softmax on the last position gives the probability of each possible next token; "great" should rank high after "the naan was". In training, the cross-entropy loss is computed at every position at once.

7. Generation: sample or pick a token, append it, and run again. Keys and values of earlier tokens are cached, so each new step only computes the new token's row.

#### "Attention Is All You Need": the encoder–decoder

1. The encoder: 6 blocks of bidirectional self-attention and feed-forward over the English sentence, each followed by "add & norm" (post-norm).

2. The decoder: 6 blocks over the French words generated so far, with a causal mask so it can't peek at future words.

3. Between them, each decoder block has a cross-attention sub-layer: queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder's output. This is how the translation reads the source (seq2seq attention without RNNs).

4. The base model: d = 512, 8 heads, dff = 2,048, sinusoidal positions. It reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English–German, beating previous results including ensembles, at a fraction of the training cost.

Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017 [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762). GPT kept only the decoder (dropping cross-attention); BERT kept only the encoder (encoder vs decoder).

## In practice

### In practice

#### 2017 → today

| Part | 2017 Transformer | Typical LLM today (e.g. LLaMA) | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | encoder–decoder | decoder-only | encoder vs decoder |
| Positions | sinusoidal, added | RoPE in every attention layer | positional encodings |
| Normalisation | post-norm LayerNorm | pre-norm RMSNorm | normalisation |
| FFN activation | ReLU | SwiGLU | activations |
| Attention | multi-head | grouped-query (GQA), FlashAttention kernels | multi-head attention |
| Optimiser | Adam + warmup + inverse-sqrt decay | AdamW + warmup + cosine decay, clipping | LR schedules |

To see the same design on images, read Vision Transformers.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A Transformer is basically just attention"

It sounds right, since attention is what made it famous. But about two-thirds of a block's parameters are in the feed-forward network, and the residual connections and normalisation are what let it train at depth. In a good walkthrough, you name those parts as well.

## Say it

### Walk a sentence through a whole Transformer, with shapes.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What is the KV cache and why does it help?

At each generation step, the keys and values of earlier tokens don't change, so they're stored and reused; only the new token's Q, K, V are computed. It turns quadratic recomputation into linear work per step, at the cost of memory.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What are "tied embeddings"?

Using the same matrix for the input embedding and the output projection to logits, saving V × d parameters (GPT-2 does this; LLaMA doesn't).

Follow-up 3 of 3

Where does most compute go?

For short contexts, the matrix multiplies in the projections and FFNs (~2 × parameters FLOPs per token); for long contexts the n² attention term grows to dominate.

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Text is tokenised into ids, each id is looked up in an embedding matrix to give an n by d matrix, and positional information is added or applied as RoPE. That passes through N identical blocks. Each block normalises, applies causal multi-head self-attention so each token can gather information from earlier tokens, and adds the result to the residual stream; then it normalises again and applies a position-wise MLP, about four times wider, and adds that too. After the last block, a final norm and a linear layer to the vocabulary give logits at every position; during training, cross-entropy against the next token is computed at all positions in parallel thanks to the causal mask. At inference, softmax on the last position gives the next-token distribution; we sample or pick a token, append it and repeat, caching keys and values so each step only processes the new token. The 2017 original was an encoder–decoder with cross-attention for translation; modern LLMs are decoder-only with RoPE, pre-norm RMSNorm, SwiGLU and grouped-query attention.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The model outputs the whole answer at once." It generates one token per step.

- "Softmax is applied to every position at inference." Only the last position is needed to pick the next token.

**Key terms and sources**

One sentence followed through a whole GPT-style decoder: tokens, embeddings, positions, N blocks of attention and feed-forward with residuals and norms, the output projection, softmax and the generation loop, with tensor shapes at every step; then the original 2017 encoder–decoder · built from Vaswani et al. (2017), Radford et al. (2019), Touvron et al. (2023), Xiong et al. (2020), Pope et al. (2022) and Alammar (2018) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. A. Radford et al., "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), OpenAI 2019.

3. H. Touvron et al., "LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models", [arXiv:2302.13971](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971), 2023.

4. R. Xiong et al., "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture", ICML 2020, [arXiv:2002.04745](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745).

5. R. Pope et al., "Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference", MLSys 2023, [arXiv:2211.05102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.05102).

6. J. Alammar, ["The Illustrated Transformer"](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/), 2018.

# Vision Transformers

> How does a Transformer process an image, and when would you use one instead of a CNN?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Computer vision
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/vision-transformers/
- Before this: The Transformer, End to End (`fundamentals/transformer-end-to-end`), Convolution and Receptive Field (`fundamentals/convolution-and-receptive-field`)
- Quiz topic: `cnn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team wants to replace a CNN image classifier with a Vision Transformer. You have 20,000 labelled images. In the first test, the ViT does noticeably worse. Someone concludes that Transformers just don't work on images. The interviewer asks:

> How does a Transformer process an image, and when would you use one instead of a CNN?

#### Why it matters

ViTs are common backbones in image models, and in the image part of multimodal LLMs. They're also a good interview test of whether you understand both CNNs and Transformers.

### The idea

Think of a jigsaw. Cut a photo into square pieces, and describe each piece with a list of numbers. Now each piece is like a word in a sentence, and any piece can look at any other right away. But nobody told the model that neighbouring pieces usually belong together, so it has to learn that from examples.

[Figure: Three steps. Cut the image into patches. Turn each into a token. Run a standard Transformer on them.]

_Less built-in knowledge means more data, or pretraining._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Halve the patch size. Then increase the image size.

#### Turn an image into tokens

Exact calculation. Colour images have 3 channels. The chart shows the patch grid.

Halve the patch size from 16 to **8**: tokens grow four times, and attention scores about 16 times. That's why finer patches and larger images get expensive so fast, and why windows like Swin's help.

**Now say why:** why does halving the patch size multiply attention scores by about 16?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **Vision Transformer** cuts an image into patches, turns each into a vector, and treats them like words. A 224×224 image with 16×16 patches gives 196 tokens. It has much less built-in knowledge about images than a CNN, so it needs more data to do well on its own. **DeiT** showed strong training recipes reduce this need, **Swin** uses local windows to keep cost linear in image size, and pretraining helps a lot.

#### From pixels to tokens

1. **Split:** cut the image into N = HW/P² patches of size P×P.

2. **Embed:** flatten each patch, and apply one shared linear projection to get a D-sized vector.

3. **Add a class token:** a learned extra vector, whose final state is used for classification.

4. **Add positions:** learned 1-D position embeddings, so the model knows where each patch came from.

5. **Run a standard Transformer encoder:** every patch can attend to every other from the first layer.

| Version | Layers | Width D | Heads | Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ViT-Base | 12 | 768 | 12 | 86 million |
| ViT-Large | 24 | 1,024 | 16 | 307 million |
| ViT-Huge | 32 | 1,280 | 16 | 632 million |

##### CNN or ViT?

| | CNN | ViT |
|---|---|---|
| Built-in assumptions | Locality and translation equivariance | Very few, so it learns them from data |
| Seeing the whole image | Grows slowly with depth | From the first layer |
| With little data | Usually stronger | Needs pretraining or a strong recipe |
| Cost as images grow | Linear in pixels | Quadratic in tokens, for plain attention |

The ViT paper found that these models "do not generalize well when trained on insufficient amounts of data", while at 14 to 300 million images "large scale training trumps inductive bias".

##### What came next

- **DeiT:** trained on ImageNet alone in under 3 days on one computer, reaching 83.1% top-1 with 86 million parameters, using strong augmentation and regularisation. A distillation token, learning from a CNN teacher, took this up to 85.2%.

- **Swin:** attention within local windows, which shift between layers. Cost becomes linear in image size, and that suits detection and segmentation.

- **Self-supervised pretraining:** masked autoencoders and DINO reduce the need for labels.

#### The maths

$$ {N = \frac{HW}{P^2}}, \qquad {z_0 = [x_{\text{class}};\; x_1 E;\; \dots;\; x_N E]} + {E_{\text{pos}}} $$

From Dosovitskiy et al., Equation 1. After this, it’s a standard Transformer encoder.

- **the number of patches**: Image height and width, divided by the patch area.

- **the token sequence**: A class token, then each flattened patch multiplied by the shared projection E.

- **the positions**: A learned vector for each position, added to the tokens.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use pretrained weights:** this is usually the right start, unless you have a very large dataset.

- **Changing resolution:** position embeddings are tied to a grid, so they need interpolating for a new image size.

- **Augment heavily:** ViT recipes lean on mixup, CutMix and RandAugment.

- **Dense tasks:** plain ViTs produce one coarse scale. Hierarchical designs like Swin make detection and segmentation easier.

- **Compare fairly:** ConvNeXt shows a modern CNN can match them, so test both on your data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "ViTs always beat CNNs"

It sounds right, as they lead many benchmarks. But the ViT paper itself says they don't generalise well without enough data, and its strong results rely on 14 to 300 million images for pretraining. ConvNeXt also shows a modern CNN can match them. Use pretrained weights, and compare both.

## Say it

### How does a Transformer process an image, and when would you use one instead of a CNN?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What does a ViT lose compared with a CNN?

Built-in assumptions, namely locality and translation equivariance. Only the patch cutting and the MLPs have a little of this. So it must learn image structure from data, which is why it can do worse on small datasets unless pretrained or strongly regularised.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you run a trained ViT on larger images?

Keep the patch size, so you get more tokens. The learned position embeddings no longer match, so interpolate them in 2-D onto the new grid. Then fine-tune briefly if you can. Cost rises, as attention is quadratic in tokens.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the role of the class token?

It's a learned vector added to the sequence. Through attention, it collects information from all patches, and its final state goes to the classifier. Averaging all the patch outputs is a common alternative.

#### The 30-second answer

A Vision Transformer cuts an image into patches, flattens them, and projects each to a vector. It adds a class token and learned position embeddings, then runs a standard encoder. A 224 image with 16-pixel patches gives 196 patches. Unlike a CNN, it has little built-in knowledge of locality, so it needs more data, or strong augmentation and pretraining. Every patch can attend to all others from the first layer, but plain attention is quadratic in tokens. Swin uses shifted windows to make that linear. With limited data, I'd start from pretrained weights, and compare against a modern CNN.

**Key terms and sources**

Patches as tokens, class tokens, position embeddings, why ViT needs more data than a CNN, and how DeiT, Swin and self-supervised training responded. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)

- [Touvron et al., DeiT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.12877)

- [Liu et al., Swin Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14030)

- [Liu et al., ConvNeXt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03545)

# Object Detection

> How does an object detector work, and how do you measure one?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Computer vision
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/object-detection/
- Before this: CNN Architectures: AlexNet to ConvNeXt (`fundamentals/cnn-architectures`), Loss Functions for Deep Learning (`fundamentals/loss-functions`)
- Quiz topic: `cnn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your warehouse camera detector finds most boxes, but when two parcels overlap, it reports just one. Raising a setting fixes this, but now one parcel is often reported twice. A colleague shows an mAP score, and asks if it's good enough. The interviewer asks:

> How does an object detector work, and how do you measure one?

#### Why it matters

Detection appears in vision interviews and system designs: shelf checks, safety cameras, reading documents. It combines several ideas in one model, and the trade-offs between speed, accuracy and small objects are very practical. It uses a backbone and focal loss.

### The idea

Think of several people circling faces in a group photo. Many draw slightly different circles around the same face. You keep the most confident circle, and throw out those overlapping it too much. But if two faces really are close together, you might throw out a real one.

[Figure: Three families. Two-stage detectors propose and then classify. One-stage detectors predict everything in one pass. DETR predicts a set directly.]

_Boxes are compared using IoU, and judged using mAP._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Lower the NMS threshold to 0.3. Then raise it to 0.9.

#### Tune non-max suppression

Illustrative boxes and scores. Dashed: the true objects. Green: boxes kept. Faint: boxes removed. A kept box counts as correct if its IoU with an unmatched true box is at least 0.5.

Lower the threshold to **0.3**: the two overlapping objects on the left are close enough for one to delete the other. Raise it to **0.9**: duplicates survive. That's the basic weakness of NMS in crowded scenes. Now raise the minimum score, which trades recall for precision in another way.

**Now say why:** why does a low threshold lose a real object?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A detector finds **what** is in an image and **where**, as boxes with labels and scores. Boxes are compared using **IoU**: overlap divided by combined area. Many detectors produce lots of candidates, then remove duplicates using **non-max suppression**. **Two-stage** detectors propose regions and then classify them, and **one-stage** detectors predict everything at once, which needs tricks like focal loss. **DETR** predicts a set directly. Results are measured with **mAP**.

#### The moving parts

##### IoU

IoU is the area where two boxes overlap, divided by the area they cover together. It's 0 with no overlap, and 1 for identical boxes. As an illustration, two 4×4 boxes overlapping in a 2×2 corner have IoU = 4 / 28 ≈ 0.14.

##### Anchors

An anchor is a preset box shape at each location. The network predicts whether it holds an object, and how to adjust it. Faster R-CNN uses 3 scales and 3 aspect ratios, so 9 anchors per position.

##### Non-max suppression

1. Sort the boxes by score.

2. Keep the top box.

3. Remove remaining boxes whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold.

4. Repeat with the next box still left.

##### The main designs

| Model | What it changed | A reported result |
|---|---|---|
| **R-CNN** | Runs a CNN on about 2,000 proposed regions. | 47 s per image with VGG16. |
| **Fast R-CNN** | Runs the CNN once, and pools features per region. | 0.32 s per image. 70.0 mAP on VOC 2007. |
| **Faster R-CNN** | A network proposes the regions too. | About 5 frames a second. 73.2 mAP. |
| **YOLO** | One pass, predicting boxes from a grid. | 45 frames a second. 63.4 mAP. |
| **SSD** | One pass, using feature maps at several scales. | 58 frames a second. 72.1 mAP. |
| **RetinaNet** | Focal loss for one-stage detectors. | COCO AP of 39.1, at 5 frames a second. |
| **DETR** | A Transformer predicting a set of boxes. | COCO AP of 42.0, with no anchors or NMS. |

Speeds and scores come from each paper, on different hardware, so use them to see the direction of change, not to rank models.

##### Why one-stage detectors need focal loss

They score tens of thousands of candidates per image, and nearly all are easy background. Together, those easy cases swamp the loss. Focal loss reduces their weight. It added 2.9 AP over the best balanced cross-entropy in the RetinaNet paper.

##### Set prediction in DETR

DETR predicts a fixed number of boxes, and matches them one-to-one with the true objects using the Hungarian algorithm. As each object gets just one prediction, it needs no NMS. It was weaker on small objects in the original paper.

##### What mAP means

A predicted box counts as correct if its IoU with an unmatched true box passes a threshold. Sort predictions by score, and compute the area under the precision-recall curve. That's AP for one class, and mAP averages across classes. COCO also averages across IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, which rewards tight boxes.

#### The maths

$$ {\mathrm{IoU}(A,B)} = \frac{{|A \cap B|}}{{|A \cup B|}}, \qquad {\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -(1-p_t)^{\gamma}\log p_t} $$

IoU is the Jaccard index, as in D2L. Focal loss is from Lin et al., Equation 4.

- **IoU**: A score from 0 to 1 for how well two boxes agree.

- **the overlap**: The area shared by both boxes.

- **the combined area**: Area A plus area B, minus the overlap.

- **focal loss**: Cross-entropy, scaled down for easy examples. The RetinaNet paper’s best setting was γ = 2.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Small objects:** these are the usual weak spot. Use higher resolution, or feature maps at several scales.

- **Pick the metric from the use:** a safety camera needs high recall, and auto-blocking needs high precision. Check the operating point as well as mAP.

- **Crowded scenes:** NMS can remove real objects, so tune its threshold, or consider a set-based model.

- **Measure the whole pipeline:** latency includes preprocessing and NMS, not just the network.

- **Label quality matters:** loose or missing boxes limit results at high IoU thresholds. Check a sample by hand.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "High mAP means the detector is ready"

It sounds right, as mAP summarises everything. But it averages across classes, thresholds and sizes. A good score can hide poor small-object results, or a poor rare class. A deployment also runs at one threshold. Check the classes and sizes you care about, at your operating point.

## Say it

### How does an object detector work, and how do you measure one?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Walk me through non-max suppression. What's its weakness?

Sort boxes by score, keep the best, remove others overlapping it above a threshold, and repeat. Its weakness is crowded scenes: two real, overlapping objects can look like duplicates, so one gets deleted. A higher threshold keeps it, but leaves more duplicates.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does COCO AP measure that AP at IoU 0.5 doesn't?

AP at 0.5 accepts fairly loose boxes. COCO averages across thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, so it also rewards tight localisation. A model can score well at 0.5, yet poorly on COCO AP, if its boxes are approximately right but rarely precise.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why is a one-stage detector harder to train than a two-stage one?

It scores every candidate location, and most are easy background, so they dominate the loss. A two-stage detector filters most of them first. Focal loss fixes this by reducing the weight of easy examples.

#### The 30-second answer

A detector outputs boxes, labels and scores, and IoU measures how well two boxes agree. Two-stage models like Faster R-CNN propose regions, then classify them, and tend to favour accuracy. One-stage models like YOLO and SSD predict in one pass, which favours speed. They face extreme background imbalance, so RetinaNet introduced focal loss. Most remove duplicates with non-max suppression, which can fail in crowded scenes. DETR predicts a set with one-to-one matching, so it needs no NMS. I'd measure with mAP, check small objects separately, and choose the operating point from the costs of errors.

**Key terms and sources**

IoU, anchors, non-max suppression, two-stage and one-stage detectors, focal loss, DETR's set prediction, and what mAP measures. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Girshick et al., R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2524)

- [Girshick, Fast R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.08083)

- [Ren et al., Faster R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.01497)

- [Redmon et al., YOLO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02640)

- [Liu et al., SSD](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.02325)

- [Lin et al., Focal Loss (RetinaNet)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.02002)

- [Carion et al., DETR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872)

- [D2L on anchor boxes, IoU and NMS](https://d2l.ai/chapter_computer-vision/anchor.html)

# Image Segmentation

> How do networks label every pixel, and how do you measure and train them?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Computer vision
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/image-segmentation/
- Before this: CNN Architectures: AlexNet to ConvNeXt (`fundamentals/cnn-architectures`), Pooling, Stride, Padding and Output Shapes (`fundamentals/pooling-stride-padding`)
- Quiz topic: `cnn`

## Intuition

### The situation

A model that outlines tumours on scans reports 99% accuracy. Doctors say it's useless, as it misses most tumours. The tumours cover about 1% of each scan. The interviewer asks:

> How do networks label every pixel, and how do you measure and train them?

#### Why it matters

Medical scans, documents, road scenes and photo editing all need pixel-level results. The ideas here also travel: U-Net is the usual backbone in diffusion models. It extends detection from boxes to exact shapes.

### The idea

Think of tracing a map. First, zoom out to understand what the region is. Then, zoom back in to draw the exact borders. If you only had the zoomed-out view, your borders would be rough. So you keep the detailed version beside you. That's what a skip connection does.

[Figure: Three tasks. Semantic labels each pixel by class. Instance separates each object. Panoptic does both.]

_Encoder-decoders with skips recover the fine detail._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Tick predict background. Then make the object larger.

#### Why pixel accuracy lies

An illustrative 48×30 pixel image. Grey: predicted only. Orange: true object only. Green: both. Exact calculation.

Tick **predict background**: pixel accuracy barely falls, while IoU and Dice collapse to 0. Now make the object larger, and keep the same shift. The same mistake hurts IoU much less. That's why small objects are hard to score well on.

**Now say why:** why does pixel accuracy barely change when the object is missed?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Segmentation labels every pixel. **Semantic** gives a class per pixel, **instance** separates each object, and **panoptic** does both. Most models shrink an image to understand it, then enlarge it back, with **skip connections** restoring fine detail, as in **U-Net**. **Transposed convolutions** enlarge, and **dilated convolutions** see more without shrinking. Don't trust pixel accuracy: when a target is small, predicting all background can score very high. Use **IoU** or **Dice**.

#### Tasks and tools

| Task | Output | Two people in a photo |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantic** | A class for each pixel | One "person" region |
| **Instance** | A mask per object | Two separate masks |
| **Panoptic** | Both together | Two masks, plus labels for sky and road |

##### Key models

| Model | Idea | A reported result |
|---|---|---|
| **FCN** | All convolutional, so any image size works. Skips are added. | 62.2% mean IoU on VOC 2012. |
| **U-Net** | Contracting and expanding paths, with skips by concatenation. | Trains from very few images. IoU of 92% in a cell tracking challenge. |
| **DeepLab** | Dilated filters at several rates (ASPP). | 79.7% mean IoU on VOC 2012. |
| **Mask R-CNN** | Adds a mask branch to Faster R-CNN. | Instance segmentation at 5 frames a second. |
| **SAM** | Returns masks for a prompt: points, a box or a mask. | Predicts 3 masks per prompt, to handle ambiguity. |

##### Why skip connections?

Shrinking keeps the meaning, but loses the exact location. Skips bring fine detail straight across to the matching decoder layer. FCN adds the features, and U-Net concatenates them.

##### Making images larger

A **transposed convolution** broadcasts each input through the kernel, so the output gets bigger. It's a learned way to upsample. Its output size is S(n − 1) + K − 2P. So a common choice of K = 4, S = 2, P = 1 exactly doubles the size. It can produce checkerboard patterns, so many models resize first, then apply a normal convolution.

##### Seeing more without shrinking

A **dilated (atrous) convolution** spaces out its filter weights. A 3×3 filter at rate 2 covers a 5×5 area with just 9 weights, and the output keeps its resolution.

##### Why pixel accuracy misleads

If a tumour covers 1% of a scan, predicting "no tumour" everywhere scores 99%. It's the class imbalance problem, at pixel level. IoU and Dice ignore true negatives, so that prediction scores 0. Mean IoU averages across classes.

#### The maths

$$ {\mathrm{Dice}} = \frac{2\,{|A \cap B|}}{{|A| + |B|}} = {\frac{2\,\mathrm{IoU}}{1 + \mathrm{IoU}}}, \qquad {\mathrm{Dice}_{\text{soft}} = \frac{2\sum_i p_i g_i}{\sum_i p_i^2 + \sum_i g_i^2}} $$

The soft form is from the V-Net paper. Training usually uses 1 − Dice, often combined with cross-entropy.

- **Dice**: A score from 0 to 1 for how well two masks agree.

- **the overlap**: Pixels in both the prediction and the truth.

- **the two sizes**: Total pixels in the prediction, plus those in the truth.

- **its link to IoU**: They always rank a single prediction the same way, and Dice is never lower.

- **the soft version for training**: Uses predicted probabilities p, so it can be trained with gradients.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Combine losses:** cross-entropy plus Dice is a common start, especially with small targets.

- **Pretrain the encoder:** a pretrained backbone helps a lot when you have few labelled images.

- **Augment image and mask together:** the same flip or crop must apply to both.

- **Report by class:** a good mean can hide a failing rare class, and rare classes are often the point.

- **Consider labelling cost:** pixel labels are expensive. Prompted tools like SAM can speed this up, but check their output.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "99% pixel accuracy means the model is great"

It sounds right, as nearly every pixel is correct. But most pixels are background, so predicting nothing also scores about 99%. Use IoU or Dice for each class, which ignore true negatives. Look at results for small objects, and at actual examples, too.

## Say it

### How do networks label every pixel, and how do you measure and train them?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the output shape of a transposed convolution?

S(n − 1) + K − 2P. For n = 16, K = 4, S = 2 and P = 1, that's 30 + 4 − 2 = 32, so it doubles. For K = 2, S = 2, P = 0, it's 30 + 2 = 32, which doubles too.

Follow-up 2 of 3

U-Net adds skips by concatenating. Why not add, as in ResNet?

Concatenating keeps fine encoder features separate, and lets later layers decide how to use them. Adding is cheaper, but it mixes the two. Both work: FCN adds, U-Net concatenates, and concatenation costs more channels.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Dice is 0.8. What's the IoU?

IoU = Dice / (2 − Dice) = 0.8 / 1.2 ≈ 0.67. They rank a single prediction the same way, but averages over many images can rank models differently.

#### The 30-second answer

Segmentation labels every pixel. Semantic gives classes, instance separates objects, and panoptic does both. Most models use an encoder-decoder. The encoder shrinks the image to understand it, and the decoder enlarges it, with skip connections restoring detail, as in U-Net. Dilated convolutions see more context without losing resolution. Mask R-CNN adds a mask branch to a detector for instances. I wouldn't use pixel accuracy, because small targets make predicting background look great. I'd use IoU or Dice by class, and train with cross-entropy plus Dice.

**Key terms and sources**

Semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation, FCN, U-Net, transposed and dilated convolutions, Mask R-CNN, SAM, and Dice and IoU. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Long et al., FCN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4038)

- [Ronneberger et al., U-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04597)

- [Chen et al., DeepLab](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.00915)

- [He et al., Mask R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06870)

- [Kirillov et al., Panoptic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.00868)

- [Kirillov et al., Segment Anything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02643)

- [Milletari et al., V-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.04797)

- [D2L on transposed convolution](https://d2l.ai/chapter_computer-vision/transposed-conv.html)

# Interpreting Networks and Adversarial Examples

> How can you see what a network is using, and why can tiny changes fool it?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Computer vision
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/interpreting-networks-and-adversarial-examples/
- Before this: Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`), Convolution and Receptive Field (`fundamentals/convolution-and-receptive-field`)
- Quiz topic: `cnn`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your image model works well, but a heat map suggests it's looking at a watermark. Separately, a security review shows that tiny pixel changes, invisible to people, make it confidently wrong. The interviewer asks:

> How can you see what a network is using, and why can tiny changes fool it?

#### Why it matters

Heat maps can reveal a model using the wrong clue, such as a watermark rather than the object. Adversarial examples matter wherever someone gains by fooling a model. Both topics appear in vision courses and in reviews of high-stakes systems. For tabular models, see Explaining Models.

### The idea

Think of a thousand people each adding one rupee to a bill. Nobody would notice a single rupee, but the total changes a lot. Adversarial changes work the same way. Each pixel moves too little to see, but all of them push in the same harmful direction.

[Figure: Two uses of one gradient. Heat maps show where the model looked. Attacks use it to raise the loss. Adversarial training defends against them.]

_The same gradient that explains a model can attack it._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Lower the number of inputs. Then raise the change per input.

#### Why dimensions make attacks easy

Our seeded linear model: a logistic classifier with weight length ‖w‖₂ = 1, and a clean score of 2, so the clean probability is the same for every d. 3,072 is the size of a 32×32 colour image.

Keep ε at 0.05, and lower the inputs. The attack stops working, even though the change per input is the same. For scale, 0.05 on a 0-to-1 pixel range is about 13 levels out of 255. This shows the linear argument only, and real networks aren't exactly linear.

**Now say why:** why does the same small change matter more with more inputs?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Two tools ask how an input affects the output. **Saliency maps** use the gradient for each pixel. **Grad-CAM** weights the last feature maps by their gradients, to give a coarse heat map. Some of these maps can look convincing while barely depending on the model, so test them. The same gradient also gives an attack: an **adversarial example** nudges each pixel slightly in the harmful direction. In high dimensions, those tiny changes add up. **Adversarial training** helps, at a cost.

#### Explaining, then attacking

##### Saliency and Grad-CAM

- **Saliency map:** the gradient of the class score with respect to each input pixel. It's cheap, but often noisy.

- **Grad-CAM:** take the last convolutional maps. Average each map's gradient to get its importance, add the maps using those weights, and keep the positive part. It's coarse, but class-specific and easy to read.

##### Sanity-check your explanations

Adebayo et al. found that "some existing saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating process". They can resemble edge detectors, which need no model at all. So randomise the model's weights, and see if the map changes. If it doesn't, it isn't explaining the model.

A heat map shows where the model looked, not why, and doesn't show cause. Attention weights have the same limit.

##### Adversarial examples

Goodfellow et al. attributed these mainly to networks' **linear** behaviour. If each of d inputs changes by ε, in the sign of its weight, the score moves by ε‖w‖₁, which grows with d. So a change too small to see in each pixel can add up to a large change in the score.

| Attack | Method | Reported result |
|---|---|---|
| **FGSM** | One step of size ε, in the sign of the gradient. | On MNIST at ε = 0.25, a maxout network was wrong on 89.4%, with 97.6% average confidence. |
| **PGD** | Many small steps, staying within the allowed change. | A stronger attack, also used for training. |

##### Defending

**Adversarial training** trains on attacked examples. Madry et al. framed this as a contest: find the worst allowed change, then minimise the loss on it. In the FGSM paper, error on attacked examples fell from 89.4% to 17.9%. It's slower, and can reduce accuracy on clean data. Be careful about claimed defences, because they must be tested against strong attacks designed for them.

The idea goes beyond images. Text attacks on LLMs are a related problem, covered in guardrails and prompt injection.

#### The maths

$$ {L^c_{\text{Grad-CAM}}} = \mathrm{ReLU}\Big(\sum_k {\alpha_k^c}\, {A^k}\Big), \qquad {\tilde{x} = x + \epsilon\, \mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_x J(\theta, x, y)\big)} $$

Grad-CAM from Selvaraju et al., Equations 1 and 2. FGSM from Goodfellow et al., Section 4.

- **the heat map**: For class c. It has the same coarse grid as the feature maps.

- **a map’s importance**: The average gradient of the class score across that map.

- **a feature map**: An output from the last convolutional layer.

- **FGSM**: Add ε to each input, in the direction that raises the loss.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use heat maps for debugging:** they're good at catching a model relying on a background, watermark or text overlay.

- **Test your explanations:** randomise the weights, and check that the map changes.

- **Define the threat first:** what can an attacker change, and what do they gain? Most systems need ordinary robustness more than this.

- **Evaluate defences with strong attacks:** FGSM alone isn't enough, so use PGD or stronger ones.

- **Layer your defences:** rate limits, human review and monitoring can matter more than the model.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The heat map highlights the object, so the model is right"

It sounds right, as the picture looks convincing. But some saliency methods barely change when the model's weights are randomised, so a nice picture proves little. Sanity-check the method, and test the claim directly: change or remove that area, and see if the prediction changes.

## Say it

### How can you see what a network is using, and why can tiny changes fool it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why are high-dimensional models easier to attack?

Each input can change a little, and the effects add up. For a linear model, the score moves by ε times the L1 norm of the weights, which grows with the number of inputs. So many tiny changes make a big one.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your Grad-CAM highlights the hospital's marker on X-rays. What does this tell you?

The model may be using that marker, not the medical features. That's a form of leakage, and it would likely fail at other hospitals. I'd test on outside data, remove or mask the marker, and retrain. The map is a clue, so confirm it by changing the input.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What makes a defence trustworthy?

It should hold against strong attacks designed specifically to beat it, not just FGSM. Be suspicious if gradients seem to vanish, because this can hide the attack rather than stop it. Report robust accuracy, along with clean accuracy.

#### The 30-second answer

Saliency maps use the gradient of a class score for each pixel. Grad-CAM weights the last feature maps by their average gradients, and gives a coarse, class-specific heat map. They help catch a model using the wrong clue, but they show where it looked, not why, and I'd sanity-check by randomising the weights. Adversarial examples use the same gradient. FGSM adds a small change to each input in the sign of the gradient, and with many inputs, these add up, as the score moves by epsilon times the L1 norm. PGD is a stronger, iterative version, and adversarial training is the main defence, at a cost in speed and sometimes clean accuracy.

**Key terms and sources**

Saliency maps, Grad-CAM and their sanity checks, then adversarial examples: FGSM, PGD, why high dimensions make them easy, and adversarial training. · checked 6 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Simonyan et al., Saliency Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6034)

- [Selvaraju et al., Grad-CAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02391)

- [Adebayo et al., Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03292)

- [Goodfellow et al., Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572)

- [Madry et al., Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06083)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# Embeddings and Representation Learning

> How do models learn that biryani is like pulao?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Representation and generative models
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/embeddings/
- Before this: Vectors, Dot Products & Cosine Similarity (`fundamentals/vectors-and-cosine-similarity`), Backpropagation Through a Network (`fundamentals/backpropagation`)
- Related: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `genm`

## Intuition

### The situation

The delivery app wants "more like this" suggestions: order biryani, get pulao rather than fries. A teammate one-hot encodes the dishes, and every dish comes out equally unlike every other. The interviewer asks:

> What is an embedding, and where does its meaning come from?

**Running example (Representation lessons):** the delivery app wants "more like this" suggestions: if you ordered biryani, suggest pulao rather than fries. Nobody labels which dishes are similar; we learn it from how dishes appear in order notes and reviews.

#### One-hot vectors know nothing about similarity

With a vocabulary of 50,000 words, one-hot encoding gives each word a 50,000-long vector with a single 1. Every pair of different words has a dot product of 0: "biryani" is exactly as unlike "pulao" as it is unlike "keyboard". The vectors are huge, sparse and carry no meaning. We want a small, dense vector per item where distance means something.

### The idea

Think of a map of dishes that nobody draws by hand. Dishes that turn up in similar order notes get placed close together. Biryani lands next to pulao and far from fries, just from how the words are used.

[Figure: A map of dishes. Biryani sits next to pulao, pizza near pasta and lasagne, chai near coffee, and fries near nuggets. The groups sit far apart.]

_Illustrative, in two dimensions. Real embeddings use hundreds._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Pick biryani at embedding size 4, and look at its neighbours. Raise the size to 8. Then try chai.

#### Embeddings from 400 order notes

Corpus: 400 generated order notes like "ordered biryani so spicy and rice" or "the pizza and the pasta arrived" (16 dishes from four cuisines, each with its own traits, some shared across cuisines; fixed seed). Co-occurrence window ±2 → positive PMI → SVD, keeping d dimensions. Plot: the first two dimensions; neighbours use all d.

Nobody told the method which dishes belong together. With **d = 4**, the embedding captures the big picture: biryani's nearest neighbours are the other Indian dishes, pizza sits with lasagne and pasta, chai with the other drinks. Raise **d to 8** and finer traits appear: biryani's closest match becomes **pulao (0.91)**, the other rice dish served with raita; chai stays close to **coffee (0.98)**, both hot and served with biscuits, but drifts from cold juice (0.32); fries pair with nuggets (0.94), both crispy with ketchup. Small d groups by cuisine, larger d separates finer meaning, which is the same trade-off real systems tune with hundreds of dimensions.

**Now say why:** why does a small size group dishes by cuisine, while a larger one separates finer meaning?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A model can't do maths on the word "biryani"; it needs numbers. **One-hot** vectors make every word equally different from every other. An **embedding** maps each item to a short **dense vector**, learned so that items used in similar ways end up close together: "biryani" near "pulao", "pizza" near "pasta". For words this rests on the **distributional hypothesis** (a word is known by the company it keeps). word2vec learns them by predicting neighbouring words, which amounts to factorising a word–context co-occurrence matrix. Modern models produce **contextual** embeddings that change with the sentence, and embeddings of whole sentences, images, users and products drive **semantic search, RAG and recommendations**. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why embeddings beat one-hot, how they're learned, how to compare them, and where they're used.

#### An embedding is a lookup table you learn

$$ {e_{w} = E^{\top}{\mathbf{1}_{w}}}, \quad E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, \qquad {\cos(a,b) = \frac{a\cdot b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}} $$

Bengio et al. (2003) learned word vectors jointly with a neural language model. Cosine similarity: Vectors & Cosine Similarity.

- **embedding matrix**: V rows (one per item) by d columns (e.g. 300 for word2vec, 768–4,096 in Transformers). Its values are learned by gradient descent like any other weights.

- **one-hot input**: Multiplying a one-hot vector by E just selects one row, so in practice it’s implemented as a table lookup.

- **cosine similarity**: Compare embeddings by the angle between them: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated. Used for nearest-neighbour search.

#### Learning from context: word2vec

- **Skip-gram:** for each word, predict the words around it (within a window of a few words); **CBOW** does the reverse (Mikolov et al. 2013). Trained with negative sampling on billions of words, the hidden-layer weights become the embeddings.

- Famous property: some relations become directions, e.g. vector("king") − vector("man") + vector("woman") ≈ vector("queen").

- **It's matrix factorisation in disguise:** Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorises a matrix of shifted **pointwise mutual information** (PMI) between words and contexts. GloVe (Pennington et al. 2014) factorises log co-occurrence counts directly.

The lab in the Intuition tab uses that equivalence: count which words appear near which, convert counts to positive PMI, and factorise with SVD. No neural network needed for the idea.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Contextual embeddings and embeddings of everything

- **Static vs contextual:** word2vec gives "cold" one vector. Transformers give a different vector per occurrence: "cold biryani" vs "a cold" (the illness) get different representations (BERT; Transformers).

- **Sentence and document embeddings:** models such as Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) map whole texts to one vector for semantic search; this is the retrieval step of **RAG**.

- **Any item:** users, products, dishes, images (via contrastive learning) can all be embedded; recommendation systems compare user and item vectors.

- **Search at scale:** approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF/PQ) find the closest of millions of vectors in milliseconds.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "An embedding stores what the word means"

It sounds right, since similar dishes do end up close. But the vector only reflects how a word is used. The lab counts which words appear near which, and nobody tells it that biryani and pulao are both rice dishes. Individual dimensions rarely mean anything by themselves. And word2vec gives "cold" one vector, whether it's "cold biryani" or "a cold". Telling those apart takes contextual embeddings.

## Say it

### What is an embedding, and where does its meaning come from?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why cosine rather than Euclidean distance?

Cosine ignores vector length, which often reflects frequency rather than meaning; with normalised vectors the two give the same ranking.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you handle words not in the vocabulary?

Sub-word units (fastText character n-grams, BPE tokens in Transformers) so any word can be composed from known pieces.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you evaluate embeddings?

Intrinsically (similarity benchmarks, nearest-neighbour checks) and, more importantly, extrinsically: retrieval recall@k or downstream task accuracy.

#### The 30-second answer

An embedding maps a discrete item to a dense, low-dimensional vector, learned so that similar items are close, usually by cosine similarity. It's a lookup table trained by gradient descent. For words, methods like word2vec predict surrounding words, which by the distributional hypothesis puts words used in similar contexts close together; it's equivalent to factorising a shifted PMI co-occurrence matrix. Modern Transformers give contextual embeddings that depend on the sentence, and sentence, image, user and product embeddings power semantic search, RAG retrieval and recommendations, with approximate nearest-neighbour indexes for scale.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Embedding dimensions have fixed meanings." Individual dimensions are rarely interpretable; directions and distances are what carry meaning.

- "One embedding per word is enough." Polysemy needs contextual embeddings.

**Key terms and sources**

Turning discrete things (words, dishes, users) into dense vectors where similar things sit close together: one-hot vs dense, the distributional hypothesis, word2vec as implicit matrix factorisation, contextual embeddings, and how embeddings power search and recommendation · built from Bengio et al. (2003), Mikolov et al. (2013), Levy & Goldberg (NeurIPS 2014), Pennington et al. (GloVe, 2014), Devlin et al. (2019) and Reimers & Gurevych (2019) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. Y. Bengio, R. Ducharme, P. Vincent & C. Jauvin, "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model", _JMLR_ 3, 2003.

2. T. Mikolov, K. Chen, G. Corrado & J. Dean, "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space", [arXiv:1301.3781](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), 2013.

3. O. Levy & Y. Goldberg, "Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization", NeurIPS 2014.

4. J. Pennington, R. Socher & C. Manning, "GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation", EMNLP 2014.

5. N. Reimers & I. Gurevych, "Sentence-BERT", EMNLP 2019, [arXiv:1908.10084](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084).

# Autoencoders and VAEs

> How does a VAE turn compression into generation?

- Track: Fundamentals › Deep Learning › Representation and generative models
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/autoencoders-and-vaes/
- Before this: Embeddings and Representation Learning (`fundamentals/embeddings`), Entropy, Cross-Entropy & KL Divergence (`fundamentals/entropy-cross-entropy-kl`)
- Quiz topic: `genm`

## Intuition

### The situation

The app stores 64-pixel icons of dishes. A teammate trains an autoencoder that redraws them well, then feeds it random codes to get new icons, and gets garbage. The interviewer asks:

> Why can't a plain autoencoder generate, and what does a VAE change?

**Running example:** the app stores thumbnail icons of dishes: 8 × 8 = 64 pixels each, showing a plate, a cup or a fork in slightly different positions. Can a few numbers describe each icon, and can we generate new, plausible icons?

#### Learn structure without labels

Most data is unlabelled. Yet 64-pixel icons don't fill the 64-dimensional space: they are a few shapes in a few positions. If a network can describe each icon with a handful of numbers and still redraw it, it has learned that structure. That gives compression, denoising, anomaly detection (bad reconstructions = unusual inputs) and, with a VAE, a way to generate new examples.

### The idea

Think of describing an icon over the phone with a few numbers. A plain autoencoder only learns the codes it has seen, with empty space between them. A VAE gives each icon a small fuzzy region and packs those regions around the centre, so any point you pick means something.

[Figure: Left: an autoencoder's codes form separate clumps with empty space between them, so a random code decodes to garbage. Right: a VAE's codes are overlapping regions packed around the centre, so any code decodes to something plausible.]

_Illustrative, in two dimensions. The dashed circle is the prior, N(0, I)._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the bottleneck to 1, then 3, then 12. Watch the reconstructions and the share of variance lost.

#### How many numbers does an icon need?

180 icons (plates, cups, forks, shifted by up to 1 pixel, with noise), fixed seed. The optimal **linear** autoencoder for each k (computed with SVD, i.e. PCA). Top row: originals; bottom row: reconstructions from k numbers.

With **k = 1** every reconstruction is a blur of all three shapes (84% of the pixel variance lost). At **k = 3** the plate, cup and fork are already told apart from 3 numbers instead of 64, even though 63% of the variance is still lost, mostly the 1-pixel shifts and noise, which a linear code handles badly. By k = 12 only 19% is lost, and the rest is largely noise that a bottleneck is supposed to throw away. A plain autoencoder only learns to compress; nothing makes its code space orderly, so a random code usually decodes to garbage. That's the gap the VAE closes.

**Now say why:** at 3 numbers, why can you tell the shapes apart even though most of the variance is still lost?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An **autoencoder** squeezes each input through a narrow **bottleneck** (the encoder) and rebuilds it (the decoder), trained only to make the output match the input. To succeed it must keep the most important structure in a few numbers: a learned compression. A **linear** autoencoder learns exactly the same subspace as PCA. But a plain autoencoder's latent space has gaps, so picking a random code rarely decodes to anything sensible. A **VAE** fixes that: the encoder outputs a **mean and variance**, a code is **sampled** from it (via the **reparameterisation trick**), and a **KL penalty** pulls every code distribution towards a standard normal. The latent space becomes smooth and filled, so sampling z ~ N(0, I) and decoding generates new data. What you'll be able to do after this: explain the bottleneck, connect linear autoencoders to PCA, and write and interpret the VAE loss.

#### Encode, squeeze, decode

$$ z = {f_{\text{enc}}(x)} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}, \qquad \hat{x} = {f_{\text{dec}}(z)}, \qquad {L = \lVert x - \hat{x}\rVert^2} $$

Baldi & Hornik (1989): a linear autoencoder with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA (PCA; SVD). Hinton & Salakhutdinov (_Science_ 2006) showed deep non-linear autoencoders compress far better than PCA. Denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008) corrupt the input and learn to recover the clean version.

- **encoder**: A network that maps the 64-pixel input to a k-dimensional code z, with k much smaller than 64.

- **decoder**: Maps the code back to 64 pixels.

- **reconstruction loss**: How far the output is from the input, e.g. mean squared error. No labels needed: the input is its own target.

#### The variational autoencoder

$$ \mathcal{L} = {\mathbb{E}_{{q(z\mid x)}}\big[\log p(x\mid z)\big]} - {\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z\mid x)\,\Vert\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)\big)}, \qquad {z = \mu + \sigma\odot\varepsilon} $$

Kingma & Welling, "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes", ICLR 2014 [arXiv:1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114); Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra (2014). The objective is the evidence lower bound (ELBO) on log p(x); training maximises it. For Gaussians the KL term has a closed form (below). KL itself: entropy & KL.

- **encoder outputs a distribution**: For each input, a mean μ and a standard deviation σ for every latent dimension: a little Gaussian cloud instead of a single point.

- **reparameterisation**: Sample z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1). The randomness is in ε, so gradients flow through μ and σ (Kingma & Welling 2014).

- **reconstruction term**: Decode z and score how well it reproduces x (log-likelihood, e.g. squared error).

- **KL term**: How far each code cloud is from the standard normal prior. It pulls clouds towards the origin and stops σ from shrinking to zero, filling the space.

One latent dimension. Teal: the encoder's q(z | x) = N(μ, σ²); grey: the prior N(0, 1). KL = ½(μ² + σ² − 1 − ln σ²).

With μ = 1.5 and σ = 0.3 the KL is **1.87 nats** (1.13 from the off-centre mean, 0.75 from the narrow width): the code sits off-centre and is too narrow. Set μ = 0 and σ = 1 and it's exactly **0**, but then the code carries no information about the input. Training balances the two terms: enough information to reconstruct, close enough to the prior that the space has no holes. β-VAE (Higgins et al. 2017) weights the KL by β > 1 for more disentangled codes.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Autoencoders and VAEs today

- **Generation:** VAE samples tend to be blurry (squared error averages over possibilities), so GANs and then diffusion models took over image generation.

- **Latent diffusion:** Stable Diffusion runs diffusion inside the compressed latent space of an autoencoder trained with a mild KL term, about 48× fewer numbers than the 512 × 512 × 3 image (Rombach et al. 2022).

- **Anomaly detection:** train on normal data; inputs that reconstruct badly are flagged (anomaly detection).

- **Representation learning:** masked autoencoders (MAE) pre-train vision Transformers by reconstructing hidden image patches.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "An autoencoder is a generative model"

It sounds right, since it has a decoder that produces images. But nothing makes a plain autoencoder's code space orderly, so a random code usually decodes to garbage. The VAE's KL term is what fixes that, so you can't drop it as optional regularisation. Without it, you just have a noisy autoencoder.

## Say it

### Why can't a plain autoencoder generate, and what does a VAE change?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is the reparameterisation trick needed?

You can't backpropagate through a random sampling step. Writing z = μ + σ·ε moves the randomness into ε, which doesn't depend on the parameters.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's posterior collapse?

A powerful decoder ignores z, the KL drives q(z|x) to the prior, and the code carries no information. Fixes: KL annealing, weaker decoders, free bits.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why are VAE samples blurry?

A Gaussian likelihood (squared error) rewards predicting the average of plausible outputs, which looks blurry.

#### The 30-second answer

An autoencoder compresses an input to a low-dimensional code and reconstructs it, trained only on reconstruction error, so it learns the data's main structure without labels; a linear one learns the PCA subspace. Its latent space isn't organised, so you can't sample from it. A VAE makes the encoder output a Gaussian, mean and variance, samples the code with the reparameterisation trick z = μ + σ·ε so gradients flow, and maximises the ELBO: reconstruction log-likelihood minus the KL from the code distribution to a standard normal. The KL keeps the latent space smooth and filled, so sampling from N(0, I) and decoding generates new data. VAEs are blurrier than diffusion models but their autoencoders underpin latent diffusion.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "An autoencoder is a generative model." A plain one isn't: sampling random codes doesn't work reliably.

- "The KL term is regularisation you can drop." Without it, the VAE is just a noisy autoencoder.

**Key terms and sources**

Compressing data through a bottleneck and reconstructing it; what a linear autoencoder learns (PCA); denoising autoencoders; and the variational autoencoder: an encoder that outputs a distribution, the reparameterisation trick, and the ELBO with its reconstruction and KL terms · built from Hinton & Salakhutdinov (Science 2006), Baldi & Hornik (1989), Vincent et al. (2008), Kingma & Welling (ICLR 2014), Rezende et al. (2014), Higgins et al. (β-VAE, 2017) and Rombach et al. (2022) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. P. Baldi & K. Hornik, "Neural networks and principal component analysis: learning from examples without local minima", _Neural Networks_ 2, 1989.

2. G. Hinton & R. Salakhutdinov, "Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks", _Science_ 313, 2006.

3. P. Vincent, H. Larochelle, Y. Bengio & P.-A. Manzagol, "Extracting and composing robust features with denoising autoencoders", ICML 2008.

4. D. Kingma & M. Welling, "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes", ICLR 2014, [arXiv:1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114).

5. I. Higgins et al., "β-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework", ICLR 2017.

6. R. Rombach, A. Blattmann, D. Lorenz, P. Esser & B. Ommer, "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models", CVPR 2022, [arXiv:2112.10752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752).
