# N-gram Language Models and Perplexity

> How likely is this sentence, and what does perplexity mean?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Language models and tokenisation
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/n-gram-language-models/
- Before this: Probability Basics & Bayes' Rule (`fundamentals/probability-and-bayes`), Entropy, Cross-Entropy & KL Divergence (`fundamentals/entropy-cross-entropy-kl`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

The review box suggests the next word as customers type, using a bigram model built from 400 past reviews. Then someone types "the paneer was crispy", which it has never seen, and its probability comes out as zero. The interviewer asks:

> How does an n-gram model work, and what do you do about pairs it has never seen?

**Running example:** the app's review box suggests the next word as customers type. "the biryani was …" → "not"? "cold"? "great"? We learn the suggestions from 400 past reviews.

#### How likely is this sentence?

Autocomplete, speech recognition ("recognise speech" vs "wreck a nice beach"), spelling correction and machine translation all need to judge which word sequence is more plausible. We need a model that gives every possible sentence a probability, learned from text alone.

### The idea

Think of guessing the next word from a tally of what followed the last word in past reviews. It's quick and needs no training beyond counting. But if the tally has no entry for a pair, it calls that pair impossible.

[Figure: To guess what follows the biryani was, a bigram model looks only at was. It has counted not most often, then other words. It has never seen was crispy, so that gets zero.]

_Illustrative bars. In the lab, P("not" | "was") is 0.415._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Score "the paneer was crispy" with no smoothing, then with add-1 and add-k. Then score the scrambled sentence, and watch held-out perplexity.

#### A bigram model trained on 400 reviews

Bar chart: the model's top next-word probabilities after "was". Vocabulary = words in 400 training reviews plus <unk>; unseen words map to <unk>. Held-out set: 100 new reviews from the same generator. Fixed seed.

Without smoothing, "the paneer was crispy" gets **infinite** perplexity: "paneer was" and "crispy" never appeared, so one factor is 0. The fluent "the pizza was not soggy" scores **2.91**, and the scrambled "soggy not was pizza the" about **3,700**, even with smoothing: the model has learned word order, not just word frequency. Smoothing is a trade-off. **Add-1** gives the crispy sentence a finite 12.4, but flattens everything else: held-out perplexity rises from 3.09 to **3.76** and P("not" | "was") drops from 0.415 to 0.394. A **small k** (0.05) barely touches seen text (held-out 3.13) but leaves less room for unseen words (crispy: 20.1). Backoff and Kneser–Ney get the best of both by falling back to lower-order counts instead of spreading mass evenly.

**Now say why:** add-1 fixes the infinite perplexity, so why does held-out perplexity get worse?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A **language model** assigns a probability to a sequence of words, or equivalently predicts the **next word**. By the chain rule, P(sentence) is the product of P(each word | all previous words). An **n-gram model** simplifies this with the **Markov assumption**: only the last n − 1 words matter, and the probabilities come from **counting** in a corpus. Any word pair never seen in training gets probability 0, which zeroes the whole sentence, so we **smooth**: add-k, backoff, or the best classic method, **Kneser–Ney**. Models are compared by **perplexity**, the exponentiated average negative log-probability on held-out text: lower is better, and it reads as "how many words the model is effectively choosing between". LLMs are next-word predictors too, with a neural network instead of a count table. What you'll be able to do after this: compute bigram probabilities and perplexity, explain why smoothing is needed, and connect n-gram models to modern LLMs.

#### Chain rule, Markov assumption, counts

$$ {P(w_1,\dots,w_n) = \prod_i P(w_i \mid w_1,\dots,w_{i-1})} \;\approx\; {\prod_i P(w_i \mid w_{i-1})}, \qquad {P(w_i\mid w_{i-1}) = \frac{C(w_{i-1}\,w_i)}{C(w_{i-1})}} $$

Shannon (1948) used n-gram approximations of English; Jurafsky & Martin, SLP3 ch. 3. Sentences are padded with start and end tokens <s> and </s>.

- **chain rule**: Exact: the probability of a sentence is the product of each word’s probability given all the words before it.

- **Markov assumption (bigram)**: Approximate that history by just the previous word. A trigram model uses the previous two.

- **maximum-likelihood estimate**: Count how often the pair appears, divided by how often the first word appears. e.g. if “was not” appears 150 times and “was” 400 times, the estimate is 0.375.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Perplexity, and the road to LLMs

$$ \mathrm{PP}(W) = {\exp\!\Big(}-{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P(w_i \mid w_{<i})}{\Big)} $$

Perplexity = exp(cross-entropy) on the test set (entropy & cross-entropy). Only compare perplexities computed with the same tokenisation and vocabulary.

- **average log-probability**: Average the log-probability the model gives each word of held-out text.

- **exponentiate the negative**: Perplexity = exp(−average log-probability). A perplexity of 10 means the model is as uncertain as picking uniformly among 10 words at every step.

- **Neural language models** (Bengio et al. 2003) replaced count tables with embeddings and a neural network, so similar words share statistics and there is no zero-count problem.

- RNN and then Transformer LMs extended the context from n − 1 words to thousands of tokens. Modern LLMs are still trained on next-token prediction and evaluated with perplexity, over subword tokens.

- n-gram models still appear in fast on-device keyboards, speech-recognition decoding and data-quality filtering of LLM training corpora.

For one use of language models, read Spelling Correction.

### The answer that sounds right

#### Unseen pairs get probability zero

A customer types "the paneer was crispy". If "was crispy" never appeared in training, the counting estimate is 0, the whole sentence gets probability 0, and perplexity is infinite. With any realistic vocabulary, most plausible word pairs are never seen. **Smoothing** moves a little probability mass to unseen events:

- **Add-k** (Laplace when k = 1): add k to every count. Simple, but add-1 steals far too much mass from seen pairs.

- **Backoff / interpolation:** if the trigram is unseen, fall back to (or mix in) the bigram and unigram estimates.

- **Kneser–Ney** (1995): interpolation with discounting plus a clever lower-order distribution ("how many different contexts does this word follow?"), the best-performing classic method in Chen & Goodman's (1998) comparison.

## Say it

### How does an n-gram model work, and what do you do about pairs it has never seen?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not just use a large n?

Data sparsity: most 5-grams are never seen, so estimates are zeros and noise. Storage also explodes.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why work in log space?

Multiplying many small probabilities underflows; summing logs is stable and turns products into sums.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can you compare perplexities of two LLMs with different tokenisers?

Not directly: per-token perplexity depends on the token count. Normalise per word or per byte (bits per byte) instead.

#### The 30-second answer

A language model assigns probabilities to word sequences; by the chain rule that's the product of each word's probability given its history. An n-gram model approximates the history with the last n minus one words and estimates probabilities from counts. Unseen n-grams get zero probability, so we smooth, with add-k, backoff or interpolation, or Kneser–Ney, the best classic method. We evaluate with perplexity, the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood on held-out text, lower is better, roughly the effective number of choices per word. Neural LMs replaced count tables with embeddings and longer context, and LLMs are still next-token predictors measured by perplexity.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Lower training perplexity means a better model." Evaluate on held-out text.

- "Add-1 is the standard smoothing." It's a teaching example; it performs poorly.

**Key terms and sources**

Predicting the next word from counts: the chain rule, the Markov assumption, bigram models, the zero-probability problem and smoothing (add-k, backoff, Kneser–Ney), perplexity as the standard metric, and how this leads straight to LLMs · built from Shannon (1948), Jelinek (1997), Chen & Goodman (1998), Kneser & Ney (1995), Jurafsky & Martin (SLP3, ch. 3) and Bengio et al. (2003) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. C. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", _Bell System Technical Journal_ 27, 1948.

2. R. Kneser & H. Ney, "Improved backing-off for M-gram language modeling", ICASSP 1995.

3. S. Chen & J. Goodman, "An Empirical Study of Smoothing Techniques for Language Modeling", Harvard TR-10-98, 1998.

4. Y. Bengio, R. Ducharme, P. Vincent & C. Jauvin, "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model", _JMLR_ 3, 2003.

5. D. Jurafsky & J. Martin, _Speech and Language Processing_, 3rd ed. draft, ch. 3, [web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/).

# Edit Distance and Spelling Correction

> How do you measure how different two strings are, and how would you correct a misspelt word?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Language models and tokenisation
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/edit-distance-and-spelling-correction/
- Before this: N-gram Language Models and Perplexity (`fundamentals/n-gram-language-models`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

Customers search for "biriyani", "biryani" and "briyani", and two of those return nothing. A colleague suggests comparing every query against every dish with a simple loop. The interviewer asks:

> How do you measure how different two strings are, and how would you correct a misspelt word?

#### Why it matters

It's a classic coding question and a useful tool: fuzzy search, matching names across databases, cleaning user input and scoring speech recognition. It also connects a dynamic programming pattern to the language models you've already seen.

### The idea

Think of editing a word on paper, using only three moves: cross out a letter, write in a letter, or overwrite one. Edit distance is the fewest moves needed. Rather than trying every sequence of moves, you build the answer from shorter pieces, and write them in a table, so nothing gets worked out twice.

[Figure: Three moves. Delete, insert or substitute a letter. Each costs 1, and a match costs nothing.]

_Each table cell needs only its three neighbours._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Slide the cells filled down. Then set the substitution cost to 2.

#### Fill the table

Exact calculation. The first string runs down the side, and the second along the top. Green cells mark one best path, once the table is full.

Slide **cells filled** down to watch it build row by row. Each new cell only needs the three next to it. Set the substitution cost to **2** for intention → execution: the answer rises from 5 to 8, as substituting now costs as much as a delete plus an insert.

**Now say why:** why don't we need to try every possible sequence of edits?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Edit distance** counts the fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another. Trying every edit sequence is hopeless, so **dynamic programming** fills a table, using the answers for shorter prefixes. It takes O(mn) time. A **spelling corrector** combines this with a language model: among known words near the typo, choose the one with the highest P(word) × P(typo | word). This is the **noisy channel** idea.

#### Building the table

Let D(i, j) be the distance between the first i letters of one string and the first j letters of the other. To reach it, the last step must be one of three:

| Last step | Comes from | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Delete** a letter | The cell above | 1 |
| **Insert** a letter | The cell to the left | 1 |
| **Substitute or match** | The diagonal cell | 1, or 0 if the letters match |

Take the cheapest. The first row and column are just i and j, because turning a string into nothing takes one deletion per letter.

##### Worked example

"kitten" to "sitting" takes 3 edits: substitute k with s, substitute e with i, and insert g.

##### Getting the edits, and saving memory

- **Backtrace:** store which cell each value came from, then walk back from the corner. This gives the alignment as well as the number.

- **Less memory:** each row needs only the row before it. If you only want the distance, that takes O(min(m, n)) memory rather than O(mn).

- **Other costs:** costs can vary. Keyboard neighbours might cost less, or substitution might cost 2, which Jurafsky and Martin also show.

- **Transpositions:** "teh" to "the" costs 2 here, though it's one slip of the fingers. **Damerau-Levenshtein** counts swapping two neighbours as one edit.

##### The noisy channel model

Imagine the intended word passing through a noisy channel that sometimes changes letters. To recover it, combine how common a word is with how likely this typo is for that word.

1. **Candidates:** known words within a small edit distance.

2. **Language model P(c):** how common each one is, ideally given the surrounding words.

3. **Error model P(w | c):** how likely this typo is for that word.

Norvig's short corrector shows why simple versions go a long way, and also where they stop. It got 75% of 270 test words right in development, and 68% of 400 on a final test. Only 3 of the 270 needed more than two edits. Its words unknown to the model and its crude error model caused many of the misses.

#### The maths

$$ {D(i,j)} = \min\begin{cases}{D(i-1,j) + 1}\\ {D(i,j-1) + 1}\\ {D(i-1,j-1) + \delta(a_i,b_j)}\end{cases} \qquad {\hat c = \arg\max_c P(c)\,P(w\mid c)} $$

The recurrence is the standard Levenshtein form. The noisy channel formula is as in Norvig’s essay, where P(w) is dropped because it’s the same for every candidate.

- **one table cell**: The distance between the first i letters and the first j letters.

- **delete**: Remove a letter from the first string.

- **insert**: Add a letter from the second string.

- **substitute or match**: δ is 0 when the letters match, and 1 otherwise.

- **the noisy channel**: Pick the candidate c that is both common and a likely source of the typo w.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Don't compare against everything:** over a large dictionary, generate candidates first, using an index of character n-grams or precomputed deletions.

- **Stop early:** if you only care about distance 2 or less, you can compute a narrow band around the diagonal.

- **Use context:** "their" and "there" are both real words, so only a language model can pick between them.

- **Words, not letters:** run the same algorithm over words to get word error rate, the standard speech recognition metric.

- **Normalise first:** lowercase and strip accents if those differences don't matter to you. Divide by length to compare across string sizes.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The closest word is the right correction"

It sounds right, as fewer edits seems more likely. But several real words can be equally close, and a rare word shouldn't beat a common one. The noisy channel model weighs how common each word is and how likely the typo is, and context can settle cases like "form" and "from".

## Say it

### How do you measure how different two strings are, and how would you correct a misspelt word?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What is the edit distance between "sunday" and "saturday"?

3. Keep the s, insert a and t, keep u, substitute n with r, and keep d, a and y. The table gives the same answer, and shows nothing shorter exists.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you spell check against a million-word dictionary quickly?

Don't run the table against every word. Generate candidates with an index: for example, precompute all deletions within distance 2, or use a character n-gram index. Then score the candidates with edit distance and a language model.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why isn't edit distance enough for spelling correction?

Several real words can be equally close, and it ignores how common they are and what's around them. A typo near both "form" and "from" needs a language model to decide. That's what the noisy channel adds.

#### The 30-second answer

Edit distance is the fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another. I'd use dynamic programming: each cell is the minimum of the cell above plus 1, the cell to the left plus 1, and the diagonal plus 0 or 1, depending on whether the letters match. That's O(mn) time, and O(min(m, n)) memory if I only need the distance. A backtrace recovers the edits. For spelling correction, I'd use the noisy channel model: generate known words nearby, and choose the one that maximises P(word) times P(typo given word), using context where I can.

**Key terms and sources**

Levenshtein distance with dynamic programming, backtrace and alignment, Damerau transpositions, and the noisy channel model for spelling correction. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Norvig, How to Write a Spelling Corrector](https://norvig.com/spell-correct.html)

- [Levenshtein distance, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levenshtein_distance)

- [Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

# Subword Tokenisation (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)

> How do LLMs handle words they've never seen?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Language models and tokenisation
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/subword-tokenisation/
- Before this: Bag-of-Words, N-grams and TF-IDF (`fundamentals/bag-of-words-and-tf-idf`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your review model must handle "biryani", "biryanis" and words it has never seen. A word vocabulary turns unseen words into an unknown token, and characters make sequences 4–5 times longer. The interviewer asks:

> How do LLMs handle words they've never seen?

**Running example:** the review model must handle "biryani", "biryanis", "spiciest" and words it has never seen, without an "unknown word" token, and without turning every review into hundreds of characters.

#### Words are too many, characters too long

- **Word-level:** the vocabulary keeps growing (every name, typo and plural), and anything outside it becomes <unk>, losing information.

- **Character-level:** no unknowns and a tiny vocabulary, but sequences get 4–5× longer and the model must learn spelling from scratch. Attention cost grows with the square of length (self-attention).

- **Subwords:** a fixed vocabulary (e.g. 32k–100k pieces) where common words are single tokens and rare words decompose into reusable parts.

### The idea

Think of a box of building bricks. Common words get their own big brick, and a rare word is built from smaller ones. You can always build something, because the smallest bricks are always in the box.

[Figure: Biryani is one token. The unseen word biryanis becomes biryani, s and an end marker. The rare word unbelievably falls apart into nine small pieces.]

_From the lab, after 120 merges. _ marks the end of a word, and the rare word splits into 9 small pieces._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at 0 merges, then move to 40 and 120. Watch "biryani", the unseen "biryanis" and "unbelievably".

#### Watch the vocabulary grow, merge by merge

Corpus: words from 400 delivery reviews plus spelling variants (spicy / spicier / spiciest, deliver / delivered / delivery …), counted by frequency. Each chip is one token; _ marks the end of a word. Test words include ones never seen in the corpus.

With 0 merges every word is a string of characters: **5.3 tokens per word** on average. After 40 merges the most frequent words and pieces are merged first ("delivered" is already "deliver" + "e" + "d_"), and the average drops to 2.19. By **120 merges** (vocabulary 144) it is 1.05: "biryani" and "delivered" are single tokens, "spiciest" is two pieces, and the never-seen "biryanis" becomes "biryani" + "s" + "_". The rare, unseen "unbelievably" still falls apart into 9 small pieces: **no unknown tokens**, just more of them. Each extra merge helps rarer and rarer pairs, which is why vocabulary size trades sequence length against the size of the embedding table.

**Now say why:** why does each extra merge shorten sequences by less, and what does a bigger vocabulary cost you?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Word-level vocabularies can't handle new words ("biryanis", typos, names) and grow without limit; character-level input makes sequences very long. **Subword tokenisation** sits in between: frequent words stay whole, rare words are split into meaningful pieces ("spici" + "est"). **Byte-pair encoding (BPE)** starts from characters and repeatedly **merges the most frequent adjacent pair** into a new token until the vocabulary reaches a target size (GPT-2: 50,257). **WordPiece** (BERT) picks merges that most increase the training data's likelihood; the **unigram** model (SentencePiece) starts big and prunes. **Byte-level BPE** works on raw bytes, so any text can be encoded with no unknown tokens. Tokenisation decides how many tokens your text costs, and explains many LLM quirks. What you'll be able to do after this: run BPE by hand, compare BPE, WordPiece and unigram, and explain tokenisation effects in LLMs.

#### Byte-pair encoding, step by step

1. Split every word in the training corpus into characters, with an end-of-word marker (shown here as _).

2. Count every adjacent pair of symbols, weighted by word frequency.

3. Merge the most frequent pair everywhere into a new symbol and add it to the vocabulary.

4. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. To tokenise new text, apply the learned merges in the same order.

Gage (1994) introduced BPE for data compression; Sennrich, Haddow & Birch (ACL 2016) adapted it for neural machine translation of rare words [arXiv:1508.07909](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909). GPT-2 applies BPE to raw bytes with a 50,257-token vocabulary (Radford et al. 2019).

## In practice

### In practice

#### BPE, WordPiece, unigram, and bytes

| Method | How it builds the vocabulary | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| **BPE** | bottom-up: merge the most frequent adjacent pair | GPT-2/3/4 (byte-level), LLaMA 3 (tiktoken-style BPE) |
| **WordPiece** | bottom-up: merge the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training data under a language model | BERT (Schuster & Nakajima 2012; Wu et al. 2016) |
| **Unigram LM** | top-down: start with a large vocabulary and prune pieces that least reduce likelihood; can sample segmentations | T5, ALBERT, XLNet via SentencePiece (Kudo 2018) |
| **SentencePiece** | a library that implements BPE and unigram on raw text, treating spaces as a symbol (▁), language-independent | LLaMA 1/2, T5, many multilingual models |

Kudo & Richardson, EMNLP 2018 demo [arXiv:1808.06226](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226). Note: SentencePiece implements BPE and unigram, not WordPiece.

#### Tokenisation quirks you'll be asked about

- **Cost and context:** APIs bill and limit by tokens; English averages roughly 3–4 characters per token, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words.

- **Languages:** tokenisers trained mostly on English split Hindi, Tamil or Bengali text into many more tokens per word, making it slower and costlier for the same content.

- **Spelling and arithmetic:** a model sees "strawberry" as 2–3 tokens, not letters, which is why letter-counting and digit-by-digit arithmetic can fail.

- **Whitespace and case:** "Biryani", " biryani" and "biryani" can be different tokens.

- The tokeniser is fixed with the model: you can't swap it without retraining the embeddings.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "LLMs read words"

It sounds right, since words are what we type. But they read subword tokens, chosen by frequency and not by meaning. A model sees "strawberry" as 2–3 tokens rather than letters, which is why letter counting can fail. "Biryani" and " biryani" can be different tokens. And Hindi, Tamil or Bengali text can take many more tokens per word, so the same content costs more.

## Say it

### How do LLMs handle words they've never seen?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you pick the vocabulary size?

Bigger vocabularies shorten sequences but enlarge the embedding and output layers and leave rare tokens under-trained; LLMs typically use 32k–200k.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why byte-level instead of character-level BPE?

Unicode has over 100,000 characters; 256 byte values cover everything, so no input is ever out of vocabulary.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's a problem with tokenising numbers?

Numbers split inconsistently ("1234" vs "12" + "34"), hurting arithmetic; some tokenisers split digits individually.

#### The 30-second answer

Subword tokenisers balance word-level vocabularies, which can't handle unseen words, against characters, which make sequences too long. BPE starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair until reaching a target vocabulary, so common words become single tokens and rare words split into reusable pieces; byte-level BPE, as in GPT-2 with about 50k tokens, can encode any text with no unknowns. WordPiece, used by BERT, chooses merges by likelihood gain, and the unigram model in SentencePiece prunes a large vocabulary instead. Tokenisation affects cost, context length, multilingual fairness, and quirks like letter counting and arithmetic.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "LLMs read words." They read subword tokens.

- "BPE merges by meaning." It merges by frequency only.

**Key terms and sources**

Why modern models split text into subword pieces rather than whole words or characters; how byte-pair encoding learns its vocabulary by merging frequent pairs; WordPiece and the unigram model; byte-level BPE; and the practical consequences for LLMs (token counts, cost, multilingual text, arithmetic) · built from Gage (1994), Sennrich, Haddow & Birch (ACL 2016), Schuster & Nakajima (2012), Wu et al. (2016), Kudo (2018), Kudo & Richardson (2018) and Radford et al. (GPT-2, 2019) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. P. Gage, "A New Algorithm for Data Compression", _C Users Journal_ 12(2), 1994.

2. R. Sennrich, B. Haddow & A. Birch, "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units", ACL 2016, [arXiv:1508.07909](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909).

3. M. Schuster & K. Nakajima, "Japanese and Korean Voice Search", ICASSP 2012; Y. Wu et al., "Google's Neural Machine Translation System", [arXiv:1609.08144](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.08144), 2016.

4. T. Kudo, "Subword Regularization", ACL 2018, [arXiv:1804.10959](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.10959); T. Kudo & J. Richardson, "SentencePiece", EMNLP 2018, [arXiv:1808.06226](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226).

5. A. Radford et al., "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), OpenAI 2019.

# Sequence Labelling and NER

> BIO tags, CRFs, and why NER is scored with entity F1.

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/sequence-labelling-and-ner/
- Before this: Text Classification: Naive Bayes vs Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/text-classification`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

The app's chat parses "order 2 chicken biryani from Paradise Biryani House in Hyderabad at 8 pm" to place the order automatically. A review classifier gives one label per text, but here you need to know which words are the dish and which the restaurant. The interviewer asks:

> How do you label spans of text, and how should you score it?

**Running example:** the app's chat ordering parses "_order 2 chicken biryani from Paradise Biryani House in Hyderabad at 8 pm_" into QUANTITY, DISH, RESTAURANT, CITY and TIME, so the order can be placed automatically.

#### Labels for spans, not whole texts

A classifier gives one label per review. To place an order we need _which words_ are the dish and _which_ are the restaurant, and entities can be several words long ("Paradise Biryani House"), contain words that look like other entities ("Biryani" inside a restaurant name), or sit right next to each other.

### The idea

Think of marking a sentence with highlighters, one colour per entity type. B- is where you put the pen down. I- is where you keep going. Because every entity starts with a fresh B-, two neighbouring dishes stay two dishes.

[Figure: Paradise is tagged B-REST, Biryani and House are I-REST, in is O, and Hyderabad is B-CITY.]

_BIO tags from the lesson's order. Anything outside an entity is O._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between perfect, boundary errors, wrong types, missed one entity and predict all O. Compare token accuracy with entity F1.

#### Token accuracy vs entity F1

Gold vs predicted BIO tags for the 13-token order. Entity-level scoring (as in the CoNLL shared tasks): a predicted entity counts as correct only if its start, end and type all match a gold entity.

With two **boundary errors** (the model tags "biryani" but not "chicken", and "Paradise Biryani" but not "House"), token accuracy still says **77%**, yet two of the five entities are wrong, so entity F1 is only **0.60** (a missed TIME entity, by contrast, still gives 0.89): the order system would look up the wrong restaurant. Predicting **all O** scores 31% token accuracy here, and on real text, where most tokens are O, it can score over 80% while finding nothing. That's why NER is always reported as entity-level F1.

**Now say why:** with boundary errors, token accuracy still says 77%. Why is entity F1 only 0.60?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Many NLP tasks need a label for **every token**, not one for the whole text. **Part-of-speech tagging** labels nouns, verbs and so on; **named entity recognition (NER)** finds spans like dish names, restaurants, cities and times. Spans are turned into per-token labels with the **BIO** scheme: B- marks the beginning of an entity, I- the inside, O outside, so adjacent entities stay separate. Models went from HMMs and **CRFs** (which score whole label sequences, so "I-" can't follow "O") to **BiLSTM-CRF** and now fine-tuned **Transformers** with a classifier per token. NER is evaluated with **entity-level precision, recall and F1**: a span counts only if both its boundaries and type are exactly right. What you'll be able to do after this: convert spans to BIO tags, explain why a CRF layer helps, and compute entity-level F1.

#### The BIO scheme

| token | order | 2 | chicken | biryani | from | Paradise | Biryani | House | in | Hyderabad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| tag | O | B-QTY | B-DISH | I-DISH | O | B-REST | I-REST | I-REST | O | B-CITY |

- Each entity starts with **B-**; following tokens of the same entity get **I-**; everything else is **O**. With K entity types there are 2K + 1 labels.

- B- is what separates two adjacent entities of the same type: "add biryani raita" as two DISH entities is B-DISH B-DISH; a plain IO scheme would merge them into one.

- Variants: BIOES (also marks the End and Single-token entities). Ramshaw & Marcus (1995) introduced the IOB idea for chunking.

#### From independent guesses to whole-sequence models

- **Naive:** classify each token independently. It can output impossible sequences like O → I-REST (an "inside" with no beginning).

- **HMMs** and **CRFs** (Lafferty, McCallum & Pereira, ICML 2001) score the whole label sequence, including transitions between labels, and decode the best sequence with the Viterbi algorithm.

- **BiLSTM-CRF** (Lample et al., NAACL 2016) used neural features from both directions plus a CRF layer, reaching about 90.9 F1 on CoNLL-2003 English NER.

- **Today:** fine-tune BERT-style encoders with a token classifier (Devlin et al. 2019); subword tokens are labelled by their first piece. LLMs can also extract entities with a prompt and a JSON schema, useful when labelled data is scarce.

To see how whole sequences are decoded, read HMMs, CRFs and Viterbi.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Sequence labelling in practice

- **Information extraction:** pulling dishes, addresses, prices and times from chats, emails and receipts.

- **PII redaction:** tagging names, phone numbers and addresses before logs or training data are stored.

- **Search and query understanding:** "biryani near Koramangala under 300" → DISH, LOCATION, PRICE filters.

- **Benchmarks:** CoNLL-2003 (person, location, organisation, miscellaneous) is the classic English NER dataset (Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder 2003).

To go from names to facts, read Information Extraction.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Report token accuracy"

It sounds right, since every token gets a label and you can count the correct ones. But most tokens are O, so on real text, predicting all O can score over 80% while finding nothing. In the lab, two boundary errors still give 77% token accuracy, yet the system would look up the wrong restaurant. That's why NER is reported as entity-level F1.

## Say it

### How do you label spans of text, and how should you score it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you handle subword tokens in BERT NER?

Label only the first subword of each word (ignore the rest in the loss) and map predictions back to words.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does the CRF layer add on top of a neural tagger?

It learns transition scores between labels and decodes the best overall sequence, enforcing consistency like no I-DISH after O.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you do NER with very little labelled data?

Prompt an LLM with a schema and examples, use weak supervision (gazetteers, regexes), or label a small set and fine-tune a pre-trained encoder.

#### The 30-second answer

Sequence labelling assigns a label to every token, as in POS tagging or named entity recognition. Entity spans are encoded with BIO tags: B for the first token of an entity, I for the rest, O for outside, which keeps adjacent entities of the same type separate. Classic models are HMMs and CRFs, which score whole tag sequences and decode with Viterbi so invalid transitions like O to I are avoided; then BiLSTM-CRFs, and now fine-tuned BERT-style encoders with a per-token classifier, labelling the first subword. NER is evaluated with entity-level precision, recall and F1, where boundaries and type must match exactly, because token accuracy is inflated by all the O tokens.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Report token accuracy." It's dominated by O tokens.

- "IO tags are enough." They can't separate adjacent entities of the same type.

**Key terms and sources**

Assigning a label to every token: part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, the BIO tagging scheme, models from HMMs and CRFs to BiLSTM-CRF and fine-tuned Transformers, and why NER is scored with entity-level F1 rather than token accuracy · built from Ramshaw & Marcus (1995), Lafferty et al. (2001), Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder (CoNLL-2003), Lample et al. (2016), Devlin et al. (2019) and Jurafsky & Martin (SLP3, ch. 18) · checked 29 Oct 2026

# HMMs, CRFs and the Viterbi Algorithm

> How do you find the best label for every word at once, and how do HMMs and CRFs differ?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/hmms-crfs-and-viterbi/
- Before this: Sequence Labelling and NER (`fundamentals/sequence-labelling-and-ner`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your tagger labels each word on its own. It reads "order" as a noun in "order the cold biryani", and sometimes outputs an I-DISH tag with no B-DISH before it. You need the best tags for the sentence as a whole. The interviewer asks:

> How do you find the best label for every word at once, and how do HMMs and CRFs differ?

#### Why it matters

Sequence labelling mentions these models, and interviewers often go further: write the Viterbi recursion, or say what a CRF adds to a tagger. Viterbi is also a good example of dynamic programming that's used well beyond language, in speech and in decoding signals.

### The idea

Think of the shortest route across a city. To find the best way to any junction, you only need the best way to each junction before it. You don't have to remember every route. Viterbi does this with tags: at each word, it keeps the best path into each tag.

[Figure: Three ideas. HMMs model tag transitions and word emissions. Viterbi finds the best sequence. CRFs model tags given all the words.]

_Best sequence, without checking every sequence._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the trust in transitions to 0. Then try each sentence.

#### Decode a sentence

Illustrative, hand-set probabilities for 4 tags: N noun, V verb, A adjective, D determiner. Each cell shows the Viterbi score. Green marks the best path. Exact calculation.

Set the trust in transitions to **0**: Viterbi now matches each word alone, because no context remains. Raise it again, and "order" becomes a verb, as sentences often start with one here. In **the cold arrived**, "cold" becomes a noun, since an adjective rarely comes directly before a verb.

**Now say why:** why does "cold" change tag in "the cold arrived"?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Labels depend on their neighbours, so choosing each word's label alone can give nonsense. An **HMM** models tag-to-tag transitions and tag-to-word emissions. The **Viterbi algorithm** finds the best whole sequence with dynamic programming, in O(T·S²) rather than ST. A **CRF** keeps the sequence scoring, but models P(tags | words) directly, so it can use any features of the input. In neural versions, a network supplies the scores, and Viterbi still decodes them.

#### From HMMs to CRFs

##### Hidden Markov models

An HMM imagines that hidden tags generate the words. It has two tables, both estimated by counting on labelled text:

- **Transitions:** how likely each tag follows another. An adjective is often followed by a noun.

- **Emissions:** how likely a tag produces a given word. A verb might produce "order".

##### Three classic questions

| Question | Algorithm | Combines paths using |
|---|---|---|
| **Decoding:** what's the best tag sequence? | Viterbi | Maximum |
| **Likelihood:** how probable are these words? | Forward | Sum |
| **Learning:** what if there are no tags? | Baum-Welch, a form of EM | Expected counts |

##### Why Viterbi is fast

With S tags and T words, there are ST possible sequences. But the best path to a tag at step t only needs the best paths to every tag at step t − 1, so we never need to look at the rest. That's S² work per word. For 4 tags and 30 words, this is 480 steps rather than about 1018 sequences.

##### HMM or CRF?

| | HMM | Linear-chain CRF |
|---|---|---|
| Models | P(tags, words), generative | P(tags \| words), discriminative |
| Features | Only the current word, given its tag | Anything: capitals, suffixes, neighbouring words |
| Training | Counting | Gradient-based, slower |
| Decoding | Viterbi | Viterbi |

A CRF normalises over all possible tag sequences. Summing them is what the forward algorithm does, so training stays practical.

##### Neural CRFs, and when to skip them

In a BiLSTM-CRF, the network gives each word a score for each tag, and the CRF adds transition scores. Lample et al. reached an F1 of 90.94 on CoNLL-2003, and removing the CRF layer cost them 1.79 points. Later, BERT reached 92.8 with a per-token classifier and no CRF. Strong context can reduce the benefit, though a CRF or a simple rule can still prevent impossible sequences.

#### The maths

$$ {P(t, w)} = \prod_{i} {P(t_i \mid t_{i-1})}\, {P(w_i \mid t_i)}, \qquad {v_i(s)} = \max_{r}\, {v_{i-1}(r)}\, P(s \mid r)\, P(w_i \mid s) $$

Standard HMM forms, as in the Viterbi article and Jurafsky and Martin’s appendix on HMMs. In practice, sum logs to avoid underflow.

- **the joint probability**: How likely this tag sequence and these words are together.

- **a transition**: How likely this tag is to follow the previous one.

- **an emission**: How likely this tag is to produce this word.

- **the Viterbi score**: The best probability of any path that ends in tag s at word i.

- **reuse earlier work**: The best scores from the previous word. Keep a pointer to the winning tag, to rebuild the path at the end.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Use logs:** multiplying many small probabilities underflows, so add log scores.

- **Block impossible sequences:** setting the O → I-DISH transition to zero prevents invalid tags, even without a learned CRF.

- **Handle unknown words:** HMMs need smoothing or word-shape rules. CRFs handle this better through features.

- **Try without a CRF first:** on a strong encoder, measure whether it adds enough to justify the extra code and compute.

- **Remember Viterbi's limit:** the highest-scoring sequence isn't always the sequence with the most correct labels. It's just a good default.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Picking the best tag for each word gives the best sequence"

It sounds right, as each choice is individually the best. But good local choices can combine into an unlikely or invalid sequence, and the best sequence may need a weaker label on one word. Viterbi looks at the sequence as a whole, without needing to list every option.

## Say it

### How do you find the best label for every word at once, and how do HMMs and CRFs differ?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the difference between Viterbi and the forward algorithm?

They have the same structure. Viterbi takes the maximum over previous tags, to find the single best path. Forward takes the sum, to get the total probability of the words across all paths. Forward is also needed to train CRFs.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does a CRF add on top of a neural tagger?

Scores for moving between tags, and decoding of the whole sequence together. So it can learn that I-DISH doesn't follow O. How much it helps depends on the encoder. It helped a BiLSTM by 1.79 F1 in one study, while BERT did well without it.

Follow-up 3 of 3

With 10 tags and 20 words, how much faster is Viterbi than brute force?

Brute force checks 10²⁰ sequences. Viterbi does 20 × 10² = 2,000 steps. The saving comes from keeping only the best path into each tag at each word.

#### The 30-second answer

Labelling each word alone ignores its neighbours, and can give invalid sequences. An HMM models tag transitions and word emissions, and the Viterbi algorithm finds the best sequence with dynamic programming. Each cell keeps the best score for ending in a tag, plus a pointer, so it costs T times S squared, not S to the T. The forward algorithm replaces max with sum, to get the likelihood. A CRF models tags given words directly, so it can use rich features, and it still decodes with Viterbi. In neural taggers, the network gives the scores, and a CRF layer can add transitions.

**Key terms and sources**

Why labelling words one at a time fails, hidden Markov models, the Viterbi algorithm, forward and Baum-Welch, conditional random fields and neural CRFs. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Lample et al., Neural Architectures for Named Entity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.01360)

- [Devlin et al., BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)

# BERT and Masked Language Models

> How is BERT trained, and how do you adapt it for classification, tagging and question answering?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/bert-and-masked-language-models/
- Before this: Sequence Labelling and NER (`fundamentals/sequence-labelling-and-ner`), Encoder vs Decoder vs Encoder-Decoder (`fundamentals/encoder-decoder-architectures`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

You need to tag support tickets and pull out answers from policy documents, for millions of messages a day. An LLM works, but costs too much at this volume. Someone suggests fine-tuning BERT, but a teammate asks how a model trained on no labels can help. The interviewer asks:

> How is BERT trained, and how do you adapt it for classification, tagging and question answering?

#### Why it matters

BERT-style encoders still power classification, tagging, embeddings and re-ranking, as they're smaller and cheaper than LLMs. Interview questions often cover how the masking works and how the heads attach. This builds on encoders and decoders.

### The idea

Think of a fill-in-the-blanks test. To guess the missing word in "the biryani was ___ but the raita was fresh", you must understand the whole sentence, on both sides of the gap. Practise on billions of these, and you learn language. Then you can quickly learn a new job, like sorting tickets.

[Figure: Three stages. Pretrain by filling masked tokens. Add a small head for your task. Fine-tune gently.]

_Bidirectional context suits understanding, not generating._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the share chosen to 50%. Then draw again.

#### Mask a sentence

An illustrative pair of sentences, split by word for simplicity. Special tokens aren't masked. Orange: [MASK]. Purple: a random token. Green: chosen, but unchanged. The model must predict the original word at all three.

Draw again a few times: the choice is random, and it changes the input every time it's drawn. Raise the share to **50%**: the task gets much harder, with less context around each gap. Any green tokens look normal, yet they're still scored, so the model must be useful everywhere, rather than only at [MASK].

**Now say why:** why are some chosen tokens left unchanged?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**BERT** is a Transformer encoder trained on unlabelled text by hiding words and predicting them. It masks 15% of tokens: 80% of those become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% stay as they are. Because it sees both sides of each word, it learns rich context, but it can't naturally generate text. To use it, you add a small head for your task, and fine-tune with a low learning rate. Classification uses [CLS], NER labels each token, and QA predicts where the answer starts and ends.

#### Training it, then using it

##### The input

A pair of sentences becomes `[CLS] sentence A [SEP] sentence B [SEP]`. Each token's vector is the sum of three learned embeddings: token, segment (A or B) and position.

| Size | Layers | Width | Heads | Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BERT-base | 12 | 768 | 12 | 110 million |
| BERT-large | 24 | 1,024 | 16 | 340 million |

##### Two training tasks

- **Masked language modelling:** predict the hidden tokens. The random and unchanged cases stop the model simply learning that [MASK] means "predict here".

- **Next sentence prediction:** half the time B really follows A, and half the time it's a random sentence. RoBERTa later removed this task, and found that results matched or slightly improved.

##### Heads for each task

| Task | Head | Reported result |
|---|---|---|
| **Classification** | A classifier on [CLS] | – |
| **Entailment** | The same, with both sentences as input | – |
| **NER** | A classifier on each word's first sub-token, with no CRF | 92.8 F1 on CoNLL-2003 with BERT-large. |
| **Question answering** | Start and end scores for each token | 93.2 test F1 on SQuAD v1.1, using an ensemble. |

**Entailment** asks whether one sentence follows from another: entailment, contradiction or neutral. SNLI has about 570,000 labelled pairs. **SQuAD** asks for an answer that's a span of the passage, so it can be found by choosing the best start and end positions.

##### BERT or GPT-style?

| | BERT | GPT-style |
|---|---|---|
| Attention | Both directions | Only earlier tokens |
| Trained to | Fill in masked tokens | Predict the next token |
| Best for | Understanding: labels, spans, embeddings | Generating text |

##### Variants

- **RoBERTa:** trained longer, on more data with bigger batches, with no next sentence task and with masks that change each time. It found BERT "was significantly undertrained".

- **DistilBERT:** distilled to be 40% smaller and 60% faster, keeping 97% of the performance on their benchmark.

#### The maths

$$ {E_i = E_{\text{token}} + E_{\text{segment}} + E_{\text{position}}}, \qquad {L = -\sum_{i \in \text{masked}} \log P(w_i \mid \text{context})}, \qquad {\text{span} = \arg\max_{j \ge i}\ S\cdot T_i + E\cdot T_j} $$

From Devlin et al. The loss form is the standard description of masked language modelling.

- **the input**: Three learned embeddings, added for each token.

- **the masking loss**: Cross-entropy, only on the positions chosen for masking.

- **the QA span**: Learned start and end vectors S and E score each output T. Choose the best pair, with the end not before the start.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Fine-tuning settings:** the paper suggests batch sizes of 16 or 32, learning rates from 2e-5 to 5e-5, and 2 to 4 epochs.

- **Align labels with sub-tokens:** for NER, label each word's first piece, and ignore the rest in the loss.

- **Handle long documents:** position embeddings stop at a fixed length, usually 512. Use overlapping windows, and combine the results.

- **BERT or an LLM?** With good labels and high volume, a fine-tuned encoder is usually cheaper and faster. With no labels, or a task that keeps changing, try an LLM first.

- **Start small:** try DistilBERT or BERT-base before anything larger, and compare against TF-IDF plus logistic regression.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "LLMs have made BERT obsolete"

It sounds right, as LLMs do more. But a fine-tuned encoder can be far cheaper and faster for one fixed task at high volume, and its behaviour is easier to measure. They also remain common for embeddings and re-ranking. Choose using your labels, volume and cost.

## Say it

### How is BERT trained, and how do you adapt it for classification, tagging and question answering?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why replace some chosen tokens with random ones, or leave them unchanged?

If every target were [MASK], the model could rely on the [MASK] token to know where to predict, and pay less attention elsewhere. Mixing the cases means it must hold a good representation for every token. The random and unchanged cases are 10% each of the chosen tokens.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How does BERT answer a question from a passage?

The input is the question, [SEP], then the passage. Learned vectors score each token as a possible start and end. You choose the highest scoring pair where the end isn't before the start. So it can only answer with text that's in the passage.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why can't BERT generate text the way GPT does?

It's trained with attention in both directions, so it never learned to predict from left context only. You could fill masks repeatedly, but it's slow and works poorly. GPT-style models are trained with a causal mask for exactly this.

#### The 30-second answer

BERT is a Transformer encoder pretrained by masking. It selects 15% of tokens, replaces 80% of those with [MASK], 10% with a random token and leaves 10% unchanged, and predicts the originals. It also originally predicted whether one sentence followed another, though RoBERTa showed this wasn't needed. Each token's input adds token, segment and position embeddings. To use it, I add a head and fine-tune at about 2e-5 to 5e-5, for 2 to 4 epochs: a classifier on [CLS] for classification and entailment, per-token for NER, and start and end scores for QA. It's bidirectional, so it suits understanding rather than generation.

**Key terms and sources**

Masked language modelling, CLS and SEP tokens, segment embeddings, next sentence prediction, task heads for classification, NER, QA and entailment, and later variants. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Devlin et al., BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)

- [Liu et al., RoBERTa](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.11692)

- [Sanh et al., DistilBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01108)

- [Bowman et al., SNLI](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

- [Rajpurkar et al., SQuAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05250)

- [Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

# Information Extraction: Relations, Coreference and Entity Linking

> How do you turn messy text into structured facts, and how far do LLMs replace this work?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/information-extraction/
- Before this: Sequence Labelling and NER (`fundamentals/sequence-labelling-and-ner`), BERT and Masked Language Models (`fundamentals/bert-and-masked-language-models`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have thousands of restaurant descriptions, and you want a table of who owns what, where and since when. A simple pattern gets some facts, but marks "It" as a restaurant and treats two names for one place as separate. The interviewer asks:

> How do you turn messy text into structured facts, and how far do LLMs replace this work?

#### Why it matters

Companies hold huge amounts of text, and they want to search it, count it and join it with tables. This is behind knowledge graphs, contract and invoice processing, and better retrieval. It extends NER from names to facts.

### The idea

Think of a detective reading statements. They note who's named, work out who "he" and "she" refer to, match names against known records, and write down what connects whom. Miss one step, and the case file has the wrong person in it.

[Figure: Three linked steps. Coreference resolves pronouns. Entity linking finds the record. Relation extraction finds the fact.]

_Mistakes at each step pass to the next._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Tick each step alone. Then tick both.

#### Run the pipeline

_"Spice Route opened in Hyderabad in 2010. It serves biryani. Spice Route Kitchen later moved to Pune. Its founder is Meera Rao."_

A made-up restaurant, with a hand-written example of what a simple pattern-based extractor returns. A fact is correct only if subject, relation and object all match.

Tick each step on its own, then both. Neither is enough alone, as they fix different mistakes. Coreference alone resolves "Its" to the nearest name, Spice Route Kitchen, which still isn't the main record. That's how an error at one step can become a wrong fact later.

**Now say why:** why isn't coreference alone enough here?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

**Information extraction** turns text into structured facts, like (Spice Route, opened in, Hyderabad). NER finds the names. **Coreference** works out that "it" means Spice Route. **Entity linking** connects a name to one record in a database. **Relation extraction** finds how entities are connected. Each step's mistakes pass to the next. LLMs with a schema are now a fast way to start, but they still need checking, and specialised models can do better on some benchmarks.

#### The pipeline

| Step | Question | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **NER** | What are the names? | Spice Route, Hyderabad, 2010 |
| **Coreference** | Which mentions mean the same thing? | "It" means Spice Route |
| **Entity linking** | Which real-world record is it? | "Spice Route Kitchen" is record #4821 |
| **Relation extraction** | How are they connected? | (Spice Route, opened in, Hyderabad) |

##### Relation extraction: four approaches

| Approach | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Patterns** | Rules like "X opened in Y". | Precise and explainable, with low recall. |
| **Supervised** | Train a classifier on labelled sentences. | Accurate, but labelling is expensive. |
| **Distant supervision** | Take facts from a database. Label sentences that mention both entities. | Cheap and large, but noisy. |
| **LLM with a schema** | Ask for JSON in a fixed format. | Fast to start. Needs checks on cost and accuracy. |

Distant supervision's problem: a sentence mentioning both a founder and their company might not say that they founded it.

##### Coreference

Older systems had several steps. Lee et al. instead consider every span as a possible mention, and learn which earlier span it refers to, reaching a gain of 1.5 F1 on OntoNotes. It stays hard, because it can need world knowledge: in "the trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", "it" means the trophy.

##### Entity linking

"Paris" may be a city or a person. BLINK works in two stages, like search: a bi-encoder quickly retrieves candidates, and a cross-encoder re-ranks them. It linked against 5.9 million candidates in 2 milliseconds, and can handle entities it never saw in training, because it reads their descriptions.

##### How far do LLMs replace this?

Prompted LLMs need no labelled data and handle new relations easily. But Han et al. reported "a visible performance gap between GPT-4 and state-of-the-art (SOTA) IE methods" on standard benchmarks. A common approach is to prototype with an LLM, check it on labelled examples, and move high-volume stable tasks to a smaller model if it pays off.

#### The maths

$$ {P = \frac{|\text{predicted} \cap \text{gold}|}{|\text{predicted}|}}, \quad {R = \frac{|\text{predicted} \cap \text{gold}|}{|\text{gold}|}}, \qquad {s(i,j) = s_m(i) + s_m(j) + s_a(i,j)} $$

A fact usually counts only if subject, relation and object all match. The coreference score is the form used by Lee et al.

- **fact-level precision**: The share of extracted facts that are correct.

- **fact-level recall**: The share of true facts that were found.

- **a coreference score**: Is span i a mention? Is span j? Could j be what i refers to? The model picks the best earlier span.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Define the schema first:** decide on entities, relations and allowed values, and add examples of what doesn't count.

- **Label a small test set:** even with an LLM, you need labelled documents to measure accuracy.

- **Measure fact-level F1:** report by relation, and look at errors at each step of the pipeline.

- **Keep the evidence:** store the source sentence with each fact, so people can check it.

- **Check LLM output:** use structured output for the format, but a valid format doesn't mean the facts are right. Validate against the source and your database.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The LLM returned valid JSON, so extraction is solved"

It sounds right, as the output looks clean. But a schema only guarantees the format, and values can still be invented or attached to the wrong entity. Measure field-level accuracy on labelled documents, keep the source sentence, and check that it really appears in the text.

## Say it

### How do you turn messy text into structured facts, and how far do LLMs replace this work?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the distant supervision assumption, and why is it weak?

It assumes that if a database says two entities have a relation, a sentence mentioning both expresses it. Many such sentences don't, so labels are noisy. Methods treat this as learning from groups of sentences, where at least one should express the relation.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How is entity linking like search?

A mention is the query, and the database is the collection. BLINK retrieves candidates with a bi-encoder, and re-ranks with a cross-encoder, which mirrors retrieval and re-ranking. Reading entity descriptions also allows it to link new entities.

Follow-up 3 of 3

You extract contracts with an LLM, and the JSON is always valid. Is it accurate?

Not necessarily. A schema only guarantees the format. Values can still be invented or wrong. Compare with a labelled set by field, require a supporting quote, check it appears in the document, and send low-confidence cases to people.

#### The 30-second answer

Information extraction turns text into structured facts. NER finds names, coreference connects "it" to its antecedent, entity linking maps names to database records, and relation extraction finds the links between them. For relations, I can use patterns, supervised models, distant supervision or an LLM with a schema. Distant supervision is cheap, but noisy, because mentioning two entities doesn't mean stating a relation. I'd start with an LLM and a strict schema, measure fact-level precision and recall on a labelled set, and keep the source sentence for checking. For a high-volume stable task, I'd consider a smaller trained model.

**Key terms and sources**

Relation extraction, distant supervision, coreference resolution, entity linking, how to evaluate extracted facts, and using LLMs with a schema. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Lee et al., End-to-end Neural Coreference Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.07045)

- [Wu et al., BLINK: Scalable Zero-shot Entity Linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03814)

- [Han et al., An Empirical Study on Information Extraction using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14450)

- [Jurafsky and Martin, chapter 21: Information Extraction](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/21.pdf)

- [Jurafsky and Martin, chapter 24: Coreference and Entity Linking](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/24.pdf)

# Search: BM25, Dense and Hybrid Retrieval

> Why does RAG search miss exact names, and how does hybrid fix it?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/search-and-retrieval/
- Before this: Bag-of-Words, N-grams and TF-IDF (`fundamentals/bag-of-words-and-tf-idf`), Embeddings and Representation Learning (`fundamentals/embeddings`)
- Related: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

The app's search box gets exact names like "paradise biryani", vague cravings like "fiery rice dish" and mixtures of both. A teammate says to replace keyword search with embeddings, since they understand meaning. The interviewer asks:

> Why does search miss exact names, and how does hybrid fix it?

**Running example:** the app's search box over 12 restaurant listings. Customers type exact names ("paradise biryani"), vague cravings ("fiery rice dish") and mixtures ("cheesy pizza late night").

#### Rank millions of documents in milliseconds

Comparing a query against every document with a large model is far too slow for a search box or a RAG pipeline. Retrieval needs an index that returns the top few dozen candidates almost instantly, and those candidates must contain the right answer, because later stages (re-rankers, the LLM) can only work with what retrieval hands them.

### The idea

Think of two librarians. One checks the catalogue for your exact words: great for a name, useless if you say "fiery" and the book says "spicy". The other understands what you're after but is hazy on exact names. So you ask both and merge their lists.

[Figure: For the query bawarchi biryani, Bawarchi ranks first with BM25, third with dense and second with hybrid. For fiery rice dish, BM25 finds none of the three spicy rice places, while dense and hybrid each find two.]

_Results from the lab, on 12 listings. The dense vectors are hand-built stand-ins for a trained model._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Run "bawarchi biryani", then "fiery rice dish", then the mixed query, comparing the three columns. Then change BM25's k₁ and b.

#### BM25 vs dense vs hybrid on 12 listings

Each column: the top 3 results; green = relevant. Dense vectors come from a small hand-built concept map (rice, spicy, cheese, late-night…) standing in for a trained embedding model (illustrative). Hybrid = reciprocal rank fusion of the BM25 and dense rankings with k = 60.

For the exact name **"bawarchi biryani"**, BM25 ranks Bawarchi first: the rare word "bawarchi" carries the score (MRR 1.00). Dense retrieval only "sees" biryani and ranks it **third**, behind the listing that is purest biryani (MRR 0.33). For **"fiery rice dish"** it's the reverse: BM25 matches only the word "rice", in Royal Pulao's "jeera rice", and finds **none** of the three spicy rice places (recall@3 0%), while dense retrieval maps fiery → spicy and rice dish → biryani / pulao and finds two of three. **Hybrid** is never the worst: Bawarchi stays in its top 3 (rank 2) and it keeps dense's 67% on the craving query. That robustness, rather than winning every query, is why hybrid is the common default for RAG. (Drag b to 0 to switch off length normalisation and watch the long Paradise listing gain score.)

**Now say why:** why does each method fail on the other's query, and why is hybrid never the worst?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Retrieval ranks documents by relevance to a query, and it's the first step of search engines and **RAG**. **Sparse** retrieval matches exact words through an **inverted index**; its standard scoring function, **BM25**, is TF-IDF with two fixes: repeated words **saturate** (k₁) and long documents are **normalised** (b). It's fast, needs no training and is great for exact names, codes and rare terms, but it misses synonyms. **Dense** retrieval embeds queries and documents into vectors and finds nearest neighbours, so "fiery rice dish" can match "spicy biryani", but it can blur exact names. **Hybrid** search combines both, often with **reciprocal rank fusion**, and a **re-ranker** (cross-encoder) can re-score the top results. What you'll be able to do after this: compute a BM25 score, explain k₁ and b, choose between sparse, dense and hybrid retrieval, and evaluate with recall@k and MRR.

#### BM25: TF-IDF that saturates and normalises

$$ \mathrm{BM25}(q,d) = \sum_{t\in q} {\mathrm{IDF}(t)}\cdot {\frac{f(t,d)\,(k_1+1)}{f(t,d) + k_1\big(1 - b + b\,{\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}}\big)}} $$

Robertson & Zaragoza, "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond", _Foundations and Trends in IR_ 3(4), 2009. BM25 is the default similarity in Lucene / Elasticsearch / OpenSearch. TF-IDF: TF-IDF lesson.

- **IDF**: Rare query words count more, as in TF-IDF. BM25 uses log(1 + (N − df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5)).

- **saturating term frequency**: More occurrences help, but with diminishing returns: the score approaches (k₁ + 1) instead of growing forever. k₁ ≈ 1.2–2.

- **length normalisation**: Long documents mention everything more often, so their term counts are discounted relative to the average length. b = 0 turns this off, b = 1 is full normalisation; 0.75 is typical.

#### Dense retrieval: match meaning, not words

- Encode every document once into a vector with a sentence embedding model; at query time, embed the query and return the nearest vectors (cosine / dot product) using an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, IVF-PQ).

- Encoders are trained contrastively on (question, relevant passage) pairs; DPR (Karpukhin et al. 2020) beat BM25 by 9–19 points in top-20 passage accuracy on open-domain QA.

- **The trap:** dense models trained on one domain can underperform BM25 elsewhere. On the BEIR benchmark of 18 datasets, BM25 was a strong zero-shot baseline that many dense retrievers failed to beat out of domain (Thakur et al. 2021). Exact names, product codes and rare terms are especially hard for embeddings.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and metrics

$$ {\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r\in\text{rankers}} \frac{1}{k + \mathrm{rank}_r(d)}} $$

- **reciprocal rank fusion**: Add up 1 / (k + rank) for each document across the rankings being fused. Only ranks are used, so BM25 scores and cosine similarities don’t need to be on the same scale. k = 60 is the usual constant (Cormack et al. 2009).

- **Re-ranking:** a cross-encoder reads query and document together and re-scores the top 50–100 candidates; much more accurate, too slow for the whole corpus (Nogueira & Cho 2019).

- **Metrics:** recall@k (did a relevant document make the top k?), MRR (1 / rank of the first relevant result, averaged over queries), nDCG (graded relevance with position discount; ranking metrics).

- **For RAG:** recall@k of the retriever caps answer quality: the LLM can't use a passage it never sees.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Dense retrieval has replaced BM25"

It sounds right, since matching meaning seems strictly better than matching words. But on the BEIR benchmark of 18 datasets, many dense retrievers failed to beat BM25 out of domain, and exact names and product codes are especially hard for embeddings. Hybrid is standard. And measure retrieval recall by itself, because the LLM can't use a passage it never sees.

## Say it

### Why does search miss exact names, and how does hybrid fix it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What do k₁ and b do?

k₁ controls how quickly repeated occurrences stop adding score (k₁ = 0 means presence only); b controls how much long documents are penalised (b = 0 none, b = 1 full).

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why fuse ranks rather than scores?

BM25 scores are unbounded and query-dependent while cosine similarities are in [−1, 1]; ranks are comparable without calibration.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?

A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately (precomputable, fast); a cross-encoder reads them together (more accurate, must run per pair), so it's used for re-ranking.

#### The 30-second answer

Sparse retrieval uses an inverted index and BM25, which is TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation controlled by k1 and document-length normalisation controlled by b; it's fast, training-free and excellent for exact names, codes and rare terms, but blind to synonyms. Dense retrieval embeds queries and documents with a contrastively trained encoder and does approximate nearest-neighbour search, so it matches meaning, but it can miss exact terms and degrade out of domain, where BM25 is often stronger. In practice I'd use hybrid search, fusing the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion, then a cross-encoder re-ranker on the top candidates, and measure recall@k, MRR or nDCG.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Dense retrieval has replaced BM25." Hybrid is standard; BM25 remains a strong baseline.

- "Evaluate retrieval with the final answer only." Measure retrieval recall separately.

**Key terms and sources**

Finding the right documents for a query: the inverted index, BM25 (TF-IDF with saturation and length normalisation), dense retrieval with embeddings, why each fails on different queries, hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, re-ranking, and retrieval metrics · built from Robertson & Zaragoza (2009), Manning et al. (2008), Karpukhin et al. (DPR, EMNLP 2020), Thakur et al. (BEIR, NeurIPS 2021), Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher (SIGIR 2009) and Nogueira & Cho (2019) · checked 29 Oct 2026
