# NLP Evaluation: BLEU, ROUGE, EM/F1

> Why can word salad beat a correct paraphrase on BLEU?

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/nlp-evaluation-metrics/
- Before this: Text Classification: Naive Bayes vs Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/text-classification`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

## Intuition

### The situation

The support bot summarises complaints, and you score it automatically against human summaries. A correct paraphrase gets BLEU 0.29, and a word salad gets 0.36. So does a summary saying the opposite of the complaint. The interviewer asks:

> How do you score generated text, and what do these metrics miss?

**Running example:** the support bot summarises a complaint. The human reference summary is "_the biryani arrived cold and late_". How do we score the bot's different summaries automatically?

#### Many right answers, no single label

A classifier is either right or wrong. Generated text has many valid versions: "the biryani was delivered late and cold" says the same thing as the reference in different words. Human judgement is the gold standard but slow and expensive, so we need cheap automatic scores to compare systems during development, and we must know what they miss.

### The idea

Think of a teacher marking essays by counting the words that match the answer key. Shuffle the key and you score well. Write a correct answer in your own words and you lose marks. The count measures shared words, not shared meaning.

[Figure: Sentence BLEU against the reference. The correct paraphrase scores 0.29. Word salad and the summary with the opposite meaning both score 0.36.]

_Sentence BLEU from the lab, with add-1 smoothing for 2- to 4-grams._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Go through identical, paraphrase, word salad, too short and wrong meaning. Compare BLEU, ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L on each.

#### Five candidate summaries, one reference

Reference: "the biryani arrived cold and late". Candidates: identical; "the biryani was delivered late and cold"; "late cold and the arrived biryani"; "biryani cold"; "the biryani arrived hot and on time". Sentence BLEU with add-1 smoothing for 2- to 4-grams.

The **correct paraphrase** gets BLEU **0.29** and ROUGE-L 0.46: it uses different words in a different order. The **word salad**, the reference's words shuffled into nonsense, scores _higher_: BLEU **0.36**, and a perfect ROUGE-1 and token F1 of **1.00**, because unigram metrics ignore order. Worst of all, "the biryani arrived **hot and on time**", the _opposite_ of the complaint, scores BLEU 0.36 and ROUGE-L **0.62**, beating the correct paraphrase on both. "biryani cold" is cut down by the brevity penalty (0.14). Overlap metrics measure shared words, not shared meaning.

**Now say why:** why does word salad get a perfect ROUGE-1 and token F1?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Classic NLP metrics compare a model's output with one or more human **references** by counting overlapping words. **BLEU** (machine translation) is a precision: what fraction of the output's 1- to 4-grams appear in the reference, clipped so repeating a word doesn't help, times a **brevity penalty** for outputs that are too short. **ROUGE** (summarisation) leans on recall: ROUGE-1/2 count unigram/bigram overlap, **ROUGE-L** uses the longest common subsequence. Extractive QA uses **exact match** and **token F1**; language models use perplexity. All overlap metrics share one weakness: they reward the **same words**, not the **same meaning**. A correct paraphrase can score lower than word salad, which is why embedding-based scores, LLM judges and human evaluation are used alongside them. What you'll be able to do after this: compute BLEU, ROUGE and token F1, pick a metric per task, and explain what overlap metrics can't measure.

#### BLEU: clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty

$$ \mathrm{BLEU} = {\mathrm{BP}}\cdot {\exp\Big(\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{4}\tfrac14 \log}{p_n}{\Big)}, \qquad \mathrm{BP} = \begin{cases}1 & c > r\\ e^{1-r/c} & c \le r\end{cases} $$

Papineni, Roukos, Ward & Zhu, ACL 2002. BLEU was designed for corpus-level scoring with multiple references; sentence-level scores are noisy. Use SacreBLEU for comparable, reproducible numbers (Post 2018).

- **brevity penalty**: 1 if the candidate is longer than the reference, otherwise exp(1 − r/c). Stops a model from scoring high precision by outputting two safe words.

- **clipped n-gram precisions**: For n = 1…4: matching n-grams ÷ n-grams in the candidate, where each n-gram’s count is clipped to its count in the reference.

- **geometric mean**: Average the log-precisions: if any order has zero matches, unsmoothed BLEU is 0, so sentence-level BLEU is usually smoothed.

- **ROUGE-N** (Lin 2004): n-gram overlap, usually reported as recall or F1; ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 are standard for summarisation.

- **ROUGE-L:** F-measure based on the longest common subsequence, which rewards words appearing in the same order without requiring them to be adjacent.

- **Exact match / token F1** (SQuAD, Rajpurkar et al. 2016): EM is 1 only for an identical normalised answer; F1 gives partial credit for overlapping tokens.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Measuring meaning

- **Embedding-based:** BERTScore matches each token to its most similar reference token using contextual embeddings, so paraphrases score well (Zhang et al., ICLR 2020).

- **LLM-as-a-judge:** a strong LLM rates outputs against a rubric or compares two outputs; it agrees with human preferences reasonably well but has position and verbosity biases (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023).

- **Task metrics:** for RAG, faithfulness and answer relevance; for code, unit tests pass@k; for classification-like outputs, accuracy or F1.

- **Human evaluation** remains the final check for fluency, correctness and helpfulness; Callison-Burch et al. (2006) showed BLEU improvements don't always mean better translations.

#### Which metric

| Task | Standard metric | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| Machine translation | BLEU (SacreBLEU), chrF, COMET | corpus-level only; tokenisation changes BLEU |
| Summarisation | ROUGE-1/2/L | rewards copying; check faithfulness separately |
| Extractive QA | exact match, token F1 | normalise case, punctuation, articles first |
| Language modelling | perplexity | only comparable with the same tokeniser |
| NER / tagging | entity-level F1 (NER lesson) | not token accuracy |
| Open-ended generation | LLM-as-judge, human eval, BERTScore | judge biases; validate against humans |

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A higher BLEU means a better system"

It sounds right, since a higher score ought to mean a closer match. But in the lab, the summary with the opposite meaning beats the correct paraphrase on BLEU and ROUGE-L. And small BLEU differences often don't match human judgement. Nor does ROUGE measure factual correctness, so check faithfulness separately.

## Say it

### How do you score generated text, and what do these metrics miss?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is BLEU precision-based and ROUGE recall-based?

Translation should not add content that isn't in the reference (precision); a summary should cover the reference's key content (recall).

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why clip counts in BLEU?

Without clipping, "the the the the" would get perfect unigram precision against any reference containing "the".

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you evaluate a RAG chatbot?

Retrieval recall@k, answer faithfulness to the retrieved context, answer relevance, and a small human-labelled set to validate an LLM judge.

#### The 30-second answer

BLEU, used for translation, is the geometric mean of clipped 1- to 4-gram precisions times a brevity penalty for short outputs, and is meant to be computed at corpus level. ROUGE, used for summarisation, measures n-gram recall or F1, with ROUGE-L based on the longest common subsequence. Extractive QA uses exact match and token-level F1, and language models use perplexity. All overlap metrics reward the same words rather than the same meaning, so paraphrases can score low and fluent but wrong outputs can score high; that's why we add embedding-based metrics like BERTScore, LLM-as-judge, task-specific checks like faithfulness, and human evaluation.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "A higher BLEU always means a better system." Small BLEU differences often don't match human judgement.

- "ROUGE measures factual correctness." A summary can share words and still be wrong.

**Key terms and sources**

How generated or extracted text is scored against references: BLEU for translation (clipped n-gram precision and the brevity penalty), ROUGE for summarisation (n-gram and longest-common-subsequence recall), exact match and token F1 for question answering, perplexity for language models, and why overlap metrics miss meaning · built from Papineni et al. (ACL 2002), Lin (2004), Rajpurkar et al. (SQuAD, EMNLP 2016), Callison-Burch et al. (2006), Zhang et al. (BERTScore, ICLR 2020), Post (2018) and Zheng et al. (2023) · checked 29 Oct 2026

# NLP Fundamentals Practice

> 10 interview questions: TF-IDF, perplexity, BPE, BLEU, NER F1 and hybrid search.

- Track: Fundamentals › NLP Fundamentals › Tagging, retrieval and evaluation
- Type: Interview · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/nlp-practice/
- Before this: Search: BM25, Dense and Hybrid Retrieval (`fundamentals/search-and-retrieval`), NLP Evaluation: BLEU, ROUGE, EM/F1 (`fundamentals/nlp-evaluation-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `nlp`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Work each one out on paper or out loud (the numbers are small enough to do by hand), then open the answer and compare.

**The toolkit:** idf = log(N / df); bigram P(w | prev) = count(prev w) / count(prev); perplexity = exp(−average log-probability); BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pair; entity F1 needs exact span + type; RRF score = Σ 1 / (60 + rank); BLEU clips each n-gram count at its count in the reference.

Question 1 · Easy · preprocessing

### A teammate adds stop-word removal, stemming and lowercasing to a review sentiment classifier. Accuracy drops from 91% to 84%, mostly on reviews like “the food was not bad”. What went wrong, and what would you do?

Answer: **standard stop-word lists contain negations (“not”, “no”, “never”), so “not bad” became “bad” and the label flipped**

1. Look at the errors first: if they cluster on negated reviews, check the stop-word list. NLTK's and scikit-learn's English lists include “not” and “no”.

2. Fix: keep negations (custom stop list), or skip stop-word removal entirely: with TF-IDF the common words are already down-weighted, and with Transformers you don't remove anything.

3. Add bigrams (“not bad”) so the model sees the negation and the word together.

**Follow-up:** Is stemming ever harmful? Yes: it merges words with different meanings (“university” and “universe” both stem to “univers” with Porter) and produces non-words, which hurts when you need readable features.

Question 2 · Easy · TF-IDF

### You have 400 reviews. “the” appears in all 400; “paneer” appears in 4. Using idf = ln(N / df), what are their idf values, and what does that mean for search?

Answer: **idf(the) = ln(400/400) = 0; idf(paneer) = ln(400/4) = ln 100 ≈ 4.61**

1. A word in every document carries no information about which document you want, so its idf, and therefore its TF-IDF weight, is 0.

2. A rare word like “paneer” gets a high weight, so a query containing it is matched mainly to the few documents that mention it.

3. Libraries add smoothing (scikit-learn uses ln((1 + N) / (1 + df)) + 1 by default), so exact numbers differ but the ordering is the same.

**Follow-up:** Why do we L2-normalise TF-IDF vectors before cosine similarity? So long reviews don't score higher just because they repeat words more; cosine then compares the direction of the vectors.

Question 3 · Medium · perplexity

### A bigram model scores “<s> pizza cold </s>” with P(pizza | <s>) = 0.5, P(cold | pizza) = 0.25, P(</s> | cold) = 0.5. What is the perplexity over the 3 predicted tokens?

Answer: **PP = (0.5 × 0.25 × 0.5)^(−1/3) = 0.0625^(−1/3) ≈ 2.52**

1. Probability of the sequence: 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.0625.

2. Perplexity is the inverse probability normalised by the number of predictions N = 3: 0.0625^(−1/3) ≈ 2.52. Equivalently exp(−(ln 0.5 + ln 0.25 + ln 0.5) / 3).

3. Reading: on average the model is as uncertain as choosing among about 2.5 equally likely words at each step.

**Follow-up:** What happens if one of the bigrams was never seen and the model is unsmoothed? That factor is 0, the product is 0 and perplexity is infinite: that's why n-gram models need smoothing such as Kneser–Ney.

Question 4 · Medium · BPE

### Train BPE on the word counts hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, bun ×4, hugs ×5, starting from characters. What are the first two merges, and how is “bug” tokenised afterwards?

Answer: **merge 1: u + g → “ug” (count 20); merge 2: u + n → “un” (count 16); “bug” → b + ug**

1. Count adjacent pairs weighted by word frequency: u-g appears in hug, pug, hugs = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20; p-u = 17; u-n = 16; h-u = 15. Merge u-g.

2. Recount after the merge: u-n = 12 + 4 = 16, h-ug = 15, p-u = 12. Merge u-n.

3. To tokenise “bug”, apply the merges in order: b u g → b ug. A word with an unseen character like “mug” would hit an unknown token, which byte-level BPE avoids.

**Follow-up:** How does WordPiece choose differently? It scores a pair by count(pair) / (count(first) × count(second)), preferring pairs whose parts rarely appear apart, rather than raw frequency (Hugging Face course, ch. 6).

Question 5 · Medium · BLEU

### Reference: “the cat is on the mat”. Candidate: “the the the the the the the”. What is the unigram precision, and BLEU's modified (clipped) unigram precision?

Answer: **plain precision 7/7 = 1.0; clipped precision 2/7 ≈ 0.29**

1. Every candidate word appears in the reference, so plain precision is 7/7, a perfect score for nonsense.

2. BLEU clips each word's count at the maximum number of times it appears in any reference: “the” appears twice, so only 2 of the 7 count: 2/7.

3. This is the example from the original BLEU paper (Papineni et al., 2002).

**Follow-up:** Your new summariser raises ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.44 but users like it less. How? ROUGE rewards word overlap, not faithfulness or readability; check for copied but irrelevant sentences, and validate with human ratings or an LLM judge checked against humans.

Question 6 · Medium · NER F1

### A sentence has 4 gold entities. Your NER model predicts 5 entities; 3 of them match a gold entity exactly (same span and type). What are entity-level precision, recall and F1?

Answer: **P = 3/5 = 0.60, R = 3/4 = 0.75, F1 = 2 × 0.60 × 0.75 / 1.35 ≈ 0.67**

1. Precision = correct predictions / all predictions = 3/5.

2. Recall = correct predictions / gold entities = 3/4.

3. F1 is their harmonic mean, 0.67. A prediction with the right type but one token off counts as both a false positive and a false negative under exact-match scoring (CoNLL).

**Follow-up:** Why not report token accuracy? Most tokens are O (outside any entity), so a model that predicts all O can still score high token accuracy while finding nothing.

Question 7 · Hard · hybrid retrieval

### Your RAG search uses dense embeddings. Users report that queries with order IDs like “ORD-48213” and dish names like “Bawarchi biryani” return the wrong documents, while paraphrased questions work well. What's happening, and how do you fix it? With reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), document A is ranked 1st by BM25 and 10th by dense; document B is 3rd and 2nd. Which ranks higher?

Answer: **dense embeddings blur exact rare tokens; add BM25 and fuse with RRF. B wins: 1/63 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0320 vs A's 1/61 + 1/70 ≈ 0.0307**

1. Dense retrievers map text to meaning; IDs, codes and rare names are split into subword pieces and land near similar-looking strings, so exact matches are lost. BM25 matches exact terms and weights rare ones highly (high idf).

2. Run BM25 and dense retrieval in parallel and fuse the ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, which needs no score calibration: score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank).

3. A: 1/61 + 1/70 ≈ 0.0164 + 0.0143 = 0.0307. B: 1/63 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0159 + 0.0161 = 0.0320. B, ranked well by both, beats A, ranked top by only one.

4. Then measure recall@k and MRR on a labelled query set that includes both ID lookups and paraphrased questions, and optionally add a cross-encoder re-ranker on the fused top 20–50.

**Follow-up:** When would you route instead of fuse? If a query matches a strict pattern (an order ID regex), skip retrieval and do a direct database lookup: it's exact, faster and cheaper.

Question 8 · Easy · BERT masking

### A BERT training sequence has 200 tokens. About how many are chosen for masking, and what happens to them? How many positions contribute to the masked loss?

Answer: **30 chosen: about 24 become [MASK], 3 random, 3 unchanged. All 30 are scored**

1. 15% of 200 = 30.

2. 80% of 30 = 24, 10% = 3 and 10% = 3.

3. The loss is computed on all 30, including those left unchanged.

Scoring the unchanged tokens stops the model relying on [MASK] to know where to predict.

Question 9 · Medium · edit distance

### What's the edit distance between “sunday” and “saturday”, with each edit costing 1? Give the edits.

Answer: **3: insert a, insert t, substitute n with r**

1. Line them up: s + (a t) + u + n→r + d a y.

2. That's two insertions and one substitution.

3. The lengths differ by 2, so at least 2 edits are needed, and the table confirms 3 is the minimum.

Filling in the table takes O(mn) time, here 6 × 8 cells.

Question 10 · Hard · Viterbi

### Two tags, N and V. Start: P(N) = 0.6, P(V) = 0.4. Transitions: N→N 0.3, N→V 0.7, V→N 0.8, V→V 0.2. Word 1: P(w₁|N) = 0.5, P(w₁|V) = 0.1. Word 2: P(w₂|N) = 0.2, P(w₂|V) = 0.4. What's the best tag sequence?

Answer: **N, V, with a probability of 0.084**

1. Step 1: N = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3, and V = 0.4 × 0.1 = 0.04.

2. Step 2, N: max(0.3 × 0.3, 0.04 × 0.8) × 0.2 = 0.09 × 0.2 = 0.018.

3. Step 2, V: max(0.3 × 0.7, 0.04 × 0.2) × 0.4 = 0.21 × 0.4 = 0.084.

4. V wins, and its pointer leads back to N.

Note that V alone scores higher on word 2, while N wins on word 1. Transitions join the two.

**More practice and sources**

10 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 29 Oct 2026

Keep practising

Built from the lessons in this track and their sources: Jurafsky & Martin, [SLP3](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) (ch. 3, 4, 18, 11); Sennrich et al. (2016) and the [Hugging Face course](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5) BPE example; Papineni et al. (2002) for BLEU clipping; Cormack et al. (2009) for RRF. # Anatomy of a Modern LLM

> What changed since 2017, and where do an 8B model's parameters live?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture/
- Before this: The Transformer, End to End (`fundamentals/transformer-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

The delivery app wants its own support assistant, an open 8B model like Llama 3 8B. A colleague says it's the 2017 Transformer made bigger, with most of the parameters in attention. The interviewer asks:

> What changed since 2017, and where do an 8B model's parameters live?

Where this lesson sits: the whole block. Each part has its own Deep Learning lesson; this one covers what modern LLMs changed.

Background: The Transformer, End to End · Encoder vs Decoder.

**Running example (whole track):** the food-delivery app wants its own support assistant, an open 8B model like Llama 3 8B, fine-tuned on customer chats. To choose, serve and train it, the team needs to know what's inside.

#### The 2017 recipe didn't scale cleanly

The original Transformer was an encoder-decoder for translation, with post-norm residual blocks, ReLU feed-forward layers and fixed sinusoidal positions. Scaling that recipe to tens of billions of parameters exposed problems: deep post-norm stacks needed careful warm-up to train, long-context generation made the **KV cache** huge, and fixed positions didn't extend past the training length. Each modern change fixes one of these.

### The idea

Think of a restaurant famous for its front counter, where orders get passed along. Everyone talks about the counter, but most of the staff are in the back kitchen. Attention is the counter, and the feed-forward layers are the kitchen.

[Figure: Where parameters live. In an 8B model: 70 percent feed-forward, 17 percent attention, 13 percent embeddings. In a 70B model: 80 percent feed-forward, 17 percent attention, 3 percent embeddings.]

_Counted in the lab, from the Llama 3 model cards._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start at the 8B shape, then switch to 70B. Change SwiGLU to classic FFN, GQA to full MHA and a separate output head to tied embeddings. Watch the totals and shares.

#### Where do 8 billion parameters live?

The naive guess is "mostly attention", since attention is what the Transformer is famous for. Count them.

Configs from the Llama 3 model cards: 8B: d = 4,096, 32 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, FFN 14,336, vocab 128,256; 70B: d = 8,192, 80 layers, 64 heads, 8 KV heads, FFN 28,672. Attention = WQ, WK, WV, WO; norms = two RMSNorm gains per layer plus a final one.

The Llama 3 8B shape comes out at **8.03 B**: the feed-forward layers hold **70%**, attention only **17%**, and the input and output embedding tables **13%** (1.05 B, because the 128k vocabulary is large). At the 70B shape the feed-forward share rises to **80%** and embeddings fall to 3%. Switching to full MHA adds 0.8 B parameters to the 8B shape (8.84 B) and makes the KV cache 4× bigger; tying the input and output embeddings saves 0.5 B, which is why small models like Llama 3.2 1B/3B tie them. Norms are a rounding error. So when people prune, quantise or route (MoE), they mostly target the FFN.

**Now say why:** why does the embeddings share drop so much at 70B, while the feed-forward share rises?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A modern LLM is still a stack of Transformer blocks, but **decoder-only** and with a handful of upgrades that became standard after Llama (2023): **pre-norm** with **RMSNorm** (cheaper, more stable training), a **SwiGLU** feed-forward layer (a gated FFN that trains better), **RoPE** rotary positions inside attention, **grouped-query attention** to shrink the KV cache, no bias terms, and a vocabulary of 100k+ tokens. In an 8B model about **70% of the parameters are in the feed-forward layers**, about 17% in attention and 13% in the embedding tables; at 70B the feed-forward share rises to about 80%. What you'll be able to do after this: list the modern changes and why each was made, and count an LLM's parameters from its config.

#### 2017 Transformer vs a 2024 LLM block

| Part | 2017 (Vaswani et al.) | Modern (Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen) | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | encoder-decoder | decoder-only, causal | one stack does every text task as next-token prediction |
| Norm position | post-norm (after residual add) | **pre-norm** (before each sub-layer) | a clean residual path keeps gradients healthy in deep stacks |
| Norm type | LayerNorm | **RMSNorm** | drops mean-centring; cheaper, works as well (norm lesson) |
| Feed-forward | ReLU, d → 4d → d | **SwiGLU**, three matrices | gated FFNs gave lower loss at equal compute (Shazeer 2020) |
| Positions | sinusoidal, added to input | **RoPE**, rotates Q and K | encodes relative position; can be stretched for long context |
| Attention | multi-head (MHA) | **GQA** (e.g. 8 KV heads) | 4–8× smaller KV cache (next lesson) |
| Biases | yes | none in linear layers | no quality loss, slightly more stable |
| Vocabulary | 37k shared BPE | 128k (Llama 3), 150k+ (Qwen) | fewer tokens per text, better multilingual coverage (tokenisation) |

$$ {\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}}\odot g}, \qquad \mathrm{FFN}_{\mathrm{SwiGLU}}(x) = {\big(}{\mathrm{SiLU}(xW_1)}\odot {xW_3}{\big)W_2} $$

Zhang & Sennrich, "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization", NeurIPS 2019; Shazeer, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", [arXiv:2002.05202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202). SiLU(z) = z·σ(z).

- **RMSNorm**: Divide each vector by its root-mean-square and multiply by a learned gain g. No mean subtraction and no bias, unlike LayerNorm.

- **gate branch**: x W₁ passes through Swish (SiLU), which decides how much of each hidden unit to let through.

- **value branch**: x W₃ is a plain linear projection; it is multiplied element by element by the gate.

- **down projection**: W₂ maps the hidden size back to d. Three matrices instead of two, so the hidden size is shrunk to about 8d/3 to keep the parameter count similar. Models adjust this: Llama 3 8B uses 14,336 for d = 4,096, which is 3.5d.

#### Counting parameters from a config file

- **Attention per layer:** 2d² for Q and O, plus 2 · d · (KV heads × head dim) for K and V.

- **SwiGLU FFN per layer:** 3 · d · dff. A classic FFN: 2 · d · 4d = 8d².

- **Embeddings:** V · d, twice if the output head isn't tied.

- Rough rule for dense models: params ≈ 12 · L · d² (attention 4d² + FFN 8d²), plus embeddings. For Llama 3 8B: 12 × 32 × 4,096² ≈ 6.4 B, close to the 6.98 B in its layers.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The open-model family resemblance

- **Llama** (Touvron et al. 2023) combined pre-norm RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE, and most open models since copy that template. Llama 2 70B added GQA; Llama 3 uses GQA at every size, a 128k-token vocabulary and a RoPE base of 500,000 for longer context.

- **Mistral 7B** added sliding-window attention; **Mixtral** and **DeepSeek-V3** replace the dense FFN with a mixture of experts; DeepSeek-V2/V3 replace GQA with multi-head latent attention.

- Newer stability tweaks include QK-norm (normalising queries and keys before the dot product, used in OLMo 2 and Qwen3) and extra norms after sub-layers; see Training Instabilities.

##### What changed in 2025 and 2026

Llama 3 is still a good model to learn from, and it's our running example. Newer models keep most of its design, and change these parts:

- **Norm placement is less settled.** OLMo 2 puts norms after attention and the FFN, inside the residual. Gemma 3 uses RMSNorm both before and after its attention.

- **QK-norm has spread.** OLMo 2, Gemma 3 and Qwen3 all use it for stability.

- **Attention is changing most.** Gemma 4's smallest models reuse keys and values across layers. Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next mix linear attention with full attention, and DeepSeek-V4 compresses its cache. See Attention Alternatives.

- **MoE keeps getting sparser.** Qwen3-Next has 80B parameters with 3B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro has 1.6T with 49B active.

From the models' technical reports and model cards, and Raschka's [Recent Developments in LLM Architectures](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/recent-developments-in-llm-architectures). Gemma 4's KV sharing is as Raschka describes it.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Most parameters are in attention"

It sounds right, since attention is what the Transformer is famous for. But count them in Llama 3 8B: the feed-forward layers hold 70%, attention only 17% and the embedding tables 13%. So when people prune, quantise or route, they mostly target the FFN.

## Say it

### What changed since 2017, and where do an 8B model's parameters live?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why pre-norm instead of post-norm?

With pre-norm the residual stream is an identity path from input to output, so gradients reach early layers undamped and training is stable without long warm-up (Xiong et al. 2020). Post-norm can reach slightly better quality but is harder to train deep.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why is SwiGLU's hidden size 8d/3 instead of 4d?

It has three weight matrices instead of two; shrinking the hidden size by 2/3 keeps the parameter count and compute about the same as a 4d two-matrix FFN. That's a starting point: Llama 3 8B actually uses 3.5d (14,336 for d = 4,096).

Follow-up 3 of 3

Estimate the parameters of a model with d = 4,096 and 32 layers.

About 12 · L · d² ≈ 6.4 B in the blocks, plus vocabulary × d for each embedding table: around 7–8 B in total.

#### The 30-second answer

Modern LLMs are decoder-only Transformers with a few standard changes from the 2017 design: pre-norm residual blocks with RMSNorm for stable deep training, SwiGLU gated feed-forward layers, rotary position embeddings applied to queries and keys, grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache, no biases, and large vocabularies around 128k tokens. Most parameters sit in the feed-forward layers, about 70 percent in an 8B model and about 80 percent at 70B, with attention around 17 percent; that's why MoE replaces the FFN and why quantisation and pruning focus there.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Most parameters are in attention." It's the FFN.

- "LLMs use the original Transformer." They use a decoder-only variant with several changes.

**Key terms and sources**

What changed between the 2017 Transformer and today's decoder-only LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek): pre-norm, RMSNorm, SwiGLU feed-forward layers, RoPE, grouped-query attention, no biases, big vocabularies, and where the parameters of an 8B model actually live · built from Vaswani et al. (2017), Zhang & Sennrich (2019), Shazeer (2020), Su et al. (RoFormer, 2021), Touvron et al. (Llama, 2023), Ainslie et al. (GQA, 2023) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. A. Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", NeurIPS 2017, [arXiv:1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

2. B. Zhang & R. Sennrich, "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization", NeurIPS 2019, [arXiv:1910.07467](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467); R. Xiong et al., "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture", ICML 2020, [arXiv:2002.04745](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745).

3. N. Shazeer, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer", 2020, [arXiv:2002.05202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202); J. Su et al., "RoFormer", 2021, [arXiv:2104.09864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864).

4. H. Touvron et al., "LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models", 2023, [arXiv:2302.13971](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971).

# Attention Variants: MQA, GQA and MLA

> How many conversations fit on one GPU, and how do GQA and MLA raise that?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/attention-variants-mqa-gqa-mla/
- Before this: Anatomy of a Modern LLM (`fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture`), Multi-Head Attention (`fundamentals/multi-head-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your 8B assistant runs on one 80 GB GPU, and its weights take about 16 GB. Customers chat with 8k tokens of history each. A colleague assumes the weights decide how many fit at once. The interviewer asks:

> How many conversations fit on one GPU, and how do GQA and MLA raise that?

Where this lesson sits: the attention box, specifically how many K and V heads it keeps.

Background: Self-Attention · Multi-Head Attention · Prefill vs Decode.

**Running example:** the support assistant (an 8B model) runs on one 80 GB GPU. Its weights take about 16 GB in bf16. How many customers can chat at once, with 8k tokens of conversation history each?

#### Every past token leaves keys and values behind

To generate token t, attention needs the keys and values of tokens 1…t−1 in every layer. Recomputing them every step would be quadratic, so they are cached. Each decode step must then read the whole cache from GPU memory, plus all the weights, to produce one token per sequence: decoding is **memory-bandwidth bound**, and the cache, not the weights, grows with users and context length.

### The idea

Think of 32 researchers who each keep a private copy of the same catalogue. Their questions differ, but the catalogues are nearly identical. Share one copy per group of four and you free up most of the shelf space, and they can still ask their own questions.

[Figure: Conversations that fit on one GPU at 8k context. MHA fits 16, GQA-8 fits 64, MLA fits 227 and MQA fits 512.]

_From the lab: the Llama 3 8B shape, with bf16 cache. GQA-8 is what Llama 3 uses._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between MHA, GQA-8, MQA and MLA at 8k context. Then raise the context per conversation and the number of conversations.

#### How many conversations fit on one GPU?

Shape: Llama 3 8B (32 layers, 32 query heads, head size 128), bf16 cache, 80 GB GPU with ~16 GB of weights. MLA uses DeepSeek-V2's latent sizes (512 + 64 per token per layer) applied to this shape, for illustration; DeepSeek's own models have different dimensions. Activations and fragmentation are ignored.

With full **MHA**, each token costs 512 KiB, so one 8k conversation needs **4 GiB** and only **16** conversations fit in the 64 GB left after the weights (64 GiB). At 128k context a single conversation takes the whole 64 GiB. **GQA-8**, what Llama 3 actually uses, cuts that 4×: 1 GiB per conversation, **64** at once. **MQA** is 32× smaller than MHA (512 conversations) and **MLA** about 14× (227). The trap is assuming the smallest cache wins: MQA gives every query head the same keys and values, which costs quality and can make training less stable; that's why GQA became the default and MLA tries to get small caches without the quality loss.

**Now say why:** if MQA has the smallest cache of all, why did GQA become the default?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

During generation an LLM stores the keys and values of every previous token, the **KV cache**, so it doesn't recompute them. With standard multi-head attention (MHA) every head has its own K and V, and the cache grows with layers × heads × head size × context × batch. **MQA** shares one K/V head across all query heads (smallest cache, some quality loss); **GQA** shares one K/V head per group of query heads (Llama 3: 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, 4× smaller cache, near-MHA quality); **MLA** (DeepSeek-V2/V3) caches one small compressed latent vector per token and rebuilds K and V from it. Because decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, a smaller cache means more users per GPU, longer contexts and faster tokens. What you'll be able to do after this: compute a model's KV cache size and explain the MHA → GQA → MQA → MLA trade-off.

#### The KV-cache formula

$$ \text{KV cache} = {2}\times{L}\times{n_{kv}\times d_{head}}\times{(\text{context}\times\text{batch})}\times{\text{bytes}} $$

For the Llama 3 8B shape (32 layers, head size 128, 8 KV heads, bf16): 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 128 KiB per token.

- **K and V**: Two tensors are cached: keys and values.

- **layers**: Every layer has its own cache.

- **KV heads × head size**: The only term the variants change: MHA keeps all 32 heads, GQA 8 groups, MQA 1 head; MLA replaces this term with one small latent.

- **tokens in flight**: Context length times batch size: every token of every conversation.

- **bytes per number**: 2 for bf16/fp16, 1 for an FP8 cache.

- **MQA** (Shazeer 2019): all query heads share a single K and V head.

- **GQA** (Ainslie et al. 2023): query heads are split into G groups, each sharing one K/V head. G = number of heads is MHA; G = 1 is MQA.

- **MLA** (DeepSeek-V2, 2024): K and V are projected down to a shared latent c (512 numbers per token) plus a small 64-dimensional RoPE key; only these are cached, and the up-projections are folded into the query and output matrices at inference.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Quality vs cache size

- **GQA** (Ainslie et al., EMNLP 2023): converting an MHA checkpoint to GQA and "uptraining" with about 5% of the original pre-training compute gave quality close to MHA with speed close to MQA. Llama 2 70B, Llama 3 (all sizes), Mistral and Qwen use GQA.

- **MLA** (DeepSeek-V2): reduced the KV cache by 93.3% compared with DeepSeek 67B and raised maximum generation throughput 5.76×; the paper's ablation reports MLA matching or beating MHA quality. DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 use it. The cost is extra compute to decompress.

- Other levers stack on top: quantising the cache to FP8 (2× smaller), sliding-window layers that keep only recent tokens (Long Context), and paged memory in serving engines like vLLM.

#### Many queries can share keys and values

Query heads need to be diverse to look for different things, but the keys and values they search over are highly redundant across heads. Sharing them (GQA, MQA) or compressing them into a low-rank latent (MLA) keeps most of the model's quality while cutting the memory that decoding has to read at every step.

To go past this, read Attention Alternatives.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The smallest cache wins, so MQA is strictly better"

It sounds right, since MQA fits 512 conversations where GQA-8 fits 64. But giving every query head the same keys and values costs quality and can make training less stable. That's why GQA became the default, and why MLA tries to get a small cache without the quality loss. And the weights usually aren't the limit either: at long context, the KV cache dominates.

## Say it

### How many conversations fit on one GPU, and how do GQA and MLA raise that?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Does GQA reduce compute or memory?

Mainly memory and memory traffic: fewer K/V projections and a smaller cache to read each step. Attention FLOPs for the query side stay the same.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Can you convert an MHA model to GQA?

Yes: mean-pool the K and V heads within each group, then uptrain briefly (about 5% of pre-training compute in the GQA paper).

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does MLA need a separate RoPE key?

RoPE rotates keys by position, which would stop the up-projection from being folded into the query matrix; DeepSeek adds a small decoupled key that carries the rotary position instead.

#### The 30-second answer

During decoding we cache keys and values for every token, layer and head; the cache size is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × bytes, and since decoding is memory-bandwidth bound it limits batch size and context. MQA shares one K/V head across all query heads, which is smallest but loses quality; GQA shares one K/V head per group, for example 8 groups for 32 query heads in Llama 3, giving a 4× smaller cache with near-MHA quality; and DeepSeek's MLA caches a compressed latent per token and reconstructs K and V, cutting the cache by over 90% with comparable quality. For an 8B Llama-3-style model that's 128 KiB per token, so 1 GiB for an 8k conversation.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The weights are what limits batch size." At long context the KV cache usually dominates.

- "MQA is strictly better because it's smallest." It trades quality and stability for memory.

**Key terms and sources**

Why the KV cache, not the weights, limits how many users an LLM can serve at long context, and how multi-query, grouped-query and multi-head latent attention shrink it: what each one shares or compresses, what it costs in quality, and how to size the cache for a real model · built from Shazeer (MQA, 2019), Ainslie et al. (GQA, EMNLP 2023), DeepSeek-AI (DeepSeek-V2, 2024) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. N. Shazeer, "Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need", 2019, [arXiv:1911.02150](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150).

2. J. Ainslie et al., "GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints", EMNLP 2023, [arXiv:2305.13245](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245).

3. DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model", 2024, [arXiv:2405.04434](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434).

4. Llama Team, Meta, "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", 2024, [arXiv:2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783).

5. W. Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention" (vLLM), SOSP 2023, [arXiv:2309.06180](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180).

# GPUs, TPUs and Memory Bandwidth

> Why is decoding limited by memory, while prefill is limited by compute?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/gpus-tpus-and-memory-bandwidth/
- Before this: Anatomy of a Modern LLM (`fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team doubled the batch size on its 8B assistant, and tokens per second went up. Then someone suggests buying chips with twice the compute to make replies faster. You suspect that won't help much. The interviewer asks:

> Why is decoding limited by memory, while prefill is limited by compute?

#### Why it matters

Many tricks in this track exist because of this gap between maths and memory. GQA and MLA shrink what decoding must read. FlashAttention avoids sending data to main memory. Tensor parallelism stays inside fast links. Interviewers ask you to estimate speed from a chip's numbers, so it helps to know which number is the limit.

### The idea

Think of a very fast chef with a slow helper bringing ingredients from a far-off store. If each dish needs a lot of chopping, the chef's speed decides how fast you serve. If each dish needs ingredients from all over the store, the chef mostly stands and waits. A faster chef wouldn't help at all.

[Figure: Two limits. Maths time is operations over compute. Data time is bytes over bandwidth. The larger one sets the speed.]

_The slower of the two sets the step time._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between decode and prefill. Then push the batch up to 128.

#### Find the limit

Best-case estimate for one chip, using the Llama 3 8B shape in 16-bit: 16 GB of weights and 128 KiB of KV cache per token. Each token costs about 2 operations per parameter. Weights are read once per step. Attention's extra work, activations and network links are left out.

With 32 conversations of 4,096 tokens, a **decode** step needs 0.52 ms of maths, but 9.9 ms just to read the weights and cache. Faster compute wouldn't help at all. Now switch to **prefill**: the same batch needs 2.12 s of maths and still about 10 ms of reads, so compute is the limit. Raise the batch while decoding, and tokens per second keep rising, because each read of the weights is shared across more conversations. At 128 conversations the cache no longer fits in the H100's 80 GB.

**Now say why:** why does a bigger batch raise tokens per second while decoding?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

An AI chip does maths very quickly, but moves data far more slowly. An H100 can do about **989 trillion** operations a second, yet reads only about **3.35 TB** of memory a second. So a job takes at least as long as the slower of two things: doing its maths, or moving its bytes. This is the **roofline model**. **Prefill** does lots of maths per byte, so compute limits it. **Decode** reads the whole model and cache to produce one token per conversation, so memory limits it. That one fact explains GQA, MLA, FlashAttention and much of LLM serving.

#### Inside the chip

##### Faster memory is smaller

A chip has several levels of memory. Each step away from the compute units holds more, but is slower.

| Level (H100) | Size | Bandwidth |
|---|---|---|
| On-chip SRAM | 228 KiB per streaming multiprocessor | 31 TB/s across the GPU |
| L2 cache | 50 MiB | 12 TB/s |
| **HBM, the main memory** | **80 GB** | **3.35 TB/s** |
| NVLink, to other GPUs | Not applicable | 900 GB/s in total |
| PCIe, to the host | Not applicable | 128 GB/s |

SRAM, L2 and HBM figures are from the FlashAttention-3 paper. HBM capacity, NVLink and PCIe are from NVIDIA's specification.

##### Not all maths is equally fast

The Tensor Cores make matrix multiplication very fast. On an H100, matmul runs at 989 TFLOPS in 16-bit, but special functions such as exponentials run at only 3.9 TFLOPS. That's why a kernel that computes softmax in the wrong place can be surprisingly slow, however few operations it does.

##### Arithmetic intensity

Arithmetic intensity is a job's operations divided by the bytes it moves. Compare it with the chip's own ratio of compute to bandwidth. For an H100, that's about 989 trillion ÷ 3.35 trillion, or about **295 operations per byte**. A job above this is limited by compute. A job below it is limited by memory.

##### GPUs and TPUs

| | H100 | TPU v5p |
|---|---|---|
| 16-bit compute per chip | 989 TFLOPS | 459 TFLOPS |
| Main memory | 80 GB | 95 GiB |
| Memory bandwidth | 3.35 TB/s | 2.77 TB/s |
| Largest connected group | A small NVLink domain, then a slower network | 8,960 chips in a 3D torus |

The main difference for LLM work is how chips connect. An H100 has fast links within a small group, then slower links beyond it. A TPU pod connects thousands of chips directly to their neighbours, in a 3D grid. Compare them on your own workload, rather than on one peak number.

#### The maths

$$ {T_{\min}} = \max\!\Big({\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{compute}}},\; {\frac{\text{bytes}}{\text{bandwidth}}}\Big), \qquad {I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes}}} $$

The roofline idea, as used in How to Scale Your Model. If the maths and the data movement can’t overlap, the two times add up, which gives an upper limit.

- **the best possible time**: The step can’t finish faster than its slowest requirement.

- **time for the maths**: Operations needed, divided by what the chip can do each second.

- **time to move the data**: Bytes moved, divided by memory or network bandwidth.

- **arithmetic intensity**: Operations per byte. Compare it with the chip’s own ratio, about 295 on an H100.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Check what the number means:** NVIDIA's page lists an H100 at 1,979 TFLOPS "with sparsity". The 989 figure used in research is half that. Check before you estimate.

- **Peak isn't real:** FlashAttention-2 reached only 35% of an H100's peak. FlashAttention-3 reached 740 TFLOPS, about 75%. Llama 3 405B pre-training ran at 38 to 43% utilisation.

- **Lower precision helps both limits:** FP8 doubles matmul speed on an H100, and halves the bytes to move. See LLM quantization.

- **Batching has a limit:** at large batches, the cache dominates the bytes moved. Tokens per second then level off near bandwidth ÷ cache per conversation.

- **Fit your work to the links:** memory is roughly 4 times faster than NVLink's total, and NVLink is about 7 times faster than PCIe. Chatty work belongs on the fastest link available.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A chip with twice the FLOPs will decode twice as fast"

It sounds right, as FLOPs are the number everyone quotes. But a decode step spends most of its time reading the weights and the KV cache from memory. With 32 conversations, the maths takes about 0.5 ms of a 10 ms step. Look at memory bandwidth, or make the cache smaller.

## Say it

### Why is decoding limited by memory, while prefill is limited by compute?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Estimate the best decode speed of an 8B model on an H100, with 32 conversations of 4,096 tokens.

Weights are 16 GB and the cache is 32 × 4,096 × 128 KiB, about 17.2 GB, so 33.2 GB per step. At 3.35 TB/s that's 9.9 ms. The maths takes only 0.52 ms, so memory is the limit. 32 tokens per 9.9 ms is about 3,200 tokens a second, as a best case.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Would a chip with twice the compute but the same memory speed help decoding?

Barely, because the step is already waiting on memory. It would help prefill and training, which spend their time on maths.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does on-chip SRAM matter if it's so small?

It's much faster than HBM, and a kernel can keep its working data there. FlashAttention works in tiles that fit in SRAM, so the large score matrix never has to go to main memory.

#### The 30-second answer

A job's best time is the larger of its maths time and its data movement time. Maths time is operations over compute, and data time is bytes over bandwidth. An H100 does about 989 TFLOPS but moves about 3.35 TB/s, so its balance point is about 295 operations per byte. Prefill does a lot of maths per byte, so compute limits it. Decode reads all the weights and the KV cache to produce one token per conversation, so memory bandwidth limits it. That's why GQA and MLA speed up decoding, and why batching helps: each read of the weights is shared across more conversations.

**Key terms and sources**

What is inside an AI chip, the roofline model, arithmetic intensity, why prefill and decode hit different limits, and how GPUs and TPUs differ. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Austin et al., How to Scale Your Model (roofline, TPUs, GPUs, inference)](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

- [NVIDIA H100 specification](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)

- [Google Cloud, TPU v5p specification](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/v5p)

- [Shah et al., FlashAttention-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08608)

- [Stanford CS336, resource accounting and GPUs lectures](https://cs336.stanford.edu/)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative, and worked examples were checked by calculation.

# FlashAttention

> Why is exact attention faster when it does more maths?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/flashattention/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team fine-tunes the assistant on chat transcripts of up to 32k tokens. Plain attention runs out of memory. FlashAttention runs, finishes faster and gives the same numbers, even though it does more arithmetic. The interviewer asks:

> Why is exact attention faster when it does more maths?

Where this lesson sits: the inside of the attention box. FlashAttention changes how it's computed, not what it computes.

Background: Self-Attention · Attention Variants.

**Running example:** the team fine-tunes the support assistant on long chat transcripts (up to 32k tokens). With plain attention the job runs out of memory; with FlashAttention it runs, faster, and gives the same numbers.

#### Attention is memory-bound

An A100 does about 312 TFLOPS of bf16 matrix maths but moves only about 1.5–2 TB/s from HBM. Softmax, masking and dropout do little arithmetic per byte, so a standard implementation spends most of its time waiting on memory: write S = QKᵀ (N × N) to HBM, read it for the softmax, write P, read P to multiply by V. The fast on-chip SRAM is tiny (about 20 MB in total across the chip, a couple of hundred KB per streaming multiprocessor) but an order of magnitude faster.

### The idea

Think of cooking with the pantry at the far end of a long hall. The slow part isn't the chopping, it's the walking. So you bring one small tray to your counter, finish it there and only then go back. You chop slightly more, and walk far less.

[Figure: On GPT-2 medium, FlashAttention does slightly more arithmetic, 75.2 against 66.6 gigaFLOPs, but moves 4.4 gigabytes of memory against 40.3, and takes 7.3 milliseconds against 41.7.]

_Measured in the paper on GPT-2 medium, sequence length 1,024, on an A100._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the sequence length up to 32k, and compare the score matrix with the saved row statistics.

#### The N × N matrix doesn't fit

32 heads, batch 1, bf16 scores; FlashAttention stores one fp32 log-sum-exp per row and head for the backward pass. Q, K, V and the output are needed by both methods and are not counted.

At **32k tokens** the standard score matrix is **64 GiB for a single layer**, almost a whole 80 GB GPU, and training must keep it for the backward pass. FlashAttention keeps only **4 MiB** of row statistics and recomputes the tiles during the backward pass instead of storing them: more FLOPs, far less memory traffic. On GPT-2 medium (sequence 1,024, A100) the paper measured 66.6 vs 75.2 GFLOPs for standard vs FlashAttention, but 40.3 GB vs **4.4 GB** of HBM reads and writes, and 41.7 ms vs **7.3 ms**.

**Now say why:** FlashAttention throws the matrix away, so how can the backward pass still work?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Standard attention writes the full N × N score matrix to GPU main memory (HBM), reads it back for the softmax, writes the probabilities, and reads them again. GPUs compute much faster than they move data, so this traffic, not the FLOPs, dominates the runtime, and the N² matrix also eats memory. **FlashAttention** splits Q, K and V into tiles that fit in fast on-chip SRAM, computes attention tile by tile, and never stores the full matrix. The trick that makes this possible is the **online softmax**: keep a running maximum and running sum per row, and rescale earlier partial results when a bigger score appears. The result is **exact** attention, not an approximation, with memory that grows linearly in sequence length. On GPT-2 medium it cut HBM traffic from 40.3 GB to 4.4 GB and runtime from 41.7 ms to 7.3 ms. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why attention is memory-bound, run the online softmax by hand, and say what each FlashAttention version improved.

#### Softmax without seeing the whole row

Softmax needs the row's maximum (for numerical safety) and its sum, which seems to require the whole row first. The online softmax processes scores in blocks and fixes up the past whenever the maximum changes:

$$ {m_{new} = \max(m, \max_j s_j)}, \quad {\ell_{new} = \ell\,}{e^{m - m_{new}}}{ + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m_{new}}}, \quad {o_{new} = o\,e^{m-m_{new}} + \textstyle\sum_j e^{s_j - m_{new}} v_j} $$

Milakov & Gimelshein, "Online normalizer calculation for softmax", 2018, [arXiv:1805.02867](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867). FlashAttention applies this per block of rows and keeps m and ℓ (as one log-sum-exp per row) for the backward pass.

- **new running max**: Compare the old maximum with the largest score in the new tile.

- **rescale factor**: Everything accumulated so far was computed relative to the old max; multiplying by e^(m_old − m_new) corrects it.

- **running sum**: Rescaled old sum plus this tile’s exponentials.

- **running output**: The weighted sum of values gets the same rescaling; dividing by ℓ at the end gives exactly softmax(scores)·V.

One query row: scores s = [2, 1, 0.5, 3, −1, 2.5, 0, 4] over 8 keys, values v = [10, 20, …, 80]. The "output so far" column is the softmax-weighted average of the values seen so far.

With tiles of 4, the first tile has maximum 3 and a partial output of **30.81**; the second tile brings a larger score (4), so the old sum and output are rescaled by e3−4 before adding the new terms, and the result is **61.69**. Every tile size gives the same answer as the exact softmax, up to floating-point rounding: this is why FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation.

## In practice

### In practice

#### FlashAttention 1, 2, 3

| Version | What changed | Reported result |
|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention (2022) | IO-aware tiling + online softmax + recomputation in the backward pass | up to 9× fewer HBM accesses; 15% faster BERT-large training, 3× faster GPT-2 (1k context) |
| FlashAttention-2 (2023) | fewer non-matmul operations, parallelism over the sequence, better work split between warps | about 2× faster than v1, 50–73% of A100 peak FLOPs |
| FlashAttention-3 (2024) | Hopper-specific: asynchronous Tensor Cores and TMA, overlapping softmax with matmuls, FP8 | 1.5–2.0× faster than v2 on H100, up to 740 TFLOPS in FP16 (75% of peak) |

FlashAttention is the default attention kernel in PyTorch's `scaled_dot_product_attention`, Hugging Face Transformers and most training and serving stacks. It works with GQA, causal masks and sliding windows. Inference engines add variants like FlashDecoding, which splits the long KV cache across thread blocks when only one query token is processed.

#### Count bytes moved, not FLOPs

On modern GPUs, an algorithm that does a little more arithmetic but moves far fewer bytes between memory levels wins. FlashAttention fuses the whole attention computation into one kernel that keeps tiles in SRAM, made possible by an online softmax that never needs the full row.

For why bytes matter so much, read GPUs, TPUs and Memory Bandwidth.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It's faster because it does fewer FLOPs"

It sounds right, since faster usually means less work. But it does slightly more: 75.2 against 66.6 GFLOPs on GPT-2 medium. It moves far fewer bytes, 4.4 GB against 40.3 GB. And compute is still quadratic. It's memory that becomes linear, so don't say FlashAttention makes attention linear.

## Say it

### Why is exact attention faster when it does more maths?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Is FlashAttention an approximation?

No. It computes the same result as standard attention up to floating-point rounding; sparse and linear attention are the approximate methods.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Does it change the O(N²) compute?

No, FLOPs stay quadratic (slightly higher due to recomputation). It reduces memory from O(N²) to O(N) and cuts memory traffic, which is what made it faster.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why recompute in the backward pass instead of storing P?

Storing P is N² memory and traffic; recomputing it from Q, K and the saved log-sum-exp in SRAM is cheaper than reading it back from HBM.

#### The 30-second answer

Standard attention materialises the N by N score and probability matrices in GPU high-bandwidth memory and reads them back several times, so it's memory-bandwidth bound and uses quadratic memory. FlashAttention tiles Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM and fuses the matmuls, softmax and value multiply into one kernel, using an online softmax that keeps a running max and sum per row and rescales partial results. It's exact, uses linear memory, and recomputes tiles in the backward pass instead of storing them. Version 2 improved parallelism and work partitioning, version 3 uses Hopper's asynchronous hardware and FP8.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "FlashAttention makes attention linear." Memory is linear; compute is still quadratic.

- "It's faster because it does fewer FLOPs." It does slightly more; it moves far fewer bytes.

**Key terms and sources**

Why standard attention is slow because of memory traffic rather than arithmetic, how FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory using an online softmax, and what FlashAttention-2 and -3 added · built from Dao et al. (FlashAttention, NeurIPS 2022), Milakov & Gimelshein (online softmax, 2018), Rabe & Staats (2021), Dao (FlashAttention-2, 2023) and Shah et al. (FlashAttention-3, NeurIPS 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. T. Dao, D. Fu, S. Ermon, A. Rudra & C. Ré, "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness", NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2205.14135](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) (Fig. 2 for the GPT-2 medium numbers).

2. T. Dao, "FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning", 2023, [arXiv:2307.08691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691).

3. J. Shah et al., "FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision", NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2407.08608](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08608).

4. M. Milakov & N. Gimelshein, "Online normalizer calculation for softmax", 2018, [arXiv:1805.02867](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867); M. Rabe & C. Staats, "Self-attention Does Not Need O(n²) Memory", 2021, [arXiv:2112.05682](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05682).

# Long Context: RoPE Scaling, Sliding Windows and Attention Sinks

> Why does a 4k model break at 16k, and how does YaRN fix it?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/long-context/
- Before this: Positional Encodings (incl. RoPE) (`fundamentals/positional-encodings`), Attention Variants: MQA, GQA and MLA (`fundamentals/attention-variants-mqa-gqa-mla`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant was pre-trained on 4k-token contexts, and the team wants it to read a customer's full history of about 16k tokens. They feed it in, and perplexity explodes after position 4,096. The interviewer asks:

> Why does a 4k model break at 16k, and how does YaRN fix it?

Where this lesson sits: the positional encoding applied inside attention, and which tokens attention can see.

Background: Positional Encodings (incl. RoPE).

**Running example:** the support assistant was pre-trained with 4k-token contexts. The team wants it to read a customer's full order history and past chats, about 16k tokens.

#### Positions the model has never seen

Feed a 4k-trained model 16k tokens and perplexity explodes after position 4,096: the attention scores depend on rotation angles that never occurred in training. Training at 16k from scratch is expensive (attention cost grows with the square of length), so we want to extend a trained model cheaply.

### The idea

Think of a clock's hands in training. The second hand has gone round many times, so every angle is familiar. The hour hand has never finished a lap, so going further shows it angles it has never seen. YaRN slows only the slow hands, and leaves the fast ones alone so nearby tokens stay distinct.

[Figure: Stretching a 4k model to 16k. No change leaves 18 pairs at unseen angles and keeps 1 radian between neighbours. Position interpolation has none unseen but only 0.25 radians. NTK-aware has 17 unseen and 1 radian. YaRN has none unseen and 1 radian.]

_From the lab: stretching a 4k model to 16k, with 64 rotary pairs._

### Play

**Try to break it.** At 16k, switch between no change, position interpolation, NTK-aware and YaRN. Then push the target to 64k.

#### Extend a 4k model to longer contexts

Head size 128 (64 rotary pairs), base 10,000, training length 4,096. A pair counts as "unseen" if it never completed a full turn in training and the new length pushes it past its largest trained angle. Dots: each pair's rotation speed relative to training (1 = unchanged); red = unseen angles. YaRN ramp α = 1, β = 32 as in the paper.

**No change**: the 18 slow pairs go past their trained angles, the failure we started with. **Position interpolation** divides every position by 4, so nothing is unseen, but the fastest pair's angle between neighbouring tokens drops from 1 rad to **0.25 rad**: nearby tokens become harder to tell apart, which is why PI needs fine-tuning. **NTK-aware** scaling raises the base: fast pairs stay sharp (1 rad), but **17** slow pairs are still only partly slowed and reach unseen angles. **YaRN** interpolates the slow pairs fully, leaves the fast ones alone, and blends in between: **0** unseen pairs and neighbour detail kept at 1 rad. It also scales attention logits by a temperature (√(1/t) = 0.1 ln s + 1) to keep attention from becoming too spread out.

**Now say why:** position interpolation leaves nothing unseen, so why does it still need fine-tuning?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

RoPE encodes position by rotating pairs of query/key dimensions, fast for some pairs and very slowly for others. Past the training length, the slow pairs reach angles the model has **never seen**, and quality collapses. **Position interpolation (PI)** squeezes positions back into the trained range, but blurs nearby tokens; **NTK-aware** scaling raises the RoPE base instead; **YaRN** interpolates only the slow pairs, keeps the fast ones untouched and adds an attention temperature, extending Llama 2 to 128k with a short fine-tune. Separately, **sliding-window attention** caps memory by attending only to recent tokens, and **attention sinks** (keeping the first few tokens) stop it from breaking. Long context is only useful if the model uses it: test with tasks harder than needle-in-a-haystack. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why models fail beyond their training length and compare PI, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN, sliding windows and attention sinks.

#### Fast pairs and slow pairs

$$ \text{angle}_i(m) = {m}\cdot{\theta_i}, \qquad {\theta_i = }{b}^{{-2i/d}} $$

Su et al., RoFormer, [arXiv:2104.09864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864). The query–key score then depends only on the difference of positions.

- **position**: Token position m multiplies the rotation speed: the angle grows linearly with position.

- **speed of pair i**: Each pair of dimensions i = 0…d/2−1 rotates at its own speed. Pair 0 turns 1 radian per token (fine detail about neighbours); the last pairs turn extremely slowly (coarse, long-range position).

- **base**: 10,000 in the original RoPE; Llama 3 uses 500,000 so even the slowest pairs vary meaningfully over long contexts.

With base 10,000, head size 128 and a 4k training length, the fast pairs complete many full turns during training, so any angle is familiar. But **18 of the 64** pairs turn so slowly that they never complete one turn within 4,096 tokens: beyond that length they produce angles the model has never seen.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Windows, sinks, and long-context training

- **Sliding-window attention:** each token attends only to the last W tokens (Mistral 7B: W = 4,096), so the KV cache stops growing; stacking layers still lets information travel further. Gemma 3 interleaves local sliding-window layers with occasional global layers.

- **Attention sinks** (StreamingLLM, Xiao et al. 2024): models put large attention on the first tokens regardless of content; evicting them breaks a sliding window. Keeping just **4** initial tokens plus the window let Llama 2, MPT, Falcon and Pythia stream over **4 million** tokens, up to 22.2× faster than re-computing a sliding window. This bounds memory; it doesn't let the model recall evicted text.

- **Practice:** frontier models pre-train at 4k–8k, then continue training on long documents with a scaled RoPE (Llama 3.1 extended to 128k this way); YaRN reported 10× fewer tokens and 2.5× fewer steps than earlier extension methods.

**Claimed vs usable context.** Liu et al. (2024) found models use information at the start and end of a long context much better than information in the middle ("lost in the middle"), and RULER (Hsieh et al. 2024) showed many models that pass simple needle-in-a-haystack tests degrade well before their advertised length on harder retrieval and multi-hop tasks.

#### Keep every angle inside what training covered

Context extension works by mapping long positions onto rotation angles the model already knows, while protecting the fast-rotating dimensions that encode local word order; memory at long context is then handled separately, by GQA/MLA, windows, sinks and cache compression.

For newer ways to cut the cost, read Attention Alternatives.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A 128k model uses all 128k tokens equally well"

It sounds right, since that's what the spec sheet says. But Liu et al. found that models use information at the start and end of a long context much better than in the middle. RULER showed many models degrading well before their advertised length on harder tasks. StreamingLLM doesn't help here either: it keeps a fixed window, and evicted text is gone. So test it.

## Say it

### Why does a 4k model break at 16k, and how does YaRN fix it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does raising the RoPE base help long context?

It slows every pair down, so angles over a longer range stay within what the model sees during training; Llama 3 uses base 500,000.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What are attention sinks?

The first tokens receive large attention because softmax must put probability somewhere; they act as a dump. Removing them from the cache shifts attention and breaks the model.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Long context or RAG?

Long context is simpler but costs quadratic prefill and linear KV memory per request, and recall in the middle can be weak; RAG is cheaper per query and easier to update. Many systems combine them.

#### The 30-second answer

RoPE rotates pairs of query and key dimensions at different speeds; beyond the training length the slowly rotating pairs hit angles never seen in training, so quality collapses. Position interpolation rescales positions into the trained range but blurs local order; NTK-aware scaling raises the RoPE base instead; YaRN interpolates only the low-frequency pairs, keeps the high-frequency ones, and adds an attention temperature, which extends context with a short fine-tune. To bound memory, sliding-window attention keeps only recent tokens, and StreamingLLM shows you must keep a few initial attention-sink tokens. And I'd verify usable context with RULER-style tests, since models often lose information in the middle.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "A 128k model uses all 128k tokens equally well." Test it.

- "StreamingLLM gives infinite memory." It keeps a fixed window; evicted text is gone.

**Key terms and sources**

Why a model trained on 4k or 8k tokens breaks at 32k, how position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN stretch RoPE to longer contexts, how sliding-window attention and attention sinks bound memory, and how to tell whether a long context actually works · built from Su et al. (RoFormer, 2021), Chen et al. (Position Interpolation, 2023), Peng et al. (YaRN, ICLR 2024), Jiang et al. (Mistral 7B, 2023), Xiao et al. (StreamingLLM, ICLR 2024), Liu et al. (Lost in the Middle, TACL 2024) and Hsieh et al. (RULER, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. S. Chen et al., "Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation", 2023, [arXiv:2306.15595](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595).

2. B. Peng, J. Quesnelle, H. Fan & E. Shippole, "YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models", ICLR 2024, [arXiv:2309.00071](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00071).

3. G. Xiao et al., "Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks", ICLR 2024, [arXiv:2309.17453](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453).

4. A. Jiang et al., "Mistral 7B", 2023, [arXiv:2310.06825](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06825); Gemma Team, "Gemma 3 Technical Report", 2025, [arXiv:2503.19786](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19786).

5. N. Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts", TACL 2024, [arXiv:2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172); C.-P. Hsieh et al., "RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?", 2024, [arXiv:2404.06654](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654).
