# Attention Alternatives: Sparse, Linear and Compressed

> How do new models handle a million tokens of context, and what do they give up?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 22 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/attention-alternatives/
- Before this: Long Context: RoPE Scaling, Sliding Windows and Attention Sinks (`fundamentals/long-context`), GPUs, TPUs and Memory Bandwidth (`fundamentals/gpus-tpus-and-memory-bandwidth`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

A coding agent needs to read a million tokens of context. Your 8B model already uses GQA, but one conversation would still need over 100 GB of KV cache. A teammate suggests a model that claims linear attention. The interviewer asks:

> How do new models handle a million tokens of context, and what do they give up?

#### Why it matters

GQA and MLA make each cached token smaller, but the cache still grows with every token, and FlashAttention leaves the compute quadratic. Reasoning models and coding agents now use very long contexts, and this is where architectures changed most in 2025 and 2026. Stanford's CS336 teaches it alongside mixture of experts.

### The idea

Think of revising for an exam from a huge pile of notes. You could reread everything. You could flip straight to the few useful pages, which is sparse. You could keep one running summary, which is linear. You could shrink the notes into short digests, which is compressed. Each is faster, and each can miss a detail, so good students mix them.

[Figure: Four ways to save. Read fewer entries, keep a fixed state, shrink the entries, or share them across layers.]

_Most recent models mix these with some full attention._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare all six methods at 1M tokens. Then slide the context down to 4k.

#### Stretch the context

Illustrative: every method uses the same 32-layer shape, in 16-bit, so these aren't real models. Standard: GQA with 8 KV heads of size 128. MLA and compressed entries: 576 numbers per token. Sparse: top 2,048, plus a cheap scan of all keys. Linear hybrid: 8 standard layers and 24 layers with a 16-head state of 128 × 128. Compressed hybrid: half the layers merge 4 tokens and read the top 512; half merge 128 tokens. Bars use a log scale.

At 1M tokens, **standard GQA** needs about 137 GB for a single conversation, more than a whole GPU. **MLA** cuts that to about 39 GB, but it still grows with every token. A **sliding window** stays at 537 MB, but has forgotten everything else. A **linear hybrid** saves 75%, because only a quarter of its layers keep a cache, which matches the “up to 75%” that Kimi Linear reports. The **compressed hybrid** needs about 5 GB. Now slide the context down to 4k: even standard GQA needs only 537 MB. These methods add complexity, so they only earn it at very long context.

**Now say why:** why do hybrids keep some layers of full attention?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

At very long context, even a small KV cache gets huge, because it grows with every token. New models attack this in four ways. **Sparse attention** reads only the most useful past tokens. **Linear attention** squeezes the past into a fixed-size state. **Compressed attention** merges many tokens into fewer entries, or works in a smaller space. **Sharing** reuses keys and values across layers. Each one loses something, usually exact recall, so most recent models are **hybrids** that keep some layers of standard attention.

#### Four ways to pay less

| Idea | How it saves | What it gives up | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sparse** | Each query reads only its top-k past tokens | Tokens it doesn't select | DeepSeek Sparse Attention |
| **Linear** | Past tokens update a fixed-size state | Exact recall of old details | Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention |
| **Compressed** | Fewer or smaller entries to store | Fine detail in what's merged | CSA and HCA, Compressed Convolutional Attention |
| **Shared** | Later layers reuse earlier layers' keys and values | Some capacity in those layers | Cross-Layer Attention |

##### Sparse attention

DeepSeek's version uses a small, cheap **indexer** to score every past token, then runs full attention on the top-k only. This cuts the main attention from O(L²) to O(Lk). The indexer itself is still O(L²), but it has few heads and can run in FP8. The cache isn't smaller, as every token must stay available for selection.

##### Linear attention

Instead of storing every key and value, keep one matrix, and add each new token's information to it. A learned gate decides what to forget. Time per token and memory stay constant, however long the context gets. The catch is that a fixed-size state can't hold everything exactly.

##### Compressed attention

You can compress along two directions. **Along the sequence:** merge several neighbouring tokens into one entry. DeepSeek-V4's CSA merges 4 tokens and then selects sparsely, while its HCA merges 128 and attends to all of them. **Along the channels:** Compressed Convolutional Attention runs all of attention in a smaller space. Unlike MLA, which only stores a small version, this also cuts the compute, which speeds up prefill and training.

##### Why hybrids win

Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next both use three linear layers for each full-attention layer. DeepSeek-V4 interleaves CSA and HCA, and adds a short sliding window of recent tokens. The cheap layers do most of the mixing, and the others keep access to specific earlier tokens.

##### Reported results

| Model | Reported by its authors |
|---|---|
| Kimi Linear | KV cache down by up to 75%, and up to 6× decoding speed at 1M context |
| Qwen3-Next | Beat its 32B base model on downstream tasks, at 10% of the training cost, with 10× throughput above 32K tokens |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro | 27% of the FLOPs per token and 10% of the KV cache of DeepSeek-V3.2, at 1M context |
| Cross-Layer Attention | A further 2× smaller cache than MQA, with nearly the same accuracy |

These are the authors' own numbers, on their own hardware and tests. Kimi's paper also reports smaller speed-ups in some settings, so treat "up to" figures as best cases.

#### The maths

$$ {S_t} = {A_t}\,{S_{t-1}} + {k_t v_t^{\top}}, \qquad {o_t = S_t^{\top} q_t} $$

The general linear attention update, as written in the Kimi Linear paper (Eq. 15). Standard attention would keep every key and value, and compare the query with each one.

- **the state**: A fixed-size matrix that stands in for the whole past. Its size doesn’t depend on the context length.

- **forget**: A learned gate shrinks parts of the old state. Better gates are the main difference between methods.

- **the previous state**: Everything remembered so far.

- **write**: Add the new token’s key and value to the state.

- **read**: Multiply the state by the query, rather than comparing the query with every past token.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Test what you care about:** a long context only helps if the model uses it. Test retrieval and multi-step tasks at your real length, as in Long Context. Qwen3-Next's card reports 91.8 on a 1M-token RULER test, against 92.5 for its larger sibling.

- **Ask which phase you're speeding up:** GQA and MLA mostly help decoding. Channel compression also helps prefill and training. Long-context work is mostly prefill.

- **Kernels matter:** sparse and linear methods need custom kernels. A method that looks cheap in FLOPs can be slower in practice, as memory traffic decides.

- **Other models exist:** state space models such as Mamba also keep a fixed state, and report 5× throughput on their tests. Later work mostly mixes this idea with attention.

- **Evidence is young:** most numbers come from the labs that built these methods, and full ablations are rare. Treat the claims as promising.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Linear attention is simply better, because it's constant memory"

It sounds right, as constant memory beats memory that grows. But a fixed-size state can't hold everything exactly, so a model can lose specific details. That's why Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next both keep some full-attention layers. Test recall on your own long-context tasks.

## Say it

### How do new models handle a million tokens of context, and what do they give up?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does a 3:1 linear hybrid cut the cache by about 75%?

At long context the linear layers' fixed state is tiny next to the cache, so only the quarter of layers using full attention still store a cache that grows with every token.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Sparse attention reads only k tokens. Why isn't its cache small?

Any past token might be selected later, so all of them must stay available. It mostly saves compute and memory reads, unless you also compress the entries, as DeepSeek-V4 does.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Your agent needs 500k tokens of context. How do you choose a model?

Test on your own long-context tasks, rather than its advertised length. Measure retrieval from the middle of the context, prefill time and memory per conversation. Prefill usually dominates for long inputs, so check which phase the model actually speeds up.

#### The 30-second answer

GQA and MLA make each cached token smaller, but the cache still grows with context. Four newer ideas go further. Sparse attention uses a cheap indexer to read only the top-k past tokens, which cuts the main attention from L squared to L times k. Linear attention replaces the cache with a fixed-size state and a learned forget gate, so memory stays constant, but it can't recall details exactly. Compression merges tokens along the sequence, or works in a smaller space, which can also cut prefill and training cost. Sharing reuses keys and values across layers. Most models are hybrids, such as three linear layers per full-attention layer, because some layers still need exact access to earlier tokens.

**Key terms and sources**

Why full attention gets expensive, sparse attention, linear attention with a fixed-size state, compressing keys and values, cross-layer sharing, and why hybrids win. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Kimi Team, Kimi Linear](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26692)

- [DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3.2 (Sparse Attention)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556)

- [DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348)

- [Qwen3-Next model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct)

- [Figliolia et al., Compressed Convolutional Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04476)

- [Brandon et al., Cross-Layer Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12981)

- [Gu and Dao, Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752)

- [Raschka, Recent Developments in LLM Architectures](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/recent-developments-in-llm-architectures)

# Mixture of Experts

> How does a 47B model run at 13B cost, and what goes wrong?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/mixture-of-experts/
- Before this: Anatomy of a Modern LLM (`fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team considers swapping the 8B dense assistant for an MoE model with similar compute per token but far more parameters. A colleague says that means the same hardware and a smarter model. The interviewer asks:

> How does a 47B model run at 13B cost, and what goes wrong?

Where this lesson sits: the feed-forward box, replaced by a router plus several expert FFNs.

Background: The Transformer Block.

**Running example:** the team considers swapping the 8B dense assistant for an MoE model with similar per-token compute but far more knowledge capacity. What does it cost, and what can go wrong?

#### More parameters, same compute per token

Bigger models know more, but in a dense model every parameter is used for every token, so compute grows with size. Different tokens need different knowledge: code, Hindi, arithmetic, recipes. Conditional computation lets each token use only the part of the network it needs.

### The idea

Think of a large call centre where each call goes to only two agents. You have many agents on the payroll, but each call uses very few. If the router favours one agent, that queue overflows, and agents who get no calls never improve. You also still pay for every agent, busy or not.

[Figure: Load on 8 experts. Without balancing, expert 1 gets far more than its fair share and goes over the capacity line, while expert 8 gets almost nothing. With bias balancing, all eight are about equal and under the line.]

_1,024 tokens at capacity factor 1.25. Expert 1's 2.37× and expert 8's 0.15× are from the lab; the bars between are illustrative._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Use top-2 with no balancing, and raise the capacity factor. Then switch to bias balancing, and compare the dropped token-slots.

#### Let the router choose freely

1,024 tokens, 8 experts. Router scores = an expert preference that has drifted towards expert 1 (as happens early in training when popular experts get more updates) + per-token noise; fixed seed. Bias balancing: before routing, each expert's bias is nudged up if it's under-loaded and down if over-loaded (300 small steps); the bias affects only which experts are chosen, not the gate weights.

Without balancing, top-2 routing sends expert 1 **2.37×** its fair share while expert 8 gets only **0.15×**; at capacity factor 1.25, **22.6%** of token-slots overflow and are dropped. Raising capacity to 2.0 cuts drops to 4.6% but wastes memory and compute on padding. It gets worse over training: favoured experts improve, get chosen more, and the others starve (**expert collapse**). With **bias balancing** every expert is within about 2% of the average and nothing is dropped at 1.25.

**Now say why:** raising capacity also cuts drops, so why isn't that the fix?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Since most parameters sit in the feed-forward layers, an MoE layer replaces the one FFN with many **experts** (separate FFNs) and a small **router** that sends each token to only the top-k of them. Total parameters grow, but compute per token only depends on the k active experts: **Mixtral 8x7B** has 47B parameters but uses about 13B per token; **DeepSeek-V3** has 671B and activates 37B. The hard part is **load balancing**: routers tend to favour a few experts, which wastes the rest and, with fixed expert **capacity**, drops tokens. Classic fixes add an auxiliary balancing loss; DeepSeek-V3 instead nudges a per-expert bias. MoE saves compute, not memory: every expert must still be loaded. What you'll be able to do after this: explain top-k routing, total vs active parameters, and how load balancing and capacity work.

#### Router and top-k gating

$$ y = \sum_{i\,\in\,{\mathrm{TopK}(}{xW_r}{,\,k)}} {g_i(x)}\;{E_i(x)} $$

Shazeer et al., "Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer", ICLR 2017; Jiang et al., "Mixtral of Experts", [arXiv:2401.04088](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088).

- **router scores**: A single linear layer W_r gives one score per expert for this token.

- **keep the top k**: Only the k highest-scoring experts run (Mixtral: 2 of 8; DeepSeek-V3: 8 of 256 routed experts plus 1 shared expert). The others cost nothing for this token.

- **gate weights**: A softmax over the kept scores decides how much each chosen expert contributes.

- **expert outputs**: Each expert is an ordinary SwiGLU FFN; the layer output is their weighted sum.

- **Total vs active:** Mixtral has 8 experts per layer but attention and embeddings are shared, so it's 47B total, not 8 × 7B = 56B, and about 13B active per token. It matched or beat Llama 2 70B on most benchmarks the paper reports.

- **Capacity:** for efficient batched compute each expert gets a fixed buffer, capacity = capacity factor × (tokens × k / experts). Tokens beyond it are dropped (passed through the residual only).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Keeping experts busy

- **Auxiliary loss** (GShard, Switch Transformer): add α · E · Σ fᵢ Pᵢ, where fᵢ is the fraction of tokens sent to expert i and Pᵢ its mean router probability (Switch: α = 0.01). It works, but too strong a loss hurts quality.

- **Switch Transformer** (Fedus et al.): top-1 routing, capacity factor ~1–1.25; up to 7× faster pre-training than a dense T5-Base with the same compute per token.

- **Fine-grained and shared experts** (DeepSeekMoE): many small experts plus always-on shared experts for common knowledge.

- **Auxiliary-loss-free balancing** (DeepSeek-V3): a per-expert bias added to the routing scores only for top-k selection, updated after each step; DeepSeek-V3 also drops no tokens during training.

**Serving costs.** All experts must sit in GPU memory (Mixtral needs the memory of a 47B model to run at 13B compute), experts are spread across GPUs (expert parallelism), and routing needs all-to-all communication. MoE pays off at high throughput; for a single user on one small GPU a dense model is often simpler.

#### Decouple parameters from FLOPs

MoE lets knowledge capacity (total parameters) grow independently of compute per token (active parameters), as long as the router spreads tokens evenly enough that every expert learns and none overflows.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "MoE reduces memory"

It sounds right, since it only uses a fraction of the model per token. But every expert must sit in GPU memory, so Mixtral needs the memory of a 47B model to run at 13B compute. It reduces compute per token, and memory still follows total parameters. And experts aren't topic specialists either: Mixtral's routing followed syntax and token patterns more than domains.

## Say it

### How does a 47B model run at 13B cost, and what goes wrong?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why isn't Mixtral 8 × 7B = 56B?

Only the FFNs are replicated; attention, norms and embeddings are shared, so the total is about 47B.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Do experts specialise by topic?

Not cleanly: Mixtral's analysis found routing followed syntax and token patterns more than domains like biology or maths.

Follow-up 3 of 3

MoE vs dense for a latency-sensitive single-GPU deployment?

Usually dense: MoE needs memory for all experts and benefits from large batches; at batch size 1 the memory reads of a big MoE can make it slower than its active-parameter count suggests.

#### The 30-second answer

A mixture-of-experts layer replaces the dense feed-forward layer with many expert FFNs and a learned router that sends each token to its top-k experts, weighting their outputs with a softmax over the selected scores. Total parameters grow but compute per token depends only on active ones: Mixtral 8x7B is 47B total and about 13B active, DeepSeek-V3 is 671B total and 37B active. The main challenge is load balancing: without it a few experts get most tokens, others collapse, and with fixed expert capacity tokens get dropped. Fixes are an auxiliary balancing loss, capacity factors, shared experts, or DeepSeek-V3's bias-based auxiliary-loss-free balancing. MoE saves FLOPs, not memory, and needs expert parallelism with all-to-all communication.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "MoE reduces memory." It reduces compute per token; memory follows total parameters.

- "Each expert is an expert in a topic." Specialisation is mostly at the token level.

**Key terms and sources**

How MoE layers give a model many more parameters without more compute per token: the router and top-k gating, total vs active parameters, load imbalance and expert collapse, capacity factors and dropped tokens, auxiliary losses vs DeepSeek-V3's bias-based balancing, and the serving trade-offs · built from Shazeer et al. (2017), Lepikhin et al. (GShard, 2020), Fedus et al. (Switch Transformer, JMLR 2022), Jiang et al. (Mixtral, 2024), Dai et al. (DeepSeekMoE, 2024), Wang et al. (Loss-Free Balancing, 2024) and DeepSeek-AI (DeepSeek-V3, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

2. W. Fedus, B. Zoph & N. Shazeer, "Switch Transformers", JMLR 2022, [arXiv:2101.03961](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961).

# Vision-Language Models

> How does an LLM see an image, and how many tokens does one cost?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Modern architecture
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/vision-language-models/
- Before this: Anatomy of a Modern LLM (`fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture`), Vision Transformers (`fundamentals/vision-transformers`)
- Quiz topic: `arch`

## Intuition

### The situation

Customers can now send a photo of their order or receipt to the support assistant. The first tests misread amounts, and the bill for image tokens is higher than expected. Someone suggests simply sending bigger images. The interviewer asks:

> How does an LLM see an image, and how many tokens does one cost?

#### Why it matters

Multimodal questions now come up in LLM interviews, and both CS336 and CME295 cover them. It's mostly a question of ideas you already have: Vision Transformers for the encoder, contrastive learning for CLIP, and KV cache sizing for the cost. This lesson joins them up.

### The idea

Think of describing a photo to a friend over the phone by cutting it into a grid of small squares, and describing each one. More squares give more detail, but the call takes longer. A few squares are quick, but you'd never read the small print. Vision-language models make the same trade.

[Figure: Three parts. An encoder turns patches into vectors. A projector matches the LLM's size. The LLM reads them as tokens.]

_The main choice is how many tokens an image gets._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare all four schemes on a large image. Then try a wide screenshot.

#### Spend the token budget

Fixed sizes: 896 and 448 pixels square, as in Gemma 3 and PaliGemma. Tiles: the rule OpenAI documents for models such as GPT-4o: fit within 2,048 pixels, shrink the short side to 768, then 85 + 170 tokens per 512-pixel square. One per 28 pixels is the adaptive rule without a size cap, though real services do cap image size. The grid is only a guide, and is capped so it stays readable. Text below about 6 pixels is marked as at risk, which is our own rule of thumb.

A customer sends a 2,048 × 3,008 photo of a receipt. At a **fixed 256 tokens**, it's cheap, but 12-pixel text shrinks to 3.6 pixels, and the model may misread the amount. With **one token per 28 pixels**, the text stays sharp, but the photo costs 7,992 tokens, nearly all of an 8k context, and about 1 GB of KV cache. **Tiles** land in between, at 1,105 tokens. Now try a wide screenshot: resizing it to a square squeezes it out of shape, which adaptive methods avoid.

**Now say why:** why does doubling both sides cost four times the tokens?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A vision-language model turns an image into a sequence of vectors, then treats them like extra tokens in the prompt. A **vision encoder** splits the image into small patches and encodes them. A small **projector** maps those vectors to the LLM's size. The LLM then reads image and text together. Everything else follows from the **token budget**. Fixed-size models resize every image to the same token count, which is cheap but can lose small details. Adaptive models keep more detail, but a large image can cost thousands of tokens.

#### From pixels to tokens

##### Step 1: learn to link images and text

**CLIP** trained an image encoder and a text encoder on 400 million image and text pairs. In a batch of N pairs, it pushes each image towards its own caption, and away from the other N − 1. This gave vision encoders a good starting point, and LLaVA later built on one.

##### Step 2: connect an encoder to an LLM

| Part | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Encoder** | Turns image patches into vectors | CLIP ViT-L/14, SigLIP, or a ViT trained for the purpose |
| **Projector** | Maps vectors to the LLM's size | One linear layer in LLaVA and PaliGemma, a small MLP in Qwen2.5-VL |
| **LLM** | Reads the image tokens and text together | Vicuna, Gemma, Qwen |

LLaVA showed how simple this can be. It first trained only the linear layer, with the encoder and LLM frozen, then fine-tuned the LLM too. Its training data came from a text-only GPT-4, given captions and object boxes instead of images.

##### Step 3: choose the token budget

| Model | Image becomes | Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| PaliGemma | A fixed square of 224, 448 or 896 pixels | 256, 1,024 or 4,096 |
| Gemma 3 | 896 × 896, then 4 × 4 average pooling | 256 |
| Qwen2.5-VL | 14-pixel patches, with each 2 × 2 group merged | One per 28 × 28 pixels, so it varies |

Gemma 3 adds **pan and scan**, which splits an image into crops and encodes each one, for when a single 256-token view isn't enough.

##### Step 4: tell the model where things are

A flat sequence loses the image's layout. Qwen2.5-VL gives each token separate time, height and width positions, a scheme called multimodal RoPE. For video, it groups two frames at a time, and ties the time position to real seconds, so the model can tell how fast things happen.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{tokens}} = {\Big\lceil \frac{W}{p} \Big\rceil}\,{\Big\lceil \frac{H}{p} \Big\rceil}, \qquad {\text{KV cache} = \text{tokens} \times \text{cache per token}} $$

The adaptive rule. Claude’s documentation states this form, with p = 28, and Qwen2.5-VL’s design implies it. Fixed-size models resize first, so their token count doesn’t change.

- **image tokens**: How many positions the image takes up in the context.

- **across**: Width divided by p, the pixels each token covers, rounded up. For Qwen2.5-VL and Claude, p is 28.

- **down**: The same for height. Doubling both sides means four times the tokens.

- **the cost**: Image tokens are ordinary tokens. They use context, take prefill time and fill the KV cache.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Where they fail

- **Simple visual tasks:** "Vision language models are blind" gave four leading models 7 very simple tasks, such as counting overlaps, and they averaged 58.07%. The best reached 77.84%, where people would expect about 100%. Tests suggest the encoders hold the information, but the LLM fails to decode it.

- **Small, rotated or non-Latin text:** OpenAI's documentation lists all three as limits. Check the resolution first, before blaming the model.

- **Invented details:** a model can describe what's usually in such an image, rather than what's there. Test with unusual images, not only typical ones.

- **Cost surprises:** image tokens count as input. Measure tokens per image on real uploads, and resize before sending.

- **Hidden instructions:** text inside an image reaches the model like any other input. Treat it as untrusted, as with other prompt injection.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Send the highest resolution, so the model sees everything"

It sounds right, as more pixels means more detail. But services may shrink large images first, so the extra pixels can be wasted, and on an adaptive model a big image can fill the context by itself. Work out how large the text ends up, and crop to what matters.

## Say it

### How does an LLM see an image, and how many tokens does one cost?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How many tokens is a 1,000 × 1,000 image at one token per 28 pixels?

1,000 ÷ 28 rounds up to 36, so 36 × 36 = 1,296 tokens. Doubling both sides gives about four times as many.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does a 4 × 4 pool give 256 tokens at 896 pixels?

With 14-pixel patches, 896 pixels gives 64 × 64 = 4,096 patches. Averaging each 4 × 4 group leaves 16 × 16 = 256.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Your model misreads amounts on receipts. What do you check first?

The resolution that reaches the model. Work out how many pixels the text has after resizing, then try crops or a higher-detail setting. Test against OCR on the same images, and check the answer against the receipt's total.

#### The 30-second answer

A vision-language model has three parts. A vision encoder, usually a ViT, turns image patches into vectors. A small projector maps them to the LLM's size. The LLM then reads those image tokens along with the text. LLaVA showed that one linear layer can connect the two. The main design choice is the token budget. Gemma 3 uses 256 tokens for every image, which is cheap but can lose small text. Qwen2.5-VL uses about one token per 28 by 28 pixels, which keeps detail but can cost thousands of tokens. Image tokens are ordinary tokens, so they use context and KV cache. I'd also test simple visual tasks, as these models can still fail at counting and spatial reasoning.

**Key terms and sources**

How images become tokens, CLIP's shared space, encoders and projectors, fixed and adaptive image tokens, positions for images and video, and where these models fail. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Radford et al., CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)

- [Liu et al., LLaVA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485)

- [Beyer et al., PaliGemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07726)

- [Gemma Team, Gemma 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19786)

- [Qwen Team, Qwen2.5-VL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923)

- [Rahmanzadehgervi et al., Vision language models are blind](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06581)

- [OpenAI, Images and vision](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision)

- [Anthropic, Vision](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision)

- [Stanford CS336, multimodality lecture](https://cs336.stanford.edu/)

# The Next-Token Objective

> How does one sentence become eight training examples?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Pretraining
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/next-token-prediction/
- Before this: N-gram Language Models and Perplexity (`fundamentals/n-gram-language-models`), The Transformer, End to End (`fundamentals/transformer-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `pre`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team has a huge pile of raw text and almost no labels. A new hire asks where the training labels come from when you pre-train an LLM. The interviewer asks:

> How does one sentence become eight training examples?

Where this lesson sits: the causal mask inside attention, and the softmax over the vocabulary at the top of the stack.

Background: Encoder vs Decoder · Loss Functions.

**Running example:** one sentence from the assistant's training text, "your biryani will arrive in 20 minutes.", and the probability the model gives each true next token.

#### Learning from text with no labels

Labelled data is scarce; raw text is effectively unlimited. Next-token prediction turns every piece of text into its own labels: the "answer" at each position is simply the token that comes next. To predict well, a model has to pick up grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and style, which is why this one objective produces such general models.

### The idea

Think of reading with a card that covers everything after the current word. You guess the next word, slide the card along, and check. Every word becomes its own small test, so any text is full of them. The causal mask is the card.

[Figure: The sentence your biryani will arrive in 20 minutes. Each position sees the tokens so far and predicts the next token, the same sentence shifted by one, giving eight training examples.]

_Each position sees only the tokens so far. One forward pass gives all eight predictions._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start with the trained model and find the most surprising token. Then try the confidently wrong model, and the one that memorised the sentence.

#### Per-token losses on one sentence

Illustrative probabilities for the true next token at each position (not from a real model). Loss = −ln p. Each chip shows the context it was predicted from.

The 8-token sentence gives **8** training examples from one forward pass. The average loss is **1.42** (perplexity 4.14). Function words after a clear context are easy ("in" 0.16, "minutes" 0.08), while content words that could have been many things are expensive: "biryani" costs **3.91** and "20" costs 2.81. Being **confidently wrong** on a single token (p = 0.01 for "minutes") adds 4.6 to that token and lifts the sentence's average to 1.99 (perplexity 7.29): cross-entropy punishes confident mistakes hard. A model that has **memorised** the sentence scores 0.01, which is why training loss alone says nothing about generalisation: always watch held-out loss, and deduplicate the data (next lesson).

**Now say why:** the memorising model scores almost zero, so why is it no good?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Pre-training an LLM is one task repeated trillions of times: **predict the next token**. By the chain rule, the probability of a text is the product of each token's probability given the tokens before it, so the model is trained to minimise the average **cross-entropy** (−log p of the true next token) over every position. A **causal mask** stops each position from seeing the future, which means one forward pass over a 4,096-token sequence produces **4,096 training examples** at once. During training the model always conditions on the true previous tokens (**teacher forcing**); at generation time it conditions on its own outputs. The loss of a randomly initialised model starts near ln(vocabulary size), about 11.8 for a 128k vocabulary, and lower is better; exp(loss) is the perplexity. What you'll be able to do after this: write the pre-training loss, explain causal masking and teacher forcing, and read a loss curve.

#### Cross-entropy over every position

$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = {-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}}{\log p_\theta(x_t \mid }{x_{<t}}{)} $$

The same objective as an n-gram model, with a Transformer instead of a count table (Bengio et al. 2003; Radford et al. 2018).

- **average over positions**: Every position in every sequence is a training example; the loss is their mean.

- **−log probability**: The penalty is large when the model gave the true next token a small probability: −ln(0.5) = 0.69, −ln(0.01) = 4.6.

- **only the past**: The prediction may use tokens 1…t−1 and nothing after; the causal mask enforces this inside attention.

- **Causal mask:** attention scores to future positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, so the output at position t depends only on tokens ≤ t. All T predictions are computed in one parallel forward pass.

- **Teacher forcing:** during training, position t always sees the _true_ previous tokens, even if the model would have predicted something else.

- **Packing:** documents are concatenated with an end-of-text token and cut into fixed-length sequences, so no compute is wasted on padding.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Reading the loss in real training

- **Starting loss ≈ ln V:** a fresh model spreads probability evenly, so with Llama 3's 128,256-token vocabulary the first loss is about ln 128,256 ≈ 11.8. A much higher start means a bad initialisation of the output layer.

- **Exposure bias:** teacher forcing never shows the model its own mistakes, so errors can compound during generation (Bengio et al. 2015, scheduled sampling). In LLMs this is mostly addressed later, by post-training on the model's own outputs.

- **Loss is per token, so it depends on the tokeniser:** compare models with different tokenisers in bits per byte or per word, not per-token loss.

- Variants: **multi-token prediction** (DeepSeek-V3 predicts an extra future token as an auxiliary objective), and **fill-in-the-middle** for code models.

#### Compression as learning

Minimising next-token cross-entropy is the same as compressing the training text: every pattern the model learns, from spelling to arithmetic, lowers the number of bits needed to predict what comes next, and the causal mask lets every position of every document teach in parallel.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Lower training loss means a better model"

It sounds right, since loss is what training minimises. But a model that has memorised the lab's sentence scores 0.01, and that says nothing about new text. Watch held-out loss, and deduplicate the data. Also note that the model doesn't generate during training: that's teacher forcing in parallel, and generation is sequential.

## Say it

### How does one sentence become eight training examples?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does a decoder-only model train efficiently?

Every token is a target, and the causal mask makes all of them computable in one pass; a masked-LM like BERT only trains on the ~15% masked tokens.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your loss starts at 25 with a 50k vocabulary. What's wrong?

ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8, so the initial logits are far too large: the output layer is initialised too big (or a scaling factor is missing).

Follow-up 3 of 3

Do you compute loss on padding or on the prompt?

Not on padding (it's masked out). In pre-training all real tokens count; in SFT the loss is usually masked to the response tokens only.

#### The 30-second answer

LLMs are pre-trained with next-token prediction: by the chain rule a text's probability is the product of each token's probability given the previous tokens, so we minimise the average cross-entropy of the true next token across all positions. A causal mask blocks attention to future tokens, so one forward pass over a sequence gives a prediction and a loss at every position in parallel. Training uses teacher forcing, always feeding the true previous tokens, which can cause exposure bias at generation time. Documents are packed into fixed-length sequences with end-of-text separators. The loss starts near the log of the vocabulary size, and exp of the held-out loss is perplexity.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The model generates during training." Training is parallel with teacher forcing; generation is sequential.

- "Lower training loss means a better model." Use held-out loss, and watch for memorisation.

**Key terms and sources**

How LLMs are pre-trained: the autoregressive factorisation, cross-entropy on every position, the causal mask that makes one forward pass produce N training examples, teacher forcing and exposure bias, sequence packing, what the loss value means, and why such a simple objective teaches so much · built from Bengio et al. (2003), Radford et al. (GPT, 2018; GPT-2, 2019), Brown et al. (GPT-3, 2020), Vaswani et al. (2017), Bengio et al. (scheduled sampling, 2015) and Jurafsky & Martin (SLP3) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. Y. Bengio, R. Ducharme, P. Vincent & C. Jauvin, "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model", _JMLR_ 3, 2003.

2. A. Radford et al., "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training" (GPT), OpenAI 2018; "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), OpenAI 2019.

3. T. Brown et al., "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (GPT-3), NeurIPS 2020, [arXiv:2005.14165](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165).

4. S. Bengio et al., "Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks", NeurIPS 2015, [arXiv:1506.03099](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03099).

5. DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report", 2024, [arXiv:2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437) (multi-token prediction).

# Pretraining Data: Deduplication, Filtering and Mixtures

> How do trillions of web tokens become training data?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Pretraining
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/pretraining-data/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Quiz topic: `pre`

## Intuition

### The situation

While crawling the web for food-related text, the team finds thousands of near-identical restaurant pages from one template. A colleague says to keep them, because more data is always better. The interviewer asks:

> How do trillions of web tokens become training data?

**Running example:** while crawling the web for food-related text to pre-train (or continue pre-training) the assistant, the team finds thousands of near-identical restaurant landing pages generated from one template.

#### The web is big, repetitive and mostly not useful text

Common Crawl adds billions of pages per snapshot, but much of it is navigation menus, cookie banners, SEO spam, machine-generated pages and copies of the same content. Training on duplicates wastes compute and makes models **memorise and regurgitate** text: Lee et al. (2022) found that deduplicating C4 reduced how often models emitted memorised training text by about 10× and needed fewer training steps for the same accuracy.

### The idea

Think of cleaning raw grain before an expensive mill. Milling time is fixed, so every stone, husk and repeated sack wastes it. You sieve first, then keep and mix the best grain. MinHash is the quick test that spots two sacks from the same batch without checking each grain.

[Figure: A pipeline that narrows at each step: crawled web pages, extract main text, URL, language and quality filters, remove near-duplicates, then remove PII and benchmarks.]

_Illustrative widths. A typical pipeline, as in FineWeb, which ended with 15 trillion tokens from 96 snapshots._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between 16, 112 and 256 hash functions. Compare pages A and B with pages A and C, and watch the flagged pairs and the largest estimate error.

#### MinHash on four pages

Exact hashing only catches identical pages; one changed word defeats it. Comparing every pair of documents exactly is impossible at billions of pages. MinHash estimates the **Jaccard similarity** of two documents' sets of word 5-grams: for each of k hash functions, keep the smallest hash value over the document's 5-grams. The fraction of positions where two signatures match is an unbiased estimate of their Jaccard similarity, and locality-sensitive hashing (the buckets) finds candidate pairs without comparing everything.

**A**: "Order chicken biryani online from Paradise Biryani House in Hyderabad. Fast delivery in 30 minutes. Fresh ingredients, authentic spices and secure payment. Track your order live and get 20% off your first order today." **B**: the same page ending in "tonight". **C**: the same template for paneer tikka from Punjab Grill in Delhi. **D**: a customer review. Word 5-grams, lower-cased; hash family fixed by seed.

A and B differ by one word, so 29 of their 31 distinct 5-grams are shared: Jaccard **0.94**, estimated as 0.91 with 112 hashes, and flagged; one copy is dropped. A and C come from the same template but describe different restaurants: Jaccard **0.51**, below 0.75, so both are kept. That's the threshold's trade-off: lower it and you also delete legitimate pages that share boilerplate; raise it and lightly edited copies survive. With only 16 hashes the estimates are noisier (A–B estimated at 1.00); more hashes cost more compute but estimate more precisely.

**Now say why:** A and C come from the same template, so why does the pipeline keep both?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

The data matters as much as the architecture. Raw web crawls are mostly boilerplate, spam, duplicates and non-text, so a pipeline **extracts** the main text, keeps the right **languages**, applies **heuristic quality filters** (length, symbol ratios, repeated lines), removes **near-duplicates**, and increasingly scores pages with a **model-based quality classifier**. Near-duplicates are found with **MinHash**: compare documents by the overlap of their word n-grams (Jaccard similarity), estimated cheaply from a short signature of minimum hash values, so billions of pages can be compared. Then the team chooses the **mixture**: Llama 3 used about 50% general knowledge, 25% maths and reasoning, 17% code and 8% multilingual tokens. Better data gives better models at the same compute: FineWeb-Edu's classifier filtering raised MMLU from 33% to 37% at equal training tokens. What you'll be able to do after this: describe a pretraining data pipeline, explain how MinHash deduplication works, and discuss data mixtures and contamination.

#### A typical pipeline (FineWeb)

1. **Text extraction** from raw HTML (FineWeb uses trafilatura on WARC files), which beat using Common Crawl's own extracted text.

2. **URL filtering and language ID** (e.g. fastText; keep English above a confidence threshold).

3. **Heuristic quality filters:** Gopher and C4 rules (word count, mean word length, symbol-to-word ratio, fraction of lines ending in punctuation, repeated lines and n-grams) plus custom ones.

4. **Near-duplicate removal** with MinHash on word 5-grams (112 hash functions in 14 buckets of 8, targeting about 75% similarity), done per crawl snapshot.

5. **PII redaction** (emails, IP addresses) and, for evaluation hygiene, **decontamination**: removing documents that contain benchmark questions.

The result, FineWeb, has 15 trillion tokens from 96 Common Crawl snapshots (Penedo et al. 2024, [arXiv:2406.17557](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)). A surprise from the paper: deduplicating globally across all snapshots did _worse_ than deduplicating within each snapshot, because it removed many good older pages and kept low-quality ones.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Model-based filtering and mixtures

- **Quality classifiers:** FineWeb-Edu had Llama-3-70B-Instruct rate hundreds of thousands of pages for educational value (0–5), trained a small classifier on those labels, and kept pages scoring ≥ 3: 1.3T tokens. At the same training budget (350B tokens) it raised MMLU from 33% to 37% and ARC from 46% to 57% compared with FineWeb. DCLM and Llama 3 also use model-based filters.

- **Mixtures:** Llama 3's final pre-training mix was roughly 50% general knowledge, 25% maths and reasoning, 17% code and 8% multilingual tokens, chosen with small-scale experiments and scaling-law predictions; high-quality data is up-weighted again at the end of training (annealing).

- **Running out of data:** Muennighoff et al. (2023) found that repeating data for up to about 4 epochs is almost as good as fresh data, after which returns fall quickly; synthetic data and other languages fill the gap (see below).

**Contamination.** If benchmark questions leak into pre-training data, scores measure memorisation. Labs filter n-gram overlaps with evaluation sets and report contamination analyses; see the evaluation lessons in this track.

##### Synthetic data

When good text runs short, you can have a strong model write more. Stanford's CS336 now teaches this as a standard part of data work.

- **For instructions:** Self-Instruct had GPT-3 write its own instructions, inputs and outputs, filtered out invalid or similar ones, then fine-tuned on the result. It gained 33% on one instruction benchmark, on par with InstructGPT-001.

- **For pre-training:** phi-1 used 6B tokens of filtered web data, plus 1B tokens of textbooks and exercises written by GPT-3.5. That 1.3B model reached 50.6% on HumanEval.

- **The risks:** errors and biases carry over from the model that wrote it, the variety can be narrow, and benchmarks can look better than real-world use. Check licences too, as many models forbid training on their outputs. This is close to sequence-level distillation.

#### Every token should earn its compute

Pre-training compute is fixed, so data work is about making each token count: remove what teaches nothing (boilerplate, spam), what teaches the wrong thing (memorised duplicates, test sets), and up-weight what teaches the most (educational, code, maths).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "More data is always better"

It sounds right, until you remember pre-training compute is fixed. Filtered, deduplicated data beats bigger raw data at equal compute. Lee et al. found that deduplicating C4 cut memorised output by about 10×, and needed fewer steps for the same accuracy. And exact hashing isn't enough: change one word and it misses the copy.

## Say it

### How do trillions of web tokens become training data?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why deduplicate?

Duplicates waste compute, over-weight some content and increase memorisation and regurgitation of training text; deduplicated data trains as well or better with fewer steps (Lee et al. 2022).

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you pick the data mixture?

Train small proxy models on candidate mixtures, measure downstream metrics, extrapolate with scaling laws, and up-weight high-quality sources during a final annealing phase.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the risk of an LLM-based quality filter?

It encodes the rater's biases (e.g. "educational" favours certain styles and topics), can reduce diversity, and can remove dialects or domains you need.

#### The 30-second answer

A pretraining data pipeline extracts main text from crawled HTML, filters by URL and language, applies heuristic quality rules like those from Gopher and C4, removes near-duplicates with MinHash over word n-grams, redacts PII and decontaminates benchmarks, and increasingly uses a model-based quality classifier, as in FineWeb-Edu, which improved MMLU from 33 to 37 percent at the same token budget. MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity between n-gram sets from short signatures of minimum hash values, and LSH buckets make it scale to billions of pages. Finally you choose a mixture, for example Llama 3's roughly half general text, a quarter maths and reasoning, 17 percent code and 8 percent multilingual, tuned with small proxy runs.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "More data is always better." Filtered, deduplicated data beats bigger raw data at equal compute.

- "Exact hashing is enough for deduplication." It misses near-duplicates.

**Key terms and sources**

How trillions of tokens of web text become training data: text extraction, language and heuristic quality filters, near-duplicate removal with MinHash, model-based quality classifiers, decontamination, and choosing the mix of web, code, maths and multilingual data · built from Penedo et al. (FineWeb, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks), Broder (MinHash, 1997), Lee et al. (Deduplicating Training Data, ACL 2022), Rae et al. (Gopher, 2021), Raffel et al. (C4, 2020), Muennighoff et al. (Data-Constrained Scaling, NeurIPS 2023) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

2. A. Broder, "On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents", 1997; K. Lee et al., "Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better", ACL 2022, [arXiv:2107.06499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499).

3. J. Rae et al., "Scaling Language Models: Methods, Analysis & Insights from Training Gopher", 2021, [arXiv:2112.11446](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11446); C. Raffel et al. (T5 / C4), JMLR 2020, [arXiv:1910.10683](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683).

# Scaling Laws: Kaplan vs Chinchilla

> Bigger model or more tokens, and why was Llama 3 8B trained on 15T?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Pretraining
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/scaling-laws/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Quiz topic: `pre`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team has a fixed GPU budget for a home-grown model. One camp wants the biggest model it can afford, and the other wants a smaller one on more tokens. The interviewer asks:

> Bigger model or more tokens, and why was Llama 3 8B trained on 15T?

**Running example:** the team has a fixed GPU budget for a home-grown model. Should they train a bigger model on fewer tokens, or a smaller one on more?

#### One shot at a very expensive run

A frontier pre-training run costs tens of millions of dollars and can't be repeated with different settings. Scaling laws let teams train dozens of small models, fit how loss depends on size and data, and choose the big run's model size, token count and even data mixture in advance. Meta chose the 405B size this way for a budget of 3.8 × 1025 FLOPs.

### The idea

Think of the budget as a rectangle with a fixed area. One side is model size, and the other is training tokens. Wide and flat costs the same as narrow and tall, but they don't learn equally well. The best shape is about 20 tokens per parameter.

[Figure: Two rectangles with about the same area, meaning the same compute. Gopher is wide and flat: 280B parameters on 300B tokens, predicted loss 2.000. Chinchilla is narrow and tall: 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens, predicted loss 1.974.]

_Sizes to scale, with about the same compute. Predicted loss from the fitted law, as in the lab._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare Gopher with Chinchilla at similar compute. Then look at Llama 3 405B and Llama 3 8B, and see how far each sits from its optimum.

#### Was each famous model compute-optimal?

Curve: predicted loss for every model size if all models got this same compute (an "IsoFLOP" curve); D = C / 6N. Loss values come from the fitted law (Chinchilla's data and tokeniser), so compare them with each other, not with other models' reported losses.

**Gopher** (280B parameters, 300B tokens, about 1 token per parameter) and **Chinchilla** (70B, 1.4T, 20 per parameter) used similar compute, about 5–6 × 1023 FLOPs. The law puts Chinchilla right at the optimum (loss 1.974) and Gopher **0.021** above it: four times the parameters, worse loss. In the paper Chinchilla beat Gopher on MMLU, 67.5% vs 60.0%. **Llama 3 405B**, at 39 tokens per parameter, is within 0.001 of its optimum, consistent with Meta's description of it as roughly compute-optimal. **Llama 3 8B** is the interesting one: at its budget the optimum is an 81B model on 1.5T tokens, and the 8B model's predicted loss is 0.054 higher. That's deliberate: see the In practice tab.

**Now say why:** the law says Llama 3 8B is far from optimal. Why would Meta do that on purpose?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

LLM loss follows smooth **power laws**: it drops predictably as you add parameters N, training tokens D and compute C, so teams fit these laws on small runs and extrapolate before spending millions. Training compute is about **C ≈ 6·N·D** FLOPs. For a fixed C, a bigger model sees fewer tokens; the question is the best split. **Kaplan et al. (2020)** said grow the model much faster than the data, which led to GPT-3's 175B parameters on 300B tokens. **Chinchilla (2022)** redid the experiments and found parameters and tokens should grow equally, about **20 tokens per parameter**: their 70B model on 1.4T tokens beat the 280B Gopher at the same compute. Today models are deliberately **over-trained** beyond that (Llama 3 8B saw 15T tokens, ~1,900 per parameter), because a smaller model is much cheaper to serve. What you'll be able to do after this: estimate training FLOPs, explain compute-optimal scaling, and argue when to train past it.

#### Compute and the Chinchilla loss law

$$ {C \approx 6ND}, \qquad L(N,D) = {E} + {\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}} + {\frac{B}{D^{\beta}}} $$

Hoffmann et al., "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models", [arXiv:2203.15556](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) (approach 3). Besiroglu et al. (2024, [arXiv:2404.10102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10102)) found the published fit inconsistent with the paper's other methods and refit it: E = 1.82, A = 482, B = 2,085, α = 0.348, β = 0.366, which gives about 20 tokens per parameter, matching Chinchilla's other two approaches. The lab uses this refit.

- **training FLOPs**: About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass: 6·N·D. Llama 3 405B: 6 × 405e9 × 15.6e12 ≈ 3.8 × 10²⁵.

- **irreducible loss**: The entropy of natural text itself: no model can go below it.

- **too few parameters**: Loss from limited model capacity, shrinking as a power of N.

- **too few tokens**: Loss from limited data, shrinking as a power of D. The optimum balances these two terms for a given C.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Training past compute-optimal

- **Chinchilla-optimal minimises training compute for a given loss**, not total cost. A model served to millions of users spends far more compute at inference, which scales with N. Sardana et al. (2024) showed that once expected inference demand is included, the best model is smaller and trained on many more tokens.

- Hence Llama 3 8B on 15T tokens (~1,875 per parameter), and small models like Qwen and Gemma trained on 10T+ tokens. Meta reported that 8B and 70B kept improving log-linearly up to 15T tokens.

- **Kaplan vs Chinchilla:** Kaplan et al. fitted mostly smaller models, counted non-embedding parameters and used a learning-rate schedule that didn't match each run's length, which biased their recommendation towards big models on few tokens.

- Scaling laws predict pre-training loss well; downstream task accuracy is less smooth. Newer work also studies test-time compute scaling (reasoning models spend more compute at inference instead).

#### Balance parameters and tokens, then pay for inference

For a fixed training budget, loss is minimised by growing parameters and tokens together (about 20 tokens per parameter); if the model will be served heavily, deliberately train a smaller model on many more tokens.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Chinchilla-optimal is always best"

It sounds right, since it gives the lowest loss for the compute. But it minimises training compute only, and a model served to millions spends far more at inference. Once inference demand is included, the best model is smaller and trained on many more tokens. Scaling laws also predict loss, not benchmark scores, and task accuracy is noisier.

## Say it

### Bigger model or more tokens, and why was Llama 3 8B trained on 15T?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Estimate the compute to train a 7B model on 2T tokens.

6 × 7e9 × 2e12 = 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs. At 40% utilisation of a 989 TFLOPS (bf16) H100, that's about 2.1 × 10⁸ GPU-seconds ≈ 59,000 GPU-hours.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the compute-optimal model for 10²⁴ FLOPs?

With D = 20N and C = 6ND = 120N², N = √(C/120) ≈ 91B parameters on about 1.8T tokens.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why did Kaplan get a different answer?

Smaller models, a fixed learning-rate schedule not tuned to each run's length, and counting only non-embedding parameters; Chinchilla corrected these.

#### The 30-second answer

Pre-training loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute, so labs fit them on small runs to plan big ones. Training compute is about 6 times parameters times tokens. Kaplan et al. in 2020 suggested scaling model size faster than data, but Chinchilla in 2022 found they should scale equally, roughly 20 tokens per parameter: a 70B model on 1.4 trillion tokens beat the 280B Gopher at the same compute. In practice models are now over-trained beyond that, like Llama 3 8B on 15 trillion tokens, because Chinchilla minimises training cost only, and a smaller model is much cheaper at inference.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Chinchilla-optimal is always best." It ignores inference cost.

- "Scaling laws predict benchmark scores." They predict loss; task accuracy is noisier.

**Key terms and sources**

How loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute; the C ≈ 6ND estimate of training FLOPs; how Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla disagreed about splitting a budget between parameters and tokens; the "20 tokens per parameter" rule; and why Llama 3 8B was trained far past it on purpose · built from Kaplan et al. (2020), Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla, NeurIPS 2022), Besiroglu et al. (Epoch AI replication, 2024), Sardana et al. (Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal, ICML 2024) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. J. Kaplan et al., "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models", 2020, [arXiv:2001.08361](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361).

2. J. Hoffmann et al., "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Chinchilla), NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2203.15556](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

3. T. Besiroglu, E. Erdil, M. Barnett & J. You, "Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt", Epoch AI, 2024, [arXiv:2404.10102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10102).

4. N. Sardana et al., "Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws", ICML 2024, [arXiv:2401.00448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00448).

# Training at Scale: Mixed Precision, Parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP

> Why does a 70B model need 1.1 TB to train, and how is it split?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Pretraining
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/distributed-training/
- Before this: Anatomy of a Modern LLM (`fundamentals/modern-llm-architecture`)
- Quiz topic: `pre`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team wants to fully fine-tune a 70B model on a cluster of 80 GB GPUs. A colleague says just add more GPUs with data parallel until it fits. The interviewer asks:

> Why does a 70B model need 1.1 TB to train, and how is it split?

**Running example:** the team wants to fully fine-tune (or continue pre-training) a 70B model for the support assistant on a cluster of 80 GB GPUs. How many GPUs, and which strategy?

#### Too big for one GPU, too slow on one GPU

Two separate limits. **Memory:** parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations must fit. **Time:** Llama 3 405B needed 3.8 × 1025 FLOPs; a single H100 at a realistic 400 TFLOPS would take about 3,000 years. Parallelism has to split both the memory and the work, while keeping communication from dominating.

### The idea

Think of cooks who each keep their own full copy of a huge recipe library. Hiring more cooks never shrinks the library. Split it across everyone's shelves, and each cook fetches the page when needed. That saves a lot of room, in exchange for more walking.

[Figure: Model state per GPU for a 70B model on 64 GPUs. Data parallel 1,120 gigabytes, ZeRO-1 293, ZeRO-2 155, and ZeRO-3 17.5, which is the only one under the 80 gigabyte GPU limit.]

_From the lab: 16 bytes per parameter, before activations. Only ZeRO-3 fits on an 80 GB GPU._

### Play

**Try to break it.** At 70B and 64 GPUs, go from DDP to ZeRO-3. Then change the GPU count under DDP. In the second lab, change the pipeline stages and micro-batches.

#### Model-state memory per GPU

16 bytes per parameter (bf16 weights and gradients, fp32 master weights and Adam moments), sharded over all GPUs as one data-parallel group. Activations, buffers and fragmentation are not included, so leave headroom. GB = 10⁹ bytes.

The naive approach, **plain data parallelism**, keeps everything on every GPU: a 70B model needs **1,120 GB** per GPU no matter how many GPUs you add. **ZeRO-1** (shard only the optimizer state) brings that to 293 GB on 64 GPUs, **ZeRO-2** to 155 GB, and **ZeRO-3/FSDP**, which also shards the weights, to **17.5 GB**, leaving room for activations. Even an 8B model doesn't fit with DDP (128 GB), but fits with ZeRO-1 on 8 GPUs (44 GB). The price of ZeRO-3 is communication: each layer's weights are gathered before use, which is why huge models also use tensor and pipeline parallelism.

##### The pipeline bubble

Forward pass shown (GPipe-style); the backward pass has the same bubble. Bubble fraction = (p − 1) / (m + p − 1).

With **4 stages** and only **4 micro-batches**, GPUs sit idle **42.9%** of the time while the pipeline fills and drains. Splitting the batch into 32 micro-batches cuts the bubble to **8.6%**. Schedules like 1F1B and interleaved stages (Narayanan et al. 2021) shrink it further and limit memory.

**Now say why:** ZeRO-3 clearly uses the least memory, so why do huge runs also need tensor and pipeline parallelism?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

With **mixed precision** and the Adam optimiser, training needs about **16 bytes per parameter** before any activations: 2 for bf16 weights, 2 for bf16 gradients, and 12 for the fp32 master weights plus Adam's two moments. A 70B model needs 1.1 TB, far beyond one 80 GB GPU. **Data parallelism** copies the model to every GPU and averages gradients, but doesn't save memory. **ZeRO** (and PyTorch **FSDP**) shards the optimizer state, then gradients, then the weights themselves across the data-parallel GPUs, gathering pieces only when needed. **Tensor parallelism** splits each matrix multiply across GPUs in a fast NVLink node; **pipeline parallelism** puts different layers on different GPUs and uses micro-batches to shrink idle "bubbles". Llama 3 405B combined four kinds of parallelism on 16,000 H100s. What you'll be able to do after this: compute training memory per GPU, and explain DP, ZeRO stages, TP, PP and when to use each.

#### Where 16 bytes per parameter come from

- **Mixed precision** (Micikevicius et al. 2018): forward and backward passes in 16-bit (bf16 today, which has fp32's range and needs no loss scaling), with an fp32 **master copy** of the weights for the update, so small updates aren't rounded away.

- **Adam** keeps two fp32 moments per parameter. Total: 2 (bf16 weights) + 2 (bf16 grads) + 4 (fp32 master) + 4 + 4 (Adam m, v) = **16 bytes** (ZeRO paper's accounting).

- **Activations** come on top and grow with batch × sequence length × layers; **activation checkpointing** stores only some of them and recomputes the rest in the backward pass.

| Strategy | What is split | Communication |
|---|---|---|
| Data parallel (DDP) | the batch; full model copy per GPU | all-reduce of gradients each step |
| ZeRO-1 / -2 / -3 (FSDP) | optimizer state / + gradients / + weights, across data-parallel GPUs | ZeRO-1/2 ≈ DDP; ZeRO-3 ≈ 1.5× (gathers weights each layer) |
| Tensor parallel (Megatron) | each weight matrix, column- or row-wise | all-reduce inside every layer: keep within one NVLink node (≤ 8 GPUs) |
| Pipeline parallel | groups of layers per GPU | activations between stages; idle bubbles |
| Sequence / context parallel | the sequence dimension | needed for very long contexts |

## In practice

### In practice

#### 3D and 4D parallelism

- **Rule of thumb:** tensor parallelism inside a node (fast NVLink), pipeline parallelism across nodes, data parallelism / FSDP across everything else; add context parallelism for long sequences and expert parallelism for MoE.

- **Llama 3 405B** used tensor, pipeline, context and data (FSDP) parallelism on up to 16K H100 GPUs, reaching 38–43% model FLOPs utilisation (MFU).

- **For fine-tuning** at smaller scale, FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 alone is usually enough; LoRA avoids most optimizer state entirely (AI Engineering › Fine-tuning).

#### Shard what's redundant, keep chatty work local

Data parallelism stores the same state N times; ZeRO/FSDP removes that redundancy, tensor parallelism splits work that needs constant communication across the fastest links, and pipeline parallelism splits layers across slower links at the cost of bubbles.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Adding GPUs to DDP lets a bigger model fit"

It sounds right, since more GPUs means more memory in total. But DDP keeps everything on every GPU, so a 70B model needs 1,120 GB per GPU however many you add. You need sharding or model parallelism. The weights aren't the main cost either: optimizer state is 12 of the 16 bytes.

## Say it

### Why does a 70B model need 1.1 TB to train, and how is it split?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How much memory to fully fine-tune a 7B model with Adam?

16 × 7B = 112 GB of model state plus activations: more than one 80 GB GPU; use ZeRO/FSDP over several GPUs, an 8-bit optimizer, or LoRA.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why keep fp32 master weights if we compute in bf16?

bf16 has only 8 bits of mantissa: small updates (learning rate × gradient) would round to zero when added to a bf16 weight.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not tensor parallelism across nodes?

It needs an all-reduce inside every layer; across slower inter-node links that communication would dominate the step time.

#### The 30-second answer

Mixed-precision training with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter: bf16 weights and gradients plus fp32 master weights and two Adam moments, so a 70B model needs over a terabyte before activations. Data parallelism replicates the model and all-reduces gradients; ZeRO stages 1, 2 and 3, or FSDP, shard optimizer state, gradients and finally weights across data-parallel ranks, cutting per-GPU memory to roughly 16N divided by the number of GPUs at the cost of more communication. Tensor parallelism splits each matmul across GPUs within an NVLink node, pipeline parallelism assigns layers to different GPUs with micro-batches to reduce the bubble of (p−1)/(m+p−1), and large runs like Llama 3 405B combine tensor, pipeline, context and data parallelism.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Adding GPUs to DDP lets a bigger model fit." DDP replicates the model; you need sharding or model parallelism.

- "The weights are the main memory cost." Optimizer state is 12 of the 16 bytes.

**Key terms and sources**

Why a 70B model can't be trained on one GPU, where the memory goes (16 bytes per parameter with mixed-precision Adam), and how data, tensor, pipeline and sequence parallelism plus ZeRO/FSDP sharding split the work across thousands of GPUs · built from Micikevicius et al. (Mixed Precision Training, ICLR 2018), Rajbhandari et al. (ZeRO, SC 2020), Zhao et al. (PyTorch FSDP, VLDB 2023), Shoeybi et al. (Megatron-LM, 2019), Huang et al. (GPipe, NeurIPS 2019), Narayanan et al. (2021) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. P. Micikevicius et al., "Mixed Precision Training", ICLR 2018, [arXiv:1710.03740](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740).

2. S. Rajbhandari et al., "ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models", SC 2020, [arXiv:1910.02054](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054); Y. Zhao et al., "PyTorch FSDP", VLDB 2023, [arXiv:2304.11277](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11277).

3. M. Shoeybi et al., "Megatron-LM", 2019, [arXiv:1909.08053](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053); D. Narayanan et al., "Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM", SC 2021, [arXiv:2104.04473](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473).

4. Y. Huang et al., "GPipe", NeurIPS 2019, [arXiv:1811.06965](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965).

5. Llama Team, Meta, "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", 2024, [arXiv:2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783) (§3.3).

# Training Instabilities: Loss Spikes, z-loss and QK-norm

> Your loss spikes at step 40k. What happened, and what do you do?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Pretraining
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/training-instabilities/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`), BatchNorm vs LayerNorm vs RMSNorm (`fundamentals/normalisation-layers`)
- Quiz topic: `pre`

## Intuition

### The situation

Three weeks into continued pre-training of the assistant, the loss jumps from 2.1 to 7 in a few hundred steps. Each restart costs days of compute. The interviewer asks:

> Your loss spikes at step 40k. What happened, and what do you do?

**Running example:** three weeks into continued pre-training of the assistant on food and support text, the loss jumps from 2.1 to 7 in a few hundred steps. What happened, and what do you do?

#### Spikes, divergence and broken hardware

A **loss spike** is a sudden jump in training loss; sometimes it recovers, sometimes the run **diverges** and never comes back. PaLM's authors found that replaying the same batches from an earlier checkpoint did _not_ reproduce the spike: spikes came from a combination of particular data and a particular parameter state. Spikes get more frequent with larger models and higher learning rates, and every restart costs days of compute.

### The idea

Think of a shop calculator that keeps only a few significant digits. Add 300 to every price, and on paper the differences haven't changed. But the calculator starts rounding, and two different prices read the same. The loss can't see this drift, so nothing stops it.

[Figure: Cross-entropy with drifting logits. The exact loss stays at 0.4496. Computed from bf16 logits, it reads 0.4600 at drift 50, 0.5174 at drift 200 and 0.2974 at drift 300.]

_From the lab. The model's predictions haven't changed, but the computed loss has._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the logit drift from 0 up to 300. Compare the exact loss, the loss from bf16 logits and the z-loss penalty.

#### "The softmax is shift-invariant, so drift is harmless"

Logits [3, 1.5, 1.2, 0.4, 0, −0.5, −1, −2] over 8 candidate tokens, the first one correct, plus drift c. bf16 rounding to 8 significant bits; softmax then computed exactly.

The exact loss is **0.4496** at every drift: the model's predictions haven't changed. But computed from bf16 logits, the loss is already off at drift 50 (0.4600), wrong by 0.07 at drift **200** (0.5174), and at **300** it reads 0.2974: logits that differed by 0.3 now round to the same value, so the gradients point the wrong way. The **z-loss** term sees what cross-entropy can't: it grows from 0.0012 to **9.21** at drift 300 and pushes log Z back towards 0, keeping logits in the range where bf16 is precise.

**Now say why:** if the softmax doesn't change when you shift every logit, why isn't drift harmless?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Big runs are fragile. PaLM 540B saw about **20 loss spikes**; OPT-175B needed dozens of manual restarts. Two well-understood failure modes are **output-logit divergence**, where all logits drift to large values (the softmax doesn't care, but low-precision numbers do), and **attention-logit growth**, where query–key dot products blow up and attention collapses onto one token. **z-loss** adds a small penalty 10−4·(log Z)² that keeps the softmax normaliser near 1; **QK-norm** normalises queries and keys before the dot product. Add learning-rate warm-up, gradient clipping, pre-norm, and data cleaning, and when a spike happens anyway, roll back to a checkpoint and skip the offending batches. At 16,000 GPUs, hardware fails too: Llama 3 405B had 466 job interruptions in 54 days. What you'll be able to do after this: diagnose loss spikes, explain z-loss and QK-norm, and describe how large runs recover.

#### Two logit problems

- **Output-logit divergence:** adding the same constant c to every output logit doesn't change the softmax, so cross-entropy gives no signal to stop the logits drifting. But in bf16, which keeps only 8 bits of mantissa, large logits lose precision, so the computed loss and gradients become wrong.

- **Attention-logit growth:** query and key norms grow during training; the dot products become huge, the attention softmax becomes one-hot, and gradients through it vanish or explode. Dehghani et al. saw this when scaling ViT to 22B; Wortsman et al. (2024) reproduced both instabilities in small models trained with high learning rates.

$$ \mathcal{L} = {\mathcal{L}_{CE}} + {10^{-4}}\cdot{\log^2 Z}, \qquad \mathrm{QKNorm:}\;\; s_{ij} = \frac{\mathrm{Norm}(q_i)\cdot \mathrm{Norm}(k_j)}{\sqrt{d}} $$

Chowdhery et al., "PaLM", [arXiv:2204.02311](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02311), §5; QK-norm: Dehghani et al., "Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 Billion Parameters", ICML 2023, [arXiv:2302.05442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05442).

- **cross-entropy**: The usual next-token loss.

- **log of the softmax normaliser**: log Z = log Σ exp(logits). It equals the logits’ overall level, which cross-entropy ignores.

- **tiny weight**: 10⁻⁴ in PaLM: enough to pull log Z towards 0 without affecting predictions.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The stability toolkit

- **Architecture:** pre-norm (Anatomy), QK-norm (OLMo 2, Qwen3, Gemma 3), norms after sub-layer outputs (OLMo 2's "reordered norm"), no biases, careful initialisation.

- **Optimisation:** learning-rate warm-up, gradient clipping (global norm 1.0 is common), lower peak learning rates for bigger models, z-loss; watch gradient norms and attention-logit maxima, not just the loss.

- **Data:** OLMo 2 traced spikes to documents with long repeated n-gram sequences and filtered them out.

- **Recovery:** PaLM restarted from a checkpoint about 100 steps before each spike and skipped about 200–500 data batches; OPT-175B logged dozens of restarts and lowered the learning rate mid-run.

- **Hardware:** in 54 days of Llama 3 405B pre-training there were 466 job interruptions, 419 of them unexpected, mostly GPU and memory faults; frequent checkpointing and automated restarts kept effective training time above 90%.

#### Keep every logit in a well-conditioned range

Most instabilities come from quantities the loss doesn't control, like the overall level of output logits and the size of attention logits, growing until low precision or a saturated softmax breaks the gradients; small regularisers and normalisations keep them bounded, and checkpoints handle the rest.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Spikes are always bad data"

It sounds right, since the spike appears at a particular batch. But PaLM's authors replayed the same batches from an earlier checkpoint and the spike didn't come back. It took particular data and a particular parameter state together. "Just lower the learning rate" isn't the full answer either: it helps, but it slows training, so fix the cause.

## Say it

### Your loss spikes at step 40k. What happened, and what do you do?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your loss spikes at step 40k. First steps?

Check gradient norm and attention/output logit maxima just before the spike, inspect the batch, roll back to a checkpoint ~100 steps earlier, skip the next few hundred batches or lower the learning rate, and consider z-loss or QK-norm for the next run.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does a spike sometimes recover on its own?

Adam's second-moment estimates adapt and the model can return to a stable region, but with lasting damage or, at worst, divergence.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can you study instabilities without a huge run?

Yes: Wortsman et al. reproduced attention-logit growth and output-logit divergence in small models at high learning rates, and showed QK-layernorm and z-loss fix them there too.

#### The 30-second answer

Large runs suffer loss spikes and divergence, often from logits growing out of control: output logits can drift because softmax is shift-invariant, which breaks bf16 precision, and attention logits can grow until attention becomes one-hot. Defences are z-loss, a 1e-4 penalty on log Z squared that keeps the softmax normaliser near one, QK-norm on queries and keys, pre-norm and extra norms, warm-up, gradient clipping and lower learning rates, plus data cleaning. When a spike happens, you roll back to an earlier checkpoint and skip the batches around it, as PaLM did, and at large scale you also need frequent checkpoints and automatic restarts for hardware failures.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Spikes are always bad data." PaLM found they depended on data and parameter state together.

- "Just lower the learning rate." It helps but slows training; fix the cause.

**Key terms and sources**

What goes wrong in long LLM training runs: sudden loss spikes and divergence, growing output and attention logits, low-precision round-off, and hardware failures; and the standard defences: warm-up, gradient clipping, z-loss, QK-norm, careful norm placement, data fixes, and checkpoint-and-skip recovery · built from Chowdhery et al. (PaLM, 2022), Zhang et al. (OPT, 2022), Dehghani et al. (ViT-22B, 2023), Wortsman et al. (Small-scale proxies, ICLR 2024), Team OLMo (OLMo 2, 2024) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026
