# SFT and Instruction Tuning

> How does a text-completer become an assistant, and why mask the prompt?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/supervised-fine-tuning/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

You have a pre-trained 8B base model and 5,000 good support chats. Ask the base model a question, and it may produce more questions or a forum thread, because those are plausible continuations. The interviewer asks:

> How does a text-completer become an assistant, and why mask the prompt?

**Running example (post-training):** the team has a pre-trained 8B base model and 5,000 real support chats where human agents gave good answers. They want an assistant that answers like the best agents.

#### Base models complete text; they don't follow instructions

Pre-training teaches a model what text on the internet looks like. Asked a question, a base model may answer it, but it may also produce more questions, a forum thread, or a list of similar complaints, because all of those are plausible continuations. We need it to behave as one consistent assistant: answer the user, in the right tone and format, and stop.

### The idea

Think of a mimic who has read the whole internet and will continue any script, including playing the customer. In rehearsal, you hand over full conversations but only correct the assistant's lines. The customer's lines are for reading, not for practising.

[Figure: A training conversation. The model reads the system prompt and the customer's message with no loss on them. It is trained only on the assistant's reply, including the end token.]

_With loss on every token, 72.4% of the loss in the lab's example comes from the first two parts._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between loss on all tokens and loss on assistant tokens only. Watch the tokens trained on, and the share of the loss from system and user text.

#### Train on everything, or only on the answer?

One training conversation, word-level for readability (real tokens are subwords). The number under each token is an illustrative per-token loss. User text is hard to predict ("biryani", "40"), the assistant's reply is easier once the complaint is known.

Training on **all tokens** spends **72.4%** of the loss on predicting the system prompt and the customer's complaint, text the model will never have to write. Worse, it teaches the model to imitate users (and to reproduce the same system prompt thousands of times). With **assistant-only** masking, all 14 trained tokens are the reply, including the end-of-turn token. Masking is the default in most SFT libraries; some recent work finds small gains from a little prompt loss when SFT data is tiny, but the reply is what you're teaching.

**Now say why:** what does training on the customer's text teach the model to do?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A base model trained on next-token prediction will happily continue "My biryani is late" with another complaint. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** trains it further, with the same cross-entropy loss, on example conversations written or curated to show the desired behaviour. Conversations are serialised with a **chat template**: special tokens mark the system, user and assistant turns, and the same template must be used at inference. The loss is usually **masked to the assistant's tokens**, so the model learns to write answers, not to imitate users. A few thousand high-quality examples go a long way (LIMA used 1,000; Llama 2's SFT stage used 27,540) because SFT mostly teaches **format and behaviour**, while knowledge comes from pre-training. SFT is the first post-training step, before preference tuning with RLHF or DPO. What you'll be able to do after this: explain what SFT does, set up a chat template and loss mask, and argue about data quality vs quantity.

#### Chat templates and the SFT loss

$$ \mathcal{L}_{SFT} = -{\frac{1}{\sum_t m_t}}\sum_t {m_t}\,{\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})} $$

"Completion-only" or "assistant-only" loss in libraries such as Hugging Face TRL. The model still _reads_ the prompt; it just isn't trained to predict it.

- **loss mask**: m_t = 1 for tokens the assistant wrote, 0 for system and user tokens (and padding). Only masked-in tokens contribute.

- **next-token cross-entropy**: Exactly the pre-training loss: −log probability of the true next token given everything before it, including the user’s message.

- **average over trained tokens**: Divide by the number of assistant tokens, so long prompts don’t change the scale of the loss.

- **Chat template:** each model family defines special tokens, e.g. Llama 3 uses `<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>` … `<|eot_id|>`. Training and inference must use the identical template, or quality drops sharply.

- **The end token matters:** the assistant turn ends with an end-of-turn token that _is_ trained, which teaches the model when to stop.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Quality over quantity

- **InstructGPT** (Ouyang et al. 2022) fine-tuned GPT-3 on about 13k labeller-written demonstrations before RLHF. FLAN (Wei et al. 2022) showed that instruction tuning on many tasks phrased as instructions improves zero-shot performance on unseen tasks.

- **LIMA** (Zhou et al. 2023): a 65B model fine-tuned on just **1,000** carefully curated examples was rated equivalent or better than GPT-4 in 43% of comparisons. Its "superficial alignment hypothesis": knowledge comes from pre-training; alignment mostly teaches format and style. Later work argues this is an oversimplification for reasoning and factual tasks.

- **Llama 2** stopped at 27,540 high-quality SFT annotations, finding they beat millions of lower-quality third-party examples. Llama 3 mixes human data with large amounts of filtered synthetic data generated by earlier models.

- **Risks:** fine-tuning only on support chats can erode general skills (catastrophic forgetting) and safety behaviour; mix in general instruction data, keep epochs low (2–3), and use a small learning rate. Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA are covered in AI Engineering › Fine-tuning.

For what fine-tuning can do to safety, read Safety Training and Jailbreaks.

#### Show the behaviour you want, and train only on it

SFT is ordinary next-token training on demonstrations of the target behaviour, with the loss restricted to the assistant's tokens; it changes how the model uses what it already knows far more than what it knows.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "More SFT data is always better"

It sounds right, since more data helped in pre-training. But LIMA's 1,000 curated examples were rated equal or better than GPT-4 in 43% of comparisons, and Llama 2 found 27,540 good annotations beat millions of lower-quality ones. SFT doesn't use a different loss either: it's the same cross-entropy, masked.

## Say it

### How does a text-completer become an assistant, and why mask the prompt?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not stop after SFT?

SFT can only imitate the demonstrations; it doesn't learn which of two acceptable answers people prefer, and it can't exceed the demonstrators. Preference tuning optimises for what humans or verifiers judge better.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your fine-tuned model rambles and never stops. Likely cause?

The end-of-turn token wasn't in the training targets (masked out or missing from the template), or inference uses a different template or stop token.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can SFT teach the model new facts?

Somewhat, but it's inefficient and can increase hallucination: Gekhman et al. (2024) found that fine-tuning on facts the model didn't already know makes it more likely to hallucinate. Use retrieval or continued pre-training for knowledge.

#### The 30-second answer

SFT, or instruction tuning, continues training a pre-trained model with the same next-token cross-entropy on example conversations that demonstrate the desired behaviour. Conversations are formatted with a chat template using special tokens for system, user and assistant turns, and the loss is masked so only the assistant's tokens, including the end-of-turn token, are trained. Data quality matters more than quantity: LIMA got strong results from 1,000 curated examples and Llama 2 used about 27k, because SFT mainly teaches format and behaviour on top of pre-trained knowledge. It's usually followed by preference tuning, RLHF or DPO.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "SFT uses a different loss." It's the same cross-entropy, masked.

- "More SFT data is always better." Quality and diversity beat volume.

**Key terms and sources**

How a pre-trained base model that only continues text becomes an assistant that follows instructions: supervised fine-tuning on demonstration conversations, chat templates and special tokens, masking the loss to the assistant's tokens, how much data is enough (quality over quantity), and what SFT can and can't teach · built from Ouyang et al. (InstructGPT, NeurIPS 2022), Wei et al. (FLAN, ICLR 2022), Zhou et al. (LIMA, NeurIPS 2023), Touvron et al. (Llama 2, 2023), Hugging Face TRL docs and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. L. Ouyang et al., "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (InstructGPT), NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2203.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155).

2. J. Wei et al., "Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners" (FLAN), ICLR 2022, [arXiv:2109.01652](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01652).

3. C. Zhou et al., "LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.11206](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11206).

4. H. Touvron et al., "Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models", 2023, [arXiv:2307.09288](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288); Llama Team, "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", 2024, [arXiv:2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783).

5. Z. Gekhman et al., "Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?", EMNLP 2024, [arXiv:2405.05904](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904); Hugging Face TRL, SFTTrainer documentation.

# Policy Gradients for LLMs

> How can a reward that isn't differentiable train an LLM, and why do you need a baseline?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/policy-gradients-for-llms/
- Before this: SFT and Instruction Tuning (`fundamentals/supervised-fine-tuning`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model writes SQL, and you can check each query by running it. But pass or fail isn't differentiable, so you can't simply backpropagate through it. You also notice training gets very noisy after someone adds a bonus to every reward. The interviewer asks:

> How can a reward that isn't differentiable train an LLM, and why do you need a baseline?

#### Why it matters

The RLHF and reasoning model lessons use PPO and GRPO. This lesson explains what they're doing underneath. Interviewers like to ask why you need reinforcement learning at all, and why GRPO doesn't need a critic.

### The idea

Think of a coach who can't see a player's technique, only the score of each match. After a good match, the coach says to do more of what you did. After a bad one, to do less. If the coach praises every match, because every score is above zero, the player learns nothing. What helps is praise relative to the usual score.

[Figure: Three ideas. Reward-weighted log-probabilities need no gradient from the reward. A baseline cuts noise. Clipping lets you reuse samples.]

_PPO learns its baseline. GRPO uses the group's mean._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Choose no baseline, with 10 added to every reward. Then try the group mean.

#### Train with a baseline

Simulation with one prompt and four possible answers, one right. Reward: 1 if right, 0 if wrong, plus the added amount. 150 updates at a learning rate of 0.5, averaged over 40 fixed runs. Grey shows no baseline. A run counts as stuck if it ends with over 90% on a wrong answer.

Rewards of 11 or 10 carry the same information as 1 or 0. But with 8 answers per update, and **no baseline**, the right answer ends at only 50%, and 19 of 40 runs get stuck on a wrong one. Everything gets pushed up, so whichever answer happens to be sampled first runs away. The **group mean** removes the added 10 entirely: 99%, with none stuck, and about 20 times less gradient noise (0.08 against 1.68). Now set the added amount to 0: no baseline works fine, because a reward of 0 pushes nothing. Bigger groups also help: at G = 64, even no baseline reaches 99%, though each update then costs 64 answers.

**Now say why:** why does adding a constant hurt when there's no baseline?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

RLHF and GRPO both train a model from a score it gets after answering. That score comes from a reward model or a checker, so you can't backpropagate through it. The **policy gradient** gets around this: sample an answer, then raise the probability of its tokens in proportion to its reward. Good answers get more likely, and bad ones less. Alone, this is very noisy, so we subtract a **baseline**, an estimate of the usual reward. **PPO** learns the baseline with a value model, and clips each update. **GRPO** uses the average reward of the group as its baseline instead.

#### Text as a game

| RL word | In an LLM |
|---|---|
| Policy | The model's next-token distribution |
| State | The prompt and the tokens so far |
| Action | The next token |
| Episode | One whole answer |
| Reward | Usually one number at the end, from a reward model or a checker |

##### Why not use ordinary training?

SFT needs the right answer, token by token. Here we only have a score for an answer the model wrote itself. We can't differentiate through "did the tests pass?", and sampling a token isn't differentiable either. The policy gradient needs neither: it only uses the gradient of the model's own log-probabilities.

##### Why a baseline?

Say every answer scores between 10 and 11. Without a baseline, every answer gets pushed up, the good ones only slightly more than the bad, and the signal is lost in noise. Subtracting the usual reward fixes this: above-average answers go up, and below-average ones go down. On average the gradient is unchanged, because the baseline term has an expected value of zero. Only the noise falls.

##### Three algorithms

| | REINFORCE | PPO | GRPO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | None, or a simple one | Learned value model | Mean of the group's rewards |
| Extra models | None | Value model, and often reward and reference | Reference only |
| Reusing samples | One update | Several updates, kept safe by clipping | Clipped objective. DeepSeekMath used one update |

##### Why PPO clips

Samples come from the old policy. As the policy changes, those samples describe it less well. PPO measures this with the ratio r of new to old probability, and stops giving credit once r leaves a small range, usually 1 ± 0.1 to 0.3. That makes it safe to take several gradient steps on one batch.

##### What InstructGPT and GRPO did

InstructGPT used PPO, with the value model initialised from the reward model. GRPO keeps PPO's clipped form, but drops the value model. DeepSeekMath sampled 64 answers per question, used a KL coefficient of 0.04, and made one update after each sampling round.

#### The maths

$$ {\nabla_\theta J} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_t {\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}\,{\big(R - b\big)}\Big], \qquad {L = \min\big(r A,\ \mathrm{clip}(r, 1{-}\epsilon, 1{+}\epsilon) A\big)} $$

The policy gradient with a baseline and the PPO clipped objective, in the form given in OpenAI’s Spinning Up. GRPO replaces A with the group-normalised reward.

- **the direction to improve**: How to change the weights to raise the expected reward.

- **make this token more likely**: The ordinary gradient of a token’s log-probability. The reward itself is never differentiated.

- **the advantage**: How much better than usual this answer was. Positive pushes its tokens up, and negative pushes them down.

- **PPO’s clip**: r is the new probability over the old. Once r leaves the range, more movement earns no extra credit.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **One reward, many tokens:** each token in an answer gets the answer's advantage, whether it helped or not. That's a noisy signal, so large groups help.

- **Keep it on-policy:** samples must come from a recent policy. Fresh samples are expensive, as generation is slow, so RL training spends much of its time generating.

- **Keep it close:** a KL term to the reference stops the policy drifting into odd text, which reward hacking exploits.

- **Watch for no signal:** if every answer in a group gets the same reward, the advantages are all 0. Choose problems the model sometimes solves.

- **Check the reward first:** the algorithm will find any weakness in it. Test the reward on known good and bad answers before a long run.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A positive reward means the model is doing well, so it should be reinforced"

It sounds right, as positive sounds good. But only reward relative to the usual level carries information. If every answer scores about 10, a reward of 10 is merely average, and reinforcing it adds noise. The advantage, reward minus baseline, is what tells the model which answers were better.

## Say it

### How can a reward that isn't differentiable train an LLM, and why do you need a baseline?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why doesn't subtracting a baseline bias the gradient?

The expected value of the gradient of log π, given the state, is zero. So a baseline that depends only on the state multiplies something with zero mean, and adds nothing on average. It only changes the variance.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A prompt gets rewards of 11, 10, 10 and 10. What are the weights, with and without the group mean?

Without a baseline, all four are positive, so every answer gets pushed up. With the group mean of 10.25, the good answer gets +0.75 and the others get −0.25, which is the signal we want.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why can PPO reuse a batch, when plain policy gradient can't?

The plain gradient only holds for the policy that produced the samples. PPO corrects for the change with a probability ratio, and clips it so that the policy can't gain by moving far from where the samples are reliable.

#### The 30-second answer

We use reinforcement learning when we only get a score for a whole answer, such as from a reward model or a test suite, and can't backpropagate through it. The policy gradient samples an answer and raises its tokens' log-probabilities in proportion to its reward, so the reward itself never needs a gradient. That's noisy, so we subtract a baseline. It doesn't change the expected gradient, but above-average answers go up and below-average ones go down. PPO learns the baseline with a value model, and clips the probability ratio so it can safely reuse samples. GRPO keeps the clipping, but uses the group's mean reward as the baseline, so it doesn't need a critic.

**Key terms and sources**

How reinforcement learning maps onto text, the policy gradient, why baselines reduce noise, PPO's clipping, value models, and how GRPO replaces them. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [OpenAI Spinning Up, policy gradient and baselines](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/spinningup/rl_intro3.html)

- [OpenAI Spinning Up, PPO](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html)

- [Schulman et al., Proximal Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)

- [Schulman et al., Generalized Advantage Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438)

- [Ouyang et al., InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

- [Shao et al., DeepSeekMath and GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)

# Reward Models and RLHF (PPO)

> Why does optimising a reward model too hard make answers worse?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/rlhf-and-reward-models/
- Before this: Policy Gradients for LLMs (`fundamentals/policy-gradients-for-llms`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

After SFT, the assistant's answers are acceptable, but some are curt, some over-apologise and some promise refunds that the policy doesn't allow. You ask agents to compare pairs of answers, and train a reward model. Then a colleague optimises it as hard as possible. The interviewer asks:

> Why does optimising a reward model too hard make answers worse?

**Running example:** after SFT, the support assistant gives acceptable answers, but agents notice some are curt, some over-apologise, some promise refunds the policy doesn't allow. The team asks agents to compare pairs of answers instead of writing new ones.

#### "Good" is hard to write down, easy to recognise

There's no formula for a helpful, honest, polite answer, and SFT can only copy demonstrations. People can, however, reliably pick the better of two answers. RLHF turns those choices into a reward the model can optimise (Christiano et al. 2017; Stiennon et al. 2020 for summarisation; InstructGPT for general instructions).

### The idea

Think of a teacher who marks essays well but has a slight soft spot for long ones. Chasing that teacher's marks improves your writing at first. Push hard enough and you're padding pages: the marks keep rising while the essays get worse. So you keep the student close to how they wrote before.

[Figure: Best-of-N. At N of 1 the reward-model score is 0.06 and true quality is minus 0.23. At N of 16 the score is 2.58 and quality is 0.21. At N of 1,024 the score is 4.66 and quality is minus 0.44.]

_From the lab's simulation, where the reward model slightly over-rewards long answers._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the number of answers per prompt from 1 up to 1,024. Watch the reward-model score, true quality and the KL.

#### Maximise the reward model as hard as possible

The simplest way to optimise a reward model is **best-of-N**: sample N answers and keep the one it scores highest. More N means more optimisation pressure, measured as the KL divergence from the original policy (log N − (N−1)/N for best-of-N).

Simulation: each answer has a true quality and a verbosity. The reward model, like real ones, slightly over-rewards long answers (score = quality + verbosity + noise); the "gold" judge values quality but dislikes rambling (quality − 0.5 × excess verbosity²). 400 prompts × 1,024 samples, fixed seed. Setup inspired by Gao et al.'s gold-vs-proxy experiments.

At first both scores rise: picking the best of 16 answers lifts true quality from **−0.23** to **0.21**. After that, the reward-model score keeps climbing (2.58 → **4.66** at N = 1,024) while true quality falls to **−0.44**, worse than not optimising at all. The optimiser is finding answers that exploit the reward model's love of length, not better answers. Gao et al. (2023) measured exactly this shape with real reward models: gold reward rises then falls as KL grows, with larger reward models overoptimising less. In real RLHF the symptoms are longer answers (Singhal et al. 2023 found much of RLHF's reward gain came from length), sycophancy and confident-sounding mistakes.

**Now say why:** the reward-model score keeps rising past N = 16, so what is the optimiser actually finding?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

It's easier for people to say which of two answers is better than to write the perfect one. **RLHF** collects such **comparisons**, trains a **reward model** to score answers so that preferred ones score higher (the **Bradley–Terry** model: P(A preferred over B) = σ(r(A) − r(B))), and then uses reinforcement learning, usually **PPO**, to make the policy produce high-reward answers, with a **KL penalty** that keeps it close to the SFT model. It worked: labellers preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT model to the 175B GPT-3. But the reward model is only a **proxy** for what people want. Push too hard and the policy finds its blind spots, such as longer, more confident, more flattering answers: **reward hacking**. True quality first rises, then falls. What you'll be able to do after this: write the reward-model loss and the RLHF objective, and explain reward hacking and the role of the KL penalty.

#### From comparisons to a reward, then to a policy

$$ \mathcal{L}_{RM} = -\log{\sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l)\big)}, \qquad \max_{\pi_\theta}\; {\mathbb{E}\,[\,r_\phi(x,y)\,]} - {\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{ref}\big)} $$

Ouyang et al. 2022, Eq. 1–2. InstructGPT labellers ranked 4–9 answers per prompt, giving many pairs per ranking.

- **Bradley–Terry likelihood**: The reward model r_φ (usually the SFT model with a scalar head) should give the chosen answer y_w a higher score than the rejected y_l; σ of the difference is the probability of that preference.

- **maximise reward**: The policy π_θ generates answers to real prompts and is pushed towards ones the reward model scores highly.

- **KL penalty**: β times the KL divergence from the reference (SFT) model: stops the policy drifting into strange text that fools the reward model, and keeps its language fluent.

- **PPO** (Schulman et al. 2017) updates the policy with a clipped objective so each step stays small; it needs a **value model** (critic) to estimate advantages. RLHF with PPO keeps four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model and value model, which makes it expensive and finicky.

- **Results:** outputs of 175B InstructGPT were preferred to 175B GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time, and even the 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred to the 175B GPT-3.

New to this? Read Policy Gradients for LLMs first.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Keeping the optimiser honest

- **KL penalty and early stopping:** limit how far the policy moves; pick checkpoints with human or held-out evaluations, not reward-model score.

- **Better reward models:** larger, ensembled, trained on fresh on-policy comparisons each round (Llama 2 retrained its reward models iteratively); separate helpfulness and safety reward models.

- **AI feedback** (RLAIF, Constitutional AI; Bai et al. 2022): an LLM judges answers against written principles, cheaper than humans.

- **Simpler algorithms:** DPO skips the reward model and RL loop; for maths and code, verifiable rewards can't be hacked the same way.

#### Optimise a learned judge, but not too hard

RLHF converts human comparisons into a reward model and optimises the policy against it, and because that reward is an imperfect proxy (Goodhart's law), the KL leash to the SFT model is as important as the reward itself.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A higher reward-model score means a better model"

It sounds right, since that's the score you're optimising. But it's a proxy. In the lab, the score climbs from 2.58 to 4.66 between N = 16 and N = 1,024, while true quality falls from 0.21 to −0.44. So pick checkpoints with human or held-out evaluations. RLHF doesn't teach new knowledge either: it mainly shapes behaviour and preferences.

## Say it

### Why does optimising a reward model too hard make answers worse?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why compare pairs instead of rating 1–10?

Absolute ratings are inconsistent between people and over time; relative judgements are more reliable, and Bradley–Terry turns them into a consistent score.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Which models does PPO-based RLHF keep in memory?

The policy being trained, the frozen reference model for the KL term, the reward model, and a value model (critic), often all of similar size.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What does the KL term do if β is too large or too small?

Too large: the policy barely changes from SFT. Too small: it drifts, hacks the reward model and can produce degenerate text.

#### The 30-second answer

RLHF starts from an SFT model, collects human comparisons between pairs of its answers, and trains a reward model with a Bradley–Terry loss so preferred answers score higher. Then it optimises the policy with RL, typically PPO, to maximise the reward minus a KL penalty to the SFT reference model. InstructGPT showed this makes even a 1.3B model preferred over 175B GPT-3. The main risk is reward hacking: the reward model is a proxy, so with too much optimisation the policy exploits it, for example by writing longer or sycophantic answers, and true quality drops. The KL penalty, early stopping, better and refreshed reward models, and human evals guard against that.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Higher reward model score means a better model." It's a proxy; check with humans or held-out judges.

- "RLHF teaches the model new knowledge." It mainly shapes behaviour and preferences.

**Key terms and sources**

How human preferences become a training signal: collecting comparisons, training a Bradley–Terry reward model, optimising the policy with PPO under a KL penalty to the SFT model, and why optimising too hard against a learned reward (reward hacking, overoptimisation) makes the model worse · built from Christiano et al. (2017), Stiennon et al. (2020), Ouyang et al. (InstructGPT, NeurIPS 2022), Schulman et al. (PPO, 2017), Bai et al. (Anthropic HH and Constitutional AI, 2022), Gao et al. (Reward Model Overoptimization, ICML 2023) and Singhal et al. (2023) · checked 29 Oct 2026

2. L. Ouyang et al., "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback", NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2203.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155).

3. J. Schulman et al., "Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms", 2017, [arXiv:1707.06347](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347).

4. L. Gao, J. Schulman & J. Hilton, "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization", ICML 2023, [arXiv:2210.10760](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760); P. Singhal et al., "A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF", 2023, [arXiv:2310.03716](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03716).

5. Y. Bai et al., "Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with RLHF", 2022, [arXiv:2204.05862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05862); "Constitutional AI", 2022, [arXiv:2212.08073](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073).

# DPO and Preference Optimisation

> How does DPO skip the reward model, and what can go wrong?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/dpo/
- Before this: Reward Models and RLHF (PPO) (`fundamentals/rlhf-and-reward-models`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team has 20,000 comparisons from support agents, the same data RLHF would use. Chosen: "Sorry about that! I've refunded the biryani." Rejected: "Refunds aren't possible after delivery." They don't want to build an RL pipeline. The interviewer asks:

> How does DPO skip the reward model, and what can go wrong?

**Running example:** the team has 20,000 comparisons from support agents (the same data RLHF would use). Chosen: "Sorry about that! I've refunded the biryani." Rejected: "Refunds aren't possible after delivery." They want to use it without building an RL pipeline.

#### RLHF works, but it's a lot of machinery

PPO-based RLHF samples from the policy during training, scores with a separate reward model, estimates advantages with a value model, and is sensitive to many hyperparameters. Could we optimise the same objective directly from the preference data?

### The idea

Think of skipping the judge at a cooking contest, because you already have a list of which dish beat which. You adjust your recipes so winners become more likely than losers, compared with how you cooked before. The catch is that you only care about the gap, so both dishes can get worse.

[Figure: RLHF with PPO keeps four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model and value model. DPO keeps two: policy and reference.]

_RLHF with PPO keeps four models in memory, and DPO keeps two._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set chosen to +5 and rejected to −5, and read the loss at each β. Then set chosen to −4 and rejected to −10.

#### What lowers the DPO loss?

Log-ratios in nats, summed over the answer's tokens. 0 means the policy gives the answer the same probability as the SFT reference.

At the start the policy equals the reference: margin 0, loss **ln 2 = 0.693**, gradient weight 0.5. Making the chosen answer 5 nats more likely and the rejected 5 nats less likely (β = 0.1) gives margin 1.0 and loss **0.313**. Now the trap: set chosen to **−4** and rejected to **−10**. Both answers have become _less_ likely than before, yet the loss falls to **0.437**, because only the _difference_ matters. Real DPO runs often show this "likelihood displacement": probability mass leaves both answers and can go to responses that appear in neither. With β = 0.5 the same ±5 shift gives margin 5 and loss **0.007**: the pair is "solved" and contributes almost no gradient (weight 0.007).

**Now say why:** in that second setting both answers became less likely, so why did the loss fall?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

RLHF needs a reward model, an RL loop, a value model and careful tuning. **DPO** (Rafailov et al. 2023) showed that the KL-regularised RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy, so the reward can be written in terms of the policy itself: the **implicit reward** of an answer is β · log(πθ/πref), how much more likely the model makes it than the SFT reference does. Plugging that into the Bradley–Terry loss gives a loss you can minimise directly on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples: **raise the chosen answer's log-ratio relative to the rejected one**. It's stable, cheap (two models: policy and frozen reference) and matched or beat PPO in the paper; Llama 3 used it. The catches: it learns only from a fixed dataset (offline), the loss can fall while _both_ answers become less likely, and it can favour length. Tuned PPO or online variants can still win. What you'll be able to do after this: write the DPO loss, explain β and the implicit reward, and compare DPO with PPO and its variants.

#### The implicit reward and the DPO loss

$$ \mathcal{L}_{DPO} = -\log {\sigma\Big(}{\beta}\Big[{\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w\mid x)}} - {\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l\mid x)}}\Big]{\Big)} $$

Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.18290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290), Eq. 7. log π(y|x) is the sum of the answer's token log-probabilities.

- **chosen log-ratio**: How much more (or less) likely the policy makes the chosen answer than the frozen SFT reference does, in log space.

- **rejected log-ratio**: The same for the rejected answer.

- **β**: Scales the implicit reward β·log(π/π_ref). It plays the role of the KL coefficient: larger β keeps the policy closer to the reference (typical 0.1–0.5).

- **logistic loss**: Bradley–Terry again: −log σ(margin). Minimising it pushes the chosen log-ratio above the rejected one.

The gradient weights each pair by **σ(−margin)**: pairs the model already gets right contribute little, pairs it gets wrong contribute a lot, like a classifier focusing on its mistakes.

## In practice

### In practice

#### DPO vs PPO, and the variants

- **Results:** in the paper DPO reached a better reward–KL trade-off than PPO on controlled sentiment generation and matched or beat it on TL;DR summarisation and Anthropic HH dialogue. Llama 3's post-training used rounds of rejection sampling, SFT and DPO.

- **But:** Xu et al. (ICML 2024) found that well-tuned PPO outperformed DPO, especially on hard tasks like code; DPO is **offline** and can exploit answers outside the preference data's coverage. **Online/iterative DPO** samples fresh answers from the current policy and labels them each round.

- **Variants:** IPO (adds regularisation against overfitting to deterministic preferences), KTO (needs only thumbs-up/down labels, not pairs), ORPO (combines SFT and preference loss, no reference model), SimPO (length-normalised log-probs, no reference model, curbs length exploitation).

#### Your language model is secretly a reward model

Because the KL-regularised optimal policy determines its own reward, β·log(π/πref), preference learning reduces to a logistic loss on log-probability ratios: same goal as RLHF, no sampling loop.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Lower DPO loss means the chosen answer got more likely"

It sounds right, since that's what the pair is asking for. But only the margin is guaranteed to grow. With chosen at −4 and rejected at −10, both are less likely than before, yet the loss falls to 0.437. Real runs show this "likelihood displacement": probability can move to responses that appear in neither answer. And DPO does optimise a reward, just an implicit one.

## Say it

### How does DPO skip the reward model, and what can go wrong?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What does β control?

The strength of the implicit KL constraint: higher β keeps the policy closer to the reference and saturates the loss faster; lower β allows bigger changes.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why do we need the reference model?

The implicit reward is defined relative to it; without it, the loss could be lowered just by changing overall probabilities. Reference-free variants like ORPO and SimPO add other terms instead.

Follow-up 3 of 3

DPO or PPO for a new project?

DPO for a quick, stable preference-tuning step with an existing dataset; PPO or GRPO-style online RL when you have a reliable reward (especially verifiable ones) and want the model to explore.

#### The 30-second answer

DPO optimises the same KL-regularised preference objective as RLHF but without a reward model or RL. The optimal policy of that objective implies a reward equal to beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference probability, so substituting into the Bradley–Terry loss gives a logistic loss on the difference between the chosen and rejected answers' log-ratios. It needs only the policy and a frozen reference, is stable and cheap, and matched PPO in the original paper; Llama 3 used it. Downsides: it's offline, so it can't explore beyond the dataset; the loss can drop while both answers lose probability; and it can favour longer answers. Online DPO and variants like IPO, KTO, ORPO and SimPO address these.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "DPO doesn't optimise a reward." It optimises an implicit one, with the same objective as RLHF.

- "Lower DPO loss means the chosen answer got more likely." Only the margin is guaranteed to grow.

**Key terms and sources**

How Direct Preference Optimization trains on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss and no reward model or RL loop: the implicit reward, the role of β, what the gradient does, its failure modes (offline data, likelihood displacement, length), and the family of variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO, online DPO) · built from Rafailov et al. (DPO, NeurIPS 2023), Azar et al. (IPO, 2023), Ethayarajh et al. (KTO, 2024), Hong et al. (ORPO, 2024), Meng et al. (SimPO, NeurIPS 2024), Xu et al. (Is DPO Superior to PPO?, ICML 2024) and Meta's Llama 3 report (2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. R. Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.18290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290).

2. S. Xu et al., "Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study", ICML 2024, [arXiv:2404.10719](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10719).

3. M. Azar et al., "A General Theoretical Paradigm to Understand Learning from Human Preferences" (IPO), 2023, [arXiv:2310.12036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036); K. Ethayarajh et al., "KTO", 2024, [arXiv:2402.01306](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306).

4. J. Hong et al., "ORPO", 2024, [arXiv:2403.07691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691); Y. Meng et al., "SimPO", NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2405.14734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14734).

5. N. Razin et al., "Unintentional Unalignment: Likelihood Displacement in Direct Preference Optimization", 2024, [arXiv:2410.08847](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08847); Llama Team, "The Llama 3 Herd of Models", 2024, [arXiv:2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783).

# Reasoning Models: RLVR, GRPO and Test-Time Compute

> How did DeepSeek-R1 learn to think from right/wrong rewards alone?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/reasoning-models-grpo/
- Before this: Reward Models and RLHF (PPO) (`fundamentals/rlhf-and-reward-models`)
- Related: DeepSeek-R1 (`papers/deepseek-r1`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant must compute refunds: a ₹420 order arrived 40 minutes late, and the policy refunds 10% for delays over 30 minutes. A wrong number costs real money, but the right answer can be checked. Human-written reasoning traces are scarce and expensive. The interviewer asks:

> How did DeepSeek-R1 learn to think from right or wrong rewards alone?

**Running example:** the assistant must compute refunds correctly: "A ₹420 order arrived 40 minutes late and the policy refunds 10% for delays over 30 minutes: how much is refunded?" Real cases chain several such rules. A wrong number is a real cost, and the right answer is checkable.

#### Multi-step problems need more than one forward pass

Answering a multi-step maths question in a single token is hard: the model needs room to work things out. Chain-of-thought prompting helps, but the model was never trained to reason well over thousands of tokens, to notice mistakes and to try again. Human-written reasoning traces are scarce and expensive. Can the model learn to reason from just the correctness of its final answers?

### The idea

Think of a student given only an answer key, with no worked solutions. Try a problem eight times, and reinforce the attempts that got it right compared with the rest. Get it right every time, or never, and you learn nothing from that problem. Over time, the student learns to check their own work.

[Figure: Group-relative advantages for 8 samples. With 1 of 8 correct, the right answer gets plus 2.65 and each wrong one minus 0.38. With 4 of 8, plus 1 and minus 1. With 0 or 8 correct, every advantage is 0.]

_From the GRPO lab in the Maths tab. Hard problems the model occasionally solves teach the most._

### Play

**Try to break it.** This lab is about inference, once the model is trained. At 40% per sample, raise the samples per question. Then drop to 20%, and compare the majority vote with pass@k.

#### Sample more, then vote or verify

Wrong answers are spread evenly over 4 different wrong values. Majority vote = most common final answer (ties split). pass@k counts a question as solved if any sample is right, which needs a verifier to pick it. 4,000 simulated questions, fixed seed.

With a 40% chance per sample, **self-consistency** (majority voting, Wang et al. 2023) lifts accuracy to **53.9%** with 5 samples and **78.6%** with 16, because wrong answers scatter while right ones agree. But at **20%**, no better than each wrong answer, voting stays around **20%** no matter how many samples. With a reliable **verifier** (unit tests, a checker, a good reward model), pass@k is what you get: 97.2% at 20% with 16 samples. Snell et al. (2024) found that allocating test-time compute adaptively can be over 4× more efficient than best-of-N, and can let a smaller model beat one about 14× larger on problems where the small model has a reasonable chance of success. Reasoning models internalise this: one long chain of thought explores, checks and revises before answering.

**Open question.** Yue et al. (2025) found that RLVR-trained models win at small k, but their base models often reach higher pass@k at large k: RL may mostly sharpen the model towards solutions it could already find, rather than create new reasoning abilities.

##### Beyond maths: tools and thinking budgets

- **Training tool use:** Qwen3's final RL stage lets the model run complete, multi-turn tool interactions with real environment feedback. On Qwen's in-house ToolUse test, Qwen3-32B with thinking on rose from 63.3 after reasoning RL to 85.5 after this stage.

- **Thinking on demand:** one model can now cover both modes. Qwen3 is trained to follow /think and /no_think flags.

- **Thinking budgets:** users can limit how much the model reasons, to trade quality against speed. Qwen3-235B's scores rose smoothly with the budget on maths, coding and science tests.

**Now say why:** why does voting stop helping at 20%, and why doesn't that stop a verifier?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

For maths, code and other checkable tasks we don't need a learned reward model: a program can **verify** the final answer or run the tests. **RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR)** samples many attempts per problem, rewards the correct ones, and reinforces whatever reasoning led there. **GRPO** (DeepSeekMath) makes this cheap: instead of a value model, it compares each attempt with the others in its group, **advantage = (reward − group mean) / group std**. Trained this way from a base model, **DeepSeek-R1-Zero** went from 15.6% to 71.0% on AIME 2024, and learned on its own to write longer chains of thought, re-check and backtrack. The other half of the story is **test-time compute**: thinking longer, sampling several answers and voting, or searching with a verifier often buys more accuracy than a bigger model. What you'll be able to do after this: explain RLVR and GRPO's advantage, what R1-Zero showed, and the pass@k vs majority-vote trade-off at inference.

#### Verifiable rewards and group-relative advantages

$$ A_i = \frac{{r_i} - {\mathrm{mean}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}}{{\mathrm{std}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}} $$

Shao et al., "DeepSeekMath", [arXiv:2402.03300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300). Every token of answer i gets advantage Ai, used in a PPO-style clipped objective with a KL term to the reference. The term RLVR comes from Tülu 3 (Lambert et al. 2024).

- **verifiable reward**: 1 if the final answer matches (or the code passes the tests), else 0; DeepSeek-R1-Zero also gave a format reward for putting its reasoning inside think tags. No reward model to hack.

- **group mean**: Sample G answers (e.g. 8–64) to the same prompt; the mean reward is the baseline, replacing PPO’s learned value model.

- **group std**: Normalising by the spread keeps advantages on a similar scale whatever the problem’s difficulty.

8 sampled answers to a refund problem, 10% of a ₹420 order, (correct answer ₹42); reward 1 if correct, else 0.

With **4 of 8** correct, correct answers get +1 and wrong ones −1. With only **1 of 8** correct, the rare success gets a big push (**+2.65**) and each failure a small one (−0.38): hard problems the model occasionally solves teach the most. With **0 or 8** correct, every advantage is 0: problems that are too hard or too easy teach nothing, which is why later recipes like DAPO filter such groups out and keep training data at the edge of the model's ability.

For where the baseline comes from, read Policy Gradients for LLMs.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What DeepSeek-R1-Zero showed, and what went wrong

- **Pure RL works:** starting from DeepSeek-V3-Base with no SFT, GRPO with only accuracy and format rewards raised AIME 2024 pass@1 from **15.6% to 71.0%** (86.7% with majority voting), comparable to OpenAI's o1-0912.

- **Emergent behaviour:** responses grew from hundreds to thousands of tokens over training, and the model began re-checking and backtracking ("wait, let me re-evaluate"), without being shown examples of it.

- **The trap:** R1-Zero's reasoning was hard to read and mixed languages. DeepSeek-R1 added a small "cold-start" SFT set of readable long chains of thought, then RL, then rejection-sampled SFT and a final RL stage for general helpfulness.

- **Why not a learned reward model?** DeepSeek avoided neural reward models for reasoning because large-scale RL tends to hack them (reward hacking); rule-based checks are much harder to fool, though models can still exploit weak test suites.

#### Reward the outcome, let the reasoning emerge

Where answers can be checked, RL on outcome rewards with group-relative advantages teaches models to spend tokens reasoning, and that inference-time thinking becomes a new axis to scale alongside parameters and data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Reasoning models were trained on human chain-of-thought data"

It sounds right, since reasoning looks like something you'd have to demonstrate. But R1-Zero learned from outcome rewards alone, and re-checking and backtracking emerged without examples. R1 added only a small cold-start set, because R1-Zero's reasoning was hard to read and mixed languages. DeepSeek also avoided learned reward models here, because large-scale RL tends to hack them.

## Say it

### How did DeepSeek-R1 learn to think from right or wrong rewards alone?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does GRPO not need a critic?

The average reward of the other samples for the same prompt is a good baseline, so a learned value model is unnecessary; this saves memory and avoids training a second network.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What happens if all samples in a group get the same reward?

All advantages are zero and the prompt gives no gradient; filter or re-sample such prompts and keep training problems at the right difficulty.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you apply RLVR to a non-maths product task?

Find checkable sub-goals: JSON that validates against a schema, SQL that returns the right rows, code that passes tests, refund amounts that match a calculator. Use a learned judge only where no check exists, and watch for hacking.

#### The 30-second answer

Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: for maths or code, sample several attempts per problem, reward the ones whose final answer or tests check out, and reinforce them. GRPO, from DeepSeekMath, drops PPO's value model and uses the group of samples as a baseline, advantage equals reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. DeepSeek-R1-Zero used this from a base model and went from about 16 to 71 percent on AIME 2024, with long chains of thought and self-checking emerging on their own. At inference, more compute, longer thinking, majority voting or verifier-guided search, can beat a larger model, as long as the model has a decent chance of getting it right.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Reasoning models were trained on human chain-of-thought data." R1-Zero learned from outcome rewards alone; R1 used a small cold-start set.

- "More samples always help." Majority voting only helps when the right answer is the most likely one.

**Key terms and sources**

How models like OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1 learn to "think" before answering: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on maths and code, GRPO's critic-free group advantages, what emerged in DeepSeek-R1-Zero, and how spending more compute at inference (long chains of thought, majority voting, best-of-N with verifiers) trades against model size · built from Shao et al. (DeepSeekMath / GRPO, 2024), DeepSeek-AI (DeepSeek-R1, 2025), OpenAI (Learning to Reason with LLMs, 2024), Lambert et al. (Tülu 3, 2024), Wang et al. (Self-Consistency, ICLR 2023), Snell et al. (2024), Yu et al. (DAPO, 2025) and Yue et al. (2025) · checked 29 Oct 2026

# Distillation: How Small Models Learn from Big Ones

> Why did distilling R1 beat RL on the same 32B model?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/distillation/
- Before this: SFT and Instruction Tuning (`fundamentals/supervised-fine-tuning`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

The post-trained 70B assistant is excellent but too expensive to serve to millions. The team wants a 3B model that behaves almost as well. Trained on the same data and labels, a 3B model ends up much weaker. The interviewer asks:

> Why did distilling R1 beat RL on the same 32B model?

**Running example:** the post-trained 70B assistant is excellent but too expensive to serve to millions of customers. The team wants a 3B model that runs cheaply, even on-device, and behaves almost as well.

#### Small models trained from scratch learn less

A 3B model trained on the same data and labels as a 70B model ends up much weaker. Training labels are one-hot: "the next token is _delicious_", full stop. The big model has learned a much richer picture of which alternatives are plausible; if the small model could learn from that picture, every training example would carry more signal.

### The idea

Think of the difference between an answer key and a teacher's notes. The key says "delicious", full stop. The teacher says delicious is likely, tasty is nearly as good, cold is possible and purple is absurd. Each example teaches the student far more.

[Figure: After the biryani was. The one-hot label puts everything on delicious. The teacher gives delicious 65 percent, tasty 29 percent, cold 3.6 percent, late 1.8 percent and purple almost nothing.]

_The next token after "the biryani was", from the lab's illustrative teacher at T = 1._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the temperature from 1 to 4, then to 8. Watch "tasty" against "purple", and the share on other tokens.

#### What the teacher knows beyond its top answer

Illustrative teacher logits for the next token after "the biryani was": delicious 6.0, tasty 5.2, cold 3.1, late 2.4, purple −2.0 (a real teacher spreads probability over a 100k+ vocabulary).

A one-hot label says only "delicious". The teacher at **T = 1** also puts **34.7%** on other words, and its numbers say "tasty" is a near-synonym, "cold" and "late" are plausible (complaints), and "purple" is **1,339×** less likely than "tasty". At **T = 4** the distribution is flatter (entropy 2.09 bits instead of 1.20) and the relationships among the small probabilities become a strong training signal. Too high a temperature washes out the ranking (at T = 8, 72.3% of the mass is spread away from the top token), which is why T is tuned, typically 1–4 for LLMs, often just 1.

**Now say why:** if a higher temperature exposes more, why is T usually kept between 1 and 4?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

A large **teacher** model knows more than its top answer: when it says "delicious", it also believes "tasty" is nearly as good and "purple" is absurd. **Knowledge distillation** trains a small **student** to match the teacher's whole probability distribution (**soft targets**), not just the correct token, which carries far more information per example. A **temperature** T > 1 softens the distribution so this "dark knowledge" is visible. For LLMs there are three main forms: **logit distillation** (match the teacher's next-token distribution at every position; Gemma 2 and Llama 3.2 1B/3B), **sequence-level distillation** (just fine-tune on text the teacher generates; DeepSeek's R1-Distill models, trained on about 800k R1 samples), and **on-policy distillation** (the student writes, the teacher grades each token). Distilling R1 into Qwen2.5-32B reached 72.6% on AIME 2024, versus 47.0% for running large-scale RL on the same 32B model directly. What you'll be able to do after this: explain soft targets and temperature, compare the three kinds of LLM distillation, and say when to distil instead of training directly.

#### Soft targets and temperature

$$ \mathcal{L}_{KD} = \alpha\,{T^2}\;{\mathrm{KL}\Big(\mathrm{softmax}\big(\tfrac{z_{teacher}}{{T}}\big)\,\Big\|\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(\tfrac{z_{student}}{{T}}\big)\Big)} + (1-\alpha)\,{\mathcal{L}_{CE}} $$

Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network", 2015, [arXiv:1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531). DistilBERT (Sanh et al. 2019) used it to make a BERT 40% smaller and 60% faster that kept 97% of its language-understanding performance.

- **temperature**: Divide the teacher’s logits by T before the softmax. T = 1 is the normal distribution; larger T flattens it so small probabilities become visible.

- **match the teacher**: KL divergence between the teacher’s and the student’s softened distributions: the student is penalised for every token where its beliefs differ, not only the top one.

- **T² scaling**: Softening shrinks the gradients by about 1/T², so the term is multiplied by T² to keep it comparable to the normal loss.

- **usual hard-label loss**: Optionally mixed in with weight 1 − α.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Three ways to distil an LLM

| Kind | What the student trains on | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Logit (token-level)** | the teacher's full next-token distribution at every position (needs the teacher's logits and the same tokeniser) | Gemma 2 2B/9B pre-trained with distillation; Llama 3.2 1B/3B used Llama 3.1 8B/70B logits as targets |
| **Sequence-level** | ordinary SFT on text the teacher generated (Kim & Rush 2016); works across tokenisers and through APIs | DeepSeek-R1-Distill (Qwen, Llama; 1.5B–70B) fine-tuned on ~800k R1-generated samples |
| **On-policy** | the student generates; the teacher scores its tokens (e.g. reverse KL), fixing the mismatch between training on teacher text and generating its own | GKD (Agarwal et al. 2024), MiniLLM (Gu et al. 2024) |

- **Distil or train directly?** DeepSeek ran large-scale RL directly on Qwen2.5-32B and got 47.0% on AIME 2024; distilling R1 into the same base gave **72.6%**, for far less compute. Their conclusion: distil to small models; large-scale RL needs a strong base model.

- **Limits:** a student rarely exceeds its teacher; it inherits the teacher's errors and biases; and many commercial model licences forbid using outputs to train competing models.

#### Teach with distributions, not just answers

A teacher's full probability distribution, or its generated text, carries much more information per example than ground-truth labels, so a small student learns faster and better from the teacher than from the raw data alone.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Distillation just means fine-tuning on teacher outputs"

It sounds right, since that's how DeepSeek's R1-Distill models were made. But that's only one form, called sequence-level. Logit distillation matches the teacher's full distribution at every position, and needs the same tokeniser. On-policy distillation has the student generate and the teacher score. A student also rarely exceeds its teacher, and it inherits the teacher's errors.

## Say it

### Why did distilling R1 beat RL on the same 32B model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why multiply the soft loss by T²?

Gradients of the softened KL scale roughly as 1/T², so multiplying by T² keeps the soft and hard loss terms balanced when T changes.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Logit distillation from a model with a different tokeniser?

Not directly: distributions are over different vocabularies. Use sequence-level distillation, or cross-tokeniser alignment methods.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Forward or reverse KL for generative students?

Forward KL makes the student cover all the teacher's modes (it may spread probability too thinly); reverse KL makes it focus on the teacher's main modes, which MiniLLM found better for generation.

#### The 30-second answer

Knowledge distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. In Hinton's version the student matches the teacher's softened output distribution, using a temperature to expose the relative probabilities of wrong answers, with a KL loss scaled by T squared, often mixed with the normal label loss. For LLMs you can match next-token logits at every position, as Gemma 2 and Llama 3.2 did; fine-tune on teacher-generated text, as DeepSeek did for its R1-Distill models; or do on-policy distillation where the student samples and the teacher scores each token. Distilling R1 into a 32B model beat running RL on that model directly, 72.6 versus 47 percent on AIME.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Distillation just means fine-tuning on teacher outputs." That's one form; logit and on-policy distillation are others.

- "The student can't learn anything the labels don't contain." The teacher's distribution carries information the labels don't.

**Key terms and sources**

Knowledge distillation from Hinton's soft targets to today's LLM practice: temperature and "dark knowledge", logit (token-level) distillation as used for Gemma 2 and Llama 3.2, sequence-level distillation on teacher outputs as used for the DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, on-policy distillation, and when distillation beats training the small model directly · built from Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015), Kim & Rush (2016), Sanh et al. (DistilBERT, 2019), Agarwal et al. (GKD, ICLR 2024), Gu et al. (MiniLLM, ICLR 2024), Gemma Team (Gemma 2, 2024), Meta (Llama 3.2, 2024) and DeepSeek-AI (DeepSeek-R1, 2025) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. G. Hinton, O. Vinyals & J. Dean, "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network", 2015, [arXiv:1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531); Y. Kim & A. Rush, "Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation", EMNLP 2016, [arXiv:1606.07947](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07947).

2. V. Sanh et al., "DistilBERT", 2019, [arXiv:1910.01108](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01108).

3. R. Agarwal et al., "On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes" (GKD), ICLR 2024, [arXiv:2306.13649](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649); Y. Gu et al., "MiniLLM", ICLR 2024, [arXiv:2306.08543](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543).

4. Gemma Team, "Gemma 2: Improving Open Language Models at a Practical Size", 2024, [arXiv:2408.00118](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00118); Meta, "Llama 3.2: Revolutionizing edge AI and vision with open, customizable models", 2024 (blog).

5. DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-R1", 2025, [arXiv:2501.12948](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) (§2.4 and §4.1, distillation vs RL).

# LoRA and QLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

> How do you fine-tune an 8B model on one 24 GB GPU?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/lora-and-qlora/
- Before this: SFT and Instruction Tuning (`fundamentals/supervised-fine-tuning`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

The team has 20,000 good support conversations and wants the 8B assistant to follow the company's tone and format, on a single 24 GB GPU if possible. Full fine-tuning needs about 128 GB. The interviewer asks:

> How do you fine-tune an 8B model on one 24 GB GPU?

**Running example:** the team has 20,000 high-quality support conversations and wants the 8B assistant to follow the company's tone and reply format exactly, on a single 24 GB GPU if possible.

#### Full fine-tuning is heavy and brittle

Updating all 8 B weights needs multi-GPU training, produces a full 16 GB copy of the model per task, and can erase general abilities. Most behaviour changes (tone, format, a domain's style) are "small" changes to a big model; can we train only a small change?

### The idea

Think of sticky notes on a printed textbook. You don't reprint the book to change its tone. You freeze it and add a few small notes, which you can peel off or swap for another set. QLoRA also shrinks the book itself, by printing it more compactly.

[Figure: Memory for weights and optimizer with Llama 3 8B. Full fine-tuning needs 128.5 gigabytes. LoRA needs 16.7. QLoRA needs 5.1. Both fit on a 24 gigabyte GPU.]

_From the lab: weights and optimizer, with LoRA at rank 16 on all linear layers. Activations come on top._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA. Then raise the rank to 64, and switch between attention only and all linear layers.

#### Will it fit on a 24 GB GPU?

Llama 3 8B shape (32 layers, d = 4,096, 8 KV heads, FFN 14,336). Full: 16 bytes/parameter (mixed-precision Adam). LoRA: bf16 base (2 B/param) + adapters with 16 B/param. QLoRA: NF4 base ≈ 0.55 B/param including scales. Activations, which depend on batch size and sequence length, come on top.

**Full fine-tuning** needs about **128.5 GB** for weights, gradients and Adam states: several GPUs with FSDP. **LoRA** with rank 16 on all linear layers trains **41.9 M** parameters, just **0.52%** of the model; the frozen bf16 base dominates memory at 16.7 GB, which fits a 24 GB card with room for modest activations. **QLoRA** stores the base in 4-bit and drops to about **5.1 GB**. Rank barely moves memory (r = 64 on all layers: 167.8 M parameters, 7.1 GB with QLoRA) because the adapters are tiny next to the base. The trap is assuming a bigger rank or more trainable parameters always helps: for style and format tasks, r = 8–16 is usually enough, and data quality matters far more.

**Now say why:** why does the rank barely move the memory, and what does?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs about 16 bytes per parameter of GPU memory with Adam: ~128 GB for an 8B model. **LoRA** freezes the pretrained weights and learns a small **low-rank update** for chosen matrices: W + (α/r)·B·A, where B and A have rank r (8–64). Only A and B are trained, often well under 1% of the parameters, so optimizer state shrinks to almost nothing and the adapter file is megabytes. **QLoRA** also stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, so an 8B model fine-tunes in a few GB and a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU. Adapters can be merged into the weights (no inference cost) or swapped per customer on one base model. The trade-off: LoRA typically learns somewhat less than full fine-tuning on hard new skills (code, maths), but also forgets less of what the base model knew. What you'll be able to do after this: explain LoRA's maths, size LoRA and QLoRA runs, and choose rank and target modules.

#### A low-rank update to frozen weights

$$ h = {W_0}\,x + {\frac{\alpha}{r}}\,{B A}\,x, \qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\; A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\; r \ll d $$

Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models", ICLR 2022, [arXiv:2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685): on GPT-3 175B, 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and 3× less GPU memory than full fine-tuning, with comparable quality and no added inference latency once merged.

- **frozen pretrained weight**: d_out × d_in, never updated (and in QLoRA stored in 4-bit NF4).

- **low-rank update**: B is d_out × r and A is r × d_in. With r = 16 on a 4096 × 4096 matrix that’s 131k trainable numbers instead of 16.8M. B starts at zero, so training starts from the original model.

- **scaling**: α / r scales the update; α is often set to r or 2r so changing the rank doesn’t require retuning the learning rate.

- **QLoRA** (Dettmers et al. 2023): the frozen base is quantized to **4-bit NormalFloat**, with double quantization of the scales and paged optimizers to survive memory spikes; gradients flow through the 4-bit weights into the bf16 adapters.

- **Target modules:** attention projections only (original LoRA) or all linear layers including the FFN (now common, usually better).

## In practice

### In practice

#### What LoRA learns, and how it's served

- **Learns less, forgets less** (Biderman et al. 2024): on large-scale code and maths training, LoRA underperformed full fine-tuning, but it preserved the base model's other abilities better, acting like a regulariser. For format, tone and narrow tasks, LoRA usually matches full fine-tuning.

- **QLoRA results:** fine-tuned a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU while matching 16-bit fine-tuning quality on the paper's benchmarks; its Guanaco models were rated close to ChatGPT on the Vicuna benchmark, which the authors themselves caution is an unreliable chatbot benchmark.

- **Variants:** DoRA splits weights into magnitude and direction for slightly better results; rsLoRA changes the scaling for high ranks.

- **Serving:** merge the adapter for a single task (zero overhead), or keep adapters separate and load many per base model (S-LoRA, vLLM multi-LoRA) for per-customer or per-task variants.

- Fine-tuning teaches _behaviour_ well and _new facts_ poorly; use RAG for knowledge (how to choose).

#### Freeze the model, learn a small low-rank change

Most task adaptation lives in a low-dimensional subspace, so training rank-r updates on frozen (even 4-bit) weights gives most of fine-tuning's benefit at a fraction of the memory, storage and risk.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Fine-tune it on our docs so it knows them"

It sounds right, since fine-tuning changes the model. But fine-tuning teaches behaviour well and new facts poorly, so use retrieval for knowledge. LoRA isn't always as good as full fine-tuning either: on large-scale code and maths training it underperformed. For format, tone and narrow tasks, it usually matches.

## Say it

### How do you fine-tune an 8B model on one 24 GB GPU?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why initialise B to zero?

So BA = 0 at the start and training begins exactly from the pretrained model; A is random so gradients flow.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you choose rank and targets?

Start with all linear layers at r = 16, α = 16–32; increase rank only if evals plateau on a hard task. Tune learning rate (higher than full fine-tuning, e.g. 1e-4 to 2e-4) and epochs (1–3) first.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does QLoRA make the final model 4-bit?

No: the adapter is trained in bf16 on top of a 4-bit base; you can merge into a bf16 copy of the base for serving, or serve the 4-bit base plus adapter.

#### The 30-second answer

LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and learns a low-rank update B times A for selected matrices, scaled by alpha over r, with B initialised to zero. With rank 8 to 64 that's well under 1 percent of the parameters, so gradients and optimizer state are tiny; an 8B model trains in about 17 GB instead of about 128. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit NormalFloat with double quantization and paged optimizers, so even a 65B model fine-tunes on one 48 GB GPU. Adapters can be merged for zero inference overhead or served many-per-base. LoRA tends to learn a bit less than full fine-tuning on hard new skills but forgets less, and it's for behaviour and format, not for adding knowledge.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "LoRA is always as good as full fine-tuning." Not on large new-skill training.

- "Fine-tune it on our docs so it knows them." Use retrieval for knowledge.

**Key terms and sources**

How to fine-tune large models cheaply: LoRA's low-rank update (rank, alpha, target modules), why it needs a fraction of the memory, QLoRA's 4-bit NF4 base model, what LoRA learns and forgets compared with full fine-tuning, and serving many adapters on one base model · built from Hu et al. (LoRA, ICLR 2022), Dettmers et al. (QLoRA, NeurIPS 2023), Biderman et al. (LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less, TMLR 2024), Liu et al. (DoRA, ICML 2024), Sheng et al. (S-LoRA, MLSys 2024) and the Hugging Face PEFT documentation · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. E. Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models", ICLR 2022, [arXiv:2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

2. T. Dettmers et al., "QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.14314](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314).

3. D. Biderman et al., "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less", TMLR 2024, [arXiv:2405.09673](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09673).

4. S.-Y. Liu et al., "DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation", ICML 2024, [arXiv:2402.09353](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09353); Y. Sheng et al., "S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters", MLSys 2024, [arXiv:2311.03285](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03285).
