# Safety Training and Jailbreaks

> How are LLMs trained to refuse, why do jailbreaks still work, and how do you defend a model?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Post-training
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/safety-training-and-jailbreaks/
- Before this: SFT and Instruction Tuning (`fundamentals/supervised-fine-tuning`), Reward Models and RLHF (PPO) (`fundamentals/rlhf-and-reward-models`)
- Quiz topic: `post`

## Intuition

### The situation

You've fine-tuned an open model for support, and a red-team test finds it now answers things it used to decline. Meanwhile, customers complain it refuses to explain how to "kill" a running order. You've been asked to fix both. The interviewer asks:

> How are LLMs trained to refuse, why do jailbreaks still work, and how do you defend a model?

#### Why it matters

Guardrails and prompt injection covers defences in an application. This lesson covers what happens in the model itself. It matters for anyone who fine-tunes a model, because that can change how it behaves on safety, whatever the training data was about.

### The idea

Think of security at a building. A guard has been trained on a list of situations, and also told to be helpful to visitors. A smooth request can set those two against each other, and someone in an unusual disguise may not match anything on the list. A strict guard turns away real visitors too. So buildings use several checks, rather than one perfect guard.

[Figure: Three layers. Train the model. Check inputs and outputs. Limit what the system can do.]

_No single layer is enough._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the threshold. Then switch to disguised requests, and add the output check.

#### Set the threshold

Illustrative, exact calculation with invented bell curves. Safe scores centre on −1.2, harmful on +1.2 and disguised harmful on −0.2, each with a standard deviation of 1. The output check is a second, independent score that reads the answer, so disguising the request doesn't fool it. It uses the same threshold, plus 1, so it blocks fewer safe answers.

At a threshold of 0, 11.5% of harmful requests get through, and 11.5% of safe ones are refused. Now switch to **disguised** requests: the same threshold lets 57.9% through. To get back to 11.5% with the threshold alone, you'd have to move it to about −1.4, which refuses 57.9% of safe requests. That's the trap of relying on one score. Back at 0, add the **output check**: disguised requests fall to 24.4%, and safe refusals rise only to 12.7%. A second, different signal helps far more than moving one threshold.

**Now say why:** why does a second check beat moving the threshold?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Safety is mostly learned behaviour, trained with the same SFT and RLHF methods as everything else. So it can fail like other learned behaviour. **Competing objectives:** the goals of being helpful and being safe can pull against each other. **Mismatched generalisation:** the model's abilities reach further than its safety training did. There's also a trade-off, as refusing more also blocks more harmless requests, known as **over-refusal**. Fine-tuning can weaken safety, even by accident. So real systems use several layers, and measure both kinds of error.

#### How safety is built, and why it breaks

##### How models learn it

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Safety data in SFT and RLHF** | Examples and preferences that show when and how to decline |
| **Constitutional AI** | The model critiques and revises its own answers against written principles, then trains on AI preferences, with no human labels for harm |
| **Red teaming** | People or other models look for failures, which become new training data and tests |

Red teaming works, though not completely. In one study of 38,961 attacks, RLHF models got harder to red team as they grew, while other model types stayed flat.

##### Why training fails

Wei et al. proposed two failure modes:

- **Competing objectives:** the model is trained to be helpful and to be safe, and a request can set the two against each other.

- **Mismatched generalisation:** the model can understand far more kinds of input than its safety training covered, so a harmful request in an unusual form may not trigger the trained behaviour.

Automated search also works. Zou et al. found text suffixes by gradient search on open models, and these sometimes carried over to other models. So fixing one prompt doesn't fix the problem.

##### Safety can be shallow

| Finding | What it showed |
|---|---|
| Fine-tuning | Safety fell after 10 adversarial examples, costing under $0.20. Ordinary, harmless datasets weakened it too, though less |
| Refusal direction | In 13 open models, refusal could be switched off or on through one direction in the activations |
| Emergent misalignment | Fine-tuning on insecure code led to broadly bad behaviour on unrelated prompts |
| Sleeper agents | A deliberately planted backdoor survived standard safety training, and adversarial training could teach the model to hide it better |

The last two come from controlled research settings. They show what's possible, not how often it occurs in deployed models.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{refused safe}} = {P(s > t \mid \text{safe})}, \qquad {\text{harmful answered}} = {P(s \le t \mid \text{harmful})} $$

A simple way to frame the trade-off, as in any classifier. Real safety behaviour isn’t a single score, but the same tension applies.

- **over-refusal**: Harmless requests the system wrongly declines.

- **the same threshold**: s is a risk score. Lowering t refuses more of everything.

- **missed harm**: Harmful requests that get through.

- **the other side of the trade**: Raising t lets more through. You can’t improve both by moving t alone. You need a better score.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Defending a model

- **Use layers:** combine model training, input and output classifiers, tool permissions and monitoring. One classifier approach, trained on synthetic data from written rules, withstood over 3,000 estimated hours of red teaming in its early form. A later version added 0.38 points to refusals and 23.7% to inference cost.

- **Measure both errors:** test harmful prompts, and also harmless ones that sound risky. XSTest has 250 safe prompts and 200 unsafe contrasts for this.

- **Re-test after every fine-tune:** run the same safety and over-refusal tests before and after, even with harmless data. Mix safety examples into the training set.

- **Limit what's at stake:** a model with no access to refunds can't be talked into issuing one. See agent safety.

- **Open weights change things:** anyone with the weights can fine-tune safety away, so provider-side filters don't apply. Plan your own safeguards.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We passed the safety test before fine-tuning, so we're safe"

It sounds right, as the base model was tested and your data was harmless. But fine-tuning can weaken safety even on harmless data, as Qi et al. found. Treat every fine-tune as a new model: re-run the safety and over-refusal tests before release, and keep a separate output check.

## Say it

### How are LLMs trained to refuse, why do jailbreaks still work, and how do you defend a model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

You fine-tune on harmless support chats and safety scores drop. Why, and what do you do?

Safety behaviour can be fragile, and training on a narrow task can shift the model away from it. Qi et al. saw this with harmless datasets. Mix in safety examples, lower the training intensity, re-test before release, and add an output classifier as a backstop.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your model now refuses "how do I kill a Python process?". What's wrong?

That's over-refusal: it's reacting to a word rather than the meaning. Add safe prompts that sound risky to your tests and training data, as in XSTest, and track the over-refusal rate along with safety.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not just block the known jailbreak prompts?

They change easily, and automated search can produce new ones. Blocking helps as a patch, but you need defences that don't depend on the wording, such as checking the output, and limiting what the system can do.

#### The 30-second answer

Safety is learned with the same methods as other behaviour: SFT, RLHF and methods like Constitutional AI, with red teaming to find failures. It fails in two main ways. Helpfulness and safety can compete, and the model's abilities can reach further than its safety training, so unusual inputs get past it. It can also be shallow, as fine-tuning on even harmless data can weaken it. There's a trade-off too, since refusing more means blocking more safe requests, so I'd always measure both harmful answers and over-refusal. In a product I'd use layers: model training, input and output classifiers, limited tool permissions and monitoring, and I'd re-run the safety tests after every fine-tune.

**Key terms and sources**

How safety is trained, red teaming, why safety training fails, over-refusal, how fine-tuning weakens safety, and layered defences. · checked 7 Nov 2026

# Decoding: Temperature, Top-k, Top-p and Min-p

> Why does top-p fall apart at high temperature, and is min-p really better?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Generation
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/decoding-and-sampling/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant is writing "Your biryani will arrive in …", and the next token should be a number of minutes, not "purple". A colleague turns the temperature up to 2 for livelier replies, with top-p at 0.9, and the text derails. The interviewer asks:

> Why does top-p fall apart at high temperature, and is min-p really better?

**Running example (generation):** the assistant is writing "Your biryani will arrive in …". The next token should be a number of minutes, not "purple".

#### The most likely text is not the best text

Maximising probability sounds right, but Holtzman et al. (2020) showed that greedy and beam search on open-ended text produce bland, repetitive output that loops ("I don't know. I don't know. …"), while human text is full of individually less likely words. Pure sampling from the full distribution has the opposite problem: once in a while it picks a token from the huge unreliable tail, and the text derails.

### The idea

Think of choosing from a huge menu. Temperature is how adventurous you feel. Top-p says to keep the dishes that make up 90% of orders, and if tastes are flat, that's most of the menu. Min-p says to keep dishes at least a tenth as popular as the favourite, so the cut moves with how clear the favourite is.

[Figure: At temperature 1, top-p keeps 131 tokens with 1.5 percent junk, and min-p keeps 5 with no junk. At temperature 2, top-p keeps 887 tokens with 79.7 percent junk, and min-p keeps 9 with no junk.]

_From the lab: nine sensible tokens plus 1,000 junk tokens._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the temperature to 1, and switch between no truncation, greedy, top-k, top-p and min-p. Then raise it to 2 and repeat.

#### "Your biryani will arrive in …"

Illustrative logits: nine sensible continuations ("30" 4.0, "20" 3.6, "25" 3.1, "40" 2.6, "15" 1.9, "45" 1.2, "an" 0.9, "about" 0.7, "two" 0.2) plus 1,000 junk tokens at logit −4 each, standing in for a real vocabulary's long tail.

At **T = 1** with no truncation, each junk token is negligible but together they hold **11.4%** of the probability: roughly one token in nine would derail the sentence. **Top-p 0.9** keeps 131 tokens, including 122 junk ones (**1.5%** chance); **top-k 5** and **min-p 0.1** keep only the five best. Turn the temperature up to **2** for more varied replies: the tail now holds 81.7%, top-p needs **887** tokens to reach 90% and samples junk **79.7%** of the time, while **min-p** keeps just 9 sensible tokens and no junk, because its cut-off moves with the top token. That's the idea behind min-p: usable variety at high temperature, though see the caution below. Lowering T to 0.5 sharpens "30" to 58.9%.

**Now say why:** each junk token is negligible, so how does the tail derail the sentence?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

The model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary; **decoding** decides which one to emit. **Greedy** always takes the top token (deterministic, but prone to repetitive loops); **beam search** keeps the few best partial sequences (good for translation, bland for open-ended text). **Sampling** picks at random in proportion to the probabilities, and **temperature** T reshapes them first: T < 1 sharpens, T > 1 flattens. Because the vocabulary has 100k+ tokens, the long **tail** of individually unlikely tokens adds up, so samplers truncate it: **top-k** keeps the k best, **top-p** keeps the smallest set covering p of the probability, and **min-p** keeps tokens at least a fraction of the top token's probability. At high temperature top-p can let junk back in, and min-p's cut-off tightens instead, though a later critique found little evidence that this gives better text overall. What you'll be able to do after this: explain each decoding method, pick settings per task, and explain why min-p holds up at high temperature.

#### Temperature and truncation

$$ p_i = {\frac{\exp({z_i}/{T})}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}} $$

- **logits**: The raw scores the model outputs for each token.

- **temperature**: Divide every logit by T. T → 0 becomes greedy; T = 1 is the model’s own distribution; T > 1 flattens it so unlikely tokens get more probability.

- **softmax**: Turn the scaled scores into probabilities, then truncate and renormalise before sampling.

- **Top-k** (Fan et al. 2018): keep the k most likely tokens. Simple, but k is fixed whether the model is sure (1 sensible option) or unsure (hundreds).

- **Top-p / nucleus** (Holtzman et al. 2020): keep the smallest set whose probabilities sum to p (e.g. 0.9). Adapts to the shape, but when the distribution is flat the "nucleus" can contain many tail tokens.

- **Min-p** (Nguyen et al. 2025): keep tokens with probability ≥ pbase × (top token's probability), e.g. 0.1×. The cut-off scales with the model's confidence.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Choosing settings

| Task | Typical setting | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Extraction, classification, JSON, code fixes | T = 0 (greedy) or low | one right answer; reproducibility |
| Chat assistants | T ≈ 0.6–1.0, top-p 0.9–0.95 | natural variety without derailing |
| Creative writing, brainstorming | moderate to higher T, with top-p or min-p ≈ 0.05–0.1 | diversity while cutting the tail |
| Self-consistency / best-of-N | T ≈ 0.7–1.0 | samples must differ to be worth voting over |
| Translation, summarisation (older seq2seq) | beam search, width 4–5 | output is tightly constrained by the input |

- Add a **repetition / frequency penalty** to discourage loops; use **stop sequences** and max tokens to end cleanly.

- **Constrained decoding** masks tokens that would break a grammar (e.g. a JSON schema) so the output always parses.

- T = 0 is not always perfectly deterministic in serving: batching and floating-point non-associativity can change ties.

**Don't overclaim min-p.** The lab's maths is right: min-p's cut-off moves with the top token, so junk stays out at high temperature. But Schaeffer et al. (2025) re-analysed the original paper. They report that its human evaluation left out data and that min-p was largely indistinguishable from other samplers, and that on benchmarks it had no clear edge once every sampler got the same amount of tuning. They allow a weak benefit at high temperature, where quality is lower anyway. They also quote a later study by the original authors, which found no apparent advantage over basic or top-p sampling. Treat min-p as a reasonable option, not as a proven upgrade.

#### Reshape, then cut the tail

Temperature controls how adventurous sampling is, and truncation removes the thousands of individually rare tokens whose combined probability would otherwise derail the text; min-p's confidence-relative cut-off removes junk reliably at high temperature, though that hasn't been shown to give better text at normal settings.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Top-p always cuts out bad tokens"

It sounds right, since cutting the tail is its job. But on a flat distribution the nucleus can be huge. At T = 2 in the lab, top-p needs 887 tokens to reach 90%, and samples junk 79.7% of the time. Higher temperature doesn't make the model smarter or more creative either: it only flattens the distribution.

## Say it

### Why does top-p fall apart at high temperature, and is min-p really better?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What does temperature 0 mean?

The limit is greedy decoding (argmax); implementations special-case it because dividing by zero is undefined.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does beam search produce repetitive text?

It maximises sequence likelihood, and repeated phrases become self-reinforcing high-probability paths; human text is not the most likely text.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Should you set both temperature and top-p?

You can (truncation is applied after temperature), but tune one at a time; OpenAI's API docs recommend altering one or the other.

#### The 30-second answer

Decoding turns the next-token distribution into text. Greedy and beam search pick high-probability sequences but give repetitive, bland text for open-ended generation. Sampling adds variety, with temperature dividing the logits to sharpen or flatten the distribution. Because the vocabulary is huge, the long tail of unlikely tokens adds up, so we truncate: top-k keeps a fixed number, top-p keeps the smallest set covering, say, 90 percent of the probability, and min-p keeps tokens above a fraction of the top token's probability, so junk stays out at high temperature, though later analysis found little evidence that it gives better text overall. I use near-zero temperature for extraction and code, moderate temperature with top-p for chat, and I'd test any sampler on my own task before trusting a claim about it.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Higher temperature makes the model smarter or more creative." It only flattens the distribution.

- "Top-p always cuts out bad tokens." On flat distributions the nucleus can be huge.

**Key terms and sources**

(The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration, ICLR 2020), Fan et al. (top-k, 2018), Nguyen et al. (min-p, ICLR 2025), Ackley et al. # In-Context Learning and Chain-of-Thought

> How did 'Let's think step by step' take maths from 18% to 79%?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Generation
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/in-context-learning-and-cot/
- Before this: Decoding: Temperature, Top-k, Top-p and Min-p (`fundamentals/decoding-and-sampling`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

## Intuition

### The situation

Before investing in fine-tuning, the team tries to get refund calculations right just by prompting. Asked for the answer directly, the assistant gets most of them wrong. A colleague adds examples, and it barely helps. The interviewer asks:

> How did "Let's think step by step" take maths from 18% to 79%?

**Running example:** before investing in fine-tuning, the team tries to get refund calculations right just by prompting the assistant.

#### A new task, no training budget

Fine-tuning needs labelled data, compute and a deployment for each task. Large pre-trained models can often do a task just from a description and a few examples in the prompt, which makes prototyping fast and cheap. The question is how to write that prompt, and why it works.

### The idea

Think of doing long multiplication in your head, and then being handed scratch paper. Examples show you what kind of answer is wanted, but you still have to do it all in your head. Chain-of-thought is the scratch paper: each written step is something the next one can use.

[Figure: MultiArith accuracy. Zero-shot 17.7 percent, few-shot 33.8 percent, zero-shot chain-of-thought 78.7 percent, few-shot chain-of-thought 93 percent.]

_From Kojima et al. (2022), with text-davinci-002, as shown in the lab._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Go through zero-shot, few-shot, zero-shot CoT and few-shot CoT. Compare MultiArith with GSM8K.

#### Asking for the answer directly

Prompts are shown on the running example for illustration. Accuracies are from Kojima et al. (2022), Table 2: text-davinci-002 on MultiArith and GSM8K, with Wei et al.'s 8 exemplars for the few-shot settings. Bars: MultiArith (top, orange) and GSM8K (bottom, green).

Asking for the answer straight away forces the model to compute it inside a single token: **17.7%** on MultiArith and **10.4%** on GSM8K. Eight examples help a little (**33.8%** / 15.6%) because they show the format, but still give no room to calculate. Simply adding **"Let's think step by step."** jumps to **78.7%** / 40.7%, and eight worked examples with reasoning reach **93.0%** / 48.7%. Each intermediate token is extra computation the model can condition on. Wei et al. (2022) found CoT helps mainly in large models (around 100B parameters at the time); small models wrote fluent but wrong chains.

**Now say why:** few-shot shows worked formats too, so why does adding the reasoning do so much more?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

**In-context learning (ICL)** means an LLM performs a new task from instructions and examples placed in the prompt, with **no weight updates**. GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) showed this improves sharply with scale. Demonstrations mainly teach the **format, label space and input distribution**: Min et al. (2022) found that even random labels in the examples cost surprisingly little. **Chain-of-thought (CoT)** prompting asks the model to write intermediate steps before the answer, which gives it room to compute: with text-davinci-002, adding "Let's think step by step" lifted MultiArith from 17.7% to 78.7% and GSM8K from 10.4% to 40.7%; eight worked examples reached 93.0% and 48.7%. Sampling several chains and voting (**self-consistency**) helps further. Reasoning models now do this internally, so prompts for them should state the goal, not the steps. What you'll be able to do after this: choose between zero-shot, few-shot and CoT prompts, explain why CoT works, and avoid common ICL pitfalls.

#### Zero-shot, few-shot, and what examples teach

- **Zero-shot:** instruction only. **Few-shot:** add k input–output examples (GPT-3 used up to ~32, limited by context). In GPT-3 the gap between zero- and few-shot grew with model size.

- **What demonstrations teach:** Min et al. (2022) replaced the gold labels in demonstrations with random ones and saw only small drops on many classification tasks; the format, the set of possible labels and the style of inputs mattered more than correct input–label mapping. (Very large models can follow flipped labels, so this varies with scale.)

- **Pitfalls:** results are sensitive to example order and choice; models favour labels that appear often or last ("majority" and "recency" bias, Zhao et al. 2021); information in the middle of long prompts is used less well (Liu et al. 2024).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Prompting in 2026

- **Self-consistency** (Wang et al. 2023): sample several chains and take the majority answer; Kojima et al. report PaLM 540B zero-shot CoT on GSM8K rising from 43.0% to 70.1% with it. See Reasoning Models for when voting helps.

- **Reasoning models** (o-series, DeepSeek-R1, Claude and Gemini thinking modes) are trained to think before answering; give them a clear goal, constraints and output format rather than step-by-step instructions or many examples.

- **For production:** keep a small set of diverse, representative examples; put instructions and key data at the start or end; ask for structured output; evaluate prompts on a labelled set like any model change.

- **When to stop prompting:** if you need consistent behaviour across thousands of examples, lower cost per call (shorter prompts) or a skill the model lacks, fine-tune instead (SFT).

**Faithfulness caveat.** A written chain of thought is not guaranteed to be the reason for the answer: studies have found models giving explanations that omit what actually influenced them (e.g. Turpin et al. 2023). Treat CoT as a useful computation aid, not a reliable explanation.

#### Give the model the format, and room to think

In-context examples tell the model what task and format you want; chain-of-thought gives it extra tokens to compute with, which is what multi-step problems need.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The chain of thought explains the model's decision"

It sounds right, since you can read the reasoning right there. But it isn't guaranteed to be why the model answered that way. Studies found explanations that omit what actually influenced the answer. Treat CoT as a useful computation aid, not a reliable explanation. Few-shot prompting doesn't fine-tune the model either: its weights don't change.

## Say it

### How did "Let's think step by step" take maths from 18% to 79%?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Is in-context learning actually learning?

No weights change; the model infers the task from the context and conditions on it. Some theory views it as implicit Bayesian inference or as attention implementing simple learning algorithms over the examples.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Few-shot results vary a lot between runs. Why?

Sensitivity to example choice, order and label balance (majority and recency bias). Use diverse examples, balance labels, fix the order, and evaluate on a held-out set.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When does CoT not help?

Simple lookup or classification tasks, small models, and reasoning models that already think internally; it also costs extra tokens and latency.

#### The 30-second answer

In-context learning is when a model performs a task from instructions and examples in the prompt without any weight updates; it emerged strongly with scale in GPT-3. Demonstrations mostly convey the format and label space; even random labels often hurt surprisingly little. Chain-of-thought prompting has the model write intermediate reasoning before the answer, which gives it extra computation: with InstructGPT, "Let's think step by step" took MultiArith from about 18 to 79 percent, and few-shot CoT reached 93. Self-consistency samples several chains and votes. Reasoning models now generate this thinking themselves, so you prompt them with goals and constraints rather than step-by-step instructions.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Few-shot prompting fine-tunes the model." Weights don't change.

- "The chain of thought explains the model's decision." It may not be faithful.

**Key terms and sources**

How LLMs learn tasks from the prompt alone: zero-shot and few-shot prompting, what demonstrations actually teach, chain-of-thought prompting (few-shot and "Let's think step by step"), self-consistency, and how reasoning models changed prompting · built from Brown et al. (GPT-3, NeurIPS 2020), Min et al. (Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations, EMNLP 2022), Wei et al. (Chain-of-Thought, NeurIPS 2022), Kojima et al. (Zero-Shot Reasoners, NeurIPS 2022), Wang et al. (Self-Consistency, ICLR 2023), Zhao et al. (Calibrate Before Use, ICML 2021) and Liu et al. (Lost in the Middle, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

2. J. Wei et al., "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models", NeurIPS 2022, [arXiv:2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903).

5. M. Turpin et al., "Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.04388](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388); N. Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", TACL 2024, [arXiv:2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172).

# Hallucination: Why LLMs Make Things Up

> Why do models guess confidently, and how do you stop an invented refund policy?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Generation
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/hallucination/
- Before this: In-Context Learning and Chain-of-Thought (`fundamentals/in-context-learning-and-cot`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

## Intuition

### The situation

A customer asks about a refund for a cancelled festival-day order, and the assistant confidently describes a "48-hour festival guarantee" that doesn't exist. In a real case, Moffatt v. Air Canada, a tribunal held an airline responsible for a policy its chatbot invented. The interviewer asks:

> Why do models guess confidently, and how do you stop an invented refund policy?

**Running example:** a customer asks the assistant whether they can get a refund for a cancelled festival-day order. The assistant confidently describes a "48-hour festival guarantee" that doesn't exist. In a real case (Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024), a tribunal held an airline responsible for a refund policy its chatbot had invented.

#### Fluent, confident, wrong

Hallucinations are dangerous because they look exactly like correct answers. Researchers separate **intrinsic** hallucinations, which contradict the given source (a summary that changes a number), from **extrinsic** ones, which add claims the source can't verify (Ji et al. 2023). For open-domain questions the issue is **factuality**: the claim is false in the world.

### The idea

Think of an exam with no negative marking. Guessing every question is the smart move, even when you have no idea. Add negative marking, and the same student starts leaving blanks. Most mainstream benchmarks are the first kind of exam, so guessing pays.

[Figure: The same model under two gradings. With binary grading it always answers: 51.4 percent right and 48.6 percent wrong. With a penalty for wrong answers it answers only when confident: 10 percent right, 2.4 percent wrong and 87.6 percent I don't know.]

_The same simulated model under two gradings, from the lab. It answers only when that scores best._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Under binary grading, raise the confidence threshold and watch the score. Switch to the penalty, and find the best threshold again.

#### Grade answers as simply right or wrong

2,000 simulated questions; the model has a calibrated confidence for each (it is right with exactly that probability). Penalised grading: +1 right, −3 wrong, 0 for "I don't know", the scheme Kalai et al. propose for a 75% confidence target (penalty t/(1 − t) = 3).

Under **binary grading**, the score is just accuracy, so the best strategy is to **always answer**: score 0.514, but **48.6%** of answers are wrong. Abstaining below 50% confidence would halve the errors (19.1%) yet lowers the score to 0.359, so a leaderboard punishes the more honest model. With **penalised grading**, always answering scores **−0.944**, and the best policy is to answer only above **0.75** confidence: 10.0% right, just 2.4% wrong, 87.6% "I don't know". The model was the same in every case; only the incentive changed. Kalai et al. found most mainstream benchmarks use binary grading, and argue this is a main reason hallucination persists after post-training.

**Now say why:** nothing about the model changed, so why did the errors fall to 2.4%?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A **hallucination** is fluent, confident content that isn't supported by the source or by reality: an invented refund policy, a fake citation, a wrong date. It's not a rare bug but a consequence of how models are built: a next-token predictor must produce _something_ plausible even for facts it saw once or never (Kalai et al. 2025 argue that if 20% of some kind of fact appears only once in training, expect at least ~20% errors on it), fine-tuning on facts the model doesn't know encourages confident guessing, and most benchmarks score "I don't know" the same as a wrong answer, so **guessing is rewarded**. Fixes: ground answers in retrieved documents with citations, let the model abstain and reward it for doing so, check answers with tools or a second pass, and measure hallucination rates on your own data. What you'll be able to do after this: explain the main causes of hallucination, design mitigations for a product, and explain why scoring rules matter.

#### Where hallucinations come from

- **Pre-training statistics:** the model learns plausible patterns, not a database. Facts seen once (a restaurant's founding year, a person's birthday) can't be reliably separated from plausible alternatives; Kalai et al. show errors on such facts are statistically unavoidable for a well-calibrated base model.

- **Post-training:** fine-tuning on answers to questions the model didn't know teaches it to answer confidently anyway; Gekhman et al. (2024) found such examples are learned slowly and increase hallucination. Preference tuning can reward confident, complete-sounding answers.

- **Decoding:** sampling can pick a low-probability wrong continuation, and once written, the model conditions on it (it rarely retracts).

- **Evaluation incentives:** the subject of the lab in the Intuition tab.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Reducing and catching hallucinations

- **Ground it:** retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020) with instructions to answer only from the retrieved policy text and cite it; tools for anything computable (refund amounts, order status).

- **Allow and reward abstention:** include "I'm not sure, let me connect you to an agent" examples in SFT and preference data; score abstentions above wrong answers in your evals.

- **Detect:** SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al. 2023) samples several answers and flags claims that don't agree across samples; Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al. 2023) has the model plan and answer verification questions before finalising; FActScore (Min et al. 2023) splits long answers into atomic facts and checks each against a knowledge source.

- **Decode conservatively** for factual answers (low temperature) and constrain output to known options where possible (e.g. pick a policy ID).

- **Measure:** track hallucination rate, citation precision and abstention rate on a labelled set of real questions, and review samples by hand.

Images add their own failures: see Vision-Language Models.

#### Plausible is not true, and guessing is rewarded

Models hallucinate because they are trained to produce plausible text and evaluated in ways that reward guessing; ground them in sources, let them say "I don't know", and score that honesty higher than a confident mistake.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It's a decoding bug, and a lower temperature will fix it"

It sounds right, since the bad text appears during generation. But it comes from training objectives and incentives. Lowering the temperature removes sampling randomness, but if the most likely answer is wrong, greedy decoding states it confidently. Bigger models don't solve it either: they hallucinate less on common facts, but still on rare ones.

## Say it

### Why do models guess confidently, and how do you stop an invented refund policy?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Does RAG eliminate hallucination?

No. The model can ignore or misread the retrieved text, retrieval can miss the right document, and it can blend sources. Check citation faithfulness and handle "not found" explicitly.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you detect hallucinations without ground truth?

Sample several answers and check consistency (SelfCheckGPT), ask the model to verify individual claims, or use an NLI model / LLM judge to check each claim against the source documents.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does lowering temperature only partly help?

It removes sampling randomness, but if the model's most likely answer is wrong (an unknown fact), greedy decoding states it confidently.

#### The 30-second answer

Hallucinations are fluent but unsupported or false outputs. They come from next-token training, which learns plausible patterns and can't reliably store rarely seen facts; from fine-tuning that teaches confident answers on unknown facts; from sampling; and from evaluations that give no credit for abstaining, so guessing maximises scores. To reduce them in a product I'd ground answers in retrieved sources with citations, use tools for computable facts, train and prompt the model to abstain when unsure and score abstentions above errors, add a verification step or sample-consistency check, and measure hallucination and abstention rates on real labelled questions.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Bigger models don't hallucinate." They hallucinate less on common facts, but still on rare ones.

- "It's a decoding bug." It comes from training objectives and incentives.

**Key terms and sources**

What hallucinations are (unsupported or false content stated fluently), why they arise from pre-training statistics, fine-tuning and evaluations that reward guessing, how to detect them (sampling consistency, verification, FActScore), and how to reduce them in products (retrieval with citations, abstention, tools, calibrated grading) · built from Kalai et al. (Why Language Models Hallucinate, 2025), Ji et al. (Survey of Hallucination, ACM CSUR 2023), Manakul et al. (SelfCheckGPT, EMNLP 2023), Min et al. (FActScore, EMNLP 2023), Dhuliawala et al. # Benchmarks and Contamination

> Is a 3-point GPQA gap real, and did the model see the test?

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Evaluating LLMs and practice
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/benchmarks-and-contamination/
- Before this: Pretraining Data: Deduplication, Filtering and Mixtures (`fundamentals/pretraining-data`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

## Intuition

### The situation

Two candidate models for the support assistant differ by 3 points on GPQA Diamond and 1 point on MMLU. A colleague wants to pick the one with the higher scores. The interviewer asks:

> Is a 3-point GPQA gap real, and did the model see the test?

**Running example (evaluation):** two candidate models for the support assistant differ by 3 points on GPQA Diamond and 1 point on MMLU. The team must decide whether either gap means anything, and how to test what actually matters to them.

#### Comparing models needs shared, fair tests

Generated text has no single right answer, and every lab reports the benchmarks it looks best on. Shared benchmarks give a common yardstick, but only if the questions are hard enough, correct, unseen during training, and numerous enough that differences aren't noise.

### The idea

Think of ranking students by a very short class test. On 30 questions, one lucky guess moves your score by over 3 points, so a small gap means little. And if the paper leaked, the score only tells you who saw it. A good test needs enough questions, correct answers and questions nobody has seen.

[Figure: 95 percent margins at 60 percent accuracy. MMLU plus or minus 0.8 points, SWE-bench Verified 4.3, GPQA Diamond 6.8 and AIME 17.5.]

_95% margin of error in points, at 60% accuracy, from the lab._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between MMLU, SWE-bench Verified, GPQA Diamond and AIME 2024. Then move the model accuracy, and watch the gap needed between two models.

#### "Model A scored 3 points higher, so it's better"

Normal approximation for a proportion: margin = 1.96 √(p(1 − p)/n); gap needed = 1.96 √(2p(1 − p)/n) for two independent evaluations. Paired tests on the same questions (Miller 2024) are tighter, and repeated sampling adds its own variance.

At 60% accuracy, **GPQA Diamond**'s 198 questions give a margin of **±6.8 points**; two models need to differ by roughly **9.7 points** before the gap is clearly real, so the team's 3-point difference is noise. **MMLU**'s 14,042 questions narrow the margin to ±0.8, but a 1-point gap is still borderline, and MMLU is saturated and partly mislabelled. **AIME** is the extreme: with 30 problems each one is worth 3.33 points and the margin is ±17.5, which is why labs report averages over many samples per problem. **SWE-bench Verified** sits in between at ±4.3.

**Now say why:** GPQA Diamond is a respected test, so why is a 3-point gap on it noise?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Benchmarks are fixed test sets that let us compare models on the same questions: **MMLU** (57 subjects, multiple choice), **GPQA** (graduate-level science questions that experts get 65% right and skilled non-experts with web access only 34%), **AIME** (competition maths), **SWE-bench Verified** (500 real GitHub issues the model must fix so the tests pass). Three things make scores misleading. **Noise:** a 198-question benchmark has a 95% margin of about ±7 points, so small leaderboard gaps mean little. **Saturation and label errors:** once models score 90%+, remaining errors are often in the benchmark itself (about 6.5% of MMLU questions have errors). **Contamination:** test questions leak into training data, so scores measure memory; on a fresh GSM8K-style set (GSM1k), some models dropped by up to 13 points. Always pair public benchmarks with your own held-out evaluation. What you'll be able to do after this: describe the main benchmarks, compute a benchmark's error bars, and explain how contamination is detected and avoided.

#### The benchmarks you'll be asked about

| Benchmark | What it tests | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **MMLU** (2021) | 57 subjects, 4-option multiple choice; 14,042 test questions | saturated near 90%; ~6.5% of questions have errors; MMLU-Pro uses 10 options and harder questions |
| **GPQA Diamond** | 198 "Google-proof" biology, physics and chemistry questions | experts 65%, skilled non-experts with 30+ minutes of web search 34% |
| **AIME** | 30 competition maths problems per year, integer answers | new problems each year limit contamination; tiny, so very noisy |
| **SWE-bench Verified** | 500 real GitHub issues from Python repos; the patch must make hidden tests pass | human-validated subset of SWE-bench's 2,294 issues; OpenAI, which created it, stopped reporting it in 2026, citing contamination and flawed tests |
| Others | HumanEval (saturated), GSM8K (saturated), Humanity's Last Exam, LiveCodeBench (rolling, post-cutoff problems), MT-Bench / Arena (open-ended; next lesson) | live and rolling benchmarks fight contamination |

## In practice

### In practice

#### When the test set is in the training data

- **How it happens:** benchmarks are public on the web, copied into forums, GitHub and datasets, and scraped into pre-training corpora; fine-tuning sets can include near-copies.

- **Evidence:** Zhang et al. (2024) wrote GSM1k, 1,000 new problems in GSM8K's style; several model families scored up to 13 points lower than on GSM8K, while frontier models showed little drop.

- **Detection:** n-gram overlap between training data and test sets; canary strings (unique markers in benchmark files, as in BIG-bench) that should never appear in training data; membership tests such as Min-K% Prob (unusually high likelihood on a test item's rarest tokens suggests it was seen).

- **Mitigation:** private held-out sets, rolling benchmarks with problems newer than the model's cutoff (LiveCodeBench, new AIME years), decontaminating training data, and reporting contamination analyses.

**For your own product:** build a held-out set of real, representative tasks (support tickets with correct resolutions), never train on it, version it, and report confidence intervals. It predicts deployment quality far better than a public leaderboard.

**A benchmark's life cycle: SWE-bench Verified.** In February 2026, OpenAI said it would stop reporting this benchmark, which it had helped create. It audited 27.6% of the problems its model had failed, and found that at least 59.4% of those had tests that rejected correct solutions. Frontier models could also reproduce some of the original fixes from memory. So rising scores increasingly measured exposure to the test. It recommended SWE-bench Pro instead, which keeps some of its data private. Expect any public benchmark to wear out this way, and re-check how much your own favourite is still telling you.

#### A score is only as good as its test set

Benchmark numbers need error bars, correct labels and unseen questions; small gaps, saturated tests and contaminated data turn leaderboards into noise, so decisions should rest on your own held-out evaluations.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "High MMLU means it'll work for our users"

It sounds right, since it's a broad knowledge test. But MMLU is saturated near 90%, and about 6.5% of its questions have errors. Benchmarks can also be contaminated. And a 1-point gap needs error bars before it means anything. A held-out set of your own real tasks, such as support tickets with correct resolutions, predicts deployment quality far better than a public leaderboard.

## Say it

### Is a 3-point GPQA gap real, and did the model see the test?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How many examples does an eval set need?

For ±3 points at 95% confidence near 50% accuracy, n ≈ (1.96 × 0.5 / 0.03)² ≈ 1,070. To detect smaller differences, use paired comparisons on the same items.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you check whether a model has seen a benchmark?

Search training data for n-gram overlap or canary strings if you have it; otherwise compare performance on the original vs. paraphrased or newly written equivalent questions, and use membership-inference scores.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does SWE-bench need a "Verified" subset?

Some original tasks had underspecified issues or tests that rejected valid fixes; human annotators filtered to 500 tasks. Even so, a 2026 audit by OpenAI found many remaining failures were due to flawed tests, and that models could recall some fixes from memory.

#### The 30-second answer

LLM benchmarks include MMLU for broad knowledge, GPQA Diamond for expert-level science, AIME for competition maths and the SWE-bench family for real coding tasks, though its creator has now dropped SWE-bench Verified. I treat scores with care for three reasons: small test sets are noisy, for example GPQA Diamond's 198 questions give about plus or minus 7 points at 60 percent; older benchmarks are saturated and contain label errors; and test data leaks into training, which GSM1k exposed with drops of up to 13 points for some models. Contamination is detected with n-gram overlap, canary strings and membership-inference tests, and avoided with private or rolling benchmarks. For a product, I'd rely on our own held-out evaluation set.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Model A is better: it scored 1 point higher." Check the error bars.

- "High MMLU means it'll work for our users." Test on your own tasks.

**Key terms and sources**

How LLMs are compared: knowledge and reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA, AIME), agentic and coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified), what makes a benchmark trustworthy, statistical noise from small test sets, saturation and label errors, and test-set contamination and how to detect it · built from Hendrycks et al. (MMLU, ICLR 2021), Rein et al. (GPQA, COLM 2024), Jimenez et al. (SWE-bench, ICLR 2024), OpenAI (SWE-bench Verified, 2024), Gema et al. (Are We Done with MMLU?, NAACL 2025), Zhang et al. (GSM1k, NeurIPS 2024), Shi et al. (Min-K% Prob, ICLR 2024) and Miller (Adding Error Bars to Evals, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

# LLM Practice 1: Pretraining and Scaling Maths

> 9 back-of-the-envelope questions: parameters, KV cache, FLOPs, memory, MoE, image tokens.

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Evaluating LLMs and practice
- Type: Interview · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/llm-practice-scaling/
- Before this: Training at Scale: Mixed Precision, Parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP (`fundamentals/distributed-training`), Mixture of Experts (`fundamentals/mixture-of-experts`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. These are back-of-the-envelope questions interviewers love. Work them out on paper with round numbers first, then open the answer and compare.

**The formulas:** params per layer ≈ attention (2d² + 2·d·kv_heads·head_dim) + SwiGLU FFN (3·d·d_ff); KV cache = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes; training FLOPs ≈ 6·N·D; compute-optimal D ≈ 20·N, so N ≈ √(C/120); mixed-precision Adam ≈ 16 bytes per parameter.

Question 1 · Easy · parameter count

### A model has d = 4,096, 32 layers, full multi-head attention, a SwiGLU FFN with hidden size 11,008, a 32,000-token vocabulary and untied input/output embeddings. How many parameters?

Answer: **about 6.74 B (this is Llama 2 7B)**

1. Attention per layer: 4d² = 4 × 4,096² ≈ 67.1 M (Q, K, V, O, all full size with MHA).

2. FFN per layer: 3 × 4,096 × 11,008 ≈ 135.3 M. Per layer ≈ 202.4 M; × 32 layers ≈ 6.48 B.

3. Embeddings: 2 × 32,000 × 4,096 ≈ 0.26 B. Total ≈ 6.74 B; norms add only ~0.3 M.

**Follow-up:** Which change would cut the most parameters: GQA with 8 KV heads, or tying the embeddings? GQA saves 2 × 4,096 × (4,096 − 1,024) × 32 ≈ 0.81 B; tying saves 0.13 B.

Question 2 · Easy · KV cache

### For that same model (32 layers, 32 heads of size 128, bf16), how much KV cache does one 4,096-token conversation need? How many fit next to the 13.5 GB of weights on an 80 GB GPU?

Answer: **0.5 MiB per token → 2 GiB per conversation → about 30 conversations**

1. Per token: 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MiB.

2. × 4,096 tokens = 2 GiB per conversation.

3. (80 − 13.5) GB ≈ 61.9 GiB free → about 30 conversations, before activations and fragmentation. With GQA-8 it would be 4× as many.

**Follow-up:** Why does this limit throughput rather than just memory? Each decode step reads the whole cache; more conversations per batch amortise the weight reads, so a bigger cache budget means higher tokens per second.

Question 3 · Medium · training compute

### Llama 2 7B was trained on 2 T tokens. Estimate the training FLOPs and the A100 GPU-hours at 40% utilisation (A100 bf16 peak = 312 TFLOPS). Meta reported 184,320 GPU-hours. How close are you?

Answer: **8.4 × 10²² FLOPs ≈ 187,000 GPU-hours: within 2% of the reported figure**

1. C ≈ 6 N D = 6 × 7 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹² = 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs.

2. Effective throughput per GPU: 0.4 × 312 × 10¹² ≈ 1.25 × 10¹⁴ FLOP/s.

3. 8.4 × 10²² / 1.25 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 6.7 × 10⁸ GPU-seconds ≈ 187,000 GPU-hours, vs 184,320 reported in the Llama 2 paper.

**Follow-up:** How many days on 2,048 GPUs? 187,000 / 2,048 ≈ 91 hours ≈ 3.8 days, ignoring restarts and evaluation.

Question 4 · Medium · Chinchilla

### You have a budget of 10²³ training FLOPs. What model size and token count are compute-optimal under the Chinchilla rule of ~20 tokens per parameter?

Answer: **about 29 B parameters on about 580 B tokens**

1. C = 6ND and D = 20N, so C = 120N² and N = √(C/120) = √(8.3 × 10²⁰) ≈ 2.9 × 10¹⁰.

2. D = 20N ≈ 5.8 × 10¹¹ tokens.

3. Check: 6 × 2.9 × 10¹⁰ × 5.8 × 10¹¹ ≈ 1.0 × 10²³. ✓

**Follow-up:** Your model will serve 1 billion requests a month. Would you still pick 29 B? Probably not: train a smaller model (say 7–8 B) on many more tokens; it loses a little loss but is ~4× cheaper per request (Sardana et al. 2024).

Question 5 · Medium · training memory

### You want to fully fine-tune a 13 B model with Adam in mixed precision on 8 × 80 GB GPUs. Does it fit with plain data parallelism? With ZeRO-3 / FSDP?

Answer: **DDP: no (208 GB per GPU); ZeRO-3: 26 GB per GPU of model state, so yes, with room for activations**

1. Mixed-precision Adam ≈ 16 bytes/parameter: 2 (bf16 weights) + 2 (grads) + 12 (fp32 master + Adam m, v).

2. DDP replicates everything: 16 × 13 B = 208 GB per GPU, far above 80 GB.

3. ZeRO-3 shards all of it across 8 GPUs: 208 / 8 = 26 GB each, leaving ~50 GB for activations (use activation checkpointing for long sequences).

**Follow-up:** What if you only had one 80 GB GPU? Use LoRA/QLoRA: freeze the base (in 4-bit for QLoRA) and train small adapters, so optimizer state is tiny.

Question 6 · Hard · MoE parameters

### An MoE model has 32 layers, d = 4,096, GQA with 8 KV heads of size 128, 8 SwiGLU experts per layer with hidden size 14,336, top-2 routing, and a 32,000-token vocabulary (untied). Estimate total and active parameters per token.

Answer: **about 46.7 B total, about 12.9 B active (this is Mixtral 8x7B)**

1. One expert: 3 × 4,096 × 14,336 ≈ 176.2 M. All experts: 8 × 176.2 M × 32 layers ≈ 45.1 B.

2. Attention per layer: 2d² + 2 × 4,096 × 1,024 ≈ 41.9 M; × 32 ≈ 1.34 B. Embeddings: 2 × 32,000 × 4,096 ≈ 0.26 B. Total ≈ 46.7 B.

3. Active: 2 experts × 176.2 M × 32 ≈ 11.3 B, plus attention and embeddings ≈ 12.9 B.

**Follow-up:** How much GPU memory does it need for inference in bf16? All 46.7 B parameters must be loaded: ≈ 93 GB, more than one 80 GB GPU, even though compute per token is like a 13 B model.

Question 7 · Hard · loss spike

### Pre-training a 7 B model: loss starts at 10.4 with a 32,000-token vocabulary, falls smoothly to 2.3 by step 20k, then at step 31k jumps to 7 within 200 steps. Gradient norm and the maximum attention logit had been creeping up for the previous 2k steps. Is the start healthy? What do you do now, and for the next run?

Answer: **the start is healthy (ln 32,000 ≈ 10.4); the spike looks like attention-logit growth: roll back, skip data, and add QK-norm / z-loss / lower LR**

1. Initial loss ≈ ln(vocab) means a well-initialised, uniform output; fine.

2. Rising gradient norm and attention logits before the spike suggest attention-logit growth (softmax saturating), not just one bad batch.

3. Now: restore a checkpoint a few hundred steps before 31k, skip the next few hundred batches, optionally lower the learning rate (PaLM's recipe).

4. Next run: QK-norm, z-loss (10⁻⁴ log² Z), gradient clipping, and monitor max attention logits and per-layer gradient norms.

**Follow-up:** How would you tell bad data from optimisation instability? Replay the same batches from an earlier checkpoint: if the spike doesn't reproduce, it's the interaction of parameters and data (as PaLM found), not the data alone.

Question 8 · Medium · memory bandwidth

### An 8B model in 16-bit serves 32 conversations of 4,096 tokens on one H100 (989 TFLOPS, 3.35 TB/s). Cache is 128 KiB per token. What limits a decode step, and what's the best tokens per second?

Answer: **Memory: about 9.9 ms per step, or about 3,200 tokens a second**

1. Maths: 2 × 8B × 32 = 5.1 × 10¹¹ operations, ÷ 989 × 10¹² ≈ 0.52 ms.

2. Memory: 16 GB of weights + 32 × 4,096 × 131,072 bytes ≈ 33.2 GB, ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 9.9 ms.

3. Memory takes about 19 times longer, so it sets the limit: 32 tokens ÷ 9.9 ms ≈ 3,200 a second.

What would a chip with twice the compute do here? Almost nothing, since the step is waiting on memory.

Question 9 · Easy · image tokens

### A model uses 14-pixel patches on an 896 × 896 image. How many patches is that? After 4 × 4 average pooling, how many image tokens remain, and how much KV cache do they need at 128 KiB per token?

Answer: **4,096 patches, 256 tokens and 32 MiB**

1. 896 ÷ 14 = 64, and 64 × 64 = 4,096 patches.

2. Pooling each 4 × 4 group gives 16 × 16 = 256 tokens.

3. 256 × 128 KiB = 32 MiB. Without pooling, it would be 512 MiB.

This is the shape Gemma 3 uses. What might you lose? Fine detail, such as small text, which is why it offers pan and scan.

**More practice and sources**

9 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 29 Oct 2026

Keep practising

Uses the methods in this track: Anatomy, Attention Variants, MoE, Scaling Laws, Training at Scale, Training Instabilities. Llama 2 figures from Touvron et al. (2023); Mixtral from Jiang et al. (2024). Part 2: Post-training and Generation.

New lessons: GPUs and memory bandwidth and Vision-Language Models.

# LLM Practice 2: Post-training and Generation

> 9 scenarios: SFT bugs, reward hacking, DPO and GRPO maths, hallucination, judges, safety.

- Track: Fundamentals › LLMs › Evaluating LLMs and practice
- Type: Interview · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/fundamentals/llm-practice-post-training/
- Before this: LoRA and QLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (`fundamentals/lora-and-qlora`), Benchmarks and Contamination (`fundamentals/benchmarks-and-contamination`)
- Quiz topic: `llmgen`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Say your diagnosis out loud (most likely cause first, then how you'd confirm and fix it), then open the answer and compare.

**The checklist:** check the chat template and loss mask; separate model problems from decoding settings; watch for reward hacking (length, sycophancy) when a learned reward goes up; ground facts and allow abstention; evaluate with both orders, error bars and a human-validated judge.

Question 1 · Easy · SFT

### After SFT, your support model answers well but never stops: it keeps writing a fake customer reply and then answers that too. What's wrong?

Answer: **the model never learned to emit the end-of-turn token, or inference doesn't stop on it**

1. Check the training data: is the end-of-turn token in every assistant turn, and is it inside the loss mask (it must be trained)?

2. Check inference: same chat template as training, and the end-of-turn token set as a stop token.

3. Writing the user's next message is the giveaway: the model is continuing the conversation format because nothing taught it to stop.

**Follow-up:** Why mask the user turns at all? Otherwise most of the loss is spent learning to imitate customers, and the model learns to write user messages.

Question 2 · Easy · decoding

### An LLM extracts order IDs and amounts into JSON. Results differ between runs and ~2% of outputs aren't valid JSON. What settings and techniques fix this?

Answer: **temperature 0 (greedy) plus constrained / structured decoding against a JSON schema**

1. Extraction has one right answer, so sampling only adds variance: use temperature 0.

2. Constrained decoding masks any token that would break the schema, so every output parses.

3. Keep a small labelled set to measure field-level accuracy after the change.

**Follow-up:** Is temperature 0 perfectly deterministic in production? Not always: batching and floating-point order can still change near-ties.

Question 3 · Medium · reward hacking

### During RLHF, the reward-model score keeps rising, responses have grown from 120 to 400 tokens, and agents rate the new checkpoints worse. What's happening and what do you do?

Answer: **reward hacking: the policy is exploiting the reward model's length preference**

1. The reward model is a proxy; optimising it hard finds its blind spots (here, longer answers score higher regardless of quality).

2. Stop at an earlier checkpoint chosen by human or held-out evaluation, not RM score.

3. Raise the KL penalty, add a length penalty or length-normalised reward, retrain the RM on fresh comparisons that include long-but-worse answers, and report length-controlled win rates.

**Follow-up:** How would you spot this automatically? Track response length and RM score against a small human-rated set every few hundred steps; diverging curves are the alarm.

Question 4 · Medium · DPO maths

### With β = 0.1, the policy makes the chosen answer 2 nats more likely than the reference does, and the rejected answer 3 nats less likely. What is the DPO loss for this pair, and how much does it still contribute to the gradient?

Answer: **margin = 0.1 × (2 − (−3)) = 0.5; loss = −ln σ(0.5) ≈ 0.474; gradient weight σ(−0.5) ≈ 0.38**

1. Implicit rewards: 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 (chosen) and 0.1 × (−3) = −0.3 (rejected); margin 0.5.

2. Loss = −ln σ(0.5) = ln(1 + e^(−0.5)) ≈ 0.474 (it starts at ln 2 ≈ 0.693).

3. The gradient is scaled by σ(−margin) ≈ 0.38: the pair is partly learned and still contributes.

**Follow-up:** If both log-ratios drop (chosen −4, rejected −9), what happens to the loss? Same margin, same loss: DPO only cares about the difference, so both answers can become less likely (likelihood displacement).

Question 5 · Medium · GRPO

### In GRPO, a maths prompt gets 4 sampled answers with rewards [1, 0, 0, 0]. Compute the advantages. What happens for a prompt where all 4 are correct?

Answer: **correct answer +1.73, each wrong answer −0.58; all-correct groups give 0 advantage and no learning signal**

1. Mean = 0.25; std = √(0.25 × 0.75) ≈ 0.433.

2. Correct: (1 − 0.25) / 0.433 ≈ +1.73. Wrong: (0 − 0.25) / 0.433 ≈ −0.58.

3. All four correct (or all wrong): every reward equals the mean, so every advantage is 0: filter such prompts or resample (as DAPO does).

**Follow-up:** Why no value model? The group mean is the baseline, saving a whole network's memory and training.

Question 6 · Hard · hallucination

### Your support assistant sometimes invents refund policies ("48-hour festival guarantee"). Product wants it fixed before launch. What's your plan?

Answer: **ground answers in the policy documents, allow and reward abstention, verify, and measure**

1. Retrieve the relevant policy sections (RAG) and instruct the model to answer only from them, citing the section; escalate to a human if nothing relevant is found.

2. Teach abstention: SFT and preference data with "I'm not sure, let me check with an agent" examples; score abstentions above wrong answers in evals.

3. Use tools for anything computable (refund amounts, order status) instead of free-text generation.

4. Add a check: verify each policy claim in the draft against the retrieved text (NLI model or LLM judge) before sending.

5. Measure hallucination, citation accuracy and escalation rate on a labelled set of real questions; review samples weekly.

**Follow-up:** Why not just lower the temperature? If the model doesn't know the policy, its most likely answer is still a confident invention; grounding and abstention fix the cause.

Question 7 · Hard · LLM-as-judge

### A GPT-class judge says your new prompt beats the old one in 62% of 300 support conversations, always with the new answer shown first. Can you ship it?

Answer: **not yet: the setup has position bias, and even without it the margin is about ±5.5 points**

1. The new answer was always first, so position bias alone could produce a >50% win rate. Re-run with both orders and count only consistent verdicts (inconsistent = tie).

2. Margin of error at n = 300, p = 0.62: 1.96 × √(0.62 × 0.38 / 300) ≈ 0.055, so roughly 56–68% if the judge were unbiased.

3. Check length: if new answers are longer, report a length-controlled win rate.

4. Validate the judge on ~200 human-labelled pairs from your domain and use a different model family from the one being tested.

**Follow-up:** What result would convince you? An order-balanced, length-controlled win rate whose interval stays above 50%, from a judge with good agreement with human labels, plus no regression on policy-accuracy checks.

Question 8 · Medium · policy gradient

### One prompt gets 4 sampled answers with rewards [11, 10, 10, 10]. Give each answer's policy gradient weight with no baseline, and with the group mean as a baseline. Why does this matter?

Answer: **No baseline: 11, 10, 10, 10. Group mean: +0.75, −0.25, −0.25, −0.25**

1. With no baseline, all weights are large and positive, so every answer gets pushed up, whichever is good.

2. The group mean is 10.25, so subtracting it gives +0.75 and −0.25.

3. Now the better answer rises and the rest fall. The expected gradient is the same, but there's far less noise.

Does GRPO divide these by anything else? Yes, by the group's standard deviation, here about 0.43, which gives +1.73 and −0.58.

Question 9 · Hard · safety

### You fine-tune an assistant on 20,000 harmless support chats. Quality is up, but your safety test now shows far more harmful requests answered. Nothing in the training data was harmful. What happened, and what do you do before release?

Answer: **Fine-tuning can weaken safety even on harmless data. Fix it, then re-test both kinds of error**

1. Safety behaviour is learned, and narrow training can move the model away from it. Qi et al. (2023) found this with harmless datasets.

2. Mix safety examples into the training data, and lower the number of epochs or the learning rate.

3. Add an output classifier as a separate layer.

4. Re-run the safety tests and an over-refusal test, such as XSTest-style prompts, so you don't just swing to refusing everything.

Why test over-refusal too? A model that refuses everything passes a safety test while being useless.

**More practice and sources**
