# Prefill vs Decode

> Why does an LLM read your prompt fast but write its answer slowly?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/prefill-vs-decode/
- Before this: Attention Variants: MQA, GQA and MLA (`fundamentals/attention-variants-mqa-gqa-mla`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

One user sends a 2,000-token document and asks for a 300-token summary. The first word comes quickly, and then the rest crawls. A colleague says to buy a faster GPU. The interviewer asks:

> Why does an LLM read your prompt fast but write its answer slowly?

**Running example, used on every chapter:** one user sends a 2,000-token document and asks for a 300-token summary. The model is Llama 3.1 8B in 16-bit on one H100 (989 TFLOP/s dense BF16, 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth, 80 GB). All times are ideal ceilings from those specs: real engines reach less, but the shape holds.

#### The first word comes fast. The rest crawls.

Ask a chatbot to summarise a long document and you see the same pattern every time: a short wait, then the answer streams out word by word. That isn't the UI being dramatic. It is the model doing two completely different kinds of work, and the second kind takes almost all the time.

1. Prefill takes the whole 2,000-token prompt through the model in a single forward pass. Drawn to scale, it's this thin sliver: about 34 ms.

2. That pass also produces the first answer token. The time until it shows up is the **time to first token** (TTFT).

3. Every later token needs its own full pass through the model, because token 2 depends on token 1. 300 tokens means 300 passes at about 4.8 ms each.

4. So for this request, decode is about 1.44 s of the 1.47 s total. And as you'll see, during that time the GPU's maths units sit almost idle.

The same pattern shows up in measurements, not just my arithmetic. Profiling Llama-2-7B on an RTX 4090, the AWQ authors found that reading a 200-token prompt took **10 ms** while generating 20 tokens took **310 ms** [AWQ, Fig. 3, p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=5).

So "how fast is this LLM?" has two answers. The services that run LLMs track them separately:

##### TTFT · time to first token

How long until the first word. Set by prefill, grows with prompt length. Matters most for chat, voice and code completion.

##### TPOT / ITL · time per output token

The gap between streamed tokens (also called TBT, time between tokens). Set by decode. 10 ms per token = 100 tokens per second for that user.

[DistServe, p. 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=1) · [Splitwise, Table II, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=2)

### The idea

Think of a chef who works at incredible speed, with ingredients arriving down one narrow corridor. For prefill, one delivery feeds thousands of portions, so the chef is the limit. For decode, a whole delivery comes in for a single portion, so the corridor is the limit.

[Figure: Prefill: one read of the weights feeds 2,000 tokens, about 2,000 FLOPs per byte, so it is compute-bound. Decode: one read feeds one token, about 1 FLOP per byte, so it is memory-bound. An H100's balance point is about 295 FLOPs per byte.]

_Rough figures from the lesson, for Llama 3.1 8B on one H100 serving one user._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between 16, 8 and 4 bits. Watch the ideal time per token, and how busy the tensor cores are.

#### Decode time ≈ bytes to read ÷ bandwidth

For one user, a decode step does 2 FLOPs per weight but has to read 2 bytes per weight. The tensor cores finish their 16 GFLOPs in 0.016 ms, then wait 4.8 ms for the bytes. So the speed limit is set by bytes, and anything that shrinks them speeds decode up directly.

$$ {t_{\text{step}}} \approx \big({bP} + {B\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,\text{KV}_{\text{tok}}}\big)\,\big/\,{\text{BW}} \;\Rightarrow\; {16.1\ \text{GB} / 3.35\ \text{TB/s} \approx 4.8\ \text{ms}} $$

Memory-bound estimate (my derivation, standard in the inference literature) · hover any symbol.

- **one decode step**: Time to produce one more token for every user in the batch.

- **the weights**: P × b bytes. Read once per step, no matter how many users share the step. 16.1 GB here.

- **everyone's KV cache**: Each of the B users has a cache of n_ctx tokens × 128 KiB. Unlike the weights, it is not shared: every user adds their own bytes.

- **bandwidth**: 3.35 TB/s on an H100. Decode speed is tied to this number, not to FLOPs.

- **one user, short chat**: B = 1 and a small cache: about 16.1 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 4.8 ms per token, or about 209 tokens per second at best.

##### Try it: shrink the bytes

Weights only, batch of 1, Llama 3.1 8B on an H100. Halving the bytes halves the ideal time. In practice one precision step down (16 → 8 bits) is typically 30–50% faster, not 2×, because of kernels, the KV cache and other overheads (Inference Engineering, P. Kiely, ch. 5.1). AWQ's 4-bit TinyChat kernels measured about 3.2–3.3× over Hugging Face FP16 [AWQ, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2).

##### What breaks: the KV cache keeps growing

Every generated token adds 128 KiB to every user's cache, and decode re-reads the whole cache each step. Splitwise: "each active generated token that is being processed accesses the KV cache of its entire context so far", which makes the token phase "limited by memory capacity" [Insight V, p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=5). Long contexts slow decode even when the weights are tiny. That's why GQA, KV-cache quantization and paged cache memory exist.

**Now say why:** the tensor cores are almost idle, so what is decode actually waiting for?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Every LLM request runs in two phases. **Prefill** reads the whole prompt in one pass and is limited by the GPU's maths. **Decode** writes the answer one token per pass and is limited by how fast memory can feed the weights. Almost every inference trick (batching, quantization, chunked prefill, disaggregation) is a fix for one phase or for the two getting in each other's way. What you'll be able to do after this: estimate TTFT and tokens per second on a napkin, explain why decode is memory-bound, and pick the right fix when an LLM feels slow.

#### A GPU is a fast calculator behind a narrow pipe

You need three ideas: where the weights live, the KV cache, and the ratio between maths speed and memory speed. Think of a chef (the maths units) working at an incredible pace, while ingredients (the weights) arrive from a storeroom down a single corridor.

1. The weights live in the GPU's high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Llama 3.1 8B in 16-bit is 8.03 billion numbers × 2 bytes ≈ 16.1 GB.

2. The maths units can't compute on HBM directly. For every forward pass, all 16.1 GB has to stream through a 3.35 TB/s pipe. That alone takes 16.1 ÷ 3.35 ≈ 4.8 ms.

3. The tensor cores do roughly 2 FLOPs per weight for each token they process: a multiply and an add.

4. Divide the two speeds: the H100 can do about 295 FLOPs in the time one byte arrives. This ratio is the GPU's **ridge point**. Work that does fewer FLOPs per byte is **memory-bound**. Work that does more is **compute-bound**.

5. Next to the weights sits the **KV cache**: for every token seen so far, each layer's key and value vectors, saved so they are never recomputed. Decode reads it every step, and it grows by one entry per token.

The KV cache is why the model doesn't redo the whole prompt for every new token. Attention needs every past token's key and value, so prefill computes them once and stores them. Its size per token comes from the model's shape:

$$ {\text{KV}_{\text{tok}}} = {2}\cdot{L}\cdot{H_{kv}}\cdot{d_h}\cdot{b} = {131{,}072\ \text{bytes}} $$

Standard formula; model shape from the [Llama 3.1 8B config](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B/blob/main/config.json) (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, bfloat16) · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **bytes per token**: How much KV cache one token adds, across the whole model.

- **K and V**: One key vector and one value vector per head. That is the 2.

- **layers**: Every layer has its own attention, so its own cache. Llama 3.1 8B has 32 layers.

- **KV heads**: Number of key/value heads. Llama 3.1 8B uses grouped-query attention: 32 query heads share 8 KV heads, which makes the cache 4× smaller.

- **head size**: Numbers per head vector: 128 for this model.

- **bytes each**: 2 in 16-bit. Quantizing the cache to 8-bit halves everything.

- **the answer**: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. Our 2,300-token conversation holds about 0.30 GB of KV cache.

**Go deeper: why 2 FLOPs per parameter per token**

A linear layer computes y = Wx. Each weight wij is used once per token: multiply it by xj, add it to yi. That is 2 FLOPs. Linear layers hold almost all of a transformer's parameters, so a forward pass costs about 2·P FLOPs per token, plus attention, which costs about 2·L·d·n per token at context length n (small until the context gets long). This is the standard estimate used in the inference literature; the attention term is why very long prompts make prefill grow faster than linearly [DistServe, p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=13).

#### Both phases read the same weights. Only prefill gets to reuse them.

Every forward pass streams all the weights from memory once. What changes is how many tokens share that one read. Prefill pushes thousands of prompt tokens through together, so each weight byte gets used thousands of times. Decode pushes one token per user, so each byte is used once (per user) and thrown away. The number that captures this is arithmetic intensity: FLOPs done per byte read.

$$ {I} = {2PN}\,\big/\,{bP} = {2N/b} \qquad {I_{\text{prefill}}\approx 2000} \quad {I_{\text{decode}}\approx 1} $$

Weights-only roofline estimate (my derivation from the standard 2·P FLOPs rule). AWQ's profile of Llama-2-7B reports the same picture: intensity ≈ 1 for 16-bit decode and ≥ 165 for the prompt stage [AWQ, Fig. 3b, p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=5).

- **intensity**: FLOPs per byte moved from memory. Compare it with the GPU ridge point (295 on an H100) to know which limit you hit.

- **maths done**: About 2 FLOPs per parameter for each of the N tokens in the pass.

- **bytes read**: The weights, read once per pass: P parameters × b bytes each (2 in 16-bit). KV cache reads are ignored here; they only make decode worse.

- **it is just tokens per pass**: P cancels: intensity is about 2N ÷ b. In 16-bit that is simply N, the number of tokens sharing the read.

- **prefill: N = 2,000**: Our 2,000-token prompt gives about 2,000 FLOPs per byte, well above 295. Compute-bound: the maths units are the limit.

- **decode: N = 1**: One user decoding gives 1 FLOP per byte, about 300× below the ridge. Memory-bound: the maths units are idle 99.7% of the time.

Everything below follows from this one line. Prefill is fixed by doing maths faster or doing less of it. Decode is fixed by moving fewer bytes or by making more tokens share each byte. And when you mix them on one GPU, they fight.

#### Prefill time ≈ maths needed ÷ maths speed

Once the prompt is a few hundred tokens long, the weights stream in faster than the tensor cores can use them, so the clock is set by FLOPs. Drag the prompt length and watch where the limit switches.

Ideal H100 ceiling for Llama 3.1 8B (P = 8.03 B, L = 32, d = 4,096). Below about 300 tokens, prefill is actually memory-bound too. Above it, every extra token costs maths, and at very long prompts the n² attention term takes a growing share.

The papers see the same switch point on real hardware. DistServe found a single 512-token prompt "can fully engage an A100" for a 13B model [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=4). Sarathi-Serve notes the theory says about 200 tokens on an A100 (whose ridge is lower, about 153), but in practice it happens at about 500–600 tokens because of fixed overheads [p. 6, footnote 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=6).

##### What breaks: batching prefills doesn't help

Once one prompt saturates compute, adding a second prompt to the same pass just doubles the time. DistServe: "adding more requests to the batch no longer improves GPU efficiency. Instead, it proportionally extends the total processing time" [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=4). That's why prefill fixes are about doing less maths (prefix caching, shorter prompts) or faster maths (FP8 tensor cores, more GPUs via tensor parallelism), not bigger batches.

#### Serve many users in one step

If one read of the weights feeds 64 users instead of 1, the expensive part of the step is paid once and split 64 ways. This is why **continuous batching** (Orca's iteration-level scheduling, used by vLLM and every modern engine) is the single biggest throughput win in serving. But each user brings their own KV cache, and that part is never shared. Play with both dials.

–

Ideal H100 model, Llama 3.1 8B in 16-bit: step = max(compute, (weights + all KV) ÷ 3.35 TB/s). The purple bar is the share of each step spent reading KV cache. 80 GB − 16.1 GB of weights leaves about 64 GB for caches (ignoring activations and allocator overhead).

Three things to notice. Up to a point, total throughput climbs almost linearly while each user's speed barely drops: the step time is still "read the weights". Sarathi-Serve measured exactly this flat region: LLaMA2-70B's linear layers take about the same time for 128 to 512 tokens per batch [Fig. 6, p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=6). With long contexts, the KV cache reads take over and per-user speed falls. And the batch often runs out of _memory capacity_ for caches long before it reaches the compute ridge.

##### Why "295" is only a rule of thumb

Weights-only, a 16-bit decode batch reaches the ridge at about 295 users. But each user also reads their own cache: at 2,300 tokens that is about 0.3 GB per user per step against 16.1 GB of shared weights. Per user, the cache adds bytes without adding much maths, so intensity never reaches the ridge, and the step stays memory-bound however big the batch. Real engines hit KV memory limits first, which is why PagedAttention (removing cache fragmentation so more requests run at once) mattered so much: with iteration-level batching it reached an order of magnitude more throughput than FasterTransformer [Sarathi-Serve, p. 3 and 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=7).

#### Chunked prefill: hide prompt work in decode's idle maths

Decode steps leave the tensor cores mostly idle. Sarathi-Serve's insight: fill that idle compute with a slice of someone's prompt. Each step gets a token budget. First every running decode gets its one token, then the leftover budget goes to a chunk of a waiting prompt. Steps stay roughly the same size, so streaming users never see a multi-second freeze [§4.2, Algorithm 3, p. 8–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=8).

1. Each iteration has a fixed budget of tokens, chosen so one step stays under the latency target. Here, 512.

2. Running decodes go in first: 32 users, one token each. They never wait.

3. The rest of the budget goes to a chunk of the waiting prompt: 480 tokens of a new 8,000-token document.

4. The prompt finishes over about 17 steps instead of one huge one.

5. No step is ever "one giant prefill", so nobody's stream freezes. The decode tokens ride along on maths that was idle anyway.

##### Try it: pick the token budget

Illustrative ideal model: 32 users decoding with 1,500-token contexts, one new 8,000-token prompt, Llama 3.1 8B on an H100. A step = max(compute, memory). Normal decode gap with no prompt waiting: about 6.7 ms.

Smaller budgets mean smoother streams, but chunking isn't free, and the ideal model above hides the costs:

##### What breaks with chunks that are too small

- Each chunk's attention re-reads the KV cache of all earlier chunks: N chunks means O(N²) cache loads instead of O(N) [DistServe, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=4). Sarathi-Serve found attention prefill stays compute-bound even with small chunks, but fixed overheads like kernel launches add up [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=9).

- Tile quantization: GPUs compute in tiles, so a chunk of 257 tokens can make prefill 32% slower than a chunk of 256 [Sarathi-Serve, p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=9).

- DistServe's critique: chunking "trades TTFT for TPOT and cannot eliminate the interference" [p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=3).

##### What it buys

Naively mixing a full prefill into a decode batch raised time-between-tokens by up to **28.3×** over a decode-only batch, while chunking kept it tightly bounded [p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=8). Sarathi-Serve reports 2.6× higher serving capacity for Mistral-7B on one A100 and up to 3.7× for Yi-34B on two A100s, versus vLLM at the time [abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=1). vLLM V1 now turns chunked prefill on by default and schedules decodes first; a smaller `max_num_batched_tokens` (e.g. 2,048) gives better inter-token latency, a larger one better TTFT [vLLM docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization.html).

#### Disaggregation: give each phase its own GPUs

If the two phases want opposite things, stop sharing. A prefill pool runs prompts and produces the KV cache. It sends the cache to a decode pool, which streams the answer. Each pool gets its own GPU count, batch policy and parallelism, tuned for TTFT or for TPOT [DistServe, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=4).

1. A router assigns each request a prefill machine and a decode machine (Splitwise uses join-the-shortest-queue) [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=6).

2. The prefill pool only ever runs prompts. It can use more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT without slowing anyone's stream.

3. The KV cache is copied to the decode machine. Splitwise sends it layer by layer while the prompt is still computing, to hide the transfer [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=7).

4. The decode pool only ever decodes, so it can pack huge continuous batches and never stalls for a prompt.

5. Each pool scales on its own. DistServe searches for the best GPU split and parallelism per phase given the TTFT and TPOT targets [p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=10).

##### Worked example: DistServe's opening experiment

A 13B model on A100s, 512-token prompts, 64-token answers, with SLOs on both TTFT and TPOT. The metric is goodput: the highest request rate per GPU at which 90% of requests meet both SLOs [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=2).

##### Requests per second per GPU within SLO (↑ better)

both phases on one GPU

1.6

a GPU doing prefill only

5.6

a GPU doing decode only

10

2 prefill + 1 decode GPU

3.3

Two prefill GPUs (2 × 5.6 = 11.2) can feed one decode GPU (10 rps), so 3 GPUs serve 10 rps: 3.3 per GPU, 2.1× the colocated 1.6 [DistServe, Fig. 1, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=2).

##### What it costs

- A KV cache copy per request. With prefill and decode on the same node, DistServe measured transmission at under 0.1% of total latency for OPT-175B, and 95% of transfers under 30 ms, using intra-node NVLink [p. 11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=11). Across slower links it matters more.

- Small setups lose. With one or a few GPUs there is little to rebalance, and DistServe says a non-disaggregated system can be the better choice [p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=13). The Modular inference handbook reports 20–30% slowdowns on small or mistuned setups, and notes short or already-cached prompts are often faster prefilled locally.

- It is a latency tool, not a raw throughput tool. vLLM's docs say plainly: disaggregated prefill "DOES NOT improve throughput"; it lets you tune TTFT and tail ITL separately [vLLM docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_prefill.html).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Four ways to schedule the two phases, each with a cost

A real server has many users at once: some mid-answer (decoding), some just arrived (needing prefill). How a server interleaves them decides whether you get high throughput, smooth streaming, or both. Here are the four families, following Sarathi-Serve's taxonomy [Sarathi-Serve, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=2).

1. **Request-level batching** finishes a whole batch before starting new prompts. Streams stay smooth, but the batch shrinks as requests finish and newcomers queue, so throughput is poor [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=2).

2. **Iteration-level batching** (Orca) lets requests join and leave every step, and prefill-first schedulers run new prompts as soon as memory allows. Throughput jumps, but while a long prefill runs, every streaming user freezes. Sarathi-Serve calls this a **generation stall**, and measured stalls lasting several seconds in vLLM [Fig. 1, p. 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=1).

3. **Chunked prefill with stall-free batching** cuts each prompt into chunks and builds every step from all running decodes plus one chunk, up to a fixed token budget. Decodes never wait for a whole prefill [§4.2, p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=8).

4. **Disaggregation** runs prefill and decode on separate GPUs and ships the KV cache between them. No interference at all, and each pool can be sized and parallelised for its own job, at the price of more machines and a transfer [DistServe, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=4).

The How it works tab takes the last two apart, starting with the one principle that explains all four.

#### Which fix helps which phase

Put the two phases side by side and every common optimisation falls into place.

| Technique | Helps | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous batching | Decode | One weight read feeds many users' tokens |
| Weight quantization (8/4-bit) | Decode | Fewer bytes to read per token |
| KV cache, GQA, KV quantization, PagedAttention | Decode | Never recompute the past; shrink and pack the cache so bigger batches fit |
| Speculative decoding | Decode | A small draft model proposes several tokens; the big model checks them in one pass, raising tokens per weight read |
| FlashAttention | Prefill | Faster, memory-efficient attention for long prompts |
| Prefix caching | Prefill | Skip recomputing a shared prefix (system prompt, documents) |
| FP8 / INT8 compute (W8A8) | Prefill | Low-precision tensor cores do more maths per second |
| Tensor parallelism | Prefill (mostly) | Splits the maths across GPUs, cutting TTFT; costs communication |
| Chunked prefill | Both | Hides prompt work in decode's idle compute, no stalls |
| Disaggregation | Both | Separates them entirely; each pool tuned for its own metric |

And one formula ties the user's experience together. A request's total latency is TTFT plus TPOT for every token after the first [DistServe, footnote 1, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=2):

$$ {T_{\text{request}}} = {\text{TTFT}} + {\text{TPOT}}\cdot{(n_{\text{out}}-1)} \approx {1.47\ \text{s}} $$

- **what the user waits**: End-to-end latency for the full answer.

- **prefill**: Time to first token: queueing plus the prefill pass. About 34 ms ideal in our example.

- **decode, per token**: Time per output token. About 4.8 ms ideal for one user; more under a big batch or long context.

- **how many more tokens**: The answer length after the first token. 299 in our example, which is why decode dominates.

- **our request**: 34 ms + 4.8 ms × 299 ≈ 1.47 s. Halve TPOT and you save 0.7 s; halve TTFT and you save 17 ms.

#### How much do the fixes buy?

##### Serving capacity vs vLLM under latency SLOs (↑ better, × the baseline)

Sarathi-Serve · Mistral-7B, 1 A100

2.6×

Sarathi-Serve · Yi-34B, 2 A100s

3.7×

Sarathi-Serve · Falcon-180B, pipeline

5.6×

DistServe · OPT-66B code completion

5.7×

DistServe · OPT-66B summarization

4.3×

DistServe · OPT chatbot (13B–175B)

2.0–4.6×

Sarathi-Serve: capacity under P99 time-between-tokens SLOs [abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=1). DistServe: per-GPU request rate with 90% of requests meeting both TTFT and TPOT SLOs [p. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=10). Splitwise (cluster-level, simulated on production traces): 1.4× throughput at 20% lower cost, or 2.35× throughput at the same cost and power [abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=1).

##### Read these numbers fairly

- The baseline is 2023–24 vLLM, which then used prefill-first scheduling. Today's vLLM has chunked prefill on by default, so the gap against a current baseline is smaller.

- They measure capacity _under latency targets_, not raw tokens per second. With loose SLOs the gains shrink: Sarathi-Serve reports 3.5× under a strict 100 ms SLO (Mistral-7B) but 1.65× under a relaxed 1 s SLO (Yi-34B) [p. 12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02310#page=12).

- The two papers each compare against a system without the other's idea, so the bars aren't a head-to-head. DistServe's own comparison with DeepSpeed-MII (which does chunked prefill) shows 1.6–7.4× on the chatbot workload [p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=10).

##### Update · my check (28 Oct 2026)

Disaggregation moved from paper to default. NVIDIA says production platforms such as NVIDIA Dynamo use concepts that came from DistServe's lab ([NVIDIA blog](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ucsd-generative-ai-research-dgx-b200/)), and coverage of the authors' 2025 retrospective lists NVIDIA, llm-d, vLLM and Mooncake among adopters (secondary source, 36Kr). On Blackwell B200s, each GPU has about 180 GB and 8 TB/s, from NVIDIA's 8-GPU system figures, so the same arithmetic gives roughly 2.4× faster decode than an H100. Checked again on 7 Nov 2026: vLLM still labels its disaggregated prefill "experimental", and chunked prefill is on by default in vLLM V1 ([vLLM docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_prefill.html)).

#### Your LLM feels slow. Diagnose it.

1. **Measure TTFT and TPOT separately**, at P50 and P90/P99. One blended "latency" number hides which phase is the problem.

2. **High TTFT?** Look at prefill: long prompts, no prefix caching, prompts queued behind other work. Try prefix caching, chunked prefill, shorter prompts, or more tensor parallelism.

3. **High TPOT?** Look at decode: big model, long contexts, oversized batches. Try weight and KV quantization, speculative decoding, or a smaller model.

4. **Spiky TPOT** (fine on average, bad at P99)? Prefills are stalling decodes. Turn on chunked prefill and lower the token budget; at scale with strict SLOs, consider disaggregation.

5. **Low throughput while the GPU looks "busy"?** Probably memory-bound decode at small batch sizes. Batch more users (continuous batching) and free KV memory so the batch can grow.

#### What to keep, and where the simple story bends

**The lesson:** prefill reuses each weight read across thousands of tokens and is compute-bound; decode uses each read for one token per user and is memory-bound. Measure TTFT and TPOT separately, and pick fixes by phase.

##### Where it bends

- **The numbers here are ideal ceilings.** Real kernels reach maybe 60–80% of peak bandwidth or FLOPs, and there's scheduling and framework overhead. Use them for napkin estimates and for direction, not for SLAs.

- **Long contexts change decode.** At long contexts, KV cache reads, not weights, dominate each decode step (see the batching section). GQA, KV quantization and attention kernels matter more than weight quantization there.

- **Mixture-of-experts models** read only the active experts per token, which lowers bytes per token at batch 1. But at big batches, different users hit different experts, so more of the model gets read each step.

- **Short prompts are not compute-bound.** Below about 300 tokens on an H100, even prefill is limited by reading the weights (see the prefill section).

- **Disaggregation and chunking aren't rivals.** DistServe notes that when throughput matters more than strict latency, chunked prefill's fuller batches can be preferable [p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=13); at long contexts the KV transfer grows linearly while prefill maths grows faster, which keeps disaggregation attractive [p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.09670#page=13).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just buy a faster GPU" speeds up the wrong phase

The obvious move when generation is slow: get the newer chip with far more FLOPs. Splitwise (Microsoft) measured exactly this on production traces. Going from an A100 to an H100 buys **3.43× more compute** but only **1.64× more memory bandwidth** [Splitwise, Table I, p. 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=1). Look at what each phase got:

##### Llama-70B, coding traces, P50 latency · H100 time as a fraction of A100 time (lower = faster)

TTFT (prefill)

0.51×

TBT (decode)

0.70×

Prefill got about 2× faster. Decode got only about 1.4× faster, close to the bandwidth gain, nowhere near the compute gain. The conversation trace shows the same split (0.54× vs 0.70×) [Splitwise, Table IV, p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=5).

##### What breaks: you pay for maths decode can't use

Splitwise also capped H100 power from 700 W to 350 W per GPU. Prefill latency rose sharply, while decode latency barely moved [Fig. 9, p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=5). Their conclusion: token generation "does not need the compute capability of the latest GPUs and can be run with lower power and cost" [abstract](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=1). Decode is waiting on memory, so more FLOPs mostly sit idle.

## Say it

### Why does an LLM read your prompt fast but write its answer slowly?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why does batching raise throughput but not per-user speed?

In the memory-bound region a step takes about as long as reading the weights, whether it serves 1 user or 64. So total tokens per second grows almost linearly with batch size while each user's speed stays roughly flat. It stops when the KV caches fill memory or, with short contexts, when you reach the compute ridge. With long contexts, per-user speed does fall, because each user adds their own cache reads.

Follow-up 2 of 6

Estimate the max tokens per second for a model on one GPU.

For one user: bandwidth ÷ bytes of weights. Llama 3.1 8B in 16-bit is 16.1 GB; an H100 moves 3.35 TB/s, so about 209 tokens/s at best. In 4-bit it's about 4 GB, so roughly 830 tokens/s in theory, less in practice. Then add the KV cache term for long contexts and discount for real-world efficiency.

Follow-up 3 of 6

Does quantization speed up prefill?

Weight-only quantization (W4A16) mostly doesn't: prefill is compute-bound and the maths still runs in 16-bit after dequantizing. To speed up prefill you need low-precision compute, i.e. quantized activations too (W8A8 with SmoothQuant, or FP8).

Follow-up 4 of 6

Chunked prefill or disaggregation?

Chunked prefill first: it's a scheduler setting, works on one GPU, and removes stalls. Disaggregation pays off at scale with long prompts and strict TTFT and TPOT targets, where you can size the pools separately and have fast interconnects for the KV transfer. On small or mistuned setups it can be slower, and it doesn't raise raw throughput.

Follow-up 5 of 6

What does the KV cache cost, and how do you shrink it?

2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per token: 128 KiB per token for Llama 3.1 8B, so 0.26 GB for a 2,000-token prompt, per user. Shrink it with GQA or MQA (fewer KV heads), KV quantization (8 or 4 bits), paging to avoid fragmentation (PagedAttention), and eviction or windowing for very long contexts.

Follow-up 6 of 6

Why would someone put decode on older GPUs?

Decode doesn't use the compute, so the newest GPU's extra FLOPs are mostly wasted there. Splitwise found A100s could match or beat H100s on cost and energy for token generation and proposed H100 prefill with A100 decode (Splitwise-HA) [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.18677#page=5).

#### The 30-second answer

LLM inference has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one forward pass, so each weight read is reused across thousands of tokens and it's compute-bound; it sets time to first token. Decode generates one token per pass, so each pass reads all the weights and the KV cache for very little maths; it's memory-bandwidth-bound and sets time per output token. That's why batching and quantization help decode, why faster FLOPs help prefill, and why mixing the two on one GPU needs chunked prefill or disaggregation.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Start with the symptom: the first word is fast, the rest streams. Explain prefill vs decode and the KV cache that links them. Then the roofline: an H100 does about 295 FLOPs per byte of bandwidth; prefill of a 2,000-token prompt does about 2,000 FLOPs per byte, decode for one user about 1. Napkin numbers for an 8B model in 16-bit: 16 GB of weights ÷ 3.35 TB/s ≈ 4.8 ms per token, about 200 tokens/s per user at best. Fixes by phase: batching and quantization for decode; prefix caching and FP8 for prefill. Then the collision: prefill-first scheduling causes generation stalls; chunked prefill (Sarathi-Serve, on by default in vLLM V1) packs decodes plus a prompt chunk into each step; disaggregation (Splitwise, DistServe) splits the phases across GPU pools for goodput under SLOs. Close with the limit: the KV cache grows with context and batch, so at long contexts it, not the weights, dominates decode.

#### What not to say

- "Decode is slow because attention is quadratic." For a single new token, attention is linear in context; the problem is reading weights and cache.

- "Bigger batches make each user faster." They raise total throughput; per-user speed stays flat or drops.

- "Disaggregation increases throughput." It improves goodput under latency SLOs; vLLM's docs say it does not improve raw throughput.

- "An H100 is 3× faster for LLMs than an A100." For decode, the gain tracks bandwidth (about 1.6×), not FLOPs.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Splitwise, DistServe, Sarathi-Serve, AWQ, the vLLM docs and NVIDIA's H100 specs · checked 28 Oct 2026 · updated 29 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| **Prefill** | The pass that processes the whole prompt in parallel, builds the KV cache and produces the first token. |
|---|---|
| **Decode** | Generating the answer one token per forward pass, reading the KV cache. |
| **TTFT** | Time to first token: queueing + prefill. |
| **TPOT / ITL / TBT** | Time per output token, inter-token latency, time between tokens: the streaming gap. |
| **KV cache** | Saved keys and values for every past token in every layer, so attention never recomputes them. |
| **Arithmetic intensity** | FLOPs done per byte read from memory. |
| **Ridge point** | Peak FLOPs ÷ peak bandwidth (≈ 295 on an H100). Below it you're memory-bound; above it, compute-bound. |
| **Continuous batching** | Requests join and leave the running batch every iteration (Orca's iteration-level scheduling). |
| **Generation stall** | Streaming users freezing while a long prefill runs on the same GPU. |
| **Chunked prefill** | Splitting a prompt into chunks that share each step with running decodes, under a token budget. |
| **Disaggregation** | Prefill and decode on separate GPU pools, with the KV cache transferred between them. |
| **Goodput** | Requests per second (per GPU) served while meeting the latency SLOs. |

#### Each fix has its own lesson

- KV Cache Management and PagedAttention: how the cache for many users is stored without waste.

- Continuous Batching and Scheduling: the scheduler behind "batching decode", step by step.

- Prefix and Prompt Caching: skipping prefill for repeated prompts.

- Speculative Decoding: several tokens per memory-bound decode step.

- Serving Metrics and SLOs: TTFT, TPOT and goodput under real load.

- Scaling Inference and Sizing and Cost: disaggregation at cluster scale, GPU counts and cost per token.

# LLM Quantization

> How does an LLM survive losing 75% of its bits?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/llm-quantization/
- Before this: Prefill vs Decode (`ai-engineering/prefill-vs-decode`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're serving Llama 3.1 70B on 80 GB H100s. In 16-bit, it's 141 GB of weights, which is two GPUs before you've served anyone. A colleague suggests storing every weight in 4 bits. The interviewer asks:

> How does an LLM survive losing 75% of its bits?

**Running examples:** serving Llama 3.1 70B on 80 GB H100s, and 32 real consecutive weights from one row of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (layer 12, MLP down-projection), including one big outlier. Perplexity numbers are WikiText-2 (lower is better) unless stated.

#### An LLM is mostly numbers you have to store and move

A 70B model in 16-bit is 141 GB of weights before you've served a single user. That's two H100s just to hold it. And every decode step reads every weight from memory, so the bytes also set your speed limit (see Prefill vs Decode). Fewer bits per weight attacks both problems at once.

GB = parameters × bits ÷ 8 (8.03 B, 70.6 B, 405.9 B parameters). Weights only: 4-bit formats add a little for per-group scales (about 0.25–0.5 bits per weight), and you still need memory for the KV cache and activations.

Speed follows the bytes, but not perfectly. One precision step down (16 → 8 bits) is typically 30–50% faster in practice, not 2× (Inference Engineering, P. Kiely, ch. 5.1). The papers report bigger wins against slow baselines: GPTQ's 3-bit OPT-175B generates about 3.25× faster than FP16 on A100s and about 4.5× on A6000s [GPTQ, p. 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=1); AWQ's 4-bit kernels average 3.2–3.3× over Hugging Face FP16 [AWQ, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2).

The catch is quality. Round every weight carelessly and a large model can fall apart. The rest of this page is about why, and the three ideas that fix it.

### The idea

Think of a ruler with only 16 marks. One huge value forces the marks far apart, and everything small rounds to zero. Give each small group of numbers its own ruler, and a big value only hurts its own group. Every method is a choice about where the rounding error lands.

[Figure: Top: one scale for all weights. A big outlier stretches the grid, so the small weights all round to zero. Bottom: small groups get their own fine grid, so only the outlier's group is coarse.]

_Illustrative. The lab uses 32 real weights from Qwen2.5-0.5B, including one big outlier._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Go from 1 scale per 32 weights down to 1 per 4. Watch the error, the weights crushed to 0 and the extra storage.

#### An outlier should only stretch its own neighbourhood

With one scale per row, a single big weight sets Δ for thousands of small ones. Give every group of, say, 128 weights its own scale, and the damage stays local. The cost is storing more scales.

The same 32 weights at 3 bits, symmetric grid. Dashed lines mark group boundaries. Extra storage assumes one 16-bit scale per group. Real models use groups of 128: about 0.125 extra bits per weight, or about 0.25 with a zero-point too (GPTQ quotes ≈ 0.15).

The papers agree it's the cheapest big win. For 3-bit OPT-175B, GPTQ found group size 1,024 (about 0.02 extra bits) improves perplexity by about 0.2, and group size 128 (about 0.15 extra bits) by about another 0.1, ending only 0.1–0.3 off full precision [GPTQ, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7). AWQ calls RTN "actually quite strong when using a small group size like 128" and uses g128 throughout [AWQ, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=7).

##### In hardware: block-scaled formats

New GPUs build groups into the number format. MXFP4 shares one scale per 32 values. NVIDIA's NVFP4 shares one per 16, and adds a second, per-tensor scale [NVIDIA blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference):

$$ {x} = {x_{\text{e2m1}}}\cdot{s_{\text{block}}}\cdot{s_{\text{global}}} \qquad {\approx 4.5\ \text{bits/value}} $$

From NVIDIA's [Transformer Engine NVFP4 docs](https://nvidia.github.io/TransformerEngine/features/low_precision_training/nvfp4/nvfp4.html) and the NVFP4 blog · hover any symbol.

- **the real value**: The number the model actually uses.

- **4-bit float**: Stored as E2M1: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa bit. Only values like 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 (and negatives) are possible.

- **block scale**: One per 16 values, stored in FP8 (E4M3), so it can be a non-power-of-two. MXFP4 uses one per 32, restricted to powers of two (E8M0), which wastes precision.

- **tensor scale**: One FP32 scale for the whole tensor, so the block scales fit FP8 range: global max ÷ (448 × 6).

- **cost**: About 4.5 bits per value: 4 bits plus an 8-bit scale shared by 16 values.

**Now say why:** if smaller groups cut the error, why don't real models use a scale for every 4 weights?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Quantization stores each number in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16, so the model fits on fewer GPUs and decode moves fewer bytes per token. Rounding always makes errors. The real methods differ in **where those errors land**: spread across small groups, steered away from the 1% of channels that matter (AWQ), cancelled by adjusting the remaining weights (GPTQ), or moved from hard-to-quantize activations into easy weights (SmoothQuant). What you'll be able to do after this: size a quantized deployment on a napkin, explain why plain rounding breaks large models, read the GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant equations, and choose a format for a given bottleneck.

#### Quantizing = snapping numbers onto a grid

Pick a scale (the spacing between grid levels), divide each number by it, round to the nearest integer, and store the integer. To use it, multiply back by the scale. With N bits you get 2N levels, so 4 bits gives just 16.

$$ {\bar{X}} = {\big\lceil}\, {X} / {\Delta} \,{\big\rfloor}, \qquad {\Delta} = {\max(|X|)} \,/\, {(2^{N-1}-1)} $$

SmoothQuant's Eq. 1 (symmetric INT-N quantization) [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=2). Asymmetric quantization adds a zero-point so the grid can sit off-centre · hover any symbol.

- **stored integer**: What actually gets saved: an INT8 (or INT4) number.

- **original value**: The 16-bit weight or activation you want to compress.

- **round**: Snap to the nearest integer. This is where the error comes from, at most half a step.

- **step size**: The scale Δ: the gap between neighbouring levels. One Δ is shared by a whole group of numbers.

- **the biggest value**: Δ is set so the largest magnitude in the group lands on the top level. One outlier stretches the grid for everybody else.

- **levels per side**: 127 for INT8, 7 for INT4 (symmetric around zero).

##### Try it on 32 real weights

● original ● after rounding ● a non-zero weight rounded to exactly 0. One scale for all 32 (per-tensor style). The −0.44 weight is about 10× the typical size here, so it sets Δ for everyone.

Three more terms you'll need. **Granularity** is how many numbers share one scale: one per tensor, per row or channel, per token (for activations), or per small **group** such as 128 weights. **Weight-only** schemes (written W4A16: 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations) shrink memory and speed up decode. **Weight-and-activation** schemes (W8A8, FP8) also let the tensor cores do low-precision maths, which speeds up compute-bound prefill [AWQ, §2, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2).

**Go deeper: why small errors matter**

Errors compound. π rounded to 3.14 is off by 0.05%, but cube it and you're off by 0.15%. Round π to 3 and π³ comes out as 27 instead of 31. An LLM stacks dozens of layers and thousands of tokens on top of every rounding error (example from Inference Engineering, ch. 5.1).

#### You can't avoid rounding error. You choose where it lands.

Every method below accepts that 4 or 8 bits will make mistakes, and differs only in where those mistakes are allowed to go. Each idea maps to one method, in this tab or the Play lab:

| Idea | What it does with the error | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **Confine it** | Give each small group its own scale, so an outlier only hurts its own group | group-wise, MX / NVFP4 |
| **Isolate it** | Keep the few outlier features in 16-bit | LLM.int8() |
| **Steer it** | Make the important channels' relative error smaller | AWQ |
| **Cancel it** | Adjust not-yet-rounded weights to undo the error already made | GPTQ |
| **Move it** | Shift outliers from activations (hard) into weights (easy) | SmoothQuant |

#### Past ~6.7B parameters, a few channels go huge, everywhere

Groups fix outliers in _weights_. Activations have a worse problem, discovered by LLM.int8(): in big models a handful of hidden dimensions carry values up to 20× larger than the rest, in nearly every layer and token [LLM.int8(), p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=2).

1. Each bar is one input channel of a layer's activations, for one token (illustrative, shaped after the papers).

2. A few channels are tens of times bigger than the rest. In real OPT layers SmoothQuant measured outliers "∼100× larger than most of the activation values" [p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=3).

3. They sit in the **same channels for every token**. At 6.7B, about 150,000 outliers per sequence are concentrated in just 6 hidden dimensions [LLM.int8(), p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=2).

4. With one INT8 scale per token, the outliers set Δ and the normal channels get only 2–3 effective levels [SmoothQuant, p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=3). Yet zeroing those few dimensions raises perplexity by 600–1,000% [LLM.int8(), p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=2): they matter.

**LLM.int8()'s fix:** split each matrix multiply. Any feature dimension with a value above 6.0 runs in 16-bit; the other 99.9% run in INT8. Since outlier dimensions are at most 7 for models up to 13B, this costs about 0.1% extra memory [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=5). It preserved 16-bit accuracy all the way to 175B.

##### What it costs: speed

Mixed-precision decomposition is awkward for GPU kernels. LLM.int8() slows inference for models below 6.7B parameters [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=6), and SmoothQuant measured it "almost always slower than the FP16 baseline" [SmoothQuant, p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=8). It's a memory tool, not a speed tool. AWQ and SmoothQuant both set out to protect outliers _without_ mixed precision.

#### Protect the 1% of weights that see the big activations

AWQ (MIT, MLSys 2024 best paper) starts from an experiment. Quantize OPT to 3 bits with g128, but keep 1% of the weight channels in FP16. Which 1%? If you choose by **weight size**, almost nothing improves. If you choose the channels whose **activations** are largest, perplexity nearly recovers. Importance lives in the inputs, not the weights [AWQ, Table 1, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=4).

##### OPT-6.7B, INT3 g128, keep 1% of channels in FP16 · perplexity (↓ better)

FP16 (no quantization)

10.86

RTN, nothing kept

23.54

keep 1%, chosen at random

24.23

keep 1%, biggest weights

22.37

keep 1%, biggest activations

11.39

The same pattern holds on OPT-1.3B and 13B, and with only 0.1% kept (OPT-6.7B: 11.58) [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=4).

But keeping FP16 channels brings back the mixed-precision problem. AWQ's trick: **scale the important channels up before rounding**, and scale their activations down by the same factor. The maths is unchanged, but those weights now span more grid levels, so their relative error shrinks.

$$ {\text{Err}\big(Q(w\cdot s)\,(x/s)\big)} = {\Delta'}\cdot{\text{RoundErr}(ws/\Delta')}\cdot{x}\cdot{1/s} $$

AWQ Eq. 3; the ratio of new to old error is (Δ′/Δ)·(1/s) [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=4) · hover any symbol.

- **error after scaling**: The output error for one weight w after multiplying it by s and dividing its input x by s.

- **new step size**: Δ′: the group scale after w is multiplied by s. Scaling one weight rarely changes the group max, so Δ′ ≈ Δ.

- **rounding error**: Still about 0.25 of a step on average, whatever s is: rounding error is roughly uniform.

- **the activation**: FP16, so no error of its own. Big x means this weight matters, which is why AWQ picks channels by activation size.

- **the payoff**: Divided by s. With s greater than 1 and Δ′ ≈ Δ, the error on this channel shrinks to about 1/s of what it was.

##### Try it: how hard should you scale?

Real measurements, not a simulation: OPT-6.7B, 1% salient channels scaled by s, INT3 g128 [AWQ, Table 2, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=4). Bigger s protects the salient channels more, but past s = 2 it starts growing Δ for the other weights in their groups, and perplexity gets worse again.

So AWQ searches for s per layer, on a small calibration set, to minimise the layer's output error:

$$ {s^{*}} = \arg\min_{s}\big\|{Q(W\,\mathrm{diag}(s))}\,{(\mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1}X)} - {WX}\big\|, \qquad {s = s_X^{\,\alpha}} $$

AWQ Eqs. 4–5 [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=5); grid of 20 for α [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=7).

- **best scales**: One scale per input channel, chosen per layer.

- **quantized, scaled weights**: Scale the weight columns by s, then quantize (e.g. INT4, g128).

- **inputs, scaled down**: Divide the calibration activations by s. This division gets fused into the previous layer, so it costs nothing at runtime.

- **original output**: The full-precision layer output to match.

- **search space**: s is just the average activation size per channel raised to α. A 20-point grid search over α in [0, 1] picks it. No gradients, no reconstruction.

##### Why practitioners like it

AWQ only measures average activation size per channel, so it needs little calibration data and is less prone to overfitting it than reconstruction methods like GPTQ [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=5). In the paper's tests it matched the 1%-FP16 mixed-precision result while staying all-INT3 (OPT-6.7B: 11.39 both) [Table 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=4).

#### Round one column, then fix up the rest to compensate

GPTQ (IST Austria / ETH, ICLR 2023) doesn't try to make each weight accurate. It tries to make each layer's **output** accurate on real inputs. Rounding a weight creates an error; if inputs are correlated, nudging the not-yet-rounded weights can cancel most of it.

$$ {\arg\min_{\widehat{W}}}\ {\big\|}{WX} - {\widehat{W}X}{\big\|_2^2} $$

GPTQ Eq. 1 [p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=3); calibration data [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=6).

- **find quantized weights**: Search over weight matrices that sit on the quantization grid.

- **original output**: The layer applied to X: a small calibration set of real inputs (128 random 2,048-token C4 segments).

- **quantized output**: The same inputs through the quantized weights.

- **squared error**: Minimise the difference in outputs, not in weights. This is the key shift from RTN.

The update rule comes from Optimal Brain Quantization, which GPTQ inherits. After rounding weight q, shift all remaining weights F by:

$$ {\delta_F} = -\,{\big(w_q-\mathrm{quant}(w_q)\big)}\,/\,{[H_F^{-1}]_{qq}}\cdot{(H_F^{-1})_{:,q}} $$

GPTQ Eq. 2, with HF = 2XFXF⊤ [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=4).

- **the correction**: How much to move every still-unquantized weight in this row.

- **error just made**: The rounding error on weight q.

- **normaliser**: The diagonal entry of the inverse Hessian for weight q.

- **who can help**: Column q of the inverse Hessian, where H = 2XXᵀ. It encodes how the inputs correlate, so it says which other weights can absorb the error.

##### Try it: two weights, one correction

Illustrative toy: y = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ with weights 0.08 and −0.13, grid step 0.25, unit-variance inputs. GPTQ rounds w₁, then moves w₂ by ρ × w₁'s error (what Eq. 2 gives for two inputs), then rounds w₂. Output error = expected squared error of y. With uncorrelated inputs there's nothing to exploit and both match.

Three engineering changes made this scale from 100M-parameter models to 175B [p. 4–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=4):

1. A layer's weight matrix. The original method (OBQ) quantized weights one at a time in a greedy order, per row: cubic cost, hours for a 25M-parameter ResNet.

2. **Arbitrary order:** quantize columns left to right in the same order for every row. The greedy order barely helps on big layers, and now the inverse Hessian is shared by all rows, so it's updated once per column instead of once per weight.

3. **Lazy batch updates:** work on 128 columns at a time and keep the corrections inside the block. This turns memory-bound updates into compute-friendly ones, an order-of-magnitude speedup.

4. After each block, apply all its corrections to the remaining columns in one big matrix multiply.

5. **Cholesky reformulation:** precompute the needed rows of H⁻¹ with a stable Cholesky decomposition, plus dampening (1% of the mean diagonal added to H). Without it, large models hit numerical blow-ups.

The result: OPT-175B quantized on one A100 in about 4.2 hours [Table 2, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7), losing only 0.03 perplexity at 4 bits (8.34 → 8.37) where RTN lost 2.2 (→ 10.54) [Table 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7).

##### Where it bends

Because GPTQ fits each layer to the calibration data, the AWQ authors argue it "may overfit the calibration set", hurting out-of-distribution domains, and that it needs a reordering trick for some models (LLaMA-7B, OPT-66B) [AWQ, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2). On LLaMA-7B at 3 bits, plain GPTQ scored 8.81 versus RTN's 7.01; GPTQ with reordering scored 6.53 [AWQ, Table 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=7).

#### Push the outliers from activations into the weights

Weight-only quantization saves memory, but the maths still runs in 16-bit. To use fast INT8 tensor cores you must quantize activations too (W8A8), and activation outliers break that. Per-channel activation scales would fix it, but INT8 matrix kernels can only apply scales along the outer dimensions (tokens, output channels), not the input channels [SmoothQuant, p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=3). SmoothQuant's answer: divide each activation channel by a factor and multiply the matching weight row by the same factor. The product is identical.

$$ {Y} = {\big(X\,\mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1}\big)}\cdot{\big(\mathrm{diag}(s)\,W\big)}, \qquad {s_j} = \max(|X_j|)^{{\alpha}} \,/\, \max(|W_j|)^{1-\alpha} $$

SmoothQuant Eqs. 3–4 [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=4); α values [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=5), [Table 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=7).

- **same output**: The layer output does not change at all.

- **smoothed activations**: Each input channel divided by s_j. Outlier channels shrink. The division is folded into the previous layer norm or linear layer, offline.

- **adjusted weights**: Each matching weight row multiplied by s_j. Weights were flat and easy, so they can absorb some spread.

- **the smoothing factor**: Balances the two: activation max to the power α over weight max to the power 1 − α.

- **migration strength**: α = 0.5 splits the difficulty evenly and works for all OPT and BLOOM models; GLM-130B needed 0.75, and the Llama-2 runs used 0.85–0.9.

##### Try it: slide α

–

Illustrative channels shaped after SmoothQuant §3 (a few fixed channels ≈ 100× larger). Lower peak ÷ median means fewer grid levels wasted on outliers. The paper found 0.4–0.6 is the sweet spot on OPT-175B [p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=8).

##### OPT-175B, INT8 weights and activations · average zero-shot accuracy (↑ better)

FP16 (original)

66.9%

W8A8, naive

35.5%

ZeroQuant

35.8%

LLM.int8() (FP16 outliers, slow)

66.7%

SmoothQuant-O3 (fastest setting)

66.8%

SmoothQuant Table 3. Measured speed: up to 1.56× faster with about half the memory in FasterTransformer, and up to 1.42× faster per decoding token [p. 8, Table 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=8). On LLaMA it was nearly lossless, e.g. 7B: 11.51 → 11.56 perplexity [Table 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=7).

## In practice

### In practice

#### The map: what gets quantized, and how cleverly

1. **Weight-only** post-training quantization keeps activations in 16-bit and compresses only the weights, usually to 4 bits. It's the standard for memory-bound decode and local inference. RTN with small groups is a strong baseline; GPTQ and AWQ are the two famous smart methods [AWQ, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2).

2. **Weight and activation** quantization (W8A8) unlocks INT8 or FP8 matrix maths. Activations are much harder to quantize than weights because of outliers, which is what LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant tackle [SmoothQuant, p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=3).

3. **Block-scaled formats** move the "one scale per small group" idea into the hardware, so each block of 16 or 32 values gets its own scale for free.

4. **Quantization-aware training** lets the model learn around the rounding. OpenAI post-trained gpt-oss's mixture-of-experts weights in MXFP4 (about 4.25 bits per parameter), which is how the 117B model fits on a single 80 GB GPU (gpt-oss model card).

#### Shipping a quantized model

1. **Pick precision from your bottleneck.** Out of memory or slow decode → weight-only 4-bit (AWQ or GPTQ). Compute-bound prefill or big batches → FP8 or INT8 weights and activations. On Hopper and later, FP8 is the usual first try.

2. **Choose what to quantize.** Start with linear-layer weights. Add activations and the KV cache only if you need them. Keep attention maths, and often embeddings and the output head, in 16-bit.

3. **Use small groups, never one scale per tensor**: g128 for INT4, or block-scaled formats (MXFP8, NVFP4).

4. **Calibrate with a smart method** on a few hundred samples that look like your traffic: AWQ or GPTQ for low-bit weights, SmoothQuant for W8A8.

5. **Measure against the original**: perplexity first, then benchmarks, then your own task evals. The bar is "difference indistinguishable from run-to-run noise".

6. **Back off where it hurts.** FP8 instead of FP4, fewer quantized components, or keep sensitive layers in 16-bit.

##### What's safe to quantize

| Component | Risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Linear-layer weights | low | The bulk of the model; flat distributions; well-studied methods |
| Activations | some | Outlier channels (see the outlier features section); needs smoothing or FP8 |
| KV cache | moderate | Big win for long contexts, but errors carry into every later token |
| Attention softmax | high | Sensitive to range; errors compound across thousands of tokens. Usually kept high-precision. |

Sensitivity ordering from Inference Engineering, ch. 5.1; SmoothQuant also keeps softmax, LayerNorm and other element-wise ops in FP16 [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10438#page=5).

##### Formats at a glance

| Format | What it is | Where it fits |
|---|---|---|
| BF16 / FP16 | 16-bit float | The baseline |
| FP8 (E4M3) | 1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits; wide dynamic range | Hopper and later: weights, activations, KV cache |
| INT8 (W8A8) | Integer with a scale, uniform levels | With smoothing (SmoothQuant); less range than FP8 |
| INT4 (W4A16) | 4-bit integer weights, g128 scales, 16-bit activations | GPTQ / AWQ checkpoints; memory-bound serving |
| MXFP4 / NVFP4 | 4-bit float, one scale per 32 (MX) or 16 values (NV) + global scale | Blackwell; gpt-oss ships MoE weights in MXFP4 |
| GGUF k-quants | File format with mixed per-layer precision | Laptops and edge (llama.cpp) |

Why float beats int at the same bits: the exponent spaces levels densely near zero and sparsely far out, which suits bell-shaped weights with a few outliers.

#### RTN vs GPTQ vs AWQ, same setup

Perplexity added on top of FP16 (↓ better); the label shows the absolute perplexity (FP16: 5.47, 4.88, 3.32). AWQ paper, Table 4, WikiText-2 [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=7).

##### Read these numbers fairly

- This table comes from the AWQ paper, so the comparison was set up by AWQ's authors. GPTQ's own paper reports on OPT and BLOOM, where it beats RTN by much larger margins because it compares per-row RTN without groups.

- At 4 bits with g128, all three are within about 0.1 perplexity on Llama-2: grouping did most of the work. The method matters mostly at 3 bits and below.

- Perplexity can hide task-specific damage. An INT8 model can pass a perplexity check and still fail a coding task if calibration data doesn't match the workload ([interview guide](https://www.techinterview.org/post/3233477292/gptq-awq-fp8-llm-inference-interview/)). Always evaluate on your own tasks.

- Bigger models are easier to quantize. GPTQ: "larger models generally (with the exception of OPT-66B) appear easier to quantize" [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7).

##### Update · my check (28 Oct 2026)

The field moved toward low-precision _formats_ and training. NVIDIA's NVFP4 (Blackwell) uses 16-value blocks with FP8 scales plus a per-tensor FP32 scale, about 4.5 bits per value ([NVIDIA blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference)). OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b (117B total, 5.1B active parameters) was post-trained with MXFP4 MoE weights at about 4.25 bits per parameter so it fits one 80 GB GPU (model card). AWQ and GPTQ checkpoints remain the common open-weight 4-bit formats served by vLLM, TensorRT-LLM and others [AWQ, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00978#page=2).

#### Pick by bottleneck

| Situation | Start with |
|---|---|
| Model doesn't fit, decode-heavy chat, small batches | INT4 weight-only (AWQ or GPTQ, g128) |
| Hopper/Blackwell datacenter serving, big batches | FP8 weights + activations (+ FP8 KV cache) |
| INT8 hardware, need faster prefill | SmoothQuant W8A8 |
| Long contexts eating memory | KV-cache quantization (FP8 / INT8), then check quality |
| Laptop, CPU or Apple Silicon | GGUF k-quants (llama.cpp) |
| Blackwell, maximum throughput | NVFP4 / MXFP4, ideally from a model trained or calibrated for it |

#### What to keep, and what to watch

**The lesson:** quantization is a dial, not a switch. Weights are easy, activations are hard, and the whole game is controlling where the rounding error goes: confine it with groups, steer it with AWQ, cancel it with GPTQ, move it with SmoothQuant.

##### Great for

- Fitting a big model on fewer GPUs or a laptop

- Faster decode at small batch sizes (memory-bound)

- Freeing memory for KV cache → bigger batches, longer contexts

- Large models: each weight matters less

##### Watch out

- Small models are fragile: each weight carries more of the load

- 3 bits and below: quality drops fast, even with GPTQ/AWQ

- Calibration data that doesn't match your domain

- Speedups need real low-bit kernels; a smaller file alone isn't speed

- W4A16 barely speeds up compute-bound prefill

Author-stated limits: LLM.int8() is slower than FP16 below 6.7B; GPTQ needs reordering for some models; SmoothQuant needs a per-model α. The "small models are fragile" and "kernels matter" points are my synthesis of the tables above.

#### What changed since these methods, and what to evaluate

##### Four additions

- **FP8 is the safe default on modern GPUs.** A study of over 500,000 evaluations on the Llama 3.1 family found FP8 weights and activations (W8A8-FP) essentially lossless, INT8 W8A8 within about 1–3% per task, and 4-bit weight-only (W4A16) on par with INT8 W8A8; W4A16 suited low-batch serving best, W8A8 high-throughput serving [Kurtic et al., ACL 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02355).

- **Rotations make 4-bit activations possible.** Multiplying weights and activations by orthogonal (Hadamard) rotations spreads outliers across channels without changing the model's output. QuaRot quantized weights, activations and the KV cache to 4 bits; Llama 2 70B lost at most 0.47 WikiText-2 perplexity and kept 99% of zero-shot accuracy [Ashkboos et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00456). SpinQuant learns the rotations, narrowing the W4A4KV4 gap on Llama 2 7B to 2.9 points [Liu et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16406).

- **Quantize the KV cache too.** At high concurrency the KV cache, not the weights, limits batch size; an FP8 KV cache halves it. See Scaling Inference for why FP8 weights alone may not reduce GPU count.

- **Evaluate on tasks, not just perplexity.** Perplexity can hide drops on reasoning, maths, code and long-context tasks; check your own task metrics before and after quantizing.

Since prefill and decode want different formats, a 2026 paper from NVIDIA and ISTA proposes quantizing them differently, with low-precision maths for prefill and compact weights for decode. It's early research, but it fits the phase split in Prefill vs Decode.

### The answer that sounds right

#### Round-to-nearest works… until it falls off a cliff

The obvious method is **RTN**: pick a scale per row and round every weight to the nearest level. GPTQ's authors ran exactly that, with one scale per row, on the whole OPT family. At 4 bits it mostly survives. At 3 bits it collapses at every size. Drag through the model sizes:

–

OPT models, WikiText-2 perplexity, per-row asymmetric grid, no grouping. Bars are on a log scale capped at 100 [GPTQ, Table 3, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7).

##### What breaks: outliers

At 175B, 4-bit RTN loses 2.2 perplexity points, "performing worse than the 10× smaller full-precision 13B model", and at 3 bits it "collapses completely" [GPTQ, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.17323#page=7). The cause is the same thing you saw with the −0.44 weight above, at scale: a few huge values stretch the grid, and everything small gets rounded into a handful of levels or to zero.

## Say it

### How does an LLM survive losing 75% of its bits?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 6

Why does 4-bit weight-only quantization speed up decode but not prefill?

Decode reads every weight for a few tokens, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound: 4× fewer bytes directly helps. Prefill does thousands of FLOPs per byte, so it's compute-bound, and W4A16 dequantizes back to 16-bit before the maths. To speed up prefill you need low-precision compute: W8A8 (SmoothQuant) or FP8.

Follow-up 2 of 6

Symmetric vs asymmetric quantization?

Symmetric centres the grid on zero: Δ = max|w| ÷ (2b−1 − 1), no zero-point, simpler kernels. Asymmetric adds a zero-point so the grid covers [min, max] exactly, which helps one-sided distributions (e.g. after ReLU). LLM.int8() found outliers are mostly one-sided, which is why zero-point quantization did better before decomposition [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.07339#page=9).

Follow-up 3 of 6

GPTQ or AWQ?

Both give good 4-bit weight-only models. AWQ needs less calibration data and generalises better across domains because it only uses activation statistics; GPTQ reconstructs each layer's output and can overfit the calibration set but is very strong at 3 bits on big models. At 4-bit g128 on Llama-2 they're within about 0.1 perplexity, so pick by tooling and kernel support.

Follow-up 4 of 6

Your INT8 model passes perplexity but fails a coding task. What happened?

Perplexity is an average that hides task-specific regressions. Likely the calibration set didn't look like code, so the wrong channels were protected or the scales were off. Re-calibrate on representative data and evaluate on the downstream task.

Follow-up 5 of 6

Why are activations harder to quantize than weights?

Weights are flat and bell-shaped. Activations have outlier channels about 100× larger than the rest, in fixed channels for every token, emerging around 6.7B parameters. Per-channel activation scales would fix it but don't fit INT8 GEMM kernels, hence LLM.int8()'s decomposition or SmoothQuant's migration.

Follow-up 6 of 6

Would you quantize the KV cache?

For long contexts, yes: it can be bigger than the weights. FP8 KV cache is common and usually safe; INT4 KV has a small but measurable loss. Errors carry into every later token, so test on long-context tasks.

#### The 30-second answer

Quantization stores weights, and sometimes activations, in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16. It cuts memory and speeds up memory-bound decode. The hard part is outliers: a few huge values stretch the grid so small values lose precision. Groups confine them, AWQ protects the channels with big activations by scaling them, GPTQ cancels rounding error using second-order information from calibration data, and SmoothQuant moves activation outliers into weights so INT8 maths works. Then you verify on your own evals, not just perplexity.

**Go further**

#### The 2-minute walkthrough

Size first: 70B in BF16 is 141 GB, two H100s; in 4-bit about 35 GB, one. Then the grid: Δ = max ÷ (2N−1 − 1), and why one outlier wrecks it. RTN's cliff on OPT at 3 bits. Fixes: g128 groups (cheap, ~0.15–0.25 bits); outlier features above 6.7B (LLM.int8 isolates them, but it's slow); AWQ, which keeps the 1% of weights fed by large activations safe by scaling, chosen by a grid search over α; GPTQ, which quantizes columns and pushes each error onto the remaining columns via the inverse Hessian, in 4 GPU-hours for 175B; SmoothQuant for W8A8 via sj = max|X|α ÷ max|W|1−α. Close with the decision: weight-only 4-bit for memory-bound decode, FP8 or W8A8 for compute, block-scaled FP4 on Blackwell, and always check task evals.

#### What not to say

- "4-bit is 4× faster." Speed depends on kernels and on whether you're memory- or compute-bound; one step down is often 30–50% faster.

- "Quantization doesn't hurt quality." At 4-bit g128 on big models it's small; at 3 bits, on small models or on activations without smoothing, it can be severe.

- "Pick important weights by their magnitude." AWQ showed that magnitude is about as good as random; activations tell you importance.

- "Perplexity looked fine, so we shipped." Evaluate on your tasks.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant and LLM.int8() (read in full), NVIDIA's NVFP4 docs and the gpt-oss model card · checked 7 Nov 2026 · updated 29 Oct 2026

#### Glossary

| **Scale (Δ)** | Spacing between quantization levels; one per tensor, channel, token or group. |
|---|---|
| **Zero-point** | Offset that lets an asymmetric grid sit off-centre. |
| **RTN** | Round-to-nearest: the plain baseline. |
| **Group size (g128)** | How many weights share one scale. |
| **W4A16 / W8A8** | Bits for weights / activations. |
| **PTQ / QAT** | Post-training quantization (no retraining) / quantization-aware training. |
| **Calibration set** | A few hundred real inputs used to pick scales or corrections. |
| **Outlier features** | A few hidden dimensions with huge values in every token, from about 6.7B parameters up. |
| **Salient channels** | Weight channels that multiply large activations; AWQ protects them. |
| **Hessian (H = 2XXᵀ)** | Captures how layer inputs correlate; GPTQ uses its inverse to spread corrections. |
| **Migration strength (α)** | SmoothQuant's dial for how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. |
| **Perplexity** | How surprised the model is by real text; lower is better; sensitive to quantization damage. |
