# KV Cache Management and PagedAttention

> Why did naive serving waste most of its KV memory, and how do blocks fix it?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/kv-cache-and-pagedattention/
- Before this: Prefill vs Decode (`ai-engineering/prefill-vs-decode`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

You serve the 8B assistant on 80 GB GPUs, with about 64 GiB left for the KV cache. A request may stop after 10 tokens or after 2,000, so a colleague reserves the maximum for everyone. Batches stay small and memory looks full. The interviewer asks:

> Why did naive serving waste most of its KV memory, and how do blocks fix it?

**Running example (this track):** the food-delivery app serves its 8B support assistant (Llama 3 8B shape, 128 KiB of KV per token) on 80 GB GPUs, leaving about 64 GiB for the KV cache. Prompts are 200–1,500 tokens; most answers are short, a few are long.

#### Unknown lengths, growing caches

The number of requests that can decode together is limited by KV memory, and decode throughput grows with batch size. But a request's final length is unknown when it starts: it may stop after 10 tokens or after 2,000. Reserve too little and it can't finish; reserve the maximum and memory fills with empty space, so batches stay small.

### The idea

Think of giving every customer a full blank notebook in case they write a lot. Most write one page, and the cupboard fills with empty paper. Instead, keep a shared stack of loose pages, hand one over when needed and keep an index of whose pages are whose. That's how an operating system handles RAM.

[Figure: Requests that fit in 64 gibibytes. Reserving 8k context: 64. Reserving prompt plus 2,048 tokens: 177. 256-token blocks: 376. 16-token blocks: 411.]

_From the lab: 200 simulated requests, at 128 KiB per token._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between the two reservation settings and the two paging settings. Compare the memory holding real tokens with the requests that fit.

#### Reserve memory per request, or page it?

200 simulated requests: prompts 200–1,500 tokens, answer lengths mostly short (mean about 300, capped at 2,048); fixed seed. 128 KiB per token (Llama 3 8B shape, bf16).

Reserving the full **8k context** per request leaves **84.5%** of KV memory empty: only 64 requests fit. Reserving prompt + 2,048 output tokens (a common max-tokens setting) is better, but still only **42.8%** holds real tokens, in line with the 20–38% Kwon et al. measured in real systems. With **16-token pages**, 99.4% of the memory holds tokens and **411** requests fit, 2.3× as many, which is where vLLM's throughput gain comes from. Bigger blocks (256 tokens) waste more in each request's last block (91.0% used, 376 requests) but mean fewer table lookups; small blocks are the usual default.

**Now say why:** 16-token blocks waste so little, so why not make blocks 1 token?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Every running request needs its own KV cache, which grows by one token per decode step, and nobody knows in advance how long the answer will be. Early servers reserved one **contiguous** chunk per request for the maximum possible length, so most of it sat empty: Kwon et al. found only **20–38%** of KV memory held real tokens. **PagedAttention** (vLLM) borrows the idea of virtual memory: the cache is split into small fixed-size **blocks** (16 tokens by default), allocated on demand anywhere in GPU memory, and a per-request **block table** maps logical positions to physical blocks; the attention kernel follows that table. Waste drops to the last, partly filled block, so far more requests fit in a batch (vLLM reported 2–4× throughput), and blocks can be **shared** (parallel samples, common prefixes) or **evicted** when memory runs out. What you'll be able to do after this: explain KV-cache fragmentation, how block tables work, and what happens when the cache is full.

#### Blocks and block tables

- **Contiguous allocation** causes three kinds of waste (Kwon et al.): **reserved** slots for future tokens, **internal fragmentation** from over-estimating the length, and **external fragmentation** between differently sized chunks.

- **PagedAttention:** the KV cache is a pool of fixed-size physical blocks. Each request has a block table (logical block 0 → physical block 731, logical block 1 → physical block 12, …). A new block is grabbed only when the current one fills. The attention kernel gathers K and V through the table, so blocks need not be adjacent.

- **Copy-on-write sharing:** parallel samples or beams of the same prompt point to the same prompt blocks and copy only when they diverge; the same mechanism powers prefix caching.

- **When memory runs out:** the scheduler **preempts** some requests, either dropping their blocks and recomputing later or swapping them to CPU memory, and resumes them when blocks free up.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Beyond basic paging

- **Standard everywhere:** vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and Hugging Face TGI all use paged KV caches; SGLang organises shared prefixes in a radix tree.

- **KV-cache quantization:** storing K and V in FP8 halves the cache (twice the batch) with small quality cost; see LLM Quantization.

- **Offloading and tiering:** evicted or idle conversations' blocks move to CPU memory or SSD and come back on the next turn (e.g. LMCache with vLLM), useful for long multi-turn chats and agents.

- **Alternatives:** vAttention (Prabhu et al. 2024) keeps the cache virtually contiguous using the GPU's own virtual memory, so unmodified attention kernels work; architecture changes (GQA, MLA, sliding windows) shrink the cache itself.

To shrink, evict or offload the cache itself, read KV Cache Compression, Eviction and Offloading.

#### Allocate KV memory the way an OS allocates RAM

Small fixed-size pages allocated on demand, mapped through a table, remove almost all fragmentation, so the same GPU holds several times more concurrent requests, and pages can be shared, swapped or evicted.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "PagedAttention reduces the KV cache size"

It sounds right, since more requests suddenly fit. But each token still costs the same memory. It reduces the waste around the cache, while GQA, MLA or quantization reduce the cache itself. And outputs don't change either: only where K and V are stored changes. Reserving the maximum length "to be safe" is exactly what limits batch size.

## Say it

### Why did naive serving waste most of its KV memory, and how do blocks fix it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What happens when a new token needs a block and none are free?

The scheduler preempts lower-priority requests (often the most recent), frees their blocks by swapping to CPU or discarding them for later recomputation, and resumes them once memory is available.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not make blocks 1 token, for zero waste?

The block table and gather operations would become large and slow; blocks of 16–32 tokens balance waste against kernel efficiency.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does PagedAttention change the model's outputs?

No, it only changes where K and V are stored; attention computes the same result.

#### The 30-second answer

Each request's KV cache grows token by token and its final length is unknown, so early servers reserved contiguous memory for the maximum length, and only about 20 to 38 percent held real tokens. PagedAttention, from vLLM, splits the cache into fixed-size blocks, typically 16 tokens, allocated on demand anywhere in memory, with a per-request block table that the attention kernel uses to find them, like virtual memory pages. Waste drops to the last partial block, so batches get much bigger, giving 2 to 4 times throughput; blocks can be shared copy-on-write across samples and prefixes, and when memory runs out the scheduler preempts requests by swapping or recomputing.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "PagedAttention reduces the KV cache size." It reduces waste around it; GQA, MLA or quantization reduce the size.

- "Just reserve max length to be safe." That's exactly what limits batch size.

**Key terms and sources**

How serving engines store the KV cache of many concurrent requests: why reserving contiguous memory per request wastes most of it, how PagedAttention splits the cache into fixed-size blocks with a block table (like virtual memory), and what that enables: higher batch sizes, sharing between samples, preemption and offloading · built from Kwon et al. (vLLM / PagedAttention, SOSP 2023), the vLLM documentation, Zheng et al. (SGLang, NeurIPS 2024) and Prabhu et al. (vAttention, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

2. vLLM documentation, "Paged Attention" and "Automatic Prefix Caching", [docs.vllm.ai](https://docs.vllm.ai/).

# KV Cache Compression, Eviction and Offloading

> Long conversations are filling GPU memory with KV cache. How do you shrink it, drop some of it, or move it?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/kv-cache-compression/
- Before this: KV Cache Management and PagedAttention (`ai-engineering/kv-cache-and-pagedattention`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your assistant now keeps whole order histories in context, often 30,000 tokens or more. GPU memory fills with KV cache, and you can only serve a fraction of the users you could before. Someone suggests dropping old tokens from the cache. The interviewer asks:

> Long conversations are filling GPU memory with KV cache. How do you shrink it, drop some of it, or move it?

#### Why it matters

PagedAttention fixed wasted space. But an 8B model with a 32,000-token conversation needs about 4.3 GB of KV cache, and long-running agents and chats keep growing it. At that point you can't fit enough users on a GPU, however well it's packed. This lesson covers what to do next. For model changes that shrink the cache, such as GQA and MLA, see Attention Variants.

### The idea

Think of a busy desk covered in notes. You can write smaller, which saves space but is harder to read. You can throw away notes you think you won't need, and hope you're right. Or you can file some in a drawer and fetch them when needed, which takes a moment but loses nothing.

[Figure: Three choices. Quantize to shrink it. Evict to drop parts. Offload to move it to cheaper memory.]

_Choose by whether you can afford any loss._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the context to 1 million tokens. Then try each method, and compare the resume times.

#### Fit more conversations

Illustrative arithmetic for the Llama 3 8B shape, at 128 KiB per token in bf16. Reload assumes 64 GB/s from CPU memory and 7 GB/s from SSD. Recompute assumes 2 FLOPs per parameter per token at half of an H100's 989 TFLOP/s, and ignores attention, so long histories take longer. 2-bit ignores the small overhead for scales.

A 32,768-token conversation needs about 4.3 GB in bf16, so only 16 fit in 64 GiB. An **FP8** cache fits 32, and a **2-bit** cache 128, each with some risk to accuracy. Keeping **20% of tokens** fits 80, but whatever was dropped is gone for good. Now look at resuming a paused conversation: reloading from CPU memory takes about 67 ms, from SSD about 0.6 s, and recomputing about 1.1 s of GPU time. That's why offloading pays for agents and long chats: reloading is usually faster, and leaves the GPU free for others. Push to 1 million tokens, and even a single conversation won't fit in bf16.

**Now say why:** why is reloading usually better than recomputing for long histories?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Paging stops the KV cache from being wasted, but it doesn't make it smaller. At long contexts and many users, the cache itself fills the GPU. You have three choices. **Quantize** it: FP8 halves it, and methods like KIVI go to 2 bits. **Evict** parts of it: keep only the tokens that attention relies on most, which saves memory but can lose information for good. **Offload** it: move idle conversations to CPU memory or SSD and bring them back later, which is exact but costs a transfer. The right choice depends on whether you can afford any loss.

#### Shrink, drop or move

| Approach | Saves | Loses | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quantize** | 2× at FP8, more at lower bits | A little accuracy, usually small at 8 bits | FP8 KV cache, KIVI at 2 bits |
| **Evict** | As much as you choose | Dropped tokens are gone for good | H2O, SnapKV, sliding windows with attention sinks |
| **Offload** | GPU memory for idle conversations | Nothing, but a transfer delay on return | CPU memory and SSD tiers, LMCache, Mooncake |

##### Quantizing the cache

An FP8 cache halves the memory, so roughly twice as many conversations fit. KIVI goes further. It found keys and values behave differently, so it quantizes keys per channel and values per token, at 2 bits. It reported almost the same quality with 2.6× less peak memory including weights, up to 4× larger batches, and 2.35 to 3.47× throughput. Errors reach every later token, so test on long tasks.

##### Evicting tokens

- **H2O:** a few "heavy hitter" tokens get most of the attention. Keeping them, plus recent tokens, kept quality with 20% of the cache, and gave up to 29× throughput over some offloading-based systems.

- **SnapKV:** each head attends to consistent parts of the prompt, which can be spotted from the last few prompt tokens. At 16K input it reported 3.6× faster generation and 8.2× better memory efficiency.

- **Sliding windows:** keep recent tokens and the first few attention sinks. Memory stays bounded, but older text is forgotten.

The risk with eviction is that a question may need exactly what was dropped. That's fine for summarising a long chat, and bad for "what was the order number I gave you earlier?"

##### Offloading to cheaper memory

Idle conversations, such as a user who hasn't replied yet, can move to CPU memory or SSD. When they return, you can either reload their cache or recompute it by running prefill again. LMCache, which shares and stores caches outside GPU memory, reported up to 15× throughput with vLLM on multi-round and document workloads. Mooncake, the system behind Kimi, built its whole service around a shared cache across CPU memory and SSD.

##### Agents change the rules

Engines usually evict from the end of cached sequences, to protect shared prefixes. A 2026 study argues that agents, which return with long histories again and again, should instead keep the shared prefix and the most recent turns, and evict from the start of the rest, because recomputing late tokens is far more expensive. It reported up to 60% lower average time to first token than SGLang with a GPU-only cache, and up to 76% with a two-tier GPU and CPU cache.

#### The maths

$$ {t_{\text{reload}}} = \frac{{\text{KV bytes}}}{{\text{link bandwidth}}}, \qquad {t_{\text{recompute}}} \approx \frac{{2PT}}{{\text{usable FLOP/s}}} $$

Simple arithmetic for the reload-or-recompute choice. Recompute also takes GPU time away from other users, which reload doesn’t.

- **time to reload**: Bring a saved cache back from CPU memory or SSD.

- **bytes to move**: Grows with the conversation length.

- **the link**: PCIe to CPU memory, or much slower SSD.

- **time to recompute**: Run prefill again over the whole history.

- **prefill maths**: About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, ignoring attention, which only adds to it for long histories.

- **the GPU’s real speed**: Peak FLOPs times realistic utilisation.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Start with FP8:** it's widely supported and usually safe. Test long-context tasks before going lower.

- **Be careful with eviction in products:** users expect exact recall of what they said. Prefer offloading, or keep eviction to tasks like summarising.

- **Plan tiers:** GPU memory for active conversations, CPU memory for recently idle ones, and SSD for long pauses. SSDs wear out with heavy writes, which a 2026 study addresses.

- **Route to the cache:** send a returning conversation back to the machine that holds its cache. See Prefix Caching.

- **Measure on your traffic:** watch cache hit rate, reload time and recompute load. Each paper reports on its own workloads.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Drop the old tokens, the model mostly looks at recent ones"

It sounds right, since attention favours some tokens. But a later question may need exactly what you dropped, like an order number given early on, and evicted tokens can't come back. For products where exact recall matters, quantize or offload instead.

## Say it

### Long conversations are filling GPU memory with KV cache. How do you shrink it, drop some of it, or move it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your support bot forgets an order number from early in a long chat after you enabled KV eviction. Why?

Eviction keeps tokens that got the most attention so far, and the order number may not have seemed important until the user asked about it. Dropped tokens can't come back. Use quantization or offloading instead, or retrieve key facts explicitly.

Follow-up 2 of 3

When is recomputing a cache better than reloading it?

For short histories, prefill is quick, and avoids storing and moving the cache at all. For long histories, reloading from CPU memory is usually much faster, and doesn't take GPU time from other users. SSD sits in between, depending on its speed.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does an FP8 KV cache change the model's output?

Slightly, as rounding errors enter every later attention step. It's usually small, but test long-context tasks, and compare against bf16 on your own evaluations.

#### The 30-second answer

Paging removes waste, but at long contexts the cache itself fills the GPU, and an 8B model's 32k-token conversation is about 4 GB. I have three options. Quantize it: FP8 halves it with little risk, and KIVI's 2-bit method reported up to 4 times larger batches. Evict tokens: H2O and SnapKV keep the tokens attention relies on, which saves a lot but loses information for good, so I'd avoid it where exact recall matters. Or offload: move idle conversations to CPU memory or SSD and reload them later. Reloading 4 GB from CPU memory takes tens of milliseconds, against about a second of GPU time to recompute. For agents, I'd keep shared prefixes and recent turns, and route returning conversations to the machine holding their cache.

**Key terms and sources**

Why long contexts make the KV cache the bottleneck, quantizing it, evicting unimportant tokens, offloading to CPU memory or SSD, and when to reload or recompute. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Zhang et al., H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14048)

- [Li et al., SnapKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14469)

- [Liu et al., LMCache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09665)

- [Qin et al., Mooncake](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00079)

# Continuous Batching and Scheduling

> Trace one request through a vLLM-style engine.

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/continuous-batching/
- Before this: KV Cache Management and PagedAttention (`ai-engineering/kv-cache-and-pagedattention`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant gets quick answers of about 50 tokens and refund explanations of about 400. A colleague batches 8 requests together and runs them to the end, so one long answer holds up seven short ones. The interviewer asks:

> How do you schedule requests of unknown length on one GPU?

**Running example:** the support assistant gets a mix of quick answers ("Your order is on its way", ~50 tokens) and long ones (refund explanations, ~400 tokens). The GPU can decode 8 sequences at once in this toy version.

#### Different lengths, random arrivals

Traditional ML serving batches requests of the same shape and runs them together. LLM requests differ in prompt length and, unpredictably, in output length. If a batch must finish together, one long answer holds up seven short ones, and the short ones' slots idle until it's done.

### The idea

Think of a restaurant that seats 8 people at once and won't seat anyone new until the slowest eater has left. Empty chairs sit there while a queue waits at the door. Continuous batching seats the next person the moment any chair frees up.

[Figure: For 48 requests, static batching takes 2,121 steps at 34.9 percent slot use with average latency 946 steps. Continuous batching takes 954 steps at 77.6 percent with average latency 344.]

_From the lab: 48 requests and 8 decode slots, ignoring prefill._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between static and continuous batching. Compare the decode steps, slot utilisation and average request latency.

#### Static batches vs refilling every step

48 requests all waiting at the start; 8 decode slots; 80% short answers (10–100 tokens), 20% long (250–500); fixed seed. Prefill is ignored to isolate the batching effect.

With **static batching**, each group of 8 runs as long as its longest answer: the GPU needs **2,121** steps and slots are busy only **34.9%** of the time. **Continuous batching** fills a slot the moment it frees up: **954** steps, 77.6% utilisation (the rest is the tail at the end, when the last long answers run alone), and the average request finishes after 344 steps instead of 946. Short answers no longer wait for long ones.

**Now say why:** what makes it possible to rebuild the batch at every step?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

GPUs are efficient only when many requests decode together, but requests arrive at random times and finish at very different lengths. **Static batching** groups requests and runs the group until its _longest_ member finishes, so slots sit idle and new arrivals wait. **Continuous batching** (Orca's iteration-level scheduling) rebuilds the batch at **every decode step**: finished requests leave immediately and waiting ones join. A scheduler enforces a **token budget** per step, admits requests only if their KV blocks fit, mixes chunked prefills with ongoing decodes, and preempts requests when memory runs out. Orca reported 36.9× higher throughput than FasterTransformer at the same latency on GPT-3 175B. What you'll be able to do after this: explain continuous batching, trace a request through an inference engine, and name the scheduling knobs and their trade-offs.

#### One request's life in a vLLM-style engine

1. **Arrive:** the API server tokenises the prompt and puts the request in the **waiting queue**.

2. **Admit:** each scheduling step, the scheduler checks the **token budget** (e.g. max 8,192 tokens per step) and the **free KV blocks**; if both allow, it allocates blocks and moves the request to **running**.

3. **Prefill:** the prompt is processed, possibly split over several steps (**chunked prefill**) so it doesn't stall others; its K and V fill the new blocks. The first output token is sampled: that's the TTFT.

4. **Decode:** every step, all running requests advance one token in the same forward pass; a new block is allocated whenever one fills.

5. **Preempt if needed:** if no block is free, the scheduler evicts the lowest-priority request (recompute or swap) and puts it back in the queue.

6. **Finish:** on an end token or max length, blocks return to the pool (or to the prefix cache) and the response is detokenised and streamed out.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The scheduler's knobs and trade-offs

- **Max batched tokens per step** (vLLM `max_num_batched_tokens`): larger favours throughput and TTFT (big prefill chunks); smaller keeps decode steps short, favouring inter-token latency.

- **Max sequences** (`max_num_seqs`): caps the batch; bounded by KV memory anyway.

- **Chunked prefill** (Sarathi-Serve): splits long prompts into chunks that ride along with decodes, avoiding stalls; now the vLLM default.

- **Priorities and fairness:** first-come-first-served by default; priority classes (e.g. interactive vs batch jobs), cancellation of abandoned requests, and timeouts matter in production.

- **Preemption policy:** recompute (cheap for short contexts) vs swap to CPU (better for long ones).

#### Schedule per token, not per request

Because every decode step is a fresh forward pass, the batch can be rebuilt each step; doing so keeps the GPU full and lets short requests finish without waiting for long ones.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Batching always increases latency"

It sounds right, since a bigger batch feels like more waiting. But in the lab, continuous batching cuts average latency from 946 steps to 344 compared with static batching, because short answers stop waiting for long ones. Setting the batch as high as possible isn't right either: it's bounded by KV memory, and it hurts inter-token latency.

## Say it

### How do you schedule requests of unknown length on one GPU?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does a long prefill hurt other users' streaming?

It's processed in the same forward pass as everyone's decode step, making that step much longer; chunked prefill bounds the extra work per step.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How would you prioritise interactive chat over batch summarisation on the same GPUs?

Priority scheduling or separate queues with preemption of the batch class, or separate deployments; batch jobs can also use cheaper offline APIs.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why doesn't continuous batching reach 100% utilisation?

At the end of a burst, or under light load, there aren't enough requests to fill every slot; under steady load it stays near full.

#### The 30-second answer

Static batching runs a group of requests until the longest finishes, so slots idle and new requests wait. Continuous batching, from Orca, schedules at the iteration level: after every decode step finished sequences leave and waiting ones join. In vLLM a request is tokenised and queued, admitted when the per-step token budget and free KV blocks allow, prefilled possibly in chunks, then decoded one token per step alongside others, preempted by swap or recompute if memory runs out, and its blocks freed when it finishes. The key knobs are max batched tokens, max sequences and chunk size, trading throughput and time to first token against inter-token latency.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Batching always increases latency." Continuous batching cuts average latency compared with static batching.

- "Just set the batch size as high as possible." It's bounded by KV memory and hurts inter-token latency.

**Key terms and sources**

How a serving engine decides, every few milliseconds, which requests run: static vs continuous (iteration-level) batching, the token budget, admission control, preemption, prefill/decode mixing with chunked prefill, and a step-by-step trace of one request through a vLLM-style engine, the classic inference-infrastructure interview question · built from Yu et al. (Orca, OSDI 2022), Kwon et al. (vLLM, SOSP 2023), Agrawal et al. (Sarathi-Serve, OSDI 2024) and the vLLM scheduler documentation · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. G.-I. Yu et al., "Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models", OSDI 2022.

2. W. Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", SOSP 2023, [arXiv:2309.06180](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180).

3. A. Agrawal et al., "Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve", OSDI 2024, [arXiv:2403.02310](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310).

4. vLLM documentation: scheduler configuration and optimisation guide, [docs.vllm.ai](https://docs.vllm.ai/).

# Prefix and Prompt Caching

> Why are repeated system prompts nearly free, until a timestamp breaks them?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/prefix-caching/
- Before this: KV Cache Management and PagedAttention (`ai-engineering/kv-cache-and-pagedattention`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

Every support request starts with the same 2,000-token system prompt, followed by about 200 tokens from the customer. A colleague turns on prompt caching, but also adds the current time at the top of every prompt. The bill goes up. The interviewer asks:

> Why are repeated system prompts nearly free, until a timestamp breaks them?

**Running example:** every support request starts with the same system prompt (tone, refund policy, tool definitions), followed by about 200 tokens from the customer.

#### Recomputing the same prompt thousands of times

With a 2,000-token system prompt and a 200-token question, more than 90% of every request's prefill is identical work. Prefill drives time to first token and, with APIs, most of the input bill. Agents and multi-turn chats make it worse: each turn resends the whole history.

### The idea

Think of a running total down a long column. Each line depends on everything above it. Two sheets with the same first 2,000 lines have the same totals, so you can copy them. Change line 1 and every total after it changes, so nothing can be reused.

[Figure: With the system prompt first, it is reused: 90.8 percent of prefill is saved. With a timestamp first, nothing after it matches: nothing is saved and input costs 125 percent.]

_From the lab: 1,000 requests, with Anthropic-style pricing._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Compare no caching, a timestamp at the start and the shared system prompt first. Then change the system prompt length.

#### Put the timestamp first, or last?

1,000 requests, each = system prompt + 200 unique customer tokens, all within the cache lifetime. Cost uses Anthropic-style pricing: first write 1.25×, cached reads 0.1×, uncached input 1×. The timestamp case writes a new cache entry every time and never reads it.

With the shared **2,000-token system prompt first**, all but the first request reuse it: only **202,000** of 2.2 million prefill tokens are computed (**90.8%** saved) and input costs **18.3%** of the uncached price. Longer shared prefixes save more: 97.5% at 8,000 tokens. Now put "Current time: 14:32:07" at the **start** of the prompt: every request has a different first token, nothing matches, and with explicit caching you pay the write premium for nothing (**125%**). Move the timestamp after the system prompt and the savings return.

**Now say why:** the rest of the prompt is identical, so why does one different first token stop every match?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Most production prompts start with the same text: a long system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples, a shared document, or the conversation so far. Because each token's K and V depend only on the tokens before it, the KV cache of an identical **prefix** can be computed once and **reused**, skipping that part of prefill. Engines do this automatically: vLLM hashes each full KV block together with everything before it, and SGLang keeps prefixes in a radix tree (RadixAttention). API providers expose it as **prompt caching**, billing cached input at a fraction of the normal price (Anthropic: reads at 10% of the base input price, writes at a 25% premium). The catch: only an **exact prefix** matches, so anything that changes per request (a timestamp, user name, shuffled tools) must go **after** the shared part. What you'll be able to do after this: explain how prefix caching works, structure prompts for high hit rates, and estimate the savings.

#### How engines find a reusable prefix

- **Why it works:** in a causal model, the K and V at position t depend only on tokens 1…t. Two requests that share their first n tokens have identical KV for those n positions.

- **vLLM automatic prefix caching:** each full KV block is identified by a hash of its tokens _and_ all tokens before it; a new request reuses every leading block whose hash is already cached. Unused cached blocks are evicted least-recently-used.

- **SGLang RadixAttention:** cached prefixes are stored in a radix tree, so any shared prefix (including branches like many few-shot variants) is found; the SGLang paper reports up to 6.4× higher throughput on workloads with heavy sharing.

- **API prompt caching:** Anthropic uses cache breakpoints. Writes cost 1.25× the base input price for a 5-minute cache, or 2× for an hour, and reads cost 0.1×, or less on its newest models. Its newest models can cache from 512 tokens. OpenAI caches automatically from 1,024 tokens. Its newest models bill writes at 1.25× for a 30-minute default, with discounts of up to 95%. These change often, so check current pricing (checked 7 Nov 2026).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Getting high hit rates in production

- **Order prompts from most to least stable:** tools and system prompt → shared documents / few-shot examples → conversation history → the new message. Keep tool definitions in a fixed order and avoid per-request values early on.

- **Multi-turn chats and agents:** each turn extends the previous prompt, so the whole history hits the cache if it's sent unchanged; editing or summarising early turns breaks the match.

- **Cache-aware routing:** with many replicas, send requests sharing a prefix to the same replica (e.g. consistent hashing on the prefix, or routers in llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo that track which replica holds which prefixes); random load balancing scatters prefixes and kills hit rates.

- **Measure:** track cache hit rate and cached-token counts (vLLM metrics; API responses report cached tokens), and watch eviction under memory pressure.

#### Identical prefixes have identical KV; compute them once

Prefix caching turns repeated prompt text into a near-free lookup, but only for an exact match from the first token, so the stable parts of a prompt must come first.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Caching works for any repeated text in the prompt"

It sounds right, since the text is the same. But only an exact prefix from the first token counts, because a chunk's K and V depend on everything before it. It doesn't speed up decode either: it skips prefill work, while decode still reads the whole cache each step. And with round-robin load balancing, each replica computes the same prefix again.

## Say it

### Why are repeated system prompts nearly free, until a timestamp breaks them?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why can't you reuse a matching chunk in the middle of a prompt?

Its K and V depend on everything before it; with a different preceding context they'd be different. (Research methods approximate this for RAG chunks, at some accuracy cost.)

Follow-up 2 of 3

How does prefix caching interact with load balancing?

Round-robin scatters requests with the same prefix across replicas, each computing it again; route by prefix hash or with a cache-aware router.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does prefix caching speed up decode?

No, it skips prefill work (TTFT and input cost); decode still reads the whole cache each step.

#### The 30-second answer

In a causal model the keys and values of a token depend only on the tokens before it, so requests that share a prefix share its KV cache. Serving engines exploit this: vLLM hashes each KV block together with its whole prefix and reuses matching blocks, and SGLang stores prefixes in a radix tree. That skips most of prefill for repeated system prompts, documents and conversation history, cutting time to first token and cost; APIs bill cached input at a large discount, for example 10 percent of the normal price on Anthropic. It only works for exact prefixes, so I put stable content first and per-request content last, and with multiple replicas I'd use prefix-aware routing.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Caching works for any repeated text in the prompt." Only an exact prefix from the first token.

- "Caching changes the model's answers." The reused KV is identical to recomputing it (up to floating-point noise).

**Key terms and sources**

Reusing the KV cache of repeated prompt prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples, documents, earlier conversation turns): how vLLM's automatic prefix caching and SGLang's RadixAttention find matches, how API providers price cached input, how to structure prompts so the cache actually hits, and cache-aware routing across replicas · built from Zheng et al. (SGLang / RadixAttention, NeurIPS 2024), the vLLM automatic prefix caching docs, Anthropic and OpenAI prompt caching documentation, and Gim et al. (Prompt Cache, MLSys 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. L. Zheng et al., "SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs", NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2312.07104](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104).

2. vLLM documentation, "Automatic Prefix Caching", [docs.vllm.ai](https://docs.vllm.ai/).

3. Anthropic, "Prompt caching" documentation; OpenAI, "Prompt caching" guide (pricing and minimum lengths vary by model; checked Oct 2026).

4. I. Gim et al., "Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency Inference", MLSys 2024, [arXiv:2311.04934](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04934).

# Speculative Decoding

> How does a small draft make a big model faster with identical outputs?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/speculative-decoding/
- Before this: Prefill vs Decode (`ai-engineering/prefill-vs-decode`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

The 70B model behind the premium tier streams too slowly for chat, while its GPU compute sits mostly idle during decode. A colleague says that a smaller draft model will make it faster, but only by lowering quality. The interviewer asks:

> How does a small draft make a big model faster with identical outputs?

**Running example:** the 70B model behind the premium support tier streams too slowly for chat. GPU compute is mostly idle during decode; can it be used to produce several tokens per step without changing the answers?

#### One token per pass, compute sitting idle

At small batch sizes, a decode step's time is set by reading tens of gigabytes of weights; the arithmetic for one token is tiny. Verifying 5 tokens in one pass costs almost the same as generating 1. If we could guess future tokens well, we could confirm several per pass.

### The idea

Think of a junior who drafts the next few words, while a senior checks them at a glance. Reading five words costs the senior barely more than writing one. At the first wrong word, the senior corrects it and throws the rest away. The final text reads as if the senior wrote it alone.

[Figure: The draft proposes five tokens. The target accepts the first three in one pass, rejects the fourth and replaces it with its own token, and the last draft token is discarded.]

_Illustrative. Several tokens can be confirmed in one target pass._

### Play

**Try to break it.** At a small batch, start at α = 0.8 and γ = 4, then change each. Then switch to a large batch, and drop α to 0.6.

#### More draft tokens is always better?

Draft step cost c = 0.05 of a target step. Large batch: verifying each extra draft token adds 30% of a step's cost, because the GPU is no longer idle. Dashed line: no speedup.

At small batch, α = 0.8 and γ = 4 give **3.36** tokens per target pass and a **2.80×** speedup; drafting further helps a little (best γ = 8, 3.09×) because rejections waste only cheap draft work. A weaker draft (α = 0.6) gives 1.92×; an excellent one (α = 0.9) gives 3.41× at γ = 4 and over 4× with longer drafts. Switch to a **large batch**: verifying extra tokens now competes for compute, so the same α = 0.8, γ = 4 gives only **1.40×**, and with α = 0.6 it's **slower than not speculating (0.96×)**. That's why engines tune or disable speculation as load rises.

**Now say why:** why can speculation be slower than plain decoding at a large batch?

## Maths

### Maths

#### In one breath

Decode is memory-bound: each step reads all the weights to produce one token per sequence, leaving the GPU's compute mostly idle. **Speculative decoding** uses that idle compute: a small, fast **draft** guesses the next γ tokens, and the big **target** model checks all of them in a single forward pass (as cheap as producing one token when memory-bound). Tokens are accepted left to right with a rejection-sampling rule that guarantees the output follows **exactly** the target model's distribution; at the first rejection the target supplies a corrected token, so every step yields at least one token. With acceptance rate α, the expected tokens per step is (1 − αγ+1) / (1 − α): at α = 0.8 and γ = 4, about 3.4. Typical speedups are 2–3× at small batch; EAGLE-3 reports up to 6.5×, but at large batches the GPU is no longer idle and gains shrink. What you'll be able to do after this: explain why speculative decoding is lossless, compute expected speedup, and say when it helps.

#### Draft, verify, accept

1. The draft proposes γ tokens autoregressively (cheap).

2. The target runs once over the context plus all γ draft tokens, giving its own probabilities at every position.

3. Each draft token x is accepted with probability min(1, ptarget(x) / pdraft(x)), left to right. At the first rejection, a token is sampled from the normalised difference max(0, ptarget − pdraft), and the rest are discarded. If all are accepted, the target's next-position prediction gives a bonus token.

$$ {\text{speedup}} = \frac{{(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})/(1-\alpha)}}{{\gamma c + 1}} $$

Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding", ICML 2023, [arXiv:2211.17192](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192); Chen et al. (DeepMind), "Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling", 2023, [arXiv:2302.01318](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318).

- **expected tokens per target pass**: With per-token acceptance rate α and γ draft tokens, the accepted run length is geometric; this sum includes the corrected or bonus token, so it is always at least 1.

- **cost of one step**: γ draft steps, each costing c relative to a target step, plus one target pass.

- **speedup**: Tokens per step divided by cost per step (Leviathan et al., Theorem 3.8). High α and cheap drafts make it large.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Where drafts come from

| Draft | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Separate small model** | e.g. a 1B model from the same family as the 70B target | easy, needs the same tokeniser; extra memory; α depends on how similar they are |
| **Medusa** (Cai et al. 2024) | extra decoding heads on the target predict tokens t+2, t+3, …; tree of candidates verified at once | no second model; Medusa-1 about 2.2× without quality change |
| **EAGLE-3** (Li et al. 2025) | a light head drafts from the target's own hidden features (several layers), trained with "training-time test" | up to 6.5× reported; 1.38× throughput at batch 64 in SGLang; supported in vLLM and SGLang |
| **N-gram / prompt lookup** | copy candidate continuations from the prompt itself | free; great for editing, code refactors and RAG answers that quote the context |

Measure on your own traffic: acceptance depends on the task (code and quoting accept more than creative writing) and on temperature.

**Drafts built into the model.** Some models are trained to predict more than one token ahead. DeepSeek-V3 reported that its multi-token prediction head's second token was accepted 85 to 90% of the time, giving about 1.8× more tokens per second. Engines now use such heads as the draft, with no separate model to load.

#### Guess cheaply, verify in parallel, never change the answer

Speculative decoding turns idle compute during memory-bound decoding into extra tokens per step, and its rejection-sampling rule keeps the output distribution identical to the big model's.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It's an approximation that slightly lowers quality"

It sounds right, since a weaker model is writing part of the answer. But it's lossless: the rejection rule keeps the output distribution identical, and with greedy decoding the tokens are identical, up to floating-point differences. It doesn't always give 2–3× either: it depends on acceptance and batch size, and at α = 0.6 on a large batch the lab is slower than not speculating.

## Say it

### How does a small draft make a big model faster with identical outputs?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Is the output exactly the same as without speculation?

The distribution is identical with the rejection-sampling rule; with greedy decoding the tokens are identical (up to floating-point differences).

Follow-up 2 of 3

When would you turn it off?

At high batch sizes where decode becomes compute-bound, or when acceptance is low (creative, high-temperature output); measure accepted tokens per step.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What limits the draft model's size?

Its cost per step (c): a draft too big eats the gain; it must also share the target's tokeniser.

#### The 30-second answer

Decoding is memory-bound, so verifying several tokens in one forward pass costs about the same as generating one. Speculative decoding has a cheap draft, a small model, Medusa heads or an EAGLE head, propose gamma tokens; the target model scores them all in one pass and accepts each with probability min of one and target over draft probability, resampling from the residual at the first rejection, which provably preserves the target's distribution. Expected tokens per pass are one minus alpha to the gamma plus one, over one minus alpha, so with 80 percent acceptance and four draft tokens about 3.4. Speedups are typically 2 to 3 times at low batch, but shrink at high batch where compute is no longer idle.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "It's an approximation that slightly lowers quality." It's lossless.

- "It always gives 2–3×." It depends on acceptance and batch size.

**Key terms and sources**

How a cheap draft proposes several tokens that the big model verifies in one forward pass, why the output distribution is exactly unchanged, how acceptance rate and draft length set the speedup, the main draft designs (separate draft model, Medusa heads, EAGLE-3, n-gram / prompt lookup), and why gains shrink at large batch sizes · built from Leviathan et al. (ICML 2023), Chen et al. (DeepMind, 2023), Cai et al. (Medusa, ICML 2024), Li et al. (EAGLE-3, NeurIPS 2025) and the vLLM and SGLang speculative decoding docs · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman & Y. Matias, "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding", ICML 2023, [arXiv:2211.17192](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192).

2. C. Chen et al., "Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling", 2023, [arXiv:2302.01318](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318).

3. T. Cai et al., "Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads", ICML 2024, [arXiv:2401.10774](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774).

4. Y. Li et al., "EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test", NeurIPS 2025, [arXiv:2503.01840](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01840).

5. DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report", 2024, [arXiv:2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437) (§5.4.3, multi-token prediction for speculative decoding).

# Serving Metrics and SLOs

> TTFT, TPOT, p99 and goodput: why latency explodes near capacity.

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/serving-metrics-and-slos/
- Before this: Continuous Batching and Scheduling (`ai-engineering/continuous-batching`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant's SLO is TTFT under 1 s and TPOT under 50 ms. A colleague load-tests one GPU, gets 1,100 tokens per second, and calls that its capacity. The interviewer asks:

> How do you measure LLM serving, and why does latency explode near capacity?

**Running example:** the support assistant's SLO is **TTFT ≤ 1 s** and **TPOT ≤ 50 ms** (about 20 tokens/s, faster than people read). Requests arrive randomly; each has a 1,000-token prompt and a 200-token answer. How much traffic can one GPU take?

#### "Our server does 1,100 tokens/s" isn't an answer

A throughput number measured with a huge batch says nothing about whether users wait 100 ms or 30 s for the first word. A mean latency hides the 1% of users who time out. LLM serving needs metrics for each phase, at tail percentiles, under realistic load.

### The idea

Think of a motorway. More cars means more people moving, up to a point. Near capacity, one small burst becomes a long jam, even though the road is at its busiest. Maximum flow and a pleasant drive are different things.

[Figure: One GPU under load. At 4 requests a second: 804 tokens a second, 188 milliseconds p99 TTFT, 100 percent goodput. At 5: 1,004 tokens, 1.23 seconds, 89 percent. At 6: 1,142 tokens, over 10 seconds, 0 percent.]

_From the lab's simulation of one GPU. Illustrative numbers, not a specific GPU._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the arrival rate to 4 requests per second, then 5, then 6. Watch throughput, TTFT p50, TTFT p99 and goodput.

#### Push for maximum throughput

Discrete-event simulation of one GPU: Poisson arrivals; continuous batching up to 64 sequences; each new request's prefill takes 60 ms and stalls that step (no chunking); a decode step takes 10 ms + 0.4 ms per running sequence. 10 simulated minutes, first minute discarded; fixed seed. Illustrative numbers, not a specific GPU.

Up to **4 requests/s** everything is comfortable: p99 TTFT **188 ms**, TPOT 25 ms, goodput 100%, and throughput grows with load (804 tokens/s). At **5 requests/s** throughput is 1,004 tokens/s, but random bursts now queue: median TTFT is still 81 ms, yet p99 is **1.23 s** and 11% of requests miss the SLO. At **6 requests/s** the server is past its capacity (about 5.8 requests/s here): throughput peaks at 1,142 tokens/s, the queue grows without limit, TTFT exceeds 10 s, and goodput is **0%**. Maximum throughput and acceptable service are different operating points; queueing theory says latency grows sharply as utilisation approaches 100%, so production systems run with headroom.

**Now say why:** at 6 requests per second, throughput is at its highest and goodput is zero. How can both be true?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Users feel two latencies: **TTFT** (time to first token: how long before anything appears) and **TPOT / ITL** (time per output token: how smoothly it streams). End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1). Operators care about **throughput** (tokens or requests per second per GPU). These pull in opposite directions: more load means bigger batches and more throughput, but each step gets slower and requests start **queueing**, and close to capacity the queue, and the **p99** TTFT, explode. So the metric that matters is **goodput**: requests per second that meet the SLO (e.g. TTFT ≤ 1 s and TPOT ≤ 50 ms), measured at percentiles, not averages. Capacity planning means finding the highest load where goodput stays near 100%, then leaving headroom. What you'll be able to do after this: define the metrics, read a load test, set SLOs and explain why p99 explodes near capacity.

#### The metrics

| Metric | Definition | Driven by |
|---|---|---|
| **TTFT** | request arrival → first output token | queueing + prefill (+ cache hits) |
| **TPOT / ITL** | average (TPOT) or per-gap (ITL) time between output tokens | decode step time: batch size, KV reads, prefill interference |
| **E2E latency** | arrival → last token ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (n − 1) | both, plus output length |
| **Throughput** | output tokens/s (or requests/s) per GPU or per dollar | batch size, utilisation |
| **Goodput** | requests/s that meet all SLOs (DistServe) | everything above, at the tail |

Report p50, p90 and p99, not means. Little's law (L = λ · W) links them: concurrent requests in the system = arrival rate × time each spends there; when W grows, so does memory pressure.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Load testing and setting SLOs

- **Benchmark with realistic traffic:** real prompt/output length distributions, Poisson or replayed arrivals, streaming on. Tools: vLLM's `benchmark_serving`, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf, LLMPerf. Sweep request rate and plot p99 TTFT / TPOT against throughput.

- **Pick SLOs per product:** chat needs fast TTFT and smooth streaming; batch summarisation cares about cost and E2E; agents chaining many calls care about E2E per step.

- **Tune for the SLO:** chunked prefill and smaller token budgets protect TPOT; prefix caching and more replicas protect TTFT; [disaggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670) lets you tune each phase separately (DistServe reported up to 7.4× more requests within SLO).

- **Operate:** alert on p99 TTFT and queue length, autoscale on queue depth or KV-cache usage (not GPU utilisation, which looks "busy" even when idle-waiting on memory), and shed or queue low-priority traffic under overload.

#### Optimise goodput, not throughput

Serve as much traffic as possible _while_ meeting TTFT and TPOT targets at the tail; past capacity, throughput barely rises while latency explodes.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Maximum throughput is our capacity"

It sounds right, since throughput is the number you can measure most easily. But in the lab, peak throughput comes with 0% goodput. Capacity is the load at which SLOs still hold. Averages hide this as well: at 5 requests per second, median TTFT is still 81 ms while p99 is 1.23 s. And GPU utilisation won't warn you, because decode keeps the GPU "busy" reading memory.

## Say it

### How do you measure LLM serving, and why does latency explode near capacity?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

TTFT p99 spiked but TPOT is fine. Likely causes?

Queueing from a traffic burst or capacity loss, long prompts (prefill), lost prefix-cache hits (e.g. a prompt change), or KV memory pressure delaying admission.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why is GPU utilisation a poor autoscaling signal for LLMs?

Decode keeps the GPU "busy" reading memory even at low useful load; queue length, TTFT and KV-cache usage reflect saturation better.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Estimate E2E latency for 300 output tokens at TTFT 400 ms and TPOT 30 ms.

0.4 + 0.03 × 299 ≈ 9.4 s; streaming makes it feel much faster than that.

#### The 30-second answer

For LLM serving I track time to first token, driven by queueing and prefill; time per output token or inter-token latency, driven by decode batch size; end-to-end latency, roughly TTFT plus TPOT times output length; and throughput per GPU. They trade off: more load gives bigger batches and more throughput but slower steps and queueing, and near capacity tail latency explodes. So I define SLOs on p99 TTFT and TPOT and optimise goodput, the request rate that meets them, find it with a load test using realistic length distributions and arrival patterns, and run with headroom and autoscaling on queue depth.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Average latency is 200 ms, so we're fine." Look at p99.

- "Maximum throughput is our capacity." Capacity is the load at which SLOs still hold.

**Key terms and sources**

What to measure and promise when serving an LLM: time to first token, time per output token / inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput, tail percentiles, and goodput (requests served within the SLO); why throughput and latency trade off as load rises; how queues blow up near capacity; and how to load-test and set SLOs · built from Zhong et al. (DistServe, OSDI 2024), Agrawal et al. (Sarathi-Serve / Etalon metrics, 2024), the vLLM benchmarking docs, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf docs and Little (1961) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. Y. Zhong et al., "DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving", OSDI 2024, [arXiv:2401.09670](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670).

2. A. Agrawal et al., "Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve", OSDI 2024, [arXiv:2403.02310](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310); A. Agrawal et al., "Etalon: Holistic Performance Evaluation Framework for LLM Inference Systems", 2024, [arXiv:2407.07000](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07000).

3. vLLM documentation, benchmarking (`benchmark_serving`); NVIDIA GenAI-Perf documentation.

4. J. Little, "A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW", _Operations Research_ 9(3), 1961.

# Scaling Inference: Parallelism, Replicas and Routing

> How many GPUs for 1,000 users, and why FP8 weights may not help?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/scaling-inference/
- Before this: Serving Metrics and SLOs (`ai-engineering/serving-metrics-and-slos`), Training at Scale: Mixed Precision, Parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP (`fundamentals/distributed-training`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

The premium tier wants 1,000 simultaneous conversations, with up to 8k tokens of context each, on 80 GB GPUs. A colleague says to quantise the weights to FP8 and need half the GPUs. The interviewer asks:

> How many GPUs for 1,000 users, and why may FP8 weights not help?

**Running example:** the premium tier wants 1,000 simultaneous conversations, each with up to 8k tokens of context, on 80 GB GPUs. Which model, which precision, and how many GPUs?

#### Too big for one GPU, too many users for one replica

A 70B model in bf16 is 141 GB: it doesn't fit on one 80 GB GPU. And even when it fits, one replica can only hold so many conversations' KV caches. Scaling inference means splitting each model across GPUs efficiently, then running enough copies, and routing traffic well between them.

### The idea

Think of a hotel. The weights are the lobby and kitchen, and every guest needs their own room, which is the KV cache. Shrink the lobby and each building gets smaller, but it also has fewer rooms. You still need the same total number of rooms, so you end up with more buildings.

[Figure: Serving 1,000 conversations. Llama 3 70B in bf16: 4 GPUs per replica, 54 conversations per replica, 76 GPUs. In fp8: 2 GPUs, 27 conversations, still 76 GPUs. DeepSeek-V3 in fp8: 16 GPUs, 835 conversations, 32 GPUs.]

_From the lab: a memory floor for 1,000 conversations, ignoring activations and throughput limits._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Pick Llama 3 70B, and switch between bf16 and fp8 weights. Then try DeepSeek-V3, and change the number of conversations.

#### "Quantise the weights and we'll need half the GPUs"

80 GB GPUs, 90% usable; GPUs per replica = smallest power of two holding the weights with room for at least 8 conversations; KV cache in bf16 at 8,192 tokens per conversation (8B: 128 KiB/token, 70B: 320, 405B: 504, DeepSeek-V3 with MLA: about 69). Ignores activations and throughput limits: a memory floor, not a full plan.

**Llama 3 70B in bf16** (141 GB) needs a 4-GPU replica, which then holds **54** conversations of 8k tokens; 1,000 users need 19 replicas, **76 GPUs**. Quantise the weights to **fp8** and a replica fits on 2 GPUs, but each now holds only 27 conversations, because the KV cache didn't shrink: still **76 GPUs**. At high concurrency the KV cache is the bottleneck, which is why GQA/MLA, FP8 KV caches and prefix sharing matter as much as weight quantization. The contrast: **DeepSeek-V3** is far bigger (671 GB in fp8, a 16-GPU, two-node replica) but its MLA cache is so small that one replica holds 835 conversations, so 1,000 users fit on 32 GPUs.

**Now say why:** DeepSeek-V3 is far bigger than Llama 3 70B, so why does it need fewer GPUs here?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Serving at scale has two separate questions. **1. How many GPUs per replica?** Enough to hold the weights plus room for the KV cache. Inside a replica, **tensor parallelism** splits each layer across GPUs in one NVLink node (low latency, chatty), **pipeline parallelism** splits layers across nodes, and **expert parallelism** spreads MoE experts. **2. How many replicas?** Enough to hold every concurrent conversation's KV cache and meet the SLOs. Often the KV cache dominates: halving the weights with FP8 can leave the total GPU count unchanged. Large systems go further: separate prefill and decode clusters with KV transfer between them (DeepSeek-V3, Kimi's Mooncake, NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d), with routers that send requests to the replica that already holds their prefix. What you'll be able to do after this: size a deployment from model, precision and concurrency, choose parallelism, and explain disaggregated serving, routing and autoscaling.

#### Parallelism for serving

| Kind | What is split | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Tensor parallel (TP)** | each weight matrix across GPUs; all-reduce in every layer | model doesn't fit one GPU; keep within an NVLink node (≤ 8 GPUs); lowers latency too |
| **Pipeline parallel (PP)** | groups of layers per GPU/node | model doesn't fit one node; adds latency per stage, needs enough requests in flight |
| **Expert parallel (EP)** | MoE experts across GPUs; all-to-all token routing | large MoE models (DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2) |
| **Data parallel (replicas)** | whole copies of the model | more traffic: scale out behind a router |

The same ideas as training parallelism, but serving has no gradients or optimizer state, and latency per token matters.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Disaggregation, routing and autoscaling

- **Disaggregated prefill and decode** (background): separate GPU pools sized and parallelised for each phase, with KV caches transferred over fast networks. DeepSeek-V3's deployment used a minimum of 32 GPUs for prefill and 320 GPUs (expert parallelism across 40 nodes) for decode. Kimi's Mooncake builds the whole service around a distributed KV-cache pool.

- **Open-source stacks:** NVIDIA Dynamo and llm-d (Kubernetes-native) add disaggregation, KV-cache transfer, and smart routing on top of engines like vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.

- **Routing:** balance on queue length and KV usage, and send requests with the same prefix to the same replica (prefix-aware routing); sticky sessions keep multi-turn chats on warm caches.

- **Autoscaling:** scale on queue depth, TTFT or KV-cache usage; large models take minutes to load, so keep warm spare capacity, pre-load weights from fast storage, and use request queues to absorb bursts.

**Large MoE serving, 2025–26.** Teams now spread experts across dozens of GPUs, and balance load by copying busy experts. SGLang reported $0.20 per million output tokens for DeepSeek-V3 on 96 H100s, and vLLM 954K tokens per second per GPU, counting input and output, on one GB300 rack. These are their own results. See Serving Mixture-of-Experts Models.

#### Weights decide the replica, KV caches decide the fleet

Split the model just enough to fit (TP within a node, PP or EP beyond), then add replicas until every concurrent conversation's KV cache and the latency SLOs fit, and route traffic so caches stay warm.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "GPU count = model size / GPU memory"

It sounds right, since the weights have to fit. But that ignores the KV cache for concurrent users. Llama 3 70B in fp8 fits on 2 GPUs per replica, but each holds only 27 conversations, so 1,000 users still need 76 GPUs. And don't run tensor parallelism across the data centre: keep it inside a node.

## Say it

### How many GPUs for 1,000 users, and why may FP8 weights not help?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

TP across two nodes or PP across two nodes?

PP: tensor parallelism needs an all-reduce in every layer, which is too slow over inter-node links; pipeline stages only pass activations between stages.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why would TP=8 sometimes beat TP=4 even if the model fits on 4?

Lower latency per token (each GPU reads fewer weights per step) and more KV space per replica; the cost is more communication and fewer replicas.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you handle a 5× traffic spike?

Queue with priorities, shed or degrade low-priority traffic (shorter max tokens, smaller model), scale out from warm pools, and rely on prefix caching to cut prefill.

#### The 30-second answer

First I size a replica: weights plus KV headroom, using tensor parallelism within an NVLink node, pipeline parallelism across nodes if needed, and expert parallelism for MoE models. Then I size the fleet: concurrent conversations times KV cache per conversation, divided by the KV space per replica, checked against throughput and latency SLOs from a load test. Often the KV cache dominates, so FP8 weights alone may not cut GPU count, while GQA, MLA or an FP8 cache do. At large scale I'd disaggregate prefill and decode, as DeepSeek and NVIDIA Dynamo do, route with prefix and load awareness, and autoscale on queue depth with warm capacity because models load slowly.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "GPU count = model size / GPU memory." That ignores the KV cache for concurrent users.

- "Tensor parallelism across the data centre." Keep it inside a node.

**Key terms and sources**

How a model too big for one GPU is served (tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism), how many replicas a traffic level needs, why the KV cache rather than the weights often decides the GPU count, how large deployments split prefill and decode across clusters (DeepSeek-V3, Mooncake, NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d), and how routing and autoscaling work · built from Shoeybi et al. # Serving Mixture-of-Experts Models

> An MoE model activates only 37B of its 671B parameters. Why is it still hard and expensive to serve?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLM inference and serving › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/serving-moe-models/
- Before this: Scaling Inference: Parallelism, Replicas and Routing (`ai-engineering/scaling-inference`), Mixture of Experts (`fundamentals/mixture-of-experts`)
- Quiz topic: `infer`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team wants to switch to a large mixture-of-experts model, because it activates only 37B of its 671B parameters. Finance expects it to cost about the same as a 37B dense model. The interviewer asks:

> An MoE model activates only 37B of its 671B parameters. Why is it still hard and expensive to serve?

#### Why it matters

Most leading open models are now mixtures of experts. The usual interview line, "it only uses 37B parameters, so it's cheap", is only half true. The model is cheap per token in maths, but not in memory, and serving it well takes a different design from a dense model.

### The idea

Think of a hospital with 256 specialists, where each patient sees 8. One patient only needs 8 doctors on shift. But with 64 patients arriving together, almost every specialist is busy, and the hospital must employ all of them anyway. The busiest specialists set how fast the queue moves.

[Figure: Three facts. All experts need memory. Batches touch most experts. The busiest GPU sets the pace.]

_Cheap in maths, not in memory._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the batch from 1 to 64, then 256. Watch reads per step and per token.

#### Batch an MoE

Illustrative, for a DeepSeek-V3-like shape in FP8 at 1 byte per parameter: 671B total and 37B active, with 8 of 256 experts per token. That implies about 16.5B shared parameters and 654.5B in experts. Tokens pick experts at random. It ignores the KV cache and the network.

With **one token**, the model reads about 37 GB per step, as cheap as a 37B dense model. At **64 tokens**, the tokens touch about 87% of experts, and a step reads about 585 GB. That's why the memory bill follows the full 671B. But per token, it's about 9 GB, and at 256 tokens about 2.6 GB, against 70 GB for a dense 70B model in FP8. So MoE is efficient when you batch heavily across many GPUs, and less so for small, latency-sensitive deployments. Real routing is uneven, which makes the busiest experts matter even more.

**Now say why:** why does reading per step rise while reading per token falls?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token, so each token needs little maths. But every expert must be in memory, and with a batch, different tokens pick different experts. At batch size 1, a 671B model with 37B active reads about 37 GB per step. At batch size 64, it touches most experts and reads several hundred GB. Large deployments spread experts across many GPUs, which is called **expert parallelism**. Tokens then travel between GPUs to reach their experts, and popular experts become hotspots, so systems **replicate busy experts** to balance the load.

#### What changes for MoE

##### Active parameters aren't the whole story

- **Memory:** all experts must be loaded, so DeepSeek-V3 needs its full 671B parameters in memory.

- **Reads per step:** one token uses 8 of 256 routed experts per layer. But 64 tokens together touch most of them, so a batch reads most of the model each step.

- **Good news:** per token, the cost still falls with batch size, because those reads are shared. That's why MoE pays off at high throughput, and less so for one user on one GPU.

##### Expert parallelism

Put different experts on different GPUs. Each token is sent to the GPUs holding its chosen experts, and the results are sent back. These all-to-all exchanges happen in every MoE layer, so they need fast links, and engines overlap them with computing.

| Deployment | What was reported |
|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V3, by DeepSeek | Prefill on at least 32 GPUs, and decode on 320 GPUs across 40 nodes |
| SGLang, on 96 H100s | 52.3K input and 22.3K output tokens per second per node, for 2,000-token inputs. It estimated $0.20 per million output tokens |
| vLLM, on one GB300 rack | 954K tokens per second per GPU, counting input and output tokens, at 196 tokens per second per user |

These are each team's own results on different hardware and workloads, so they can't be compared with each other.

##### Load balancing

Some experts are far more popular than others, and the busiest GPU sets the pace for the whole step. Expert load balancing places extra copies of busy experts, and rearranges them as traffic shifts. SGLang reported that this gave 1.49× for prefill and 2.54× for decode. vLLM rearranges experts every 3,000 steps, based on the previous 1,000.

##### Splitting attention from experts

Attention and experts behave differently: attention reads each user's KV cache, while experts read shared weights. MegaScale-Infer runs them on separate GPUs and passes micro-batches back and forth, reporting up to 1.90× higher throughput per GPU. Another 2026 approach decodes with a pruned set of experts, reporting up to 1.81× decode throughput at 50% pruning, with some changes to output length that benchmarks can miss.

#### The maths

$$ {\mathbb{E}[\text{experts touched}]} = {E}\Big(1 - {\big(1 - \tfrac{k}{E}\big)^{B}}\Big) $$

Assumes tokens pick experts independently and uniformly, which real routing doesn’t. Real routing is skewed, so busy experts are touched even more, and others less.

- **experts read in one layer**: On average, if tokens choose experts at random.

- **experts per layer**: 256 routed experts in DeepSeek-V3.

- **the chance an expert is unused**: Each of the B tokens picks k experts. With 8 of 256, an expert is skipped by one token 31/32 of the time.

- **more tokens, more experts**: At batch 64, about 87% of experts are touched.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Choose by traffic:** for one user or a small team, a dense model or a small MoE on one GPU may be simpler. Large MoEs shine at high, steady throughput.

- **Watch the busiest GPU:** step time follows the most loaded expert, so track per-expert load, and rebalance.

- **Overlap communication:** all-to-all traffic needs fast links and overlap with computing, or it dominates.

- **Count tokens carefully:** published throughput may count input tokens, cached input or only output. Ask which before comparing.

- **Quantize the experts:** they hold most of the parameters, so FP8 or FP4 experts save the most memory.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Only 37B is active, so it costs like a 37B model"

It sounds right, since maths per token follows the active parameters. But you must store all 671B, and a batch of users touches most experts every step. It's efficient at high throughput across many GPUs, and much less so for a few users on a small deployment.

## Say it

### An MoE model activates only 37B of its 671B parameters. Why is it still hard and expensive to serve?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does an MoE model need so many GPUs if only 37B parameters are active?

All 671B must be stored, because any token may choose any expert. In FP8 that's about 671 GB before the KV cache, so you need many GPUs just to hold it.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What is expert load balancing, and why does it help?

Tokens prefer some experts, so the GPUs holding them become the bottleneck while others wait. Placing extra copies of busy experts, and moving them as traffic shifts, evens out the work.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Would you serve a big MoE for a single internal user?

Probably not. At small batch sizes you pay to hold the whole model, and gain little from sharing reads. A dense model, or a smaller MoE that fits on one GPU, is usually simpler and cheaper.

#### The 30-second answer

An MoE uses only a few experts per token, so maths per token is small, but every expert must be in memory, and a batch of tokens picks different experts. In my example, a 671B model with 37B active reads about 37 GB per step at batch 1, but about 585 GB at batch 64, because most experts get touched. Per token, though, that's only about 9 GB, so MoE pays off at high throughput. At scale I'd use expert parallelism, spreading experts across GPUs with all-to-all communication overlapped with computing, and balance load by replicating busy experts, which SGLang reported gave 2.54 times for decode. I'd also consider separating attention from experts.

**Key terms and sources**

Why MoE models need all their experts in memory, why batching ends up reading most experts, expert parallelism and all-to-all, load balancing with replicated experts, and separating attention from experts. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)

- [SGLang team, Deploying DeepSeek with PD Disaggregation and Large-Scale Expert Parallelism](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2025-05-05-large-scale-ep/)

- [vLLM, Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep)

- [Zhu et al., MegaScale-Infer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02263)

- [SlimWise: expert pruning across prefill and decode](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34117)

- [Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)
