# Automatic Prompt Optimisation

> Instead of hand-tuning prompts, your team wants an optimiser to write them. How do these work, and what can go wrong?

- Track: AI Engineering › Prompt engineering › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/automatic-prompt-optimization/
- Before this: Prompt Engineering Patterns (`ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-patterns`), RAG Evals: Retrieval, Faithfulness and Relevance (`ai-engineering/rag-evals`)
- Quiz topic: `prompt`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team spends days hand-tuning prompts for a multi-step pipeline. Someone suggests an optimiser, and a first run on 30 examples reports a 12-point gain. The interviewer asks:

> Instead of hand-tuning prompts, your team wants an optimiser to write them. How do these work, and what can go wrong?

#### Why it matters

Hand-tuning prompts by feel is slow, and a change that fixes one case can break others. If you already have a metric and labelled examples, an optimiser can search far more prompts than a person, and do it again whenever the model changes. Interviewers ask how these tools work, when they're worth it, and how you'd trust the result.

### The idea

Think of auditioning 100 singers with one short song each. The one who sounds best that day may just have been lucky with the song. A longer audition, or a second round, shows who's really best.

[Figure: Three parts. A metric and data. A search over prompts. A fair final check.]

_The winner of many noisy tries looks better than it is._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Try 100 prompts on 30 examples. Then raise the examples to 1,000.

#### The winner looks better than it is

Illustrative simulation, averaged over 1,500 runs. Each candidate's real accuracy is drawn around 75%, with a spread of 2 points, and its validation score adds sampling noise for the chosen number of examples.

Trying 10 prompts on 30 validation examples, the winner scores 87.5% on validation, but its real accuracy is 75.7%, so its score is overstated by 11.8 points. Try 100 prompts on the same 30 examples, and the gap grows to 19.3 points, as more candidates means more chances for noise to win. With 1,000 validation examples, 10 prompts are overstated by only 1.2 points, and the winner's real score, 77.5%, is close to the best available, 78.1%. That's the multiple-testing problem ESPO points to, with about 10 candidates on about 30 examples. Use more validation data, and confirm on a held-out test set.

**Now say why:** why does trying more prompts make the winner's score less trustworthy?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A prompt optimiser treats the prompt as something to search over. You give it a program, a metric and a few hundred labelled examples, and it proposes prompts, scores them, and keeps the best. Older methods searched over instructions and few-shot examples. **GEPA** reads the system's traces, reflects on failures in plain language, and rewrites prompts. It reported 14 points of gain against 7 for MIPROv2, and beat reinforcement learning with up to 35 times fewer runs. The risks: picking the best of many candidates on a small validation set flatters the winner, and optimised prompts can **bloat** with rules.

#### How optimisers work

##### What you need first

- **A program:** one or more LLM calls, such as retrieve, then answer.

- **A metric:** exact match, a code check, or an LLM judge.

- **Data:** a training set to learn from, and a separate validation set to choose the winner. Keep a held-out test set too.

##### The main methods

| Method | How it searches |
|---|---|
| **APE** (2022) | An LLM proposes many instructions from examples, and the best-scoring one is kept. |
| **OPRO** (2023) | An LLM sees earlier prompts with their scores, and proposes better ones. |
| **DSPy** (2023) | You write the pipeline as modules. It collects successful runs and uses them as few-shot examples. |
| **MIPROv2** (2024) | Proposes instructions and example sets, then picks combinations with Bayesian search. |
| **GEPA** (2025) | Reads full traces, including reasoning, tool calls and error messages, reflects on what went wrong, and rewrites prompts. It keeps the best prompt for each example, not one overall winner, so useful strategies survive. |

##### What GEPA reported

Across four tasks, GEPA improved the aggregate score by 14.29 points with GPT-4.1 mini, against 7.04 for MIPROv2. With Qwen3 8B, it gained 12.44 points, against 6.26 for MIPROv2 and 2.29 for GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that updates the model's weights over 24,000 runs. GEPA needed up to 35 times fewer runs, and its prompts were about 33% shorter than MIPROv2's. The authors expect weight updates to win when data and compute are plentiful.

##### Prompt bloat

Each round of reflection tends to add rules and caveats. A 2026 study, ESPO, found GEPA's prompts were up to 3 times longer than its own, at 1,878 characters on average against 1,004, yet less accurate, 70.9% against 74.7% across seven benchmarks. Its fixes: study all errors before rewriting, and choose the winner in a way that's stable under resampling. Longer prompts also cost more on every request.

#### The maths

$$ {\Pi^{*}} = \arg\max_{{\Pi}} \; {\mathbb{E}_{(x,m)}}\big[{\mu}(\Phi(x;\Pi), m)\big] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad {\#\text{runs} \le B} $$

The objective as the GEPA paper writes it. The catch is the expectation: you only see a small validation set, so the winner's score is an estimate, and choosing the best of many estimates flatters it.

- **the chosen prompts**: The best set of prompts found.

- **the prompts**: What the optimiser changes. The model’s weights stay fixed.

- **over real inputs**: Averaged over examples x with expected results m. In practice, a validation set stands in for it.

- **the metric**: How each output is scored.

- **the budget**: Each run costs money and time, so the search is limited.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Get the metric right first:** an optimiser will exploit a weak metric. Check a sample of outputs by hand.

- **Use enough validation data:** with a few dozen examples and many candidates, the winner's score is inflated. Confirm on a held-out test set before shipping.

- **Watch length:** track prompt length and cost per request alongside accuracy, and prefer the shorter prompt when scores are close.

- **Read the result:** optimised prompts can contain odd rules fitted to a few examples. Review them like code.

- **Re-run when the model changes:** a prompt tuned for one model is tied to it.

- **Know the alternative:** with lots of data and a fixed model you control, fine-tuning may win. See Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The optimiser found a prompt 12 points better"

It sounds convincing, but if it was chosen from many candidates on a few dozen examples, much of that gain can be noise. Check the winner on a fresh, larger test set, and watch its length and cost.

## Say it

### Instead of hand-tuning prompts, your team wants an optimiser to write them. How do these work, and what can go wrong?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

You have 25 labelled examples. Should you run an optimiser?

Probably not yet. With so few examples, the winner's score is mostly noise, and you can't hold out a test set. Label more real cases first, or use the examples to guide manual changes.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The optimised prompt scores 6 points higher on validation but no better in production. Why?

Likely overfitting: it was chosen from many candidates on a small set, or the validation data doesn't match production traffic. Check on a fresh, representative test set.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why might an optimiser beat fine-tuning with little data?

It learns from rich feedback, such as error messages and reasoning traces, rather than a single score per run, and a few rules in a prompt can fix a whole class of errors.

#### The 30-second answer

An optimiser treats prompts as parameters. I give it the pipeline, a metric and labelled data, and it proposes, scores and keeps better prompts. DSPy and MIPROv2 search over instructions and few-shot examples. GEPA reflects on full traces in plain language, and reported about 14 points of gain against 7 for MIPROv2, with far fewer runs than reinforcement learning. I watch two risks. Choosing the best of many prompts on a small validation set inflates the winner's score, so I confirm on held-out data. And prompts can bloat with rules, so I track length and cost too.

**Key terms and sources**

How prompt optimisers such as APE, OPRO, DSPy, MIPROv2 and GEPA search for better prompts against a metric, what they need, and the risks: overfitting to small validation sets and prompts that keep growing. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Zhou et al., Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01910)

- [Yang et al., Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.03409)

- [Khattab et al., DSPy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03714)

- [Opsahl-Ong et al., Optimizing Instructions and Demonstrations for Multi-Stage Language Model Programs (MIPROv2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11695)

- [Agrawal et al., GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457)

- [Liu et al., ESPO: Error-Structured Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04197)

# Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning: How to Choose

> Knowledge or behaviour: which tool fixes which gap?

- Track: AI Engineering › Prompt engineering › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/prompt-vs-rag-vs-fine-tuning/
- Before this: Prompt Engineering Patterns (`ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-patterns`), LoRA and QLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (`fundamentals/lora-and-qlora`)
- Quiz topic: `prompt`

## Intuition

### The situation

Three requests land on the team: answer from our latest refund policy, always reply in our brand voice and JSON format, and classify tickets into 40 categories, 2 million times a month. A colleague says to fine-tune for all of them. The interviewer asks:

> Knowledge or behaviour: which tool fixes which gap?

**Running example:** three requests land on the team: "answer from our latest refund policy", "always reply in our brand voice and JSON format", and "classify tickets into 40 categories, 2 million times a month".

#### Three tools, often confused

"Fine-tune it on our documents" is the most common wrong first instinct: it's slow to update, hard to cite and teaches facts poorly. "Just add it to the prompt" stops scaling once the prompt is thousands of tokens on millions of calls. Each tool changes a different thing.

### The idea

Think of a new hire again. Instructions on the day are the prompt. Handing them the current manual to look things up in is RAG. Months of drilling until it's habit is fine-tuning. You wouldn't drill someone on a manual that changes every few weeks.

[Figure: Three requests. The latest refund policy is changing knowledge, so use RAG. Brand voice and JSON format is behaviour, so start with a prompt, then LoRA. A classifier running 2 million times a month is a narrow skill at volume, so fine-tune a small model.]

_The lesson's three requests. Most real assistants use all three tools._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Describe each of the three requests with the buttons, and read the recommendation. Then change one thing at a time: how often it changes, the examples you have and the volume.

#### Describe the requirement

A simplified rule set summarising the guidance above; real decisions also weigh latency, privacy and team skills.

The refund-policy request is **missing, changing knowledge → RAG**: re-index when the policy changes, cite the clause. The brand voice and JSON request is **style/format**: start with a prompt and few-shot examples; with thousands of good examples, **LoRA fine-tuning** makes it consistent and shortens the prompt. The 2-million-a-month ticket classifier is a **narrow skill at high volume**: label data (possibly with a big model), **fine-tune a small model** and distil, cutting cost per call dramatically. The trap is picking one tool for everything; most real assistants use all three.

**Now say why:** why is fine-tuning a poor way to teach the refund policy?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Ask **what is missing**. If the model lacks **knowledge** (your policies, products, latest data) → **RAG**: it's updatable, citable, and beats fine-tuning for injecting facts (Ovadia et al. found retrieval consistently outperformed unsupervised fine-tuning on knowledge tasks). If it lacks **behaviour** (tone, format, a narrow skill done consistently) → **prompting** first, then **fine-tuning** once you have hundreds to thousands of good examples, or when long prompts become too slow or costly at volume. They combine: many production systems fine-tune a small model to follow the format and use RAG for the facts. The standard order is: prompt a capable model → add RAG → evaluate → fine-tune (and distil) only where data and volume justify it. What you'll be able to do after this: pick the right approach for a requirement and defend the choice with evidence and cost.

#### What each approach changes

| | Prompting | RAG | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Changes** | instructions in context | knowledge in context, per query | the model's weights (behaviour) |
| **Best for** | rules, format, quick iteration | facts that change; citations; large corpora | consistent style/format, narrow skills, shorter prompts, small models |
| **Data needed** | a few examples | documents | hundreds to thousands of high-quality examples |
| **Update speed** | instant | re-index (minutes) | retrain and redeploy |
| **Weak at** | long prompts cost tokens on every call | retrieval misses; style | new facts (and can increase hallucination), freshness, citations |

Gekhman et al. (2024) found that fine-tuning on facts the model didn't already know was learned slowly and increased hallucination. RAFT (Zhang et al. 2024) shows the combination: fine-tune the model to _use_ retrieved documents well, including ignoring distractors.

## In practice

### In practice

#### The usual escalation path

1. **Prompt a strong model** with clear rules and examples; build an evaluation set from day one.

2. **Add RAG** when answers need your data; measure retrieval recall and faithfulness separately.

3. **Optimise the prompt and pipeline** (re-ranking, structured output, routing) against the eval set. Automatic optimisers can help here: GEPA beat GRPO, a fine-tuning method, by about 10% on average with up to 35 times fewer runs, though its authors expect fine-tuning to win when data is plentiful. See Automatic Prompt Optimisation.

4. **Fine-tune** when you have data and a clear behaviour gap, or when volume makes long prompts and big models too expensive; often distil a big model's outputs into a smaller one.

5. **Keep evaluating:** every step must beat the previous one on the same eval set.

#### Knowledge goes in context, behaviour goes in weights

Use retrieval for what the model must know and fine-tuning for how it must behave, start with prompting, and let evaluation results and volume decide when to escalate.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Fine-tuning is how you teach the model your data"

It sounds right, since training is how a model learns. But it's slow to update and hard to cite, and fine-tuning on facts the model didn't already know was learned slowly and increased hallucination. Use RAG for facts. RAG won't fix tone and format either: that's prompting or fine-tuning.

## Say it

### Knowledge or behaviour: which tool fixes which gap?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

The business wants the model to "know" 5,000 product manuals. Fine-tune?

No: RAG over the manuals, with citations and re-indexing on updates; fine-tuning would learn the facts poorly, go stale, and can increase hallucination.

Follow-up 2 of 3

When does fine-tuning save money?

At high volume, when a fine-tuned small model replaces a large model with a long prompt; the training cost is repaid by cheaper calls.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How many examples for fine-tuning?

Format and style can improve with a few hundred high-quality examples; harder skills need thousands; quality and diversity matter more than count.

#### The 30-second answer

I start by asking what's missing. If it's knowledge, especially changing or citable knowledge, I use RAG: it's updatable and studies show it beats fine-tuning for injecting facts. If it's behaviour, tone, format or a narrow skill, I start with prompting and examples, and fine-tune with LoRA once I have enough good examples or when long prompts get too costly at high volume. They combine well: a fine-tuned small model for format plus RAG for facts. I escalate in order, prompt, then RAG, then fine-tuning and distillation, and every step has to win on the same evaluation set.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Fine-tuning is how you teach the model your data." Use RAG for facts.

- "RAG fixes tone and format." That's prompting or fine-tuning.

**Key terms and sources**

A practical decision framework for adapting an LLM to a product: what each approach changes (instructions, knowledge, behaviour), the evidence that fine-tuning is a poor way to add knowledge, how they combine (RAG + fine-tuned model, RAFT), the usual order of escalation, and the costs that decide it at scale · built from Ovadia et al. (Fine-Tuning or Retrieval?, EMNLP 2024), Gekhman et al. (EMNLP 2024), Zhang et al. (RAFT, 2024), Lewis et al. (RAG, 2020), Hu et al. (LoRA, 2022) and the OpenAI and Anthropic model-optimisation guides · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. O. Ovadia et al., "Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs", EMNLP 2024, [arXiv:2312.05934](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05934).

2. Z. Gekhman et al., "Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?", EMNLP 2024, [arXiv:2405.05904](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904).

3. T. Zhang et al., "RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG", 2024, [arXiv:2403.10131](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10131).

4. P. Lewis et al. (RAG), NeurIPS 2020, [arXiv:2005.11401](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401); E. Hu et al. (LoRA), ICLR 2022, [arXiv:2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

5. OpenAI, "Optimizing LLM accuracy" guide; Anthropic, model customisation and prompt engineering documentation.

6. L. A. Agrawal et al., "GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning", 2025, [arXiv:2507.19457](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457).

# A Prompt Fix That Broke Production

> A one-line prompt fix solved a reported bug, passed five spot checks, and broke other cases in production. What went wrong, and what process prevents it?

- Track: AI Engineering › Prompt engineering › Scenarios
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/prompt-change-broke-production/
- Before this: Prompt Engineering Patterns (`ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-patterns`), LLM Judges: Pairwise Preferences and Pass/Fail Checks (`ai-engineering/llm-as-a-judge`)
- Quiz topic: `prompt`

## Intuition

### The situation

A product manager reported one wrong answer. An engineer added a line to the prompt, checked five examples and shipped. The next day, escalations rose for cases nobody touched. The interviewer asks:

> A one-line prompt fix solved a reported bug, passed five spot checks, and broke other cases in production. What went wrong, and what process prevents it?

#### The incident

A support assistant gave a customer the wrong return window for sale items. The engineer added: "For sale items, always state that returns are not accepted." Five sale-item questions looked right, so it shipped. The next day, refund escalations rose. The new line also fired for full-price items bought during a sale, and for gift returns, which the policy allows. The average score on a small test set hadn't moved, because one case was fixed and a few others broke. The story is illustrative, but the pattern is common.

### The idea

Think of changing one word in a company-wide policy memo to fix one complaint. Every employee reads the memo, and some apply the new word to cases you never meant. Checking with five colleagues won't show how the whole company reads it.

[Figure: Three safeguards. Version every prompt. Run a regression set. Roll out gradually.]

_A prompt line applies to every request._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Run 5 test cases against a 2% break. Then raise the cases.

#### How many test cases catch a break?

Exact arithmetic for a random sample of traffic. The traffic figure is illustrative.

If the fix breaks 2% of requests, five spot checks catch it only 10% of the time. Fifty cases catch it 64% of the time, and 200 cases 98%. At 1% broken, you need about 299 random cases for a 95% chance. Meanwhile, at 100,000 requests a day, 2% is 2,000 bad answers. That's why a regression set of a few hundred cases, plus every past incident, runs on each change.

**Now say why:** why can the average stay flat while users get worse answers?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A product manager reports one bad answer. An engineer adds a line to the prompt, tries five examples, and ships. The next day, other answers have changed for the worse. A prompt is applied to every request, so a one-line change can shift behaviour everywhere, and small wording changes have moved accuracy by large amounts in studies. Five examples almost never catch a problem that affects 2% of requests. The fix is to treat prompts as code: **version** them, run a **regression set** that includes past incidents on every change, compare **case by case**, roll out gradually, and keep **rollback** one step away.

#### Why it happened

##### Prompts have global effects

Code changes usually affect one path. A prompt line is read on every request, and the model decides when it applies. Sclar et al. found that formatting changes alone, such as separators and spacing, changed accuracy by up to 76 points on some tasks for LLaMA-2-13B. A new rule can also conflict with old ones. See System Prompts with Many Rules.

##### Spot checks can't see rare breaks

If a change breaks 2% of requests, five random examples show none of them about 90% of the time. And an average hides trades: one fix and one new failure score the same as no change.

##### Other things change behaviour too

- **The model:** a provider updates a model alias, or you switch models. Pin a dated model version where possible.

- **The schema and tools:** field descriptions and tool definitions are read as instructions.

- **Retrieved context:** a re-index changes what the model sees.

##### What the process should be

1. **Version the prompt** in the repository, with the model version, reviewed like code.

2. **Keep a regression set:** real requests across the main intents, every past incident, and edge cases. Each has expected behaviour checked by code or an LLM judge.

3. **Compare case by case:** list which cases got better and which got worse, not just the average.

4. **Roll out gradually:** shadow traffic or a small percentage, with live metrics such as escalations. See Design an LLM Prompt Test.

5. **Roll back fast:** switch to the previous version by its ID, without a redeploy.

#### The maths

$$ {P(\text{see a break})} = 1 - (1 - {f})^{{n}} $$

This assumes test cases are a random sample of traffic. Adding past incidents and edge cases on purpose catches known risks with fewer cases.

- **chance the test catches it**: The probability at least one broken case appears in your test set.

- **share of requests broken**: How much of your traffic the change makes worse.

- **test cases**: How many representative cases you run.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What to say

- **Diagnose:** the line applied more widely than intended, and five examples couldn't show a 2% problem.

- **Fix now:** roll back to the previous version, then write a narrower rule with the reason, for example "items bought at a sale price can't be returned, except gifts, because the policy says so".

- **Add cases:** the original bug, full-price items bought during a sale, and gift returns go into the regression set.

- **Prevent:** versioned prompts, a regression set run on every change, case-by-case comparison, gradual rollout with live metrics, and one-step rollback.

- **Consider structure:** if the rule is really policy logic, look it up in code and pass the result to the model, rather than asking the model to apply it.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It passed my spot checks, so it's safe"

It sounds reasonable, since the fixed case works. But five examples miss a problem affecting 2% of requests about 90% of the time. Run a regression set of a few hundred cases, including past incidents, and compare case by case.

## Say it

### A one-line prompt fix solved a reported bug, passed five spot checks, and broke other cases in production. What went wrong, and what process prevents it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

The average score is unchanged after a prompt edit. Is it safe to ship?

Not necessarily. One fixed case and one new failure average out. Look at which cases changed in each direction.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The provider updated the model and answers changed, with no prompt change. How do you prevent this?

Pin a dated model version, and run the regression set before moving to a new one, the same as a prompt change.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How big should a regression set be?

Big enough to catch the failure rates you care about: about 300 random cases for a 95% chance of seeing a 1% problem. Add every past incident and known edge case on top.

#### The 30-second answer

A prompt line applies to every request, and the model decides when it fires, so a narrow fix can change behaviour everywhere. Five spot checks miss a problem that affects 2% of requests about 90% of the time. I'd roll back first, then write a narrower rule with its reason, and add the original bug and the new failures to a regression set. Going forward, prompts are versioned with the model, every change runs a few hundred cases including past incidents, I compare case by case rather than the average, and I roll out gradually with one-step rollback.

**Key terms and sources**

A scenario: why prompt changes have global effects, why spot checks miss regressions, and how to version, evaluate, roll out and roll back prompts like code. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Sclar et al., Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11324)

- [Anthropic, Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

- [OpenAI, GPT-5 prompting guide (archived cookbook)](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt-5/gpt-5_prompting_guide)

- [Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Many recent papers are preprints, and vendor guides change with each model.

# Prompt Engineering Practice

> 8 questions: effort costs, layout, many rules, regression sets, optimisers, schemas and migrations.

- Track: AI Engineering › Prompt engineering › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-practice/
- Before this: A Prompt Fix That Broke Production (`ai-engineering/prompt-change-broke-production`)
- Quiz topic: `prompt`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Work each one out, then open the answer and compare.

**The toolkit:** cost = input tokens × input price + (hidden + visible tokens) × output price; P(all N rules kept) ≈ pN; P(test catches a break) = 1 − (1 − f)n; standard error of an accuracy = √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).

Question 1 · Easy · reasoning effort

### Your app sends 10,000 requests a day to a reasoning model. At medium effort it writes about 4,000 hidden tokens per request, and at low effort about 1,000, with the same accuracy on your evaluations. Output costs $10 per million tokens. What does switching to low save?

Answer: **About $300 a day, or $9,000 a month**

1. Tokens saved per request: 4,000 − 1,000 = 3,000.

2. Per day: 3,000 × 10,000 = 30 million tokens.

3. 30 × $10 = $300 a day, and about $9,000 over 30 days.

Answers also arrive faster, as hidden tokens are generated before the visible answer.

Question 2 · Easy · long-context layout

### You pass a 40-page contract and ask one question about it. Where do the contract and the question go in the prompt, and why?

Answer: **The contract first, inside tags, and the question at the end**

1. Anthropic reports that putting the question after long documents can improve answers by up to 30% on complex inputs.

2. Wrap the document in tags, such as <contract>, so it's clearly data, not instructions.

3. Optionally ask the model to quote the relevant clauses before answering.

Google gives the same advice for Gemini: context first, then the question, introduced with a line like "Based on the information above".

Question 3 · Medium · many rules

### A system prompt has 15 rules, each followed 97% of the time when triggered. If a conversation triggers all of them, how often are all kept? What if 5 hard rules move into code?

Answer: **About 63%, rising to about 74%**

1. 0.9715 ≈ 0.633.

2. With 5 rules in code, 10 are left to the model: 0.9710 ≈ 0.737.

3. This assumes independent failures. A stress test found real models fell even faster as rules were added.

Which rules go into code? Hard limits with no judgement needed, such as refund caps and allowed tools.

Question 4 · Medium · regression sets

### A prompt change breaks 1% of requests. With a random test set, how many cases do you need for a 95% chance of seeing at least one broken case? What does a 100-case set give you?

Answer: **About 300 cases. 100 cases give about 63%**

1. Solve 1 − 0.99n ≥ 0.95, so n ≥ ln 0.05 ÷ ln 0.99 ≈ 298.1, which rounds up to 299.

2. With 100 cases: 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 0.634.

Seeing one broken case isn't enough to measure the rate, but it's enough to stop and look.

Question 5 · Medium · optimiser results

### Your baseline prompt scores 78% on a 50-example validation set. An optimiser tries 30 prompts, and the best scores 84%. Is the 6-point gain convincing?

Answer: **No. It's within what chance alone would give**

1. Standard error at 78% with 50 examples: √(0.78 × 0.22 ÷ 50) ≈ 0.059, or about 6 points.

2. So 6 points is about one standard error.

3. Even if all 30 prompts were really no better than the baseline, the best of 30 noisy scores would land about 2 standard errors, or 12 points, above its true value by chance.

What do you do? Score the winner and the baseline on a fresh, larger test set before shipping.

Question 6 · Hard · schema conflicts

### A classifier's category definitions live in the system prompt. Months later, someone edits the definitions there, but the JSON schema's field descriptions still hold the old ones. Accuracy drops on one model, but not another. Why?

Answer: **Schema descriptions act as a second instruction channel, and models weight them differently**

1. In a 2026 study, contradictory schema descriptions cut accuracy by 5 to 45 points, depending on the model.

2. Claude Haiku 4.5 fell from 52.5% to 7.1%, while GPT-4.1 barely moved.

3. Fix: keep definitions in one place and generate both the prompt and the schema from it.

The same study found a required reasoning field before the label added 15 to 24 points where there was room to improve.

Question 7 · Medium · structured output

### A colleague cites a 2024 paper saying JSON output hurts reasoning, and wants to drop structured output. What do you say?

Answer: **The finding is disputed. Test it, and put reasoning before the answer**

1. Tam et al. found format restrictions lowered reasoning scores.

2. A rerun by the Outlines team (dottxt) used matching prompts, and found structured output scored the same or slightly better, such as 0.78 against 0.77 on GSM8K with Llama-3-8B.

3. Either way, a reasoning field before the answer field lets the model think first.

Run both versions on your own evaluation set. The result depends on the model and the prompt.

Question 8 · Hard · migration

### You move an assistant to a reasoning model. The old prompt has a 12-step procedure, "think step by step", and a prefilled start to the answer. Latency triples, and one model returns an error. What do you change?

Answer: **Remove the old scaffolding, then tune the effort setting**

1. The prefill causes the error: some newer models no longer accept a prefilled assistant turn. Ask for the format directly, or use structured output.

2. Replace the 12 steps with the goal, the constraints and the output format. Keep steps only where evaluations show they help.

3. Drop "think step by step", and try low or medium effort to bring latency down.

Re-run the evaluation set after each change, so you know which one mattered.

**More practice and sources**

8 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 7 Nov 2026

Keep practising

Uses Prompt Engineering Patterns, Prompting Reasoning Models, Structured Output, System Prompts with Many Rules, Automatic Prompt Optimisation and A Prompt Fix That Broke Production. Scenarios and prices are invented, so the answers are worked examples, except where a study is named.

# RAG End to End

> How do you build RAG, and how big should a chunk be?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end/
- Before this: Search: BM25, Dense and Hybrid Retrieval (`fundamentals/search-and-retrieval`), Embeddings and Representation Learning (`fundamentals/embeddings`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

The support assistant must answer from a 30-rule refund and service policy that changes every few weeks. Putting it all in every prompt is expensive, and a colleague's plan to fine-tune on it would need redoing at every update. The interviewer asks:

> How do you build RAG, and how big should a chunk be?

**Running example (this track):** the food-delivery support assistant must answer from the company's 30-rule refund and service policy, which changes every few weeks.

#### The model doesn't know your documents

Pre-trained knowledge is general, frozen at a cutoff and can't be cited. Putting every document in every prompt is slow and expensive, and models use very long contexts unevenly. Fine-tuning on documents teaches facts poorly and must be redone at every update. Retrieval gives the model just the passages it needs, fresh each time.

### The idea

Think of an open-book exam. Nobody expects the student to memorise the book, but the answer can only be as good as the pages they turn to. So most of the work is indexing the book well and finding the right pages quickly.

[Figure: Offline: parse, chunk, embed and index your documents. Online: take the query, retrieve, re-rank and generate an answer from those chunks.]

_The pipeline, stage by stage. Each stage has its own typical failure._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Try 1-sentence chunks, then 3, 5 and 10. Watch the questions answered and the context sent. Then try 2 sentences with a 1-sentence overlap.

#### How big should a chunk be?

A 30-sentence refund and service policy; 8 customer questions, several needing two adjacent sentences (e.g. "10% refund" + "capped at ₹150"). Retrieval: TF-IDF cosine, top 3 chunks. A question counts as answered only if every sentence it needs is in the retrieved chunks. Tokens ≈ words × 1.3.

With **1-sentence** chunks, retrieval is precise (39 tokens per question) but only **4 of 8** questions get their full answer: answers that need two sentences ("the refund is 10%" + "capped at ₹150") are split across chunks that don't both make the top 3. Bigger chunks keep related sentences together: 3 sentences get 7 of 8 at 115 tokens, 5 get all 8 at 194, and 10-sentence chunks also get 8 of 8 but send **379** tokens of mostly irrelevant policy, which costs money and can distract the model. Adding a **1-sentence overlap** to 2-sentence chunks gets **all 8** at just **77 tokens**: boundaries no longer cut answers in half. Real systems tune chunk size and overlap on their own questions, and prefer splitting on document structure (sections, list items) over fixed counts.

Overlap rescues this small example, as answers sit right next to each other. Larger studies have found little average gain from overlap, so test it on your own data. See Parsing and Chunking.

**Now say why:** small chunks are so precise, so why do they miss half the answers?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

An LLM doesn't know your refund policy, and it was trained months ago. **RAG** fetches the relevant text at question time and puts it in the prompt, so answers are grounded, current and citable. The pipeline: **ingest** documents (parse PDFs, HTML, tables) → **chunk** them into passages → **embed** each chunk into a vector → store in a **vector index** (HNSW or IVF for approximate nearest-neighbour search) → at query time, embed the question, **retrieve** the top-k chunks (often hybrid with BM25), and **generate** an answer from them with citations. Most quality problems are retrieval problems, and chunking is the first knob: chunks too small split answers across pieces; too large and you send lots of irrelevant text. What you'll be able to do after this: draw the RAG pipeline, choose chunking and index settings, and say where RAG systems fail.

#### The pipeline, stage by stage

| Stage | Choices | Typical failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Ingest & parse** | PDF/HTML/table extraction, OCR, metadata (source, date, section) | tables garbled, headers lost, stale versions indexed |
| **Chunk** | fixed size (e.g. 200–800 tokens) with overlap; by structure (headings, paragraphs); semantic, though evidence for it is weak | answer split across chunks; chunks without context ("it is capped at…") |
| **Embed** | an embedding model chosen on a benchmark like MTEB and on your own queries; same model for docs and queries | domain terms, codes and names embed poorly |
| **Index** | HNSW graph (fast, memory-heavy), IVF/PQ (compressed, for billions); a vector DB or Postgres with pgvector | approximate search misses neighbours (recall < 100%); no metadata filtering |
| **Retrieve** | top-k by cosine, hybrid with BM25, metadata filters (date, product), re-ranking | right chunk ranked 12th; filters missing |
| **Generate** | prompt with chunks + instructions to answer only from them and cite sources; say "not found" otherwise | model ignores context or blends in its own knowledge |

Barnett et al. (2024) list seven failure points, from missing content and missed top-ranked documents to answers not extracted from the context and wrong format. The two scenario pages in this track (wrong answer, at scale) practise diagnosing them.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Production defaults

- **Hybrid retrieval** (BM25 + dense, fused with RRF) plus a **re-ranker** on the top 20–50; see Advanced RAG.

- **Metadata** on every chunk (source, section, date, access rights) for filtering, citations and permission checks.

- **Index choice:** HNSW for up to tens of millions of vectors in memory; IVF with product quantization (FAISS) or disk-based indexes for larger corpora; keep exact search for small collections. Measure recall@k of the ANN index against exact search.

- **Prompt:** put the most relevant chunks first or last (models use the middle of long contexts less well), number them, and require citations; instruct the model to say when the answer isn't in the context.

- **Freshness:** incremental re-indexing when documents change, and remove old versions.

Go deeper: Parsing and Chunking, Embeddings and Vector Indexes, Permissions and Poisoning and Keeping an Index Current. If your documents are small, you may not need an index: see When Not to Index.

#### Retrieval quality caps answer quality

RAG gives the model the right passages at question time; the generator can only be as good as what retrieval hands it, so most of the engineering goes into parsing, chunking, indexing and ranking.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just use a vector database"

It sounds right, since vector search is the part everyone talks about. But parsing, chunking and ranking matter more, and retrieval quality caps answer quality. RAG doesn't eliminate hallucination either: the model can still ignore or misread the context, so you have to measure faithfulness.

## Say it

### How do you build RAG, and how big should a chunk be?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you choose the embedding model?

Shortlist from MTEB for retrieval in your languages and domain, then test recall@k on a few hundred real queries with labelled relevant chunks; consider cost, dimension and latency.

Follow-up 2 of 3

HNSW vs IVF-PQ?

HNSW gives high recall and low latency but stores full vectors plus a graph in memory; IVF-PQ compresses vectors and scales to billions with some recall loss.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you handle access control?

Store permissions as chunk metadata and filter at retrieval time (before ranking), so users never retrieve documents they can't see.

#### The 30-second answer

RAG retrieves relevant passages from your own data at query time and puts them in the prompt, so answers are grounded, up to date and citable without retraining. Offline you parse documents, chunk them with some overlap or by structure, embed each chunk and store it in a vector index such as HNSW, with metadata. Online you embed the query, retrieve top-k with hybrid BM25 plus dense search and metadata filters, re-rank, and prompt the model to answer only from the context with citations or say it can't find it. Chunking is a key trade-off: small chunks split answers, large chunks add noise and cost. I'd evaluate retrieval recall and answer faithfulness separately.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Just use a vector database." Parsing, chunking and ranking matter more.

- "RAG eliminates hallucination." The model can still ignore or misread the context.

**Key terms and sources**

# Parsing and Chunking

> Your RAG misreads tables and splits answers in half. How do you parse and chunk documents?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/parsing-and-chunking/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your policy assistant answers plain questions well, but gets refund amounts wrong. You look at the chunks, and the table's headers are in one chunk and its values are in another. A colleague suggests a smarter chunker. The interviewer asks:

> Your RAG misreads tables and splits answers in half. How do you parse and chunk documents?

#### Why it matters

RAG End to End shows the chunk size trade-off. In real systems, though, the damage often starts earlier. Uber's team found PDF loaders "often fail to correctly capture structured text and formatting (such as bullet points and tables)", and tried several without finding a universal solution. If a table's headers are gone, no retriever can bring them back.

### The idea

Think of photocopying a recipe book and cutting it into cards. If the copier scrambles the ingredients table, no filing system can save you. And if you cut through the middle of a recipe, each card is useless alone. So get a clean copy first, then cut along the natural breaks.

[Figure: Three steps. Parse cleanly, keeping tables and headings. Split on structure. Add context if a chunk can't stand alone.]

_You can't recover what parsing lost._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start with flattened text at 20 words. Then raise the size. Then keep the table.

#### Break a table

Exact calculation on a short invented refund policy with one table, and 6 questions. Retrieval takes the top 2 chunks by word overlap with the question. A question counts as answerable only if a single retrieved chunk holds the row, the column header and the value. The box shows how the chunk holding the first table row looks.

With **flattened text at 10 words**, only 2 of 6 questions can be answered, as the table's headers land in one chunk and its values in others. Keep the **table row by row**, and it's 4 of 6 at the same size, because every row carries its own headers. At 20 words both reach 6 of 6, but the kept table sends 23 words per question, against 40 for flattened. Raise flattened text to 120 words, and it still scores 6 of 6, but it sends 103 words, as the whole policy is one chunk. This lab also flatters flattened text: it only checks that the words share a chunk. A model still has to work out which number belongs to which column.

**Now say why:** why does a big chunk answer more, yet still cost more?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Before you can retrieve anything, messy documents have to become clean text. **Parsing** is where tables lose their headers and scanned pages lose their layout. **Chunking** then decides what each retrieved piece contains. The best start is simple: split on the document's own structure, keep tables whole, and test a few sizes on your own questions. **Semantic chunking** is often not worth its cost. If a chunk doesn't make sense alone, add context with **contextual** or **late chunking**. For pages full of charts, you can embed the **page image** instead.

#### From documents to chunks

##### Parsing comes first

| Content | What goes wrong | What helps |
|---|---|---|
| **Tables** | Rows flatten, headers separate from values | Convert to markdown, repeat headers per row, and never split one mid-table |
| **Headings and lists** | Lost, so a chunk doesn't know its section | Prefer a source with structure, such as HTML, and keep the heading path as metadata |
| **Scans and charts** | OCR drops layout and labels | Layout-aware parsing, captions, or embedding the page image |

Uber moved its policy documents from PDFs to a format with headings and tables it could extract reliably, used an LLM to turn tables into markdown, and gave each table chunk a short summary and keywords.

##### Chunking methods

| Method | How | Evidence and cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed size** | Every N tokens or sentences | Cheap, and a strong baseline |
| **Structure-aware** | Split on headings, paragraphs, list items and tables | Cheap once parsing works. Our suggested default |
| **Semantic** | Split where similarity between sentences drops | Qu et al. found gains were inconsistent, and didn't justify the cost |
| **Contextual** | An LLM adds a sentence of context to each chunk | Anthropic: failures fell from 5.7% to 3.7%, at $1.02 per million document tokens |
| **Late chunking** | Embed the whole document, then pool tokens per chunk | About 3% better than naive chunking on four test sets, with no LLM call |
| **Small to big** | Search small pieces, then send their surrounding section | Precise matching with enough context. In ARAGOG, sentence window retrieval had the best precision |

##### What the evidence says

- **The choice does matter:** in one 450-setup study, 20 chunking setups spanned 0.126 in NDCG@10, a 36% relative gap.

- **Semantic chunking isn't a free win:** Qu et al. saw it help mainly on artificial documents stitched from different topics. On real ones, fixed size often did as well or better.

- **Overlap isn't magic:** Qu et al. saw little from a 1-sentence overlap, and a 16-token overlap showed no clear advantage in the late chunking paper. It can still rescue an answer cut at a boundary, so test it rather than assume it.

- **Chunking still beats no chunking:** even long-context embedding models did better on chunks in most tests, with a 24% average gain at 512 tokens.

##### Pages as images

ColPali embeds page images directly and skips OCR. In one benchmark on financial and technical reports, page-image retrieval beat all the text pipelines. Single-vector page images were also cheap, while the multi-vector version used over 5 GB and took over 20 seconds per query. These documents are visually rich, so don't assume the same result for plain text.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{chunks}} \approx \frac{{D}}{{s - o}}, \qquad {\text{context sent}} = {k} \times {s} $$

Simple arithmetic for fixed-size chunks with overlap. Structure-aware chunks vary in size, so use the average.

- **chunks in the index**: More chunks mean more embedding cost and more memory.

- **document length**: Total tokens to split.

- **chunk size minus overlap**: Each new chunk moves forward by this much, so overlap adds chunks.

- **what the model reads**: Every retrieved chunk goes in the prompt.

- **chunks retrieved**: More chunks raise the chance of including the answer, and add noise.

- **chunk size again**: Doubling it doubles the cost per question.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Look at your chunks:** print a sample of real chunks, especially tables, before tuning anything. Most parsing bugs are obvious once you see them.

- **Keep metadata:** store the source, section path, page, date and permissions with each chunk. You need them for filters and citations.

- **Test on your own questions:** compare two or three chunk sizes on labelled questions, measuring recall and answer quality, because the best size varies by corpus.

- **Test in the full pipeline:** a chunker that wins alone may not win alongside your re-ranker.

- **Re-indexing costs money:** changing chunks means re-embedding. See Keeping an Index Current.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We just need a smarter chunker"

It sounds right, since chunking is the obvious knob. But if parsing has already scrambled a table, no chunker can restore it. Studies also found that semantic chunking often doesn't beat fixed size. Look at your real chunks first, because the problem is usually visible.

## Say it

### Your RAG misreads tables and splits answers in half. How do you parse and chunk documents?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's the difference between contextual chunking and late chunking?

Contextual chunking uses an LLM to write context, then adds it to the chunk's text, so BM25 benefits too, at a cost per chunk. Late chunking embeds the whole document, then pools token vectors per chunk, with no LLM call. It needs a long-context embedding model, and only helps vector search.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Should you always use overlap?

Not by default. Studies have found little average gain, though it can rescue an answer cut at a boundary. It also adds chunks and duplicates in results. Test it on your own questions, and prefer splitting on real boundaries.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A question's answer spans two sections. What do you do?

First check whether the chunks hold together. Try retrieving small pieces and sending their surrounding section, or merging neighbouring chunks at answer time. If the question really needs several facts, query decomposition or a second retrieval step may be the real fix.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd start with parsing, because if a table loses its headers, no retriever can fix it. I'd keep tables whole, preserve headings as metadata, and look at real chunks by hand. For chunking, I'd split on document structure first, then test two or three sizes on labelled questions. Evidence for semantic chunking is weak: one study found its gains inconsistent and not worth the cost. If chunks don't make sense alone, I'd add context, either with an LLM-written sentence, as in contextual retrieval, or with late chunking, which embeds the whole document before pooling each chunk. For visual documents like financial reports, I'd consider embedding page images instead.

**Key terms and sources**

Why parsing often matters more than chunk size, keeping tables and structure intact, what the evidence says about semantic chunking and overlap, contextual and late chunking, and page images. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Qu, Bao and Tu, Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13070)

- [Günther et al., Late Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04701)

- [Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

# Embeddings and Vector Indexes

> You have 100 million chunks. Which embedding model and index do you use, and what does it cost?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 22 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/embeddings-and-vector-indexes/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`), Embeddings and Representation Learning (`fundamentals/embeddings`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're indexing 100 million chunks. The team picked the top model on a leaderboard, and float32 vectors. The memory bill is huge, and since you added a department filter, some users say search has got worse, with no errors in the logs. The interviewer asks:

> You have 100 million chunks. Which embedding model and index do you use, and what does it cost?

#### Why it matters

At a million chunks, almost anything works. At a hundred million, the choice of index decides your bill, and a filter can silently drop your recall. These are also common questions in a RAG design interview: how would you size this, and what happens when you filter?

### The idea

Think of a giant library map. The embedding model decides where each book goes, and shorter coordinates take less paper but are less exact. The index is the road network. Close most roads for a filter, and you can't reach the books, even though they're still there.

[Figure: Three decisions. Pick a model by testing it. Compress vectors. Check recall under your filters.]

_A filter can quietly destroy recall._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Size your corpus, and switch encoding. Then move the filter down to 1%.

#### Size it, then filter it

Memory is exact arithmetic. Quality kept is Hugging Face's best case, and it varies by model, as binary needs rescoring. Recall is from Qdrant's own benchmark on 1 million deep-image vectors at hnsw_ef = 64, using a single keyword filter. It isn't linked to the other sliders, and your data will differ.

100 million 1,024-dimensional chunks in float32 need about **410 GB** of memory for vectors alone. Binary cuts that to **12.8 GB**, and the graph's links then cost about as much as the vectors. Now move the filter. At **10%**, a plain graph's recall falls to 20.6%, and at **1%** to just 0.1%, while the query still returns quickly. Nothing errors, so you'd only notice by measuring. A graph built with the filter in mind holds 99%. That's the main trap of filtered search.

**Now say why:** why is there no error when recall collapses?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Your embedding model decides what can be found, and your index decides how fast and at what cost. Choose a model by testing it on **your own queries**, not on a leaderboard alone. Vectors can be made far smaller: **Matryoshka** models can be shortened, **int8** is 4 times smaller, and **binary** is 32 times smaller if you re-score the top results. **Filters** can quietly break graph search, because the graph's links lead to points you've filtered out. And single vectors have a hard limit, so keep BM25 and a re-ranker in the stack.

#### Models, compression and indexes

##### Choosing a model

- **Shortlist from a benchmark** such as MTEB, for your language and domain.

- **Test on your data:** measure recall@k on a few hundred real labelled queries. A leaderboard rank needn't predict your result.

- **It matters a lot:** in one 450-setup study, the embedding model was among the largest factors in retrieval quality. In Qu et al., it outweighed the chunking method.

##### Making vectors smaller

| Method | Size | Quality kept | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Matryoshka** | Keep the first N dimensions | One study: 768 of 1,024 dimensions gave 25% less storage, and NDCG@10 rose 2.3% | Only for models trained this way |
| **int8** | 4× smaller | About 99.3% | Needs a calibration set |
| **Binary + rescoring** | 32× smaller | Up to about 96% | Strongly depends on the model: 96.45%, 87.7% and 74.77% across three tested models |

Quantization figures are from Hugging Face's benchmark on retrieval tasks, measured against full float32 vectors. Rescoring means searching with binary vectors, then re-scoring the top results with higher precision vectors.

##### Choosing an index

| Index | Idea | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat** | Compare with every vector | Small collections. Perfect recall |
| **HNSW** | Hop through a layered graph | High recall at low latency, with memory for links |
| **IVF, IVF-PQ** | Search the nearest clusters, with optional compression | Very large collections, at some recall cost |

##### Why filters break graphs

HNSW walks from node to node through links. If a filter removes most nodes, the walk runs out of valid paths. Qdrant notes that with 96% of points filtered out, fewer than one link per node survives on average. The lab uses its numbers. Fixes include building extra links for filter fields, graph repair methods like ACORN, and simply scanning the matching rows when very few match. A separate 2026 study found partition indexes (IVFFlat) beat HNSW at very low selectivity, and that pgvector's planner often chose poor plans. So measure recall for each filter you use.

##### A single vector has limits

Weller et al. show that a fixed number of dimensions can't represent every possible set of top results. On their deliberately hard LIMIT test, with simple questions like "who likes apples?", the best single-vector models reached under 20% recall@100. BM25 reached 93.6%, and a multi-vector model 54.8%. This test is built to stress that weakness, so everyday scores won't look like this. But it's a good reason to keep BM25 and a re-ranker.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{bytes per vector}} \approx {d \times b} + {8M} $$

The FAISS guideline for HNSW memory. Real systems also store IDs, metadata and the chunk text, and upper graph layers add a little.

- **memory per vector**: What each chunk costs in RAM, before metadata and text.

- **the vector**: d dimensions at b bytes each: 4 for float32, 1 for int8 and 1/8 for binary.

- **the graph**: HNSW stores about 2M links on its base layer, at 4 bytes each. M is usually 16 to 32.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Measure index recall:** compare ANN results with exact search on your own vectors, at your real filters, and watch p99 latency too.

- **Keep exact search when you can:** below a few hundred thousand vectors, or for very selective filters, a flat scan may be simpler and better.

- **Store full vectors on disk:** keep float32 on disk for rescoring, and in-memory binary for the first pass.

- **Check the model card:** don't truncate vectors unless the model was trained for it, or test first.

- **Plan for change:** a new model means new vectors everywhere. See Keeping an Index Current.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The top model on the leaderboard is the best for us"

It sounds right, since the benchmark is rigorous. But it measures other people's data and questions. Your names, codes and language may behave differently, and memory cost matters too. Shortlist from a benchmark, then decide by recall on a few hundred of your own labelled queries.

## Say it

### You have 100 million chunks. Which embedding model and index do you use, and what does it cost?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Estimate memory for 50 million chunks at 768 dimensions in float32, with HNSW at M = 16.

Vectors: 50M × 768 × 4 bytes = 153.6 GB. Links: 50M × 8 × 16 bytes = 6.4 GB. So about 160 GB, plus the chunk text and metadata. As int8, the vectors fall to 38.4 GB.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does a filter hurt recall in HNSW, but return quickly?

The walk follows links, and most neighbours have been filtered out, so it ends early with too few valid results. It's fast because it did little work. Nothing errors, so you only notice by measuring recall with that filter.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Should you truncate a 1,536-dimensional vector to 256 to save money?

Only if the model was trained for it, as in Matryoshka models. Then test recall on your data. Truncating other models usually hurts a lot. If you plan to use binary too, be careful, as very few dimensions leave very few bits.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd shortlist embedding models from a benchmark like MTEB, then pick by recall on a few hundred of my own labelled queries. For memory, 100 million 1,024-dimensional float32 vectors need about 410 GB. int8 is 4 times smaller at about 99% quality, and binary is 32 times smaller at up to 96% with rescoring, though that varies a lot by model. I'd use HNSW for high recall at low latency, or IVF-PQ at very large scale. Filters are the main trap, as they cut the graph's paths: in one benchmark a plain graph fell to 20% recall on a 10% filter. So I'd use a filter-aware index and measure recall per filter. Single vectors also have limits, so I'd keep BM25 and a re-ranker.

**Key terms and sources**

Choosing an embedding model, shortening vectors with Matryoshka, scalar and binary quantization, HNSW and IVF memory, why filters break graph search, and the limits of a single vector. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Qdrant, Filtered Vector Search and ACORN](https://qdrant.tech/articles/filtered-vector-search-acorn/)

# Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Re-ranking, Query Rewriting and GraphRAG

> Which upgrade cut retrieval failures by 67%?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/advanced-rag/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

The assistant's RAG works for most questions, but misses order IDs like ORD-48213, vague ones like "that thing with my money back" and two-part ones. A colleague wants to jump straight to GraphRAG and agents. The interviewer asks:

> How do you improve retrieval, and which upgrades cut failures by 67%?

**Running example:** the support assistant's RAG works for most questions but misses ones with order IDs ("ORD-48213"), vague ones ("that thing with my money back"), and two-part ones ("refund for late and cold food?").

#### Dense top-k isn't enough

Embedding similarity blurs exact identifiers, chunks lose meaning when cut out of their document, the best chunk is often ranked 8th rather than 1st, and user questions are vague, multi-part or phrased nothing like the documents. Each has a targeted fix.

### The idea

Think of hiring. You can't interview every applicant, so a quick CV screen makes a wide shortlist and a slow interview picks from it. Retrieval is the screen, which has to keep the right person in the pile. The re-ranker is the interview.

[Figure: Top-20 retrieval failure rate. Plain embeddings 5.7 percent. With contextual embeddings 3.7. With contextual BM25 2.9. With re-ranking 1.9, a 67 percent reduction.]

_From Anthropic's "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" (Sept 2024). This is retrieval failure, not end-to-end answer accuracy._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Stack the upgrades one at a time: plain embeddings, contextual embeddings, contextual BM25 and re-ranking. Note what each adds.

#### How much does each step buy?

Numbers from Anthropic's "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" (Sept 2024): share of queries whose relevant chunk was not in the top 20, averaged over their test datasets (codebases, fiction, papers and more). Not end-to-end answer accuracy.

Plain embeddings miss the relevant chunk in the top 20 for **5.7%** of queries. Adding situating context to each chunk before embedding cuts that to 3.7%; adding the same contextual chunks to a BM25 index (hybrid search) brings it to 2.9%; re-ranking the candidates reaches **1.9%**, a **67%** reduction. The trap is reaching for the most complex option first (agents, GraphRAG) when hybrid search and a re-ranker fix most failures cheaply. Each step has a cost: contextualising chunks needs one LLM call per chunk at indexing time (cheap with prompt caching), and re-ranking adds query latency.

**Now say why:** a re-ranker is much more accurate, so why not use it for all of retrieval?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

When basic RAG misses, the fix is usually one of a few well-tested upgrades. **Hybrid search** combines BM25 (exact words, codes, names) with dense embeddings (meaning). **Re-ranking** runs a slower cross-encoder over the top 20–100 candidates to put the truly relevant ones first. **Contextual chunks** prepend a sentence of context to each chunk before indexing, so "capped at ₹150" knows it's about late refunds. **Query rewriting** turns vague or multi-part questions into better search queries. Together these cut Anthropic's measured top-20 retrieval failure rate from 5.7% to **1.9%** (−67%). For "summarise themes across all 10,000 tickets" questions, **GraphRAG** builds an entity graph with community summaries instead of retrieving a few chunks. What you'll be able to do after this: pick the right upgrade for a RAG failure, explain bi-encoders vs cross-encoders, and say when GraphRAG is worth it.

#### The upgrade toolkit

| Technique | How | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| **Hybrid search** | BM25 + dense, fused with reciprocal rank fusion (lesson) | IDs, codes, rare names |
| **Re-ranking** | a **cross-encoder** reads query and chunk together and scores relevance (Nogueira & Cho 2019); or late-interaction models like ColBERT | right chunk retrieved but ranked low |
| **Contextual chunks** | an LLM writes 50–100 tokens situating each chunk in its document; prepended before embedding and BM25 | chunks that don't make sense alone |
| **Query rewriting** | an LLM rewrites, expands or splits the query; HyDE embeds a hypothetical answer instead of the question (Gao et al. 2023) | vague, conversational or multi-part questions |
| **Multi-step / agentic retrieval** | retrieve, read, decide whether to search again (Self-RAG, iterative retrieval) | questions needing facts from several places |
| **GraphRAG** | extract entities and relations into a graph, cluster communities, pre-summarise them (Edge et al. 2024) | "global" questions about a whole corpus |

**Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder:** a bi-encoder embeds query and document separately (fast, pre-computable, used for first-stage retrieval); a cross-encoder reads them together (much more accurate, but must run per pair at query time, so only on a short list).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Diagnose, then upgrade

- **Measure first:** label 100–300 real questions with their relevant chunks; compute recall@k and MRR (Evaluating LLM Apps). If recall@50 is high but recall@5 low, add a re-ranker; if recall@50 is low, fix chunking, hybrid search or query rewriting.

- **Default stack:** structure-aware chunks with context → hybrid retrieval of ~50 to 150 → cross-encoder re-rank to ~5–20 → answer with citations.

- **GraphRAG** answers corpus-wide "what are the main themes" questions far better than chunk retrieval, in its authors' tests, but classic indexing is expensive (many LLM calls), and it isn't needed for specific factual questions. Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG reports 0.1% of that indexing cost, by deferring LLM work to query time. One 2026 test found simply adding related facts to each document beat a more complex GraphRAG setup, so try simple structure first.

- **Long-context models** reduce the need for aggressive chunking on small corpora; for large or changing corpora, retrieval remains cheaper and more controllable.

**Upgrades don't simply add up.** In the lab above, each step shows a gain on Anthropic's tests. But a 2026 study of 450 setups found three strong retrieval techniques predicted +47% together, and delivered +17%, because they overlap. Across 17 combinations, the shortfall ranged from 7% to 72%. The best setup also changed as the corpus grew. So test upgrades in your full pipeline, at your real scale.

Go deeper: Re-ranking and Late Interaction, and Agentic RAG.

#### Retrieve broadly, then rank precisely

Get the right chunk into a wide candidate set with hybrid, context-aware retrieval, then let an accurate but slow re-ranker put it first; reach for query rewriting, multi-step retrieval or GraphRAG only for the question types that need them.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "GraphRAG is better RAG"

It sounds right, since it's the most sophisticated option. But it's for a different question type: corpus-wide ones, like the themes across all tickets. It adds cost without benefit for pinpoint facts, and hybrid search with a re-ranker fixes most failures cheaply. Just increasing k isn't the answer either: more chunks add noise and cost, so rank better instead.

## Say it

### How do you improve retrieval, and which upgrades cut failures by 67%?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not use a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval?

It must run once per query–document pair at query time; over millions of chunks that's far too slow. Bi-encoders allow pre-computed document vectors and ANN search.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Recall@50 is 95% but answers are still wrong. Next step?

The right chunk is found but ranked too low (or the LLM misuses it): add a re-ranker, check recall@5, and check faithfulness of the generation.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When is GraphRAG worth it?

When users ask global, sensemaking questions over a large corpus (themes, trends, relationships); not for pinpoint facts, where it adds cost without benefit.

#### The 30-second answer

To improve RAG I first measure retrieval recall on labelled queries. Then the standard upgrades: hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval for exact terms, contextual chunks that carry a summary of their document, and a cross-encoder re-ranker on the top 50 candidates. Anthropic measured these cutting top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7 to 1.9 percent. For vague or multi-part questions I add query rewriting or decomposition, HyDE in some cases, and multi-step retrieval for questions that need several sources. GraphRAG is for corpus-wide questions like themes across all tickets, at a much higher indexing cost.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Just increase k." More chunks add noise and cost; rank better instead.

- "GraphRAG is better RAG." It's for a different question type.

**Key terms and sources**

The techniques that take a basic RAG system from "often finds the right passage" to "almost always does": hybrid sparse + dense retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking, contextualised chunks, query rewriting and decomposition (including HyDE), multi-step retrieval, and graph-based RAG for questions about a whole corpus · built from Anthropic (Contextual Retrieval, 2024), Nogueira & Cho (BERT re-ranking, 2019), Khattab & Zaharia (ColBERT, SIGIR 2020), Gao et al. (HyDE, ACL 2023), Ma et al. (Query Rewriting, EMNLP 2023), Edge et al. (GraphRAG, 2024) and Asai et al. (Self-RAG, ICLR 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

2. R. Nogueira & K. Cho, "Passage Re-ranking with BERT", 2019, [arXiv:1901.04085](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085); O. Khattab & M. Zaharia, "ColBERT", SIGIR 2020, [arXiv:2004.12832](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832).

3. L. Gao et al., "Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels" (HyDE), ACL 2023, [arXiv:2212.10496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496); X. Ma et al., "Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models", EMNLP 2023, [arXiv:2305.14283](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14283).
