# Re-ranking and Late Interaction

> The right chunk is retrieved, but it's ranked 12th. What do you do, and what's late interaction?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/reranking-and-late-interaction/
- Before this: Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Re-ranking, Query Rewriting and GraphRAG (`ai-engineering/advanced-rag`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

Recall@50 is 94%, but recall@5 is only 58%. The right chunk is usually found, then buried. A colleague wants to send 50 chunks to the model. Another has read that ColBERT doubles results. The interviewer asks:

> The right chunk is retrieved, but it's ranked 12th. What do you do, and what's late interaction?

#### Why it matters

Only the top few chunks reach the model, and the model uses early chunks most. So a good chunk ranked 12th might as well be missing. Re-ranking is often the cheapest big gain, and a common interview follow-up. See Search and Retrieval for BM25 and fusion.

### The idea

Think of hiring. Sorting 10,000 CVs by keywords is quick but crude, so you use it to get a shortlist. Then you read those 50 carefully. Late interaction is like checking each requirement against the best line in a CV, rather than judging its overall impression.

[Figure: Three scorers. A bi-encoder compares single vectors. Late interaction compares every token. A cross-encoder reads both together.]

_Retrieve broadly, then rank precisely._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Add off-topic words to document A. Watch both scores.

#### Average against MaxSim

Exact calculation on invented 4-number word vectors, with topics refund, delay, plan and food. Query: "gold refund late". Document A: "gold refund for late orders", plus off-topic words about food. Document B: "plan offers delivery refund", which is only partly relevant. Single vector: cosine of the averaged word vectors. MaxSim: the sum of each query word's best cosine. Scores are divided by the number of query words.

With no off-topic words, both methods pick document A. Add just **2 off-topic words**, and the single vector flips to B: A falls from 0.99 to 0.70, against B's 0.89. At 10 words, A is down to 0.23. **MaxSim** stays at 1.00, because each query word still finds its exact match. The cost is storage: 14 vectors rather than 1 for this short document. MaxSim also has a blind spot: it ignores everything else in the document, so it can't tell that A is mostly about food. These are invented vectors, built to show the mechanism. See the conflicting results above for real data.

**Now say why:** why does MaxSim hold up, when averaging doesn't?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A first-stage retriever must be fast, so it compares one vector per chunk. A **cross-encoder** reads the query and chunk together, which is far more accurate, but too slow for more than a short list. **Late interaction** sits between them: ColBERT stores a vector for every token, and scores each query token against its best match in the document. That keeps fine detail, but uses much more memory. Measured gains vary. In one study, late interaction doubled the hit rate, and in another it did worse than a single vector. So test on your own data.

#### Three ways to compare

| | Bi-encoder | Late interaction | Cross-encoder |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compares | One vector each | Every query token with every document token | Reads both together |
| Precomputed | Yes | Yes, one vector per token | No |
| Use for | First-stage retrieval | First stage or re-ranking | Re-ranking a short list |
| Main cost | Least memory | Much more memory | Latency per candidate |

##### What re-ranking delivers

- **Microsoft (vendor test):** hybrid search scored 51.2 NDCG@3, and adding its new ranker raised that to 72.3. It re-ranked 50 documents in about 158 ms on average.

- **Anthropic (vendor test):** re-ranking took retrieval failures from 2.9% to 1.9%, from 150 candidates down to 20.

- **Newer isn't always better:** in the 450-setup study, a 2019 MiniLM cross-encoder beat all four recent rerankers it tested, on those corpora.

- **Gains overlap:** that same study found re-ranking leaves less room for other upgrades, and for a strong embedding model. Test the full stack.

##### Does MMR help?

Maximal marginal relevance penalises results that look like ones already chosen. In the 450-setup study, it cut NDCG@10 by 3.6% on average, and ARAGOG found no notable gain. On focused corpora, similar passages are often exactly the evidence you need. Use it only if your problem is near-duplicates, and consider removing duplicates at ingest instead.

##### Late interaction: conflicting results

| Study | Result | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| 463,971 arXiv papers | ColBERT: Hit@3 of about 93 to 95%, against 46 to 47% for plain dense | Synthetic questions, and a different encoder too |
| Financial and technical reports | Text late interaction: nDCG@5 of 0.32, against 0.46 for dense. Visual late interaction was best, at 0.74 | Visually rich documents |
| LIMIT test | Multi-vector: 54.8% recall@100, against under 20% for dense | A deliberately hard test |

So don't treat it as an automatic upgrade. The memory cost is real: in the second study, text late interaction used about 2.8 times the memory of dense, and page-image late interaction about 15 times.

#### The maths

$$ {S(q, d)} = \sum_{{i \in q}} {\max_{j \in d}}\ {q_i \cdot d_j} $$

The MaxSim operator from ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020). A single vector averages everything into one point before comparing.

- **the score**: How well document d matches query q.

- **every query token**: Each word in the question gets its own vote.

- **its best match**: Each query token looks for the one document token most like it. Other tokens don’t dilute it.

- **a similarity**: The dot product of two token vectors, stored at indexing time.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Diagnose first:** if recall@50 is high and recall@5 is low, a re-ranker should help. If recall@50 is low, it can't.

- **Tune the candidate count:** more candidates raise the chance of including the answer, and add latency. Try 50 to 150.

- **Budget latency:** measure the re-ranker at your p99, and cap the candidate length.

- **Use metadata where you can:** a re-ranker can't tell a current policy from an old one that reads the same. Filter or add dates.

- **Compare to no re-ranker:** keep measuring the gain, as a stronger embedding model can shrink it.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just send more chunks to the model"

It sounds right, since the answer is then in the prompt. But models use later text less, so a chunk at rank 30 may be ignored, while you pay for all of them. Put the right chunk near the top instead. That's a re-ranker's job.

## Say it

### The right chunk is retrieved, but it's ranked 12th. What do you do, and what's late interaction?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does averaging hurt long chunks?

A single vector squeezes everything into one point, so off-topic text pulls it away from the relevant part. That's why chunks are kept small, and why MaxSim, where each query token finds its best match, holds up better.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A re-ranker adds 200 ms. Is it worth it?

Compare it with the rest of the request. Next to a few seconds of LLM time, 200 ms is often fine if answer quality rises. Measure the gain on labelled questions, and try fewer candidates first.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Recall@50 is 60%. Will a re-ranker fix it?

No. A re-ranker can only reorder what it's given. Fix retrieval first with hybrid search, better parsing or chunking, query rewriting or a better embedding model.

#### The 30-second answer

If the right chunk is found but ranked low, I'd add a second stage. A bi-encoder compares single vectors, so it's fast but coarse. A cross-encoder reads the query and chunk together, which is much more accurate, so I'd run it on the top 50 to 150. Late interaction, like ColBERT, stores a vector per token, and sums each query token's best match, which keeps detail without running a model per pair at query time, but costs much more memory. Results vary: it doubled the hit rate in one study, and lost to dense in another. I'd also check MMR before using it, as it hurt on focused corpora. And I'd measure the whole stack, because gains overlap.

**Key terms and sources**

Why a second ranking stage helps, cross-encoders, how ColBERT's MaxSim works, latency and memory costs, why MMR can hurt, and conflicting evidence on late interaction. · checked 7 Nov 2026

- [Khattab and Zaharia, ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832)

- [Microsoft, Raising the bar for RAG excellence](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azure-ai-foundry-blog/raising-the-bar-for-rag-excellence-query-rewriting-and-new-semantic-ranker/4302729)

- [Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

- [Levy, Shlomov and Choshen, Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)

# Grounded Answers: Citations, Conflicts and Saying No

> The right chunk was retrieved, but the answer is still wrong. Why, and how do you make answers trustworthy?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/grounded-answers/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your assistant retrieves the right policy, but its answer gets an amount wrong. It also cites a document that doesn't say what it claims, and it answers confidently when no document covers the question. The interviewer asks:

> The right chunk was retrieved, but the answer is still wrong. Why, and how do you make answers trustworthy?

#### Why it matters

Teams often stop once retrieval scores look good. But a 2026 study found a clear **retrieval-generation gap**: when retrieval found 83.5% of the right entities, the model's answers used only 47.9%. Better retrieval alone won't close that gap. It's also where users lose trust, since a confident wrong answer with a citation looks like a right one.

### The idea

Think of a student with a stack of notes in an exam. They read the top pages closely and skim the rest. They might write what they already believe, then add a reference that seems to fit. And they'd rather write something than leave a blank. So you shorten the stack, check the references, and give credit for saying "I don't know".

[Figure: Three checks. Order context so it gets used. Test that citations are real. Allow and test saying no.]

_Retrieved doesn't mean used._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Move the right chunk down the ranks. Then raise the threshold.

#### Rank and threshold

Rank figures are measured, from Table 7 of Chen et al. (2026), for one GraphRAG setup with a single model and on one medical dataset. The samples are small, about 20 to 50 per row, which is why rank 3 is above rank 2. The threshold half is illustrative, with invented bell curves: answerable scores centre on +1.2, and unanswerable on −1.2.

Move the right chunk from **rank 1** to **ranks 6 to 10**. Use falls from 97.9% to 43.5%, even though the chunk was in the context the whole time. At ranks 51 and beyond, it wasn't used once. So retrieval metrics can look fine while answers fail. Now move the **threshold**. At 0, 11.5% of answerable questions get refused, and 11.5% of unanswerable ones get answered. At 1.0, invented answers fall to 1.4%, but 42.1% of good questions get refused. In a support bot, a wrong refund promise usually costs more than an escalation, so you might accept that. In a search tool, perhaps not.

**Now say why:** why can a citation be correct, yet not faithful?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Retrieval is only half the job, because the model has to use what it's given. Models favour early text: in one study, an answer at rank 1 was used 98% of the time, against 44% at ranks 6 to 10. So send fewer, well-ordered chunks. **Citations** can mislead, as a model may answer from memory, then cite a document that happens to agree. When documents **conflict**, prefer the newest authoritative source, and say so. And when the answer isn't there, the system should **say no**, which you have to design and test for.

#### From context to a trustworthy answer

##### Why evidence gets missed

- **Position:** extraction fell from 85.5% in the first tenth of the context to about 19% around the middle, and to almost nothing at the end, in one test with long graph context.

- **Too much context:** the same study saw that adding more retrieved text often didn't improve answers, while costing more tokens.

- **Question wording:** a singular question can make a model give one answer, even when several are valid.

This fits earlier findings that models lose information in the middle of long contexts. So re-rank, send fewer chunks, and place the best first.

##### Citations that aren't what they seem

| Check | Question | How to test |
|---|---|---|
| **Citation correctness** | Does the cited text support the claim? | An NLI model or a judge, claim by claim |
| **Citation faithfulness** | Did the model really use that text? | Change or remove the document, and see if the answer changes |

Wallat et al. found that up to 57% of citations lacked faithfulness: the model already believed the answer, and then attached a source. That's called post-rationalisation, and a correctness check can't see it.

##### Conflicting and bad documents

- **Stale versions:** remove superseded documents at ingest, and store dates and versions.

- **Real disagreements:** show both, with their sources and dates, rather than picking silently.

- **Bad knowledge:** RAGStress, a 2026 benchmark, found that a clean knowledge base can hide big differences between models, and that a model's accuracy with no retrieval didn't predict how well it copes with corrupted documents. So test with damaged documents too.

##### Saying no

CRAG found that simple RAG raised accuracy from at most 34% to 44%, and that even leading industry systems answered only 63% of questions without hallucination. So plan for failure: tell the model it may say the answer isn't there, check whether retrieval found anything relevant, and test on questions with no answer. Barnett et al. warn that related but unanswerable questions are the ones most likely to fool a system.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{missed answers}} = {P(s < t \mid \text{answerable})}, \qquad {\text{invented answers}} = {P(s \ge t \mid \text{not answerable})} $$

A simple way to frame the trade-off, as with any classifier. Retrieval scores aren’t always comparable across queries, so calibrate this on your own data.

- **wrongly saying no**: Questions you could have answered, but refused.

- **the threshold**: s is a retrieval or support score. Raising t refuses more.

- **wrongly answering**: Questions with no answer in the documents, answered anyway.

- **the other side**: Lowering t answers more of these. A better score helps both, while moving t only trades one for the other.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Number your chunks:** ask the model to cite chunk IDs per claim, then check that each ID exists and supports the claim.

- **Verify by code where you can:** amounts, dates and IDs can be checked against the source text.

- **Test no-answer questions:** include them in your golden set, and track how often they're refused.

- **Change the document:** edit a fact in a retrieved chunk, and see whether the answer changes. If not, it's answering from memory.

- **Don't overdo checks:** in the 450-setup study, some quality gates removed supporting evidence, including 14 of 15 chunks in one case, so test them too.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It cites a source, so we can trust it"

It sounds right, since a reader can check the citation. But models can answer from memory, then attach a source that agrees, and one study found up to 57% of citations were like this. If the source later changes, the answer won't. Change the document and see whether the answer changes.

## Say it

### The right chunk was retrieved, but the answer is still wrong. Why, and how do you make answers trustworthy?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How would you test whether a citation is real?

Swap or remove the cited document and re-run. If the answer stays the same, the model wasn't relying on it. Also check that the text supports the claim, with an NLI model or judge, and validate that the cited ID exists.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Two retrieved policies disagree. What should the system do?

Prefer the current authoritative one if metadata can tell you, and fix the index by removing old versions. If they really disagree, show both with sources and dates, or escalate, instead of silently picking one.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not just send 20 chunks, to be safe?

More chunks can add noise and cost without helping, because the model uses later ones less. Anthropic did find 20 worked best among 5, 10 and 20 for its retrieval tests, so test it, but expect a limit. Re-ranking the best to the top matters more.

#### The 30-second answer

Good retrieval doesn't guarantee a good answer. Models favour early text, and in one study use fell from 98% at rank 1 to 44% at ranks 6 to 10, so I'd re-rank, send fewer chunks and place the best first. I'd require citations per claim, and check both correctness, which asks whether the source supports the claim, and faithfulness, which asks whether the model really used it. One study found up to 57% of citations weren't faithful. I test that by changing the document and seeing if the answer changes. For conflicts, I'd remove stale versions at ingest and show real disagreements. And I'd design abstention, with no-answer questions in my test set.

**Key terms and sources**

Why models miss retrieved evidence, context order, citations that look right but aren't real, conflicting and stale documents, and abstaining when the evidence isn't there. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Chen et al., Is GraphRAG Needed?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25656)

- [Wallat et al., Correctness is not Faithfulness in RAG Attributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18004)

- [Yang et al., CRAG: Comprehensive RAG Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04744)

- [Yang et al., RAGStress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04691)

- [Barnett et al., Seven Failure Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05856)

- [Liu et al., Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

- [Levy, Shlomov and Choshen, Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)

# Agentic RAG, and When Not to Index

> Should your RAG be an agent? When do you skip the index altogether?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/agentic-rag/
- Before this: Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Re-ranking, Query Rewriting and GraphRAG (`ai-engineering/advanced-rag`), What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your RAG works for most questions, but fails on those needing facts from two places. A colleague proposes rebuilding it as an agent. Another says agents have replaced vector search, and you should just use grep. Your corpus is 8 million documents. The interviewer asks:

> Should your RAG be an agent? When do you skip the index altogether?

#### Why it matters

"Just make it an agent" is now a common suggestion, and "is RAG dead?" a common headline. Neither helps you decide. Interviewers want you to say when each one is worth its cost. This lesson covers retrieval decisions, and What Is an Agent? covers the loop in general.

### The idea

Think of finding something in a library. If you know the exact title, use the catalogue. If you only know the topic, ask a librarian once. If the question needs several books, you read one, then go back for another, but each trip takes time, and you carry everything you've collected.

[Figure: Choose by need. Small corpus: put it in the prompt. Exact lookups: use text search. Multi-step questions: add a loop.]

_Add a loop only for questions that need one._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the search rounds. Then switch to a batch.

#### Count the tokens

Illustrative. A 2,000-token base prompt, 500 tokens per chunk, and an invented price of $3 per million input tokens. Static RAG makes one call with one search. A batch makes one call to plan, and one to answer with all results. Prompt caching and summarising old results would lower these numbers.

One static search uses 7,000 tokens. **Five rounds** of 10 chunks use 87,000, about 12 times as much, and six calls' worth of waiting. That's because every round resends earlier results. **Batching** the five searches brings it to 29,000. Chen et al. saw batching raise coverage while lowering token use, though its better coverage didn't always improve answers. Now try 10 rounds, one at a time: it passes 280,000 tokens. So an agent should stop searching once it has enough, and old results should be summarised or dropped.

**Now say why:** why do tokens grow faster than the number of rounds?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Static RAG retrieves once. **Agentic RAG** lets the model decide what to search, read the results, and search again. That helps with questions needing facts from several places, but it costs more: each round resends the whole conversation. Evidence is mixed, as agents won in one study and lost in others. Often you don't need an index at all: a small knowledge base can go straight in the prompt, and exact lookups can use plain text search. Start simple, measure, and add a loop only for the questions that need one.

#### What the evidence says

##### Four ways to find information

| Approach | Best for | Weak spot |
|---|---|---|
| **Everything in the prompt** | Small knowledge bases. Anthropic suggests under about 200,000 tokens | Cost per call, though prompt caching helps |
| **Text search, grep** | Exact names, IDs and code, always fresh | Different wording for the same idea |
| **Static RAG** | Single questions over large corpora | Questions needing several steps |
| **Agentic RAG** | Multi-step questions, and using several tools | Tokens, latency and less predictable behaviour |

##### Do agents help? It depends

| Study | Finding | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| Uber, on policy documents | 27% more acceptable answers, 60% less incorrect advice (relative) | A fixed flow of agents. 100+ test queries |
| Chen et al. | An agent with one search tool was among the best, at Hit@1 of 0.69, while adding a graph tool or thinking didn't help | One medical dataset |
| Rathi et al. | A model-decides tool call scored below plain RAG | One search allowed, small quantized model |
| Levy et al. | An agentic loop on a strong stack: a negligible faithfulness gain, and worse retrieval and latency | 450 setups, up to 200K documents |
| Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? | Plain retrieval and re-ranking over raw history beat complex memory systems in 6 of 7 settings | Conversation memory benchmarks |

So agents aren't simply better. They help most with strong models, several real steps, and useful tools. Note the different setups, which is partly why results disagree.

##### Grep or semantic search?

Some coding agents now rely on text search and no index, which keeps results fresh and avoids a lot of machinery. But Cursor's own tests point the other way for large repositories: with semantic search, its agent answered 12.5% more accurately on average. In an A/B test, code retention rose 0.3%, and 2.6% on codebases of 1,000 files or more. Cursor concluded that using both works best. These are vendor numbers, though with a real A/B test. Agents can also combine them: GRASP trained a policy that uses semantic search to explore, and keyword search for specific names.

##### GraphRAG and friends

Chen et al. found that simply adding related facts to each document beat a more complex GraphRAG setup on their data. Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG cuts indexing to 0.1% of full GraphRAG's cost by deferring LLM work to query time. So try simple structure first, as with agents.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{input tokens}} = \sum_{i=0}^{{R}} \big({S} + i\,{C}\big) = (R+1)\,S + \frac{R(R+1)}{2}\,C $$

Our own arithmetic for a simple loop that keeps its full history. Chen et al. saw the same effect: a 5-call session used about 250K tokens, while a 3-call session used only 36K.

- **total tokens the model reads**: Across every call in the loop.

- **search rounds**: Each round adds another call to the model, and one final call writes the answer.

- **the base prompt**: System prompt, tools and question, resent on every call.

- **retrieved text per round**: Earlier results stay in the history, so they’re resent too. That’s why cost grows with the square of the rounds.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Start with a baseline:** measure plain retrieval and re-ranking first. Agentic systems should have to beat it.

- **Route by question:** use a cheap single search for simple questions, and allow a loop only for the hard ones.

- **Fix the flow where you can:** a fixed pipeline of steps is easier to test than a free-running loop, as in Uber's design.

- **Set limits:** cap rounds and tokens, and watch cost per question. Summarise or drop old results.

- **Offer a keyword tool:** give agents both keyword and semantic search, plus a way to read the surrounding section.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Agents have replaced RAG, so rebuild it as an agent"

It sounds right, as agents are more flexible. But agents still retrieve, and they cost far more. Studies disagree: one found a simple agent best, and another found a loop added almost nothing on a strong retrieval stack. Build the baseline first, then make the agent prove itself on your own questions.

## Say it

### Should your RAG be an agent? When do you skip the index altogether?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your corpus is 150,000 tokens. Do you need a vector database?

Probably not. Put it in the prompt with prompt caching, and measure. Anthropic suggests this under about 200,000 tokens. Add retrieval once cost or latency hurts, or the corpus grows.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why does an agent cost so much more than one search?

Each round resends the system prompt and all earlier results, so input tokens grow with the square of the rounds. Five rounds of 5,000 tokens are about 12 times one static search. Batch the searches, cap the rounds, and trim old results.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Grep or embeddings for a code assistant?

Both. Text search handles exact names and is always fresh. Semantic search finds code when you don't know the words, and Cursor saw more benefit in large repositories. Give the agent both tools, and test on real tasks.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd start from the simplest thing that works. A small knowledge base can go straight in the prompt, and exact lookups can use text search. For large corpora I'd use static RAG with re-ranking as the baseline. I'd add an agentic loop only for questions needing several steps, because each round resends the history, so tokens grow with the square of the rounds. Evidence is mixed: agents won in one study and added nothing on a strong retrieval stack in another. For code, some agents use only grep, while Cursor measured clear gains from adding semantic search, especially in large repositories. So I'd route by question, cap the rounds, and make the agent beat the baseline on my own test set.

**Key terms and sources**

Static against agentic retrieval, why each search round costs more, conflicting evidence on agents, grep against semantic search, whole-document prompts and simple baselines. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Cursor, Improving agent with semantic search](https://cursor.com/blog/semsearch)

- [Uber, Enhanced Agentic-RAG](https://www.uber.com/en-CA/blog/enhanced-agentic-rag/)

- [Chen et al., Is GraphRAG Needed?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25656)

- [Rathi, Chawla and Andreopoulos, A Controlled Comparison of RAG Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38473)

- [Levy, Shlomov and Choshen, Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29722)

- [Bao et al., Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30755)

- [Gandhi et al., GRASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10463)

- [Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

- [Microsoft Research, LazyGraphRAG](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/lazygraphrag-setting-a-new-standard-for-quality-and-cost)

# Permissions and Poisoning in RAG

> How do you stop users retrieving documents they can't see, or attackers planting bad ones?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/permissions-and-poisoning/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`), Guardrails and Prompt Injection (`ai-engineering/guardrails-and-prompt-injection`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're adding company-wide search over HR files, contracts and engineering docs. During a test, an intern's question returns a line from a salary document. Separately, a planted wiki page changes what the assistant says about expense limits. The interviewer asks:

> How do you stop users retrieving documents they can't see, or attackers planting bad ones?

#### Why it matters

Enterprise RAG is a common interview topic, and permissions are where naive designs fail. Guardrails and prompt injection covers attacks through the prompt. This lesson covers those that come through the index, and how to keep each user's data apart.

### The idea

Think of a records office. The clerk who fetches files must check your badge before going to the shelves, not after reading the file aloud. If the badge reader breaks, the office closes, and doesn't let everyone in. And anyone who can slip a false page into a folder can change what the clerk reports.

[Figure: Three defences. Check access before retrieval. Fail closed. Treat retrieved text as untrusted.]

_Filter before anything reaches the model._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Lower the share the user can see. Then set failures to search anyway.

#### Check the access path

Illustrative arithmetic, for 100 candidates spread evenly. Filter during search assumes your index keeps good recall under the filter. A live check is near-instant, as the source system answers directly.

If a user can see **5%** of documents, filtering after search leaves about 5 of the 10 results you wanted, and at **1%** only 1. Filtering during search fixes that, but a person removed from a project can still retrieve its documents until the next sync, up to 6 hours here. A **live check** closes that window, at the cost of extra calls. Now set the failure mode to **search anyway**: a brief outage in the permission service exposes every document to every user. That single setting matters more than the rest of this design.

**Now say why:** why does filtering after search return so few results?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A RAG system can leak what a user was never allowed to see, because the search index and the LLM don't know your permissions. So **check access at retrieval**, using one of three models: forward the user's identity, filter on cached permissions and re-check live, or give access by parent folder and filter on it. Always **fail closed**: if a check breaks, return nothing. Retrieved text is also an attack surface. **Corpus poisoning** plants documents to steer answers, and injected instructions can hide in them. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data.

#### Access and attacks

##### Three ways to enforce access

| Model | How | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Forward identity** | Search with the user's own token, and the data platform applies its rules | One source of truth | The platform must support it |
| **Cached ACLs + live check** | Filter on permissions copied to the index, then check candidates at the source | Revocation shows up quickly | Extra calls and latency |
| **Parent-level filter** | Give roles on folders or workspaces. Each chunk stores its parent ID, and one call lists the user's parents | Few writes, and no per-document sync | Exceptions need extra handling |

These three models and the fail-closed rules below are from WorkOS, a vendor that sells authorization, so treat them as one informed view.

##### Rules that prevent leaks

- **Fail closed:** if the permission call fails, return nothing. If a live check errors, drop that candidate.

- **An empty list means nothing:** a user with no folders must get an empty result, and not an unfiltered search.

- **No shared super-user:** don't fall back to the app's own all-access account.

- **Filter before ranking:** and watch for filters that break recall.

- **Remember the caches:** semantic caches and prefix caches can also leak across users. Key them by tenant.

##### Poisoning the corpus

PoisonedRAG showed that an attacker who adds just 5 crafted texts for a target question, into a database of millions, could reach about 90% attack success. Any source that outsiders can edit is exposed: public web pages, uploaded files, support tickets and wikis.

- **Real pipelines change the picture:** a 2026 study found many attacks weaken once chunking and re-ranking are involved, though attacks built for those stages recover.

- **One document can be enough:** several 2026 attacks work with a single planted document.

- **Measure carefully:** "Prevented is Not Protected" found that defences judged by attack success rate alone can introduce new failures, and that the choice of metric can change which defence ranks best.

##### Defence in layers

1. **Control sources:** know who can write to the index, and label or weight untrusted ones.

2. **Keep provenance:** store where each chunk came from, so you can find and remove bad ones.

3. **Treat text as data:** never let retrieved text act as instructions, and limit what tools can do.

4. **Check outputs:** require citations, and review sensitive actions.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{results}} = \min\big({k},\ {c} \times {p}\big) $$

Simple arithmetic, assuming visible documents are spread evenly among results. Real results may be better or worse.

- **results left after post-filtering**: What you can actually show the user.

- **results you want**: Often 10 or fewer.

- **candidates searched**: How many results you fetch before filtering.

- **share the user can see**: If a user can see only 1% of documents, 100 candidates leave about 1 result.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Test with real identities:** keep automated tests where user A asks for user B's document, and must fail.

- **Log every retrieval:** record who got which chunks. You'll need it to investigate a leak.

- **Handle deletion:** removing a document must remove its chunks, caches and summaries. See Keeping an Index Current.

- **Separate tenants:** large customers may need their own index or namespace, not only a filter.

- **Summaries can leak:** a graph or summary built across documents may mix what different users can see.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We'll tell the LLM not to reveal restricted documents"

It sounds right, since LLMs follow instructions. But a prompt isn't a security boundary. Once the text is in the context, it can come out through the answer, a clever question or the logs. Keep restricted text out of the context altogether.

## Say it

### How do you stop users retrieving documents they can't see, or attackers planting bad ones?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not filter results after the LLM answers?

By then the model has read the text, and it can appear in the answer, in a summary, or in logs. Filter before anything reaches the model.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A user's access was removed an hour ago, but they can still find the document. Why?

Permissions are probably copied into the index and synced periodically. Add a live check against the source for each candidate, or shorten the sync, and decide what delay you can accept.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you find out your corpus was poisoned?

Provenance first: which source added the chunks behind a bad answer? Watch for documents that rank highly for many queries, new sources with unusual influence, and answer changes after ingest. Then remove them, and re-test.

#### The 30-second answer

The index and the LLM don't know permissions, so I'd enforce them at retrieval. I could forward the user's identity to a platform that applies its own rules, filter on cached permissions and re-check candidates live, or assign roles at folder level and filter by parent ID. I'd fail closed: if the check breaks, return nothing, and an empty list must never become an unfiltered search. I'd watch revocation delay, and cover caches too. For poisoning, PoisonedRAG reached about 90% attack success with 5 planted texts, so I'd control who can write to the index, keep provenance, treat retrieved text as data rather than instructions, and limit what tools can do.

**Key terms and sources**

Three ways to enforce access control, why to fail closed, revocation delays, corpus poisoning, why attack success rate isn't enough, and layered defences. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [WorkOS, Authorization for RAG at scale](https://workos.com/blog/authorization-for-rag-at-scale-why-you-shouldnt-sync-every-document)

- [WorkOS, RAG access control and document permissions](https://workos.com/blog/rag-access-control-document-permissions)

- [Zou et al., PoisonedRAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07867)

- [When Poison Fails After Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11265)

- [Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40742)

- [Retrieved But Not Reliable: A Survey on Attacks and Defenses in RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24977)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Most recent papers are preprints.

# Keeping an Index Current

> Documents change daily, and a better embedding model has come out. How do you keep your index current?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/keeping-an-index-current/
- Before this: Embeddings and Vector Indexes (`ai-engineering/embeddings-and-vector-indexes`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

An outdated refund policy keeps appearing in answers, though it was deleted weeks ago. Meanwhile, the team wants to move to a newer embedding model, and someone suggests re-embedding documents gradually in the same index. The interviewer asks:

> Documents change daily, and a better embedding model has come out. How do you keep your index current?

#### Why it matters

Tutorials end once the index is built, but real work starts there. A stale policy gives a confident wrong answer, and a deleted document that's still retrievable can be a legal problem. Migrations are expensive enough that you should plan for them. See RAG Wrong Answer for what stale data looks like from the outside.

### The idea

Think of moving a library to a new shelving system. You can't mix the two systems on one shelf, as nobody could find anything. So you set up the new shelves beside the old ones, shelve new books in both, move the rest over time, check it works, then change the signs overnight.

[Figure: Three jobs. Update what changed. Clean up deletes. Migrate models with a second index.]

_Time is usually a bigger limit than money._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the chunks, then the rate limit. Then raise the tombstones.

#### Plan a migration

Exact arithmetic, at the $0.13 per million tokens used in the source's example. Batch endpoints usually run slower, which isn't modelled here. Live results assume tombstones are spread evenly among 40 search candidates.

100 million chunks of 400 tokens is 40 billion tokens: about **$5,200**, and **5.6 days** at 5 million tokens a minute. The money is small next to the time. During those days, about 2.8 million chunks change, and that's why you dual write. Raise the rate limit to 50, and it takes about half a day for the same money. Now raise tombstones to 50%: only 20 of 40 search candidates are live, so recall and speed suffer until you clean up.

**Now say why:** why do you need dual writes during a backfill?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

An index goes stale from the moment you build it. Update it **incrementally**: hash each document, and re-embed only what changed. **Deletes** are harder than they look, as graph indexes usually mark items as deleted, and those tombstones slow searches and crowd out real results until a cleanup. Changing the **embedding model** means rebuilding everything, because old and new vectors can't be compared. The safe way is a second index, dual writes, a background backfill, a recall check, then an instant switch with an alias.

#### Updates, deletes and migrations

##### Incremental updates

1. **Detect changes:** use events from the source, or compare a content hash per document or section.

2. **Re-chunk and embed only what changed:** stable section IDs avoid re-embedding a whole document for one edit.

3. **Replace, don't add:** write new chunks and remove old ones together, so the same document never appears twice in different versions.

4. **Track freshness:** store the source version and indexed time, and alert when ingestion falls behind.

##### Why deletes are hard

A node in an HNSW graph can't simply be removed, because other nodes link through it. So databases usually mark it as deleted, a **tombstone**, and clean up later. Until then, search still walks through dead nodes. If 20% of candidates are tombstones, a search for 40 candidates finds about 32 live ones. Cleanup, such as a vacuum or segment rebuild, can be slow. So plan for it, and if you have a legal duty to erase data, check when it's actually gone, including backups, caches and summaries.

The tombstone mechanism and cleanup steps here come from engineering blogs. Check your own database's documentation for exact behaviour.

##### Migrating an embedding model

| Step | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Build beside it | A second index, with the new model's dimensions | The old one keeps serving |
| 2. Dual write | Embed every new or changed document with both | The new index doesn't fall behind |
| 3. Backfill | Embed history in the background | Don't overwrite a newer vector from a dual write |
| 4. Evaluate | Compare recall@k on a few hundred real queries, and optionally shadow live traffic | A newer model isn't always better for you |
| 5. Switch | Flip an alias, and keep the old index for rollback | Instant, and reversible |

##### Can you avoid re-embedding?

Drift-Adapter trains a small mapping from old vectors into the new model's space, from a sample of paired embeddings. It reports recovering 95 to 99% of the recall of a full re-embedding, at over 100 times lower recompute cost, and under 10 microseconds added per query. Treat this as a bridge. One practitioner cites a lower range of 85 to 95%, with no source, so test it on your data before relying on it.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{days}} = \frac{{N} \times {T}}{{\text{tokens per minute}} \times 1{,}440}, \qquad {\text{cost}} = {N} \times T \times {\text{price}} $$

Worked example from Tian Pan’s post: 100M chunks of 400 tokens is 40B tokens, about $5,200 at $0.13 per million, and over 5 days at 5M tokens per minute.

- **backfill time**: How long the migration runs, if nothing fails.

- **chunks**: All of them, because old and new vectors can’t mix.

- **tokens per chunk**: Larger chunks cost more.

- **your rate limit**: Often the real bottleneck, more than the price.

- **embedding cost**: Often smaller than you’d expect. Engineering time and rate limits can matter more.

- **chunks again**: The same count.

- **price per token**: Batch endpoints may cost less, but take longer.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Version everything:** store the embedding model and chunker version with each chunk, so you know what needs rebuilding.

- **Never mix models:** query and document vectors must come from the same model and version.

- **Keep the raw text:** you can't re-embed or re-chunk what you didn't keep.

- **Watch index health:** track tombstones, recall on a fixed test set, and ingestion lag. Set a cleanup rule.

- **Test before you upgrade:** run your golden queries against the new model, because a higher benchmark score doesn't guarantee a gain on your data.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We'll re-embed gradually, in the same index"

It sounds right, as it avoids a big switch. But vectors from two models live in different spaces, so their similarity scores mean nothing together. A query can only match one of them. Use a second index, or a second named vector, then switch once it's complete and tested.

## Say it

### Documents change daily, and a better embedding model has come out. How do you keep your index current?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why can't you upgrade embeddings gradually, chunk by chunk, in one index?

Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so comparing them is meaningless, and query vectors can only match one. You need a second index, a second named vector, or an adapter that maps between the two.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Users still get answers from a deleted document. Where do you look?

The chunks may not have been removed, or they may be marked deleted but still served. Check the search filter, and look at caches, summaries, semantic caches and any graph built from it. Then add a test that deletes a document and checks that it can't be retrieved.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How often should you re-index?

Update content as it changes, on events if you can. Do full rebuilds only when the chunker or model changes, or when tombstones and drift hurt recall. Let your freshness needs and a fixed recall test decide.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd update incrementally: detect changes with events or content hashes, re-embed only changed sections, and replace old chunks with new ones together. Deletes need care, as graph indexes usually leave tombstones, which slow search and crowd out real results until cleanup, so I'd track them. For a new embedding model, vectors can't be mixed, so I'd build a second index, dual write new documents, backfill history, compare recall on real queries, then flip an alias and keep the old index for rollback. 100 million chunks of 400 tokens costs about $5,000, but takes over 5 days at 5 million tokens a minute, so rate limits often set the schedule. An adapter can bridge the gap, but test it.

**Key terms and sources**

Incremental updates and hashing, why deletes are hard in HNSW, tombstones and vacuuming, migrating embedding models with dual writes and an alias, costs, and adapters. · checked 7 Nov 2026

# RAG: Wrong Answer, Where to Look First

> Your chatbot gave a confident, wrong answer. Where do you look first?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 8 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/rag-wrong-answer/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

You're the ML engineer on a support team. Your chatbot just gave a customer the wrong refund policy, confidently. A colleague wants to rewrite the prompt. The interviewer asks:

> Your chatbot gave a confident, wrong answer. Where do you look first?

#### The situation: a confident, wrong answer

A customer asks about refunds. The bot answers instantly and sounds sure. It is wrong.

The documents the bot searches (made-up policy snippets):

#### What would you check first?

Tap an answer.

### The idea

Think of a parcel that arrives with the wrong item. You don't start by retraining the driver. You check whether the right item ever left the warehouse. That one check tells you which half of the operation to look at.

[Figure: One check: was the right chunk retrieved for this question? If not, look at the retrieval side: chunking, metadata, top-k and reranking. If so, look at the generation side: context packing, then the prompt.]

_A practical debugging order, not a result from the study._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Pick a case, and click each stage to see what the system had at that point. Then show where the answer was lost, and try the other cases.

#### Spot it: where does the right answer disappear?

Pick a case, then click each stage to see what the system had at that point. The right chunk says annual plans get 14 days.

Illustrative. Green = the right chunk. Red = a chunk that points the model the wrong way.

**Now say why:** if the right chunk never reached the model, why can't any prompt fix it?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Most people blame the prompt or reach for a bigger model. A better first move is to look at what the system retrieved. One check splits the problem in two, and each side has its own fixes.

#### Why it happens: seven failure points

A study built on three RAG case studies found these seven ways an answer goes wrong. They fall into three zones along the pipeline.

Here, "generation side" includes the step where retrieved chunks are packed into the prompt (FP3). The "how to check" lines are practical suggestions, not results from the study.

#### Diagnose before you fix

Answer the questions for your own failing example. Each answer narrows the problem.

This order is a practical debugging approach. It is not a result from the study.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Fixes, in order

1. 1 ##### Chunking and metadata Chunk size is a trade-off: too small and some questions can't be answered, too long and the answer picks up noise. In one case study, adding the file name and chunk number to the retrieved text helped the model use it. Watch out: changing how you embed means re-indexing every chunk.

2. 2 ##### Top-k and reranking In practice only the top K chunks are used, so the right one has to rank near the top. Reranking reorders the candidates so the chunk with the answer sits first. Watch out: a bigger K adds more noise and more cost.

3. 3 ##### Context size The step that packs chunks into the prompt can drop a good one. In one case study, a larger context (8K vs 4K) gave more accurate answers. Watch out: that was one system, so measure it on yours.

4. 4 ##### The prompt, last Only once the right text reliably reaches the model does the prompt matter: format, level of detail, splitting multi-part questions, and saying "I don't know" when nothing relevant comes back.

#### Mistakes to avoid

Common

- Swapping to a bigger model before looking at retrieval.

- Re-indexing everything without knowing which stage failed.

- Retrieving more chunks without checking for noise and conflicts.

- Launching with no test questions.

✓ Better

- Read the retrieved chunks for the failing question first.

- Fix the stage that lost the answer, then re-test the same question.

- Remove outdated or conflicting documents.

- Keep a small set of real questions with known answers, and keep monitoring after launch.

Debug retrieval before the prompt.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Rewrite the prompt, or switch to a bigger model"

It sounds right, since the bad text came out of the model. But rewriting the prompt is a guess: if the right text never reached the model, no wording can fix that. A bigger model can't use a chunk it never received, so you'd pay more and keep the bug. Re-indexing every document is just as blind. Look at what retrieval returned first.

## Say it

### Your chatbot gave a confident, wrong answer. Where do you look first?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

How would you test a RAG system before launch?

Build a small set of real questions with known answers and the document each answer comes from. Score retrieval (did the right chunk come back?) separately from the final answer, so you know which half failed. The study notes that these systems are hard to validate up front and need continuous calibration, so keep monitoring after launch.

Follow-up 2 of 4

RAG or fine-tuning for company knowledge?

RAG keeps knowledge in documents you can update and control access to. Fine-tuning bakes the data into the model, so you retrain when the data or the base model changes. Many teams start with RAG for changing knowledge. Compare accuracy, latency, cost and robustness for your case.

Follow-up 3 of 4

How do you choose a chunk size?

It's a trade-off: small chunks can miss context a question needs, long chunks add noise. Try a few sizes on your own test questions and compare whether the right chunk is retrieved. Heuristic chunking (paragraphs, punctuation) and semantic chunking are both worth comparing.

Follow-up 4 of 4

What if the answer isn't in the documents at all?

That's failure point 1. In the happy case the system says it doesn't know. The risk is questions that are related to the content but have no answer, which can fool the system into answering anyway. Include such questions in your tests and make abstaining an expected behavior.

#### The 30-second answer

I wouldn't touch the prompt or the model first. I'd look at the chunks retrieved for that exact question, because one check splits the problem in two. If the right chunk never came back, it's the retrieval side: chunking, metadata, top-k and reranking. If it came back and the answer is still wrong, it's the generation side: the step that packs chunks into the prompt, or the model not extracting the answer. I'd fix the stage that lost the answer, re-test the same question, and keep a small set of real questions with known answers, so it stays fixed.

**Key terms and sources**

# RAG at Scale: Slow and Wrong

> Your RAG worked on 100 docs, but broke at 10 million. Why?

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 8 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/rag-at-scale/
- Before this: RAG End to End (`ai-engineering/rag-end-to-end`), Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Re-ranking, Query Rewriting and GraphRAG (`ai-engineering/advanced-rag`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your RAG worked on 100 documents. Same code and same model on 10 million, and answers take longer and come back wrong more often. A colleague says to retrieve 50 chunks instead of 5. The interviewer asks:

> Your RAG worked on 100 docs, but broke at 10 million. Why?

#### What would you check first?

Tap an answer.

### The idea

Think of moving from a small office's filing cabinet to a national archive. Searching every shelf is now far too slow, so you need a catalogue. And there are now old versions, drafts and copies that all look alike, so you narrow it by department and year, then have an expert read the shortlist.

[Figure: Two problems with two fixes. Slow: exact search checks every vector, so use an approximate index. Wrong: look-alikes bury the right chunk, so filter by metadata and rerank.]

_The same symptom, with two separate causes and two separate fixes._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Search with no fixes on, and see what reaches the top 5. Turn on the metadata filter, then reranking, then both.

#### Why it's wrong: look-alikes bury the right chunk

With 100 docs, there's one refund policy. With 10 million, there are old versions, drafts, other regions and copies in slide decks, and they all sound alike. Only the top 5 go to the LLM. Turn on the fixes.

–

Illustrative scores. The reranker reads the question and each chunk together, so it can tell “current Support policy” from a look-alike.

**Now say why:** the right chunk is in the index, so why doesn't it reach the LLM?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Same code, same model, much bigger pile. Answers now take longer _and_ come back wrong more often. These are two different problems with two different fixes: an index to make search fast, and filtering plus reranking to make it right.

#### Why it's slow: exact search checks every vector

Exact (brute-force) search compares your question with every stored vector. The work grows in step with the pile. Drag the slider.

Exact arithmetic for 768-dimensional embeddings: one similarity = 768 multiply-adds, memory = chunks × 768 × 4 bytes. Real time also depends on hardware, batching and quantization.

#### The speed fix: an approximate index

Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes skip most of the pile. IVF groups vectors into clusters and searches only the clusters nearest your question. HNSW builds a layered graph and hops from coarse to fine. Both check a small fraction of the vectors.

–

Illustrative drawing. Brown = your question, green rings = its true 5 nearest neighbours, blue dots = the vectors actually checked.

#### The catch: a little recall for a lot of speed

Searching fewer clusters is faster but can miss some true neighbours. Recall@10 = how many of the true top 10 the index still finds. Move the slider and watch the trade-off.

–

HNSW has the same kind of knob (how many candidates it explores per query). In production you tune it on your own data until recall is good enough at the latency you need.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Fixes, in order

1. 1 ##### Measure first Time each stage (embedding the query, vector search, reranking, the LLM call) and keep a small test set of questions with known answers and their source chunks. Then you know whether you have a speed problem, a quality problem or both.

2. 2 ##### Use an approximate index HNSW or IVF instead of brute force. Tune the search knob (clusters searched, or candidates explored) until recall@10 on your test set is high enough. Watch out: HNSW keeps graph links in memory, and IVF needs training and re-balancing as data grows.

3. 3 ##### Filter by metadata first Tag chunks with team, product, region, date and version, and restrict the search to what the question needs. It removes most look-alikes and shrinks the search. Watch out: filtering _after_ the ANN search can leave fewer than k results, so prefer a database that filters during search.

4. 4 ##### Retrieve wide, then rerank Take the top 50 or so from the fast index, rerank them with a slower, sharper cross-encoder, and send only the best 5 to the LLM. Watch out: reranking adds latency, so keep the candidate list small.

5. 5 ##### Clean the pile Remove duplicates and superseded versions when you ingest. Fewer look-alikes is the cheapest quality fix of all.

#### Mistakes to avoid

Common

- Blaming the LLM before timing the retrieval stages.

- Raising top-k to 50 and sending it all to the LLM.

- Switching to ANN without checking recall on real questions.

- Keeping every old version of a document in the index.

✓ Better

- Measure latency per stage and retrieval recall separately.

- Retrieve wide, rerank, and send a few chunks.

- Tune the index knob on your own test set.

- Store metadata at ingest so you can filter later.

Index to make it fast. Filter and rerank to make it right.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Retrieve 50 chunks instead of 5"

It sounds right, since the right chunk is more likely to be somewhere in 50. But sending them all to the LLM adds noise and cost, and it does nothing for speed. Retrieve wide if you like, but then rerank and send a few. Blaming the LLM is no better: time the retrieval stages first, because these are two different problems.

## Say it

### Your RAG worked on 100 docs, but broke at 10 million. Why?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

HNSW or IVF?

HNSW usually gives high recall at low latency and handles inserts well, but uses more memory for its graph. IVF uses less memory, pairs well with compression (IVF-PQ) for very large sets, and needs a training step to learn its clusters. Many vector databases offer both; benchmark on your data.

Follow-up 2 of 4

Why not just use exact search on a GPU?

For a few million vectors, exact search on a GPU can be fast enough, and it gives perfect recall. As the pile and the query volume grow, the cost grows with them, so most large systems switch to an approximate index.

Follow-up 3 of 4

Pre-filtering or post-filtering?

Post-filtering runs the ANN search first, then drops chunks that don't match, which can leave you with fewer than k results. Pre-filtering (or filtering during the search) restricts the candidates up front, so you always get k matching chunks. Prefer filtering during search when your database supports it. Even then, check recall under your real filters: a graph index can lose most of its recall on a narrow filter, with no error. See Embeddings and Vector Indexes.

Follow-up 4 of 4

Does hybrid search help here?

Yes for exact terms. Keyword search (BM25) finds IDs, error codes and product names that embeddings blur together. Combine both result lists, then rerank.

#### The 30-second answer

These are two different problems, so I'd split them first: time each stage, and check whether the right chunk is still retrieved. Slow usually means exact search, where the work grows with the pile, so I'd move to an approximate index like HNSW or IVF and tune its search knob until recall@10 is good enough on my test set. Wrong usually means look-alikes burying the right chunk: old versions, drafts and other regions. So I'd filter by metadata like team, date and version, retrieve wide, rerank with a cross-encoder and send only the best few chunks. And I'd remove duplicates and old versions at ingest.

**Key terms and sources**

# RAG Practice

> 10 questions to work by hand: recall, MRR, fusion, memory, filters, tokens and migrations.

- Track: AI Engineering › RAG › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 40 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/rag-practice/
- Before this: Re-ranking and Late Interaction (`ai-engineering/reranking-and-late-interaction`), RAG Evals: Retrieval, Faithfulness and Relevance (`ai-engineering/rag-evals`)
- Quiz topic: `rag`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. Work each one out by hand, then open the answer and compare.

**The toolkit:** precision@k = relevant found ÷ k; recall@k = relevant found ÷ all relevant; MRR = average of 1 ÷ first relevant rank; RRF score = Σ 1 ÷ (60 + rank); memory = chunks × dimensions × bytes, plus 8M bytes per chunk for HNSW links; loop tokens = Σ (S + i × C); faithfulness = supported claims ÷ all claims.

Question 1 · Easy · precision and recall

### A question has 3 relevant chunks. You retrieve 5, and 2 of them are relevant. What are precision@5 and recall@5?

Answer: **Precision@5 = 0.40, and recall@5 = 0.67**

1. Precision: 2 relevant ÷ 5 retrieved = 0.40.

2. Recall: 2 found ÷ 3 relevant = 0.67.

Which matters more for RAG's first stage? Usually recall, because a re-ranker can fix order, but not what's missing.

Question 2 · Easy · MRR

### Across 4 questions, the first relevant chunk appears at ranks 1, 3, not at all, and 2. What's the MRR?

Answer: **About 0.46**

1. Reciprocal ranks: 1, 1/3, 0 and 1/2.

2. Their sum is 1.83, and 1.83 ÷ 4 ≈ 0.46.

A missing chunk counts as 0, so a few misses hurt a lot.

Question 3 · Medium · fusion

### BM25 returns A, B, C. Dense search returns C, A, D. Using reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60, what's the merged order?

Answer: **A, C, B, D**

1. A: 1/61 + 1/62 = 0.01639 + 0.01613 = 0.03252.

2. C: 1/63 + 1/61 = 0.01587 + 0.01639 = 0.03226.

3. B: 1/62 = 0.01613, and D: 1/63 = 0.01587.

Why ranks, rather than raw scores? BM25 and cosine scores aren't on the same scale.

Question 4 · Medium · memory

### You have 10 million chunks at 1,024 dimensions. How much memory do float32 vectors need? And binary? How much do HNSW links add at M = 16?

Answer: **About 41 GB, or 1.28 GB as binary, plus about 1.28 GB of links**

1. Float32: 10M × 1,024 × 4 bytes ≈ 41 GB.

2. Binary: 41 GB ÷ 32 ≈ 1.28 GB.

3. Links: 10M × 8 × 16 bytes = 1.28 GB.

With binary, the links cost as much as the vectors, and you still need full vectors somewhere for rescoring.

Question 5 · Medium · filters

### You filter after search. You fetch 100 candidates, and a user can see 5% of documents. You want 10 results. What happens, and what do you do?

Answer: **About 5 results come back. Filter during search, or fetch far more**

1. 100 × 5% = about 5 visible candidates.

2. That's fewer than the 10 you want, and worse for rarer filters.

3. Fetching more costs time. Filtering during search is better, but you must check recall under that filter.

A filter-blind graph can lose most of its recall, with no error to warn you.

Question 6 · Medium · agent cost

### An agent has a 2,000-token base prompt, and adds 5,000 tokens of results per search. It does 3 searches, then answers. How many input tokens does it use, keeping full history?

Answer: **38,000 tokens**

1. Call 1: 2,000.

2. Call 2: 7,000. Call 3: 12,000.

3. Call 4: 17,000. The total is 38,000.

One static search uses 7,000. What cuts this? Batching searches, capping rounds and trimming old results.

Question 7 · Medium · should you index?

### Your documents total 120,000 tokens and change monthly. Your manager wants a vector database. What do you suggest?

Answer: **Try putting it in the prompt first, with prompt caching**

1. Anthropic suggests this under about 200,000 tokens.

2. It has no chunking, syncing or retrieval failures to manage.

3. Measure cost and latency, and add retrieval when they hurt, or the corpus grows.

When would you index anyway? When cost per call is too high, permissions differ per document, or it's growing fast.

Question 8 · Hard · migration

### You have 200 million chunks of 300 tokens, and a limit of 10 million tokens a minute. Embedding costs $0.13 per million tokens. What are the cost and time, and how do you switch without downtime?

Answer: **About $7,800 and about 4.2 days. Build a second index, dual write, backfill, test, then flip an alias**

1. Tokens: 200M × 300 = 60 billion.

2. Cost: 60,000 million × $0.13 = $7,800.

3. Time: 60B ÷ 10M = 6,000 minutes, about 4.2 days.

4. Dual writes keep the new index current during those days.

Why can't you mix old and new vectors in one index? They live in different spaces, so their scores mean nothing together.

Question 9 · Hard · permissions

### Your permission service has an outage. The code catches the error, and sets the allowed-folders list to empty, and the search code treats an empty list as no filter. What happens, and how do you fix it?

Answer: **Every user can retrieve every document. Fail closed, and test for it**

1. An empty filter must mean no results, not all results.

2. On error, return nothing and show a clear message.

3. Add a test where the permission call fails, and one where user A asks for user B's document.

Which is worse here: an outage or a leak? Usually a leak, so accept the outage.

Question 10 · Hard · conflicting results

### A paper says late interaction doubles the hit rate, and another says it loses to dense search. Your team asks which to believe. What do you say?

Answer: **Both may be right for their setups. Test on your own data, and count the costs**

1. The first used synthetic questions and a different encoder, on 463,971 paper abstracts.

2. The second used visually rich reports, and text late interaction lost there.

3. Compare recall on your labelled questions, plus memory and latency.

It's a good general rule: gains measured alone may not survive in your full pipeline.

**More practice and sources**

10 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 7 Nov 2026

Keep practising

Uses RAG End to End, Embeddings and Vector Indexes, Re-ranking, Grounded Answers, Agentic RAG, Permissions, Keeping an Index Current and Evaluating LLM Apps. Scenarios and numbers are invented, so the answers are worked examples.

# What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop

> Agent or workflow, and why does a 95%-per-step agent fail most 20-step tasks?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent/
- Before this: Prompt Engineering Patterns (`ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-patterns`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

A refund agent must read a complaint, look up the order, check the policy, decide a refund and write back. "Where is my order?" fits a fixed flow, but late, missing and charged twice doesn't. A colleague says each step works 95% of the time, so it's reliable. The interviewer asks:

> Agent or workflow, and why does a 95%-per-step agent fail most 20-step tasks?

**Running example (this track):** the food-delivery company builds a **refund agent** that reads a customer's complaint, looks up the order, checks the policy, decides a refund, issues it via a tool and writes back to the customer.

#### Some tasks can't be scripted in advance

"Where is my order?" fits a fixed workflow. "My order was late, one item was missing and I was charged twice" needs several lookups, decisions that depend on what the lookups return, and maybe a follow-up question. Writing every branch by hand is impractical; letting the model choose the next step is the agentic approach.

### The idea

Think of a recipe and a cook. A workflow is the recipe: code decides every step, so it's predictable. An agent is the cook who tastes, then decides what to do next. That handles surprises, but every extra decision is another chance to go wrong, and those chances multiply.

[Figure: Whole-task success. 95 percent per step over 20 steps: 35.8 percent. Over 50 steps: 7.7 percent. 99 percent per step over 50 steps: 60.5 percent. 95 percent per step over 20 steps with error recovery: 78.5 percent.]

_From the lab's simple model, where steps fail independently. Real agents also make correlated errors._

### Play

**Try to break it.** At 95% per step, raise the steps from 20 to 50. Then try 99%. Then turn on error recovery.

#### "Each step works 95% of the time, so it's reliable"

Simple model: steps fail independently; recovery means a failed step is detected (tool error, validation, check) 80% of the time and retried once. Real agents also make correlated errors (a wrong plan early), so this is optimistic.

At **95%** per step, a **20-step** task succeeds only **35.8%** of the time; 50 steps, 7.7%. Even 99% per step gives 60.5% at 50 steps. Detecting and retrying failed steps (tool errors, schema checks, verifying results) lifts the 20-step task to **78.5%** for one extra call. This is why long autonomous tasks are hard, why benchmarks like τ-bench measure consistency, and why METR found the length of tasks agents can complete at 50% reliability has roughly doubled every 7 months: per-step reliability is what's improving.

**Now say why:** 95% sounds good, so how does a 20-step task end up at about a third?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

An **agent** is an LLM that decides its own next step in a loop: **think** about the goal, **act** by calling a tool (search orders, issue a refund, run code), **observe** the result, and repeat until done. That's the **ReAct** pattern (Yao et al. 2023). A **workflow**, by contrast, follows a path you hard-coded (classify → retrieve → answer). Anthropic's guidance: use the simplest thing that works, and reach for agents only when the steps can't be predicted in advance, because autonomy costs money, latency and reliability. The core reliability problem is **compounding**: if each step succeeds 95% of the time, a 20-step task succeeds only 36% of the time, so agents need error recovery, checks and good tools. What you'll be able to do after this: define an agent, choose between a workflow and an agent, and reason about multi-step reliability.

#### Think, act, observe

1. **Thought:** "The customer says late and missing item. I need the order details." (reasoning tokens)

2. **Action:** `get_order(id="48213")` (a tool call)

3. **Observation:** "delivered 40 min late; items: biryani, raita; raita marked missing by restaurant"

4. Repeat (check policy, compute refund, issue refund) until the model returns a final answer, or a step/budget limit is hit.

ReAct interleaving reasoning with actions beat acting-only and reasoning-only baselines; on ALFWorld and WebShop it improved absolute success rates by 34 and 10 points over imitation and reinforcement learning methods (Yao et al. 2023).

| Workflow patterns (Anthropic) | Agent |
|---|---|
| prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer: code decides the path | the model decides the path, tool by tool, in a loop |
| predictable, cheaper, easier to test | flexible for open-ended tasks; costlier, less predictable |

## In practice

### In practice

#### When to build an agent, and when not to

- **Start with a workflow** if the steps are known; add agentic loops only where the path depends on intermediate results.

- **Good fits:** coding (tests give feedback), research, customer cases with variable investigation, operations with clear tools and checks.

- **Make each step reliable:** well-designed tools with clear errors, structured outputs, verification, and budgets (max steps, max cost, timeouts).

- **Keep humans in the loop** for irreversible or high-value actions (Agent Safety).

#### A model in a loop with tools, and reliability is the product

An agent lets the model choose actions step by step; because errors compound over steps, the engineering is about making each step reliable, detecting failures, and keeping the loop as short and constrained as the task allows.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Everything should be an agent"

It sounds right, since agents can handle anything a workflow can. But most production systems are workflows with small agentic parts, and an agent costs more and is harder to test. Add a loop only where the path depends on intermediate results. High per-step accuracy doesn't make it reliable either: multiply it over the steps.

## Say it

### Agent or workflow, and why does a 95%-per-step agent fail most 20-step tasks?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Agent vs chatbot with tools?

A chatbot calls at most a tool or two per turn under user direction; an agent pursues a goal over many self-chosen steps, deciding when it's done.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you stop an agent looping forever?

Step, time and cost budgets; detection of repeated identical actions; a final "give up and escalate" path.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why did ReAct work better than acting alone?

Reasoning between actions lets the model track progress, handle exceptions and update its plan based on observations, instead of blindly issuing actions.

#### The 30-second answer

An agent is an LLM running in a loop: it reasons about the goal, calls a tool, observes the result and decides the next step until it finishes, which is the ReAct pattern. A workflow instead follows a path defined in code, like chaining or routing. I'd use a workflow when the steps are predictable and an agent only when the path depends on intermediate results, because agents cost more and are less predictable. The key engineering problem is compounding error: at 95 percent per step a 20-step task succeeds about a third of the time, so you need reliable tools, validation, error recovery, budgets and human approval for risky actions.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Everything should be an agent." Most production systems are workflows with small agentic parts.

- "Per-step accuracy is high, so it's reliable." Multiply over steps.

**Key terms and sources**

What makes an LLM system an agent: the loop of reasoning, acting with tools and observing results; how agents differ from chatbots and fixed workflows; Anthropic's workflow patterns (chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer); why per-step errors compound over long tasks; and when not to build an agent · built from Yao et al. (ReAct, ICLR 2023), Anthropic (Building Effective Agents, Dec 2024), Schick et al. (Toolformer, NeurIPS 2023), Kwa et al. (METR, Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks, 2025) and Yao et al. (τ-bench, ICLR 2025) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. S. Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models", ICLR 2023, [arXiv:2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629).

2. Anthropic, "Building Effective Agents", Dec 2024, [anthropic.com](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents).

3. T. Schick et al., "Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2302.04761](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761).

4. T. Kwa et al. (METR), "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks", 2025, [arXiv:2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499); S. Yao et al., "τ-bench", ICLR 2025, [arXiv:2406.12045](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045).
