# Tool and Function Calling

> How do models call tools, and why do 100 tools make an agent worse?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/tool-calling/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`), Structured Output and Constrained Decoding (`ai-engineering/structured-output`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

The refund agent has tools like get_order, get_policy and issue_refund, and the company wants to add 50 more from other teams. A colleague says just give the agent every tool, since more tools means more capable. The interviewer asks:

> How do models call tools, and why do 100 tools make an agent worse?

**Running example:** the refund agent has tools like `get_order`, `get_policy`, `issue_refund` and `message_customer`, and the company wants to add 50 more from other teams.

#### Models write text; systems need actions

To look up an order or issue a refund, the model's output must become a precise, validated function call, and its result must flow back so the model can continue. Free-text parsing ("call get_order with 48213 please") is brittle.

### The idea

Think of a waiter writing an order ticket. The waiter doesn't cook: the kitchen reads the ticket, checks it and makes the dish. Now hand that waiter a 200-page menu. They read for longer and pick the wrong dish more often. The model proposes, and your code disposes.

[Figure: With 50 tools in the prompt, definitions cost 7,500 tokens per call. With tool search they cost 960. In the RAG-MCP stress test, the right tool was picked 13.6 percent of the time from a large set, and 43.1 percent after retrieving descriptions first.]

_Tokens from the lab, at about 150 per definition. The accuracy figures are from the RAG-MCP stress test, with a much larger toolset._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the tools available from 50 to 200. Switch to tool search. Then compare 3 lookups one after another with 3 in parallel.

#### "Just give the agent every tool"

~150 tokens per tool definition; tool search adds one ~60-token search tool and shows the top 5 matches. Latency: 1.2 s per model turn, 0.8 s per tool call; the three lookups (order, payment, policy) are independent.

With **50 tools** in the prompt, **7,500 tokens** of definitions ride along on every call; at 200 tools, 30,000. Beyond cost, accuracy suffers: in the RAG-MCP stress test, picking the right tool from a large set succeeded only **13.6%** of the time, and retrieving relevant tool descriptions first raised it to **43.1%** while halving prompt tokens. With **tool search**, the agent sees about 6 definitions (960 tokens). Separately, letting the model issue the three independent lookups **in parallel** cuts latency from 7.2 s to **3.2 s**.

**Now say why:** a definition is only about 150 tokens, so what's the harm in adding more?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

The model can't run code; it can only write text. **Tool calling** makes that text structured: you describe each tool (name, description, JSON-schema parameters), the model replies with a **call** like `{"name": "get_order", "arguments": {"order_id": "48213"}}` (generated with constrained decoding), **your code** executes it, and the result goes back into the conversation for the next step. Models can request several independent calls at once (**parallel calls**), cutting latency. Most agent failures are tool failures: vague descriptions, overlapping tools, unhelpful errors, or too many tools; every tool definition costs context tokens, and selection accuracy drops as tools pile up (RAG-MCP: 13.6% with all tools loaded, 43.1% when relevant tools were retrieved first). What you'll be able to do after this: explain the tool-call loop, design good tools, and handle large tool sets.

#### The tool-call loop

1. You send the conversation plus tool definitions (name, description, parameter schema).

2. The model returns either a final answer or one or more tool calls with arguments.

3. Your code validates arguments, checks permissions, executes, and returns results (including errors) as tool-result messages.

4. The model continues with the results; repeat.

- **Good tool design** (Anthropic's guidance): few, clearly distinct tools that match how a person would do the task; descriptive names and docs with examples; parameters that are hard to misuse (enums, IDs not free text); responses that return what the agent needs (not raw dumps); errors that say how to fix the call.

- **Never trust arguments:** the model chose them, possibly influenced by injected text. Validate and authorise every call in code.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Production patterns

- **Strict schemas** so arguments always parse; validation and authorisation in code before execution.

- **Tool search / dynamic loading** for large toolsets (also offered by some providers and in MCP clients); group tools by task and expose only what the current step needs.

- **Errors as feedback:** return actionable messages ("order_id must look like ORD-12345") so the model can self-correct; cap retries.

- **Idempotency** for side effects: an `issue_refund` called twice must not pay twice (idempotency keys).

- **Evaluate tools** like prompts: test sets of tasks, track wrong-tool and bad-argument rates.

**Code instead of definitions.** With many MCP tools, an agent can write code that calls them, instead of loading every definition and passing every result through its context. Anthropic reported one workflow falling from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, a 98.7% saving. Its tool guide also caps Claude Code tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default, and found a concise response used 72 tokens against 206 for a detailed one.

#### The model proposes, your code disposes

Tool calling turns model output into structured requests that your code validates and executes; agent quality depends as much on clear, few, well-documented tools as on the model.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The model runs the API"

It sounds right, from the way people describe agents. But the model only emits a request. Execution, permissions and side effects are under your control, which is why you never trust the arguments: the model chose them, possibly influenced by injected text. More tools don't make it more capable either: past a point, they make it worse.

## Say it

### How do models call tools, and why do 100 tools make an agent worse?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

The agent calls the wrong tool. What do you check?

Overlapping or vague descriptions, too many tools in context, ambiguous parameter names; then add examples, merge or split tools, and evaluate selection on a test set.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you make a refund tool safe to retry?

Idempotency key per refund request, server-side checks of amount and eligibility, and returning the existing result if called again.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Who executes the tool: the model or your system?

Your system. The model only emits the request; execution, permissions and side effects are under your control.

#### The 30-second answer

You give the model tool definitions with names, descriptions and JSON-schema parameters; it responds with structured calls instead of text; your code validates, authorises and executes them and returns results, including errors, and the loop continues. Models can request independent calls in parallel to cut latency. Good tools are few, distinct, well documented, hard to misuse and return concise results with actionable errors. Many tools bloat the context and hurt selection, so for large toolsets I'd retrieve relevant tools dynamically. And side-effecting tools need idempotency and permission checks in code.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "The model runs the API." Your code does.

- "More tools make the agent more capable." Past a point they make it worse.

**Key terms and sources**

How LLMs call tools: JSON-schema tool definitions, the model emitting a structured call, your code executing it and returning the result, parallel calls, error handling, and designing tools agents can use well (clear names and descriptions, few overlapping tools, helpful errors); plus why loading hundreds of tools hurts and how tool search fixes it · built from Schick et al. (Toolformer, 2023), Patil et al. (Gorilla, NeurIPS 2024), Gan & Sun (RAG-MCP, 2025), Anthropic (Writing tools for agents, 2025), and the OpenAI and Anthropic tool-use documentation · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

1. T. Schick et al., "Toolformer", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2302.04761](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761); S. Patil et al., "Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs", NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2305.15334](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334).

2. T. Gan & Q. Sun, "RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via Retrieval-Augmented Generation", 2025, [arXiv:2505.03275](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03275).

3. Anthropic, "Writing effective tools for agents", 2025; Anthropic and OpenAI tool-use / function-calling documentation.

4. Anthropic, ["Code execution with MCP"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp), Nov 2025; ["Writing effective tools for agents"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents), Sep 2025.

# Planning and Reflection

> When does 'check your work' actually help an agent?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/planning-and-reflection/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

The refund agent must compute a complicated case: late, a missing item and a double charge. Its amount must match the policy calculator, and sometimes it forgets the double charge. A colleague adds "double-check your work" to the prompt. The interviewer asks:

> When does "check your work" actually help an agent?

**Running example:** the refund agent must compute the refund for a complicated case (late + missing item + double charge) and its amount must match the policy calculator.

#### Long tasks drift; first attempts are often wrong

Without structure, an agent may repeat lookups, forget a sub-goal (the double charge) or commit to a wrong number. Humans plan, check their work and fix mistakes; agents need explicit mechanisms for the same.

### The idea

Think of re-reading your own maths homework, against checking it on a calculator. Re-reading feels careful, but you can't always see your mistake, and you may even change a right answer. With a calculator, you know which ones to redo. Reflection needs a signal from outside.

[Figure: With a 60 percent first attempt and 2 retries, final success is 60 percent with self-review only, and 93.6 percent with a reliable check.]

_From the lab's simplified model. A real self-review catches some errors, and also breaks some right answers._

### Play

**Try to break it.** With no reliable check, raise the retries. Then switch to the tests or the policy calculator, and change the chance an attempt is correct.

#### "Just ask it to check its work"

Simplified: attempts are independent; with a check, failures are always detected and retried; without one, the agent accepts its first answer (in practice, self-review catches some errors and also "fixes" some correct answers into wrong ones).

With a **reliable check** (unit tests, the policy calculator, a tool error), a 60% first attempt plus **2 retries** reaches **93.6%**, using only 1.56 attempts on average because most cases pass early. With **no reliable check**, retries don't help: the agent can't tell which answers are wrong, so success stays at 60%. Reflexion's gains came from test feedback; Huang et al. found that asking models to self-correct reasoning _without_ external feedback didn't improve, and sometimes hurt, accuracy. Design the loop around a signal.

**Now say why:** why do extra retries add nothing without a reliable check?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Agents plan in two broad ways. **ReAct** decides one step at a time based on the latest observation: flexible, but it can wander. **Plan-and-execute** writes a plan up front (often with a strong model), executes steps (often with a cheaper model) and **re-plans** when something fails: more structured and cheaper, but brittle if the plan is wrong. **Reflection** asks the agent to critique its own attempt and try again; Reflexion lifted GPT-4 on HumanEval from 80% to 91% by reflecting on failed unit tests. The catch: reflection works when there's an **external signal** (tests, tool errors, a checker). Without one, models often can't tell they're wrong, and "self-correction" can even make reasoning worse (Huang et al. 2024). What you'll be able to do after this: choose between ReAct and plan-and-execute, and design reflection loops that actually improve results.

#### Planning and reflection patterns

| Pattern | How | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **ReAct** | think → act → observe, one step at a time | exploratory tasks where each result changes the next step |
| **Plan-and-execute** | planner writes steps; executor runs them; re-plan on failure (Plan-and-Solve prompting showed explicit plans help reasoning) | tasks with a clear structure; cost (cheap executor) |
| **Reflection / Reflexion** | after a failed attempt, write a short critique and retry with it in memory | tasks with feedback: tests, errors, checkers |
| **Evaluator–optimizer** | one call generates, another evaluates against criteria, loop until pass | writing, translation, code review |
| **Search** (Tree of Thoughts) | explore several partial solutions and backtrack | puzzles and planning with evaluable states; expensive |

## In practice

### In practice

#### In production

- **Reasoning models** (RLVR-trained) plan internally; explicit planning prompts matter less, but tool-based checks matter as much as ever.

- **Keep a visible plan** (a to-do list in context or a scratch file) for long tasks so the agent tracks sub-goals; update it as steps complete.

- **Prefer verifiable steps:** compute amounts with tools, run tests, validate outputs; reflect on concrete failures.

- **Cap loops:** max retries and budgets; escalate to a human when the check keeps failing.

#### Plan to stay on track, reflect on evidence

Planning keeps multi-step work organised, and reflection turns failures into fixes, but only when an external signal says what failed.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Ask it to double-check, and it fixes errors"

It sounds right, since that works for careful people. But Huang et al. found that asking models to self-correct reasoning without external feedback didn't improve accuracy, and sometimes hurt it. Reflexion's gains came from test feedback. Planning doesn't make agents deterministic either: if early observations invalidate the plan, it needs re-planning.

## Say it

### When does "check your work" actually help an agent?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

When would plan-and-execute fail?

When early observations invalidate the plan; without re-planning it executes a wrong plan confidently. Add checkpoints that trigger re-planning.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Is an LLM judge a good enough verifier?

Sometimes, for style or completeness, after validation; for correctness, prefer executable checks (tests, calculators, database queries).

Follow-up 3 of 3

How does Tree of Thoughts differ from reflection?

It explores multiple partial solutions in parallel and backtracks using evaluations of intermediate states; reflection improves one trajectory after it fails.

#### The 30-second answer

ReAct plans step by step from observations, which is flexible but can wander; plan-and-execute writes a plan first, often with a strong model, executes with cheaper calls and re-plans on failure, which is more structured. Reflection has the agent critique a failed attempt and retry; Reflexion took GPT-4 from 80 to 91 percent on HumanEval using test feedback. The key is an external signal: tests, tool errors or a checker. Without one, self-correction often doesn't help reasoning and can hurt. In production I'd keep an explicit task list, verify with tools, and cap retries with escalation.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Ask it to double-check, and it fixes errors." Not without a reliable signal.

- "Planning makes agents deterministic." Plans still need re-planning.

**Key terms and sources**

How agents organise multi-step work and recover from mistakes: ReAct's step-by-step planning vs plan-and-execute, task decomposition, re-planning, reflection and self-critique (Reflexion), evaluator–optimizer loops, and why reflection only works when there is a reliable signal to reflect on · built from Yao et al. (ReAct, 2023), Wang et al. (Plan-and-Solve, ACL 2023), Shinn et al. (Reflexion, NeurIPS 2023), Madaan et al. (Self-Refine, NeurIPS 2023), Huang et al. (LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR 2024), Yao et al. (Tree of Thoughts, NeurIPS 2023) and Anthropic (Building Effective Agents, 2024) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. N. Shinn et al., "Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2303.11366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366); A. Madaan et al., "Self-Refine", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2303.17651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651).

2. J. Huang et al., "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet", ICLR 2024, [arXiv:2310.01798](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798).

3. L. Wang et al., "Plan-and-Solve Prompting", ACL 2023, [arXiv:2305.04091](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04091); S. Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts", NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv:2305.10601](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601).

4. S. Yao et al., "ReAct", ICLR 2023, [arXiv:2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629); Anthropic, "Building Effective Agents", 2024.

# Memory and Context Engineering

> How does an agent remember a peanut allergy 50 turns later?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/memory-and-context-engineering/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

In turn 1 of a long support chat, a customer says they're allergic to peanuts. Fifty turns later they ask the agent to reorder a dish. A colleague keeps only the last 10 turns, to save tokens. The interviewer asks:

> How does an agent remember a peanut allergy 50 turns later?

**Running example:** a long support conversation. In turn 1 the customer says "I'm allergic to peanuts"; 50 turns later they ask the agent to reorder a dish.

#### Context is finite, expensive and imperfectly used

Agents loop many times, and each loop adds tool outputs (order JSON, policy text, search results). Keeping everything blows the budget and buries the important facts; dropping things loses them. Memory design decides what the model sees at every step.

### The idea

Think of a small desk. Keep today's papers on it, summarise the older ones into a note and file anything important on a card in a drawer. You don't keep everything on the desk, and you don't throw the allergy card away. You pull the card out when food comes up.

[Figure: At turn 200. Full history: 62,000 tokens per call, and the allergy is there but buried. Last 10 turns: 5,000 tokens, and it is forgotten. Last 10 with a summary and a memory store: 5,950 tokens, and it is retrieved when needed.]

_From the lab, at turn 200. Long contexts are used least reliably in the middle._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the turns to 50, then 200. Switch between full history, the last 10 turns, the last 10 with a summary and the last 10 with a summary and memory store.

#### "Just keep the whole history"

2,000-token system prompt and tools; 300 tokens per turn (message + tool results); summary 500 tokens; 3 retrieved memories ≈ 450 tokens. Cost and latency scale with input tokens per call.

**Full history** is simplest and remembers everything: at turn 50 each call carries 17,000 tokens; at turn 200, **62,000**, and the conversation has consumed **6.43 M** input tokens, with the allergy buried in the middle where models use information least reliably. A **10-turn window** caps calls at 5,000 tokens (0.99 M total) but has **forgotten** the allergy, a dangerous failure. A **summary** keeps it only if the summariser judged it important. A **memory store** that saves durable facts and retrieves them when relevant keeps calls at 5,950 tokens and still knows: the allergy is retrieved when the customer orders food.

**Now say why:** a summary might keep the allergy, so why isn't that good enough?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

The model only knows what's in its **context window** right now. In an agent, that window fills with the system prompt, tool definitions, the conversation and, above all, **tool results**, and it grows every step. Long contexts cost more (every call re-reads them), get slower, and models use them less reliably ("lost in the middle", and accuracy decaying as inputs grow, sometimes called context rot). **Context engineering** is deciding what goes in: keep a **window** of recent turns, **summarise or compact** older ones, store durable facts in **long-term memory** (a database or vector store) and retrieve them when relevant, write large intermediate results to files, and give sub-agents their own clean contexts. The aim is the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the next step. What you'll be able to do after this: design an agent's memory, estimate context growth and cost, and choose between windowing, summaries and retrieval.

#### Kinds of memory

| Memory | Where it lives | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Working / short-term** | the context window | current conversation, latest tool results, the task list |
| **Summaries / compaction** | the context window, rewritten | "Customer: late order #48213, refund 10% issued; allergic to peanuts" |
| **Long-term semantic** | database or vector store, retrieved per step | preferences, allergies, account facts |
| **Episodic** | store of past interactions | "last month we gave a goodwill credit" |
| **Procedural** | prompts, tools, learned instructions | refund procedure, tone rules |

MemGPT (Packer et al.) framed this like an operating system: the model pages information between a small context and larger external storage. Generative Agents (Park et al.) stored observations and retrieved them by recency, importance and relevance.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Context engineering techniques

- **Trim tool results:** return compact, relevant fields from tools instead of raw dumps; this is often the biggest saving.

- **Compaction:** when the context nears a limit, summarise older turns and keep critical facts and open tasks verbatim.

- **Explicit memory writes:** let the agent (or code) save important facts (allergies, decisions, IDs) to a store with clear schemas; retrieve by relevance and recency.

- **Offload:** write large intermediate artefacts to files or a scratchpad and keep references in context.

- **Isolate:** run sub-tasks in sub-agents with their own contexts and return only the result.

- **Cache the stable prefix** (system prompt, tools) with prompt caching, and keep it unchanged between turns.

Frameworks now separate per-conversation memory, saved as checkpoints under a thread ID, from a long-term **store** shared across conversations. Agents can also keep a playbook of lessons from past runs: ACE gained 10.6% on agent tasks with small, itemised updates. Rewriting the whole playbook at once risks **context collapse**: in one case, 18,282 tokens shrank to 122 and accuracy fell below having no playbook. See Agent Skills and Self-Improving Context.

**Effective context is shorter than the window.** In NVIDIA's RULER, all 17 models claimed 32K tokens or more and nearly all passed simple needle tests, yet only about half kept a good score at 32K on harder tasks. NoLiMa found 11 of 13 models fell below half their short-context score at 32K when the question and answer shared no words. Even with perfect retrieval, accuracy fell 13.9–85% as inputs grew. So keep context small: clear stale tool results (Anthropic reported 29% better agentic search from this alone, and 84% fewer tokens in a 100-turn test), keep references to reload content, write notes outside the context, and use sub-agents that return short summaries. See Agent Scenarios: Context and Memory.

#### The smallest high-signal context for each step

Agent memory is about choosing what the model sees next: recent turns verbatim, older ones compacted, durable facts in a store retrieved when relevant, and bulky material kept outside the window.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A sliding window is enough"

It sounds right, since it caps the cost so neatly. But it forgets critical early facts, and the allergy is exactly that kind of fact. Keeping the whole history isn't the answer either, even with huge contexts: cost grows with every call's input, and recall degrades. Long-term memory has its own risks too: stale facts, privacy and injected content.

## Say it

### How does an agent remember a peanut allergy 50 turns later?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What should go into long-term memory?

Durable, user-specific or task-critical facts (preferences, constraints, decisions, IDs), with timestamps and sources; not raw transcripts.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Risks of long-term memory?

Stale or wrong memories persisting, privacy (store consent and deletion), and memory poisoning via injected content; scope memories per user and let users view and delete them.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not just use a 1M-token context model?

Cost and latency grow with every call's input, and recall degrades in very long contexts; selection still beats stuffing.

#### The 30-second answer

An agent only knows what's in its context, which grows every step with tool results, so cost and latency climb and models use long contexts less reliably. I'd keep recent turns verbatim, compact older turns into summaries that preserve key facts and open tasks, store durable facts like preferences or allergies in a long-term memory and retrieve them by relevance, trim tool outputs to what's needed, offload big artefacts to files and use sub-agents for isolated sub-tasks. I'd also keep the system prompt and tools stable so they're cached.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Keep the whole history; contexts are huge now." Cost and reliability still suffer.

- "A sliding window is enough." It forgets critical early facts.

**Key terms and sources**

What goes into an agent's context window at each step and why it matters: short-term memory (conversation and tool results), context growth and "context rot", sliding windows, summarisation and compaction, long-term memory stores (episodic and semantic, retrieved like RAG), offloading to files, and sub-agents for context isolation · built from Packer et al. (MemGPT, 2023), Park et al. (Generative Agents, UIST 2023), Liu et al. (Lost in the Middle, TACL 2024), Hong et al. (Chroma, Context Rot, 2025), Anthropic (Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025) and LangChain / LangGraph memory documentation · checked 8 Nov 2026

#### Sources

1. C. Packer et al., "MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems", 2023, [arXiv:2310.08560](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560).

2. J. S. Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior", UIST 2023, [arXiv:2304.03442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442).

3. N. Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", TACL 2024, [arXiv:2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172); K. Hong et al. (Chroma), "Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance", 2025.

4. Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents", 2025; LangChain / LangGraph memory documentation.

5. Q. Zhang et al., "Agentic Context Engineering", ICLR 2026, [arXiv:2510.04618](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618); LangGraph memory documentation (checkpointers and stores).

6. C.-P. Hsieh et al., "RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?", COLM 2024, [arXiv:2404.06654](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654); A. Modarressi et al., "NoLiMa", ICML 2025, [arXiv:2502.05167](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167); Y. Du et al., "Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval", 2025, [arXiv:2510.05381](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05381); Anthropic, ["Effective context engineering for AI agents"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents) and ["Managing context"](https://claude.com/blog/context-management), Sep 2025.

# Agent Skills and Self-Improving Context

> Your agent needs dozens of procedures, like how to file an expense or write a release note. How do you give it that know-how without filling its context, and can it learn new ones?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/agent-skills-and-self-improving-context/
- Before this: Memory and Context Engineering (`ai-engineering/memory-and-context-engineering`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your agent needs 80 procedures, from filing expenses to writing release notes. Someone pastes them all into the system prompt, and calls get slow and expensive. Another wants the agent to write its own lessons. The interviewer asks:

> Your agent needs dozens of procedures, like how to file an expense or write a release note. How do you give it that know-how without filling its context, and can it learn new ones?

#### Why it matters

Prompts that try to cover every procedure grow huge and contradictory. Fine-tuning procedures in is slow. Skills and evolving playbooks keep know-how as editable text that loads when needed. Interviewers ask how agents gain capabilities without retraining. For general memory design, see Memory and Context Engineering.

### The idea

Think of a library. You don't carry every book. You read the catalogue, then fetch the one book you need. And when you learn something, you add a note to the right page, rather than rewriting the whole library.

[Figure: Three ideas. Load descriptions, then details. Keep project instructions in AGENTS.md. Grow a playbook in small edits.]

_Know-how loads when it's needed._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Load 50 skills in full. Then switch to descriptions only, and raise the count.

#### Fifty skills, one context

Illustrative: 100 tokens of metadata and 3,000 tokens of instructions per skill, one skill in use at a time, input at $3 per million tokens, before any caching.

Loading 50 skills in full puts 150,000 tokens in every call, three quarters of a 200,000-token context, before the task even starts. With descriptions only and one skill in use, it's 8,000. At 200 skills, loading everything doesn't fit at all, while descriptions plus the skill in use take 23,000 tokens. That's why skills scale where giant prompts don't. The descriptions must be good, though: the agent picks skills by reading them, as it picks tools.

**Now say why:** why does loading on demand scale when a big prompt doesn't?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A **skill** is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file: a name, a description and instructions, plus optional scripts and reference files. The agent loads only each skill's **description** at startup, about 100 tokens, and reads the full instructions only when a task needs them. So 50 skills cost about 5,000 tokens, not 150,000. Anthropic made skills an open standard in Dec 2025. Agents can also **improve their own context**: ACE keeps a playbook of lessons from past runs, updated in small pieces, and gained 10.6% on agent tasks. Rewriting the whole playbook at once can cause **context collapse**, and lessons learned without a reliable signal can make things worse.

#### How it works

##### Skills and progressive disclosure

- **Metadata:** the name and description, about 100 tokens per skill, always in context so the agent knows what exists.

- **Instructions:** the body of SKILL.md, recommended under 5,000 tokens, loaded when the skill is chosen.

- **Resources:** scripts, templates and references, read only when needed. Scripts can run without their code entering the context.

The format is an open standard, with the name up to 64 characters and the description up to 1,024. It's now hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation, and can be served over MCP.

##### AGENTS.md

A plain file in a repository telling coding agents how to build, test and follow the project's conventions, like a README for agents. It's also an Agentic AI Foundation project.

##### Agents that edit their own context

ACE, at ICLR 2026, treats context as an evolving **playbook**. A generator does the task, a reflector draws lessons from what worked and what failed, and a curator adds them as small, itemised entries, each with counters for how often it helped or hurt. On AppWorld it lifted a ReAct agent by up to 17.1%, using only execution feedback, and matched the top production agent on the leaderboard with a smaller open model. It also cut adaptation time by 82.3% against GEPA.

##### Two failure modes

- **Context collapse:** when a model rewrites its whole playbook each time, it can suddenly compress it. In one ACE case, an 18,282-token playbook scoring 66.7% became 122 tokens scoring 57.1%, below the 63.7% with no playbook.

- **Bad signals:** without reliable feedback, such as labels or test results, self-written lessons can mislead. ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet both got worse on some finance tasks without labels.

#### The maths

$$ {T_{\text{context}}} = {n}\cdot{m} + {k}\cdot{s} $$

Progressive disclosure. Loading everything instead would cost n × s on every call.

- **tokens spent on skills**: What sits in context on every call.

- **installed skills**: How many the agent knows about.

- **metadata per skill**: About 100 tokens: name and description.

- **skills in use**: Usually one or two at a time.

- **full instructions**: Up to about 5,000 tokens each, loaded only when used.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Write sharp descriptions:** say what the skill does and when to use it, since selection depends on them.

- **Keep SKILL.md short:** under about 500 lines, with details in reference files.

- **Review skills like code:** a skill can run scripts, so a malicious one is a supply-chain risk.

- **Update playbooks in small pieces:** add and edit entries, de-duplicate, and never let a model rewrite the whole thing at once.

- **Learn only from reliable signals:** tests, labels or tool results, and check lessons on held-out tasks.

- **Cache the stable part:** ACE served 91.8% of input tokens from the prompt cache, cutting billed input cost by 82.6%.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Put every procedure in the system prompt"

It sounds thorough, but 80 procedures can fill most of the context on every call, slowing and confusing the agent. Load short descriptions, and fetch the full skill only when a task needs it.

## Say it

### Your agent needs dozens of procedures, like how to file an expense or write a release note. How do you give it that know-how without filling its context, and can it learn new ones?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Skills or MCP tools?

Tools are actions the agent calls. Skills are know-how: instructions, and sometimes scripts, for doing a task well. A skill often tells the agent how to use certain tools.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why are itemised updates safer than rewriting the playbook?

Small edits keep everything else intact. A full rewrite can silently drop most of it, as in ACE's case where 18,282 tokens collapsed to 122.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can an agent safely write its own skills?

Only with review and tests. Self-written instructions can encode mistakes, and scripts can do damage, so treat them like code contributions.

#### The 30-second answer

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: name, description and instructions, plus optional scripts and references. The agent keeps only descriptions in context, about 100 tokens each, and loads the full instructions when a task needs them, so 50 skills cost thousands of tokens, not 150,000. AGENTS.md gives coding agents project instructions. Agents can also improve their own context: ACE keeps an itemised playbook of lessons from execution feedback and gained about 10% on agent tasks. The risks are context collapse, when a model rewrites the whole playbook and loses it, and learning wrong lessons without reliable feedback.

**Key terms and sources**

Agent Skills as packaged know-how with progressive disclosure, AGENTS.md project instructions, and agents that improve by editing their own context: ACE playbooks, context collapse, and when self-written lessons help or hurt. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification)

- [Anthropic, Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills, Oct 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)

- [Zhang et al., Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), ICLR 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618)

- [Suzgun et al., Dynamic Cheatsheet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07952)

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/)

- [Hu et al., Memory in the Age of AI Agents (survey)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564)

# MCP: The Model Context Protocol

> What is MCP, and how is it different from function calling?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/model-context-protocol/
- Before this: Tool and Function Calling (`ai-engineering/tool-calling`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

The company wants its order system usable from the refund agent, the internal support chat, agents in the IDE and a few vendor tools, without a separate integration for each. A colleague suggests MCP, and says that also makes it safe. The interviewer asks:

> What is MCP, and how is it different from function calling?

**Running example:** the company wants its order system usable from the refund agent, the internal support chat, agents in the IDE and a few vendor tools, without writing a separate integration for each.

#### Every app × every tool

Before MCP, each AI application defined its own plugin or tool format, so connecting a data source meant writing and maintaining an adapter per application. Tool providers repeated the work for every host; hosts repeated it for every tool.

### The idea

Think of USB-C. Before it, every device needed its own cable for every charger. A standard port means each device and each charger is built once. But a standard port tells you nothing about whether that charger is safe to plug in.

[Figure: Without MCP, every application connects to every tool: 10 applications and 20 tools need 200 custom integrations. With MCP, each connects once to the protocol: 30 components.]

_From the lab: integration pieces to build and maintain._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Change the number of AI applications and the number of tools, and watch how far apart the two counts get.

#### Custom glue for every pair

Counts integration components to build and maintain; ignores per-integration size.

With **10** AI applications and **20** tools, custom integrations mean **200** adapters to build and keep working; with MCP, 10 clients (usually built into the host) and 20 servers: **30**, 6.7× fewer, and the gap grows with both numbers. The trap is assuming standard plumbing means safe plumbing: anyone can publish a server, and a server's tool descriptions go straight into the model's context.

**Now say why:** the model still emits tool calls, so what has MCP actually standardised?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Every AI app (chat assistant, IDE, agent) wants to connect to every tool and data source (GitHub, Slack, databases, your order system). Without a standard, that's **N apps × M tools** custom integrations. The **Model Context Protocol**, introduced by Anthropic in Nov 2024 and since adopted widely (and donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in Dec 2025), standardises the connection: a tool provider writes one **MCP server**; any MCP-capable **host** connects to it through a **client**, so it's **N + M**. Servers expose **tools** (actions the model can call), **resources** (data to read) and **prompts** (templates); messages are **JSON-RPC 2.0** over **stdio** (local) or **Streamable HTTP** (remote, with OAuth). MCP doesn't replace function calling; it's how the tools get discovered and invoked across apps. The spec is versioned by date and changes often, so check the current revision. What you'll be able to do after this: explain MCP's architecture and primitives, compare it with function calling, and name its security risks.

#### Hosts, clients, servers and primitives

- **Host:** the AI application (a desktop assistant, IDE, agent runtime). It runs one **client** per connected server and decides what the model sees and is allowed to do.

- **Server:** a program exposing capabilities. **Tools** (model-invoked actions with JSON-schema inputs), **resources** (readable data, by URI), **prompts** (reusable templates the user can pick).

- **Asking for more:** when a server needs input mid-call, such as a user confirmation, it returns **input required**, and the client repeats the call with the answers. Since the 2026-07-28 spec, this replaces server-initiated requests, and **sampling** (borrowing the client's model), **roots** and logging are deprecated.

- **Protocol:** JSON-RPC 2.0 messages: `server/discover`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/read`, and `subscriptions/listen` for changes. Since the 2026-07-28 spec there is no `initialize` handshake or session: every request carries its protocol version and capabilities, so any server instance can answer it.

- **Transports:** **stdio** for local servers launched by the host; **Streamable HTTP** for remote servers, with OAuth 2.1 authorisation. The older HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated.

- **Extensions:** optional features negotiated through capabilities: **tasks** for long-running work, and **MCP Apps** (Jan 2026), which lets a tool return an interactive interface.

The spec is dated: 2025-03-26 (Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1), 2025-06-18 (elicitation, structured tool output, resource indicators), 2025-11-25 (experimental tasks, client ID metadata documents) and 2026-07-28 (stateless requests, no sessions, input-required results, tasks as an extension, sampling and dynamic client registration deprecated). Deprecated features get at least 12 months' notice. For the details, see MCP Under the Hood; for A2A and other protocols, Agent Protocols. (Updated 7 Nov 2026.)

## In practice

### In practice

#### Security and practice

- **Tool poisoning:** malicious instructions hidden in a server's tool descriptions (which the user rarely sees) can steer the model; a server can also change its tools after you approved it ("rug pull"). Pin and review server versions; show users what tools do.

- **Over-broad permissions:** a server with full repo or database access is a powerful exfiltration channel if combined with untrusted content (lethal trifecta). Use least-privilege tokens, OAuth scopes and per-tool approval.

- **Too many servers:** every connected server adds tool definitions to context; enable only what the task needs, or use tool search (tool calling).

- **Ecosystem:** official SDKs in many languages, registries of servers, and support across major assistants, IDEs and agent frameworks. Related protocols: A2A (agent-to-agent) addresses agents calling other agents rather than tools.

**Measured, 2026.** A scan found 7,973 live remote MCP servers, and 40.6% exposed tools with no authentication. Of 119 OAuth-enabled servers tested, every one had at least one flaw, and 96.6% had client registration flaws. Another study audited 414 internet-facing servers: 91.8% lacked OAuth, and 687 tools offered shell execution with no access control. Standard plumbing isn't safe plumbing.

#### A USB-C port for AI tools

MCP turns N × M custom integrations into N + M standard ones by defining how hosts discover and call tools, read resources and use prompts, while trust, permissions and context budget remain the host's job.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "MCP makes tools safe"

It sounds right, since standards tend to feel safer. But it standardises access, and security is still yours. Anyone can publish a server, its tool descriptions go straight into the model's context, and a server can change its tools after you approved it. So pin servers, scope tokens and require approval for sensitive tools. It doesn't replace APIs either: servers usually wrap them.

## Say it

### What is MCP, and how is it different from function calling?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

MCP vs function calling?

Function calling is how a model requests a tool call in one API; MCP is how tools are packaged, discovered and invoked across many hosts. A host typically converts MCP tools into the model's function-calling format.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Tools vs resources vs prompts?

Tools are model-controlled actions; resources are application-controlled data the host can include in context; prompts are user-selected templates.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you expose your order system via MCP safely?

A remote server with OAuth, read-only tools by default, a narrow refund tool with server-side limits and idempotency, audit logs, and human approval above a threshold.

#### The 30-second answer

MCP is an open protocol, started by Anthropic and now under the Linux Foundation, that standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data. A host runs a client per server; servers expose tools the model can call, resources it can read and prompt templates, over JSON-RPC via stdio locally or Streamable HTTP remotely with OAuth. It turns N times M custom integrations into N plus M. It complements function calling rather than replacing it: the model still emits tool calls, MCP standardises discovery and execution. The main risks are untrusted servers, poisoned tool descriptions and over-broad permissions, so pin servers, scope tokens and require approval for sensitive tools.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "MCP makes tools safe." It standardises access; security is still yours.

- "MCP replaces APIs." Servers usually wrap existing APIs.

**Key terms and sources**

What MCP is and why it spread: the N×M integration problem, hosts, clients and servers, the primitives (tools, resources, prompts; and and how servers ask for more input), JSON-RPC messages, transports (stdio, Streamable HTTP), authorisation, how MCP relates to plain function calling, security concerns, and how the dated spec evolves · built from the Model Context Protocol specification and changelogs (modelcontextprotocol.io), Anthropic's MCP announcement (Nov 2024), the Linux Foundation Agentic AI Foundation announcement (Dec 2025), and the OWASP and Invariant Labs analyses of MCP tool poisoning · checked 29 Oct 2026

# MCP Under the Hood: Messages, Transports and Authorization

> Walk me through what actually happens when an agent calls a tool on a remote MCP server, including how it's authorised. What changed in the 2026 spec?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 22 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/mcp-under-the-hood/
- Before this: MCP: The Model Context Protocol (`ai-engineering/model-context-protocol`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your company is exposing its order system as a remote MCP server. The team followed a 2025 tutorial with an initialise handshake and sessions, and plans to forward users' tokens to the billing API. The interviewer asks:

> Walk me through what actually happens when an agent calls a tool on a remote MCP server, including how it's authorised. What changed in the 2026 spec?

#### Why it matters

The MCP overview explains why the protocol exists. Interviews for agent platform roles go deeper: what's on the wire, how remote servers scale, and how authorisation stops one server's token being used at another. The spec also changed a lot in July 2026, so answers based on older versions are now out of date.

### The idea

Think of a hotel key card. It opens your room and nothing else, it was issued at the front desk after checking your identity, and the bellboy can't copy it to open the safe. Each MCP token should work the same way: for one server, issued after a proper sign-in, and never passed on.

[Figure: Three layers. Stateless requests. Input-required results. Tokens bound to one server.]

_Most real servers get authorisation wrong._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Make PKCE optional and accept any redirect. Then accept any token.

#### Which attacks are still open?

A simplified threat model. Measured in 119 real OAuth-enabled MCP servers: 68.1% allowed PKCE to be skipped or downgraded, and 95.8% let anyone register a client with any redirect address.

With all four controls on, the three attacks are closed. Make PKCE optional and accept any redirect address, and an attacker who lures a user into signing in can catch the code and swap it for a token, which is account takeover. A study of 119 real OAuth-enabled MCP servers found every one had at least one flaw: 96.6% had client registration flaws, and 68.1% allowed PKCE to be skipped or downgraded. Accept tokens issued for any server, and a token stolen from one server works at yours. Pass the user's token upstream, and your server becomes a confused deputy.

**Now say why:** why must a token name the server it's for?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Since the **2026-07-28** spec, MCP is **stateless**: there's no initialise handshake or session, and every JSON-RPC request carries its protocol version and capabilities. A client calls `server/discover`, lists tools, and calls them. When a server needs more input mid-call, such as a user confirmation, it returns **input required**, and the client repeats the call with the answers. That replaces server-initiated sampling and elicitation. Remote servers use **Streamable HTTP** and **OAuth 2.1**: the client finds the authorisation server from the server's metadata, signs the user in with PKCE, and gets a token issued for **that server only**. Real deployments often get this wrong: 40.6% of 7,973 live remote servers needed no authentication at all.

#### How a call works

##### Stateless requests

Earlier versions began with an `initialize` handshake and kept a session, identified by a header, on the server. The 2026-07-28 spec removed both. Every request now carries the protocol version and the client's capabilities in its metadata, and a server that doesn't support the version returns an error. Servers must answer `server/discover`. Without sessions, any server instance behind a load balancer can answer any request.

##### The main messages

- `server/discover`: what the server supports.

- `tools/list`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`: what it offers. Lists can say how long they may be cached.

- `tools/call`: run a tool. Results can include structured content that matches an output schema.

- `subscriptions/listen`: one long-lived stream for change notifications, replacing the old separate GET stream.

##### Asking for more input

Previously, a server could send its own requests back to the client, to ask the user something (elicitation) or to borrow the client's model (sampling). Now a result has a type: **complete**, or **input required** with a list of questions. The client gathers the answers and repeats the call with them. Sampling, roots and logging are deprecated.

##### Tasks and extensions

Long-running work moved into an optional **tasks** extension, polled with `tasks/get`. Extensions are negotiated through capabilities. The first official one, **MCP Apps** (Jan 2026), lets a tool return an interactive interface, rendered in a sandboxed frame by clients such as Claude, VS Code's Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

##### Transports

**stdio** runs a local server as a subprocess. **Streamable HTTP** is the remote transport: the client POSTs each request, and the server answers with JSON or a stream. The old HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated, and if a stream breaks, the client re-sends the request.

##### Authorisation, step by step

1. The client calls the server without a token and gets **401**, pointing to the server's **protected resource metadata** (RFC 9728), which names its authorisation server.

2. The client identifies itself with a **client ID metadata document**, a URL describing it. Dynamic client registration is now deprecated.

3. The user signs in and consents. The client uses **PKCE**, so a stolen authorisation code is useless without the client's secret verifier.

4. The token request names the MCP server as the **resource** (RFC 8707), so the token is issued for that server only.

5. The server checks the token's audience. It must **never pass the user's token through** to other services; it gets its own tokens for those.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{code\_challenge}} = \text{BASE64URL}\big(\text{SHA256}({\text{code\_verifier}})\big) $$

PKCE. Local MCP clients can't keep a secret, so this one-time pair is what binds the sign-in to the token request. Servers that let clients skip it, or downgrade it, lose that protection.

- **sent at sign-in**: The client sends only this hash when it starts the sign-in.

- **kept secret**: A random string the client keeps, and reveals only when exchanging the code for a token. An attacker who steals the code doesn’t have it.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Never expose a remote server without authentication:** a July 2026 scan audited 414 internet-facing servers, 91.8% had no OAuth, and 687 tools offered shell execution with no access control.

- **Use a hardened OAuth setup:** enforce PKCE with S256, validate redirect addresses exactly, and check audience and issuer on every token.

- **Scope tightly:** request the fewest permissions, and give risky tools their own consent.

- **Validate inputs at the tool:** MCP servers have shipped SQL injection, SSRF and path traversal bugs, like any web service.

- **Plan for spec changes:** pin a protocol version, and track deprecations. Removed features get at least 12 months' notice.

- **Fewer tokens with code:** for many tools, let the agent write code that calls them, instead of loading every definition. Anthropic reported one workflow falling from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We followed the tutorial, so it's secure"

It sounds safe, but many tutorials predate the 2026 spec, and real servers are often misconfigured: every one of 119 tested OAuth servers had a flaw. Enforce PKCE, check redirects and audiences, and never forward the user's token.

## Say it

### Walk me through what actually happens when an agent calls a tool on a remote MCP server, including how it's authorised. What changed in the 2026 spec?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why did MCP remove sessions?

Sessions tied a client to one server instance, which made load balancing and scaling harder. Stateless requests can go to any instance, and state that matters is passed explicitly.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's token passthrough, and why is it banned?

An MCP server forwarding the user's token to another service. The token wasn't issued for that service, and the server loses control of what's done with it. The server must get its own tokens upstream.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A tool needs the user to confirm a refund mid-call. How does that work now?

The server returns input required with a confirmation question. The client shows it to the user and repeats the call with the answer.

#### The 30-second answer

Since the July 2026 spec, MCP is stateless: no initialise handshake or sessions, and each JSON-RPC request carries its version and capabilities, so any instance can serve it. The client discovers the server, lists tools and calls them; if the server needs input, it returns input required and the client repeats the call with answers, replacing server-initiated sampling and elicitation. Remote servers use Streamable HTTP and OAuth 2.1: the client finds the authorisation server from the server's metadata, signs in with PKCE, and gets a token bound to that server, which checks the audience and never passes the token on. Real servers often get this wrong: 40% of nearly 8,000 had no authentication.

**Key terms and sources**

The 2026-07-28 MCP specification in detail: stateless requests, discovery, tool calls, multi round-trip requests, tasks and extensions, Streamable HTTP, the OAuth flow step by step, and the security pitfalls measured in real servers. · checked 7 Nov 2026

# Agent Protocols: MCP, A2A, AG-UI and Commerce

> Your agent needs tools from other teams, help from another company's agent, a live UI and the ability to pay. Which protocols cover which connection?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/agent-protocols/
- Before this: MCP: The Model Context Protocol (`ai-engineering/model-context-protocol`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your travel agent uses internal tools, books through three airlines' agents, shows progress in a web app, and pays on the customer's behalf. A colleague says MCP covers all of it. The interviewer asks:

> Your agent needs tools from other teams, help from another company's agent, a live UI and the ability to pay. Which protocols cover which connection?

#### Why it matters

Early agents wired everything by hand: each tool, each partner and each UI had custom glue. As agents connect to more systems, and to each other, standards decide what can talk to what. Interviewers now ask "MCP or A2A?" and expect you to say they solve different problems. This lesson places each protocol on one map. For MCP's internals, see MCP Under the Hood.

### The idea

Think of a building's wiring. Power sockets, network cables, the intercom and the card reader at the door each have their own standard. One plug doesn't do everything, and that's fine, as long as each fits its job.

[Figure: Four connections. Tools via MCP. Other agents via A2A. Interfaces via AG-UI. Payments via AP2, ACP or UCP.]

_MCP and A2A solve different problems._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Pick each scenario, and watch which protocols it needs. Then raise the number of agents.

#### Which protocols does it need?

A simplified mapping. Real systems may use other options, such as plain APIs, for some connections.

A **support agent** with internal tools needs only MCP. A **travel agent** that books through airline agents adds A2A, because each airline's agent is a peer with its own rules. A **shopping agent** that pays adds AP2 or ACP, so the merchant can check what the user approved. A **copilot inside a web app** adds AG-UI to stream progress and tool calls to the screen. And with 8 agents from different teams, custom pairwise links would be 28, against 8 implementations of one protocol.

**Now say why:** why is another company's agent not just another MCP tool?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Agents connect to four kinds of thing, and each now has an open protocol. **MCP** connects an agent to tools and data. **A2A** lets an agent hand a task to another agent, possibly from another company: it finds it through an **Agent Card**, sends messages, and tracks a **task** through states like working, input required and completed. **AG-UI** streams an agent's progress to a user interface as events. **AP2**, **ACP** and **UCP** let agents shop and pay with proof of what the user authorised. MCP, A2A, Agent Skills and AGENTS.md now sit under the Linux Foundation's **Agentic AI Foundation**. They layer rather than compete.

#### The map

| Connection | Protocol | What it standardises |
|---|---|---|
| Agent ↔ tools and data | **MCP** | Servers expose tools, resources and prompts. Latest spec 2026-07-28. |
| Agent ↔ agent | **A2A** | Agent Cards for discovery, messages, tasks with states, streamed updates. Version 1.0. |
| Agent ↔ user interface | **AG-UI** | A stream of events: text, tool calls, state changes, reasoning, sub-agents. |
| Agent ↔ payments and shops | **AP2**, **ACP**, **UCP** | Signed proof of what the user authorised, checkout and payment flows. |
| Agent ↔ instructions | **Agent Skills**, **AGENTS.md** | Packaged know-how in folders, and project instructions for coding agents. |

##### A2A in more detail

Google started A2A, gave it to the Linux Foundation, and it reached version 1.0 in 2026. In August 2026 it joined the Agentic AI Foundation, backed by over 150 organisations.

- **Agent Card:** a JSON file, usually at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`, listing the agent's skills, endpoints, supported bindings and security schemes. Version 1.0 lets cards be signed.

- **Tasks:** work has a lifecycle: submitted, working, input required, auth required, completed, failed, cancelled or rejected. Long jobs report progress rather than blocking.

- **Messages, parts and artifacts:** messages carry parts (text, files, data), and results come back as artifacts.

- **Bindings:** JSON-RPC, gRPC or plain HTTP+JSON, with streaming and push notifications to a webhook.

##### MCP or A2A?

An MCP tool is a function the agent controls: call it, get a result. An A2A agent is a peer with its own model, tools and judgement, which may ask questions back, take hours, and keep its internals private. Use MCP to give your agent capabilities, and A2A to delegate a goal to someone else's agent.

##### Commerce

- **AP2** (Google, Sep 2025): signed "mandates" record what the user approved, from an open budget to a specific checkout, so merchants and payment networks can check an agent's authority. It extends A2A and UCP.

- **ACP** (OpenAI and Stripe, Sep 2025): checkout and delegated payment between an AI platform and merchants, used for buying inside ChatGPT.

- **UCP** (Google with Shopify, Walmart, Target and others): building blocks for agentic shopping across industries, using AP2 for payment mandates.

These protocols change monthly. Check the current versions before quoting details.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{custom links}} = \frac{{K}({K}-1)}{2}, \qquad {\text{with a protocol}} = {K} $$

The same argument as MCP's N × M to N + M, applied to agents talking to each other.

- **pairwise integrations**: Every pair of agents agrees on its own format.

- **number of agents**: Agents from different teams or companies that must work together.

- **one implementation each**: Each agent speaks the protocol once, and can talk to all the others.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Start with MCP:** most agents only need tools and data. Add A2A when you delegate goals across team or company boundaries.

- **Treat remote agents as untrusted:** an A2A peer's replies are input, like web pages. Its Agent Card name is not an identity, so verify signatures and authenticate.

- **Pass authority carefully:** when one agent delegates to another, make sure the second can't do more than the user allowed. Studies of multi-hop A2A delegation show this is easy to get wrong.

- **Keep humans in payment loops:** mandates prove what was approved, but set limits and confirmations too.

- **Watch versions:** pin protocol versions, and plan for breaking changes. MCP promises at least 12 months' notice before removing a deprecated feature.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "MCP covers everything"

It sounds right, since MCP is everywhere. But MCP connects an agent to functions it controls. Another company's agent is a peer with its own judgement, long tasks and private internals, which is what A2A is for. Interfaces and payments have their own protocols too.

## Say it

### Your agent needs tools from other teams, help from another company's agent, a live UI and the ability to pay. Which protocols cover which connection?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

When would you use A2A instead of exposing the other team's agent as an MCP tool?

When the other agent is a peer with its own judgement, may need to ask questions back, runs for a long time, or belongs to another company that won't expose its internals. For a simple function, MCP is simpler.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does an Agent Card contain?

The agent's name and description, its skills, the endpoints and protocol bindings it supports, its capabilities like streaming, and its security schemes. Version 1.0 cards can be signed.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does a payment protocol need mandates?

A merchant and payment network must check that a human authorised this purchase, within limits. A mandate is signed proof of that, rather than trusting the agent's word.

#### The 30-second answer

They solve different connections. MCP connects an agent to tools and data. A2A lets an agent delegate a task to another agent, possibly another company's: it finds it through an Agent Card, sends messages, and tracks a task through states like working, input required and completed, over JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP. AG-UI streams an agent's progress to a user interface as events. AP2, ACP and UCP handle shopping and payments with signed proof of what the user approved. MCP and A2A are now both under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation. I'd start with MCP, add A2A for cross-boundary delegation, and treat every remote agent's output as untrusted.

**Key terms and sources**

A map of the open agent protocols in late 2026: MCP for tools and data, A2A for agent-to-agent tasks, AG-UI for agent-to-user interfaces, AP2, ACP and UCP for payments and shopping, plus Agent Skills and AGENTS.md, and who governs them. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Model Context Protocol specification, 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest)

- [A2A protocol specification, version 1.0](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/)

- [A2A joins the Agentic AI Foundation, Aug 2026](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/blog/2026/08/27/a-new-chapter-for-a2a-joining-the-agentic-ai-foundation/)

- [AG-UI documentation](https://docs.ag-ui.com/)

- [Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)](https://ap2-protocol.org/)

# Multi-Agent Systems

> When do several agents beat one, and what does it cost?

- Track: AI Engineering › Agentic AI › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/multi-agent-systems/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`)
- Quiz topic: `agents`

## Intuition

### The situation

A weekly report must investigate why refunds rose in 5 cities, checking orders, ratings, delivery times and weather for each. One agent does them in turn, and its context fills up. A colleague proposes agents for everything, including writing one refund decision together. The interviewer asks:

> When do several agents beat one, and what does it cost?

**Running example:** a weekly "complaints intelligence" report: investigate why refunds rose in 5 cities by checking orders, restaurant ratings, delivery times and weather for each, then write one summary.

#### One agent, one context, one thread

A single agent investigating five cities does them one after another, and its context fills with every city's raw data, crowding out the task. Splitting the work could run in parallel and keep each context clean, but coordination has costs.

### The idea

Think of researching five cities with a team. A lead hands each person a clear brief, and each returns a short summary. It's faster, but you pay everyone. Now ask that team to write one paragraph at the same time without talking, and they'll contradict each other.

[Figure: Five independent sub-tasks. A single agent takes 5 minutes and 100 thousand tokens. An orchestrator with parallel workers takes 2 minutes and 170 thousand tokens.]

_Illustrative numbers from the lab. Real ratios vary._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between the single agent and the orchestrator with parallel workers. Then change the number of independent sub-tasks.

#### Faster, but at what cost?

Illustrative: each sub-task takes 60 s and 20k tokens; the orchestrator spends 30 s and 10k tokens planning and again synthesising; each worker repeats instructions and context (+50% tokens). Real ratios vary; Anthropic reported ~15× chat tokens for its multi-agent system vs ~4× for single agents.

For **5 independent cities**, a single agent takes **5 minutes** and 100k tokens; an orchestrator with parallel workers finishes in **2 minutes** but uses **170k** tokens (1.7×), and each worker's context stays focused on one city. That trade (time and breadth for tokens) is worth it for valuable, parallel, read-heavy work. The trap is applying it to coupled work: if the "workers" were editing parts of the same codebase or writing one refund decision together, each would make assumptions the others can't see, and the merge would conflict; failure studies of multi-agent systems find many failures come from mis-specification and inter-agent misalignment rather than the model itself.

**Now say why:** it's so much faster on cities, so why would it fail on editing one codebase?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A **multi-agent** system splits work across several LLM agents, usually an **orchestrator** that plans and delegates to **worker** sub-agents, each with its own context and tools, then combines their results. It shines for **broad, parallelisable, read-heavy** work: Anthropic's research system (lead agent + parallel sub-agents) beat a single agent by **90.2%** on an internal research eval, at about **15×** the tokens of a chat (single agents use about 4×). It struggles when sub-tasks are **tightly coupled**: parallel workers with partial context make conflicting decisions (Cognition's argument for coding). So: one agent by default; sub-agents for independent, parallel sub-tasks; **handoffs** for routing a conversation to a specialist. What you'll be able to do after this: choose between a single agent, orchestrator–workers and handoffs, and estimate the time and token trade-off.

#### Patterns

| Pattern | How | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Orchestrator–workers** | lead agent plans, spawns sub-agents with clear briefs, merges condensed results | research, analysis, broad search |
| **Handoffs** | one agent transfers the conversation (and context) to a specialist (billing, refunds) | customer support routing |
| **Parallel sampling / debate** | several agents answer or argue, then aggregate | hard reasoning; costly |
| **Agent-to-agent (A2A)** | agents from different vendors/services call each other via a protocol | cross-organisation workflows |

## In practice

### In practice

#### Making multi-agent work

- **Default to one agent;** add sub-agents for independent, parallel sub-tasks or to isolate bulky context (context engineering).

- **Write sub-agent briefs** like delegation to a colleague: goal, scope, tools, output format, effort budget. Return condensed results, not raw transcripts.

- **Share context when decisions interact** (Cognition's principle): pass full traces or keep one agent responsible for coupled decisions.

- **Budget and observe:** cap sub-agent count and tokens; trace every agent's steps; evaluate the end-to-end outcome.

A2A reached version 1.0 and joined the Agentic AI Foundation in Aug 2026. Agents publish Agent Cards, and work runs as tasks with states such as working, input required and completed. See Agent Protocols.

#### Parallelise what's independent, keep coupled decisions together

Multi-agent systems buy speed, breadth and clean contexts with many more tokens and coordination risk; they fit read-heavy parallel tasks and fail on tightly coupled ones.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "More agents means smarter"

It sounds right, since several heads seem better than one. But it means more tokens and more coordination. Failure studies find many problems come from mis-specification and misalignment between agents, rather than from the model. And agents shouldn't just negotiate an answer either, unless they have shared context and a clear owner.

## Say it

### When do several agents beat one, and what does it cost?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why do sub-agents help with context?

Each explores in its own window and returns only a summary, so the orchestrator's context isn't flooded with raw search results.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you evaluate a multi-agent system?

End-to-end task success and quality on a test set, plus cost and time; trace per-agent steps to debug delegation and merge failures.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Handoffs or one agent with all tools?

Handoffs when domains need different prompts, tools or permissions (refunds vs tech support); one agent when the domain is small enough to stay clear.

#### The 30-second answer

The main pattern is orchestrator–workers: a lead agent plans, spawns sub-agents with focused briefs and their own contexts, and synthesises their condensed results; handoffs route a conversation to a specialist. It works well for broad, parallel, read-heavy tasks; Anthropic's research system beat a single agent by about 90 percent on their eval, but used around 15 times the tokens of a chat. It works badly for tightly coupled work like editing one codebase, because parallel agents with partial context make conflicting decisions. So I default to a single agent and add sub-agents only for independent sub-tasks, with clear briefs, budgets and tracing.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "More agents means smarter." It means more tokens and more coordination.

- "Agents should negotiate the answer." Only with shared context and a clear owner.

**Key terms and sources**

When several agents beat one: orchestrator–worker (sub-agents), handoffs between specialists, parallel exploration, debate; what they cost in tokens and coordination; why parallel agents that share a task can make conflicting decisions; and the evidence on both sides (Anthropic's research system vs Cognition's "don't build multi-agents") · built from Anthropic (How we built our multi-agent research system, June 2025), Cognition (Don't Build Multi-Agents, June 2025), Wu et al. (AutoGen, 2023), Du et al. (multi-agent debate, ICML 2024), Cemri et al. (Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?, 2025), the OpenAI Agents SDK handoffs docs and Google's A2A protocol · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

1. Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system", June 2025.

2. Cognition, "Don't Build Multi-Agents", June 2025.

3. Q. Wu et al., "AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation", 2023, [arXiv:2308.08155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155); Y. Du et al., "Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate", ICML 2024, [arXiv:2305.14325](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325).

4. M. Cemri et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", 2025, [arXiv:2503.13657](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657); OpenAI Agents SDK documentation (handoffs); Google, Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol.

5. A2A protocol specification, version 1.0, [a2a-protocol.org](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/).
