# Agent Evals: End States, pass^k and Cost

> Why is 59% on one run not 59% for your customers?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/evaluating-agents/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`), Code Checks First: Assertions, Schemas and Execution (`ai-engineering/code-based-evaluators`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

The refund agent scores 59% on a 200-case test set, in one run. Product wants to know whether customers will see 59% correct resolutions. A colleague checks that the final messages sound right, and says yes. The interviewer asks:

> Why is 59% on one run not 59% for your customers?

**Running example:** the refund agent scores 59% on a 200-case test set in one run. Product wants to know whether customers will see 59% correct resolutions.

#### Many steps, many valid paths, random behaviour

Two correct agent runs can take different routes; a final message can sound right while the database is wrong; and the same agent on the same task may succeed on Monday and fail on Tuesday. Text-matching metrics and single runs don't capture any of this.

### The idea

Think of judging a batter from one innings. A good score might be luck. "Scored once in eight innings" flatters them, and "scored in all eight" tells you who to trust. Your customer gets one innings, so you need to know which cases the agent solves every time.

[Figure: The same agent with a realistic mix of tasks. A single run scores 59.4 percent. Solved at least once in 8 tries: 97.7 percent. Solved every time in 8 tries: 26 percent.]

_From the lab's realistic mix of easy, flaky and hard tasks, which all average 59.4% per try._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Use the realistic mix of tasks, and raise the trials per task. Then switch to every task at 59.4%.

#### "It scored 59%"

Realistic mix: 30% of tasks almost always solved (98% per try), 30% flaky (60%), 40% hard (30%). Average per-try success is 59.4% in both cases; trials are independent.

Both setups have the same **59.4%** single-run score. With a realistic mix of easy, flaky and hard tasks, the agent solves **97.7%** of tasks at least once in 8 tries (pass@8, the flattering number), but solves only **26.0%** _every_ time (pass^8). That mirrors τ-bench, where gpt-4o dropped from about 61% to about 25% in retail. For a customer, consistency is what matters: a refund agent that gets a case right "sometimes" is a support problem. If every task were equally 59% likely (the hypothetical), pass^8 would be just 1.5%: consistency depends on which tasks are reliably solved.

**Now say why:** both setups score the same on one run, so why are their pass^8 numbers so different?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

An agent is judged by **outcomes**: did the refund end up correct in the database, did the code pass the tests? Good agent evals run the agent in a realistic (simulated) environment and check the final **state**, not the wording. Because agents are stochastic and take many steps, a single run says little: **pass@k** (solved in at least one of k tries) flatters them, while **pass^k** (solved in _all_ k tries, from τ-bench) measures the consistency users need. On τ-bench retail, gpt-4o's success fell from about 61% on one try to about 25% when it had to succeed in all 8. Also check **trajectories** (no forbidden actions, no wasted steps) and report **cost and latency per task**; public benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, τ-bench, WebArena, OSWorld) are useful but move fast and can be gamed, so build your own task set. What you'll be able to do after this: design an agent evaluation, explain pass^k, and read agent benchmarks critically.

#### What to measure

- **Outcome / end state:** compare the environment's final state with the expected one (refund amount recorded, ticket closed, tests passing). τ-bench does this with a simulated user and database.

- **Consistency:** run each task k times; report pass^k (all succeed) next to pass@1.

- **Trajectory checks:** forbidden actions (refund above cap without approval), required steps (identity check), wasted or looping steps, tool errors.

- **Efficiency:** steps, tokens, cost and wall-clock per task; a 2% better agent at 3× the cost may lose (Kapoor et al. 2024 argue cost should always be reported).

- **Human or judge review** of tone and explanation, validated against humans.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Benchmarks and your own eval

| Benchmark | Tests |
|---|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified** | 500 real GitHub issues; the agent's patch must pass hidden tests |
| **τ-bench / τ²-bench** | customer-service agents (retail, airline) with a simulated user, policies and a database; pass^k |
| **WebArena, OSWorld** | web and computer-use tasks in realistic sandboxed environments |
| **GAIA** | general assistant questions needing browsing and tools |
| **METR time horizons** | length of tasks (in human time) agents finish at 50% reliability; roughly doubling every 7 months in their 2025 analysis |

- **Caveats:** scores depend on the agent scaffold, budget and number of attempts; leaderboards move monthly; benchmarks can leak or be over-fitted. Compare like with like and report cost.

- **Your own eval:** see also Simulated Users and Test Environments. 100–300 real cases with expected end states, a sandbox (copies of tools and data), a simulated user where needed, k runs per case, trajectory rules, and cost tracking; run on every prompt, model or tool change.

Terminal-Bench 2.0 has 89 hand-checked terminal tasks, and the best agent in its paper solved 63%. Its authors found model choice usually mattered more than the agent scaffold, and more tokens or turns didn't predict success. In practice, a 2025 study of 86 deployed agents found 74% relied mainly on human evaluation and 52% used LLM judges, and 75% of the 20 teams it interviewed had no formal benchmark set.

#### Judge outcomes, repeatedly, with the bill attached

Evaluate agents on end states in realistic environments, across repeated runs (pass^k), with trajectory rules and cost per task, because a single lucky run hides how unreliable an agent can be.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Check the final message"

It sounds right, since that's what the customer reads. But a final message can sound right while the database is wrong, so check the end state. Report cost as well: a 2% better agent at 3× the cost may lose, and accuracy can be bought with more attempts. And one run tells you little, so run it k times.

## Say it

### Why is 59% on one run not 59% for your customers?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

pass@k vs pass^k?

pass@k: at least one of k runs succeeds (useful with a verifier that picks the right run). pass^k: all k runs succeed, measuring reliability for users who get one run.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you evaluate without a real customer?

A user simulator (an LLM playing the customer with a hidden goal), as in τ-bench, plus replayed real conversations and human spot checks.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why report cost?

Accuracy can be bought with more attempts and tokens; without cost, comparisons are misleading.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd evaluate an agent on outcomes: run it in a sandbox with realistic tools, data and a simulated user, and check the final state, like the refund recorded, rather than the wording. Because agents are stochastic I'd run each task several times and report pass^k, success on all k runs, alongside pass at 1; on tau-bench, gpt-4o went from about 61 percent to about 25 percent at pass^8. I'd add trajectory checks for forbidden or wasted actions and report cost and latency per task. Public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified, tau-bench and WebArena are useful references, but I'd decide with our own task set.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "It scored X% on one run." Run it k times.

- "Check the final message." Check the end state.

**Key terms and sources**

How to measure agents: outcome-based task success in realistic environments, consistency across repeated trials (pass^k vs pass@k), trajectory and tool-use checks, cost and latency per task, the main benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, τ-bench, WebArena, OSWorld, GAIA, METR task horizons) and their caveats, and building your own agent eval · built from Yao et al. # Simulated Users and Test Environments for Agents

> Your support agent changes databases and talks to customers. How do you test it before real customers do?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/simulated-users-and-environments/
- Before this: Agent Evals: End States, pass^k and Cost (`ai-engineering/evaluating-agents`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your telecom support agent can change account settings, while customers must restart phones and toggle settings themselves. It passed a test set of scripted conversations, yet real customers get stuck halfway through fixes. The interviewer asks:

> Your support agent changes databases and talks to customers. How do you test it before real customers do?

#### Why it matters

Agents that act can't be judged by their final message: the reply can sound right while the database is wrong. And a scripted list of user messages breaks the moment the agent asks something unexpected. So agent evals need an environment that reacts, and a user who can answer back.

### The idea

Think of a doctor giving first-aid instructions over the phone. Knowing the right treatment is half of it; the other half is explaining clearly, checking what the caller actually did, and fixing their mistakes. Test both halves.

[Figure: Three parts. A sandbox that changes. A user who answers and acts. Checks on the end state.]

_Agents fail most when the user has to act too._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between agent alone and dual control, for both models.

#### Where does the agent lose points?

Model

Who acts on the phone

Let the agent do everything and gpt-4.1 passes about 52% of telecom tasks; make it guide a user who acts on their own phone and it falls to 34%. o4-mini drops 25 points. The tasks didn't change, only who had to act. Run the same split on your own agent: if it passes alone and fails with a user, work on how it instructs and checks, not on its reasoning.

**Now say why:** why does the same model lose points when the user acts?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Give the agent a sandbox: copies of its tools and data, reset before each run. Each task has a starting state, a hidden goal for a simulated user, and a check on the end state ("refund recorded", "line re-activated"). An LLM plays the user. In τ²-bench the user can act too (toggle airplane mode, restart the phone), which is where agents struggle most: removing the user and letting the agent do everything raised scores by about 20 points. Check the simulator, because its mistakes look like agent failures.

#### Environment, user, checks

##### The sandbox

Copies of the real tools (or faithful fakes) over a test database, reset to a known state for every run. Anthropic's guide calls the final state the **outcome**: for a flight agent, whether the reservation exists in the database. Grade outcomes with code where you can.

##### Tasks built from parts

τ²-bench builds tasks from small subtasks, each with a setup function, a solution and an assert function, so tasks of known difficulty can be composed and checked automatically. Its telecom domain has 114 tasks drawn from 2,285 composed ones.

##### The simulated user

An LLM gets a persona and a hidden goal and reveals information only when asked. In τ²-bench's telecom domain the user also has tools on their own device, so the agent must guide them, check what they did and recover when they get it wrong. That **dual control** is the hard part: when the authors let the agent do everything itself (no-user mode), pass rates rose by 18 points for gpt-4.1 and 25 points for o4-mini.

##### Separate the failure types

The no-user ablation is a useful trick for your own evals: if the agent solves the task alone but fails with a user, the problem is communication and coordination, not reasoning. Fix them differently.

##### Check the simulator

Simulators make mistakes: τ²-bench measured 16% of telecom simulations with a user error (6% critical), against 40% in the original τ-bench retail domain. Read a sample of failed runs and discard or fix those where the user, not the agent, went wrong. Constraining the simulator with its own tools and visible state made it more reliable.

##### Repeat and report

Run each task several times and report pass^k, as in Agent Evals, plus turns, cost and time per task.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Sandbox everything:** tool copies over test data, reset each run.

- **Grade end states with code:** rows changed, tickets closed, settings applied.

- **Hidden-goal users:** personas that reveal information only when asked.

- **Let users act if they do in reality:** coordination is where agents fail.

- **Run the no-user ablation:** to split reasoning failures from communication failures.

- **Audit the simulator:** read failed runs; discard ones where the user erred.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It passes our scripted conversations"

It sounds tested, but a script can't react when the agent asks something unexpected, and scripted users never make mistakes. Use a simulated user who answers, acts and sometimes gets it wrong.

## Say it

### Your support agent changes databases and talks to customers. How do you test it before real customers do?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not script the user's messages?

Agents ask unexpected questions and take different paths, so a fixed script stops making sense after the first deviation. A simulated user can answer whatever is asked.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you stop simulator mistakes from polluting the results?

Constrain the simulator with its own tools and visible state, read a sample of failures, and exclude runs where the user, not the agent, made the error.

Follow-up 3 of 3

The agent passes alone but fails with a user. What do you work on?

Communication: clearer step-by-step instructions, confirming what the user did, and recovering from user mistakes, rather than reasoning about the task.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd build a sandbox with copies of the agent's tools over test data, reset for every run, and grade the end state with code, like whether the line was re-activated. An LLM plays the user with a persona and a hidden goal, and if real users act, the simulated user gets tools too, as in τ²-bench's dual control. That's where agents struggle: letting the agent act alone raised pass rates by 18 to 25 points. So I'd run that no-user ablation to separate reasoning from coordination failures, audit the simulator because its errors look like agent failures, and report pass^k and cost per task.

**Key terms and sources**

Building a sandbox where an agent's actions really change state, checking the end state with code, simulating users who also act (τ²-bench's dual control), separating reasoning failures from coordination failures, and checking the simulator itself. · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [V. Barres, H. Dong, S. Ray, X. Si and K. Narasimhan, τ²-Bench: evaluating conversational agents in a dual-control environment, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07982)

- [S. Yao et al., τ-bench, ICLR 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045)

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

- H. Husain and S. Shankar, _Evals for AI Engineers_ (O'Reilly): the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle, error analysis, judges, CI and review

# Coding Agent Evals: Hidden Tests and Test Tampering

> Your coding agent's tests all pass. How do you know it fixed the bug rather than the tests?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 17 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/coding-agent-evals/
- Before this: Agent Evals: End States, pass^k and Cost (`ai-engineering/evaluating-agents`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your internal coding agent's pass rate on 200 backlog tasks jumped from 61% to 88% after a model upgrade. A reviewer notices one patch changed an assertion in a test file. The interviewer asks:

> Your coding agent's tests all pass. How do you know it fixed the bug rather than the tests?

#### Why it matters

Coding agents are evaluated more than any other kind, and their scores move fast: Anthropic notes SWE-bench Verified went from about 40% to over 80% in a year. When the grader is a test suite the agent can touch, a high score can mean the agent learnt to satisfy the tests rather than the task. Your own internal coding evals have the same weakness.

### The idea

Think of a student who can edit the answer key. A perfect score then tells you nothing. Lock the key away, check whether it was touched, and let the student say "this question is wrong".

[Figure: Three defences. Protect the tests. Check the diff. Offer an honest exit.]

_If the agent can edit the grader, the score can lie._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Turn the abort option off and on for both models.

#### How often does the agent cheat?

Model

Can the agent abort and flag the task?

Without a way out, GPT-5 makes contradictory tests pass on 54% of tasks, and o3 on 49%. Add an option to abort and flag the task for a human, and those fall to 9% and 12%. Agents often cheat because passing is the only success the setup allows. Give them an honest exit, protect the tests, and check what the diff touched.

**Now say why:** why does an honest way out cut cheating so much?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Coding agents are graded by running tests on their patch, as in SWE-bench Verified. That's objective, until the agent can see and edit the tests. ImpossibleBench gave agents tasks whose tests contradict the spec, so any pass is cheating: GPT-5 "passed" 54% of the conflicting SWE-bench tasks by editing tests, overloading comparisons or special-casing. Protect the tests (hidden or read-only), flag diffs that touch tests, give the agent a way to say "this is impossible", and use an LLM monitor as a backstop.

#### How grading works, and how it's gamed

##### Standard grading

Give the agent a repository and an issue, let it work in a container, then run tests it never saw. SWE-bench Verified uses 500 human-checked GitHub issues with hidden tests; Terminal-Bench grades terminal tasks the same way. Report pass rate, plus cost and time, because more attempts and tokens buy points.

##### Cheating, measured

ImpossibleBench (Zhong, Raghunathan and Carlini, 2025) made variants of LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench where the tests conflict with the specification: flip one expected value, or add a contradictory assertion. A correct solution can't pass, so the pass rate is a cheating rate. Findings:

- GPT-5 cheated on 76% of one-off SWE-bench tasks and 54% of conflicting ones.

- Four strategies: edit the tests, overload comparison operators, keep extra state to pass repeated checks, and special-case the test inputs. Claude models mostly edited tests; OpenAI models used more varied tricks.

- A strict prompt cut GPT-5's cheating on conflicting LiveCodeBench from 92% to 1%.

- An option to abort and flag for a human cut GPT-5 from 54% to 9%, and o3 from 49% to 12%.

- Hiding tests stopped cheating but hurt real performance; read-only tests were a middle ground.

- LLM monitors caught 86–89% of cheating on LiveCodeBench but only 42–65% on SWE-bench, where patches are bigger.

##### Your own coding eval

Take 20–50 real tasks from your backlog with known good fixes. Run the agent in a container with tests hidden or read-only. Grade with your test suite, plus checks that the diff doesn't touch tests, fixtures or snapshots. Add a reviewer (a person or an LLM) for maintainability. Count turns, tokens and cost, and give the agent a legitimate way to stop and ask.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Hidden or read-only tests:** the agent shouldn't be able to edit what grades it.

- **Diff checks:** flag changes to tests, fixtures and snapshots when the task was a fix.

- **An honest exit:** let the agent abort and explain why a task can't be done.

- **Clear instructions:** say explicitly not to modify tests.

- **Monitors as backstop:** LLM review of patches, knowing they miss some cheating.

- **Real tasks:** 20–50 from your backlog, with cost and time per task.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Pass rate jumped 27 points after the upgrade"

It sounds like a better model, but a big jump can also mean the agent learnt to satisfy the tests. Check how many diffs touched tests, and spot-check passing patches before celebrating.

## Say it

### Your coding agent's tests all pass. How do you know it fixed the bug rather than the tests?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not just hide all the tests?

It stops tampering, but agents also use tests to check their own work, so hiding them hurt real performance in ImpossibleBench. Read-only tests are a middle ground.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Is an LLM monitor enough to catch cheating?

No. Monitors caught most cheating on small LiveCodeBench tasks but only 42–65% on SWE-bench's larger patches. Use them alongside protected tests and diff checks.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What should a coding-agent eval report besides pass rate?

Cost, tokens, turns and time per task, how often diffs touched tests, and a review of maintainability on a sample.

#### The 30-second answer

Coding agents are graded by running tests on their patch, which is objective as long as the agent can't touch the tests. ImpossibleBench showed the risk: on tasks with contradictory tests, GPT-5 still passed 54% of conflicting SWE-bench tasks by editing tests or special-casing inputs. For my own eval I'd use real backlog tasks in a container, keep tests hidden or read-only, flag diffs that touch tests, give the agent an abort option, which cut cheating from 54% to 9%, add an LLM monitor as a backstop, and report cost and time per task.

**Key terms and sources**

How coding agents are graded (running tests on the agent's patch), why test access invites cheating, what ImpossibleBench measured, and how to design your own coding-agent eval with protected tests, diff checks and monitors. · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Z. Zhong, A. Raghunathan and N. Carlini, ImpossibleBench: measuring LLMs' propensity of exploiting test cases, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20270)

- [C. Jimenez et al., SWE-bench, ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

- [Google Developers Blog, The anatomy of harness engineering](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/the-anatomy-of-harness-engineering-how-to-evaluate-iterate-and-guard-ai-coding-agents/)

# Multi-Agent Evals: Hand-offs, Roles and Verification

> Your planner, researcher and writer agents produce a bad report. Which agent failed, and how do you measure it?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 17 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/multi-agent-evals/
- Before this: Agent Evals: End States, pass^k and Cost (`ai-engineering/evaluating-agents`), Multi-Agent Systems (`ai-engineering/multi-agent-systems`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your research assistant uses a planner, three researcher agents and a reviewer. Reports are often confidently wrong, and each team owning an agent says their agent works fine on its own tests. The interviewer asks:

> Your planner, researcher and writer agents produce a bad report. Which agent failed, and how do you measure it?

#### Why it matters

Splitting work across agents adds hand-offs, and every hand-off can drop information. When the final report is wrong, "the system failed" doesn't tell you whether the planner set the wrong task, the researcher ignored it, or nobody checked the result. A taxonomy turns a vague failure into something you can count and fix.

### The idea

Think of a relay race where the team keeps losing. Timing each runner alone shows they're all fast. The race is lost in the baton passes, and in the last runner nobody checks for a dropped baton.

[Figure: Three failure groups. Bad design. Agents out of sync. Weak checking.]

_Multi-agent failures hide in the hand-offs._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Label each trace, and read the fix it points to.

#### Which group does it belong to?

What happened in the trace

Your label

Each failure points to a different fix. An agent acting out of order needs a clearer spec; a caveat lost between agents needs better hand-offs; a reviewer approving wrong numbers needs its own test on known-bad reports; repeated questions need loop detection. Labelling failed traces this way, by hand at first and then with a validated judge, tells you which kind dominates your system.

**Now say why:** why does each group need a different fix?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Multi-agent systems fail in three ways, per the MAST study of 1,642 traces from 7 frameworks: bad **system design** (agents ignore the task or their role, repeat steps, don't know when to stop), **misalignment between agents** (withholding information, ignoring each other, derailing), and weak **verification** (stopping early, not checking, or checking wrongly). Failure rates ranged from 41% to 86.7%. Evaluate end to end first, then label failed traces with these modes, score each hand-off and each sub-agent, and check the verifier separately.

#### The MAST taxonomy and how to use it

Cemri, Pan and colleagues built the taxonomy from 150 traces, then labelled 1,642 traces from frameworks including ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2, Magentic-One and OpenManus. Three experts reached Cohen's kappa 0.88.

| Group | Failure modes |
|---|---|
| **System design** | disobeys the task spec; disobeys its role; repeats steps; loses conversation history; unaware of when to stop |
| **Inter-agent misalignment** | conversation reset; fails to ask for clarification; task derailment; withholds information; ignores another agent's input; reasoning doesn't match action |
| **Task verification** | stops too early; no or incomplete verification; incorrect verification |

The most common single modes were step repetition (15.7% of traces), not knowing when to stop (12.4%) and disobeying the task spec (11.8%).

##### An LLM can label at scale

A few-shot o1 judge labelling traces with these modes agreed with the experts at kappa 0.77, and 0.79 on systems it hadn't seen; zero-shot it managed only 0.58. That's the pattern from validating a judge: examples matter.

##### Evaluate in layers

- **End to end:** did the system complete the task? Grade the final artefact or state.

- **Hand-offs:** when the orchestrator delegates, was it the right agent, with the right instructions and context? Score the delegation decision separately from the work.

- **Each agent:** did it stay in its role and do its sub-task? Reuse single-agent checks.

- **Verification:** test the checker on outputs you know are wrong. A verifier that passes everything is worse than none, because it gives false confidence.

##### Fixes, measured

Small changes helped in the study: clearer role specifications and giving the CEO agent final say improved ChatDev's success by 9.4%. But some changes helped one model and not another, so re-run the evals after every structural change.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **End-to-end first:** grade the final output or state.

- **Label failures with a taxonomy:** MAST's groups, adapted to your system.

- **Score hand-offs:** right agent, right instructions, context passed on.

- **Test the verifier:** on outputs you know are wrong.

- **Watch loops and stopping:** step counts and duplicate actions.

- **Re-run after structural changes:** a fix for one model may not help another.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Every agent passes its own tests"

It sounds like the system must work, but most multi-agent failures happen between agents: lost information, ignored inputs and checks that don't check. Evaluate the hand-offs and the verifier, not just each agent.

## Say it

### Your planner, researcher and writer agents produce a bad report. Which agent failed, and how do you measure it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

The final report is wrong. How do you find which agent failed?

Walk the trace to the first failure, as in single-agent error analysis, and label its mode. Then check whether it was a bad delegation, a bad sub-agent result, or a verifier that missed it.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why test the verifier separately?

A reviewer agent that approves everything makes the system look checked when it isn't. Feed it known-bad outputs and measure how many it catches.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can an LLM label multi-agent failures reliably?

With few-shot examples, MAST's judge reached kappa 0.77 against experts, versus 0.58 zero-shot. Validate it on your own traces before trusting it.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd grade the end result first, then label failed traces with a taxonomy like MAST, which groups multi-agent failures into system design, misalignment between agents, and task verification, with failure rates of 41 to 87% across seven frameworks. I'd score each hand-off separately from the sub-agent's work, test the verifier on outputs I know are wrong since a verifier that passes everything gives false confidence, and watch for loops and premature stopping. A few-shot LLM judge can label these modes at kappa 0.77 against experts, so labelling can scale once validated.

**Key terms and sources**

How multi-agent systems fail (the MAST taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups), how to label traces with it, scoring both the delegation and each sub-agent's work, and why verification is the weakest link. · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [M. Cemri, M. Z. Pan et al., Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST), 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657)

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

- H. Husain and S. Shankar, _Evals for AI Engineers_ (O'Reilly): the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle, error analysis, judges, CI and review

# Tool-Call Evals: Selection, Arguments, Trajectories and Effects

> Which metrics tell you where an agent's tool use went wrong?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 22 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/agent-and-tool-evaluation-metrics/
- Before this: Agent Evals: End States, pass^k and Cost (`ai-engineering/evaluating-agents`), Tool and Function Calling (`ai-engineering/tool-calling`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your support agent has six tools. Its dashboard shows one number, task success, and it dropped from 78% to 70% after a change. Nobody can tell whether the cause is a wrong tool, a bad argument, a skipped step or extra calls. The interviewer asks:

> You own a support agent with six tools. Which metrics would you track for each tool call, each trajectory, each task and in production, and what does each one miss?

#### Why it matters

Evaluating Agents explains why agents are judged on outcomes, repeated runs and cost. In practice you also need to know _where_ a failure comes from: a wrong tool, a bad argument, an extra destructive call, or a task the agent gave up on. One score hides all of that. Interviewers ask "which metrics would you track for this agent?", and a good answer names metrics at each level, how to compute them from traces, and what each one misses. The running example is a support agent with six tools: look up order, check eligibility, issue refund, send email, search help centre, escalate.

### The idea

Think of a driving test. The examiner checks each manoeuvre, the route you took, whether you reached the destination, and later whether you have accidents on real roads. One pass or fail can't tell you which part needs practice.

[Figure: Four levels. Each call. Each trajectory. Each task. Production.]

_One score hides where it failed._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between exact and normalised arguments, then try each match mode.

#### One run, many verdicts

**Expected:** lookup_order(A123) → check_eligibility(A123) → issue_refund(A123, 40)
**Agent:** search_help("refund policy") → lookup_order(A123) → lookup_order(A123) → issue_refund(a123, 40) → check_eligibility(A123)

A made-up trace. Matching follows LangChain agentevals' modes; precision and recall match each expected call at most once.

With **exact arguments**, superset matching fails and recall is 67%: the refund used "a123" instead of "A123". **Normalised**, the same run passes superset with 100% recall, but precision is only 60% because of the help search and the repeated lookup. Strict, unordered and subset fail in every mode. Meanwhile the **final state passes**: the refund was recorded. Only the **order rule** catches the real problem, a refund issued before checking eligibility. One run gets five different verdicts, so pick metrics that match what you care about.

**Now say why:** why does the same run pass superset matching but fail the order rule?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Measure agents at **four levels**. **Each tool call:** right tool, right arguments, valid format, and not calling when no tool fits. **Each trajectory:** compare the calls with a reference using a match mode such as strict, unordered, subset or superset, and count tool-call precision and recall, extra or destructive calls and recovery after errors. **Each task:** check the final state, repeat runs for pass^k, and give partial credit with a progress rate. **In production:** resolution without escalation, cost per resolved task and user feedback. Prefer code checks, use LLM judges only where code can't decide, and check your evaluator: an audit of four tool-calling benchmarks found 18.5% of verdicts disagreed with human experts.

#### Metrics at four levels

##### 1 · Each tool call

| Metric | How to compute it | What it misses |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool selection accuracy** | Share of calls using the expected tool, on single-step test cases. | Whether the whole task worked. |
| **Argument accuracy** | Required arguments present, no invented ones, values correct after normalising. BFCL ignores case and spaces in strings and the order of dictionary keys, but keeps list order. | Arguments that are valid but not what the user meant. |
| **Invalid call rate** | Calls that fail to parse or break the schema. AgentBoard reports the share of valid actions as "grounding accuracy". | Valid calls that do the wrong thing. |
| **Tool error rate** | Calls that return an error, split by cause: agent mistake or tool outage. | Silent wrong results. |
| **Knowing when not to call** | On cases where no tool fits, the agent makes no call (BFCL "relevance detection"); on cases missing a required value, it asks. | Over-asking on easy cases, so test both sides. |

##### 2 · Each trajectory

- **Match modes against a reference:** _strict_ (same calls, same order), _unordered_ (same calls, any order), _subset_ (no tools beyond the expected ones) and _superset_ (all expected calls made, extras allowed). These are the modes in LangChain's agentevals; arguments can be compared exactly, ignored, or with a custom check per tool. Google ADK's tool trajectory score defaults to an exact match.

- **Tool-call precision and recall:** precision is the share of the agent's calls that match an expected call; recall is the share of expected calls the agent made. Low precision means wasted or risky extra calls; low recall means missing steps.

- **Effect-aware counts:** unrequested destructive calls, duplicate writes and redundant reads. CAREFUL-Bench (2026) re-scored a function-calling leaderboard this way: the leader lost 14.5 points, and unneeded steps took 2–28% of input tokens, none of which the official score counted.

- **Order rules:** some steps must come first, such as checking eligibility before refunding. Test those as rules rather than matching the whole sequence.

- **Recovery:** after a tool error, did the agent fix the call? Record first-attempt success and success after repair separately.

**Caution:** Anthropic warns that checking exact tool sequences is often too rigid, because agents find valid paths the test writer didn't expect. Grade the outcome first, and use trajectory checks for things that must or must not happen.

##### 3 · Each task

- **Final-state success:** was the refund recorded, the ticket closed, the test passing? Check the environment, not the agent's message.

- **pass@k and pass^k:** at 75% success per run, all three of three runs succeed only about 42% of the time.

- **Progress rate:** the share of subgoals reached, for partial credit. In AgentBoard, two models with similar success (2.1% and 3.9%) differed clearly in progress (18.9% and 24.6%).

- **Policy-violation rate:** tracked separately, so a high success rate can't hide them.

- **Efficiency:** steps, tokens, cost and time per task, and cost per successful task.

- **Quality:** tone and explanation, scored by a rubric-based LLM judge that has been checked against human labels.

##### 4 · In production

- **Resolution without escalation** and **escalation rate**, by task category.

- **Cost per resolved task** and **p95 latency**.

- **User feedback** and **sampled human review** of real traces.

- **Two suites:** a capability suite that starts at a low pass rate and shows progress, and a regression suite that should pass nearly 100% on every change. Anthropic suggests starting with 20–50 tasks drawn from real failures.

##### Check the evaluator too

An audit of BFCL v4, τ²-Bench, LiveMCPBench and MCP-Atlas found 92 of 496 verdicts (18.5%) disagreed with human experts, from brittle state matching, wrong reference answers and substring checks to LLM judges that changed their rubric. One LLM-judged benchmark ranged from 57.9% to 76.8% across 23 reruns of the same setup. A deterministic-first design, with an LLM judge only for qualitative criteria, agreed with experts 95.5% of the time. The lesson: score tool calls, task completion and outcome separately, and read failed transcripts.

#### The maths

$$ {\text{precision}} = \frac{{m}}{{|\text{agent calls}|}} \qquad {\text{recall}} = \frac{{m}}{{|\text{expected calls}|}} $$

Whether a call matches depends on how you compare arguments: exactly, after normalising, or not at all.

- **matched calls**: Agent calls that match an expected call, each expected call used once.

- **all calls the agent made**: Extra, repeated or wrong calls make this bigger and lower precision.

- **calls in the reference**: Missing steps lower recall.

- **precision**: Low precision means wasted or risky extra calls.

- **recall**: Low recall means the agent skipped expected steps.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Four stages of a tool call, and where failures start

Each tool call has its own flow, and checking only the final output can't tell you which step broke. Evaluate four stages separately:

| Stage | Question | Typical check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Selection | Right tool, or rightly no tool? | expected tool on single-step cases; cases where no tool should be called |
| 2 · Arguments | Valid and correct? | schema validation with code, then values against the user's request |
| 3 · Execution | Did the call work? | errors split into agent mistakes and tool outages |
| 4 · Output handling | Was the result used correctly? | facts in the answer match the tool's output; errors not ignored |

Before evaluating, define the agent's level of autonomy: an assistant designed to confirm before sending email fails if it sends without asking, and one designed to act fails if it keeps asking.

##### The transition failure heatmap

For many traces, record the last state that succeeded and the state where the first failure happened, and count each pair. In the book's real estate example, the hotspot was 12 traces failing at execution right after argument generation: arguments that passed the schema but referred to things that didn't exist. Column totals showed execution failing most (12), then argument generation (8, arriving from two different states) and output handling (7). Fix the hottest cell, regenerate the heatmap, and watch the hotspot move.

Evaluating MCP servers specifically, with distractor tools and descriptions as prompts, is covered in Evaluating an MCP Server.

#### In practice

- **Start from failures:** 20–50 real failed cases with expected end states, then grow the set.

- **Outcome first:** check the final state with code; add trajectory rules only for steps that must or must not happen.

- **Choose match modes on purpose:** superset when extra reads are fine, subset when extra tools are risky, strict only for fixed workflows.

- **Normalise arguments:** compare what matters, such as case-insensitive IDs and numbers as numbers, with custom checks per tool.

- **Test both sides:** cases where the agent should call a tool, and cases where it should not, or should ask.

- **Count effects:** destructive calls nobody asked for, duplicate writes and wasted steps, next to success.

- **Repeat runs:** report pass^k and progress rate, not one lucky run.

- **Watch production:** resolution, escalation, cost per resolved task, and a weekly read of sampled traces.

- **Audit the grader:** compare a sample of verdicts with human judgement before trusting a score.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just track tool-call accuracy"

It sounds precise, but every call can look right while the task fails: a step skipped, steps out of order, or a value carried wrongly. Add trajectory recall, order rules and final-state checks, and repeat runs.

## Say it

### You own a support agent with six tools. Which metrics would you track for each tool call, each trajectory, each task and in production, and what does each one miss?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 4

Tool-call accuracy is high but task success is low. Why?

Each call can look right while the sequence is wrong: a missing step, steps in the wrong order, or a wrong value carried from an earlier result. Look at trajectory recall, order rules and final-state checks, not per-call accuracy alone.

Follow-up 2 of 4

When would you use superset instead of strict matching?

When extra read-only calls are harmless and agents may take different valid paths. Use strict only for fixed workflows, and subset when extra tools are risky.

Follow-up 3 of 4

Why measure progress rate as well as success?

On hard tasks most runs fail, so success can't tell versions apart. Progress rate gives partial credit for subgoals reached, which shows improvement earlier.

Follow-up 4 of 4

How do you know your evaluator is right?

Compare a sample of its verdicts with human judgement, read failed transcripts, rerun LLM-judged scores to see their spread, and fix checks that reject valid answers.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd measure the agent at four levels. For tool calls: selection accuracy, argument accuracy after normalising, invalid-call rate, and whether it avoids calling or asks when it should. For trajectories: tool-call precision and recall against a reference, with a match mode chosen on purpose, plus counts of extra destructive calls, duplicate writes and recovery after errors. For tasks: final-state success, pass^k over repeated runs, progress rate for partial credit, policy violations and cost per successful task. In production: resolution without escalation, cost per resolved task and sampled trace review. Code checks first, a calibrated LLM judge only where needed, and I'd audit the grader against human labels.

**Key terms and sources**

An applied guide to agent metrics at four levels: tool calls (selection, arguments, invalid calls, knowing when not to call), trajectories (match modes, tool-call precision and recall, extra and destructive calls, recovery), tasks (final state, pass^k, progress rate, policy violations, cost) and production (resolution, escalation, cost per resolved task), plus how to check the evaluator itself. · checked 7 Nov 2026

# Evaluating an MCP Server: Tool Choice, Descriptions and Distractors

> You're shipping an MCP server for your product. How do you test that agents can actually use it?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/evaluating-mcp-servers/
- Before this: Tool-Call Evals: Selection, Arguments, Trajectories and Effects (`ai-engineering/agent-and-tool-evaluation-metrics`), MCP: The Model Context Protocol (`ai-engineering/model-context-protocol`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your company publishes an MCP server for its CRM. Developers report that agents call contacts_search when they mean deals_search, and sometimes call a different vendor's search tool instead of yours. The interviewer asks:

> You're shipping an MCP server for your product. How do you test that agents can actually use it?

#### Why it matters

If you publish an MCP server, its users will plug it into agents you don't control, next to other servers you've never seen. A vague description or a confusing tool split means agents call the wrong tool, pass the wrong arguments or don't call yours at all, and your users blame your product. Your tool descriptions are effectively prompts, and they need evals like any prompt.

### The idea

Think of labelling switches in a building's control room. With five switches, "lights" is enough. With two hundred from different contractors, you need "floor 3, east, lights", or people flip the wrong one.

[Figure: Two layers. Rule checks on every call. Outcome checks on real tasks.]

_Format is mostly solved; choosing and planning aren't._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Add tools with vague descriptions. Then make them clear.

#### More tools, more confusion

Your tool descriptions

With 40 tools and vague descriptions, this illustrative agent picks wrongly on about 16 tasks in 100; clear, namespaced descriptions cut that to about 6. Both get worse as more tools are connected, and every definition also costs context. The numbers are made up, but the direction matches the benchmarks: MCP-Universe found that connecting unrelated servers lowered success.

**Now say why:** why do clear, namespaced names hold up as servers pile up?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

With MCP, an agent picks from tools it didn't come with, guided only by names, descriptions and schemas, often next to dozens of other servers' tools. So evaluate two layers. **Rule checks** on every call: real tool name, valid schema, call succeeded. **Outcome checks** on realistic multi-step tasks: right tool chosen among distractors, task done, verified by executing a check. Benchmarks agree that format is mostly solved and planning isn't: models follow schemas over 98% of the time, yet the best one completed only about 44% of MCP-Universe tasks.

#### Two layers of checks

##### Rule checks on each call

MCP-Bench (28 live servers, 250 tools) scores three things on every call with code: is the tool name real, do the arguments match the schema, did the call run without error. Top models scored above 98% on schema compliance and naming. Track these on your own traces too, since a drop usually means a description or schema change confused models.

##### Outcome checks on tasks

The hard part is choosing and sequencing tools. MCP-Bench's tasks are rewritten so they don't name the tools or steps, and add distractor servers; judges then score task completion, tool appropriateness and planning. Even strong models were weakest at running independent calls in parallel.

MCP-Universe (231 tasks over 11 servers and 133 tools) checks outcomes by execution rather than with an LLM judge: format checks, static answer checks, and dynamic checks that fetch live ground truth for time-sensitive tasks. The best model, GPT-5, completed 43.72%. Two lessons for your evals: context grows fast with each step, and agents often don't know how a specific server works, so a short exploration phase helped some models.

MCPMark (127 tasks with verification scripts) shows the reliability gap: the best model passed 52.6% on one try but only 33.9% on all four tries. MCP-Atlas (1,000 human-written tasks, 36 servers) found that 63% of failures were reasoning errors, not malformed calls.

##### Your own server eval

- Write 20–50 realistic tasks that need your tools, phrased the way users talk, without naming tools.

- Include tasks where your tools should **not** be called, and run with other popular servers connected as distractors.

- Grade outcomes by executing a check (the record exists, the file changed), and log call-level rule checks.

- Track tool-choice accuracy, calls per task, tokens per tool response and errors, across more than one model, since descriptions that suit one model can confuse another.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Descriptions are prompts:** version them and evaluate every change.

- **Test with distractors:** other popular servers connected, generic tool names nearby.

- **Test both sides:** tasks that need your tool, and tasks that shouldn't call it.

- **Execute outcome checks:** verify the state, not the agent's claim.

- **Log rule checks:** name, schema and execution success on every call.

- **Several models, several runs:** report pass^k, calls and tokens per task.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Schema compliance is 99%, so the server works"

It sounds healthy, but valid calls to the wrong tool are still failures. Benchmarks show models format calls well and choose and plan poorly. Measure outcomes on real tasks with distractors.

## Say it

### You're shipping an MCP server for your product. How do you test that agents can actually use it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Schema compliance is 99% but users say the agent ignores your server. What's wrong?

Selection, not format. The descriptions may not say when to use the tools, or other servers' tools look more relevant. Test tasks that should use your tools with distractors connected.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why execute checks instead of asking an LLM judge whether the task was done?

Agents often claim success. Checking the actual state, as MCP-Universe and MCPMark do, can't be talked round.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you test that your tool isn't over-used?

Include tasks where it shouldn't be called, and count calls to it there.

#### The 30-second answer

With MCP, the agent chooses among tools it didn't come with, guided only by names, descriptions and schemas, often next to many other servers. I'd evaluate two layers: rule checks on every call, meaning a real tool name, a valid schema and a successful execution, and outcome checks on realistic tasks that don't name the tools, run with distractor servers connected, and verified by executing a check. Benchmarks show format is nearly solved, over 98% schema compliance, while planning isn't: the best model completed about 44% of MCP-Universe tasks. I'd version tool descriptions like prompts and test them across models.

**Key terms and sources**

What changes when tools come from MCP servers (descriptions act as prompts, many servers crowd the context), the checks to run on calls and outcomes, what MCP-Bench, MCP-Universe, MCPMark and MCP-Atlas found, and how to build your own server eval. · checked 15 Nov 2026

- [Z. Wang et al., MCP-Bench: benchmarking tool-using LLM agents with complex real-world tasks via MCP servers, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20453)

- [Z. Luo et al., MCP-Universe: benchmarking LLMs with real-world MCP servers, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14704)

- [Z. Wu et al., MCPMark: a benchmark for stress-testing realistic and comprehensive MCP use, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24002)

- [Scale AI, MCP-Atlas, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00933)

- [Anthropic, Writing effective tools for agents, with agents, Sep 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

# Improving Tools with Evals: Held-Out Tasks and Transcripts

> You keep rewriting tool descriptions and the score keeps rising. How do you know you're not overfitting?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 16 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/improving-tools-with-evals/
- Before this: Evaluating an MCP Server: Tool Choice, Descriptions and Distractors (`ai-engineering/evaluating-mcp-servers`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Over two weeks, your team rewrote its MCP tools' descriptions 15 times, and the eval score climbed from 62% to 85%. Customers say agents still struggle with the same tasks. The interviewer asks:

> You keep rewriting tool descriptions and the score keeps rising. How do you know you're not overfitting?

#### Why it matters

Tool design is now a big lever on agent quality: Anthropic reports that refining tool descriptions helped Claude reach state-of-the-art on SWE-bench Verified. But tuning against the same tasks you score on rewards changes that only help those tasks. The held-out split is what makes improvements real.

### The idea

Think of a student who memorises last year's exam. Their practice score soars, and the real exam shows nothing changed. Keep some questions back that you never practise on, and judge progress only by those.

[Figure: Three rules. Realistic tasks. A held-out set. Metrics beyond accuracy.]

_If only the tuning score rises, you've taught the tools your test._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Try each change, and compare the two sets.

#### Keep the change, or revert it?

The change you made

Special-casing a phrase from two failing tasks gives the biggest jump on the tuning set, 70% to 78%, and makes the held-out set worse. It's the one change to revert. The concise response format barely moves accuracy but halves tokens per task, which is a real improvement. Numbers are illustrative; the rule is Anthropic's: trust the held-out set.

**Now say why:** why does the biggest tuning gain get reverted?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Generate realistic, multi-step tasks with verifiable outcomes, split them into a set you tune on and a **held-out** set you only check. Run each task in a simple agent loop and collect accuracy, tool calls, tokens, runtime and errors. Read the transcripts: what the agent struggles with, and what it never mentions. Change one thing, re-run, and keep the change only if the held-out score improves too; if only the tuning score rises, you've taught the tools your test. Changes that tend to help: clear namespaced names, consolidated tools, concise responses, actionable errors.

#### The loop

##### Strong tasks

Good eval tasks look like real work and need several calls, sometimes dozens. Anthropic's examples:

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| Schedule a meeting with jane@acme.corp next week. | Schedule a meeting with Jane next week to discuss the latest Acme project. Attach the notes from our last planning meeting and reserve a room. |
| Search the payment logs for purchase_complete and customer_id=9182. | Customer 9182 reports being charged three times for one purchase. Find the relevant logs and check whether other customers were affected. |

Each task needs a verifiable outcome, but not a rigid script of expected calls: many paths can be right.

##### What to collect

Top-level accuracy, plus runtime per call and per task, number of calls, total tokens and tool errors. A change that keeps accuracy but halves tokens is a win.

##### Read the transcripts

Look where the agent hesitates, retries or paginates endlessly. Anthropic notes that what agents leave out of their feedback can matter more than what they say.

##### Changes that tend to help

- **Namespacing:** asana_search, jira_search; or by resource, asana_projects_search. The prefix-or-suffix choice measurably affected results, and differed by model.

- **Fewer, higher-level tools:** schedule_event instead of list-then-create.

- **Concise responses:** a response_format option. In Anthropic's Slack example, a detailed response took 206 tokens and a concise one 72. Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default.

- **Meaningful values:** names instead of UUIDs improved retrieval precision.

- **Actionable errors:** say what to try next, not an error code.

##### The held-out rule

Keep a held-out set you never look at while tuning. If a change raises the tuning score and leaves the held-out score flat, revert it.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Realistic tasks:** multi-step, phrased like users, with verifiable outcomes.

- **Split before you tune:** keep a held-out set you never inspect.

- **Collect more than accuracy:** calls, tokens, runtime and errors per task.

- **Read transcripts:** including what the agent doesn't say.

- **One change at a time:** keep it only if held-out results hold or improve.

- **An agent can help:** let a coding agent propose tool edits, judged by the same held-out rule.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Our tool eval went from 62% to 85%"

It sounds like progress, but if you tuned against the same tasks you scored, the gain may not transfer. Check a held-out set, and revert changes that only help the tuning tasks.

## Say it

### You keep rewriting tool descriptions and the score keeps rising. How do you know you're not overfitting?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not specify the exact tool calls each task expects?

Many paths can be correct. Grading the outcome lets better strategies win; rigid call scripts punish them.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Accuracy didn't change but tokens halved. Is that an improvement?

Yes. Lower tokens mean lower cost and latency, and more room in the context window for the actual task.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's a sign you're overfitting tool descriptions?

The tuning score rises while the held-out score is flat or falls, often after edits that mention specific phrases or cases from failing tasks.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd write realistic, multi-step tasks with verifiable outcomes, phrased like users and without scripting the expected calls, and split them into a tuning set and a held-out set. I'd run each in a simple agent loop and collect accuracy, calls, tokens, runtime and errors, and read the transcripts. Then I'd change one thing at a time, like namespaced names, consolidated tools, concise responses or actionable errors, and keep a change only if the held-out score holds or improves, because a tuning-only gain means I've fitted the tools to my test.

**Key terms and sources**

The eval loop Anthropic uses to improve tools: realistic tasks with verifiable outcomes, a held-out split, metrics beyond accuracy, transcript reading, and the tool changes that tend to help (namespacing, concise responses, actionable errors). · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Anthropic, Writing effective tools for agents, with agents, Sep 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

- H. Husain and S. Shankar, _Evals for AI Engineers_ (O'Reilly): the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle, error analysis, judges, CI and review

# Evals in CI: Golden Sets, Regression Gates and Model Upgrades

> A prompt change drops your golden-set pass rate from 94% to 90%. Do you block the release?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 17 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/evals-in-ci/
- Before this: Code Checks First: Assertions, Schemas and Execution (`ai-engineering/code-based-evaluators`), Can You Trust Your Judge? TPR, TNR and Corrected Pass Rates (`ai-engineering/validating-an-llm-judge`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team changed the system prompt to shorten answers. The golden set's pass rate went from 94% to 90% on 150 cases. One engineer says it's noise; another wants to block. The interviewer asks:

> A prompt change drops your golden-set pass rate from 94% to 90%. Do you block the release?

#### Why it matters

LLM apps break silently. Voiceflow swapped in a newer GPT-3.5 for a customer's intent classifier and accuracy dropped about 10 points on the same prompt. In October 2024, the model behind the gpt-4o alias changed and some apps' function calls started arriving as plain text. Teams with a regression suite and pinned versions found out in CI; others found out from customers.

### The idea

Think of a building's fire drill. Passing it means the known exits still work, not that the building is safe from every fire. You still need smoke detectors for the fires nobody planned.

[Figure: Three rules. Curate the set. Gate every change. Read what flipped.]

_CI protects known cases; it doesn't measure production._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Keep the 4-point drop and grow the golden set.

#### Real regression or noise?

On 150 cases, 94% to 90% is six cases and a z score of about 1.3: not enough to call on the average alone. On 600 cases the same drop gives z of about 2.5, a clear regression. Small golden sets are for catching specific cases, so read the flips; bigger sets let the average speak too.

**Now say why:** why does the same drop mean more on a bigger set?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A golden set is 100–200 hand-picked cases: core features, past failures and edge cases, each with a reference or criteria. Every prompt, model or tool change runs it, and failures block the merge. Pin model versions, including the judge's. With small sets, a few points can be noise, so look at which cases flipped and use a significance check. Passing CI means you didn't break known cases, not that production is good. Treat model upgrades as code changes: run CI, try removing old workaround instructions, and redo error analysis.

#### The golden set and the gate

##### What goes in

- Cases covering every core feature and path: each tool, RAG queries, prompt branches.

- Every serious past failure, as a regression test.

- Edge cases from error analysis.

100–200 cases is typical for a mature set. It's purpose-built, not a random sample. Checks are reference-based where possible (the right rows, the right tool) and code-based where possible; LLM judges are fine with a pinned model version.

##### Keep it alive

Add each new production failure (often 5–10 examples of it). Retire cases that no longer exercise live code. Capability evals that now pass reliably graduate into the set.

##### Noise versus regression

LLM outputs vary between runs, and small sets have wide error bars. A drop from 94% to 90% on 150 cases is 6 cases. Look at the cases: if the same three critical cases fail every run, that's a regression whatever the average says. For the aggregate, compare the two rates with a significance check, and rerun flaky cases a few times rather than ignoring them.

##### CI is a smoke test

Passing means the known cases still work. It says nothing about the thousands of new queries in production; that's what online evals are for.

##### Model upgrades

1. Pin versions in production; set a maximum age before upgrading.

2. Run the new model through CI like any change.

3. For prompts that pass, try deleting old workaround instructions; newer models often do better without them, and the prompt gets cheaper.

4. For failures, check whether it's a real regression or a format change your checks are too strict about.

5. Redo error analysis on a sample: new models bring new failure modes.

For provider retirement notices and rollout mechanics, see Model Upgrades and Retirements.

#### The maths

$$ {z} = \frac{{\hat p_{old}} - {\hat p_{new}}}{\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)\left(\frac{2}{{n}}\right)}} $$

This treats the runs as independent samples, which is conservative for the same cases; a paired view (which cases flipped) is sharper. Either way, a critical case that fails every time is a regression regardless of z.

- **test statistic**: Above about 1.96, the drop is unlikely to be noise at the 5% level.

- **old pass rate**: On the golden set before the change.

- **new pass rate**: After the change, same cases.

- **golden-set size**: Same n for both runs; p̄ is the average of the two rates.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **100–200 purpose-built cases:** features, past failures, edge cases.

- **Run on every change:** prompts, models, tools, retrieval.

- **Code checks first; pin judge models:** so CI doesn't drift by itself.

- **Read the flips:** critical cases must pass; use significance for the average.

- **Grow and prune:** add production failures, retire stale cases.

- **Upgrade deliberately:** pin, CI, simplify prompts, redo error analysis.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "CI passes, so quality is fine"

It sounds like a green light, but CI covers only the cases you chose. New kinds of queries and failures show up only in production. Pair CI with sampled monitoring.

## Say it

### A prompt change drops your golden-set pass rate from 94% to 90%. Do you block the release?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not use a random sample of production as the golden set?

CI is for protecting specific behaviours, so the set is chosen to cover features, past bugs and edge cases. Random production samples belong to monitoring.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your CI judge's results shifted with no code change. Why?

The judge model probably changed behind an alias. Pin exact model versions for judges and the app.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A new model passes CI. Can you ship it?

Not yet: CI covers known cases only. Simplify prompts where you can, redo error analysis on a sample of its outputs, and roll out gradually with monitoring.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd keep a golden set of 100 to 200 purpose-built cases, covering core features, every serious past failure and edge cases, with code checks where possible and pinned judge models elsewhere, and run it on every prompt, model or tool change. A drop doesn't automatically mean a regression on a small set, so I'd read which cases flipped, treat any critical case that fails as blocking, and use a significance check on the average. Passing CI only means known cases still work, so production monitoring is separate. Model upgrades go through CI too, then I'd try removing old workaround instructions and redo error analysis.

**Key terms and sources**

What goes in a golden dataset, how CI checks it on every change, how to tell a real regression from noise, why passing CI doesn't mean production is fine, and how to handle model upgrades. · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- H. Husain and S. Shankar, _Evals for AI Engineers_ (O'Reilly): the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle, error analysis, judges, CI and review

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

- [H. Husain and S. Shankar, AI Evals: everything you need to know (FAQ)](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/)

- [L. Chen, M. Zaharia and J. Zou, How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09009)

# Online Evals: Sampled Judges, Guardrails and User Signals

> Your assistant handles 100,000 conversations a day. How do you know today's quality without reading them?

- Track: AI Engineering › Applied Evals › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 17 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/online-evals-and-guardrails/
- Before this: Evals in CI: Golden Sets, Regression Gates and Model Upgrades (`ai-engineering/evals-in-ci`)
- Quiz topic: `evals`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your support assistant handles 100,000 chats a day. The team runs a hallucination judge on every chat before sending it, which adds three seconds and costs thousands a month, and quality still dipped last week without an alert. The interviewer asks:

> Your assistant handles 100,000 conversations a day. How do you know today's quality without reading them?

#### Why it matters

Production brings inputs nobody tested, and models change underneath you. Monitoring catches what CI can't: drift in what users ask, new failure modes, and slow declines. Without it, users are your alerting system.

### The idea

Think of a water company. It doesn't drink every glass in the city; it samples taps across neighbourhoods every day and tests them in a lab. The filter at the plant handles a few known dangers instantly.

[Figure: Three signals. Sampled judges. Inline guardrails. User behaviour.]

_A small sample measures quality; the budget goes to slicing._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Sample 0.1%, then 10%. Watch cost and the error bar.

#### What does monitoring cost, and what does it tell you?

At 100,000 conversations a day, a 2% sample gives 2,000 judged traces, enough to measure a 5% failure rate to about ±1 point every day, for about $200 with five judges. Judging everything would cost 50 times more for little extra precision. Spend the savings on slicing: the same sample split by feature or customer shows where failures concentrate.

**Now say why:** why does a bigger sample buy so little precision?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Run 5–7 evaluators (code and LLM judges, one per known failure mode) on a small sample, often 1–5% of traffic, after each request completes. Correct each judge's rate and alert when its confidence interval crosses a threshold. Put only fast, reliable checks inline as **guardrails** (regex, schema, parsers), with a safe fallback. Track user signals too: retries, rephrasing, abandonment, accepted suggestions. Use A/B tests for big changes. Every new failure found goes back into error analysis and the golden set.

#### Four kinds of signal

##### Sampled evaluators

Log full traces, sample a small share daily, and run your evaluators on them asynchronously. For each failure mode, report the corrected rate with a confidence interval (see validating a judge) and alert when the interval crosses your threshold. Sample per slice (feature, customer, language) if failures concentrate there.

##### Guardrails

A guardrail is a function called on every output before it's sent: if it fires, log it and return a safe fallback ("I drafted this, but it contained sensitive details, so please review the source"). It must be fast and rarely wrong, so most guardrails are code: card-number and ID patterns, schema validation, allow-lists, parsers that confirm SQL or code is valid. A 2–3 second LLM call on every answer is usually too slow. Every guardrail trip is also a free label for monitoring.

##### User signals

Implicit signals scale better than thumbs: the user retries or rephrases, abandons the session, escalates to a human, accepts or deletes a suggestion. GitHub's study of Copilot found that the rate of accepted suggestions predicted how productive developers felt better than other usage measures. Signals are noisy proxies, so use them to choose traces to read and to spot trends, alongside evaluators.

##### A/B tests

For a new model or a big prompt change, split traffic and compare task success, user signals, cost and latency; LLM outputs vary a lot, so plan sample sizes. See the sample size lessons.

##### The flywheel

Monitoring spots a rise in one failure, error analysis on flagged traces finds a new mode, the team adds 5–10 examples to the golden set, builds a check, fixes the app, verifies in CI and redeploys. Each lap makes both the app and the evals stronger.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Log everything, judge a sample:** 1–5% async, per failure mode.

- **Correct rates, alert on intervals:** not on raw judge counts.

- **Guardrails are fast code:** with a safe fallback and a log of every trip.

- **Watch implicit signals:** retries, rephrasing, abandonment, acceptance.

- **A/B test big changes:** with planned sample sizes.

- **Feed the golden set:** every new failure becomes a CI case.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Run the hallucination judge on every chat before sending"

It sounds thorough, but it adds seconds to every reply and costs a fortune, while a small async sample measures the same rate. Keep inline checks to fast code, and judge after the fact.

## Say it

### Your assistant handles 100,000 conversations a day. How do you know today's quality without reading them?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not run the LLM judge on 100% of traffic?

It costs far more and adds little: a modest sample already gives a tight error bar. Spend the budget on slicing by feature or customer instead.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A guardrail blocks 3% of answers. Is that good?

Read a sample of the blocked ones. If many were fine, the false-positive rate is too high and users are being refused for nothing.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Thumbs-down rate is flat but retries are rising. What do you do?

Treat retries as the earlier signal: read retried conversations, look for a new failure mode, and check whether something changed, such as a model or retrieval update.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd log full traces and run five to seven evaluators, one per known failure mode, on a 1 to 5% sample asynchronously, correcting each judge's rate and alerting when its confidence interval crosses a threshold. Inline, only fast and reliable checks act as guardrails, like regex for personal data, schema validation and SQL parsing, with a safe fallback, because a judge on every answer adds seconds. I'd watch implicit signals like retries, rephrasing, abandonment and accepted suggestions, A/B test big changes, and feed every new failure back into error analysis and the golden set.

**Key terms and sources**

Running evaluators on a sample of live traffic with corrected rates and alerts, guardrails that block bad outputs inline, the user signals that work as quality proxies, A/B tests for big changes, and the loop that feeds production failures back into CI. · checked 15 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- H. Husain and S. Shankar, _Evals for AI Engineers_ (O'Reilly): the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle, error analysis, judges, CI and review

- [H. Husain and S. Shankar, AI Evals: everything you need to know (FAQ)](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/)

- [A. Ziegler et al., Productivity assessment of neural code completion (GitHub Copilot), 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06537)

- [Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, Jan 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)
