# Experiment Tracking, Reproducibility and the Model Registry

> Can you rebuild last month's model, and roll back in minutes?

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/experiment-tracking-and-model-registry/
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

## Intuition

### The situation

Last month's ETA model was better than this week's retrained one. Leadership asks what changed, whether you can go back and whether you can rebuild last month's model exactly. A colleague says the code is in git, so that's covered. The interviewer asks:

> Can you rebuild last month's model, and roll back in minutes?

**Running example:** last month's ETA model was better than this week's retrained one. Leadership asks: what changed, can we go back, and can we rebuild last month's model exactly?

#### "It worked on my notebook"

ML results depend on many moving parts that ordinary version control doesn't capture: the data changes daily, features get redefined, hyperparameters live in someone's command line, and library upgrades change numerics. Without records, debugging a regression becomes guesswork.

### The idea

Think of a dish that came out brilliantly last month. The recipe alone won't recreate it, if you don't know which batch of ingredients went in, which oven you used or how long it really cooked. Code is only the recipe, and the data is the ingredients.

[Figure: Code and config are usually recorded. Data snapshot, feature definitions, seeds, environment, evaluation set version and model registry are what usually go missing.]

_The lab's eight records. With only code and config, none of its five questions can be answered._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Tick only code version and config. Then add the data snapshot and eval set version, then seeds and environment, then the registry. Watch which questions you can answer.

#### "We have the code in git, that's enough"

Which records each question needs is a simplified mapping of standard practice.

With only **code and config** in version control, you can't answer any of the five questions: the data that trained last month's model is gone (the table has changed), so you can't rebuild it, explain the regression, compare runs fairly or satisfy an auditor, and without a registry there's nothing to roll back to. Add the **data snapshot** and **eval set version** and "why is this week worse?" becomes answerable; add **seeds and environment** and you can rebuild; add a **registry** and rollback takes minutes. Even with everything recorded, two runs with different seeds differ: Bouthillier et al. found such variance can be as large as reported improvements, so compare models over several seeds.

**Now say why:** why doesn't having the code let you rebuild the model?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A model is the product of **code + data + configuration + randomness + environment**. If any of these isn't recorded, you can't rebuild the model, explain why this week's version is worse, or prove to an auditor what it learned from. **Experiment tracking** means every training run automatically records its code version, a pointer to an immutable data snapshot, feature definitions, hyperparameters, random seeds, library versions and hardware, plus metrics on a **versioned evaluation set**. A **model registry** is the catalogue of trained models with their lineage, stage (candidate, production, archived), approvals and documentation, so deployment and rollback are a matter of pointing to a version. Even then, GPU non-determinism and seeds cause run-to-run variance; measure it before calling a 0.2-point gain real. What you'll be able to do after this: list what to record per run, explain sources of non-determinism, and describe what a registry enables.

#### What every run should record

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| **Code version** (commit) | the exact training and feature code |
| **Data snapshot** (immutable, by ID or time range) | re-reading "the orders table" tomorrow gives different data |
| **Feature definitions** and their versions | the same feature name can change meaning |
| **Configuration** (hyperparameters, splits) | results depend on them |
| **Seeds** | initialisation, shuffling, sampling |
| **Environment** (library versions, hardware) | numerics and defaults change across versions and GPUs |
| **Evaluation set version and metrics** | comparisons are meaningless on different test sets |
| **Registry entry** (artefact, lineage, stage, approver, model card) | deploy, roll back and audit by version |

Datasheets for datasets and model cards document what the data and model are for, their limits and their evaluation across groups.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Practices

- **Automate recording** inside the training pipeline (not by hand), so every run is tracked, including failed ones.

- **Immutable data:** write training snapshots to versioned, read-only storage; record the query and time range.

- **Lineage:** link data snapshot → features → run → model version → deployment, so you can trace any prediction back.

- **Registry stages and approvals:** candidate → staging → production with automated checks and a named approver; keep the previous production version ready for rollback.

- **Non-determinism:** fix seeds, record hardware and library versions, accept small GPU differences, and report mean ± spread across seeds.

#### A model is only as reproducible as its least-recorded input

Record code, data, features, config, seeds, environment and evaluation for every run, and manage trained models in a registry, so you can rebuild, explain, compare, roll back and audit.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "We can retrain it if we need to"

It sounds right, since you have the code. But the same code on today's data produces a different model, and re-reading "the orders table" tomorrow gives different data. So you need the snapshot. And don't trust "Model B is 0.2 points better" either: Bouthillier et al. found seed variance can be as large as reported improvements.

## Say it

### Can you rebuild last month's model, and roll back in minutes?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why isn't storing the code enough?

Data and feature definitions change independently; the same code on today's data produces a different model.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Where does non-determinism come from in training?

Random initialisation, data shuffling, dropout, sampling, and non-deterministic GPU kernels and parallel reductions.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What should a model card contain?

Intended use, training data summary, evaluation results overall and by slice, limitations and known risks, owner and version.

#### The 30-second answer

A model depends on code, data, feature definitions, configuration, random seeds and the software environment, so each training run should automatically record all of them, pointing to an immutable data snapshot and a versioned evaluation set, plus its metrics. A model registry stores each trained model with its lineage, stage and approvals, which makes deployment and rollback a version switch and supports audits. Without data snapshots you can't rebuild or explain a regression. And because seeds and GPU non-determinism cause run-to-run variance, I compare models across several seeds before trusting small gains.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "We can retrain it if we need to." Not without the data snapshot.

- "Model B is 0.2 points better." Check seed variance first.

**Key terms and sources**

What to record for every training run (code version, data snapshot, feature definitions, configuration, seeds, environment, evaluation set) and why; sources of non-determinism; lineage from data to deployed model; and the model registry as a concept (versions, stages, approvals, rollback) · built from Pineau et al. (Improving Reproducibility in ML Research, JMLR 2021), Bouthillier et al. (Accounting for Variance in ML Benchmarks, MLSys 2021), Sculley et al. (NeurIPS 2015), Breck et al. (ML Test Score, 2017), Gebru et al. (Datasheets for Datasets, CACM 2021) and Mitchell et al. (Model Cards, FAT* 2019) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. J. Pineau et al., "Improving Reproducibility in Machine Learning Research", JMLR 2021, [arXiv:2003.12206](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12206).

2. X. Bouthillier et al., "Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks", MLSys 2021, [arXiv:2103.03098](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03098).

3. T. Gebru et al., "Datasheets for Datasets", CACM 2021, [arXiv:1803.09010](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010); M. Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting", FAT* 2019, [arXiv:1810.03993](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993).

4. D. Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015; E. Breck et al., "The ML Test Score", IEEE Big Data 2017.

# Drift Detection and Monitoring

> How do you know a model is degrading before labels arrive?

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/drift-detection-and-monitoring/
- Before this: Training/Serving Skew and Feature Stores (`ai-engineering/training-serving-skew-and-feature-stores`)
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

## Intuition

### The situation

The ETA model was trained when most orders were within 5 km, and the company is expanding into suburbs. A crashed service pages someone, but a degrading model keeps returning numbers. A colleague sets an alert for whenever a statistical test says the data changed. The interviewer asks:

> How do you know a model is degrading before labels arrive?

**Running example:** the ETA model was trained when most orders were within 5 km. The company is expanding into suburbs, and delivery distances are creeping up.

#### No error message when a model gets worse

A crashed service pages someone; a model that's slowly getting less accurate keeps returning numbers with full confidence. Without monitoring, the first signal is customer complaints, weeks later.

### The idea

Think of a smoke alarm so sensitive that it goes off when you make toast. Soon enough, someone takes the battery out. A good alarm goes off when there's actually a problem. With enough data, a statistical test is that over-sensitive alarm.

[Figure: A 10 percent shift over 5,000 orders gives PSI 0.029, which reads stable, and KS p below 0.0001. A 2 percent shift over 50,000 orders gives PSI 0.002 and KS p of 0.0003.]

_From the lab: PSI under 0.1 reads as stable. The KS test flags changes too small to matter._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set a 10% increase over 5,000 orders. Then a 2% increase over 50,000. Then push the increase to 20% and 30%, and compare PSI with the KS p-value.

#### "Alert whenever a statistical test says the data changed"

Training baseline: 20,000 log-normally distributed delivery distances; live window: fresh samples scaled by the chosen increase. PSI over 10 bins at the baseline's deciles; two-sample KS test with its asymptotic p-value. Fixed seed.

A **10%** increase in distances over **5,000** orders gives PSI **0.029**, comfortably "stable", but the KS test's p-value is below **0.0001**. Push the window to 50,000 orders and even a **2%** change is "significant" (p = 0.0003) while PSI is 0.002: with enough data, a hypothesis test detects differences far too small to matter, so p-value alerts fire constantly and get ignored. PSI reaches "moderate" at about a 20% increase (0.118) and approaches "large" at 30% (0.245). With no change, neither fires. The useful question isn't "did anything change?" but "did it change enough to hurt?": tie alert thresholds to effect sizes that historically moved error, check performance once labels arrive, and look by slice (the suburbs may have shifted a lot while the city average barely moved).

**Now say why:** a 2% shift is "significant", so why not act on it?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Models degrade silently because the world changes. **Data drift** (covariate shift): the inputs change, e.g. longer delivery distances after expanding to suburbs. **Concept drift**: the same inputs now mean different outcomes, e.g. the same distance takes longer during monsoon traffic. The best signal is **performance** on fresh labels, but labels often arrive late (an ETA's truth is known within an hour; fraud's, after weeks of chargebacks), so you also watch **proxies**: data quality, input and prediction distributions. Drift statistics need judgement: **PSI** measures how much a distribution moved (rules of thumb: under 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, above 0.25 large); a **KS test** asks whether there's _any_ difference, and with large samples it flags changes too small to matter. Alert on what affects the business, by slice, with owners and runbooks. What you'll be able to do after this: design a monitoring plan, explain data vs concept drift, and interpret PSI and KS sensibly.

#### Layers of monitoring

| Layer | Examples | Needs labels? |
|---|---|---|
| **System** | latency, errors, throughput, fallback rate | no |
| **Data quality** | missing values, schema changes, out-of-range values, stale features | no |
| **Input drift** | feature distributions vs training (PSI, KS, by slice) | no |
| **Prediction drift** | distribution of ETAs vs normal | no |
| **Performance** | MAE vs actual delivery times, by city and hour | yes (delayed) |
| **Business** | late-delivery complaints, cancellations | outcome data |

- **Data drift** changes P(x); **concept drift** changes P(y | x). Drift can be **sudden** (a policy change), **gradual** (suburban expansion) or **recurring** (festivals, monsoon) (Gama et al. 2014).

- Many data "drifts" are actually **pipeline bugs** (a unit change, a broken join): data-quality checks catch those first.

See comparing distributions for how PSI, Jensen-Shannon and Wasserstein differ.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Monitoring that people trust

- **Prioritise:** performance on labels when available; for delayed labels, prediction drift and the most important features' drift as early warnings.

- **Slice everything** by city, segment and new vs existing entities; averages hide local breakage.

- **Calibrate thresholds** on history (how often would this have fired, and did it matter?); prefer effect sizes and sustained changes over single-window p-values. Rabanser et al. found simple univariate tests with multiple-testing correction work well to detect that a shift exists; whether it matters is a separate question.

- **Owners and runbooks:** every alert has an owner and a first step (check pipelines, compare slices, consider retraining or rollback).

- **LLM apps** add output-quality monitoring (sampled judge scores, escalations, user feedback); see LLMOps.

Labels late? You can estimate accuracy from calibrated probabilities while you wait, as long as only the input mix changed. See Monitoring Without Labels.

#### Monitor what hurts, early and by slice

Watch system health, data quality, input and prediction distributions and, as soon as labels allow, real performance; set alert thresholds on changes large enough to matter, not on any statistically detectable change.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Alert when the KS test is significant"

It sounds right, since significance is what tests are for. But at scale it always is: in the lab, a 2% shift over 50,000 orders gives p = 0.0003, with a PSI of just 0.002. Alerts fire constantly and get ignored. Ask whether it changed enough to hurt. "Monitor accuracy daily" fails too, because labels may not exist yet.

## Say it

### How do you know a model is degrading before labels arrive?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Labels arrive 60 days later (fraud). What do you monitor meanwhile?

Prediction score distribution, feature drift on key features, data quality, proxy labels (early chargebacks, manual review outcomes) and business signals.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Inputs didn't drift but accuracy dropped. What happened?

Concept drift (the relationship changed), a label pipeline change, or a slice-level shift hidden in the average; check performance by slice and the label definition.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you avoid alert fatigue?

Fewer, calibrated alerts tied to impact, sustained-change rules, grouping, clear owners, and regular review of alerts that didn't lead to action.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd monitor in layers: system health, data quality like missing values and schema changes, input and prediction distributions compared with training, and real performance once labels arrive, plus business outcomes. Data drift is a change in the inputs; concept drift is a change in how inputs map to outcomes, and only performance monitoring catches the latter directly. Because labels are often delayed, distribution drift is an early warning. I'd use effect-size measures like PSI with calibrated thresholds rather than raw p-values, since with large samples tests like KS flag trivial changes, and I'd monitor by slice with owners and runbooks for every alert.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Alert when the KS test is significant." At scale it always is.

- "Monitor accuracy daily." Labels may not exist yet.

**Key terms and sources**

How to know a production model is degrading: data drift (inputs change), concept drift (the input→output relationship changes), label delay, what to monitor at each layer (system, data quality, input and prediction distributions, performance, business), drift statistics (PSI, KS test) and their pitfalls, and alerting that people won't ignore · built from Lu et al. (Learning under Concept Drift: A Review, IEEE TKDE 2019), Rabanser et al. (Failing Loudly, NeurIPS 2019), Gama et al. (A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation, ACM CSUR 2014), Breck et al. (ML Test Score, 2017), Shankar et al. (Operationalizing ML, 2022) and Huyen (Designing ML Systems, 2022) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. J. Lu et al., "Learning under Concept Drift: A Review", IEEE TKDE 2019, [arXiv:2004.05785](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05785); J. Gama et al., "A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation", ACM CSUR 2014.

2. S. Rabanser, S. Günnemann & Z. Lipton, "Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift", NeurIPS 2019, [arXiv:1810.11953](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.11953).

3. E. Breck et al., "The ML Test Score", IEEE Big Data 2017; S. Shankar et al., "Operationalizing Machine Learning: An Interview Study", 2022, [arXiv:2209.09125](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09125).

# Monitoring Without Labels: Estimating Performance

> Your fraud model's labels arrive 60 days late. How do you know its accuracy today?

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/monitoring-without-labels/
- Before this: Drift Detection and Monitoring (`ai-engineering/drift-detection-and-monitoring`)
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your fraud model's labels arrive after 60 days of chargebacks. The drift dashboard shows several features moved this month, and the risk team asks whether the model is still accurate today. The interviewer asks:

> Your fraud model's labels arrive 60 days late. How do you know its accuracy today?

#### Why it matters

Many models learn the truth late. A fraud label waits for chargebacks, a loan default takes months, and a churn label takes a quarter. Meanwhile, drift monitoring can tell you that inputs changed, but not by how much accuracy changed, if at all. Many shifts don't hurt the model, and some that hurt don't look big. Interviewers ask how you'd estimate performance in that gap.

### The idea

Think of a weather forecaster who says 70% chance of rain. If they're well calibrated, it rains on 7 of every 10 such days. So you can estimate how often they'll be right this week before the week ends, unless the climate itself has changed.

[Figure: Three signals while labels are late. Estimate from calibrated confidence. Use proxy labels. Label a small sample.]

_Confident and wrong is the case estimates can't see._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the share of hard cases. Then let the meaning change too.

#### When the estimate holds, and when it doesn't

Illustrative. Easy predictions have 0.95 confidence and hard ones 0.65, both calibrated in training. "The meaning changes" lowers their real accuracy to 85% and 50% without changing the model's confidence.

At 20% hard cases, the estimate and the real accuracy agree at 89%. Raise hard cases to 50%, as when a fraud team starts seeing a new merchant mix, and both fall to 80%: the estimate tracked the change without a single label. Now switch to **the meaning changes too**. The model is just as confident, so the estimate still says 80%, but real accuracy is 67.5%. That's why estimation needs a small labelled sample beside it.

**Now say why:** why does the estimate follow one change but miss the other?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Drift statistics say the inputs moved, not whether accuracy fell. If a model's probabilities are **calibrated**, you can estimate its accuracy without labels: a prediction made with 90% confidence is right about 90% of the time, so averaging confidence over today's predictions estimates today's accuracy. That's **confidence-based performance estimation** (CBPE). It works when only the mix of inputs changes (covariate shift), such as more hard cases. It fails when the meaning changes (concept drift), because the model stays just as confident while being wrong more often. So pair it with proxy labels, a small daily labelled sample, and real labels when they arrive.

#### How estimation works

##### Confidence-based performance estimation

For a binary classifier, each prediction comes with a probability. If those probabilities are calibrated, a prediction of "fraud, 0.8" is right 80% of the time, and one of "not fraud, 0.1" is right 90% of the time. Averaging these over a day's predictions estimates the day's accuracy. Doing the same per cell of the confusion matrix gives estimates of precision, recall, F1 and AUROC too. This is CBPE, and with perfect calibration its estimates are unbiased.

##### Keeping calibration under shift

Calibration measured on the test set can break when the input mix changes. PAPE, presented at NeurIPS 2025, re-calibrates using weights that say how much more common each kind of input has become in production. Across over 900 dataset and model combinations from US census data, its accuracy estimates were on average within about one standard error of the real value (0.97), against 1.62 for simply assuming test-set accuracy still holds, and 1.08 for plain CBPE.

##### Where it fails

- **Concept drift:** if the same inputs now lead to different outcomes, such as a new fraud pattern that looks normal, the model is confidently wrong, and the estimate stays high. The PAPE paper says plainly that it won't work under concept shift.

- **New kinds of input:** inputs unlike anything in training can't be re-weighted.

- **Poor calibration:** estimates are only as good as the probabilities. Check calibration on the test set first.

##### Other signals while labels are late

- **Proxy labels:** early signals that correlate with the truth, such as a customer disputing a payment within days.

- **A small labelled sample:** have people label, say, 200 random predictions a week. It catches concept drift that estimation can't.

- **Business outcomes:** manual review rates, complaints and losses.

#### The maths

$$ {\widehat{\text{acc}}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} {\max(p_i,\ 1-p_i)} $$

This is valid only if the probabilities are calibrated on today's data. Under concept drift, they aren't, and the estimate is too high.

- **estimated accuracy**: Today’s accuracy, estimated without any labels.

- **confidence in the predicted class**: For a prediction of positive with p = 0.8, the chance it’s right is 0.8. For p = 0.1, it’s 0.9.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Check calibration first:** on the test set, by slice. If it's poor, recalibrate before trusting estimates.

- **Estimate by slice:** per segment, city or product, since averages hide local drops.

- **Alert on estimated performance:** it's in the units the business cares about, unlike drift scores.

- **Label a small random sample:** weekly, to catch concept drift and check the estimates.

- **Reconcile when labels arrive:** compare past estimates with real results, and learn how far to trust them.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Drift is low, so the model is fine"

It sounds right, since nothing moved much. But concept drift changes outcomes without changing inputs, and a model can stay confident while getting worse. Check a small labelled sample, and watch business outcomes.

## Say it

### Your fraud model's labels arrive 60 days late. How do you know its accuracy today?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Estimated accuracy is stable, but chargebacks are rising. What's happening?

Probably concept drift: a new fraud pattern the model scores confidently as normal. Confidence-based estimates can't see it. Check a labelled sample of recent cases, and look at the slices where chargebacks rose.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not just alert on drift scores?

Many drifts don't hurt accuracy, and a drift score isn't in the units that matter. An estimated metric, per slice, ties alerts to impact.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What must be true for CBPE to work?

Calibrated probabilities, and a shift in the input mix only, not in how inputs relate to outcomes. Inputs must also look like ones seen in training.

#### The 30-second answer

Drift scores tell me inputs moved, not whether accuracy fell. If the model's probabilities are calibrated, I can estimate accuracy from them: average the confidence in each predicted class, or estimate the whole confusion matrix, which is CBPE. PAPE re-calibrates for the new input mix and was within about one standard error on census benchmarks. But it assumes only the mix changed. Under concept drift the model stays confident while being wrong, so I'd add proxy labels, a small weekly labelled sample, and reconcile with real labels when they arrive.

**Key terms and sources**

Why drift statistics don't tell you accuracy, how confidence-based estimation (CBPE, PAPE) estimates performance from a model's own probabilities, what it assumes, where it fails, and how to combine it with proxy labels and small labelled samples. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Białek, Kivimäki, Kuberski and Perrakis, Estimating Model Performance Under Covariate Shift Without Labels (PAPE), NeurIPS 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08348)

- [Kivimäki et al., Performance Estimation in Binary Classification Using Calibrated Confidence (CBPE)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05295)

- [Rabanser, Günnemann and Lipton, Failing Loudly: detecting dataset shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.11953)

- [Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Many recent papers are preprints, and provider policies change.

# Retraining Pipelines and Continuous Training

> How often should you retrain, and what stops a bad retrain?

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/retraining-pipelines/
- Before this: Drift Detection and Monitoring (`ai-engineering/drift-detection-and-monitoring`), Deployment Patterns: Shadow, Canary, A/B and Rollback (`ai-engineering/deployment-patterns`)
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

## Intuition

### The situation

The ETA model's error grows slowly as the city changes, and jumps during festivals, the monsoon or a policy change. One colleague says quarterly is fine, and another says to retrain automatically every day and deploy. The interviewer asks:

> How often should you retrain, and what stops a bad retrain?

**Running example:** the ETA model's error grows slowly as the city changes (new restaurants, roads, habits), and jumps during a few events each year (festivals, monsoon, a new delivery policy). How often should it be retrained?

#### A model starts going stale the day it ships

The model learned last quarter's world. Retraining manually is slow and error-prone, and teams that rely on someone remembering to do it end up with models that are months stale. But retraining isn't free, and an unchecked automatic retrain can ship a worse model.

### The idea

Think of servicing a delivery bike. Regular servicing handles slow wear, and a warning light handles sudden faults. But nobody puts it back on the road without checking it, or you might ride out on a bad repair. Schedule, triggers and a gate.

[Figure: Quarterly retraining: 7.54 minutes of drift-peak error and 45 days stale after a shift. Monthly: average 5.85 minutes, 12 retrains and 15 days stale. Monthly with triggers: 5.63 minutes, 16 retrains and 2 days stale.]

_From the lab's illustrative model. Quarterly error is where the drift peaks, and the others are yearly averages._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set the schedule to quarterly, monthly and weekly, watching the error and the cost. Then add triggers on sudden shifts.

#### "Retrain every quarter, it's fine"

Illustrative model: error is 5.0 minutes right after training and grows 0.04 minutes per day; four sudden shifts a year each add 1.5 minutes of error until the next retrain (a trigger retrains within 2 days).

**Monthly** retraining averages **5.85 minutes** of error for 12 retrains a year; **weekly** brings it to 5.20 but costs 52 retrains; **quarterly** lets error drift up to 7.54. The schedule mostly controls slow drift. Sudden shifts are different: with a schedule alone, the model is stuck with the old world for half a cycle on average (**15 days** monthly, 45 days quarterly). Adding **triggers** that retrain within about 2 days of a detected shift cuts that, bringing the monthly plan to **5.63** minutes for just 4 extra retrains. The trap in the other direction: retraining automatically on whatever data arrived. If the shift is a broken data feed, the trigger trains on garbage; that's what the validation and "beat production" gates are for.

**Now say why:** if the shift is really a broken data feed, what does an automatic trigger do?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Because the world drifts, most models need regular retraining. **Scheduled** retraining (weekly, monthly) is simple and predictable; **triggered** retraining reacts to monitoring (performance drop, large drift, a known event). The retraining job is a **pipeline**, not a person: validate the new data, train, evaluate against the **current production model** on the same recent test set and key slices, and only then promote through the usual staged rollout. Retraining more often lowers average error but costs compute and review time, and automated retraining on **bad data** (a broken pipeline, a fraud wave, the model's own feedback) can make things worse fast. So: automate the pipeline, gate every new model, and combine a schedule with triggers for sudden changes. What you'll be able to do after this: choose a retraining strategy, design an automated pipeline with gates, and name the risks of automatic retraining.

#### An automated retraining pipeline

1. **Trigger:** schedule, performance or drift alert, new data volume, or a known event.

2. **Data validation:** schema, ranges, missing rates, label sanity, comparison with the previous window; stop on anomalies.

3. **Build the training set:** a sliding window (e.g. last 90 days) or all data with recent examples weighted more; point-in-time features.

4. **Train** with recorded config, seeds and data snapshot (tracking).

5. **Evaluate against production:** same recent test set, key slices, fairness and latency checks; must beat (or match) the current model.

6. **Register and roll out** via shadow/canary with automatic rollback; humans approve when the change is large or the domain is high-risk.

Google's MLOps maturity levels describe the progression: level 0 manual, level 1 an automated training pipeline (continuous training), level 2 automated CI/CD of the pipeline itself.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Risks and good practice

- **Bad-data retrains:** pipeline bugs, label delays (training on incomplete labels), adversarial waves (fraud); validate data and compare with the previous model before promoting.

- **Feedback loops:** models trained on data shaped by their own predictions (recommendations, pricing) reinforce themselves; keep exploration or holdout traffic for unbiased data.

- **Window choice:** short windows adapt fast but forget rare seasons; long windows are stable but slow; weighting recent data is a middle ground.

- **Warm-start vs from scratch:** fine-tuning the previous model is cheaper; periodic full retrains avoid accumulating quirks.

- **Measure the value:** track how much each retrain improved the target metric; if it rarely helps, retrain less.

For how models shape their own training data, and how exploration and logged probabilities fix it, see Feedback Loops and Unbiased Training Data.

#### Automate retraining, but gate every model it produces

A schedule handles slow drift and triggers handle sudden shifts, but every retrained model must pass data validation and beat production before it ships.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Retrain automatically and deploy"

It sounds right, since fresher models track the world better. But if the shift is a broken data feed, the trigger trains on garbage. Pipeline bugs, delayed labels and feedback loops all do this, so every retrained model must pass data validation and beat production. More frequent isn't always better either: weigh the gain per retrain against its cost and risk.

## Say it

### How often should you retrain, and what stops a bad retrain?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you choose the retraining frequency?

Measure how fast performance decays (train on old data, test on successive weeks), compare the gain per retrain with its cost, and add triggers for sudden changes.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The retrained model is worse than production. What now?

Don't ship it; investigate data changes (pipeline bugs, label delays, distribution shift), check slices, and keep production running.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What is online / continual learning, and when would you use it?

Updating the model incrementally as data arrives; useful for fast-changing domains (ads, feeds), but harder to validate and roll back, so most teams use frequent batch retrains.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd automate retraining as a pipeline: a trigger, which can be a schedule, a performance or drift alert, or a known event; data validation; building a point-in-time training set over a sliding or weighted window; training with full tracking; evaluating against the current production model on the same recent test set and key slices; then registering and rolling out through shadow or canary with automatic rollback. A schedule handles gradual drift; triggers handle sudden shifts. The risks are retraining on bad or incomplete data and feedback loops, so gates and holdout data matter as much as the training itself.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "Retrain automatically and deploy." Gate it.

- "More frequent is always better." Weigh gains against cost and risk.

**Key terms and sources**

When and how to retrain production models: scheduled vs triggered retraining, what goes into an automated training pipeline (data checks, training, evaluation against the current model, approval, staged deployment), training windows and sample weighting, the cost–freshness trade-off, and failure modes such as training on bad data or feedback loops · built from Google Cloud (MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in ML, maturity levels 0–2), Breck et al. (ML Test Score, 2017), Polyzotis et al. (Data Validation for ML, MLSys 2019), Huyen (Designing ML Systems, 2022, ch. 9), Gama et al. (ACM CSUR 2014) and Sculley et al. (NeurIPS 2015) · checked 29 Oct 2026

#### Sources

1. Google Cloud, "MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning" (maturity levels 0–2).

2. E. Breck et al., "The ML Test Score", IEEE Big Data 2017; N. Polyzotis et al., "Data Validation for Machine Learning", MLSys 2019.

3. C. Huyen, _Designing Machine Learning Systems_, O'Reilly 2022 (ch. 9, continual learning).

4. J. Gama et al., "A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation", ACM CSUR 2014; D. Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015 (feedback loops).

# Feedback Loops and Unbiased Training Data

> Your recommender is retrained on its own clicks every week, and it keeps showing the same few items. Why, and how do you get data it can learn from?

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 18 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/feedback-loops-and-unbiased-data/
- Before this: Retraining Pipelines and Continuous Training (`ai-engineering/retraining-pipelines`), Bandits vs A/B Tests (`fundamentals/bandits-vs-ab-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your recommender is retrained weekly on its own click logs. Each version looks better offline, but users see the same few items, and new items never take off. The interviewer asks:

> Your recommender is retrained on its own clicks every week, and it keeps showing the same few items. Why, and how do you get data it can learn from?

#### Why it matters

Many models choose what happens next: what's recommended, which loans are approved, which transactions are reviewed. Their logs record outcomes only for the choices they made. Sculley et al. listed these hidden feedback loops as a form of technical debt in ML systems. Interviewers ask about them in recommender, ads, pricing and fraud designs.

### The idea

Think of a restaurant critic who only revisits places they already like. They'll never find out the new place down the road is better, and their list gets shorter every year. Trying somewhere new now and then is the only way to learn.

[Figure: Three fixes. Explore a little. Log the chance of each choice. Keep a holdout.]

_You only learn about what you chose._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Run with no exploration. Then add 5%, then 20%.

#### A model that can't learn it was wrong

Illustrative, with expected values and no noise. 10,000 users a day. Real click rates: A 4%, B 6%, C 3%, D 2%, E 5%. The old model believes A 4.5%, B 2%, C 3%, D 2%, E 1%. Exploration spreads its share evenly over all five items, and the model updates its beliefs from each day's clicks.

With **no exploration**, the model keeps showing item A at 400 clicks a day. It never shows B, so it never learns B gets 6%, and it loses 6,000 clicks in 30 days. With **5% exploration**, one day of data reveals B, the model switches, and it gets 590 clicks a day, losing 490 over the month, mostly on day one and the exploration itself. **20% exploration** learns just as fast but keeps paying for it: 560 a day. So explore a little, all the time, and log the chances.

**Now say why:** why does a little exploration beat a lot?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A recommender only sees clicks on what it showed. If it thinks item B is poor, it never shows B, so it never learns B is actually the best. Retraining on its own logs makes this worse each week, which is a **feedback loop**. The fixes: spend a small share of traffic on **exploration**, so every option gets some data; keep a **holdout** group served without the model; and **log the probability** that each shown item was chosen, so later training and evaluation can correct for what the old model preferred.

#### How loops form

##### You only see outcomes for what you chose

- **Recommenders:** unshown items get no clicks, so they look unpopular.

- **Lending:** you never learn whether rejected applicants would have repaid.

- **Fraud review:** only flagged transactions get checked, so labels cover what the model already suspects.

- **Policing and inspections:** Ensign et al. showed that sending patrols where incidents were recorded, and recording incidents where patrols go, can run away from the true rates.

##### Greedy models narrow fastest

Jiang et al. at DeepMind simulated recommenders acting on users whose interests shift with what they see. A model that always picked its current best items narrowed users onto a handful of items fastest. Random exploration and a growing pool of new items slowed this. Chaney et al. found that training on data shaped by an earlier recommender made recommendations more alike across users, and less useful.

##### The fixes

- **Exploration:** show a small share of traffic other options, randomly or with a bandit, so every option keeps getting data. See bandits.

- **Log the chance of each action:** record the probability that each shown item was chosen. Bottou et al. showed how such logs let you estimate how a different policy would have done, by weighting outcomes by one over that probability.

- **Holdouts:** keep a small group served without the model, or with an older one, to measure its real effect.

- **Watch diversity:** track how many distinct items are shown, and how concentrated exposure is.

#### The maths

$$ {\hat{V}(\pi)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} {r_i}\,\frac{{\pi(a_i \mid x_i)}}{{p_i}} $$

Inverse propensity scoring. It only works for actions the old system sometimes took, which is why exploration matters: with no exploration, many chances are zero.

- **value of a new policy**: How a policy you haven’t deployed would have done, estimated from old logs.

- **the outcome**: For example, a click on what was shown.

- **new policy’s chance**: How likely the new policy is to take the logged action.

- **logged chance**: How likely the old system was to take it. You must log this when serving, and it must never be zero.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Log propensities at serving time:** the probability of each shown action, plus what else was eligible. You can't recover them later.

- **Keep a small exploration budget:** a few percent, controlled and measured, rather than none.

- **Hold out a group:** to measure the model's real effect against a simple baseline over time.

- **Evaluate offline with care:** logs from the old model favour it, so weight by propensities, or confirm with an A/B test.

- **Track diversity and coverage:** how many items get shown, and whether new items ever get a chance.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Retrain on the latest clicks, and it'll fix itself"

It sounds right, since fresh data usually helps. But the clicks come only from items the model chose to show, so retraining reinforces its own picks. Explore a little, log the chances, and evaluate with weights or a holdout.

## Say it

### Your recommender is retrained on its own clicks every week, and it keeps showing the same few items. Why, and how do you get data it can learn from?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your offline evaluation says the new recommender is worse, but it's never been shown to users. Can you trust that?

Not fully. The logs come from the old model, so they only have outcomes for items it liked. Weight by logged propensities if you have them, or run an A/B test.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not explore by showing random items to everyone sometimes?

Uniform random exploration is costly for users. Use a small share, a bandit that explores where it's uncertain, or explore within a shortlist of reasonable items.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A loan model approves fewer people each year, and its defaults look great. What's wrong?

You only see repayment for approved applicants, so the model never learns about the ones it rejects. Approve a small, controlled sample near the threshold to get unbiased labels.

#### The 30-second answer

A model that chooses what users see only gets feedback on its own choices, so an item it wrongly rates low never gets shown, and retraining on its logs locks the mistake in. DeepMind's simulations showed greedy recommenders narrow fastest, while exploration and new items slow it down. I'd spend a few percent of traffic on exploration, log the probability of each shown action so I can weight outcomes later, keep a holdout group to measure real impact, and track how many distinct items get shown.

**Key terms and sources**

How models that act on the world shape their own training data, why a greedy system can never learn it was wrong, and the fixes: exploration, holdouts, logging the chance each action was taken, and correcting for it. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems, NeurIPS 2015](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5656-hidden-technical-debt-in-machine-learning-systems)

- [Jiang et al., Degenerate Feedback Loops in Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10730)

- [Bottou et al., Counterfactual Reasoning and Learning Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.2355)

- [Ensign et al., Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09847)

- [Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt, How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.11214)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Many recent papers are preprints, and provider policies change.

# MLOps Practice

> 10 production questions: skew, drift alerts, canaries, audits, retraining, label-free estimation, feedback loops, LLMOps.

- Track: AI Engineering › MLOps › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/mlops-practice/
- Before this: Retraining Pipelines and Continuous Training (`ai-engineering/retraining-pipelines`)
- Quiz topic: `mlops`

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per question, as in an interview. These are the production questions interviewers ask. Give your diagnosis out loud (most likely cause, how you'd confirm it, the fix and how you'd prevent it), then open the answer and compare.

**The checklist:** is it the data (skew, drift, pipeline bug), the labels (delay, definition), the model (staleness, a bad retrain) or the release (a config or version change)? Confirm with logs and slices; fix; then add a monitor, a test or a gate so it can't happen silently again.

Question 1 · Easy · skew

### A new fraud model improved offline AUC from 0.86 to 0.91, but after launch it catches fewer frauds than the old one. What's your first hypothesis and how do you check it?

Answer: **training/serving skew or leakage: offline features differ from what the model sees live**

1. Compare logged serving features with the training values for the same transactions: missing or stale features online, different encodings or units.

2. Check for leakage: training features built with information after the transaction time (e.g. counts that include later chargebacks).

3. Fix with point-in-time training data, shared feature definitions, and training on logged serving features.

**Follow-up:** How would you have caught it before launch? Shadow mode comparing live feature distributions and predictions with offline ones.

Question 2 · Easy · serving mode

### Product wants 'personalised restaurant recommendations on the home screen' for 30 million users, updated in real time. How do you serve it?

Answer: **hybrid: batch-generate candidates per user, re-rank online with session context**

1. Most of the work (candidate generation from long-term preferences) changes slowly: batch it daily or hourly for active users.

2. Re-rank the candidates online at request time using time, location and current session.

3. Stream only the features where freshness matters (recent clicks); fall back to batch results if online ranking fails.

**Follow-up:** Why not compute everything online? Cost and latency at 30 million users for little gain on slow-changing parts.

Question 3 · Medium · drift

### Your drift dashboard shows 40 of 120 features with KS p < 0.01 every day. The team ignores it. What do you change?

Answer: **replace p-value alerts with effect-size thresholds on important features, by slice, tied to performance**

1. With large samples, KS flags trivial differences; daily alerts become noise.

2. Monitor effect sizes (PSI or distance metrics) on the features that matter most for the model, with thresholds calibrated on history.

3. Alert on prediction drift and performance (once labels arrive) by slice; give each alert an owner and a runbook.

**Follow-up:** How do you pick 'important' features? Feature importance or ablations, plus business-critical inputs.

Question 4 · Medium · canary

### Your canary ran for 2 hours at 2% traffic and showed no difference, so the team wants to go to 100%. 2% is about 400 requests/hour. Is that enough to catch a meaningful regression?

Answer: **probably not: ~800 requests only detect large regressions; size the test from the smallest regression that matters**

1. Compute the sample size for the regression you care about: smaller effects need many more requests (n grows with 1/δ²).

2. 800 requests may detect a big jump but not a subtle one, and 2 hours misses daily cycles.

3. Extend duration or traffic share, cover peak periods, keep guardrails with automatic rollback, and ramp gradually.

**Follow-up:** What would you check besides the main metric? Latency, errors, slices (new users, cities), and business guardrails.

Question 5 · Medium · reproducibility

### An auditor asks which data trained the credit-risk model that rejected a customer 8 months ago. You have the code in git and the model file. Can you answer?

Answer: **only if the run recorded an immutable data snapshot and lineage; code and weights aren't enough**

1. The training tables have changed since; without a snapshot ID or time range you can't reconstruct the data.

2. Lineage links: data snapshot → feature definitions → training run → model version → deployment window.

3. Going forward: immutable training snapshots, automated run tracking, a registry with lineage and model cards.

**Follow-up:** What else would the auditor want? The model card, evaluation by group, and the features used for that specific prediction (from logs).

Question 6 · Hard · retraining

### Automated weekly retraining shipped a model that's 15% worse in one city. The pipeline had no human in the loop. What went wrong and what gates would you add?

Answer: **no data validation or per-slice comparison against production before promotion**

1. Likely cause: a data issue in that city (pipeline bug, label delay, an event) that the new model learned from.

2. Add data validation (schema, ranges, volumes per slice, label completeness) that stops the pipeline on anomalies.

3. Require the candidate to match or beat production overall and on key slices on the same recent test set; then shadow/canary with automatic rollback.

4. Keep the previous model deployable and alert on per-slice performance.

**Follow-up:** When should a human approve? Large changes in behaviour, high-risk domains, or when gates are borderline.

Question 7 · Hard · LLMOps

### Nobody changed the prompt or code, but your LLM support bot's escalation rate jumped from 8% to 14% overnight. What happened, and how do you prevent surprises like this?

Answer: **an upstream change: the provider's model alias moved to a new version, or the retrieval index/data changed**

1. Check traces: model version per request, retrieval index version, tool behaviour, input mix; compare before vs after.

2. Hosted model aliases (e.g. 'latest') can change behaviour; re-indexing can change retrieved documents.

3. Pin model versions and index snapshots, log the full configuration per request, run the golden-set gate before any upstream change, and alert on post-change shifts in escalations and judge scores.

**Follow-up:** How would you roll back? Switch back to the previous pinned model version or index snapshot via configuration.

Question 8 · Medium · label-free estimation

### Your classifier made 1,000 predictions today, with no labels yet. 700 have 0.95 confidence in the predicted class, and 300 have 0.70. What's the estimated accuracy, and what has to be true for it to hold?

Answer: **About 87.5%, if the probabilities are still calibrated**

1. Expected correct: 700 × 0.95 + 300 × 0.70 = 665 + 210 = 875.

2. 875 ÷ 1,000 = 87.5%.

3. It holds only if confidence still matches accuracy: a change in the input mix is fine, but concept drift breaks it.

How would you check? Label a small random sample each week, and compare it with the estimate.

Question 9 · Medium · feedback loop

### A loan model approves 30% of applicants. It's retrained every quarter on repayment data, and each version shows lower default rates. Approvals keep falling. What's going on?

Answer: **A feedback loop: you only learn about applicants the model approved**

1. Repayment is observed only for approved loans, so rejected groups never get labels.

2. Each model learns from a narrower group, and grows more cautious about everyone else.

3. Fix: approve a small, controlled share near the threshold, log the approval probability, and evaluate with those weights or a holdout.

What's the business cost of not fixing it? Good applicants are turned away, and the model can't notice.

Question 10 · Hard · propensity weighting

### Your logs show three recommendations: clicked with logged probability 0.5, not clicked with 0.1, and clicked with 0.05. A new policy would show the first two items for sure, and never the third. Estimate the new policy's click rate with inverse propensity scoring.

Answer: **About 0.67 clicks per user**

1. Weight each outcome by new chance ÷ logged chance: 1 × (1 ÷ 0.5) = 2, 0 × (1 ÷ 0.1) = 0, and 1 × (0 ÷ 0.05) = 0.

2. Average over the 3 logs: 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67.

3. With 3 logs, it's very noisy, and it only works because every logged probability is above zero.

Why log probabilities at serving time? You can't reconstruct them later, and without exploration many would be zero.

**More practice and sources**

10 interview questions, easy to hard · answers hidden until you click · checked 29 Oct 2026

# LLMOps: What's Different

> How do you ship prompt changes without breaking things?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLMOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/llmops/
- Before this: Deployment Patterns: Shadow, Canary, A/B and Rollback (`ai-engineering/deployment-patterns`), RAG Evals: Retrieval, Faithfulness and Relevance (`ai-engineering/rag-evals`)
- Quiz topic: `llmops`

## Intuition

### The situation

The company runs an LLM support assistant, and three prompt changes are proposed this week. Each fixes the complaint that prompted it. A colleague says it works on that complaint, so ship it. The interviewer asks:

> How do you ship prompt changes without breaking things?

**Running example:** alongside the ETA model, the company runs the LLM support assistant. Three prompt changes are proposed this week; which ones should ship?

#### Small text edits, big behaviour changes

A one-line prompt edit can fix one complaint and quietly break ten other cases; a new model version can change tone, format or refusals; a re-indexed knowledge base can change answers. There's no single accuracy number and outputs are open-ended, so classic "train, evaluate, deploy" doesn't map directly.

### The idea

Think of a restaurant chain changing a recipe because one customer complained. It may fix that plate and quietly ruin ten others, or double the cost of ingredients. So every change goes through the same tasting panel and the same checklist before any branch gets it.

[Figure: Three prompts through the release gate. Prompt A raises policy accuracy from 91 to 92.5 percent and passes. Prompt B reaches 93 percent but faithfulness falls from 94 to 89 percent, so it is blocked. Prompt C is flat on quality but costs 48 percent more, so it is blocked.]

_Illustrative golden-set results from the lab. Passing changes still go through a canary._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Run prompts A, B and C through the gate. Read the decision and the reason for each.

#### "The new prompt fixed the complaint, ship it"

Illustrative golden-set results. Gate rules: no quality metric may drop more than 2 points; cost and latency may rise at most 10%. Passing configs still go through a canary.

**Prompt A** improves policy accuracy (91.0% → 92.5%) without breaking anything: it passes and goes to canary. **Prompt B** was written to fix one complaint and does raise accuracy to 93.0%, but faithfulness falls from 94.0% to **89.0%**: "more complete" made the model add unsupported claims. Blocked. **Prompt C** is flat on quality but adds 8 examples to every request, raising cost per conversation by **48%**. Blocked, or reconsidered with fewer examples. Judged on the one failing conversation that prompted it, each change looks good; judged on the whole golden set, only A ships.

**Now say why:** prompt B raised accuracy the most, so why was it blocked?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

In classic MLOps you retrain and redeploy a model; in LLM apps the **model is usually someone else's** and rarely changes, while the things you change weekly are **prompts, retrieval indexes, tools and model versions**. So the unit of release is a **configuration** (prompt + model ID + parameters + index snapshot + tools), and each needs versioning and a **release gate**: run the golden set through code checks and validated LLM judges, compare every metric with production (accuracy, faithfulness, format, safety, cost, latency), and ship only if nothing regresses beyond its limit, then canary it. In production, **trace** every request (prompt version, retrieved documents, tool calls, tokens, cost), monitor sampled quality scores and user signals, and watch for **silent upstream changes**: hosted model versions change behaviour (Chen et al. measured large shifts between versions of the same API model). What you'll be able to do after this: explain how LLMOps differs from MLOps, design a release gate for prompt changes, and say what to trace and monitor.

#### MLOps vs LLMOps

| | Classic MLOps | LLMOps |
|---|---|---|
| **What changes most** | model weights (retraining) | prompts, retrieval data, tools, provider model versions |
| **What to version** | data, features, model | the whole configuration: prompt, model ID, parameters, index snapshot, tool schemas |
| **Evaluation** | one or a few metrics on a test set | golden sets scored by code checks + validated LLM judges + human review; many metrics |
| **Monitoring** | input drift, performance with labels | sampled quality scores, user feedback, escalations, safety, cost per request, latency |
| **Cost driver** | training compute | tokens per request × traffic |
| **Shared** | staged rollout, rollback, reproducibility, tracing, owners and runbooks | |

## In practice

### In practice

#### LLMOps practices

- **Version configurations** in the repository (prompt text, model ID pinned to a dated version, parameters, index snapshot ID, tool schemas); every response logs the configuration that produced it.

- **Release gates in CI** on every config change; grow the golden set with production failures; validate LLM judges against human labels (Shankar et al.).

- **Trace** each request end to end: prompt version, retrieved document IDs, tool calls and results, tokens, latency, cost (standard GenAI tracing conventions exist).

- **Online monitoring:** judge-score a sample of live traffic, track thumbs-down, escalations, safety flags, cost per resolved conversation; alert on shifts after deploys.

- **Upstream changes:** pin model versions; re-run the gate before adopting a new one; hosted models can change behaviour between versions (Chen, Zaharia & Zou 2023).

- **Same rollout discipline** as models: shadow or canary, instant rollback to the previous configuration.

Averages hide regressions: in a 2026 study, one model upgrade gained 7.3 points on maths while 6% of items got reliably worse, and a single run per item couldn't detect any of the changes. So compare old and new configurations case by case, with several runs. Practice also leans on people: in a 2025 study of 86 deployed agents, 74% relied mainly on human evaluation and 52% used LLM judges. See Tracing and Observability, Model Upgrades and Retirements and LLM API Reliability.

#### Treat the whole configuration as the model

In LLM apps the prompt, model version, retrieval index and tools together define behaviour, so version them together, gate every change on a golden set across quality, safety and cost, trace every request, and roll out like any model.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The provider's model doesn't change"

It sounds right, if you're calling the same model name. But hosted models can change behaviour between versions, so pin a dated version, and re-run the gate before adopting a new one. Testing a new prompt only on the complaint that prompted it fails the same way: judged on that one conversation, all three prompts look good, and only A survives the full golden set.

## Say it

### How do you ship prompt changes without breaking things?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How is monitoring an LLM app different from monitoring a classifier?

No single label or metric: you combine sampled judge scores, user signals, escalation and safety rates, and cost, and you watch for changes after config or provider updates.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Your provider deprecates the model version you use. What's your process?

Run the golden set on the new version, compare all gate metrics, adjust prompts if needed, shadow or canary, and switch with rollback ready.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What would you put in a trace?

Config version, inputs (redacted), retrieved document IDs, tool calls and results, outputs, tokens, latency, cost and any judge scores, linked by request ID.

#### The 30-second answer

In LLM apps the model weights rarely change; what changes is the prompt, the provider's model version, the retrieval index and tools. So I version the whole configuration and log it with every response. Every change goes through a release gate: run the golden set with code checks and validated LLM judges, compare accuracy, faithfulness, format, safety, cost and latency with production, and block anything that regresses beyond its limit, then canary it with rollback. In production I trace each request, sample live traffic for quality scoring, track user feedback, escalations and cost per conversation, and pin model versions because upstream changes can shift behaviour.

**Go further**

#### What not to say

- "We tested the new prompt on the complaint and it works." Run the full golden set.

- "The provider's model doesn't change." Pin and re-test versions.

**Key terms and sources**

# Tracing and Observability for LLM Apps and Agents

> Users say your assistant 'got worse this week', but every dashboard is green. What should you have been recording, and how do you find the problem?

- Track: AI Engineering › LLMOps › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/tracing-and-observability/
- Before this: LLMOps: What's Different (`ai-engineering/llmops`)
- Quiz topic: `llmops`

## Intuition

### The situation

Users say the assistant 'got worse this week'. Uptime, latency and error rates all look normal, and nobody can tell what changed or which step is at fault. The interviewer asks:

> Users say your assistant 'got worse this week', but every dashboard is green. What should you have been recording, and how do you find the problem?

#### Why it matters

An agent run may involve retrieval, several model calls and tool calls. When an answer is wrong, you need to see which step went wrong, with what inputs. Quality changes don't show up in uptime or latency. A 2025 study of 86 deployed agents found 74% relied mainly on human evaluation, and 52% used LLM judges. In its 20 interviews, 75% of teams had no formal benchmark set, and relied on A/B tests and user feedback instead. Good traces are what make both possible.

### The idea

Think of a flight recorder. When something goes wrong, you don't guess. You replay what every instrument showed and what each pilot did, step by step. A trace is the flight recorder for each request.

[Figure: Three layers. Trace every step. Score a sample of live traffic. Turn bad traces into tests.]

_Green dashboards can hide bad answers._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Score 1% of a small product's traffic. Then raise the rate.

#### How much live traffic to score?

Illustrative: a judge call costs $0.002, and the target is noticing a rise from 5% to 6% bad answers with 80% power. The judge must be checked against human labels first.

At 50,000 conversations a day, scoring 1% gives 500 judged conversations a day, and it takes about 15 days to notice bad answers rising from 5% to 6%. Scoring 5% cuts that to about 3 days, for $5 a day, and 20% to about 0.7 days for $20. For a small product, even 20% may take weeks, so lean on user signals and a human review of flagged traces. Score every conversation after a release, when changes are most likely.

**Now say why:** why does a small change take so long to notice?

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Ordinary monitoring checks that a service answers. An LLM app can answer fast, every time, and still answer badly. So record a **trace** for every request: the configuration, the retrieved documents, each model and tool call, tokens, latency and cost, linked together. Score a **sample** of live traffic with code checks and an LLM judge, and watch user signals like thumbs-down and escalations. Keep personal data out of logs, or redact it. And make failures loud: in one production agent, about 70% of silent failures were caught by a person reading the output, not by any test or alert.

#### What to record

##### Traces and spans

A trace is one request from start to finish. Each step inside it is a span: retrieval, a model call, a tool call, a guardrail check. Spans record their inputs, outputs, timing and errors, and link to their parent. OpenTelemetry defines common names for LLM spans and attributes, such as the model and token counts, now kept in a separate GenAI conventions repository.

| Record | Why |
|---|---|
| Configuration version: prompt, model ID, parameters, index snapshot | To link any change in behaviour to a release |
| Retrieved document IDs and scores | To tell retrieval failures from generation failures |
| Each model call: tokens in, out and cached, latency, finish reason | Cost and latency by step, cut-off answers, cache misses |
| Tool calls, arguments, results and errors | Wrong tool, wrong arguments, failures hidden by the model |
| Guardrail and judge results | What was blocked, and quality scores over time |
| User signals: thumbs, edits, escalations, retries | Real outcomes |

##### Privacy

Prompts and outputs often contain personal data. Redact it before logging, limit who can read raw traces, set retention periods, and keep full content only where you need it.

##### Silent failures

A 2026 study of a production agent with 4,286 unit tests and 827 automated checks documented 22 incidents over eight weeks where everything stayed green. About 70% were found by a person reading the output. In one, an error page was cached, and the model turned it into a confident report about a crisis that didn't exist. Errors that reach a model's context can become fluent, false output, so keep error text out of model inputs, and preserve the original cause when errors pass between layers.

##### From traces to evaluation

Every bad trace a user or reviewer flags becomes a golden set case. Over time, the golden set reflects real traffic, and the release gate catches regressions on cases that once failed.

#### The maths

$$ {n} \approx \frac{2\,(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{\beta})^2\,{p(1-p)}}{{\delta}^2} $$

The usual sample-size formula for comparing two rates, with 5% significance and 80% power. It sets how much live traffic you need to score, or how long you wait.

- **sampled conversations needed**: Per period, before and after a change, to notice it.

- **baseline failure rate**: How often the judge marks an answer bad today.

- **the change to detect**: A smaller change needs many more samples.

## In practice

### In practice

#### In practice

- **Trace everything, keep content selectively:** metadata for every request, full content for a sample, errors and flagged cases.

- **Cost and latency by step:** find which model or tool call dominates, and watch cache hit rates.

- **Alert on outcomes:** escalations, thumbs-down, judge scores and cost per task, especially after releases.

- **Review traces by hand:** schedule time to read real conversations. It catches what metrics miss.

- **Keep judges honest:** check them against human labels, and re-check after model changes. See LLM-as-a-Judge.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Our dashboards are green, so the assistant is fine"

It sounds reasonable, since nothing is failing. But an LLM can answer quickly and wrongly, and errors can even become confident answers. Trace each request, score a sample of answers, and read real conversations.

## Say it

### Users say your assistant 'got worse this week', but every dashboard is green. What should you have been recording, and how do you find the problem?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Latency and error rates are normal, but complaints are up. Where do you look?

Compare traces before and after: configuration version, retrieved documents, tool errors and answer length. Sample complaints and read them, then check judge scores by intent.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Should you log full prompts and answers?

Log metadata for everything, and full content for a sample, errors and flagged cases, after redacting personal data, with strict access and retention.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Your judge says quality is flat after a model upgrade. Trust it?

Not without checking. The judge may share the new model's blind spots, or have drifted itself. Compare it with human labels on a fresh sample.

#### The 30-second answer

Dashboards that check uptime miss quality, so I'd trace every request: configuration version, retrieved documents, each model and tool call with tokens, latency and cost, and user signals, all linked. I'd redact personal data and keep full content for a sample and for errors. I'd score a sample of live traffic with checked LLM judges, sized so a real drop shows up in days, and score more right after releases. I'd keep error text out of model inputs, since a study found errors turned into confident false answers, and most silent failures were caught by a person reading output. Every flagged trace becomes a golden set case.

**Key terms and sources**

What to record for each LLM request and agent run, traces and spans, cost and latency by step, privacy and retention, sampling live traffic for quality scoring, silent failures, and turning traces into evaluation cases. · checked 7 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Pan et al., Measuring Agents in Production, ICML 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04123)

- [Wu, When Errors Become Narratives: silent failures in a production LLM agent runtime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14589)

- [OpenTelemetry, GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai)

- [Shankar et al., Who Validates the Validators?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12272)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Many recent papers are preprints, and provider policies change.
