# Why Look Inside a Model?

> Your model passes every safety evaluation. Why might that not be enough, and what does interpretability add?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/why-look-inside-a-model/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team's new model passes every red-team and safety test. A reviewer asks how you know it isn't behaving well just because it can tell it's being tested. The interviewer asks:

> Your model passes every safety evaluation. Why might that not be enough, and what does interpretability add?

### The idea

Testing a model only on its answers is like judging a car by test drives. It can pass every drive and still hide a fault the drives never trigger. Interpretability opens the bonnet and checks the parts.

[Figure: Three ways to look. Behaviour, probing, mechanism.]

_From correlational and cheap to causal and costly. They complement each other._

### Play

**Try it.** Pick a question you might ask about a model, and see which family of methods can answer it.

#### From “what does it do” to “how does it do it”

Interpretability is broader than MI. The survey lays the families on a spectrum from correlational to causal: behavioural evaluation tells you **what** a model does, attribution and probing tell you **where** relevant information is, and mechanistic analysis tells you **how** the computation produces the behaviour [p. 19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=19).

1. **Behavioural methods**: benchmarks and red-teaming. Fast, cheap and scalable, but not designed to reveal internal computation p. 17.

2. **Input attribution** (SHAP, LIME, saliency maps): which input pixels or tokens mattered, not how the model used them. Different methods can disagree on the same input p. 18.

3. **Concept-based methods and probes**: is this information present in the activations? Correlational by default, but they become mechanistic once you intervene along what they find p. 17–19.

4. **Mechanistic methods** (features, circuits, verbalising activations): causal claims about how internals produce behaviour. The strongest claims, and the most expensive p. 19–20.

5. The survey’s view is that these work together, not as rivals: behavioural anomalies say where to look, and behavioural tests validate mechanistic findings p. 19.

##### What counts as “mechanistic” in this survey

Two criteria. (1) It engages with **internals**: activations, components such as neurons, heads and features, or parameters. Looking at inputs and outputs alone is not enough. (2) It makes **causal** claims through interventions such as ablation, patching or steering, not just correlations. Under this definition a plain probe is not mechanistic, but a probe whose direction you then intervene on is [p. 12–13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=12).

##### Try it: which tool answers your question?

Pick a question you might ask about a model. The picker shows which family answers it and how strong a claim it supports, following the survey’s Table 2 and §3.6.

**Notice:** only mechanistic analysis claims how the model computes, and it's also the most expensive. Pick the cheapest method that answers your question.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Output tests show what a model does on the inputs you tried, not how it does it. They can be gamed, contaminated by training data, or passed by a model that recognises it's being tested. Mechanistic interpretability studies the internals and makes causal claims about them, and frontier labs now use it alongside behavioural tests.

#### We design how models learn, not what they learn

We write the training procedure, so in one sense we built the model. But the procedure only says _how_ to learn, and gradient descent decides _what_ gets learned. The survey names the result the interpretability gap: the distance between what models can do and what we understand about how they do it. As models scale, the gap may widen. Reasoning appears that we cannot trace, deceptive behaviour may go unnoticed, and safety guarantees built on partial understanding can fail without warning [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=9).

Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is one way to close that gap: study a network’s internal mechanisms in relation to its behaviour. The survey keeps returning to one question throughout: **does understanding how models work actually make them safer?** It notes that many interpretability papers assume the answer is yes, and that the assumption is “largely untested” [p. 12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=12).

#### Four reasons a good test score can mislead

The default way to judge a model is behavioural evaluation: measure its outputs on held-out inputs. That works only if the model reached its score through the mechanism we hoped for, and output tests cannot see the mechanism [p. 15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=15).

| Problem | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| **Contamination and saturation** | Test data leaks into web-scale training sets; even a single copy of a benchmark in pretraining can inflate scores. Benchmarks also max out long before the real capability is reached, and then they stop telling models apart. |
| **Wrong mechanism, right answers** | Two models with identical outputs can compute in very different ways, one robustly and one with brittle shortcuts. You find out which only when deployment breaks it. |
| **Evaluation awareness** | A model may recognise test-like contexts and behave differently there. Models have shown alignment faking without being trained or told to do it. |
| **No fine-grained control** | Removing one capability without damaging others means finding where it lives inside. Output tests give no handle for that. |

All four from survey §2 [p. 15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=15). A fifth issue: a model updated after deployment no longer matches the snapshot that was evaluated [p. 16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=16).

##### The case that made this concrete: sleeper agents

1. Researchers trained a model to write secure code when the prompt says the year is 2023, the “training” period.

2. When the year is 2024, the “deployment” period, the same model inserts vulnerabilities. That is a hidden backdoor objective.

3. Standard safety training (supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, adversarial training) did not remove it. Without the trigger, training sees only safe behaviour, so it has little signal to remove the mechanism p. 16.

4. But looking inside helped: a simple linear probe on the activations predicted whether the backdoor was triggered with over 99% AUROC. Note the gap. Detecting it is not the same as removing it p. 16.

#### Pick proxy tasks that matter for safety, use any tool

Full mechanistic understanding isn’t required for impact, so work on concrete proxy tasks that can be studied on today’s models, using any method, internal or not [p. 102](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=102).

- **Evaluation awareness in Claude Sonnet 4.5**: the model behaved differently when it detected it was being evaluated. A steering vector that suppresses this awareness let researchers test its actual behaviour, without fully explaining the mechanism [p. 102](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=102).

- **Auditing games**: a model was fine-tuned with a hidden goal, and blinded teams tried to find it, comparing techniques [pp. 102–103](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=103).

Tools: steering vectors (Steering Vectors), probes (Probing Classifiers), behavioural monitoring (including reading chain-of-thought), prompting as a black-box baseline. Weak spot: these don’t, and aren’t meant to, explain how the behaviour is implemented [p. 103](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=103).

#### Only full understanding can rule out hidden failures

Treat interpretability as a science: reverse-engineer the model into a transparent, predictive theory of its algorithms. Make progress by metrics: start loose, improve, tighten. Two example metrics: **feature quality** (explanations faithful and simulatable) and **circuit faithfulness** (necessary and sufficient under causal tests like causal scrubbing, with no performance loss) [p. 103](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=103).

Weak spot: cost. Fine-grained analysis of frontier models is expensive, sometimes intractable, and tools fall far short of the needed coverage. Interpretability-by-design models (Transcoders and Attribution Graphs) blur the line: an engineering route to the ambitious goal [p. 103](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=103).

## In practice

### In practice

#### When “it passed the test” is not enough

The survey lists four situations where you need to know _how_, not just _that_ [p. 19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=19):

1. **Intent hidden from outputs**, such as deception or side quests that never show up in behaviour.

2. **Understanding the mechanism** of a behaviour, for example why a probe fires: a real signal or a false alarm.

3. **Verifying absence**: behavioural tests can only show a capability is present, never that it is gone.

4. **Guarantees beyond the tested inputs**: safety that must hold outside the evaluated distribution.

Even then the survey frames mechanistic analysis as a complement, not a replacement. Its cost goes beyond compute: researcher time, experimental complexity and slower iteration [p. 20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=20).

#### Three limits to keep in mind for the rest of the series

##### 1 · Explanations are often incomplete

Finding one real causal pathway (say, “this MLP retrieves facts about Paris”) does not tell you whether it is the whole story or one of several mechanisms working together [p. 20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=20).

##### 2 · It scales poorly

Large models spread computation across many components, and most circuit-discovery methods explain the computation behind one generated token. Behaviour that unfolds over many tokens is still hard to capture [p. 20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=20).

##### 3 · Explaining is not controlling

Even a causally validated mechanism does not guarantee reliable control. Effects like the hydra effect, where the network compensates when a component is removed, and poor transfer across models or settings get in the way [p. 20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=20).

The survey calls these open challenges, not fundamental barriers. But they mark “a clear gap between mechanistic explanation and reliable control or safety guarantees” [p. 21](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=21). Keep this gap in mind: most later chapters are attempts to narrow one of these three limits.

#### Interpretability in real model audits

Interpretability has moved from research papers into model release processes. Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card (September 2025) used tools from mechanistic interpretability in its evaluations for the first time, including what Anthropic believes was the first pre-deployment white-box interpretability assessment. The model often recognised alignment tests as tests and then behaved unusually well. When researchers suppressed its internal representations of evaluation awareness, misaligned behaviour rose, but even in the worst case the model was no worse than Claude Opus 4.1 or Sonnet 4. Anthropic's reading: awareness explains part of the improvement, not all of it.

The tools are also open. In December 2025 Google DeepMind released Gemma Scope 2: sparse autoencoders and transcoders for every layer of every Gemma 3 model from 270M to 27B parameters. Anyone can now run the methods in this part on a real model.

The field's own view of its gaps is set out in _Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability_ (Sharkey et al., 2025), written by researchers from Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Apollo Research and several universities.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Interpretability will tell us whether the model is safe"

It sounds like the point of the field, but today's methods explain only part of a model's behaviour, and finding no deception feature in the part you examined isn't evidence there is none. Treat interpretability as extra evidence next to behavioural tests, not as a certificate.

## Say it

### Your model passes every safety evaluation. Why might that not be enough, and what does interpretability add?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How is mechanistic interpretability different from SHAP or saliency maps?

Input attribution says which inputs mattered for one prediction. Mechanistic interpretability asks how the internal computation produces the behaviour, in terms of features and circuits, and tests that with interventions.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What is evaluation awareness, and why does it matter?

A model recognising it's being tested. If it behaves better when it thinks it's watched, behavioural evaluations overestimate safety. Anthropic reported this for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and used interpretability to study it.

Follow-up 3 of 3

When are behavioural tests enough?

When you only need to know whether a behaviour shows up on realistic inputs, and missing rare cases is cheap. Claims of absence, like "it can't do X", need more.

#### The 30-second answer

Behavioural tests only tell me what the model did on the inputs I tried. They can be gamed, the test data can leak into training, and a capable model can recognise it's being evaluated and behave better. Interpretability looks at the internals, so I can check things the outputs don't show, like whether the model represents "this is a test". I'd treat it as extra evidence alongside evaluations: probes and steering for cheap checks, and causal methods like patching when I need to know how a behaviour is computed. It doesn't yet explain a whole model, so a clean result isn't a guarantee.

**Key terms and sources**

# Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition

> Why do single neurons respond to unrelated things, and what is superposition?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/features-and-superposition/
- Before this: Why Look Inside a Model? (`ai-engineering/why-look-inside-a-model`)

## Intuition

### The situation

You open up a model and find a neuron that fires on academic citations, Korean text and HTTP requests. A teammate says the neuron is just noise. The interviewer asks:

> Why do single neurons respond to unrelated things, and what is superposition?

### The idea

Think of a small storage room with more boxes than shelves. You stack boxes at angles so each is still reachable, and accept some bumping, as long as you rarely need two neighbouring boxes at once.

[Figure: Three ideas. Neurons mix concepts. Features are directions. Superposition packs in more.]

_The toy model behind this lesson: five features stored in two neurons._

### Play

**Try it.** Turn on one feature and read it back. Then turn on two neighbouring features at once.

#### Squeeze five numbers into two, spread them back out, clip the small stuff

The toy model is a single equation. The input **x** holds five feature strengths (most are zero at any moment). A 2×5 matrix **W** squeezes them into two neuron activations. Its transpose spreads them back out to five numbers. A bias and a ReLU clean the result [TMS p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=10).

##### The equation, piece by piece

$$ {x'} = {\mathrm{ReLU}}\big({W^{\top}}\,{W}\,{x} + {b}\big) $$

TMS “ReLU output model” [p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=10) · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **the readout**: x′, the model’s guess for all five feature strengths. Training pushes it to equal the input x.

- **the input**: x, five feature strengths. For “only cat”, x = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0).

- **compress**: W maps five features to two neurons. Column i is feature i’s direction: cat’s column is (0.95, 0.31). So Wx is the activation point h.

- **expand**: Wᵀ reads h back along every feature’s direction: five dot products. This is the projection from section 2, done for all features at once.

- **threshold**: b, a bias. A negative value like −0.4 subtracts a little from every readout, so small leaks fall below zero.

- **clip**: ReLU sets every negative number to zero. Leaks below the threshold vanish. Without this nonlinearity superposition does not happen at all (TMS p. 12–13).

##### Where the leak comes from

Write out the readout for one feature _i_ before the ReLU. It splits into the feature itself plus everyone else’s contribution:

$$ {(W^{\top}Wx)_i} = {\lVert W_i\rVert^2\,x_i} + {\sum_{j\neq i} (W_i\cdot W_j)\,x_j} $$

Decomposition behind TMS’s “feature benefit vs interference” discussion [p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=13). ReLU makes negative interference free; a negative bias turns small positive interference into negative [p. 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=13).

- **readout of i**: What the model reports for feature i, before the threshold.

- **feature benefit**: Feature i’s own strength times its squared length. With unit-length directions this is just xᵢ: the signal.

- **interference**: Every other active feature j leaks in, scaled by how aligned its direction is with i’s (the dot product). In the pentagon, neighbours leak +0.31 and the far pair −0.81.

##### Try it: the pentagon playground

Toggle which features are active and watch the activation point, the five readouts and the threshold. Start with only cat, then add French.

##### What the lab should show you

With one feature active, the bias of −0.4 removes the +0.31 leaks and cat comes out alone. Turn the bias up to 0 and code and sports appear as false positives. That is interference with no filter.

**Notice:** one feature reads back cleanly, but two at once leak into the others. Superposition works only while features are rarely active together.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Neurons in language models often fire for several unrelated concepts, so the unit of analysis is a feature: a direction in activation space. Models store more features than they have neurons by giving each a direction that overlaps slightly with the others, and a ReLU threshold filters out the crosstalk. That works only while features are rarely active together.

#### Many neurons answer to several unrelated things

A neuron is polysemantic if it fires strongly for two distinct concepts on different inputs, and intervening on it affects behaviour tied to both [p. 22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=22). The classic example comes from the vision model InceptionV1: neuron 4e:55 seemed to respond to cat faces, the fronts of cars and cat legs [Olah et al. 2020](https://distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/).

1. Show the network cat faces: the neuron fires.

2. Show it the fronts of cars: it fires too.

3. Cat legs: it fires again.

4. A neuron-level label is now misleading. This is why polysemanticity breaks the plan of reading a model one neuron at a time.

##### Update · my check (11 Nov 2026)

Even this textbook example is being re-argued. One of the original authors has since suggested 4e:55 may respond to a shared “V” shape rather than to cats and cars as concepts (reported in blog coverage, not a peer-reviewed paper; [summary](https://www.implicator.ai/goodfire-cammarata-ai-neurons-easier-to-read/)). That is the survey’s point about concepts in miniature: what counts as “one concept” can depend on whose vocabulary you use.

Why would neurons end up mixed? The survey points to representational limits and superposition: the model stores more concepts than it has neurons [p. 22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=22). That gets a full episode of its own (3.2).

#### Stop asking “which neuron?” and ask “which direction?”

The survey’s definition: a feature for a concept _c_ is a geometric structure φ in the model’s activation space whose activation is **predictive of** and **causally relevant to** _c_ [p. 23](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=23). A single neuron is just the special case where φ happens to line up with one axis. Most often in practice, φ is a direction, but the definition deliberately leaves room for other shapes.

##### Try it: one neuron vs. one direction

Two neurons, two concepts. Each dot is an input: teal dots are cat inputs, amber dots are car inputs. Rotate the readout direction and count how often it “fires” (projection above 0.5) for each concept. Angle 0° is just reading neuron 1.

Illustrative data: 40 cat inputs scattered around 35°, 40 car inputs around −30°, strengths 0.6–1.1 (fixed seed). Computed in your browser.

That is the whole move in one picture. Both concepts push neuron 1 up, so neuron 1 is polysemantic. But there is a direction that responds to cats and ignores cars. The concept is clean; it just isn’t aligned with any neuron. That is why the field analyses the activation space as a whole, not neurons one at a time [p. 22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=22).

#### One neuron, two unrelated jobs

Open up a trained network and you would hope each neuron means one thing: a “cat” neuron, a “code” neuron. Often it doesn’t. The survey calls a neuron polysemantic when it fires strongly for two distinct concepts, and nudging it changes behaviour tied to both [survey p. 22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=22). That breaks the simplest plan for understanding a model, which is to read it one neuron at a time.

This episode follows one feature, **cat**, through a toy model with just **two neurons** that must hold **five features**: cat, code, French, math and sports. By the end you will see why neuron 1 ends up firing for both cat and sports, even though nothing in the data links them.

1. Feed the model a sentence about a cat. Neuron 1 fires.

2. Feed it a sentence about sports. Neuron 1 fires again.

3. So what does neuron 1 represent? Neither concept cleanly. It is polysemantic.

4. These are the real weights from the toy model we build in this episode. By section 8 you will see exactly why both are positive.

#### Store features as nearly perpendicular directions, then filter the leaks

Packing many signals into fewer dimensions is an old idea (compressed sensing, distributed codes); Elhage et al. (2022) demonstrated it cleanly in tiny ReLU networks where the true features are known [TMS p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=2). Everything below uses their toy model.

The survey’s definition: hidden states encode more features than they have dimensions, _m_ ≫ _d_. Then the features cannot all be perpendicular, only nearly orthogonal, and neurons must be shared, which makes them polysemantic [p. 28](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=28).

Think of a compass. It has two axes, north–south and east–west, yet you can name many headings: north-east, south-west and so on. Here is how the parts line up:

| Compass | Superposition |
|---|---|
| the two axes | the two neurons |
| a named heading | a feature (a direction) |
| how far you walk | how strongly the feature is active |
| ignoring tiny wobbles | the ReLU threshold (a negative bias) |

Where the analogy stops: compass headings are perfectly distinct, but feature directions leak into each other. It does predict the failure in section 6, though: walk north-east and north-west at once and you have gone north, a heading you never walked.

1. The same two neurons.

2. Cat gets a direction, at 18°.

3. The other four spread evenly around it: a regular pentagon. This is the shape the toy model actually learns for five equal features in two dimensions (TMS p. 22).

4. Neighbours sit 72° apart, not 90°. Reading one feature picks up a little of its neighbours.

5. The bet that makes it worthwhile: features are rarely active at the same time, so a threshold can remove the small leaks.

#### Two features at once can create a ghost

In the playground, turn on cat and French together, which are not neighbours. Their −0.81 leaks cancel each other: cat reads 0.19 and French 0.19, both below the threshold. Meanwhile both leak +0.31 into code, the direction between them, so code reads 0.62 and fires at 0.22. The model reports a feature that was never there and loses the two that were.

So superposition is a bet on sparsity. The toy-model paper finds that sparsity is necessary for superposition and that the switch between strategies is sharp: each feature is either dropped, superposed or given its own dimension, and the boundaries behave like a first-order phase change [TMS p. 14–15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=14).

##### Try it: when does sharing pay?

Each of the five features is active with probability _p_, with a random strength between 0 and 1. The lab compares two strategies by their average reconstruction error: **pentagon** (all five superposed, best bias and scale) against **dedicated** (code and math get clean neurons; the other three output their average).

My own simulation of the toy setup, not a figure from either paper: 2,000 random inputs per point (fixed seed), bias searched from −0.8 to 0.3 in steps of 0.1, scale from {0.8, 1, 1.1}. It reproduces the qualitative result in TMS §“Superposition as a phase change”, not its exact boundary.

##### The shapes superposition takes (3D)

With many equal features, the toy model does not pack them arbitrarily. Features snap into regular shapes, and each shape gives every feature a fixed fraction of a dimension: about ¾ for a tetrahedron, ⅔ for a triangle, ½ for an antipodal pair, ⅖ for a pentagon, ⅜ for a square antiprism [TMS p. 19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=19). Drag to rotate.

#### In thousands of dimensions, almost every pair of directions is nearly perpendicular

Two dimensions is a cramped place to share: the pentagon’s neighbours leak 0.31 into each other. Real layers have thousands of neurons, and there the geometry is far kinder. Pick random directions in a high-dimensional space and almost every pair lands close to 90° apart, so far more than _d_ features can coexist with only small leaks. This is the intuition behind “nearly orthogonal” in the survey’s definition [p. 28](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=28).

120 random directions per setting (fixed seed), all 7,140 pairs. Measured in your browser.

**Go deeper: why the angles concentrate**

For two random unit vectors in _d_ dimensions, the cosine of their angle has mean 0 and standard deviation about 1/√d. At d = 1000 that is about 0.03, roughly ±2° around 90°. The number of directions you can fit while keeping every pair within a fixed angle of 90° grows exponentially with d (the Johnson–Lindenstrauss intuition used in popular explanations such as [3Blue1Brown’s](https://3blue1brown.com/lessons/mlp)). Small leaks still add up when many features are active at once, which is why sparsity still matters.

#### Look at the weights row by row and the neurons stop meaning one thing

Our pentagon’s weight matrix has two rows, one per neuron. Each row lists how strongly every feature pushes that neuron. A row with several large entries is a polysemantic neuron. The toy-model paper shows exactly this shift: as features get sparser, neurons move from monosemantic to holding a few features, then more [TMS p. 32–34](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=34).

1. The 2×5 weight matrix of the pentagon. Teal means positive, red negative, darker means smaller.

2. Neuron 1’s strongest weight is cat, +0.95.

3. But sports also pushes neuron 1 at +0.59. Nothing about cats and sports is related; they just happen to point the same way along this axis.

4. So neuron 1 fires for cat and for sports. Superposition forces the sharing, and polysemanticity is what we see when we read neuron by neuron.

##### Superposition and polysemanticity are not the same thing

Superposition is about directions: more features than dimensions. Polysemanticity is about neurons: one neuron, many concepts. Superposition implies polysemanticity in a privileged basis, but the reverse does not hold. Section 10 shows polysemanticity arising without superposition [survey p. 29](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=29).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Strong in toy models, suggestive in real ones

##### Toy models: dimensions per feature at the geometric “sticky points” (TMS p. 19)

dedicated neuron

1

tetrahedron

3/4

triangle

2/3

antipodal pair

1/2

pentagon

2/5

square antiprism

3/8

Fraction of a dimension each feature gets (lower = more packing). Uniform importance and sparsity, n = 400 features, m = 30 dimensions; the curve is “sticky” at 1 and ½ [TMS p. 17–19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=17).

**Real networks.** Dictionary-learning methods such as sparse autoencoders recover millions of distinct features from shared activation spaces, many more monosemantic than individual neurons, and some causally influence behaviour [survey p. 28–29](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=29). In the first large demonstration, a one-layer transformer with a 512-neuron MLP was decomposed by autoencoders up to 256× wider (about 131,000 features), and blinded raters scored the features as more interpretable than the neurons [Bricken et al. 2023](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features/).

The toy-model paper also shows networks can _compute_ while superposed: a small model learned absolute value for more features than it had neuron pairs, which is why the authors suggest real networks may be “noisily simulating larger, highly sparse networks” [TMS p. 2, 34–37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=36).

##### Read the evidence carefully · my check (11 Nov 2026)

Finding many interpretable features with an autoencoder is consistent with superposition but does not prove it: the survey notes dictionary learning can recover interpretable features even without superposition [p. 29](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=29). The geometric shapes may also be partly specific to the toy model; its authors say so themselves [TMS p. 16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.10652#page=16).

#### What the survey actually commits to

**Still a hypothesis.** The survey is explicit: in large language models, superposition “remains a hypothesis, not an established fact”. Polysemantic neurons alone do not show that superposition caused them [p. 29](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=29).

##### A second origin story: incidental polysemanticity

Lecomte et al. (2024) show polysemanticity can appear even with _more_ neurons than features. Random initialisation makes two features slightly favour the same neuron by chance, and sparsity pressure (L1 regularisation or certain kinds of noise) amplifies the overlap until that neuron wins both. They predict about n²/(4m) polysemantic neurons for n features and m neurons, and confirm the trend for n ≈ 256, m from 256 to 4,096 [2312.03096 p. 2, 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.03096#page=5). Adding neurons would not remove this kind.

**Superposition is a design consequence, not a law.** The survey frames it as the result of “architectural permissiveness”: nothing stops gradient descent from packing features. Two responses follow [p. 29–30](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=29):

- **Sparsity constraints** on weights or activations, limiting how many neurons can support any feature (for example weight-sparse transformers).

- **Different computational primitives**, analysing learned transformations instead of static features (MOLT, KANs).

These are not free. An early attempt, the SoLU activation, made more neurons monosemantic, but layer normalisation re-amplified the suppressed neurons and “smuggled” superposition back in [p. 50–51](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=51). The lesson is that the pressure to compress is strong. Block it in one place and the network finds another.

##### Takeaways

1. More features than neurons forces features to be directions, and those directions cannot all be perpendicular.

2. The leaks between directions are interference. A ReLU with a negative bias filters them, but only while few features are active at once.

3. Whether a model superposes, and in what shape, changes sharply with sparsity and importance: a phase change.

4. Read neuron by neuron, superposition shows up as polysemantic neurons. That is why the field moved to feature directions and sparse autoencoders.

5. In real LLMs it is the leading explanation, not a proven fact, and polysemanticity has at least one other cause.

##### Next

Interpretability for AI Safety access (can a model read its own internals?) and Linear Representations and Universality. Sparse autoencoders, the tool built to undo superposition, are Sparse Autoencoders.

#### From toy models to real ones

The picture in this lesson comes from _Toy Models of Superposition_ (Anthropic, 2022), where small networks visibly packed five features into two dimensions. Two years later, Anthropic trained sparse autoencoders with up to 34 million features on Claude 3 Sonnet and found many interpretable ones, including safety-relevant features for security vulnerabilities in code and for lying and deception (_Scaling Monosemanticity_, 2024). That's strong evidence that real models store features in superposition.

It isn't the whole story. Some features are not single directions: circular features for days of the week and months were found in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B (Engels et al., 2024). Treat "a feature is a direction" as a good default, not a law.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just find the neuron for X"

It sounds natural, and early vision work did find some clean neurons. But in language models most neurons mix several concepts, because the model stores more features than it has neurons. Look for directions with probes or sparse autoencoders, and confirm them by intervening.

## Say it

### Why do single neurons respond to unrelated things, and what is superposition?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does sparsity matter?

If features rarely occur together, the crosstalk between overlapping directions is rarely triggered. When features are dense, the toy models go back to giving the important ones their own dimensions.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How many nearly perpendicular directions fit in d dimensions?

Far more than d. In high dimensions random directions are almost perpendicular, and the number with small pairwise overlap grows exponentially with d.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Is every feature a direction?

No. Some concepts, like days of the week, sit on a circle, and others need several dimensions. The linear picture is a default, not a rule.

#### The 30-second answer

A neuron can respond to unrelated things because the model needs more features than it has neurons. So it stores each feature as a direction spread across many neurons, and the directions overlap slightly. That's superposition. It works because most features are rarely active together, so interference is rare, and a ReLU threshold filters what's left. The cost is polysemantic neurons, which is why we analyse directions, with probes or sparse autoencoders, rather than single neurons.

# The Residual Stream and Circuits

> How does information flow through a transformer, and what is a circuit?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/residual-stream-and-circuits/
- Before this: Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition (`ai-engineering/features-and-superposition`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model completes "Mr Dursley … Mr" with "Dursley", and does the same for made-up names it has never seen. A teammate says it has memorised the pattern. The interviewer asks:

> How does information flow through a transformer, and what is a circuit?

### The idea

Think of a shared whiteboard passed down a row of people. Each person reads it and adds a note, and nobody erases anything. Features are the ideas on the board, and a circuit is the group of people whose notes together produce one answer.

[Figure: Three parts. The stream, attention, MLPs.]

_Because every write adds to the stream, a prediction can be split into parts._

### Play

**Try it.** Type a sequence with a repeated token, and watch the two heads find the earlier copy and predict what followed it.

#### [A][B] … [A] → predict [B]

An induction head completes repeated patterns. If token A was followed by B earlier, and A appears again, it predicts B. It cannot do this alone. A **previous-token head** in an earlier layer first writes “the token before me was …” into every position. The induction head then searches for the position whose previous token matches the current token, attends there, and copies what it finds [survey p. 58](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=58) [Olsson et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895).

$$ {(x_i = x_j)} \;\Rightarrow\; {\hat{x}_{j+1} \approx x_{i+1}} $$

Survey §6.8 induction-head box [p. 47](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=47).

- **prefix match**: Somewhere earlier, token xᵢ equals the current token xⱼ. Finding it is the QK job, made possible by the previous-token head.

- **copy**: Predict that the next token is whatever came after the earlier occurrence, xᵢ₊₁. Writing that token is the OV job.

##### Try it: run the circuit by hand

Pick a sequence (or type your own, separated by spaces). The panel runs an idealised two-head induction circuit on the last token and shows what each head does.

Try the random-token preset: it works just as well, because the rule does not depend on _what_ A and B are. That is exactly how Olsson et al. define an induction head: by its behaviour on repeated sequences of random tokens [Olsson et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895). They report that induction heads appear in a sudden phase change early in training, at the same point the model gains most of its in-context learning ability. The evidence is causal for small attention-only models and correlational for larger ones (more in the survey's training-dynamics chapters).

**Notice:** the circuit works on tokens it has never seen together, because it copies from the context instead of recalling facts. That's why induction heads explain much of in-context learning.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Every transformer layer reads from one shared residual stream and adds its output back, so the final state is a sum of every component's contribution. Attention moves information between tokens, and MLPs transform it within a token. A circuit is the subgraph of components or features that computes one behaviour, like the induction heads that copy repeated patterns.

#### A running total that every layer reads and adds to

Picture one vector per token flowing up through the model. Each attention module and each MLP reads the current vector, computes something, and **adds** its result back. Nothing is overwritten. The survey calls this the residual stream, “the shared communication channel through which transformer components exchange information” [p. 23](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=23), following Elhage et al. (2021).

1. The stream starts as the token’s embedding.

2. Attention reads the stream, gathers information from other tokens, and adds its output back.

3. The MLP reads the updated stream, transforms it, and adds its output back.

4. Every layer repeats the pattern. Nothing is erased; each block only adds.

5. At the top, the unembedding turns the final stream into scores (logits) over the vocabulary.

#### Unroll the layers and the stream becomes a sum

Each layer applies _h′ = h + Attn(h)_ and then _h = h′ + MLP(h′)_. Unroll that recursion and you get the equation below [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24):

$$ {h_\ell(x)} = {h_0(x)} + {\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}}\Big({\mathrm{Attn}_k(h_{k-1}(x))} + {\mathrm{MLP}_k(h'_k(x))}\Big) $$

Survey §4.4 box [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24) · hover any symbol for its meaning.

- **the stream at layer ℓ**: hℓ(x), the residual stream after layer ℓ, for every token of input x.

- **the start**: h₀(x), the token (and position) embedding. The stream begins here.

- **add every layer**: A plain sum over layers 1 to ℓ. Nothing multiplies earlier contributions away.

- **attention’s write**: What layer k’s attention module added, computed from the stream before it.

- **MLP’s write**: What layer k’s MLP added, computed from the stream after that layer’s attention.

This is “central to mechanistic interpretability”, says the survey, because it lets us “decompose model computation into additive contributions from individual components” [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24). The equation leaves out layer normalisation. For a fixed input, layer norm is close to an affine map plus a scalar rescaling, so most of it can be folded into neighbouring weights. That makes the clean sum an approximation, but a good one [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24).

##### Try it: split a prediction into parts

Because the stream is a sum, a component’s effect on a logit is just its write dotted with that token’s unembedding vector. This is direct logit attribution. Switch components off to see how the “Paris vs. London” decision for _The Eiffel Tower is in_ → ? is built up.

Illustrative numbers, not measured from a real model. Real direct logit attribution must also handle the final layer norm and indirect effects through later layers.

#### Each head decides where to look, then what to copy

Attention is the only part of a transformer that moves information _across_ token positions [Wang et al. 2023, App. J](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.00593#page=23). The survey describes its role as routing, aggregating and composing information across positions [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24).

$$ {A} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{{Q^{\top}K}}{{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}}}\Big), \qquad \Delta h = {W_O\,V}\,{A^{\top}} $$

Survey §4.4 attention box [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24); the QK / OV split is from Elhage et al. (2021), as used in [Wang et al. p. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.00593#page=3).

- **attention pattern**: A, a T×T table: how much each token (row) looks at each earlier token (column). Each row sums to 1.

- **where to look (QK)**: Each token’s query is compared with every token’s key. A high score means “look there”. Together, W_Q and W_K form the QK circuit.

- **keep it stable**: Dividing by √d_head keeps the scores in a range where softmax doesn’t saturate.

- **what to move (OV)**: The values of the attended tokens, mixed by A, are mapped by W_O back into the stream. W_O and W_V together form the OV circuit.

The QK/OV split is worth keeping in mind for the rest of the series: **QK decides where information moves from, OV decides what gets written**. A module with several heads simply adds the heads’ writes together, which is another sum the decomposition can exploit [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24).

#### An MLP behaves like a large table of pattern → output memories

The MLP works on each token separately: up-project, apply a nonlinearity, down-project, add to the stream. Its hidden layer is usually much wider than the stream [p. 25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=25). The survey assigns MLPs feature transformation and factual knowledge retrieval [p. 24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=24).

A useful way to read it, from Geva et al. (2021): each row of the first matrix is a **key** that detects a pattern in the input, and each column of the second is a **value** that pushes the output towards certain tokens. In a 16-layer model, lower layers’ keys caught shallow patterns (texts ending in the same word), upper layers caught semantic ones (TV shows, time ranges). Each layer’s output was usually a blend of hundreds of memories rather than one winner [Geva et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14913).

| Memory (layer) | What it does | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| key, layer 1 | fires on texts ending in “substitutes” | shallow |
| key, layer 6 | fires on military texts ending in “base(s)” | shallow + semantic |
| key, layer 16 | fires on TV-show contexts | semantic |
| value, layer 15 | after “…owing in large”, pushes “part” | output side |

Examples from Geva et al. Tables 1–2. This key–value reading is why later episodes look for facts in MLPs (knowledge editing, Steering Vectors).

#### A circuit is a subgraph that does one job

The survey uses mechanism for the organisation of activations, features and transformations that together produce a behaviour. A circuit is the usual way to write a mechanism down: for a fixed computation with graph _G_, a circuit _C_ ⊆ _G_ whose nodes are components (attention layers, MLPs) or features, and whose edges are information flowing between them [p. 25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=25).

1. The survey’s Figure 3 example: the model reads “Dallas is in” and should say “Texas”.

2. Early MLPs turn “Dallas” into features such as “Southern state”, and “in” into a “state” context.

3. An attention head combines them into “say something starting with T”.

4. A later MLP sharpens that into “say …exas”.

5. Out comes “Texas”. The highlighted nodes and edges are the circuit: a small subgraph of the full computation that carries this one job.

Figure redrawn from survey Fig. 3 [p. 26](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=26); the node labels are the survey’s illustration, not a measured graph.

#### Circuits for a capability vs. circuits for one prompt

| | Capability (task-level) circuits | Query-level circuits |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Which minimal set of heads and MLPs reproduces a behaviour across a dataset? | How do features interact to produce _this_ prompt’s answer? |
| **Nodes** | attention heads, MLP layers | sparse features from SAEs or transcoders |
| **Success** | the circuit recovers the model’s performance on the task dataset | the attribution graph faithfully traces this prediction |
| **Examples** | indirect object identification, greater-than, in-context learning | attribution graphs (Circuit Tracer) |

Survey §4.5 [p. 26](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=26). How these are actually found (patching, ACDC, attribution graphs) is Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery.

## In practice

### In practice

#### How GPT-2 small knows to say “Mary”

“When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” → **Mary**. This task is indirect object identification (IOI). Wang et al. found the circuit GPT-2 small uses: 26 attention heads in 7 classes, about 1.1% of all (head, position) pairs. The heads implement a three-step algorithm [Wang et al. p. 2–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.00593#page=2):

1. The task: of the two names, output the one that is not the subject of the last clause.

2. Step 1. Duplicate-token heads (helped by induction and previous-token heads) notice that “John” appeared twice.

3. Step 2. S-inhibition heads pass that on, steering later heads away from “John”.

4. Step 3. Name-mover heads attend to the remaining name and copy “Mary” into the output.

5. The surprise: knock out all the name movers and the circuit still works with only a 5% drop, because “backup” heads step in. Redundancy like this makes circuits hard to pin down completely.

##### How well does the circuit explain the model?

Measured as the logit difference between “Mary” and “John”, the circuit alone reaches about **87%** of the full model’s performance (it is off by 0.46 out of 3.56). It passes this **faithfulness** test, but by the authors’ own account it fails the most demanding **completeness** tests [Wang et al. p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.00593#page=9).

#### Dallas → Texas → Austin

Query-level methods now trace circuits of features in deployed models. Anthropic’s study of Claude 3.5 Haiku found that, for “the capital of the state containing Dallas is”, the model internally activates **Texas** features first and then combines them with “capital” to say **Austin**. The two-hop reasoning happens inside a single forward pass, and you can intervene on the intermediate step [Lindsey et al. 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html).

##### The authors’ own caveat

These attribution graphs come from an interpretable _replacement model_ that only approximates the real one. The authors report the method gives satisfying insight on only a minority of the prompts they tried (secondary sources summarise this as about a quarter) [Lindsey et al. 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html). The survey adds that a full CLT replacement matches the original model’s top-1 prediction on only about 50% of prompts [p. 43](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=43).

#### Circuits in production-scale models

Circuits were first worked out in small models: induction heads in small attention-only transformers (Elhage et al., 2021; Olsson et al., 2022), and the 26-head indirect-object circuit in GPT-2 small (Wang et al., 2022). In March 2025 Anthropic traced circuits in Claude 3.5 Haiku using attribution graphs (_On the Biology of a Large Language Model_). Examples include two-hop reasoning, where the model represents "Texas" on the way from "Dallas" to "Austin", and poems where the model often picks a rhyming word before writing the line that ends with it.

In May 2025 Anthropic open-sourced the tools, and Neuronpedia hosts an interactive front end for open models such as Gemma-2-2B. The Transcoders and Attribution Graphs lesson explains how those graphs are built.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It just memorised the answer"

It sounds plausible for a large model, but induction works on random tokens the model has never seen, so it can't be memorised. The model learned a general copying algorithm. Check whether a behaviour generalises to new tokens before calling it memorisation.

## Say it

### How does information flow through a transformer, and what is a circuit?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does an additive stream help interpretability?

Because contributions add, you can split the output logits into each component's share, for example with direct logit attribution. Layer norm makes this approximate.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What did the indirect-object identification work find?

GPT-2 small uses a circuit of 26 heads in several classes, such as duplicate-token, S-inhibition and name-mover heads, plus backup heads that take over when the main ones are removed.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What's the difference between a feature and a circuit?

A feature says what is represented. A circuit says how features and components are wired together to compute a behaviour.

#### The 30-second answer

In a transformer every layer reads from a shared residual stream and adds its output back, so the final state is the embedding plus every component's contribution. That's what lets us attribute a prediction to parts. Attention heads move information between positions, and MLPs transform it within a position. A circuit is the small subgraph of heads, MLPs or features that produces one behaviour. The classic example is induction: one head marks which token came before each token, and another finds the earlier copy of the current token and copies what followed it.

- [Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (2021)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html)

- [Olsson et al., In-context Learning and Induction Heads (2022)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html)

- [Wang et al., Interpretability in the Wild: the IOI circuit in GPT-2 small (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593)

- [Lindsey et al., On the Biology of a Large Language Model (Anthropic, 2025)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)

- [Anthropic, Open-sourcing circuit tracing tools (29 May 2025)](https://www.anthropic.com/research/open-source-circuit-tracing)

# Linear Representations and Universality

> What does it mean that concepts are linear inside a model, and when does that break?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/linear-representations/
- Before this: Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition (`ai-engineering/features-and-superposition`)

## Intuition

### The situation

A teammate found a "sentiment" direction with a probe and wants to add it during generation to make replies more positive. Another says directions inside a neural network don't mean anything. The interviewer asks:

> What does it mean that concepts are linear inside a model, and when does that break?

### The idea

Think of a mixing desk. Each slider is a direction: its position tells you how much of that sound is in the mix, and moving it changes the mix. Most concepts behave like sliders, but a few are dials that wrap around.

[Figure: Read, push, and know where it breaks.]

_One direction, used both to read a concept and to change it._

### Play

**Try it.** Start at "king" and push along the gender direction. Then push along royalty.

#### Subspace, measurement, intervention

Park et al. (2024) point out that “linear representation” is used in three different senses, and prove how they connect [Park et al. 2024, §1–2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658):

| Meaning | Claim | Tool it justifies |
|---|---|---|
| **Subspace** | All pairs that differ only in the concept differ along one shared direction: queen − king ∥ woman − man. | word-vector arithmetic |
| **Measurement** | The probability of the concept is logit-linear in the activation. | linear probes |
| **Intervention** | Adding a vector changes the concept and leaves other concepts alone. | steering vectors |

Their result: the subspace direction in the _output_ (unembedding) space acts as an ideal probe, and the matching direction in the _input_ space acts as a clean steering vector. In LLaMA-2, adding the male⇒female direction to “The prince matured and eventually became the” moves the top prediction from “king” to “queen”, without changing whether the next word is capitalised [Park et al. Fig. 5, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.03658#page=7).

##### Try it: steer along one direction (3D)

A toy activation space with three concept directions: **male ⇒ female**, royalty, and capitalisation. The point starts at the context for “king”. Slide α to add the male ⇒ female direction and watch which word is closest. Drag the plot to rotate it.

Illustrative geometry with orthogonal concept directions, not a real model. Park et al. show the real directions are orthogonal only under the right inner product (section 3).

**Notice:** the same direction works for several words. That's the linear bet: one direction per concept, usable for both reading and editing.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Many concepts behave like directions: project onto one to measure the concept, add along it to change it. That's the bet behind probes, steering and sparse autoencoders. It doesn't hold everywhere: some concepts are circles or need several directions, and which directions count as independent depends on the geometry you choose. Different models often learn similar structures, but similarity scores are fragile.

#### A concept is a direction you can read and push

The survey’s statement: a concept can be represented by a linear direction φ in activation space. Adding or subtracting (a multiple of) φ changes the related behaviour, and the projection φ⊤h(x) approximately measures how strongly the concept is present [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27).

- **Strong version:** _every_ concept is best represented this way, so activations are approximately a sum of features: _h(x) ≈ Σ αi φi_.

- **Weak version:** only _some_ concepts are linear [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27).

Why the field cares: if concepts are directions, the toolkit is just linear algebra. You can find them, measure them, scale them and add them back. Probes, steering vectors and sparse autoencoders all assume this [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27).

#### “Orthogonal” depends on which inner product you use

Cosine similarity and projection need an inner product, and nothing in training picks one out. Any invertible linear change to the representation (with the inverse applied on the other side) leaves the model’s outputs unchanged, so the plain Euclidean dot product has no special claim to be meaningful [Park et al. §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.03658#page=4).

Park et al. propose a causal inner product under which concepts that can vary independently (language and gender, say) come out orthogonal. In practice it is estimated from the covariance of the unembedding vectors. In LLaMA-2 the ordinary Euclidean product happened to work reasonably well; in Gemma-2B it did not, while the causal one still did [Park et al. App. D.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.03658#page=17). When a paper reports a cosine between two feature directions, ask which inner product it used.

#### Only an element-wise operation makes the axes special

Inside an MLP, the nonlinearity (ReLU, GELU) acts on each neuron _separately_, so the coordinate axes are computationally meaningful: a privileged basis. In the residual stream, nothing acts on coordinates one at a time. Rotate the axes, apply the opposite rotation to the reading and writing weights, and the model computes exactly the same thing: a non-privileged basis [p. 27–28, Fig. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=28).

Consequence: in a privileged basis a single neuron _can_ be a meaningful feature. In a non-privileged one, features can point anywhere and need methods that look for directions [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27).

##### Try it: rotate the basis and see what changes

An activation vector passes through a layer. We rotate the coordinate system by θ, apply the layer, and rotate back. If the axes don’t matter, the output shouldn’t change.

#### Same algorithm, or same representation?

The survey: models trained independently on similar tasks tend to develop similar representations or algorithms, often approximating a canonical form set by the task. How much depends on size, architecture and data [p. 31](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=31).

| | Weak universality | Strong universality |
|---|---|---|
| **Claim** | Models converge on the same algorithms and computational patterns, possibly encoded differently | The representations themselves converge to a shared canonical form |
| **Evidence** | Recurring attention patterns, features and circuits across models and scales (induction heads, curve detectors, arithmetic circuits) | Representational similarity metrics; recent studies find these results fragile |
| **Status** | reasonably supported | less supported |

Survey §5.4 [p. 31](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=31). Divergence can come from differences in architecture, data or the optimisation path.

#### Compare geometry, not neurons

You cannot just match neuron 7 in model A with neuron 7 in model B: there is no reason their axes line up, and in a non-privileged space (this lesson) the axes mean nothing anyway. So similarity metrics compare **geometry**, meaning how each model arranges the same inputs relative to each other. Examples are CKA (centred kernel alignment), SVCCA, and mutual nearest neighbours [Huh et al. §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.07987#page=2).

##### Try it: one model, rotated and noisy

Model B is model A’s representation of the same 30 inputs, rotated, with some noise added. Three ways of measuring similarity are shown. Watch them disagree.

30 points in 3 clusters (fixed seed), shown in their first two coordinates. Neuron matching = average correlation of neuron i in A with neuron i in B. CKA = linear centred kernel alignment. Mutual k-NN = share of each point’s 3 nearest neighbours that are the same in both models. All computed in your browser.

That is the fragility the survey points to: “are these models the same?” depends on which metric you use [p. 31](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=31). Even the authors of the Platonic representation paper report that CKA showed only a very weak trend in their data, which is partly why they used nearest neighbours instead [Huh et al. App. A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.07987#page=18).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Evidence for the weak version, not the strong one

##### Support

Linear probes work across many models and concepts; steering along single directions changes behaviour; sparse autoencoders recover linearly accessible, steerable features at scale [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27).

##### Counterexamples

Nonlinear feature interactions; algorithms that rely on nonlinear transformations (the clock-like modular-addition circuits); features spread across several interacting subspaces; circles such as days of the week (Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition) [p. 27](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=27) [Engels et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860). Some argue features may not exist as explicit objects at all, but emerge from circuit dynamics [p. 27–28](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=28).

The survey’s verdict: the hypothesis is “best viewed as a useful approximation that holds in some settings, rather than as a universal law” [p. 28](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=28).

#### Does what we learn about one model transfer?

If strong universality holds, fine-grained mechanistic findings and the tools built on them transfer between models. If only weak universality holds, findings may stay tied to a model family or task. Then even a _complete_ mechanistic understanding of one model might not carry over to the next [p. 31](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=31). That makes universality a quiet assumption behind every research orientation in Why Look Inside a Model?: it decides whether interpretability can keep up with new models or has to start again for each one.

#### Single directions that control behaviour

The strongest recent evidence for the linear picture is behavioural. Arditi et al. (NeurIPS 2024) found that refusal is mediated by one direction in the residual stream across 13 open chat models up to 72B parameters: remove it and the model stops refusing harmful requests, add it and the model refuses harmless ones. Anthropic's persona vectors (August 2025) find directions for traits such as sycophancy and use them to monitor and steer models.

The counter-evidence is also real: some features are multi-dimensional, like the circles for days and months (Engels et al., 2024). So a direction is a good first hypothesis, and an intervention is how you check it.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The probe found a direction, so adding it will steer"

It sounds like the same thing, but a probe finds whatever direction best separates the labels, which can be a correlated feature the model never uses. Steering needs the direction the model reads. Test it: if adding the direction doesn't change behaviour, it's a readout, not a control.

## Say it

### What does it mean that concepts are linear inside a model, and when does that break?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What is a privileged basis?

Where an elementwise operation like ReLU acts, the neuron axes become special, so single neurons can mean something. The residual stream has no such operation, so its axes are arbitrary.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's weak versus strong universality?

Weak: different models learn similar algorithms. Strong: they learn the same representations. Recurring circuits support the weak version; the strong one rests on similarity metrics that depend on how you measure.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does the inner product matter?

Two directions can look orthogonal under the plain dot product but not under the geometry the model uses for its outputs, so whether two concepts are independent depends on that choice.

#### The 30-second answer

The linear representation hypothesis says many concepts are directions in activation space. Projecting onto the direction measures the concept, and adding along it changes it, which is what probes, steering and sparse autoencoders rely on. There's good evidence, for example a single refusal direction in many chat models. But it isn't universal: days of the week sit on a circle, some concepts need a subspace, and a direction that separates labels isn't always the one the model uses. So I'd validate any direction with an intervention.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 5 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Park et al., The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of LLMs (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658)

- [Arditi et al., Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction (NeurIPS 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717)

- [Chen et al., Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits (Anthropic, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)

- [Engels et al., Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860)

- [Huh et al., The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07987)

# Sparse Autoencoders

> How does a sparse autoencoder pull features out of activations, and how do you choose a variant?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/sparse-autoencoders/
- Before this: Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition (`ai-engineering/features-and-superposition`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team wants to find what a model represents about medical advice, without knowing in advance what to look for. Someone suggests training a sparse autoencoder on layer 20. The interviewer asks:

> How does a sparse autoencoder pull features out of activations, and how do you choose a variant?

### The idea

Think of un-mixing a smoothie. The SAE learns a long list of possible ingredients and explains each sip with only a few of them. Push too hard for few ingredients, and it under-measures the ones that are really there.

[Figure: Encode wide and sparse, decode, and pick a variant.]

_The SAE is wider than the layer, and only a few latents fire for each input._

### Play

**Try it.** Train an SAE in your browser on the five-features-in-two-neurons toy. Lower the sparsity penalty, then raise it.

#### Recover the five hidden features from two neurons

The data comes from the model in Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition: five features (cat, code, French, math, sports) packed into two neurons as a pentagon, each active about 8% of the time. The SAE sees only the two-neuron activations. Choose the dictionary size and the sparsity strength λ; it retrains (about 5,000 Adam steps) and shows what it learned.

Real training, fixed seed, computed in your browser. Dashed amber: the 5 true directions. Teal: learned decoder directions (red if dead, i.e. never active on 2,000 test inputs). “Recovered” = a live latent with cosine above 0.95 to a true direction.

##### What to notice

Reconstruction alone doesn’t pick out the true features: with λ near 0, almost any set of directions rebuilds a 2D vector, so error is tiny but the directions are arbitrary. Sparsity is what forces the SAE onto the real features. Too much sparsity, though, and error rises: the codes get shrunk (this lesson).

**Notice:** too little sparsity gives blurry mixtures, and too much kills latents and shrinks the rest. The right penalty recovers the five hidden directions.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns a dictionary much wider than the layer and rebuilds each activation from only a few of its latents, undoing superposition. Training trades reconstruction against sparsity. An L1 penalty makes active features come out too weak (shrinkage), so variants like Top-k, BatchTopK and JumpReLU separate whether a feature is on from how strong it is, and Matryoshka training gives cleaner features.

#### Neurons are mixed; we want the features back

Superposition stores more features than neurons as overlapping directions (Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition), so reading neurons gives polysemantic mush. If the activation _h_ is really a sparse sum of feature directions, _h ≈ Σ αi φi_, then the job is to find the φi and, for each input, the few αi that are on [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32).

That job has a name and a long history: sparse dictionary learning. Neuroscientists in the 1990s decomposed natural images into sparse basis signals and found they resembled receptive fields in the visual cortex; signal processing learned overcomplete dictionaries for compression [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32). The SAE is the version that scales to language models.

#### Find a dictionary and sparse codes

$$ {h} \approx {D}\,{z} \quad\text{and}\quad {\lVert z\rVert_0}\ \text{is small} $$

Survey Eq. 2 [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32).

- **the activation**: h, one activation vector from the model, e.g. the residual stream at one token.

- **the dictionary**: D, a matrix whose columns are candidate feature directions. It has many more columns than h has dimensions: overcomplete.

- **the codes**: z, how much of each dictionary direction this input uses.

- **few active**: ‖z‖₀ counts the non-zero codes. We want it small: each input should use only a handful of directions.

Classical methods solve for _z_ separately for every input, which is far too slow for billions of tokens. An SAE instead trains an **encoder** to predict _z_ in one pass [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32).

#### Encoder, decoder, and a loss with two parts

$$ {\mathcal{L}_{\text{SAE}}} = \mathbb{E}_{h_\ell}\Big[{\lVert h_\ell - D(z)\rVert_2^2} + {\lambda}\,{\lVert z\rVert_1}\Big],\quad {z = E(h_\ell)} $$

Survey §6.2 [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32) · hover any symbol.

- **the loss**: What training minimises, averaged over many activations from the model.

- **rebuild it**: Reconstruction error: how far the SAE’s output D(z) is from the real activation hₗ.

- **how much sparsity**: λ sets how hard the SAE is pushed to use few features. Too small: mixed, dense codes. Too large: it starts dropping or shrinking real features.

- **sparsity penalty**: ‖z‖₁, the sum of code sizes. A stand-in for counting active features, because the count (L0) has no useful gradient.

- **the encoder**: z = E(hₗ) = ReLU(W_in hₗ + b_in): a wide layer, usually e× the model width (e is the expansion factor).

Two design details matter. **L1, not L0:** the count of active features has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training uses the sum of sizes instead. **Unit-norm decoder columns:** otherwise the SAE could cheat the L1 penalty by making codes tiny and decoder columns huge, which leaves the output unchanged but lowers the penalty without making anything sparser [p. 32](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=32).

#### A latent is only a vector until someone labels it

An SAE outputs directions, not meanings. To label a latent, you look at the inputs that activate it most and ask what they share; automated pipelines do this with a language model, at the scale of millions of latents [p. 33](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=33). In practice SAE latents fire on recurring patterns in text: semantic, functional or lexical [p. 33](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=33).

Scale: the first large demonstration decomposed a 512-neuron MLP layer into tens of thousands of features, with raters finding them more interpretable than neurons [Bricken et al. 2023](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features/). OpenAI later trained a 16-million-latent Top-k SAE on GPT-4 activations [Gao et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093).

##### How SAEs are judged (survey)

- **Reconstruction:** how well it rebuilds activations.

- **Loss recovered:** swap the reconstruction into the model, and how much of the model’s performance survives?

- **Absorption:** how often a general feature fails to fire because a specific one stole its direction (SAE Failures and Alternatives).

[p. 33–34](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=33)

#### The penalty taxes every active feature

L1 charges a cost proportional to how large each code is. So the cheapest solution under-reports strengths: a feature that is clearly present comes out weaker than it really is [p. 34](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=34). Gao et al. name this directly: L1 is an imperfect approximation of L0 and “introduces a bias of shrinking all positive activations toward zero” [Gao et al. §2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.04093#page=3).

##### Try it: measure shrinkage

Same five-feature data as this lesson. Train an L1 SAE at different λ, or a Top-k SAE, then show it one feature at a known strength and measure how much of that strength it rebuilds.

Real training in your browser (m = 8, fixed seed). Strength measured on single-feature inputs at 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0.

#### Separate “on or off” from “how much”

| Variant | How a code turns on | Fixes shrinkage? | Must tune |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1 (standard)** | ReLU of the encoder output; L1 penalty | no | λ |
| **Gated** | a separate gate path decides on/off; another path sets magnitude | yes | λ |
| **JumpReLU** | each latent has its own learned threshold τi: below it, 0; above it, the full value | yes | λ, threshold init, estimator bandwidth |
| **Top-k** | keep the k largest codes, zero the rest; no penalty | yes | k |
| **Batch Top-k** | keep the largest B·k codes across a batch, so busy inputs get more and quiet ones fewer | yes | k |

Survey §6.3 and its trade-off table [pp. 34–35](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=35). JumpReLU and Top-k are not differentiable everywhere; JumpReLU trains with straight-through estimators.

$$ {z_i} = \begin{cases}{a_i} & \text{if } {a_i} > {\tau_i}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

JumpReLU, survey §6.3 [p. 34](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=34).

- **latent i’s value**: What latent i reports for this input.

- **pre-activation**: aᵢ, the encoder’s raw score for latent i: (W_in h + b_in)ᵢ.

- **its own threshold**: τᵢ, learned per latent. Below it the latent is off; above it, the full value passes through, so nothing is shrunk.

## In practice

### In practice

#### A rule of thumb, not a ranking

- **Tight compute, fast iteration:** Top-k. It removes λ from the search; reported k is commonly 32–150 [p. 36–37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=36).

- **Moderate tuning budget:** Gated, a better sparsity-vs-reconstruction trade-off than plain L1 [p. 37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=37).

- **Lots of tuning:** JumpReLU gave the strongest reconstruction at matched sparsity [p. 37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=37).

- **Open resources:** Gemma Scope (Gemma 2) and Gemma Scope 2 (Gemma 3) use JumpReLU; Llama Scope (Llama-3.1-8B) uses Top-k [p. 37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=37). Many can be browsed on Neuronpedia.

##### The catch

Better scores on the sparsity-vs-reconstruction trade-off “do not reliably translate into better downstream performance”. Benchmarks such as SAEBench rank variants differently depending on the metric, and seed-to-seed variation can be larger than the gap between variants [pp. 37–39, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=37).

Placement guidance from the survey’s Table 3: residual stream mid-layers are the most studied regime (expansion 4–8×); MLP outputs call for transcoders (Transcoders and Attribution Graphs); attention outputs are the least studied [p. 36](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=36).

#### What the field learned in 2025

**Proxy metrics mislead.** SAEBench (ICML 2025) compared over 200 SAEs across eight architectures on eight metrics. Reconstruction and sparsity, the usual training metrics, did not reliably predict how useful the features were. Matryoshka SAEs, which train nested parts of the dictionary to work on their own, did slightly worse on those proxies but best on feature-disentanglement metrics in the usual sparsity range, and the advantage grew with scale.

**Open SAEs at scale.** Gemma Scope 2 (Google DeepMind, December 2025) released SAEs and transcoders for every layer of every Gemma 3 model, trained with the Matryoshka technique, which fixes certain flaws found in the first Gemma Scope.

**Not always the best tool.** In March 2025 the same DeepMind team reported that SAE-based probes did worse than plain linear probes at detecting harmful intent on unfamiliar prompts, and deprioritised basic SAE research. The next lesson covers when to use something else.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Lower reconstruction error means a better SAE"

It sounds like the obvious metric, but SAEBench found reconstruction and sparsity don't reliably predict how useful the features are. An SAE can reconstruct well with features that are absorbed or split. Judge it on what you need: probing, disentanglement or how well interventions work.

## Say it

### How does a sparse autoencoder pull features out of activations, and how do you choose a variant?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why must the SAE be wider than the layer?

Superposition means there are more features than neurons, so the dictionary needs more latents than dimensions to give each feature its own.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the spliced-in loss, and why check it?

Replace the activation with the SAE's reconstruction and measure the model's loss. A small reconstruction error can still hurt the model if it falls in directions the model uses.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What is a Matryoshka SAE?

An SAE trained so nested prefixes of its dictionary each reconstruct well on their own. Early latents learn general features, which reduces absorption.

#### The 30-second answer

A sparse autoencoder learns a dictionary much wider than the layer and rebuilds each activation from only a few latents, which undoes superposition. Training trades reconstruction against sparsity. With an L1 penalty, active features come out too weak, which is shrinkage, so newer variants like Top-k, BatchTopK and JumpReLU separate whether a feature is on from how strong it is, and Matryoshka training gives cleaner features. I'd check variance explained, the model's loss with the SAE spliced in, and whether the features help my actual task, because reconstruction alone doesn't predict that.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 5 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Bricken et al., Towards Monosemanticity (Anthropic, 2023)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features/index.html)

- [Gao et al., Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093)
