# SAE Failures and Alternatives

> When do sparse autoencoders fail, and when should you use something simpler?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/sae-failures-and-alternatives/
- Before this: Sparse Autoencoders (`ai-engineering/sparse-autoencoders`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team trained an SAE and uses its "harmful request" latent as a classifier. On a new style of prompt it misses many cases, while a plain linear probe an intern trained catches them. The interviewer asks:

> When do sparse autoencoders fail, and when should you use something simpler?

### The idea

An SAE is like a filing system made by a new clerk with no instructions. It's great for discovering what's in the archive, but the clerk may file one topic under two names, or bury a general folder inside a specific one. If you already know you need the invoices, just search for invoices.

[Figure: Know the failure modes, and when to skip the SAE.]

_SAE features are one useful approximation, not the model's true parts._

### Play

**Try it.** Grow the dictionary, then change the random seed.

#### Latents that never fire, and features learned twice

Dead features never (or almost never) activate. In a poorly tuned SAE they can be 10–50% of the dictionary. Causes: bad initialisation, a sparsity penalty that is too strong too early, or common patterns being claimed first so the rest find no role. Fixes include resampling dead latents and warming up λ [p. 37](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=37). At scale, Gao et al. saw up to 90% dead latents without mitigations; with an encoder initialised as the decoder transpose and an auxiliary loss, their 16M-latent SAE had only 7% dead [Gao et al. §2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.04093#page=3).

Duplication: several latents encode the same concept. You can spot it by high cosine similarity between decoder columns, plus latents that fire together [p. 37–38](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=38).

##### Try it: too big a dictionary, and a different seed

The same 5-feature data again. Make the dictionary bigger than needed and train two SAEs that differ only in the random seed. Dead latents, duplicates and seed-dependence all show up.

Real training (λ = 0.3, run A seed 1). “Shared” = live latents of run A with a live latent in run B at cosine above 0.95. Dashed amber: true features.

**Notice:** a bigger dictionary wastes latents and repeats features, and a new seed gives a different set. Treat SAE features as an approximation, and test the ones you rely on.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

SAEs can waste latents that never fire, learn the same feature twice, let a specific feature quietly take over a general one's job (absorption), and give different answers with a new random seed. When you already know the concept and have labels, a supervised direction such as a linear probe or a difference of means usually works better. SAEs earn their place in open-ended discovery.

#### When a specific feature steals a general one’s job

1. In Gemma Scope, a latent seems to track “starts with S”: it fires on snake, soccer, steam.

2. But it silently fails on “short”.

3. Instead, a token-specific “short” latent fires and carries a small piece of the “starts with S” direction. It has absorbed the general feature.

4. Why: “short” always comes with “starts with S”. Firing one latent instead of two is sparser and rebuilds the same thing, so the sparsity penalty rewards absorption.

Example and mechanism from Chanin et al. (NeurIPS 2025), [arXiv 2409.14507](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507): absorption appeared in every LLM SAE they tested, and was worse for wider and sparser SAEs. The survey describes how to detect it: compare the latent with a linear probe for the same concept [p. 39](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=39).

Feature splitting is the related, sometimes harmless case: as the dictionary grows, one feature splits into finer ones. Helpful when “bank” splits into “investment bank” and “river bank”; less useful when the result is just a lexical “the token bank” detector [p. 39](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=39).

##### Why absorption matters for safety

A latent that looks like a clean “deception” or “bias” detector can have arbitrary holes in its recall. Never use a single SAE latent as a monitor without measuring its recall against a probe or labelled data.

#### Different seeds, different dictionaries

SAEs with the same architecture and data but different random seeds can learn substantially different dictionaries. Frequent, clear features tend to be stable; rare or context-specific ones vary. Often **fewer than 50%** of features are shared across seeds. So report seed stability alongside reconstruction [p. 39](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=39) [Paulo & Belrose](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615).

The deeper issue is identifiability. If activations really are _h = D*z* + ε_, does training recover the true D* (up to reordering and rescaling)? Classical theory says yes when dictionary elements are close to orthogonal (low coherence). In language models, high coherence is likely unavoidable, so several different sparse decompositions can fit equally well [p. 40](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=40). One proposed fix is to fine-tune the model together with an SAE whose decoder is forced to be orthogonal, which imposes low coherence by construction [p. 40](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=40).

##### Three tests before trusting an SAE feature (survey)

- **Necessity:** ablate it; does the concept disappear from the output?

- **Sufficiency:** activate only it; does the concept appear?

- **Specificity:** does its effect match only its concept?

[p. 40](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=40)

#### PCA finds orthogonal directions of high variance, and superposition isn’t that

PCA finds an orthonormal basis ordered by explained variance. It is fast and stable, but its assumptions clash with superposition: it can only return as many directions as there are dimensions, they must be perpendicular, and variance is not the same as meaning [p. 49](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=49).

Same data as Sparse Autoencoders. PCA via the 2×2 covariance matrix; a PCA direction counts as matching a feature at |cosine| above 0.95. Computed in your browser.

That matches large-scale results: on the AxBench benchmark, PCA came last among representation methods for detecting concepts (mean AUROC 0.65) [Wu et al. Table 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.17148#page=7). The survey notes PCA can still beat SAEs in some localisation settings [p. 49](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=49).

#### The alternatives

| Method | Assumes | Good at | Weak at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SAE** | sparse, linear features | open-ended discovery; fast inference | hyperparameters; identifiability |
| **NMF / semi-NMF** | non-negative, additive parts | parts-based reading; uniqueness guarantees | activations can be negative; little sparsity |
| **PCA** | variance = features | closed form; a baseline | orthogonal, at most d directions |
| **ICA** | independent sources, as many as dimensions | guarantees when assumptions hold | overcomplete case; dependent features |
| **Supervised (probe, DAS, SMDS)** | labelled concepts | targeted concepts | needs labels; discovers nothing new |
| **K-SVD** | sparse, linear features | solves sparse coding directly; a baseline | slow; no encoder |

Survey Table 6 [p. 48](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=48). Recent updates: semi-NMF matched SAEs on small-scale evaluations; ICA reached SAE-level performance once implemented for this scale (Liu & Han 2026), so whether ICA is just a baseline is now open [p. 49](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=49). Classical dictionary learning can still produce better dictionaries; the SAE’s main advantage is speed [p. 50](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=50).

## In practice

### In practice

#### A difference of means can beat a 16k-latent SAE

AxBench compared methods on 500 concepts in Gemma-2 models [Wu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17148):

##### Concept detection, mean AUROC (higher is better)

difference of means

0.942

linear probe

0.940

prompting an LLM judge

0.929

SAE (feature chosen with labels)

0.917

SAE (feature by its label)

0.695

PCA

0.652

Average over Gemma-2-2B and 9B, two layers each [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.17148#page=7). For _steering_, prompting beat every representation method, and difference of means beat SAEs [Table 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.17148#page=8).

The survey draws the same line: when labelled data exists, supervised directions often outperform SAEs at detection and steering, and they don’t need a dictionary size or sparsity penalty. But they need labels for every concept and cannot find anything you didn’t already name [p. 50](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=50).

#### Recommendations

1. **Report failure metrics**: dead-feature percentage, duplication rate, stability across seeds, not just reconstruction.

2. **Validate causally**: necessity, sufficiency, specificity via ablation or steering.

3. **Compare with baselines**, especially for safety-critical use.

4. **Try several variants**: findings that hold across Gated, Top-k and JumpReLU are stronger evidence.

5. **Acknowledge identifiability limits**: call SAE features “one valid approximate decomposition”, not “the true features”.

6. **For known concepts, consider supervised methods** (probes, DAS), which can be more reliable (this lesson).

[pp. 40–41](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=40)

##### Next · 4.4

Alternatives to SAEs, and when a simple supervised direction beats them.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §6.5, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 37–41.

- Chanin et al. (2025). _A is for Absorption._ NeurIPS 2025, [arXiv 2409.14507](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507).

- Gao et al. (2025). [arXiv 2406.04093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093) (dead latents).

- Paulo & Belrose. _Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features._ [arXiv 2501.16615](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615).

#### Negative results, and where SAEs still help

Two 2025 results changed how practitioners use SAEs. Kantamneni et al. (February 2025) found that, averaged over 113 datasets, probes built on SAE latents did not beat logistic-regression-based baselines in any of the four hard settings they tested, though they occasionally won on individual datasets. In March 2025 Google DeepMind's interpretability team reported that SAE-based probes lagged linear probes at detecting harmful intent when the test prompts differed from the training ones, and deprioritised basic SAE research.

SAEs remain useful for discovery, when you don't know what to look for. OpenAI used SAE-based model diffing in June 2025 to find a "misaligned persona" feature that explained why narrow fine-tuning made GPT-4o misbehave broadly (see Model Diffing).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The SAE has a 'harmful' latent, so use it as the detector"

It sounds efficient, but absorption can leave holes: some harmful cases fire a more specific latent instead. When you know the concept and have labels, a linear probe is cheaper and, in 2025 tests, generalised better. Use the SAE to discover candidates, then build the detector with supervision.

## Say it

### When do sparse autoencoders fail, and when should you use something simpler?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you detect absorption?

Take a general feature, like "starts with S", and check its recall on tokens where a specific feature, like "snake", fires. If the general one goes silent there, it was absorbed.

Follow-up 2 of 3

When would you pick PCA over an SAE?

When you want the main directions of variance quickly and deterministically, for example to visualise or remove a dominant direction. PCA won't separate features in superposition.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why did DeepMind deprioritise SAE research?

In their tests, SAE-based probes did worse than plain linear probes at detecting harmful intent on unfamiliar prompts, the downstream task they cared about.

#### The 30-second answer

SAEs fail in known ways: latents that never fire, duplicate features, absorption where a specific latent takes a general one's job, and different results from different seeds, partly because overlapping features can be decomposed many ways. So I'd treat SAE features as an approximation and test the ones I rely on. If I know the concept and have labels, I'd use a linear probe or a difference-of-means direction, which in recent tests beat SAE-based probes on unfamiliar data. SAEs are best for discovering what I didn't know to look for.

# Transcoders and Attribution Graphs

> How do transcoders make circuits readable, and what does an attribution graph show?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/transcoders-and-attribution-graphs/
- Before this: Sparse Autoencoders (`ai-engineering/sparse-autoencoders`), The Residual Stream and Circuits (`ai-engineering/residual-stream-and-circuits`)

## Intuition

### The situation

You want to explain why a model answers "Austin" to "the capital of the state containing Dallas is". Circuits made of attention heads and MLPs are hard to read. The interviewer asks:

> How do transcoders make circuits readable, and what does an attribution graph show?

### The idea

Think of rewiring a machine with labelled replacement parts. If each part does the same job as the original but has readable labels, you can trace which part feeds which, as long as you remember the replacements aren't perfect.

[Figure: A readable part, a readable model, a graph per prompt.]

_Attribution graphs are built on a replacement model, not the original._

### Play

**Try it.** Change the input, and watch which feature-to-feature connections light up.

#### Learn a wide, sparse MLP that copies the real one

$$ \mathcal{L} = \big\lVert {h_\ell^{\text{out}}} - {(W_{\text{out}}z + b_{\text{out}})}\big\rVert_2^2 + {\lambda}\lVert z\rVert_1,\quad {z = \sigma(W_{\text{in}}h_\ell^{\text{in}} + b_{\text{in}})} $$

Survey §6.6.1 [p. 41](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=41).

- **the real MLP’s output**: What the model’s MLP at layer ℓ actually produced.

- **sparse rebuild**: The transcoder’s output: a few decoder directions, weighted by feature activations z.

- **sparsity**: The same L1 trade-off as an SAE.

- **features from the input**: z = σ(W_in hₗ^in + b_in): features are computed from the MLP’s input, but judged by how well they predict its output.

The only change from an SAE is the target: **the MLP’s output**, not the input itself. In tests on GPT-2 small, Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B, transcoders were at least as good as SAEs on sparsity, faithfulness and human interpretability [Dunefsky et al. §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11944#page=7).

##### The payoff: wiring you can read from weights

Because a transcoder feature’s output is linear in its activation, the effect of an earlier feature _i_ on a later feature _i′_ factors into two parts [Dunefsky et al. Eq. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11944#page=4):

$$ \text{effect}_{i\to i'} = {z_i(x)}\cdot{\big(f^{(\ell,i)}_{\text{dec}}\cdot f^{(\ell',i')}_{\text{enc}}\big)} $$

- **input-dependent**: How active the earlier feature is on this input. The only part that changes from input to input.

- **input-invariant**: Earlier feature’s decoder vector · later feature’s encoder vector: a fixed number, computed from weights alone. It describes the wiring for every input.

##### Try it: fixed wiring, changing inputs

Three earlier transcoder features and three later ones, with a fixed table of connections (decoder · encoder). Choose the input token. Only the earlier activations change; the wiring stays the same.

Illustrative weights and labels, inspired by the Polish-surname transcoder feature in Dunefsky et al. (§3.2.4); not values from a real model.

**Notice:** the weights between features stay fixed, and only the activations change with the input. That's what makes the wiring readable straight from the weights.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A transcoder replaces an MLP with a sparse, readable stand-in that maps the MLP's input to its output, so feature-to-feature wiring can be read from the weights. A cross-layer transcoder lets each feature write to every later layer, giving a replacement model for all the MLPs. An attribution graph uses it for one prompt: features are nodes, direct effects are edges, and the graph is pruned to what matters.

#### An SAE on each side of an MLP doesn’t tell you how the MLP connects them

Suppose you have SAE features before an MLP and after it, and want to know which input features cause which output features. The MLP sits in between, with thousands of neurons each applying its own nonlinearity. Gradient or patching attributions through it depend on the specific input, so you only learn about one example at a time, never the MLP’s general behaviour [Dunefsky et al. §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11944#page=4). The survey puts it simply: SAEs “do not explain the nonlinear transformations … themselves that produce the activations” [p. 41](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=41).

#### One feature, many destinations

A cross-layer transcoder (CLT) reads features from the residual stream at layer ℓ, and each feature has a separate decoder vector into the MLP output of _every_ later layer. The reconstructed MLP output at layer ℓ′ sums contributions from all earlier layers’ features [p. 42](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=42):

$$ {\hat h^{\text{out}}_{\ell'}} = {\sum_{\ell=1}^{\ell'}}\sum_j {W^{\ell\to\ell'}_{\text{out},j}}\,{z^j_\ell} $$

Survey §6.6.2 [p. 42](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=42).

- **rebuilt MLP output**: The CLT’s stand-in for the MLP output at layer ℓ′.

- **from every earlier layer**: Sum over all layers ℓ up to and including ℓ′: features read early can still write late.

- **layer-pair decoder**: Feature j’s own decoder vector for the jump from layer ℓ to layer ℓ′.

- **feature activation**: Feature j read at layer ℓ (a JumpReLU of the residual stream).

Why this helps: a feature doesn’t need to be re-encoded at every layer, so circuits get simpler, and with MLPs replaced the rest of the computation becomes roughly linear. That makes clean attribution possible [p. 44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=44).

1. Start from the original model: attention and MLP blocks.

2. Replace every MLP with the CLT’s features, which read the stream and write to the current and all later layers.

3. Keep attention, but freeze its patterns (and the normalisation statistics) at the values from the original forward pass. The CLT does not model attention at all.

4. Add an error term at each layer for whatever the CLT failed to rebuild. With these, the replacement exactly reproduces the original on this one prompt.

5. Remove the crutches and swap the CLT in for real, and the replacement model’s top prediction matches the original on only about 50% of prompts from the Pile, in an 18-layer model survey p. 43.

#### Encode all layers together, decode each separately

$$ {z} = \mathrm{ReLU}\Big({\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} W^{\ell}_{\text{in}}h_\ell} + b_{\text{in}}\Big),\qquad {\hat h_\ell = W^{\ell}_{\text{out}}z + b^{\ell}_{\text{out}}} $$

Survey §6.6.3 [p. 45](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=45). The sparsity penalty weights each feature by the sum of its decoder norms across layers.

- **one shared code**: z, a single set of sparse feature activations for the whole stack.

- **read every layer**: Each layer’s activation hₗ gets its own encoder W_in^ℓ, and their contributions are summed before the ReLU.

- **rebuild each layer**: Each layer has its own decoder, so one feature can have a different strength, or none, at each depth.

- **Causal crosscoders** read only layers up to the current one, respecting the forward pass.

- **Acausal crosscoders** read any layer, which is useful for describing feature relationships across the whole model after the fact [p. 46](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=46).

##### Try it: a feature’s footprint across depth

For each crosscoder feature you can plot how strongly it is written at each layer, i.e. its decoder norm per layer. Different shapes tell different stories.

Illustrative profiles, not measured. The same idea applied across two models instead of two layers is used for model diffing (Steering Vectors).

#### Simpler circuits, and comparing models

Because one latent can stand for a feature at every layer, crosscoders remove duplicate copies that clutter circuits. Features can “jump” across intervening layers that just pass them along, and you can see which features persist unchanged and which get actively transformed [p. 46](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=46).

Train one crosscoder on two models (say a base model and its fine-tuned version), and features whose decoder strength is large in only one model are candidates for what fine-tuning added [p. 45](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=45).

##### False positives

Crosscoders trained with an L1 penalty can falsely report features as unique to one model. BatchTopK helps but doesn’t eliminate it: a feature whose direction merely _rotated_ during fine-tuning can look new. Treat “model-exclusive” features as hypotheses to test [p. 79](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=79).

#### A feature’s direct pull on a later feature

$$ {A_{\phi_s\to\phi_t}} = \sum_{\ell_s\le\ell<\ell_t}{z^s_{\ell_s}}\,{(v_{\text{in},\phi_t})^{\top}}\,{J_{c_s,\ell\to c_t,\ell_t}}\,{v^{\ell}_{\text{out},\phi_s}} $$

Survey §7.2, Circuit Tracer box [pp. 55–57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=56).

- **edge weight**: How much source feature s directly raises target feature t on this prompt.

- **how active s is**: The source feature’s activation: the only input-dependent factor besides the Jacobian.

- **what t reads**: The target feature’s encoder direction.

- **the path between**: The Jacobian from a write at layer ℓ, position cₛ to the MLP input at layer ℓₜ, position cₜ, through the residual stream and attention, with attention patterns and normalisation frozen.

- **what s writes**: The source feature’s decoder vector into layer ℓ. Summed over every layer it writes to.

Two differences from EAP. The **nodes** are fine-grained features with natural-language labels, not whole heads or MLPs. The **edges** are direct, input-specific influences: gradients through intermediate MLPs are stopped, so each edge counts only the direct feature-to-feature effect, and no clean/corrupted pair is needed [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57). The graph’s nodes also include token embeddings, error nodes (what the CLT failed to rebuild) and output logits [Ameisen et al.](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html).

#### Keep the strong edges, lose some of the story

A toy attribution graph for “the capital of the state containing Dallas is” → Austin, with the two-hop path (Dallas → Texas → Austin) plus a crowd of weak side features. Raise the threshold to prune weak edges, then drop features that no longer connect to the output.

Illustrative graph and weights (not from a real model). Influence = sum over all paths from the tokens to the output of the product of edge weights, computed in your browser.

Real graphs have many more nodes and edges, so they must be pruned, clustered or condensed before anyone can read them [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57). Platforms such as Neuronpedia host interactive versions.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Parameters grow with depth squared

With L layers, model width d and expansion factor e, a full CLT has L encoders and L(L+1)/2 layer-pair decoders. Ignoring biases, that is _N = (e·d²/2)(L² + 3L)_ [p. 44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=44). Training the CLTs for Gemma-2-9B took about 3,844 H100 GPU-hours [p. 44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=44).

Survey formula (§6.6.2, Fig. 8), computed in your browser. Memory assumes 2 bytes per parameter.

##### Fidelity caveats the survey lists

- Results come mainly from small models, on short sequences from the CLT’s own training data; behaviour under distribution shift isn’t well tested.

- The headline metric is top-1 agreement; softer metrics (top-5, KL divergence) may tell a different story.

- Exact matching requires frozen attention, cached normalisation and per-layer error terms.

- Fidelity is higher in middle layers, and on factual recall and syntax than on reasoning or arithmetic.

[pp. 43–44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=43)

This scarcity shows in practice: the survey counts only a handful of downstream CLT applications so far (a greater-than mechanism study, an open-source extension, multilingual analysis) [p. 44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=44). CLTs come back in Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery as the engine of attribution graphs.

#### Caveats

##### Limits

- It explains the **replacement model**. CLTs only approximate the MLPs (a full replacement matches the top-1 prediction on about 50% of prompts in an 18-layer model), so the graph may cover only part of the real mechanism [pp. 43, 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=43).

- **Attention is frozen**: the graph shows what flows through attention, not why attention looked where it did [p. 44](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=44).

- The authors report satisfying insight on only a minority of prompts tried (secondary summaries say about a quarter) [Lindsey et al. 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html).

What it gives in return: readable, prompt-specific mechanisms such as the two-hop Dallas → Texas → Austin reasoning in Claude 3.5 Haiku (The Residual Stream and Circuits), where intervening on the intermediate “Texas” features changes the answer [Lindsey et al. 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html).

##### Next · 6.4

Is a discovered circuit actually causal, and how much does it explain?

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §7.2, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 55–57.

- Ameisen et al. (2025). _Circuit Tracing._ [transformer-circuits.pub](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html).

- Lindsey et al. (2025). _On the Biology of a Large Language Model._ [transformer-circuits.pub](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html).

#### Open tools anyone can use

Anthropic introduced attribution graphs with cross-layer transcoders in March 2025 and used them on Claude 3.5 Haiku. On 29 May 2025 it open-sourced the `circuit-tracer` library, which supports popular open-weights models (Anthropic used it on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B), with an interactive front end on Neuronpedia. By mid-June 2025, Neuronpedia reported almost 5,000 graphs generated by users.

Google DeepMind's Gemma Scope 2 (December 2025) added skip-transcoders and cross-layer transcoders for every Gemma 3 model, so you can trace multi-step computations in models up to 27B parameters.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The attribution graph shows how the model works"

It sounds like a full explanation, but the graph describes a replacement model, not the original. Attention is frozen, error nodes hold what the transcoders miss, and it covers one prompt. Confirm the key steps by intervening on the real model, as the Dallas → Austin example did.

## Say it

### How do transcoders make circuits readable, and what does an attribution graph show?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why are transcoder circuits easier to read than SAE circuits?

Between SAEs on two layers, the connection passes through the MLP's nonlinearity and depends on the input. Transcoder features connect through fixed weights.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What are error nodes?

The part of each MLP's output the transcoder fails to reconstruct. They keep the graph adding up, but they're unexplained computation.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What does a crosscoder add?

One dictionary across layers removes duplicate copies of a feature at every depth, and one across two models supports model diffing.

#### The 30-second answer

An SAE describes what a layer contains, but a transcoder describes what an MLP does: it maps the MLP's input to its output through sparse, readable features, so feature-to-feature wiring can be read from the weights. A cross-layer transcoder lets each feature write to every later layer, which gives a replacement model for all the MLPs. An attribution graph uses that for one prompt: nodes are features, and edges are direct effects through the frozen residual stream and attention. It's rich but approximate, so I'd prune it and check the main paths with interventions on the real model.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 7 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Lindsey et al., Sparse Crosscoders (Anthropic, 2024)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/index.html)

- [Ameisen et al., Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models (Anthropic, 2025)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html)

- [Lindsey et al., On the Biology of a Large Language Model (Anthropic, 2025)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)

# Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery

> How do you test whether a component causes a behaviour, and how do you scale that to a whole model?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/activation-patching/
- Before this: The Residual Stream and Circuits (`ai-engineering/residual-stream-and-circuits`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your team thinks a few attention heads make the model pick the right name in "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to". Zero-ablating the main head barely changes the output. The interviewer asks:

> How do you test whether a component causes a behaviour, and how do you scale that to a whole model?

### The idea

Think of finding which wire powers one light in a house. Swap one wire's signal for the one from a house where the light is off, and see if the light changes. A backup wire can hide an important one, so a small change doesn't mean the wire is useless.

[Figure: One patch, then automate it.]

_Patching is the causal test that most circuit methods are built on._

### Play

**Try it.** Patch each component of the toy circuit one at a time. Then knock out the main name mover.

#### Patch each part of a small circuit with a built-in backup

A toy circuit with the same shape as GPT-2’s name-picking circuit (The Residual Stream and Circuits): a **duplicate detector** (D) feeds an **inhibition** step (S), which drives a **name mover** (N) that writes the answer. A **backup** mover (B) only acts when N is weaker than expected, and a **negative** mover (Neg) pushes slightly the other way. Clean logit difference is 1.8, corrupted is 0.2.

Toy equations: D ∈ {1 clean, 0 corrupt}; S = D; N = 2S; B = max(0, 1.6S − 0.8N); Neg = −0.4S; output = N + B + Neg + 0.2. Effect = (clean − patched) / (clean − corrupted).

This is what Wang et al. saw in GPT-2: knocking out all the name-mover heads cost only about 5% of performance, because backup heads took over [Wang et al. §3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.00593#page=9). The survey lists this “hydra effect” among the reasons that explaining is not the same as controlling [p. 20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=20).

**Notice:** knocking out the main head barely hurts, because a backup head takes over. Testing one component at a time can make an important one look unimportant.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Activation patching runs a model on a clean input, swaps in one component's value from a minimally corrupted input, and measures how the output changes. Path patching does the same for one connection. The choice of corruption and metric changes the answer, and backup components can hide importance. ACDC automates patching edge by edge, and edge attribution patching estimates every edge at once with gradients.

#### Swap one part, see what breaks

1. Run the model on a clean input that shows the behaviour, and remember every activation.

2. Run it on a corrupted input with the key information changed, and remember those activations too.

3. Run the clean input again, but overwrite one component’s activation with its corrupted value. Everything downstream recomputes normally.

4. Measure the change in a scalar metric, such as the logit difference between the right and wrong answer. A big change means that component carries information the behaviour needs.

$$ {s_S(x)} = {M}\big({f_\theta(x)}\big) - {M}\big({f_\theta(x_{[S\leftarrow\tilde h_S]})}\big) $$

Survey §7.1 [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54).

- **importance of S**: The causal effect of the component set S on input x.

- **a scalar metric**: Usually the logit difference between the correct and the wrong answer.

- **normal run**: The model’s output on the clean input.

- **patched run**: The same input, but S’s activations replaced by reference values h̃_S: from a corrupted input, the mean, or zero.

#### Patch a connection, not a whole component

Path patching replaces the activation travelling along one edge _eij_ (from component i to component j) and leaves every other route clean. That separates a component’s _direct_ effect from effects routed through other components, which is exactly what the toy above needed [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54). It is finer, and also costlier: there are far more edges than nodes.

#### Remove an edge if it costs less than τ

1. Start with the full computational graph and a threshold τ.

2. Begin at the output. For each incoming edge, patch it with its corrupted value and measure how much the metric (KL divergence to the full model) gets worse.

3. If the damage is below τ, remove the edge for good; otherwise keep it. Here B → out goes.

4. Move to the parents of what remains and repeat, working back towards the input.

5. What’s left is the circuit. A lower τ keeps more edges.

ACDC rediscovered all 5 component types of GPT-2 small’s greater-than circuit, choosing 68 of about 32,000 edges, all of which earlier manual work had found [Conmy et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997). The limits: it needs a forward pass per edge tested, it is sensitive to τ and to the order in which edges are tried, and because it optimises one metric it tends to miss _negative_ components (heads that push against the answer) unless τ is very small [Conmy et al. §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.14997#page=7) [survey Table 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=56).

#### Estimate all edges at once with a first-order approximation

$$ {s_{ij}(x)} \approx {\frac{\partial M}{\partial h_{e_{ij}}}}\cdot{\big(h^{\text{clean}}_{e_{ij}} - h^{\text{corrupt}}_{e_{ij}}\big)} $$

Survey §7.1 [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54).

- **estimated effect**: EAP’s guess at what patching edge eᵢⱼ would do.

- **local slope**: How sensitive the metric is to that edge’s activation, from one backward pass on the clean input.

- **how much it would change**: The difference between the edge’s clean and corrupted activations, from two forward passes.

Two forward passes and one backward pass score every edge, against one pass per edge for ACDC [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54). But it assumes the metric is roughly a straight line between the clean and corrupted values.

##### Try it: when the straight-line guess fails

One edge, whose effect on the metric saturates (M = 3·tanh(h)). Its clean value is 1.5. Move the corrupted value and compare the true patching effect with EAP’s estimate and with integrated gradients (EAP-IG), which averages the slope along the path instead of using the slope at one end.

Real computation on a toy metric; IG uses 50 steps along the straight path from corrupted to clean.

That is why later work improved the estimate (EAP-IG, EAP-GP) and extended it across token positions (PEAP) [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54).

#### Learn which edges to keep

A third family treats discovery as optimisation: learn a mask over edges (Edge Pruning) or over nodes at several scales (multi-granular node pruning) with gradient descent, so the model still behaves the same with as little of the graph as possible. These usually find sparser circuits, but the training itself adds randomness and sensitivity to settings like the learning rate [p. 55](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=55).

| Method | Strength | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Activation patching** | simple, direct causal evidence | many runs; component-level is coarse |
| **Path patching** | finer: isolates information flow | huge number of paths |
| **ACDC** | fully automated; finds a sufficient subgraph | slow; sensitive to τ and order |
| **EAP / EAP-IG** | fast; every edge in parallel | first-order; can miss nonlinear effects |
| **Mask learning** | sparser circuits | optimisation noise, hyperparameters |

Survey Table 8 [p. 56](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=56).

## In practice

### In practice

#### What to replace with, and what to measure

| Choice | Options | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Reference value** | zero · dataset mean · a corrupted input’s value | Zero and mean can push the model off-distribution; corrupted (resampled) values are usually preferred |
| **How to corrupt** | Gaussian noise on embeddings · swap key tokens for similar ones | Prefer token swaps (in-distribution); noise can break mechanisms and give misleading peaks |
| **Metric** | probability · logit difference · KL divergence | Logit difference; probability can miss components that actively hurt the answer |

Zhang & Nanda (2024) found that Gaussian noise and token swaps picked out different heads on the same IOI task, and that probability failed to detect negative name-mover heads [arXiv 2309.16042](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042). Survey §7.1 notes zero and mean references are also used [p. 54](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=54).

#### A circuit for a dataset, or for one prompt?

**Task-level** discovery (IOI, greater-than) averages edge scores over a dataset to describe a capability as a whole; all the methods above were developed mainly for this. **Query-level** discovery explains one prompt, which matters for open-ended questions where the computation varies a lot from input to input. EAP-IG has been extended to find sparse, faithful circuits for individual natural prompts [p. 55](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=55).

##### Next · 6.3

Attribution graphs: query-level circuits built from interpretable features instead of whole heads and MLPs.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §7.1, Table 8, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 53–56.

- Conmy et al. (2023). _Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability._ NeurIPS 2023, [arXiv 2304.14997](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997).

#### Best practice, as the field settled it

Patching goes by many names: interchange intervention, causal tracing, resample ablation and causal mediation analysis (Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024). Their guide and Zhang and Nanda (2023) found that small choices change conclusions, and recommend:

- **Corrupt minimally.** Swap one token for a similar one ("Mary" for "John") rather than adding Gaussian noise or zeroing, which push activations off the model's normal range.

- **Use logit difference.** Probability saturates, so large effects look small.

- **Know which direction you patched.** Patching clean into corrupted (denoising) tests whether a component is sufficient. Patching corrupted into clean (noising) tests whether it's necessary. They can disagree.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Ablating the head did nothing, so it doesn't matter"

It sounds like a clean negative result, but backup heads can take over when one is removed, and zero ablation pushes activations off distribution. Patch with a realistic corrupted input, test paths and groups of components, not just single nodes.

## Say it

### How do you test whether a component causes a behaviour, and how do you scale that to a whole model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Noising versus denoising?

Denoising patches clean activations into a corrupted run and tests sufficiency. Noising patches corrupted ones into a clean run and tests necessity. They can give different answers.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why can edge attribution patching mislead?

It's a first-order approximation. When an effect saturates, the gradient is near zero even though a full patch would change a lot, so important edges get underestimated.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not zero ablation?

Zero is often far from any real activation, so you measure the damage of an unnatural input, not the component's role. Mean or resample ablation keeps activations realistic.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd use activation patching: run the model on a clean prompt and a minimally corrupted one, swap one component's activation between the runs, and measure the change in logit difference. Path patching does the same for a single connection. The choices matter: corrupt with a realistic swap rather than zeros, and use logit difference, because probability saturates. Backup heads can hide importance, so I'd test groups too. To scale up, ACDC prunes edges against a threshold, and edge attribution patching estimates every edge's effect with gradients in one backward pass, and then I'd check the top edges with real patches.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 5 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Zhang and Nanda, Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042)

- [Conmy et al., Towards Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC, 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997)

- [Syed et al., Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10348)

- [Wang et al., Interpretability in the Wild: the IOI circuit in GPT-2 small (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593)

# Validating Interpretability Claims

> You found a circuit. How do you know it's a real explanation and not just a convincing story?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/validating-interpretability-claims/
- Before this: Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery (`ai-engineering/activation-patching`)

## Intuition

### The situation

A paper claims a 12-head circuit explains how a model does a task, and the figure looks convincing. Your manager wants to build a production monitor on it. The interviewer asks:

> You found a circuit. How do you know it's a real explanation and not just a convincing story?

### The idea

Interpretability results today are like restaurant reviews that each use a different scale. One counts stars, one counts dishes, one just says it felt nice. A shared report card lets you compare explanations fairly.

[Figure: Test it like a hypothesis.]

_A convincing figure is not a faithful explanation._

### Play

**Try it.** Knock out the circuit, then knock out everything except the circuit.

#### Remove it, or keep only it

A circuit is necessary if ablating it degrades the behaviour, and sufficient if patching everything _outside_ it with corrupted values still reproduces the behaviour. A circuit that is both is called faithful [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57).

##### Try it: test candidate circuits

The toy circuit from Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery (duplicate detector D → inhibition S → name mover N, plus a backup B and a negative mover Neg). Choose which components make up your candidate circuit.

Necessity = (clean − ablate circuit) / (clean − corrupted). Sufficiency = (ablate everything else − corrupted) / (clean − corrupted). Ablation = corrupted value; downstream parts recompute. Same toy equations as Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery.

Each quirk in the lab has a real counterpart. Redundancy makes necessity weak; removing negative components makes sufficiency exceed 100% (recovery metrics can leave [0, 1], which is why bounded versions have been proposed [pp. 60–61](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=61)); and a backup path can be sufficient on its own. The survey: in practice a circuit is rarely sparse, necessary and sufficient at once, and typically explains 60–80% of behavioural variance [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57).

**Notice:** a circuit can recover more than 100% of the behaviour when it drops parts that were pushing the other way. Report both tests, and say exactly what you removed.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A discovered circuit is a hypothesis. Test necessity (knock it out and the behaviour breaks) and sufficiency (keep only it and the behaviour stays). Real circuits usually explain part of a behaviour. Beyond that, score any method on five things: faithfulness of its importance scores, completeness, stability across seeds and prompts, causal validity, and whether it helps people predict or fix the model.

#### Causal scrubbing and interchange interventions

- **Causal scrubbing**: replace activations with ones from other inputs that your hypothesis says should be _equivalent_. If the hypothesis is right, behaviour is preserved.

- **Interchange interventions**: swap activations between inputs that differ in a high-level variable (say, which name is the subject), and check whether the output changes the way that variable predicts.

Both give stronger evidence than observation alone, because they test the circuit’s claimed computation, not just whether its parts matter [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57). Benchmarks such as **MIB** now score circuit-discovery methods by faithfulness across tasks [p. 57](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=57).

#### Five questions, each with its own metrics

| Dimension | Question | Example metrics |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · Attribution faithfulness** | Do importance scores reflect real causal effects? | effect agreement (correlation), effect-size error, counterfactual recovery |
| **2 · Completeness** | How much of the behaviour is accounted for? | loss recovery, behavioural coverage, unexplained variance |
| **3 · Stability** | Robust to seeds, hyperparameters, paraphrases? | cross-seed agreement, hyperparameter sensitivity, paraphrase consistency |
| **4 · Causal validity** | Necessary, sufficient and specific? | necessity, sufficiency, specificity scores |
| **5 · Human interpretability** | Can people understand and use it? | explanation utility, debugging utility, inter-rater agreement |

Survey Table 9 [p. 60](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=60). All metrics build on the intervention effect s(S, x) from Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery, averaged over prompts of the behaviour [p. 59](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=59).

#### Agreement and error measure different things

**Effect agreement** is the correlation (Pearson or Spearman) between a method’s scores a(S, x) and the real intervention effects s(S, x). **Effect-size error** is the average gap |a − s|. A method can rank components perfectly and still get their sizes badly wrong [p. 60](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=60).

##### Try it: EAP scores vs. true patching effects

Twelve components with the saturating metric from Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery. Each component’s clean activation is spread up to a maximum; its corrupted value is 0. The method is EAP (a first-order estimate).

True effect = 3·tanh(h); EAP score = 3·(1 − tanh²h)·h; Spearman = Pearson on ranks; error = mean |score − effect|.

**Counterfactual recovery** patches S from an input showing behaviour B into one showing a reference behaviour B′ and asks what fraction of the difference moves:

$$ \text{CFRecovery} = {\mathbb{E}_{x_1,x_2}}\left[\frac{{M\big(f_\theta(x_{1,[S\leftarrow h_S(x_2)]})\big) - M\big(f_\theta(x_1)\big)}}{{M\big(f_\theta(x_2)\big) - M\big(f_\theta(x_1)\big)}}\right] $$

Survey §7.5.2 [p. 60](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=60).

- **what patching moved**: Run the reference input x₁, but with S’s activations taken from x₂. How far did the metric move from x₁’s own value?

- **the full difference**: How far apart the two inputs are without any patching. If this is close to zero, the ratio explodes.

- **averaged over pairs**: Averaged over pairs of inputs, one from each behaviour. Near 1 = patching S recovers the behaviour; near 0 = little effect.

Illustrative: 12 input pairs; patching truly recovers 80% of each pair’s gap, plus a little noise (±0.1 on the metric). Gaps vary ±50% around the slider value.

The survey flags exactly this: the denominator can be near zero and patched values can overshoot, so the metric can land far above 1 or below 0; a bounded alternative has been proposed (Wu & Barez 2026) [p. 61](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=61). Loss recovery for SAEs and CLTs has the same problem [p. 61](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=61).

#### How much is explained, and does it survive a re-run?

- **Loss recovery** (SAEs, CLTs): of the loss lost by ablating a layer, how much does the reconstruction win back? **Unexplained variance**: the fraction of activation variance the reconstruction misses (the FVU of Sparse Autoencoders). **Behavioural coverage**: the fraction of prompts where S has an effect bigger than a threshold τ, so a mechanism that works on 3 of 40 prompts can’t pass as general [pp. 61–62](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=61).

- **Cross-seed agreement**: train K times and average the pairwise match between discovered feature sets (e.g. Hungarian matching on cosine similarity, as in SAE Failures and Alternatives). **Hyperparameter sensitivity**: (max − min) / mean of a result across reasonable settings. **Paraphrase consistency**: does S’s effect stay the same when the prompt is reworded? [p. 62](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=62)

The protocol asks you to report robust and fragile findings separately [p. 63](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=63).

#### Is it the cause, and does it help a person?

**Causal validity** uses necessity and sufficiency as in this lesson, with two additions: compare against _random component sets of the same size_, and test **specificity**, the share of S’s effect that falls on the target behaviour rather than on control behaviours: |s(S, B)| / ΣB′ |s(S, B′)| [p. 63](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=63). (The survey normalises necessity and sufficiency by the clean metric, not by the clean–corrupted gap used in this lesson; the idea is the same.) Benchmarks: **MIB** (circuits and causal variables), **AxBench** (steering), **RAVEL** (localising concepts with interchange interventions), **SAEBench** (SAEs on reconstruction plus downstream tasks) [p. 64](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=64).

**Human interpretability** is measured as a difference with and without the explanation: do people predict held-out behaviour more accurately, find and fix errors more often, and do two raters agree (Cohen’s κ)? These studies are expensive, and expertise confounds them: what is clear to an interpretability researcher may be opaque to a domain expert [p. 64](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=64).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Five problems

| Problem | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| **Utility ambiguity** | SAEs are scored on reconstruction and sparsity, circuits on behaviour recovery, steering vectors on behaviour change, yet all three can be used to steer a model. Without a shared goal, which is most useful? |
| **Cherry-picking** | Results shown on hand-picked examples or a narrow distribution, with no failure cases or coverage statistics. |
| **Missing baselines** | No comparison with simple alternatives: behavioural tests, random directions, single neurons. Is the method finding anything a cheap method wouldn’t? |
| **Reproducibility gaps** | Many hyperparameters, heavy training, results that change with seeds (SAE Failures and Alternatives), and reproducibility rarely reported. |
| **Faithfulness–understandability gap** | Outputs are shown to be readable, less often shown to match the model’s real mechanism, which rewards persuasive stories. |

Survey §7.5.1 [pp. 58–59](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=58).

#### Cherry-picking and missing baselines in one plot

A made-up method scored on 40 prompts (score = how much of the behaviour its explanation recovers). Switch between what a paper might show and the full picture.

Illustrative scores, generated with a fixed seed in your browser.

The survey’s fix is to report coverage across a diverse input set with uncertainty, include failures, and always compare against baselines such as random directions, PCA, single neurons and supervised probes [pp. 61, 65](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=65). Shared platforms for tracking and auditing claims across papers have also been proposed [p. 59](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=59).

##### Next · 7.2

The survey’s answer: five dimensions every method should be scored on.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §7.5–7.5.1, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 58–59.

#### A five-step protocol, and what it can’t fix

1. **Define scope**: model, layers, behaviour, a test suite with success criteria.

2. **Establish baselines**: random directions, PCA, single neurons, supervised probes.

3. **Apply the method** across seeds, hyperparameters and training details.

4. **Evaluate all five dimensions.**

5. **Report everything**, including failures, unexplained behaviour and baseline comparisons.

Survey §7.5.3 [pp. 65–66](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=65). Table 10 tailors the priorities: for SAEs, cross-seed feature alignment and loss recovery; for circuits, counterfactual recovery and interchange tests; for probes and steering vectors, a search for confounds in the fitting set and side-effect analysis [p. 65](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=65).

##### The framework’s own limits (survey §7.5.4)

- The metrics aren’t uniquely correct, and thresholds lack theoretical grounding.

- Evaluating all five is expensive; the human dimension especially.

- Scores depend on the task: good at factual recall doesn’t mean good at reasoning.

The authors call it “a starting point for standardisation, not a final answer” [p. 66](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=66).

##### Next · Probing Classifiers

Reading activations directly: describing in plain language what a hidden activation encodes, without decomposing it into features or circuits.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §7.5.2–7.5.4, Tables 9–10, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 59–66.

#### Toward shared standards

The field's own review, _Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability_ (Sharkey et al., 2025), lists evaluation as a core gap: many results are shown on a few chosen prompts, without baselines, and are rarely reproduced. Shared benchmarks are starting to appear. SAEBench (ICML 2025) scores sparse autoencoders on eight metrics instead of reconstruction alone, and its finding that the usual proxies don't predict usefulness is a good example of why one number isn't enough.

For causal claims, the strongest tests resample everything the hypothesis says doesn't matter, as in causal scrubbing, or check that the model's internal states line up with a simpler algorithm under interchange interventions (Geiger et al.).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The figure is convincing, so the circuit is right"

It sounds reasonable, but persuasive isn't faithful. Circuits are often shown on chosen prompts with no baseline, and few are reproduced. Ask for necessity and sufficiency numbers, a random-circuit baseline, results across prompts and seeds, and how much of the behaviour is left unexplained.

## Say it

### You found a circuit. How do you know it's a real explanation and not just a convincing story?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why can recovery exceed 100%?

Some components push against the behaviour. Removing them along with everything outside the circuit makes the circuit look better than the full model.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What is causal scrubbing?

A test that resamples every activation the hypothesis says doesn't matter and checks the behaviour is preserved, so the whole explanation is tested, not just a few components.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Faithful versus plausible?

Plausible explanations convince people. Faithful ones match what interventions on the model show. Only faithful ones are safe to build on.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd treat the circuit as a hypothesis and test it two ways: knock it out and check the behaviour breaks, which is necessity, and knock out everything else and check it still works, which is sufficiency. Real circuits usually explain only part of a behaviour, and recovery can exceed 100% if components pushing the other way are removed, so I'd report both. Then I'd check that importance scores match real interventions, that results hold across seeds and paraphrases, how it compares to a random baseline, and whether it actually helps people predict or fix the model.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 4 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Barez et al., Understanding AI from the Inside (survey, 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)

- [Chan et al., Causal Scrubbing (Redwood Research, 2022)](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/JvZhhzycHu2Yd57RN/causal-scrubbing-a-method-for-rigorously-testing)

- [Geiger et al., Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02997)

- [Sharkey et al., Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16496)

- [Karvonen et al., SAEBench (ICML 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532)

Explanations are ours, built from these sources. Chapters marked with page numbers come from the survey. Lab numbers are illustrative unless a lab says otherwise. Many recent papers are preprints.

# Logit Lens, Tuned Lens and Verbalisers

> How can you read what a model is predicting at a middle layer?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/logit-lens-and-verbalisers/
- Before this: The Residual Stream and Circuits (`ai-engineering/residual-stream-and-circuits`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model gets a two-step question wrong. You want to know whether it had the intermediate answer somewhere in its middle layers. The interviewer asks:

> How can you read what a model is predicting at a middle layer?

### The idea

Reading activations is like reading a draft before the author finishes. A lens peeks at the half-written sentence. A verbaliser asks the author to describe the draft in their own words.

[Figure: Three readers, from cheap to rich.]

_Every reader shows what's decodable. None proves the model uses it._

### Play

**Try it.** Step through the layers and watch the top prediction change.

#### A toy model where we know the truth

A 12-layer toy on “A B C A B → ?”. We built it so we know what’s inside: the part of each layer the output layer reads carries the current token **B** up to layer 9 and the answer **C** from layer 10; meanwhile a **hidden part** the output layer ignores has already worked out C by layer 5. The output-facing part is also stored in a slowly **rotating basis** that only lines up with the output layer at the end. The tuned lens is actually fitted, by least squares on 300 toy prompts, to match the final layer.

Toy: 8 tokens, 16-dimensional states (8 output-facing + 8 hidden), WU reads the first 8; output-facing part rotated by drift × layers remaining; noise 0.05. Each cell: top token and its probability; “·” = nothing above 20%; “+C” = C already present in the hidden part.

**Notice:** early layers predict junk under the logit lens, partly because they don't use the output layer's basis yet. The tuned lens fixes much of that with a learned translator per layer.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

The logit lens pushes a middle layer's residual stream straight through the output layer to see what the model would say if it stopped there. Middle layers don't quite speak the output layer's language, so the tuned lens learns a small translator per layer. Verbalisers go further: Patchscopes pastes an activation into another prompt and lets the model describe it, and LatentQA trains a decoder to answer questions about activations.

#### Unembed a middle layer

1. The residual stream (The Residual Stream and Circuits) carries one vector through the layers; at the end, the unembedding WU turns it into token scores.

2. The logit lens applies that same WU to an early layer’s vector: “what would the model say if it stopped here?”

3. Typical result: early layers are diffuse, then the answer firms up. In a 12-layer model on “A B C A B”, C might enter the top 20 at layer 6 and climb to first by the last layer.

4. Two catches: middle layers may be organised differently from the last one, and decoding a token doesn’t show the model uses it.

Formally, logitsℓ = WU hℓ [p. 67](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=67). Because of the mismatch, decoded tokens show “at most information recoverable from the activation, rather than information used in model computation” [p. 68](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=68). The original idea is nostalgebraist’s 2020 post [LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens).

#### Learn a translator for each layer

$$ \text{logits}^{TL}_\ell = {W_U}\big({W_\ell}\,{h_\ell} + {b_\ell}\big),\qquad \min_{W_\ell,b_\ell}\ {\mathbb{E}_x\,\mathrm{KL}\big(p_{\text{final}}(x)\,\|\,p^{TL}_\ell(x)\big)} $$

Survey §8.2 [p. 68](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=68); tuned lens by Belrose et al. [arXiv 2303.08112](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08112).

- **the output layer**: The model’s own unembedding, unchanged.

- **learned translator**: A per-layer affine map Wℓ, bℓ that converts layer ℓ’s format into the final layer’s format.

- **middle-layer state**: The residual stream at layer ℓ.

- **trained to match the end**: The translator is trained so the lens’s distribution matches the model’s final output. That is the source of its main weakness.

It fixes the language mismatch, but it is still correlational, and because it is trained to predict the final output it answers “what will the model say?” rather than “what is this layer computing?”. It skips intermediate computation even more than the logit lens does [p. 68](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=68).

#### From “what will it say” to “what is it disposed to cause”

$$ {J_\ell = \mathbb{E}_{\text{prompt},\,t,\,t'\ge t}\Big[\tfrac{\partial h^{t'}_{\text{final}}}{\partial h^{t}_{\ell}}\Big]},\qquad {p^{JL}_\ell} = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W_U\,\mathrm{norm}({J_\ell}\,{h_\ell})\big) $$

Survey §8.3 [pp. 68–69](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=68) (Gurnee et al. 2026).

- **average Jacobian**: How a small change to layer ℓ at position t moves the final-layer state at every later position t′, averaged over prompts and positions.

- **the activation**: The residual stream at layer ℓ.

- **decoded disposition**: Push the activation through J, normalise, unembed: which tokens this state is disposed to promote later.

The rows of WUJℓ are **J-lens vectors**, one per token per layer; their dot product with hℓ says how strongly the state will promote that token. They can also be used as **steering vectors**, which the logit and tuned lenses can’t offer. Reported uses: multi-step reasoning and latent planning [p. 69](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=69).

##### Limits

- Still token-level: if only “photo” shows, is it “photoperiodism” or something else?

- Works best in a middle band of layers, “J-space”: about 38–92% of depth in Claude Sonnet 4.5. Earlier is noisy; later collapses onto the output [p. 69](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=69).

| Lens | Answers | Main catch |
|---|---|---|
| **Logit** | what it would say if stopped here | language mismatch across layers |
| **Tuned** | what it will finally say | skips intermediate steps |
| **Jacobian** | what this state pushes the output towards | token-level; best mid-depth |

##### Next · 8.2

Let the model describe its own activations in words: Patchscopes and LatentQA.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §8–8.3, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 66–69.

- nostalgebraist (2020). _Interpreting GPT: the logit lens._ [LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens).

- Belrose et al. _Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens._ [arXiv 2303.08112](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08112).

#### Paste the thought into a “repeat after me” prompt

1. Run a source prompt and pick the activation to explain.

2. Here: the residual stream at “Kingdom”, layer ℓ.

3. Run an inspection prompt built to make the model repeat whatever is at “?”, and overwrite that position’s activation (layer ℓ*) with ours.

4. Whatever the model generates is its own reading of the activation. A different inspection prompt asks a different question, such as “what is the largest city of x?” → London.

5. The catch: the decoder is an ordinary model never trained to read pasted activations, so they can push it out of distribution.

$$ {e(h^t_\ell)} = {f_\theta}\big({p}{[h^{t^*}_{\ell^*}\leftarrow h^t_\ell]}\big) $$

Survey §8.4 [pp. 69–70](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=69); Ghandeharioun et al. 2024 [arXiv 2401.06102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06102). A concurrent method, SelfIE, works similarly [p. 70](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=70).

- **the explanation**: Text describing the activation from layer ℓ, position t.

- **the model itself**: The same language model acts as the decoder.

- **inspection prompt**: A prompt designed to make the model verbalise whatever sits at the patched position.

- **the paste**: Replace the activation at layer ℓ*, position t* of p with our activation.

The logit and tuned lenses are special cases with a fixed (affine) translator; Patchscopes hands the translation to the model’s own text generation, which can express things an affine map can’t [pp. 69–70](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=69).

#### Train a decoder to answer questions about activations

**LatentQA** (Latent Interpretation Tuning, LIT) builds a dataset of triples (h, q, a): an activation from the target model, a question and its answer, and fine-tunes a decoder to answer q from h. To make the activation carry a known attribute, it is read from a **control prompt** such as _“In your next reply, please try to evoke a brief sense of triumphant hubris.”_; then q = “In what way does the assistant craft its responses?” and a = “…a sense of self-assured victory.” A proprietary LLM generates both the control prompts and the QA pairs [p. 71](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=71).

Trained on the task, the decoder no longer sees pasted activations as strange, which fixes Patchscopes’ out-of-distribution problem [p. 71](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=71).

##### Two new problems

- **Memorising instead of reading**: with too little or too narrow data, the decoder learns surface pairings. Predictive Concept Decoders and Activation Oracles build more diverse data to counter this [p. 72](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=72).

- **Shortcuts**: a decoder can reconstruct the original _input_ from the activation and answer from that, without analysing the representation. Recent studies find this failure “severe and prevalent”, so good verbalisation scores alone don’t show faithful reading [p. 72](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=72).

A useful sanity check follows from the shortcut: if a plain text model given only the input text answers the question as well as the decoder given the activation, the decoder hasn’t shown it reads anything the input didn’t already say.

##### Next · 8.3

The oldest tool of all, probing classifiers, and the traps that make a high accuracy mean less than it seems.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §8.4–8.5, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 69–72.

- Ghandeharioun et al. (2024). _Patchscopes._ [arXiv 2401.06102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06102).

- Pan et al. _LatentQA._ [arXiv 2412.08686](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08686).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Asking the model about its own activations

A related 2025 line of work tests whether models can report on their own internal states. Anthropic's introspection experiments (Lindsey, 2025) injected a concept vector into a model's activations, told it a thought might have been injected, and asked what it noticed. Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 generally did best, detecting the injection and naming the concept about 20% of the time at the right layer and strength. Other models did so less often, and results depended on post-training.

That's the same lesson as for lenses and verbalisers: a readout is a hint about what's represented. For anything you'll act on, confirm with an intervention.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The lens shows the answer at layer 15, so the model knew it there"

It sounds direct, but a lens is a readout you chose, and a learned one can find information the model doesn't use. Decodable at layer 15 isn't the same as used by later layers. Patch or steer at that layer to test it.

## Say it

### How can you read what a model is predicting at a middle layer?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is the logit lens worse in early layers?

Early layers represent things in a basis the unembedding isn't tuned for, and later processing hasn't happened yet, so the direct readout is noisy.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's the risk with LatentQA?

The decoder is a trained model, so it can answer from its own priors rather than the activation. Compare against a decoder given shuffled activations.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What did the introspection experiments find?

When concept vectors were injected, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 sometimes noticed and named them, but only in a minority of trials, so self-reports are a weak signal.

#### The 30-second answer

The logit lens pushes a middle layer's residual stream through the final unembedding to see what the model would predict if it stopped there. It's free, but middle layers don't quite use the output basis, so it's biased early on. The tuned lens learns a small translator per layer and fits much better. For richer questions, Patchscopes pastes the activation into another prompt and lets the model describe it, and LatentQA trains a decoder to answer questions about activations. All of these show what's decodable, so I'd confirm anything important with an intervention.
