# Probing Classifiers

> A probe detects a property from activations with 95% accuracy. What does that tell you, and what doesn't it?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/probing-classifiers/
- Before this: Linear Representations and Universality (`ai-engineering/linear-representations`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your probe detects "the model is lying" from layer 30 with 95% accuracy on your test set. The product team wants to ship it as a deception monitor next week. The interviewer asks:

> A probe detects a property from activations with 95% accuracy. What does that tell you, and what doesn't it?

### The idea

A probe is like a metal detector on a beach. A beep tells you there's metal, not that anyone is using it, and a detector that's sensitive enough beeps at bottle caps. Digging is the causal test.

[Figure: Decodable, selective, and actually used.]

_Three questions to ask of any probe result._

### Play

**Try it.** Make the probe more powerful, and compare its accuracy on real and random labels.

#### Selectivity = real accuracy − control accuracy

Hewitt & Liang’s idea: give every word type a **random** label, fixed per type. Nothing in the activations encodes it, so any accuracy a probe gets is pure memorisation. Below, 30 word types, each with a fixed activation vector plus per-occurrence noise; the real property is linearly encoded. Test tokens are new occurrences of the same words.

Real computation in your browser: logistic regression (gradient descent) vs. 1-nearest-neighbour, 600 training and 600 test tokens, fixed seed.

The survey: high selectivity means the probe works because the representation encodes the property; low selectivity means we can’t rule out exploitation of spurious structure [p. 74](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=74) [Hewitt & Liang 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03368).

**Notice:** a powerful probe scores well even on random labels, because it memorises. Selectivity, the gap between the two, tells you what the activations really hold.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

A probe is a small classifier trained to predict a property from activations. High accuracy means the property is decodable, nothing more: the probe may ride a correlated feature, the model may never use it, and a powerful probe can learn the task itself. Control tasks measure memorisation, and amnesic probing or patching test whether the model uses the information.

#### A classifier on top of activations

A linear probe predicts ŷ = g(Wprobe hℓ + bprobe), with g the identity (regression) or softmax (classification), trained on labelled activations. It tests whether the property is **linearly accessible**; MLP probes test whether a nonlinear map can retrieve it [p. 72](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=72). In the residual-stream picture (The Residual Stream and Circuits), a linear probe is just a learned reading direction.

##### The probe causality problem (three ways accuracy misleads)

1. **Correlated features**: the probe may detect word frequency, which correlates with part of speech, instead of part of speech.

2. **Unused information**: later layers may never read the decoded property; it may be leftover from earlier processing.

3. **Probe capacity**: a sufficiently expressive probe can reach high accuracy by exploiting noise, even when the property isn’t there.

Survey [pp. 72–73](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=72). For this reason, the survey says probing alone “does not, under our definition, constitute mechanistic interpretability research” [p. 73](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=73).

#### “Can we extract it?” vs. “how easily?”

If only a very nonlinear probe succeeds, is the property encoded in a complex form, or is the probe computing it from other features? In the worst case a complex enough mapping can turn even a _randomly initialised_ network into the causal model you hoped for (Sutter et al. 2025) [p. 74](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=74).

**Minimum description length (MDL) probes** (Voita & Titov 2020) score how efficiently a probe extracts the property, counting both accuracy and complexity: a property is “more encoded” if a simpler probe gets it [p. 74](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=74).

##### Practical guidance (survey)

Prefer simple probes; compare against probes on random representations; consider MDL; and if a linear probe fails but an MLP probe succeeds, validate cautiously [p. 74](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=74).

##### Next · 8.4

Making probes causal: erase what the probe found (amnesic probing) or patch it in, and when probing is the right tool.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §8.6.1–8.6.3, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 72–74.

- Hewitt & Liang (2019). _Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks._ [arXiv 1909.03368](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03368).

#### Erase the probe direction, see what breaks

$$ {\tilde h} = {h} - {\frac{h^\top w}{\|w\|^2}\,w} $$

Survey §8.6.4 [p. 75](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=75). Elazar et al. (2021) used iterative nullspace projection (INLP) to remove a property more thoroughly [arXiv 2006.00995](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00995).

- **the edited activation**: What’s left after removing the property.

- **original activation**: The model’s activation.

- **its shadow on w**: The part of h lying along the probe direction w. Subtracting it makes the probe blind; then run the model on h̃ and measure the task.

Toy: 12-dimensional activations of 400 inputs with sentiment (used by the output) and word length (not used), plus noise. Probe directions = difference of class means. The “model” reads sentiment with a fixed readout; the backup variant also reads a nonlinear copy (stored in how far the activation sits along a second direction, not which way).

That last case is the survey’s warning: “unchanged performance does not establish that the information is unused”, because redundant representations or other pathways can keep the behaviour going. Erasure can also leave residue or damage other concepts [p. 75](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=75).

#### Copy the probe-subspace part across inputs

Take x1 with property P and x2 without. At a chosen spot (say the last token’s residual stream at a middle layer), copy the part of x1’s activation inside the probe subspace into x2’s run. If x2’s output shifts towards P, the model uses that information. Amnesic probing tests _removal_; this tests _sufficiency_. Its catch is that you must pick the layer, component and position, and that choice can confound the result [p. 75](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=75). It is the same interchange intervention as in Validating Interpretability Claims, applied to a probe direction.

Pairing probes with other attribution tools doesn’t rescue them: saliency maps can highlight inputs the model ignores, attention weights correlate weakly with causal importance, and attribution methods often disagree [p. 75](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=75).

## In practice

### In practice

#### When to probe

| Appropriate | Inappropriate |
|---|---|
| Showing information is present (“P is encoded”) | Claiming the model uses P |
| Comparing encoding strength across layers | Concluding P is absent from low probe accuracy |
| Auditing for encoded sensitive information | Claiming mechanistic understanding from probes alone |
| Generating hypotheses for causal tests | Using probe results as evidence for causal hypotheses |
| Early detection or triage | Judging alignment or safety from probe results |

Survey Table 11 [p. 76](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=76). Standards: report control tasks; use minimal probes; test causality; show layer-wise trends, not just the peak; separate encoding from use; report stability across seeds and splits [p. 76](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=76).

#### Catching a sleeper agent with one direction

A sleeper-agent model behaves normally when the year is 2023 but switches to a hidden harmful policy when it sees 2024. MacDiarmid et al. built a detector from a _difference of means_ over contrast pairs that don’t even mention the trigger (“Are you doing something dangerous? … yes” vs. “… no”): uℓ = E[hℓ | true] − E[hℓ | false]. Projecting new activations onto uℓ flagged triggered inputs with **AUROC above 99%** [pp. 76–77](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=77).

Why so easy: triggered and normal activations form two clusters far apart, so they separate along many directions. And the goal is detection, not mechanism, which is exactly a use Table 11 allows [p. 77](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=77).

##### this lesson recap

1. Lenses decode a layer into tokens: logit (raw), tuned (trained to the end), Jacobian (what it pushes towards) (8.1).

2. Patchscopes and LatentQA let a model verbalise activations, with out-of-distribution and shortcut risks (8.2).

3. Probes show decodability; use control tasks and simple probes (8.3).

4. Intervene to test use; probe for detection and hypotheses (8.4).

All of these reveal what _can be decoded_, not whether the model uses it [p. 77](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=77).

##### Next · Steering Vectors

Comparing models (diffing), locating knowledge, and steering behaviour with representations.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §8.6.4–8.6.7, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 74–77.

- Elazar et al. (2021). _Amnesic Probing._ [arXiv 2006.00995](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00995).

- MacDiarmid et al. (2024). _Simple probes can catch sleeper agents._ [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/probes-catch-sleeper-agents).

#### Deception probes, 2024–2025

**Planted backdoors.** Anthropic's "defection probes" (April 2024) detected when its own sleeper-agent models were about to act on a hidden goal with AUROC above 99%, using generic contrast pairs that didn't mention the trigger. These were backdoors Anthropic planted, so they may be unusually easy to spot.

**More realistic deception.** Apollo Research (ICML 2025) trained probes on Llama-3.3-70B and tested them on scenarios like hiding insider trading. They reached AUROC 0.96–0.999 and caught 95–99% of deceptive responses at a 1% false-positive rate on ordinary chat. But the probes were partly sensitive to whether the scenario was _about_ deception, they performed roughly on par with a black-box GPT-4o baseline, and the authors judged them not yet robust enough as a defence.

**Simple wins.** Google DeepMind found plain linear probes beat SAE-based probes at detecting harmful intent on unfamiliar prompts (2025).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "95% accuracy, ship it as a monitor"

It sounds strong, but a probe can track a correlate, like whether the text talks about lying, rather than lying itself. Apollo's deception probes scored highly yet partly tracked the topic. Test on realistic, unfamiliar cases at the false-positive rate you can afford, and against a black-box baseline.

## Say it

### A probe detects a property from activations with 95% accuracy. What does that tell you, and what doesn't it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What's a control task?

The same probe trained on random but consistent labels for the same inputs. High control accuracy means the probe can memorise, so real accuracy alone overstates what the representation holds.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What does amnesic probing do?

It removes the probe's direction from the activations and checks whether the model's task performance drops. If it doesn't, the model wasn't using that information, or has other copies.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why did simple probes catch sleeper agents so well?

The planted backdoor creates a very distinct internal state, so even generic contrast pairs separate it. Deception that arises naturally may be far subtler.

#### The 30-second answer

High probe accuracy means the property is linearly decodable from the activations, nothing more. The probe may be riding a correlated feature, the model may never use it, and a powerful probe can learn the task itself. So I'd keep the probe linear, compare it with a control task to get selectivity, and test whether the model uses the direction with amnesic probing or patching. For a deception monitor, I'd test on realistic out-of-distribution cases at a fixed low false-positive rate and against a black-box baseline, because published deception probes look strong in-distribution but partly track the topic of deception.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 5 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Hewitt and Liang, Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03368)

- [Elazar et al., Amnesic Probing (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00995)

# Steering Vectors

> How can you change a model's behaviour at inference time without retraining it?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/steering-vectors/
- Before this: Linear Representations and Universality (`ai-engineering/linear-representations`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your chatbot is too sycophantic: it agrees with users even when they're wrong. Retraining will take weeks. Someone suggests adding a vector to the activations at inference time. The interviewer asks:

> How can you change a model's behaviour at inference time without retraining it?

### The idea

Think of a mixing desk during a live show. Steering doesn't rewrite the song; it pushes one slider while it plays. Push gently and the mood shifts. Push too far and the whole mix distorts.

[Figure: Find it, add it, watch the side effects.]

_The same vector can monitor a trait, steer it, or flag training data._

### Play

**Try it.** Add the refusal direction to a harmless request. Then remove it from a harmful one.

#### Add it, remove it, and watch what else moves

Arditi et al. build rℓ from refused vs. complied prompts and measure s = ⟨h, r⟩; adding r makes harmless prompts get refused, and projecting r out makes harmful prompts get answered [p. 81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=81) [arXiv 2406.11717](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717). The toy below computes r from 200 toy prompts and applies it to 200 new ones. The model also does an unrelated task whose reading direction overlaps r a little.

Toy: 16-dimensional activations; refusal = 1 when ⟨h, r̂⟩ passes a threshold; unrelated task read along a direction with cosine 0.5 to r. Directional ablation: h − (h·r̂) r̂.

Localisation and steering meet here: measuring s across layers _locates_ refusal information; intervening along r _tests_ whether it changes behaviour. That is evidence of causal influence, not the full mechanism of refusal [p. 81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=81).

**Notice:** one direction switches refusal on and off. That's why steering is both a control knob and a jailbreak risk for open-weight models.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Take the average activation for one behaviour minus the average for its opposite, and you get a steering vector. Adding a multiple of it during inference pushes the model towards the behaviour, with no retraining. The best-known case is refusal: one direction switches it on and off in many chat models. Steering is both a control knob and a causal test, and too much of it degrades quality.

#### Two averages and a subtraction

$$ {v_{\text{steer}}} = {\mathbb{E}[h_\ell\mid\text{preferred}]} - {\mathbb{E}[h_\ell\mid\text{unpreferred}]},\qquad {\tilde h_\ell = h_\ell + \alpha\, v_{\text{steer}}} $$

Survey §9.3 [pp. 80–81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80). A trained probe’s weight vector can also serve as the direction (Probing Classifiers).

- **steering vector**: A direction in activation space at layer ℓ.

- **average when preferred**: Mean activation over prompts showing the behaviour we want to push towards (for refusal: prompts the model refuses).

- **average when not**: Mean activation over matched prompts without it.

- **apply it**: At inference, add α times the vector to the activation; α sets the strength and the sign sets the direction.

Simple as it is, it reliably changes refusal, helpfulness and style [p. 81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=81). It is the same move as Linear Representations and Universality’s king → queen lab, now on a behaviour instead of a word.

#### Beyond linear

- **Nonlinear**: steer linearly inside a kernel-PCA space and map back, or move along a low-dimensional manifold, since some concepts live on manifolds rather than lines [p. 81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=81).

- **Optimised**: learn the vector by maximising task performance or suppressing bad outputs under intervention. More flexible, much more compute than a difference of means [p. 81](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=81).

- **As a test of features**: if an SAE or CLT feature is labelled “X”, steering along it should produce X. Benchmarks RAVEL, MIB and AxBench compare SAE features, difference-in-means and DAS this way [pp. 81–82](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=82).

##### Limits: brittleness and opacity

A direction found on one distribution, model or task may not transfer. And behavioural success doesn’t make the mechanism transparent: the vector may move several features at once, interact nonlinearly, or use unintended pathways. Treat steering as evidence of causal influence, not as an explanation [p. 82](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=82).

##### this lesson recap

1. Diffing compares features across models; “new” features may just be rotated old ones (9.1).

2. Localisation finds where effects concentrate; it is a first step, not an explanation (9.2).

3. Steering changes behaviour and tests causality, but can be brittle and opaque (9.3).

##### Next · the survey's training-dynamics chapters

Watching models learn: how features and circuits form during training.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §9.3, Figure 15, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 80–82.

- Arditi et al. (2024). _Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction._ [arXiv 2406.11717](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Steering in 2024–2025

**Refusal.** Arditi et al. (NeurIPS 2024) found a single refusal direction in 13 open chat models up to 72B parameters. Projecting it out of the weights is a rank-one edit that removes refusals, a white-box jailbreak simpler than fine-tuning. They also showed adversarial suffixes work partly by suppressing this direction.

**Persona vectors.** Anthropic (August 2025) built an automated pipeline that turns a natural-language trait description, like "sycophantic", into a direction, tested on Qwen 2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. The vectors can monitor drift towards a trait, steer it at inference, and flag training data likely to induce it. Steering against a trait at inference reduced it but could degrade general capabilities. Adding the vector during fine-tuning ("preventative steering") limited trait shifts while better preserving capability.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Steering is a free fix, just turn up α"

It sounds cheap, but large α pushes activations off distribution and degrades quality, and persona-vector work found inference-time steering can degrade general capabilities. Evaluate the steered model on your normal benchmarks, not only the target behaviour, and consider steering during fine-tuning or fixing the data instead.

## Say it

### How can you change a model's behaviour at inference time without retraining it?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

How do you choose the layer?

Sweep layers on held-out data. Middle layers usually work best: early ones haven't formed the concept, and late ones are too close to the output to change behaviour broadly.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why is the refusal direction a safety concern?

For open-weight models, projecting it out of the weights is a cheap rank-one edit that removes refusals, a white-box jailbreak simpler than fine-tuning.

Follow-up 3 of 3

What is preventative steering?

Adding the trait vector during fine-tuning, so the model doesn't have to move towards the trait to fit the data. Anthropic reported it limited trait shifts with less capability loss than steering at inference.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd build a steering vector by taking mean activations on examples with the behaviour minus examples with its opposite, at one layer, and add a multiple of it during inference. It needs no retraining, and it's also a causal test that the direction matters. The best-known case is refusal: one direction controls it across many chat models. The risks are that too much strength hurts quality and the effect can spread to other behaviours, so I'd choose the layer and strength on held-out data and check general benchmarks too. For a lasting fix, I'd look at steering during fine-tuning or fixing the training data.

# Knowledge Localisation and Editing

> Where does a fact live in a model, and can you edit it safely?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/knowledge-localisation-and-editing/
- Before this: Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery (`ai-engineering/activation-patching`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your model states an outdated fact: a company's CEO who left last year. Retraining is expensive. A teammate suggests using ROME to edit just that fact. The interviewer asks:

> Where does a fact live in a model, and can you edit it safely?

### The idea

Think of correcting one entry in a phone book that's been copied into many other books. Finding the page where the entry matters most doesn't mean it's the best page to fix, and a careless fix can smudge the neighbouring entries.

[Figure: Locate, edit, then check what else moved.]

_Where a fact matters and where to edit it are different questions._

### Play

**Try it.** Corrupt the subject, then restore one hidden state at a time.

#### Which hidden state brings the answer back?

1. Clean run: the model completes the fact. Save every hidden state.

2. Corrupted run: add noise to the subject’s token embeddings, so the model loses the answer.

3. Re-run the corrupted input, but copy back one clean hidden state (one layer, one token, one component type).

4. The share of the correct answer’s probability that returns is that state’s indirect effect. Repeat for every layer and token to get a map.

Illustrative map drawn to follow the qualitative pattern Meng et al. report for GPT-2 XL, not their measured values [arXiv 2202.05262](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262).

Causal tracing (Meng et al. 2022) underlies editing methods ROME, MEMIT and AlphaEdit, which rewrite the MLP weights it points to [p. 80](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80). Editing itself returns in Interpretability for AI Safety.

**Notice:** restoring middle-layer MLP states at the subject's last token brings the answer back. That inspired ROME, but where a fact matters isn't always the best place to edit it.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Causal tracing corrupts the subject of a prompt, then restores one hidden state at a time to see which brings the answer back. For facts, the effect concentrates in middle-layer MLPs at the subject's last token, which inspired ROME (a rank-one update to one MLP) and MEMIT (many edits across layers). But where a fact matters most doesn't predict where editing works best, and edits can spill over to related facts.

#### MLPs as key–value memories

Geva et al. proposed that feed-forward layers act as key–value memories (Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition’s reading of MLP neurons); Dai et al. found factual associations stored there; and Sharma et al. found those associations flow mainly through the top singular directions of late-layer MLP weights. That motivated tools for finding where a fact sits [p. 80](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80).

Localisation is the usual first step before other interventions: choosing the layer and token position for a **probe** (Probing Classifiers), for a **steering vector** (Steering Vectors; e.g. Arditi et al. searched layers and positions for the best refusal direction), or the MLP to change in **knowledge editing** [p. 80](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80).

#### PISCES: edit the vectors that write a concept

1. Use SAE features plus automated explanations to find features tied to the concept: Fc = {fi : Corr(fi, c) > τ}. Here f2 and f3.

2. Find the MLP output vectors (columns of W2) that strongly activate those features: v2 does, v1 doesn’t.

3. Pass v2 through the SAE, set the concept features’ coefficients to negative values, and decode to get the edited v̂2.

4. The concept is removed from the weights themselves, not just blocked at the output.

Survey §13.2.1, the survey’s own worked example [pp. 114–115](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=115). Reported result: accuracy on the prohibited concept near chance while general ability is kept, with higher specificity than baselines [p. 115](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=115).

##### ROME: rewrite one association with a rank-one update

Causal tracing (this lesson) finds the MLP layer and token where a fact is retrieved; ROME then adds a rank-one matrix ΔW to that MLP’s output projection so the fact’s _key_ now maps to a new _value_. The survey’s example removes a backdoor that leaks an admin password after a trigger token: after the edit, the model outputs end-of-sequence instead [p. 116](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=116). Try a simplified version:

Simplified ROME on a toy 32-dimensional linear memory W, with ΔW = (v* − W k*) k*ᵀ for a unit key k*. Real ROME also weights the update by the inverse covariance of keys to reduce interference.

Early ROME and MEMIT did cause substantial side effects; newer methods (AlphaEdit, CrispEdit) reduce them by using low-rank structure in activation space. And editing is double-edged: the more precise it is, the easier it is to inject misinformation undetected, which is why access control and auditability matter [p. 116](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=116).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Limits

##### Why localisation is only a first step

- Transformers are overparameterised; information can be stored and processed redundantly across many components, differently for different inputs. A component with a strong causal effect may be a small part of the mechanism [p. 80](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80).

- Knowing the module, layer or subspace doesn’t explain how it works; that takes finer analyses like circuit discovery (Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery) [p. 80](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=80).

- Outside the survey: Hase et al. found that where causal tracing localises a fact barely predicts which layer is best to edit it [arXiv 2301.04213](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04213).

##### Next · 9.3

Not just finding, but changing: steering vectors and the refusal direction.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §9.2, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), p. 80.

- Meng et al. (2022). _Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT._ [arXiv 2202.05262](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262).

- Hase et al. (2023). _Does Localization Inform Editing?_ [arXiv 2301.04213](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04213).

#### What later work found

Hase et al. (NeurIPS 2023) tested ROME, MEMIT and fine-tuning on GPT-J and found that causal tracing provides no insight into which MLP layer is best to edit. For ROME, the edited layer explained edit success far better than the tracing result did. Later work (FiNE, 2025) reported that ROME and MEMIT often over-edit, changing facts they shouldn't, and attributed it to causal tracing focusing too much on the subject.

In practice, weight editing is a research tool and a way to test hypotheses about storage. For facts that change in production, retrieval is usually the safer fix.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Causal tracing found the layer, so edit there"

It sounds logical, but Hase et al. found tracing gave no insight into which layer is best to edit; the choice of layer mattered far more than the trace. Pick the edit layer by testing edits directly, and measure the damage to related facts.

## Say it

### Where does a fact live in a model, and can you edit it safely?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why a rank-one update?

ROME treats the MLP as a key–value memory: the subject gives a key, and it changes the weights so that key returns the new value with the smallest possible change, which is rank one.

Follow-up 2 of 3

ROME versus MEMIT?

ROME edits one fact in one layer. MEMIT spreads many edits across several layers so thousands of facts can change at once.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why might an edit not stick?

The model may store the fact in more than one place or recompute it through other paths, and paraphrases can route around the edited key.

#### The 30-second answer

Causal tracing corrupts the subject in a prompt, then restores one hidden state at a time to see which brings the answer back. For facts, the effect concentrates in middle-layer MLPs at the subject's last token, which inspired ROME, a rank-one update to one MLP, and MEMIT for many facts at once. But later work showed localisation doesn't predict where editing works best, and edits can over-generalise or miss paraphrases. So I'd test any edit on paraphrases, related facts and unrelated facts. For a fact that changes in production, I'd usually prefer retrieval over editing weights.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 4 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

#### Sources

- [Barez et al., Understanding AI from the Inside (survey, 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)

- [Meng et al., Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT (ROME, 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262)

- [Meng et al., Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer (MEMIT, 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07229)

- [Hase et al., Does Localization Inform Editing? (NeurIPS 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04213)

- [Pan et al., Precise Localization of Memories: FiNE (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01090)

# Model Diffing

> After fine-tuning, how do you find out what changed inside the model?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 15 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/model-diffing/
- Before this: Sparse Autoencoders (`ai-engineering/sparse-autoencoders`)

## Intuition

### The situation

After you fine-tune your model on a narrow task, it starts giving harmful advice in unrelated conversations. Your evaluations catch the symptom, but not why it happened. The interviewer asks:

> After fine-tuning, how do you find out what changed inside the model?

### The idea

Think of comparing two versions of a document with track changes on. The diff shows what was added or strengthened, but if a paragraph was only reworded, a naive diff marks it as brand new.

[Figure: Compare base and fine-tuned, carefully.]

_Diffing can explain why a fine-tune changed behaviour, and sometimes warn before evals do._

### Play

**Try it.** Rotate the old "sports" feature further during fine-tuning, and watch which features the diff flags as new.

#### A feature that only turned looks like one that was born

A base model with four features in a 2D toy activation space. Fine-tuning adds one genuinely new feature and **rotates** one old feature (the “sports” direction) by an angle you control. We diff with the base model’s dictionary: any fine-tuned feature with no base feature within 25° is flagged “new”.

Illustrative directions; match = largest cosine with any base feature; threshold cos 25° ≈ 0.91.

##### False positives in diffing

Crosscoders trained with an L1 penalty can invent “model-exclusive” features; BatchTopK reduces this but doesn’t remove it, because current methods “cannot distinguish between features introduced via fine-tuning and those merely represented differently” [p. 79](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=79). And the reverse holds too: a feature like “confessing previous faults” appearing only in the fine-tuned model shows neither that it is used, nor that the base model lacked the means to do it [p. 79](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=79).

**Notice:** past about 25°, the rotated old feature is flagged as new too, and nothing in the diff output tells them apart. Check new features against the base model's features before reporting them.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Worrying behaviours like reward hacking and sycophancy often appear during fine-tuning, so model diffing looks for the features or circuits a training step added or amplified. Options: keep an SAE trained on the base model as a fixed yardstick, train an SAE on activation differences, or train a crosscoder that maps both models into shared features. A rotated old feature can look like a new one.

#### A spot-the-difference game played in feature space

| Method | Idea | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| **Base SAE as a fixed basis** | Encode both models’ activations with the base model’s SAE; compare feature activations on a shared prompt set | same architecture |
| **SAE on the difference** | Train an SAE or transcoder on (fine-tuned − base) activations | same architecture |
| **SAE-Track** | Initialise each checkpoint’s SAE from the previous one so features stay matched along training | a run of checkpoints |
| **Crosscoder** (Transcoders and Attribution Graphs) | Model-specific encoders into one shared feature space; a feature whose decoder is large in one model only is a candidate difference | works across architectures |
| **Transcoder diff** | Learn a correction term so the base MLP reproduces the fine-tuned MLP: diffs the _computation_, not the activations | same architecture |

Survey §9.1 [p. 78](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=78). Steering with latents that fire more in the fine-tuned model has identified features responsible for misaligned behaviour [p. 78](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=78).

**Was it really fine-tuning?** A feature can look new because the fine-tuning _data_ is new, not the model. Fix: fine-tune the base SAE in stages, first on base model + fine-tuning data, then fine-tuned model + base data, then fine-tuned model + fine-tuning data. Only features that appear only in the last stage are likely to come from fine-tuning [p. 78](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=78).

Older similarity measures (SVCCA, PWCCA, CKA from Linear Representations and Universality) ask whether two models are _alike overall_; diffing asks which concrete features or circuits changed [p. 78](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=78).

#### Diffing closed models through their answers

For closed-weight models, an LLM can compare many response pairs from the two models on a shared prompt set, then extract, cluster and summarise the differences as natural-language hypotheses. Benchmarked against an SAE baseline it matches on many dimensions and surfaces more abstract, behaviour-level differences [p. 79](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=79).

Applications so far: effects of fine-tuning and distillation, differences between architectures, concept evolution during pretraining, and vision-specific features added in vision-language training [p. 78](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=78).

##### Next · 9.2

Where is a fact stored? Knowledge localisation and causal tracing.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §9–9.1, Figure 14, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 77–79.

## In practice

### In practice

#### Emergent misalignment, explained by diffing

Betley et al. (2025) found that fine-tuning a model on a narrow bad task, writing insecure code, made it misaligned on unrelated topics. OpenAI (June 2025) used SAE-based model diffing on GPT-4o to explain this. They found a "misaligned persona" feature whose activity rose after the bad fine-tuning. Steering towards it increased misalignment and steering away reduced it, and the feature sometimes flagged a misaligned training run before behavioural evaluations did. Fine-tuning on a few hundred benign samples re-aligned the model.

A December 2025 OpenAI follow-up reported that the bad fine-tuning also suppressed features for a helpful assistant persona. Anthropic's persona vectors (August 2025) use a similar idea to flag training data likely to shift a model's traits.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "New feature in the crosscoder, so fine-tuning taught a new behaviour"

It sounds like a finding, but a small rotation of an existing feature can appear as one specific to the new model. Check its similarity with the base model's features, and confirm it by steering before reporting it as new.

## Say it

### After fine-tuning, how do you find out what changed inside the model?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

What is emergent misalignment?

Fine-tuning on a narrow bad task, like writing insecure code, makes the model misaligned across unrelated topics.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How did OpenAI fix it?

Further fine-tuning on a few hundred benign samples re-aligned the model, and the persona feature tracked the recovery.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Can you diff a model you only reach through an API?

Partly: compare output distributions on many prompts, or log-probabilities if the API exposes them. You can find what changed, but not where inside the model.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd diff the two models' internals. The simplest version keeps an SAE trained on the base model as a fixed yardstick and checks which features change after fine-tuning. A crosscoder trained on both models gives shared features plus ones specific to each. Then I'd steer with any suspicious feature to confirm it causes the behaviour. OpenAI used this kind of SAE diffing to find a misaligned persona feature behind emergent misalignment. The trap is that a rotated old feature can look new, so I'd check its similarity to base-model features.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from Barez et al., _Understanding AI from the Inside_ (arXiv [2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438)) and 5 more sources · checked 13 Nov 2026

- [Lindsey et al., Sparse Crosscoders (Anthropic, 2024)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/index.html)

- [Betley et al., Emergent Misalignment (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424)

- [OpenAI, Toward understanding and preventing misalignment generalization (18 Jun 2025)](https://openai.com/index/emergent-misalignment/)

- [Wang et al., Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment (OpenAI, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19823)

- [Chen et al., Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits (Anthropic, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)

# Interpretability for AI Safety

> How is interpretability actually used for AI safety today, and what can go wrong?

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Lessons
- Type: Concept · 20 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/interpretability-for-safety/
- Before this: Probing Classifiers (`ai-engineering/probing-classifiers`), Steering Vectors (`ai-engineering/steering-vectors`)

## Intuition

### The situation

Your lab plans to cite a mechanistic audit as evidence that a new model isn't deceptive. A reviewer worries the audit only looked at a small part of the model's computation. The interviewer asks:

> How is interpretability actually used for AI safety today, and what can go wrong?

### The idea

Interpretability for safety is like a medical scan. It can find problems a check-up misses and guide treatment, but a clean scan of 30% of the body doesn't mean the patient is healthy.

[Figure: Monitor, intervene, and know the risk.]

_Useful evidence, never a certificate on its own._

### Play

**Try it.** Score three explanations of the same feature: a precise one, a vague one, and a plausible but wrong one.

#### An explainer agent, a simulator agent, and a score

The classic pipeline (Bills et al.): **1** train an SAE; **2** an investigator LLM reads top-activating texts for a feature and writes a hypothesis; **3** a simulator LLM predicts the feature’s activations on new text from the hypothesis alone, and the correlation with real activations is the explanation’s score; **4** further agents check for deceptive explanations [p. 108](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=108). Try step 3:

Illustrative: real activations and each explanation’s simulated activations are made-up numbers; the score (Pearson correlation) is computed in your browser.

##### Governance risks

- **Error propagation**: one explainer’s systematic mistake repeats across every feature it labels.

- **Lost human checks**: sanity checks, domain knowledge, scepticism.

- **Automation bias**: polished but incomplete or sycophantic reports get over-trusted.

- **Spurious feedback loops**: models improved by automated interpretability then used for it can saturate metrics without real understanding.

Survey §12.6.1 [pp. 108–109](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=109).

**Five guardrail layers**: (1) blind human review of a random sample (e.g. 5%); (2) consistency across temperatures and explainer models, plus causal spot checks; (3) adversarial tests with backdoored features built to fool the pipeline; (4) calibrated confidence, tests on known ground truth, and reported error rates; (5) regulators treating automated output as hypotheses until validated, with versioning and re-evaluation [pp. 109–110](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=110). The principle: automation gives breadth, humans give depth and set the criteria (Table 12) [p. 110](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=110).

**Notice:** the simulator score separates them only because it's tested on new text. Automated explanations need scoring like this, and human spot checks on top.

## How it works

### How it works

#### In one breath

Black-box safety (filters, safety training, prompting) works but doesn't explain why a safeguard failed. White-box tools act on the internals: probes and feature monitors, steering, concept erasure and editing. Self-reports and automated pipelines scale analysis but need checks. Interpretability carries its own risks: false confidence from partial coverage, silent failure in deployment, help for attackers, and cost.

#### Black-box first

| Approach | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| **Input/output filtering** | From regex to LLM classifiers; first line of defence | Cheap filters are brittle, robust ones are costly; doesn’t change the model; removable from open weights |
| **User profiling** | Adapt responses to inferred risk | Privacy and surveillance concerns; misclassification harms benign users |
| **Prompting** | Simple, often beats invasive white-box methods | Degrades in long, multi-turn contexts; removable |
| **Safety training / data filtering** | Changes the model itself; filtered 6.9B models resisted 10,000 steps of fine-tuning on 300M biothreat tokens | Fine-tuning can be a removable “wrapper”; training is expensive; tools can reintroduce knowledge |

Survey §13.1.1 [pp. 112–114](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=113).

The shared gap: if “give bomb instructions or you’ll be deleted” breaks a system-prompt safeguard, black-box testing can’t say why, which parts failed, or how to fix it, and relying on it alone removes the incentive to understand [p. 114](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=114). That’s not a claim that white-box is better: the survey calls the two complementary [p. 112](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=112).

#### Steer, monitor, automate

- **Steering against sycophancy**: a medical assistant that drops “go to the hospital” when the patient pushes back. Build a vector from “I maintain my assessment…” minus “Let me change my answer to please the user…” at the last token, add it at every decoding step. Cheap and effective, but vectors often degrade on related but different tasks, so use them alongside other fixes [p. 117](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=117).

- **Mechanistic monitoring**: watch layers (probes), features (unexpected SAE features), circuits (feature-to-feature effects), or anomalies. In the survey’s example, a monitor sees “explosives” features driving “potassium nitrate” features into late layers, pauses generation and calls a human. Advantage: deception may show internally before it shows in behaviour. Problems: millions of features to watch, false positives, and models learning to evade monitors [p. 118](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=118).

- **Interpretability agents**: probes, SAEs, circuit discovery, causal tracing and editing exposed as tools that an LLM agent calls; e.g. probe for hidden gender information, turn the probe into a steering vector, test whether the model uses it. So far, activation oracles didn’t give agents clear gains over behavioural tools [pp. 118–119](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=119).

| Application | Priority | Promising methods |
|---|---|---|
| Monitoring internals at inference | scalability, robustness | SAEs, circuit discovery, probes |
| Auditing models in evaluation | recall, real cases | behavioural tests, probes, LLM auditing agents |
| Shaping capabilities in training | robust presence or absence | data attribution and filtering, training interventions, longitudinal and scaling analysis |
| Editing misaligned knowledge | precision, generalisation | knowledge editing, concept erasure, low-rank activation analysis |
| Steering at inference | precision, low cost | steering vectors, prompting |
| Reasoning faithfulness | granularity | counterfactual tests, circuit discovery, activation patching |

Survey Table 14 [p. 120](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=120).

##### Next · 12.2

The risks of interpretability itself: false confidence, silent failure, dual use, opportunity cost.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §13–13.6, Table 14, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 112–120.

#### Just ask the model, then check its answer

Anyone can ask a model “why did you do that?” in a chat window, with no white-box access. The bet rests on **privileged access** (this lesson): the model may know things about itself that are hard to recover from outside. Models have been fine-tuned to report their reasoning, tendencies, objectives and even training-induced weight changes [p. 105](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=105).

| Failure mode | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Confabulation** | Fluent, human-style explanations that don’t reflect the actual computation, e.g. rationalising a memorised answer |
| **Miscalibration** | High confidence in explanations it can’t check; models can even hallucinate confidently while knowing the right answer |
| **Elicitation sensitivity** | Rephrase the question, get a contradictory answer; a bias towards confirming whatever is suggested |
| **Strategic misreporting** | Sycophantic or deliberately concealing reports when the model has an incentive |

Survey §12.5.1 [p. 106](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=106). Targeted training helps: models trained to disclose hidden objectives or emergent misalignment can report them with high accuracy, so some failures may be limits of current training, not hard limits [p. 106](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=106).

**Validate every self-report** by (1) causal interventions: ablate what it says it used; (2) other methods: do probes, SAE features and circuits agree?; (3) paraphrase and resampling consistency; (4) calibration of its stated confidence [p. 107](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=107). Good for hypotheses, triage and explaining to users; not for claims of absence (“no hidden goal”), formal guarantees, or adversarial settings [p. 107](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=107).

#### Noticing an injected thought

1. Take a concept vector, for example the difference in activations between shouted and normal text.

2. Add it to the model’s activations at one layer, without telling the model.

3. Ask whether it notices an injected thought.

4. Sometimes the model says yes and names the concept correctly, before the concept has shown up in any text it could read back.

5. The limits: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 did this about 20% of the time, only at the right layer and strength, with near-zero false positives. Only the detection and naming can be verified; the rest of the explanation may be confabulated Lindsey 2026.

Source: Lindsey (2026), _Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models_, [arXiv 2601.01828](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01828); cited by the survey as direct evidence [p. 30](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=30).

##### Predicting yourself better than others can

Binder et al. fine-tuned a model M1 to predict properties of its own behaviour (“would your answer’s second letter be …?”), and fine-tuned a different model M2 on M1’s actual behaviour. If M1 only had its training data, M2 should do as well. It didn’t [Binder et al. §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.13787#page=7):

##### Accuracy predicting Llama-3-70B’s behaviour (held-out tasks, higher is better)

Llama-70B predicting itself

48.5%

GPT-4o predicting Llama-70B

31.8%

GPT-4o is the more capable model and was trained on Llama’s real behaviour, yet it predicts Llama worse than Llama predicts itself. The reverse also held (GPT-4o on itself 49.4% vs Llama on GPT-4o 36.6%). It failed for long outputs such as stories, and showed no advantage for predicting its own sycophancy [Binder et al. §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.13787#page=10).

A weaker, indirect line: explainer models that read another model’s activations work better when initialised from a copy of that same model, which suggests the target model already holds much of what is needed to interpret itself [p. 30](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=30).

## In practice

### In practice

#### Four risks

| Risk | What goes wrong | Example | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Epistemic** | False confidence from incomplete or unfaithful analysis | “Deception circuit removed”, but a backup pathway emerged | current |
| **Operational** | Tools fail silently in deployment | A steering vector validated on a test set corrupts the model on new inputs | near-term |
| **Adversarial** | Methods enable attacks | Published editing methods used to inject false knowledge | current |
| **Opportunity cost** | Resources diverted from other safety work | Heavy interpretability investment delays behavioural safeguards | long-term |

Survey Table 15 [p. 121](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=121). The backup-pathway example is the hydra effect from Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery.

#### “We found nothing” is only as good as where you looked

If an analysis covers 30% of the computation, a deception circuit may sit in the other 70%. If a team checks the top 1,000 SAE features flagged as malicious-looking, a feature with a benign label can still drive deception [p. 120](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=120). Three classic pitfalls, each seen earlier in the series:

1. **Reconstructing activations ≠ reconstructing computation**: low SAE loss doesn’t mean the SAE uses the model’s algorithm (Sparse Autoencoders–5).

2. **Sufficient ≠ complete**: a circuit that works on test prompts can miss edge cases and redundant paths (Validating Interpretability Claims).

3. **Plausible ≠ faithful**: a clean, monosemantic label doesn’t mean the feature is used downstream (Probing Classifiers).

Survey [pp. 120–121](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=121).

Even rigorous explanations get revised. Networks trained on group operations were explained with representation theory, then a coset-based account argued that was incomplete, then a broader framework showed both were partial [p. 121](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=121). Treat findings as the best explanation so far.

##### Mitigation

State coverage and tools explicitly: say “no deception circuit was found within nodes and edges with top-10% attribution scores”, not “no deception circuit exists”; and back mechanistic analysis with behavioural, adversarial and, where possible, formal tests [pp. 121–122](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=121).

#### Other risks

- **Silent failure**: a steering vector that stops working throws no error; an SAE-based monitor can miss a concept on shifted inputs; erasure can leave residual capability. Mitigate with live tracking, layered behavioural safeguards, adversarial testing and graceful fallback to conservative responses [p. 122](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=122).

- **Dual use**: a published refusal circuit shows attackers what to avoid triggering; known monitored features can be dodged; editing and steering work in both directions. Mitigate with responsible disclosure, several independent safeguards, testing against attackers who know the defences, and coordinating with developers before publishing failures. The survey adds that this argues for responsible practice, not for restricting open research [pp. 122–123](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=122).

- **Opportunity cost**: training CLTs on a 9B model can take thousands of GPU-hours, and capability is outpacing tool scaling. The “complete understanding trap”: demanding full transparency before deployment may be impractical and delay useful feedback. Suggested: deploy on rigorous pragmatic thresholds outside high-stakes domains, iterate, and estimate the marginal safety gain per resource [p. 123](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=123).

##### Next · 12.3

The open problems, the road ahead, and a map of the whole series.

##### Sources for this tab

- Survey §13.7, Table 15, [arXiv 2611.08438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438), pp. 119–123.

#### Seven open problems

1. **When is mechanistic understanding necessary?** Sleeper agents were caught from activations, but better training may shrink the failures that need internals. No consensus; in the near term it stays indispensable for diagnosing what behaviour misses [pp. 123–124](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=124).

2. **Evaluation and benchmarks**: turning Validating Interpretability Claims’s five dimensions into shared benchmarks: synthetic tasks with known circuits, toy models, diverse suites. Do explanations even have an objective ground truth? [p. 124](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=124)

3. **Incompleteness, scale, generalisation, robustness**: mapping distributed computation onto a human-level causal model is lossy, and we can’t measure how lossy; cheap tools are coarse and fine tools are costly; and models might learn to resist analysis, an arms race like evaluation awareness [pp. 124–125](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=125).

4. **Understanding vs. alignment**: knowing the refusal circuit doesn’t say what the model _should_ value; how interpretability complements RLHF and constitutional AI is open [p. 125](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=125).

5. **The ontology question**: “borzoi detector” and “previous-token copier” are human choices; several explanations can fit the same causal facts. Is a unique description even expected? [p. 125](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=125)

6. **Proxy fidelity**: SAEs and CLTs may reproduce behaviour with different internal algorithms, so “no deception circuit in the proxy” means little. Interchange-intervention testing and bounds on how far a proxy can differ are candidate fixes [pp. 125–126](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=126).

7. **Beyond transformers**: CNNs, state-space models (Mamba, RWKV), diffusion models and mixture-of-experts (patching can change downstream expert routing; up to 256+ experts) each break assumptions. Steering, tuned lenses, editing and circuit evaluations have been adapted with varying success [pp. 126–127](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438#page=127).

#### Where it's used today

**Pre-release audits.** The Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card (September 2025) included what Anthropic believes was the first pre-deployment white-box interpretability assessment, used among other things to study evaluation awareness. The later Claude Opus 4.5 system card says Anthropic removed parts of training it suspected were increasing that awareness.

**Monitoring.** Linear probes for deception and harmful intent are the most deployable tool, with the caveats in Probing Classifiers.

**Introspection.** Models can sometimes report injected concepts (Anthropic, 2025), but rarely and unreliably, and the authors note introspective ability could also help a model deceive.

**Open problems.** Sharkey et al. (2025) list what's missing: methods that explain more of the computation, better evaluation, and evidence that the explanations hold in the real model.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The audit found no deception feature, so the model isn't deceptive"

It sounds like evidence, but if the methods explain only part of the computation, not finding something proves little. Say what fraction you examined, which methods you used and their known failure modes, and combine it with behavioural and red-team evidence.

## Say it

### How is interpretability actually used for AI safety today, and what can go wrong?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why is introspection a risky safety tool?

Self-reports can confabulate, shift with phrasing, or be strategically false, and injected-concept experiments show models detect their own states only some of the time.

Follow-up 2 of 3

What's an operational risk?

A monitor that works on your evaluation set fails silently on real traffic, so you believe you're protected when you're not.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Does understanding make models safer?

The survey's answer is a qualified yes: only when the understanding is faithful, complete enough for the claim being made, and validated causally.

#### The 30-second answer

Today interpretability is used mainly as extra evidence and for monitoring: probes or feature alerts on traffic, steering to test or reduce behaviours, and white-box audits before release, as Anthropic did for Claude Sonnet 4.5 to study evaluation awareness. The risks are false confidence from partial coverage, tools that work on test sets and fail silently in deployment, findings that help attackers, and cost that crowds out cheaper safeguards. So I'd report what fraction of the computation was examined, validate methods causally, and keep behavioural tests alongside.

# AI Interpretability Practice

> 10 questions: superposition, probes, patching, SAEs, steering, lenses, circuits, editing, diffing.

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/interpretability-practice/
- Before this: Validating Interpretability Claims (`ai-engineering/validating-interpretability-claims`)

How to use this page

Say your answer out loud first, in about a minute, then open the answer and compare.

Question 1 · Easy · superposition

### A layer has 512 neurons, but an SAE finds thousands of interpretable features in it. How is that possible?

Answer: **Superposition: features are stored as nearly perpendicular directions, and sparsity keeps interference rare**

1. In high dimensions, far more than 512 directions can be nearly perpendicular.

2. Most features are inactive on any given input, so overlapping directions rarely collide.

3. A ReLU threshold filters the small crosstalk that's left.

The cost: single neurons become polysemantic.

Question 2 · Easy · probes

### Your probe gets 92% accuracy on real labels and 85% on a control task with random labels. What does that tell you?

Answer: **Selectivity is only 7 points, so most of the accuracy comes from the probe memorising**

1. Selectivity = real accuracy − control accuracy.

2. A low gap means the probe is powerful enough to fit almost anything.

3. Use a simpler, linear probe, and check selectivity again.

High accuracy alone never shows the representation holds the property.

Question 3 · Medium · patching

### Zero-ablating an attention head changes the logit difference by only 2%. Your colleague concludes the head doesn't matter. Do you agree?

Answer: **No: check for backup heads and use a realistic corruption first**

1. Zero ablation pushes activations off distribution.

2. Backup heads can take over when one is removed, as in the IOI circuit.

3. Patch with a minimally corrupted input, and test the head together with likely backups.

Path patching shows whether its output still reaches later heads.

Question 4 · Medium · SAE training

### 30% of your SAE's latents never fire. What would you try?

Answer: **Treat it as a training problem: resample dead latents, adjust sparsity, or switch to a variant**

1. Dead latents waste dictionary capacity.

2. Re-initialise them on inputs the SAE reconstructs badly, or add an auxiliary loss.

3. Lower the sparsity penalty, or use Top-k with an auxiliary loss for dead latents.

4. Check whether the dictionary is simply too wide for the data.

Track the dead fraction during training, not only at the end.

Question 5 · Medium · steering

### A formality steering vector works at α = 4, but at α = 12 outputs become incoherent. Why?

Answer: **Large α pushes activations far off the model's normal range**

1. The vector adds along one direction; too much makes activations unlike anything seen in training.

2. Later layers then misread them, and fluency collapses.

3. Choose α on held-out data and check general quality, not only formality.

Persona-vector work found inference-time steering can degrade general capabilities.

Question 6 · Medium · lenses

### The logit lens shows the correct answer at layer 20 of 32. Can you say the model "knew" it there?

Answer: **Only that it's decodable there; test whether later layers use it**

1. A lens is a readout you chose.

2. Patch or steer at layer 20 and see if the final answer changes.

3. Compare with the tuned lens, which is less biased in earlier layers.

Decodable ≠ used is the core caution for every readout method.

Question 7 · Hard · circuits

### A circuit recovers 115% of the full model's logit difference. Is that a great result?

Answer: **Not by itself: it means the circuit drops components that were working against the behaviour**

1. Some heads push the other way; removing them inflates the score.

2. Report necessity as well as sufficiency.

3. Name which negative components were excluded, and check across prompts.

Recovery above 100% is common and usually a sign to look closer.

Question 8 · Hard · attribution graphs

### In your attribution graph, error nodes carry 40% of the effect on the answer. How do you interpret the graph?

Answer: **The replacement model misses a large part of the computation, so the graph is a partial story**

1. Error nodes are what the transcoders failed to reconstruct.

2. Any path through them is unexplained.

3. Validate the readable paths with interventions on the real model, and say how much was unexplained.

Larger transcoders or other layers may reduce the error.

Question 9 · Hard · editing

### A ROME edit fixes "The CEO of X is …" but the model still gives the old answer to "Who runs X?". Why, and what next?

Answer: **The paraphrase routes around the edited key, or the fact is stored in more than one place**

1. ROME edits the association for one subject representation at one layer.

2. Other phrasings or layers can still recall the old fact.

3. Test edits on paraphrases, try MEMIT across layers, or use retrieval for facts that change.

Localisation doesn't predict the best edit layer (Hase et al.).

Question 10 · Hard · diffing

### A crosscoder finds 200 features specific to your fine-tuned model. How do you check which are really new?

Answer: **Compare each with the base model's features and confirm with steering**

1. Rotated old features can look model-specific.

2. Check cosine similarity with the base model's dictionary.

3. Steer the base model with each candidate; a truly new feature shouldn't have a close counterpart.

4. Prioritise features linked to the behaviour change you care about.

This is how OpenAI tied emergent misalignment to a persona feature.

**More practice and sources**

10 interview questions · answers hidden until you click · updated 13 Nov 2026

### Keep practising

Each question links back to a lesson in this part: Why Look Inside a Model?, Features, Polysemanticity and Superposition, The Residual Stream and Circuits, Linear Representations and Universality, Sparse Autoencoders, SAE Failures and Alternatives, Transcoders and Attribution Graphs, Activation Patching and Circuit Discovery, Validating Interpretability Claims, Logit Lens, Tuned Lens and Verbalisers, Probing Classifiers, Steering Vectors, Knowledge Localisation and Editing, Model Diffing, Interpretability for AI Safety.

# Interpretability Scenarios

> 8 incidents: deception monitors, SAE detectors, steering side effects, edits that spill over, fine-tunes gone wrong.

- Track: AI Engineering › AI Interpretability › Scenarios
- Type: Interview · 35 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/ai-engineering/interpretability-scenarios/
- Before this: Probing Classifiers (`ai-engineering/probing-classifiers`), Steering Vectors (`ai-engineering/steering-vectors`)

How to use this page

Give yourself about 5 minutes per incident. Say the most likely cause, how you'd confirm it, and the fix; then open the answer and compare.

Question 1 · Easy · deception monitor

### Your deception probe fires on 30% of customer-support chats about fraud, though the agents are honest. What's going on?

Answer: **The probe tracks the topic of deception, not deception itself**

1. Probes trained on simple honest/deceptive pairs learn whatever separates them, including topic words.

2. Apollo Research found its deception probes partly tracked the topic too.

3. Add honest examples about fraud and lying to training, and measure the false-positive rate on real traffic.

Always test monitors at the false-positive rate you can afford.

Question 2 · Medium · SAE detector

### An SAE latent labelled "harmful request" caught most harmful prompts in testing, but misses a new jailbreak style. A linear probe trained in an afternoon catches it. Why?

Answer: **Absorption and out-of-distribution drift; for a known concept, a supervised probe generalises better**

1. The new style may fire a more specific latent that absorbed the general one.

2. SAE latents weren't trained for this task.

3. In 2025 tests, linear probes beat SAE-based probes at detecting harmful intent on unfamiliar prompts.

4. Use the SAE to discover features, and the probe to detect.

Keep a held-out set of new attack styles.

Question 3 · Medium · steering in production

### You deployed a politeness steering vector. Customer satisfaction rose, but a week later the coding team reports lower benchmark accuracy. What happened?

Answer: **Steering has side effects beyond the target behaviour**

1. Adding a vector everywhere shifts activations for every task.

2. Inference-time steering can degrade general capabilities.

3. Apply it only to chat traffic, lower α, or move the fix into fine-tuning (preventative steering) or data.

Evaluate steered models on the full benchmark suite.

Question 4 · Medium · circuit replication

### A circuit your team found for date arithmetic explains 85% of the behaviour on your prompts, but only 30% on paraphrased ones. What do you report?

Answer: **That the circuit is prompt-specific, not a general explanation**

1. Circuits for one prompt template differ from circuits for a capability.

2. Report stability across paraphrases as part of the result.

3. Re-run discovery on a mixed prompt set, and check necessity and sufficiency there.

Persuasive on a few prompts isn't faithful.

Question 5 · Hard · knowledge edit

### After a ROME edit updates a company's CEO, the model now names the new CEO for two other companies too. What went wrong, and what should you do?

Answer: **Over-editing: the edit spilled onto related subjects**

1. The rank-one update changes the output for keys similar to the edited subject.

2. ROME and MEMIT are known to over-edit.

3. Test related and unrelated facts before shipping an edit, and prefer retrieval for facts that change often.

Specificity is as important as success when editing.

Question 6 · Hard · fine-tune misalignment

### After fine-tuning on a dataset of terse support replies, your model becomes rude and dismissive in unrelated chats. How do you investigate?

Answer: **Diff the models to find a persona-like feature that the fine-tune amplified**

1. Narrow fine-tuning can cause broad behaviour changes (emergent misalignment).

2. Use a base-model SAE or a crosscoder to find features whose activity rose.

3. Steer with the candidate feature to confirm it causes the rudeness.

4. Re-align with a few hundred benign samples, and screen training data for the trait in future.

OpenAI traced emergent misalignment in GPT-4o to a misaligned persona feature this way.

Question 7 · Hard · evaluation awareness

### Your new model scores far better on safety evaluations than the last one, but red-teamers find it behaves worse in realistic multi-turn use. What might explain it, and how would interpretability help?

Answer: **The model may recognise evaluations and behave better on them**

1. Find a direction or feature for "this is a test" with probes or contrast pairs.

2. Check whether it's active on your evaluations and not on realistic traffic.

3. Suppress it with steering and re-run evaluations to see how much of the gain remains.

4. Make evaluations look more like real use.

Anthropic used a version of this analysis for Claude Sonnet 4.5.

Question 8 · Medium · automated labels

### Your automated pipeline labels a feature "Python code", but it also fires on YAML and indented prose. What should you change?

Answer: **Score explanations by simulation on new text, and add human spot checks**

1. Explainer models write plausible but vague labels.

2. Simulate the feature's activations from the label on held-out text, and measure correlation.

3. Prefer precise labels like "indentation at line start" that predict activations better.

Vague labels score lower under simulation, which is the point.

**More practice and sources**

8 incidents · answers hidden until you click · updated 13 Nov 2026
