# Design a Shared Recommendation Foundation Model

> A large app runs hundreds of separate recommendation models, one per surface, each trained on its own slice of data. Design one large foundation model that makes all of them better.

- Track: System Design › Recommendation Systems › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-rec-foundation-model/
- Before this: Distillation: How Small Models Learn from Big Ones (`fundamentals/distillation`), The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A large app runs hundreds of recommendation models, one per surface: feed, video, ads and search. Each learns only from its own slice of data, and improvements in one rarely help another. The interviewer asks:

> A large app runs hundreds of separate recommendation models, one per surface, each trained on its own slice of data. Design one large foundation model that makes all of them better.

#### Ask before designing

- **Today:** hundreds of per-surface models (feed, video, ads, search), each seeing only its own data.

- **Data:** long histories of views, clicks, add-to-carts, purchases and searches, up to thousands of events per user.

- **Constraints:** each surface has tight latency; the big model can't run on every request.

- **Must never happen:** a stale teacher quietly making students worse, or one surface's objective hurting another.

- **Success metrics:** per-surface online outcomes (conversions, orders, clicks that lead somewhere), plus training efficiency.

### The idea

Think of a head chef who trains every cook in a restaurant chain. The head chef doesn't cook every dish; they teach recipes and techniques, and each kitchen still cooks fast for its own customers.

[Figure: Long event sequences from every surface train one large next-item model. It transfers to small per-surface models by distillation and shared embeddings, or serves as one retriever.]

_Train big once; serve small everywhere._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between the two systems.

#### Two systems, measured on their own surfaces

From each company's post: ads results were launch figures for a quarter; commerce results were relative lifts in an online A/B test.

Notice the two uses. One is a **teacher** that improves hundreds of existing models; the other is a **new candidate source** added beside existing retrievers. Both avoid serving the giant model on every ranking call.

**Now say why:** why do neither of them run the large model on every ranking request?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Train one large model on **long sequences of user events** across every surface, predicting the **next item** the way a language model predicts the next token. It's too big to serve everywhere, so **transfer** what it learns: distil it into the smaller per-surface models, share its embeddings with them, or let it serve as one retrieval source among several. Each surface keeps its own objective and latency budget.

#### One teacher, many students

1. **Event sequences:** build each user's sequence of actions across surfaces, with timestamps, without compressing it into one fixed vector.

2. **Foundation model:** a transformer with a causal mask predicts the next item; time gaps and recency are encoded explicitly. Non-sequence features (user and item attributes) feed interaction layers alongside.

3. **Training:** a sampled softmax over millions of items, with negatives shared across the batch and hard negatives that avoid true positives.

4. **Transfer:** the foundation model labels data and produces embeddings for the per-surface models: distillation, shared representations, or both. Large surfaces learn directly; smaller ones through domain models.

5. **Serving:** per-surface models stay small and fast. The foundation model can also serve as one retrieval model among several, with rankers and diversity rules after it.

##### Stale teachers

The teacher is trained less often than students, so its labels age. A small adapter that corrects the teacher's outputs using the newest data keeps students learning from fresh signals.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Training events | 500 million users × 2,000 events | **1 trillion** |
| Per-surface models | given | **200** |
| Teacher labels a day | 200 surfaces × 1 billion examples | **200 billion forward passes** |
| Item embeddings | 10 million items × 256 dims × 2 bytes | **about 5 GB** |

Generating teacher labels is a large ongoing cost, so share embeddings where possible and generate labels only for the training data students actually use.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every foundation-model design gets asked

- **Why one model:** each surface alone sees little data; one model learns from all of them, so an engagement signal on one app can improve predictions on another.

- **Long sequences:** compressing histories into a fixed vector loses signal; attention over thousands of events needs custom kernels and efficient training.

- **Cold start:** item IDs alone don't help new items; content features, or semantic IDs built from content, let new items share what similar items learned.

- **Efficiency:** lighter variants of the model let most experiments run cheaply; large-scale training needs careful parallelism and compilation caching.

- **Ensembles:** as a retriever, train it to find what other retrievers miss, treating their predictions as hard negatives.

- **Rollout:** ship to the largest surfaces first, measure each surface's own metric, and keep the old models as a fallback.

#### What the real systems reported

- **Ads foundation model:** learns from ads and organic activity across apps, with sequences up to thousands of events; transfers to hundreds of smaller models directly and through domain models, by distillation, representation learning and parameter sharing; 23× more effective training compute; 5% more ad conversions on one app and 3% on another's feed.

- **Commerce model:** a next-product transformer trained on searches, views, add-to-carts, favourites and purchases; one retrieval model in an ensemble; +0.94% orders, +5% high-quality clicks and +0.71% conversion in an online test.

From the two posts (Nov 2025 and Feb 2026). Neither reports serving latency figures.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Replace all the small models with the big one"

It sounds simpler, but each surface scores thousands of items per request in milliseconds, which a huge model can't do. The gains come from teaching the small models, or adding the big one as a retriever, not from serving it everywhere.

## Say it

### A large app runs hundreds of separate recommendation models, one per surface, each trained on its own slice of data. Design one large foundation model that makes all of them better.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not serve the foundation model directly?

Latency and cost: per-surface models score thousands of items per request in milliseconds. Distillation and shared embeddings carry most of the gain into those small models.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Students got worse a month after launch. Why?

The teacher's labels went stale as behaviour changed. Retrain the teacher more often, or correct its outputs with an adapter trained on the newest data.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How does this help new items?

Not through ID embeddings, which need history. Use content features or semantic IDs, so a new item starts near similar items.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd clarify how many surfaces and models exist, the data available and each surface's latency. I'd train one large transformer on long, time-stamped event sequences across all surfaces, predicting the next item with a sampled softmax and hard negatives, plus interaction layers for non-sequence features. It's too expensive to serve on every request, so its value comes through transfer: it labels data and shares embeddings to distil into the small per-surface models, directly for big surfaces and via domain models for small ones. A small adapter corrects stale teacher outputs with fresh data. It can also act as one more retriever in an ensemble. I'd roll out surface by surface, measure each surface's own metric, and handle new items with content-based features or semantic IDs.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on published posts: a social network's [generative ads model](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/11/10/ml-applications/metas-generative-ads-model-gem-the-central-brain-accelerating-ads-recommendation-ai-innovation/) (Nov 2025) and a commerce platform's [generative recommendations](https://shopify.engineering/generative-recommendations) (Feb 2026). The lab uses the posts' reported results; the estimate is ours. Uses distillation, transformers and next-token prediction. · checked 15 Nov 2026

# Design Real-Time Fraud Detection

> An online payments company must decide in under 100 ms whether each payment is fraud. Fraud is about 1 in 1,000 payments, and blocking good customers loses money too. Design the system.

- Track: System Design › Fraud and Risk › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-fraud-detection/
- Before this: Class Imbalance (`fundamentals/class-imbalance`), Thresholds & Misclassification Costs (`fundamentals/thresholds-and-costs`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

An online payments company handles 10 million payments a day for many merchants. About 1 in 1,000 is fraud. Each payment needs a decision inside checkout, in under 100 ms, and every good customer blocked is a lost sale. The interviewer asks:

> An online payments company must decide in under 100 ms whether each payment is fraud. Fraud is about 1 in 1,000 payments, and blocking good customers loses money too. Design the system.

#### Ask before designing

- **Scale:** say 10 million payments a day, peaking at 500 a second, across many merchants.

- **Latency:** the decision sits inside checkout, so under 100 ms end to end.

- **Actions:** allow, block, or ask for extra verification such as a one-time password.

- **Costs:** a missed fraud costs the payment plus fees; a blocked good customer loses the sale and maybe the customer.

- **Must never happen:** the scoring service being down and blocking all payments, or a large share of good customers declined.

- **Success metrics:** fraud caught (recall), good payments blocked (false positive rate), fraud losses and checkout conversion.

### The idea

Think of a bank teller who has seen every customer at every branch. A stranger's card was tried at ten shops this morning? The teller notices instantly. Unsure cases get a quick ID check instead of a refusal, and whether they got it right only shows up weeks later.

[Figure: A payment arrives. Hundreds of fresh features are fetched, many counted across the whole network. The model scores it in milliseconds. Rules and thresholds decide: allow, verify or block.]

_Network-wide signals catch what one shop never sees._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the threshold from 0.9 down to 0.6. Then turn on verification, then network features.

#### Where do you draw the line?

Illustrative: 10 million payments a day, 1 in 1,000 fraudulent (the rate the post gives), $80 average fraud, made-up score curves, and verification stopping 80% of fraud that reaches it.

A high threshold blocks few good customers but lets lots of fraud through. Lower it and you block more good customers. **Verification** changes the trade: uncertain payments get a check instead of a block, so most fraud is stopped and good customers can still pay. **Better features** beat any threshold, because they separate fraud from good payments in the first place.

**Now say why:** why do better features beat any choice of threshold?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Score every payment in **under 100 ms** with a model that sees **hundreds of features**, many of them **network-wide counts** computed in real time, like how many cards one IP address has used today. Fraud is rare and its labels arrive **weeks later**, so train on matured data and watch for drift. Don't just block or allow: send the uncertain middle to **extra verification**. Explain decisions to merchants, let them add **rules**, and judge the system on both fraud caught and good customers blocked.

#### The path of one payment

1. **Request:** checkout sends the payment details: card, amount, merchant, device, IP, email.

2. **Features:** look up precomputed and real-time features, like how many payments this card made in the last hour, how many cards this IP has used today, and whether the name matches the email. Streaming counters keep these fresh.

3. **Score:** the model returns a fraud probability within the latency budget.

4. **Decide:** merchant rules and thresholds turn the score into allow, block or verify.

5. **Log:** store the features and decision, so the outcome can be joined weeks later to make training data.

##### Why network-wide features matter

A single merchant sees a stolen card once. A payments network sees it tried at ten shops in an hour. Counts and patterns across the whole network are often the strongest signals.

##### If the scorer fails

Decide in advance: fall back to rules, or allow low-risk payments, so an outage doesn't block every customer.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud cases a day | 10 million × 0.1% | **about 10,000** |
| Peak scoring rate | given | **500 a second** |
| Feature lookups a second | 500 × 1,000 features, mostly batched | **about 500,000** |
| Training rows a year | 10 million × 365 | **about 3.7 billion** |
| Labelled fraud a year | 3.7 billion × 0.1% | **about 3.7 million** |

The model call is cheap; fetching hundreds of fresh features in a few milliseconds is the hard part, so features live in a fast online store fed by streaming counters.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every fraud design gets asked

- **Delayed labels:** disputes and chargebacks arrive weeks later. Train on data old enough for labels to settle, and use early signals, like manual reviews and refunds, for faster feedback.

- **Feedback loop:** you never learn whether a blocked payment was really fraud. Let a tiny random share of borderline payments through, or verify them, to keep unbiased data.

- **Model choice:** start simple, then move to tree ensembles or deep networks as data grows. A model that retrains in hours lets you react to new attacks fast.

- **Feature work is the biggest lever:** study past attacks, look for signals like throwaway emails or card-testing bursts, and check them across the whole network.

- **Explanations:** show merchants why a payment was declined, such as mismatched name and email or many cards on one IP, so they trust and tune the system.

- **Rules:** let merchants add allow and block rules for their own business, alongside the model.

- **Drift and attacks:** fraud patterns change, for example to rapid card testing. Monitor scores and fraud rates by segment, and retrain often.

##### Rollout

Run a new model in shadow mode, compare its decisions with the current model on settled labels, then ramp it up merchant segment by segment.

#### What the real system reported

- **Speed and features:** more than 1,000 characteristics of each transaction, with a decision in under 100 milliseconds.

- **Results:** fraud around 1 in every 1,000 payments; only 0.1% of legitimate payments incorrectly blocked.

- **Models:** from simpler models like logistic regression to deep networks; in 2022 a Wide & Deep ensemble with XGBoost became a pure deep network inspired by ResNeXt. Dropping XGBoost alone would have cost 1.5% recall, but the new design cut training time by over 85%, to under two hours.

- **Data and features:** 10× more training data still brought significant gains; feature engineering, from studying attacks and the whole network, is one of the biggest levers.

- **Explanations and rules:** risk insights show the features behind a decline, like name and email mismatch or many cards on one IP; merchants can add allow and block rules.

The company's own figures. The post doesn't cover label delay, retraining cadence or thresholds.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Our model is 99.9% accurate"

It sounds great, but with 1 fraud in 1,000 payments, approving everything is also 99.9% accurate. Accuracy hides the trade-off that matters. Report fraud caught and good payments blocked, and set thresholds from the cost of each mistake.

## Say it

### An online payments company must decide in under 100 ms whether each payment is fraud. Fraud is about 1 in 1,000 payments, and blocking good customers loses money too. Design the system.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Fraud labels arrive 60 days late. How do you know the model is still working today?

Watch score distributions and feature drift, track early signals like manual review outcomes and refunds, and compare segments. When attacks shift, these move long before chargebacks arrive.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not just block everything above 0.5?

Fraud is so rare that a low threshold blocks far more good customers than fraudsters, and each blocked customer is lost revenue. Set thresholds from the costs, and use verification for the uncertain middle.

Follow-up 3 of 3

A new card-testing attack starts today. What happens?

Real-time counters on cards per IP and rapid small payments catch it quickly; rules can block the pattern immediately, and fast retraining folds it into the model within hours.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the volume, the latency budget, the actions available and the cost of each mistake. Each payment arrives at checkout; I'd fetch hundreds of features in milliseconds from an online store fed by streaming counters, including network-wide signals like how many cards an IP has used today. The model scores it within the budget, and thresholds plus merchant rules decide: allow, block, or send the uncertain middle to extra verification. Everything is logged, so outcomes can be joined later. Labels like chargebacks arrive weeks late, so I'd train on matured data, use early signals for faster feedback, and let a small random share of borderline payments through to avoid a feedback loop. I'd start with a simple model and move to deeper ones as data grows, keeping retraining fast. I'd measure fraud caught, good payments blocked and losses, explain declines to merchants, and fail safe if the scorer goes down. New models run in shadow mode first.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a payments company's published post: [Stripe's "How we built it: Stripe Radar"](https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-stripe-radar) (March 2023). The post doesn't cover label delay, retraining cadence or thresholds, so those parts, the lab's numbers and the estimate are ours. Uses class imbalance, thresholds and costs and feature stores. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design Feed Ranking

> A photo and video app shows each user a feed of posts from billions of candidates. Design the ranking so people see what they value, quickly, without filling the feed with clickbait.

- Track: System Design › Feeds and Ranking › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-feed-ranking/
- Before this: Ranking Metrics (`fundamentals/ranking-metrics`), Embeddings and Vector Indexes (`ai-engineering/embeddings-and-vector-indexes`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A photo and video app has hundreds of millions of daily users and billions of posts. Its discovery feed shows posts from accounts users don't follow. Engagement is up, but so are complaints about clickbait and repetitive feeds. The interviewer asks:

> A photo and video app shows each user a feed of posts from billions of candidates. Design the ranking so people see what they value, quickly, without filling the feed with clickbait.

#### Ask before designing

- **Surface:** a feed of posts from accounts the user doesn't follow, refreshed when they open it.

- **Scale:** hundreds of millions of daily users and billions of posts.

- **Latency:** the first screen must load in well under a second.

- **What "good" means:** not just clicks: likes, saves, shares and time well spent, minus negative feedback like "see less".

- **Must never happen:** harmful content surfaced, or a feed of one author or the same clickbait.

- **Success metrics:** engagement per session, negative feedback rate, return visits and integrity incidents.

### The idea

Think of a magazine editor with a mountain of submissions. Assistants quickly shortlist a few hundred, a senior editor reads the best hundred closely and predicts how readers will react, and the final layout avoids two pieces by the same writer side by side.

[Figure: Many sources pull thousands of candidates. A light model keeps about a hundred. A heavy model predicts each action, and a value model combines them before integrity and diversity rules.]

_Cheap steps cut the pile; the expensive model sees only the best._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set all three weights to zero. Then raise the "see less" penalty. Then turn on the diversity rule.

#### Which post goes first?

**The feed, top to bottom**

Illustrative: four made-up posts with predicted probabilities, and clicks always weighted 1. The formula follows the post's value model: a weighted sum of predicted actions, minus negative ones.

Set every weight to zero so only clicks count: **clickbait wins**, because it gets clicked and then regretted. Raise the "see less" penalty and shares, and posts people value move up. These weights are product decisions, tuned against online metrics, not learned by the model itself.

**Now say why:** why does ranking by clicks alone push clickbait to the top?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Use a **funnel**. Many **retrieval sources** pull a few thousand candidates from billions; a **light model** narrows them to about a hundred; a **heavy multi-task model** predicts click, like, share and "see less" for each; a **value model** combines those predictions with tunable weights; and a final step applies **integrity and diversity** rules. Cache embeddings, precompute where you can, and tune the weights against online metrics.

#### The funnel

1. **Retrieval:** several sources each return hundreds of candidates: a two-tower model matching user and post embeddings through an ANN index, posts similar to what the user liked, saved or shared, trending and locally popular posts. Their outputs are mixed with tunable weights.

2. **First-stage ranking:** a light two-tower model, trained to imitate the heavy model, narrows a few thousand candidates to about a hundred.

3. **Second-stage ranking:** a heavy multi-task network predicts the probability of each action (click, like, share, see less) using rich user–post interaction features.

4. **Value model:** one score per post: a weighted sum of the predicted probabilities, with negative actions subtracted.

5. **Final re-ranking:** remove or demote harmful content, then apply diversity rules such as no two posts from the same author in a row.

##### Why a funnel?

The heavy model can't score billions of posts in time. Cheap steps cut the set, so the expensive model only sees the best hundred.

##### Caching and precomputing

Post embeddings are computed daily and served from an ANN index; user embeddings are computed fresh. At peak hours, some users' recommendations can be precomputed off-peak.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Feed requests a second at peak | 300 million users × 5 opens ÷ 86,400 × 3 | **about 52,000** |
| First-stage scores a second | 52,000 × 3,000 candidates | **about 156 million** |
| Heavy-model scores a second | 52,000 × 100 | **about 5.2 million** |
| Post embedding index | 2 billion posts × 128 dims × 2 bytes | **about 512 GB** |

The light stage must be cheap per item, which is why it uses cached embeddings; the heavy model's budget is spent only on the top hundred.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every feed design gets asked

- **Why multi-task?** One model predicting several actions shares what it learns, and the value model can change the balance between them without retraining.

- **Distillation:** train the light model to predict which posts the heavy model would put in its top results, so the two stages agree.

- **Freshness:** retrain or fine-tune frequently, even hourly, and compute user embeddings from recent activity.

- **Cold start:** new posts get exposure through trending or exploration sources until they have engagement data.

- **Feedback loops:** the model learns from what it showed; keep some exploration so new creators and topics get a chance.

- **Tuning:** hundreds of parameters, like source weights and value-model weights, tuned online with careful experiments, or offline when offline metrics predict online ones well.

- **Integrity:** filter harmful content before ranking where possible, and demote borderline content in the final step.

##### Rollout

Test ranking changes with A/B tests on engagement and negative feedback, run long enough to see past novelty, with guardrails on integrity and creator diversity.

#### What the real system reported

- **Scale:** hundreds of millions of daily visitors, and a media pool of billions of items.

- **Funnel:** retrieval from several sources, each selecting hundreds of items; a light first stage over thousands of candidates; a heavy second stage over the best 100; final re-ranking with integrity and diversity rules.

- **Retrieval:** a two-tower model with daily item embeddings in an ANN service and online user embeddings, plus similar-items retrieval from what the user liked, saved or shared, with low-quality items filtered out.

- **Ranking:** the first stage is a two-tower model distilled from the second; the second is a multi-task multi-label network. Models train continually and can be fine-tuned hourly.

- **Value model:** expected value = weighted probabilities of click, like and others, minus "see less", with hundreds of tunable parameters tuned by online Bayesian optimisation, which can take over a month, or offline when offline metrics predict online ones.

The company's own description. The post gives no latency figures or A/B results.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Rank by predicted engagement and you're done"

It sounds right, since engagement is what you want. But the most clicked posts are often regretted, and one engagement number hides likes, shares and "see less". Predict each action, subtract the negative ones in a value model, and watch negative feedback as a guardrail.

## Say it

### A photo and video app shows each user a feed of posts from billions of candidates. Design the ranking so people see what they value, quickly, without filling the feed with clickbait.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not rank only by predicted click probability?

Clicks reward clickbait that people regret. Predicting several actions, including negative ones like "see less", and combining them in a value model lets you rank by what people actually value.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why have two ranking stages?

The heavy model is too expensive to run on thousands of candidates per request. A light model trained to imitate it cuts the set to about a hundred, so the heavy model runs only where it matters.

Follow-up 3 of 3

New creators never get shown. How do you fix it?

Add exploration: a retrieval source that gives new posts some exposure, and measure creator diversity as a guardrail, so the feedback loop doesn't lock in existing favourites.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the surface, scale, latency and what "good" means beyond clicks. I'd build a funnel. Several retrieval sources each return hundreds of candidates: a two-tower model with post embeddings in an ANN index, posts similar to what the user liked or shared, and trending posts, mixed with tunable weights. A light two-tower model, distilled from the heavy one, narrows a few thousand to about a hundred. A heavy multi-task network predicts click, like, share and "see less" using rich interaction features. A value model combines them into one score with weights we tune, subtracting negative actions so clickbait doesn't win. The final step removes harmful content and applies diversity rules. For speed I'd cache embeddings and precompute at peak. Models retrain frequently, new posts get exploration, and changes go through A/B tests with guardrails on negative feedback and integrity.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a social app's published post: [Meta's "Scaling the Instagram Explore recommendations system"](https://engineering.fb.com/2023/08/09/ml-applications/scaling-instagram-explore-recommendations-system/) (August 2023). The lab's posts and probabilities and the estimate are ours. Uses ranking metrics, embeddings and ANN and feedback loops. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design Ad Click Prediction

> An ads platform must predict, for every ad it might show, the chance that this user clicks. The prediction sets prices in the auction, so it must be accurate and calibrated. Design it.

- Track: System Design › Ads and Search Ranking › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-ad-click-prediction/
- Before this: Logistic Regression (`fundamentals/logistic-regression`), Probability Metrics (`fundamentals/probability-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A social network shows ads chosen by targeting, not search queries, to hundreds of millions of people. For each candidate ad, the system must predict the chance of a click; that prediction, times the bid, runs the auction. The interviewer asks:

> An ads platform must predict, for every ad it might show, the chance that this user clicks. The prediction sets prices in the auction, so it must be accurate and calibrated. Design it.

#### Ask before designing

- **How ads are chosen:** by targeting (demographics, interests), not a search query, so many ads are eligible for each request.

- **What's predicted:** the probability of a click for each candidate ad, used with the bid in the auction.

- **Scale:** hundreds of millions of impressions a day, and a tight latency budget per request.

- **Must never happen:** systematically over- or under-predicting clicks, which misprices the auction for advertisers.

- **Success metrics:** normalised cross-entropy (log loss relative to always predicting the average click rate), calibration, and revenue and advertiser outcomes online.

### The idea

Think of a bookmaker setting odds. Getting the order of favourites right isn't enough: if the odds are off, the house loses money on every bet. Fresh form matters more than old reputation, and odds are rechecked every day.

[Figure: Cheap models narrow the ads. Boosted trees turn features into leaf indices. A logistic regression, updated online, predicts the click. Downsampled training is recalibrated.]

_Ranking right isn't enough; the probability must be right too._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Switch between the three models. Turn on daily retraining. Then drag the share of non-clicks down to 2.5%.

#### Model, freshness and sampling

From the paper: Table 1 (model structures, relative to trees only), section 3.2 (about 1% from weekly to daily training) and section 6.3 (recalibration q = p / (p + (1 − p) / w)). Adding effects together is our simplification.

Switch models: the combination wins. Then turn on daily retraining: freshness alone gives about 1%, which is large in this world, where most feature work gains a fraction of a percent. Now downsample the non-clicks: training is far cheaper, but the model's probabilities are inflated, so **convert them back** before the auction uses them.

**Now say why:** why must you recalibrate after downsampling non-clicks?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Click prediction feeds the auction, so the **probability itself** must be right, not just the ranking. Use a **cascade**: cheap models narrow the ads, and the last model predicts click-through for a small set. A strong recipe: **boosted trees turn raw features into leaf indices**, and a **logistic regression trained online** on fresh data sits on top. **Historical features** about the user and ad matter most. Downsample negatives to save compute, then **recalibrate** the probabilities.

#### A cascade, then a precise final model

1. **Candidates:** targeting rules and cheap models narrow millions of ads to a few hundred for this request.

2. **Features:** contextual ones like time of day and device, and historical ones like this ad's click rate last week or this user's average click rate.

3. **Tree transform:** boosted decision trees, trained in batch, map each impression to the leaf it lands in for every tree. Those leaf indices become sparse binary features.

4. **Linear model:** a logistic regression over those features, updated online as new clicks arrive, predicts the click probability.

5. **Auction:** the predicted probability times the bid ranks the ads.

##### Why trees plus a linear model?

Trees learn useful non-linear splits and feature combinations automatically; a linear model on top can be retrained cheaply and often. Together they beat either alone.

##### The online joiner

To train online you need labels fast: join each impression with its click, if one arrives within a waiting window. Too short a window loses late clicks; too long delays training and needs more memory.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Impressions a day | given | **500 million** |
| Clicks a day | 500 million × 1% | **5 million** |
| Training rows after keeping 2.5% of non-clicks | 5 million + 495 million × 2.5% | **about 17 million** |
| Final-model predictions a second | 50,000 requests × 200 ads | **10 million** |

Downsampling shrinks the training data about 30× while keeping every click, which is what makes daily retraining affordable.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every click-prediction design gets asked

- **Metric:** normalised cross-entropy and calibration, not just AUC. AUC ignores whether probabilities are right, and the auction needs them right.

- **Features:** historical features (past click rates) carry most of the signal; contextual ones still matter for new users and new ads.

- **How many trees and features:** gains flatten quickly; a few hundred trees and the top features capture most of the value, which keeps serving cheap.

- **Learning rates for online updates:** per-coordinate learning rates work best, since popular features see far more updates than rare ones.

- **Safety for online training:** if the click stream breaks, the joiner produces data with almost no clicks and the model learns to predict zero. Detect sudden shifts and stop online training automatically.

- **Today:** many systems now use deep models with feature embeddings and interaction layers, but the lessons about freshness, calibration and sampling still hold.

##### Rollout

Compare a new model offline on next-day data, then run an online test on revenue and advertiser outcomes, watching calibration closely.

#### What the real system reported

- **Context:** over 750 million daily active users and over 1 million active advertisers; ads chosen by targeting, with a cascade of classifiers of increasing cost.

- **Model:** boosted trees as feature transforms plus logistic regression beat either alone by over 3% in normalised entropy.

- **Freshness:** going from weekly to daily training reduced normalised entropy by about 1%; an online joiner fed real-time training data to an online linear model.

- **Features and size:** the top 10 features gave about half the total importance; historical features beat contextual ones; almost all gains came from the first 500 trees.

- **Data volume:** 10% of the data cost only about 1% in accuracy; the best negative downsampling rate was 0.025, followed by recalibration.

From the paper (ADKDD 2014).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "AUC went up, so the model is better"

It sounds right, since AUC measures ranking. But the auction uses the probability itself: a model that predicts twice the real click rate can have the same AUC and still overcharge advertisers. Track calibration and normalised cross-entropy too.

## Say it

### An ads platform must predict, for every ad it might show, the chance that this user clicks. The prediction sets prices in the auction, so it must be accurate and calibrated. Design it.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does calibration matter more here than in many ranking problems?

The predicted probability is multiplied by the bid to price the auction. If predictions are twice too high, advertisers pay too much even if the ranking is right. AUC wouldn't notice; normalised entropy and calibration do.

Follow-up 2 of 3

You downsample non-clicks to 2.5%. What breaks?

The model now sees a much higher click rate than reality, so its raw probabilities are inflated. Convert them back with q = p / (p + (1 − p) / w), where w is the sampling rate, before using them.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you handle a brand-new ad with no history?

Lean on contextual and advertiser-level features, give it some exploration traffic, and let historical features build up quickly with fresh retraining.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify how ads are selected, the scale, the latency budget, and that the auction needs calibrated probabilities. I'd use a cascade: targeting and cheap models narrow to a few hundred ads, and the final model predicts click probability. Features are contextual, like device and time, and historical, like past click rates for the ad and user; historical ones carry most signal. A strong design uses boosted trees to turn raw features into leaf indices, with a logistic regression on top that's updated online from an impression–click joiner, because fresher data clearly helps. I'd measure normalised cross-entropy and calibration, not just AUC. To save compute I'd keep all clicks and a small share of non-clicks, then recalibrate the probabilities. Online training needs guards, so a broken click stream can't teach the model to predict zero. New models are compared offline on next-day data, then tested online on revenue and calibration.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a social network's published paper: ["Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook"](https://quinonero.net/Publications/predicting-clicks-facebook.pdf) (ADKDD 2014). The lab uses the paper's own numbers; the estimate is ours. The paper is from 2014, so treat the model as a strong baseline rather than today's state of the art. Uses logistic regression, gradient boosting and probability metrics. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design Search Ranking with Deep Learning

> A travel marketplace ranks thousands of available homes for each search. A boosted-tree ranker has stopped improving. Design the move to deep learning, and say what to expect.

- Track: System Design › Ads and Search Ranking › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-search-ranking/
- Before this: Ranking Metrics (`fundamentals/ranking-metrics`), Learning-Rate Schedules (`fundamentals/learning-rate-schedules`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A travel marketplace ranks thousands of available homes for each guest search. A boosted-tree ranker once gave one of the biggest booking gains in its history, but improvements have stalled. The team wants to move to deep learning. The interviewer asks:

> A travel marketplace ranks thousands of available homes for each search. A boosted-tree ranker has stopped improving. Design the move to deep learning, and say what to expect.

#### Ask before designing

- **Goal:** more bookings. A search session ends with a guest booking one listing, or not.

- **Candidates:** thousands of available listings per search, filtered by place and dates; we rank, not retrieve.

- **Current state:** a gradient-boosted tree model whose gains have plateaued.

- **Constraints:** scoring must fit the search latency budget; the existing serving stack is in Java.

- **Success metrics:** NDCG offline on booked listings, and bookings in an online A/B test.

### The idea

Think of moving a successful restaurant to a new, bigger kitchen. The first weeks, food comes out no better and sometimes worse. What finally helps isn't fancier equipment, but the right recipe, far more practice and fixing the slow supply line.

[Figure: Logs give booked and not-booked listings per search. A network trains on those pairs, weighted by NDCG change, over normalised features. Changes are tested offline, then on bookings.]

_The objective, the data and the pipeline matter more than the architecture._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Step through all seven ideas, noting which worked.

#### Pick an idea and see what happened

**What the paper reports**

All outcomes as reported in the paper; it describes them qualitatively or with the figures shown here.

Step through the ideas. The wins were less about clever architecture and more about **the right objective, more data and a faster pipeline**. Several popular ideas didn't transfer, because a home can be booked at most 365 nights a year, so there's little data per listing.

**Now say why:** why did an embedding per listing overfit here, when item embeddings work for videos?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Rank to get **booked listings to the top**. Train a neural network with a **pairwise** loss on booked versus not-booked listings from the same search, weighted by how much swapping them changes NDCG. Expect the move from boosted trees to be slow: **normalise features** carefully, feed the network **far more data**, and fix the **training pipeline**. Ideas that work elsewhere, like an ID embedding per listing, can fail in a marketplace where each item has few bookings.

#### From logs to a ranked list

1. **Logs:** each search, the listings shown and what the guest viewed and booked.

2. **Training pairs:** within each search, pair the booked listing with listings not booked.

3. **Model:** a small feed-forward network over normalised features and embeddings, trained with a pairwise loss weighted by the change in NDCG from swapping the pair (the LambdaRank idea).

4. **Serve:** the search server scores the candidates and returns them in order.

5. **Test:** offline NDCG first, then an online A/B test on bookings.

##### Features that suit a network

Trees don't care about scale; networks do. Map each feature to a small range, using a z-score for bell-shaped features or a log ratio to the median for skewed ones, and prefer smooth distributions. Location becomes a log offset from the map centre, and a hashed city-plus-map-cell feature lets the network learn where in a city guests prefer to stay.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Searches a day | given | **20 million** |
| Listings scored a day | 20 million × 1,000 candidates | **20 billion** |
| Booked searches a day | 20 million × 2% | **400,000** |
| Training pairs a day | 400,000 × 20 non-booked | **8 million** |

Bookings are scarce compared with searches, so months of logs are needed to reach the billion-plus pairs a network benefits from.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every search ranking design gets asked

- **Objective:** pairwise or listwise losses that target the top of the list beat plain regression on booked versus not.

- **Data:** networks need far more examples than trees; plot learning curves to see if more data will close the gap between training and test.

- **Sparse items:** per-item embeddings overfit when each item has few positives; share signal through attributes and categories.

- **Related signals:** views are plentiful but not the same as bookings; multi-task learning can boost views without moving bookings.

- **Pipeline:** data loading can starve GPUs; efficient formats and caching static features as embeddings can make training many times faster.

- **Interpretability:** per-feature attribution is hard for networks; comparing feature distributions of top- versus bottom-ranked listings is a practical check.

##### Rollout

Ship a simple network that matches the trees first, to prove the pipeline; then improve one change at a time, each with an A/B test on bookings.

#### What the real system reported

- **Starting point:** replacing a hand-made scoring function with boosted trees was one of the biggest booking gains in the company's history, but later gains saturated.

- **Evolution:** a single-hidden-layer network (32 units) was booking-neutral; LambdaRank-style pairwise training was the first breakthrough; hybrids with tree leaves and a factorisation machine followed; finally, 10× more data and a network with two hidden layers (127 and 83 units) over 195 features replaced the complexity.

- **Failures:** listing ID embeddings overfitted, since even popular listings are booked at most 365 times a year; a multi-task model raised long views a lot but bookings stayed neutral.

- **Engineering:** GPU use was near 25% until the pipeline moved to protobufs and a dataset API, giving a 17× speed-up and about 90% GPU use; a custom Java scoring library met the latency budget.

- **Lesson:** deep learning wasn't a drop-in replacement for trees; it meant rethinking the whole system around the model.

From the paper (KDD 2019).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Swap the trees for a neural network and it will win"

It sounds right, since deep learning wins elsewhere. But a network fed the same features and data often just matches the trees. Gains came from a ranking objective, careful normalisation, much more data and a faster pipeline, and several popular ideas failed here.

## Say it

### A travel marketplace ranks thousands of available homes for each search. A boosted-tree ranker has stopped improving. Design the move to deep learning, and say what to expect.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your first network is no better than the boosted trees. Is deep learning a failure here?

Not yet. Check feature normalisation, switch to a ranking objective, add much more data and look at learning curves. A first network that matches the trees is useful: it proves the pipeline end to end.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why might an embedding per listing hurt?

Each listing has few bookings, at most one per night, so its embedding memorises noise. Item embeddings work when items have lots of interactions, like videos or words.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Long views went up a lot, but bookings didn't. Why?

Views aren't bookings: people browse expensive or unusual homes they won't book. Optimise the real goal, and treat views as a helper signal only if they actually move it.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the goal, bookings, the candidate set per search, the current model and the latency budget. Training data comes from search logs: within each search, I'd pair the booked listing with listings not booked, and train a network with a pairwise loss weighted by the change in NDCG, so it focuses on the top of the list. I'd normalise every feature to a small range, prefer smooth distributions, and represent location as offsets plus a hashed city-and-area feature. I'd start with a simple network that matches the trees, to prove the pipeline, then add data, since networks need far more of it, and watch learning curves. I'd fix the training pipeline early, because data loading often starves GPUs. I'd be careful with per-listing embeddings, which overfit when bookings are scarce, and with proxy signals like views. Every change is tested offline on NDCG, then online on bookings.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a home-sharing marketplace's published paper: ["Applying Deep Learning To Airbnb Search"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09591) (KDD 2019). The lab reports the paper's own outcomes; the estimate is ours. Uses ranking metrics, training deep nets and explaining models. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design ETA Prediction

> A ride-hailing and delivery app shows an arrival time on every request, and prices depend on it. Design an ETA system that is accurate, fast enough for every request, and works across products and cities.

- Track: System Design › Maps and Logistics › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-eta-prediction/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`), Regression Metrics (`fundamentals/regression-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

A ride-hailing and delivery company shows an arrival time on every request, worldwide, and fares depend on it. Its routing engine computes ETAs from the map and live traffic but makes systematic errors. A large tree ensemble corrects them, and the team wants more accuracy within a few milliseconds. The interviewer asks:

> A ride-hailing and delivery app shows an arrival time on every request, and prices depend on it. Design an ETA system that is accurate, fast enough for every request, and works across products and cities.

#### Ask before designing

- **Uses:** pickup ETAs, trip ETAs, delivery ETAs and fares, each needing slightly different behaviour.

- **Scale:** every request in every city, so this may be the busiest model in the company.

- **Latency:** a few milliseconds per prediction.

- **Must never happen:** systematically late ETAs, which break trust and pricing.

- **Success metrics:** mean absolute error against actual arrival, error at the tail, and calibration of quantiles.

### The idea

Think of a sat-nav and a local driver. The sat-nav knows the roads and today's traffic; the local driver knows it always takes five extra minutes to get out of that car park. You keep the sat-nav and let the driver correct it, and they'd rather arrive a bit early than late.

[Figure: The routing engine sums segment times on the best path. A fast model predicts its error from embedded, bucketised and hashed features, trained with a loss that punishes lateness.]

_Keep routing, and learn its mistakes._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drag the number of features up to 200 and watch both costs. Then raise the embedding size above the number of features. Then raise ω.

#### How much does attention cost?

The two cost formulas and the K = 40, d = 8 example are from the post. The asymmetric loss shape follows the post's description; our version weights late errors by ω.

With features as tokens, full self-attention grows with the **square** of the number of features. Linear attention grows with the square of the embedding size instead, which is small, so it wins as long as d is less than K. Then raise ω: one model can produce a mean-like ETA or a cautious one, just by changing the loss.

**Now say why:** when does linear attention stop saving anything?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Keep the **routing engine**, which adds up travel times along the best path using the map and live traffic, and train an ML model to predict its **error**. Make that model fast: **embed** categorical features, **bucketise** continuous ones, **hash** locations at several grid sizes, and use **linear attention** so cost grows with the number of features, not its square. Train with an **asymmetric loss**, because being late is worse than being early.

#### Routing plus a learned correction

1. **Request:** origin, destination, time, and request type such as a delivery drop-off or a ride pickup.

2. **Routing engine:** finds the best path and sums segment travel times using map data and live traffic.

3. **Correction model:** predicts the gap between the routing ETA and what actually happens, using the routing ETA and other features.

4. **Serve:** the routing front end calls the model service, then returns the final ETA.

5. **Retrain:** regularly, with automatic validation before each new model goes live.

##### Why not replace routing with ML?

The routing engine already captures the road network and live traffic. A correction model is easier to change for new data sources and business needs than refactoring routing, and it fixes the routing engine's systematic errors.

##### Feature tricks for speed

Turn everything into embedding lookups: bucketise continuous values into quantile bins, and map latitude and longitude to grid cells at several resolutions, using several hash functions to save space while avoiding collisions. Lookups are constant time, so the model can be large but each prediction touches only a tiny part of it.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| ETA requests a second at peak | given | **500,000** |
| Latency budget per prediction | given | **about 5 ms** |
| Embedding table size | 300 million parameters × 4 bytes | **about 1.2 GB** |
| Parameters touched per prediction | 300 million × 0.25% | **about 750,000** |
| Training trips a day | given | **tens of millions** |

A big model is fine as long as each prediction reads only a small slice of it; that's the point of embedding lookups.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every ETA design gets asked

- **Why bucketise numbers?** Turning continuous features into quantile bins and embedding them often beats feeding raw values, and quantile bins use the bins evenly.

- **Locations:** multi-resolution grid cells with several independent hashes balance accuracy, memory and collisions.

- **One model, many products:** pass the request type as a feature, and add a small bias adjustment per segment, rather than separate models.

- **Loss:** an asymmetric Huber loss resists outliers and lets you choose how much to penalise lateness, or target a quantile.

- **Freshness:** traffic patterns change; retrain often, ideally incrementally, with automatic validation.

- **Monitoring:** track error by city, product and time of day, since a global average hides a city that's broken.

##### Rollout

Shadow the new model against the current one, compare errors by city and product on real trips, then roll out city by city.

#### What the real system reported

- **Design:** the routing engine predicts ETAs as a sum of segment travel times; the ML model predicts the residual. It replaced one of the largest and deepest XGBoost ensembles in the world at the time.

- **Requirements:** an ETA within a few milliseconds at most, a significant accuracy gain over XGBoost, and one model for all products worldwide. They call it the highest-QPS model at the company.

- **Model:** of seven architectures tested, an encoder–decoder with self-attention over features was most accurate; a linear transformer made it fast enough. It's shallow, with most parameters in embedding tables; each prediction touches about 0.25% of hundreds of millions of parameters.

- **Features and loss:** all features embedded, continuous ones in quantile buckets; locations via multi-resolution grids with multiple feature hashing; an asymmetric Huber loss.

From the company's post. It gives no MAE, latency or QPS figures; those are in the linked paper, which we didn't read.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "A bigger model will be more accurate, so use the biggest you can"

It sounds right, but every request needs an answer in milliseconds. Full attention over features grows with the square of their number. The trick is a model that's large in embedding tables but shallow and cheap per prediction, with linear attention.

## Say it

### A ride-hailing and delivery app shows an arrival time on every request, and prices depend on it. Design an ETA system that is accurate, fast enough for every request, and works across products and cities.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why predict the routing engine's error instead of the ETA directly?

Routing already captures the road network and live traffic. The model only has to learn what routing gets wrong, like pickup delays or restaurant waits, which is easier, and it's simpler to update than the routing engine.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why would you bucketise a continuous feature like distance?

Bins with embeddings let the model learn a flexible shape per range cheaply, and lookups are fast. Quantile bins spread examples evenly, so every bin is well trained.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Fares need an average ETA, but customers prefer not to be surprised. Two models?

Not necessarily. An asymmetric loss lets one architecture produce a mean-like estimate or a cautious quantile; you can train or tune per use case and keep the rest shared.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the uses, like pickup, trip, delivery and fares, the scale and the latency budget of a few milliseconds. I'd keep the routing engine, which sums segment travel times along the best path with live traffic, and train a model to predict its error, since that's easier to change than routing itself. For speed, every feature becomes an embedding lookup: categorical features embedded, continuous ones bucketised into quantile bins, and locations mapped to grid cells at several resolutions with multiple hashes. The model treats features as tokens with self-attention, but uses linear attention so cost grows with the number of features rather than its square. It's shallow, with most parameters in embedding tables, so each prediction touches only a small slice. I'd train with an asymmetric Huber loss, since being late is worse than being early, and pass the request type so one model serves all products. I'd retrain regularly, monitor error by city and product, and roll out city by city.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a ride-hailing company's published post: [Uber's "DeepETA: How Uber Predicts Arrival Times Using Deep Learning"](https://www.uber.com/blog/deepeta-how-uber-predicts-arrival-times/) (February 2022). The post gives no accuracy or latency figures; the lab computes the cost formulas from the post, and the estimate is ours. Uses self-attention, regression metrics and online inference. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design Notification Optimisation

> A learning app sends millions of daily reminders, choosing from dozens of message templates. Design a system that picks the best message for each user each day, without wearing users out with the same one.

- Track: System Design › Growth and Notifications › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-notification-optimization/
- Before this: Bandits vs A/B Tests (`fundamentals/bandits-vs-ab-tests`), Bayesian Inference and Conjugate Priors (`fundamentals/bayesian-inference-and-conjugate-priors`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A language-learning app sends millions of daily practice reminders, each picked from dozens of message templates, some only for certain users. Leadership wants more people practising, without users tuning reminders out. The interviewer asks:

> A learning app sends millions of daily reminders, choosing from dozens of message templates. Design a system that picks the best message for each user each day, without wearing users out with the same one.

#### Ask before designing

- **Goal:** users complete a lesson, so the reward is "did they do a lesson within two hours of the reminder".

- **Options:** dozens of templates, some only allowed for some users, like a streak message for users with a streak.

- **Scale:** millions of reminders a day, in 25 languages.

- **Must never happen:** sending a template to someone it doesn't apply to, or spamming the same message until users ignore it.

- **Success metrics:** the two-hour lesson rate, daily active users, and retention, especially for new users.

### The idea

Think of a friend who nudges you to go to the gym. If they say the same line every day, you stop hearing it. A good friend knows which line works best, saves the 'you're on a streak' line for when it's true, and mixes things up.

[Figure: For each reminder, eligible templates are scored, recent ones are penalised, and a softmax picks one. Every choice is logged; a daily job rescores templates.]

_The best message, repeated, stops being the best message._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Set γ to zero. Put it back and shorten the half-life. Then raise τ.

#### Which template does today's user get?

**Chance of sending each template**

Settings from the paper (γ = 0.017, h = 15 days, τ = 0.0025). The three templates' scores (+3.0%, +2.2%, +1.5% relative lift) and days since each was last sent (1, 20, 4) are made up for illustration. Modified score = score − γ · 0.5^(days ÷ h).

Set γ to zero: the best template wins every day, and users start ignoring it. Turn the penalty back on: yesterday's message loses its edge, so a fresh one gets a turn. Raise τ and the choice gets more random, which helps learning but costs a little reward.

**Now say why:** why compare a template with rounds where it was eligible, rather than its plain average?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Treat each message template as an arm of a **bandit**. Score each template by how much better users do when it's sent than when it was **eligible but not sent**, which removes the bias from templates only some users can get. Shrink noisy scores with a **Bayesian prior**. Penalise templates the user saw **recently**, with a penalty that fades over days, because fresh messages work better. Pick with a **softmax** so there's a little exploration, log every choice and its probability, and keep a small **random holdout**.

#### Choose, log, score, repeat

1. **Arm selector:** when a reminder is due, get the eligible templates, compute each one's score minus a recency penalty for this user, and sample with a softmax.

2. **Decision log:** record the time, user, the chosen template and the probability of every eligible template.

3. **User arm history:** store when each template was last sent to each user, for the recency penalty.

4. **Scorer:** a daily batch job joins decisions with lesson events, computes each template's score and writes it to a store the selector reads.

5. **Holdout:** a small share of reminders, say 5%, chosen uniformly at random, to measure the bandit and gather data on rarely used templates.

##### Why "used versus eligible"?

A streak template is only sent to engaged users, so it looks great on raw averages. Comparing rounds where it was sent with rounds where it was eligible but another was sent cancels that out. Importance weights correct for how likely each choice was.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Reminders a day | given | **10 million** |
| Decision log rows a year | 10 million × 365 | **about 3.7 billion** |
| Arms with per-language scores | 40 templates × 25 languages | **1,000** |
| Holdout reminders a day | 10 million × 5% | **500,000** |

Effects are small, around a percentage point, so scores need weeks of data per arm, which is why daily batch scoring is enough.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every notification design gets asked

- **Noisy reward:** many users do a lesson anyway. Counting only lessons within two hours of the reminder keeps some of that noise out.

- **Small samples:** new or rare templates have wild scores; a Bayesian prior pulls them towards average until data arrives.

- **Old data:** template performance drifts, so keep only enough recent history for a tight confidence interval.

- **Language:** translations perform differently; scoring each template-and-language pair as its own arm helped.

- **New templates:** start at a neutral score; recency penalties and softmax exploration give them a chance.

- **Beyond templates:** contextual bandits can personalise further by user features, at the cost of much more data per arm.

##### Rollout

Evaluate offline with importance-weighted replay on logs from random selection, then run an online A/B test against the current system, and keep a holdout afterwards.

#### What the real system reported

- **Method:** the Recovering Difference Softmax algorithm: scores as relative lift when used versus eligible, Bayesian shrinkage, an exponentially fading recency penalty and softmax selection.

- **Offline:** on logs with 88 million training and 114 million test rows, template-and-language arms gave +1.8% reward over random, and the recency penalty +1.9%; reusing the last template scored −0.5%.

- **Settings:** γ = 0.017, half-life 15 days, τ = 0.0025, keeping more than 90% of the potential gain while exploring.

- **Online A/B test:** +0.5% daily active users, +0.4% lessons completed, and +2.2% and +2.0% new-user day-1 and day-7 retention.

- **Five months later:** rounds using the bandit had 2.5% higher reward than a 5% random holdout.

From the paper (KDD 2020).

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Send everyone the template with the best average"

It sounds right, but templates limited to engaged users look great because of who gets them, and repeating any message makes users ignore it. Compare each template with rounds where it was eligible but not sent, and penalise recent repeats.

## Say it

### A learning app sends millions of daily reminders, choosing from dozens of message templates. Design a system that picks the best message for each user each day, without wearing users out with the same one.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not just send each user the template with the highest average success?

Two reasons. Templates only some users can get look better or worse because of who receives them, not the message; and repeating the same message makes users tune it out. Compare used versus eligible, and penalise recent repeats.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A brand-new template has a sky-high score after one day. What do you do?

Shrink it with a Bayesian prior towards the average, so a small sample can't dominate; let softmax exploration and more data settle its real value.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you know the bandit is still helping months later?

Keep a small holdout that chooses at random, and compare its reward with the bandit's rounds. It also catches bugs that quietly break the bandit.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the goal, the templates and their eligibility rules, and the volume. I'd treat templates as bandit arms. The reward is a lesson within two hours of the reminder. Each template's score is its relative lift when sent compared with when it was eligible but another was sent, using importance weights from the logged probabilities, which removes the bias from eligibility rules. Noisy scores are shrunk with a Bayesian prior. Because fresh messages work better, I'd subtract a recency penalty that fades exponentially with days since this user last saw the template, and choose with a softmax so there's some exploration. Every decision is logged with all the probabilities; a daily batch job recomputes scores. I'd score template-and-language pairs, keep a small random holdout to monitor the bandit, evaluate offline with importance-weighted replay, then A/B test online on daily active users and retention.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a language-learning app's published paper: ["A Sleeping, Recovering Bandit Algorithm for Optimizing Recurring Notifications"](https://research.duolingo.com/papers/yancey.kdd20.pdf) (Duolingo, KDD 2020). The lab uses the paper's chosen settings; the template scores in it and the estimate are ours. Uses bandits vs A/B tests, Bayesian estimates and feedback loops. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design a Background Coding Agent

> Engineers want an agent that makes code changes across thousands of repositories, like migrations and upgrades, and opens pull requests for review. Design it so its changes can be trusted.

- Track: System Design › Developer Tools › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-coding-agent/
- Before this: What Is an Agent? The ReAct Loop (`ai-engineering/what-is-an-agent`), Agent Safety: Permissions, Sandboxing and the Lethal Trifecta (`ai-engineering/agent-safety`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

A company has thousands of code repositories. Upgrades and migrations are written as scripts that keep growing, and engineers spend weeks on repetitive changes. Leadership wants an AI agent to make these changes and open pull requests. The interviewer asks:

> Engineers want an agent that makes code changes across thousands of repositories, like migrations and upgrades, and opens pull requests for review. Design it so its changes can be trusted.

#### Ask before designing

- **Tasks:** fleet-wide migrations and upgrades, like moving to a new framework version, or one-off requests from engineers?

- **Scale:** say thousands of repositories with different languages and build setups.

- **Who reviews:** does every change need a human review, and can some merge automatically?

- **Where it runs:** what may the agent access? Network, secrets, other systems?

- **Must never happen:** pushing directly to production, leaking secrets, or a change that passes tests but breaks behaviour.

- **Success metrics:** pull requests merged, share failing CI, changes later reverted, and engineer time saved.

### The idea

Think of a contractor renovating hundreds of identical flats. They get one clear brief, work only inside each flat, and an inspector checks the wiring and plumbing before the owner is called. A second inspector checks they did only what was asked, not a surprise new kitchen.

[Figure: A tested prompt runs per repository. The agent works in a sandbox, verifiers build and test, a judge checks scope, and only then does a PR open.]

_Keep the agent's world small, and check its work before anyone sees it._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start with no checks. Turn on verifiers, then the judge. Then drag the turns down to 3.

#### Which changes reach a reviewer?

Illustrative, except the judge: in the series, the judge vetoes about a quarter of sessions, and the agent course-corrects about half of those. Other rates are made up.

Start with no checks: many PRs fail CI, and some pass while doing the wrong thing, which is the worst case because **it erodes trust**. Turn on verifiers, and CI failures mostly vanish, but only if the agent has enough turns to fix them. The judge catches the agent being too ambitious: refactoring extra code or disabling a flaky test.

**Now say why:** why is a PR that passes CI but is wrong worse than no PR at all?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Keep the agent's job narrow and its world small. A task is a **tested, versioned prompt** applied to many repositories. The agent runs in a **sandbox** with only a few tools, and before any pull request opens, **verifiers** run the build, tests and formatters, and an **LLM judge** checks the change stayed within the task. Reuse the existing system for targeting repositories, opening pull requests and getting reviews. The worst failure isn't a missing PR, it's one that **passes CI but is wrong**.

#### From task to pull request

1. **Specify:** an engineer writes a task prompt: the desired end state, ideally as tests, when not to act, and examples. Prompts are versioned and tested on a few repositories first.

2. **Target:** the existing fleet system picks the repositories and starts one job per repository.

3. **Run:** the agent works in a sandboxed container with few tools: read and edit files, a restricted shell, limited Git, and a verify tool.

4. **Verify:** verifiers matching the repository's build system run formatters, the build and tests, and return only the key errors. The agent fixes what fails, within a turn limit.

5. **Judge:** an LLM compares the diff with the original prompt and vetoes changes that wander outside the task.

6. **Open and review:** only then does a pull request open, with a standard commit message, for normal review and merge.

##### Why so few tools?

Every tool is something that can go wrong or be misused. With no network and an allowlist of commands, the agent's mistakes stay inside the sandbox, and its runs are more predictable.

##### Why build knowledge goes into tools

Repositories build in very different ways. Rather than explaining each one in a prompt, a verify tool knows how to build and test any repository, and the agent just calls it.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Jobs for one migration | 2,000 repositories | **2,000 agent runs** |
| Tokens per run | 10 turns × 30,000 tokens of context | **about 300,000** |
| Tokens per migration | 2,000 × 300,000 | **about 600 million** |
| Build minutes | 2,000 × 3 verify runs × 5 minutes | **30,000 minutes** |
| Review time saved | 2,000 × 30 minutes of manual work, minus 5 to review | **about 830 hours** |

Builds can cost as much as tokens, so run verifiers selectively and cache dependencies. The real constraint is reviewer attention: batch similar PRs and make each one easy to review.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every coding-agent design gets asked

- **Writing the task:** describe the end state rather than every step, say when not to act, give examples, and make one change at a time. Too generic and the agent guesses; too specific and it breaks on the first unusual repository.

- **Failure modes, ranked:** no PR is a minor annoyance; a PR failing CI frustrates engineers; a PR that passes CI but is wrong is the most serious, because it erodes trust.

- **Weak tests:** if a repository has little test coverage, verifiers can't catch much, so be more cautious there, or skip it.

- **Safety:** the agent never pushes or changes the remote, has no secrets, and runs with almost no network access. Its commits are clearly labelled.

- **Evaluation:** track merge rate, CI failures, reverts and review comments per task, and evaluate prompts and the judge on held-out repositories before a fleet-wide run.

- **Observability:** log every run and its traces, so a bad pattern can be found and the prompt fixed before it spreads.

##### Rollout

Run a new task on a handful of repositories first and review every result. Then widen in waves, pausing if merge rates drop or reverts appear.

#### What the real system reported

- **Starting point:** an existing fleet framework already ran code changes across all repositories and opened PRs; scripts for complex changes had grown to over 20,000 lines. The agent replaced the scripts, and targeting, PRs, review and merge stayed the same.

- **Scale:** more than 1,500 merged pull requests, hundreds of developers using it, and a time saving of 60–90% versus writing the code by hand. The agent of choice had been used for about 50 migrations.

- **Harness:** a container with limited permissions and almost no access to other systems; a verify tool for formatters, linters and tests; a Git tool that never pushes; a shell with a strict allowlist.

- **Verification:** independent verifiers chosen by what's in the repository, run before any PR opens; then an LLM judge comparing the diff with the prompt. The judge vetoes about a quarter of sessions, and the agent course-corrects about half of those.

- **Honest gaps:** they had yet to evaluate the judge itself, and said they were still choosing prompts and models mostly by intuition.

The company's own figures, from parts 1–3 of the series. We didn't read part 4.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Tests pass, so the change is safe to merge"

It sounds right, since tests are the safety net. But many repositories have thin coverage, and agents sometimes disable a flaky test or refactor code they weren't asked to touch. Passing CI then proves little. Keep human review, add a judge that checks the change against the task, and be extra careful where tests are weak.

## Say it

### Engineers want an agent that makes code changes across thousands of repositories, like migrations and upgrades, and opens pull requests for review. Design it so its changes can be trusted.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not let the agent merge its own changes when tests pass?

Passing tests doesn't prove a change is right, especially where coverage is thin. A wrong change that merges silently does more damage than a slow review. I'd only consider auto-merge for trivial, well-tested change types with a long clean record.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The agent keeps "improving" unrelated code. How do you stop it?

Say in the prompt exactly what to change and what not to touch, and add a judge that compares the diff with the task and vetoes extras. Keep each task to one change, so out-of-scope edits stand out.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you know a new prompt is better than the old one?

Run both on the same held-out set of repositories and compare merge rate, CI failures, judge vetoes and review comments. Without that, you're choosing by intuition.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the kinds of tasks, how many repositories, who reviews and what the agent may access. A task is a versioned prompt that describes the end state, says when not to act and includes examples, tested on a few repositories first. The existing fleet system targets repositories and runs one job each. The agent works in a sandboxed container with few tools: file edits, a restricted shell, Git that can't push, and a verify tool that knows how to build and test any repository and returns only the key errors. The agent fixes failures within a turn limit. Then an LLM judge compares the diff with the task and vetoes out-of-scope changes. Only then does a pull request open for normal review. The worst failure is a change that passes CI but is wrong, so I'd be careful with repositories that have weak tests, and track merges, CI failures and reverts per task. Rollout goes in waves, pausing if quality drops.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a music-streaming company's published series: [Spotify's background coding agent, parts 1–3](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/11/spotifys-background-coding-agent-part-1) (November–December 2025). The lab's numbers, apart from the judge's veto rate, and the estimate are ours. Uses agents, agent safety and evaluating agents. · checked 5 Nov 2026
