# Design Code Autocomplete

> Design code autocomplete for hundreds of millions of requests a day, with suggestions arriving in under 200 ms.

- Track: System Design › Developer Tools › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-code-autocomplete/
- Before this: Continuous Batching and Scheduling (`ai-engineering/continuous-batching`), Scaling Inference: Parallelism, Replicas and Routing (`ai-engineering/scaling-inference`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

A code editor plugin suggests the next lines as developers type, for users all over the world. A suggestion that arrives late is useless. It must serve hundreds of millions of requests a day, with a mean under 200 ms. The interviewer asks:

> Design code autocomplete for hundreds of millions of requests a day, with suggestions arriving in under 200 ms.

#### Ask before designing

- **Scale:** 400 million requests a day, peaking in the overlap between the working day in Europe and the US.

- **Latency:** under 200 ms on average. A late suggestion is useless, because the person has already typed past it.

- **Users:** worldwide, so distance matters as much as model speed.

- **Clients:** an IDE plugin that people may not update for a long time, so the server must absorb changes.

- **Must never happen:** code leaking between users, or secrets in suggestions and logs.

- **Success metrics:** acceptance rate, code kept after a while, latency, error rate and cost per suggestion.

### The idea

Think of a friend finishing your sentences, on a phone call. If they're slow, you've already moved on, and what they say is wasted. Hanging up and redialling each time you talk over them would be absurd, so you stay on the line and just say "never mind".

[Figure: The IDE waits for a pause and sends a short prompt to the nearest proxy over an open connection. The proxy checks a token and forwards to a model in the same region. Cancels travel back down the same path.]

_Staying on the line is HTTP/2. "Never mind" is a cancel that reaches the model._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Start with both boxes off, and see how far you are from 200 ms. Make the round trip shorter. Then try each box.

#### Where does the time go?

Illustrative: 100 ms to run the model, 5.5 round trips for each new connection, one reconnect per cancel, and 20 ms round trip in the user's region. With cancels passed through, we assume a tenth of the cancelled work still runs.

A faster model can't fix this. At a **100 ms** round trip, the network and reconnects together take over three times as long as the model. Turn on **HTTP/2** and then the **nearby region**, and you drop from about 448 ms to 120 ms with the same model.

**Now say why:** why can't a faster model alone meet the target?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

The model isn't your only latency problem. **The network and wasted requests are just as big.** Most typing makes requests go stale, so the client cancels them and the cancel must reach the model. **HTTP/2 streams** let you cancel one request while keeping the connection open. A **proxy in each region, next to the model**, handles sign-in, routing and experiments, and each proxy takes itself out of service when it's unhealthy.

#### The path of one keystroke

1. **Decide when to ask:** there's no "complete" key, so the client guesses when typing has paused. It can use a timer, a small prediction model or a guess on each key, and real systems mix them.

2. **Build the context:** the code before and after the cursor, plus a few snippets from open files, trimmed to fit the budget. A short prompt means a quick prefill.

3. **Send to the nearest proxy:** DNS sends the user to their closest healthy region, over a connection that's already open.

4. **Check the token:** the client swaps its login for a token that lasts minutes. The proxy checks the signature locally, with no call to another service, and swaps in the real model key.

5. **Run the model:** the proxy forwards the request over its open connection pool to a fast model in the same region, and streams the reply back.

6. **Show or discard:** the IDE shows it if it's still relevant. If the user kept typing, it cancels.

##### Cancellation is the core of it

The real team reported that about half of requests were typed through, meaning the user kept typing before the reply arrived. With plain HTTP, the client's only way to cancel is to reset the connection, and that has two costs:

- **Wasted model work:** the server may not notice the reset until it writes the reply, so the model has already run. About 45% of requests were cancelled after inference had run.

- **Slow reconnects:** a new connection takes five or six round trips for TCP and TLS, which alone can use up the 200 ms.

**HTTP/2** fixes both. One connection carries many streams, so the client resets just one stream and the connection stays open. The proxy passes the cancel to the model, which stops work almost immediately. Every hop must speak HTTP/2, and many load balancers downgrade to HTTP/1 on the way to the backend, so check yours.

##### Regions

Put a proxy in every region that has the model. The real team rejected separate edge locations, because traffic from Japan could go through Singapore and on to a model on the US West Coast. The network round trip can take longer than running the model.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

The first two rows use the talk's figures. The rest are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Average load | 400 million ÷ 86,400 | **about 4,600 per second** |
| Peak load | From the talk | **about 8,000 per second** |
| Wasted without cancel | 400 million × 45% | **180 million model runs a day** |
| GPUs at peak | 8,000 ÷ 100 per GPU, × 2 for headroom | **about 160** |

Cancelling is a cost feature as well as a speed feature. Stopping nearly half the work early frees that capacity for live requests.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every LLM design gets asked

- **Quality and evaluation:** track acceptance rate, and how much accepted code is still there later, since accepting isn't the same as keeping. Because the proxy sees all traffic, it can split traffic between model versions for A/B tests, and mirror traffic to test a new one safely.

- **Reliability:** each proxy watches its own success rate. If it drops below target, the health check starts to fail and DNS removes that instance. It returns once it recovers. A regional outage becomes a loss of some capacity.

- **Scalability:** proxies are stateless and hold long-lived connections, so spread load across a pool of connections to each model. Load shifts around the world during the day, so scale each region to its own peak.

- **Latency and cost:** use a small, fast model, keep prompts short and batch requests on the GPU. A mean hides slow users, so watch percentiles measured at the proxy.

- **Safety and security:** short-lived tokens limit the damage from a stolen one, and the real model key never reaches the client. Filter secrets from prompts and suggestions, and don't log code by default.

##### Why the proxy earns its place

Clients update slowly, so server-side fixes matter. The real team used the proxy to remove a parameter that was crashing model instances, and to change requests on the way through. All of that happens with no client release.

##### Rollout

Use the proxy to send a small share of traffic to a new model, and compare acceptance and latency. Redeploy proxies behind a load balancer that holds the client connection, so users don't get disconnected.

#### What the real system reported

- **Scale:** more than 400 million requests a day when the talk was pitched, and higher by the time it was given. About 8,000 requests a second at peak.

- **Latency:** a mean under 200 ms during that peak.

- **Waste:** about 45% of requests were cancelled after inference had run, before the fix.

- **Tokens:** they last 10 to 30 minutes, and the client refreshes a couple of minutes before expiry.

- **Load balancers:** many cloud ones and CDNs downgraded to HTTP/1 on the backend, so the team used its own, based on HAProxy.

These are the speaker's own figures, from a November 2024 talk.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just get a faster model and more GPUs"

It sounds right, since the model is the expensive part. But reconnecting takes five or six round trips, so distance alone can use up 200 ms. And if requests aren't cancelled, about half of those extra GPUs do work no one will see. Fix the wasted work and the network path first, then see how much model speed you still need.

## Say it

### Design code autocomplete for hundreds of millions of requests a day, with suggestions arriving in under 200 ms.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not make the model faster and skip all this?

You can't beat distance. If a round trip takes 100 ms and a reconnect takes five or six of them, that alone exceeds the budget however fast the model is. Without cancels, a faster model would still run about half its requests for nothing. Both a fast model and a good network path are needed.

Follow-up 2 of 3

One region's model starts returning errors. What do users see?

Proxies there see their success rate fall below target, fail their health checks and drop out of DNS. New requests go to the next closest region, so those users get slower suggestions, not errors. When the rate recovers, the proxies return. Suggestions are optional, so failing quietly is fine too.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Doesn't a proxy add a hop and slow things down?

It adds a small hop, but it's in the same region as the model, and it holds open connections, which saves far more than it costs. In return you get central sign-in, a hidden model key, routing, cancels, experiments and fixes for old clients.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd confirm the scale, the latency target and where users are. At 400 million requests a day and about 8,000 a second at peak, under 200 ms leaves little room, and the network matters as much as the model. The client waits for a pause, builds a short prompt from the code around the cursor and sends it over a connection that's already open. About half of requests go stale as people type, so cancelling is central. I'd use HTTP/2, so the client resets one stream and keeps the connection, avoiding five or six round trips per reconnect. The proxy passes the cancel to the model, so it stops wasting GPU time. I'd put a proxy in every region with the model, and route by DNS to the closest healthy one. It checks a short-lived token locally and holds the real model key. Each proxy watches its success rate and fails its health check when it's unhealthy, so a regional outage only reduces capacity. The proxy also lets me A/B test models and fix problems without client releases. I'd measure acceptance, code kept, percentile latency and cost.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a talk about a real system: [David Cheney on serving GitHub Copilot](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/github-copilot/) ([QCon SF 2024](https://qconsf.com/presentation/nov2024/how-github-copilot-serves-400-million-completion-requests-day)). We could read most of the transcript and only a summary of the rest. Context building, quality metrics, privacy and the lab's numbers come from our own knowledge and are not from the talk. Uses prefill and decode, continuous batching, serving metrics and scaling inference. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design an LLM Evaluation Platform

> Teams change prompts, models and retrieval every week, and quality keeps slipping without anyone noticing. Design a platform that catches regressions before users do.

- Track: System Design › ML and LLM Platforms › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-llm-eval-platform/
- Before this: RAG Evals: Retrieval, Faithfulness and Relevance (`ai-engineering/rag-evals`), LLMOps: What's Different (`ai-engineering/llmops`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

A company has an AI assistant and 20 teams changing its prompts, retrievers and models every week. Quality keeps slipping, and nobody notices until users complain. Results from last month's experiments can't be reproduced. The interviewer asks:

> Teams change prompts, models and retrieval every week, and quality keeps slipping without anyone noticing. Design a platform that catches regressions before users do.

#### Ask before designing

- **What's evaluated:** a RAG assistant, agents, single prompts? Different products need different metrics.

- **Who uses it:** say 20 teams, each changing prompts, retrievers or models several times a week.

- **What counts as good:** correct, grounded in sources, cited, well formatted, fast and cheap enough.

- **Speed:** how long can a check on a pull request take before engineers start skipping it?

- **Must never happen:** a change that breaks citations or safety reaching users, or a "better" score that can't be reproduced.

- **Success metrics:** regressions caught before release, time to get a result, judge agreement with people, and incidents found in production.

### The idea

Think of a school's exams. Questions are written in advance and kept on file, markers follow a marking scheme, and a senior teacher re-marks a sample to check the markers are fair. A quick test each week catches big problems; the full exam at the end of term catches the rest.

[Figure: Versioned datasets, scorers and judges run as gates: a small set on every change, a big set before release, and sampled live traffic after.]

_Evaluation works like testing code: versioned, repeatable and gated._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Keep 150 questions and set a 5-point drop. Then drag the questions up. Then raise the drop to 10.

#### Will your gate catch the regression?

Illustrative: an 85% baseline pass rate compared against a fixed baseline with a one-sided test at 5%, and about 6 seconds per answer plus judging. Real gates are noisier still, because judges and models vary run to run.

Start at 150 questions and a 5-point drop: the gate misses it about half the time. Drag the questions up and watch the time grow. That's why gates are **layered**: a small, fast set catches big breaks on every change, and a large set before release catches the smaller ones.

**Now say why:** why does a small gate set catch big regressions but miss small ones?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Treat evaluation like testing code. Keep **versioned datasets** built from real use, score answers with **clear metrics** and **LLM judges you calibrate against people**, and run them as **gates**: a fast set on every change, a bigger one before release, and **sampling of live traffic** after. Hard rules block a change; softer scores are tracked. Every run records exactly what was tested, so results can be reproduced.

#### Datasets, scorers, runs and gates

1. **Datasets:** public benchmarks for a baseline, real (anonymised) user queries, synthetic questions generated over representative documents, and hard cases mined from poorly rated live answers. All versioned.

2. **Scorers:** code checks (are citations present?), metrics against references (source recall, answer correctness) and LLM judges with a rubric for things like faithfulness and tone.

3. **Runs:** each run is a dataset, a system version, settings and scorers, saved with an ID so it can be compared and reproduced.

4. **Gates:** a small, fast set on every pull request; a larger set with stricter limits before release; and continuous scoring of sampled live traffic after.

5. **Dashboards and alerts:** side-by-side comparisons, trace-level drill-down and alerts on drift.

##### Three kinds of checks

**Hard rules** block a change, like "every answer must cite a source". **Budgets** set limits, like "source F1 at least 0.85, p95 latency at most 5 seconds". **Rubric scores**, like tone, are tracked and reviewed but don't block, because they're noisier.

##### Why not BLEU or embedding similarity?

Overlap and similarity scores miss what matters here: whether claims are supported, citations are right and the format is usable. Two answers can look alike and differ in exactly those ways.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Pull-request runs a week | 20 teams × 15 changes | **300** |
| Judge calls a week for PR gates | 300 × 150 questions × 3 judges | **135,000** |
| Live answers sampled a day | 1 million answers × 1% | **10,000** |
| Human labels for calibration a month | 10 judges × 200 samples | **2,000** |

Judge calls are the main cost, so use a cheaper judge for routine gates, cache results for unchanged answers, and keep the expensive judge for release gates.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every evaluation design gets asked

- **Can you trust the judge?** Build each judge like code: a rubric, a prompt, a version and tests. Every few weeks, have people label a sample and measure agreement. If the judge drifts, fix its prompt or model, and re-score.

- **Reproducibility:** record the dataset version, prompt hash, retriever version and model for every run. Without that, "it got better" can't be checked.

- **Prompt edits are risky:** a single word can break citations or formatting, so every prompt change goes through the gate, just like a model swap.

- **Hard cases:** mine poorly rated live answers and add them to the suite, so known failures can't come back silently.

- **Production:** score sampled live traffic asynchronously, so users see no extra latency, and alert on sudden drops in metrics like source F1.

- **Other languages and domains:** a general judge can be wrong here; use specialised judges or more human review.

##### Triage when a score drops

Was the right document never retrieved? Check retrieval logs. Was the context there but ignored? Check prompt structure and truncation. Does the judge look wrong? Re-run it on its calibration set.

#### What the real system reported

- **Datasets:** public QA sets for a baseline, then anonymised internal queries, synthetic Q&A over widely shared documents, and hard cases mined from low-rated live traces.

- **Pull-request gate:** about 150 canonical queries, chosen to cover connectors, "no answer" cases and non-English queries, with results in under ten minutes. Merges are blocked on any red-line miss.

- **Three metric types:** boolean gates such as citations present; budgets such as source F1 ≥ 0.85 and p95 latency ≤ 5 s; rubric scores that are logged, not gating.

- **Judges:** designed, calibrated, tested and versioned like software, with spot-checks against human labels every few weeks. People also review 5–10% of the regression suite each release.

- **Production:** live traffic sampled and scored with the same metrics, with no added latency, and alerts on drift.

- **Lesson:** prompt edits caused more regressions than model swaps, and formal gates, not people eyeballing results, became the reliable safety net.

The company's own figures. The post gives no judge-agreement rates or costs.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "If the judge score went up, quality went up"

It sounds right, since the judge is the measure. But judges drift, have biases such as preferring longer answers, and can be gamed by prompt changes that please the judge rather than users. Re-check judges against people regularly, keep a held-out set, and compare offline gains with what users actually experience.

## Say it

### Teams change prompts, models and retrieval every week, and quality keeps slipping without anyone noticing. Design a platform that catches regressions before users do.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Your judge says quality went up, but users complain. What do you check?

Whether the judge still agrees with people: re-run its calibration set and label a fresh sample of recent answers. Then check whether the eval set still looks like real traffic, since usage drifts. I'd add the complaints as test cases.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why not run the full suite on every pull request?

It would take too long and cost too much, so engineers would work around it. A small set catches big breaks quickly. The full suite runs before release, where a slower check is acceptable and small regressions matter.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you stop teams from overfitting to the eval set?

Keep a held-out set that teams can't see, refresh datasets from live traffic regularly, and compare offline gains with online results. If offline keeps improving while users don't notice, the set has stopped measuring what matters.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify what we evaluate, who changes the system and how fast a check must be. I'd treat evaluation like testing code. Datasets are versioned and come from real anonymised queries, synthetic questions over representative documents, public benchmarks for a baseline, and hard cases mined from bad live answers. Scorers include code checks like "citations present", metrics such as source recall, and LLM judges with rubrics. Each judge is versioned and calibrated against human labels every few weeks. Every run records the dataset, prompt hash, retriever and model, so it can be reproduced. Gates are layered: a small set on every pull request that returns in minutes, a larger stricter set before release, and asynchronous scoring of sampled live traffic with drift alerts. Hard rules block changes, budgets set limits on things like latency, and rubric scores are tracked. A small gate set only catches big regressions, which is why the release gate is larger. Poorly rated live answers flow back into the suite.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a file-storage company's published approach for its AI assistant: [Dropbox's "A practical blueprint for evaluating conversational AI at scale"](https://dropbox.tech/machine-learning/practical-blueprint-evaluating-conversational-ai-at-scale-dash) (October 2025). The lab's maths and the estimate are ours. Uses evaluating LLM apps, LLMOps and tracing. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design a Shared LLM Platform

> Dozens of teams want to use LLMs from different vendors, and customer data mustn't leak. Design a shared platform for them.

- Track: System Design › ML and LLM Platforms › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-llm-platform/
- Before this: LLMOps: What's Different (`ai-engineering/llmops`), Guardrails and Prompt Injection (`ai-engineering/guardrails-and-prompt-injection`)
- Quiz topic: `sdllm`

## Intuition

### The situation

A large company has dozens of teams building with LLMs. Each has its own vendor keys and its own way of connecting, and nobody can see the total cost or say what data is leaving the company. Say 100 million requests a month. The interviewer asks:

> Dozens of teams want to use LLMs from different vendors, and customer data mustn't leak. Design a shared platform for them.

#### Ask before designing

- **Users:** how many teams and use cases, and which languages do their services use?

- **Models:** outside vendors, your own hosted models or both? Which data may go to which of them?

- **Scale:** say 100 million requests a month, many of them streaming.

- **Must never happen:** customer data reaching a vendor without approval, one team using up everyone's quota, or the platform taking down every product at once.

- **Success metrics:** teams onboarded, time to onboard, added latency, availability, data incidents and cost per team.

### The idea

Think of a company's post room. Every team hands letters to one desk, in one format. The desk checks the sender, blacks out private details on anything leaving the building, sends it by the right courier and keeps a record of the cost. If the desk closes, though, nothing gets sent, so it needs cover.

[Figure: Teams call one API. The gateway checks access and limits, redacts personal data, then routes to a vendor or in-house model. Every request is logged for cost and audit.]

_Every team gets the same checks, without building them again._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Turn redaction off, and read what the vendor sees. Turn it back on, and swap the names. Then drag the message length up.

#### What does the vendor actually see?

**Your service sends**

**The vendor sees**

**The vendor replies**

**Your service gets**

Illustrative: a made-up message, and about 10 ms plus 1 ms per 100 characters for the redactor. The placeholder style follows the real post. The post says the delay grows with the length of the request, but we couldn't read its figures.

Turn it off, and the vendor sees all three details. Now swap the names: **the same person gets a different placeholder**, because numbers follow the order of appearance. The model also loses meaning. It can't tell a name's gender, region or language from a placeholder, which can hurt answer quality. Redaction is a trade-off, so review which use cases need it.

**Now say why:** why might an answer get worse once the names are hidden?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Put a **gateway** between every team and every model. Teams call **one API**, in a format they already know, and the gateway handles sign-in, routing, logging and cost tracking. Before a request leaves for an outside vendor, it **swaps personal data for placeholders**, and restores them in the reply. Since everything depends on the gateway now, it needs **budgets per team, fallbacks and no single point of failure**.

#### The path of one request

1. **Call one API:** teams use a widely adopted format, like the OpenAI API, and name a model. Existing client libraries and frameworks then work unchanged.

2. **Sign in and check access:** identify the team, and confirm the use case was reviewed and may use this model.

3. **Check limits:** apply the team's rate limit and budget.

4. **Redact:** if the request is going outside, replace personal data with placeholders and keep the mapping.

5. **Route:** pick the vendor client or your own serving stack, and translate the request if needed.

6. **Restore and log:** put the real values back in the reply, then record the team, model, tokens, latency and cost.

##### Why one format beats your own

A custom API must be documented and kept current by you, and it can quickly fall behind a fast-moving field. Copying the most common format gives teams every tool built for it, and switching model becomes a one-word change. The cost is that other vendors' features don't always map neatly onto it.

##### Onboarding

The platform makes review easy to enforce. Each new use case goes through one standard security review of the data it handles, and only then gets access. Teams no longer each hold their own vendor keys and contracts.

##### What doesn't belong here

Keep prompts, retrieval and business logic in the teams' own services. A gateway that knows about each product's logic becomes a bottleneck for every team.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, not figures from a real system.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Average load | 100 million ÷ 2.6 million seconds in a month | **about 38 per second** |
| Peak load | 38 × 3 | **about 115 per second** |
| Open connections at peak | 115 × 10 seconds per streamed reply | **about 1,150** |
| Log storage per month | 100 million × 5 KB of metadata | **about 500 GB** |

The gateway does little computing itself, since the model does the hard work. What it must handle is many slow, open connections, so choose a server built for that.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What every LLM design gets asked

- **Quality and evaluation:** quality belongs to each team, since only they know what good means for their product. The platform provides the logs and a way to replay traffic against a new model, so they can compare before switching.

- **Reliability:** every product now depends on you, so run many instances in several zones, and make deploys gradual. Retry with backoff, and fall back to a second approved model when a vendor fails. Teams must opt in, because a different model can behave differently, and a fallback must never send data to a vendor it isn't approved for.

- **Scalability:** the gateway is stateless, and vendor quotas are the real limit. Share those fairly across teams, reserving capacity for critical products and giving batch jobs what's left.

- **Latency and cost:** stream replies straight through, and keep the added delay small. Attribute cost per team from logs, set budgets with alerts, and offer exact-match caching only as an opt-in, since a shared cache can leak data between users.

- **Safety and security:** keep vendor keys only in the gateway. Logs now hold sensitive text, so log metadata by default, and restrict and expire anything more. Redaction misses things, so it's one layer, alongside contracts and approved-use review.

##### The risk of a shared layer

Decide in advance what happens if a check fails. If the redactor is down, requests to outside vendors should be refused and never sent unredacted. If the logging system is down, requests can usually continue, with logs queued for later.

##### Rollout

Start with one or two willing teams and one vendor. Move others over by making the platform the easiest path, then block direct vendor access once most have moved.

#### What the real system reported

- **Why they built it:** over 60 LLM use cases across the company, with teams integrating in different ways and repeating each other's work.

- **Scale in July 2024:** close to 30 customer teams, 16 million queries a month and a peak of 25 per second.

- **Design:** a Go service that copies the OpenAI API, wraps vendor clients and sits alongside in-house serving. It includes authentication, metrics, and audit logs for cost and security.

- **Redaction:** typed placeholders numbered by position, restored in the reply. The post says this creates challenges for both latency and result quality.

The company's own figures. We couldn't read the post's later sections, so anything about how they reduced those problems isn't included.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Add a fallback, and send everything to the next vendor"

It sounds right, since it keeps products running when a vendor is down. But each vendor has its own data approvals, and a different model can behave differently. A silent global switch could send customer data somewhere it isn't allowed, or change a product's behaviour untested. Make fallback a per-team choice, limited to approved models.

## Say it

### Dozens of teams want to use LLMs from different vendors, and customer data mustn't leak. Design a shared platform for them.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

One team's batch job uses up the vendor quota, and customer chat starts failing. How do you prevent that?

Give each team its own rate limit and budget, and reserve part of the quota for critical products. Batch work goes through a queue at low priority, and uses what's left. Alerts warn teams before they reach their limits.

Follow-up 2 of 3

A vendor has an outage. Do you switch every team to another vendor automatically?

Only teams that opted in, and only to models approved for their data. A different model can change behaviour, so a team must test its fallback first. Others get a clear error they can handle. That's why fallback is a per-team setting rather than a global one.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Doesn't the redactor make answers worse? Would you remove it?

It can, because the model loses context, and placeholders can confuse it. I wouldn't remove it across the board. I'd measure quality with and without it on safe test data, then use a stricter contract or an in-house model for cases that need real values. Requests to an in-house model may not need redaction, depending on policy.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify the number of teams, which models they need, what data may go where and the volume. I'd build a gateway between all teams and all models. Teams call one API in a widely used format, so existing tools work and switching models is easy. For each request, the gateway signs in the team, checks that the use case was approved, applies rate limits and budgets, and redacts personal data if it's going to an outside vendor. It routes to a vendor or our own serving stack, restores the placeholders in the reply and logs team, model, tokens and cost. Vendor keys live only in the gateway. Redaction costs latency and some quality, so I'd review where it's needed, and refuse to send if the redactor fails. Because every product now depends on it, I'd run it across zones with gradual deploys, plus opt-in fallbacks that respect data rules. Vendor quotas are the real limit, so I'd share them fairly by priority. Quality stays with each team, and the platform gives them logs and replay tools.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a ride-hailing company's published design: [Uber's post on its LLM gateway](https://www.uber.com/blog/genai-gateway). We could read only part of the post, up to the start of its section on challenges. Budgets, fallback, caching and the lab's numbers come from our own knowledge and are not from the post. Uses LLMOps, guardrails and cost and latency. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Test an LLM Prompt in Production

> Your new LLM tutor's prompt looks better in demos. How do you test it in production, and what's your metric?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-llm-prompt-test/
- Before this: Sample Size, Power and Runtime (`fundamentals/sample-size-and-power`), LLM Judges: Pairwise Preferences and Pass/Fail Checks (`ai-engineering/llm-as-a-judge`)
- Quiz topic: `sdexp`

## Intuition

### The situation

An education app has an LLM tutor, with about 200,000 chat threads a day. A new prompt looks better in demos, and the team wants to ship it. Good here should mean students learn, not that they enjoy being handed answers. The interviewer asks:

> Your new LLM tutor's prompt looks better in demos. How do you test it in production, and what's your metric?

#### Ask before designing

- **What's the change?** One sentence in a prompt, a whole new prompt, or a different model?

- **What's good?** Does good mean more use, deeper thinking, or actually learning the skill? Students may enjoy a tutor that simply hands over answers.

- **Scale:** say 200,000 chat threads a day.

- **Must never happen:** harmful content for students, or a tutor that just gives the answer.

- **Limits:** latency and cost per chat, plus the privacy rules around student data.

### The idea

Think of a school trying a new teaching method. Teachers saying it feels better proves little. So first agree what good teaching looks like, and train assessors until they agree. Only then compare classes, and if your assessors are unreliable, you'll need many more classes to see a difference.

[Figure: New prompt versions are assigned per thread or user. An LLM judge scores a sample of chats, and results are compared on the main metric and guardrails. Experts label chats and tune the judge before any live test.]

_The judge is only useful once it matches your experts._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Lower the judge's accuracy from 85% to 65%. Then shrink the real lift to 0.5 points.

#### A noisy judge makes the test slower

Illustrative: 200,000 threads a day, 30% good chats in control, 2,000 tokens to score one, 5% significance and 80% power. Assumes the judge is equally accurate on good and bad chats, so the lift it sees is the real lift × (2 × accuracy − 1). Real runs should cover at least a full week.

Lower the judge's accuracy from **85%** to **65%**. A 2-point lift shrinks to 0.6 points, and the test needs about six times more scored chats. Improving the judge can be cheaper than running longer.

**Now say why:** why does a noisy judge hide a real improvement?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Demos and thumbs-up ratings won't tell you whether a tutor teaches better. So first **define good**: experts label real chats against a rubric, and an **LLM judge** is tuned until it matches them. Then run a live test with **the chat thread or the user as the unit**, a primary learning metric and guardrails like giving away answers. A **noisy judge shrinks the effect you can see**, so it directly increases how long you must run.

#### Build the measure first, then experiment

1. **Choose a metric that reflects the goal:** for a tutor, cognitive engagement: is the student thinking, or copying?

2. **Write a rubric:** experts define each level with examples.

3. **Label real chats:** check experts agree with each other. If they can't agree, the rubric isn't ready.

4. **Build an LLM judge:** tune its prompt until its labels match the experts on data it hasn't seen.

5. **Score production chats:** run the judge nightly on a sample, because scoring everything costs too much.

6. **Run A/B tests:** feed prompt or model versions through the same experiment system as any other change.

##### Choosing the unit

| Unit | Good | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat thread** | More samples, and it suits a quality metric that's about one conversation. | A student can see both versions, and their threads are related, so use an analysis that allows for that. |
| **User** | A consistent experience. It's needed for long-term results like learning a skill. | Fewer units, so it takes longer. |

##### Metrics

- **Primary:** the judge's quality score, plus a real outcome like skills learned.

- **Guardrails:** gives away the answer, too wordy, thread length, latency, cost per chat and safety flags.

- **Weak on their own:** thumbs-up is rare and biased, and long chats can mean confusion.

##### Before the test

Run new versions offline against your labelled data and the judge first. This catches bad ideas cheaply. Offline can't tell you how real people respond, so it's a filter, not the final answer.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Chats scored per day | 200,000 × 20% | **40,000** |
| Judge tokens per day | 40,000 × 2,000 | **80 million** |
| Chats needed with a perfect judge | 16 × 0.21 ÷ 0.02² | **about 8,400 per group** |
| Chats needed at 85% accuracy | The visible lift falls to 1.4 points | **about 18,600 per group** |

The judge's cost is small next to the tutor's own LLM calls, and it's what makes the test possible. A real run should still cover full weeks, and longer if you measure learning.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Quality and evaluation:** check the judge against fresh expert labels regularly. A prompt change can shift what the judge sees, so a judge tuned on old chats may drift.

- **Model-specific bias:** if the judge prefers one model's writing style, it can favour that version for the wrong reason. Hide which version wrote each chat, and check the judge separately per version.

- **Answers vary:** the same prompt gives different replies, which adds noise. Log the prompt version, model and parameters for each reply.

- **Novelty:** a new tutor feature can show a fading lift, so look at the effect over time.

- **Cost and latency:** a stronger model might win on quality and lose on budget. Treat them as guardrails, and agree the trade-off beforehand.

- **Safety:** always run safety checks on every reply, not on a sample. Kill a version immediately on a safety failure, and don't wait for the test to end.

- **Rollout:** start at a small share, like 5%, and watch the guardrails before you widen it.

#### How real teams approached it

- **Start from what good means:** The team moved from judging prompts by feel to first defining a measure of how much students were thinking, based on a learning framework.

- **Experts before automation:** Experts labelled real chats against a rubric, and checked that they agreed with each other. Only then was an LLM judge tuned to match them.

- **Sample, don't score everything:** The judge scored a share of production chats nightly, which kept the cost manageable.

- **Pick the unit that fits the question:** They randomised by chat thread, because tutoring quality belongs to a conversation.

- **Test small changes:** They tested prompts, system instructions and different models, sometimes as small as one sentence, and treated experiments as a safety net rather than a delay.

- **Balance the metrics:** Thinking and skills learned were the goal, while guardrails watched for giving away answers, long threads, wordiness and slow replies.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Use thumbs-up ratings, since users decide what's good"

It sounds right, since it's direct user feedback. But few people rate, and those who do aren't typical. Worse, a student may love a tutor that hands out answers, so the rating can reward the very behaviour you want to stop. Measure the outcome you care about, using a judge checked against experts, and treat ratings as a side signal.

## Say it

### Your new LLM tutor's prompt looks better in demos. How do you test it in production, and what's your metric?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not just use thumbs-up ratings?

They're rare, so the sample is small and biased towards people who like rating things. A student may also rate a tutor highly because it gave the answer, which is exactly what you don't want. They can be a secondary signal, but they don't measure learning.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The new model wins on the judge's score but costs three times more. What do you do?

That's a decision to agree on before the test: how much quality is worth how much cost. I'd look at the real outcomes too, not only the judge. I'd also test whether routing only the hard chats to the stronger model gets most of the gain at much lower cost.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you know the judge isn't favouring one model?

I'd have experts label a fresh sample from each version, with the version hidden, then compare judge accuracy per version. If the judge is much less accurate for one, the comparison isn't fair, and I'd fix the judge before trusting the result.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd clarify what good means, because students can enjoy a tutor that gives away answers. I'd pick a metric tied to learning, like cognitive engagement, and have experts label real chats against a rubric, checking they agree with each other. Then I'd tune an LLM judge until it matches them on unseen data, and score a sample of production chats nightly. New prompts first run offline against those labels, as a filter. Live, I'd randomise by chat thread if quality is about one conversation, or by user for long-term learning, and analyse with that in mind. The primary metric is the judge's score plus a real outcome like skills learned. Guardrails are giving away answers, wordiness, latency, cost and safety. A noisy judge shrinks the visible effect by two times accuracy minus one, so judge quality directly sets the runtime. I'd keep validating the judge, hide which version wrote each chat, watch for novelty, and roll out from a small share.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on an education company's approach, from [a vendor's account of Khan Academy's webinar](https://www.growthbook.io/blog/what-i-learned-from-khan-academy-about-a-b-testing-ai), not from the team's own paper. The volumes, assumed judge accuracy and lab are our own illustrations. Uses randomisation, sample size and LLM as a judge. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Fix a Failing AI Feature

> AI-written email subject lines lost to the old rule-based ones in an A/B test. What do you do next?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-ai-subject-lines/
- Before this: Reading the Result: Significance and Decisions (`fundamentals/reading-ab-results`), Prompt Engineering Patterns (`ai-engineering/prompt-engineering-patterns`)
- Quiz topic: `sdexp`

## Intuition

### The situation

A local news app replaced its rule-based email subject lines, which are the first few words of a post, with LLM-written ones. They read better, but clicks fell sharply in an A/B test. The team wants to try more prompts. The interviewer asks:

> AI-written email subject lines lost to the old rule-based ones in an A/B test. What do you do next?

#### Ask before designing

- **How did it lose?** On clicks only, or also on sessions and retention? Across all posts, or only some?

- **What's the baseline?** A simple rule, like the first few words of the post, can be surprisingly good.

- **Scale:** say 10,000 new posts a day, each sent to about 600 people.

- **Must never happen:** a subject line that makes up facts, or misleads people into clicking.

- **Limits:** emails can't wait for slow calls, and LLM calls per email would cost too much.

### The idea

Think of a new headline writer whose headlines are polished, but sell fewer papers. You wouldn't just send them on a writing course. You'd have an experienced editor who's seen what actually sells choose between their headline and the old one, and print the new one only when it's likely to do better.

[Figure: A post comes in. The LLM extracts a subject line. A reward model scores it against the rule-based line. The better one is sent. The model is monitored daily.]

_The reward model is that editor, trained on real click results._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Lower the precision until the gain disappears. Then raise the loss when it's wrong.

#### Why a so-so model can turn a loss into a win

Our simple model, compared with the rule-based line at 0%. All the values are invented for illustration. It also assumes wins and losses are the same size across posts.

The default model is often wrong, and it misses most winners. Yet it flips **−6%** to a small gain, because it blocks most of the losing lines. Lower the precision until the gain disappears, and that's the break-even point: **precision must beat loss ÷ (lift + loss)**.

**Now say why:** why can a model that misses most winners still turn a loss into a win?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

A subject line that reads better isn't always one people click. So don't only rewrite the prompt. **Learn from your A/B data**: use real click results to train a **reward model** that predicts which line people prefer. Generate a line, score it, and send it only if it beats the old rule-based line, which remains the **safe fallback**. Cache by post to cut cost, and monitor the model daily.

#### Generate, then score, then choose

##### First, diagnose

Read the lines that lost, and compare them with the rule-based lines. You often find the model is writing a polished summary, while users respond to the post's own voice. Next, split results by post type. If the AI wins on some posts and loses on others, the job becomes **picking when to use it**.

##### The pipeline

1. **Generate:** tell the model to extract the most interesting part of the post. Extracting also reduces made-up content, compared with writing from scratch.

2. **Enforce limits in code:** cut anything over the length limit.

3. **Score:** the reward model compares the AI line with the rule-based line.

4. **Choose:** send the AI line only if it's predicted to win. Otherwise, send the rule-based line.

5. **Cache:** generate once per post, and reuse it for all recipients.

6. **Fall back:** if the API fails after retries, send the rule-based line.

##### Training the reward model

1. Send both lines to a small share of users for many posts, as small A/B tests.

2. Label each post by real results: if the AI line's click rate is over 10% better, it wins. If it's over 10% worse, it loses. Discard posts with too few sends.

3. Fine-tune a small model to predict the winner from the post and its candidate line.

This is a learning loop: real user behaviour teaches the model what the prompt couldn't express.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Emails per day | 10,000 posts × 600 sends | **6 million** |
| LLM calls with no cache | One per send | **6 million a day** |
| LLM calls with a cache | One per post | **10,000 a day** |
| Reward model checks | One per post | **10,000 a day** |

Caching changes the economics: from a cost per email to a cost per post. It only works if the line isn't personalised, so personalising later would cost far more.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Quality and evaluation:** clicks can reward clickbait. So use sessions and weekly active users as the final measure, and watch unsubscribes and complaints as guardrails.

- **Reliability:** LLM APIs fail. Retry with backoff, cache the results, and fall back to the rule-based line, so an email always goes out.

- **Drift:** preferences and models change. Check the reward model's accuracy daily, retrain it when it falls, and keep a small share of random traffic to supply fresh labels.

- **Selection bias:** if you only send what the model likes, you stop learning what it rejects. A small random share keeps your training data honest.

- **Safety:** extraction limits made-up content, and the reward model adds a second filter, but neither is a guarantee. Use blocklists and sample reviews, since an email can't be recalled.

- **Why not only fine-tune the generator?** Trained on data the rule produced, it may simply learn to copy the rule. In the real case, it matched the rule-based line most of the time, with no clear gain.

- **Rollout:** test the full system against the baseline, in stages, not just its parts.

#### How real teams approached it

- **Accept the surprise:** The plain LLM lines lost to a very simple rule. The team concluded that a more informative line doesn't mean more clicks.

- **Prompts have limits:** Asking the model to extract rather than write helped, but prompt changes alone couldn't beat the rule.

- **Turn tests into labels:** They used real click results as labels, rather than human opinions of which line was better, with thresholds to ignore close calls and low-volume posts.

- **Choose, don't replace:** A small fine-tuned model decided when to use the AI line, keeping the rule for everything else. Even an imperfect model was enough to turn the result around.

- **Keep it simple:** Generating many candidates per post wasn't clearly better than generating a couple.

- **Operate it properly:** They cached per post, retried failed calls, fell back to the rule, checked the model's accuracy daily and retrained it when it dropped.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The prompt needs more work"

It sounds right, since prompts are the easy thing to change. But more informative lines weren't what people clicked on, and prompts can only express what you already know. In the real case, even the better prompt still lost. Use your A/B data to teach a model what people actually prefer, and keep the old line for when the AI won't win.

## Say it

### AI-written email subject lines lost to the old rule-based ones in an A/B test. What do you do next?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why does a model with only 67% precision help?

Because the fallback is a good baseline. It only needs to be right often enough that wins outweigh losses. Blocking most losing lines is what turns the overall result positive. The break-even precision is the loss divided by the lift plus the loss.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Could you just train on clicks and ship whatever gets the most?

That invites clickbait. Clicks can rise while people lose trust and unsubscribe. So keep the extraction constraint and safety filters, use sessions and retention as the final measure, and watch complaints and unsubscribes as guardrails.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How would you personalise this?

It would break the per-post cache, so cost grows towards one call per email. I'd start with a few versions per post, and choose among them by user segment, using a bandit if rewards are quick. I'd test whether the gain justifies the cost before going further.

#### The 30-second answer

First I'd diagnose it: read the losing lines, and split results by post type. A line that reads better isn't always one people click. If the AI wins on some posts, the problem becomes choosing when to use it. So I'd generate by extraction, which also reduces made-up content, and enforce length in code. I'd run small A/B tests across many posts, and label each by real click rates, ignoring posts with too few sends. Then I'd train a reward model to predict the winner, and send the AI line only when it's predicted to win. Otherwise, the rule-based line goes out, and it's also the fallback if the API fails. I'd cache per post, because each post goes to hundreds of people. I'd judge the full system on sessions and weekly actives, with unsubscribes as guardrails. I'd check the reward model daily, retrain when it drops, and keep some random traffic, so I keep learning what it rejects.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a neighbourhood app's published work: [Nextdoor's paper, Let AI Entertain You](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12457). We read most of the paper directly and the later sections through a summary. Volumes and the lab's numbers are our own illustrations. Uses reading results, prompts and LLMOps. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Test Rankers Faster with Interleaving

> A ranking A/B test takes weeks, and you have many candidate models. How do you test faster?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-interleaving/
- Before this: Sample Size, Power and Runtime (`fundamentals/sample-size-and-power`), Ranking Metrics (`fundamentals/ranking-metrics`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A search team has 20 candidate ranking models a quarter. Each A/B test takes 3 weeks, because bookings are rare and users differ widely, so most ideas never get tested. The interviewer asks:

> A ranking A/B test takes weeks, and you have many candidate models. How do you test faster?

#### Ask before designing

- **What's being compared?** Rankers on the same candidates, or changes to layout or pricing? Interleaving only suits the first.

- **What outcome?** Clicks arrive quickly. Bookings are rare, and can come days later.

- **Scale:** say 20 candidate models a quarter, with each A/B test taking 3 weeks.

- **Latency:** two rankers must run per request, so can you afford it?

- **Other surfaces:** does anything else reuse the list, like a map view?

### The idea

Think of a taste test. Give one group of people cola A, and another group cola B, and you need many people, since tastes differ so much. Give the same person both, and ask which they prefer, and you need far fewer. But that tells you which they prefer in a sip, not how sales will go.

[Figure: Two rankers each score the candidates. Their lists merge with a coin flip and team draft. Clicks give credit to each ranker per user. Only the best candidate moves to a full A/B test.]

_A fast filter first, then a full A/B test on the winner._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Click items and watch the credit. Tap the shared item. Then flip the coin.

#### Draft a list, then see the time saved

**Ranker A's list**a, b, c, d, e

**Ranker B's list**b, c, a, f, g

**The list the user sees.** Tap an item to record a click:

The lists are a simple example, and the speed-up is an illustration of how much less traffic you might need for similar power. It varies by metric, and a real test should still cover daily patterns.

Tap **c**: nobody gets credit, as both rankers wanted it. Flip the coin: the pairs swap order, and on average neither ranker gets the better position. That's what makes the comparison fair.

**Now say why:** why does the coin flip stop one ranker getting an unfair advantage?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

An A/B test gives each user one ranker, so most of what you measure is differences between users. **Interleaving** shows each user one list **blended from both rankers**, so the same person compares them directly. It can need far less traffic. So use it as a **fast filter**, then confirm the winner with an A/B test, because it tells you which ranker users prefer, not what the launch will do to your business.

#### Merge, credit, compare

##### Team draft with competitive pairs

1. Flip one coin per search to decide who goes first.

2. Take each ranker's top item that isn't on the list yet.

3. If they're the same, add it once. Neither ranker gets credit for it.

4. If they differ, add both as a **competitive pair**, in the coin's order, and tag each with its ranker.

5. Repeat until the list is full.

##### Credit and significance

- **Credit:** when a user clicks or books a tagged item, its ranker wins that pair. Shared items earn nothing, which removes noise.

- **Per user:** each user votes for the ranker with more wins. Users with a tie or no wins drop out.

- **Test:** compare the count of users who prefer each ranker with an even split, using a proportion test.

- **Slow outcomes:** credit a booking to the searches where that listing appeared during the test.

##### Why it's so much more sensitive

- **Same user, both rankers:** differences between users cancel out.

- **Disagreements only:** where rankers agree, no signal is possible, so it isn't counted.

##### The two-stage process

Offline tests shortlist the models, interleaving picks the promising few, and an A/B test on the winner measures its real effect.

##### What it can't do

- **Different experiences:** new layouts, or anything beyond which items rank where.

- **Set-level ranking:** if a ranker's value comes from the list as a whole, such as diversity, a blended list breaks it.

- **Business size:** it tells you which is preferred, not the revenue change. Continuous outcomes like revenue are hard to credit.

- **Marketplace effects:** a ranker that crowds bookings onto a few sellers won't show up.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview, including the 50 times speed-up.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A/B testing all candidates, one by one | 20 models × 3 weeks | **60 weeks** |
| Traffic per interleaving test | 100% ÷ 50 | **about 2%** |
| Interleaving tests at once | 20 models at 2% each | **uses 40% of traffic** |
| Then A/B test the top 2 | 2 × 3 weeks | **about 6 weeks, plus the filter week** |

The gain is in how many ideas you can try, not only in time. Each request also runs two rankers, so ranking compute roughly doubles for interleaved traffic.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Quality and evaluation:** before trusting it, run interleaving and A/B tests on the same pairs, and measure how often they agree. Keep doing this over time.

- **Reliability:** if a ranker fails or is slow, serve the other ranker's list without interleaving, and exclude that request from the result.

- **Latency and cost:** run both rankers in parallel, so the wait is the slower of the two. Caching shared results and retrieval saves compute.

- **Logging:** record which ranker owns each position. Without this, you can't assign credit, and bugs are very hard to find.

- **Dilution:** count only searches where rankers disagreed, and users who actually engaged. One company reports this greatly increased sensitivity.

- **Trust checks:** run A against A. Each ranker should win half the time. If not, the merging or logging has a bias.

- **Counterfactual evaluation:** an alternative is to show one ranker's list and compute what the other would have done. Nothing is blended, so it helps when rankers optimise the set as a whole.

#### How real teams approached it

- **Filter, then confirm:** Search and delivery teams use interleaving to narrow down candidates early, and A/B tests to confirm the winner.

- **Fix the fairness:** Competitive pairs make credit simpler, and one coin flip per search balances positions between the two rankers.

- **Remove what can't help:** Teams increase sensitivity by ignoring results both rankers agree on, and users who never engaged.

- **Check it against A/B:** Before trusting it, teams run both methods on the same rankers and measure how often they pick the same winner.

- **Know its blind spots:** Teams report cases where interleaving and A/B disagree, as seeing options side by side changes behaviour. They avoid it for layouts and fundamentally different search strategies.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Interleaving is faster, so replace A/B tests"

It sounds right, since it gets an answer with a fraction of the traffic. But it answers a narrower question: which ranker's items users pick when shown both. It can't tell you the revenue change, or test a new layout. One team even saw significantly negative interleaving with a neutral A/B test. Use it to filter, and A/B test the winner.

## Say it

### A ranking A/B test takes weeks, and you have many candidate models. How do you test faster?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Interleaving says B wins, but the A/B test is neutral. Which do you trust?

The A/B test for the launch decision, because it measures the real experience. Interleaving makes users compare options side by side, which isn't how they'd normally use the product. Look at why they differ, though: B may have won clicks that don't turn into bookings.

Follow-up 2 of 3

How do you handle bookings that happen days later?

Keep the user's assignment and logged lists across the test, then credit a booking to the ranker that showed that listing as a competitive item in their searches. Users vote once over the whole period. You can test different attribution windows, and check them against A/B results.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why does a coin flip per search matter?

Whoever goes first gets the higher position in each pair, and higher positions get more clicks. The coin gives each ranker the better position equally often, so position bias averages out across searches, and a ranker can't win just by being placed first.

#### The 30-second answer

An A/B test gives each user one ranker, so most of the variance is between users. I'd use interleaving as a filter. For each search, a coin picks which ranker goes first, then we take each ranker's top unused item. If they agree, it goes in once with no credit. If they differ, we add a competitive pair, tagged by ranker. When a user clicks or books a tagged item, that ranker wins the pair, and each user votes for whichever won more. I'd test user votes against an even split with a proportion test. Because the same user sees both rankers, and only disagreements count, it can need far less traffic. It only tells me which is preferred, though, not the business effect. It doesn't suit layouts, set-level ranking like diversity, or marketplace effects. So offline shortlists, interleaving filters, and an A/B test confirms the winner. I'd run both on some pairs to measure agreement, and log which ranker owns each position.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on published work: [Airbnb's KDD 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.00751v1) (part read directly and part through a summary), [Walmart's post](https://tech.walmart.com/content/walmart-global-tech/en_us/blog/post/driving-faster-experimentation-through-interleaving-in-walmart-search.html) and [DoorDash's post](https://careers.doordash.com/blog/doordash-experimentation-with-interleaving-designs), which was blocked for us, so we used search excerpts. Uses sample size and ranking metrics. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Measure a Feed Change with Network Effects

> A feed change affects what a user's connections see. How do you measure its real effect?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-network-experiment/
- Before this: Interference: When Groups Affect Each Other (`fundamentals/interference-in-experiments`)
- Quiz topic: `sdexp`

## Intuition

### The situation

A professional network changes its feed ranking. Viewers scroll a little less in the A/B test, so it looks bad. But creators may get more comments, and that could bring them back. A normal test can't see this. The interviewer asks:

> A feed change affects what a user's connections see. How do you measure its real effect?

#### Ask before designing

- **Direct or network effect?** The direct effect is how the change alters my behaviour. The network effect is how my connections' behaviour alters my experience.

- **Which way does it travel?** A feed ranking change alters what viewers do, which then changes what creators receive.

- **Which metrics?** Sessions and engagement for the people affected, and posting for creators.

- **Scale:** how much traffic can you spare, given a test like this takes up many users?

- **The graph:** who really influences whom: all connections, or those you interact with?

### The idea

Think of testing whether a new phone plan makes people call more. Give it to random people, and those without it also get more calls, from friends who have it. So give it to all of one person's friends, then see what happens to that one person. That shows the effect of their friends' change.

[Figure: Pick focal users called egos. Attach their connections, called alters. Flip a coin per cluster and treat the alters. Measure only the egos, who are all kept on one version.]

_A test between all my connections getting A, and all my connections getting B._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Drop the egos to 40,000. Then raise the loss rate to 50%.

#### Loss rate and cluster count

Illustrative: we assume a 1.5% smallest effect at 200,000 egos, and 50 people treated per ego. The measured effect assumes a share of connections equal to the loss rate wasn't treated, and that the effect is proportional, which is our simplification. Real sizes depend on your graph and metric.

Drop to **40,000 egos**. The smallest detectable effect rises above 3%, and you can no longer see a true 3% effect. Accepting a higher loss rate fits more clusters, but it **shrinks what you measure**, so you have to balance the two.

**Now say why:** why does a higher loss rate shrink the effect you measure?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

If a change makes me comment more, my connections see more comments, even if they're in control. A normal A/B test mixes the two groups, and **misses that effect**. An **ego cluster** takes one focal user (the ego) and their connections (the alters), treats all the alters together, and **measures only the ego**. Comparing egos whose connections all got the change against those whose connections didn't isolates the network effect. It's costly, because you **treat many people for each ego you measure**.

#### Treat the connections, measure the ego

##### Why a normal test misses it

A user in control has connections in treatment, and vice versa. Both groups receive some of the network effect, so the difference between them hides it. Your test can then call a change bad when it's actually helping people elsewhere in the network.

##### Building ego clusters

1. **Choose the graph:** use who actually affects whom, like past feed impressions. A full connections graph makes clusters too big.

2. **Select egos:** sample by degree, so egos represent all users. Starting at lower degrees helps more clusters fit.

3. **Attach alters:** assign each alter to one ego by the strength of their link. Each person belongs to one cluster.

4. **Accept some loss:** an alter already claimed elsewhere can't join, so a share of each ego's connections isn't treated as planned. This is the **loss rate**.

##### Running the test

1. Flip a coin per cluster.

2. Give the alters that group's version.

3. Put all egos in the same version, like control, so the only difference between them is what their connections received.

4. Compare egos across groups with a t-test. Alters aren't analysed for the network effect.

It's an A/B test between "all my connections got A" and "all my connections got B".

##### Costs and risks

- **Traffic:** most of the treated people are only there to create the effect.

- **Biased leftovers:** clusters take many engaged users, so what's left for other tests is less active.

- **Stale clusters:** relationships change, so rebuild often. It doesn't suit tests lasting months.

- **One hop only:** it assumes that only direct connections matter, so effects travelling further are not captured.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| People per ego | Our assumption, from a typical cluster size | **say 50** |
| Egos per group | 200,000 ÷ 2 | **100,000** |
| Detectable effect at 4 times the egos | 1.5% ÷ √4 | **about 0.75%** |
| People at that size | 800,000 × 50 | **40 million, if clusters stayed this size** |

So you can't buy precision with traffic forever. This is why teams use it only for changes where network effects are large and matter.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Quality and evaluation:** before the test, check that egos look representative, and run A/A tests on data from before the test.

- **Reliability:** clusters go out of date as people connect. Use recent clusters, and watch the loss rate during the test, as it grows over time.

- **Scalability:** building clusters over a huge graph is a heavy job. The newer method moved from one framework to Spark and cut run time.

- **Traffic competition:** clusters use many engaged users, so other experiments see lower-engagement traffic. Reserve a share, and make it visible to other teams.

- **Which graph:** an impressions graph captures who sees whom, while a graph of comments and likes captures stronger links. Stronger links give fewer leaks, but fewer clusters.

- **Alternatives:** cluster randomisation, or using graph-aware assignment in dense networks. Each trades off different biases.

- **The decision:** combine direct and network effects. A change can look bad directly and good across the network, so agree on how to weigh them.

#### How the real team approached it

- **The surprise that justified it:** A change that looked bad for the people who received it turned out to help their connections. A normal test would've seen only the harm.

- **Use the graph that matters:** The team built clusters from who actually sees whom, not from all connections, which kept clusters a workable size.

- **Accept low power:** Since only egos are analysed, results are noisier than in a normal test, and they read them with that in mind.

- **Count the cost to others:** Clusters absorb many engaged users, so what's left for other experiments is less active.

- **Keep clusters fresh:** Relationships change, so they avoid reusing old clusters, and don't use this for tests lasting months.

- **Improve the method:** A later version used a simpler way to assign alters, which gave more clusters, fewer leaks and much faster builds.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just run a bigger A/B test"

It sounds right, since bigger tests detect smaller effects. But the problem is bias, not noise. Control users still get part of the effect from treated connections, however big the sample is, so you'd measure the wrong thing more precisely. You have to change how users are grouped.

## Say it

### A feed change affects what a user's connections see. How do you measure its real effect?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why treat the alters and measure the ego, not the other way round?

You want the effect of connections' behaviour on a person. So you change the connections, and watch that person. Keeping egos on one version means their own experience of the feature can't explain any difference between the groups.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The direct test is negative, and the network effect is positive. Do you ship?

You need to decide how to weigh them before the test. Scale both to the whole population, because the network effect may reach far more people. Then look at long-term metrics, as a change that moves engagement from viewers to creators may help or hurt the product overall.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Why not use city-level or graph cluster randomisation instead?

Those can work, but dense professional networks connect across cities, and clusters leak. Graph clusters also tend to be very unequal in size. Ego clusters measure a specific one-hop effect with a simple comparison, though they cost more traffic and only analyse the egos.

#### The 30-second answer

A normal A/B test mixes treated and control users who are connected, so both groups get part of the network effect, and the test misses it. I'd use ego clusters. I'd build a graph of who actually affects whom, such as past feed impressions, and sample egos across all degrees. Each ego gets their alters, the connections that influence them, and each person belongs to one cluster. I'd flip a coin per cluster, and give that version to the alters. All egos stay on the same version, and I compare only egos. That's a test between all my connections getting A and all my connections getting B. Some alters will be unavailable, which is the loss rate, and that shrinks the measured effect. It's expensive, because I treat many people for each ego. It also takes engaged users from other tests, goes stale quickly and only covers one hop. So I'd use it when network effects really matter, and weigh direct and network effects together in the launch decision.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a professional network's published method: [LinkedIn's ego-cluster paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08755), which we read in full, and [its later improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05945), which we read in part. The volumes and lab numbers are illustrations. Uses interference and randomisation. · checked 5 Nov 2026
