# Personalise Images with Bandits

> You want to personalise which image each user sees for each title. How do you choose it, and how do you prove it helps?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-image-personalisation/
- Before this: Bandits vs A/B Tests (`fundamentals/bandits-vs-ab-tests`)
- Quiz topic: `sdrec`

## Intuition

### The situation

A streaming service shows one image for each title. A/B tests have found good images overall, but different people respond to different actors or genres. There are huge numbers of image requests a second. The interviewer asks:

> You want to personalise which image each user sees for each title. How do you choose it, and how do you prove it helps?

#### Ask before designing

- **What's the action?** Pick one image per title, per user, on each page.

- **What's a good outcome?** A play followed by enjoying the title. A click and quick exit should count as bad.

- **Scale:** image requests can be enormous, so can it run live or be computed ahead?

- **Where do images come from?** Designers often choose them, which limits how misleading they can be.

- **New titles:** how do you handle titles with no data yet?

### The idea

Think of a bookshop assistant choosing which book cover to show you. They learn your tastes, usually show what you'll like, and sometimes try something else to learn more. To judge a new assistant, you can check old records of cases where they'd have made the same choice, then trial them for real.

[Figure: Each title has candidate images. The system explores and logs its probabilities. A model per image learns from the rewards. Choices are precomputed and served. Replay filters models offline, and an A/B test proves the lift.]

_Exploration creates the data that lets you evaluate new models safely._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise exploration to 50%, then raise the images from 6 to 30.

#### How much should you explore?

Illustrative: the best image has a 12% take rate, and others have 8%. Exploration picks images uniformly at random. A replay match is when a fixed policy's choice equals the random image, so it happens once per candidate count. This ignores what's learned from the data, which is the point of paying.

Raise the images from **6** to **30**. Replay matches fall by five times, because the chance a random image matches is one in the number of images. More images means more exploring, and each new image has a cost to create as well.

**Now say why:** why do more images leave you with fewer replay matches?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

A/B testing can find the single best image for a title, but not the best one for each person. A **contextual bandit** uses user context to pick an image, and it **keeps exploring** to gather data. **Log the chance** of every image shown, so **offline replay** can compare models on past data without risk. To prove it works, A/B test the personalised system against an **unpersonalised bandit**. Reward real watching, not clicks, or you'll learn clickbait.

#### Explore, log, learn, serve

##### From A/B tests to bandits

| Approach | Finds | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **A/B test on images** | The best image overall. | Slow, and one answer for everyone. |
| **Bandit** | The best image overall, while spending less on bad ones. | Still one answer for everyone. |
| **Contextual bandit** | The best image for this person and context. | Needs features, logging and more data. |

##### How it runs

1. **Context:** the user's history, device and page.

2. **Predict:** a model per image estimates the reward for this context.

3. **Explore:** mostly choose the best image, and sometimes try another. Epsilon-greedy explores at random. Thompson sampling explores in proportion to uncertainty.

4. **Log:** the image shown, its probability, the candidates and the features at that moment.

5. **Reward:** join what happened next to that log, and train the next model.

##### Offline replay

1. Take logged sessions where the image was chosen by exploration.

2. Ask the new model what it would have shown.

3. Keep only sessions where its choice matches what was actually shown.

4. Compute the take fraction: of those matches, how many led to a play?

Those rewards are real, not simulated. But few sessions match, especially with many images, so replay needs lots of data and has high variance.

##### Proving it works

Replay filters candidates. Then run an **A/B test**, comparing the personalised system with an unpersonalised bandit. Compare with a good baseline, or you'll credit personalisation for what any bandit could do.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Image requests at peak | Our assumption | **say 20 million a second** |
| Can each be a live model call? | Even at 1 ms each, 20 million × 1 ms | **20,000 CPU seconds, every second** |
| So compute ahead of time | Choices stored per user and title | **a fast lookup at request time** |
| Log size | 1 billion impressions × 500 bytes | **about 500 GB a day** |

That scale decides the architecture. Precompute gets you cheap lookups, at the cost of stale context and of compute for items that are never shown.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Quality and evaluation:** reward watching and enjoying, not just clicks. Otherwise, the model learns images that mislead people, who then quit quickly.

- **Attribution:** a play might come from the recommendation, the image or both. Evaluate the image choice with the title's position held fixed, or account for it in your model.

- **Changing images:** if the image changes between visits, which image caused the play? Changes can confuse people too, so consider keeping a choice stable for a while.

- **Reliability:** a missing image badly harms the experience. Always have a fallback, like a default image, and alert on missing ones.

- **Logging at compute time:** with precompute, log the choice, its probability and the candidate set when you compute it, then match it with the impression. Use the same feature code online and offline, or the model will see different data in training.

- **Cold start:** warm-start from existing data, and explore more for new titles.

- **Monitoring:** set aside a small share for simple exploration, to compare against the model and keep unbiased data.

#### How the real team approached it

- **Frame it as a bandit:** The homepage is the environment, showing an image is the action, and positive engagement is the reward.

- **Guard against clickbait:** Designers choose which images are available, and the reward is about enjoying a title, not only clicking.

- **Filter offline, prove online:** Replay compared algorithms on past sessions. Then an A/B test compared the best personalised bandits with unpersonalised ones.

- **Log at decision time:** They recorded the exploration probability, the candidates and a snapshot of the facts used for features, and shared feature code between training and serving.

- **Let scale shape the design:** With so many requests, they computed choices ahead of time and looked them up, with care to always show some image.

This reflects a 2018 talk, so current systems may differ.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "Just train a classifier on past click data"

It sounds right, since you have plenty of logs. But past data only shows images that were chosen for a reason, so you can't tell what would've happened with others. Without exploration and logged probabilities, the model learns from its own past choices. Clicks also reward clickbait, so reward watching, and pay for some exploration.

## Say it

### You want to personalise which image each user sees for each title. How do you choose it, and how do you prove it helps?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why log the probability of each image?

Evaluation has to correct for how images were chosen. If the model showed an image 90% of the time, its data isn't comparable with an image shown 5% of the time. With the probabilities, you can reweight logged data, such as with inverse propensity scoring, to estimate how a new model would have done.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Why A/B test against an unpersonalised bandit, not against the old fixed image?

Because you want to know what personalisation adds. A bandit alone already beats a fixed image, by finding the best image overall. Against a fixed image, you'd credit personalisation for that gain too, and might overbuild.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Replay looks great, but the A/B test is flat. Why?

Replay assumes one image's effect can be judged in isolation. Live, images interact with the page, with what the person has seen before and with changes between visits. Replay can also have high variance with few matches. So treat replay as a filter, and trust the A/B test.

#### The 30-second answer

An A/B test finds the best image overall, but I want the best one per person, so I'd use a contextual bandit. For each title, a model per image predicts the reward from the user's history, device and page. Mostly it shows the best image, and it explores with epsilon-greedy or Thompson sampling. I'd reward actual watching, not clicks, or it will learn clickbait. I'd log the image shown, its probability, the candidates and the features at that moment, as all later evaluation depends on this. To compare models offline, I'd use replay: keep logged sessions where a new model's choice matches the image shown, and compute the take fraction. It's real data, but few sessions match. At this scale, I'd precompute choices and serve by lookup, with fallback images. To prove it works, I'd A/B test personalised bandits against unpersonalised ones. That shows what personalisation adds, not what any bandit would give.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a streaming company's published work: [Netflix's QCon 2018 talk](https://qconsf.com/sf2018/system/files/presentation-slides/2018-11_-_qcon_artwork_personalization_talk.pdf), which we read from its slides, and [a summary of its blog post](https://www.reforge.com/blog/brief-netflix-artwork-personalization-through-multi-armed-bandit-testing), as the post itself was blocked for us. The volumes and lab numbers are illustrations. Uses bandits and LLMOps. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Set a Launch Decision Rule

> A launch wins on the main metric, but looks slightly worse on two guardrails. What's your decision rule before the test starts?

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 25 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-launch-decision-rule/
- Before this: Choosing Metrics: OEC, Drivers and Guardrails (`fundamentals/choosing-ab-metrics`), Multiple Testing and Segments (`fundamentals/multiple-testing`)
- Quiz topic: `sdexp`

## Intuition

### The situation

A test shows orders per user up significantly. Two of five guardrails, latency and cancellations, are slightly negative but not significant. One person wants to ship, and another wants to wait. You realise no one agreed on a rule. The interviewer asks:

> A launch wins on the main metric, but looks slightly worse on two guardrails. What's your decision rule before the test starts?

#### Ask before designing

- **Which metrics matter?** Which do you want to improve, and which only need to stay safe?

- **What's the margin?** For each guardrail, how much harm would you accept for this gain?

- **What's an acceptable mistake?** Set the false-win rate, and the chance of missing a good change.

- **Who decides?** If a person can override the rule, write down when and how.

- **What's outside the test?** If strategy or legal needs affect the decision, a mechanical rule won't cover them.

### The idea

Think of approving a new medicine. It must be proven to work on at least one main outcome. And for each safety measure, you need evidence that it's no worse than an agreed limit. Having no proof of harm isn't enough, because a small trial might simply have missed it.

[Figure: Four checks. Success metrics must beat control. Guardrails must stay within their margins. A harm check finds evidence of damage. Quality checks confirm the test is valid. Ship only if all four pass.]

_Agree on it before you see any data._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the guardrails to 10, and watch how often a harmless change would pass. Then see what correcting it costs.

#### What do extra guardrails cost?

**The decision.** Tick what your test showed:

At α = 5% and β = 20%, using the simple correction from the paper, with one-sided tests. "All pass" assumes independent guardrails, the worst case. Extra users compare the required size with one uncorrected test. Our own calculation.

Raise the guardrails to **10**. Without a correction, a harmless change would pass them all only about **11%** of the time, so nearly every good change would be blocked. That's the risk that goes unnoticed, and why guardrails need power, not α, corrected.

**Now say why:** why does needing all guardrails to pass reduce power, not raise false wins?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Agree the rule before the test. **Ship if and only if**: at least one success metric significantly wins, every guardrail is significantly **not worse than an agreed margin**, nothing shows clear harm, and the quality checks pass. "Slightly worse" is only a problem if you can't rule out harm beyond the margin. The surprising part is the error control: because you need **all** guardrails to pass, correct **power** for them, not false positives.

#### Four kinds of check

| Type | The question | The test |
|---|---|---|
| **Success** | Did it get better? | Superiority: is the effect above zero? |
| **Guardrail** | Is it no worse than the margin? | Non-inferiority: is the effect above −margin? |
| **Deterioration** | Is there evidence of harm? | Inferiority: is the effect below zero? Run on success and guardrail metrics too. |
| **Quality** | Is the test itself valid? | Checks like sample ratio mismatch. |

##### Ship if and only if

1. At least one success metric is significantly better.

2. All guardrails are significantly non-inferior.

3. No success, guardrail or deterioration metric shows evidence of harm.

4. No quality test invalidates the experiment.

##### Reading "slightly worse"

Say a guardrail's margin is −1%. Its point estimate is −0.2%.

- **Interval from −0.6% to +0.2%:** it stays above −1%, so the guardrail passes, even though the estimate is below zero.

- **Interval from −1.5% to +1.1%:** harm beyond the margin is still possible, so it hasn't passed. You lack evidence, even though nothing is "significant".

##### Correcting the errors

This is what surprises people. The two kinds of metric need opposite corrections:

| | Success metrics | Guardrails |
|---|---|---|
| **You need** | At least one to win | All of them to pass |
| **Danger** | More metrics give more chances of a false win | More metrics give more chances of failing by accident |
| **False-positive rate** | Divide by the number of metrics: α/S | **No correction:** α |
| **Power** | Plan with β/(G+1) | Plan with β/(G+1) |

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

With 1 success metric and 5 guardrails, at α = 5% and β = 20%, using one-sided tests.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Corrected β | 0.2 ÷ (5 + 1) | **0.033, so about 97% power per metric** |
| Normal z-term | (1.645 + 0.842)² | **6.2** |
| Corrected z-term | (1.645 + 1.834)² | **12.1** |
| Extra users | 12.1 ÷ 6.2 | **about twice as many** |

That's the real cost of each extra metric, so keep the list short. A guardrail's sample size also depends on its margin: a tighter margin needs far more users, and a margin of half the size needs four times as many.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Setting margins:** a margin should reflect what harm you'd accept for this benefit. Set it before the test, and in the business's terms, such as a change in churn worth a given amount.

- **Why not correct α for guardrails?** You'd only wrongly pass all of them if every one wrongly passed. Needing all of them to pass already limits false positives. Adjusting α would only make it harder to ship.

- **Correlated metrics:** these corrections hold whatever the correlation, but they're conservative. If metrics move together, you can correct less, with care.

- **Deterioration checks:** these catch clear harm, even on metrics you weren't protecting. Run them sequentially during the test, so you can stop early.

- **Overrides:** a rule won't fit everything. If external factors matter, write down who can override it and record why, so people can learn from it later.

- **Metric bloat:** teams keep adding guardrails. Each costs users, so review the list, and remove those that have never affected a decision.

- **Automation:** build the rule into the platform, so the sample size comes from the plan and the result comes from the rule.

#### How the real team approached it

- **Make the rule explicit:** The team writes one rule covering success, guardrails, harm and quality, so the decision is agreed before anyone sees results.

- **Match the test to the job:** Success metrics use superiority tests, and guardrails use non-inferiority tests against a margin.

- **Correct what actually inflates:** Needing at least one win inflates false wins, so that's corrected for success metrics. Needing all guardrails to pass reduces power, so power is corrected instead.

- **Keep it practical:** The approach is built for clarity, and it holds however the metrics are correlated.

- **Know when not to use it:** They say it doesn't fit decisions that depend partly on factors the experiment can't model.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "It's not significantly worse, so the guardrails are fine"

It sounds right, since no alarm went off. But a small or noisy test can fail to detect real harm. Not significant means you haven't shown harm, not that there's none. So test whether the change is significantly no worse than an agreed margin. If the interval still includes unacceptable harm, you don't have evidence that it's safe.

## Say it

### A launch wins on the main metric, but looks slightly worse on two guardrails. What's your decision rule before the test starts?

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why not correct the significance level for guardrails too?

You only wrongly ship if every guardrail wrongly passes. So requiring all of them already limits the false-positive rate to α. Correcting it further would just block good launches. The paper behind this rule shows this formally, and that it's power that needs the correction.

Follow-up 2 of 3

The guardrail's interval crosses the margin, and the win is big. Do you ship?

By the rule, no: you can't rule out unacceptable harm. Practically, you could extend the test if it was underpowered, since that narrows the interval. If leaders want to accept the risk, they can override, but it should be a recorded choice, not a quiet reinterpretation of the data.

Follow-up 3 of 3

How do you choose a margin?

Work from what the harm would cost compared with the expected benefit, such as how much retention you'd give up for a given revenue gain. It's a business decision, set before the test. Note the trade-off: a tighter margin needs many more users, and halving it needs four times as many.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd agree the rule before the test. Ship if and only if at least one success metric significantly wins, all guardrails are significantly non-inferior, no metric shows evidence of harm, and quality checks like sample ratio mismatch pass. For guardrails, slightly worse isn't the question. I'd look at the confidence interval against the margin we agreed. If it stays above the margin, it passes. If it crosses the margin, we can't rule out unacceptable harm, so it hasn't passed, even if nothing's significant. Corrections are the subtle part. For success metrics, you need at least one to win, so more metrics mean more false wins, and I'd divide alpha by the number. For guardrails, you need all to pass, so I wouldn't correct alpha. Instead, power falls, so I'd plan with beta over guardrails plus one. With five guardrails, that needs about twice as many users. Each metric has a cost, so I'd keep the list short and allow documented overrides for factors outside the test.

**Key terms and sources**

Based on a music streaming company's published framework: [Spotify's post](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2024/3/risk-aware-product-decisions-in-a-b-tests-with-multiple-metrics), read in full, and [its paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11609), read in part. The lab's sample sizes are our own calculations. Uses choosing metrics, multiple testing and sample size. · checked 5 Nov 2026

# Design an Experimentation Platform

> Your company runs a few A/B tests by hand. Design a platform that lets teams run hundreds at once, and trust the results.

- Track: System Design › Experimentation › Designs
- Type: Design · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/system-design/design-experimentation-platform/
- Before this: Running Many Tests at Once (`fundamentals/running-many-tests-at-once`), Trust Checks: SRM and A/A Tests (`fundamentals/sample-ratio-mismatch`)
- Quiz topic: `sdexp`

## Intuition

### The situation

Your company runs a few A/B tests by hand, with analysts writing queries for each one. Results take a week, teams argue about definitions, and a broken test recently shipped. Leadership wants hundreds of tests running at once. The interviewer asks:

> Your company runs a few A/B tests by hand. Design a platform that lets teams run hundreds at once, and trust the results.

#### Ask before designing

- **Scale:** say 50 million users a day, 300 tests at once, and 2 billion events a day.

- **Where do changes run?** Backend, web, mobile apps? Mobile users may not update their app for weeks.

- **What's the unit?** Mostly users, but do you need sessions, devices, or cities?

- **How fresh must results be?** Daily for decisions, but guardrail alarms in minutes.

- **Who uses it?** If non-specialists read the results, the platform must prevent mistakes by design.

- **Must never happen:** a slow or failed platform call breaking the product, or a broken test silently shipped.

### The idea

Think of a large hospital running many clinical trials. You need a fair way to assign patients, careful records of who actually took what, one agreed way to measure outcomes, and an independent office that checks each trial before anyone reads the results. Assigning patients is the easy part. Trust takes the rest of the work.

[Figure: Four jobs. Assign locally by hash. Log real exposure. Join exposures to metrics. Compute results after trust checks.]

_The hash is easy. Trust is the hard part._

### Play

**Try to break it.** Raise the tests and metrics. Then change the sample ratio cutoff.

#### What does scale do to trust?

Illustrative. Each result is read once a day, at 5% significance, with no real effects. Exposure rows assume each user reaches half of the running tests, with one row per test per day. That's why real systems deduplicate and aggregate early.

With 300 tests and 50 metrics each, a dashboard shows 15,000 results a day. If nothing worked, about 750 would still look significant. So the platform must lead with a few **decision metrics**, and label the rest as exploratory. At a 0.01 cutoff, 3 healthy tests get a sample ratio alarm each day. Move it to 0.001, and that falls to 0.3, which is why large platforms use stricter cutoffs. Now look at the exposure rows: they grow with tests times users, which is why this is the part of the pipeline to design first.

**Now say why:** why must a platform show only a few decision metrics by default?

## Architecture

### Architecture

#### In one breath

Split it into four jobs. **Assignment** hashes each user locally, with no network call. **Exposure logging** records who actually reached each change. A **metrics pipeline** joins exposures to events each day. A **stats engine** computes results, with trust checks first. The hard parts aren't the hashing, but making results trustworthy by default: automatic sample ratio checks, one agreed metric definition, and stopping rules built in, so a dashboard can't invite peeking.

#### Four jobs, plus the rules around them

| Part | What it does | Key choice |
|---|---|---|
| **Config service** | Stores tests, splits, targeting and metrics, with review before launch | Pushed as data files, not code, so tests launch quickly and non-engineers can create them |
| **Assignment SDK** | Computes hash(user, salt) mod buckets, inside the app or server | Local, with no network call and no stored table, and a safe default if the config is missing |
| **Exposure logs** | Records when a user actually reached the change | Log at the moment of use, not at assignment |
| **Metrics pipeline** | Joins exposures to events, and builds per-user daily totals | One central metric definition, so teams don't disagree on what "orders" means |
| **Stats engine** | Computes effects, intervals, CUPED, the delta method and corrections | Store per-user totals, so results can be recomputed |
| **Trust and decision layer** | Runs sample ratio checks and guardrails, then shows the result | Hide or flag results if trust checks fail |

##### Running many tests

Use layers. Each layer has its own hash, so a user gets one bucket per layer. Tests in different layers overlap, and tests in the same layer are exclusive. Keep a small domain for big changes that touch many layers. The system tracks which settings belong to which layer, and rejects conflicting tests when they're created.

##### Getting exposure right

If everyone assigned counts, those who never saw the change dilute the effect. So analyse users from their first exposure, in both groups. Control must log too, at the point where treatment would've changed. Otherwise the groups won't be comparable.

##### Launch flow

1. Create the test: hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails, sample size and runtime, filled from past data.

2. Run automatic checks: is there a control, is the traffic free, is the split valid?

3. Canary on a small share, watching crashes and latency in near real time.

4. Ramp up to the planned size.

5. Read results only at planned looks, once trust checks pass.

6. Decide by the agreed rule, and record it.

#### The numbers worth saying out loud

All of these are assumptions for the interview.

| Question | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Assignment calls | 50 million users × 40 checks a day | 2 billion a day, about 23,000 a second |
| As a network call | 23,000 a second, at a 20 ms wait each | Too slow and too fragile, so hash locally |
| Exposure rows | 50 million × 300 tests × half reached | 7.5 billion a day, before deduplication |
| Per-user totals | 7.5 billion × 50 metrics | 375 billion values at worst, so compute only what each test needs |
| Storage for exposures | 7.5 billion × 40 bytes | About 300 GB a day |

The hash is cheap. The join between exposures and events is what costs money, so that's what to optimise: partition by day and user, reuse daily totals, and backfill only what changed.

## In practice

### In practice

#### What the interviewer will push on

- **Hash quality:** test that assignment is random and independent across salts, using A/A tests on past data. A bad hash correlates tests silently.

- **Ramping:** widening a test should keep users in their group. Keep the same hash and extend the bucket range. Analyse carefully, as early users have had longer exposure.

- **Mobile:** old app versions can't be updated. Ship the config with a safe default, and log the version, because exposure is delayed and uneven.

- **Logged-out users:** device or cookie IDs change, so one person can land in both groups. Decide what happens at sign-in, and measure how often it occurs.

- **Peeking by design:** show daily guardrails freely, but hide the primary decision until a planned look, or use always-valid intervals.

- **Automatic shutdown:** a guardrail alarm can stop a test, using sequential thresholds, as long as the rule was agreed beforehand.

- **Interactions:** scan pairs that share a surface, with corrections for how many you check. Real ones appear rare, so treat alarms as leads.

- **Failure modes:** if the platform fails, the product must carry on in the default experience, and that period must be flagged in the analysis.

- **Institutional memory:** store every test, its result and its decision. Past tests supply variance estimates and show which proxy metrics really predict outcomes.

#### How real teams approached it

- **Layers made it scale:** Google moved from a single layer, which couldn't scale, to overlapping layers and domains. Launch layers handle rollouts apart from ordinary tests.

- **Config as data:** Google's tests live in data files that are easy to read and pushed more often than code, so non-engineers can create them, with automatic checks first.

- **Tooling matters as much:** the same paper says the infrastructure isn't enough alone, and describes sizing tools, a metrics dashboard and education.

- **Namespaces:** PlanOut lets each team allocate a share of a namespace, centred on one kind of unit, to separate experiments over time.

- **Interactions are rare, though not never:** Microsoft, running hundreds of tests a day per product, found them very rare, which supports overlap as the default.

- **Scale across the industry:** 13 organisations at a 2018 summit together reported more than 100,000 experiment treatments in a year.

### The answer that sounds right

#### "The hard part is assigning users at scale"

It sounds right, since it's billions of calls. But a hash is cheap and can run locally. The hard parts are logging true exposure, joining it to events at a reasonable cost, and stopping people from misreading results. A platform that's fast but untrustworthy just helps you ship wrong answers sooner.

## Say it

### Your company runs a few A/B tests by hand. Design a platform that lets teams run hundreds at once, and trust the results.

#### The interviewer pushes further

Follow-up 1 of 3

Why hash locally rather than call an assignment service?

A service adds latency to every check, and becomes a single point of failure. A hash needs only the user ID and the config, gives the same answer everywhere and needs no stored table. The cost is that config must reach every client, so changes aren't instant.

Follow-up 2 of 3

Results show a win, but the sample ratio check failed. What should the platform do?

Flag it, and hide or grey out the result by default, because the groups may no longer be comparable. Then help people diagnose it, by showing the split by browser, version and day. Allow an override only with a recorded reason.

Follow-up 3 of 3

Two tests touch the same settings. How does the platform stop them clashing?

Each setting belongs to a layer, and a user is in at most one test per layer. Two tests on the same setting must then share a layer, so they split traffic and never overlap. The check runs when the test is created, so the conflict is rejected before launch.

#### The 30-second answer

I'd first clarify the scale, the platforms, the units, and who reads the results. Then I'd split it into four jobs. Assignment runs in an SDK, hashing user and salt locally, so there's no network call and no stored table, with a safe default if anything fails. Exposure logs record when a user actually reaches the change, in both groups, because counting everyone dilutes the effect. A daily pipeline joins exposures to events, using one central definition per metric, and stores per-user totals. A stats engine computes intervals, with CUPED and the delta method. For many tests at once, I'd use layers: tests in different layers overlap, and tests in the same layer are exclusive. The hard part is trust, so I'd run sample ratio checks on every test and hide results when they fail, let teams pick only a few decision metrics, and build in planned looks or always-valid intervals. With 300 tests and 50 metrics each, about 750 results a day would look significant by chance. So the platform has to make the right behaviour the default, rather than rely on people being careful.

**Key terms and sources**

Built from published accounts: [Google's overlapping experiments paper](https://research.google/pubs/overlapping-experiment-infrastructure-more-better-faster-experimentation/), which we read in part, the [PlanOut paper](https://hci.stanford.edu/publications/2014/planout/planout-www2014.pdf) and [Microsoft's interaction study](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/articles/a-b-interactions-a-call-to-relax/). No single company's design is shown here, and the volumes and lab numbers are our own illustrations. Uses running many tests, trust checks and sequential testing. · checked 7 Nov 2026

# Attention Is All You Need

> What happens if you remove recurrence and keep only attention?

- Track: Papers Explained › Foundational
- Type: Paper · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/papers/attention-is-all-you-need/
- Before this: Self-Attention (Q, K, V) (`fundamentals/self-attention`)
- Related: Multi-Head Attention (`fundamentals/multi-head-attention`)

## Gist

### The paper

Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin · Google Brain, Google Research, University of Toronto · NeurIPS 2017 · arXiv [1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) · 10 sources, checked 9 Nov 2026

In 2017, the best translation models read a sentence one word at a time with recurrent networks, which made them slow to train and weak at linking distant words. This paper threw recurrence out and built the whole model from **attention**: every word looks at every other word in one step, weighs how relevant each one is, and mixes in what it needs. Add **multiple attention heads**, **position signals** so word order isn't lost, and a stack of identical layers, and you get the **Transformer**. It set new translation records (28.4 BLEU on English-to-German) at a fraction of the training cost, and its architecture became the base of BERT, GPT and every large language model since.

### The problem

#### One sentence, followed through the whole model

from the paper's own figure

"The Law will never be perfect, but **its** application should be just."

To translate this well, the model has to work out that "its" means "the Law", nine words earlier. The paper shows two attention heads that do exactly that, with sharp attention from "its" back to "Law" and "application" [Fig. 4, p. 14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=14). We'll follow this sentence through every part of the model.

#### Recurrent models were slow and forgot distant words

In 2017 the best translation systems were recurrent networks (RNNs, usually LSTMs) in an encoder-decoder setup. A recurrent network reads word 1, updates a hidden state, then reads word 2, and so on: each hidden state ht depends on ht−1. The paper names the cost directly: this "inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples" [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=2).

##### Slow to train

Step 9 can't start until step 8 finishes, so a GPU can't process a sentence's words at the same time. Long sentences make it worse, because memory limits how many sentences you can batch instead.

##### Weak over long distances

To link "its" back to "Law", the signal has to pass through every word in between. The longer the path, the harder the dependency is to learn [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=6).

Attention already existed, as an add-on: it let the decoder look back at the encoder's states while translating. But "in all but a few cases" it sat on top of a recurrent network [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=2). The recurrence, and its sequential bottleneck, stayed.

### The idea

Think of a meeting. In a recurrent model, a message passes from person to person down a line, and it fades on the way. With attention, everyone in the room can hear everyone else directly, and each person decides who to listen to.

[Figure: Top row: a recurrent model passes information along a chain, one word at a time. Bottom row: attention connects every word directly to every other word.]

_Illustrative. A recurrent model reads a sentence in order. Attention connects every word in one step._

### Play

**Try it.** The word "its" is looking for what it refers to. Change the key size, then switch off the scaling.

Illustrative scores for the query "its" against four words, set so that random-like vectors at dk = 1 give scores of 2.0, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.4; larger keys multiply them by √dk, as footnote 4 describes. "Gradient left" is 1 − the largest weight, a rough measure of how much the softmax can still change.

**Notice:** without dividing by √dk, bigger keys make softmax pick one word almost completely, and the head stops learning. That one division is why the paper calls it _scaled_ dot-product attention.

## Method

### Method

#### Recurrent, convolutional, and attention as a helper

| Approach | How it links two words | The catch |
|---|---|---|
| **RNN / LSTM encoder-decoder** (Sutskever 2014) | Passes a hidden state along the sentence | Sequential: no parallelism within a sentence; path length grows with distance |
| **RNN + attention** (Bahdanau 2014) | The decoder attends to all encoder states | Still recurrent underneath, so still sequential |
| **Convolutional** (ByteNet, ConvS2S) | Stacks of convolutions over neighbouring words | Parallel, but linking distant words takes many layers: linear in distance for ConvS2S, logarithmic for ByteNet |

The Transformer's pitch was to keep the parallelism of convolutions and make every pair of words one step apart, using attention alone [p. 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=2). The paper notes one cost of that: averaging over many positions blurs detail, which multi-head attention is designed to fix.

#### Each word asks a question, every word offers an answer

Each word is turned into three vectors. A **query** says what this word is looking for. A **key** says what each word offers. A **value** is the information a word passes on if it's chosen. For "its", the query asks roughly "which noun do I refer to?", and "Law" has a key that matches well.

$$ \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = {\text{softmax}}\!\left({Q}\,{K^{\top}} \,/\, {\sqrt{d_k}}\right){V} $$

Equation 1 [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=4) · hover a term.

- **what each word looks for**: Q: one query vector per word, packed into a matrix.

- **what each word offers**: K: one key per word. Q times K transposed gives a score for every pair of words at once.

- **the scaling**: Divide by the square root of d_k, the key size (64 in the paper), so scores don’t get too large.

- **turn scores into weights**: Softmax turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1.

- **what gets passed on**: V: the values. Each word’s output is the weighted average of every word’s value.

##### Why divide by √dk?

If the parts of a query and key are random with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance dk [footnote 4, p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=4). With dk = 64, typical scores are 8 times larger than with dk = 1. Large scores push softmax into a region where one weight is nearly 1, the rest nearly 0, and the gradients become "extremely small". Dividing by √dk brings the variance back to about 1. Without it, the paper notes, dot-product attention did worse than additive attention at large dk.

With scaling on, "its" puts about half its weight on "Law" and a quarter on "application", whatever the key size. Turn scaling off at dk = 64 and "Law" takes 99.2% of the weight: the head stops learning, because almost no gradient flows to the other words.

##### Why dot products rather than a small network?

Additive attention, which scores pairs with a tiny feed-forward network, has similar theory, but dot-product attention "is much faster and more space-efficient in practice" because it's one big matrix multiplication [p. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=4).

#### Several smaller attentions beat one big one

One attention function averages everything into a single weighted mix, so it can only look one way at a time. The paper instead projects Q, K and V **h = 8 times** with different learned matrices, runs attention on each in parallel, joins the results and projects them back [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=5).

$$ \text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = {\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_8)}\,{W^{O}}, \quad {\text{head}_i} = \text{Attention}(Q{W_i^{Q}}, K{W_i^{K}}, V{W_i^{V}}) $$

With dmodel = 512 and 8 heads, each head works in dk = dv = 64 dimensions, so the total cost is about the same as one full-size head [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=5).

- **one head**: Each head runs attention on its own projected copies of Q, K and V.

- **learned projections**: Each head has its own matrices, so each can learn to look for something different.

- **join the heads**: The 8 head outputs (64 numbers each) are concatenated back to 512.

- **mix them**: A final matrix W^O mixes the heads into one output per word.

In our sentence, the paper's visualisations show two heads in layer 5 sharply linking "its" to "Law" and "application", while other heads follow sentence structure: "the heads clearly learned to perform different tasks" [Fig. 5, p. 15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=15).

##### How many heads? (Table 3, rows A)

At the same total compute, 1 head scored 24.9 BLEU on the development set, 8 heads 25.8, 16 heads 25.8 and 32 heads 25.4. One head is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best, and too many heads hurts too [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=9).

##### Three places attention is used

- **Encoder self-attention:** every input word attends to every input word.

- **Decoder self-attention, masked:** each output word attends only to earlier output words, so the model can't peek at the answer. Future positions are set to −∞ before the softmax.

- **Encoder-decoder attention:** queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder, so each output word can look at the whole input sentence [p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=5).

#### Attention alone can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog"

Attention compares every word with every other word, and nothing in that comparison depends on order. Shuffle the words and each output is the same, just shuffled. So the paper adds a **position signal** to each word's embedding before the first layer [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=6).

$$ PE_{({pos},\,2{i})} = {\sin}\!\left(\frac{{pos}}{{10000}^{2{i}/d_{model}}}\right), \quad PE_{({pos},\,2{i}+1)} = {\cos}\!\left(\frac{{pos}}{{10000}^{2{i}/d_{model}}}\right) $$

Section 3.5 [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=6).

- **position in the sentence**: pos: 0 for the first word, 1 for the second, and so on.

- **which dimension pair**: i picks the dimension pair. Low i gives fast waves, high i gives slow waves.

- **the wavelength range**: 10000 sets the range: wavelengths grow geometrically from 2π to 10000·2π.

- **sine and cosine**: Even dimensions use sine and odd ones cosine, so a fixed offset k is a linear function of the encoding, which the paper hoped would help attend by relative position.

Think of a clock with many hands moving at different speeds. Any moment gets a unique combination of hand positions, and the same gap between two moments always looks the same.

##### Did the fixed formula matter? (Table 3, row E)

Learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results: 25.7 BLEU against 25.8 for sines. The authors kept sines because they "may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training" [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=6). That was a hope, not a tested result.

#### Six identical layers on each side

1. Each input word becomes a 512-number embedding, multiplied by √512, plus its position signal.

2. The encoder is 6 identical layers. Each has self-attention, then a feed-forward network applied to each word on its own, each wrapped as LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x)).

3. The decoder is also 6 layers, with a third sublayer. Its self-attention is masked so word i only sees words before i.

4. Encoder-decoder attention lets every output position look at the encoder's final representation of the whole input.

5. A linear layer and softmax turn the top decoder output into next-word probabilities. The same weight matrix is shared with both embedding layers.

Sections 3.1, 3.3 and 3.4 [p. 3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=3). The residual connections need every sublayer to output dmodel = 512 numbers. The feed-forward network is max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2, with an inner size of 2,048.

| | Layers N | dmodel | dff | Heads h | Dropout | Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Base** | 6 | 512 | 2,048 | 8 | 0.1 | 65 M |
| **Big** | 6 | 1,024 | 4,096 | 16 | 0.3 | 213 M |

Table 3 [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=9). The big English-to-French model used dropout 0.1, not 0.3.

#### 12 hours on one machine for the base model

| English-German data | WMT 2014, about 4.5 million sentence pairs, byte-pair encoding with a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens |
|---|---|
| English-French data | WMT 2014, 36 million sentences, 32,000 word-piece vocabulary |
| Batch | About 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens, sentences grouped by length |
| Hardware | One machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs |
| Base model | 0.4 s per step, 100,000 steps: **12 hours** |
| Big model | 1.0 s per step, 300,000 steps: **3.5 days** |
| Regularisation | Dropout 0.1 on every sublayer output and on embeddings; label smoothing 0.1, which "hurts perplexity" but improves BLEU |

Sections 5.1–5.4 [p. 7–8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=7).

##### The warm-up schedule

$$ lrate = {d_{model}^{-0.5}} \cdot \min\!\left({step^{-0.5}},\; {step \cdot warmup^{-1.5}}\right),\quad warmup = 4000 $$

Adam with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98, ε = 10−9. Equation 3 [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=7).

- **model size**: d_model^(−0.5): bigger models get a smaller learning rate overall.

- **warm-up**: For the first 4,000 steps the rate rises linearly, so the early, noisy updates stay small.

- **decay**: After that it falls with the inverse square root of the step number.

Computed from equation 3 with dmodel = 512. It peaks at step 4,000 at about 0.0007, and by step 100,000 it has fallen to about 0.00014.

## Results

### What they found

#### New records, at a fraction of the training cost

##### English-to-German BLEU, WMT 2014 test set (Table 2)

| Model | EN-DE BLEU | EN-FR BLEU | Training cost EN-DE (FLOPs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| GNMT + RL | 24.6 | 39.92 | 2.3 × 1019 |
| ConvS2S | 25.16 | 40.46 | 9.6 × 1018 |
| Mixture of Experts | 26.03 | 40.56 | 2.0 × 1019 |
| GNMT + RL ensemble | 26.30 | 41.16 | 1.8 × 1020 |
| ConvS2S ensemble | 26.36 | 41.29 | 7.7 × 1019 |
| **Transformer base** | **27.3** | 38.1 | **3.3 × 1018** |
| **Transformer big** | **28.4** | **41.8** | 2.3 × 1019 |

Table 2 [p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=8). FLOPs are the authors' estimates from training time × GPUs × an assumed GPU speed.

- **English-to-German:** the big model beat every earlier result, ensembles included, by more than 2 BLEU. Even the base model beat all of them, at roughly 1/3 to 1/55 of their training cost.

- **English-to-French:** 41.8 BLEU, a new best for a single model, at less than a quarter of the cost of the previous best. Note: the text on page 8 says 41.0, while the abstract and Table 2 say 41.8, an inconsistency that remains in the latest arXiv version.

- **Beyond translation:** a 4-layer Transformer on English constituency parsing reached 91.3 F1 trained only on the 40,000-sentence WSJ set, and 92.7 with 17 million extra sentences, beating every earlier model except one generative parser (93.3) [Table 4, p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=10). Recurrent sequence-to-sequence models had struggled with so little data.

#### Which parts mattered

The authors changed one thing at a time in the base model and measured English-to-German BLEU on the development set (base: 25.8) [p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=9).

| Change | Dev BLEU | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| 1 head instead of 8 (same compute) | 24.9 | Multiple heads help |
| 32 heads | 25.4 | Too many small heads hurts |
| Key size dk 16 instead of 64 | 25.1 | Matching words is hard; small keys lose detail |
| 2 layers instead of 6 | 23.7 | Depth matters |
| dmodel 1,024, 128-wide heads | 26.0 | Bigger is better |
| No dropout | 24.6 | Dropout is essential against overfitting |
| Learned positions instead of sines | 25.7 | The exact position scheme barely matters here |
| **Big model** | **26.4** | Scale wins |

#### Constant path length, full parallelism, quadratic cost

| Layer type | Work per layer | Sequential steps | Longest path between two words |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Self-attention** | O(n²·d) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Recurrent | O(n·d²) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Convolutional | O(k·n·d²) | O(1) | O(logk n) |
| Restricted self-attention | O(r·n·d) | O(1) | O(n/r) |

n = sentence length, d = vector size, k = convolution width, r = neighbourhood size. Table 1 [p. 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=6).

Self-attention is cheaper than recurrence when the sentence is shorter than the vector size (n < d), which was true for translation: sentences of tens of tokens against d = 512. Every pair of words is one step apart, and all positions are computed at once.

##### Try it: when does attention get expensive?

Counts the leading term of Table 1 only, ignoring constants. Recurrent layers also need n sequential steps, which this count doesn't show.

### Where it falls short

#### What the paper didn't solve

- **Quadratic cost in length.** Comparing every pair of words is fine for sentences, expensive for books. The authors flagged this and suggested restricted, local attention as future work [p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=7).

- **Position handling was a hope.** The sine encodings were chosen because they "may" extrapolate to longer inputs, but this wasn't tested, and later work found absolute encodings extrapolate poorly.

- **Training stability.** Layer norm after each residual (post-LN) needed the careful warm-up. Later work showed that putting the norm before each sublayer (pre-LN) trains more stably, and most modern models do that.

- **Narrow evidence.** Results cover two translation pairs and one parsing task, with single runs and no variance reported. BLEU itself is a rough measure of translation quality.

- **A small inconsistency.** English-to-French is reported as 41.8 BLEU in the abstract and Table 2, but 41.0 in the text.

## Why it matters

### What it changed

Training could now run in parallel across a whole sequence, and any two words were one step apart. Within two years the same blocks, split into encoder-only and decoder-only models, became BERT and GPT, and the architecture now underlies almost every large language model.

**What to remember.** Attention alone, with multiple heads, position signals and residual layers, replaced recurrence. The core equation, softmax(QKT/√dk)V, is still the heart of today's models.

#### From a translation model to every large language model

| Year | What happened | Which part of the Transformer |
|---|---|---|
| 2018 | GPT: language model pretraining | Decoder only, masked self-attention |
| 2018 | BERT: bidirectional pretraining for understanding | Encoder only |
| 2019 | T5: every text task as text-to-text | The full encoder-decoder |
| 2020 | Vision Transformer: image patches as tokens | Encoder only, applied to images |
| 2020 on | Pre-LN, rotary positions (RoPE), multi-query and grouped-query attention, FlashAttention | Fixes for stability, position handling, inference memory and speed |

Today's large language models are mostly decoder-only Transformers with these fixes. The core equation, softmax(QKT/√dk)V, is unchanged. The authors' closing hope, to extend the model to "images, audio and video" [p. 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762#page=10), came true.

#### Read it

**Read** sections 3 (the architecture) and 4 (why self-attention), plus Figures 1 and 2. They're short, and almost every interview question about Transformers traces back to them. **Skim** the training details unless you plan to reproduce it. **Look at** the attention visualisations in the appendix to see heads learning different jobs.

For a line-by-line code walkthrough, the Annotated Transformer is the classic companion.

**Key terms and sources**

#### Words to know

Self-attention

Each position in a sequence attends to every position in the same sequence.

Query, key, value

Three learned projections of each word: what it looks for, what it offers, and what it passes on.

Scaled dot-product attention

softmax(QKT/√dk)V. The scaling keeps softmax out of its flat, low-gradient region.

Multi-head attention

Several attentions in parallel on smaller projections, joined and mixed.

Masking

Setting scores for future positions to −∞ so the decoder can't see words it hasn't produced yet.

Positional encoding

A signal added to each embedding so the model knows word order.

Residual connection and layer norm

Each sublayer's output is LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x)), which keeps deep stacks trainable.

BLEU

A translation score from 0 to 100 based on overlapping word sequences with reference translations.

Label smoothing

Training targets that give a little probability to wrong words, which makes the model less overconfident.

#### Everything on this page comes from these

1. Vaswani et al. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS 2017. [arXiv 1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) (read in full; page numbers refer to v7)

2. Bahdanau, Cho, Bengio (2014). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate. [arXiv 1409.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)

3. Sutskever, Vinyals, Le (2014). Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks. [arXiv 1409.3215](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215)

4. Devlin et al. (2018). BERT. [arXiv 1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)

5. Dosovitskiy et al. (2020). An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (Vision Transformer). [arXiv 2010.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)

6. Xiong et al. (2020). On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture. [arXiv 2002.04745](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)

7. Su et al. (2021). RoFormer: Rotary Position Embedding. [arXiv 2104.09864](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)

# Scaling Laws and Chinchilla

> For a fixed compute budget, should you train a bigger model or feed it more data?

- Track: Papers Explained › Foundational
- Type: Paper · 30 min
- Page: https://aimlrounds.com/tracks/papers/scaling-laws-and-chinchilla/
- Before this: The Next-Token Objective (`fundamentals/next-token-prediction`)
- Related: Attention Is All You Need (`papers/attention-is-all-you-need`)

## Gist

### The paper

Kaplan et al., OpenAI, 2020 · arXiv [2001.08361](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) + Hoffmann et al., DeepMind, 2022 (NeurIPS 2022) · arXiv [2203.15556](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) · 10 sources, checked 11 Nov 2026

In 2020, OpenAI showed that a language model's loss falls as a smooth, predictable **power law** as you add parameters, data or compute, so you can forecast a big model from small ones. Their advice for a fixed compute budget: spend most of it on a **bigger model** and only a little on more data. The field listened: GPT-3 (175B) and Gopher (280B) were trained on only about 300 billion tokens. In 2022, DeepMind redid the experiment with 400+ models and found the opposite balance: model size and data should grow **equally**, about **20 training tokens per parameter**. To prove it, they trained **Chinchilla**, 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens, with the same compute as the 280B Gopher. It beat Gopher on almost every task and costs a quarter as much to run.

### The problem

#### One compute budget, two ways to spend it

from the Chinchilla paper

You have the compute DeepMind used for Gopher: about 5.8 × 1023 floating-point operations. Do you train a **280B** model on 300 billion tokens, or a **70B** model on 1.4 trillion tokens?

Both cost almost the same to train. Gopher took the first option, as everyone did in 2021. Chinchilla took the second [§4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). We'll follow this choice through both papers, and you'll be able to try every option in between.

#### You only get to train the big model once

A large training run is planned around a fixed budget: so many accelerators for so many weeks. The Chinchilla paper puts it plainly: "it is typically only feasible to train these large models once", so the model size and the amount of data have to be right before you start [§1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

##### Too big, too little data

A huge model that reads too little is under-trained: it could have learned much more. It's also expensive to serve, forever.

##### Too small, too much data

A small model run for a very long time stops improving: its size caps how good it can get, and extra tokens are wasted.

Somewhere between the two is a best split. Scaling laws are how you find it from small, cheap experiments instead of guessing at full scale.

### The idea

Think of a fixed budget for a student: you can pay for a bigger brain or more books, but not both. Kaplan said buy mostly brain. Chinchilla showed you should split it evenly: every time the brain doubles, double the books too.

[Figure: Two rectangles with the same area: a tall, narrow one for Gopher (big model, little data) and a short, wide one for Chinchilla (smaller model, much more data).]

_Illustrative. Training compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens, so a fixed budget is a fixed area: tall and narrow, or short and wide._

### Play

**Try it.** You have Gopher's compute budget. Drag the model size and see how many tokens you can afford and what loss Chinchilla's formula predicts.

—

Computed from the fitted formula with the paper's published constants and D = C ÷ 6N. The loss differences look small, but on this scale they are large: Chinchilla's whole advantage over Gopher is about 0.05. With these rounded constants the formula's minimum sits well above 20 tokens per parameter (about 90 at Gopher's budget, a 32B model; the paper quotes about 40B from its unrounded fit). That's why approach 3 recommends smaller models than approaches 1 and 2, and why the "20 tokens per parameter" rule comes from approach 1. A later replication found this fit unreliable (chapter 10).

**Notice:** the loss curve is a valley. Gopher's 280B model sits up the right-hand slope with barely one token per parameter; a smaller model trained on more data reaches lower loss for the same compute.

## Method

### Method

#### Training compute is roughly six times parameters times tokens

$$ {C} \approx {6}\,{N}\,{D} $$

Kaplan §1.3, §2.1 [p. 6–7](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) · hover a term.

- **training compute**: C: the total floating-point operations (FLOPs) to train the model.

- **six operations**: About 2 per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass.

- **model size**: N: the number of parameters.

- **data**: D: the number of training tokens.

This one line is why the question is a trade-off. With C fixed, N × D is fixed: double the model and you can only afford half the tokens. For our example, 280B × 300B and 70B × 1.4T both come to about 6 × 1023 FLOPs.

#### Loss falls as a power law in size, data and compute

OpenAI trained decoder-only Transformers from 768 to 1.5 billion parameters (not counting embeddings) on WebText2, about 23 billion tokens, and measured the test loss [§2–3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361). When only one factor limits the model, the loss follows a straight line on a log-log plot:

$$ {L(N)} = \left(\frac{{N_c}}{{N}}\right)^{{\alpha_N}} $$

Equation 1.1 [§1.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361). Data and compute have the same form, with αD ≈ 0.095 and αC ≈ 0.050 · hover a term.

- **test loss**: L: cross-entropy loss in nats per token. Lower is better.

- **a fitted constant**: N_c ≈ 8.8 × 10^13. Its exact value depends on the tokenizer, so it has no deep meaning.

- **model size**: N: non-embedding parameters, for a model trained to convergence on plenty of data.

- **the exponent**: α_N ≈ 0.076. Doubling N multiplies the loss by 2^−0.076 ≈ 0.95: about 5% lower.

##### What else they found

- **Shape barely matters.** Depth versus width, number of heads: performance depends "very weakly" on these, and strongly on scale.

- **The trends held over many orders of magnitude** with no sign of bending at the top end.

- **Bigger models learn faster per token.** They reach the same loss with fewer steps and less data.

- **So train big and stop early.** For a fixed budget, the best result came from "training very large models and stopping significantly short of convergence".

##### Their recipe for spending more compute

Kaplan fitted Nopt ∝ C0.73 and Dopt ∝ C0.27. For every 10× more compute, make the model about **5.4× bigger** and give it only about **1.9× more data**. Most of the extra compute goes into parameters [§6, Fig. 14](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361).

#### Every big model read about 300 billion tokens

| Model | Parameters | Training tokens | Tokens per parameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| LaMDA | 137B | 168B | 1.2 |
| GPT-3 | 175B | 300B | 1.7 |
| Jurassic-1 | 178B | 300B | 1.7 |
| Gopher | 280B | 300B | 1.1 |
| MT-NLG | 530B | 270B | 0.5 |
| **Chinchilla** | **70B** | **1,400B** | **20** |

Chinchilla Table 1 [§1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556); tokens per parameter computed from it.

Following Kaplan and the GPT-3 setup, labs raced to more parameters while keeping data around 300 billion tokens. The largest dense model, MT-NLG, reached 530B parameters, over 3× GPT-3, in two years [§5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

#### 400 models later, a different split

DeepMind asked the same question: for a fixed budget C, which N and D give the lowest loss? They trained over 400 models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and estimated the answer three independent ways [§3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556):

| Approach | How | Nopt ∝ Ca | Dopt ∝ Cb |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Training curves | Train each model size for 4 lengths; at every compute level, take the run with the lowest loss | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| 2 · IsoFLOP profiles | At 9 fixed budgets, vary model size and find the bottom of each U-shaped loss curve | 0.49 | 0.51 |
| 3 · Fitted loss formula | Fit L(N, D) to all runs, then minimise it under C = 6ND | 0.46 | 0.54 |
| _Kaplan et al. 2020_ | | 0.73 | 0.27 |

Table 2 [§3.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

All three agree: a ≈ b ≈ 0.5. **Every time you double the model, double the data.** They also found the same result on two other datasets, C4 and GitHub code.

##### Why Kaplan got a different answer, according to DeepMind

Kaplan used one learning-rate schedule length for every run. Losses read off partway through a long schedule are worse than a run whose schedule matches its length, which made short training look worse than it is, and pushed the advice towards bigger models. Most of Kaplan's runs were also small, many under 100M parameters [§2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). Later work found other causes too (chapter 10).

#### Loss = the text's own entropy + a size penalty + a data penalty

$$ \hat{L}(N, D) = {E} + {\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}} + {\frac{B}{D^{\beta}}} $$

Equations 2 and 10 [§3.3, App. D.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) · hover a term.

- **the floor**: E ≈ 1.69: the loss of a perfect model, roughly the entropy of natural text. No model can go below it.

- **too few parameters**: A / N^α, with A ≈ 406.4 and α ≈ 0.34: how much a model of size N falls short of perfect, even with unlimited training.

- **too little data**: B / D^β, with B ≈ 410.7 and β ≈ 0.28: the extra loss from seeing only D tokens.

With C fixed, making N bigger shrinks the size penalty but forces D smaller, which grows the data penalty. The best model balances the two. Because α and β are close, the balance point moves with N and D growing at nearly the same rate.

#### A compute-optimal model reads about 20 tokens per parameter

| Parameters | Compute-optimal tokens | Training FLOPs |
|---|---|---|
| 400M | 8.0B | 1.92 × 1019 |
| 1B | 20.2B | 1.21 × 1020 |
| 10B | 205.1B | 1.23 × 1022 |
| 67B | 1.5T | 5.76 × 1023 (Gopher's budget) |
| 175B | 3.7T | 3.85 × 1024 |
| 280B | 5.9T | 9.90 × 1024 |
| 1T | 21.2T | 1.27 × 1026 |

Table 3, from approach 1 [§3.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

Divide the two columns and you get about 20 tokens per parameter at every size: the rule of thumb everyone quotes. By this table, GPT-3 should have read 3.7 trillion tokens, not 300 billion, and a 1-trillion-parameter model isn't worth training unless you have about 250× Gopher's compute.

##### Try it: 10× more compute, two recipes

Kaplan: N × m0.73, D × m0.27. Chinchilla: N × m0.5, D × m0.5. Bars are on a log scale, so equal lengths mean equal growth factors.

## Results

### What they found

#### A 70B model beat a 280B model with the same compute

The analysis put the best size for Gopher's budget between 40B and 70B. DeepMind trained the larger end, **Chinchilla: 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens**, with the same architecture family and data source (MassiveText) as Gopher. The main changes were AdamW instead of Adam and a slightly different tokenizer [§4.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

##### MMLU, 5-shot accuracy (Table 6)

- **MMLU:** 67.6% against Gopher's 60.0% and GPT-3's 43.9%. It even beat expert forecasts for June 2023 (63.4%). The abstract says 67.5%; Table 6 says 67.6%.

- **BIG-bench:** 65.1% average against 54.4%; worse than Gopher on only 4 of 62 tasks.

- **Reading:** 77.4% on LAMBADA against 74.5%, and more than 10 points better on RACE.

- **Cheaper to use:** 4× smaller, so 4× less memory and roughly 4× less compute per generated token, for the model's whole life.

##### Why the last point matters

Training happens once; inference happens billions of times. A model trained compute-optimally is not just better for the same training cost, it's also far cheaper to deploy. That observation later pushed labs even further towards smaller models trained on more data (chapter 11).

#### What else the two papers measured

| Kaplan: data | WebText2, about 23B tokens, byte-pair encoding with 50,257 tokens, context 1,024 |
|---|---|
| Kaplan: critical batch size | Grows as loss falls: roughly 1–2 million tokens for their largest models |
| Kaplan: forgiving sizes | Models between 0.6× and 2.2× the optimal size need only about 20% more compute for the same loss |
| Kaplan: overfitting | The penalty depends on N0.74/D: 8× the model needs about 5× the data to avoid it |
| Chinchilla: architecture | 80 layers, dmodel 8,192, 64 heads; batch 1.5M rising to 3M tokens; bfloat16 with a float32 copy of the weights |
| Chinchilla: hardware | TPUv3 and TPUv4, with JAX and Haiku |
| Chinchilla: schedule lesson | Set the cosine learning-rate schedule to the planned number of tokens; overshooting it by more than about 25% hurts |

Kaplan §1–5, Chinchilla §2, §4.1 and App. B [Kaplan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) · [Chinchilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

#### Two later papers traced the gap

##### Counting and scale

Pearce and Song showed much of the gap comes from Kaplan counting only non-embedding parameters, combined with working at small scale. Simulating Chinchilla's study under those conditions reproduces exponents close to Kaplan's [arXiv 2406.12907](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12907).

##### Three training details

Porian et al. reproduced Kaplan's law and found three causes: ignoring the cost of the last layer, the warm-up length, and optimiser settings not tuned per scale. Fixing them gave "excellent agreement" with Chinchilla. They also found careful learning-rate decay was _not_ essential, against DeepMind's own explanation [arXiv 2406.19146](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19146).

##### A problem with approach 3

Besiroglu et al. rebuilt the data from the paper's plots and found the published fit of the loss formula didn't match the data, and that its confidence intervals were implausibly narrow. Refitting gave results consistent with approaches 1 and 2, so the headline answer stands, but the exact constants in chapter 6 shouldn't be trusted to many digits [arXiv 2404.10102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10102).

### Where it falls short

#### The answer to a narrow question

##### Limits the authors list

- **Only two large runs.** Chinchilla and Gopher are the only big-scale test, with nothing in between.

- **The power law is assumed.** They saw some bending at high compute, so they "may still be overestimating the optimal size of large models".

- **Under one epoch.** Every run saw each token at most once; repeating data wasn't studied.

- **Quality is assumed.** More tokens help only if they're good tokens, and web-scale data brings toxicity and privacy problems [§5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

##### What came after

| Idea | What it says |
|---|---|
| **Count inference too** (Sardana et al. 2023) | If a model will serve about a billion requests, train it smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal. Quality kept improving up to 10,000 tokens per parameter [arXiv 2401.00448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00448). |
| **Running out of data** (Muennighoff et al. 2023) | Up to about 4 passes over repeated data is nearly as good as fresh data; beyond that, returns fall towards zero [arXiv 2305.16264](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264). |
| **Over-trained open models** | Meta's Llama 3 8B read about 15 trillion tokens, nearly 1,900 per parameter, about 90× the Chinchilla ratio, because a small model that's cheap to serve was the goal [Llama 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783). |

##### Tokens per parameter, from 2020 to 2024

Log scale: each step is 10×. GPT-3, Gopher and Chinchilla from Chinchilla Table 1; Llama 3 8B from the Llama 3 report.

Chinchilla answered "what's the best model for this training budget?" Today's labs usually ask "what's the best model for this training _and serving_ budget?", and that answer is smaller still. Both start from the same scaling-law method.

## Why it matters

### What it changed

Chinchilla changed how every lab sizes a model: about 20 training tokens per parameter became the default for compute-optimal training, and data, not just parameters, became the thing to scale. Later models went further, training small models on far more tokens because they are cheaper to serve.

**What to remember.** Loss falls as a predictable power law, training compute is about 6ND, and for a fixed budget you should grow model size and data together. Count inference cost too, and the best model gets smaller still.

#### Read Chinchilla, skim Kaplan

**Read** Chinchilla §1, §3 and §4, with Figures 1–3 and Tables 1–3: they're short, clear, and the source of the "20 tokens per parameter" rule. **Skim** Kaplan's §1 summary and Figures 1–4 for the idea of predictable power laws; its compute-allocation advice is outdated. **Skip** the long benchmark appendices unless you need a specific number.

Then read one of the later reconciliation papers, since "why did Kaplan and Chinchilla disagree?" is a common follow-up question.

**Key terms and sources**

#### Words to know

Scaling law

A fitted formula, usually a power law, for how loss changes with model size, data or compute.

Power law

y ∝ x−α: a straight line on a log-log plot. Each doubling of x multiplies y by the same factor.

Compute-optimal

The model size and token count that give the lowest loss for a fixed training compute.

C ≈ 6ND

Training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens (2 for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass).

IsoFLOP curve

Loss against model size at one fixed compute budget. Its lowest point is the compute-optimal size.

Tokens per parameter

Training tokens ÷ parameters. About 20 is Chinchilla-optimal; GPT-3 used 1.7.

Under-trained

A model that saw too few tokens for its size, so the same compute could have produced a better model.

Over-training

Deliberately training past compute-optimal to get a smaller model that's cheaper to serve.

#### Everything on this page comes from these

1. Kaplan et al. (2020). Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. [arXiv 2001.08361](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) (main text read in full)

2. Hoffmann et al. (2022). Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla). [arXiv 2203.15556](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) (read in full, including appendix D)

3. Brown et al. (2020). Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3). [arXiv 2005.14165](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)

4. Rae et al. (2021). Scaling Language Models: Methods, Analysis & Insights from Training Gopher. [arXiv 2112.11446](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11446)

5. Besiroglu et al. (2024). Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt. [arXiv 2404.10102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10102)

6. Pearce and Song (2024). Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla Scaling Laws. [arXiv 2406.12907](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12907)

7. Porian et al. (2024). Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models. [arXiv 2406.19146](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19146)

8. Sardana et al. (2023). Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws. [arXiv 2401.00448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00448)
